19–20. The two verses on the perfection of skillful means. Just as a physician administers medicine to a patient according to their specific illness, so too does the Bodhisattva apply skillful means to sentient beings according to their respective dispositions. Furthermore, just as a skilled pilot leads a ship across the great ocean to its destination, so too does the Bodhisattva lead sentient beings across the ocean of existence to the shore of nirvana by means of skillful means. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the perfection of vows. Just as a great king, having made a vow to protect his subjects, never abandons them even at the cost of his own life, so too does the Bodhisattva, having made a vow to liberate all sentient beings, never abandon them even at the cost of his own life. Furthermore, just as the sun, having vowed to illuminate the world, never ceases its radiance until the end of the aeon, so too does the Bodhisattva, having vowed to bring benefit to sentient beings, never cease their compassionate activity until all have been liberated. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of vows is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the perfection of power. Just as the wind, possessing great power, can shatter mountains and move the great earth, so too does the Bodhisattva possess the power of wisdom to shatter the mountains of afflictions and move the great earth of the three realms. Furthermore, just as the fire, possessing great power, can burn dry wood and illuminate the darkness, so too does the Bodhisattva possess the power of wisdom to burn away the fuel of afflictions and illuminate the darkness of ignorance. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of power is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the perfection of gnosis. Just as space, being vast and pervasive, is not obstructed by anything, so too is the gnosis of the Bodhisattva vast and pervasive, unobstructed by any phenomena. Furthermore, just as the ocean, being deep and vast, contains immeasurable jewels, so too does the gnosis of the Bodhisattva contain immeasurable dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of gnosis is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the perfection of dharma. Just as the Dharma King, having attained the sovereignty of the Dharma, turns the wheel of the Dharma for all sentient beings, so too does the Bodhisattva, having attained the sovereignty of the Dharma, turn the wheel of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Furthermore, just as the Dharma rain, falling from the sky, nourishes all grasses and trees according to their capacity, so too does the Dharma rain of the Bodhisattva fall upon sentient beings, bringing growth according to their faculties.

Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the perfection of the ultimate fruit. Just as a precious jewel, when worn on the body, brings about all desired benefits, so too does the ultimate fruit of the Bodhisattva bring about all the benefits of liberation for sentient beings. Furthermore, just as Mount Sumeru, standing at the center of the world, supports all the lands, so too does the ultimate fruit of the Bodhisattva support all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ultimate fruit is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the summary of the perfections. Just as a great cloud, gathering all waters, rains down nectar upon the world, so too does the Bodhisattva, gathering the waters of all the perfections, rain down the nectar of the Dharma upon sentient beings. Furthermore, just as the great earth, supported by the water element, sustains all living beings, so too does the Bodhisattva, supported by the water of the perfections, sustain all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfections is supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the mutual support of the perfections. Just as the eye and other sense organs function together to perceive objects, so too do the perfections function together to achieve enlightenment. Furthermore, just as the various parts of a chariot work in concert to reach a destination, so too do the perfections work in concert to reach the city of Nirvana. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are mutually supportive. 19–20. The two verses on the classification of the perfections. Just as a great physician classifies diseases according to their symptoms and prescribes remedies accordingly, so too does the Bodhisattva classify the afflictions of sentient beings and apply the appropriate perfections as remedies. Furthermore, just as a skilled jeweler classifies gems according to their quality and price, so too does the Bodhisattva classify the perfections according to their depth and efficacy. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are to be classified. 19–20. The two verses on the sequence of the perfections. Just as one first builds the foundation and then constructs the walls and roof of a house, so too does the Bodhisattva first cultivate generosity and then gradually cultivate the subsequent perfections. Furthermore, just as one first purifies the ground and then plants seeds and harvests the fruit, so too does the Bodhisattva first purify the mind through generosity and then cultivate the remaining perfections to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said that there is a fixed sequence to the perfections. 19–20. The two verses on the causes and fruits of the perfections. Just as a seed sown in the earth produces various fruits according to its nature, so too do the perfections, when cultivated, produce various fruits of merit and wisdom. Furthermore, just as the sun and moon, shining upon the world, cause all things to flourish, so too do the perfections, when practiced, cause all sentient beings to flourish in virtue. Therefore, it is said that the perfections have both causes and fruits. 19–20. The two verses on the distinctions of the perfections. Just as the ocean contains immeasurable waters of different flavors, so too do the perfections contain immeasurable virtues of different kinds. Furthermore, just as a great tree has roots, trunk, branches, and leaves, each with distinct characteristics, so too do the perfections have distinct characteristics in their practice and realization. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are distinguished. 19–20. The two verses on the non-duality of the perfections. Just as fire and heat are not separate entities, so too are the perfections ultimately non-dual in their essence. Furthermore, just as waves arise from the same water and return to the same water, so too do the perfections arise from the same mind and return to the same mind. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are non-dual. 19–20. The two verses on the inexhaustibility of the perfections. Just as the flow of a great river is inexhaustible, so too is the practice of the perfections inexhaustible. Furthermore, just as the light of the sun is inexhaustible, so too is the illumination of the perfections inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are inexhaustible. 19–20. The two verses on the supremacy of the perfections. Just as the Dharma King is supreme among all kings, so too is the perfection of wisdom supreme among all perfections. Furthermore, just as the great ocean is supreme among all bodies of water, so too is the perfection of meditation supreme among all perfections. Therefore, it is said that the perfections are supreme. 19–20. The two verses on the inclusion of the perfections within the six. Just as all medicinal herbs are contained within the great medicinal tree, so too are all the perfections contained within the six perfections. Furthermore, just as all rivers flow into the great ocean, so too do all the practices of the Bodhisattva flow into the six perfections. Therefore, it is said that all perfections are included within the six. 19–20. The two verses on the cultivation of the perfections. Just as a farmer cultivates the land diligently to obtain a harvest, so too does the Bodhisattva cultivate the perfections diligently to attain enlightenment. Furthermore, just as a goldsmith refines gold repeatedly to make it pure, so too does the Bodhisattva refine the perfections repeatedly to make them pure. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva must cultivate the perfections. 19–20. The two verses on the obstacles to the perfections. Just as darkness obstructs the light of the sun, so too do the afflictions obstruct the light of the perfections. Furthermore, just as clouds obstruct the sky, so too do the secondary afflictions obstruct the sky of the perfections. Therefore, it is said that there are obstacles to the perfections. 19–20. The two verses on the benefits of the perfections. Just as a lamp dispels darkness and brings light, so too do the perfections dispel the darkness of ignorance and bring the light of wisdom. I worship with devotion that one Lord, the indivisible, the increate, the imperishable, who stands far beyond all speech and thought, and who has brought joy to the entire universe. 1.

Here, indeed, desiring to comment upon the *Kāṇva-Upaniṣad-Bhāṣya* for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the entire sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), the Teacher first performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) in the form of a salutation to his chosen deity— a practice authorized by the conduct of the elders— in order to remove the obstacles to the completion of his intended work. Simultaneously, he summarizes the subject matter of the commentary he intends to explain, so that it may be easily understood.

The connection is with the words "I worship that All-pervasive One with devotion," beginning with the phrase "one's own ignorance" (*svāvidyā*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the well-known status of the Supreme Being according to worldly consensus is stated. Now, an objection is raised: "If the Supreme Being is an object of common renown, then He cannot be the subject of the scripture, because He would lack the quality of being 'unobtainable through other means' (*ananyalabhya*). To this, he provides the answer by specifying the substantive (*viśeṣya*) as "the All-pervasive One" (*vibhum*). Although the Supreme Being is generally known, the Supreme One who possesses unsurpassed sovereignty is not [merely] infinite... [text fragment ends].

The sense is that its specific form, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), cannot be established except through scripture; therefore, it is appropriate that it possesses attributes which are accessible only via scripture. Thinking that since the Lord is the ultimate limit of those to be worshipped, it is fitting to offer salutation to Him, he employed this act of veneration. Intending to show that salutation, when rooted in devotion and faith, yields the desired fruit, he says: "With devotion."

But the Mīmāṃsakas, while experiencing the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, yet not perceiving a transcendent impeller, describe [the Lord] as being established by scripture—like a painting on a wall that does not exist. To them, he says: "By one's own ignorance" (*svāvidyā*). The word "own" (*sva*)...

The object of one's own [consciousness] belongs to the friend, just as "one's own" [is understood]; and that [object], which is the manifestation called ignorance residing within the self, is produced by that extensive material cause (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, it is brought about and established by the perceived secondary cause (*nimitta*), which is the expansive dualistic world (*dvaitaprapañca*) consisting of enjoyers and objects of enjoyment.
By means of that clear and very firm delusion—of the nature "there is no Lord"—[the reality] is concealed and obstructed in the Supreme.

The construction of the verse is as follows: "I bow with devotion to that Lord whom those Mīmāṃsakas—who possess the cognition of non-existence—conceive through the distinction of enjoyer and so forth. This is the intended meaning: it is not that the Lord does not exist, for He is known through the Śruti and other sources; therefore, it is logical that He is established by scripture (*śāstra*). However, some assert that He is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like milk; in response to them, he says: "partless" (*nirbhāga*).

The sense is this: for things such as milk, which possess parts, undergo transformation; however, the Supreme [Brahman] does not, because of scriptural statements regarding its partlessness (*niravayavatva*). Others, however, on the basis of the inference of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*) and scriptural texts such as "He transcended," maintain that the Lord is extrinsic (*taṭastha*); he refutes them with the words "entirely" (*sakala*). For we do not maintain, through either inference or scripture, that the Supreme—which is beyond the reach of speech and mind—is extrinsic. Indeed, as for inference: [The text continues: "Indeed, inference..."

In this regard, the reason for such a possibility is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would contradict the *Sūtra* on "birth and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*). Even scripture (*āgama*), without making Him its direct object, proclaims His state of non-attachment;
however, neither scripture nor inference can operate directly upon Him, according to the scriptural teaching that He transcends speech and mind.

Therefore, the meaning is that the Lord is not merely an external observer. Now, it may be argued: "The Lord is a specific Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), their results (*vipāka*), or latent dispositions (*āśaya*)."

Since it has been stated by the venerable Patañjali that "in that [state], there is no pleasure either, just as there is no suffering," how can it be the subject matter of the treatise? For according to your own view, if there were an absence of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) due to the lack of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), it could not be the subject of the scripture. To this, he replies: "He who has gladdened the universe.
For it is well known that he who makes others wealthy is himself possessed of limitless wealth; likewise, he who has gladdened the entire universe—[is himself the Supreme].

It is understood that he himself is one who possesses unsurpassed bliss (*ānanda*), according to the scripture which states, "He indeed is bliss. Therefore, the intention is that even in the absence of sensual pleasure—just like suffering and so forth—this [state] is rightly considered the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstra*) because of the *Yoga-sūtra*. Now, just as one who makes another wealthy does not possess wealth himself merely by virtue of that act, nor is he defined by wealth itself, so too for one who brings happiness to others, there is only the state of being a giver of happiness, but not [the possession of] happiness itself.

Likewise, bliss (*sukha*) and supreme joy (*parānanda*) possess the relationship of quality and possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇitva*), just as form and the possessor of form do; therefore, he says: "One" (*ekam*). Because of scriptural texts stating that it is "one alone," which precludes all distinctions, there is no relationship of quality and possessor of quality in the Supreme. Furthermore, because non-difference is heard in passages such as "He understood that bliss is Brahman," the meaning is that even though its essential nature is bliss, it serves as the cause of happiness when delimited by various mental modifications (*vṛtti*). However, the Buddhists [hold a different view]...

Regarding those who claim that the Lord is omniscient, naturally in a state of nirvāṇa, eternally emergent, and the sustainer of worldly activities such as the composition of scriptures, [the author] replies: "He is imperishable and unborn. For the Supreme [Lord], birth and destruction do not occur inherently; otherwise, the requirement for causes and material substrates would become useless even elsewhere, since they would be absent at the time of existence, and because He is Himself non-existent at the time [of such events]. Furthermore, if these two were established inherently, their own manifestation—

[Otherwise,] there would be the consequence of [the Self] being reduced to a mere corpse. Nor can those two [origination and destruction] be established through another, because of the lack of connection with anything else. By the negation of the modifications at the beginning and the end, all modifications existing in between are also negated. Thus, the sense is that it is appropriate for the supreme reality—which is eternal, immutable, and not perceived as it truly is—to be the subject of the scripture (*śāstra*). Alternatively, by the word "that" (*tam*), the self-evident establishment of the inner self (*pratīc*) is stated; otherwise, like a jar—(2)

Because it would follow that [the self] lacks its own nature as a self, there is the scriptural statement: "In this regard, this person is self-luminous. The Digambaras, who are proponents of the "one-sided" view, assert that it is atomic (*aṇu*) or of intermediate size; the author refutes that by stating "all-pervading" (*vibhu*). For if it were atomic, it would be impossible for it to perform functions that extend throughout the entire body.
1 kha. Regarding that; 2 ka. for they; 3 ka. which is well-known.
1 [Vol. 1, page 25]
4.2 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* (Commentary on the Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)

[Objection: Since it would follow that [the self] is non-eternal like a jar if it possessed a middle-sized dimension, we perceive through direct experience that it possesses infinite dimension; thus, "He pervaded everywhere... [is said].

The intention is that this is the scriptural statement [beginning with] "Therefore... Since there is no other object to be praised within the full Self (pratīci), it is considered appropriate to employ the verb *vandati* (to salute) as a salutation to that very Self;
and since such a salutation is not fruitful without devotion (*bhakti*) and faith (*śraddhā*), the word "with devotion" (*bhaktyā*) is used.

Now, an objection is raised: the fullness of the Self is not possible, because its differentiation is perceived in relation to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth; to this, he replies: "By one's own ignorance" (*svāvidyā*). By the word "own" (*sva-*)...

The inner self (pratyagātman) is said to be powerful when there is no subverting factor, because it is primary; its manifestation is indeed ignorance alone. For it possesses no power other than that of ignorance. And it will be stated later: "Ignorance itself is our power. Produced by that [ignorance], the vast dualistic phenomenal world (dvaitaprapañca) is expanded through the states of the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth; caused by that, a clear delusion regarding the difference between selves is produced.

The connection of the words is as follows: I bow with devotion to Him whom those living beings (*jīvas*)—whose intellects are submerged in and veiled by that [ignorance] and who are full within the inner self (*pratīci*)—contemplate through various distinctions such as "Sūtra," "Hiraṇyagarbha," and "Virāj. This is the underlying intention:

there is no real, ontological difference in the inner self, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it; since such perception is merely due to ignorance (*avidyā*), its fullness is not thereby impaired.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the distinction [of the self] exists according to its appearance, since the cognition of a distinction established by both worldly people and investigators cannot be set aside?
To this, he says: "without parts" (*nirbhāgam*). First of all, there is no distinction therein caused by space and so forth, because [the self] is omnipresent, eternal, and non-dual.
Furthermore, whatever it were to differ from would itself be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*), because it would have to differ from the very nature of the self; therefore—

The meaning is that the cognition of difference regarding that [Self] is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*). Anticipating the objection that if the Self is partless, it would manifest as such for everyone, he says: "entire" (*sakala*). Alternatively, since the Self is not an object of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) but is self-luminous, difference within it is not established by authority; for surely, when something is not an object of knowledge, its difference cannot be an object of knowledge. Thus he says: "entire. If the Self were beyond all empirical usage (*avyavahārya*), then it would not be the subject matter of the scriptures.

[Objection: Since that which is untouched by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) lacks the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), [the author] says "no," beginning with the word "delighted" (*nandita*). For the entire world has its joy brought about by the Self; such a state would be impossible for one whose nature is devoid of bliss. Furthermore, scripture states: "Other beings subsist on mere portions of this very bliss. Therefore, it is logical that the human goal, as bliss, is not touched by engagement and withdrawal.

The sense is that even the inner self (*pratyak*) is the subject matter of the scripture. Alternatively, having raised the objection that the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*)—on account of the perception "I am happy" or "I am miserable"—cannot be the subject matter of the scripture, he says: "Nandita," etc. The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), together with its reflection, is the locus of pleasure and so forth, not the inner self (*pratyagātman*), because the latter is the witness of that [organ] and is supreme bliss (*parānanda*); therefore, it is logical that the self is accessible through the scripture. If the self were... [text truncated]

Anticipating the objection that because bliss (*ānanda*) possesses states such as birth and so forth, the same would necessarily follow for the Self (*ātman*) as well, he says: "It is imperishable and unborn.

By the negation of all modifications through such passages as "It is neither born nor does it die," its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) is declared; therefore, how could this [Self] be subject to birth and the like?

Nor does that [birth and so forth] belong to bliss either, because it is not perceived when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not taken into account, whereas in the case of suffering and the like, there is no perception of them as being the Self.

The meaning is that there is no fault even if this [act of salutation] is natural. If it is argued that there can be no salutation directed toward the inner self (pratyag-abhivādana) because a distinction between the one who salutes and the one who is saluted is observed in cases such as that of the teacher and the disciple, he says in response: "One" (ekam). The sense is that although there is no difference in reality within the inner self, that salutation is performed by imagining a difference. There is another interpretation: [the text refers to] the Reality shown in such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). This Reality—

He defines that which is characterized by knowledge and so forth, the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the word "That" (*tatpada*), as follows: "Him"—the Lord of cause and effect, the Witness thereof, the one who is "Thou" (*tvam*). [Note: The manuscript variants indicate textual differences regarding the reading of the verse.]
[This is] mine. 6 ka.
[The rain-retreat] of the year. [Vol. 1, page 26]
16. Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 5 1

He shows that this [Self], which is established by such scriptural passages as "consisting of consciousness, dwelling within the vital breaths," is the meaning of the word (*padalakṣya*). By the term "all-pervading" (*vibhum*), he indicates through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words that the meaning of the sentence is the identity of the referents of "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*). By the term "one" (*ekam*), he intends to convey that the supreme reality to be expressed is the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) alone, whose apparent objectivity is merely superimposed; it is with this intention that the accusative case is employed. In that regard, through one-pointedness of speech, body, and mind—
Salutation is the act of greeting. It is stated that "with devotion" because only when performed with both devotion (*bhakti*) and faith (*śraddhā*) does that salutation become fruitful.

Now, it may be objected: the Self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer, according to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "One of them eats the sweet fruit. But the Lord (*īśvara*) is not so; for another scripture says, "The other looks on without eating. Therefore, since these two are mutually contradictory, there can be no identity between them. To this, he replies: "His own..."

Thus, by its own term (*svaśabda*), the individual soul (*pratyagbrahman*) is denoted, according to the Vedic scripture: "He becomes merged into his own (*svam apīto bhavati*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) has that [Brahman] as its locus and that [Brahman] as its object;

for it is impossible for ignorance to have anything else as its locus or object, since that would entail the status of being ignorant [in that other entity]. As they say: "The indivisible consciousness alone possesses both the state of being the locus and the state of being the object. Its manifestation consists of two powers: the power of concealment (*samācchādana-śakti*) and the other, the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*).

Nor should it be argued that for us, ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is not a power (*śakti*), because it has been stated that ignorance possesses no further power, which would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For power is indeed to be understood solely through its effects. And in the case of ignorance, two effects are observed, namely concealment (*ācchādana*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). As it has been said: "Having concealed [it], it projects the nature of the Self which is ever-shining. Therefore, it possesses two powers corresponding to those [two effects].

This is also desired by the Śakti. Nor is there an infinite regress, because there is no need to postulate another power [to produce this one]. Thus produced, the vast aggregate-form (samaṣṭirūpa) which has become twofold through the distinction between the subtle and the gross—namely, the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) consisting of the seventeen-fold subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) composed of the five unquintuplicated great elements and their effects, and the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) known as the Vairāja, composed of the five quintuplicated great elements and their effects—the state of that...

The grammatical connection is as follows: I bow with devotion to Him whom the *cidābhāsas* (reflections of consciousness)—which are the individual selves (*jīvas*)—conceive of through the distinction of "the individual soul," "the world," and "the Supreme Self. These *cidābhāsas* are those whose true nature is obscured by the ignorance that is the cause of their delusion; because they are deluded, they possess the clear error of thinking themselves to be "doers" and "enjoyers. This occurs precisely because of the superimposition of identity with the two bodies (the subtle and gross) which are placed there by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of duality and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in their individual forms. It is solely due to this superimposition of identity that they are so mistaken.

And it has been said: "The world, though not fashioned by one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), has its fundamental state (*bhūmabhāva*) defiled by the distinction between the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratva*) and the state of the individual soul (*jīvatva*). One's own ignorance is *svāvidyā*; its manifestation (*vibhava*) is that which gives rise to it. The world-process (*prapañca*) is both vast and twofold.

Those in whom a clear delusion (*spaṣṭabhrānti*) has been instilled by these two are called "those with clear delusions. The intellect whose object is the Self is *ātmamati*; that [intellect] is obscured—

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those for whom [duality] is beneficial" (*hitā yeṣām te tathā*); and they are "those to whom the extensive manifold of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*)—produced by the power of their own ignorance (*svāvidyāvibhava*)—is beneficial"; and they are "those whose errors are manifest" (*spaṣṭabhrāntayaḥ*); and they are "those whose cognition of the Self is concealed" (*tirohitātmamatayaḥ*). In this context, by the term "their own ignorance" (*svāvidyā*), the superimposition of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyādhyāsa*) upon the reality that is of a single flavor is shown;

by the word "power" (*vibhava*), its two-fold capacity is stated. By the portion beginning with "produced" (*prasūta*) and ending with "errors" (*bhrānti*), the modification of the power of projection (*vikṣepaśakti*) is indicated.

Projection (*vikṣepa*) has been explained. The division [of the powers] is as follows: by the words "hidden" (*tirohitā*) and so forth, the function of the power of concealment (*ācchādana-śakti*) is stated. He restates the delusion of difference in the Self, which has acquired the cognition of difference due to being encircled by the two cities arising from ignorance (*avidyā*), with the words: "those who conceive [the Self] as having parts.
One should infer the plural number (*bahuvacana*) based on taking this very delusion of difference as the referent. This is the intended meaning (*abhisaṃdhi*): in the Self, the enjoyer...

Since the appearance of [the self] as "thou" and so forth is due to ignorance (avidyā), its identity with the Supreme Self—established by the sentence—is not contradictory, even though it appears in a contrary form.
Now, what is the answer to the inference that "Brahman and the Self are distinct from each other because they possess contradictory attributes, like water and fire"?
To this, he says: "Nirbhāgam" (without parts). First of all, a real distinction is not the probandum here, because it would involve an unestablished qualification (aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva); nor...

The appearance is merely illusory because it involves proving what is already established; furthermore, the possession of contradictory attributes is unestablished for those who accept valid cognition, while the other [attributes] belong to the original object and its reflection.
[Vol. 1, p. 27] (Note: ka, kha, and ga manuscripts read "asminn eva" here.)
6 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*— [Introduction]

The meaning is that because [the distinction] is subject to contradiction, there is no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) even by means of inference. Furthermore, Brahman is heard in scripture to be beyond speech and mind, and the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is likewise; otherwise, it would follow that it is non-self, like a jar. Thus, he states a counter-inference: "It is not distinct from the Supreme in reality, because it is beyond speech and mind, just like That. He says "sakala... etc. Moreover, "Brahman is bliss"—thus it was clearly declared...

Brahman is bliss because of scriptural texts such as "not from the sun" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1). Furthermore, because of the hearing of passages such as "of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32), and because it is the object of supreme love, the Self is likewise [bliss]; therefore, this [Self] is not different from the Supreme in reality. He states another inference for this: "because it is supreme bliss, like that [Supreme]. Moreover, by both Śruti and Smṛti, the Supreme is indeed immutable (kūṭastha); and by those same two, the individual soul (jīva) is also [immutable]. Therefore, by that...

He says that [the individual self] is not different from the Supreme in reality because it is immutable (*kūṭastha*), just like Him; thus he states: "It is imperishable and unborn. Furthermore, the Lord is independent, for otherwise His true nature would be impossible; and the individual soul (*jīva*) is likewise so because it is of the nature of the Self (*ātman*). As for the scriptural and traditional declarations regarding dependence, they refer to the qualified entity denoted by the word "jīva. Therefore, the inner consciousness indicated by the word "Thou" is non-different from the Supreme because it is independent, just like Him. Nor is it...

He states that there is no deficiency of means (*sādhanavaikalya*) even in the example, because that which is to be characterized is intended [therein]. Or rather, he states the contradiction with scripture regarding the inference of difference by saying "one" (*ekam*). In that context, the scriptural reality—that the object and its meaning are one—is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) expressed by the scripture as "that one all-pervading"; furthermore, the relationship (*saṃbandha*) between the subject and the object is also indicated by the phrase "delighting the universe," which implies unsurpassed...

The attainment [of the goal], the fruit, and the qualified seeker who desires that [fruit] have been indicated. Therefore, it should be understood that this [treatise] is to be commenced because the fourfold preliminary conditions (*anubandha*) are established. || 1 ||

The teachers, who followed their own teachers, have composed this commentary under the guise of the Kaṇva-Upaniṣad for the purification of the meaning of the entire Veda and for the peace of the virtuous.
The elucidation of the meaning is undertaken briefly by means of discourse grounded in logic, for the purpose of utterly destroying the doubts raised by sophists. (2)

Thus, under the guise of saluting the deities, the meaning of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) has been briefly stated: that the group of non-selves, which is perceived through one's own ignorance, is superimposed and not real; rather, it is Brahman alone, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and free. Now, by declaring the freedom from all defects of the Commentary about to be explained, and thereby indicating the faultlessness of the *Vārtika* itself—which consists in the manifestation of that [Commentary’s] meaning—the author states his intended purpose:

He makes his formal promise with the words beginning "yām" and so forth. The connection is as follows: "Having commenced the manifestation of the meaning of that commentary (*vṛtti*) which the teachers have well-composed, even in its smallest parts, by means of speech resting upon logic (*nyāya*). Having raised the objection that the *bhāṣya*—denoted by the word *vṛtti*—need not be further explained because its meaning is already clear, he states its "clarity and profundity" with the word "Kāṇva. By way of providing a commentary upon it—
The commentary proceeds to state that the mere study of the Veda, as acquired through the injunction for Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), has as its ultimate purpose Brahman and the Self.

For the Karma-kāṇḍa is an indirect auxiliary to the realization of Brahman by means of the purification resulting from the performance of rituals, according to the scriptural text, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice" (*yajñena... vividiṣanti*), and the principle of the *Sarvāpekṣā* section. The Jñāna-kāṇḍa, however, is directly useful therein, because of the scriptural text stating that the Supreme is "known through the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣada*).

Furthermore, this follows from the logic of the *Samanvaya* section (Brahma-sūtra 1.1). There is also the Śruti text: "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim. Although the Vṛtti [of Upavarṣa] appears clear on the surface, its meaning is extremely profound because it reveals that the entire sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) has Brahman as its sole purport; thus, it requires further exposition—this is the sense.
By this, the connection between the modification (*vṛtti*) and its object has been stated. He says that the modification must also be explained because it was composed by [the author] himself:
"The attainment of joy."
[Vol. 1, Page 28] Vārbika,
accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Regarding the word "guravaḥ" (the teachers): he states that this [work] must also be explained because it was composed by those belonging to a traditional lineage (*sāṃpradāyika*). He says: "by those who have attended upon their teachers. The meaning is: those by whom the teachers were attended upon through service (*śuśrūṣā*) and other means are "those who have attended upon their teachers"; having obtained knowledge from them, they composed this *Vṛtti* (commentary), and therefore it must be explained. Furthermore, since there exist qualified students endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), the *Vṛtti* which has been set forth for their sake must also be explained.
He says: "Of the virtuous" (*satām*). Having raised the doubt as to how this conduct (*vṛtti*) could provide benefit to them, he states the result:

"For peace" (*śāntaye*). Peace is the removal of saṃsāra along with its cause; the meaning is that this conduct is for their attainment of that [peace]. Since there is no reason for the conduct itself to require further explanation, he asserts that it is appropriate for the *Vārttika* to proceed toward the manifestation of its meaning: "The meaning... (*artheti*).

[Objection: Is the fruit of that *vārttika* merely the fruit of the [commentary] itself, or is it a different fruit? In the first case, discerning people who have already obtained the fruit through the commentary alone would disregard that *vārttika*. In the second case, that [different fruit] must be stated. To this, he says: "By the bad logicians (*kutārkika*)," and so forth. Having abandoned the scriptural reasoning (*tarka*) that supports it, and instead relying on reasoning born of their own intellect, those proponents of difference (*bhedavādinaḥ*) who desire to establish reality are the "bad logicians. Of those [bad logicians], the [fruit is] based on their own imagination...

The intermediate fruit of the *Vārttika* is the removal of doubts, misconceptions, and so forth; however, the ultimate fruit is peace (*śānti*) itself—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Since the words of the *Bhāṣya* themselves are capable of producing the understanding of its own meaning, the intermediate fruit is also established [by them]; therefore, the *Vārttika* is useless. To this he says: "By means of logic" (*nyāya*). Because it is possible for those of dull or mediocre intellect to have contrary understandings even regarding the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*, there is a need for logic to dispel them; thus, the [logic] contained within the *Bhāṣya*...

The meaning is that its fruitfulness results from the commencement of this *Vārttika*, which consists in the clarification of the *Nyāya*. By the word "speech" (*vacasā*), it is meant that it consists of the investigation of what has been stated, what has not been stated, what has been stated twice, and so forth. And it has been said:

"Wise scholars who know the nature of a *vārttika* declare that work to be a *vārttika* in which there proceeds an investigation into what has been stated, what has not been stated, what has been stated twice, and so forth."

By stating that it is impossible to reveal all the meanings of the aforementioned conduct (*vṛtti*), he confirms its extreme profundity and indicates his lack of arrogance by saying "in brief" (*leśataḥ*). By stating that the *Bhāṣya* on the *Kāṇva Upaniṣad* is to be explained, he has also indicated that its *Vārttika* is likewise to be commenced. || 2 ||

Now, at the commencement of a work, the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and other such factors must be stated as prerequisites for engagement; for in their absence, discerning persons (*prekṣāvantaḥ*) would not engage.
As they say:
"A listener proceeds to listen to that which has a known subject matter and a known relationship [between the words]."
"Therefore, at the beginning of a treatise, the connection (saṃbandha) together with the purpose (prayojana) must be stated.

Although the qualified student (adhikārī) and the subject matter (viṣaya) are indeed stated by the commentary beginning with "for those desiring to escape from saṃsāra," nevertheless, because the fruit (phala) has not been mentioned, there is no confidence for undertaking the work. For it has been said:
"For indeed, until the purpose of any treatise or even any action whatsoever has been stated, by whom would it be grasped?

Nor does either of the two commentaries provide that [purpose], because of the split in the sentence; nor is there an absence of fault because it is provided through the sense (*arthāt*), for that which is merely implied (*ārthika*) is not...

Because it would result in a lack of reliance on the word as such; nor is the *Nāmabhāṣya* concerned with the fruit, since that [discussion] concludes solely with its etymological derivation (*nirukti*), and that alone is not the meaning in every respect. [Note: The text fragments provided appear to be footnotes or marginalia from a manuscript or printed edition. 1. *sva.* [refers to a specific reading or commentary]. 2. *kha.* [indicates a variant reading].
3. *ka.* [indicates another variant]. [Vol. 1, page 29]
In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*,

regarding the objection that "the commentary (*bhāṣya*) need not be explained because its purpose is not desired," [the author replies]: "In that regard, since all activities are for the sake of a result, that [result] is primary."

And because the commentaries on the *Dadhikārya* and others contain a profusion of topics, [the author] sets those aside and first demonstrates that the *Nāmabhāṣya* is intended for the fruit [of liberation], according to the maxim that the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger [than the sequence of words]. This is shown by the passage beginning with "And here" (*atra ca*) and ending with "liberation alone is the purpose" (*muktimātraṃ prayojanam*).
Furthermore, in this context, the word "Upaniṣad" has as its sole referent the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
And since the referent of the expression exists only in that [consciousness], how could it [exist] elsewhere? (3)

He analyzes the commentary beginning with "This very [is it]," etc., by saying "In this [context]. In this commentary—or in another work—the word *upaniṣad* is asserted to denote merely the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) when it occurs in an internal (spiritual) sense, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). He states the reason for this as expressed in the commentary beginning with "of those intent on that," by saying "Therein. Regarding the two prefixes and the root √sad with the suffix *kvip*, according to the method to be explained, the meaning of the term *brahma-* is as follows:

The meaning is that because it occurs only in the sense of "knowledge" (*vidyā*), the word *upaniṣad*—formed from the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa* with the suffix *kvip*—refers specifically to that [knowledge] which possesses its own primary meaning. In passages such as "O sir, speak of the *upaniṣad*," the particle *ca* (and) is used to include the usage of that term for the knowledge of Brahman. Since the word is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in reference to a specific portion of the Veda (*āmnāya*), why should it abandon that conventional sense and function in another sense through its etymological derivation (*avayavārtha*)? For conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)...

He raises an objection based on the maxim "one takes away the village" (*gamāpaharati*), arguing that since it is accepted that words such as *śyena* function elsewhere even without abandoning their conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), [how can they be used in a figurative sense here?].
He asks: "Why is that? (3).
A prefix (upapadapūrva) exists in a state of proximity; it reaches its completion in that which faces it.
The word "ni" is also a qualifier for the threefold true object.

Regarding the phrase "and its designation," according to the maxim that "the function of intention (*tātparya-vṛtti*) is stronger than the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vṛtti*"), one examines the intention and—setting aside the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*)—it was stated that words such as *śyena* (hawk) are names of rituals based on a similarity described in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice] seize the hating enemy. However, it is not the same here, for the function of denotation [is absent] due to the lack of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*).

Since [the meaning] is well-known from its very nature, the derivation will be explained later; intending to show that the logical principle does not apply here, he explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "of the root preceded by *upa*" (*upanipūrvasya*) by means of the four Vārttikas, stating the meaning expressed by the prefix *upa*: "Upa. He states the objective meaning of that very [prefix]: "that which is facing it" (*tatpratīci*). Proximity, which is non-intervention, culminates in the "inner-facing" (*pratīci*) which is devoid of the distinction between internal and external; thus, it is "immediate" (*anantara*) and "not external" (*abāhya*).
This is from the Śruti. And it has been said: "Since the Self is the very nature of the Self, by what could there be any separation? This will be made explicit in the *Vidyāsūtra*.

Therefore, the meaning is that consciousness (*caitanya*), characterized by the absence of separation on all sides, is the sense indicated by the prefix *upa*. He states the meaning of the other prefix and the verbal root: "of the threefold," etc. [It refers to] the verbal root *sad*, ending in the *kvip* suffix, which denotes the agency of disintegration and so forth.

The meaning is "threefold. This is because it is recorded in the traditional lexicon (*smṛti*) that the root *ṣad* signifies "dissolution," "motion," and "depression. The meaning is that, just like the word *upa*, the word *niṣ* is also a qualifier by means of imparting its threefold sense in the manner to be described hereafter. || 4 ||
Having led this Self to Brahman from which all duality has been cast away, [one attains liberation].
It destroys ignorance and that which is born from it; therefore, it is called an *upaniṣad*.

How is it that the word *upaniṣad* applies specifically to knowledge (*vidyā*), even though its etymological meaning [suggests otherwise]? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states "It brings near" (*upanīya*) etc., restating the meanings of the prefixes and the root, and asserting that because the qualifier and the qualified both reside within knowledge, that alone is the *upaniṣad*. It brings near the pure meaning of "Thou" (*tvam*). Upa... [text continues].
1. Therein, the commentary (vārtika) [begins]. [Vol. 1, page 30]

Having caused [the seeker] to grasp Brahman— which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (aprapañca) and characterized by the absence of succession— knowledge loosens ignorance along with its effects from its previous state.

And it has been said: "It is the [instruction] for those whose souls are near to that, beginning from the womb. Therefore, because the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) is fully developed (*pauṣkalya*) in her, she alone is the *upaniṣad*; this is the meaning. Here, the meaning of the prefix *upa* is expressed by the four words beginning with *imām*, while the meaning of the root *ni* is expressed by *upanīya*; thus, the distinction is that it denotes the agent of dissolution (*viśaraṇakartṛtva*). || 5 ||
Having destroyed one's own ignorance—the root of all misfortune—by means of the Supreme as the Inner Self.
Or, because it causes one to go to that which is free from all differentiation, it may be called an *upaniṣad*.

Restating the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as being the cause for the attainment [of liberation], he states another mode regarding the application of the term *upaniṣad* specifically to knowledge (*vidyā*).

He says, "having destroyed": the evil (*anartha*) consists of the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth. For it has been said: "The evil consists of the state of being a knower, headed by agency (*kartṛtva*) and enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*). Its root is ignorance (*avidyā*); having cast off that [ignorance] which is the cause of the notion that the Self is not Brahman, knowledge [reveals] the Supreme Self as non-different.

It brings about the realization of the inner self (pratyak) as characterized by pure being (bhāva). As it has been said: "Because of the conclusion, or because of going beyond, [it is so called]; for among all sciences, its object is distinct. Therefore, since the meaning of the three designators is fulfilled within that [knowledge], that alone is the Upaniṣad; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
Because it completely cuts off the root of all causes for worldly involvement.
Since this knowledge causes one to settle [in the Self], it is therefore considered an *upaniṣad*.
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Asian scripts such as Sanskrit or Tibetan typically indicate the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]

Now, reiterating the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as "that which causes exhaustion," the author adopts another perspective regarding this very application of the term *upaniṣad*. Regarding the word "in its activity" (*pravṛtti*): attachment and other such factors are the causes of auspicious, inauspicious, and mixed activities;

knowledge (*vidyā*) destroys them by means of completely dispelling ignorance, which is their cause, through mere confrontation with it. For it has been said that [the root] has the sense of causing exhaustion (*avasādana*).
And because of the absence of dejection; therefore, since this [knowledge] fulfills the meaning of its constituent parts, it alone is the Upaniṣad—this is the sense. || 7 ||
Because it awakens one to the wisdom as previously described, the text is also non-different from that [wisdom].
It would be called an "Upaniṣad" just as a plough is called "jīvana" (the means of life).

If it is argued that since *vidyā* (knowledge) alone is intended by the term *upaniṣad*, how then can that word apply to the book [containing it], and is it not improper for a single term to have multiple meanings? Anticipating this objection, he applies the commentary beginning with "Because it has that as its purpose" (*tādarthyāt*). He says: "As described. For that knowledge of the Self as Brahman is the cause of dissolution (*viśaraṇa*) and so forth; the book possesses the quality of being the means of awakening that [knowledge], namely, its capacity to explain it. Therefore, because of the metaphorical identification of the explained and the explainer, we study the *upaniṣad*.

In such passages as these, the use of the word *tat* (that) is likewise appropriate. By this, the objection that one must postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for both [the word and its referent] is refuted; this is the meaning.
He provides an example of using the word *sādhya* (the probandum) for the *sādhana* (the means of proof) through the metaphorical treatment of the two as non-different: "The plough," etc. (Verse 8).
And because it is studied in the forest, it is called the Āraṇyaka.
Because of its greatness in both text and meaning, it is considered the Bṛhadāraṇyaka.

Anticipating the objection—given that the text generates the aforementioned knowledge, why does it not arise for all its students?—the author states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "this six-chapter work" (*seyaṃ ṣaḍadhyāyī*), intending to show that such knowledge arises from the syllables studied according to the rules of forest-recitation (*araṇyānuvacana*) and so forth, only for those intent upon hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other such practices. [He says: "araṇya... [The study of] the Veda, when studied according to the aforementioned rules, is the cause of knowledge; it is not merely the Veda.
1. Not from the womb (*nāgarbhā*). 2. Also not of a name (*nāmapīti*). [Vol.

The word "and" (*ca*) signifies that [the text] has been studied according to the rules for recitation in the forest (*araṇya*) and so forth. The term "this" (*etad*) refers to the collection of works [already mentioned]. Now, having been studied according to the rules for recitation in the forest and so forth—

Anticipating the objection—"Since you yourself do not know the true nature of some of these Vedāntas, how can knowledge arise from the syllables [of this work] as described?"—the author states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "Because of its greatness" (*bṛhattvāt*). "Because of its greatness": it is great in terms of its textual extent because it exceeds other Upaniṣads;
it is great in terms of its meaning because the indivisible Brahman is the subject matter propounded here, along with the internal and external means for attaining knowledge of that [Brahman].

Because it establishes many [doctrines], because of its greatness (*bṛhattva*), and because it is a forest-treatise (*āraṇyaka*), it is called the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*. Therefore, the Vedānta, as instructed by the teacher, leads to knowledge for one whose mind has been purified by the merits of many births, who has studied the Veda under the prescribed rules, and who has accomplished hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; it does not lead to knowledge for one of impure intellect—this is the meaning. || 9 ||
Under the guise of deriving such names [as "Īśvara"], that which is appropriate to the present context [is established].
He stated that the sole purpose of all the Upaniṣads is liberation alone.
He concludes the purport regarding the name by saying "ityādi" (and so forth).

Thus, at the beginning of the work, under the guise of etymologically explaining the names *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and *Upaniṣad*, the venerable author of the commentary states that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman—which is to be produced by all the Upaniṣads and is conducive to the commencement of the present treatise—is the destruction of bondage along with its causes and the attainment of unsurpassed bliss; he asserts that this is not some other fruit to be accomplished.
The inclusion of the term "Upaniṣad" is intended to show that the two types of texts on knowledge (vidyā) share a single fruit; this is the underlying intention. || 10 ||
For the purpose of establishing their mutual opposition, [the author treats] those qualified for action and those qualified for knowledge.
The author of the Commentary declared this statement to be for those desiring to transcend cyclic existence.

An objection is raised: "If the fruit has already been stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Nāma*, then by implication the qualified person (*adhikārī*) who desires that fruit is established; therefore, the *Bhāṣya* on the qualified person is redundant. Anticipating this, he states its intended meaning with the words "mutually" (*mithaḥ*). The literal meaning is as follows: there is a mutual contradiction—that is, a difference in nature—between the one qualified for ritual action (*karmādhikārī*) and the one qualified for knowledge (*jñānādhikārī*); the *Bhāṣya* on the qualified person is for the purpose of establishing that [distinction]. Even though [the distinction] is [implied] in the *Bhāṣya* on the fruit...

Although the one entitled to the offering of curd (dadhikārī) is established [as a qualified person], the intention is that there must be a distinction between the one entitled to ritual action (karmādhikārī) and the one entitled to knowledge (jñānādhikārī); such is the sense. || 11 ||
For one who has renounced all [worldly] activity and desires to abandon the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
And only for one who desires to know the oneness of the Self does there exist eligibility for the Vedantas. || 12 ||

Now, [the author] addresses the objection that there is no difference in the qualified candidates for knowledge and action, because both constitute the subject matter of the scripture (*śāstra*), and thus it is possible for them to be performed by the same candidate—just as the *agnihotra* and *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are.

To this he says: "Having renounced... etc. For one who has attained purity of intellect through the power of auspicious karma accumulated over many births, who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal, and who, being dispassionate, intensely desires to abandon all worldly enjoyment—both of this life and the next—all duties must be performed.

The qualification for the Vedāntas belongs to that renunciant who, having abandoned ritual actions according to the injunctions like the [discarding of] the black antelope horn, remains established in tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues; who is a seeker of liberation desiring the means to liberation; and who wishes to know the single-flavored nature of the Self. One who is desirous, capable, learned, and not excluded from the injunctions is qualified for them; nor is there a single qualification for both knowledge and action merely because they are the subject matter of the scriptures, as [is argued by] Bṛhaspati.

The meaning is that, because of the deviation [of results] in the case of the *rājasūya* sacrifice and others performed by Śūdras, it is evident that there is a distinction between the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) of knowledge and ritual action. || 12 ||
1. *brahmātmavāda*. 2. *sādhyaṃ* (ka); *phalaṃ* (pha). 3. *'ranivi* (ka).
[Vol. 1, page 32] *Vārtika*.

And likewise, [the statement] "this very [Self]" is for the sake of knowing the true nature of the inner Self (*pratyag-yāthātmya*), accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
The Śruti declares that one who has renounced all ritual actions is qualified for knowledge.

Having described the qualified seeker of knowledge, he states the authoritative means [for attaining it] with the words "This very one. The Śruti, seeking a qualified seeker for the purpose of ascertaining the reality—the true nature of the Inner Self which is Brahman—speaks of the renunciant through such passages as "Desiring this world alone, mendicants renounce" and the section on tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.
In accordance with these different types of qualified seekers, she declares that the renunciant, endowed with the aforementioned qualifications, [is the one fit] for the attainment of knowledge.
The meaning is that [the author] states [this] regarding the qualified person. || 13 ||
The study of the Vedas and other such practices are for the sake of accomplishing the desire to know the inner Self.
However, for the sake of attaining Brahman, one must renounce that [worldly life], by the force of the scriptural statement: "They desire it. (11)

[Objection: But surely, since one who has abandoned action possesses the qualification for knowledge, and since such Smṛti passages as "From dharma come happiness and knowledge" state that actions—denoted by the word *dharma*—are causes of knowledge, how [is this reconciled]? To this he replies: "The inner self... etc. Ritual duties such as the study of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) are causes of wisdom (*dhī*) by means of the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) and the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), because of the Śruti passage, "They desire to know through sacrifice. Therefore, when the desire to know and so forth exist...

The point is that since those [works] have already accomplished their purpose, they are no longer effective [for liberation], and thus their abandonment is established; however, memory serves as a cause for knowledge through a traditional lineage. What, then, is the direct means (*sākṣāt-sādhana*) to knowledge? He says: "Brahman. The attainment of Brahman is knowledge; for its production, the abandonment of those works, accompanied by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, is the direct cause. [As stated in the *Yogārū*...]

The meaning is that this is because of the Smṛti text: "The pacification of that very [mind] is the cause. He states another means of knowledge (*māna*) for the fact that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is a direct cause of knowledge: "Because of the Śruti text, 'Desiring... According to the Mādhyandina Śruti, "Desiring this very world, mendicants renounce," there is the proof of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on the literal sense of scripture) regarding renunciation being the direct cause for attaining the realization of the Self; for [otherwise], the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*)...

If that [action] were not a means to that [end], then one desiring it would not resort to it; for one who desires that end would not engage in its cause if they lacked the desire for it. The point is that a person desiring a village does not engage in eating merely because their desire for the village has ceased and they have developed a desire for something else, such as a new experience. || 14 ||
This has been stated for the purpose of understanding the subject matter of the aforementioned section.
The statement "the cause of saṃsāra" is supported by clear reasoning. || 15 ||

Having explained the commentary (*bhāṣya*) concerning the qualified student (*adhikārī*), he introduces the commentary that presents the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and other elements with the words "It has been said" (*ukta*). The "qualification" (*adhikāra*) mentioned in the opening words of the commentary—"The [present] discourse is commenced"—refers to the commencement of the work itself. The subject matter required for that is non-duality, which is accessible through the Vedānta; the commentary exists for the sake of the knowledge of that. Alternatively, "one whose qualification has been stated" (*uktādhikāra*) refers to the means (*sādhana*) taught in the immediately preceding commentary and so forth.

The qualified seeker is distinguished by four attributes; his subject matter is direct realization, which is the cognition of identity; and the commentary (bhāṣya) exists for that purpose. Alternatively, the qualification has been stated, and the fruit is that which is stated in the Māṇḍūkya [Upaniṣad]; for knowledge is applied toward that fruit, and the means to that fruit—which consists in the cessation of ignorance—is the realization of the subject matter of the Vedānta, namely the cognition of identity; thus the commentary exists for that purpose. In this way, there are three types of meaning for the commentary.

He states how there is the capacity for the expression of that meaning: "clearly" (*sphuṭa*). The clarity of the reasoning (*nyāya*) consists in its being free from fallacious appearance (*anābhāsatva*). || 15 ||
For there is no other subject for the words of the Vedānta than the nature of the one Self.
A certain object is apprehended; therefore, the cognition thereof dispels darkness.

Now, it might be argued that unity is not the subject matter of the Vedāntas, because they are devoted to such things as meditative identification (*saṃpad*); and thus, since they would lack the status of being a valid cognition regarding the nature of unity, they would be fruitless.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Introduction]:

Regarding this, he says: "Aikātmya" (the oneness of the Self). Since it is understood through the marks of purport—such as the uniformity of the opening and the conclusion—that the Vedāntas have oneness as their primary aim, they cannot possibly have the nature of mere meditative identification (*saṃpad*) or the like; therefore, the knowledge of oneness possesses fruitfulness by virtue of being valid cognition (*pramā*). This is the meaning. || 16 ||
For the sake of attaining the knowledge that destroys ignorance, the cause of saṃsāra.
This [work], devoted to the Upaniṣads of the Vedānta, has been commenced with great effort. [Objection:
Even if it removes ignorance (*tamas*), the knowledge of oneness (*aikyadhi*) remains as good as fruitless because it does not remove the causes of saṃsāra, namely merit and demerit (*dharmādharma*).

For merit and demerit are the causes of bondage, according to such scriptural passages as "Verily, by merit one becomes meritorious," and so forth; yet, because they are objective entities (*vastu*), they cannot be parts of knowledge. Therefore, he says: "Transmigration... etc. Indeed, merit and demerit are not the causes of that [bondage] for the unattached Self, since there can be no connection between it and them without ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, ignorance alone—acting through the medium of merit and so forth—is the cause of that [bondage]. And since ignorance is the opposite of the knowledge of the identity of the Self, it is logical that it is the destroyer of the cause of bondage.

The sense is: "You [are that]. Now, one might object: since bondage is still perceived even by one who has attained knowledge, self-knowledge cannot be the destroyer of the ignorance that is its cause; for when a cause is destroyed, its effect cannot persist. To this, he says: "the destroyer. For it is not indirect or common self-knowledge that destroys the cause of bondage, but rather the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; and it is for the sake of achieving that [realization] that this work, in the form of an *upaniṣad*, has been composed with such intent. And when...

The meaning is that in that [state], the perception of bondage is a mere appearance (*ābhāsa-mātra*). To the question, "How can even that produce direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding that which is beyond the range of words? he says: "Supreme" (*parā*). The meaning is that it is indeed pre-eminent (*atiśayavatī*), by virtue of which it may instill an understanding—even regarding that which is beyond the range [of words]—through both primary and secondary modes of operation (*mukhyetaravṛtti*). Alternatively, having stated the purport (*tātparya*) of that which is to be realized as the bestower of the object and so forth, this is connected with the statement that the meditative process (*vṛtti*) is now being commenced.
That which joins syllables is called "saṃsāra. || 17 ||
Only the knowledge of the true nature of the inner self effects the destruction of ignorance regarding that inner self.
And that [knowledge], by its very arising, does not depend on anything else for the destruction of darkness. || 18 ||

The proponent of the doctrine of combination (samuccaya-vādī) maintains that the cognition of the Self, which depends upon ritual action, destroys ignorance; in response to him, [the author] says: "pratyak... (referring to the verse beginning with *pratyag*).

Since ritual action is not opposed to ignorance, it cannot serve as an auxiliary to the knowledge that destroys it; furthermore, the doctrine of combination will be refuted later, and thus such a combination is impossible. Even if knowledge does not have ritual action as its auxiliary in the destruction of ignorance, one might argue that constant meditation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) will be its auxiliary.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "And that [is]... [meaning] another practice (*prasaṃkhyāna*). The sense is that a means of valid cognition does not depend upon anything other than itself for its own result. || 18 ||
The means of accomplishment and the qualified practitioner belong to the two sections of ritual action and knowledge.
Now, regarding their establishment through mutual contradiction, an objection is raised therein. || 19 ||

He restates the meaning of the three commentaries with the words "and the means" (*sādhanaṃ ca*). Action preceded by non-discrimination and so forth is the means to the human goal in the *Karmakāṇḍa*; in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, knowledge preceded by discrimination and so forth is the means. Thus, the means are established as distinct from one another according to the difference between the two sections. Furthermore, the distinction between the qualified aspirants (*adhikāribheda*) was mentioned here for the purpose of establishing their mutual opposition. By the repetition of the word "and" (*ca*), he implies the difference in subject matter (*viṣaya*) and other factors.

Thus, the meaning is that in both cases, the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth are established as being distinct. Now, he raises an objection regarding the distinction between the means of proof and the rest.
"Now" (*adhunā*) [introduces this]. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the indication of the means of proof and so forth. || 19 ||
Vārttika [Vol. 1, p. 34]
Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 13.
But surely we understand liberation to be characterized by injunction, just like worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Without the performance of the rite, there is neither eligibility nor attainment of the fruit of the sacrifice.

Thinking that, just as the attainment of heaven and other such worldly prosperities (*abhyudaya*) is accomplished through ritual action (*karman*), liberation (*mukti*) must also be accomplished by it because it is a fruit prescribed by the scriptures (*śāstra*), and thus the means and the qualified person (*adhikārī*) are identical, he elaborates upon the objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). By the etymological derivation from *karman*, "that which is characterized by injunction" (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the means (*sādhana*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, the meaning is that [liberation] is something whose means are rituals characterized by injunction. Even though it is a fruit prescribed by the scriptures...

To the objection that there would be no loss [to the seeker] if liberation were not achievable through action, he replies: "The effect" (kārya). Even in the world, an eligible person (*adhikārī*), though independent of scripture, does not achieve success without an object of cognition regarding what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*)—that is, the effect; for the activity of the eligible person has that as its object. The word *ijyā* denotes sacrifice (*yāga*) and refers to the means [of accomplishment]. || 20 ||

Even worldly [attainment] is obtained here; how much more so that which relies on the scriptures? Furthermore, there are Vedic statements for the purpose of establishing the characteristics of ritual injunctions.

The meaning is that even the worldly relationship between means and ends is not tenable without an effect (*kārya*), because the cognition of that [relationship] does not exist in what is not an effect; therefore, if liberation were not achievable through action (*akarmasādhyatva*), its status as a fruit taught by the scriptures would be untenable, which serves as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). By the word "also" (*api*), he states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic indicated [by it]: "What then, my friend... Here, "my friend" (*aṅga*) is an address to either an inferior or a middling person. This is the underlying intention (*ākūta*) here: when...

In the world as well, there is no acquisition of office or the like without a task; therefore, that which relies upon the Veda cannot be established without a task, according to the principle of the "Topic of the World and the Veda" (*lokavedādhikaraṇanyāya*), because the Veda follows the world. Thus, in the injunction for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma-codanā*), both heaven and the corresponding *niyoga* (directive) appear as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Consequently, a person’s mastery over action depends on both; and even therein, the *niyoga* holds primacy—up to [the point where...]

However, it is established in the *Jīvanādhikaraṇa* that in the injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvaj-jīva*), the mandate is produced solely by the *niyoga* itself. Furthermore, in the sentence concerning the "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*), the *niyoga* understood as pertaining to the sacrifice for the sake of the enjoined person qualified by the goal of heaven does not reach its conclusion without establishing that the sacrifice is a means to the heaven intended by the desirer; thus, through the implication of the *niyoga*, the sacrifice—though momentary—is understood to be a means to the fruit.

Because it is impossible for that [action] to be the cause of a fruit that arises at a later time, it is accepted—according to the logic of the *Apūrva* section—that it acts through the medium of the *apūrva*. Furthermore, it was stated in the *Bādari* section that the connection between a Vedic sacrifice and its fruit is dependent upon something to be accomplished (*kārya*). Therefore, even for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), liberation results only from the performance of ritual action;
thus, it is the effect of that [action]. He states that the fact that absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) is the effect of ritual action is supported not only by inference but also by scripture.

Regarding the word "vidhi": like [the rule] *yekayordvivacanaikavacane*, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) here has its primary meaning as an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). The sense is that there are indeed Vedic statements intended to establish that liberation is achievable through ritual action (*karma*). || 21 ||
One should perform the seasonal sacrifice (ṛtu), and so forth; such is the injunction for the sake of prosperity (abhyudaya).
And likewise, the injunction "one should worship" is observed even in the state of liberation.

He states those [points] by way of examples: "One should perform," etc. Just as an injunction (vidhi) is observed regarding sacrifices and the like when heaven and so forth are the intended objects, so too is that [injunction] seen to have meditation and the like as its domain even when liberation is the intended object; therefore, the meaning is that liberation results from meditation and so forth performed according to injunction. Furthermore, the meaning includes the collection of passages such as those concerning the instrument of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*). || 22 ||
[Vol. 1, p.
35] 14 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the Connection]:
Prosperity and liberation are, respectively, that which is to be accomplished and that which is not to be accomplished; they are constant and inconstant.
1. Due to this difference, the equality of their means of proof is not tenable. || 23 ||

Since liberation is to be accomplished through action, and since there exists a gradation among its fruits, it might follow that there is no distinction between those qualified for the means and the fruits in both sections [of the Vedas]. To this, he replies with the words beginning "No" (*na*). He clarifies the aforementioned negation by means of the stated reason with the words "of prosperity" (*abhyudayasya*). It is not proper to claim that prosperity and liberation have identical means, because of the difference between the two.

The logical connection is that [the two differ] due to the distinction between what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and what is not to be accomplished (*asādhya*), and so forth. Indeed, it is not reasonable to infer that [liberation] possesses the fruit of scriptural injunction (*śāstrīyaphala*). This is because it is sublated by the two limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) and being non-eternal (*anityatva*). Furthermore, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the means of proof, because liberation is not something to be accomplished—since its status as something to be accomplished will be refuted—and because it is eternal. Therefore, the intended meaning is that when there is a difference between the means and the fruit, one must recognize a difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). || 23 ||
The beneficial is one thing, and the pleasant is indeed another; both, having different aims, bind a person.
Of these two, for him who chooses the higher good, it becomes beneficial; but he who chooses the pleasant is deprived of his true purpose. 24.

He asks: "Is your inference contradicted by scripture? and replies: "The other. This means that *śreyaḥ*—knowledge, which is the means to liberation (*apavarga*)—is different from, or distinct from, *karman*, which is the cause of [attaining] heaven and so forth. He says that *preyaḥ*—action (*karman*), which is the means to prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—is likewise distinct from knowledge, which is the cause of liberation. And those two, *śreyaḥ* and *preyaḥ*, namely knowledge and action, [lead] a single person in succession...

He says that these two are distinct in their fruits because they are the means to heaven and liberation respectively: "Those two... Among them, for one who is intent on hearing [the scriptures] and so forth and thereby accomplishes the higher good (*śreyaḥ*), which is knowledge, there arises a fruit that is auspicious and free from rebirth. But he who chooses what is called *preyaḥ*—action—and is devoted to its performance while turning away from knowledge, by implication attains only an impermanent fruit.

He states the resulting fruit with the words beginning "of those two" (*tayor*), and so forth. The distinction is that in the first half [of the verse] the difference between cause and fruit is stated, whereas elsewhere the distinction lies in the difference between the fruit and the qualified recipient (*adhikārī*). || 24 ||

But surely, like prosperity (*abhyudaya*), liberation must be something to be accomplished, because it is of a nature not yet attained.
