It was stated that inference cannot function because it is based on a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*) and because it contradicts scripture. Now, an objection is raised: "The liberation under dispute is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because it has the nature of being unattained, like heaven"—thus, by this inference, the probans is pervaded by the limiting condition of being "to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*). [The author] replies: "Not so. Is the unattained nature of liberation real or illusory? It cannot be the first, because it would be unproven for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddhi*). Thus he says: "Not so."

In the second [alternative] as well, one may propose the options that it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), or the manifestation of what was previously non-existent, or the destruction of non-attainment or error; he refutes the first of these with the words "Even if it were to be accomplished" (*sādhyāpi*). Just as spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is something to be bestowed through effort, liberation (*apavarga*) is not so for us, because it is our very own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the illusory notion that liberation consists in the form of non-attainment does not bring about its status as a primary object to be accomplished (*mukhya-sādhya*), as there is an inconsistency in cases such as gold placed in one's hand that has been forgotten.
Such is the intended meaning. || 26 ||
Because darkness, whose obstacles are naturally liberated, is destroyed by knowledge.
Therefore, that absolute liberation (kaivalya) is said to be the goal to be accomplished, though only figuratively. || 27 ||

In the second [verse], he states that [the argument] is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*). Regarding the word "svataḥ" (by itself): in the sense of a non-coordinate construction (*vyadhikaraṇa*), it means "of him by whom obstacles have been abandoned as a matter of fact, there is darkness"; or, in the sense of a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it means "of him who is liberated by himself, there is darkness. [The genitive endings in both cases] refer to that [darkness].

The wise declare that although Nirvāṇa is eternally attained as one's very own nature, it is nevertheless to be accomplished through knowledge; for they say that it is as if unattained because it is destroyed by the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] sentences, and thus it is figuratively said to be an effect of knowledge. We too maintain that its status as an effect is merely figurative. Therefore, the sense is that if "being an effect" is defined as the destruction of the delusion of non-attainment, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). || 27 ||

In the same way, although liberation exists as the very nature of the knower, it is veiled by ignorance; through the realization of that [nature], ignorance is destroyed, and thus [liberation] is figuratively designated as something "attained.

He states the proof for liberation being eternally attained as the very nature of the Self: "Brahman," etc. Passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman"; "Being Brahman, he attains [Brahman]"; "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" indicate that liberation—which consists of the nature of Brahman as the Self—is eternally established, since its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is merely figurative. Therefore, [the opponent's position] is sublated by scripture (*āgama*).

The meaning is that there is an inference based on liberation being something to be accomplished in reality. He states the result [of this] regarding liberation being eternally attained by virtue of its being the Self: "In deep sleep," etc.

Since this Self is eternally liberated, therefore—just as a sleeping person is awakened by someone standing nearby through the clapping of hands and so forth, but is not made to perform an action—likewise, the seeker of liberation is also instructed by such scriptures as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) that "you are not a transmigrating being, you are indeed Brahman," and is not [instructed] to practice meditation and the like.
Therefore, because ignorance is destroyed by awakening, liberation is said to be that which is to be accomplished; such is the meaning. || 29 ||
What purpose would there be here for an injunction, given that its cause is falsehood?
Even if it were heard [in scripture], it would be meaningless here, because the purpose of an injunction is impossible.

One might raise the objection: "Even though liberation is the fruit of knowledge, knowledge itself is enjoined by such passages as 'one should cultivate wisdom' (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*). [Objection: Regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), even if an injunction (*vidhi*) were heard [in scripture], it would be purposeless because it cannot be performed; otherwise, it would be directed toward an unfit object and thus useless, like the sharpness of a razor applied to stones and the like. When there is no duty to be performed, no qualification is determined.

Having refuted the notion that liberation is like worldly prosperity by pointing out the difference between the fourfold fruits of action and liberation, [the author] stated the distinction between the two sections regarding their means and so forth; now he restates the argument expressed by the words "without an effect" (kāryaṃ vinā) and so on. "Effort" (*yatna*) is the human activity directed toward the desire to determine the intended meaning of the Veda. Since, on the plane of worldly transaction, every subject matter of the Veda culminates as either an injunction (*vidhi*), a prohibition (*niṣedha*), or a supplement to those two, ritual action alone is the cause of human goals; therefore, since even liberation (*mokṣa*) is a human goal like heaven (*svarga*), it must be accomplished by that [ritual action]. || 34 ||
Surely, I have already spoken many times in the Śruti regarding the statements previously mentioned.
Because they are not productive [of results], what has been stated by you is not logical. (35)

Therefore, how can it be claimed that ritual action alone is the cause for attaining the goals of human life? To this we reply: Since those passages lack the quality of conveying the nature of reality, it is ritual action alone that is the cause for the goals of human life.

It refutes [the objection]: "Because it is not prescriptive" (avidhāyitvataḥ). || 35 ||
Because the sacred tradition has action as its purpose, and because of the aphorism beginning with "by means of injunction."

Since it is possible for them to form a single syntactical unit as being supplementary to an injunction (vidhiśeṣatayā), one might ask: "In the absence of their having as their purport the entities heard therein, what is their purport? Those sentences such as "He wept" (so'rodīt) and others, which do not convey any action or anything related to an action, lack a meaningful subject matter because they do not establish a dharma that possesses a result. Therefore, a sentence of this kind is non-eternal;

since it depends on another means of knowledge by virtue of its dependence on an already established fact, it is not an authority [on dharma]. This is the meaning of the sūtra beginning with "Because the Veda has action as its purpose" (kriyārthatvād āmnāyasya).

Thus, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position was raised that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack authority. [The reply is: An *arthavāda* such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" is authoritative because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) ending with "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu.

There is a single syntactical unity between the injunction and the praise because the words possess mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Even though there is no action [explicitly mentioned] in passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," etc., [the connection is established through the context].

Even though neither that [result] nor its connection is understood, nevertheless, since the injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*ālabheta*) and so forth possess purpose through the meaning characterized by the fulfillment of required actions and the like, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) would be authoritative; thus it is said, "But because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction," and so on.

For those [passages] that are devoid of a fruit but desire one, it is logical that they reach their final completion by attaining syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with an injunction possessing a fruit, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). "Since it is a logical principle that when a single unified statement is possible, a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda) is not desired, they do not constitute a separate context there. Then, having raised the objection that there can be no cause for liberation because it is eternal, he says, "By means of its instrument," [implying] that it requires a means because it is a human goal, like heaven.

Consequently, when this present body falls, there is an absence of any cause for the assumption of another body; thus, for one who has practiced as described, liberation—the absolute cessation of the body—is established without effort. Nor is this [knowledge] independent of a medium with respect to the sacrifice—

To this he replies: "Of the Self. Just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇatva*) assists the sacrifice by way of the ladle (*juhū*), so too knowledge assists it by way of purifying the agent; thus, knowledge is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of that [sacrifice]. Therefore, the mention of a fruit in that context is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). But surely, passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" are seen to be explanatory passages subordinate to injunctions, yet no such thing exists in the Vedāntas?

Regarding the statement that there is no injunction (*vidhi*) in the case of knowledge because the mention of its fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), he says: "The injunction. Since knowledge is not something to be enjoined, even in the absence of an injunction for it, it is unavoidable that it be a subordinate part of an injunction as a refinement of the agent (*kāraka-saṃskāra*), like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Thus, it is logical that the mention of its fruit is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). || 45 ||
It is not so, because of the mutual contradiction between their respective causes and their respective natures.
Therefore, what has been stated by you regarding both liberation and worldly prosperity is not correct.

He refutes the opponent’s claim that liberation is achievable through ritual action (*karma*) by means of the principle of "belonging to a single birth" (*aikabhavika*), stating: "Not so. The reason for this is given as "because of their causes" (*taddhetu*).

The meaning is that since the causes of those two—liberation and worldly prosperity—are respectively knowledge preceded by discrimination and action preceded by non-discrimination, they are mutually distinct;
therefore, liberation cannot be achieved according to the logic you have proposed. Now, the opponent does not accept the reason for the distinction between those two causes.

For he maintains that both [types of karma] are to be accomplished through action; regarding this, he says: "tadrūpa" (of that nature). The meaning is that since their natures—being constant (*dhruva*) or non-constant (*adhruva*)—are distinct, the distinction between their causes is implied by implication (*ārthika*). Furthermore, the distinction between the nature and the cause of those two has already been established because...

Therefore, he states that the claim you make—that liberation is to be accomplished through action—is based on ignorance of the reasons already stated and is not correct: "In liberation... (verse 46).
It is stated by you that liberation is the abiding of the self in its own essential nature;
and the attainment of that [liberation] is described as resulting from the avoidance of desire-driven actions and the like. (47)
Having stated that the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) does not arise, he restates the objection raised by another in order to state it in yet another manner: "In its own nature," etc.
Having restated the goal (upeya), he restates the means (upāya): "Desirable [results] and so forth. (47)
In that regard, what is the nature of the self such that it was not previously established in that state, [and thus requires] its establishment?
For that which depends upon a cause through effort would not be its own inherent nature.

He entertains the doubt as to whether the self was previously established in its own nature or not, due to the performance of the stated means. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): he restates the second alternative with the words "in its own nature" (*svarūpe*).

He states the reason for the self's non-establishment in its own nature prior to the performance of the means with the words "by which" (*yena*): if, by that very reason through which the self seeks a cause for its establishment in its own nature, it were [already] established in its own nature previously—then [the seeking of a cause would be redundant].
This is for the purpose of restating [the opponent's position]. He refutes it with the words: "For the essential nature... (48).
That which is not established by itself is forcibly established there by means of a logical reason.
If this [self] is indeed already established, for what purpose is there a search for a cause? (49)

The meaning is that where [the Self] does not abide by itself, nor is it established by means of a cause through the force of practice—that is not the essential nature of the Self because it would be adventitious, like [transient] attributes (dharma) and so forth. He takes up the first [objection] with the word "Now" (atha). He refutes it, saying: "In that case, the practice of the desired means would be useless; for one who has already reached the village does not wish to go to the village. Why? [He asks: "For what purpose? (kimartham) || 49 ||
Moreover, even in the state of isolation (kaivalya), the non-release from that association would follow as a logical consequence. || 89 ||
Therefore, by avoiding prohibited acts, optional rites, and the like, there is no liberation for the self. (50)

Anticipating the objection that one who has attained the fruit does not incur fault by following the cause [of action] simply out of his own nature (*svabhāva*), he says: "Even in liberation" (*kaivalye 'pi*). Since nature persists as long as the substance exists, even a liberated person would continue to follow it; consequently, there would be no distinction between the states of liberation and bondage. Furthermore, since the avoidance of desire-driven acts and so forth depends upon the connection with the body and other such factors, if the liberated person were to perform them, he would remain connected to them. Therefore...

He says "there is no liberation" and "there is no release. Since, if [the self] were already established, the performance of further means would be useless, and if it were not established, its being an inherent nature (svabhāva) would be impossible—therefore, for the reasons stated, the establishment of liberation as the state of abiding in one's own essential nature for the self does not occur. He states the conclusion with the word "therefore. || 50 ||
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of removing the lack of composure born from habitual engagement with sense objects;
But for what reason does that contact with sense objects occur? (51)

One might object: "We do not resort to the means taught for the sake of abiding in the true nature [of the Self], but rather to pacify the sins produced by repeated experience of objects associated with the world. To this, he replies: "Regarding the objects... [The objection continues: "In the case of the unattached Self, there can be no attachment to objects because of the absence of a cause. [The response continues: "...but the mind... [and so on]. 1. *ka*. *ddhistu va*; 2. *kha* *tasthau*; 3. *kha* *to navara*.

The Lord says: "But he... Anticipating the objection that consciousness might be attached to objects by its very nature, just as it is in the self, He asks:
Because there is no prohibition even when your power is released from its causeless state.
If that were the case, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation. || 52 ||
In the second half of the verse, the author states the reason for the proposition that "without a cause, there can be no liberation for you regarding attachment to objects.
The meaning of the reason is this: if the union with objects were to arise without a cause, then the consequence would inevitably follow that such union would occur even in the state of liberation.
To establish that there is no factor to prevent this, he provides the reason: "because [you] do not deny it" (aniṣedhataḥ). || 12 ||
If it is caused by merit and demerit, then what [is the cause] in the case of the transgression of dharma?
Even for one whose nature is unattached, these two forcibly bring about contact.

In contact with sense objects, one shakes off the defect caused by the absence of a cause. Regarding the word "Dharma": one might raise the doubt whether these two [virtue and vice] produce a connection with objects for the Self—which is unattached and a non-doer—or rather for that which is the opposite of it; having thus proposed the alternatives, he refutes the first. "But what then? The word *kiṃ* (what) is used here in the sense of negation. || 53 ||
Indeed, even if it were flashing, it would not appear on a cloth marked with *bhallātaka* fruits in this world.
Even a skilled potter [cannot produce] that which has the nature of a non-pot or the like. —54‖
One should make the jar of clay cool by means of wind or water.
"If the self were of the nature of an agent and so forth, then do not desire liberation.

In this regard, he states an example by way of contrast: "Like the *bhallātaka* fruit," etc. Just as a *bhallātaka* fruit, when brought into contact with a cloth that is in reality stainless, defiles it, so too [are] merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which bring about the acquisition of objects, [not applicable] to the self which is devoid of attachment and the like.

This is the meaning. He states the incapacity of those two [space and consciousness] to impart a connection with an object to the self through both a point of similarity (*sādharmya*) and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), beginning with the words "For not... and so forth. Regarding the statement "not by force of manifestation" (*sphuranbalāt na*), there is a distinction: since it is said that one who is "skilled" (*kuśala*) explains the body's strength as "manifestation," while "skill" (*kauśala*) refers to the strength of the intellect, the former is physical power and the latter is cognitive power. Just as a potter makes a jar from clay, so too space—which is by nature not a jar or the like—does not become a jar.

It is capable of doing so; however, just as the wind, although it produces cold everywhere, does not produce it in fire, so too dharma and the other factors, though they are causes for the production of all things, do not establish a connection with the aforementioned Self. For an object contrary to one's own nature cannot be brought about even by a hundred reasons—this is the meaning. He restates the second [position]: "The Self," etc. First of all, the Self has the nature of being an agent and so forth; its...
The meaning is that the avoidance of lust and so forth is for the purpose of removing the attachment to objects and the resulting habituation to virtue and vice.

Is this [agency] of the nature of an effect such as agency and the like, or is it of the nature of the power (śakti) for that? Regarding the first case—that liberation of the self occurs upon the destruction of effects such as agency—the author says "Do not desire" (mā kāṅkṣīḥ), [refuting it] by stating that this is not the case even when those effects are not destroyed. || 14 || 11 ||
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities cannot be turned away, just as heat cannot be removed from water.
An object that has ceased from its intrinsic nature is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like a flower in the sky.

In this regard, the reason is given: "Not indeed. Anticipating the objection that even the nature of the self—such as its being an agent and so forth—might be averted from its harmful state by means of a specific cause, he says: "From its own nature" (svabhāvāt). || 16 ||
Fire is never destroyed without its heat being removed;
likewise, liberation cannot possibly occur without being freed from the agent and other such factors.

Now, even though fire is excluded from its own nature of heat when in proximity to mantras and the like, it does not thereby become devoid of nature like a sky-flower; likewise, the Self, although withdrawn from the aforementioned nature due to the stated reason, is not devoid of nature. To this, he says: "No," and so forth. Because its power is obstructed by the presence of mantras and the like, fire does not produce a burn or similar effects; it is not because of that [obstruction] that its nature as fire ceases to exist.

Furthermore, even if that [fire] ceases after some time, it is because its effect is observed from that very same [cause]; therefore, fire existing in proximity to mantras and the like might naturally deviate from its heat. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of its losing its intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*). Likewise, if the Self were to deviate from its own nature, it would follow that it lacks an intrinsic nature, and thus there would be no liberation. This is the sense. He says "nor the second" [to refute that alternative]: "And not... For liberation is indeed the destruction of suffering (*anartha*), and [the Self is] the agent...
And since non-existence (anartha) begins with "non-being" (tvat), as long as that exists, there is no liberation because bondage alone persists; this is the meaning. || 17 ||
Is it not the case that the very activity of being an agent and an enjoyer constitutes the transmigratory existence of the self?
But it is not that [the object exists] as mere power; rather, it exists as mere power in this manner. || 58 ||

Having rejected the position that [the Self] has the nature of effects such as agency (*kartṛtva*), he adopts the position that its nature is the potentiality (*śakti*) for those [effects]. He introduces this with "But surely" (*nanu*). He states what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with "but not" (*na tu*). If it is argued that even so, the impossibility of liberation remains the same, he says "no" with "In this way" (*ityevam iti*). This means: by the existence of that potentiality alone, which is devoid of effects such as agency. || 18 ||
From liberation from all that is disadvantageous, the state of self-liberation is established.
Let it not be so; for in that case, there would be a fault regarding the difference or non-difference between the power and its effect. (59)

The meaning is that "misfortune" refers to effects such as agency and so forth; even when that potential exists, there is an absence of the cognition of misfortune during states such as deep sleep. He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating, "Not so," on the grounds that liberation does not occur despite the existence of that potential. How is liberation impossible under the theory of potential? [The answer is: Because of difference. || 59 ||
Because there is no distinction between the power and its effect. || 72 ||
If there were a distinction between those two, it would follow that the impossibility of restriction [of cause and effect] would arise.

Anticipating the objection as to how there is a fault in both cases, he clarifies the fault in the difference between power (*śakti*) and its capacity (*śakya*), or between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*). He says: "Power... Since the distinction—"this is power" and "this is the effect"—is not perceived, and because the root *vid* here means "to know," the meaning is that such a distinction does not exist. Anticipating the objection that even if this difference exists, it does not appear due to unfitness for perception, he says:

He says "niyameti" (it would restrict). The meaning is that if there were a difference between the power (*śakti*) and its effect (*tatkārya*), there could be no restriction such that "this is the power" and "this is its effect," because, like a cow and a horse which are absolutely distinct, the relationship of being that [power and effect] would be impossible. || 60 ||
The relationship of cause and effect would not exist between two things that are established as distinct by their own nature.
And if there were no difference between the two, they would be one; how then could there be the relationship of cause and effect? || 61 ||
1 kha. Not so. 2 kha. Thus. Not at all.

Anticipating the objection that—just as between power (*śakti*) and its effect (*tat-kārya*)—there is no lack of restriction because a cow and a horse are neither cause nor effect of one another—he says: "The effect... (*kārya*).

The meaning is that since a causal relationship is impossible between two things that are substantially distinct, as in the case of a horse and a buffalo, the lack of restriction cannot be refuted by that [causal relationship]. [Regarding non-distinction...]
He reveals the fault in the opposing position [the view that they are non-different] with the words: "And if there were no difference" (abhede ceti). || 61 ||
A cause that does not act is never observed, nor is an effect ever seen while it is not being produced.
If, on the other hand, their non-difference is accepted, it follows that [the cause] must perish when the effect is destroyed. (62)
The destruction of that capacity [of the pot] also follows, because it is not distinct from those two.
And when the nature of the power is lost, there is the negation of the possessor of the power. || 63 ||
Because there is no distinction between the two, that very [self] arrives undesired.
Since the doctrine of selflessness has been explained previously, one should not conceive of it in such a manner.
Even though power (*śakti*) and its effect (*tat-kārya*) are one and the same reality, what loss is there if they possess the nature of cause and effect? To this, he says: "Not being an agent," etc.

For a mere entity (*vastu-mātra*) is neither the cause nor the effect, because in that case there would be no distinction between the state of being an agent (*kurvat-tva*) and the state of being acted upon (*kriyamāṇa-tva*); thus, it would not be an agent.

The meaning is that it would be contrary to worldly experience (*alaukika*) for an effect to exist while its cause is not being produced. To state another fault, he restates the position of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*) with the word "Now" (*atha*).
Having raised the dilemma—whether the effect is included within the power (*śakti*) or the power is included within the effect—the first fault [is as follows]:

[The opponent] says: "It is the effect. This means: because of that power, namely, the power which is the cause having the effect as its counter-correlative. [The author] asks: even if that power perishes—just as the effects such as agency perish—what harm is done? To this he replies: "Power... Even if there is the destruction of the power, its effect, and the possessor of the power, what is lost? To this he replies: "That very same... [The opponent asks: How can you say "that very same" when the topic under discussion is the doctrine of no-self (*nirātmavāda*)?

Regarding this, the [opponent] states the objection: "The previously mentioned," meaning "the object that has ceased from its own nature. And thus, the implication is that there is no liberation because of the absence of a fruit; for if the effect were included within the potency, then as long as the potency persists, the effect would not be destroyed, and consequently, agency—

Intending to show that there is indeed no liberation because [the distinction] exists as long as the self exists—just like the power of manifestation (vyañjaka-śakti)—he concludes the refutation of non-difference with the words "Therefore... (tasmāt).
If it is held that the non-manifestation of the effect is due to the impossibility of its cause—
namely, the power (śakti)— that is not tenable, because both the power and its cause do exist.
Avoiding the aforementioned faults regarding the positions that [liberation] consists in either the power (*śakti*) or its effect (*kārya*), he states another view: "The view" (*matam*).

Liberation is not the destruction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the effect or its power; rather, it is the non-manifestation (*anabhivyakti*) of that effect which belongs to the power—such is the view, if one accepts this.

This is the construction [of the sentence]. Anticipating the objection that there would be an over-extension of the definition because the unmanifested effect exists even during sleep and so forth, he says: "By a cause. In sleep and similar states, however, causes for manifestation—such as unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and the like—still exist; otherwise, knowledge would be purposeless.
In liberation, on the other hand, those causes are impossible, and thus there is an absolute non-manifestation of effects. Therefore, there is no over-extension; this is the meaning.

He refutes the claim that liberation is the non-manifestation of the effect while both the potency (*śakti*) and the effect exist, with the words "Not that" (*na tat*). He states the reason for this: "Potency," etc. Potency is the material cause (*upādāna*); or rather, the excellence (*atiśaya*) derived from it is the cause of that effect, such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. Because of the occurrence of these two, [liberation is impossible]. [The commentary notes: 1. *vaṃtrika*; 2. *ka. di*; *muktiri*.

This is the interpretation: those causes for the manifestation of effects which exist in *saṃsāra* are present without deficiency even in liberation; therefore, the sense is that the manifestation of effects would likewise occur there [in liberation] as well. || 65 ||
The relationship of even the causal conditions is held to exist in the form of a potency.
Therefore, by those who perceive signs, there is an equality with the heat of fire and so forth. (66)

[Objection: But surely, even though the cause and the effect exist in an unmanifest state during liberation, there is no manifestation of the effect at that time because they are not mutually connected; therefore, he says: "By power" (*śakti*). Just as the soul is connected with the efficient causes (*nimitta*) such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth through their power, and with the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) through the excellence residing therein, it must likewise be accepted as being connected with the resulting states (*naimittika*) such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and the like. Indeed, the soul exists even in liberation; therefore, at that time—

Furthermore, at that time, attributes such as *dharma* and so forth remain unmanifest (*avyakta*), just like the power (*śakti*). Therefore, the relationship between locus and located exists therein; through the excellence inherent in that [power], these [attributes] share a common substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). By this, the relationship of the power with even the occasional (*naimittika*) factors has been stated. Since the causes of those [occasional factors], such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and the rest, stand in a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittikatva*), the manifestation of agency and so forth in that state is no different from [the state of] transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); this is the meaning.

He states the resulting conclusion regarding the absence of agency (*kartṛtva*): "Thus, from that" (*iti tataḥ*). Since the unavoidable nature of the connection between dharma and so forth with their respective causes has been stated, therefore—just as the manifestation of heat and light occurs when the manifesting agent is present—the manifestation of the effect must necessarily occur even in that [state of liberation] when the obstacle of ignorance (*satyanāva*) is removed.
Thus, the position that liberation consists in the non-manifestation of that [agency] is not tenable; this is the meaning. || 66 ||
If the effect were identical with its causal capacity, then because that capacity would always be present in the cause, [the effect would also always exist].
The production of effects would occur at all times, just like heat during the summer season. || 67 ||

Furthermore, does the effect such as agency depend upon a complete set of causes, or not? Regarding this, he first restates the first position and then refutes it with the words "of the effect. *Śakti* means the entire cause; that is also the meaning of the word *kāraṇa*. That [position] is not tenable because, according to the reasoning already stated, since the complete cause exists even in liberation (*mokṣa*), the production of effects would follow there as well; thus, liberation, cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), and deep sleep (*supti*) would all result in a state of total cessation (*laya*).

The meaning is as follows: since the effect is dependent on the complete cause, liberation does not occur while that [cause] remains; regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "not in summer" (*nedāgha*). Just as there is a continuity of merit when the cause for abundant merit is present, so too, because there is no cessation of that [agency] while the totality of factors such as agency exists, the meaning is that as long as agency and the like continue, there is no liberation. || 67 ||
In the same way, this same fault would arise even if [the agent] were not dependent on power (śakti).
An effect would never arise, because its cause would never exist.

He refutes the second [position] with the word "tathā" (so too). Just as there is an impossibility of liberation in the first case, so too, even though agency and the like depend upon a collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*), since that [agency] follows [the self], its independence is untenable; this is the meaning. He demonstrates that very fault.

He says: "The effect," such as agency and so forth, [is liberation]. The meaning is that because a cause for the effect never exists, and because the effect is never dependent upon a complete set of causes, the cessation of that [effect] due to the absence of those [causes] is liberation. || 68 ||
Since this statement is as cold [unreasonable] as it is during the summer heat, it is incorrect.
For if there were the production of an effect from that which is causeless, then the arising of effects would occur at all times. (69)

For this reason...

one might object that it is incorrect to say "that which is not dependent on a cause is not born, like the Self," because there is no subverting argument against the production of an effect without a cause. Anticipating this, he says: "of that which is without a cause" (niṣkāraṇasya). || 69 ||
Or how could there be bodily action for him, if he were not dependent upon causes? (2)
And it is not possible for men to maintain this vow from birth until death. || 70 ||
Even by the most skillful, there is the avoidance of prohibited and optional rites, and so forth.

He states another refutation: that if agency and so forth were independent, they would not be occasional. [The verse begins with] "kārya" [etc.]. It was previously stated that external means are useless for the self to abide in its own nature or to prevent the restlessness born from the habitual pursuit of objects; now, wishing to eliminate such means themselves, he first declares that the renunciation of desire and so forth is difficult to accomplish. [The verse begins with] "na ca" [etc.].

"From birth until death" means during the interval between birth and death; this is to be connected with the phrase "even by men who are skillful. By the word "etcetera," the avoidance of prohibited and optional rites of sight is included. The very vow regarding the causes mentioned by you is difficult for humans to undertake, let alone its performance; the gods, however, might somehow be capable of making such a vow and performing it for that purpose—this is said for the sake of derision.

It has been stated [by others] that "this is for men. Now, [the author] says "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) to show that even if such a vow and its performance are impossible for those of small intellect like ourselves, they are not impossible for humans of great intelligence who exert extraordinary effort. The remainder of the sense is that mere greatness [of intellect] does not suffice to accomplish the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow and its performance. (70–71)
Doubt certainly arises, yet for that reason alone there is no failure of the thesis.
Now, if he is released here, it will happen for him accordingly.

[Objection: But surely, because space and time are limitless, it is not reasonable for you—who are not omniscient—to assert that no one at all is capable of practicing the means taught by me, since you lack any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to ascertain their non-existence. To this, he says: "But there is doubt. Even in the absence of a means of knowledge proving the incapacity to practice the means taught by you, [doubt arises] due to the absence of any means of knowledge that makes known its existence.

The meaning is that there is doubt in the listener regarding the reason stated. Anticipating the objection that one who is in doubt might proceed to act upon even the reason stated by me—just as one approaches an object of doubt out of curiosity—he says: "In the case of a [pro]position," etc. For although one may act out of doubt regarding matters requiring little effort, one does not act when in doubt about matters requiring great effort, such as crossing the ocean; and since the reason stated by you requires great effort, one would not engage in it.

The meaning is that activity proceeds from doubt (*saṃdeha*). He anticipates the objection that even from doubt one may achieve success in one's own position, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). He refutes the establishment of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on doubt with the words "what you have said. The literal meaning is this: if one accepts that the establishment of the position [of yours] occurs through doubt regarding these means such as the avoidance of optional rites (*kāmya*) which you have described, it would not be so. For doubt does not first determine the object, since it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) by way of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); nor can your position be established through the impossibility of that [doubt], because we observe verbal doubt even when both alternatives are unseen.

[The opponent replies: "Indeed, even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent, a word produces knowledge; such is the established principle (*nyāya*). Therefore, the meaning is that by one who asserts the establishment of a thesis (*pakṣasiddhi*) from doubt, it is actually the non-establishment of the thesis itself that has been stated. [The author asks: "But [one might argue]: 'The subject under dispute (*vimata*) is established somewhere, because it is a category of doubt, like a commonly accepted thing (*saṃmata*). To this, he says: 'In its being inexpressible' (*avaktavyatve*). In the reading *tvadukteḥ*, the connection is with this [term]. He establishes its inexpressibility.

[The author] says: "It is certain. And that which is the object of doubt is not "certain," because that would involve a contradiction; therefore, it should not be said that [the subject matter] exists somewhere simply because it is the object of doubt. The remainder of the argument is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of verbal doubt. Anticipating the objection that even that which is the object of doubt might be taught—just as agriculture and the like—he says: "[It leads to] the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Even agriculture and the like, though doubted...

The reason stated by you is fit to be taught because it has a visible fruit; however, since [the means to] the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) must be determined through valid cognition (māna), that which lacks such determination does not deserve to be taught—this is the meaning. || 73 ||
But a wise person should not speak here of success that is merely accidental.
This is indeed within the domain of destiny, but not within the domain of human effort.
Now, some teach that even what is not established by valid means of knowledge—such as climbing heated stones and the like—is a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*);
regarding this, he says: "But not... [The word] *yādṛcchikī* refers to an attainment that occurs by chance; an attainment without a valid means of knowledge does not result in a supreme fruit.

The meaning is that a discerning person should not speak to one who is angry; however, those who desire an accidental success even regarding liberation through such acts as climbing a heated stone and so forth are not wise. Having refuted the establishment of a position based on doubt, he concludes by proving the impossibility of the stated reason: "By fate... (verse 74).
If it were the case that Śakti would become a co-agent, according to the principle [stated above], then...
"Even though it is within the range of human experience, it is not so described because of the impossibility [of such a description]. (75)

An objection is raised: since it is a logical principle that for verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) which convey meaning, the capacity of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) is a necessary auxiliary factor, and because a prescription (*vidhi*) cannot function as a prescription without a qualified person capable of performing the enjoined act, a verbal suffix such as "one desiring liberation should avoid [the desire-driven rites]" conveys its own meaning with respect to a human being and thus depends upon human capacity; therefore, its applicability to gods alone is unestablished. This he [the opponent] objects to. *Saha-*...

Regarding the term "agent" (*kartṛ*): where there is a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the power of agency is desired to reside there as its correlate; however, in the case of the statement "one desiring liberation should avoid [actions] such as those performed for desire," there is no verbal suffix that expresses this. Therefore, he provides the resolution: "Not by the verbal suffix," because the reason stated does not fall within the scope of human action. || 75 ||
There is no injunction stating that one who seeks liberation must not avoid rites performed for specific desires and the like.
Is there anything in the Veda by which [the *arthavāda*] would be a part of the injunction (*vidhi*)? (76)
1 kha. by that; 2 kha. kospra; 3 kha. in verbal [cognition] saṃ; 4 ka. tā || O Lord; 5 ka. O Lord iti.
[Vol. 1, page 49] 28

Anticipating the objection that there exists a statement in our own words— namely, "one who seeks liberation should avoid rites for desired ends (*kāmya*) and so forth"— and having proposed the alternative as to whether the basis for your statement is *Śruti* or *Smṛti*, he refutes the first possibility with the words "seeking liberation" (*muktyarthī*). For nowhere in the *Śruti* is it stated as you have described—

He states the conclusion regarding the non-existence of the verb (*ākhyāta*): "By which," etc. The meaning is that since there is no such thing as a verb in the Veda—by virtue of which [your claim] it could have the status of being a part [of the Veda] through its cooperation with the verb *kartṛśakra* (the agent-power)—your statement lacks authority because it is not rooted in the Śruti. || 76 ||
However, this avoidance of optional rites and the like arises solely from one's own intellect.
Therefore, it is not in any way logical for Śakti to be a part of that.

"One who desires liberation should not engage in optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*niṣiddha*) acts; one should perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites with the desire to avoid transgression"—this authoritative statement is the basis for our own words. Anticipating this second objection, he says: "Optional and so forth. First of all, this is not an independent means of valid knowledge (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), because it contradicts the section on Smṛti (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3). Nor can perception or other means of knowledge be its source, since [the results] belong to the next world.

Because the relationship between a means and its result is the exclusive domain of the Veda, and it has been stated that no such verb as you have described exists in the Veda; therefore, since an authoritative statement would lack a foundation and thus lack validity, and since your own statement cannot possess validity by being rooted in that [Vedic authority], the verb regarding the avoidance of optional rites (*kāmya*) and so forth is merely your own imagination. Consequently, the hundredfold agents [of the sacrifice] do not serve as auxiliaries for the verb situated in your statement.

The meaning is that it is a part of that [sentence]. He indicates that whether your statement is rooted in Śruti and Smṛti or is rootless, the agency-power (kartṛśakti) does not establish its being a part of that [sentence] by means of its cooperation with the verb (ākhyāta) contained therein. "In any way whatsoever" (kathaṃcidapi). || 77 ||
Neither by performing the obligatory rites and so forth, nor by avoiding the optional rites and so forth.
The attainment of the highest good is possible, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of knowledge being fruitless. (78)

[Objection: Is it not the case that the basis for my statement is the word of a supreme authority (*āpta*), and by virtue of being based on that, the Vedic statement—which teaches the means to liberation as described—is inferred? Furthermore, according to the principle that one knows the *smṛti* from observed conduct (*ācāra*) and infers the *śruti* from the *smṛti*, [the Veda is established].

To this, he says: "Not from eternal [means]," etc. The particle *ca* has a restrictive sense and is connected with the negative particle *na*. "Having perceived Him, one is released from the mouth of death."

The sense is that the aforementioned conceptualization is contradicted by the direct scriptural statements (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) regarding the fruits of knowledge and liberation, as well as by the contradiction with the section on non-contradiction (*avirodhādhikaraṇa*). || 78 ||
Let there be no attainment of heaven or other such desired results arising from that [action] when it is not performed.
Whether it arises from a different object or from its own nature, it is not prevented. || 79 ||
"Let it be that desires and the like are avoided in some way; nevertheless, that [avoidance] is not a means to liberation," he says: "From desires and so forth.

Let there be no heaven and the like caused by desire-driven action (kāmya-karma), nor the body and so forth which are the instruments for its enjoyment, due to the avoidance of the karma that causes them.

As for "inaction" (akriyā), it refers to prohibited action; when such exists, there is the falling into hell resulting from its maturation, as well as the body and so forth which are the basis for that.

Even by avoiding what is prohibited, liberation will not be attained in that manner; for, due to another point to be stated later, or by virtue of one's own nature, or through the power of merit such as residing in a holy place, the attainment of heaven and the like resulting from sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*) is unavoidable. This is the meaning. || 79 ||
1 kha. replies: 2 kha. "tatpuṃma" [Vol.
1, page 50].
[This is] the Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 29.
If there is no pride regarding existence from another source, then let there be doubt in this matter.
Even by this much, your position remains obstructed and is not established. || 80 ||

Now, one might object: "Since there is no evidence for the occurrence of another body due to some other cause upon the fall of the present body for one who possesses the aforementioned means, liberation (kaivalya) must be inevitable. This is the doubt raised by the words "from another" (*anyataḥ*). He replies with "let it be so" (*astu*), meaning that since there is likewise no evidence for the non-occurrence of another body from another cause, there must be doubt regarding its occurrence. And he reminds [the opponent] of the previously stated failure of the position (*pakṣāsiddhi*) in the case of such doubt. "This... (*etā-*)...

He says "vateti. By the word *pakṣa* (the thesis), liberation attainable through the means belonging to others is understood; for the performance of causes pertaining to the next world depends upon certainty (*niścaya*). Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is its obstacle. Therefore, the meaning is: since the intended reason is obstructed by doubt, there is no establishment of liberation for you. || 80 ||
And likewise for those who transgress the meaning of the injunction, it is as stated in the verse beginning with "atha etayoḥ."
And there is no doubt here that pleasure, pain, and so forth are directly perceived. || 81 ||

Having stated the doubt regarding the taking of another body by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) upon the fall of the present body, [the author] now demonstrates the certainty based on the existence of a decisive factor and weakens the aforementioned doubt. "Now" (*atha*), etc.: just as for those who possess only ritual action (*karma*) and for those who practice the combined path (*samuccaya*), [there is no falling back from the state of the body]...
After the fall [of the body], a connection with the southern and northern paths is heard of; likewise, according to the observation of present happiness, suffering, and so forth,

those who are seen to be habitually transgressing injunctions and prohibitions— those whose knowledge and actions are turned away from [the Divine]— upon the fall of their current bodies, have a connection with a third place, as described by the passage beginning "nor by either of these two paths," which consists of very little happiness and is characterized by abundant suffering and delusion, and is insignificant.

Therefore, since the state of being a living being is heard [in scripture], there is no doubt that even one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), if devoid of knowledge and action, undergoes the assumption of another body; for it is heard in scripture that one entitled to perform ritual action (*karmādhikārī*) assumes another body in the absence of the causes for either of the two paths [of knowledge or action]. Nor is that [scriptural statement] restricted to subjects other than those desiring liberation, because, according to the principle that "the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) are also prescribed," he too is entitled to religious duty (*dharma-adhikṛta*), and thus a restriction [of the rule] is untenable. Nor is it forbidden for him...

Because he has abandoned what is enjoined, he does not attain the state of a "small creature" (kṣudrajantu), for it is difficult to establish that one partakes in the fruits [of actions] merely by abandoning what is prescribed. Nor is there a connection with a third place [rebirth] resulting from the performance of obligatory duties (nitya) and so forth, since such performance is admitted to be fruitless. Thus, due to the absence of both knowledge and ritual action, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) would experience neither liberation nor worldly existence; alas, he would enter into a most wretched state! This will be refuted later.

And there is the state of having only one more birth. Therefore, since a future body is certain even for one whose conduct has been described [as virtuous], the ignorant person has no hope for liberation; this is the sense. || 81 ||
Although there is no fault in performing that which is obligatory, there is indeed a fault in its non-performance.
It is not prevented by either another intrinsic nature or by a means of valid cognition (māna). || 82 ||

It has been stated that even if one completely renounces optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and the like in this life, there is no liberation because bondage is established through those same acts performed in other births.

As for the argument that no further body arises for such a person because the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth— which would otherwise cause sin— is prevented by their performance, to that he replies:

Regarding the phrase "of the eternal": even if, due to the complete performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth in this life, there is no taking up of another body caused by the demerit (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the non-performance of those same rites in the present, it is nonetheless impossible to deny the demerit arising from the non-performance of such rites in previous lives, or from the habituation to dwelling in sinful regions, or from innate nature. Therefore, because of the attainment of another birth caused by that [demerit], there is no liberation; such is the meaning. || 82 ||
1 kha. "And of these two" | 2 kha. "beginningless" | 3 kha. "removal" [Vol.
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, regarding the connection [of the treatise]:
"If the desired fruit of the obligatory (*nitya*) and other rites is the destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*), [then what of the fruit of liberation?]"
Nevertheless, apprehension regarding future faults may arise as before. (83)

One might raise the objection that the collection of evils accumulated in previous births—which have as their causes such factors as non-performance [of duty]—is destroyed by the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced from the performance of daily obligatory rites (*nitya*) in this life, and thus it does not constitute an obstacle to liberation. To this, the author replies with the words "of the *nitya* and so forth": even if the evils and the like caused by past non-performance are removed by current *nitya* rites, the suspicion remains unavoidable that one will take on another body due to defects caused by future non-performance. Thus he refutes the objection.
Rati says: "Even so. She indicates that there may still be doubt in this matter by saying, "As before. || 83 ||
And because undesirable fruits are of the nature of evil deeds, their destruction occurs.
By bowing down, there shall be the destruction of your prosperity, for it is desired by those who seek advancement.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), there must be the non-performance of actions in this life or in the next? Not the first [alternative], because there is no such non-performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and other duties already undertaken day by day; nor the second, because liberation is necessary at the end of the present body. To this, he says: "anabhīṣṭa" (unwanted), etc. According to the Vedic text, "By dharma one drives away evil," since sins are causes of what is undesirable, even if they are entirely destroyed by obligatory rites and the like, there remains the [result] of good deeds (*sukṛta*).

Because those things conducive to [worldly] life are means to what is desired and are not in conflict [with karma], therefore, for one whose path is destroyed, the production of another body by previously performed good deeds—whether uncommenced or past—is unavoidable; this is the meaning. || 84 ||
If all things were inherently defective, they could not become non-defective through ritual injunction.
Nor is there a defect due to the faultiness of the result, such as in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others. (85)

He raises an objection based on the principle of the section concerning analogical extension (*atideśādhikaraṇanyāya*): "Of all [actions]," suggesting that just as evil deeds are undesirable for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), so too are well-performed deeds equally undesirable. He replies: "No. For what is enjoined, by the very power of its injunction, is not defective even with respect to one seeking liberation.
The meaning is that what is prohibited is indeed defective, whereas what is enjoined is pacified for the ignorant person simply through experience (*bhoga*).

But surely, being enjoined is not the determinant for being non-defective, since there is a deviation in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others; to this he replies: "Nor even... By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the *saṃdaṃśa*, the *ekatrika*, and so forth are included. For *soma* sacrifices and the like are not equal to the *śyena* and others, because their fruits are not prohibited.

In the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others, however, the result is prohibited by the injunction "one should not harm. Thus, because the result is defective due to its being prohibited, there is no qualified person (adhikārī) [to perform it], and consequently, there is no injunction regarding the instrumental means (sādhana). For it has been said:
"And because it is intended as the result, the Śyena and such are not objects of injunction."
"This procedure for cultivation also ceases from the portion consisting of the fruit."
However, in the case of Soma and other such rites, because qualified practitioners exist, the injunction is complete. As they have said:
"Furthermore, that action which, even in its result, is not followed by misfortune, and which is a cause of pure joy alone, is proclaimed as Dharma."

Furthermore, the difference between the Śyena sacrifice and the Agniṣomīya sacrifice was established in the *Codanāsūtra*; therefore, since the Śyena and others are not indeed prescribed [as dharma], how can there be a deviation? This is the meaning. || 85 ||
1. From the perspective of the wicked.
[Vol.
1, page 52] *Gārtika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 31.
If the truth of the knowledge of the one Self were known, the predominance of ritual action would be rendered useless.
And the preeminence of knowledge has been demonstrated by the words "This is that. (6.16) || 86 ||

It has been stated that even for one who possesses the means [of liberation], there is no liberation without [the exhaustion of] karma, because another body arises [from it]. Having thus refuted this, the author takes up the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) and objects: "In the case of the identity of the Self" (*aikātmya*). The meaning is that for one who performs the aforementioned means and possesses a purified intellect, liberation occurs through the destruction of all karma by means of the cognition of oneness (*aikyadhiyā*). If that is so, since liberation is possible through knowledge alone—which destroys that [karma]—then the status of karma as a direct cause of liberation is not supported by evidence.

He says it is "devoid of fruit" [in the verse beginning] "in vain. With the intention that even for knowledge (*jñāna*), the status of being a direct means to liberation is not supported by authoritative evidence, he says:

"And the primacy [of knowledge]. The meaning is this: since the *vividiṣā* passage enjoins ritual actions as the means for the desire for knowledge—which itself has liberation as its fruit—the status of knowledge as a direct means to liberation is established, as is also shown by such scriptural texts as "Only by knowing Him... (*tameva viditvā*). || 86 ||
Then, by the path already described, [the rites] which effect the refinement of the agent [are performed].
It is certain that the purpose of ritual actions is the knowledge of the oneness of the self. 87.

[Objection: Since agency is dependent on the *puruṣa* (the self) and not [inherently] in desire, ritual actions have no application there; for this very reason, they also have no application in the knowledge of that which is desired. Therefore, their status as a means to liberation does not exist. To this, he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). Because sacrifices and so forth do not directly connect with desire and knowledge—which are not dependent on the self—according to the sequence taught in such scriptural injunctions as "one should sacrifice with whatever [means]," [they lead to] the purification of the intellect...
The meaning is that it has been determined in the *Puruṣārthapāda* that the third mention of the causes of increase culminates in the knowledge that is the cause of liberation. || 87 ||
Having realized the lack of substantiality in actions through that, he becomes a knower of the true principle of the Vedas.
One whose impurities have been washed away by austerity attains the knowledge of the single Self.

[Objection: But if actions are a cause of knowledge by way of purification (*saṃskāra*), then their performance would have to continue as long as knowledge lasts, because that [purification] has a visible result; therefore, the renunciation of one who desires to know (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*) would be impossible. To this he says: "By that," meaning by austerity such as the daily obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) and so forth, one whose impurity has been removed and who has studied the Vedas...

The literal meaning is as follows: one who understands the meaning of the Vedas through a superficial encounter, yet lacks discernment, realizes—by means of such [Vedic] statements as "not by action is there non-action"—that ritual acts yield impermanent fruits;

becoming detached from them, he renounces action in order to perform hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means directed toward knowledge, which is the means to liberation. Thus is established the renunciation of the seeker of knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*). For ritual acts are not direct causes of liberation, but rather [serve as causes] through the mediation of detachment and so forth. Therefore...

The sense is this: since one who is dispassionate has no further need for those [works], he does not perform them; however, those which are the direct means [to liberation], one desiring liberation performs them until knowledge is attained, according to the principle of the *āvṛtti-adhikaraṇa*. || 88 ||
But he who, through practice in previous births, has extinguished all desires—
He is qualified from the very beginning; furthermore, he does not look toward ritual action.

Even in the case of gradual renunciation (*kramasaṃnyāsa*), since that [renunciation] is absent for a perpetual student (*brahmacārin*), how can it be said that "one should go forth from the very state of studentship"? To this, the Scripture says: "But he who... This means: due to practice in previous lives—that is, due to the abundance of performing obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth in past births. The word "at first" refers to the first stage of life (*āśrama*). The qualified person, having completed hearing the scriptures and other means for the sake of knowledge, performs renunciation; this is the remainder of the sentence. Now...

Even for one who has already abandoned action, there might be a renewed performance of it out of faith, just as a youth, though devoid of sensory enjoyment in his early years, may still experience the impulse of desire for them; to this he says: "Again" (punar). [Verse 89] [Note: The commentary fragments provided appear to be scribal notes or variant readings regarding the text's transmission.]
[Volume 1,
Page 53] 32 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Introduction]
But for one who is dispassionate and desirous of knowledge, there is no dependence on anything other than the means of valid cognition.
For action is required when an object is yet to be accomplished; once the object is already established, that action is purposeless. || 90 ||

Regarding this, he states the reason: "of one who is dispassionate. Anticipating the objection that action must be required by knowledge as an auxiliary for its fruit—just as the Āgneya and other sacrifices require the Prayāja and other rites—he says: "Action... (90).
[The dialogue] of Vāmadeva, Maitreyī, and Gārgī is indeed consistent.
There is the vision [of truth], as well as the instruction on the proper measure of celibacy and other practices. || 91 ||

He establishes, by means of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on scripture), that rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are indeed auxiliary to knowledge by way of purifying the ritual acts—just as they are in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. He does so by citing the example of Vāmadeva: although there was an absence of ritual performance in this life for Vāmadeva while he was still in the womb, as well as for Maitreyī and Gārgī, the realization of reality (*tattvajñāna*) occurred for them, as evidenced by the statement "seeing this" (*tadvaitat paśyan*) in the *Maitreyī* and *Gārgī* Brāhmaṇas.
And since this is being taught, it would be logical to accept that actions belonging to other births serve as causes for knowledge through a continuous succession.
For it has been said:
"In those other births which [preceded] this one, [the action] must certainly have been performed."
"That which is the duty to be performed by a person here [in this world]—otherwise, there is no abiding in Brahman."

Therefore, even in the absence of actions performed in this life, the sense is that for some, because liberation is seen to result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), those [actions] serve as auxiliary causes for that fruit. Furthermore, the injunctions such as "on the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce," and "one should renounce even from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*)," which prescribe renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) from the stages of life (*āśrama*) starting with studentship as a means to knowledge, demonstrate that actions possess the quality of being auxiliary causes for the fruit of knowledge.
He states another logical implication (*arthāpatti*) by saying "it prevents," namely, "of celibacy and so forth. The word "tathā" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). || 91 ||
Because the causes such as sacrifices and charitable works are infinite for the sake of attaining heaven.
Therefore, the impossibility of another reason would be difficult to know only through the possibility [of such a reason]. || 92 ||

Even for one who possesses the means taught by others, there is no liberation from an external object or from its own nature, because another birth would still occur; and if the knowledge of unity is attained, liberation comes from that very knowledge alone, while ritual acts (karmāṇi) are said to be only indirectly helpful toward it. Now, he explains the "external object" (arthāntara): "The desired," etc. The "desired" (iṣṭa) is Vedic ritual, the "pūrta" is Smṛti-based ritual, and by the word "etc.," the giving of gifts (datta) is included. For it has been said:
“The Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, truthfulness, the preservation of the Vedas,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva offering— this is designated as ‘iṣṭa’ (sacrificial rites).”
The construction of step-wells, wells, tanks, and temples,
as well as the gift of food and the establishment of groves, is designated as *pūrta*.
"Protecting those who have come for refuge and non-violence toward living beings,
as well as whatever gift is given outside the sacrificial altar— this is designated as 'given' (datta)."
1 kha. 'tū | tatkṛ ṃ | 2 ka. 'taḍāgādi | — [vol 1, page 54]
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

Because there exists an infinite number of these [karmas] whose fruits have not yet begun, which serve as the cause for future bodies, even for a seeker of liberation who avoids all desire-driven action (*kāmya-karma*) in this life, there would still be another cause for a subsequent body after the fall of the present body, for the sake of experiencing heaven and other such rewards.
The meaning is that its occurrence would be difficult to discern because it occurs in the manner described. || 92 ||
In this manner, one should apply the aforementioned reasoning to prohibitive statements as well.
Thus, the statement regarding obligatory rites is exactly like that; therefore, there is no certain determination of liberation [from them].

He demonstrates the same principle that was shown regarding optional rites (*kāmya*) by applying it to prohibited acts (*niṣiddha*) as well, using the word "thus" (*evam*). That is to say, in those [scriptural] passages concerning prohibited acts—namely, the prohibitions themselves—since prohibited acts are infinite, it is possible for those whose fruits have not yet begun to become causes for future bodies; therefore, all prohibited acts in this life...

Even for one who renounces, it is impossible to know that after the fall of the present body there will be no other cause for falling into hell in another body; the meaning is that prohibited actions (*niṣiddha-karma*) may still occur. Now, [one might object]: "Prohibited actions have been cast off by obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, so they do not necessitate another body. To this, he says: *nitya*... Those in which the statement "this is an obligatory rite" applies are *nityakarman*.
The same reasoning previously stated regarding optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) acts must also be applied to the occasional (*naimittika*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites.

Since it is impossible to perform them in their entirety across previous and future births, sin is not entirely eliminated therein; consequently, because another body arises due to that [remaining] cause, how can there be liberation for one who performs only the obligatory and other such rites in this life? This is the meaning. For, by the reasoning shown above—

He concludes that liberation cannot be ascertained even for one who possesses the aforementioned means, because there exists a cause for the body in a future life; thus he says: "Not from this" (nātaḥ). || 93 ||
Of the merit and demerit of karma acquired over many lifetimes.
And because the killing of a Brahmin may occur for the sake of an infinite body. || 94 ||

As for the claim that liberation occurs because actions belong to a single lifetime and—due to the aforementioned reason—there is an absence of karma that would cause another birth, he replies with the words "aneka... (not one). The meaning is that since, in this beginningless saṃsāra, there is the possibility of various actions performed in previous births whose fruits are to be experienced in diverse bodies, the principle of "belonging to a single lifetime" does not apply; therefore, liberation cannot result from that [principle]. Furthermore, as for the claim that all accumulated actions, acting together, [produce a single body]...

It might be argued that it is logical for [karmas] to initiate a single body; to this, he replies: "Infinite," etc. For it is not the case that all karmas together initiate a single body, since it is possible for a single act of violence against a Brahmin to be the cause for assuming multiple bodies:
"Of dogs, pigs, donkeys, and camels; of cows, goats, sheep, deer, and birds..."
For the Smṛti states: "And the killer of a Brāhmaṇa enters the womb of Cāṇḍālas and Pulkasas.

Nor is it logical to hold that while other karmas, manifested at the time of death, originate a single body, this [karma], manifested at that same time, originates multiple types of bodies in succession; for the doctrine of being restricted to a single birth (*aikabhavikatva*) lacks scriptural authority.
This is the meaning. || 94 ||
Then, by the power of the remainder [of that merit], through her word, and because of this [act] performed here, it was so.
Therefore, the persistence of those whose desire for results has not yet commenced is understood. || 95 ||

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [the author] cites *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as authorities for the determination that uncommenced (*anārabdha*) karma acquired over many lifetimes persists. Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*): "The castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), established in their own duties, after departing and experiencing the fruit of their actions, then—by means of the remainder (*śeṣeṇa*)—[attain] distinguished place, birth, family, form, and lifespan..."

Based on the Smṛti passage, "Those who possess learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence attain birth in various directions, while those who are the opposite perish," and based on the Śruti passage, "Those here whose conduct has been pleasant shall enter a pleasant womb," etc., it is established that there exists a persistence of karmas whose fruits have not yet begun.
Therefore, since actions do not belong to a single lifetime alone, the aforementioned qualified person does not attain liberation through [the mere exhaustion of] karma; this is the meaning. || 95 ||
Nor, in this case, is the fruit of the eternal [practice] merely the destruction of evil deeds.
Because another fruit is heard [in scripture], it is directly [the cause], just as the memory of a mango [is the cause of salivation]. || 96 ||

As for the claim that even when obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*)—which have as their sole fruit the cessation of the demerit incurred by non-performance—are performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), they do not initiate another body, to this he replies: "The fruit," etc. The word "here" (*iha*) refers either to the scripture or to the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*). He states the reason for this: "Because of another fruit," etc. Whether there is performance or non-performance of the obligatory rites and so forth, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is unavoidable; [for] if they are performed, [the result is] the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ-loka*).

The sense is that one must perform [rites] because they are prescribed for those who have attained [the body], as the Śruti states, "By action, the world of the ancestors," and because, in the case of non-performance, there is the affliction of sin (pratyavāya) leading to a fall into hell.
He states that even Smṛti is an authority for the existence of other fruits for the obligatory (nitya) rites and so forth, saying: "It is as follows" (tadyathā). || 96 ||
"Regarding the mango tree, [it is] a sign," and so forth, is indeed a statement from the Āpastamba-smṛti.
He declares that even eternal rites possess fruitfulness. || 97 ||

It is as follows: "Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary benefits; likewise, when practicing the Dharma, various benefits arise, and even if they do not arise, there is no loss of the Dharma. Thus he analyzes mindfulness. Regarding the word "mango": [it serves as an illustration].

"Placed in the cause" (nimitte nihite) means "implanted. He states the purport of the aforementioned Smṛti by saying, "the state of having a result" (phalavattvam). The word "api" (also/even) serves either to include the occasional (naimittika) rites or to provide an illustration by means of optional (kāmya) rites and so forth. || 97 ||
This has indeed already been stated; however, this is the definitive conclusion regarding the doubt here.
Whatever power is established here initiates an action. || 98 ||

Having established that obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and others possess fruits through both Śruti and Smṛti, he states the conclusion: "It has been said. In the previous section, where it was asked whether there is no authority for liberation occurring through other means, the absence of a decisive factor was stated as the reason for the doubt—namely, whether liberation occurs immediately after the fall of the body for one who follows the prescribed means. Here, however, since the fruitfulness of obligatory rites and others is established by Śruti and so forth, [the discussion concerns] the aforementioned practice...

The conclusion is that even for such a person, there is no liberation; the meaning is that this is because of the scriptural statements regarding the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth resulting from obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and the like. Furthermore, does one who attains liberation through the performance of the causes you have mentioned possess the capacity to perform them or not? If it is not present, how can there be performance of those [rites] by one who lacks the capacity, and how, then, can there be liberation? Thinking thus, he refutes the first position with the word "kāryam" (the effect). Here, the word "iha" (here) refers to the Self (*ātman*).

Since capacity (*śakti*) persists as long as the substance exists, there would be no liberation even in the state of *mokṣa*, because it would still initiate the performance of causes [for action], just like *saṃsāra*.

For the capacity for agency and so forth is indeed equal to the capacity for performing the means [to an end]; thus, the meaning is that this [capacity] would also initiate agency and so forth in liberation. || 98 ||
Because, in the absence of an effect, this capacity itself cannot be established.
The establishment of cause and effect occurs through their mutual non-distinction. || 99 ||
