1, page 56] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 35.
And although power exists within the self, it does not possess the capacity to initiate an effect, because the persistence of the cause is possible even without initiating an effect.

Now, the author [Datta] says: "Because... The meaning is that since power (*śakti*) is to be understood through its effect (*kārya*), in the state of liberation (*mukti*) where that effect is absent, power itself would not be established;
therefore, the existence of power implies the existence of its effect. As for the claim that a cause can remain even when no effect has begun, he says in response to that:
Regarding the word "kārya" (the effect): cause and effect are established in mutual dependence; therefore, in the absence of either one, neither is established.

Thus, since the cause cannot exist in the absence of the effect, if the power (*śakti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) were to persist in liberation, the effect would also have to persist—this is the meaning. || 99 ||
Therefore, since the inner self is accepted as having the nature of both agent and enjoyer;
There is no hope for liberation by relying on the path of reasoning previously described. || 100 ||

Since the continuity of the stream of effects belongs to that which possesses the power of agency and so forth, [the author] concludes, considering it futile to desire liberation when one has identified with the inner self (pratyak) in the form of an agent and enjoyer: "The agent... etc. He recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "Do not long for that" (*mā kāṅkṣīs taḥ*).
This refers to what was previously mentioned. || 100 ||
Liberation on account of having committed an offense would necessarily result in being merely doubtful.
By your word, for the twice-born as well as for donkeys and the like, it would undoubtedly be so. (101)

Having set aside the alternatives as to whether one seeking liberation is capable or incapable of practicing the stated causes, he points out another defect regarding the imagined means: "Because of being faulty" (*sāparādhatvataḥ*). Even for those of the three higher castes who are entitled to ritual action and who practice the causes here as described, there is the possibility of being accompanied by some accidental fault consisting of the non-performance of what is enjoined or the performance of what is prohibited; consequently, [there remains] the necessity of another birth.

The meaning is that because they are [merely] honored, their liberation would remain doubtful. Furthermore, for those who are ineligible, such as donkeys and the like, that liberation would be certain;
for since actions pertain to a single birth, there is no cause for taking up another body once this body has fallen away. Thus he says, "of the donkey and so forth.
By the phrase "by your statement," the opponent's assertion regarding the subject of being confined to a single birth is referred to. || 101 ||
But has it not been stated that the self's status as the agent of sacrifice is merely a remnant of its ritual function?
This is not so, because this knowledge is not intended to be an auxiliary part of ritual action.

Having refuted the reasons stated by others and asserted that knowledge alone is the cause [of liberation], the distinction between the two sections (kāṇḍas) regarding the qualified seeker and so forth was explained; now, he restates what was said in the passage beginning with "because the Self is a supplement to ritual action" (ātmanaḥ karmaśeṣatvāt). He introduces this with "But surely" (nanu). The words "of the knowledge of the Self" (ātmajñānasya) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. To the question, "By what means does it serve as a supplement to that [ritual action]?", he replies: "Of the Self" (ātmanaḥ). This refers to either worldly or Vedic knowledge of the Self.

Having raised the alternative that [knowledge] is an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), he refutes the first [position] with the words "This is not so. Since the knowledge of the self as it is known in the world is an auxiliary to ritual action, it cannot be the cause of liberation; having thus stated the proposition with "This is not so," he states the reason for it with the word "Because" (*yataḥ*). The word "this" (*etat*) refers to the worldly knowledge of the self. Therefore, the remainder of the sense is: "Hence, what you have said is incorrect. (102)
The agency of the self is established, since it exists even in other sacrificial acts.
Because it performs its function without remainder, what was said [by you] is therefore unseemly.

As for the claim that because the self is the agent of sacrifice, knowledge of it—by means of that agency—is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, he says [in response]: "Agency... Since the empirical self is seen to possess agency not only in sacrifices and the like, but also in common worldly and Vedic activities, [the knowledge of such a self] is [useless]. (Note: *naiṃ* and *na* appear as variants.)
[vol 1, page 57] 4 36
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, regarding the connection [of knowledge with ritual action]:

because that [knowledge of the self] lacks an unerring connection with the sacrifice—unlike the *juhū* ladle and other such implements—it cannot be a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice through that medium.

This is because it is accepted that a subsidiary is that which assists while possessing a unique (non-common) character; therefore, it is untenable for worldly knowledge of the self to be a subsidiary part of ritual action.
Such is the meaning. || 103 ||
For it is not the case that one is unable to perform action due to a lack of self-knowledge.
Just as a sacrificial ladle cannot be used for offering oblations without the knowledge of the leaves [of the Palāśa tree], so it is here. || 104 ||

Now, even if Vedic self-knowledge were an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action, would that auxiliary be the knowledge of the Self as transcending hunger and so forth, or merely the knowledge of a Self distinct from the body? It is not the first case; thus he says: "For not... By the word "Self" (*ātman*), there is designated that reality which is beyond hunger and so forth, which is devoid of distinctions such as Brahmin or Kshatriya, which is non-transmigratory, and which is known through the Vedāntas. On the contrary, [such knowledge] is contradictory [to ritual action], because it destroys the notions of the agent and so forth.
The word "tvāt" (because of you) is the ellipsis. To show that it is impossible to perform action without the aforementioned knowledge of the Self, he provides a counter-example:
"parṇa," etc. "Lātum" means to take up or grasp. || 104 ||
This is for one who does not know that there exists a self connected to another body.
This activity pertaining to the next world is not appropriate for one who possesses discernment. || 105 ||

Second, he raises [the objection] by way of a negative argument (*vyatireka*) with the words "in another body" (*dehāntara*). Its meaning is as follows: for a discerning person, there can be no engagement in an action that has heaven as its fruit—[a fruit] to be enjoyed in a divine body—without knowing the self to be suitable for that body; and this [absence of engagement] is an inconsistency (*anupapatti*).
This indicates that supernormal knowledge (tiraścījñāna) serves as an auxiliary factor for that [attainment]. || 105 ||
If that is so, then action cannot be the constituent part [of liberation], because the sole cause is the excellence of the agent.
Nor is knowledge enjoined as a subsidiary to ritual action, like one who desires a fruit [desires the means to obtain it]. (106)

Even if the Self is distinct from the body, it may be either an agent or a non-agent. In the first case, knowledge of that [Self] is not an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*), because it would lead to the performance of all actions without exception; with this in mind—since it has been stated that the agent is common [to all actions], and thus it is untenable for that [knowledge] to be an auxiliary to action by way of the agent—it says: "If that is so... In the second case as well, knowledge of that [Self] is not an auxiliary to ritual action, for according to the logic already stated—that it is not due to the absence of knowledge of the Self—the agent alone [is the factor].
He says, "Because it is a cause of the agent," [and] "In that case, then. He provides an example for the fact that something common to all activities is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the action:

"The fruit" (*phala*). This is based on the etymological derivation: one who desires the fruit (*phalārthin*) is a person for whom the fruit is the object (*artha* = *viṣaya*). For that [desire], although it is a cause of all the agent’s activities, is not an auxiliary part of the ritual act because it is common [to all actions]; such is the meaning regarding the knowledge of the agent. Alternatively, the "one who desires the fruit" is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); of him, all—

The meaning is that knowledge of the cause of engagement is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to Vedic ritual; even though such knowledge may assist it, its non-auxiliary status is possible—just as in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-laying)—and the same applies to the knowledge of the agent. Furthermore, there is neither scripture (*śruti*) nor presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as proof for the claim that the knowledge of a self distinct from the body is an auxiliary to ritual action.

He states "And not... [to show] that the first [proof] is not the case; for in passages such as "the knower sacrifices," there is an injunction regarding the sacrifice following upon a restatement of the knowledge of the cause and so forth.

The intended meaning is that there is no injunction for self-knowledge to be a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), because a sentence situated within the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*) does not have self-knowledge as its subject matter. || 106 ||
But even so, would entry not be established in all ritual acts?
This is indeed by the power of self-knowledge, not by recourse to an injunction. || 107 ||

The second *vārttika* states that because activity directed toward the next world is impossible without the cognition of a self distinct from the body, such knowledge is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) for that activity.
[This is] accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
[The author] raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*). The very same objection stated previously regarding the connection with another body has been brought here by way of context.

Even if, due to the absence of an injunction and because it depends upon that [injunction], self-knowledge does not constitute an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to ritual action], let it be so; nevertheless, [regarding] activity pertaining to the next world—

The construction is as follows: by way of the aforementioned impossibility (*anupapatti*), its inclusion in all ritual acts would be established; that aforementioned impossibility constitutes the *sāmarthya* (logical force/evidence). || 107 ||
This is not so for one who has not understood the true nature of things regarding these very actions.
For [the person] distinguished by the meaning of selflessness possesses the status of being qualified [for practice], because of that very reason. || 108 ||

For it is by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that the status of the cognition of the self as being an auxiliary to [ritual] action is established. And that [cognition] must have either a qualified object or a solitary object. In the first case, since the qualified [object] is merely imagined (*kalpita*), that would not be a cognition of the [true] Self; therefore, even if that [qualified cognition] were an auxiliary to ritual action, the cognition of the Self itself would not be an auxiliary to it—thus he says: "Not so. He refutes the second alternative with the words: "Because it is unapprehended," meaning because of ignorance.

For one who is qualified for ritual actions (*karma*) is indeed distinguished [from the liberated], not merely [the self] as it is in liberation; therefore, although the knowledge of the qualified self (*viśiṣṭātmadhi*) is an auxiliary to those actions, the knowledge of the mere self (*kevalātmadhi*) is not an auxiliary to them, because there is no evidence for that. Rather, the point is that the latter is the cause of liberation. He states the reason why the ignorant person is qualified for ritual action: "anātma... (not-self...). For the self is delimited by the body and the senses, since that which is undelimited cannot be subject to qualification; such is the nature of that delimitation.
And its dependence on ignorance will be explained later. Thus, the sense is that only the ignorant person has the qualification for ritual action (karma). || 108 ||
The wise declare that abiding in the true nature of the self is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*);
any connection of the self with anything other than that is caused by ignorance. (Kārikās 89–109)

Furthermore, he states that because the knowledge of the isolated Self has liberation as its fruit, it is not an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma*). He says: "In its own nature" (*svarūpe*). The supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) of the Self is its abiding in its own nature. And that is accomplished for one whose ignorance has been dispelled by the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, since knowledge is the cause of liberation by way of removing ignorance, it is not an auxiliary to ritual action; this is the meaning. Even though knowledge is the means to final release (*apavarga*), [it does not serve] the purpose of the non-Self...

It has been stated that it is improper to say that the Self, which is distinct, possesses a distinction from the non-Self (anātman) created by its own ignorance; for that [distinction] is possible even without being prompted by that [ignorance], since it possesses a connection with ignorance. To this, he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). A connection of the Self with a non-Self other than ignorance is based on ignorance, because for that which is inherently unattached (*asaṅga*), such a connection is impossible by itself; however, the connection with ignorance does not require an external cause, as it belongs to that which already possesses ignorance.
The sense is that it is so because it is self-sustaining and because it brings about the liberation of both itself and others. || 109 ||
That which is adventitious and not of the nature of the self should be understood through its own self-awareness alone.
Therefore, for one who has attained the goal of human existence and abides in his own true nature, there is nothing further to be gained.

Furthermore, he states that the connection with the non-self is also dependent on that [Self], based on the inference: "The non-self is dependent on ignorance because it is an effect, like a snake [superimposed on a rope]. Moreover, the nature of the non-self is to be known by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin); and that [nature] cannot be known without its connection [to the Self].
There can be no association [of the Self] without ignorance (avidyā); thus, intending to show that both the non-Self and its relationship [to the Self] are dependent upon ignorance, he says:

"That" (tat). He states the result of saying that those two are dependent on ignorance: "Not from this" (nātaḥ). Since the attainment of the supreme human goal cannot occur without the practice of the cause [of knowledge], he says: "By its own nature" (svarūpa-). || 110 ||
The state of being an agent, an enjoyer, and so forth, arises from the ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna) and nothing else. || 110 ||
Karma, the enjoyment of its fruits, and the external instruments. || 111 ||
38. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction] [Volume 1, Page 59] Connection:

Anticipating the objection—"If he is established in his own nature as immutable bliss (*kūṭasthānanda*), how can there be any manifestation of him otherwise?"—the author says: "The agent" (*kartṛ*). The grammatical connection is "not from anything else. Now, one might object: "It is improper to say that agency and so forth are caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*); since the Self is conscious, it will naturally attain sovereignty over actions and become both agent and enjoyer; so what is the use of postulating ignorance? Anticipating this, [the author speaks] of being qualified for action (*adhikāritva*) and so forth.

In order to establish that [liberation] does not depend on those [means], he enumerates the causes for qualification, beginning with "action" (*karman*). First, action is the cause for qualification in ritual acts, according to such scriptural passages as, "One becomes meritorious through merit. Furthermore, the experience of the fruits of action is a cause for it, because one who has not experienced those fruits lacks qualification for them due to attachment to them; and because injunctions such as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," prescribe these rites only for one who possesses desire, [the sense organs] such as speech and the other organs of action [are likewise involved].

He says "the external [senses]" because the auditory and other organs of perception are the causes thereof; for it has been stated that if there is a deficiency in even one of them, one does not accept the qualification for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), and thus blind persons and others will not be able to perform the duties of a householder.
The mind (*manas*) is also the cause of that, as it is said: "One should meditate with the mind upon whichever deity the oblation may have been taken for."
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that it is because of scripture (śruti). || 111 ||
Beyond even that is the external body, and its inherent genus.
Old age, death, and birth, as well as the physical bodies that serve as their substrata. || 112 ||

Furthermore, those [qualities] do not engage in action without a substratum; therefore, he states that the body, which is their substratum, is also a cause in that regard by saying, "from that too. He states that the caste (jāti) such as Brāhmaṇahood is also a cause for that [action], based on Vedic injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," by saying, "caste.
He also states that birth, old age, and death are causes for that [action], since there are injunctions for the *jātakarman* and other rites with reference to them.
He causes to grow old. || 112 ||
Wife, sons, wealth, and whatever else is external to the body;
The causes for eligibility regarding ritual action belong to him by his own nature, even though he is not eligible [for other purposes]. || 113 ||

He states that even wife, son, and wealth—which are external to the body—are instrumental [in the performance of rites], for one who has a wife, has produced a son, and possesses wealth is qualified for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*). He says: "Wife" (*dāra*), etc. The word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include all things—whether already mentioned, yet to be mentioned, or merely possible—that are required for qualification. He concludes the enumerated causes of qualification with the word "action" (*karman*); the word "cause" (*hetu*) here emphasizes the state of being an action.

The meaning is that those [factors] such as karma and so forth, which possess the status of being causes for the qualification (*adhikāra*), are "thus" [referred to]. Anticipating the objection that since the Self is conscious, its qualification is established by itself and therefore the stated causes of that [qualification] are useless, he says: "by itself. Because that which is unattached, changeless, and unlimited has no qualification by itself, it is only through its connection with the non-Self (*anātman*) that this [Self] possesses qualification; therefore, the stated causes of that [qualification] are [necessary].
The sense is that they are logical. || 113 ||
Due to delusion, they consider the indivisible Self to be possessed of distinctions.
For neither the qualifier nor the essential nature can exist by itself through its own power as something distinct from the other. || 114 ||
In the world, it is seen that without ignorance there is nothing seen at all, for everything is seen only through delusion.
"He is a thief who is pursuing me"—in this way, it is a qualification of the thief. (115)
1. ka. *kartrādī*; 2. kha. *ni kāra*; 3. kha. *ni kāra*. [Vol.
1, page 60] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 39.
The ignorant person perceives a post as a man, but not one who has seen darkness without [the object].
But surely, even in the absence of ignorance, one thing is seen as the qualifier of another. (116)

If the Self is by its own nature ineligible [for inquiry], how could it be so even through another? For fire does not become non-hot through contact with wind; anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the non-different. Proponents of the view that the inner self (*pratīc*), though naturally devoid of distinctions, acquires the aforementioned means of realization (*sādhana*) as they bring about specific attributes such as agency, maintain that what is not luminous by itself [cannot be made so].

The meaning is that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in a jar becoming manifest by virtue of a lamp. [The author] refutes the notion of actual qualifiedness (saviśeṣatva) with the words "through delusion" (mohāt). By this, contradiction is also dispelled. Anticipating the objection—"If action and the rest can inherently differentiate the Self, what is the use of delusion?"—he says: "the qualification" (viśeṣaṇam). For one thing is indeed distinct from another...

Neither a qualifier nor its own nature exists [in the Self] by itself, because such is not observed in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth. Indeed, in the world, one thing being a qualifier of another is never seen without ignorance (avidyā); therefore, the meaning is that even action and the like are qualifiers of the Self only through delusion (moha). Anticipating the objection that "one thing being a qualifier of another is not seen even through delusion," he says: "through delusion" (mohāt)—[meaning] from every perspective.

"In all cases such as 'this is silver,'" and so forth; the meaning is that one thing is seen as the qualifier of another. The statement "through delusion, one thing is [taken as] the qualifier of another" is clarified by means of an example: "This is a thief. For when a person does not perceive a post standing before him as it truly is, he thinks, "This is a thief coming toward me," and [identifies] that [post] with the thief.

He distinguishes [the case]: "But he who knows the post standing before him as a post by its true nature does not qualify it. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the meaning is that the status of being a qualification of the person belongs to the post only because of delusion (moha), and so it is elsewhere as well. He raises an objection regarding a possible deviation (vyabhicāra) in the statement "but darkness is not seen without [the object]," beginning with "nanu" (but). || 114 || 115 || 116 ||
A woman, a king, as well as Śyenacit and others.
This is not so, because in that case, such self-awareness is not intended.
The relation of that which is not [directly] denoted is, in some cases, like [the expression] "I am thin. 117.

He explains that very same view: "aupagavaḥ" (the son of Upagu). In the expression "upagoḥ apatyam" (the offspring of Upagu), Upagu is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), serving as the qualifier for the meaning of the patronymic suffix (*apatya-pratyaya*). Nor is ignorance on the part of the speaker or the listener the cause in that case; likewise, in the expression "nṛpahayaḥ" (the king's horse), the king is the qualifier of the horse, and ignorance is not the motivating factor here either. In this same way, [expressions] such as "śyenacit" (the altar built in the shape of a hawk), "agnicit" (the altar built in the shape of a fire), and "daṇḍī" (one who possesses a staff) are [cases of] qualifiers...

The meaning is that since things are perceived even in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is not observed that one thing serves as a qualifier for another through non-cognition; therefore, [your argument] is not consistent. He refutes [the opponent's position], stating that the example cited by you is not similar to the case I have stated, but rather dissimilar, saying: "It is not so. He clarifies this very dissimilarity, beginning with: "Because... Just as in the case of "I am thin," where there is no apprehension of a difference between the self and [the body]...

The effect is its qualifier; likewise, the qualifiers beginning with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as stated by you are not qualifiers of that [effect], because no difference is perceived between them and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Indeed, in any example accepted by you, a qualifier is never seen as non-different from the qualified by way of identity (*pratyaktayā*); rather, in those cases, a relationship is desired between a distinct qualifier and a distinct qualified. Therefore, there is a disparity.
This is the meaning. || 117 ||
1 kha. ‘It would be so.
[Vol. 1, page 61] 40
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [the section on] the Connection [states]:
"In words such as *upagu*, the father and so forth are the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), while [the son] is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)."
The meaning of the patronymic suffix in "Aupagava," which has been split [from its base], is understood. || 118 ||

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *aupagava*, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) exists precisely between two things whose difference is not perceived. [This is supported by] the inference: "The subject under dispute—the relation of qualifier and qualified—is preceded by a non-apprehension of difference, because it is a relation of qualifier and qualified, like the thought 'I am thin'. To this, he says: "In *upagu* etc. In the word *aupagava*, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is the qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). And yet, those two—the base and the suffix—do not have their difference unperceived by those two [meanings].

Because even in a compound, there is the comprehension of a distinction between multiple word-meanings that are not redundant, as seen in the case of *cayanacetṛ* (the one who piles and the one who causes to pile), where the distinction between the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) is clear; whereas in cases such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer), the distinction is directly perceptible. Therefore, in the examples you favor, the cognition of the qualifier-qualified relationship occurs only between two things whose distinction has already been perceived; thus, the inference [of non-difference] is sublated by the apprehension of difference. || 118 ||
One should not [perceive] the agent and so forth, ending with the body, nor likewise the birth and so forth residing in the body, in such a manner.
In this world, a certain person distinguishes [himself] by way of exclusion. || 119 ||

[Objection: One might argue that just as in the case of Upagu and others, the offspring and so forth are indeed qualifiers of the self; since their distinctions are observed there, how can there be any disparity? [Response: It is not so. "The agent" refers to the ego (ahaṃkāra); those for whom this is the first are the "agents and so forth. These entities, ending with the body—

Up to this point, it is indicated that the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*)—preceded by the cognition of difference (*bhedadhī*)—among those [objects] and with respect to the Self is not within the scope of a human being.
By the word "mānava" (human), the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) is expressed as "here. || 119 ||
For this reason, he qualifies [the self] by its very nature as the self, without any further qualification.
"I am blind," "I am a young brahmin," "I am burnt," or even "I am covered. (120)

He provides his own experience as the proof for the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the body and so forth, on the one hand, and the Self, whose distinction from them is unknown, on the other.

[The verse begins with] "Since" (*yataḥ*). The meaning is: since the world qualifies the Self—which is by its very nature devoid of qualifiers—with these non-self entities such as the body and so forth, through non-difference, it is therefore logical that the qualifier, whose distinction from the qualified is not perceived, should reside therein. He explains this very point [with the words] "I act" (*karomi*).

The meaning is that since the body, the senses, and the ego-sense—which are distinct from the self due to their unseen impressions (*adṛṣṭa*)—are perceived as qualifiers of that [self], the self is also a reality among them; for otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the way things are experienced, which is preceded by a non-apprehension of their difference. || 120 ||
Without ignorance, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified among these.
This alone is to be known as the cause of the self's entitlement to ritual action.

Having established that the agent and other factors are qualifiers of the Self according to the method stated above, he states the proven point: "Not ignorance" (*nāvidyām*). Although the status of the agent and others as qualifiers of the person—just as a post is a qualifier of a man when their difference is unknown—is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), he says "this very [ignorance]" (*iyameva*) to address what follows regarding the present context of ritual action (*karmādhikāra*). For, since there is no perception of the difference between the Self and the non-Self...

The relationship of qualifier and qualified depends on the self; this very relationship is the cause for one's eligibility [to study]. Therefore, the meaning is that the eligibility for that [knowledge] belongs to one who possesses ignorance regarding the object to be known. || 121 ||
By means of this, they are authorized for rites such as the Bṛhaspatisava;
therefore, because it is the cause of eligibility for ritual action for those who have not yet realized the identity [of the self with Brahman], [it is taught]. 122cd–123a.

For this reason as well, he states that one who possesses ignorance (avidyā) is qualified for ritual action (karma): "They are qualified," etc. By which cause these Brahmins and others [are so qualified]—[this is from the Vārttika, accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled Śāstramañjarī]. 41.

The construction is as follows: in rites such as the Bṛhaspatisava, [the various castes] are connected by way of being the sacrificers; this very distinction between qualifier and qualified, which serves as the cause for their eligibility [for those rites], is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). For the eligibility for ritual action is based on the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; otherwise, if everyone were eligible for everything, there would be no specific instruction such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. And this [conceit] is indeed rooted in ignorance.
Therefore, the sense is that the ignorant person is the one entitled to perform ritual action (*karma*). Regarding this, he states the conclusion: "Hence" (*ataḥ*).

Because the ignorant person—by whom the identity of the Self has not been realized—is entitled to rituals, it follows that although knowledge of that [identity] may be an auxiliary to ritual action, the knowledge of the pure Self is not an auxiliary to it. || 122 ||
It is established in the true nature of the inner self, as ascertained by the means of knowledge such as scripture.
The knowledge born from the authority of Vedanta is that which completely cuts off all karma.

[Objection: But surely even that [knowledge of the Self] is an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), because it is a form of knowledge, just like other [ritual-related knowledges]. To this, he says: "By scripture and so forth" (*śrutyādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, the experience of the learned (*vidvadanubhava*), inference (*anumāna*), and so on are included; or else, the six criteria of interpretation—*liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, *samākhyā*, and *śruti*—as stated in the sūtra beginning with "Indicative mark, word, context," etc., are meant.
By these, the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the inner self (*pratīc*) is established as being the uprooting of all suffering and consisting solely of unsurpassed bliss.

The knowledge born from the Vedānta texts, which is established in that [Brahman] and has that as its object, is not an auxiliary to ritual action because it brings about its cessation; for this is the meaning of the Śruti passage, "And his actions perish," and the Smṛti passages such as, "The fire of knowledge consumes all actions. || 123 ||
Because knowledge is well-known in this world as that which destroys ignorance, which is the root of that [bondage]. || 124 ||
But it is not an impeller; therefore, there is no possibility of its being a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda).
But in the case of the sacrificial ladle made of *parṇa* wood, the mention of a result is appropriate because it is subordinate to the ritual action. || 125 ||

[Objection: But surely even verbal knowledge is capable of wiping away only ignorance, not action, since it is well known that there is a contradiction only between knowledge and ignorance. To this, he says: "Having that as its root" (*tanmūla*). The meaning is this: ignorance brings about the conceit of agency and so forth, which in turn produces actions; therefore, knowledge, by dispelling that [ignorance], also obstructs those [actions] which have it as their root. [Objection: Does it remove the ignorance that has already arisen, or that which has not yet arisen?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because [knowledge] arises without contradiction, whereas in the case of contradiction, it does not arise. Nor is the other [alternative] correct, because that which is unarisen and non-existent lacks the capacity to remove [ignorance]. Therefore, he says: "Of knowledge. The meaning is that there is no objection, since in both common worldly experience and the Veda, it is well-established that knowledge removes ignorance by virtue of its being inseparable from its own arising, and because a lamp is observed to remove darkness. This establishes that knowledge is capable of removing ignorance.

He states the application [of this principle] with the words "But not... The sense is that because it removes the cause for the engagement in all ritual actions (*karma*), the knowledge of the Self alone is not a subsidiary part of ritual action. Since it is not a subsidiary part of ritual action, he concludes by stating the result: because it is not subordinate to anything else, the scriptural mention of its fruit is not a mere *arthavāda* (eulogistic statement). Regarding the objection that it is like the mention of a fruit in the case of the *parṇamayī* [sacrificial ladle], he says: "In the case of the *parṇamayī*..."

"Thus [it] is fitting"—the remainder of the sentence is that it is fitting for the mention of the fruit to be an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement). He states the reason for this: "Because of the ritual act," etc.

Since the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood enters into the ritual through the *juhū* ladle, its possession of a fruit is possible by means of the fruit of that very [ladle]; therefore, the meaning is that it is logical for the separate mention of a fruit to be an *arthavāda*.
As for what you have urged, even you must accept this status of being an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
Even though it is not desired, the injunctive sense is here established as a rebuttal. || 126 ||
1 kha.
Thus it is said: [vol 1, page 63] 42
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the *Connection*]:

He restates what has already been refuted with the intention of expressing further elaboration, beginning with "As for that which... The word "api" (even/also) serves as an illustration by means of the phrase "by me alone.

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of injunctions regarding a subordinate element (*śeṣin*) in the Vedāntas, how can the mention of a fruit in relation to knowledge be considered a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)?"—he says: "Even by one who does not desire..."
Rapture. He claims a superior concentration in this regard. || 126 ||
I certainly accept the status of this statement as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because its primary intent is directed toward something else.
"Because he speaks of the meaning exactly as it was heard, there is no speaking of a non-existent meaning.

(127) — Is it merely being an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement) that is to be proven regarding the scriptural mention of results in relation to knowledge, or is it being a statement of a non-existent fact? Regarding this, he accepts the first [position] with the words "I accept. He states the reason for accepting the status of the scriptural mention of results—such as "he knows Brahman"—as being merely an *arthavāda*, with the word "anyā" (other). [The word] "mahā-"...

The meaning is this: the sentence is indeed primary because it possesses fruit by having as its object the identity of the higher and the lower; whereas that which is recited in its proximity is its subordinate member, because it is subsidiary to the activity that causes the knowledge of that [identity]. He refutes the second [position] with the words "Just as... (yathā). || 127 ||
Just as the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices are performed for the sake of the heavenly world, so too [are these two].
But it is not the speaking of what is unreal, as in the case of hearing evil verses. || 128 ||

Anticipating the objection that if [the Vedas] were speakers of the actual state of things (*bhūtārthavāditva*), they would not be mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—which would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—he says: "They are sacrificed.

For, just as the explanatory passage recited within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), namely "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are sacrificed for the sake of the heavenly world," possesses both the quality of referring to an actual fact and the status of an explanatory passage as a supplement to that rite, so too [the passage] "He knows Brahman" and so forth would possess both the quality of referring to an actual fact and the status of an explanatory passage. This is the meaning.

One might object: "Why should the Vedas not be considered non-factual in their meaning, just like the *apāpa-śloka* (the verse concerning the 'sinless' one), since it is possible for such examples to be the opposite [of what they claim]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But not... The sense is that the fruit taught by the Śruti, which is experienced immediately after knowledge [dawns], is not contradicted. || 128 ||
From what is the fruit obtained? For the fruit of the cognition of the self is indeed directly perceived.
From this it is understood that, by means of that [knowledge], action does not approach [the self]. || 129 ||

If sentences such as "He knows Brahman" (*brahma veda*) have an existing referent, another means of knowledge must be stated; for [if they were not based on perception], they would merely be restatements (*anuvāda*) by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—such as "for the sake of heaven"—of what is already established by the principal injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Since no other means of knowledge exists here, the status of these as restatements remains unestablished. Thus he objects: "Why? He replies that the fruit established by the direct perception of the learned is what is restated by the scriptural declarations of fruits: "It is perceived."

The word "hi" (for) indicates that, having accepted those [scriptural passages] as restatements (*anuvāda*), another means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding the fruit has been stated. Now, he says that even for the aforementioned reason, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). This is because the fruit of knowledge is understood through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the wise; therefore, the cognition of the pure Self does not touch upon ritual action.
For a rite such as the *darśa*, which possesses its own fruit, cannot be a subsidiary to anything else. This is the meaning. || 129 ||
Because it is contrary to active involvement and because it is an obstacle to liberation.
Therefore,

for one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), there is the qualification for the cessation of all actions. Since it has been stated that the knowledge of the absolute Self is the cause of liberation and action is the cause of worldly prosperity, there is a distinction in the means [of attainment] between the two sections (kāṇḍas) regarding their respective qualifications.

Having stated the distinction regarding the *Ṛbhus*, he provides another argument on that very point: "Because of [the nature of] activity" (*pravṛtteḥ*). The meaning is that the ritual acts preceded by the conceit of being an agent and so forth are opposed to the repetition of hearing and other means practiced by one seeking liberation; therefore, one seeking liberation does not desire them. Furthermore:
1. ka. 'dastaṃ'.
[Vol.
1, Page 64] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 83 M.

His actions, being contrary to his desired liberation because they result in bondage, do not lead him upward; for the Smṛti states: "By the rope of dharma one goes upward, by the rope of sin one goes downward. Therefore, he has no inclination toward those [actions]. Thus he says: "Liberation. Where, then, does his inclination lie?
To that he replies: "Of the seeker of liberation. Since he lacks the qualification for ritual action, he aims at knowledge through the renunciation of such action, by means of hearing (śravaṇa).
The meaning is that there is authority over the [other] directions. || 130 ||
Because the cause of active engagement has been utterly destroyed, there is no engagement whatsoever in any way.
It is easy to traverse, auspicious, and capable of leading to the attainment of the desired city. || 131 ||

[Objection: But surely, while performing those [prescribed duties], he may also perform occasional rites (karmāṇi) from time to time; therefore, does he not possess the state of a renunciant (saṃnyāsitā)? [Reply: No, as the author says: "In active engagement... etc. Attachment and the like are the causes of active engagement; for one who desires liberation, these are completely destroyed. Since he is one whose impurities such as attachment have been cast out, there is no engagement in action even in the intervals [between formal rites]. This is the meaning. Now, even one who has produced knowledge through the performance of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth—previously...

Fearing that one might perform actions out of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and thus the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) would not have entirely distinct scopes of authority, he refutes this with an illustration, beginning with "No" (*na*). [The term] *abhipretam* means desired as something to be attained; *tatprāptisamartham* means capable of attaining it, that is to say, fit for its attainment. He states that it is free from obstructions such as mountains which cause indifference; [the word] *sugamam* means easy to traverse. [It is like a path for] travelers [fleeing] from thieves and the like.
He states the absence of defects: "Auspicious" (śivam). || 131 ||
Provided with water and food, and free from all misfortunes. || 47 ||
Having abandoned the path already attained, one proceeds by a way that is contrary to it.
A wise person who desires to go [to liberation] is like a deluded traveler on a road. || 132 ||

He states its desirability by means of its possession of ponds, water-stations, and so forth, with the word "vāri" (water). That is to say, it is accompanied by water as well as provisions for the journey (*pathyadana*). He states that it is free from excessive winds and other such obstacles with the word "sarva" (all). Having raised the doubt that even such a path might be neglected due to the impossibility of reaching its end—just like the route leading to Mount Kailāsa, which spreads out above the peak of Meru—he says "prāpta" (attained) to dispel that concern.

For no wise person whatsoever, disregarding the path already described, desires to reach their intended destination by another path that is contrary to what has been stated; thus he says, beginning with "the path," and expresses this very point by means of a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) with the word "just as. || 132 ||
Likewise, it is devoid of such attributes as an agent arising from ignorance, and is immutable.
Having understood that which is devoid of action and agent, which bestows the entirety of the goals of human existence.
He states the illustrative example with the words "In that way," and so forth. The connection is: having known the Self, how could one apply the mind to ritual action?

For the eligibility for ritual action belongs to the knower [only] through a connection with the non-Self, or else by itself; it is not the first case, as he says: "Through ignorance. The sense is that there is no inherent connection with the non-Self for him because of his being unattached (*asaṅga*), nor is there a connection through ignorance because his ignorance has been destroyed.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "unchanging" (*avikriyam*). The sense is that for that which is all-pervading and partless, there can be neither vibration (*parispanda*) nor transformation (*pariṇāma*). Furthermore, he states with the word "actionless" (*akriya*) that for one who perceives the Self as devoid of contact with action and its factors (*kāraka*), there is no qualification for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*).

Is this for the sake of attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*) by one who knows the ritual, or for the realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), or for the attainment of the Supreme Self already realized? Or is it for...?

Whether for the sake of attaining the human goal through that knowledge, or for its direct realization, or for liberation (*apavarga*), or for the increase of that [knowledge], first— [vol 1, page 65]— there is absolute difference.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Section on the Connection], verse 133:

He rejects [the objection] with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The sense is that for the knower, ritual action is not for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), because for him—who is free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*) and is of unsurpassed bliss (*anatiśayānanda*)—there is no unattained prosperity to be attained.
Relying on self-conviction, one should directly perceive oneself as a god.
And when that [state] is established, the desired fruit is eternal and devoid of further means. || 134 ||

He refutes the second [view]: "The Self. For one who possesses knowledge and is free from ignorance, action is not required for the sake of attaining the Supreme, because that [attainment], being innate, does not depend upon causal factors (kārakas); this is the meaning. He refutes the third [view]: "The Self. For a knower does not resort to action for the sake of attaining the nature of knowledge, since that is his very own nature and is therefore eternally attained.

This is the meaning. He refutes the fourth [view] with the words "the deity" (*devam*). For there is no dependence on ritual action for the sake of making knowledge the goal of man, because knowledge—which consists of supreme, unlimited bliss—is inherently so by its own nature; this is the meaning. He rejects the fifth [view] with the words "directly" (*añjasā*). For there is no ritual action for the sake of the direct realization of knowledge, which has consciousness as its essence, because there is no direct realization other than that of knowledge. Indeed, by means of knowledge...

The meaning is that, according to the Bhāṣya’s statement that Brahman is "that which is desired to be known by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*), even though there is a distinction [between them], action is not the cause of knowledge, because knowledge is independent with respect to its own fruit. He rejects the sixth [alternative] with the words, "And while that [Brahman] persists. For action does not serve for the sake of liberation for the knower, since that [liberation] consists in abiding in one's own Self and because the destruction of ignorance along with its effects depends solely upon knowledge. He replies to the seventh [alternative]:

Regarding the word "eternal" (*nitya*): it is not logical to claim that ritual action (*karman*) serves the purpose of increasing liberation—which is attained through knowledge—on the grounds of the maxim that "an abundance of means results in an abundance of fruit. This is because, unlike heaven, an increase in liberation cannot be achieved there; for liberation is eternal, whereas [heaven] is distinguished by being non-eternal. Furthermore, since liberation does not depend on any means, there is no ritual action for the knower. He states this with the words "means," etc. Alternatively, by this [verse], its eternality is [established].
It is established. || 134 ||
In the case of external means that produce results contrary to that [desire] and involve multiple causal factors, [the agent's knowledge is not considered valid].
How could an omniscient being apply his mind to action, even while laughing? (135)

Anticipating the objection that a wise person might perform ritual action for the sake of results other than heaven or liberation, he says: "contrary to that. The meaning is this: since there is a scriptural tradition stating, "A living being is bound by action," action that yields a result contrary to liberation cannot be undertaken by a wise person out of a desire for some other fruit, because such a person lacks even the expectation of such a result. Furthermore, for one in whom knowledge has arisen and whose ignorance along with its products have been destroyed, external requisites...

He says that because of the absence of various causes for action, there is no engagement in actions. [Regarding the verse beginning with] "External": although an ignorant person requires external means, he anticipates the objection that a knower might perform action even without such requirements, and thus says: "Aneka... (many). Action depends upon causal factors (*kāraka*), such as animals and so forth; without each of these, no one can engage in action. Furthermore, [regarding] non-discrimination...

The prior activity [of the world] does not belong to one in whom knowledge has arisen; for such a person, whose ignorance and its products have been dispelled and whose own nature is realized as unobscured, there is no object to be perceived [as external]. Thus he says: "All... Now, one might object: even though the knower has accomplished all that was to be done, he will still perform action for the sake of sporting with the Self. To this he says: "Even while playing... Indeed, even for the sake of sport, it is not fitting for a knower to perform action, because...
The sense is that this is because [the Lord] is the instrumental cause and because his desires are already fulfilled. || 135 ||
1 kha. From form. 2 kha. "And because of being...
[Vol.
1, page 66] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 45.
And for one whose entire darkness has been rubbed away by right understanding, it is no longer as it was before.
Furthermore, ignorance and the like can be produced again, because they lack the nature of an agent. || 136 ||

If it be argued that even for one whose ignorance has been destroyed by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), there might again arise an entitlement to action through the application of causal factors (kāraka-yoga) due to another instance of ignorance, [the author] says "no," providing the reason: "because of the state of being a non-agent" (akārakatvataḥ). This is because, since the Self is immutable (kūṭastha), it is impossible for it to be the cause of ignorance and so forth; furthermore, there is no other cause, and the production of an effect without a cause is a logical contradiction.
Such is the meaning. || 136 ||
One who possesses the knowledge of reality as it truly is, as established by the means of valid cognition such as scripture, and its fruit.
Because it is contrary [to his nature], the wise man does not strive for actions here. || 137 ||

Having stated that one who knows the Self, by the removal of the qualification for ritual action, becomes dispassionate and—having renounced all actions according to injunction—is qualified for liberation, he says [the following] regarding the opposite case, namely that one is qualified for worldly prosperity: "Śruty-ādi... (verse 137).
Therefore, it is the member [of the path] itself that is to be completely abandoned by those desiring liberation.
The self’s engagement in action belongs to that which is not a property of the self, such as an agent and so forth. (138)

Anticipating the objection that even one characterized by ignorance would not be entitled to perform ritual action—since such entitlement would otherwise follow even for one who is asleep—the author says: "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The meaning is this: the entitlement to ritual action belongs to one characterized by non-self-sense (anātman) extending from the agent up to the body, and not to one characterized by ignorance alone; thus there is no over-extension [of the rule] to the sleeping person, because he lacks the identification with the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth. If that is so, then even for the knower (vidvān), due to the momentum of commenced karma (ārabdhakarman), there remains identification with the body and so on...

Regarding that, he states [the reason] for why there is no qualification for ritual action: "The seeker of liberation," and so forth. Even for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), the non-self is desired to be abandoned; how much more so for the knower who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta)?

Therefore, even though the body and so forth may appear to him, he has no qualification for ritual action, because of the absence of identification with the body, which is the cause thereof—this is the sense. || 138 ||
And because knowledge and the delusion of the self, along with their respective effects, are mutually contradictory.
Because it is undesirable, like disease and so forth, the agent and other factors are to be abandoned. (139)

He states the reason why the agent and so forth are not the Self for the wise person: "Knowledge" (vidyā). Because knowledge and self-delusion (ātmamoha) are mutually opposed both in their essential nature and in their effects, the agent and so forth must be abandoned by means of the knowledge of the Self; this is the meaning. The word "that" (tat) refers to the essential nature [of the agent]. Now he states the reason why the agent and so forth are to be relinquished by one seeking liberation: "Like a disease, etc. By the word "etc.," [the author intends] the snake, the thorn, and so on.
The letter *ka* and so forth are included. || 139 ||
To say that this is the very nature of one who desires to abandon [suffering] is the talk of a child.
If the agent and so forth were its intrinsic nature, [it would contradict] that which has the form of a non-agent as perceived by direct perception. (240)
There would be contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, and likewise, there would be no liberation.
Let it be that there is no liberation, since the Seer possesses the nature of modification. (80, 141)
If, by virtue of being the enjoyer of the fruit like fire, there were a state resembling space;
Thus, because the self is eternal, modification is logically untenable. || 142 ||

1, page 67] 46. *Sureśvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikaṃ* [Saṃbandha-]
Anticipating the objection that "since the agent and so forth are the very nature of the Self, nothing could be desired to be abandoned," he says: "of the one who desires to abandon.
Anticipating the objection that "the agent and so forth are the essential nature of the Self because they are perceived therein, just like consciousness," he says: "the agent and so forth.

The Self is experienced by the direct perception of the wise as being of the nature of a non-agent and so forth; if it were otherwise, [it would contradict] the direct perception of the wise and the inference to be stated hereafter.

The meaning is that there would also be a contradiction with the scriptural statement, "The whole is indeed a mass of pure consciousness. Anticipating the objection that the perception of the wise cannot be sublated because it is subject to disagreement, he states another defect: "There would be no liberation. If the nature of being an agent and so forth were not removed, liberation would be impossible; in the first case (if it were not removed), there would be no liberated one, and in the second case (if it were removed), there would still be the existence of evil. Therefore, the Self is of the nature of an agent and so forth.

84. "It remains as it was stated before" means that it stands exactly as previously described. In this regard, the Lokāyata challenges [the position] with the words "Let it be so. He provides the reason why the consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*) constitutes an *iṣṭāpatti* (an undesired conclusion accepted by the opponent) with the word "transformation" (*vikriyā*). The meaning is that, just as fire possesses transformations such as burning and cooking, the Self likewise possesses transformations such as birth; therefore, because it would be impermanent, liberation—which is eternally established—would not exist. [This refers to] the transformation of birth and so forth belonging to the body...
Having raised the doubt that [the Self] cannot be the agent because of its immutability (*sthātva*), [the author] intends to show that this is not so because there is no Self other than the body.

Then, having proposed the alternative as to whether that [Self], even if admitted, possesses the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) or not, he refutes the first position with the words "phalet" (it would bear fruit). The remainder of the sense is that since enjoyment does not occur without modification (*vikriyā*), the possession of such modification by the enjoyer is inevitable. He follows up on the second position with the words "no cet" (if not). In that case, for the conscious Self—

He states that it is indeed non-existence (*asattvam*), because in the absence of being an enjoyer, there is the inclusion within the portion of the enjoyed. He says "of space" (*ākāśa*) etc.; since space consists of the absence of material form (*mūrtābhāvatva*), its similarity to this [unmanifest] should be understood as being precisely non-existence. Refuting the idea that the Self possesses modification (*vikriyāvattva*), he rejects the notion that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is actually desired.
He says "no" (*na*). Possession of modification is pervaded by impermanence (*anityatva*); for even in the case of atoms and the like, which possess such modification, permanence is not admitted.

And it will be stated that the self is eternal. The meaning is that the exclusion of changeability—which is pervaded by [non-eternality]—from the self also excludes from it its own pervader, namely, the state of being subject to modification. || 140 || 141 || 142 ||
How could there be any modification of the inner self, which is devoid of both form and formlessness?
For the state of being an enjoyer consists indeed in the application of valid cognition, and valid cognition belongs to the Self eternally. (I.1.143)

Furthermore, modification is observed in the phenomenal world consisting of the elements and their derivatives, which are both formed and formless; however, the Self is the witness of that world and is distinct from it, and therefore it does not possess those qualities—this is what he states in the verse beginning with "mūrta" (formed). Alternatively, by this [verse], the eternity of the Self is established.

Having established its permanence, he states the conclusion: "Modification," etc. Regarding the claim that the Self, being immutable and a non-enjoyer, is like space, he replies: "Cognition," etc. Enjoyment consists in the experience of pleasure and so forth, as well as the experience of objects which are the causes thereof; the connection with that constitutes the seer's status as an enjoyer. This would exist even for one who is devoid of activity; therefore, it is not like space. For one who is devoid of activity, there is no cognition—

Anticipating the objection that [the self] might also be unperceived in space like a cow, he says: "And it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramā*). For the Self experiences its own nature without depending on anything else, and it knows objects by way of being delimited by the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) assuming their respective forms.

Therefore, the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) belongs to the Self because of its connection with the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, which consist of the nature of experience. For it has been said: "The state of being an enjoyer would belong to that which is changeless..."
The meaning is that because it arises from a delusion of the intellect, it does not possess similarity to space. || 143 ||
The modification is not like that of wind or fire, because [in those cases] prior non-existence and so forth are impossible.
But because fire and the like possess parts, they are [overpowered] by their powerful fuels. (144)

For those whose true nature has been overcome [by impurities], [it is attained] by means such as the friction of wood.
Their manifestation is indeed always appropriate, because they consist of action. || 145 ||

Furthermore, transformation occurs only in that which possesses prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth, as is the case with fire and other such things; and since the possession of prior non-existence and so forth is excluded from the Self,
it follows that its state of possessing transformation is also excluded from it— thus he states the immutability of the Self by way of another method.

"Like wind and fire": the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth of the self are not perceived by the self, because it is impossible for those two to exist at the same time; nor can they belong to another self, because a distinction between such selves is unestablished. Nor can one's own prior non-existence and so forth be inferred by oneself, because there is a counter-inference: "The subject under dispute is possessed of my existence, because it is time, like a time that is agreed upon. Therefore, the self [is eternal], due to the absence of prior non-existence and the rest.

The meaning is "action" (*kriyā*). Alternatively, even by this [verse], permanence itself is established. Now, one might object: "The Self possesses transformation because it undergoes manifestation and disappearance, like fire and other such things"—thus its possession of transformation is inferred. To this, he says: "Of fire and the rest. These [things] possess parts; their inherent nature is suppressed by fuel and other substances which also possess parts and are capable of suppressing them, through the friction of wood and so forth.

The meaning is that it is not logical for manifestation to occur through some part [of the object] due to a cause such as impact; nevertheless, the possession of change by those [entities] is not caused by their possessing the state of manifestation and so forth, but rather is produced by their having parts—thus, the reason is one that possesses a limiting condition (sopādhika). How do fire and the others have parts? He says: "Because they are substances while being effects. He states: "Eternal... [144, 145].
But because the self is partless, these two [divisions] cannot exist in any primary sense whatsoever.
And because manifestation and disappearance are established by their own nature. || 146 ||
He refutes the pervasion of the probans with the words "But not... Furthermore, are the manifestedness and disappearance posited as causes imagined or non-imagined?
If the former, is the probandum—the state of possessing modification—also imagined or non-imagined? Not the first, because it would result in proving what is already established;
nor the second, because there is a deviation from the rule due to the manifestedness and disappearance of things like cities of Gandharvas. Thinking thus, [he considers] the alternative...

In order to refute [the opponent's] objection, he says: "The two primary [powers]" (*mukhyau*). There is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the preceding negative particle (*nañ*). Now, even for that which is partless, as long as the causal complex for manifestation (*āvirbhāva-sāmagrī*) does not exist, there is real concealment (*tirobhāva*); subsequently, manifestation occurs. To this, he replies: "Because it is established by itself" (*svataḥ siddheḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to dispel doubt. || 146 ||
Even if manifestation is admitted, it does not constitute a modification of that which is manifested.
In whatever way it may be, there is a lack of manifestation for all disputants alike. (147)

Even if it were granted that manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and disappearance (*tirobhāva*) do not cause modification (*vikriyā*) in the Self, they themselves would still be modifications; yet this is not so.

For these two, being unimagined (*akalpita*), cannot coexist simultaneously in one place, nor can they occur sequentially in the self-luminous Self. Even if they were possible, they do not constitute a modification of the Self.
Thus he says: "Even if admitted... [The meaning is: manifestation and the like do not possess the nature of a modification of that which is manifested and so forth.
He states that this [work] possesses the status of being the established conclusion of all systems with the words: "Of all... (verse 147).
Therefore, by those who do not accept that the self possesses an agent and so forth in liberation, [the following must be admitted].
It should be known as imagined through ignorance, for it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 148 ||
1 kha. Vadāvi | [vol 1, page 69] 48
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, regarding the section on the "Connection" (*saṃbandha*):
If the Self is devoid of modification, what is the status of the modifications such as agency that are nevertheless perceived in it? To this he replies with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).
Because the presence of modification in the Seer contradicts the reasoning already stated, that modification—such as being an agent and so forth—which appears, is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Having thus stated the proposition, he states the reason: "by those who do not accept [it]. For proponents of liberation do not accept agency and so forth in liberation;

therefore, because this [agency] is fallacious, its nature is imagined (*kalpita*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—this is the sense. Furthermore, because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), agency and so forth are imagined, like a snake [superimposed on a rope]; thus he says: "For not... (148).
Because that which has the nature of being the self of the agent and so forth is directly perceived, it does not exist within [the self].
The means of knowledge that cognizes the mother and so forth [does not apply] to the inner self, the witness.
It cannot be set in motion, just as a firebrand cannot be used to burn a fire.

[Objection: Since agency and so forth are attributes of the Self (ātman), like consciousness, they are not produced by ignorance; thus, bondage and liberation would consist in the arrival and departure of those [attributes] from the substrate (dharmin). [The author] says "no" and states: "agency and so forth... He provides the reason for why agency and the rest are not attributes belonging to the substrate, the Self.

"Self" (ātman): consciousness (*caitanya*) is the intrinsic nature of the self, insofar as this [agency and so forth] is perceived as dependent upon it. Is agency and the rest perceived by the self, or not? In the first case, it cannot be a property of the self because it is subject to it, like a jar. In the second case, there is no proof; this is the sense—that [the property] is unestablished. The inference that agency and the rest are not properties of the self is sublated by the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which grasps them as being properties of that [self].
Anticipating the objection that [the opponent] might apprehend either the mother and so forth, or their witness, he offers the first alternative as a counter-argument:

"The mother and so forth. The meaning is this: if the perception imagined by you were to reveal the mother and so forth, it would not sublate the inference under discussion; for such [perception] does not exclude the fact that agency and other qualities are attributes of the mother and so forth. He then refutes the second alternative: "The inner self (pratyag). For that...

Is [the action] performed by an agent such as the mother, or is it performed by the Witness (sākṣin)? It cannot be the first, because it is logically impossible for the Inner Self (pratyañc) to be the object of an action whose agent is its own mother or other [external factors]. For fire is not the object of the action of its own fuel-stick (ulmuka), which it consumes. Nor can it be the second, because the Witness, being changeless, cannot possibly possess agency. Therefore, the meaning is that inference is not sublated by the cognition "I" (ahaṃdhī). || 149 || 150 ||
Just as there is a relationship between the witness and the object witnessed, so it is with the knower and the rest.
It could not exist as an object of perception within the nature of pure experience alone.
[Objection: Is the witness of the subject (mātr) and others a seer or a non-seer? In the first case, he too would be cognizable by a witness because he is a seer, just like the subject;

and thus, since agency and so forth are established in the witness by that very [witness], inference—which is sublated by the witness’s direct perception—would be defeated. In the second case, [the witness] would be insentient, like a pot or similar objects.

To the objection that [the Self] cannot be a witness because it is not an object of perception, he says: "The Witness. In inert objects such as the body and so forth, which invariably require the illumination of something other than themselves, there is the state of being an object (*sākṣyatva*); whereas in the conscious Self, there is the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*). While this relationship between witness and object is thus possible in those cases, it is not possible in the case of the Self. This is because the Self is of the nature of pure conscious light, lacks dependence on an object for its own manifestation, and because any other object would necessarily be inert, [rendering the relationship untenable].

Since non-inertness [cannot arise] from conjunction because a distinction [between them] is untenable, the conscious Self is indeed the witness; the meaning is that its nature as a seer is like the sun's nature as an illuminator. || 111 ||
By means of the realization that the body, the enjoyer, the agent, and so forth, are all composite and exist for the sake of another.
Because of this contradiction, how could an object contrary to that [perception] be perceived by cognition? (152)
1. [The cognition] of this [object] is from perception. 2. Cognition.
Those people consider that very cognition which makes known the object to be the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). 3.
[This is] the definition.
