1, Page 70] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 49 M.

[Objection: Surely the Self is the object of the cognitions of the subject (mātr) and so forth, because it is not distinct from them, just like they themselves; thus, the means of knowledge that makes known the subject and so forth would be what subverts the inference. To this, he says: "For the sake of another" (*parārtha*), etc. The Witness of the subject and so forth is not an object of the cognition of the subject and so forth, because He is distinct from them. Whatever is distinct from something is not an object of the cognition of that thing, just as the sky, being distinct from a jar, is not an object of the cognition of that jar.

The meaning is that there is no non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) because [the witness] is distinct from the *mātrās* and so forth, due to being for the sake of another (*aparārthatvāt*), just like that [house]. Thus, by means of this negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*), the reason—being non-distinct from the *mātrās* and so forth—is not unestablished. To avoid the objection that the example of the *mātrās* and so forth lacks the exclusion of the probans (*sādhanāvyāvṛttatva*), he establishes its being for the sake of another with the words "saṃhata" (composite). The meaning is: "The subject of dispute is for the sake of another, because it is composite, like a house. Furthermore, the witness is the *mātrā*... [and so on].

[The opponent argues: "It is like that [the body], because it possesses the nature of a self (ātmatva) which is distinct from [the witness]. [The author replies: "And the example is not excluded from the probans (sādhana), for its non-selfhood (anātmatva) is established by its being a composite.

Thus he says: "Anātma" (it is not the self). Furthermore, the witness is distinct from that [the body] because it is an enjoyer (bhoktṛ), unlike that [body]; nor is there an exclusion from the probans on the grounds that the sense-organs (mātra) and so forth are also enjoyers, because, according to the logic stated in the passage "For the connection with cognition... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14], they are included within the objects of enjoyment (bhogya). Thus he says: [the witness is] "not the self."

Regarding the term "bhogyā" (the object of experience): because it is not an agent, the Witness (*sākṣin*) is distinct from the mere-measure (*mātra*) and so forth; yet, one might argue that its non-agency is no different [from theirs]. To this he says: "kartṛ-ādi" (agent, etc.). He states: "bodhinā" (by the cognizer), meaning that the Witness, who is distinct from the cognizer of the aforementioned form of the mere-measure and so forth, cannot be made an object by that cognition, because external means of knowledge (*parāṅ-māna*) are opposed to functioning toward the inner self (*pratīc*). Thus he says: "bodhinā."
Day by day. || 152 ||
In this same way, let desire, aversion, and so forth also not be accepted as attributes of the Self.
Desire, volition, and so forth—because they thus depend upon the nature of the mind. (153)

"Desire and the rest must reside in something, because they are qualities, like color and so forth. From this inference, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the self (*ātman*) is established as their substratum. Furthermore, agency and other such attributes will also belong to that [self] since they are dependent upon desire and the rest. To those who hold this view, he replies with the word "desire" (*icchā*). For they [the qualities] must be either independent or dependent; not the first, because the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddhi*); nor the other, because of the lack of a substratum.

Because [the self] is being characterized [as the locus], the substratum is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Nor are they established by themselves, because they are insentient (*jaḍatva*); nor are they established by another, because if that [other] were non-self, it could not be a prover; and if it were the self, then since desire and so forth—which are objects of perception by that [self]—are not established as its attributes (just like color and so forth), the same applies to agency and the rest: they too are not attributes of the self. This is the meaning. Now, if desire and so forth were to reside in a substance distinct from the eight substances, since they are impossible in those [eight], [they must reside in a ninth].

Having raised the objection that these [desires] are qualities of the self because they possess the nature of being qualities, like sound— an inference based on their being qualities— he says "Desire" (kāmaḥ) [in verse 993], stating that this is not so because it contradicts scripture.
For if [the world] were caused by itself, by another, or by both, there would follow the consequence of no liberation.
And when these are correctly examined, they are indeed merely the effects of ignorance.

Furthermore, regarding these [bondages], do they have the nature of being produced (*kāryatva*) or not? First, they cannot be unproduced; for if that were the case, they would exist eternally, which would result in the impossibility of liberation. Even if they are produced, does their cause exist or not? If it does not exist, then they must either always exist or never exist at all;

in the first case, the impossibility of liberation has already been stated, and in the second, bondage itself is unestablished. If a cause does exist, is it desire and so forth, or is it something else?

It cannot be both; for the first alternative [that desire and so forth are eternal], since a thing already established cannot be the cause of its own establishment, it would follow that they are self-dependent. If, on the other hand, what is unestablished were the producer, then because such a state is possible even in liberation (*mokṣa*), there would be no liberation at all. Nor can it be the second [that they are produced by something else], because no other cause is observed; or if one were observed, if it were occasional, then in the search for its cause there would be an infinite regress. If it were eternal, then because it would always produce desire and so forth, there would be no liberation. Nor can it be the third. For in that case:
[Vol. 1, Page 71] 50 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Section on the Connection] (Saṃbandha)

The second [alternative] is whether it is insentient or sentient. In the first case, is its capacity to generate desire and so forth its inherent nature or not? It cannot be the former, because that would entail the impossibility of liberation. Nor can it be the latter, because it would follow that it could never produce them; for according to the maxim, "a power that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another. Therefore, considering that desire and the like must be admitted as being products of ignorance (*avidyā*), he says:

"Self and other," etc. Furthermore, these [distinctions] cannot first of all be different from the Self, because it is impossible for them to possess the nature of attribute (dharma) and substrate (dharmin). For this very reason, they are not non-different, nor are they both different and non-different, due to contradiction. Nor can they be unreal (tuccha), because they are directly perceived. Therefore, since they cannot withstand inquiry yet are directly perceived, they are of the nature of ignorance (āvidyaka), like the blueness of the sky; thus he says: "Correctly," etc. (verse 154).
If desire and the rest have their own causes, how could they themselves produce what is harmful?
Therefore, it is not logical for the self to know the enemy as being oneself. || 155 ||

If both [the self and the other] are the cause of desire and the rest, and if the second is sentient, is it the individual soul (*jīva*) or another? Or are there two? If it is the individual soul, does it perceive that desire and the rest are harmful or not? Regarding this, he refutes the first alternative with the words "of desire and the rest. "Of its own" means by itself. He provides a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for the principle that one who acts with forethought does not bring about harm to oneself, using the word "just as."
He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ). If the individual soul (jīva) does not know their harmful nature, then it follows that they are the product of ignorance;
therefore, it is not logical for them to arise from the Self. This is the meaning. || 155 ||
Likewise, because there is no avoidance of misfortune when it has another as its cause.
The result would not be certain, just as in the case of the avoidance of disease and so forth. || 156 ||

If it is argued that the other [the Lord] is sentient, he says: "In that case... If the other were to produce such evils as desire and so forth, would He do so for Himself or for another? Not the first, because it would contradict His omniscience and other attributes. In the second case, just as He brings about evil for those in saṃsāra, He would likewise bring it about for the liberated; and thus, since their avoidance of that [evil] would not be a constant result, liberation would be untenable. Now, [an objection]: "But..."

An opponent might argue that an omniscient being will not inflict harm upon those who are liberated, because such harm would obstruct the means to their liberation; therefore, [the author] says "no. For neither the knowledge nor the action that causes liberation exists within liberation itself; thus, since there is no obstruction to it, there is no one to prevent the infliction of harm by another. Consequently, just as worldly adversities are destroyed, the destruction of suffering would not be absolute. This is the intended meaning. || 116 ||
If [the self] moves about by means of the collection of instruments, how can there be an escape for the vision?
Likewise, if both [causes] were the cause, there would be no certain emergence of the result. || 157 ||

If it is argued that the liberated self will avoid the harm being inflicted by another because of its similarity [to that other], he says "no," with the words "by means of instruments" (*karaṇaiḥ*). The meaning is that for the liberated self, the avoidance of harm caused by another and the cause thereof is not established, because it is devoid of the aggregate of body and organs; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its remaining in saṃsāra, and because the Lord possesses *māyā*.

Now, neither the Supreme Self alone nor the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the cause of desire and so forth; rather, both are. Therefore, these do not arise in the state of liberation, because the soul is liberated and [desire] is not conducive to that state. To this, he says: "In the same way. Just as there would be no liberation if desire and so forth were produced solely by the Supreme Self, so too it would be in the view that they are produced by both. For, due to the independence of the Lord, [desire] would be brought about in accordance with the soul's own inclination—[and thus bondage would persist].
The meaning is that he will bring about misfortune; therefore, there is no liberation. || 157 ||
[Vol.
1, page 72] Vārtika. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 51 Ari.
Because the intentions of others are not fixed, there can be no certainty regarding liberation;
however, no fault whatsoever exists in the postulation of ignorance as being without a cause. (158)

Now, one might object: "Surely the Lord, having perceived the liberated soul and thinking, 'Let there be no further bondage for him,' would not inflict any harm upon it; thus, liberation is certain. To this, he replies with the words "parā" (the other). Anticipating the doubt that these two defects of alternative views apply equally even to your own position, he states that in the view where desire and so forth are considered non-real (avidyamāna), there is no fault such as the impossibility of liberation, by saying "nirhetu" (without cause). || 118 ||
Because the complete accomplishment of avoiding that [fault] is achieved by resorting to well-known means.
That which is commonly regarded as the fruit among external objects of knowledge;
According to the authority of the Vedāntic teachings, consciousness alone is the object to be known here. (159)

To the question of how desire and the like, which originate from ignorance (*avidyā*), could be impossible at the time of liberation—such that there would be the undesirable consequence of non-liberation—the [author] says in response: "Of its abandonment," etc. Since the abandonment of ignorance exists in liberation, its effects, such as desire and the like, are impossible there, for without the material cause (*upādāna*), the effect cannot exist.

The sense is that there is an absence of anything to be given. Now, [one might ask: is the removal of ignorance (avidyā) brought about by ignorance itself, or by its effect, or by the inner self (pratīc), or by some other cause? It cannot be the first, because that would involve a contradiction regarding ignorance’s capacity to subvert itself. Nor can it be the second, because its effect cannot logically be the remover of that very cause; for a jar does not remove the clay [from which it was made]. Nor can it be the third, because if the Self were the remover of ignorance, then ignorance could not be perceived therein.

[This is] not [the case] because of existence. It is not the latter [alternative], because no other cause is perceived; therefore, he says: "well-known" (*prasiddha*). The inner self (*pratyagātman*) is well-known as being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*);

that very [self] is the means for the removal of ignorance through its recourse. For one who possesses the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), who has performed positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and who is qualified for hearing [the scriptures], when the knowledge of unity arises from the heard sentence, the seeing-self (*dṛg-ātman*) manifested therein [destroys] its own ignorance along with its effects.

The meaning is that after burning [ignorance], one becomes established in one's true self (*svastha*). Now, an objection is raised: since the cessation of ignorance is nothing other than the Self itself, it cannot serve as a means toward it; for the relationship between a means and its goal depends upon duality. To this, he says: "parāk" (outward-turned). The meaning of this is as follows: those means of knowledge such as perception, whose objects of cognition (*prameya*) are external things such as sound and so forth, are "those for which the objects of cognition are external things" (*parāgarthaprameyāṇi*). Among these, that consciousness (*saṃvit*) which is accepted as the result—[is the subject of the following].

"In reality, however, [the fruit] is not the non-arising of birth; rather, that very [Self], whose nature is the Supreme Self, is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by the statements of the Vedānta, and is the goal reached through their intended meaning (*tātparya*). Thus, it possesses a dual nature: it is a means (*upāya*) by virtue of its aspect as the adversary of ignorance (*avidyā*), and it is the end (*upeya*) by virtue of being the self-nature of the cessation of that [ignorance]. Therefore, within the one and the same Self, there is this twofold state due to the difference in aspects. || 159 ||
Furthermore,
if one were to assume a meaning other than this, there would follow the consequence of invalidity.
Therefore, one should not conceive of any other meaning for the Vedāntas than this. || 160 ||

Having accepted that perception and the other means of knowledge have as their object that which is "other" (parāg), it was stated that the undivided consciousness which is their fruit is the object of the Vedāntas.

Now, he states that those [means of knowledge] do not have "other" things as their objects, beginning with the words "aprāmāṇya-". If perception and the others were to take as their domain an object that is "other," then the Vedāntas would not be a valid means of knowledge regarding Brahman, who is characterized by the absence of all difference. Therefore, from this—

If one were to conceive of an object external to the Self—which is the nature of the second [experience] and is to be known through the Vedāntas—as being cognizable by perception and other means of knowledge, then the Vedāntas would lose their authority. Therefore, one should not conceive of an object other than that which is known through the Vedāntas as being within the scope of perception and the like;
rather, the meaning is that Brahman with attributes (*sopādhika*) is the object of those [other means], while Brahman without attributes (*nirupādhika*) is the object of the Vedāntas. || 160 || 216

Not accepting that the Vedāntas have as their object the experience of non-duality, he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but). The meaning is: even if the Vedāntas possess authority regarding Brahman, which is the self of the experience of non-duality, the Karma-kāṇḍa would lack authority, because it relies upon distinctions such as the factors of action (*kāraka*), and because such distinction has been sublated by the Vedāntas, which teach non-duality. For the proponent of non-duality, the lack of authority for the Karma-kāṇḍa [follows] solely from the Vedāntas...

Fearing that one who desires validity [for the Vedas] would not accept what is undesirable, he says: "In the Vedāntas," etc. The meaning is that if those [Vedāntas] were invalid, then because they are a part of the Veda, there would be a lack of confidence in the Vedāntas as well; therefore, the invalidity of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is not desired. || 169 ||
This is not so, because even all means of knowledge without exception possess the status of being valid cognizers.
"Until the realization of the Supreme Self, [the scripture] remains valid there because everything is subsumed within it.

(162) Does its validity as ultimate reality (*tāttvika*) suffer contradiction, or its validity as conventional (*vyāvahārika*)? Having accepted the first, he refutes the second with the words "Not this," etc. Is its conventional validity destroyed prior to the arising of knowledge?
He says "or not at all" regarding the first alternative, meaning "because of that. The ellipsis is: "therefore, prior to that knowledge, there is no sublation of that [injunction].

He refutes the second alternative with the word "there. Since all non-self (anātman) is destroyed upon the arising of supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), it is indeed accepted that injunctions and the like lack authority after knowledge has arisen.
However, their lack of authority does not extend to their empirical (*vyāvahārika*) validity; for the Vedāntas also possess such [empirical] validity, as their subject matter is reality (*tattva*).

The sense is that [the Veda] possesses ultimate validity because it is based on direct revelation (śruti). || 162 || There is no descent of other means of knowledge here, because all are subsumed within the single unity of the one [Vedic authority].
There would be a sublation of injunctions such as those for the Śyena sacrifice by the injunction of non-violence, just as [in the case of the prohibition of killing]. || 163 ||

Now, even though the knower continues to engage in empirical activity through the means of knowledge (*māna*) as before until the fall of the body, how is it that injunctions and the like lack authority after the dawn of knowledge? To this, he says: "Not from that" (*nātaḥ*). After the dawn of knowledge, because the ignorance that causes the operation of perception and other means has been exhausted by being reduced to the state of pure subjectivity (*pratyag-mātratayā*), there is no further operation of those means. Nor is it impossible for the knower to act without the means of knowledge; for such activity can occur through the persistence of what has already been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛttyā*).

The meaning is "from existence. Now, one might object: "The knowledge of identity is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is itself a means of valid cognition, just like other means of valid cognition. To show the fallacy (vyabhicāra) in that argument, he says: "Śyena, etc. The word "etc. refers to [the sacrificial animals such as] cows and so forth. Thus, by the knowledge arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), previously operative injunctions and the like are sublated; this is because of the maxim: "In a sequence of prior and posterior, the prior is weaker, as in the case of the archetypal sacrifice" (paurvāparye pūrvadaurbalyaṃ prakṛtivat). This is the remainder of the sense. || 163 ||
Therefore, ritual actions are prescribed for the person who possesses ignorance,
but not for the twice-born one who has destroyed all causes of action.

Furthermore, since ritual actions are prescribed for one who possesses ignorance and harbors the conceit of being a human agent, the authority of the *karmakāṇḍa* (the section on rituals) is merely conventional; this is because there is no contradiction regarding its authority as long as [true] knowledge has not arisen. Thus he says: "Ritual actions... Anticipating the objection that "the subject under dispute reveals reality because it is a means of valid cognition, like what is already accepted," he says: "But not... [The world] is entirely destroyed along with its cause.

For one who possesses the conceit of being a Brahmin and so forth—wherein karma is the cause—the injunctions of ritual acts are not prescribed with respect to that "twice-born" man (dvija) who is [actually] possessed of knowledge, because he is no longer subject to such prescriptions. Furthermore, if "authoritativeness" (mānatva) means the capacity to reveal reality (tattvāvedakatva), then it is indistinguishable from the probandum; if it means being a factor in worldly transaction (vyavahārāṅgatva), then there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of waking from dreams and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedic injunctions and so forth do not possess ultimate (tāttvika) authority. || 164 ||

The meaning is that, according to the principle that "one who acts [in a contrary manner] has no authority [to engage]," because [the injunctions] are not conducive to what they desire due to being opposed to their inclination toward worldly activity, the injunction of action is intended only for the undiscriminating; therefore, it does not reveal the ultimate reality (tattva) to him. || 165 ||
For in the conventional usage of causal factors, a pure reality is not perceived.
And likewise, when the object is established as pure, there is the activity of the agent. || 166 ||

[Objection: Surely, even for one who possesses discrimination and is dispassionate, as long as knowledge has not been attained, there is no possibility of abandoning ritual action (*karman*), because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating, "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—this action must not be abandoned; it must indeed be performed. Therefore, even one who desires to know (*vividiṣu*) remains qualified for ritual action. [Reply: No; he says: "By the agent," etc. [The word *kāraka* refers to] the agent and so forth.

The so-called "transaction" (*vyavahāra*) of the causal factors (*kāraka*) is action (*karman*); when that exists, the desire to know the Self (*ātmajijñāsā*) does not arise at all. Even if such a desire were present, one who is desirous of knowing would not be capable of perceiving the pure reality, because the intellect has been carried away by action; therefore, until discrimination (*viveka*) is attained, there must be the performance of action. Upon the attainment of discrimination, however, there is its abandonment, according to the Smṛti passage beginning, "For the sage who desires to ascend to Yoga," and so forth. And thus, for one who desires to know, there is no [obligation to] action.

The phrase "sacrifice, charity, and austerity" (*yajña-dāna-tapaḥ-karma*) and so forth, however, is intended as a praise of obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves to draw back the negative particle (*nañ*). The meaning is that when the non-manifest reality (*niṣprapañca-tattva*) has been made the object of discernment, there is no qualification for [ritual action] in that person, because the conceit caused by karma has become lax. || 166 ||
The cognitions of "agent" and "non-agent" cannot coexist at one time regarding a single object.

Because [the Veda] is authoritative by virtue of being the source (*tantra*), a cognition of difference that contradicts it cannot arise; therefore, the meaning is that an entity is either different or non-different, but not both.
He addresses the position that the state of being both different and non-different for a single thing is unreal with the words "If not" (*na cet*).

If the cognition of difference and non-difference regarding one thing is a false cognition, then there is no fault even if one accepts that a single thing is both different and non-different. This is provided that this [cognition] is not false.

The meaning is that, in that case, there could be no such thing as cognition (dhī), because the aforementioned contradiction would be unavoidable. Alternatively, he states the defect if cognition were dependent upon an unreal object:

"If not," etc. As for the second alternative, it is refuted externally; for if difference-and-non-difference were merely imagined within the Self, there would be no harm, since non-difference alone is the reality there. || 171 ||
And how this [position] is contradictory will be explained later on.
Only the single Self is the object of knowledge, because of the lack of awakening to that very [Self]. (172)

Furthermore, he says "And as... because the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) is to be refuted in the context of explaining such passages as "These three are one Being" (*tad etat trayam sad ekam*), which establish that the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is indeed of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Regarding the phrase "of that which is [the Self]": since only that whose nature is of a single flavor (ekarasa) is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), it alone possesses reality, and not the phenomenal world (prapañca). For the latter cannot be "unknown" in the same way as Brahman; therefore, the world is superimposed upon That. And this will be demonstrated in the section on the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta-prakriyā).
This is the meaning. || 172 || i. 1.4.179 ||
In this world, objects are loved when they are distinguished from one another.
Therefore, what has been stated by you is contradicted by the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva).
Now, is this identity [of the means of knowledge] with perception and so forth, or with scripture, or with both? It is not the first; thus he says: "entities.

Here, "here" refers to the sphere of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). "By non-existence" means by that which is other than it, namely by perception and the rest. Nor is it the second, because of duality—

Because, in the case of a contradiction with the Himālaya, it is impossible for the scripture to have oneness as its object; for this very reason, he says "by that" [in verse 173] that the third [alternative] is not [the case].
Whether there is difference or non-difference between transmigratory existence and Brahman;
Similarly, there would be the non-Brahmanhood of Brahman, as well as the futility of knowledge and the possession of parts. (174)

As for the claim that because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) lacks the status of being unknown, it is superimposed upon the Self which is not an object of knowledge (*ameya*), [the author] refutes the first alternative by considering the options of whether there is a difference or non-difference between that [world] and Brahman. He says, "Or if there is a difference. The ellipsis is that "in both cases there is a fault.
He clarifies the position of difference with the words, "Of Brahman," meaning: if the phenomenal world of saṃsāra were other than Brahman, then there would be a limitation of its reality...

The meaning is that [the world] is Brahman. Regarding the position of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), there are two alternatives: either the world is non-different from Brahman, or Brahman is non-different from it. In the first case, knowledge (*vidyā*) would be useless, because it is impossible for the transmigratory world—which is non-different from Brahman—to be removed by knowledge in the same way that Brahman is. In the second case, Brahman would possess manifoldness (*anekarasa-tva*) due to its non-difference from such a manifold world, just like the world itself; thus he says: "tadvat" (like that). || 174 ||
If it is claimed that Brahman possesses ignorance, then indeed this is a great fault.
And if ignorance were non-existent, it would follow that knowledge is purposeless. || 175 ||

Now, one might object: since saṃsāra is other than Brahman, knowledge (vidyā) is not purposeless, nor does it entail a limitation of the reality of that [Brahman], because that which is characterized by ignorance (āvidya) is unreal. In this regard, one must choose among the following alternatives: does ignorance reside in Brahman, or in the individual soul (jīva), or is it independent? Taking the first alternative, he says: "In Brahman. [The opponent argues: Brahman, whose nature is knowledge and who is omniscient, cannot be assailed by ignorance, because that would involve a contradiction.

He refutes [the objection] with "But surely" (*nanu*). He addresses the second point—that even in Brahman who is devoid of ignorance, the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be the locus of ignorance because it is non-different from Brahman, otherwise Brahman’s state of being devoid of ignorance would be impossible—with the words "And [in one] devoid of ignorance. By the word "and" (*ca*), the fault [of the previous argument] is [implied].

The connection with "the Great" (Mahat) has been indicated. He addresses the third [objection]—that if [the intellect] were independent, it could not be sublated by knowledge as Brahma is, and thus [the scripture] would be purposeless—by saying: "Of knowledge... (vidyāyāḥ). || 175 ||
"It does not have ignorance"— thus, remaining within ignorance itself, it is falsely conceptualized.
But from the perspective of Brahman, this so-called "ignorance" is in no way tenable.

Since the position of absolute identity is untenable, and because difference and non-difference between the world and Brahman are perceived—just as the notions of "agent" and "non-agent" are not contradictory in a single locus—the opponent arrives at this conclusion; [the author] refutes it with "No. The meaning is: first, the non-measurability of absolute identity cannot be maintained because it will be demonstrated later; nor can the alternatives of difference and non-difference be applied to transmigratory existence, for that which consists of indeterminable ignorance and its products is unfit for such conceptual distinctions. As for that which pertains to Brahman...

Regarding the point that it is not "ignorance" (*avidyā*) because of its omniscience and its nature as knowledge (*vidyā*), he says: "of this" (*asya*). For it is not independent, like Brahman, because that would contradict its being ignorance; nor is the individual soul (*jīva*) its locus, because the soul is not distinct from Brahman. Therefore, when one considers its nature as ignorance, its connection with Brahman is inevitable; yet, in reality, since that very nature does not exist, and because Brahman is essentially of the nature of true knowledge (*vidyā*), [it is not ignorance].

The state of possessing real ignorance (*tāttvikāvidyāvattvam*) is not contradictory; however, omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is established as the sublator of that [state], according to the logic of the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Is the relationship between ignorance and Brahman real (*tāttvika*), since it is either the relationship itself or one of its relata (Brahman or ignorance), just like Brahman?
To this, he says: "Brahman... By considering the nature of Brahman, there is no ignorance in It, because It is an unattached, undivided consciousness (*asaṅgānavacchinnacid-dhātu*).

The meaning is that this inference is sublated by the following inference: "The subject under dispute is unreal, because it is characterized by the condition of not being excluded from the knowledge of reality, since it is either ignorance or the relation between ignorance and Brahman, like [the case of] ignorance. || 176 ||
For ignorance is known through direct experience, just like the experience "I am Brahman."
Therefore, that [consciousness] also, being destroyed by the consciousness arising from pride, returns to the state of the Self.

Now, one might object: what kind of knowledge dispels ignorance—is it knowledge of its own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) or knowledge derived from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*)? It cannot be the first, because that which establishes ignorance cannot be its remover. Nor can it be the second, because since ignorance, like Brahman, is an object of the means of valid cognition such as scripture, it would be impossible for it to be removed by them. Therefore, there is no pervasion with the probandum; to this he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). Ignorance is not an object of the means of valid cognition, because it cannot be removed by them.

However, that which is the object of the experience of the nature of Brahman is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), common to both valid and invalid means of knowledge; the Śruti and other authorities merely inform those who are in disagreement regarding it about its distinction from non-existence. Thus it has been said:

"In this context, since ignorance—which is known by the witness—is shown by the means of knowledge to be excluded from non-existence, there is no consequence of its being cognizable by the means of knowledge. And so it is.

The meaning is that because ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its relation [to the self] are sublated by valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*), the probans does not pervade the locus of the *upādhi*. Regarding the point that the ignorance of the Self is established by eternal experience, he provides an illustration with the word "Brahman. Knowledge arising from the [great] sentence is the experience of Brahman; it is not self-established due to its insentience (*jāḍya*), nor is it established through a means of knowledge (*māna*), as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, it is established through the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), which is the very nature of Brahman. Ignorance is likewise [established].

Such is the meaning. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that this [ignorance] is established solely through eternal experience (*nityānubhava*): "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since ignorance is not an object of valid means of knowledge (*māna*), but rather the province of eternal experience, it is therefore destroyed by the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) arising from the Great Sentence; thus, it is not real (*tāttvika*). The sense is that both ignorance and its connection are unreal. Now, does the destruction of ignorance by knowledge exist as something other than Brahman, or not? In the first case...

If Brahman were the locus of ignorance, the fall into duality would occur in the second [case], because it is that which destroys ignorance; for a cessation cannot have as its locus that which has already ceased. To this he says: "That too goes. For ignorance, when struck down by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perishes upon attaining the nature of Brahman, according to the principle:
"There is no division, on account of the scriptural statement. Therefore, since the destruction of ignorance is not distinct from Brahman, there is no fall into duality. Nor...

Brahman is not the locus of ignorance because it is its locus prior to its destruction; for although the destruction of a jar has clay as its nature, it is observed that prior to that destruction, the clay is the locus of the jar. With this intention, he says: "It also merges" (api eti). || 177 ||
When Brahman is not known, it is logically untenable that there is no ignorance (avidyā) due to the lack of realization.
Moreover, when [the object] is thoroughly cognized, there is no uncontradicted false cognition. (178)
1 kha. ...in the *Vārttika*; 2 kha. ...the state of being subject to destruction; 3 kha. ...due to the nature of non-occurrence; 4 ka. ...in that [work].
[Vol. 1, page 78] *Vārttika*.

Furthermore, regarding Brahman: are ignorance and its relationship with it cognized when Brahman is unknown, or when it is known? To refute the first position, he says: "Brahman—" [Note: The text provided appears to be an excerpt from Ānandagiri’s *Śāstraprakāśikā* commentary.]

[The author] says: "In the case of the unknown Brahman, ignorance (*avidyā*), as well as its relation [to Brahman], is established through the cognition of them; for without a cognition of the substratum (*āśraya*), a cognition of that which is supported (*āśrita*) is impossible—this is the meaning. He refutes the second [alternative] with: "And even more so... When Brahman is known, false cognition (*mṛṣādhīḥ*), which is ignorance, and its relation [to Brahman] are not established, because they have been destroyed by knowledge; and a cognition of those two through a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is utterly ruled out.
This is the meaning. || 178 ||
One who possesses ignorance is not capable of defining that very ignorance.
Therefore, with respect to the actual state of things, it is not defined as "ignorance. || 179 ||

Furthermore, regarding Brahman, does the ignorant person measure it through ignorance and its connection [to Brahman], or does the knower? Of these, he refutes the first [position] with the words "one who possesses ignorance. The meaning is that there is no means of knowledge (māna) for it; or, if such a means existed, it would contradict the very nature of possessing ignorance. He states that the second [position] is not tenable with the word "entity" (vastu). The knower (mātṛ) and the means of knowledge (māna) are entities; their "functioning" (vṛtta) is their essential nature (svarūpa). In relation to that, ignorance and its connection [cannot exist] in Brahman.
Therefore, the meaning is that those two are logically established merely through the testimony of witnesses. || 179 ||
For it is not logical for the operation of means of valid cognition to apply to anything other than a real entity.
And ignorance is not accepted as a real entity, because it cannot withstand the assault of valid cognition.

He states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in order to infer that ignorance (*ajñāna*) lacks epistemic validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*). He says: "Of a non-entity" (*vastunaḥ*). Having stated, "Whatever is a non-entity is unfit for a means of valid cognition (*māna*), just like a rabbit's horn," he says: "The subject of dispute (*vimata*) is unfit for a means of valid cognition because it is a non-entity, like that [rabbit's horn]. Regarding the phrase "and ignorance" (*avidyā ca*), the word *iti* follows immediately after the word *vastu*, and the ablative case in the word *jñānanivartyatvāt* (because of being removable by knowledge) follows after the word *iṣṭa*.
And there is an ellipsis (adhyāhāra). || 180 ||
This indeed is the defining characteristic of ignorance as ignorance.
The inability to endure insults and injuries is considered its unique characteristic. || 181 ||

One might object by proposing a counter-inference: "The subject under dispute is fit to be an object of valid cognition, because it is the meaning of the scripture, like Brahman. Anticipating this, I shall point out the non-establishment of the reason (hetvasiddhi) with the words "of ignorance" (avidyāyāḥ). It has been stated that since transmigratory existence—which is superposed upon ignorance—is manifested within the Self that is Brahman, which is established solely through eternal experience, it does not admit of the conceptual alternatives of difference or non-difference. || 189 ||
In your position, much would have to be postulated, and it would contradict all authoritative means of knowledge.
In my view, ignorance alone is to be postulated, and that is grounded in experience. (182)

[Objection: "But in your view, ignorance (*avidyā*) and its status as the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) are merely postulated. In my view, however, since the distinction and non-distinction between the already established transmigratory existence and Brahman are admitted, why is my own view not accepted, given this difference in postulation? To this, he replies: "In your position," etc. [The meaning is: For you, there is both distinction and non-distinction between the world and Brahman; the destruction of beginningless bondage—which is itself real—is liberation (*kaivalya*), which is the fruit of karma, and that is eternal.

The meaning is that because many things would have to be postulated in your position, it is not accepted due to such complexity (*gaurava*). If it is argued that complexity is not a fault according to the maxim, "Even very many unseen things must be postulated if they possess valid means of knowledge," he replies to that with the word "all. They are certainly not to be postulated.
(Note: *kha* reads *māna* for *myā*.)
58 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Introduction]—Connection of Topics—[Vol. 1, p. 79]

However, they contradict that [position]. If one thing were both different and non-different [from another], there would be a contradiction with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because existence and non-existence are accepted as residing in a single substrate (*upādhi*). Furthermore, the claim that the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) possesses an end, despite being a real entity, contradicts inference, since that which is beginningless and real cannot have an end. The view that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the fruit of ritual action (*karman*) contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti, which state that it is the fruit of knowledge alone. [The claim that it is] the fruit of ritual action...
The point is that its [the Self's] eternality contradicts both inference and scripture, which are preceded by the universal rule (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is produced is impermanent.

Now, one might object: "In your own position as well, there is much to be postulated—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), its beginninglessness, its capacity to bind, and its being removable by knowledge (*vidyā*);

thus, the two positions are equal. To this he replies: "Postulated" (*kalpyā*). This refers to [the four attributes of] ignorance: its beginninglessness, its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), its binding nature, and its being removable by knowledge.

"When the individual soul (jīva), asleep through beginningless illusion (anādimāyā), is awakened"; "Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless"; "There was neither non-existence nor existence"; "This [world] existed as darkness"; "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti."

The sense is that these [phenomena] need not be postulated as belonging to ignorance (*avidyā*), since they are established by the very words of the Śruti and Smṛti: "For this is an illusion created by me," "And again at the end, there is the cessation of the universal illusion," and "They cross over this illusion.
Furthermore, even ignorance itself is not something to be postulated, because it is established by eternal experience; thus he says: "And that... (verse 182).
Merely by the arising of the correct knowledge produced from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi).
Ignorance, together with its effects, has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist. || 183 ||
He states the established conclusion regarding the fact that the bondage consisting of aversion to ignorance and its effects is superimposed: "The [teachings] such as 'That thou art'... (verse 183).
Therefore, it is impossible to perceive through any means of valid cognition that this person possesses ignorance.
Of what nature is it, or from where does it arise, since it is experienced as having a single form? (184)

One might object: "Is it not the case that even the time of liberation is touched by ignorance and the like, because it is time, just like prior time? To this he says: "Therefore. Since the knowledge arising from the [great] statement does not tolerate the existence—pertaining even to the three periods of time—of ignorance along with its effects, therefore it is impossible to ascertain through any means of valid cognition that ignorance with its effects exists for one who is liberated; for it is unfit to say that it exists at the time of liberation.

The meaning is that this would contradict its being simultaneous with that [Brahman]. Anticipating the objection—"Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) by virtue of being conjoined with Brahman, it is possible for it to exist even in its own nature; why then is it impossible to perceive it through a means of valid cognition (*māna*)?"—he asks: "Of what kind? No means of valid cognition need be sought here to remove the desire to know (*tubhutsā*) regarding what the form of this ignorance is and how it exists in Brahman; for without such a means, ignorance is [known] through one's own experience (*svānubhava*).
The meaning is that, upon attainment, there is the cessation of the desire to know. || 184 ||
Surely, the deity, the substance, the agent, and so forth are real entities; how then can reality be non-dual?
Because non-duality is not established, as it is [only] renowned to everyone in the world. || 185 ||

By the passage beginning with "ignorance together with its effects," it is stated that duality is imagined and that the experience of the nature of Brahman is non-dual. Not accepting this, the opponent objects: "The deity... He states the reason for the reality of duality such as heaven, *apūrva*, and so forth: "all... He states the reason for the unreality of the non-dual: "of the non-dual... The word "api" (also) has the sense of "like duality," indicating a point of contrast (*vaidharmya*).
The illustration. || 185 ||
1. Kha-na-sa; 2. Ka. [It exists.

This is not correct, for the means of valid cognition do not indeed have the name "all the world."
There is no proof for that on account of which you speak in this manner regarding life.

Regarding the claim that by the power of which the very entity is a deity and so forth, rather than being non-dual—it being questioned whether that [power] is distinct from the means of knowledge such as perception known to all the world, or whether it is included within them—the first alternative is refuted with the words "This is not so. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). The meaning is: "by the power of which," namely, by the power of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. || 186 ||
And it is here that this conceit of the entire world is perceived.
The falsity of that [cognition] is asserted on the grounds that "this object is indeed perceptible. (187)

He states the second [point]: "and [the notion of] conceit. In this world, the conceit of people that "this object is perceptual" and "this is inferential" is understood; because that [conceit] is sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya-jñāna*), its falsity has been declared—like [the perception of] silver and so forth—by scriptural passages such as "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*). And thus, for the Lord, all worldly means of knowledge known as perception and so on, which are included within those [objects], [are likewise false].

The claim that such [scriptures] bring about the realization of the Truth is unestablished; the meaning is that perception and the other means of knowledge do not bring about that realization, according to the principle of the section concerning "the origin" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa). || 187 ||
And direct perception is considered to be closer to the object than indirect cognition.
Just as everything has not been abandoned [in that state], so too the awakening arising from the sentence occurs within the Self.

[Objection: "Surely, the knowledge of the Self derived from scripture does not sublate perception, because it is not perceptual, just like inference; thus, by this inference, the bondage established by perception remains unsublated. In that regard, [the opponent asks] whether the non-perceptuality of the scriptural knowledge of the Self consists in its not cognizing a proximate object, or its not cognizing an immediate object, or its not being a locus of immediacy, or its lacking independence. To [the objection] beginning with "not the first," [the author] says: "And perception... *Note: This passage is part of a commentary on the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa*, specifically addressing the relationship between scriptural testimony (*śruti*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the nature of the Self and the reality of bondage.*

Just as an object that has become a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is desired to be more proximate than an object that is imperceptible and must be inferred (*anumeya*), so too the cognition arising from the Vedāntic statements regarding Brahman and the Self (*ātman*) makes its object more proximate than anything else; for that object, being the Self, is the most immediate (*pratyaktama*). Thus, because this cognition lacks the quality of being "proximately perceived" (*saṃnihitābodhitva-pratyakṣatva*) in the ordinary sense, it is logical that it sublates the cognition of duality.
The state of being. || 188 ||
Perception and the other means of valid cognition are established by relying upon the self-experience of the self.
Since experience is established by itself, what further dependence could there be for the establishment of the self? (189)

He says that it is not the second [alternative], namely: "the self-experience" (*ātmānubhava*). First of all, perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish themselves intrinsically because they are insentient (*jaḍatva*); nor do they [establish themselves] through another means of knowledge, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*). Furthermore, what is unestablished cannot serve as a proof for its object. Therefore, the meaning is that their establishment depends upon experience (*anubhava*), which is the very nature of the Self. Anticipating the objection that the manifestation of the self-experience, like that of perception and so forth, must also depend on something else, he says:

Regarding the phrase "from experience" (anubhūteḥ): since the self’s own-nature experience—which is the cause of the establishment of everything—is incapable of being established by anything else, it is directly perceived by itself. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition arising from the sentence concerning that [self] does not fail to cognize a directly perceived object, nor is it non-perceptual. || 189 ||
Because perceptuality is preceded by the experience of the self, it is not [established] intrinsically.
The state of absolute unity, which is to be realized solely by the self, is understood in the Vedāntas. || 190 ||
1. Gains. 2. b. ‘Or not you are. [Vol. 1, page 81] *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya.

He says that it is not the third [alternative], namely, "through the relation with the experience of the Self" (*ātmānubhava*). Even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not intrinsically immediate (*aparokṣa*) due to its insentience (*jāḍya*);

rather, it is so because of its relation to the experience of the nature of the Self, which is eternally immediate. And thus, the immediacy residing in that [perception] is established by the intrinsically realized experience of the Self.

The meaning is that because the Vedic cognition regarding that [Self] is dependent on that [Self], it cannot fail to have the Self as its substrate for immediacy. He says "not the fourth" with the words "to be known by the Self alone. For it was established in the *Codanā-sūtra* that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).

Thus, since the Vedāntas, which convey the aforementioned object, cannot be dependent on anything else, it is extremely clear that the cognition of the Self produced by them is independent; this is the intended sense.
And as for what was also stated—that according to the Śruti and Smṛti, perfection is attained through action alone—
Therefore, there is no other means for liberation apart from ritual action. || 191 ||

Since the non-dual cognition arising from Śruti is independent and, being of scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*), is stronger than the aforementioned means of knowledge, it is established that it sublates duality as perceived through perception and other means.

Consequently, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) born of ignorance can be removed solely by knowledge, knowledge is the cause of liberation. Furthermore, the distinction between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) regarding their respective means and so forth has been stated: one who possesses the fourfold qualification is the qualified seeker for knowledge, which is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), while the undiscriminating person is the qualified seeker for ritual action. Now, with respect to each— [The text continues: ...presently, with respect to each—

Having restated the mere fragments of prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa) propounded by others according to the method of the *ṭīkā*, he repeats what was stated in the verse "Because action is heard in the Śruti" (*śrutatvāt karmaṇaḥ śrutau*) in order to refute them, beginning with the words "And that which... (191).
And by whom was it said that action does not become a means for liberation?
"You did not hear that very thing, nor do you remember the teaching that these are merely conditioned formations. (192)

In this regard, is action the direct cause of liberation or the indirect cause? It is not the first [option], because there is no means of attainment; for, considering that statements such as "By action alone one attains perfection" are intended to have another meaning when they appear to contradict scriptural passages such as "Not by action," he accepts the other alternative. He asks: "By what? It is accepted that action is the cause of liberation either through the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) or through purification (*saṃskāra*). Of these, regarding the first:

He cites the *vividiṣā*-passage as authority: "Regarding that very [Self]... [The passage continues: "Garbhādhāna, Puṃsavana, Sīmantonnayana, Jātakarman, Nāmakaraṇa, Annaprāśana, Caula, Upanayana, the four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*), Snāna, union with the partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī*), the performance of the five sacrifices—namely, those to the gods, ancestors, men, spirits, and Brahman—and for these [the rites of] the eight offerings (*aṣṭakā*), the *pārvaṇa* Śrāddha, the *Śrāvaṇī*, the *Āgrahāyaṇī*," and so forth.

The *Hāyaṇī*, *Proṣṭhapadī*, *Caitrī*, and *Āśvayujī*—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*. The *Agnyādheya*, *Agnihotra*, *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, *Āgrayaṇa*, *Cāturmāsya*, *Nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and *Sautrāmaṇī*—these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*. The *Agniṣṭoma*, *Atyagniṣṭoma*, *Uktha*, *Ṣoḍaśī*, *Vājapeya*, *Atirātra*, and *Aptoryāma*—these are the seven forms of the *soma* sacrifice; such are these [sacrifices].

The phrase "and the purificatory rites" (saṃskārā iti ca) indicates the view that the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) are intended, based on such Smṛti passages as: "He who possesses forty purificatory rites attains union with Brahman. || 992 ||
Although the cognition of the identity [of the individual self with Brahman] is not explicitly enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti;
Nevertheless, it is not external to those two, because the self is realized through them alone.

Having refuted [the opponent's argument] beginning with "because that [liberation] is established from actions alone," it was stated here that "only the action prescribed in Śruti and Smṛti [leads to it]. This [opponent's] objection is to be disregarded.

The commentator says: "Even though," etc. The meaning is that although knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) is not explicitly enjoined [as a ritual act], it is not non-Vedic because it is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, just like the knowledge of ritual action (*karmajñāna*);
therefore, its status as a means to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is not contradictory. || 193 ||
And you have questioned this point: that there is no entity being made known in the Veda.
That objection has been set aside, and its refutation will be stated [later]. || 194 ||

One might raise the objection: "How can the Self be known through the Śruti and Smṛti? Since those two have action as their purpose, they teach established facts only as subordinate to that [action], according to the principle of 'the past and the future' (bhūta-bhavya-nyāya). Anticipating this, he restates what was said in the passage beginning with "And not apart from action" (*na ca karmātirekeṇa*). He says, "And that," referring to the fact that this [objection] has already been refuted by the passage beginning with "established in the true nature of the inner Self as cognized by the authority of Śruti and so forth. This is because the unity [of the Self] is established by Śruti and the other means of knowledge.

Raising the objection, "How can this be refuted merely by stating that [the self] is the object of pride (*māna*), without providing a proof for it?", he says, "And it will be stated," [implying that] even what is to be explained later in the passage beginning with "All this... should be kept in mind here as well. || 194 ||
Furthermore, you have asserted that the word lacks the status of a means of valid cognition.
And he will strive to refute that [objection] with clear and logical arguments. || 195 ||

He restates what was said previously—that the meaning of the Veda consists solely of injunctions and prohibitions—beginning with the words "In an injunction... By supplying the word "iti" after the verb, it should be construed as "and that which [is prohibited]. That too has been refuted by stating that the Vedas and other authorities have the non-dual reality (*aikātmya*) as their object.

Furthermore, he says that all of this will be rejected right at the beginning of the passage starting with "All this...", through the presentation of a series of arguments that are both uncontradicted and free from doubt.
It is manifest. || 195 ||
And as it has been said: "There is no human goal [attained] merely from the cognition of the thing-in-itself."
For it is observed here that the Upanishads (the end of the three Vedas) abound in narrative accounts.

He takes up the objection intended [in the sūtra] "Because the Veda has action as its purpose" (Jaimini 1.2.1), beginning with the words "As for what was said. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "That is not so; the Vedāntas do not have as their sole purport the mere nature of reality. Anticipating the objection that even those texts whose purport is merely that might still possess authority by having happiness and the like as their fruit, he says: "By means of narratives," etc. The reason for this is that in those [Vedāntas], there is an abundance of such [narratives], as seen in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the battle between the gods and the asuras and so forth.

Therefore, the implication is that these [scriptures] do not possess the status of valid authority by virtue of having results such as pleasure, which are to be accomplished through activity and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) is an expression referring to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). || 196 ||
"Rāma became king"—this much alone does not constitute true awakening.
Therefore, a human goal (pumartha) is possible [from them], since there is an absence of any injunction (vidhi).

Now, it might be argued: from the Vedāntas arises knowledge of the thing-in-itself (vastumātra); from that, a desire; from that, activity. Thus, even though they are intent upon that [knowledge], their status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) is established because their fruit is to be accomplished through activity. To this, he says: "Rāma," etc. Just as in the aforementioned example, the Vedāntas [yield] only that...

The implication is: "If even these [other means] lack a fruit, how can they possess authority? Since one who is not intent upon an injunction does not attain the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), it follows that for that purpose, the Vedāntas must also be held to be intent upon injunctions; thus he states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Because there is no goal of human life in any sentence without an injunction (*niyoga*), an injunction must be accepted even in the Vedāntas for the sake of their authority as possessing a fruit.
This is the meaning. || 197 ||
In this context, it is observed that the very purpose of knowledge everywhere consists solely in the benefit of others.
"Because there is an injunction for performance after [the truth] has been known, even the statement 'the wise man sacrifices' [is justified]. (198)

Raising the objection that since no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard in those [Upaniṣadic passages], how can they possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) by culminating in the human goal through being intent upon that [Self], he says: "For the sake of another" (*parārthatā*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement of the scripture (*śāstra*). The meaning is that, just like the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), because the knowledge of the Self is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣatva*), it is logical that the Vedāntas are intent on enjoining that [action] by way of that [knowledge]. The context (*prakaraṇa*) is the authority for [the knowledge of the Self] being an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Anticipating the objection as to what authority there is for the knowledge of the Self being an auxiliary to that [action], he says:
"Having known" (*jñātvā*). || 198 ||
The refutation for this has already been stated, and it will also be explained further below.
Because it relies on reasons such as the perceptibility of the fruit of knowledge. || 199 ||

Since it has been established by the aforementioned method that there is no difference between the means, the qualified seeker, and so forth for the two sections (kāṇḍas), [the author] refutes this with the words "it has been stated here. By relying on the direct perception of the wise and the scriptural testimony, it was stated in the previous section that the fruit of the knowledge of the Self is the destruction of all miseries and the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss;

that is, the fruit of the knowledge of the Self is directly perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedāntas do not constitute a supplement to the injunctions for ritual action. In that regard, the tradition states:
By the words "of that which is denoted" and so forth, he indicates the future meditative absorption as well. And "above" [refers to] verse 199.
But is it not heard in the Śruti that the fruit [of knowledge] is the shaking off of sorrow and so forth?
Therefore, this is self-praise; it is merely fashioned from the desires of your own mind.

He raises an objection, setting aside the scriptural passage concerning the fruit of knowledge, such as "the knower of the Self transcends sorrow," and so forth. He does so by saying, "But surely... (nanu). The word "fruit" implies "the fruit of knowledge. The meaning is that this Self is indeed of great majesty, since its knowledge is the destroyer of all sorrow and the like; thus, this is a praise of the Self as qualified for ritual action (karma), and therefore scripture is not an authority regarding the fruit of knowledge. As for what was stated there...

He refutes that [position] which was stated as being the direct perception of the wise, beginning with the words "tvat" (your). For your imagined perception is not capable of apprehending the result as described; the meaning is that since it is established merely by your own mental wish, we do not accept it as such. || 200 ||
To this it is replied: that which is intended is indeed understood through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 201 ||
Having completely abandoned that fruit, why [is there] praise by means of figurative indication?
Just as an ignorant person imagines something that has never been heard and is not intended [by others]. (202)

He offers the following alternatives: is the reason [for rejecting the Veda’s] purpose of destroying grief and so forth that such a purpose is not intended by it, or that it is not understood directly from the sentence, or that it is known through another means of knowledge? Regarding this, he says: "Because it is intended. Since it is impossible for a result being sought—namely, "May I have happiness" and "May I not have suffering"—not to be intended, the first alternative is not tenable. It is not the second either.

Thus he says: "that which is being traversed. This means that, in the present context, because of the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*), it is seen immediately. He says that it is not the third [alternative]: "by means of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*). The sense is that it is unproven that what appears through the experience of the wise (*vidvadanubhava*) cannot be known by another means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, how can the mention of a fruit be intended as praise of the Self (*ātmastuti*) by way of being a non-factual explanatory passage (*abhūtārthavāda*); or rather, is it praise directly from the sentence itself?
Is it because [the Self] is already known, or because it is intended [as a praise], or because it is established by another means of knowledge? It is not the first; thus he says: "The fruit.

There is no direct cognition of the praise of the Self from the sentence; rather, it must be inferred through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), and there is no perception or other [means of knowledge] for this which is seen in the scripture.

*karmaṇi dvitīyā* (the second case-affix is used in the sense of the object).

The meaning is that one who acts with foresight would not abandon the fruit perceived by the wise and instead imagine that figurative [meaning]. He states the reason why self-praise does not appear here directly:
"Because it is not heard," which means because no word expressive of praise is observed.

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case]: "anabhipretām" (unintended). The meaning is that praise is not intended because it is distinct from happiness, the removal of extreme suffering, and their causes. He says that the third [alternative] is not [the case]: "kalpayasi" (you imagine). The fact that the destruction of grief and so forth constitutes self-praise is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, you behave like an ignorant person by imagining what is not supported by valid cognition. || 201 ||
And there is no single object for both perception and verbal testimony, because—
The refutation is stated by the scripture itself, because [the Self] moves through its own abodes such as the heart and so forth. (203)

It has been stated that the scriptural mention of a fruit [of knowledge] does not intend to be a praise of the Self, because that would entail the fallacies of discarding what is heard [in scripture] and imagining what is not heard. Now, it might be argued that since there is a contradiction with perception—such as the experience "I am suffering"—the scriptural mention of the fruit cannot intend the destruction of grief and so forth for the Self. To this, he replies: "Not so. Is the contradiction between perception and scripture due to their having different objects, or due to their having the same object? Regarding these two options, considering the first to lead to over-extension (*atiprasañjita*), he addresses the second: "Not so. Not.
For their object is one and the same, since they are established as having the qualified nature as their object; therefore, there is no contradiction between the two—this is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection—"The Self, characterized by attributes such as agency, is the object of the notion of 'I'; how then can the perception and the Śruti have different objects?"—he says:

"By the Śruti. By stating the movement through the three stations, [the Śruti] indicates the Witness of those stations and their presiding deities as being distinct from them, which are subject to appearance and disappearance.

Having stated that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) has the nature of the experience of eternal bliss, the Veda declares the absence of suffering and other states dependent upon its connection with the three conditions (*avasthātraya*), precisely because that self is unrelated to them.

Therefore, since the resolution of the contradiction between perception and scripture—based on their having different objects—is stated by the scripture itself, there is no room for suspicion of contradiction therein. This is the meaning. || 203 ||
By her who spoke many times with unattached words, proclaiming the state of non-attachment.
I consider all this that has been spoken by you to be like a kingdom of dreams.

He states the purport of the scripture regarding the teaching on the Self as previously described: "In many ways" (*bahuśaḥ*). Having established that the scriptural mention of results (*phalaśruti*) is intended to convey the result according to the method already stated, he takes up the objection formulated by you, which was based on mere imagination: "A kingdom of the mind" (*manorājya*). By the word "this" (*etat*), he refers to Brahman, which is exclusively composed of consciousness and bliss; superimposed upon it are agency and so forth, and the absolute destruction of those is the fruit of knowledge, which is itself known through the direct perception of the wise.
Thus he says: || 204 ||
I do not believe [in them], because the fruit is directly perceived through knowledge.
If, even from a statement heard, a fruitful understanding does not arise, [then one must seek another means].
This very point which has been stated by you might be suspected at that time.

The reason for this is "no. The sense is that this direct perception (pratyakṣa) lacks authority regarding the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā-phala*), because it is sublated by the non-apprehension of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*). He refutes the objection that the statement "direct perception is the fruit of knowledge" is merely a fanciful notion by saying "from what is heard" (*śrutāt*). If even for a qualified person (*adhikārin*) knowledge accompanied by its fruit did not arise from the heard sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), then your suspicion might be justified; but this is not the case.

For it is a logical principle that the Veda generates valid knowledge for those who are qualified; therefore, since verbal cognition is possible for such a person, there exists its fruit, namely liberation (*mokṣa*).

The realization of eternal liberation arises from the [great] sentence, and not from anything else.
The cognition of the meaning of a sentence is also preceded by the recollection of the meanings of the individual words. (18/190) [Verse 206]

Having stated that knowledge arises for the qualified seeker from the heard sentence, [the author] raises the doubt that such cognition might occur even without that [sentence], through other means of knowledge alone; he replies, "It is not so," because the reality (vastu) is unfit for other means of knowledge, stating the word "eternal" (nitya). Now, one might object: "Even a sentence may not produce knowledge regarding the aforementioned object, since it would follow that such knowledge would arise for everyone who has merely heard the sentence. Anticipating this, he addresses the [role of the] words...

He states that for those whose minds are devoid of the purity of meaning, even if they hear the words, those words are as ineffective as singing to the deaf; thus he says: "Of the sentence-meaning... (verse 206).
“By means of positive and negative concomitance, the meaning of a word is certainly remembered.”
In this way, one realizes the self to be free from suffering and inactive. || 207 ||
From such statements as "together with the gods," the valid cognition [of the Self] becomes even more manifest.
Just as from the statement "You are the tenth," [the identity is realized], so it is with respect to the inner self.

(*sadeva*) is not a means of valid knowledge regarding the reality-in-itself, because it is a sentence, like an injunctive sentence; its lack of authority therein consists either in its failure to produce certainty, or in its having a defective causal complex, or in its subject matter being sublated by another means of knowledge, or in its failing to generate immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge. Among these, he refutes the first [alternative] by appealing to the contradiction with experience, stating "Valid knowledge" (*pramā*). As for the reason of being a sentence—
He states that there is no uncertainty: "You are the tenth. || 207 || 208 ||
Because there exists the possibility of doubt regarding non-perception, and because there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition.
And this he will explain with effort by means of arguments established in the world. || 209 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "amāptatva" (unauthoritativeness). Since there is no room for the suspicion of a defective causal complex (*duṣṭasāmagrī*) in the Veda—which is not of human origin—here too, unauthoritativeness, which consists in the presence of a defective causal complex, cannot even be suspected; this is the meaning. He responds to the third [position] with "māntaraiśca" (and by other means of knowledge).

There can be no suspicion of contradiction between two [means of knowledge] that are established as having distinct specific natures as their objects; how then could the Veda have its object sublated by perception and the other [means of knowledge]?

This is the meaning. He refutes the fourth [position] with the words "he will say. For a means of knowledge (*māna*) produces a cognition of an object exactly as that object is; otherwise, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) would be impossible.

Thus, in the case of something remote (*parokṣa*), it must produce a remote cognition, and in the case of something immediate (*aparokṣa*), an immediate cognition, in accordance with the means of knowledge. Furthermore, since the Self is eternally immediate according to such scriptural texts as "That which is manifest," the sentence must produce an immediate cognition regarding It. Such is the worldly [view].
The meaning is that the author of the Bhāṣya will state that, by relying on the reasoning of established proof, immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge arises from that statement. || 209 ||
Then, by the removal of the fourfold pride, the fruit of direct knowledge [arises] from that.
