(211) [18.174] In response to the inquiry, "How will he speak? the author says: "Four-footed," etc. Regarding the cognition which has four feet—namely, word, reasoning, enumeration, and the self—some maintain that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) does not arise from the word; in the context of refuting that view, [the author states] from that sentence...

The meaning is that the author will state that direct valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). Now, one might object: "Valid cognition makes known what was previously unknown;

however, the Self is not unknown because it is of the nature of immediate consciousness (*aparokṣasaṃvit*); therefore, the Self would not be established by the authority of the Veda. Anticipating this objection, he explains the previously mentioned illustration with the words, "He does not know [it]. Just as, in reality, the tenth boy [does not know] himself, thinking, "I am Maitra, the son of so-and-so,"...

The meaning is this: although he perceives directly through his own consciousness that there are other young students (*māṇavaka*) who are about to be enumerated, his intellect is robbed of its capacity to count the ninth student; thus, without the statement "you are the tenth," he does not know "I am the tenth," due to the presence of ignorance which obstructs the realization of reality (*tattva*). || 210 || 211 || dū~.b1 ১18 (500)
"Even one who has cast off duality [is thus], without [the realization] beginning with 'That Thou Art' (tattvamasi)..."

"Or [he does not know] himself as one with the body, due to non-awakening from delusion. (212) || 18 || 115 || Thus he elaborates upon the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*) beginning with "evam" and so forth. Regarding the word "apaviddha": therefore, because the Self, though made directly manifest in its general aspect, remains unknown in its specific details, it follows that the Self has the Veda as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the implied sense. Now, [one might object]: for the tenth person, there is knowledge of his own subject...

The state of possessing existence (*bhāvavattva*) is [the nature of] ignorance; however, for the Self, which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), such ignorance is not tenable. Therefore, how could there be the authority of the Veda with respect to it? To this he says: "The inner" (*pratyak*). Delusion (*moha*) regarding the Self and that which has the Self as its locus is "inner delusion" (*pratyamoha*); because it is to be dispelled by knowledge (*vidyā*), it is itself non-awakening (*aprabodha*). Thus, the syntactical connection is: "Therefore, this [Self] does not know itself. For ignorance is certainly not the state of possessing an absence of knowledge of oneself.

Indeed, that which is the object of ignorance is itself ignorance; it is not the mere absence of knowledge, because it is the cause of the world’s delusion. Furthermore, this ignorance, being distinct from a simple absence, is experienced within the self as "I do not know myself. Therefore, the intention is that it is logical for the self to be the subject of Vedic authority.
However, if the reading is *pratipadaṃ bādhata iti* ("it sublates at every step"), then it serves as the reason for the statement "one does not know [the self]. || 212 ||
By the words "it exists in the assembly" and so forth, his desire to know is firmly severed.
The realization [of Brahman] would be inward through the sublation of the ignorance regarding the inward Self.

(213) Having raised the objection that what is desired to be known must be conveyed by words, whereas the Self— being immediate— is not such [an object], and therefore cannot be expressed by words, he says:

Regarding the term *bubhutsate*: although the Self is by nature immediate consciousness and eternal bliss, it still desires to know itself. This is because, for one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), although the Self is seen in a general way throughout the various Upanishads (*prativedānta*), it is not seen in its specific detail. Therefore, the meaning is that through a sentence which removes such expectancy, there must indeed arise an uncontradicted and non-doubtful realization of the Self. Now, [an objection]: does not a statement such as "Being, etc. (*sadādi-vākya*) take as its object a Self that is unknown?

This is incorrect, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that ignorance itself would have that [Self] as its object. For when one who possesses a staff is being brought, the staff is not left behind.

To this he replies: "The inner" (*pratyak*). The intended meaning is that when the Self is indicated through the sublation of the ignorance that characterizes it, the knowledge arising from the sentence is what is desired; therefore, ignorance is not the object of that knowledge. || 293 ||

The renunciation of all actions without exception is for the sake of generating the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence.
Because it provides assistance from a distance, it is fit to serve as an auxiliary to that [primary factor]. || 214 ||

[Objection: But surely, by stating that for one who has purified the meanings of the words and desires to know the meaning of the sentence, the cognition of that [sentence-meaning] arises from the sentence, you have disregarded the fact that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is an auxiliary means to knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus, the proposition that "its abandonment is for the sake of attaining Brahman" would be abandoned; to this, he replies with the words "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*). He states the reason why renunciation serves as an auxiliary to the means of knowledge, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), etc., with the words "of that" (*tasya*). It is prescribed—
The meaning is that, like tranquility (śama) and the other [disciplines], renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is an auxiliary factor that directly assists knowledge (jñāna). || 214 ||
For renunciation alone is indeed the supreme means for the liberation of all.
For that which is to be known must indeed be abandoned by the renouncer, [revealing] the supreme state that is within oneself.
(215) [The author] states the reason for its being the most proximate means: "Renunciation" (tyāga). By the word *mokṣa*, its cause—knowledge—is indicated.
The term "supreme" (*uttama*) expresses its proximity. Why is the renunciation of all actions a proximate means toward knowledge, rather than [other] actions?

One might ask: why could those very [actions] not be the causes for that? To this he replies: "abandoning. For one who performs actions while thinking "I am the doer" and "I am the enjoyer" is not capable of perceiving the Self as devoid of connection with action and so forth; the point is that the two are contradictory.
"Peaceful and self-controlled," and likewise, preceded by the renunciation of everything.
Śruti itself has declared the means for the self-knowledge [of the Self]. || 216 ||

He shows the agreement with the scripture that will be cited regarding the fact that the renunciation of action is the cause of knowledge, beginning with the word "tranquil" (*śānta*). In that context, by first stating the abandonment of obligatory and occasional rites through the term "ceased" (*uparata*), the scripture—teaching that one should perceive the Self preceded by that [abandonment]—has itself declared the renunciation of action to be the means for that [knowledge]. This is because, from its association with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, there arises the conviction that cessation is a means to knowledge.

The meaning is that, because the hearing [of the injunction] has ceased, this is intended as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) regarding renunciation as a means to knowledge, just like the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*) and so forth. || 216 ||
Yoga is characterized by active engagement; knowledge is characterized by renunciation.
Therefore, placing knowledge at the forefront, the wise person should renounce in this world.

(217) 2)4) Regarding that very point, he states another passage beginning with "pravṛtti. That by which one is joined is *yoga*, namely action (*karman*), for by means of it a person becomes connected to its fruit.

This also...

Having inferred the end [of the body], and having completely burnt away ignorance with the fire of knowledge—once the obstacles have been removed at that conclusion—one may attain that supreme state of the Self, which consists of the oneness of consciousness, bliss, and existence, and is unlimited; thus he says: "Having slain... Thus, preceded by the renunciation of everything, [one should understand] truth and falsehood.

Regarding its being a means to knowledge, he cites another Smṛti passage: "Having abandoned truth and untruth, pleasure and pain, as well as this world and the next, one should seek the Self. The word "tathā" (likewise) serves to indicate a conjunction. [This is because] the meaning of the Śruti is otherwise untenable...

Not one who has not desisted from misconduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed.

Now, having begun with "the renunciation of optional rites," [it is said]: "But the renunciation of obligatory action is not possible.

By saying this,

the Blessed One [Śaṅkara] indicates that even when optional rites (*kāmya*) are abandoned, the abandonment of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is not sanctioned; and thus, regarding the abandonment of optional rites—

Anticipating the objection that although knowledge is the cause [of liberation], the abandonment of the eternal [rites] is not its cause, he cites another scriptural passage beginning with "not" (na).

One who has not desisted from *duścarita*—that is, prohibited action—is not qualified for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. One who is not tranquil—that is, one habitually engaged in the performance of optional rites (*kāmya*)—is also not qualified therein. One who is not concentrated—that is, one who has not abandoned the obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth according to the injunctions—is also not [qualified].

One who possesses such [desires] is not qualified for that [knowledge]. One whose mind is unpeaceful, whose mental activity is not withdrawn from external objects, is also not qualified for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;

being unqualified for that, and thus having not performed hearing and so forth, he does not attain the eternally liberated Self through the knowledge of the oneness of the Self—the meaning is that this is because of the absence of the cause, which is the absence of knowledge. By way of stating that those devoted to ritual action lack qualification for knowledge, [it is shown that] for one who has abandoned all activities...

The eligibility of the renunciants for that [knowledge] is shown in the subsequent passages; however, the Blessed One intended this as a praise of the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth for the sake of purification. (222)
Because of the effort made in stating the application of the recitation of the Vedas and so forth.
The mark [indicating] a difference in qualification belongs to the two sections: that of ritual action and that of spiritual knowledge. || 223 ||

[Objection: But surely, since the *vividiṣā* passage enjoins actions as a means to knowledge according to the logic of the *godohana* vessel, the one qualified for knowledge is not one who has abandoned action, but rather one who is already qualified for action; therefore, [the author] says: "Veda... [etc. When it is stated that actions are enjoined as means to knowledge, the intent of the *vividiṣā* passage is seen to be that the one qualified for action is the one qualified for knowledge. However, [this applies only] to the two sections...

The mention of "residue" (*reṣa*) implies a difference in the scope of authority (*bhinnādhikāratva*). For indeed, even for one who is authorized for the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and so forth, there is no application (*viniyoga*) of the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices in that [residual] carrying of water (*appraṇayana*), because he is not authorized for that specific act. Similarly, for one who is authorized for ritual action (*karma*) but has entered the scope of knowledge (*jñāna*), there would be no application of those rituals toward that [knowledge]. However, just as for one authorized for the carrying of water, even though he is also authorized for the New Moon sacrifice and so forth, there is an application of those [sacrifices] toward that [act], so too for one authorized for ritual action...

If it be argued that even though knowledge (*jñāna*) has its own specific qualification (*adhikāra*), those [rites] might still be employed toward it, we say no. This is because knowledge lacks a separate fruit of its own, whereas rites possess fruits; thus, through the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), they are employed toward knowledge. Therefore, the sense is that the application [of rites] mentioned in the *vividiṣā* passage indicates a difference in qualification between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*). || 223 ||
Since it is inferred from such signs as the arising of knowledge and so forth, it is merely the cause thereof.
Therefore, no distinction is perceived; thus, it is not understood that [the object] is merely an action.

[Objection: Since ritual actions are enjoined as causes for knowledge, their abandonment cannot be a cause for that [knowledge]. Indeed, the presence and absence of one and the same thing cannot both be connected as causes for a single result. To this, he says: "Knowledge... etc. From dharma (merit) come both happiness and knowledge; thus, it is understood that ritual actions produce knowledge. "Thirty purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*)" refers to their nature as *saṃskāras*. "The mind of the wise becomes indeed unimpaired, for they are purifiers" refers to their capacity to effect the purification of the mind. Thus, since action is observed through the signs of the arising of knowledge, the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), and the purification of the *saṃskāras*, its status as a mere cause with respect to knowledge is understood, but not its specific character. For there is no specific cognition that action alone is the cause of knowledge.

Furthermore, this is because it would entail the contradiction of scriptural passages and other authorities that establish renunciation (*tyāga*) as a cause for that [knowledge]. Therefore, actions are causes of knowledge by way of purification.

The meaning is that since renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is directly [the means] through its role as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, the validity of both being means is established in this distinction.
The explanation of the phrase "no distinction" is: "it is not understood that action alone [is the means]. || 224 ||
Shaven-headed, free from possessions, unattached, and always pure both outwardly and inwardly.
And the Vedic scripture states: "The wandering mendicant becomes one with Brahman. (225)

Having stated that both action and its renunciation are causes of knowledge in accordance with both types of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he cites another scriptural passage regarding the renunciation being a cause of that [knowledge]: "Muṇḍa... By the term "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*), he indicates the absence of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, just as there is an absence of a tuft of hair (*śikhā*). By the term "without possessions" (*aparigraha*), he refers to the absence of possession of houses, fields, and the like; for it is said in another scriptural passage: "Having shaved his head including the tuft, the wise man should discard the external thread. [The text continues: ...the absence of possession of houses, fields, and so forth.

Attachment to those [objects] is also possible for them; therefore, he says "detached" (*asaṅga*) in order to exclude that. He states that the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) thus described becomes fit for the direct realization of Brahman through the means of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth:

"Brahman... Now, the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), clothed in ochre, shaven-headed, possessing nothing, pure, non-injurious, subsisting on alms, [realizes] Brahman— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.*

Regarding this, the Jābāla Śruti states, "He becomes for the sake of further [growth]," and here the rule "Now, the wandering mendicant" (parivrāj) is the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) for renunciation (*pāritrājya*), while from that point onward is the injunction for its duties (*dharma-vidhi*); such is the distinction. || 229 ||
Vedic statements such as these, numbering in the tens of millions along with the Smṛtis, loudly enjoin the renunciation of all actions for the sake of knowledge. (226)

Demonstrating that the cited *śruti* and *smṛti* passages concern the renunciation of one who desires knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*), he concludes the discussion on the means of knowledge and their objects with the words "and so forth" (*ityādi*).

By the word "aloud" (*uccaiḥ*), he indicates the purport of the *śruti* and *smṛti* texts regarding the injunction for renunciation. And here, a fourfold injunction is stated because they do not deviate from one another. (226)
And as for what was said: "Without a task, no qualification can be determined."
Even this fault would not exist at all in the means of knowledge as it has been described.

By stating that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is prescribed for one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) and requires knowledge as the means to liberation—according to both Śruti and Smṛti—the difference between the two sections (kāṇḍas) regarding their respective means and so forth has been stated. Now, in order to clarify that very point by resolving all objections, he restates the objection with the words "And that which... Since there is no duty (kārya), there can be no person entitled to it (adhikārī); therefore, even for one desiring liberation, there must be [an absence of] action, because sovereignty arises from action.

The meaning is that because [the qualification] depends on that, when one approaches it, there is a unity of the means of proof and so forth. Alternatively, for the sake of establishing the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), either an action is required as the means to knowledge, or [eligibility] resides in knowledge itself; of these, he refutes the first [position] with the words "this is a defect. This defect—that there is no eligibility for the previously mentioned means of knowledge, such as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and hearing (*śravaṇa*), without an action—is not applicable here. In that regard, [it is said] "one must hear" (*śrotavya*).

This is because such effects [as liberation] are observed. Nor should it be argued that the Vedānta texts likewise have an injunction regarding an action as their primary purport; for, just as in the context of the Darśa sacrifice one avoids syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) by enjoining a set of observances for a woman in her menses, here too one might accept a syntactical split. However, since a syntactical split is inadmissible when a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is possible, there is no injunction even for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. This is because, in the absence of such an injunction, the engagement of one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) would lack a scriptural basis (*avaidhatva*).
Because it would follow that [the Vedas] are arbitrary, and because it would result in the impossibility of the first sūtra, which is intended to establish the necessity of investigating the Vedānta.
Such is the meaning. || 227 ||

"Since an examination of the qualification for the path of injunction (*vidhi*) is undertaken here..."
"But when consciousness has become the fruit, no qualification is determined.

He says "not the second" [in the verse], beginning with "vidhi" (injunction). The investigation in the treatise concerns the path of injunction—that is, its object—and the qualification therein, which is the relationship between the injunction and the person, or its cause; this is because the object of an injunction possesses unseen results (*adṛṣṭaphala*). For he will say:

"One who desires [heaven], though lacking qualification, may perform the Agnihotra and other rites; so too a Śūdra," and so forth. However, there is no consideration of qualification regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), because it is unfit for injunctions and because its fruit is directly perceived (*dṛṣṭaphala*). Therefore, the sense is that the absence of a qualified person (*adhikāryabhāva*) in the case of knowledge is not caused by the absence of an action to be performed (*kāryābhāva*). Anticipating the objection—"Granted that there is an examination of qualification in the path of injunction (*vidhimārga*); why should knowledge not also be part of that path?"—he says: "The fruit... (referring to the verse beginning with *phala-*) .

The meaning is that there is no consideration regarding eligibility for that [result], because of the inference: "The object of dispute is not something to be performed, because it is a result, like heaven. || 228 ||
For deliberation regarding eligibility is not desired with respect to a real entity.
"In reality, that [liberation] is not logically tenable, even from the perspective of the human goal itself. || 229 ||

Anticipating the counter-inference (pratyanumāna): "The subject under dispute is [an object] to be enjoined, because it is either knowledge or its cause, like that cause," he says: "adhi-kāra" etc. The sense is: "It is not so, because this [counter-inference] is equal to a fallacy (ābhāsa-samānatva) and because the limiting condition (upādhi)—namely, 'being worthy of effort'—pervades the probans. Anticipating the objection that the limiting condition might pervade the probans, he says: "vastu" etc. [This concludes the] counter-inference.

Fearing that the reason for its being a fruit might be unestablished even in the absence [of a separate result], he says: "And by itself" (*svayaṃ ca*). The nature of the Self, manifested by the intellect arising from the [Vedic] sentence, is knowledge because it destroys ignorance along with its effects; nor is that destruction something distinct from it. Since it is established in various places that "the Self alone is the removal of ignorance," the meaning is that there is no lack of proof, as knowledge itself constitutes the human goal. || 229 ||
1! That which is accepted as the fruit [of cognition] with respect to an object that is not the self (anātman) and is the thing to be cognized (prameya)—
That very experience of the Self, as it is described in the Vedāntas, is here the object of knowledge (prameya). 230.

Fearing that the capacity to remove ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like does not belong to the Self (*ātman*) as described above, he recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "by resorting to well-known means" (*prasiddhopāyasaṃśrayāt*). [The verse begins with] "In the non-Self" (*anātmani*). That very experience (*anubhūti*), which constitutes the nature of the Self and is well-known as the result (*phala*) regarding objects such as sound—objects of knowledge through perception and other means—is itself manifested in the cognition (*buddhi*) born of the [great] sentence. And thus, the cognition having the form of sound and so forth—

The meaning is that, just as the experience manifested by the supernormal power (*siddhi*) is well known to be the remover of ignorance regarding that [power], so too the experience of the Self as it truly is, manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the Self, is established as the destroyer of one's own ignorance and the like. || 230 ||
For the scripture likewise states: "Consciousness is bliss; it is indeed the Self."
The object of human purpose is indeed the object of knowledge, independent of the status of being a knower and so forth. || 231 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the Vedāntas is the Supreme, which is a single, infinite consciousness (*anantacidekatāna*), whereas the experience of sound and so forth is the fruit of a means of knowledge (*mānaphala*) and is delimited? Moreover, there can be no identity between those two, because one is delimited and the other is not; such identity is absent. To this, he says: "Consciousness" (*vijñānam*). The conscious self (*cidātmā*), conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as it possesses various modifications (*vṛtti*), enters into the state of the knower (*mātṛdaśā*); and conditioned by those respective modifications, it is the means of knowledge (*māna*).

Through the medium of its respective modifications (*vṛtti*), it attains the state of being a fruit (*phala*) as delimited by its respective objects; and through the medium of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it attains the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) as delimited by those same [objects].

As it has been stated: even in the waking state, the non-mediacy (*aparokṣatā*) of the object residing within does not differ from the internal non-mediacy of the experience resulting from valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*). [Variant reading:
*vidyate*].
[Vārtika, Vol. 1, p.

92] "Because of the manifestation of form," and so forth. And that [Brahman] is blissful knowledge, according to such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" and "Bliss is indeed the Self. Thus, [it is established that Brahman is blissful knowledge].

And its intrinsic nature, being consciousness that is independent of the status of subject (*mātṛ*) and so forth, constitutes the supreme human goal by virtue of being supreme bliss; yet, through the medium of ignorance, it assumes the state of the object of knowledge (*meyādibhāva*) in various instances. Thus, since limitation is merely imagined, there is no failure of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), because it is possible for consciousness—the essence of consciousness manifested by the intellect arising from the [great] sentence—to be the fruit. This is the intended meaning. || 231 ||
For one in whom that knowledge has arisen, it has truly arisen; it is not otherwise.
For even while remaining within the womb, it was just as it was for Vāmadeva.

Furthermore, regarding the position that there is an injunction for the knowledge of the Self, [the author] states "That knowledge... and so forth, showing that [the injunction] does not apply to its sublation, nor to its connection with a fruit, nor to the destruction of obstacles thereto; it is not the first [of these]. Just as in the case of the sage Vāmadeva—who, though lying in the womb defiled by many impurities such as urine and feces, attained perfect knowledge because he was refined by the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and other means performed in a previous birth—[knowledge arose] even while still in the womb.

For it is heard that Vāmadeva spoke thus even while still in the womb; and the text will later say, "Beholding this very thing. Nor is that [knowledge] sublated by anything; likewise, for another person as well, whose intellect is pure, the knowledge that has arisen through the power of hearing and so forth does not become otherwise. For a correct perception is never sublated by a misconception, nor is a misconception [sublated] by a correct one.
The meaning is that there exists another cognition which acts as a sublater. || 232 ||
And that [ignorance] is indeed cast off by one who is anointed with the contemplation of the hunter, just as ignorance is dispelled.
Upon the recovery of his memory, the prince's state as a hunter ceases.
Just as this is so for the ignorant self through such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), [so too is it for the wise].
When the memory of the attained identity [with the Self] arises, all ignorance, along with its effects, perishes.

He says that it is not the second [alternative], namely "that" (tacceti). The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that even without being something to be enjoined (vidheya), [the knowledge of the Self is established]. The sense is that there is indeed no injunction regarding the connection of the knowledge of the Self with the fruit of destroying ignorance of that [Self], because it is a cognition produced by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇajñāna), just like the cognition of mother-of-pearl. It is not the third [alternative].
Thus he said: "The Hunter. It is said that a certain prince, having been abandoned by his royal palace immediately upon birth, entered the forest due to the influence of portents.

He was taken as a son by a certain childless hunter and, though growing up in that man's house, spent a long time with a mind conditioned by the thought, "I am a hunter. Once, [the prince] thought: "I am not the son of a hunter; I am a prince."

When told by a trusted person, "It is you," he remembers his own status as a prince. Upon regaining that memory—"I am the king's son"—his long-held state of being a hunter ceases through the arising of the contrary memory. Similarly, for the ignorant one who, though desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), has fallen into a miserable condition while possessing attributes such as humanity superimposed by ignorance, a compassionate teacher, having perceived this, [bestows] the knowledge of the Self arising from the words he has instructed.

Through such remembrance (smṛti), ignorance in all its forms, together with its effects, perishes. Thus, for one who realizes the Self as Brahman—which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—the obstacle to the fruit of knowledge is already cast aside by that very realization; therefore, even upon the destruction of that [ignorance], there is no need for an injunction. This is the meaning. ||233||234||
Since this is so, no injunction (vidhi) can be postulated here in any way;

even if one were postulated, it would be useless because it serves no purpose here. Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the Self, an injunction is neither heard in scripture nor can it be postulated. To [refute] the first [possibility], he says: "Since... [draṣṭṛ-].
1. Three [cases] in the sense of knowledge (jñāna). 2. Ka. ‘ściraṃkā’.
[Vol. 1, page 93] 72.
Since it will be stated later that words such as "he should" (vyādi) do not possess injunctive force, there is no injunction heard in the context of the knowledge of the Self.

The meaning is that, according to the logic already stated, there is no utility for such an injunction in that context. He presents the second [objection]: "It must be inferred," on the grounds that—just as in the case of "Pūṣan has the ground flour as his portion"—an injunction, though not explicitly heard, is inferred in the knowledge of the Self; otherwise, the sentence would lack authority. To this he replies: "Not so; because there is no basis for such an inference, nor is there an impossibility of the sentence's authority, since even when [the scripture] merely makes known an existing reality, its authority is possible without an injunction."

And he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that such an assumption would be useless, with the words "it is purposeless. He states the reason for the futility of assuming an injunction regarding that [Self-knowledge] with the word "of it" (*tasya*).
The meaning is: there is no utility for an assumed injunction in the case of Self-knowledge, because activity and cessation are impossible therein; therefore, the assumption of it is vain. || 235 ||

The fruit of an injunction consists of origination, acquisition, refinement, or modification; liberation is distinct from all these, and therefore an injunction is useless here [in the case of liberation]. (236) 17.50

Now, [the author] says "origination" (*utpatti*) to address the objection that a rule (*vidhi*) imagined within knowledge has no utility for liberation. The meaning is that it is well known that there are only four kinds of fruits of action: the origination of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is the fruit of the rule for kneading; the acquisition of milk, which is the fruit of the rule for milking; the consecration of the mortar and other implements, which is the fruit of the rule for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*); and the modification of rice and other grains, which is the fruit of the rule for threshing (*avaghāta*). These are the fruits of action.

Even though action (*karman*) is of four kinds, how is it that the status of liberation (*mukti*) as being produced by an injunction (*naiyogikatva*) is refuted? To this, he says: "Liberation... First of all, liberation is neither an origination nor something to be produced, because it is not an effect (*akriyatva*) and because it is beginningless (*anāditva*). Nor is it an attainment or something to be attained, because it is not a relation (*asaṃbandhatva*) and because its essential nature is already established (*prāptasvarūpatva*). Nor is it a purification (*saṃskāra*) or something to be purified, because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and because no excellence can be imparted to it (*anādheyātiśayatva*).

Nor is liberation a modification (*vikāra*) or something to be modified (*vikārya*), because it is not an effect and because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). Therefore, the meaning is that liberation is not the fruit of an injunction.
He states the consequence of its not being such a fruit with the words "by that" (*tena*). Here, "here" (*iha*) refers to knowledge. || 236 ||
Because its perfect realization does not depend on anything else, and because the reality of the self is free from ignorance.
There is neither the state of being an action nor the state of being a result, nor even the nature of an agent.

Having raised the objection that while an injunction is impossible regarding knowledge because Brahman is not subordinate to it, an injunction for meditation (*upāsti*) is possible since Brahman can be subordinate to it, [the author] says:

"Not other" (*ananya*). For the injunction for the meditation on Brahman is not a subordinate part [of anything else], because it is difficult to establish in Brahman any of the characteristics that serve as the basis for being subordinate, such as being a ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth. To begin with, Brahman does not possess the nature of an action (*kriyātva*), which consists in having its own existence dependent upon causal factors (*kāraka*), since its establishment is not dependent on anything else.

Nor does Brahman possess the status of being an agent residing in one who possesses ignorance, because it is free from ignorance; nor does it possess the status of being a fruit, because it lacks the quality of being produced by an action. Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman cannot even be a subordinate element to an injunction for meditation (upāsanā-vidhi). || 237 ||
Therefore, the absence of an injunction here is not a defect in any way whatsoever.
This is an excellent ornament, praised in the Vedāntas. || 238 ||
Thinking that the Vedāntas lack authority because they do not serve as supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*), some maintain that "the Vedāntas are barren soil for the Veda.

To those, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is this: since Brahman is established by the authority of the Vedāntas even without an injunction—just like the connection between the fruit and the riverbank—the absence of an injunction therein is not a cause for their lack of authority. It is not merely that the absence of an injunction in them [renders them unauthoritative]...

He states that there is both truthfulness and the status of being a cause for validity by saying, "It is an ornament. The sense is this: since the validity of the Vedāntas is impossible with respect to Brahman—which is pure and established only through a positive injunction—therefore, in the absence of such a [positive] entity, praise is appropriate for the sake of awakening one to the Self as Brahman, which is the goal of human life. || 238 ||
"I am enjoined by the injunctions, and likewise, I am Brahman."
Because they are mutually contradictory, two [opposites] cannot exist together in one place at one time. (239)

Furthermore, regarding injunctions for knowledge and so forth, neither the one who already knows (vidvān) nor the one who desires to know (vividiṣu) can be the person to be enjoined; thus he says: "By means of the injunctions... (verse 239).
For a master is certainly not appointed by a servant, just as a master is not appointed by another master.
He is indeed to be awakened, like a sleeping king by bards. || 240 ||

He says "not the second" [meaning the master], explaining: "The master. Even one who desires to know (the Self) is the master of the Veda because he has transcended the path of worldly existence; therefore, he is not impelled by it. Indeed, a master is not commissioned by his servant like a servant is by a master; rather, just as a sleeping king is awakened by bards and others who perceive that the time for action is passing, so too [is the Self awakened] through the realization of being the witness of the body and the like, and the cause of the world.

The meaning is that he [the seeker] is to be awakened by the Veda with the words "You are indeed Brahman"; therefore, because there is no one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), there is no injunction in the Vedāntas.

Alternatively, having established in the first half-verse the absence of the status of being enjoined for the knower (*vidvas*), the second half-verse establishes the non-enjoinability of the seeker of knowledge (*vividiṣu*). And it is considered that although such a person may be enjoined to activities like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, they do not possess that same status regarding [the attainment of] knowledge itself. || 240 ||
Let the definition of dharma as being characterized by injunction (codanā) and so forth be understood as applying to dharma alone.
Because the proposition concerns dharma alone, Brahman is not what is being accepted [as the subject]. || 241 ||

But surely, even if Brahman is not subordinate to injunction (*vidhi*) according to the investigation of the Vedānta, it might still be subordinate to injunction upon examining the context of the sūtras of the Karma-mīmāṃsā; for that [system] is engaged under the condition of being merely the meaning of the Veda, and its nature is defined by *codanā* (Vedic injunction).

He explains: Since it is established that the word *codanā* signifies an injunction—that is, "an injunction is a statement that impels one toward action"—it follows that Brahman, as the subject matter (*vedārtha*) of the Veda, must also be touched by injunctions. To this he replies with the word "codanā. He states the reason why being "established by the authority of injunction" (*vidhipramāṇakatva*), "being distinct" (*bhinnatva*), and so forth apply only to *dharma* and not to Brahman, with the words "of dharma": [it applies] only to *dharma*, which is a single portion of the Veda's subject matter.

The meaning is: because it has been proposed in this *sūtra* as the subject of investigation. Now, one might object: for one who has completed the study of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*) and is thus in doubt—wondering whether the meaning understood from the *svādhyāya* is sublated or not—the *sūtra* "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) was composed for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion through logic (*nyāya*).

Thus, four points are established: [the subject matter, the purpose, the connection, and] the independent qualification as a subsidiary. Among these, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which consists of the formulation of logical principles (*nyāya*) that serve as the means for investigating the meaning of the Veda. Regarding this, there is the doubt: "Is it not to be commenced, or is it to be commenced? In this regard, [the prima facie view is: "The study of one's own Veda..."

Since the injunction "one should study" prescribes the act of study, and because of the Vedic revelation (Śruti) stating, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age and teach him," as well as the Smṛti texts such as, "But he who, having initiated a disciple... and so forth, the purpose of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is the fulfillment of the qualification for the injunction regarding the office of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*), which has initiation as its constituent part; and since the *svādhyāya* exists for that purpose, if it were directed toward something else, its own literal meaning would not be intended. Thus, due to the absence of a subject matter and other necessary factors, [the passage in question lacks authority].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this treatise is not useless. Even though the act of study is prompted by the injunction to teach—which has initiation (*upanayana*) as its constituent element—the mere accomplishment of that teaching is not the fruit [of study], because it resides in another person and is thus extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). On the other hand, the knowledge of the meaning, although occurring subsequent to the study, is [intrinsic]. 10. ...[the intrinsic nature]... of the study. Therefore, the knowledge of the meaning is the fruit of the injunction to study. And since that [knowledge of the meaning] is the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*niḥśreyasa*), the treatise is not useless. However, in the case of the injunction to sacrifice, the mere performance of the ritual action is the fruit; the attainment of heaven is merely a secondary result (*guṇaphala*). This is because the attainment of heaven is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is therefore extrinsic, whereas the completion of the ritual action is intrinsic. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even if the knowledge of the meaning were the primary fruit of the injunction to study, it would still be necessary to explain how that [knowledge] leads to the supreme human goal. For one might object: "Even if the knowledge of the meaning is the fruit of the injunction to study, why should that lead to the supreme human goal? It is possible that the knowledge of the meaning might lead to some other fruit. To this, we reply: No, because the knowledge of the meaning is the means for attaining the supreme human goal. How so? Because the supreme human goal is attained through the practice of dharma and adharma, which are understood by means of that [knowledge of the meaning]. Therefore, regarding the *svādhyāya* (one's own Veda)...

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the treatise (*śāstra*) must be commenced because it has the intended subject matter and because it possesses the nature of a subject, object, and so forth. Thus, since the inquiry proceeds under the condition of being the meaning of the Veda, and since Brahman is also the meaning of the Veda, one might think that Brahman is declared as the object of inquiry therein; to this he says "not so" (*na tu*). The declaration of Brahman as the object of inquiry is not accepted here, because it would contradict the word "dharma. This is the meaning. (249)

for one who is qualified for the knowledge of ritual action is also qualified for the injunction to study the Veda, and thus, immediately after studying the entire Veda, one who desires heaven and other such fruits engages in the inquiry into ritual action.

Because one who desires liberation engages in the inquiry into Brahman, it follows by the force of the qualification "dharma" that the duty of inquiry applies specifically to that which is delimited by being a portion of the Veda's meaning; for this very reason, the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra) used the word "dharma" alone throughout the commentary on the first Sūtra, in such passages as "Dharma is to be desired to be known" and "one should wish to know Dharma. It is understood that [the Upanishads] are supplementary to the ritual injunctions (*vidhiśeṣatva*), because they are declared as the object to be known (*vijijñāsyatva*) within the form of the meaning of the Veda. Regarding this, four points have been set forth as the means of knowledge: the contact of the word with its meaning, and the fact that the meaning consists solely of what is to be done (*kārya*). In this context, the subject matter is the meaning of the Veda;

and when the doubt arises as to whether it is of an established nature (*siddharūpa*) or exclusively of the nature of what is to be done (*kāryarūpa*), since an established meaning is observed in passages such as "Brahman is truth, consciousness, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*), [the opponent argues that the Upanishads are not supplementary to injunctions].

Furthermore, because there is no cause for the manifestation [of meaning] and because the determination of an effect is unestablished, it is possible for the first acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) to occur even without verbal usage, as in the case of sentences regarding established facts such as "a son is born. Moreover, since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) follows that [usage], the meaning of the Veda can indeed be of an established nature.

Thus, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), since verbal usage itself is the primary path for acquiring linguistic competency, and because in the sentence "a son is born" there is a cause for joy known as that birth—

Because the state of being a communicator is difficult to ascertain, because many causes for joy are possible, and because the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) is inapplicable; and because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which is observed to have a specific object as its domain, is capable of generating the postulation of a [linguistic] capacity (*śakti*); and because that [usage] is never deviant from the effect [of understanding]; and because the grasp of that capacity occurs therein through the methods of presence and absence (*āvāpodvāpa*), whereby it is established in the specific [instance]; and because intention (*tātparya*) follows the capacity—words that touch upon the object [are thus established].

Because the accomplishment of action alone [is required], even in those sentences where no visible effect is perceived, one of the two—either *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis) or *lakṣaṇā* (indication)—is necessarily required; therefore, since the Vedāntas also have action as their purport by being, in some way or another, subordinate to injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the Veda consists solely in the form of action. [The opponent argues: "In that case, since Brahman is the subject matter of the Veda, it too must enter into the domain of injunction as a subordinate element of the 'thing-to-be-done' (kārya). To this, he replies with the words "codanā" (injunction). The meaning of the Sūtra is: "Dharma is that beneficial object, distinct from [acts such as] the Śyena sacrifice and the like, which is characterized by—that is, known through—an injunction (*codanā*), which is a statement that impels one to action. In this context, by means of the two qualifiers "injunction" and "dharma," the nature of only a portion of the Vedic subject matter is established through both scripture (*śruti*) and logical implication (*artha*).

The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are shown [here]. Otherwise, the sūtra would have been "the Veda is the means of valid cognition; the meaning of the Veda [is to be investigated]," and the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*)—which serves to exclude [prohibitions such as] the Śyena sacrifice—would be inappropriate, since that too is the meaning of the Veda. As they say: "In that context, an evil purpose might be stated as Dharma; it is for this reason that the word 'meaning' is included. Therefore, the intention is that the second sūtra is not a definition of Brahman. Now, as for the section concerning "those [words] which have become [parts of a compound]" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*)...

By logical reasoning, Brahman must be understood as being untouched by injunctions (*vidhi*). To explain: Vedic sentences are the subject matter. There arises a doubt as to whether they depend on other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) or are independent of them. In this regard, although the meaning of a sentence is understood from it in the linguistic usage of elders, in the case of the Veda, the sentence constitutes a distinct collection [of words] whose relationship with its meaning has not been previously grasped; and in the event of postulating such a relationship—

Having raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Vedic sentences lack authority because a convention must be accepted and because they depend upon other means of knowledge, [the author replies]:

since words and their meanings are not different in the world and in the Veda, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in the Veda is likewise rooted in worldly linguistic usage; and since a sentence consists of words whose capacities have been ascertained as residing in relation to what is to be accomplished (*kāryānvita*), and which delimit a specific meaning, the Vedic sentences—being independent of convention—[possess authority].

It has been established as a settled conclusion that because sentences have the capacity to produce cognition of their own meaning, those [Vedic] texts which are not of human origin possess authority through being independent. Therefore, since a sentence can convey Brahman even by means of its connection with an action well-known in the world, it follows that it is a subordinate part of an injunction due to its relation to action;

to this, he says "no," with the words: *tadbhūtānām* (of those [words] existing therein). *Tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samāmnāyo 'rthasya tannimittatvāt* (Of those [words] existing therein, there is a traditional recitation for the sake of action, because the meaning [of the whole] is caused by that).

Regarding those word-meanings (*padārtha*), there is a recitation (*samāmnāya*)—that is, an utterance as a sentence formed by the coming together of words existing within those entities—in the form of an effect which serves as the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) for the purpose of comprehending that [sentence-meaning].
This is because the meaning of each individual word, when combined, becomes the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that it is the words themselves, with the recollection of word-meanings serving as their intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), that bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

Furthermore, Brahman does not appear here as a subordinate element of an injunction; and the sentence that establishes Brahman, even while conforming to a power already established in the world, does not require an action [to be accomplished]. For the capacity [of words] is easily grasped even with respect to an already established object; indeed, children do not fail to perceive the expressive power in sentences that produce joy, sorrow, and so forth, merely because they lack the expansion of the mouth or other such physical effects, nor do they require the superimposition of an action [to complete the sense].

Therefore, the point is that even on the basis of the *tadbhūta* section [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*], Brahman does not serve as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to an injunction. Now, according to the principle of the *arthavāda* section, Brahman might be a subordinate element to an injunction. To explain: injunctions associated with *arthavādas* such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) are the subject matter. The doubt is whether these are non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) or authoritative (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, since the meaning of the *arthavāda*, such as Rudra’s weeping, is not something to be accomplished...

Because it lacks connection with the action as its object, its manner of performance, or its result, and because it is not a qualification of the person—unlike "living" [which qualifies the agent]—and because it is not a qualification of the one to be enjoined, there is no established connection as a cause here, unlike the case where "dirtiness" serves as the cause for the duty to bathe in the statement "one who is dirty should bathe. Furthermore, if it were connected by way of praise (*stuti*), there would be the consequence of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and since the duty is understood from the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself, the commencement of the action is thereby established.

In the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—that because there is no need for praise, and since [the Veda] is connected as a cause, all injunctive statements (*codanā*) joined with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack authority due to their teaching of effects dependent on that [cause]—it is argued that all words possess authority by having the "thing to be done" (*kārya*) as their purport; that the injunctive word directly denotes that [thing to be done]; that the other parts [of the injunction] have that as their purport by denoting their own meanings as connected to it; and that the meaning of the explanatory passage serves as a reason for the unprecedented thing to be done (*apūrvakārya*) mentioned in the injunctive statement.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, regarding the connection [of the explanatory passages]:

since there is no evidence for a syntactical relation (*anvaya*) [between the injunction and the explanatory passage], and because the words of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are useful for the comprehension of the action (*kārya*) by means of imparting praise, the cognition of that [action] is established from the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself when it is joined with the explanatory passage;

thus, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the authority of all injunctions is valid when accompanied by their explanatory passages, just like the case of the "red-clothed" (*raktapaṭa*) [ascetics].

Therefore, since the authority of sentences with accomplished meanings (siddhārthavākya) is established through their being syntactically one with injunctions (vidhi), and since the Vedāntas also possess authority precisely by virtue of being syntactically one with those [injunctions], it follows that Brahman must be subordinate to injunction; to this, he replies: "Of the sacred tradition" (āmnāyasya). For there, having raised the doubt regarding the lack of authority for injunctions accompanied by explanatory passages (arthavāda), [the author] establishes that because the arthavādas are syntactically one with the injunctive statements (vidhyuddeśa) by way of being eulogistic, they are connected to them.

It is established that the authority of injunctive statements [is based on their connection to an action]. However, the Vedāntas—having legs that have leapt over the context of injunctions—are purposeful through the mere knowledge of their own meaning and do not require syntactic unity with an injunction. Therefore, the point is that Brahman is not a subordinate element of an injunction even by virtue of the *arthavāda* section. || 242 ||
Words denoting action have the sense of becoming as their meaning; therefore, from them, an activity is understood.
Thus, in this matter concerning human conduct, the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī is to be understood.

But is it not the case that, according to the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, Brahman is subordinate to an injunction? For instance, in such passages as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," there arises the doubt: do each of the words contained therein individually assist the *niyoga* (the mandate), or is only one word in the sentence the assistant of the *niyoga* while the others serve its purpose?

In this doubt, since all word-meanings are for the sake of the action (*kārya*), and since a direct connection with it is possible, a mediated (indirect) connection is improper; thus, [it is seen that...]

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that because mutual connection is established by general rule (*pāṇikatvāt*), there is an imparting of the injunction (*niyoga*) for every word—[the following is argued]: if there were an imparting of the injunction for every word, the connection between the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) as they are observed would be destroyed; furthermore, since there would be a plurality of things to be accomplished (*kāryabheda*), the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanīnyāya*) would not apply. Consequently, when the application (*viniyoga*) is destroyed, the injunction dependent upon it is also destroyed. Therefore, in a single sentence, only one word imparts the injunction, while the others serve that purpose. This is the [conclusion regarding] each word (*pratipadādhi-*).

When the instrument (karaṇa) is established therein, a doubt arises as to whether words denoting substances (dravya) and qualities (guṇa) also convey that [instrumentality], or whether it belongs only to words denoting action (bhāva). Since no specific distinction is perceived and there is no contradiction in their application, a state of uncertainty prevails. Anticipating the objection that "if this [scripture] possesses purposefulness, my own position is established," he says: "Karma... Here, the phrase "in this regard" refers to the position that the soul perishes.

The sense is that for the proponent of the destruction of the living soul (jīvanāśavādin), since knowledge and action would be rendered useless, the undertaking of the scripture for the sake of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) would be unestablished. || 263 ||
If this cyclic existence were real, it could not be produced by ignorance alone.
The fault of the destruction of its own nature would occur even in a single part, as before.

Furthermore, regarding the soul (*jīva*), which is a modification of Brahman, its bondage must be either inherent or produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). To this, he first replies with the words "Not at all. If this cycle of transmigration were real, it could not be removed by the knowledge of Brahman, because it would lack the nature of being produced by ignorance; for a real entity cannot be sublated by knowledge, since it is a reality, just like the Self (*ātman*). Nor do ritual actions (*karma*) remove bondage, because they are themselves the cause of that bondage. Therefore...

The meaning is that knowledge and action would be rendered useless. Even if the individual soul (*jīva*) is considered a single part of Brahman, one must raise the same alternatives as before; regarding the first alternative, he states the defect: "In its own nature," etc.
Even if the individual soul is accepted as a single part of Brahman, if its bondage does not perish because it is a real entity (*vastu*), then there is no liberation.

If it were to perish, then the soul characterized by that [bondage] would perish, and thus—just as in the case of the theory of modification (*vikārapakṣa*)—knowledge and the rest would again be useless. This is the meaning. || 264 ||
But when transmigratory existence is superimposed by ignorance, it does not exist in reality.
In the case of a modification as well as a part, it is exactly as previously stated.
This position should be carried out by us as well, for it is approved by us. || 266 ||

He accepts the position that bondage is due to ignorance (*avidyā*) in both systems. Regarding the phrase "But when": since in both views it is accepted that being a modification, being a part, bondage, and the state of being bound—all this is merely due to ignorance regarding the Self—then the previously mentioned position, namely that the subjects and so forth differ between the two sections (*kāṇḍas*), must also be maintained by you. Just as we [have explained] the aforementioned position...
He says, "By us," [implying] that others also should strive in the same manner as he does. || 269 || 266 ||
And because it is non-contradictory in all cases from the very beginning, no positive injunction is required here.
For at that time, all conceptual constructions—consisting of modifications, parts, and so forth—[cease].

He will accomplish all these very things in this manner, quite in vain.

And for those who maintain this position, there is no contradiction with worldly experience or the Vedas; thus he says: "All," etc. Let all proponents of liberation accept that everything, such as transmigratory existence and so forth, is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), and let them maintain that liberation arises from knowledge; nevertheless, what is established for you [the opponent] by this? To this he replies: "Not therefore," etc. Since liberation results from knowledge alone, there is no possibility of an injunction in the Vedantas due to the absence of anything to be enjoined, for liberation is not of that nature.

The meaning is that, because it has heaven as its fruit, knowledge is not dependent on a person; therefore, the Vedāntas culminate in the mere reality (vastumātra). Now, an objection: if the individual soul (jīva), having abandoned being a part of Brahman and being a modification thereof, is instead merely an undivided reality, then how do [the following scriptural passages] apply: "All beings are one foot of Him," "A portion of My very self is in the world of living beings," "A portion [of the Lord], because of the various designations," and "He generates all, the breath, and the white [light]"?
Regarding the passage of the texts, such as "The Śūnya-puruṣa is distinct" and "All these selves emerge [from Him]," he states the solution:

"For then... When there is an absence of injunctions in the Vedāntas, then all the aforementioned conceptual constructions (kalpanās), being rendered purposeless, are not tenable. When liberation results from knowledge, then the previous conceptual constructions do not possess reality; for on your [opponent's] view, liberation would be impossible.

Because they are afflicted by pain, all these [scriptures] consist of ignorance; yet it is with the intention of expressing their non-difference that the Śruti and other texts designate them as such—this is the sense. || 267 ||
Therefore, that which is complete is the supreme good; it is incomplete due to ignorance.
Therefore, it appears as something false, by means of the knowledge of the self as it truly is.
When ignorance has been utterly destroyed, only the plenary remains. || 269 ||

Now, fearing that liberation might depend upon traveling to another location—as suggested by such scriptural passages as "the light beyond heaven"—and that consequently there would be no difference between the two sections (of the Vedas) regarding the qualifications of the seeker and so forth, and that the soul's status as a part (*aṃśa*) and so on would be unavoidable, he says: "The Full.

According to such scriptural passages as "Only the Full remains" and "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," the reality that is neither excluded from nor followed by anything else is denoted by the word *brahman*.

Furthermore, because it will be stated later that Brahman is all-pervading (*pūrṇa*) and that this alone is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), as supported by such scriptural passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," liberation is not dependent upon ritual action (*karman*). Moreover, the passage beginning with "Now, when... occurs within a section concerning meditative worship (*upāsti*) and does not teach that liberation depends on traveling to another location.
This is the meaning: how, then, can the status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a part (*aṃśa*) [of Brahman] be established? How, then, does the notion of Brahman being limited arise?

Therefore, he says: "That is incomplete. Now, regarding the abiding of Brahman in its own nature (svarūpa), is it for one whose limitations have not been destroyed or for one whose limitations have been destroyed?

Not the first, because that would entail the consequence of there being no distinction between saṃsāra and liberation. In the second case, the result would be the loss of distinction between deep sleep and liberation; therefore, he says: "Hence. Liberation is the abiding of Brahman in its own nature for one whose limitations have been destroyed. [This occurs] in deep sleep and so forth.

However, even when the effect is destroyed, because the cause is not destroyed, there is no equality with liberation; therefore, it is only when the distinctions between cause and effect are destroyed by knowledge that the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is attained—this is the meaning. || 268 || 269 ||
Therefore, with respect to the supreme good, every injunction is purposeless.
Thus, that which was previously urged by you has been established through reasoning.

If it is argued that even the aforementioned *niḥśreyasa* (ultimate liberation) would be the fruit of an injunction, he says "no," namely: "it is purposeless. [In that view, it remains so.

Because Brahman is full and constitutes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), it follows that it is distinct from the fourfold fruits of ritual action; this is the sense. By the word "in every respect" (*sarvaśas*), the modes of injunction regarding origin, application, qualification, and performance are included. He concludes the absence of injunction with respect to liberation and its cause with the words "this being so. "By reasoning" (*nyāyataḥ*) means by the reasoning already stated, beginning with "But in the case of knowledge, which is the fruit," and so forth. [The term] *kāryam*...

Having concluded his own established position—that the Vedāntas are not subordinate to injunctions by refuting the claim that one cannot be qualified [for them] without such [injunctions]—and in order to clarify what was stated later as "it will be explained," he restates the very objection that has already been answered: "As for that which... He says, "In this regard," because the section on *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) does not have the Upaniṣads as its subject matter, since they are not cited therein in the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, or Ṭīkā. This was also [stated] previously.
The word "also" (api) is used to indicate that this has already been refuted. || 270 ||
For in that case, there would be a designation of the Veda by means of the designation of the Veda itself.
The fact that injunctions have action as their purpose is established; it is stated here as a supporting reason. || 271 ||

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra beginning with "Because the Veda has action as its purpose" (*kiṃcāmnāyasya kriyārthatvāt*), one might wonder: does the status of the Vedāntas as subordinate to injunctions arise from the force of the word "Veda" (*āmnāya*) itself, or rather from the force of those words within it that do not have that [action] as their meaning? Having thus raised this alternative, he refutes the first position with the word "therein" (*tatra*). That is, in that sūtra...

The meaning is that, just as in the expression "the village is burnt," the term *āmnāya* (scripture) refers only to that portion consisting of injunctions; therefore, by the force of that term, the Upaniṣads do not become subordinate to injunctions. One might object: since there is no restrictive factor for the word *āmnāya* in the Bhāṣya and other texts—where it is stated that "reciters would have recited sentences so that one might know how an action is to be performed"—how can it be said that it refers only to a single part? To this, he says:

Regarding the word "vidhi" (injunction): in the *Codanāsūtra*, it was established that injunctive sentences have action as their purpose, not the Veda in its entirety, because that would contradict the meaning of the terms *codanā* and *dharma* and would result in a break in the context. Therefore, in this present section (*adhikaraṇa*), that very point is stated as the reason for the meaninglessness of those sentences that do not have action as their purpose.

Consequently, it is correct that the term *āmnāya* (Veda) refers here only to injunctions; otherwise, the reason—that they have action as their purpose—would be partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddhi*).

Nor is it the case that injunctions (*vidhi*) have action as their sole purpose; for if those [passages] not having action as their purpose were to be meaningless, that would be a non-concomitant reason (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, because injunctions have the performance of a task (*kārya*) as their purpose, it must be stated that even those situated within the context of such injunctions have that same purpose. Otherwise, since they would be meaningless, the injunctions associated with them would also lack utility—this is indeed the intended prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, because the word "Veda" (*āmnāya*) refers only to a portion of it, it does not [apply to the entire Veda].
The sense is that the Vedāntas are subordinate to injunctions. || 279 ||
Of those [words] situated in the section on ritual action (kriyāprakaraṇa), which exist as supplements to injunctions (vidhiśeṣa).

That statement [of yours] leads to the futility of those words whose meaning is not an action. (272)

He states the second [reason] with the word "action" (*kriyā*). Since words situated within the context of ritual action—which, by the course of fate, have action as their purpose, yet lack such a manifestation on the surface—are designated here by the term "words not having that meaning" (*atadartha*), this Sūtra aims to declare the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the injunctive portion associated with them, by way of stating that they are devoid of a fruitful object. Therefore, even by the force of the word "not having that meaning" (*atadartha*) contained therein, the Upaniṣads are not [included].
The meaning is that it is a subordinate element of the ritual injunction. || 272 ||
But it is not logical for the Upanishads [to have a separate purpose], since their independence is possible.
By the very same reasoning stated previously, it does not follow that [the Veda] is a subordinate element of those injunctions. || 273 ||

[The opponent] objects: "Since there is no difference in their lack of purposeful action (*akriyārthatva*), why was it not stated in the Sūtra that these [mantras] are also useless, like the passage 'He wept' (*so 'rodīt*) and so forth? [To this, the author] replies: "Because of the absence of [any other] option... [Vol. 1, p.

Regarding the term *pārthagarthya*: the state of having a separate meaning is *pārthagarthya*; because that is possible, there is no pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in the Upaniṣads—this is the sense.

[The author] refutes the unestablished reason (*hetvasiddhi*). Regarding the word "prior" (*pūrva*): because it is based on scripture (*śrauta*) and because it is directly perceived by the wise (*vidvat-pratyakṣa*), the fruit resulting from the sentence (*vākyīya-phala*) is difficult to deny; such is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Since the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*) can be explained in another way as well, for that reason, the Upaniṣads do not constitute an injunction (*vidhi*).
He concludes with the word "chateti": "Not from this," [verse 273].
As for what was also urged, namely, "because of the syntactical unity with the injunction," [that too is refuted].
Let that [non-existence] also belong to those very things, because it is enjoined as being purposeless for them. (274)

[The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that, according to the Siddhānta-sūtra *vidhinā* [JS 1.2.7], the Upaniṣads are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhiśeṣatva*)? Even if no action or anything connected to an action is understood from them, they are nonetheless authoritative because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*). To this he replies "no," stating *vidhinā tu*. This refers to those sentences situated within the context of ritual action for which futility has been suspected on the grounds that they do not have action as their purpose.

It has been stated that these [Arthavādas] possess purposefulness because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions for the sake of praising the deities and so forth required by those very injunctions; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the author of the Sūtras being unreliable, since the question and answer would lack a common purpose. Furthermore, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), while asserting that Arthavādas such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" form a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," thereby excludes the Vedānta texts situated in a different context.

[The opponent] objects: "In this way, all these passages praise or censure some object; therefore, such passages as 'Vāyu is the swiftest deity' and so forth are indeed authoritative. By saying this, [the opponent] implies that the Vedānta texts are also included. To this he replies, "Not so," with the word "tat" (that). This is because the phrases "these" and "of this kind" refer back to those very passages under discussion and their like—namely, "Vāyu is the swiftest deity"—and do not apply to the Upaniṣads.
And the meaning is that [terms] such as "that" (tyādi) are contradicted by the supplementary portions of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*). || 274 ||
But it is not [the case] because of the Vedānta statements having a perceptible purpose as their reason.
The fact that this cognition has a distinct object has already been explained at great length. // 275 //

[The opponent] objects, having forgotten what was previously stated—that because the Vedāntas lack such fruits [of action], they are subordinate to those [injunctions] due to their proximity to injunctive sentences that have fruits such as heaven, according to the maxim "that which lacks a fruit in the proximity of that which has a fruit is its subsidiary"—since such a possibility exists.
To this, he replies: "But not so. Even if those [texts] devoid of fruit, being recited in proximity to those that possess fruit, were subordinate to them, [it is not so in the case of the Vedāntas].

The meaning is as follows: according to the principle that it is not reasonable to postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) for those [texts] situated in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) which have a visible result (*dṛṣṭaphala*), how could there be a status as a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatā*) for those who are averse to an unseen heaven and so forth? One might raise the objection that the Vedāntas do not have a visible purpose, since even one who has realized the truth continues to perceive saṃsāra as before; anticipating this, he says: "Because of the cognition of that" (*tadbuddheḥ*). This means that the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence possesses a fruit distinct from the fruit of ritual action.

This has been explained in detail by the passage beginning with "not of prosperity" (nābhyudayasya). Therefore, there is no dispute regarding the independent status of the Vedāntas; rather, the meaning is that the notion of bondage persists as a residual impression even after it has been sublated, just as before. || 275 ||
And likewise, because the meaning of the Vedānta texts cannot be established otherwise.
When there is a single intended meaning, one should not assume a split in the sentence.
It is not logical that it [the Veda] is so [authorless], because it is observed [to have an author], just like sentences such as "I invoke you, O God" (devasya tvā).
