Furthermore, since the *prayāja* offerings and other such rites contribute to the fruit of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is logical that their scriptural passages constitute supplementary parts (*vākyaśeṣa*) of those [sacrificial] passages.

However, because the reality of the Self (*ātman-vastu*), which is to be known through the Vedāntas, does not contribute to ritual action, those [Vedāntic] passages do not serve as supplements to injunctions for such rites; thus he says: "For another purpose," etc. [The Vedāntas...]

The meaning is that they do not have another purpose, nor do they possess the utility of assisting a ritual action (*karma*), because such [an assistance] is untenable; thus, they cannot be subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) to a ritual injunction.

Having thus established that the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) constitute distinct sentences, the author raises an objection based on the principle that "when a single sentence is possible, a split of sentences (*vākya-bheda*) is not desired," stating "by way of being subordinate to an injunction" and so forth. [The objection begins with] "the purpose... [and continues: like the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśa* sacrifice, the two sections—

The meaning is that once the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is established through having a single fruit, it is not proper to assume a division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) on the basis of a difference in fruits. He provides an example for the unity of a sentence based on having a single purpose, stating: "because this is observed. The underlying principle is: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its purpose, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 2.1.46).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there arises the doubt as to whether the extent of the *yajus* formulas can or cannot be known. Since the extent of the *ṛc* verses is easily known through their metrical form (*chandas*) and the instruction regarding their Vedic character (*chāndasa*), and since the extent of the *sāman* chants is likewise well-known, whereas for the *yajus* there is no means of determination because they are recited in a continuous, unbroken sequence (*praśleṣapāṭha*), it is argued that their extent cannot be known. Against this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: a collection of words that conveys a single result, which, when divided, remains syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), constitutes a single [yajus].
It was established in the second [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] that "that single sentence is a *yajus*, and its extent can be known"; by this same principle,

since it is observed that the collection of words in a mantra such as "devasya tvā savituḥ" forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the word "nirvapāmi"— being mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) when separated from it and together conveying a single result— so too must the Vedāntas have a single purpose with the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*).
Since it is impossible to split a sentence when syntactic unity is possible, there is no difference in the qualified person and so forth. || 276 ||
In the same way, when two things are understood as having distinct meanings, they are expressed by separate words.
Since [the word] is observed in "iṣe tvā" and other instances, it is not logical to assume a single meaning [for it everywhere]. || 277 ||

He rejects the unity of the two sections [kāṇḍas]. "In the same way" means that just as it is not logical for there to be multiple sentences when there is oneness, so too, since a difference in purpose is observed, the assumption of a single sentence based on a single purpose is not logical, given that a difference in sentences is observed.

He provides an example for the division of sentences due to a difference in meaning: "in the case of 'iṣe tvā' and so forth. The meaning of this is: it is established in the section defining [sentence] division (Bhedalakṣaṇa).

"In the case of identical [syllables], there would be a split of the sentence. Regarding the doubt as to whether "iṣe tvorje tvā" and so forth constitute one *yajus* (sacrificial formula) or many: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because they are recited in close proximity (*praśleṣapāṭha*), and because these two—*iṣe tvā* and *ūrje tvā*—are applied respectively to the cutting of the branch and the smoothing of it while remaining mutually contiguous, they form a single sentence due to their single purpose; thus, it is one *yajus*. Having thus argued, [the sūtra states] "iṣe tvā" [is used for] cutting the branch, and "ūrje tvā" [is used for]...

Because the application of *anumārṣṭi* (he rubs) and *anumārjanam* (rubbing) is distinct due to their difference in meaning, and because a reading by *praśleṣa* (conjunction) is possible even if it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that there is more than one *yajus* (sacrificial formula), since a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through the citation of a portion (*pratīka*) of the word found in the injunctive sentence is untenable; thus, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is proper. That very same [principle] is observed regarding the split of the sentence when there is a difference in meaning in cases such as *iṣe tvā*.
Since it is logical that there is a difference in sentences when even two sections have different fruits, there is no unity of qualification and so forth. || 277 ||
Furthermore, as for the fact that the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is supplementary to the meaning of the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa):
But surely,
these two are the causes for application because of their syntactic unity as a single sentence.

You may argue that even in the established doctrine (siddhānta), it is accepted that ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*) form a single syntactical unit with the statements of knowledge (*jñānavākya*), because they serve as a supplement to them. To this, he says: "Knowledge... [referring to the passage on page 108, vol. 1]: "Furthermore, the fact that the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is subsidiary to the knowledge of the knowledge section (*jñānakāṇḍa*) by way of purification..."

[The relationship between] those two is based on the authority of the sentence "desiring to know" (*vividiṣā*), which enjoins them; since they have different meanings, they are indeed two distinct sentences in a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor.

The literal meaning is: "because it is accepted that [the injunction] forms a single syntactical unit with that [desire for knowledge]. Just as the mantras and arthavādas—which lack independent meaning—form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) does not form a single syntactical unit with the knowledge section (*jñānakāṇḍa*) by being subordinate to it; rather, just as the injunction regarding the acquisition of wealth forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctions for the sacrificial rites, the two sections form a single syntactical unit because the injunction regarding the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) assigns actions as a cause for knowledge.

Therefore, the sense is that although there is unity of sentence (*vākyaikya*) between those two—just as between the injunction for the acquisition of wealth and the injunction for the sacrifice—the means and so forth are distinct, because even that which is obtained through an injunction serves as an auxiliary to the sacrifice, just like a substance obtained through desire (*rāga*). || 278 ||
This will be explained further according to the reasoning that is about to be set forth. || 279 ||
Therefore, its distinctness is established, having set aside the characteristics of a mandatory injunction.
And for all the Upaniṣads, the knowledge of the Self is the means to liberation.

To the question, "How can the *vividiṣā*-sentence possess the power of application (*viniyojakatva*)?", he replies: "By means of reasoning" (*nyāyena*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the *vividiṣā*-sentence possesses the power of application. Anticipating the objection that while a sentence possessing a fruit may form a single syntactical unit (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with another sentence possessing a fruit—as is the case with the rules for acquiring property and the injunctions regarding sacrifices—the fact that the Upaniṣads possess a fruit is not established for us, he says: [the following].

"Furthermore" (bhūyo'pi): the meaning is that their possession of fruit has already been stated and will be stated again; thus, there is no failure to establish their possession of fruit. He concludes the separate meaningfulness of the Upaniṣads with the word "separateness" (pārthagarthyam). By the word "hence" (ataḥ), the reasoning already stated and yet to be stated is expressed. He clarifies that very point with the words "set aside" (apāsta). || 279 || 280 ||
It consists in the complete cessation of all activities of speech, mind, and body.
And their culmination should be understood here according to the path of reasoning as it has been stated. || 281 ||

Now, it has been argued that the aforementioned knowledge is not established by means of the Upaniṣads, because even among those who have studied the Upaniṣads, some do not perceive it; therefore, the stated fruit of the Upaniṣads is improbable. To this, he replies: "Niḥśeṣa... (without remainder). The culmination (*niṣṭhā*) of that knowledge consists in hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which takes the form of the cessation of all natural activities; and this is understood from the scripture as the means for attaining the knowledge in question.

And this is to be understood through both positive and negative concomitance; thus, the aforementioned knowledge arises from the Upaniṣads for him alone who possesses hearing and so forth accompanied by tranquility (śama) and the rest, and not for others even if they have studied the Upaniṣads—this is the meaning. He recalls what was stated in the passage "the tranquil one, the self-controlled one" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.14), with the words "as stated. || 289 ||
And in that [state], authority is established for one who has abandoned all ritual actions.
This applies only to one who desires to know, and not to an agent who does not always have the desire to prove [the point]. || 282 ||

[Objection: Surely there must be a qualified person (adhikārin) for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; otherwise, those would not be accomplished. Furthermore, the attainment of qualification depends upon an injunction (niyoga), and that [injunction] does not have the act of knowing as its object. Therefore, how can hearing and so forth—which are causes of knowledge—consist in the cessation of all activities? To this, he says: "Even the qualification... The phrase "from the statement regarding tranquility and so forth" is to be supplied. And the meaning is "even without an injunction. One who is established in knowledge is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī).

If one asks what the cause of that person's qualification is, he says: "of the seeker" (*jijñāsoḥ*). The qualification for the means of knowledge belongs to one who possesses the desire for knowledge, not to an agent who always desires to act, nor does it belong to a renunciant whose qualification is based on a mandate (*niyoga*);

rather, because it is produced by the desire for knowledge preceded by discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth, the meaning is that the agent’s qualification for ritual action is caused by a mandate. || 282 ||
[Vol. 1, Page 109] *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [Connection]
Qualification [for this practice] exists even by means of the mere understanding of the reality of Brahman as the Self.
In this case, it certainly arises for the seeker of knowledge, even for the ignorant one, due to their desire for liberation. || 283 ||

Now, is it one who has not yet known the nature of Brahman who is qualified for the means of its knowledge, or is it one who already knows that nature? It cannot be the first, because such a person lacks the desire to know it (*taj-jijñāsā*), since a specific cognition (*viśiṣṭa-dhī*) is preceded by a cognition of its qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa-dhī*). Nor can it be the second, because for one who already knows it, the desire to know has ceased; thus, due to the absence of a qualified candidate, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices would not need to be performed. To this, he says: "Brahman," [meaning] for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), the cause of that...

For one who has studied the Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) correctly and understands the connection between the words and their meanings, there arises in the Vedāntas an initial, superficial knowledge regarding Brahman and the Self; this knowledge, termed "understanding" (*vyutpatti*), is the motivator for inquiry (*vicāra*). Even by that much alone, eligibility for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other stages of practice is established;

therefore, since it is proven that the aforementioned eligible person—even if lacking direct realization—is required to perform those [stages], it is established that the eligible person and so forth are distinct.
The meaning is "in the two sections. || 283 ||
Do not proceed in this way, having previously considered both the commencement and the conclusion.
The unity of purpose and the single intentionality of the Veda have been declared through its status as a single syntactical whole. (284)

He raises an objection against the previously stated distinction regarding the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and so forth, by means of another method: "Not so. [This refers to] the opening passages such as *agnim īḷe purohitam* ("I praise Agni, the domestic priest"), *iṣe tvorje tvā* ("For food thee, for strength thee"), and *agna āyāhi* ("O Agni, come hither"), as well as the injunctions such as "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives" and "Only while performing [these rites] here..."

By reflecting on the concluding passages, such as "performing rituals in a pure household" and "studying one's own Veda in a sacred place," and so forth, one determines that the Veda has action (kārya) as its sole purpose; thus, the status of the two sections as a single unified whole (ekavākyatā) is established. Consequently, the previously stated claim that the subject matter and other factors differ between the two sections is incorrect. Alternatively, the objection raised regarding the attainment of a single purpose is here restated with its necessary supplements. In this regard:
And the application of syllables is indeed manifest. || 284 ||
Therefore, those who perform everything prescribed in the Vedas without exception possess the qualification for this.
Once it is established that they form a single syntactical unit, one must assume that they have different intended audiences.

Anticipating the objection that even if the two sections (kāṇḍas) form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), they still possess different subjects (*adhikārin*), he says: "By that" (*tena*). The meaning is that because they form a single syntactical unit, one who has performed the rites starting from the *darvī-homa* up to the *satra* becomes qualified for knowledge; thereafter, by performing the injunction of knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) following the complete performance of those rites, liberation is attained—thus the two sections have a single subject. One—

Having stated that there is a single subject because they constitute a single sentence (*vākya*), he states the fault in the opposing view: "For if [it were established]... The meaning is that if the two sections had different subjects, their status as a single sentence would not be established. || 285 ||
For this has already been established by us previously.
Consequently, the objection stated by you does not apply here. || 286 ||

He refutes the claim that because the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) have a single purpose, they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) and thus share a single qualified agent (*ekādhikāritva*), by saying: "Not so. Even though the two sections—each having its own independent operation culminating in its own fruit—are distinct in their qualified agents, they constitute a single syntactical unit merely through the relationship of mutual assistance via their respective purposes, just as in the case of the rules for acquiring wealth and the injunctions for the sacrifice (*kratu*). Therefore, it has been stated [in the passage beginning] with "the status of being a subordinate part of the meaning of the Knowledge-section (*jñānakāṇḍa*)," and so forth; hence, there is no [such unity] between these two.
The meaning is: how can there be a single subject of authority if they are a single syntactical unit by virtue of having a common purpose? || 286 ||
1. ‘Not of this’; 2. ‘the state of being for the sake of action.
[Vol.
1, page 110] [Vārtika] accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.
Nor is a man capable of performing the entire meaning of the Vedas in its entirety.
By means of which one might possess the qualification for self-knowledge even within the span of a human life. || 287 ||

The introduction (*prakrama*) and the conclusion (*saṃhāra*), however, have the single purpose of [establishing] action and are not explicitly stated; thus they are disregarded, because those two [introduction and conclusion] exist for the sake of knowledge as well, through the distinction of sentences in various places. As for the claim that one who performs all the rites prescribed in the Veda is qualified for knowledge, he says: "Nor even... Since it is impossible to perform all rites even in a hundred years, the qualification for knowledge would not be established; therefore, the injunction [regarding such performance] would be without a qualified subject (*niradhikāra*).
He states the result with the words "by which" (yeneti). || 287 ||
And because of that, the status of being a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) applies to the attainment [of results] within the scope of the Vedānta.
Because there is no person qualified for [the realization of] knowledge, its intrinsic validity is cast aside. (288)

Furthermore, if both sections (kāṇḍas) were for a single qualified person (adhikārī), then neither section would be an authoritative means of knowledge for one who desires heaven and so forth, nor for one who desires knowledge; thus he says, "And of the meditative identifications" (saṃpadām). Since sacrifices and the like are subsidiary to knowledge, their fruits—such as heaven—are not intended [as primary goals]; therefore, because there is no connection with a qualified person desiring those respective results, the two sections are not an authority for such a person. Not the second [alternative].

Thus he says: "By that [reason]. Because of the stated reason—that it is impossible for a single person to perform all ritual actions—there is an absence of an eligible agent (*adhikārī*) regarding the knowledge of unity produced by the Vedic statement. Consequently, the two sections (the *karmakāṇḍa* and *jñānakāṇḍa*) would not be authoritative for him; therefore, its inherent validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) would be undermined. This is the meaning: there would be a contradiction with the *Codanāsūtra*. || 288 ||
Furthermore, liberation that is not understood through pride is not desired.
When [the Self] is known, because it is one's own essential nature, there is no desire whatsoever. || 289 ||

For this reason as well, he states that its authority does not apply with respect to one who is qualified for knowledge. He says, "Furthermore... The desire for liberation (*mokṣakāmanā*) is a qualification for one qualified for knowledge; and that [desire] must exist either when liberation is unknown or when it is known. Regarding the first case, he says, "From a means of valid cognition" (*mānāt*). The meaning is that the rule is that desire arises toward what has been experienced. Regarding the second case, he says, "When [liberation] is known. [This refers to] liberation.

The connection is that when [liberation] is known, there is no desire for it. Is it known as non-self or as self? Not the first, because the notion of liberation being non-self would be an error. He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "as one's own self" (*svātma*). Liberation, when known as the self, does not admit of desire because it is already attained; for desire is possible only regarding what is unattained and exists as a mental representation (*viparivartin*). This is the sense. When it is attained...
He states the excellence [of his position] by saying "sutarām" (all the more), because the cessation of this [desire] alone follows from experience.

Therefore, since the desire for liberation—which is a qualification of the seeker—is difficult to establish in the opponent's view, there is no qualified person eligible for knowledge; thus, the overall meaning is that the Veda lacks authority. || 289 ||
It is not proper to say that there is no desire for liberation among men.
Because we observe a desire for happiness and other such things that is not restricted by place or time. || 290 ||

[Objection: "But surely, for you as well, the desire for liberation (*mokṣakāmanā*) is a qualification for one entitled to knowledge (*jñānādhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). And according to your own stated method, that [desire] is not tenable whether liberation is unknown or known. Therefore, how can the authority of the Vedānta be established in this regard? To this, he says: "It is not tenable. The reason for this is given: "Because of space," etc. Since the prayer of all living beings—"May I have happiness; may I not have suffering"—is perceived, it follows accordingly that [the desire for liberation is] unconditioned...
1. Because of being self-existent.
[Vol. 1, page 111]
90. Regarding Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the connection]:
Since desire for liberation—which consists in the destruction of all suffering and the attainment of bliss—is impossible, it is not reasonable for me to say that there is no longing for it.

Indeed, liberation, characterized by the Brahman-nature of the Self, is not unknown because it is self-luminous; nor is it known through a means of valid cognition prior to the arising of knowledge, because it is not an object of any other means of valid cognition. Therefore, since desire for liberation is possible in my view—where it is known in its own nature yet unknown through a means of valid cognition—the qualification of the seeker of specific knowledge is established, and thus there is no invalidity of the Vedāntas. Furthermore, there is no contradiction, for it is precisely with respect to such a person that the Karma-kāṇḍa applies.
The sense is that it is worthy of honor. || 290 ||

Furthermore, if knowledge were to have an unseen result (adṛṣṭārtha), like the Agnihotra and other such rites, then there would arise a consideration regarding eligibility (adhikāri-cintā) due to the doubt that the result might not be achieved even when the act is performed. (291)

Furthermore, he states that in our view, there is no lack of authority for that [knowledge] because one who is qualified for knowledge is obtained; this is expressed by the words "Moreover" (*kiṃca*). In your view, since knowledge—like the *agnihotra* sacrifice—is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), a person whose qualification remains uncertain would not engage in it due to the doubt as to whether the result will arise even when that [knowledge] is performed or not. And the determination of qualification depends upon the desire for liberation (*mokṣakāmanā*). But that [desire] exists whether that [liberation] is known or unknown.

Or rather, it is appropriate to question you regarding the absence of eligibility for knowledge; however, in our view, knowledge does not have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because—like agriculture and other such acts—it is accepted that its fruit is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and thus possesses a visible fruit. Therefore, since the existence of a fruit in the knowledge of the Self is certain—just as in the case of the knowledge of mother-of-pearl and the like—the eligibility of one who desires that fruit is established, and consequently, there is no occasion for an inquiry [into the nature of the Self] prior to that eligibility. Thus, [the inquiry] pertains to the qualified person (*adhikārin*).
The meaning is that when [the truth] is easily accessible, the Vedāntas become a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 291 ||
Even the desire for [the results of] the Agnihotra and other such rites is not permitted for a Śūdra who lacks the qualification [for them].
Even that which has been performed with effort is rendered fruitless by him; this is examined therein. || 292 ||

If [it is argued that] there is no consideration of eligibility (*adhikāra*) regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), then—alas!—since there is no difference in their being means prescribed by the Vedas, such consideration would not apply to the *agnihotra* sacrifice either.

Consequently, all determination of eligibility would be rendered invalid. Nor is there the consequence of the non-performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, for they are accomplished by one who desires heaven and the like; anticipating this objection, he says: "by one desiring [heaven]," etc. Even by a *śūdra* desiring heaven and the like, [knowledge is not attained], because of the lack of eligibility...

The meaning is that since the results of rites such as the *agnihotra* performed by an agent are not perceived, it is difficult for discerning people to engage in actions whose fruits are unseen without first considering their eligibility (*adhikāra*); therefore, such consideration is appropriate in those cases. || 292 ||
They depend solely upon the arising of knowledge that devours ignorance.
But nothing further regarding the goal of man is sought here beyond what is found in the scriptures. (293)

One might raise the objection: "Since self-knowledge is prescribed in the Veda as a means [to a goal], like the Agnihotra sacrifice, it must have an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), and thus there would be a consideration regarding eligibility for it as well.

Anticipating this, the author considers the alternative of whether such knowledge is mediate (parokṣa) or immediate (aparokṣa). Regarding the first case, he considers that it would be a proof of what is already established (siddhasādhyatva);

then, addressing the second case, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). This is because the human goal exists as being dependent solely upon the attainment of the knowledge that destroys ignorance through the scripture.
No further unseen fruit is sought; therefore, the meaning is: how can there be any consideration of qualification regarding knowledge? || 293 ||
If it is asked, "Whence comes that knowledge?", [the answer is: for it arises from the complete destruction of bondage.
And this [being] is either past, or future, or present. || 294 ||
Knowledge as taught in the treatises does not arise even for one who has studied those treatises, because it is not perceived; nor is there any other cause for its production. Thus they say.
[Vārtika] [This is] accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 91] He raises an objection with the word "kutaḥ" (whence?). He provides the resolution: "For that [knowledge]..."—that is, for one whose sins have been exhausted, true knowledge arises through the power of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
Now, is this obstacle past, future, or present? It cannot be the first, because it does not obstruct the arising of present knowledge.

[The opponent objects: "It cannot be the first [alternative], because that which is non-existent lacks the capacity to be an obstacle. Nor can it be the second, because it is untenable for something unobtained to act as an obstacle.

Nor can it be the third, because there is no evidence for the existence of a present obstacle when the cause of knowledge has been performed. Thus he [the author] raises the objection with the words "asau" (this one). || 294 ||
For this very reason, even one who has studied the Vedas and understood their meaning is not liberated.
And this very point has been demonstrated through the analogy of a hidden treasure of gold and other examples. || 295 ||

He provides the answer by stating the evidence regarding the existence of an obstacle to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, beginning with the words "Having studied... (*adhīta*). The meaning is as follows: even when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present, the fact that the absence of knowledge is observed in some cases must be due to that very obstacle under discussion. Thus, in this world, when there is no obstacle to what is currently being undertaken, the attainment of that [knowledge] is established according to the maxim of "the sight of the elephant" (*darśanārditinyāya*). As for the aforementioned obstacle—a specific sin accumulated in the past—the proof for its existence is *arthāpatti* (presumption).
Having set that aside, he cites the Śruti: "Hiraṇya... This refers to the sin which acts as an obstacle to knowledge for one who has already performed hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means.

As the Śruti says: "Just as those ignorant of the field (*akṣetrajña*), though walking right over a hidden treasure of gold, do not find it, even so all these creatures, though going there day after day, do not find this world of Brahman. By this stated analogy, the Śruti demonstrates the existence of such an obstacle.
The meaning is "he goes. || 295 ||
The knot of the heart is severed, and all doubts are rent asunder.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.

Thus, by stating that because knowledge has a visible fruit, the consideration of qualification (adhikāra)—as in the case of the *agnihotra* sacrifice—does not apply to it, he has declared its status as being perceptible to the wise (*vidvat-pratyakṣa*) due to its visible fruit. Now, he cites scripture regarding that very point: "It is shattered," and so forth. The "Supreme" is Hiraṇyagarbha; that which is "lower" than him is the Unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), or else that which is lower than the Supreme, or both the Supreme and the Lower in the form of the reflection (*pratibimba*).
The meaning is: when that [Self] has been directly realized by oneself. || 296 ||
By these and other such statements, it is also declared that consciousness does not have an unseen purpose.
Thus, it has been demonstrated by what means that [attainment] of Brahman occurs. || 297 ||

He states the purport of the scriptural passage with the words "by [the phrase] beginning with 'iti' etc. By the word "etc.," passages such as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" and "The fire of knowledge consumes all actions" are included. With the particle "api," he adds the direct perception of the wise person which was indicated previously. Regarding the fact that knowledge has a visible purpose, he cites another statement with the word "tathā": "That wise man, having attained this state, becomes a true Brāhmaṇa."

"Thus" (tīti) is the statement regarding the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*). He asks by what characteristic that [fruit] would exist, with the words "by what" (*kena*). By whatever characteristic it might be characterized, one who is established in such knowledge is of a single form, the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*); thus, by the absence of a future result to be accomplished, he explains the perceptible fruit of knowledge with the words "by which it may be, by that very same [characteristic]. By this sentence, as in the passage "the knot of the heart is severed," [knowledge is shown].
He states that its status as having visible results has been demonstrated: "Thus it has been shown. (297)

For those who desire the severance of the attainment of ultimate suffering and misfortune.
Even the excellence of joy is seen in this world; why is it not desired? || 298 ||
He raises an objection: "Even if self-knowledge has a visible purpose, whether the eligibility for it belongs to one who desires liberation is uncertain or certain?

If it is uncertain, then even one who desires heaven and the like would engage in the pursuit of knowledge; if it is certain, then by the same reasoning through which that certainty is established in your view, it is likewise established in our view as well—thus, the authority of the two sections of scripture (the ritual and the philosophical) with respect to such a person is not contradictory."

Regarding the term "ultimate": ultimate attainment of happiness and the eradication of such suffering—liberation (mokṣa) is that excellence of joy observed in the world belonging to one who desires both of these. For liberation is not something other than the attainment of the sought-after happiness and the removal of misfortune; therefore, since prayers such as "May happiness be mine" have liberation as their object even in our position, just as in yours, one who desires that [liberation]...
The sense is that because there exists a qualified person (adhikārin), the validity of both sections [of the Veda] is established with respect to him. || 298 ||
Because there is no distinction in the excellence of the joy associated with objects that are seen or unseen.
The wise man does not find rest anywhere other than in this primary bliss. || 299 ||

He states another reason why the prayer of a discerning person cannot have heaven and the like as its object: "But... The word "but" (tu) has the sense of "and. The meaning is that because pleasure born of action is impermanent—due to its being something produced, like the fruit of agriculture and so forth—the prayer of a discerning person does not culminate in anything other than liberation (mokṣa). Anticipating the objection that the probans "being produced" might be inconclusive (vyabhicāra) with respect to liberation, he says: "Because it is a manifestor... Liberation...

The meaning is: it is not something to be produced (*sādhya*), but rather something to be manifested (*abhivyaṅgya*); likewise, being dependent on a manifestor (*abhivyañjakatantra*) and not dependent on a means of production (*sādhanādhīna*), it is eternal; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. || 300 ||
All actions, indeed, function solely as formative forces (saṃskāra).
Or their entry into the section on knowledge is not something other than that [knowledge]. || 301 ||

Now, are these two sections (kāṇḍas) distinct sentences or a single sentence? Not the first, because their meanings being mutually contradictory would result in both being non-authoritative. As for the second, since the subject matter of the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) does not assist the subject matter of the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), it is merely subordinate to the latter; thus, while there might be a single sentencehood [of the two] in that sense, the qualification for knowledge belongs only to one who performs all the rites prescribed in the Veda. Therefore, no one is capable of performing the entire meaning of the Veda.

Regarding the objection that the aforementioned fault would apply [to the view that the Self is the agent], he says: "By means of the *saṃskāra* (refinement/impression). This is because actions contribute to the benefit [of the Self] by way of refining the person (*puruṣa*).

Fearing dissatisfaction [with this], he states another alternative: "By knowledge," etc. To the question, "What kind of entry of actions is there therein?

he replies: "Of them," etc. Therefore, since there is no result of liberation for those actions aimed at liberation that is distinct from the fruit of knowledge, their status as a cause toward the fruit of knowledge is what is meant by their "entry" into the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*); in that context, knowledge is primary and action is subordinate.

He says "Thus" (*evam*). He excludes the possibility of a single coherence through any other manner by saying "Not" (*na*). [This is] because [liberation results] from the performance of the entire meaning of the Veda.

The meaning is that the unity of those two—namely, that activity proceeds from knowledge upon its completion—is not accepted. It is incorrect to say that for them [the fruits of action] there is no object other than that [liberation], because even for one performing actions for the sake of liberation, heaven and so forth are merely incidental; thus, suspecting that a person who has experienced the fruits of all their karma would have the qualification for knowledge, he says: "Asāra" (insubstantial). One desiring liberation performs actions for the sake of liberation and honors knowledge.

Since he does not seek heaven through that [action], because it is so insignificant and undesired, and since liberation has been designated as his goal, the meaning is that he attains that very liberation through actions accompanied by knowledge. The meaning is that heaven and the like are not objects to be prayed for out of attachment (*prīti*). || 302 || 303 ||
The excellence of joy is also heard [in scripture] through the distinction between heaven and self-sovereignty.
Nor is the word "heaven" (svarga) a designator for such a limited measure of joy.

Having established that, according to the view of liberation through the combined performance [of rituals and knowledge], there is no lack of authority for the Vedas—since, as in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the qualification for knowledge is determined—and that there is likewise no proof of a difference in the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and so forth between the two sections [of the Veda], he states another reason for the absence of a difference in their means (*sādhana*) and so on:

"Because of the excellence of joy" (*prīteḥ*). Liberation is the excellence of joy; and that [is taught in such texts as] "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) and "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice" (*svārājyakāmo yajeta*).

The meaning is that since [liberation] is also heard to be achievable through action (*karman*), there is no difference between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) regarding their means and so forth. Anticipating the objection—"In the sentence concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), the word 'heaven' does not denote liberation, but rather refers to a particular pleasure of limited scope; how then can the idea that liberation is achievable through action arise from that sentence?"—he says: "Nor... The word 'heaven' does not denote the measure or limit of that joy.

The meaning is as follows: since specific pleasures are delimited by a finite measure, it is impossible for the word [svarga] to possess a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to them due to their infinity; rather, because its power is grasped in a general sense, it denotes mere pleasure without qualification. And since liberation (*apavarga*) consists of nothing more than that, it is logical that the word *svarga* has liberation as its sole referent.
Therefore, the point is that from the sentence "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the fact that liberation is achievable through ritual action (*karma*) is established. || 304 ||

Although the word "heaven" (svarga) has its power understood in the context of liberation (mokṣa), one might still object that a person engages in [rituals] like sacrifice by apprehending only a small amount of pleasure through that word; anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... Although someone might engage in sacrifices and the like by grasping only a small amount of pleasure as the meaning of the word "heaven," nevertheless, a discerning person seeking liberation, having investigated the meaning of that word and determined that it denotes liberation, [proceeds accordingly].

One performs those actions which are the means to that [attainment]. If the word "that" (tat) refers to specific minor pleasures that are not desired, then for a discerning seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), there would be no performance of ritual action; or else, such performance would belong only to one who is not a seeker of liberation. Alternatively, the point is that it would contradict the principle to be stated later—that all ritual actions have as their purpose the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). This applies specifically to sentences such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth.

"pleasure" (prīti). Whatever pleasure exists as a result, without its specific qualifications being intended, that alone is heaven (svarga).

If a specific distinction is desired by way of such conditions as sons, cattle, and so forth. || 306 ||

When liberation is desired as the fruit of one's actions, it is achieved by performing [the rite] only once.

Is that [heaven] colored by some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), or is it free from all limiting adjuncts? It cannot be the first, because that which is delimited by a limiting adjunct does not exist until liberation; having considered this, he refutes the second [option] with the words "Not at all. He provides the reason for why that specific pleasure devoid of limiting adjuncts would not be heaven:
"Because it is known," etc. For the word "heaven" does not apply to a specific pleasure that is devoid of limiting adjuncts.

There is no known cause for its engagement, nor is there any indicator of it, nor does it possess self-luminosity; for if that were the case, it would follow that sacrifices could not be performed with it as their objective, since it is self-established, separated only by ignorance, and thus independent of any cause other than knowledge.

Therefore, because the word "heaven" (svarga) does not refer to liberation, but rather to a particular region of the world—as in the passage beginning "that which is unmixed with suffering"—[the Vedic injunctions do not pertain to liberation].

The point is that because that [Vedic] passage is devoted to praising Him, and because it is understood from that very passage in the *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) injunction that [He] alone is to be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*), there is no identity of means and so forth between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) of the Veda. He states that even if the word "heaven" (*svarga*) in the *svargakāma* injunction were somehow to refer to liberation (*mokṣa*), liberation is not something to be accomplished by ritual action: "In liberation... Since liberation would be obtained merely through the accomplishment of optional ritual action (*kāmyakarman*), the *agnihotra* need not be repeated. Nor is its repetition for the sake of an abundance of results, because liberation consists of the unsurpassed nature of Brahman; therefore, since liberation follows from the *agnihotra* performed only once, such [repetition] is useless for that purpose.
Furthermore, because intermediate [results] are of no use, the injunctions for them lack authority; thus, the meaning is that liberation is not the fruit of optional rites (kāmyakarman). || 307 ||
"For these are like rafts," so it is said; likewise, "those who here... and so forth.
It has been demonstrated by such statements as "there is no liberation from karmas. || 308 ||

Having raised the objection that liberation is therefore the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) as established by such statements as "it is imperishable" (*akṣayyam*), [the author] replies, considering that this statement is intended as praise and is not authoritative in its literal sense due to its contradiction with other scriptural passages: "For these are rafts... (*plavā hi*).

This means that these performers of sacrifice, such as the sacrificers and others, "float"—that is, they go away or perish; therefore, they are not causes for imperishable fruits. Having examined the worlds... (*parīkṣya lokān*)—[and so forth].

In this regard, the text "not by what is done does one obtain the uncreated" serves as the basis. There, the statement declaring that "among living beings here in this world, those whose actions are beautiful attain a beautiful birth as Brahmins and so forth" effectively negates the idea that actions have *nirvāṇa* as their fruit. By the word "and" (*ca*), passages such as "those conquered by action in this world" are included. He states the purport of the aforementioned scripture: "from actions..."

Thus, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that by such statements as these, it is shown that there is no liberation from ritual actions (*karma*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), passages such as "not by action" (*na karmaṇā*) and so forth are included. || 308 ||
Because there is no reason [to reject] those things prescribed by the direct Vedic injunctions and the established ritual patterns.
I consider the renunciation involved in sacrificial rites and the like to be indeed an act of extreme daring.

He raises an objection, stating that since an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) is more powerful than explanatory sentences (*arthavāda-vākya*), one can rely upon the former to understand that liberation (*kaivalya*) is the fruit of ritual action; thus, the fact that both sections of the Veda share a single qualified agent remains established. He says: "Direct perception... etc. Just like words such as *svapnānta* (the end of a dream), an injunction itself constitutes the remainder of the injunction (*vidhyanta*), such as "One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice as long as one lives" (*yāvaj-jīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*); and because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), it does not depend on any other foundational means of knowledge (*mūla-pramāṇa*).

Because it is seen in direct Vedic texts (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the abandonment of the Agnihotra and other rites prescribed therein—without a valid reason—is mere recklessness; therefore, even the Agnihotra and such acts are causes for liberation as being subordinate to knowledge (*jñāna-śeṣatayā*). And it has been stated in the [sūtra] *karturvā śrutisaṃyogāt* that the Agnihotra and other rites are to be performed throughout one's life. As they say: "In this way, the matter will be determined by the Veda; otherwise..."

"There may be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). But even more so than that, [it is the knowledge] enjoined by the Upaniṣadic statements which are directly perceived.
Indeed, the abandonment of steadfastness in the knowledge of the one Self is an extreme act of rashness.

Renunciation is prescribed for one who has become dispassionate by means of such passages as "peaceful" (*śānta*). [The author] concludes [the verse]. Regarding the phrase "of that": fearing that because the mere relationship already promised does not reach a final conclusion, the author of the Bhāṣya might have stated even its specific nature, he says "clearly" (sphuṭam), meaning that even if that much were established, this specific identity—namely, "this is that"—is not clearly established.
The sense is that the reason for not stating the specific relationship required is being sought. || 313 ||
Even by such words as "it is denoted," that [ultimate reality] is not expressed.
Therefore, it is stated that the Veda possesses authority regarding an already established entity.

Anticipating the objection that since the specific nature of the relationship will be stated immediately in the subsequent commentary beginning with "All this," there is no need to search for the reason why it was not stated here, he says: "It is being stated, etc. [The phrase] "it is being stated" (*abhidhīyate*) is the beginning of the commentary starting with "All this" (*sarvo 'py ayam*); thus, by that statement as well, the specific nature of the relationship is not expressed.

The meaning is that, therefore, the reason for not stating that [connection] must be explained. Having raised the objection as to how it is understood that the specific connection is not mentioned in the immediately following commentary, he says: "Because in that [commentary] another meaning is perceived," namely, "it is established. || 314 ||
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, Page 118] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Since the statement of the Vedānta is authoritative, the relationship [between them] is now being explained.
Therefore, for the very sake of establishing its validity, it is said: "all of this," and so forth. || 315 ||

Anticipating the objection raised by the commentary beginning with the words "tasya" (of that), he replies: "Vedānta... and so forth. Having proposed the general connection [between the Vedas and dharma], the author of the Bhāṣya does not state the specific reason for it, even though such a specific reason is required; for, as established in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the authority of that portion of the Veda which incites action has been affirmed, whereas the Vedāntas do not possess such authority because they do not aim at action, but rather consist solely in the description of entities that are neither objects of engagement nor withdrawal. Thus...

In the *Taittirīyaka-sūtra*, although the authority of the Veda as a whole was established on the basis of its independence (*anapekṣatva*), one might suspect that this [authority] belongs only to that portion of the Veda which impels action (*pravartaka*), due to the force of the context; thus, one might doubt the authority of the Upaniṣads. Therefore, thinking that there would be no connection whatsoever with the section concerning knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*)—whose status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) remains unestablished—he first establishes the authority of the Vedānta and subsequently [connects it] with the section concerning ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Thinking that it is appropriate to state the connection [between the two treatises], he establishes their authority in the immediately following commentary; the intention is that the statement of the relationship [between them] will then be easy to accomplish. || 315 ||
Either the relation is implied, or the relation is not directly expressed.
If it is asked how [this is so], it is stated by way of breaking down the word ending in the seventh case. || 316 ||

In that case, one might object: "Having first established its authority (*prāmāṇya*), the commentary on the initial proposition (*pratijñā-bhāṣya*) should be composed when there is a desire for a connection (*saṃbandha*). Anticipating this, he states another position: "Or it is objected" (*ākṣipyate vā*). One might further object: "That objection does not appear in the *Bhāṣya*, because words such as 'not' (*na*), which would express that meaning, are not seen there. Anticipating this, he says: "The connection is not [stated]. This means that the connection between the section on knowledge (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*) and the section on dharma (*dharma-kāṇḍa*) is not stated.

The meaning is that, having split the word ending in the seventh case [“saptamyanta”] and brought forth the negative particle (*nañ*), an objection (*ākṣepa*) is to be seen. He asks for the cause of that objection: “How so? He then promises to state it: “It is said. || 316 ||
There is no connection between two things with distinct meanings, because they do not depend upon each other's meaning.
And because they have a single purpose, the sections on ritual action and the section on knowledge constitute a single unified statement.

Are these two sections (kāṇḍas) of different meaning, or are they of identical meaning? Regarding the first case, he states that there can be no connection between two things whose meanings are independent, whether by mutual expectancy or by the expectancy of only one; thus he says, "If they are different. Regarding the second case, he says, "And if they have a single purpose. By the word "and" (ca), the phrase "there is no connection" is drawn forward [from the previous sentence]. When the two sections have the same subject matter, there is no split in the sentence (vākyabheda), because, according to the principle "that which has a single purpose is a single sentence," it constitutes one sentence.
By logical necessity; for a connection exists between two things when they form a single syntactical unit, not with only one—this is the meaning. || 317 ||
Likewise, if those two were not cognized, the statement of their relationship would not be tenable.
If there were cognition of either one of the two, or of both together, then neither a relation nor anything else could be established. || 318 ||

Furthermore, are the two sections non-authoritative (*amāna*) or authoritative (*māna*)? In the first case, there would be no connection between the subject matter (*vācya*), just as in the case of the words of a deceiver;

thus he says, "In that way" (*tathā*). Even if they are authoritative, whether both are so or only one is, in neither case is there a connection. For if both were authoritative, they would be mutually ignorant of each other's discourse, and because a connection between the authoritative and the non-authoritative cannot be expressed. And if both were authoritative...

He states that if the distinction between what is real and what is unreal were established by the validity of only one of the two, then the distinctions among the means of proof and so forth would not be established: "Of the two... (318).
1. It has been said:
[vol 1, page 119]
Since that has already been stated by the Śruti itself with the effortful words "this very [path]," Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [on the connection] says: 98. [omitted].
Having kept this in mind, the teacher did not state the connection.

Intending to show that the relationship—obtained through the impossibility of a fixed sequence between the two sections—is not what is directly expressed (vācya), and thus cannot be implied by it, he states another reason for not mentioning the immediate connection: "By direct statement" (*śrutyā*). Having proposed the mere relationship in the words "of that," etc., and wishing to explain its specific nature, the Commentator, observing that [the relationship] is evident in the *vividiṣā* passage, [states] that for one who has studied the Veda and knows the words...

The meaning is that, thinking that for one who possesses a superficial understanding (*āpātajñāna*) of the relationship between categories within the Vedāntas, this [relationship] will ascend to his own intellect by itself and thus need not be explicitly taught, he does not discuss it immediately thereafter. || 319 ||
Or, having established the validity of the Vedāntas through diligent effort;
The connection with the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) will be explained properly later. || 320 ||

Fearing that the cognition of the relationship between the two sections—the one concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and the one concerning [the knowledge of Brahman]—might act as an obstacle even to what was promised therein, just as it does to the statement of its specific details, he elaborates on the phrase "because of the statement of the Vedānta. He says: "Having established... The meaning of this is as follows:

By way of an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*), the Commentator promised the relationship with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*). Therefore, that promise is not [contradicted by] the Vedānta...

Having refuted the objection that [the Vedas] lack authority by asserting their authority, [the author] stated the specific relationship known as the causality of ritual actions toward the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is established by the *śruti* on the desire to know. Therefore, there is no defect whatsoever in this commentary. || 320 ||
The study of the Vedas and other such practices are for the purpose of generating the knowledge of the oneness of the Self.
By the sentence "This very [one]," the injunction for the obligatory rites will be stated. || 321 ||

He raises an objection regarding the specific relationship intended by the Commentary (Bhāṣya) to be expressed between the two sections (kāṇḍas), as stated in the *vividiṣā* passage. [The objection begins with] "Veda... [etc.].

By the *vividiṣā* passage, only the manner in which obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites serve as means for the arising of knowledge is indicated; it does not apply to all actions, because optional (*kāmya*) rites, being causes for other fruits, cannot logically be means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). And thus, in one part of the Karma-kāṇḍa...

The meaning is that even though there is a connection with the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), the entirety [of the work] is not integrated with it. The phrase "will be stated" means that which is expressed without being intended [as the primary subject]; or rather, this reference is made in consideration of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). || 321 ||
Or rather, all ritual actions have the purpose of generating the desire to know [Brahman].
By the statement "this very [one]," because of the distinctness of the conjunction. || 322 ||

It is impossible to restrict [the rule] to the idea that only obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites are causes of knowledge, because there is no restrictive authority; furthermore, the scriptural statement "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*) is heard without qualification. Therefore, he provides the solution: by means of the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*), it is stated that all ritual actions are causes of knowledge through the mediation of the desire to know. Alternatively, those rites performed for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*), which have already been enjoined for other fruits by the statement of the injunction, cannot be further enjoined for the purpose of the desire to know.

Anticipating the objection that "there is no possibility of application for that which has already been applied," he says: "of the conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*). This is its meaning: when one thing possesses both [purposes], there is "separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktvam*). In the case of the Agnihotra, regarding the injunctions "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "One desiring sense-power should offer with curd" (*dadhendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), there arises a doubt as to whether the curd serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) or the purpose of the fruit (*phalārthatā*). In this regard, just as in the case of the *godohana* vessel and others, the phrase "for one desiring sense-power" connects it to the fruit.
