In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was argued that because a sentence devoid of an injunction of qualification (*adhikāra*) forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with an injunctive sentence of qualification, that [sentence] must indeed have human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*). However, since the injunctive sentence of qualification is established even by way of restating a worldly *dadhi*-oblation, it does not depend on another sentence; and since in the case of "one offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*) as well, the injunction of curds is made by way of restating the contextually relevant oblation (*prakṛtahoma*), the performance of the rite is accomplished through that very [injunction], and thus there is no need for an expectation of a qualification (*adhikārākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, there is a distinction in connection (*saṃyogabheda*).

In the fourth [book], it was established as a settled conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that a single thing can serve two purposes. The meaning of the sūtra is that the "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktvam*) is the reason for a single substance, such as curd (*dadhi*), being both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*); for there is one connection expressed by "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and another by "for one desiring the senses through curd" (*danendriyakāmasya*).

And thus, even for those rituals associated with heaven and other results, setting aside the fruit of heaven and so forth, they become causes of knowledge through their connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).
Thus, there is a connection between the entire section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) and the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa). || 322 ||
Having accepted from worldly convention the means such as animals, rice, and so forth, [one proceeds].
"This is to be done, this is not"—such is the scope of the Śruti concerning the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa).

Now, one might object: "The scripture of the *karmakāṇḍa* speaks of a distinction between agents such as animals and so forth, whereas the scripture of the *jñānakāṇḍa* speaks of non-dual Brahman; therefore, because of this mutual contradiction, how can there be a connection [between them]? To this, he says: "From worldly experience" (*lokataḥ*). Animals and so forth, as well as their distinctions, are established by worldly experience, and these are [the subject matter of] the *karmakāṇḍa*.
Anticipating the objection that if the Śruti merely restates [what is already known], then it lacks authority because it is a restatement (anuvādaka), he says: "This... (323).
The connection between the probandum and the probans, which has been established by another means of valid cognition;
It reveals the science of action, but it does not bring about the realization of the ultimate reality.
Nevertheless, anticipating the doubt as to how the stated objection is answered, he elaborates upon the second half [of the verse] with the words "by another means of knowledge" (*mānāntareṇa*).

The meaning is that even though the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is merely reiterative regarding the distinction between action and so forth, it is not devoid of authority, because it makes known a relationship that was previously unknown. The phrase "it manifests" implies the remainder of the sentence: "therefore, it is not unauthoritative. Now, one might object: "But by that [means of knowledge], the Self too, like the relationship, would be something distinct from the body..."

It might be argued that since one does not engage in actions pertaining to the next world without knowledge of that [Self], the subject matter has already been covered by another section (kāṇḍa) of the scripture; to this he says "No" with the words "But not... The meaning is as follows: the scripture, which makes known the relationship between words and their meanings, does not directly reveal the reality [of the Self] because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Any cognition of an additional Self that arises is merely implied (*ārthikī*) and not verbal (*śābdī*); and according to the maxim, "that which is obtained through implication is not the intended meaning of the injunction (*codanārtha*). || 324 ||
For indeed, this entire Veda exists for the sake of establishing the knowledge of the oneness of the Self.
Therefore, there is no other connection between the sections on ritual action and knowledge.

Nevertheless, one might object that there is no connection between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) because their respective effects—desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) and direct knowledge (*jñāna*)—are mutually distinct and do not culminate in the same point. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the Veda... The meaning is as follows: this entire Veda is the cause of the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self; therefore, since both sections ultimately rest upon the single cognition of that [identity], directly or indirectly, there is indeed a connection between them. Just as there can be a relationship between a rope and a jar, such a relationship is possible between these two.

Anticipating the objection—"What is the use of a relationship as the cause of the cognition of identity that is not well-established?"—the author says "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is: no relationship other than the aforementioned causality of the cognition of identity is appropriate for these two, because [other relationships] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) are difficult to maintain. || 325 ||
For here, the obligatory and occasional rites [are performed] for the purpose of purifying the agent.
They do not terminate anywhere else than in the knowledge whose object is oneness with the Self.

Unable to tolerate the word "all" being used as a coordinate term with the word "Veda," [the opponent] raises the objection introduced in the passage beginning with "of the recitation of the Vedas, etc. (vedānuvacanādīnām). 1. Section on the two divisions [vol.

[The opponent] says: "It is eternal," etc. Among the various kinds of ritual acts (*karma*), the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) ones are causes for knowledge by means of imparting a purification known as *saṃskāra* to the agent;
the optional (*kāmya*) rites are not. Therefore, the meaning is that it is unproven that the entire Veda is a cause for that [knowledge]. || 326 ||
“For these are indeed rafts,” and likewise, “those who here [in this world]...”
The necessity of performing optional rites is determined through the censure [of their non-performance]. || 327 ||

Alternatively, regarding the point that [the Vedas] are for the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), one might object: "Since it has been stated that even those [Vedic rites] performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) are causes of knowledge, why is it not the case that the entire Veda is a cause of that [knowledge]?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For they are rafts" (*plavā hi*). The meaning is that, because of scriptural censure, those [rites] do not even have the status of being something to be performed (*kāryatā*); how then could they be causes of that knowledge? || 327 ||
Even so, the inclusion of a censure of the ritual rule is not tenable.
But if it were merely an intention toward a result, it would be appropriate only as a censure. || 328 ||

He refutes [the objection] that it is improper for optional rites (*kāmya*) to be considered non-performable because they are enjoined and not prohibited, stating: "Because of the injunction," and so forth. Even though there is a coexistence of injunction and censure regarding optional rites, nevertheless, their non-performability is not at all tenable due to the injunction.

The construction is: "because there is no prohibition. Now, if a prohibition of those [rites] is also inferred from the scriptural mention of censure (*nindā*), is that censure directed at their essential nature or at the intention for a result? It cannot be the first, because since rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) are stated to be things to be done by such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the Citrā," it is impossible for censure to enter into them; otherwise, if the prohibition inferred from that censure were also to enter into that very same [rite], there would be a coexistence of injunction and prohibition in one and the same place.

The meaning is that there would be a confusion between engagement and withdrawal from action. He supports the second [position] with the words "phala-". If the intended censure applies merely to attachment to the fruit, then an injunction regarding the essential nature [of the act] is indeed possible. And thus, even a sacrifice such as the *Citrā* performed without desire for a fruit becomes a cause of knowledge; therefore, it is established that all actions are causes of that [knowledge] through a traditional succession (*pāraṃparyeṇa*). Nor is there any deficiency in sacrifices like the *Citrā* when there is an absence of desire for the fruit.

It is not the case that [the action] is non-desirable for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because even in the absence of an intention toward the fruit mentioned in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), that [action] pertains to other types of qualified persons (*adhikārin*).
Nor does it follow that it is non-desirable with respect to the seeker of liberation; for since it is a subsidiary to the means of liberation, it is performed by him as well.

Although the performance by seekers of liberation takes this same form even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth, there is a distinction in their intermediate nature, because other fruits are heard in the injunctive statements regarding those [obligatory rites].
The state of being. || 328 ||
And whatever meditation is heard in the context of a particular knowledge (vidyā), [it belongs to that specific knowledge].
That too is postulated solely for the sake of making [the self] fit for the knowledge of its identity with That. || 329 ||

Having raised the objection that while it is established by direct statement (*vākya*) that actions situated in other contexts serve as causes for knowledge through means such as purification, the fact that meditations (*upāsanā*) situated within the context of knowledge serve as causes for liberation along with that knowledge is based on the context (*prakaraṇa*), he says: "And meditation...

He includes the threefold meditation—performed for the sake of the success of ritual action, for the sake of prosperity, and for the sake of gradual liberation—with the words "whatever [meditation]... and so forth.

The suitability of knowledge consists in its being oriented toward birth; for those who have performed the required rites but have not yet developed a desire for knowledge, it is intended that meditations (*upāsana*) serve as causes for that desire and so forth by means of removing the sins that obstruct its arising. Nor is there an absence of an applicatory rule (*viniyojaka*), because the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself serves that purpose. Furthermore, one should not argue: "How can these [meditations] be subordinate to knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*) when there is a scriptural mention of another fruit? For even if a fruit is heard...

Having abandoned the pursuit of results that do not lead to excellence, one seeks the remainder of actions, just as one does for ritual acts; and thus the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*) is consistent with both [the means and the end].
[Note: The numbers in brackets refer to variant readings in manuscripts *kha* and *ka*.]

[Vārtika] The sense is that, because they are equal [in status], the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*) applies; thus, even meditations (*upāsanā*) are included by the word "austerity" (*tapas*). || 329 ||
Because of the statement "being liberated" and likewise because of the statement regarding "not long," [it is so].
It is not perceived that meditations terminate merely in their own specific objects.
Now, one might raise the doubt: "Why could the meditations (*upāsanā*) not be causes for liberation itself, just like knowledge (*vidyā*)? Anticipating this, he says:

"vimucyamāna iti" ("being liberated..."). The meditations cannot be direct causes of liberation; rather, they are indirect causes, because in the passage, "Being liberated from here, where will you go?", the destination to be reached by the meditator via the sequence [of stages] is asked about, [referring to] the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth.

And because of [the word] "renown" (*viśruti*). The sense is that the path and so forth do not exist directly in liberation, since it was established in the *Bādha* section that they have as their object only what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). He refutes the second [position] with the words "svārtha... (in its own meaning). If the means of knowledge (*upāyani*) are causes of liberation by way of attaining *Satyaloka* and so forth, then there is no contradiction with Śruti and Smṛti; for liberation is their own purpose (*svārtha*), and [only] in that respect is there a succession.
The meaning is that there is no finality regarding them without [this], because there is a lack of evidence. || 330 ||
In this way, such a connection with the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is appropriate.
If it were connected otherwise than this, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever would be observed. || 339 ||

He concludes the exposition of the relationship between the two sections (kāṇḍas), as intended by the Commentary, which establishes that while actions are causes of purification through the medium of purification, the Upaniṣads are so directly. He says: "In this way. Regarding those who claim that the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) is subservient to the section on action (karmakāṇḍa) because the knowledge of Brahman serves as a refinement of the agent (kartṛsaṃskāra) and is thus an auxiliary to ritual action, he replies: "Other than this... (331).
Nor is there any connection with ritual action, as there is in the case of knowledge concerning the udgītha and other such elements.
Because of the cognition of oneness, that door of cognition is not perceived at all.

[Objection: Surely the knowledge of the Self must enter into ritual action because it is Vedic knowledge, like the knowledge of the *udgītha* and so forth; to this he replies: "No. He states the reason for that: "Because of the cognition of that [Self]" (*tadbuddhi*). It is appropriate that the knowledge of the *udgītha* and so forth enters into ritual action—even though it is not a constituent part of the rite—by virtue of the principle of the "restriction of its determination" (*tannirdhāraṇāniyamanyāya*), since it is bound to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the rite. However, in the case of the cognition of the Self, since no such means (*dvāra*) for its entry into the rite is perceived, it does not enter into ritual action.
This is the meaning. || 332 ||
The knowledge of non-dual identity is not enjoined by scripture anywhere in the Veda.
The attendance should be as it is for Indra; nor is there any connection by means of a characteristic mark (liṅga).
And it is just as in the case of "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth. (333)

But surely, without requiring any mediation, the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) itself enjoins the knowledge of the Self for the sake of ritual action, according to the principle of the *aindra-adhikaraṇa*.

This is established in the section on the definition of subsidiary elements (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*): "On account of the specific injunction, however, the *aindrī* mantra should be used in a manner not according to its literal meaning" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.2.3). In the context of the fire-altar (*agniprakaraṇa*), regarding the injunction, "With the *aindrī* mantra—'He who is the depository, the gatherer of riches'—one worships the *gārhapatya* fire," is this mantra intended for the worship of Indra? Or...

In the doubt as to whether it is for the purpose of worshiping the *gārhapatya* fire, the second case-ending in the word "gārhapatyam" indicates through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) that the *gārhapatya* is the primary object (*śeṣin*).

Even so, because the mantra lacks the capacity to express that [meaning], and because the application (*viniyoga*) follows the nature of what is to be applied, and because of the word "Indra" [itself]... [Śureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, on the Connection].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that since the primary meaning of the word [Indra] cannot be rendered secondary (*gauṇatva*), the phrase "having approached the Gārhapatya" must be supplied as an ellipsis; thus, the mantra is for the purpose of worshipping Indra. To this, the reply is: because the accusative case-ending shows the Gārhapatya to be the primary object, and the instrumental case-ending indicates that the mantra is subordinate to it, and because the Gārhapatya—just like Indra—is a means of sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*) and is capable of being denoted by the mantra through a secondary figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), the mantra is therefore enjoined for the Gārhapatya.

Because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is understood, and because that [meaning] is established through the semantic power (*sāmarthya*) of the words, when the capacity (*śakti*) of each individual word is examined, it is possible for the word "Indra" itself to be used figuratively (*gauṇatva*). Since the Gārhapatya fire also possesses sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) with respect to its own function, the word "Indra" is applied to it etymologically (*yaugikatva*). Therefore, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that, setting aside the need for textual insertion (*adhyāhāra*), the mantra is for the purpose of worshipping the Gārhapatya fire. Thus, the term *aindrī* (belonging to Indra) is not literal; it is non-primary in its referent.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that [the meditation on the Self] must pertain to the *gārhapatya* fire, because of the statement "he worships the *gārhapatya*," and because the *gārhapatya* is understood to be the primary object through the use of the accusative case. Likewise, in the present context as well, since the knowledge of the Self is enjoined for the sake of ritual action by the scriptural statement using the instrumental case, "Whatever one performs with knowledge," he says: "By scripture. Just as [the verse] beginning with "Indra, the dweller, the gatherer of riches" is [enjoined] at some time—

The meaning is that, just as the worship of the Gārhapatya fire is performed with the first verse beginning "Canas-tarīr asi," the knowledge of the Self (ātmadhī) is not enjoined by scripture in any context or any ritual action through the medium of ritual science (vidyā), because it falls within the scope of meditations connected to specific ritual limbs (aṅgāvabaddhopāsti). Now, one might object: according to the principle of the section on the primary and the secondary (gauṇa-mukhya-adhikaraṇa), the knowledge of the Self serves as a refinement of the agent (kartṛ-saṃskāra).

The connection of the revealed scripture (*śruta*) with ritual action occurs through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), which consists in the impossibility of its realization without entering into ritual action. For instance:

"Because of the connection with the expression of meaning, there is the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) in the case of mantras; therefore, the relationship of origin is with the meaning, due to the eternal connection" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.2.1).
Thus, regarding mantras such as *barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi* ("I cut the grass, the seat of the gods"), whether in their primary or secondary sense—

In the doubt as to whether the application (*viniyoga*) is primary (*mukhya*) alone, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: that in which the cognition of the meaning arises from the word itself is primary; whereas that in which the cognition of another meaning arises through a connection with a quality related to the sentence-meaning is secondary (*gauṇa*). Since there is no distinction in the capacity [of the word] in both cases, the application belongs to both. To this, [the reply is]: even if the capacity exists for the secondary meaning, there is no application based on that alone.

Since an injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the agent of application (*viniyojaka*) regarding a task established by the context (*gātra*), and since a secondary understanding (*gauṇadhi*) is preceded by a primary understanding (*mukhyadhī*), the mantra is applied first to its primary meaning.
Because the injunction has fulfilled its purpose with that alone, there is no occasion to postulate an application to a secondary meaning as well.
Furthermore, since a secondary meaning is accepted only when a primary one is impossible, the application of mantras is based on indicative power (*liṅga*) solely in their primary sense.

It is established in the third [section]: since mantras are connected with the primary meaning when it is expressed, they possess the status of being subsidiary (śeṣatva) to the principal rite (pradhāna) mentioned in the context (prakaraṇa) among those recited therein. However, mantras should not be employed for a secondary (gauṇa) meaning; for by the very application to the primary meaning, any lack of purpose (ānarthakya) is avoided. If there were no application even there, the production of the mantra would be useless due to its failure to assist the principal rite; therefore, [the application must be] by means of the primary meaning.

The meaning of the sūtra is that because these [mantras] have a permanent connection, their relationship—characterized by arising within that specific context—is purposeful. To the objection that, in the same way, knowledge of the Self might also be enjoined toward the aforementioned ritual action by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), he replies: "Nor also... Just as in the case of the mantra beginning with "barhiḥ," this mantra is enjoined toward the cutting of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth by virtue of an indicative mark such as its capacity to manifest the manner of cutting the grass, so too is it with the knowledge of the Self.

The meaning is that because no indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the capacity to reveal the status of being a subsidiary part (*aṅgabhāva*) of the *nasya* rite—is observed, there is no connection of that [mantra] with that rite;

furthermore, its inclusion in the rite as a purifier of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*) has already been rejected and will be rejected later. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), mantras such as "Spread wide the thigh" (*ūrū prathasva*) and "Wide be your husband of the sacrifice" (*uru te yajñapatiḥ*) are included. || 333 ||

Nor does cognition proceed from a sentence by way of its agent.
It does not reside in the performance of ritual action, just as the quality of being made of parṇa-wood resides in the sacrificial ladle (juhū).

Let it be then that, according to the principle of the section on sentences (*vākyādhikaraṇa*), the status of the self as an object—subsidiary to the cognition—is derived from such sentences as "the self is to be known.

For it is established in the third book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā*]: "That [substance] serves all purposes, because there is no specific context" (*tatsarvārthamaprakaraṇāt*, Pū. Mī. 3.6.1). [As in: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report; he whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira*-wood [cuts] with the very essence of the meters..."

In such cases as "the ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," although the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇatā*) is studied independently of any specific ritual context, its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice is established through the recognition of the ritual injunction (*niyoga*) by means of its connection with the *juhū* ladle and other implements, which are invariably associated with the sacrifice. When the doubt arises—whether this injunction is for the sake of both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), or for the sake of the archetype alone—the absence of a defining context (*prakaraṇa*) would suggest it applies to both; however, because it is enjoined with reference to the *juhū* and other implements, and because these implements serve as the means for producing the respective transcendental results (*apūrva*) of those specific rites, the connection with the *juhū* and so forth [is determined].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is no distinction between the two cases—both being established through direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*)—this rule is intended for both. However, in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), because the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) and other qualities are to be enjoined with reference to the *juhū* ladles and so forth already obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), those [ladles] are brought forward by way of that [quality]. Consequently, since the *parṇatā* and other qualities would also be obtained therein, enjoining them again would result in the unavoidable fault of tautology (*dvirukti*). Furthermore, since the injunction is understood to apply to the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice) by taking the *juhū* and other implements—known through direct injunction—as its object—then the matter is settled.

Regarding the purpose [of the injunction], since there is no further operation after the connection with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) once the requirement for water has been met, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the injunction of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth applies only to the original sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

The meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra is that because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not restrictive, the injunction of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth applies to both the original and the modified sacrifices. The sūtra of the established conclusion, "Or rather, in the original sacrifice, because of the absence of double-statement" (*prakṛtau vā ’dviruktatvāt*), means that these [injunctions] should be inserted into the original sacrifice alone, as they have not [yet] been stated elsewhere.

The meaning is that by studying these very sentences in this manner, there will indeed be no redundancy. [Objection: In the same way, the knowledge of the Self (ātmadhī) is also enjoined for ritual action through the sentence.

[Reply: He says "No" to this. Just as in the case of the sentence "He whose ladle is made of parṇa-wood," the quality of being made of parṇa—though not understood from the context of the sacrifice—is connected as a subsidiary part of the ritual by way of its presence in the *juhū* ladle; it is not so with knowledge, which cannot be connected to the ritual even through the sentence by way of the agent.
The meaning is "he enters. Here, for the sake of the context of the sentence, he qualifies knowledge as "not being in operation" (aprakriyā). || 334 ||
It is capable of fulfilling the requirement for the perfection of the form of the sacrificial ladle and other implements.
One should enter the sacrifice [through the quality] of being made of parṇa wood and so forth, because of their introduction by way of the archetype (prakṛti).

He explains that the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth serves as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by means of the phrase "juhv-ādi" (the *juhū* ladle, etc.). The meaning is this: when there is a requirement for a material substance (*prakṛti-dravya*) for the production of the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the *juhū* and other such items, then qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood—which are capable of providing that specific object—would enter into the ritual through the medium of the *juhū* and so on, by way of establishing the material, based on sentences such as "The *juhū* is made of *parṇa*-wood. || 335 ||
It destroys the nature of the agent and so forth as required by karma, but it does not [destroy the karma itself].
The knowledge of the unity of the self follows [the Lord] even in His state of absolute freedom, because it possesses purposefulness.
He states the application to the subject with its supplementary explanation: "Action," etc. The connection is that the knowledge of the oneness of the Self does not follow after action.
He states another argument for the fact that the knowledge of the Self does not enter into action: "Even in the case of independence," etc. (336).
Because it is invariably concomitant with the *juhū* and other implements, one should establish the sacrifice [through the name].
The agent [is not established] because of its existence elsewhere; it is not an implied [necessity], due to the possibility of deviation.

104. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [On the Connection]:

Having stated the difference between the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and the knowledge of the Self—based on whether they serve as means required by the sacrifice or act as its sublation—with respect to their entry into the ritual (*kratu*),...

He states the disparity even between the two things considered to be the means (*dvāra*), namely the *juhū* and so forth, in the verse beginning with "juhvādi. Because it is never absent from the sacrifice (*kratu*), the *juhū* and so forth bring forward their own required material cause; thus, as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) toward qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood, it presents the sacrifice itself. However, the agent, as the subordinate element of knowledge, does not imply the ritual action (*karman*), because that [knowledge] exists even in worldly actions, and because there is no fixed connection with Vedic ritual action alone.
This is the meaning. || 337 ||
Moreover, because it is stated as not being dependent on a specific context, there is no inclusion of a particular topical section here. || 338 ||
Once the general relationship has been established through inference from ritual actions, then [the specific application follows].
It is established that the comprehension of the specific meaning of a name occurs through a sequence. || 339 ||

But is it not the case that, according to the principle of the section on context (*prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*), knowledge of the Self is subsidiary to ritual action because of its context? For instance, regarding the rule: "That which is unconnected [by direct statement, etc.

is [determined] by context, because of the requirement for a procedure" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā* 3.3.11), there arises the question: does or does not context exist as a distinct means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*)—beyond direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest—for the subsidiaries of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, such as the *prayāja* offerings, which provide assistance from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*)?

In the case of doubt, because the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the injunctive sentence denotes the supreme *apūrva* as connected with the proximate word-meanings by way of "thisness" (*aidamarthya*), and because this "thisness" is necessarily restricted to being either an instrument or a means of assistance, the *prayāja* and other rites are connected to the task already occupied by the *āgneya* and others enjoined at the stage of origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) solely as its auxiliaries; thus, since even the specific [auxiliary] enters into the stage of denoting the connection (*anvitābhidhāna*), it possesses the status of being directly expressed by the Veda (*śrautatva*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the application (*viniyoga*) is based solely on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), one first understands the general sense of "being for the sake of this" (*aidamarthya*) through such principles as "when there is a conjunction of what has a purpose and what lacks a purpose, the other [lacks a purpose] because it serves the purposeful one. Then, when there arises a desire to know the specific manner—"How so?"—one examines other means of knowledge to determine the specific connection, namely that "something functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*)" and "something functions as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In this process, the status of the *Āgneya* and other offerings as instruments is established through the principle of material necessity (*aupādānika*).

In the third [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], it was established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that because the status of being a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is contextual (*prākaraṇika*), their connection with the *darśa* and other sacrifices occurs through context (*prakaraṇa*), since no such connection is seen through direct statement (*śruti*) or other means. That which is not connected by direct statement and so forth becomes connected through context because of its requirement for a procedure; for a sentence that fulfills the requirement of something standing in proximity that requires a procedure enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it.

This is the meaning of the Sūtra. Likewise, since the cognition of the Self (*ātmadhī*) is also employed for ritual action (*karman*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), he says: "Not being commenced" (*anārabhya*).

Since a difference in context has been stated, and because the cognition of the Self is not recited there within the commencement of the ritual, it does not have the status of being a subordinate part of the ritual (*karmaśeṣatva*) through the inclusion of context, as is the case with the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; this is the meaning. Regarding the subordination of knowledge to ritual action, even the authority of position (*sthāna*) and name (*samākhyā*) is absent.

To state their scope, he says: "The established [rule]," etc. It was stated in the *Śeṣalakṣaṇa* (Book 3): "On account of indicative mark (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyāna*), that which is recited is connected with optional rites (*kāmya*). Many optional rites addressed to a single deity, such as "One who has rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and "One whose kinsmen are wasting away should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," have arisen in sequence.

Likewise, in the section known as the *Kāmyayājyānuvākyākāṇḍa*, many pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to those respective deities are recited in their sequence, such as "O Indra and Agni, [the lights] of heaven," "To the leaders among men, O Indra and Agni," and "Indra and Agni, [you shattered] ninety forts, [you slew] Vṛtra. Regarding these, there arises a doubt: is their application (*viniyoga*) according to their indicative mark (*liṅga*), or is it restricted by both sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*)?

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "because there is no distinction in the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is application everywhere," beginning with the words "It is established" (*siddha*). The meaning of this is as follows:
1. Kha na ca ni.

Since all those optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) beginning with those dedicated to Indra and Agni have been produced in sequence, and since there is no distinction in the capacity of the pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for Indra, Agni, and the others, a relationship [with all of them] would follow without distinction; [therefore], having reached this point, he states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). From that...

By these and other such statements, the following meaning is established: Once a general connection with the *grāhaka* (the recipient of the application) has been established, the injunction (*vidhi*), seeking a specific detail to bring that connection to fulfillment, considers the capacity of the mantra and determines its application (*viniyoga*) to a task consistent with that capacity. Since capacity assists by demonstrating the specific detail, and since the indicative power (*liṅga*)—which depends on a general connection—is the means of application everywhere, [it is subordinate to] the context (*prakaraṇa*).

The literal meaning is as follows: since both *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name/designation) must be sought for the sake of that [application] when the [direct] sense (*bhāva*) is present, the determination of the specific application occurs through them by means of the general;
thus, following the cognition of the general connection, there arises the specific cognition that "this pair of *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses is to be employed in this particular rite.
This is established in the section on *liṅga-krama* (indicative power and order) based on the commonality of the name *kāmya* and the force of *krama*. [End of] *liṅga*...

The meaning of the sūtra is that, because it is declared according to a systematic order, the collection of mantras and the collection of sacrifices—which are stated to be "optional" (kāmya)—are invariably connected [to the preceding]. || 338 || 339 ||
In this case, however, there is no application of the cognition of identity [with Brahman], for it is not like an optional sacrifice performed for a specific desire.
Therefore, the connection with karma does not at all arise from the cognition of a single self, because that [cognition] is not valid knowledge.

Let it be then that in the present case as well, according to the principle of the section on order (*kramādhikaraṇa*), the cognition of the Self is merely a subsidiary part of the ritual action by virtue of its sequence. For it was established in the third book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "And the order [is determined] from the commonality of location. Regarding the recitation of the principal consecratory mantras (*pradhānānumantraṇamantra*) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there arises a doubt when the mantra "O curd, thou art named" (*dadhirnāmāsi*) is recited in the sequence of the Upāṃśuyāja: does it pertain to all the principal rites, or is it for the sake of the Upāṃśuyāja alone?

Since the syntactic connection [of the mantra] with its purpose through the *niyoga* (injunctive force) is verbal, and since that [connection], being without distinction, serves as the cause for the requirement of all primary rites (*pradhāna*), while the difference based on the commonality of location is not verbal, the mantra serves the purpose of all primary rites and does not reside in the *upāṃśuyāja* solely due to its position; having thus raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: even though the syntactic connection with the purpose through the *niyoga* is verbal, it is nevertheless determined by the difference in proximity known as "position" (*sthāna*).

It has been established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that the *dhimantra* is intended solely for the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice according to its sequence. Furthermore, sequence (*krama*) is an applicator (*viniyojaka*), just like direct statement (*śruti*) and the others.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: when the consecratory mantras (*anumantraṇamantra*) for the primary rites possessing a sequence are taught in their respective order, since there exists an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) on the part of each primary rite toward the specific ritual detail (*dharma*) mentioned in its own position, they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Thus, by sequence, [the mantra belongs] to the self—

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is also subordinate to ritual action (*karman*). Alternatively, its application therein is established by its name (*samākhyā*), according to the principle of the section on names (*samākhyādhikaraṇanyāya*).

For it is stated in that very context: "And the name is thus [determined], because it is for the sake of that. Regarding the names *Ādhvaryava*, *Hautra*, *Audgātra*, and so forth, there arises a doubt as to whether there is a restriction of the ritual acts—namely, that whatever is named after a particular [priest] must be performed by that [priest] alone—or not.

Since a name (*samākhyā*) is worldly in nature, it lacks the capacity to restrict the relationship between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*aṅgin*) regarding the subject matter of the Veda; thus, when an absence of restriction would otherwise result, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that although the name is worldly, because its subject matter is the Veda, it serves as a means of inferring the application (*viniyoga*) seen in Vedic injunctions, and therefore restriction is achieved by it. Just as in common worldly usage, upon perceiving a word such as "cook" (*pācaka*), one understands its connection with the act of cooking (*pacati*), so too in the Veda—

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: upon seeing a word that expresses a relationship with something not yet established, there arises a cognition of that relationship; therefore, the name (*ākhyā*) is the allocator (*viniyoktrī*), because it is the cause of the cognition of the purpose for that [action]. Thus, even in the present case, he says "no" to the claim that the action is allocated by the name (*samākhyā*). He says: "But here... For [the mantras] denoted by the *Kāmyayājyānuvākyākāṇḍa* are not [restricted to] the *Iṣṭis*...
1. Among those well-known [persons].
106 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 127]

The meaning is that since there is neither a similarity of designation (*samākhyā*) nor a similarity of sequence (*krama*) between the knowledge of the Self (*ātmadhi*) and ritual action (*karman*), there can be no connection of the former as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the latter by means of those two. One might then argue that the status of the knowledge of the Self as a subsidiary part of ritual action is established through another means of knowledge; to this he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is because no means of knowledge other than scripture (*śruti*) and so forth—which reveals the relationship of principal and subordinate—is established either in common worldly experience or in the Veda. Thus...
He states the reason for this, saying: "Because it is immeasurable. (340)
Nor can this be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), because that would result in a syntactical split from the injunction.
And because its extraction is for a perceptible purpose, there is no assumption of an imperceptible result based on the recitation.

[Objection: But surely the scriptural statement regarding the fruit of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because it contradicts direct perception—just like the scriptural mention of "sinless verses" (*apāpaśloka*). By this inference, since the knowledge of the Self could be a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*), just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood [is subordinate to the ladle], the realization [of Brahman] is unestablished. To this, he says: "And not... The status of being an explanatory praise whose content is not a factual reality (*abhūtārthavādatva*) is pervaded by the state of being syntactically unified with an injunction (*vidhyekavākyatva*). Therefore, when that [pervader] is excluded from this [knowledge of the Self], it also excludes its own pervaded [concomitant], namely, the status of being an explanatory praise whose content is not a factual reality.

This is the meaning. The phrase "of this" (*asya*) refers to the statement regarding the fruit [of knowledge]. Nor is there any contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) here in the scriptural mention of the fruit, because for one in whom knowledge has arisen, there is no experience of suffering, and one who possesses that [suffering] is necessarily possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, since the scriptural teaching on the destruction of suffering is not a mere figurative eulogy (*abhūtārthavāda*), knowledge does not stand as a subsidiary part of ritual action even from the perspective of its fruit; such is the sense of the word "also" (*api*). As for those who hold that the Vedāntas are of contradictory meaning—like the passage concerning the "tawny cow" (*jaradgava*)—and so forth...

Those who claim that the study of that [Vedānta] by a Brāhmaṇa, like the study of the Rājasūya, is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because of its authority, say that no knowledge of oneness arises from them; in response to them, he says: "Because it has a seen purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatvāt*). Since there is no reason for the Vedāntas to lack authority, and since the fruit of the knowledge produced by them—the destruction of all suffering—is seen, their study is not for an unseen purpose. Therefore, as there is no evidence for the status of that [Vedānta] as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), it is unauthoritative.
The meaning is that the relationship between the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin) is reversed between the two sections. || 349 ||
On the contrary, according to sentences such as "This very [sacrifice]," the sacrifice and so forth are indeed subordinate members [of another rite]. (342)
But others say that one whose mind is corrupted by desire is not able [to attain it].
In order to behold that supreme non-duality, because all desires remain unfulfilled. || 343 ||

Not only is there a lack of evidence for the notion that the self-knowledge is subordinate to ritual action; on the contrary, because the *vividiṣā* passage serves as the authority for ritual actions being subordinate to that knowledge, the relationship of subordination and predominance is not the reverse. Thus he says: "Him" (*tam*). Having refuted the connection of the knowledge of unity with ritual action as its subordinate element, he has stated his own desired position: the connection of ritual action with that knowledge as its subordinate element. Now, even if ritual action is subordinate to knowledge, [the author addresses] desire—
He states the view that his status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is through liberation (*bilaya*), and not through the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), with the words "But others...

He establishes that the destruction of desires is the cause for eligibility for knowledge (*jñānādhikārahetutva*) with the words beginning "No," and so on; the meaning is that the destruction of desires is proven to be the cause of self-knowledge through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let there be eligibility for knowledge immediately upon the destruction of desires," he says:
"Of all" means: all desires, such as heaven and so forth; upon their completion, there is a turning away from passion for them, but not at the very outset because they have not yet been attained.
This is because the enjoyment of those [desires] lacks the cause for the destruction of passion for them. || 342 || 343 ||
Having attained the fruit of the Sūtrānta through the mental constructions of duality and unity, the person [is liberated].
Having enjoyed the station of Prajāpati, he then attains identity with him. || 344 ||

Then, anticipating the objection that the destruction of desire might occur through the attainment of heaven and so forth right at the outset, he says: "The notion of the identity of duality," etc. The meditation on the *sūtrātman* is the effort; and the rituals beginning with the *darvihoma* and ending with the *satra* sacrifices are performed by those various human beings.
[Regarding Kārtika:

Having begun from [the first sūtra] up to the end of the Sūtras, having attained the fruit in due order, and having experienced the enjoyments pertaining to the Sūtras, he brings that body [to its end] and [experiences] those others which have not yet been enjoyed.

Because there is an absence of the fruits of actions that are yet to be experienced, Prajāpati, with desire withdrawn from all sides, experiences his own essential nature; thus, the meaning is that the state of Prajāpati is the gateway through which actions become causes for burning [ignorance] by means of the dissolution of desire. || 344 ||
It is not so; even in hundreds of years, that destruction does not occur through the attainment of one's desires.
From service to that [object], there shall be great increase; from seeing its faults, there is cessation.

He refutes the view that actions result in the residue of wisdom (*dhīśeṣatva*) by means of the destruction of desire (*kāmadhvansa*). [The text says: "Not so. As for the claim that the destruction of desire occurs through experience (*bhoga*), he says: "No. The point is that this is sublated by the non-apprehension of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), since the destruction of desire is not observed among those who possess enjoyments. What, then, results from the enjoyment of desires? He says: "That" (referring to the aforementioned state). If one asks what, then, is the cause for the destruction of desire, he says: "The cessation... (niṣṭhā).
Thus [it is said]. || 349 ||
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of the objects of desire.
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more. || 346 ||

He cites the words of Manu and others as authoritative proof for the point that indulgence in sensual pleasure is a cause for the intensification of passion, not a means for its destruction: "Never... (346).
One might even turn away from sensual pleasures because the means for attaining them have not been accomplished.
One should also rely upon the knowledge of the self, which is the pacification of all afflictions. || 347 ||

Even though enjoyment exists within the realm of desire (*kāma*), the actions performed [for its sake] obstruct it; for desire is not able to remain within well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*), yet the cognition of the defects of sense-objects is what destroys that [desire]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It would cease. In the absence of action, the cognition thereof, and their performance, heaven and so forth are difficult to attain; thus, there might somehow arise detachment from them. But when there is knowledge of those [objects] and their performance [of actions for them], [detachment does not arise].

Since the enjoyment of those fruits is inevitable, one attains them through karma due to the intensification of passion (*rāga*); thus, there is never a transcendence of the wheel of *saṃsāra*. Therefore, the sense is that actions, like the pursuit of sense-objects, do not turn away desire. Furthermore, in the absence of the knowledge of karma and its performance, even if the desire for its fruits is somehow destroyed, one must seek the means for attaining that [liberation] through the desire for the uninterrupted bliss of Brahman.

One who desires to fully accomplish knowledge might at times engage in its causes, such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; however, this is not the case when there is the state of ritual action and knowledge. Therefore, for this reason as well, ritual actions are not the cause for the destruction of attachment; thus he says: "All... (verse 347).
Then Ānanda was heard directly, yet not made an object by the means of knowledge.
He was not even able to diminish his longing for the bliss he had seen.

Lest it be thought that actions opposed to passion might arise there, and that the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda) heard [in scripture] would suppress all other passions, the author raises this doubt and says: "Now, as for bliss. One situated in the station of Prajāpati does not hear of the bliss of Brahman, because the scriptures have human beings as their intended audience; and even if it were heard, how could that which has never been experienced suppress a passion for a fruit of a similar nature that has not been experienced?
The meaning is that since [the scripture] is not even able to weaken [attachment], let alone reject it, hearing it is not a cause for the destruction of passion for sense objects. || 248 ||
1 ka. What, then, is it?
[vol 1, page 129] 108
The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya: [Regarding the Connection]—The cultivation of the meaning that is its opposite follows for the purpose of dissolving desire.
The injunctions regarding those actions would be the causes for their opposite.

Since worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), ritual action (*karman*), and the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) do not destroy desire, he concludes that only the excellence of the practice of perceiving the defects in sense objects possesses such power. He says, "Desire... etc. The meaning is this: the opposite of that desire is the cognition of defects in sense objects; the cultivation—that is, the repeated practice—of that cognition results in the destruction of attachment to sense objects. Although desirable things are causes for the intensification of attachment to their fruits, [the obligatory rites]—even though they are...

Anticipating the objection that those [obligatory rites] do not cause the destruction of desire because they have names [denoting specific acts] and thus are not the cause of that [destruction], he says: "The injunctions. Since there is a scriptural statement without qualification—namely, "By action, the world of the ancestors"—even obligatory rites possess fruits; therefore, like optional rites, they are causes for the intensification of passion toward their own results. Thus, the "injunctions" regarding their performances—that is, their practices—are the "obstacles" (vipakṣa) to that destruction of desire.
The meaning is that the excellence of [the means] is its expenditure; likewise, because of the practice of perceiving defects, nothing else can bring about its destruction. || 349 ||
The state of Prajāpati is not the fixed gateway to liberation.
No specific distinction of reality is observed within the limiting adjuncts (upādhis). || 350 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "having enjoyed the station of Prajāpati," the question is whether that station is a cause for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) or a cause for the excellence of reality (*tattvotkarṣa*). He says it is not the first: "It is a door. This means it is a door to liberation, which is to say, to the knowledge that is its cause; the sense is that this follows from the non-specific scriptural statement, "Whosoever among the gods... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). He refutes the second alternative with: "For not... (verse 350).
There is no distinction in space itself, despite its association with limiting adjuncts such as jars, troughs, and the like.
Even among things distinguished by distance, proximity, and so forth, whether conceptualized or non-conceptualized. || 351 ||

In this regard, he provides an illustration with the word "no. There, although there is no distinction because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) possess a single uniform nature, one might suspect that there is distinction here because the adjuncts beginning from "human" and ending with "the thread" possess diverse forms; anticipating this doubt, he says "pot," etc. Furthermore, although there is no distinction among the adjuncts in close proximity, one might suspect that there is distinction among those that are remote; anticipating this doubt, he says "far," etc. [This refers to] those that have arisen, are arising, and will arise.
Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction [between the two] with respect to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he says: "Kalpitā" (imagined). || 351 ||
The non-difference of entities is not accepted with respect to the seven principles.
Because its intrinsic nature is abandoned, that distinction between them exists only externally. || 352 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say "Brahman is without distinction like space" because Brahman, being of the nature of the universal existence (*sattā-sāmānya*), possesses distinctions, [the author] raises the dilemma as to whether human beings and so forth—which are its particular manifestations—are non-different or different from Brahman due to their being that very reality (*sat-tattva*), and states the flaw in each case: "In the state of being *sat*... Human beings and others are the specific entities (*bhāva*); there can be no non-difference between them and Brahman, which is of the nature of pure existence (*sad-rūpa*). Therefore, if they were non-different...

The meaning is that, like that [universal], their status as particulars would be destroyed. He addresses the position of difference with the word "existent" (*sat*). The difference of entities is from the existent;

it cannot be by way of existence, because that would entail the non-existence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thinking thus, he refutes the second alternative with the words "by its own nature" (*svabhāva*).

Because they are distinguished from existence by way of non-existence, and because they would lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*), the entire universe would become devoid of both universals and particulars.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, are the particularities (viśeṣas) mutually non-different or different? Not the first, because it would result in the non-duality of particularities and lead to the aforementioned defects. Nor the second; for if they were different by way of existence (*sattva*), it has already been stated that this leads to the non-existence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); and if they were different by way of non-existence (*asattva*), it would follow that the substratum (*dharmin*) itself is non-existent. Thus, both [positions] are untenable. [Notes on variants: 1. kha. *satastvāṃ*; 2. kha. *satasvā*; 3. kha. *satattve*; 4. kha. [omitted].
Ṣaṣṭha | [Vol.
1, page 130] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 109.

He says that even so, there would be only one reality (bhāva) devoid of both generality and particularity; thus he states: "mutually" (*anyonyam*). The syntactical connection is: "because [they] do not have their own respective natures mutually. Then, what is the status of the particularity that appears? To this he says: "particularity" (*viśeṣaḥ*). It is the particularity such as "human" and so forth superimposed upon Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sad-rūpa*); thus, it is excluded from the form of that which is to be accepted.
This is the meaning. || 352 ||
Even in the position that there is cause and effect, the effect does not exist elsewhere than in the cause.
And there is no distinction in reality, just as there is none in gold [regardless of whether it is fashioned] into bracelets and so forth. || 353 ||

Having raised the objection that Brahman possesses attributes because it is a cause, like gold, [the author] considers the alternatives as to whether effects are non-different from or different from it.

Regarding the first alternative, thinking that those [effects] cannot be its effects because they are non-different from it—just like it itself—he refutes the second alternative with the words "kārya" (effect). The meaning is:

even though the world and Brahman stand in the relation of effect and cause, there is no absolute difference between them; for such a state [of absolute difference] does not exist between two things that are thus related, just as it does not exist between a horse and a buffalo. Why?

And are the effects themselves the specific causes within the cause, Brahman, or are they themselves the specificities? It is not the first [option], as he says: "Not... The meaning is that there is no specificity produced by the effect within the reality that is the cause, Brahman, because there is a lack of evidence. Having raised the objection—"The subject under dispute possesses specificities produced by the effect, because it is a cause, like gold"—he says: "Kaṭaka... The word "not" (*na*) is to be supplied here. Kaṭaka...

The meaning is that gold does not possess a specific quality produced by its effects; for even though qualities such as roundness are perceived in those [effects], gold lacks them. Therefore, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*). Nor are the effects themselves the specific qualities, because those things which come and go—being as illusory as a snake—are incapable of being real specific qualities; for even bracelets and the like are not real entities distinct from the nature of the gold itself.
With the intention that these are specific instances, he says: "such as bracelets, etc. (353).
Therefore, the reality in Prajāpati is not distinct from that in a worm.
This is also established through reasoning and scripture, as expressed in such passages as "whosoever he may be. (354)

He concludes the absence of differentiation in Brahman with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The connection is: "Therefore [it is so] by means of reasoning" (*tarkāt*). Fearing that the aforementioned reasoning—beginning with the impossibility of the relation between universal and particular—might be a fallacy because it does not result in a final conclusion, he says: "And from scripture" (*āgamataśca*). For here, by the force of the statement regarding the arising of knowledge without distinction among gods and others, their non-differentiation is established.
The meaning is that this was seen by Brahmā. || 354 ||
When all the desires that dwell in his heart are completely released,
Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman.
He states another scriptural indication (*śrautaliṅga*) for the fact that Brahman is without distinction in all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). [The verse begins with] "When...

Here, it should be understood that Brahman is without distinction in all limiting adjuncts because immortality is predicated of the mortal, because Brahman-hood is ascribed to one who resides in a mortal body, and because of the statement that desires are situated in the heart. || 355 ||
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
The supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities. || 356 ||

Having stated the scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that Brahman is devoid of distinctions, he cites the scripture: "One" (*eka*). [This refers to the state] as the threefold form (*mūrtitraya*). [Note:
*kha* reads *heno'sti*].
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:

The word “one” (*eka*) is used for the purpose of precluding the distinctions established in the *Purāṇas* and other texts. And he will state: “Though one, [the Lord] appears as Hari, Brahmā, Pinākin, and so forth in many ways.”
"It is sung [in scripture]"—this rejects the notion of indivisible insentience. "The God"—this precludes His being like the sun, which remains external.
"In all beings"—to the question of why, then, He is not grasped by all as the Self, He replies: "Hidden.

Anticipating the doubt that there might be a distinction based on the relationship of container and contained, He says: "Pervading all. All this exists through His existence, and is perceived through Him.

The meaning is that because there is manifestation [of this Self] within all beings, there is no real limitation due to non-manifestation. To the objection—how can there be no real limitation when this Self is the inner controller of beings, being both the one to be controlled and the controller—he says: "sarvabhūta... (He is the inner Self of all beings). The meaning is that He alone is the inner Self of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, for the scripture declares His entry into all created beings. If that is so, then what of His power of agency and so forth?

He says "no" because the inner self (*antarātman*) is of such a nature. [Objection: If that is so, then since it is distinct from that [body] by virtue of being the witness to the world's activity, the problem of difference remains;

he says "no," [answering with] "of all. This is the abode (*adhivāsa*) of all beings because it is their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); and since there is no superimposed form without that [substratum], there is no real limitation (*pariccheda*). Because it is a reality, its visibility is inferred like that of a jar.

If it is argued that there is no limitation [of the Self] because there is no dependence on another seer, he says "no," for the reason is the limiting adjunct of insentience (*jaḍatva*). He says "the Witness" (*sākṣī*). Suspecting that there might be limitation due to being the agent of seeing, he says "consciousness" (*cetana*). Suspecting that, like an ordinary seer, it would possess modification due to being a seer, he says "absolute" (*kevala*). Its "seership" consists in its being pure consciousness, as it is the cause of the world's empirical activity by mere proximity.
The meaning is that it is not subject to modification. Some maintain that knowledge and bliss are attributes (*guṇa*) of Brahman; he refutes them by stating "devoid of attributes" (*nirguṇa*).
Furthermore, the sense is that Brahman is of a single essence (*ekarasa*), devoid of all particularities (*viśeṣa*). || 356 ||
If it is said that there is a threefold conjunction of consciousness and karma, [then...]
Because of the previously stated intention that the Veda has a single unified nature, this [position] is not tenable. || 357 ||

Since Brahman is devoid of distinctions in all its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the state of Prajāpati is not necessarily the fixed gateway for attaining it. Thus, it was stated that the idea of ritual acts being causes of knowledge by way of destroying desire is unauthoritative. Now, he states the view that those acts are not causes of knowledge, but rather, when combined with it, they lead only to liberation: "Vijñāna... [Knowledge is primary, action is secondary; or the reverse; or both].

Alternatively, there is a threefold possibility regarding [the means of knowledge]: [that they have] equal primacy, or that one part is primary. Among these, the first—that the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) or the knowledge portion (*jñānabhāga*) is the authority—is not tenable, because the former has as its purport the teaching that rituals alone are the cause of heaven and so forth. Thinking thus, he refutes the second [possibility] with the words "pūrva" (the former). The meaning of the word "former" is that there is nothing other than the subject of the identity of the Self (*aikātmya*) for the words of the Vedānta, and so on. This refers to the *upaniṣad* portion of the Veda. That...

The meaning is that this combination is improper because it lacks scriptural authority; for the texts resolve themselves into the single-flavored Brahman-Self, from which all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been removed, since the indicators of the intended purport (*tātparya*), such as the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth, are perceived therein alone. || 357 ||
Because of the lack of subordination to a single sentence, and likewise because of the impossibility of a single goal to be accomplished.
How can there be a collection of knowledge and action, as there is of substance and quality? || 358 ||

Having stated the common defect regarding the threefold conjunction (*trividhasamuccaya*), he now states it specifically regarding the equal conjunction (*samasamuccaya*). "One" (*ekā*)—this is the meaning: in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, rites such as the *āgneya* are produced by such scriptural injunctions as, "The *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds [is offered] at the new moon and the full moon," and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon; he who, knowing thus, [sacrifices] at the new moon."

And it is heard in the scripture: "He sacrifices. In this regard, do these two injunctions to sacrifice enjoin two previously unknown actions (*apūrva*), or do they refer to the previously mentioned *Āgneya* and other sacrifices?
[This is from the *Śāstraprakāśikā* commentary by Ānandagiri on the *Kārtika* section, volume 1, page 132.]

When there arises a doubt as to whether [the sentences] are restatements of two groups [of acts], since—given examples such as "He offers the *samidhs*"—the injunction of distinct acts would follow from repetition (*abhyāsa*), it was concluded in the second book (PMS 2.2.3) that the acts under discussion are the basis for the two statements connected with the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices, because no difference in form (*rūpa*) has been stated; this was established in the section beginning with "But because there is no mention of form on the Full Moon day. Therefore, just as [in the case of] the sacrifice...

Because the mention of the "collection" (*samudāya*) in the phrase "by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices" serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*), the duality [of the sacrifice] is established by way of the governing injunction (*adhikāra*). Since the Āgneya and other constituent rites are connected to a single governing injunction, they are equally primary; thus, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) regarding the unseen potency (*apūrva*) and so forth. However, this is not the case for knowledge and ritual action.
Regarding that very point, he states another reason: "sādhya... (the result). This is the meaning: is there a connection with the fruit for each of the Āgneya and other rites individually, or...

In this regard, when there is a doubt as to whether these [actions] have separate fruits, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the principal acts—produced by originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) that do not depend on one another—each individually require a fruit, the single fruit mentioned in proximity to them must be connected with each one. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached through the eleventh book (*adhyāya*), starting from the sūtra "Because of the connection with a purpose, there is separateness" (*prayojanābhisaṃbandhāt pṛthaktvam*). Since the fruit is enjoined by means of the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which denotes the collection (*samudāya*) of those acts, the fruit is common (*tantra*) to them all. Thus, because they are expressed as a collective whole, the fruit belongs to the group as a unit.

It was considered that there is no identity of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) between knowledge and action—which have respectively certain and uncertain fruits; therefore, how could there be a combination (*samuccaya*) of them? Since there is no combination because they stand in the relationship of subordinate and principal, he provides a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) beginning with "dravya" (substance). Its meaning is as follows: when there is a single purpose, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) because substance and quality perform a single function. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, one buys Soma with a red, one-year-old cow (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā somam krīṇāti*); therein, the redness...

Having raised the doubt as to whether [the quality of redness] applies to the entire section or specifically to the purchase by means of the one-year-old cow (*vaikahāyanī*), it is argued that although the connection with the purchase is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*) from the instrumental case-ending in "one purchases with the red one" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), because a quality is incorporeal and thus cannot directly connect with the action, the syntactical connection must be set aside;

rather, by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is applied as a subordinate element to any substance mentioned in the context. This being the position reached, [the author replies] regarding the statement "one should sacrifice with a cow": [it refers to] the generic form (*ākṛti*).

Even though quality is formless (*amūrta*), it can be connected with the purchase because it delimits the substance that serves as the means of purchase; thus, since there is no contingency of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), the third [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] establishes that, by virtue of the sentence, there is a mutual restriction (*itaretara-niyama*) between the redness (*aruṇa*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), such that the redness is placed in the one-year-old cow specifically for the purpose of the purchase. Where the unity of purpose (*arthaikya*) of a substance and a quality is heard in scripture, there those two should be restricted to a single ritual act (*padārtha*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that because there is a single purpose, for here only one purpose—namely, the connection with the purchase—is heard in the scripture. Thus, just as there is no combination of the redness (*aruṇa*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) in the act of purchase by way of subordinate and principal elements, so too there can be no combination of knowledge and action as subsidiary and primary members when they are not understood to function as means toward a single end; he states this conclusion regarding the threefold impossibility of combination. Whence, then, could there be a combination of knowledge and [action]?
Of Rmaṇo. || 358 ||
I [am that] which, by being the locus of both difference and non-difference, [unites] knowledge and action into a single essence.
Since mutual assistance would be lost, what kind of synthesis could there be? (359)
In that very context, he states another argument: "bhedeti" (regarding difference). A conjunction (*samuccaya*) is invariably concomitant with the relationship of the benefited and the benefactor.

Here, however, there is no mutual relationship of the benefited and the benefactor between the action based on the distinctions of agency and so forth, and the cognition of the non-dual Self which is devoid of those [distinctions];
therefore, due to the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the conjunction pervaded by it also does not exist—this is the meaning. || 359 ||
The knowledge of the true nature of the deity and the sacrificial substance has become an auxiliary part of ritual action.
For indeed, that ritual action remains such only so long as the substance and the deity are not known.

Anticipating the objection that "the knowledge under discussion is eligible for combination with ritual action because it is a form of knowledge, like the knowledge of deities and so forth," he says: "The deity...
[ka. kha. omits this, stating "not having spoken of the fruit"].
112 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection]...

"Being a limb of ritual action" means being included within it, which is to say, having that as its body. The point is this: since knowledge of the deity and so forth is included within ritual action and is of the same nature as it, it cannot be combined with it; therefore, [the opponent's argument] suffers from the fallacy of lacking the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*). [Objection: But knowledge of the deity and so forth is not included within ritual action, because one can perform ritual action even without it—as seen in the Vedic text, "By that, both perform [the sacrifice]. Therefore, since it is a different thing, it must be combined with ritual action.

"No," he says, "only so long. For that is indeed action where one who knows the substance and the deity performs the sacrifice; for according to the Śruti, "Having known [the deity], one should undertake the action," and according to the Smṛti, "Having known [it], you ought to perform here the action as prescribed by the scriptural injunctions. But it is not that [action] where the substance and the deity are unknown; for [the Śruti states]:
"He who, indeed, being ignorant of the seer, the metre, the deity, and the Brāhmaṇa [of a mantra], performs a sacrifice or teaches [it]..."
The meaning is that knowledge of the deity and so forth is included within ritual action, because of the scriptural censure: "He approaches a pillar or falls into a pit. (360)
Because of the greater number of constituent parts in its specific variety, there is a greater abundance of fruit; therefore [this is so].
For him, there would be no conjunction; nor could there be a conjunction of the member with the possessor of the members. || 361 ||

If it is argued that one who does not know the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the deities and other factors would not perform ritual action (*karman*), then how can it be accepted in the passage "by that [knowledge] both perform [the sacrifice]"? To this he replies: "In its particularity" (*tad-viśeṣa*). Because of the abundance of the ritual action when it is joined with a specific auxiliary (*aṅga-viśeṣa*) consisting of the cognition of the true nature of the deities and so forth, there is also an abundance of its fruit, according to such scriptural passages as "Whatever one performs with knowledge," and so on; therefore, even for one devoid of the worship of the deity, the ritual action— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...is not entirely lacking in efficacy. Thus, while the fruit of the ritual action performed by one who knows the truth is indeed greater than that of one who does not, it is not the case that the latter's action is entirely fruitless. This is because the scripture teaches that even the mere performance of the ritual action yields some result. Therefore, the statement "both perform [it]" remains consistent. Furthermore, since the ritual action is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) to knowledge, it is logical that the fruit of knowledge is superior.
