[The opponent argues: "There would be performance [of the rite], but not an abundance of fruit, because of the principle 'for by knowledge alone' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3). To this he replies: "No," meaning that it is not so. Anticipating the objection—"In a ritual action possessing an excellence of fruit, since there is an abundance even of its subsidiaries, and because the knowledge of the deity and so forth is combined with that [action] due to having the same single fruit, how can the illustrative example be deficient in the probandum?"—he says: "Combination. By "of that" (*tasya*), the knowledge of the deity and so forth is meant. The word "subsidiary" (*aṅga*)...

The subject matter is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The term "principal" (*aṅgin*) refers to that which possesses an essential nature non-different from them. Thus, it should be understood that there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the *darśa* sacrifice and others, by way of the subsidiary acts such as the *prayāja*s—which have their own established essential natures—contributing toward the result. Alternatively, even for the *prayāja*s and other subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is no conjunction with the principal *darśapūrṇamāsa* itself; rather, [conjunction occurs] only with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as qualified by those [subsidiaries].

Since the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and others are the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for attaining heaven and so forth, they constitute the instrument (*karaṇa*) precisely when accompanied by their specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*); likewise, although knowledge of the deity and other factors is a subsidiary part of the ritual action, it is only that action as qualified by such knowledge which is the most effective means for the abundance of the fruit. Therefore, the establishment of a combination (*samuccaya*) with that [knowledge] alone is not achieved. || 369 ||
Furthermore, that knowledge of the identity of the self is the sole devourer of ignorance.
That being so, whence could there be action, or what need for an object within its range? (362)

Having stated that the example of the knowledge of deities and so forth lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*), he states a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) for the reason "because it is knowledge" (*jñānatva*): "And that which... The meaning is: the subject under dispute (*vimata*) is not conjoined with ritual action (*karman*) because it is opposed to it; whatever is opposed to something is not conjoined with it, just as light is not conjoined with darkness. Light does not depend on darkness for its own effect, whereas knowledge does depend on action for that [effect]; therefore, it is not [conjoined with it].

Anticipating the objection that the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*) because [knowledge] "wears away" [ignorance], he says: "What else? The meaning is this: the object (*gocara*) of this knowledge is liberation (*apavarga*), which consists in the identity of Brahman and the Self; in that regard, it has no dependence on anything else, for it is observed in the case of the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like that right cognition is independent with respect to its own fruit. || 362 ||
The knowledge of being a Brahmin and so forth [is the cause] of rituals such as the Agnihotra.
Whatever is seen for the sake of accomplishing the goal is indeed in accordance with that very action.

Now, one might object: "Since the subject of the inference is the knowledge belonging to the agent-self (kartṛ), how can there be a counter-inference? In that case, would it not be a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā)? To this he says: [The *Brāhmaṇavārttika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri, page 134].

"Let him eat [the sacrificial remains]. According to the Vedic scripture, "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," even Agnihotra and other rites performed by a Śūdra—who lacks such entitlement—are fruitless.

Therefore, the knowledge of a Brāhmaṇa and others regarding the results aimed at through those rites—such as that seen in texts like "A Brāhmaṇa [attains heaven] by the Bṛhaspatisava"—is auxiliary to the ritual action. Thus, the meaning is that there is no harm even if his [the Śūdra's] knowledge is combined with the ritual action. || 363 ||
Because, upon the realization of the true nature of the reality of oneness, [notions of] birth and so forth are sublated.
Not only would there be no action, but on the contrary, there would be non-action regarding all deeds.

Furthermore, regarding the combination [of knowledge] with ritual actions—whether performed after the arising of knowledge, or those acquired in previous births, or those performed in this very life prior to the arising of knowledge—the author states the defect in the first case: "aikātmya... (oneness with the Self). The word *kriyā* refers to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

Since oneness with the Self alone is the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmya*), because everything else is superimposed, when that [oneness] is realized through the verbal [instruction], there is no further realization of anything else.

Because there would be a sublation of the place, caste, and other factors that serve as the causes for those [rites], the performance of the rites prompted by them could not be established; and thus, how could there be a combination of knowledge with ritual acts that follow after it? He refutes the second [position] with the words "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*). The construction is as follows:

not only is that [combination] unestablished, but on the contrary, there is the very non-existence of rituals—denoted by the term "inaction"—which is the opposite of performance. By means of the direct realization of the Self—

The meaning is that since knowledge has been discarded, there is an absence of karma acquired in other births which would have that [ignorance] as its root; therefore, even for those [karmas], a conjunction with knowledge is impossible. || 364 ||
The cognition of a snake or similar object where none exists is the cause for fleeing.
When the cognition of the rope has destroyed the notion of the snake, one regrets even what was already done.

Anticipating the objection that while the effects of ignorance cease upon its cessation, the effects of *karman* do not—because they are not caused by ignorance—the author says: "Furthermore... First of all, a rope-snake and the like are unreal objects; the cognition thereof is "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) because it is opposed to true knowledge. That this [ignorance] is the cause for such things as fleeing from it is well-established in the world. In the same way, *karman*s are also rooted in ignorance; for it is the ignorant person who, desiring [results], performs them. Therefore...

The meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, that [bondage] is destroyed. Anticipating the third objection—that there might be a combination of knowledge with those karmas belonging to the time prior to the arising of knowledge in the very birth in which knowledge occurs—the author says: "As in the case of a rope. Just as in the world, when the knowledge arises that "this is a rope," the wise man, due to the cessation of the cause [of fear], regrets his previously performed actions such as fleeing; so too does one who has realized the truth.

One feels remorse, thinking, "For all this time, bound by bondage, I have performed actions in vain"; therefore, there can be no combination [of karma] even with those actions belonging to the present life that occurred prior to knowledge, according to the principle established in the *Adhikaraṇa* on "The Attainment of That" (*tadadhigama*). This is the intended meaning. || 369 ||
There is no activity of karma in liberation, because of the absence of acquisition and so forth.
And since the direct scriptural statements (śruti) and so forth do not apply there, there can be no combination (samuccaya).

He states another argument for the absence of a synthesis of knowledge and action in every respect: "Not action," etc. Anticipating the objection that there is indeed a synthesis—based on such scriptural passages as "Both knowledge and ignorance" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12) and such traditional texts as "Food joined with honey" (Mahābhārata)—he says: "Nor," etc. The sense is that those scriptures and traditional texts which speak of synthesis do so by way of a sequential synthesis. He then states the consequence of this lack of evidence [for simultaneous synthesis]:
"By that," [it is said]. || 366 ||

For direct knowledge (*vijñāna*) is indeed internal, because it rests solely upon the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*).
But external action would be [so called] because it depends upon external substances. || 367 ||

He states that there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action because they are respectively strong and weak, according to the maxim: "Between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger.
He says: "For the internal... (367).
When internal consciousness is present, that which is external is not established.
But ritual action is merely a purifier; it serves to destroy ignorance through knowledge. || 368 ||

Anticipating the objection that even an internal factor may depend upon an external one due to the requirements of the task at hand—just as we see that even a king, though internally powerful, depends on his chief minister for matters such as marriage—the author says: "When [it exists]. The meaning is this: when knowledge, which is the internal means to liberation, exists, ritual action, which is its external means, no longer functions; because ignorance, the cause of that [action], has been destroyed, there is no dependence on action once action is absent. Let it be so.

If it is argued that there is a combination of external action with internal knowledge for the sake of liberation because action requires knowledge, he says "no," [stating] "it is a purifier" (*saṃskārakam*).

The meaning is that if actions were a means to liberation, there would be a combination [with knowledge] by way of requiring knowledge; however, that is not the case, because it has already been stated previously that they are employed for a different purpose. Furthermore, knowledge also purifies the person, since it is a Vedic means, just like action.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From knowledge" (jñānāt). The meaning is: "The subject under dispute is the remover of ignorance, because it is knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), like the knowledge of a rope. || 368 ||
The cognition of the self as it truly is; actions are based solely on delusion.
When right knowledge has arisen, how can there be action? For action, which is the cause [of rebirth], has been destroyed. || 369 ||

Then, having raised the objection that ritual action (*karman*) must also remove ignorance because it is a means to the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), just like knowledge, he states that "being the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). He says "just as... [to illustrate]. He further states "delusion... to show that ritual action does not remove ignorance because it conforms to what is contrary to reality, like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Having raised the objection that although isolated ritual action does not remove ignorance, it might do so when combined [with knowledge], he says:

Regarding the word "rightly" (*samyak*): since it is not observed that knowledge effects the cessation of karma, how can there be an absence of karma at that time? To this, he says: "Karma... (verse 369).
And consciousness is eternally attained by the inner self, because of its constant proximity.
Action is impermanent and distinct in form, while that which is permanent sublates the impermanent. || 370 ||

Anticipating the objection that knowledge (*jñāna*), like action (*karman*), is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*) and therefore shares its same status of being and non-being, he says: "eternal" (*nitya*). The meaning is that since knowledge—consisting of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) which is the very nature of the Self—is eternal, it does not share the same status as action. He states the reason for its eternity: "of the inner witness" (*pratīcaḥ*). Because the inner witness exists everywhere and at all times as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the knowledge called the light of consciousness, which has that [witness] as its essence, is indeed eternal.

The sense is that [the seeker] shakes off bondage along with its cause only by means of the cognition arising from the statement. Anticipating the objection that action, like knowledge, must be performed eternally—otherwise the commencement of *saṃsāra* would result—he says: "Action. For action, being enjoined as something to be done, [is not the means to liberation].

The meaning is that there is no beginning to saṃsāra, because its cause—ignorance—is beginningless. He states the reason for the impermanence of karma with the word "separately" (pṛthak). The meaning is that because it depends on various causal factors, karma is manifold; therefore, it is impermanent. This [is said] in consideration of the permanence of knowledge and the impermanence of karma.

115 He states the point established by his own [arguments]: "And it is eternal," etc. The Self, which is pure consciousness (*dṛg-ātman*), when conjoined with a specific modification of the mental faculty (*dhī-vṛtti*) in the form of the non-dual Brahman (*niṣprapañca-brahma*), destroys ignorance along with its effects—which is the cause of the appearance of that which is contrary to itself. Therefore, there is no contradiction between knowledge and action, as they possess distinct natures.
The meaning is "a collection. || 370 ||
The world is produced by karma and is subject to decay; [liberation occurs] through the realization of the self up to the realm of Brahmā.
When sovereignty over the three worlds has been obtained, what man indeed would care for alms?

In that very context, he states another reason: "perishable" (*kṣayī*). The meaning is that because their fruits are contradictory, there can be no combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action, just as there is none between a painting and a mirror. Now, one might object: even when a seeker of liberation possesses knowledge, although the desire for liberation ceases, the longing for the fruits of action does not cease; therefore, since one performs action for that purpose, the establishment of their combination is secured. To this, he replies: "attained" (*labdhe*). (Verse 371)
Knowledge belongs to a different category; it is not desired through action.
And because of contradiction, that [action] is independent and subordinate to nothing else. // 372 //

Having stated the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action either as subordinate and primary or as equally primary, [the author] raises the alternative: "Is this combination—wherein action is primary and knowledge is subordinate—the one relevant to the present context, or is it known from scripture (*śruti*) and other sources? Having thus proposed the first option, he refutes it with the word "bhinnā" (distinct). He refutes the second option with the word "kāṅkṣitam" (sought); for knowledge is not sought after by means of action.

The meaning is that since the general relationship between those two is not established by their very nature, their specific relationship cannot be established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth. Furthermore, an object of assistance has a requirement for an agent of assistance; however, no such relationship exists between these two because they possess contradictory natures, and thus there can be no combination (*samuccaya*). He states this with the words "and because of contradiction. Anticipating the objection that even if knowledge is subordinate to action, it is not independent because it is subordinate toward its own fruit, he says:
Regarding the word "guṇa": the sense is that liberation (kaivalya), which is the fruit of knowledge, is non-different from that [knowledge]. || 372 ||
Because this [cognition] conforms to the object and does not depend on the will of the knower.
Therefore, knowledge is said to be independent for the sake of destroying ignorance. || 373 ||

Just as action depends on an agent, so too knowledge depends on a knower; therefore, anticipating the objection that it is not independent, he says: "Since... Even so, one might ask how that which depends on an object can be independent; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Through ignorance... The phrase "dependence on an object" is what is referred to by the word "tena" (by that). "Independent" means that, with respect to its own fruit, it does not depend on any other cause. || 373 ||
Furthermore, it is clearly not heard anywhere that there is a non-return from karmas.
However, it is heard repeatedly in the Śruti that non-return [to saṃsāra] occurs through knowledge alone. || 374 ||
Fearing that there might be a combination [of means] where action is primary and knowledge is secondary—rather than the opposite—he says:

"And non-return. The meaning is that since knowledge, which is the cause of liberation, has no requirement for actions which are not its causes, even a contrary combination is precluded. Furthermore, fearing the objection that liberation from actions is heard of in such passages as "he does not return again," he says: [the following].

"Clearly" (sphuṭam): the sense is that it is not the case that actions are the cause of non-return there, because for one who meditates [on Brahman], gradual liberation is established according to such principles as "upon the exhaustion of the effects, he, together with their presiding deity... and so forth. Having raised the objection that knowledge, like action, cannot be the cause of non-return because it is a Vedic means (*sādhana*), he says: "From knowledge" (*jñānāt*). The fact that knowledge is the means to non-return is its fruit...
1. Herein, this is the explanation:

The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that this has already been established in the chapter on the *Saṃbandha*. Having raised the doubt that the scripture (*śruti*) there might have another purpose, he says: "In many places.
This refers to such scriptural passages as, "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death," and so forth. (374)
And consciousness is of a single form, because its object of cognition is of a single form.
Actions take on diverse forms by depending upon many factors.

Having rejected the combination of knowledge and action on the grounds that one is subordinate and the other is primary, he now refutes that very same combination—this time on the grounds of their being equally primary—by means of another argument.
He says, "And of a single form," and then, anticipating the objection that actions might also possess a single uniform nature just like knowledge, he says, "Diverse. (371)
For liberation, which is of a single nature, there can be no means that is of a diverse nature.
For liberation is of a single nature, and its means of accomplishment is likewise of a single nature.
Anticipating the objection that those very manifold forms might act together toward the liberation of knowledge, he says: "of that which has a single form.
Anticipating the objection that even knowledge cannot be the means for liberation—which is eternal—because that would contradict its eternity, he says: "of that which has a single form.
He illustrates the maxim "the capable is conjoined with the capable" by means of the first particle *hi*; by the second [particle],...
This indicates that even for liberation, which is eternal, there is a dependence upon knowledge once the obstacles have been destroyed. || 376 ||
Therefore, the fruit of action is manifold, arising from manifold actions.
The scriptures have demonstrated that for the agent [of action], [rebirth] occurs among gods, humans, and animals. || 377 ||

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what is the fruit of actions?", he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is that liberation, being of a single nature, is not the fruit of action. He states the reason for the diversity of worldly pleasure: "Diverse" (*nānā*). To the question, "Whose fruit is this action?", he replies: "Of the gods" (*deva*), etc. This fruit belongs to the agent existing in various wombs, not to one who desires to know Brahman.
The meaning is that this has been stated in the scriptures with such passages as "one who desires," and so forth. || 377 ||
But others, certain proponents of profound reasoning, consider it thus.
In the Veda, the dissolution of some particular distinction is understood in certain places.

By refuting the position that [the ritual section] is a subsidiary to the knowledge-section (brahmakāṇḍa) through the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*)—which was stated by way of the alternative view that [ritual action] leads to the destruction of desire—it was established through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the ritual section is subsidiary to the knowledge-section. Now, he raises the following view: "The method of elimination is not established, because the ritual section is subsidiary to the other [knowledge-section] by way of dissolving the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This is introduced with the words "But others... He uses the term "others" to indicate that the refutation of the view about to be stated will be easy.

Regarding the term "sati" (being): it refers, in effect, to those who propound fallacious arguments (*nyāyābhāsa*). Anticipating the objection that if the scripture has as its ultimate goal the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then the mere statement "there is no conceptual proliferation" would suffice—what is the use of such extensive proliferation in the Veda? [The author] says: "of difference" (*bhedasya*).
The meaning is that because of the multiplicity of things to be negated, it is appropriate for the Veda, which performs the negation, to be likewise extensive. || 378 ||
The dissolution of the notion of the body as the self is like that in the phrase "one who desires heaven."
In this context, it is understood that the body is the agent [of action] and heaven is the object of experience. || 379 ||

Anticipating the objection that ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) inform us of their own results and do not indicate the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he says: "The body" (*deha*). Just as there is a relationship of subordinate and principal between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) according to the manner stated, so too, by way of illustration, the dissolution of the identity of the body and the self (*dehātmatva*) is understood from the sentence containing the term *svargakāma* (desiring heaven); therefore, the meaning is that its purport lies in that dissolution. Now, one might object: "This [injunction] is intended to establish that sacrifice is the means to heaven; it does not have the dissolution of anything as its purport."
[Kārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
[Page 138] "From the body," etc. For here, the qualified seeker (adhikārī) is established as one capable of experiencing heaven at another time and so forth.

Furthermore, the self is distinct from the body, because once the body has been reduced to ashes right here, the enjoyment [of results] by that [self] would be impossible; therefore, since the dissolution of the identity of the self with the body is what must be known, the purport of the statement lies precisely therein. If the statement were intent on establishing [the self], the transcendence of the body could not be known, as it would be contradicted by perception in the form "I am a human being. However, if its purport is the dissolution [of that identity], there is no such contradiction; for even when it contradicts perception, a statement by a reliable person (āpta) regarding that purport is more powerful—just as in the case of the statement, "This is not a snake"—and this applies to the sacrifice as well.

The meaning is that even by means of a sentence intended for another purpose, the fact that [the ritual] is a means to attain heaven can be known through the principle of the *Devatādhikaraṇa*; thus, the *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) passage is indeed devoted solely to dissolution (*laya*). || 379 ||
In the case of "by means of milking," here too there is the dissolution of one who has another qualification.
Because he possesses the authority over those already authorized, no other person is authorized. || 380 ||
Nevertheless, suspecting that this might be a mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*) because another sentence lacks that specific intent, he says: "By means of the *godohana* [vessel].

Regarding the statement, "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] by means of the *godohana*," he provides the reason why there is a cognition of dissolution for an independent agent distinct from the one qualified for the *darśa* and other sacrifices: "The qualified [agent]," etc. He who desires heaven is [the one qualified for] the *darśa*—

The meaning is that since the person already qualified for the [Soma] sacrifice is the same one who desires cattle, he has no independent qualification for the *godohana* vessel; therefore, it is logical that the *godohana* sentence also intends to sublate [the general injunction]. || 380 ||
The dissolution of the fluctuations arising from passion and the like occurs directly through prohibitions.
Even in the case of their dissolution during ritual procedures, it occurs due to their being assigned to other tasks.

Having stated that the purport of the injunctions for optional rites (*kāmya-vidhi*) lies in that [realization], he says that the purport of the prohibitory statements (*niṣedha-vākya*) also lies in that very same place: "From passion... (*rāgād*). He states that the injunctions for obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites also have that as their purport: "In the injunctions... (*vidhiṣu*). The meaning is that even in the injunctions for obligatory and occasional rites, the absence of natural inclinations (*svābhāvika-pravṛtti*) is manifested. If so, how then is there a distinction between injunction and prohibition? To this, he says: "The effect... (*kāryā-*)...

The meaning is as follows: by means of the injunction regarding another activity—namely, "one should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and in the morning"—those injunctions for obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth, which bring about the lack of opportunity for any other task at that time, result in the non-performance of such other tasks when they are absent. || 381 ||
And even in the world, there is the direct prevention of one from an undesired path.
Or rather, let it be understood that even in the Veda, [the absence of a thing] is established in this way by the instruction of another path.
Anticipating the objection—"Why would they not simply state non-existence itself, as that involves less conceptual complexity?"—he says: "In the world also...
The meaning is that since the world and the Veda follow the same method, the authority of the world does not fail to apply to the Veda which conforms to it. || 382 ||
Thus, by way of the path of activity and dissolution arising from causes such as passion and the rest.
All injunctions without exception are established for the purpose of qualifying one for the knowledge of the Self. (383)

He concludes that the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is subordinate to the injunction for knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) by means of the dissolution of its manifold expansion (*prapañca-laya*). [The word] "thus" (*evam*) refers to this.

The dissolution of activity (*pravṛtti-laya*) is also indicative of the dissolution of the body and so forth. "Authority" (*adhikāra*) means an injunction (*niyoga*). The term "prescription" (*vidhi*) is also indicative of prohibitions (*niṣedha*). || 383 ||
1. But he who [is the master] of these...
[vol 1, page 139] 118
This is not so, because not all injunctions regarding ritual action are found in the Śruti.
They expect another result from the action understood through their own words. || 384 ||

He refutes the position that the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is subordinate to the injunction for knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) by means of the dissolution of distinctions through the words "Not this" (*neti*).

Whether the injunctions of action are for one seeking liberation, or for one seeking heaven, or for one seeking merely the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), or for one desiring to understand the object of the injunction for knowledge, they all declare the non-existence of the phenomenal world; among these, he first rejects the initial alternative with the words "Since" (*yataḥ*). All injunctions of action are heard in the Śruti.

The meaning is that they do not require another fruit called liberation (mokṣa) distinct from the fruits such as heaven understood from their own words; therefore, they would not have taught the non-existence of the phenomenal world (prapañca) for that purpose. || 384 ||
Because the Vedas have as their primary intent the performance of ritual acts, dissolution is nowhere understood from them.
For how could the non-existence of the scriptural declaration of fruit be something to be established if it were itself fruitless? (385)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "the Veda. For nowhere in the *karmakāṇḍa* is the dissolution of any duality ever perceived, since its purpose lies in ritual performance; nor is the absence of phenomenal diversity the cause of heaven, but rather action itself. Therefore, the injunctions regarding action would not teach the absence of that [diversity] to one who desires heaven—this is the meaning. He states the reason for the focus on performance with the word "fruit" (*phala*): [namely,] heaven and so forth.

The section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is that which, upon hearing [the Vedas], is intent upon the performance of sacrifices and other rites as a means to those [results]. He replies to the third [objection] with the words "for it is a non-existence" (*abhāvo hi*). The meaning is this: the non-existence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is not something to be accomplished, because it is a non-existence, like the hair of a tortoise; and because it is not a human goal, like the non-existence of a son and so forth. Therefore, since there can be no desire for that alone, injunctions do not concern one who seeks that [non-existence], nor do they concern one who already possesses the knowledge of the non-existence of phenomenal proliferation. || 385 ||
Nor does the comprehension of an object ever arise from dissolution.
Because it is logically consistent even in the case of non-existence, and because there is no perception [of objects] even in deep sleep. || 386 ||

He refutes the fourth [position] with the words "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*). The object of the injunction to know is the means for that knowledge, just as the ritual action is the means for the injunction regarding heaven; however, the absence of the phenomenal world (*prapañcābhāva*) is not the cause for the knowledge of the Self. For the comprehension of a real entity never occurs through the dissolution [of the world] and so forth; therefore, this [absence of the world] is not the object of the injunction to know. [The meaning is: the absence of the phenomenal world [is not the object] of the knowledge of the Self—

He clarifies the nature of causality with the words "even in the absence. The meaning is this: just as the cognition of the oneness of the moon arises through authoritative testimony (*āptavākya*) and so forth even while the cognition of two moons persists, so too it is logical that the realization of Brahman occurs through scripture (*śruti*) and other means even when the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is absent and the body and such still exist; therefore, the absence of the phenomenal world is not the cause of that realization. Having stated that there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between that [realization] and that [absence], he states that there is also no positive concomitance (*anvaya*), with the words "and in deep sleep" (*suṣupte ca*).

The meaning is that even though the absence of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) exists during states such as dissolution (pralaya) or fainting (mūrchā), because the knowledge of Brahman is not observed there, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya). || 386 ||
If phenomenal manifestation were intrinsic, it could not be ceased.
If it is argued that the cessation of the effect occurs upon the destruction of the cause, [we reply] that the cessation of the effect does not occur by itself.

It has already been stated that because the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is not established by knowledge, it cannot be the object of an injunction regarding that [knowledge]. Now, having raised the alternative that the absence of phenomenal proliferation—whether beginningless or with a beginning—is the object of the injunction for knowledge, he refutes the first position with the words "if it were inherent" (*svābhāvika*). The phrase "like consciousness" (*caitanyavat*) is to be supplied as the remainder. He rejects the second position with the words "if it were produced" (*kāryaśced*). The cause of phenomenal proliferation—
1 1 ka. 'tyato | 2 kha. kārya cetkā | 3 kha. kārye cedi | [vol 1, page 140]
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

Knowledge does not exist without the destruction [of the world], nor is there its destruction without knowledge; therefore, because of the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—that the destruction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) results from knowledge, and that knowledge [results] from that [destruction]—[the argument is untenable].
The absence of conceptual proliferation is the object of knowledge and injunction; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 387 ||
The dissolution of the entire manifold world cannot be accomplished by anyone.
The dissolution of one's own senses and so forth during sleep occurs by itself, not through scriptural injunction.

Furthermore, regarding the destruction of the phenomenal world (prapañca) along with its cause—is this the destruction of the whole, or of only a portion thereof? It is not the first case; thus he says: "In its entirety" (*kṛtsna*). The phrase "without the knowledge of the Self" (*ātma-jñānaṃ vinā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The sense is that although the Lord is capable of destroying the phenomenal world without exception, He does not enter into the injunction of knowledge as one who is to be enjoined. In the second case, [if it were the destruction] of any particular part thereof—

Whether that [object] is the external object itself or the internal sense-faculty (*indriya*) and so forth, it cannot be the former; for if it were, even one who strikes a pot would experience the arising of [that] knowledge.

Thinking thus, he states another alternative: "one's own sense-faculties, etc. The meaning is that since the dissolution of one's own sense-faculties and so forth during sleep and similar states is natural (*svābhāvika*), it does not depend upon scriptural human effort (*puṃvyāpāra*); therefore, it is not an object of an injunction (*niyoga*). || 388 ||
Furthermore, because there is rebirth for one who has arisen, non-annihilation is suspected.
In that case, there would be a lack of confidence even regarding what you yourself have accepted.

In this context, one might raise the following objection: even though there is a dissolution of the senses and other faculties, that dissolution is not absolute, because for one who has awakened, those [faculties] exist just as before; therefore, since its absolute destruction depends upon an injunction, it must be the object of a mandatory command (*niyoga*). This is the doubt expressed by the words "of one who has arisen" (*utthitasya*). Whether the existence of those very same senses and so forth is postulated for one who has arisen from the perspective of the senses, or whether it is postulated for the cause of those [senses] during sleep and so on—in the first case, its manifestation...

Considering that if existence were in the form of being unmanifest, there would be a contradiction with states such as deep sleep (*svāpa*) in the first case, he addresses the second alternative, saying:

"It follows. If the senses and so forth exist in an unmanifest state during sleep and the like, then even when the senses and other factors—which are the objects of the injunctions regarding knowledge according to your own admission—dissolve, their existence would still be possible in an unmanifest form, just as in sleep; consequently, there would be no cessation of them.
The meaning is that liberation is not established due to doubt. || 389 ||
Then, by subsisting on air alone, the cause of differentiation is destroyed.
It is not the case that a cause ever perishes through the destruction of its effect.

In cases such as sleep, because there is no destruction of the cause [of the world], the subsequent emergence of the senses and so forth is logical; however, in the case of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) dependent upon knowledge and ritual injunction (*niyoga*), this is not so, because the cause of that [world] has been destroyed. Thus, resolving this lack of confidence, he takes up the second [alternative]. He says "the phenomenal world" (*prapañca*). Is the destruction of the phenomenal world the cause for the destruction of its cause—namely, knowledge and ritual injunction—or is it knowledge and ritual injunction themselves? It is not the first; he says "not so. For nowhere is there [a case of] the destruction of a cause by means of the destruction of its effect.
The cause is seen to perish; therefore, the meaning is that the destruction of phenomenal proliferation is not caused by the destruction of its cause. || 390 ||
Because even the cause, which is ignorance, is destroyed through the realization of reality.
Therefore, for the purpose of destroying ignorance, the dissolution of the phenomenal world is fruitless. || 391 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the cause" (*kāraṇasya*). The ellipsis is: "The injunction of knowledge does not destroy its cause. Nor can some real entity (*vastu*) itself be the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because even through an injunction, it would not cease, just like consciousness; this is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*). Now, one might object: since the injunction of knowledge has the purpose of removing ignorance by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world, it is indeed required. To this he replies: [the text continues...]
1. Not his "ka. 2. Kha: "at the beginning, one's own sense-faculties... 3. Kha: "he declares.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the *Saṃbandha*]:

Regarding the word "yataḥ" (since): because it is precisely the knowledge of the reality (*vastubodha*) that is required for the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), therefore the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañcalaya*) is fruitless and cannot be an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). What, then, is the need for an injunction (*niyoga*) by way of that [dissolution]? This is the meaning. || 391 ||
For it is through the knowledge of the rope and so forth that the manifestation of the snake and other such things is dissolved.
Even when the appearance of the snake has dissolved, this rope is not perceived in the darkness. || 392 ||

Anticipating the objection that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), like the application of knowledge (*jñānaniyoga*), cannot be the cause for the destruction of ignorance because the delusion of a snake is observed again even in one who has known the true nature of the rope, he says: "In the case of the rope... The sense is that since the dissolution of that [delusion] is understood from the aforementioned knowledge, it is accepted that the destruction of ignorance results from the knowledge of reality; this is the remainder of the argument. How then is there the perception of a snake there at another time? Anticipating this objection—

Thinking that [this knowledge] arises from another cognition, he states the proof for that case: "In the case of a snake," etc. Even when the appearance of a snake superimposed on a rope has subsided, if it is not perceived again at a later time while darkness persists, then—due to the influence of another error, because of the absence of the ignorance that was the cause of the previous appearance of the snake, and because of the absence of that [prior] cognition—it is understood that there is a different [subsequent] cognition. Nor is there any violation of established doctrine in accepting multiple ignorances within a single substrate.

The sense is this: because it is accepted that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions; and because even in the case of Brahman, the consequence of multiple ignorances—like that of a rope—is not a cause for non-liberation, since those two (ignorance and cognition) are distinct by virtue of being qualified and unqualified respectively, and because even in that [Brahman], a difference in their forms is admitted, and furthermore because of the scriptural text: "In the end, there is the cessation of the entire illusion. || 392 ||
For us, valid cognition is restricted to the conventional, because there is a distinction between the objects of things and [ultimate] reality.
Now, that measure applies to the object, but it would not apply to dissolution nor to duality.

It has been stated that the dissolution (*laya*)—whether of a portion or of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), whether beginningless or with a beginning—is not the object of an injunction (*niyoga*). Furthermore, is the scriptural [subject] merely the dissolution of the phenomenal world, or the reality (*vastu*) alone, or both? It is said that it is not the first; thus he says: "By dissolution... In a scripture whose subject is merely the dissolution of the phenomenal world, reality is not established, because it is distinct from that subject, and because no other means of knowledge (*māna*) establishes it.
The meaning is "you" (tvāditi). Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with "atha" (now/if). He rejects the third with "na ca" (nor). The point is this:
here, being a single sentence is pervaded by having a single meaning; since the pervader is excluded, the pervaded—namely, being a single sentence—is also excluded. || 393 ||

That which is yet to be produced cannot be destroyed; that which has already been produced ceases of its own accord; but that which is presently existing perishes by itself because it is a product. (394)

Furthermore, is the object of the injunction of knowledge the destruction of the phenomenal world (prapañca) as yet to come, already past, or currently existing? Regarding the first [option], he says: "as yet to come" (*bhāvī*). The words "because it has not been attained" (*aprāpteḥ*) are to be supplied. Regarding the second, he says: "even that which is past" (*bhūto'pi*). Regarding the third, he says: "the phenomenal world" (*prapañca*). This means [it cannot be so] by itself, without an injunction. || 394 ||
If the purpose of the scripture were dissolution, the result would be accidental.
If it were for the sake of the result, there would be no dissolution; nor could both be [the case], because that would entail a split in the sentence. || 395 ||

As for the claim that the purport of the ritual scriptures (*karma-śruti*) is the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañcābhāva*), one must ask: does their purport lie in that non-existence alone, or in results such as heaven, or in both? It is not the first case; thus he says: "Of the scripture" (*śruteḥ*). If the ritual scriptures were intent solely on the non-existence of the phenomenal world, they would have no purport regarding ritual action. Consequently, since that [non-existence] would not be performed as an object of knowledge, and because heaven and the like do not arise for a person who has not performed rituals...
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, Page 142] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 121 A.

The meaning is that [the world] would be accidental (*dākasmika*). Having restated the second [view], he refutes it with the words "phalet" (it would bear fruit). If the scriptural mention of action (*karmaśruti*)—which refers to the relationship between the means and the end regarding heaven and sacrifice—were not intended to signify dissolution (*laya*), then the assumption that there is an injunction (*niyoga*) for one desiring knowledge regarding the destruction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be contradicted; this is the meaning. He rejects the third [view] with the word "na" (no). || 399 ||
By means of the dissolution of the five alone, through the abandonment of all misfortunes.
If the human goal were fully accomplished [by other means], knowledge would result in fruitlessness. || 396 ||

He states another defect [in the view] that the scriptures (śruti) are intent upon the destruction of the phenomenal world (prapañca). He says: "In the case of the phenomenal world... The sense is that, in such a case, there would be a lack of authority for the section concerning Brahman (brahmakāṇḍa), beginning with the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1). || 396 ||
Therefore, through the knowledge of the true nature of the oneness of the Self, ignorance is abandoned.
Once the goal of human existence has been accomplished, the postulation of its dissolution is purposeless.

Anticipating the objection that "since ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, that [destruction] is not fruitless," he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). Since the destruction of ignorance through knowledge is desired for the sake of making knowledge fruitful, it follows that by that very [destruction], all evils are destroyed and the state of abiding in one's own nature free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhika-svarūpa) is attained; thus, the destruction of the world is fruitless, and its being the cause of knowledge is refuted due to the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā). This is the meaning. || 397 ||
And because the injunctions themselves have their respective purposes exhausted, they do not apply to one another.
Tell me, how can there be a single common substratum when there is an absence of mutual dependence? (398)

Regarding the claim that ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) and the injunction for knowledge (*jñāna*) share a single locus of authority (*ekādhikāratva*) because the former serve as a cause for the eligibility for the latter, he replies with the words "svakārya" (by their own effects). The syntactical connection is as follows: "Tell me, for what reason do you assert that the injunctions for ritual action and knowledge have a single locus of authority? [The answer is: Because they are exhausted by their own respective effects, they lack mutual dependence. It is the injunctions of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*) that possess a single locus of authority when they are mutually expectant (*anyonyākāṅkṣā*), not those that are independent of one another.

The meaning is: since these are injunctions of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) as opposed to injunctions of action (*kārya-vidhi*), they are mutually independent; thus, while culminating in their respective fruits, how could they have a single common qualification? || 398 ||
And likewise, of all injunctions as well as of prohibitive statements.
For if it is accepted—without any basis in valid cognition—that [the self] is established in name and so forth, [then the following ensues].
Liberation would be signless, and the scripture itself would thus be purposeless. (399)

He states another defect in the state of being intent on dissolution: "And of the injunctions," etc. [The text continues: "Of the injunctions and prohibitions, [the world] consisting of name, form, and action..."

The meaning is as follows: if [the Upanishads] were intent solely on negation, then since there would be no distinction from other Vedic texts, even the *Tattvamasi* and similar passages would be intent on that [negation]. Consequently, there would be no injunctions for hearing and so forth regarding the means to liberation;

and since what is not enjoined is not performed, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) would not be established. Thus, like heaven, liberation too would result in being accidental. Let it be so—let heaven and liberation be accidental. To this, he replies: "And the scripture... (399).
If you consider [the efficacy] of actions by way of effects such as heaven and so forth, [then...]
Just as one ascends the roof of a palace by means of a flight of stairs.
There will be an entry into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self. || 400 ||

He raises an objection: "If [you say] heaven and so forth... Because the two sections have liberation as their fruit, they are not fruitless; nor is there any arbitrariness regarding heaven and so forth, because they serve as gateways to liberation.

This is what he suggests. If you think that the Agnihotra and other rites lead to the attainment of heaven and so forth by means of the dissolution of the body and other factors, [and thereby lead to knowledge]...
[Vol. 1, p. 143] 122 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*. [The connection is as follows:

"The state of being a supplement to Yoga" is the connection. If ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) are the causes for the qualification for knowledge (*jñāna-adhikāra*) by means of heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, then regarding those [actions] in relation to heaven and so forth—
Anticipating the objection—“Since [the rites] arise from the context of the *vāvasāna* (the concluding part), how can they be subsidiary to something else?”—he says: “Like a staircase” (*sopāna*).

Just as one desiring to ascend to the roof of a palace ascends it by means of the successive steps of a staircase, so too the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) will ascend to liberation by way of heaven and the like; therefore, just as the act of going up the stairs is subsidiary to the act of ascending the palace, the meaning is that ritual acts whose fruits are heaven and so forth are subsidiary to the injunction for knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*). || 400 ||
Just as it is like giving instructions on the way to a village situated along the road to a city.
The instruction regarding the road to the city is understood to be subordinate [to the primary purpose]. || 401 ||

One might object that while it is directly perceived that ascending the stairs is supplementary to climbing the palace, it is not established by authoritative means (*prāmāṇika*) that ritual actions which have heaven and the like as their fruits are supplementary to the injunction for knowledge; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as... The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: likewise, the injunctions of ritual action are also supplementary to the injunction for knowledge by way of their own fruits, preceded by the teaching of the dissolution of the body and so forth. [The reason is: the subject of dispute is supplementary to the injunction for knowledge because it is taught for one who seeks knowledge.

The meaning is that whatever is taught to one who desires a particular goal is subordinate to that goal; for example, the instruction regarding the arrival at a village along the way to one desiring to go to the city is subordinate to the arrival at the city. || 409 ||
Since it is not desired [as an end], its status as a subordinate element (śeṣatā) is indeed appropriate for its occurrence in villages and the like.
But heaven and the like do not possess the status of being subordinate, because they have the person as their ultimate purpose.

Considering that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), he says: "No. He states that there is no inference because of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the absence of a fruit for its own sake (*svārthe phalavaikalya*). He says: "Because it is not desired" (*akāmitatvāt*). The meaning is as follows: for one who wishes to go to a city but happens to pass through villages and so forth situated on the road to the city, since he does not desire those [intermediate places], his mention of them is fruitless with respect to its own object; therefore, it is logical that such a statement is merely a subordinate part (*śeṣatā*) of the statement regarding the fruitful goal of going to the city. He dispels the charge of the reason being over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*) by saying: "Of heaven and so forth" (*svargādeḥ*). [The context concerns] ritual action (*karma*).

The meaning is that ritual injunctions do not have knowledge as their subordinate purpose (*niyogaśeṣatva*), because [injunctions] are heard to have human goals such as heaven as their intended objects; therefore, there is no pervasion by that [knowledge]. || 402 ||
Then, for the purpose of attracting [disciples], [he taught] heaven and so forth, for the sake of liberation.
It is like the description of the qualities of a village situated on that very path upon reaching a city. || 403 ||

Since heaven and the like are not intended [as the primary goal], the injunction regarding ritual action does not find its finality therein; therefore, those [injunctions] are subordinate to the injunction for knowledge. Thinking that this indeed constitutes a pervasion of the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*), he raises an objection with the words "Now" (*atha*). For those who do not desire liberation—which is distinct from worldly pleasure—the descriptions of heaven and so forth serve to inspire them toward that [liberation]; thus, the scriptural passages concerning rituals for those purposes do not terminate in their own literal meaning. [Regarding heaven...]

Anticipating the objection that if these [results] do not exist they would be like a hare’s horn and thus serve no purpose as incentives (*prarocanā*), whereas if they do exist they cannot be subordinate to the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*), he says: "In the city," etc. Just as one desiring to lead a child to a city by means of enticement points out the enjoyment of food and other requisites in the villages and such located along the way, so too the injunctions for ritual action, for the sake of inciting one toward liberation, point out heaven and the like.
The meaning is that those who possess detachment arising from the enjoyment of those [objects], having attained the application of knowledge, culminate in liberation. || 403 ||
This is not so, because [the validity] is established from another source; this is appropriate in the case of human speech.
But in the case of the Veda, because there is no speaker, the existence of intention and so forth is impossible. (404)

Whether the fact that ritual injunctions are subordinate to the injunction for knowledge is known from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or from scripture (*śabda*), it cannot be the former, because of the disparity with the illustrative example.

[Vārtika] He says: "Not so. In the case of human-authored speech, it is appropriate to mention a result for the sake of inducement, because the intention of a person can be known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is fitting that the descriptions of the qualities of villages and so forth situated on the path to the city are subordinate to the attainment of the city.

Since there is no possibility of deception or the like in that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), the mention of a fruit [of action] is not for the sake of enticement. Thus, the sense is: in the Veda, whose subject matter is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, how could there be a relationship of principal and subordinate (śeṣa-śeṣitā) without direct scriptural statement (śruti) and so forth? This is because of the absence of a speaker—that is to say, because of the non-existence of an author. || 404 ||
Or rather, the intended meaning (tātparya) lies precisely where one is led after having been enticed.
But since there is no [attainment] of the city, how could a man exert effort? (405)

Even in the second case, Upacchandaka—or the one who has understood, or the one who intends to understand—realizes that the mention of the village on the road is subordinate to the attainment of the city;
for [he thinks] that the first alternative is not tenable because the employment of words is for the sake of another, and because in the case of the illustration (the dṛṣṭānta) there is no speaker.

Intending this, he states another alternative with the words "Or else" (*yadvā*). The phrase "or else" is for the purpose of refuting the remaining position, since the person who has understood [the meaning] indeed [understands] the mention of the village on the road as referring to that very [city].

One understands the intention (tātparya) from the word itself or from another means of knowledge, and not elsewhere; for the intention of the leader to reach the city remains unknown [to others]. Furthermore, there can be no relationship of subordinate and principal (śeṣa-śeṣitā) between what is known and what is unknown. Since the village situated on the path to that city is beyond the scope of the listener's intention, even a child whose linguistic proficiency depends upon such activity does not perceive the journey through the villages on the road as being subordinate to the arrival at the city. It is the same in this case.
The sense is that, even for the injunctions regarding ritual action, there is no scriptural basis for their being subordinate to the qualification for knowledge. || 405 ||
Even when, according to the actual state of things, it is a means for attaining a city;
Even then, the attainment of the village and the attainment of the city result from the object itself, not from the means of knowledge.

One might object: "Even though the state of having reached the village on the path is not an object of the senses (such as hearing), it is in fact a subordinate part of that [reaching the city]; therefore, just as the statement 'there is no other way' intends the reaching of the city, so too the injunctions regarding ritual actions intend the mandate for knowledge. Thus, there is no disparity between the illustration and the case at hand. Anticipating this, he says: "Even when... (*yadāpi*). "The actual state of things" (*vastuvṛtta*) means the inherent capacity of a thing; by that, the attainment of the village is the means for attaining the city.

Even if it is admitted [that there is a sequence], the meaning is as follows: since the purpose known from the sentence does not terminate there, the journey to the village remains subordinate to the journey to the city;

however, it is established by the words themselves that ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) are subordinate to the injunction for knowledge (*jñānaniyoga*). Thus, a disparity certainly exists. || 406 ||
Even by implication, there is no intended meaning [of such a rule], just as in the case of the injunction for the acquisition of wealth.
For, in the Veda, the understanding of the intended meaning arises solely by following the words.

Then, anticipating the objection that for the sake of consistency with the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), the injunctions regarding ritual action (karmavidhi) must also, by implication (arthāt), be subordinate to the injunction regarding knowledge (jñānaniyoga), he says:

"By implication" (arthāt). Even by implication, there is no understanding of the intent (tātparya) of the injunctions and prohibitions toward the injunction regarding knowledge; for one who has understood their own [independent] meaning, that [subordination]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning is that there is no lack of logical consistency [regarding the connection] with the *reṇu* (dust/particles). He provides an example for the fact that the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) does not have the injunction of knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) as its purpose: "dravya... and so forth. This is its meaning: it is established in the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]: "That in which a person finds pleasure, the desire for that is characterized by the object itself, because it is inseparable [from the person].

[For example], for a Brāhmaṇa by means of receiving gifts and the like, for a Kṣatriya by means of victory and the like, and for a Vaiśya by means of agriculture and the like; by those various [means]..."

Regarding the acquisition of wealth prescribed by the *Yama* rules, there arises a doubt as to whether it is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). In this regard, since no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard in the texts concerning the acquisition of wealth, and because if one were to assume such a qualification based on a desire for wealth, the injunction would be rendered purposeless—since activity toward wealth is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*) alone—and furthermore, because if the rules were merely restrictive (*niyamārtha*), there would be the consequence of violating the scripture for one who proceeds by other means; therefore, it is logical that the acquisition is for the sake of the sacrifice, being adopted by way of obtaining the materials required by the sacrifice.
[Vol. 1, Page 145] 224 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Connection]

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it is for that purpose" (*tad-arthaṃ*): since there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) or other evidence for such a purpose, and because the connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*) is not established, it is impossible for the act to be subsidiary to it through the medium of the substance—as is the case with the *parṇa*-leaf rule. Furthermore, since the Brahmins and others, whose eligibility is understood from the power of the subject matter itself, are not left without eligibility, the injunction is accepted as a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) for one who, desiring wealth, is already engaged in seeking general means and has set out to acquire it; thus, its own eligibility is inherent.

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: although the acquisition of wealth performed according to the prescribed rules (vidhi) serves the purpose of the person—just like the eating of food that is restricted by rule—it is also possible for it to be subordinate to the sacrifice (kratvartha), since only wealth acquired through righteous means (nyāya) is fit for the ritual. Thus, the acquisition of wealth is indeed for the sake of the person, while simultaneously serving as an auxiliary to the sacrifice. For when a man experiences pleasure upon performing a certain action, his desire to obtain that object arises for the sake of maintaining the body; and it is evident that one whose body is maintained [seeks such objects].

The meaning of the sūtra is this: since he possesses wealth, the acquisition of wealth serves the purpose of man, for it is not separate from his pleasure. Thus, even though the *karmakāṇḍa* does not have the injunction regarding knowledge as its primary aim, it nonetheless has an implied intention (*ārthika-tātparya*) insofar as it is somehow conducive to knowledge.
If one objects, "If the *karmakāṇḍa* is not intended to lead to the injunction regarding knowledge, then where does its intention lie?", he says [in response]: "By the word... (*śabda...*).

The understanding of the purport in the Veda arises from indicators such as *upakrama* (introductory statements) or from the means of proof such as *śruti* (direct statement); thus, even in the *karmakāṇḍa*, when a specific relationship is not known, the purport is to be understood through *śruti* and the other indicators—this is the meaning. || 407 ||
If there were no intention toward [attaining] heaven and so forth, there would be no realization of the oneness of the Self.
If it were not [the case] regarding liberation, nor regarding heaven, because of the split in the statement; nor in both cases.
Furthermore, if the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) were subsidiary to the injunction for knowledge (jñānaniyoga), would its purport lie in [attaining] heaven and so forth, or in liberation, or in both?

In the first case, the status of being subsidiary to the injunction for knowledge is not established; thus he says: "In heaven and so forth. In the second case, however, there would be a contradiction with the cognition of a relationship that has not been previously known;
thus he says: "If it be in liberation. He refutes the third alternative by stating: "Because of the split of the sentence" (vākyabheda). || 408 ||
Furthermore, there is no equality between effects such as heaven and the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings.
An entry might be postulated for the sake of some other effect. || 409 ||

Anticipating the objection that—since the mention of fruits such as heaven is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) and thus not intended to be taken literally—it is logical that the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is subordinate to the injunction for knowledge which possesses its own fruit—the author says: "And not... The meaning is that because the fruit mentioned in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) is not, like the fruit of an *arthavāda*, unintended, the ritual section—which possesses its own fruit—is not subordinate to anything else. || 409 ||
And it must be explained how these [elements] are beneficial through perception alone.
If this is the view regarding the qualification for the knowledge of the Self: || 410 ||
Because it prohibits engagement with objects perceived through the influence of passion and other such afflictions.
Let it be so; for in the case of negations, [the cognition] is assisted by the exclusion [of the object]. (411)
Regarding the claim that injunctions and prohibitions serve as causes for the qualification to know the Self (ātmajñāna) solely through their visible utility, he says:
"And it must be stated," etc. He restates the visible means favored by the opponent with the words, "If," etc.

[The opponent argues: Injunctions and prohibitions assist the mandate of knowledge (*jñānaniyoga*) through the invisible means of specific engagement and abstention; therefore, since the door of entry into the qualification for knowledge is well-known, there is nothing [further to be established].

This is the meaning of what is to be said. He accepts that, according to the principle stated regarding prohibitions (*niṣedha*), there may be an auxiliary benefit toward the injunction of knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) because the cessation of desire for that [worldly object] is conducive to it;
thus he says: "Let it be so. (410) (411)
1 [Vol. 1, p.
146] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 125
But tell me, how do these injunctions restrain passion?
For these are not for the purpose of exclusion, nor are they restrictive rules.

Anticipating the objection that injunctions (*vidhi*), like prohibitions (*niṣedha*), serve as a subordinate part of the mandate for knowledge (*jñāna-niyoga*) because they prevent activity caused by passion and the like by warding them off, he says: "But the injunctions... Anticipating the further objection that even those [injunctions] obstruct activity dependent on passion and the like by means of expressing specific types of activity, he says: "For not... Regarding the threefold injunction consisting of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), restriction (*niyama*), and the unprecedented (*apūrva*), [he explains] both cases therein.

When [the action] is already established, it is an *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive) injunction, such as: "With the mantra 'They have taken this rein of immortality,' he takes the horse's bridle. Since the action is established in both cases, ritual injunctions do not result in the exclusion of other alternatives as their primary fruit. When [the action] is established only optionally, it is a *niyama* (restrictive) injunction, such as:

"One's own Veda is to be studied. These [injunctions under discussion], however, are not restrictive injunctions in that sense, because they do not operate by relying on an optional establishment [of the action].
Therefore, the meaning is that they do not exclude anything other than their own referent. || 412 ||
For injunctions inform us of an object that is absolutely unattained.
A rule whose object is already established is held to have the exclusion of other things as its result. (413)
What, then, is the nature of these objects? To this he replies: "Absolute," and so forth. And it has been said:

"An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when something is absolutely not otherwise established; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when there is an optionality; and when it is already established both there and elsewhere, it is called an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)."

Even though ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) are primarily concerned with enjoining what has not been previously established (*apūrvavidhi*), one might suspect that, by virtue of being injunctions, they must result in the cessation of something else, just like other injunctions. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "prāpta... (in the verse), considering that the limiting condition (*upādhi*) here is the fact that they do not have as their object something that is absolutely unestablished (*atyantāprāptārtha*). || 413 ||
And because service, conciliation, and intrigue have the same purpose as [the other means], they are not [separately enumerated].
For it is held that ritual action enjoined by scripture has its fruit at an indefinite time. (414)

Even though ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) have the *apūrva* as their purpose, [the author] raises the objection that they might result in the cessation of other activities. He says: "Service," etc. Just as service (*sevā*), such as the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, has a specific fruit (e.g., the acquisition of a village), and thus for one engaged in one thing there is a de facto cessation from another, so too here, there is a cessation from activity arising from passion (*rāga*) and so forth, in favor of scriptural activity.

And because the necklace is the fruit of *saṃsāra*, one who is engaged in scriptural activity naturally desists from anything other than that; therefore, even for injunctions regarding ritual actions (*karma-vidhi*), which concern objects not previously established [by nature], there exists the quality of obstructing natural inclinations—this is the meaning. He refutes this with the words "But it is not so. He states the reason for the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration with the words "Because... He clarifies that very disparity with the words "Unrestricted... [and] "Scriptural..."
The meaning is that activity does not necessarily have an immediate result, because its fruit may arise in either case. || 414 ||
For activities arising from passion and so forth have seen objects as their purpose, whereas those arising from ignorance have unseen objects as their purpose.
The non-contradiction of service through the means of a village by way of the *sāṃgrahaṇī* [offering]. || 415 ||

The reason for this is stated: "having an unseen purpose" (*adṛṣṭārtha*). The meaning is that because scriptural activity has an unseen purpose, its fruit—whether mediated or immediate—is possible by virtue of that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). He states the opposite regarding natural activities: "having a seen purpose" (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

Although both scriptural and natural activities result in *saṃsāra*, they do not have equal fruits like service and the like, due to the difference in their intermediate results (*avāntaraphala*). Thus [the text] concludes.

The meaning of *dāya* (inheritance). Having accepted that service (*sevā*) and *sāṃgrahaṇī* (the act of winning over) share a single fruit, it was stated that this is not the case for other scriptural activities; now, however, [this point] is being addressed. [Page 147] [Note: The text provided contains two bracketed references to manuscript variants:
"1 kha. ucyate" and "2 kha. 'dyuttha". These have been integrated into the translation as they appear to indicate editorial notes.]

Furthermore, even for those two, there is no rule of equal fruitfulness; for just as in the injunction "one desiring a village should perform the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice," service has the attainment of a village as its fruit.

He says "grāma... [etc.], meaning that because pride is absent, those two are not restricted; thus, even if there were a restriction to a single fruit, the disparity between them would be unavoidable.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction between service and the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice by way of their being means to reach the village (*grāma*), and there can be no relationship of sublated and sublator between two things that are not contradictory. || 415 ||
"The fruit arises from action"—this is the extent of my teaching.
Therefore, from this [state], there is either gradual or simultaneous attainment of both service and the comprehensive grasp [of the goal].
For one who desires the excellence of the fruit, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the performance [of the practice]. (416)

Furthermore, does the scriptural injunction such as "one desiring a village [should perform] the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice" exclude service? Or does the Sāṃgrahaṇī exclude service because service and the Sāṃgrahaṇī cannot be performed simultaneously by a single person? Or does it exclude it because the performance of the latter serves no purpose once the desired result is obtained through the former? Or is the non-performance of service implied by the circumstances? It is not the first case; thus he says: "Because of the action," meaning that the Sāṃgrahaṇī involves the inclusion of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

From the scripture, one understands only that the village is the cause; it does not follow that service is not a cause, because a single sentence cannot have an intention directed toward both simultaneously.

For it has been stated: "And in the case of optional rites, it is so because of the desire for the result" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 6.3.8). Regarding the injunction, "One desiring a village should offer the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas," there arises a doubt as to whether this rite should be performed even when deficient in its subsidiaries, or only when conjoined with all its parts—this being the case in the context of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

Since the instruction concerns the primary element alone, and since the qualification [of the agent] pertains to that which has been so instructed, it follows—by way of extended application—that even if deficient in its constituent parts, the rite should be performed in the case of obligatory rites, as if it were complete.

This being the prima facie view, we reply: because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) belongs to that which is conjoined with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because here too a result is heard, the rite must necessarily be an instrument; and since that [status of being an instrument] is impossible for one devoid of procedure, therefore, just as in the archetype, so also in a modification (*vikṛti*) performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), [the rite is to be performed only when complete].

It is established in the sixth [book]—in the sūtra "But because of the lack of connection, it would not be so"—that there is a requirement for the inclusion of all constituent parts; therefore, the meaning is that the scriptural injunction regarding the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice does not set aside [the other requirements]. He says "not the second" [meaning the second alternative is not tenable], adding "by way of sequence. This means that, unlike the movement across the eastern and western oceans which cannot be performed by a single person simultaneously (*aparyāyam*), there is no such impossibility of simultaneous performance for service and the *sāṃgrahaṇī*; for even if both are performed on the very same day, there is no contradiction. Alternatively:

In some days one performs the service (*sevā*), and in others the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice as well, since there is no contradiction between them. Therefore, the meaning is that the *sāṃgrahaṇī* does not exclude the service. He says "not the third" [alternative], namely: "the fruit. The *sāṃgrahaṇī* alone accomplishes a mere village, whereas when accompanied by the service, it accomplishes a great kingdom; thus, for one who desires a superior result at a particular time, there is the possibility of performing both means simultaneously.
The meaning is that even for fear of [rebirth], one must not fail to practice service. || 416 ||
And because it is entirely opposed to the activities arising from passion.
Even those activities based on injunctions would not exist, due to the absence of the material substance. || 417 ||
Furthermore, do these scriptural activities uproot only some natural tendencies or all of them?

In the first case, human effort would be rendered useless, because it would be possible to eliminate a few non-scriptural tendencies without difficulty; thinking thus, he refutes the second alternative with the words "rāgādi" (passion, etc.). If those scriptural activities were to eliminate all such tendencies arising from passion and the like, then...
The injunction regarding the acquisition of wealth would also be refuted, because that too serves merely to regulate activity impelled by passion. As they say:
"Not at all.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

"Because of the scriptural injunction regarding restraint, one may indeed assume an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), but not through the abandonment of a visible result (*dṛṣṭa*). And upon that cessation, because of the absence of material substance, there is no [obligation].
The meaning is that the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) would lack authority, as its activities would not proceed toward a firm foundation. || 417 ||
And there is no distinction whatsoever between actions performed for visible results and those performed for invisible results.
Because they are desired as means due to the causes impelled by passion and the like. || 418 ||

He states another reason for not obstructing worldly activity other than scriptural activity. [The verse begins with] "Dṛṣṭa" (seen). Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction—namely, that Vedic activities, which involve the unseen (adṛṣṭa), are conducive to liberation, whereas natural worldly activities (dṛṣṭa) are not—he says: "As a means" (upāyatvena). Even Vedic activities are equal to natural activities insofar as they are means to the fruits being desired.
