This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that innate activities are prompted by passion (*rāga*) and so forth, whereas scriptural (*vaidhyā*) ones are not, he says: "Passion, etc.

The meaning is that there is no difference between both types of activities insofar as they have passion and so forth as their cause; for scriptural activities cannot be accomplished without the desire for heaven and the like. || 498 ||
And even though the cause— the adherence to conceptual proliferation— is equal for both of these, [there is still a difference].
With reference to what specific distinction is a single activity conducive to liberation? (419)

Anticipating the objection that there is a distinction—namely, that while other natural activities are preceded by an attachment to worldly proliferation (*prapañca*), those [Vedic activities] are caused by an attachment to liberation—he says: "Proliferation... Just as natural activities are preceded by attachment to houses, fields, and so forth, so too Vedic activities are preceded by attachment to heaven and the like; thus, since both constitute a single category, the distinction that one is a cause for liberation while the other is not is unestablished.
This is the meaning. || 419 ||
Furthermore, if it is not desired that ritual actions serve as a means to sensual pleasure, then...
The established principle would be abandoned, and the fruit would become accidental. || 420 ||

Since it is not accepted that actions have heaven and so forth as their results, it is not logical that they are preceded by an attachment to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); thus, one might object—following the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning those desiring heaven—that ritual activities prescribed by injunctions (*vaidha-pravṛtti*) are causes for liberation. [The author] objects with the word "desire" (*kāma*). He refutes this with the logic of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) from the beginning of the sixth book: "It has been stated. This is the intended meaning: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," and so on.

When it is understood from Vedic sentences that heaven and sacrifice stand in the relationship of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), a doubt arises as to whether heaven is the subordinate factor (*guṇa*) and the sacrifice the principal (*pradhāna*), or vice versa.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: just as in the sentence "Devadatta cooks," the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is accepted as denoting the agent; thus, since the sacrifice is the principal and heaven is subordinate, heaven cannot be the goal [of the injunction]. Consequently, because its literal meaning is not intended, ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) are merely supplementary to the injunction for knowledge (*jñānaniyoga*).

Having accepted that the phrase "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) serves to designate the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—just as in the case of the injunction "having given [the cow], one should sacrifice for Devadatta"—and having established that heaven is the primary object to be accomplished while the sacrifice is subordinate, it was concluded in the *rāddhānta* (final position) that ritual injunctions have their intended meaning as independent acts and are not subsidiary to anything else.

As it has been said: "But it is not a means [to another end] because it exists for that purpose. For heaven is indeed bliss (*prīti*), since the word for it does not deviate from that [bliss]; therefore, [the sacrifice] is for its sake.

If one could not find anyone else who accomplishes the action in any other way, then—since the action exists for the sake of pleasure—the meaning of the Sūtra is that sacrifice is subordinate (guṇa) and heaven is the primary goal (pradhāna). This very reasoning, as stated, would be undermined if one did not accept that actions are the means for attaining heaven and so forth; otherwise, it would be rendered impossible.
[Vol. 1, Page 149] .128 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection— ]

Furthermore, he says "And the fruit" [verse 420]: if actions lacked fruits such as heaven, then heaven and so forth would be without cause; consequently, there would be the arrival of what was not done and the destruction of what was done. Thus he speaks.
Then, by means of the consumption of all desires and through the path of the dissolution of all desires;
If the injunctions lead toward conformity with liberation, then that is indeed a matter of common sense.

Desiring to avoid the aforementioned defects, he raises an objection by resorting to the position that desire is destroyed [by action]. He says: "All... Ritual injunctions impel a person toward action; once engaged, they cause him to experience the fruits; and through that experience, they remove his desire for those fruits.
By this means, they ultimately culminate in the qualification for the knowledge that is the cause of liberation; therefore, there is neither a contradiction with logic nor...
The meaning is that heaven and so forth would be accidental. He refutes this with the word "vārttam" (meaning "trifling" or "insignificant"). || 421 ||
How could that which is the cause of activity be its own terminator?
Even if one has set out [on the path], one should turn back from actions that employ sensual desires as a means.
Or else, one might recoil from knowledge, which devours all human enjoyments.
Likewise, how could there be such a thing as the word "empty" even in Vṛndāvana? (423)
Engagement in actions either obstructs attachment to the fruit or the enjoyment of that fruit; it is not the first case, as he says: "That which has [attachment] as its cause," etc.
For engagement in actions is caused by attachment to the fruit; it cannot itself obstruct that very [attachment], because that would contradict its own purpose.

Even in the second case, does the enjoyment of the fruit obstruct attachment to the fruit at its own time, at the time of its own prior non-existence, or at the time of its own destruction? It does not [obstruct it].

He refutes the first [position] therein with the words "yannimitta" (that which has as its cause). The meaning is that the engagement in enjoyment, occurring through the performance of action due to attachment to the fruit, is not capable of turning away from that very [attachment], because it has been shown that enjoyment is a cause for the increase of that [attachment]. He answers the second [position] with the words "pravṛtto 'pi" (even though engaged). [The argument is: the enjoyment of the fruit might ward off attachment to the fruit at the time of its own prior non-existence, but [it cannot do so] at the present time when one is engaged in actions.

Furthermore, one would also desist from those actions that serve as the means to desired fruits, because the passion for the fruit—which is the motive for engaging in them—has been cast aside by the enjoyment of future fruits; thus, there would never be any engagement in actions. He refutes the third [position] with the words "he would tremble. Even at the time of death, for one who is permeated by the enjoyment of the fruits of action and still longing for those fruits, [when faced with] that which cuts off their enjoyment...

The meaning is that one is agitated by news of one's own ignorance; therefore, at the time of its own destruction, the enjoyment of the fruit serves as the means for turning back from that speech [of ignorance]. Now, the word "atha" (then) restates the third alternative, while the word "vā" (or) negates it. The remainder of the passage is the demonstration of that [negation]; such is the division. Alternatively, he says: "That activity toward karma which is caused by the enjoyment of the fruit does not bring about the cessation of karma and so forth, because it would contradict itself," using the words "yannimittā" (caused by which).

Furthermore, even a person engaged in worldly enjoyment would not desist from the actions that serve as its means out of regard for that enjoyment, because there is a constant inclination toward action as a means for the sake of similar enjoyment; thus he says: "Even though engaged... Anticipating the objection that one might desist from it through the knowledge of the Self, he says: "One would be repelled... For one who desires to enjoy, such a reliance on the Self is impossible; on the contrary, due to the resulting agitation, he says "one would be repelled. To those blinded by passion, even the mere mention of the knowledge of the Self—
He states his pride regarding agitation with the word "even":
"Even in an empty Vṛndāvana, he would desire the state of a jackal."

"But never at any time is liberation without an object, O Gautama"—the meaning of this verse sung by Kāmi is that it indicates the distress of knowledge which turns one away from enjoyments and the like. || 422 || 423 ||
[Vārtika] Even though it has been stated that in this Veda there is the dissolution of something in some place—[this is found] in the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 129.
[Vārtika] Even though it has been stated that in this Veda there is the dissolution of something in some place... [End of fragment].
Because it is taught that one should not be intent upon that [state], there is consequently no dissolution of the body and so forth.

Having thus refuted those of his own school who maintain the doctrine of the destruction of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he restates what they have said: "It has been said. He then refutes it: "In that regard... The reason for this is: "...because it does not have that as its primary purport. First of all, the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) does not have the destruction of difference as its primary purport, because its purport is merely the establishment of a relationship [between rites and results] that was previously unknown; nor does the *jñānakāṇḍa* (the knowledge section) have that as its primary purport, because its purport is the reality that is devoid of difference. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no Veda which has the dissolution of duality as its primary purport.
Regarding the argument that the statement "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth was cited as an example for the entire Veda having non-duality as its meaning, he says: "No.
For from the sentence "one who desires heaven," the dissolution of the body and so forth is not understood; rather, only the relationship between heaven and the sacrifice and so forth is understood.
This is the meaning. || 424 ||

Even though the purpose of [the Veda] is heard to be heaven, if there is still a conceptualization [of it as a means], then [it follows that] it is [attained] by implication upon the dissolution [of the body].
Therefore, that is not established by the statement of direct perception, because the dissolution of the body and so forth [is not perceived]. || 425 ||

He raises an objection: "Even though the intention (*tātparya*) regarding its connection is understood, that [connection] is postulated upon the dissolution of the body and so forth; otherwise, it would lack the capacity to impel a person toward action for the sake of the next world. [The author replies: "Even when [the connection] is heard... For an object that cannot be established otherwise gives rise to a postulation (*kalpanā*). However, the dissolution of the identity of the body as the self is established by other means of knowledge (*māna*); since activity pertaining to the next world is based upon that [dissolution], there is no need for a postulation here.
"No," he refutes it; "that is not so. || 425 ||
Even when an elephant is seen directly before one's eyes, there is no inference of the elephant's footprint.
The statement beginning with "not gross" (asthūla) directly effects the negation of the body and so forth. || 426 ||

He provides an illustration for the point that when the dissolution of the body and so forth is possible as a direct scriptural meaning (*śābdatva*), it should not be assumed to be merely implied (*ārthikatva*). He says "directly" (*sākṣāt*). What is that statement which directly establishes the dissolution of difference and so forth? He says: "Not gross, etc. (*asthūlādi*) || 426 ||
Those who, conversely, speak of knowledge and action as they have been described [in this way].
Or rather, the measure [of their validity] should be stated as having a single common subject when they are conjoined with cognitions. (427)

Having refuted the connection between the two sections by means of the destruction of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), [the author] now restates—even though it has already been refuted—the connection with error (*viparyaya*) by way of explaining the absence of context, sentence, and indicative mark, beginning with the words "otherwise" (*ito 'nyathā*). The phrase "by way of error" (*viparyayeṇa*) refers to the inversion in which action is the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and knowledge is the principal (*śeṣin*). [This would imply] a single qualification (*adhikāritā*), being accomplished by a single person impelled by a single injunction (*niyoga*).

The meaning is "let it be stated. He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating that the proof for knowledge being a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣatva*) must be stated, because that [subsidiarity] is not established merely by the statement [of the opponent].
Thus: "must be stated" (vācyam). || 427 ||
In this case, there is no such process as there is, for example, in the sprinkling of rice and other grains.
Because its status is dependent on the indication (lakṣaṇā) of a connection with the unestablished primary matter (prakṛta-apūrva). || 428 ||

Anticipating the objection that, just as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is subsidiary to the *darśa* and other sacrifices, knowledge (*jñāna*) might likewise be contextually (*prākaraṇika*) subsidiary to ritual action, he says: "Not at all. He explains the illustrative example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) with the words: "In the case of the material... That collection of rice grains which has a connection with the *apūrva* by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the substance to be offered is what is meant by "connected with the *apūrva*"; and such [a connection] occurs within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *darśa* and other sacrifices.
17.1 What is it that is postulated?
[vol 1, page 151]

In the case of the injunction "one should offer handfuls," the word *vrīhi* (rice) in the subsequent statement "one sprinkles the *vrīhis*" functions as an indicator (*gamaka*) by virtue of its secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*). This is according to Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, in the section on the connection (*saṃbandha*).

The meaning is that, because of its context (*prakaraṇa*), it is logical for the sprinkling of rice (*vrīhiprokṣaṇa*) to be subordinate to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the primary rite. || 428 ||
For the word "vrīhi" would indeed be meaningless with respect to the essential nature of the rice itself.
It is logical that [the word] should convey a connection with the unestablished (apūrva) relevant to the context. || 429 ||

Raising the objection: "Why is it accepted that the word *vrīhi* (rice) indicates the aggregate of rice-grains as the material substance for the offering-material (*pradeya*) belonging to the apūrva, rather than the word being intended merely to denote the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of rice?"—the author replies with the word *vrīhīn*. He states that because sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is impossible upon mere rice-grains and would otherwise be purposeless, the word must indeed function as an indicator (*lakṣaka*). This is because the word *vrīhi* [denotes] the aggregate of rice-grains under discussion, which is connected to the *apūrva*.

Therefore, it is logical that the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is subordinate to the New Moon sacrifice and others; thus he concludes. [The word] "prakṛta" [is used]; the ellipsis is "the context (prakaraṇa) would make it known. || 429 ||
Nor can there be a connection by means of a sentence, as in the case of the *juhū* ladle being made of *parṇa* wood. (430)
Because of the cause consisting in the connection with the ritual action, which is invariably concomitant with the tip of the *juhū* ladle.
Therefore, even without a formal grammatical derivation, it will certainly bring forth the object.

[The author] says "Nor even... because of the apprehension that, although knowledge is not subsidiary to action due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), it might nonetheless be subsidiary to it by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is. He explains the illustrative example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "The ladle, etc. The substance such as the ladle is [subsidiary] to the ritual action...

The meaning is this: since qualities such as being made of *parṇa* wood, which are enjoined by statements such as "that which is made of *parṇa*," are invariably connected with a specific [act] intended for that purpose, therefore, in relation to that act, the *juhū* and other implements are the means;

thus, even without the context (*prakaraṇa*), they are subsidiary to the ritual action solely by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*). The word "therefore" (*tena*) refers to this syntactical connection. Because of their invariable connection with Vedic ritual acts, these *juhū* implements and others [attain their status] even without the context.

The construction is as follows: by the sentence itself, one must necessarily bring the sacrifice into connection with the leaf-nature and so forth, which constitute its own material cause. ||430||431||
It has been described that in that case, the connection of "his" is established by the sentence itself.
But self-knowledge would not be thus [attained], nor is it heard of in that context. (432)

He states, "by means of the sentence," referring to the fact that it was deliberated upon in the third [book] that even for things like the *parṇa*-leaf [used for ladles], which are studied in an isolated context (*anārabhyādhīta*), their connection to the sacrifice occurs through the sentence alone.

Although the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) has already been introduced, he clarifies the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*) beginning with "not by context" (*na tāvat prakriyā*), stating that while sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the *parṇa*-leaf quality are subsidiary to the ritual action by virtue of both context and sentence, knowledge is not subsidiary to it by those two means.

Regarding the term "Self": knowledge [of the Self] is not a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*), because it is not heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of such action; for a *prakara�ṇa* consists of that which requires a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for what is to be performed, and there is no such requirement for this knowledge to be a subsidiary of ritual action. This is the meaning. || 432 ||
Nor is the non-deviation of the self from its action observed.
Therefore, its connection with action is not established by means of measurement.

He elaborates upon the application of the illustration with the words "Nor even by a sentence," and so forth. The phrase "nor even" implies that this applies equally to both worldly and Vedic actions. Nevertheless, one might suspect that knowledge is a subordinate part of action on the basis of scripture (*śruti*) and other means of proof; anticipating this objection, he says, "By that. The connection is: "by that means of proof, namely scripture and the rest. The meaning is that knowledge is the object of the genitive case (i.e., the subordinate element), since it has been refuted by scripture and the other authorities. || 433 ||
1. For indeed, investigation... 2. Having observed the action...
[Vol.
1, page 152] Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 131.
And thus, when the benefit for another is not known, a statement of result is not an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Therefore, there is indeed a separate qualification for knowledge and action as they have been described.

He states the conclusion regarding the fact that knowledge does not have ritual action as its remainder: "And thus," etc. When the knowledge of the Self—being independent and devoid of being subordinate to anything else according to the reasoning previously stated—is established, the scriptural mention of a fruit for it is not a non-factual *arthavāda*.
As it is said: "And when its subservience to another is known, even that which is called a 'mention of a fruit'..."

The meaning is that since it has been refuted by the statement, "That [injunction] must indeed be an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*); there is no other fruit than from knowledge," knowledge is the cause of liberation and not ritual action; thus, due to the difference in the qualified persons (*adhikārī*) and other factors between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*), the connection with the opposite [conclusion] is unestablished. He states the conclusion regarding knowledge having the intended fruit: "Distinctly," etc.; [this means] that unlike ritual action, knowledge possesses a fruit...

The meaning is that it has been established that because those two subjects under discussion are distinct due to their respective inherent connections, the qualified aspirant (*adhikārī*) for the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) is different. || 434 ||
Presumption (arthāpatti) is also applicable to a capable agent and enjoyer.
But that [cognition] cannot belong to the follower of the Upaniṣads, for whom all distinctions have been destroyed.

Now, it is incorrect to claim that there is no evidence for the knowledge of the self being a subsidiary part of ritual action; for since the engagement in rituals pertaining to the next world would be impossible for one who has not ascertained the nature of the self, the knowledge [of the self] is inferred to be a subsidiary part of ritual action through *arthāpatti* (presumption), which serves here as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
To elaborate on the absence of such a logical mark in this case, he says, beginning with "artha": "Presumption [is the means of knowing] the knowledge of the self as an agent in ritual..."

He addresses the first [position], which asserts that the knowledge of the non-agent Self establishes its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) [of ritual action]. He says: "By implication" (*arthāt*). Since the Self—as either agent or enjoyer—is fit for ritual action, and since activity toward such action is impossible without knowledge of it, it is logical that the knowledge of it is implied by necessity as a subordinate element; moreover, the cognition of that [Self] is accepted as being subordinate to it. He refutes the second [position] with: "But not... [referring to that which is] knowable solely through the Upaniṣads.

The meaning is that because the Self—devoid of distinctions such as being an agent—is unfit for ritual action, knowledge of it is of no use therein and is even contradictory; therefore, it cannot be implied as a subordinate element of such action. || 435 ||
Because it relies upon the authority of the Vedic words that are directly perceived.
For it is a false tradition that one becomes fully perfected through renunciation at the very outset; [rather, there are debts to be paid]. (436)

Even though there is no connection between the two sections [of the Veda] because knowledge is merely a supplement to ritual action, another view is raised—based on such scriptural and traditional texts as "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts" and "Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation"—that ritual actions are supplements to the injunction for knowledge by way of discharging those debts. To this, he says: "Direct perception," etc., beginning with "One should renounce from the stage of studentship itself."

The meaning is this: because one relies on the authority of explicit scriptural injunctions (*śruti*), the attainment of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) belongs only to one established in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*). Since the qualification for knowledge (*jñāna*) must occur in that very birth in which the discharge of debts (*ṛṇāpākaraṇa*) takes place, there is no fixed rule; rather, the intention of both *śruti* and *smṛti* is merely that it should be performed at some time or other. However, if the intention of the *śruti* and other authorities were that the discharge of debts must be accomplished in this very birth—

In that case, it is not an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); for when there is a contradiction with an injunction, it is not authoritative, and when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), tradition (*smṛti*) is not authoritative. Thus he says: "For [it is said] 'the debts'... (436).
1. Sustenance; 2. Or, birth.
Nor is liberation logically possible from mere ritual actions alone.
And so it will be stated clearly: therefore, liberation does not arise from karma.

Now, if knowledge is the cause of liberation, one might inquire whether ritual actions (*karman*) are subordinate to the injunction for knowledge—either by way of discharging a debt (*ṛṇanirāsa*) or through some other means. Furthermore, it may be argued that knowledge is not the cause of liberation because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*); for the scriptural passage (*śruti*) merely describes an existing state and is thus not an authority, just like the verse regarding "sinless fame" (*apāpaśloka*).

On the other hand, action is its cause, based on such Smṛti texts as "By action alone, indeed, [one attains] perfection. To this, he replies: "And not... [The text continues: "...because it is a description of an existing state."

Even so, the scriptural statement that liberation arises from knowledge is not a figurative expression (nāmamātra), because it speaks of an actual fact—just like the passage beginning with "Heavenly indeed..."—and because its meaning is established by the experience of the wise and there is no non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible.

As for the Smṛti, its scope is the attainment of knowledge through the medium of purification; it does not have liberation as its direct object, for that would contradict such Śruti passages as "Liberation is not [attained] by action. This is the intended sense. What is that reasoning which does not tolerate liberation arising from mere actions?
Regarding this, he says: "And so it is. This refers to the reasoning that will be stated in the discussion on the *Bhujyu* and other passages. He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. (437).
And thus, the thorough realization of the identity of the self is not held to depend upon repeated practice.
Or for the sake of cultivation toward liberation; likewise, it will be explained further below. || 438 ||

Even if there is no liberation from karma, one might suspect that knowledge requires practice as its cause and is not sufficient by itself; anticipating this objection, he says "And not... because it would contradict such passages as "Only by knowing Him... He says "Meditative cultivation (bhāvanā)... regarding those who, wishing for the practice of knowledge to be the cause of liberation, consider knowledge to be for that purpose. The connection is: "Nor is knowledge desired for the sake of meditative cultivation. [This concerns] knowledge.

The meaning is that [the view of liberation through action] contradicts such scriptural passages as those stating that [knowledge] is the cause of the human goal by its own independence. By the phrase "tathā ca" (and likewise), he indicates the argument to be stated later in the *Bhujyu-vicāra* and other sections, namely that knowledge is the cause of liberation without depending on anything else. || 438 ||
Because the reality known as the single self is established through its own direct experience.
Furthermore, it will also be stated that there would be no knowledge produced through cultivation. || 439 ||

Now, one might ask: "Since the knowledge of the Self is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it is produced by the *Upaniṣads*, like the knowledge of the fire in a woman [as a sacrificial substitute], how can it be a means to liberation? To this, he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). The meaning is that since inference is impossible due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of having a superimposed object, the aforementioned cognition of the Self is rightly the cause of liberation. Anticipating the objection that the reason is over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*), he states that the validity of the cognition of the Self consists in its having a non-superimposed object; thus, everyone—
He says that this should be understood on the occasion of the commentary beginning with "pīti" etc., stating: "And this... (439).
Others say that because it is an object (*padārtha*), it must be cognizable through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The self is not established through scripture, like any other category of object asserted by an opponent.

In the context of refuting the position that the discharge of debts [is a means to liberation], it was already stated that neither mere ritual acts (*karma*) nor their repeated practice are causes for liberation. Now, since the Vedāntas enjoin the cessation of impressions (*vāsanā*) such as waking and dreaming, or the cessation of the mind (*manonirodha*), he states the view that the two sections [of the Veda] are connected because those injunctions regarding ritual acts are subordinate to that [cessation]. He says: "Others... [and so on]. Now, [it may be objected]: the Vedāntas do not [enjoin] cessation...

He says "no" because [the Upanishads], like injunctions, would terminate in their own [literal] meaning, as in the case of perception; for this reason he states: "because they are [merely] word-meanings. The meaning is that since the Self, like rice and other such things, is an already established object (*siddhārtha*), it is accessible through other means of knowledge; therefore, it cannot be known through the Vedāntas alone due to the possibility of agreement or disagreement with those other means. || 440 ||
1 [Vol. 1, p.
154] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 233
Through positive and negative concomitance, [this is known] by means of the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states.
Therefore, having discerned one's own self through such recognition, [one attains liberation].
Because its activity has reached completion, there is no further dependence upon it.

Now, one might object: "In the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the author of the Bhāṣya refuted the view that the Self is an object of other means of knowledge by stating, 'Because no relation [is grasped] when it is not an object of the senses,' and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he speaks after first analyzing that point, beginning with the words "anvaya" (positive concomitance). The three states are variable and are objects of perception, whereas the Self is non-variable and is the witness; such are the forms of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and by means of these—

One who, having discerned the Self as distinct from the body and other such things during the waking state and so forth, recognizes it as one and the same through such acts of recognition as "I am he who was asleep" and "I am now awake," does not require any further means of knowledge called scripture (*āgama*) regarding that [Self]. This is because the manifestation of the Self—which is the very operation of that [scripture]—is established by recognition and the like precisely through the removal of ignorance concerning it. Therefore, the inner self (*pratyak*) is not accessible through another means of knowledge.
The sense is that, because of the difficulty of warding off that [objection], the Sūtra beginning with "birth and so forth" (janmādi) must also be considered. || 441 ||
Therefore, for the sake of ceasing those latent impressions, the person is enjoined by the scripture.
This occurs either through the cessation of the mind, but not through the comprehension of the reality of things.
Since that is established by another means of knowledge, speech does not function here [to establish it]. || 443 ||

Anticipating the objection—"If the Vedāntas are not authoritative regarding the inner self (pratyak), which is capable of being known through other means of knowledge, how can they possess authority when they are included within the injunction to study?"—he says: "The impression of that" (*tadvāsanā*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the three states are meant. "By the scripture" refers to such passages as "One should restrain speech and mind. It is not that this person is enjoined by the scripture for the purpose of cognizing a real object; rather, [the scripture serves] the purpose already stated. Regarding the reason previously mentioned:

It reminds [the reader]: "by another means of knowledge" (*mānāntareṇa*). Here, the word "that" (*tat*) and the locative case refer to the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth mentioned previously as that other means of knowledge. || 442 || 443 ||
Because its nature is self-luminous, it has extinguished the latent impressions of the internal mind.
Even though independent of other means of valid cognition, the self manifests by itself.

Now, one might object: "If the Self were cognizable through other means of knowledge (*māna*), it would follow that it is non-Self, like a jar; and since it is not accessible to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like, it must be known only through the Vedāntas. To this he says: "By itself" (*svayam*). Even though the Self does not depend on recognition and so forth when established by reasoning, there is no dependence on scripture for its own direct realization; otherwise, like *dharma*, it would result in being a non-Self. Therefore, for one whose all mental impressions (*vāsanā*) have been removed by discrimination and the like, [the Self is] free from [external] proof—
Because it is proximate and of the nature of consciousness (cit-svabhāva), it shines forth by itself; thus, the meaning is that it is not something to be known through the Vedānta. || 444 ||
Thus, it is precisely by way of the effect (kārya), just like the sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices.
The authority of the Vedāntas is not held to reside in an object in the same manner as that of the senses. || 445 ||

[Objection: But surely, since no injunction for cessation (*nirodha*) is perceived in those [Upaniṣadic texts], they cannot have authority by virtue of being devoted to that [cessation]; nor can they be entirely without authority, because they are included within the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), just like injunctive sentences. Therefore, their status as a means of knowledge must be grounded in reality (*vastuniṣṭha*), just like perception. To this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*).

First of all, the Vedāntas do not possess the status of a means of knowledge regarding reality in the same manner as the eye, because it has been stated that, being [already] established entities (*padārtha*), they are accessible through other means of knowledge; rather, [they concern] the self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument as presented.*

Furthermore, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the reality [of Brahman] through the acceptance of its ownership (*tvātmya*), and because their authority is established solely by way of the injunction of cessation (*nirodha-niyoga*)—as proven by such statements as "having become composed" (*samāhito bhūtvā*) which are similar to ritual injunctions (*karma-vākya*)—the meaning is that these [Upanishadic texts] are included within the scope of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). || 449 ||
134 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Relation—] [Vol. 1, p. 155]
Because the self's connection with misfortune is caused solely by latent impressions (vāsanā).
Whether other means exist or not, liberation occurs through cessation alone.

Is the fruit [of the Vedāntas] the knowledge of the injunction for cessation (*nirodha-niyoga*), or is it liberation? It cannot be the first, because that [knowledge] is established through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth alone; nor can the injunction for cessation have knowledge as its purpose by being subordinate to it, because if the relationship between the subordinate and the principal were as you desire, the reverse would result. Nor can it be the second, because the fact that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation is established by Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore, how can the authority of the Vedāntas be based on their being subordinate to the injunction for cessation? Thus [the objection].

He says: "It is the latent impression (*vāsanā*). Since the connection of the self with misfortune is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be caused solely by latent impressions, liberation results precisely from their cessation, which is what is being enjoined; this is the logical connection (*anvaya*). To the question, "If it is established that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, how can it be so [in this case]? he replies: "Other... Even for the knower (*jñānin*), because the appearance of transmigratory existence persists, there must be the cessation of latent impressions, and [only then] does knowledge...

The sense is that since it is possible to lead [the self] to that [state], the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures find their purpose by having that as their object; therefore, that alone is the means to liberation. || 446 ||
Independence [of the Veda] cannot be established, because in some cases there is an absence of an injunction (niyoga).
And since the operation of the word is established [otherwise], there is no possibility of a mandate (niyoga). || 447 ||

He states another reason for the authority of the Vedāntas precisely as being subordinate to the method of cessation (*nirodhavidhi*). [The word] "possible" (*saṃbhāvyam*) means this: in both worldly and Vedic usage, the independence—and thus the authoritative status—of a word being employed is not possible without an injunction (*niyoga*), because it is observed that such independence belongs only to that which culminates in one.

Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedāntas possess authority only by virtue of being subordinate to that [injunction]. Even if they possess authority through being subordinate to it, [the point remains].

If it is argued that the realization of the state of being one who has attained his goal (*siddhārthabodhitva*) remains unimpaired for us, [the author] says "no," beginning with "And if [it were] established" (*siddhe ceti*). The meaning is this: an injunction (*niyoga*) whose instrument is the sense of becoming (*bhāvārtha*) and which has that [becoming] as its object is not established in the case of what is already established; therefore, the Vedāntas, being subordinate to an injunction, could not make known an already established reality. || 447 ||
And an example is not intended for the status of being a means of valid cognition with respect to a real entity.
The injunction is for the sake of a quality, because that [quality] also has its operation as its object. || 448 ||

One might object: since in the injunction "one desiring sense-power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), only a subordinate factor (*guṇamātra*) is being enjoined for the sake of a fruit within the context of an already established ritual, even that [injunction]—though centered on a *niyoga* (obligation)—has as its object an already established fact (*siddhārthaviṣayatva*). By the same logic, the Vedāntas, which are subordinate to that [ritual], must likewise have established facts as their object. Anticipating this doubt, he says "And not... (*na ca*), following the principle of the section concerning "one desiring sense-power through curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmādhikaraṇanyāya*). The meaning of this is: "But because of the scriptural mention of a fruit, the action... (*phalaśrutestu karma...*) [is the primary element].

"Because the fruit is connected with the action" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 2.2.29). With reference to the Agnihotra, it is heard in scripture: "One desiring sensory power should offer curd. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is a different action qualified by an accessory enjoined here, or is the injunction of an accessory for the sake of a fruit within the context of the original action? In that case, the offering of curd would indeed be a different action from the Agnihotra offering, because a fruit is heard of here.

And that [result] is logically connected to the ritual action; for the result of the *homa* is indeed directly stated in the *śruti*, whereas the result of the curd is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Since direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection, and because the result is connected to the ritual action, it follows from the mention of the result that this is a distinct ritual action. It is not a prescription of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the result within the context of the original ritual based on syntactical connection—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is not a distinct ritual action, but rather the result arises from the accessory: one who desires heaven [should offer] to Agni...

Because the two statements— "One should offer the *hotṛ* oblation"— and "One should offer for one desiring sensory power (*indriya*)"— are not equal, in the former the fruit is mentioned in connection with the ritual action (*karman*),

whereas in the latter it is mentioned in connection with a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, in the statement regarding the desire for sensory power, the cognition of the fruit arises as being caused by a quality.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 135.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that in the present case of ritual action, it is an injunction regarding a quality for the sake of the fruit. As it has been stated in the section on the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*): "But because the two sentences are not equal, the [quality] should be understood there as a quality. And thus, since even an injunction regarding a quality has as its object a quality that is entered into by an operation, it does not [contradict] the Veda—
The status of these as examples is due to their being established by scripture and their capacity to convey already established meanings. || 448 ||
Furthermore, the status of an object as a human goal (puruṣārtha) belongs to that which is being experienced.
In all cases, it is understood in the Veda; by no means is it [understood] from direct experience. 449.

He states another reason for the Vedāntas lacking authority regarding an established, pure [Brahman], beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). In the world, it is observed everywhere that only that which is experienced constitutes the goal of human life (*pumartha*); even pleasure is such only when it is perceived as residing within oneself. The Veda, moreover, follows worldly convention; therefore, even there, only that which is an object of knowledge (*vedya*) constitutes the goal of human life, not the realization of the self-luminous Self (*svaprakāśātman*). Nor can the Veda possess authority regarding that which is fruitless, because its authority is invariably connected to a result.
And thus, the sense is that the Vedāntas are authoritative precisely as being subordinate to an injunction for the sake of a fruit. || 449 ||
And therefore, what arises from a word is mere intuition, not a valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, it is established that the human goal (puruṣārtha) is indeed what is being perceived. || 450 ||

If the experience of a self-luminous reality were not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), what would be the status of such scriptural passages as "consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānānanda*) which illuminate its being a human goal?

To this he replies: "And therefore... Since it is observed that only that which is an object of experience can be a human goal, words such as "consciousness" and so forth give rise to a mere mental appearance (*pratibhā*) and not to valid knowledge (*māna*).

This is because he accepts that the suffix *-tas* (in *vijñānatas*) functions as a substitute for all case endings; however, it does not constitute valid knowledge, as that would contradict common worldly experience—this is the meaning.

The word *iti* serves to refer back to the passage beginning with "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). He states the conclusion: that if experience were not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then the mandate (*niyoga*) and so forth would be its goal instead. He provides the reason for this by saying "because it is perceived," meaning that it is established that only that which is being experienced constitutes the human goal in all cases;
thus he says "on account of its being well-known. || 410 ||
Furthermore, an entity that is being appropriated is not established as the object of an action.
That which is observed to accomplish the purpose of man, even when its status as a constituent part [of the means] is not yet fully recognized.

Anticipating the objection that if things to be experienced, such as ritual injunctions (*niyoga*), can constitute human goals (*puruṣārtha*), then even established entities (*siddhavastu*) understood through words would likewise be established as human goals—thereby undermining the rule that words have only things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as their objects—the author says "also" (*api*). Even an established entity, though cognized from the Veda, is not seen to accomplish a human goal unless it is understood through scripture (*śruti*) and other means as being subordinate to ritual action; therefore, a word does not [function] toward a pure, established object.
Such is the construction [of the sentence]. || 451 ||
And that which is not being grasped does not possess the status of being a known constituent part.
If the self were not subordinate to it, its subordination toward the injunction would not be possible. || 452 ||

In that regard, he says [the following] concerning the fact that the Self also possesses the status of being established by verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇaka*) as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being a subordinate element of an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatva*): "And when it is not being enjoined... (Anupādīyamānaśca). For the Self is not made known by the Veda, because its nature is self-luminous experience (*svaprakāśānubhava-svabhāvatva*); nor is its status as a subordinate element of action known through scripture (*śruti*) and so forth. And if this is so, then its being a human goal by way of being a subordinate element of an injunction lacks any basis of proof (*mānābhāva*).
This is the meaning. || 452 ||
1. nāṃ śuddhasiddhā; 2. kha.
saṃcita [vol 1, page 157]
The Siddhas, 136 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Introduction]...
For there is the direct scriptural statement: "One should worship one's own Self."
If you claim that it is a constituent part therein, then you have entered my own path from here. || 453 ||

He raises the objection that the scriptural statement is the authority for the self being a subordinate element of ritual action, by saying, "One should meditate" (*upāsīta*). The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) excludes the possibility that the statement is merely to be inferred; for this very reason, it was said, "because such a word is heard. In that context, the expression "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the injunction regarding meditation. This refers to the position that the self's status as a human goal is derived from its being a subordinate element of the injunction, and that the Vedāntas possess authority with respect to that [self].

The proponent of the Vedic injunction (*niyogavādin*) says: "If [the Veda] were established as being pure, then its authority would belong to that [purity], which would result in the destruction of your position; whereas if its authority is held to exist solely by virtue of being subordinate to an injunction, then my own position is attained. He says, "You have followed my path," meaning that you have come to this path by taking me, the proponent of the injunction, as your guide. Alternatively, the suffix rule for compound endings may be considered non-eternal (*anitya*). (453)
The authority of the word is established on the basis of its being intent upon the performance of ritual action.
Thus some explain it, being solely devoted to the meaning of the injunction (niyoga). || 454 ||

He distinguishes his own path with the words "kriyā" (action). Since the Vedāntas are subordinate to the injunctions for cessation [of action], and since ritual actions also exist within that very context, the connection between the two sections is established; thus he concludes with the words "iti vyācakṣate" (thus they explain). Of this...
The phrase "niyoga" indicates that the position [of the opponent] is to be rejected because it is rooted in attachment. || 454 ||
This was not well stated so emphatically, even because of the absence of a formal injunction.
When the desired object is fully accomplished through ordinary worldly means alone. || 455 ||

He asserts that it is incorrect to claim that liberation occurs solely from cessation (*nirodha*). He states: "This is not so. The connection is as follows: that which was loudly and emphatically proclaimed by the proponent of the injunction for cessation—that [position] is not sound. Regarding the view that liberation results from the cessation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even without a formal injunction (*niyoga*), the attainment of the desired goal—which consists of the removal of what is harmful and its causes, and the attainment of human goals and their causes—is established through ordinary means of knowledge (*laukika-pramāṇa*) alone; therefore, the Vedic word would be rendered useless. Thus, [the opponent's position] is unsound.
He accomplishes that very [state] in this way: "By means of application" (niyoga). || 455 ||
Because it exists when that [object] exists, and because it has the latent impression as its sole basis, it serves as the inferential mark.
The connection of the self with misfortune is known [to be adventitious], but it is not real.
Anticipating the question of how suffering and its cause are established by worldly experience, he says: "tadbhāve... (In the presence of that...).

The connection of the Self with suffering—such as being a mother and so forth—which appears, arises from the support of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), based on the evidence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): namely, that it exists when those awakened latent impressions of waking states and the like exist, and it does not exist when they do not. Thus, it is known to be of the nature of the non-Self.
Since the body does not manifest during sleep and so forth, the meaning is that through both direct experience and inference, there is no cognition of the object nor of its cause. || 456 ||
Therefore, because the cause of connection with saṃsāra is established.
Therefore, through that very sign, when it is destroyed, misfortune ceases.

Nevertheless, as to how there can be a proposition regarding the futility of the Vedic words, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The connection with what follows is this: since the bondage of the Self to its objects and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is its cause are established by the very evidence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on the aforementioned experience, the word [of scripture] is fruitless. The sense is that a word is not purposeful regarding an object already established by evidence such as inference, because there is no subject matter that has not yet been known.
1. *Caritrati* | i | 2. kha. *vameva sā* | 3. kha. *vastutaḥ* | [Vol.
1, page 158] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 137.

Now, one might object: "Even if speech lacks purposefulness because its objects are neither the human goal nor its causes, it may still possess purposefulness by having as its object the human goal and its causes. To this, he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). Through *samādhi*, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of waking and other states are restrained, but not otherwise; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that only by means of the restraint of the mind (*manonirodha*)—as the sole method—is there the destruction of that cause of bondage called *vāsanā*. According to the principle that "in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect," [the goal is attained].

By which [knowledge] that which is called bondage—an evil—is removed; and thus, since the human goal and its cause are established even without the scripture, the opponent's objection regarding the uselessness of the scripture is unavoidable. This is the meaning. || 417 ||
Even without a verbal statement, [the proof is established] through logical demonstration, as in the case of the Buddhists and others.
Therefore, the teaching regarding liberation as the goal of human endeavor would be fruitless. || 458 ||

He states the resulting conclusion—that even for you, like that of the Buddhists and others, the Vedas are purposeless—on the grounds that the human goal called liberation, as well as its cause, the cessation of mental impressions (*manovāsanā*), are established through inference and other means even without Vedic speech. [The verse says: "Without... and so on. The connection is: "because it is established from this" (*ataḥ siddhitaḥ*). || 498 ||
Because of the infinity of latent impressions arising from many past births that have already passed.
Their cessation is impossible for human beings within a single lifetime. (459)

As for the claim that "therefore, a person is enjoined by scripture to restrain those latent impressions (*vāsanā*)," one must consider whether these impressions to be restrained are past, present, or future. Regarding the first case, he says: "The past... Since the latent impressions acquired in past births are infinite and have already passed away, their restraint is difficult to accomplish. For even gods and others can only with great difficulty restrain such aforementioned impressions.

The meaning is that human beings, who are the subjects of the scriptures, do not [act] in this manner. The second [alternative] is not tenable, because since present latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are occasional, their cessation is established even without an injunction (*niyoga*). The third is also not tenable; it should be understood that because future latent impressions have not yet arrived, their cessation is difficult to accomplish. || 459 ||
If [this is not achieved] through the direct realization of the Self, which cuts away the darkness regarding the innermost reality;
If the cultivation of suffering and so forth has been destroyed, how could that cultivation dispel it? || 460 ||
Furthermore, regarding the cessation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is knowledge, its repeated practice, or application toward its object the cause?

To refute the first, he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). The sense is that if liberation occurs through the cessation of latent impressions by means of the destruction of ignorance regarding the Self—via the direct realization of the Self—then you have merely accepted our own position. He rejects the second [alternative] with: "If not. Knowledge is [the destroyer of] ignorance.

If the cultivation of knowledge does not dispel the latent impression (*vāsanā*), or if it dispels both [the impression and its object], then how could the cultivation of knowledge—which has been destroyed by long-standing and extremely dense cultivations of suffering and so forth—dispel ignorance along with its effects? For the meaning is this: a cultivation that is itself sublated is not capable of sublating another. || 460 ||
And thus, by way of the path of ritual injunction (niyoga), this liberation is not accomplished.
We shall explain accordingly at the appropriate occasion by means of a clear path of reasoning. (461)

He refutes the third position—that the application of the practice of knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa-niyoga*) is the cause of liberation by way of the removal of ignorance and so forth—with the words "niyoga" (application). [Vol. 1, p.
159] 1. Because it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
138 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]
He says, "We shall explain," [referring to the passage] beginning with "Liberation does not result from the power of *niyoga*; this is another means of experience. || 461 ||
Since this Self is in reality neither the meaning of a word nor the meaning of a sentence, because its true nature is realized precisely through the scripture that negates those [concepts]. (462)

The view that liberation occurs precisely through cessation (*nirodha*) and so forth has been refuted. As for the argument that because the Self is a category (*padārtha*), it must be cognizable by other means of knowledge—just like rice and the like—the author replies with the words beginning with "No" (*na*). Since the meaning of a sentence consists either of related categories or their mutual relation, how can the Self, which is the meaning of the sentence, be something that is not a category? To this he says: "No. If that is so, then how is it the subject matter of the Veda? To this he replies:
Regarding the word "tat": all particularities, such as being an object of a category (padārthatva) and so forth, constitute the meaning of that word. The second "tat" refers to the Self.
The meaning is that, by means of negating all superimposed particularities, that which is solely consciousness is the subject matter of the Veda. || 462 ||
Even in the absence of latent impressions (vāsanās), as in deep sleep and similar states, there is no liberation.
Nor is there destruction of the self of vision due to the absence of the activity of a sentient being or a person. || 463 ||

Having dispelled the suspicion that the Self might be accessible through other means of knowledge by virtue of being a *padārtha* (an objective category), he states another objection regarding the claim that liberation occurs solely through cessation:
"Of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*)... Nor should it be argued that latent impressions of waking and so forth exist there [in deep sleep] because of a subsequent re-emergence;

for that would entail the collapse of the very nature of deep sleep and the like. Nor can it be said that they exist there in the form of their cause, since this specific character [of causality] is present in the other states as well.

Furthermore, it is not correct to say that even in such states as deep sleep there is no liberation because the cause—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—still exists; for if that were the case, liberation would result solely from the destruction of that cause, rather than from the destruction of the latent impressions, and the destruction of the cause would itself result from knowledge. This is the intended meaning. As for the argument that because the Self is by nature self-luminous, its manifestation must necessarily occur once the latent impressions have been suppressed—that too applies to states such as deep sleep.

He states that [the definition] is too broad (*vyabhicārī*) by saying "māna" (cognition). By the word "vā," the negative particle (*nañ*) is drawn back [into the compound]. The intended meaning is that even when the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa-prathana*) occurs, its practical usage (*tad-vyavahāra*) is not possible without cognition (*māna*). || 463 ||
For ignorance alone is the cause of its connection with all that is harmful.
For even in the conjunction of latent impressions (vāsanās), that very same [causal efficiency] is required. || 464 ||
Regarding the statement, "Because the self's connection with misfortune has *vāsanā* alone as its cause," it was said therein that *vāsanā* is the cause of misfortune.

To this, he says: "All... [etc.]. One might object: "Since it is possible for even those *vāsanās* that possess ignorance (*avidyā*) to be causes, how can there be such a restriction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the *vāsanās*... [etc.]. The meaning is that because they cannot function as material causes—due to their being effects themselves and the resulting infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—ignorance alone, together with the *vāsanās*, is the cause of misfortune.
It is stated as "that very [avidyā]" in order to demonstrate that for the unattached Self, there can be no association with latent impressions (vāsanā) without avidyā. || 464 ||
Independence is also conceivable on account of the absence of a mandatory injunction (niyoga).
And we shall explain it accordingly, by way of a clear and logical path. (465)

Regarding the statement that "it is possible [for there to be] independence [of the word], yet there is no independence of the word's authority without entry into an injunction," he replies with the words "It is possible. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "we shall explain this in the passage beginning with 'Every [word]' and so forth" (verse 465).
This is perceived by you as well, solely through the power of your own direct experience.
88. An injunction and the like constitute the object of a means of valid cognition, but experience does not [arise] from an injunction. || 466 ||
[Vol. 1, p.
160] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Regarding the objection that "once [the object] is established, the application (*niyoga*) is not possible," he replies with the words "svānubhūti" (one's own experience). [The proponent of] *niyoga*—

An insentient object such as an injunction (*niyoga*) is understood only through the power of the conscious self (*cidātman*); likewise, the conscious principle (*cid-dhātu*), which establishes that object, does not depend upon an injunction for its own realization. For the sun, which illuminates forms and other objects, does not illuminate by depending on them.
Therefore, the objection that an injunction is impossible once the conscious self has been established is not a fault, because it is [already] accepted [by us]. This is the meaning. || 466 ||
That whose non-establishment is not due to ignorance, nor is its establishment due to a means of valid cognition.
How can that reality of experience be said to be dependent? || 467 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the establishment of an object of knowledge depends upon a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and no other means of knowledge is accepted for the Self? Furthermore, the scripture (*āgama*) is intent upon injunction (*niyoga*) and does not have as its scope the Self untouched by injunction. Therefore, the dependence on injunction for the establishment of the Self is unavoidable. [Reply: He says "of whom... to show this is not so. He states the reason why there is neither establishment nor non-establishment through knowledge or ignorance: "because its nature is experience" (*anubhavatattvasya*). [This refers to] that which has neither risen nor set...

He says, "Why? [verse 467], meaning that once the single essence of the immutable, innate consciousness (mitakūṭasthabodha) is established, there is not even the slightest suspicion of a requirement for injunctions (niyoga) and the like.
For that which is other than it is established solely through the cognition of its own self as primary.
This is due to dependence upon the cognition of an effect, and not because of the reality of the self as an experienced entity. || 468 ||

In that very context, he states another reason: "svapradhāna... (independent). The self-substance (*ātman-vastu*) is independent, not dependent on anything else, and autonomous. Intellect (*buddhi*) is of the nature of that [self], which is consciousness (*caitanya*). Since the entire category of non-self, which is distinct from itself, has its existence obtained only through that very self, there is no requirement for an injunction or other such mental constructs for the sake of the self-establishment of this conscious reality. For the cognition of a rope does not depend upon the cognition of a snake; therefore, the establishment of the self [does not require them].
The meaning is "dependent upon yoga. || 468 ||
Who indeed has considered that which is being experienced to be the goal of man?
Because the fruit of pride alone is consistently associated with the human goal [of liberation]. || 469 ||

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of that which is being experienced," it was stated there that only the object of experience (*anubhāvya*) constitutes the human goal (*pumarthatva*). To this, he replies: "Which? The meaning is that the status of the human goal belonging to an isolated experience (*niṣkṛṣṭānubhava*) as such has never been apprehended through any means of valid cognition (*māna*). Then, of what, indeed, does the status of the human goal consist?

To this he replies: "Of the fruit of knowledge" (*mānaphalasya*). Because experience is connected with the human goal by way of being a qualification of the desired object, it is that very [experience] which persists [through time] that possesses the status of being that goal.

For a garland or the like, though desired as such, does not possess that status if it has not ascended into experience; thus, the status of being a human goal belongs only to the experience that is non-deviant [with respect to the object], and not to the object which is mutually deviant [from the experience]. This is the meaning. || 469 ||
And since cognition has no fruit other than itself, how can it be restricted solely to the object?
This connection between action and its fruit does not exist, because the mother is the enjoyer.

If it is argued that because experience (*anubhūti*) is dependent upon that which is experienced (*anubhāvya*), it too—like color and other qualities residing therein—is itself merely an object of experience, and therefore the object alone constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), [the author] says "no," for [it is established by] "cognition" (*pratīteḥ*). The meaning is as follows: experience is the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*māna*); the object is not its substrate, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). For there can be no relationship of substrate and superstrate between the insentient and the sentient; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Objection: Since a fruit cannot exist independently, a substrate must be stated; in that case, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*)...

He says "no" to the idea that [the self] is dependent on the means of knowledge (*meya*). He states: "Not by action. For the fruit of the means of knowledge (*māna*) rests upon the knower (*mātṛ*), whereas the fruit of an action rests upon the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
And these two are not distinct; therefore, the connection with that fruit—which is metaphorically called "experience" (*anubhava*)—belongs to that very self which is one with it.

The meaning is that Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [is composed]; since it is metaphorically attributed [to him], the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*), because it is not proven that the fruit of a means of knowledge resides in the object of knowledge. || 470 ||
And no object whatsoever is held to exist apart from the self's own experience.
This applies even to all means of valid cognition; how much more so in the case of the Vedānta teaching? || 471 ||

Regarding the point that the Vedāntas do not possess the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an object in the same way as the senses do, he says: "And not... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because there is no other [object] unknown [to it]. He states what is indicated by the word "also" (*api*): "What more need be said? The meaning is: since there is no object in the Vedāntas other than the Self, whose nature is experience in the form of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), what further need is there to say anything? For that [Self] alone is the unknown [object]. || 471 ||
All worldly and Vedic conventional practice in the world as well.
Therefore, the purpose of the Pradhāna is solely for the sake of the enjoyer; nothing else is intended for it. || 472 ||

Regarding the fact that the authority of the Vedāntas rests solely upon the Supreme Self, the conscious essence, which is the supreme human goal untouched by [the injunctions of] *niyoga*, he states another reason:
"In the world," etc. All worldly activity everywhere has the enjoyer as its purpose, not any other;

for the experience of the nature of the enjoyer is primary as the end to which everything else is subordinate. Since that very [Self], being the object of supreme love, is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and since there is no new human goal [other than this]...
This is the purport of the word; thus, the meaning is that the authority of the Vedāntas rests upon the inner self (pratīc) whose nature is bliss. || 472 ||
"Verily, O Maitreyī, [the husband is not dear for the sake of the husband]; rather, it is this Self that is dearer. Thus it is also said.
In this entire world, there is nothing superior to the Self.

He states the proof for the fact that the inward-facing Self (pratīc) is unsurpassed bliss: "Or rather not... In this world, among the entirety of things such as wife and son, the Self is the primary [object of affection], and nothing other than the Self—such as a wife—is so; for it is heard in scripture that "the wife is not dear for the sake of the wife, but for the sake of the Self she is dear," and so forth. Furthermore, since the primary Self is the object of love that is free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhi), how could It not be supreme bliss?
The meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "This is dearer than a son" declares its status as supreme bliss by virtue of its being the object of unsurpassed affection. || 473 ||
Neither the knower, nor the means of knowledge, nor the activity, the object of knowledge, or the fruit are considered primary here; for it is the enjoyer alone who is primary. (474)

To the question of how the enjoyer (bhoktṛ) can be primary when the material cause and so forth are primary, he replies: "No. Here, "here" refers to the sphere of empirical experience (vyavahārabhūmi).

The reason for this is given as "of the enjoyer. The meaning is that because the enjoyer is desired as the sovereign of all, it is logical that he possesses primacy; whereas for the other [the material cause], such primacy is untenable since it exists only as a subordinate element (śeṣatayā). || 474 ||
It is certain that even the agent-state of the self exists for the sake of the experiencer.
Therefore, this other [element] as well is employed for the sake of the enjoyer. || 475 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the state of being an agent is primary because it is the locus of action? How then can the enjoyer alone be primary? To this he says: "Of the Self. [Objection: But a person who is intent upon sense objects considers his son and so forth to be primary. To this he says: "Since... Since agency exists for the sake of the enjoyer, everything else—such as sons and so forth—is for his sake; therefore, nothing other than the enjoying Self is primary.
The meaning is that attachment to anything other than that is indeed an error. || 475 ||
1 kha. ‘is seen’; 2 kha. ‘and’. [Vol.
1, page 162] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstramañjarī composed by Ānandagiri. 141.
Nor is there any other entity, distinct from the Self, that falls within the scope of valid cognition.
How this is possible will be explained further below.

Furthermore, there exists nothing that is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) as being distinct from the Self, such that one might suspect it possesses primacy and so forth; thus he says, "Nor... He explains how an entity other than the Self is imagined: "And just as... The word *udarka* refers to the investigation into the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so on. || 476 ||
Disregarding the meaning as it was stated, they are solely intent upon the meaning of the injunction.
Some proclaim that the Vedāntas have as their sole purpose the accomplishment of a task.

Thus, since the immutable experience of the Self as Brahman—which is the ultimate human goal—is established by the authority of the Vedāntas, it is impossible for those [Vedāntic texts] to be subordinate to injunctions regarding cessation (*nirodha*).

Furthermore, the connections between the two sections (karmakāṇḍa and jñānakāṇḍa) as proposed by others are untenable. Therefore, having accepted the connection based on the *vividiṣā* passage—that actions are the cause of knowledge by way of purification, whereas the Upaniṣads are the direct cause—the commentary beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) has been explained. Now, however...

He states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which is to be refuted by the commentary beginning with "sarvo'pi" (everyone...). By the words "anādṛtya" (disregarding) and so forth, the meaning is as follows: some people, having rendered everything stated—including the distinction between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) regarding the qualified aspirants (*adhikārī*) and so on, the specific relationship (*saṃbandha*), and the reality known as identity (*aikātmya*)—as lacking scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*), assert that the Vedāntas terminate solely in action (*kārya*). He indicates the fallacious nature of the prima facie position about to be discussed by [the word] *niyo*...
The way of entry. || 477 ||
Because the means of valid cognition consisting of scripture is restricted solely to the object to be accomplished.
Whence, then, comes this abiding in oneness that was previously asserted by you? (478)

Anticipating the objection that the statement beginning with "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) has been declared to be intent upon identity and that there is no reason to disregard it, he says: "kārya... (It is concerned with what is to be done).

The meaning is that even this [sentence] is directed toward an action (*kāryaniṣṭha*), because it is a scriptural statement of authority (*pramāṇavākya*), like an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*). Anticipating the further objection that if all of the Veda were directed toward action, it might also be directed toward an existing reality (*vastuniṣṭha*), he says: "eka... (One...). Indeed, a single sentence cannot have two purposes when there is a difference in meaning.

The sense is that [the two] would constitute a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Anticipating the objection that, according to the principle of "the past and the future" (*bhūtabhavyanyāya*), even the teaching regarding an existing entity (*bhūta*) might be subordinate to an action (*kāryaśeṣatayā*), he says "only" (*mātra*), considering that even an existing entity which is subordinate to an action is itself nothing but an action. || 478 ||
For its independence is not established by the fact that it makes known an already existing thing.
For that which is measured by another means of knowledge is called an established entity. || 479 ||

[The author] establishes that scripture does not have as its final aim an already established fact (*siddhārtha*). [He says: "For not... The meaning is this: since scripture, which is accepted as having an established fact as its object, reveals that very fact, its authority is not independent; for it is capable of being verified by other means of knowledge (*māna*), and what terminates in such [a fact] cannot be independent.
[An objection: But even if scripture were to terminate in an action (*kārya*), the loss of independent authority would be the same. [The author] says "no," for... [he continues: "Since..."

That which is an established entity (*siddha-vastu*) is said to be suitable for other means of knowledge (*mānāntara-yogya*), whereas that which is an effect (*kārya*) is not so suitable; therefore, because it is accepted as being "unprecedented" (*apūrva*)—not having been previously known through other means of knowledge—the validity of [the Vedic injunction] resting upon that [effect] is independent (*anapekṣya*). This is the meaning. || 479 ||
The restriction of the expressive power of words is understood from worldly usage alone.
In the world, an object established through other means of knowledge is expressed solely for the sake of action.
[Page 163] Because its validity [is derived from that].
142 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Introduction]—

He states another reason for the position that the entire Veda is intent upon action (*kāryaniṣṭha*) and is not an authority regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*). [The verse begins with] "By words" (*śabda*). A word whose power (*śakti*) is known is the sublater [of doubt], in the sense that its power regarding this specific meaning is ascertained; that [ascertainment] is understood solely from the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and therefore it culminates in action—this is the meaning. From the evidence (*liṅga*) of the usage of elders, the power of a word is grasped even in the case of an established fact.

Anticipating this objection and considering that a linguistic sign (liṅga) is dependent upon a cognition that prompts action—therefore, such [an objection] is not valid—he says: "In the world" (loke).

The meaning is that since, on the plane of worldly transaction, an established entity (siddhārtha) proven by perception and other means is spoken of only as a supplement to what is to be done (kārya), the apprehension of its expressive power (śakti) occurs in relation to that which is connected to it; thus, the Veda is intent solely upon that [action]. || 480 ||
For there is no speech that is devoid of both engagement and withdrawal.
Since no object is perceived here, there can be no validity regarding the thing-in-itself.

Furthermore, the validity of verbal testimony depends upon its intended meaning (tātparya), and that [intended meaning] resides in what is beneficial to man (puruṣārtha). That [benefit] is accomplished through engagement or avoidance, and those two depend upon injunction and prohibition; moreover, these two relate to what is to be done (kārya). Therefore, he states with the words "No" and so forth that the Veda does not have as its primary aim an already established fact (siddhārtha).
Thus, the restriction of both linguistic capacity (śakti) and intended meaning (tātparya) to what is to be done has been demonstrated. || 489 ||
