Nor is there an understanding of the relationship [between word and meaning] from a word that expresses an already existent object.
From the activity initiated by the prompter, the cognition regarding the object is inferred. || 482 ||
Therefore, the capacity of the word is determined from the cognition [it produces].
Therefore, this [sentence] has only the task [to be accomplished] as its object, according to valid cognition.

[Objection: But surely *śakti* (the expressive power of a word) does not reside solely in that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), because it is established even from sentences that convey an already established fact (*siddhārtha*)—such as "A son has been born to you"—which are not impelling (*pravartaka*). Since such [impulsion] is impossible there, one must either supply an implied *kārya* or resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) even in those cases. Intending to address this, he says: "By relation" (*saṃbandha*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because there is an absence of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) due to the absence of activity. He then states how the cognition of *śakti* occurs in such cases:

Regarding the phrase "from the inciter": immediately after hearing the inciting speech uttered by an elder (uttamavṛddha), a child infers that the middle-aged person’s (madhyamavṛddha) activity is preceded by a cognition of the object that prompts action. [The inference is: "The activity under discussion is preceded by a cognition of the inciter, because it is an activity preceded by cognition, like a [previously] agreed-upon case. Furthermore, since that cognition of the inciter is perceived to follow the presence and absence of the word, it is determined to have arisen from that word. Thus, the inciter—

Having generally ascertained the capacity of a word for its meaning through the methods of presence (*anvaya*) and absence (*vyatireka*), it is understood that words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denote that which prompts action (*pravartaka*), while other words denote their own meanings as connected to that [prompting]. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of the word's power resides in the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished).

Anticipating the objection that even if the power of words is known to reside in the *kārya*, a sentence might still possess authority regarding an already established fact (*siddha-artha*), he says: "In the *kārya*... [and so forth].

Since words whose powers are known convey their own respective meanings, and since the power [of the word] is known with respect to the action (kārya), therefore the meaning of the word is the action. || 482 ||
Even by those who maintain that the meaning of a sentence is the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka), [the same principle applies].
Because they involve reiteration and contradiction, those [scriptures] lack authority. || 484 ||

But surely, a sentence is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the meaning of a sentence—the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*); how then can the authority of a sentence have only the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*) as its object? [Note: Variants *mahā* and *veṃ* appear in manuscripts; the reading is based on the context of the argument.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 143] Regarding that, he says: "Action" (*kriyā*). In cases such as "he cooks rice," the connection between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is capable of being apprehended through other means of knowledge; therefore—
The meaning is that, since a sentence lacks authority in those cases due to agreement and disagreement, its authority resides in the *niyoga* (the injunction). || 484 ||
But it is not possible for the effect to enter into the interior [of its cause].
For the comprehension of the purpose of the ritual act arises from the word alone, not from worldly usage.

[Objection: But even in that case, since it is an object of action (*kāryātman*), other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) are possible—just as with worldly objects of action—and thus the aforementioned defect remains the same. [Response: No; he says this with the words "by another means of knowledge" (*māntareti*). He states the reason for this with the words "from verbal testimony" (*śabdāditi*). According to the principle that "an object of action distinct from mere activity (*kriyā*) which is to be known cannot be known by other means of knowledge," the sentence is the authority regarding an injunction (*niyoga*) not previously established by other means of knowledge; for even though it is an object of action, it does not [function] like a worldly object of action.

Since it would follow that being an object of another means of knowledge applies equally to "action-ness" (kriyātva) as well, and since it will be stated later that the mandate (niyoga) is distinct from that, the point is that the authority of the sentence resides in the cognition of the impelling effect produced by words such as the optative suffix (liṅ). || 485 ||
The word "pravartana" (causing to proceed) is expressed by the term "pravartaka" (the prompter).
Since a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) functions by making [an object] known, it would become an instigator (kāraka) by impelling [action]. || 486 ||

[Objection: But surely, since the Bhāṣya states that "the Vedic injunction (codanā) is the cognition that impels [one to act], arising from words such as the optative suffix (liṅ)," the optative suffix itself must be the impeller;

therefore, [the author] says: "[It is] the impelling. Why should one assume that the author of the Bhāṣya calls the optative suffix an "impeller" only because it makes known the impelling? Why might its being an impeller not be intended directly? To this, he says: "making known..."

"Because it is a means of knowledge (pramāṇa)"—since a means of knowledge is informative (jñāpaka) and not a causal agent (kāraka) like passion and so forth, if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others were the instigator (*pravartaka*), they would be causal agents and not a means of knowledge; yet they are accepted as a means of knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that the statement in the Bhāṣya regarding their being "instigators" is made solely by way of their expressing the instigation. || 486 ||
Nor is it suspected that passion and the like arise from the word when there is a cognition of incitement.
Passion and the like are the instigators; sound is the communicator of the instigation. || 487 ||

If it is argued that even if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers denote an instigator (*pravartaka*), let the instigator be desire (*rāga*) and the like, and not the "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*), [the author] says "no," and states: "From the word" (*śabdāt*). When the understanding of an instigator arises from the word containing the optative suffix and so forth, desire and the like cannot be suspected of being the instigator; he states the reason for this as: "Desire and the like" (*rāgādi*). Even though desire and the like are not themselves instigators because they do not constitute the instigator itself, they nevertheless follow upon the activity (*pravṛtti*).

One might object that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth do not possess such a nature [of being a motivator], because, like desire and the like, they are causes of causes; thus, their positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established otherwise, as they lack direct causal agency (*akārakatva*).

Anticipating this, he says "preraṇā" (impulsion), meaning: since it would follow that [the suffix] must be a causal factor (*kāraka*) if it were the actual motivator, this is not the case. A "sound" (*dhvani*) refers to words such as the optative suffix;
it is not itself the motivator, but rather conforms to activity by making known the meaning of impulsion, which is the motivator.
This is the meaning of what was stated. || 487 ||
Because the Lord is observed to possess the quality of agency in the accomplishment of the purpose once he has commanded it.
And since the object such as passion is not established, the activity of the agent does not arise from passion.

It has been stated that because desire (*rāga*) and the like, as well as verbal expression (*śabda*), cannot logically function as motivators, it is only the "task" (*kārya*) that serves this purpose. Alternatively, although in common worldly experience desire and the like are indeed the motivators, when defining the meaning of words, such is not the case for them; thus he says: "Commanded," etc. When a student or similar person carries out tasks such as bringing a cow—which are the objects of a command from a teacher or the like—even in the absence of desire and so forth, the activity (*kṛti*) arises solely through the power of the command.
1 sva. can be accomplished; 2 kha. for the sake of the meaning of the suffix *rya*; 3 kha. having measured; 4 kha. two masculine [forms].

The meaning is that since the activity of a master, a servant, or the like is observed to be preceded by effort involving deliberation, the activity occurring immediately after the word does not arise from passion (*rāga*) or similar factors. || 488 ||
Through the perception of the master’s anger, favor, and so forth, as well as his inner intentions and heart's desire.
Nor would there be any inclination on the part of the listener [to act] based on the word, because anger and so forth are not perceived from it.

Even though it does not incite passion or hatred residing in the listener, one might suspect that because anger and the like of an authoritative elder (uttamavṛddha)—which are established by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers—are absent [in the listener], the [optative] does not have the capacity to incite action.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "The master," etc. The word "etc. refers to joy, sorrow, and so forth;

the meaning is that even from knowing his internal intention (*ākūta*), which is the very purpose residing in his heart, there is no inclination to act. He states the reason for this: "From the word," etc.

The meaning of the reason is that, unlike the case of an injunction (*niyoga*), no anger on the part of a master or similar [sentiment] is perceived from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. || 489 ||
The optative suffixes and others are not recorded in tradition as being expressive of anger and the like.
For those [objects] are measured by other means of knowledge, and they indeed incite men to action. || 490 ||
It establishes the reason: "the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth. This means that they are traditionally remembered as conveying only injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like.

Since it is well known that even the anger of a master and similar factors act as motivators, if [injunction] were not verbal in nature, by what would its status as a motivator be understood? Indeed, something that is unknown cannot be a motivator.
Anticipating the objection that this consequence would apply even to what is already known through other means—such as the anger of a master—he says: "By another means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*).
The sense is that since they do not possess a meaning unobtainable by other means, they lack the capacity to incite action toward an object that has already come into being. || 490 ||
In this context, they are indicated by signs such as the names of the Ganges and other rivers.
Passion and the other [defilements] serve as the means for accomplishing the object in order to bring about the fulfillment of the injunction.
What is that other means of knowledge? He states it: "Fie! and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sūtras for anger, favor, joy, sorrow, and so on are indicated.

The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the hearing of the sentence. "Being inferred from gestures" (*iṅgitatva*) means being inferred. The ellipsis is: "those [gestures] are not the denotative meanings (*śabdārtha*) of those words.

Now, if neither the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so on, nor passion (*rāga*) and so on, nor anger (*kopa*) and so on possess the capacity to instigate action, then by process of elimination, the *kārya* (the thing-to-be-done) alone must be the instigator.

The statement that passion (*rāga*) and so forth are the instigators (*preraṇākārī*) because they are obtained from the [Vedic] text is incorrect; for the injunction (*niyoga*) known as instigation is dependent upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and is therefore not produced by passion and the like. To this, he says: "Passion and so forth. The meaning is: by accomplishing the meaning of the verbal root for the sake of fulfilling the injunction, they also accomplish that [injunction] known as instigation; thus, it is logical that passion and the like are the instigators. || 491 ||
And for this very reason, even though it is associated with passion and the like, it is distinguished [from them].
Since one who is told "Go!"—the meaning of the imperative and other such moods—proceeds toward his own purpose without [any other] purpose [of the word itself], [the word is not the cause]. || 492 ||

[Objection: "But surely, since in worldly sentences it is observed that the *niyoga* (injunction) is always associated with passion (*rāga*) and the like, and since in every case where activity follows immediately upon hearing the words, it is perceived that the *niyoga* as thus associated is the motivator, it is impossible to distinguish that the motivator is the *niyoga* alone and not passion and so forth; therefore, [the author] says:
'For this very reason. For there is no rule that in worldly sentences the observation of the *niyoga* is necessarily associated with passion and the like."

The meaning is as follows: since a listener addressed by a master with the command "Go! proceeds toward his own goal even without a desire for the fruit [of that action], it follows that even in cases where verbal activity (*śābdapravṛtti*) occurs through passion and the like, the mandate (*niyoga*)—being conjoined with those [passions]—is nevertheless distinguished from them. Therefore, the certainty is established that the mandate alone, following along [with the person], is the motivator, and not passion or the like. || 492 ||
1. *abdo darpaśo*; 2. *kale pra*; 3. *gato ni*.
[Vol.
1, page 166] The Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 145.
But surely [this is known] through inference from the great sentences connected with giving and so forth.
When only a portion is stated, such as "Go," one proceeds to act solely out of desire. || 493 ||

He raises the objection that since no one ever engages in action without a desire for a result (*phalarāga*), and since it is only an injunction (*niyoga*) conjoined with such desire that possesses the power to impel, the distinction between the stated power to impel [the injunction] is unestablished. This is introduced with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). When an elder person utters a portion of a sentence such as "Go! or "Stay!", there arises a great [injunction] connected to giving and so forth, in the form of "Go to the village, I will give you wealth," or "Stay here, you shall obtain clothing and the like."

The speech of the middle-aged elder is inferred [to be as follows]: "The disputed activity of speech culminates in a result for the listener, because it is a specific instance of speech-activity, like that which is commonly agreed upon; therefore, activity proceeds from the mandate (niyoga) alone when accompanied by an attachment to substances and so forth. The meaning is that there is no extraction of a separate motivator [other than the mandate]. || 493 ||
Even when employing the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), if there is no discernment of the meaning of the constituent words (padārtha).
However, this activity of a person is observed to arise from the imperative mood (*loṭ*) and so forth alone, and not from anything else. (494)

He refutes [the objection] with the words "in the case of a great sentence" (*mahāvākya*). Where a great sentence is employed even without the utterance of a portion of that sentence, the activity of a person—such as a middle-aged elder—is observed; and in the discernment of what prompts action, it is determined that this proceeds from the injunction (*niyoga*) alone, expressed by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) and so forth, and not from passion (*rāga*), because the passion of the listener is difficult to establish there. Therefore, [it is established] by means of the sentence...

The meaning is that even when a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is inferred from the statement of a single part, the establishment of that [sentence] occurs through the determination of the impelling factor (*pravartaka*), namely the specific injunction (*niyoga*). || 494 ||
Since only the optative and other such [moods] are heard, there is no possibility of passion or the like in that case.
The child engages in that [activity], and thus the nature of instigation (preraṇā) is known.

This clarifies what has already been stated: "of the imperative (loṭ) and so forth. Even in cases such as a stick, where desire and the like are impossible for the child, he nevertheless engages in it upon hearing the imperative and other forms such as "bring" (ānaya), because he knows their meaning; therefore, the word consisting of the imperative and so forth possesses instigation—
The meaning is that, because it is understood to have the purpose of an injunction (niyoga) that impels one to action, it alone is determined to be the impeller in all cases. || 495 ||
He said: "It is claimed that this object is not understood by means of another cognition."
And it is known from the word itself that [the relation] is unknown; thus there is a contradiction. (496)

Now, is *niyoga* (an injunction) apprehended through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? In the first case, there would be an admission that the "task" (*kārya*) enters the domain of another means of knowledge, which contradicts the stated position. In the second case, however, since the relationship [between the word and its meaning] is unknown, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth cannot convey the *niyoga*; thus he objects with the words "He says. If *niyoga* is not within the scope of another means of knowledge, then the power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix and so forth could not be grasped therein.

Furthermore, for one who does not know [the relationship], the understanding of the injunction (*niyoga*) from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth depends upon the cognition of that relationship; and since the child likewise lacks knowledge of the [inherent] power [of words], the same undesirable consequence would follow. Therefore, the meaning is that the injunction, as a verbal object, is not the motivator. || 496 ||
If even a word whose relationship [to its meaning] is unknown were to convey an object, [then there would be no need for instruction].
What hatred do you have toward us, that you should direct this reproach? (497)
And it is understood from this as well.
19 [vol 1, page 167]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]...

He raises the objection: "This is the power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that even when its own potency is unknown, it causes one to understand an injunction (*niyoga*). [The author] says "If... and then, considering that this would be a transgression of the nature of words, he asks: "What is this aversion? For an aversion toward the proponents of Brahman on the part of the proponent of injunction (*niyoga-vādin*) is not appropriate, since words such as "Brahman" convey their meaning even when their potency is unknown; and in the apprehension of that potency, there is no scope for other means of knowledge regarding Brahman.

The meaning is that the objection—that the Vedāntas lack authority because they conflict with or contradict worldly usage—is cast aside by the fact that even words such as "Brahman" can possess the aforementioned power, just like verbal suffixes (liṅ) and the like. || 497 ||
When it is understood that there is no other cause for one's own activity.
And when the word is clearly understood, its meaning is then discerned. (498)

The proponent offers a rebuttal: "When... When no other cause—distinct from words such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth—is perceived to indicate the motive for activity that occurs immediately after the word, and when the optative and such words are known to be the indicators of the motive for activity, then the meaning of the optative and so forth, namely the *niyoga* (an injunction), is distinguished from the meanings of nouns because it is unfit for other means of knowledge; and that [injunction], being thus extracted, is clearly [perceived] from the word.
The meaning is that the Blessed One is the cause of activity. || 498 ||
But positive and negative concomitance are preceded by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.
"But the meaning of the sentence does not depend on that [the mere action]; thus it is distinguished from others.

(Verse 499) Even if the capacity (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is grasped with respect to the mere action (*kāryamātra*), since that alone is not an injunction (*niyoga*), one might raise the objection: "How could this [suffix], whose relation [to its object] has not been established, cause one to understand an injunction (*niyoga*) that is not accessible through other means of knowledge? Anticipating this, he says: "By concomitance" (*anvaya*). [This refers to] the speech uttered by an elder...

When the middle-aged man issues an injunction regarding that object, an inference known as *anvaya-vyatireka* (positive and negative concomitance) arises in the child through the mark of the middle-aged man’s purposeful activity preceded by knowledge: "The activity under dispute is preceded by a cognition that is the opposite of the absence of activity, because it is a specific kind of activity, like my own activity. And that object, which is the opposite of the absence of activity, is understood from the word itself, since its presence and absence correspond to the presence and absence of the word.

He determines: "In this way, since the middle-aged person who understands the word acts as an instigator for the child, there is no apprehension of the *śakti* (denotative power) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; thus, the instigating *niyoga* (injunction) is not cognizable by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Nor does a word whose *śakti* is unknown possess the capacity to convey meaning—this is the sense. [The opponent objects: "If one apprehends the *śakti* of the optative suffix and so forth after having inferred the instigator, how can it be said that the instigating *niyoga* is not cognizable by another means of knowledge? This is the objection.

He says: "But as for the meaning of the sentence... Just as Rāhu, when conjoined with the moon and so forth, becomes an object of perception, so too it is only the *niyoga* (injunction) as qualified by [the agent’s] knowledge and so forth that falls within the scope of inference and other means of knowledge; it is not the *niyoga* in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*) that is the meaning of the sentence.

Thus, its distinctness from other nominal meanings—which are suitable [to be grasped] in their own form—consists in this: that the *niyoga* is not accessible through other means of knowledge except by way of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The sense is that the position of *niyoga* (the mandatory injunction) is logical, because the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) enter into the [cognition] there by virtue of the apprehension of their power (*śakti*), and because they do not enter [into the cognition] in their own form through any other means of knowledge, thereby establishing their Vedic character. || 499 ||
Indeed, even from sentences, it is understood that there is an intention to express what ought to be done.
The intention to speak is not an effect [of the word], for it has the meaning of the word as its object.

Now, even if desire and the like are not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it does not follow that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is their meaning, because the intention (*vivakṣā*) is what constitutes its meaning. For it has been stated by Kīrti: [1kha] "In its capacity as such..."
[Vol. 1, p.
168] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"Because there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) between words and things..."

"Therefore, there is no accomplishment of the object [intended], for those [words] merely indicate the intention of the speaker. To this, he replies: "The state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*). Is it mere intention that is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, or is it intention qualified by the state of being something to be done? It cannot be the first, because in the case of the non-human-authored Veda, such [intention] is absent; thus it is impossible for that [mere intention] to be the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth in human-authored sentences.

Even when that [cognition] is apprehended, it is apprehended as qualified by "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*); therefore, that alone is not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Nor is the second [alternative] correct, because the possibility of intending a qualified [meaning] is equally present in the impersonal Veda; and if that [intention] were the meaning, then—by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not—the meaning of the word would have to be "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) alone. This is the sense. Since intention and "what is to be done" are identical, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified; therefore...
Fearing that if "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) were the meaning of the word, then the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) alone would become its meaning, he says: "Of the intention.
He states the reason for the absence of non-difference between those two [the intention and what is to be done] as follows: "Because of the word-meaning... (100).
But the meaning of the word is not dependent on that [the sentence], for it is understood first.
Therefore, even an object associated with injunctions and the like is established through discernment. || 501 ||

Based on the maxim that "the application of a word is preceded by the speaker's intention," one might suspect a distinction [in the case of Vedic injunctions], namely that because the application of words in the world occurs by virtue of intention, it is intention alone that must be the cause [of the application] there as well. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By virtue of that" (*tadvaśāt*). For the application of words cannot be restricted by virtue of intention due to the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); nor can the determination of the meaning of a word be dependent upon intention, since [if it were so] in the restriction of intention...

It should be stated that this is according to the principle: "The cause [of usage] is convention (*saṃketa*) for the purpose of manifesting that [meaning]. However, because that [convention] depends upon intention (*sāmarthya*), and because it has been stated that the possibility of intention is absent in the Veda, the sense of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*) is one thing and "intention" (*vivakṣā*) is another. As Kīrti said: "For everywhere, a word is restricted to its meanings by intention. Thus, there is no suspicion of non-difference [between them]. This is the point regarding the difference between intention and what ought to be done.

He states another reason: "For that [is so]," etc. The meaning is that the word-meaning called "what-is-to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*) is understood by the mere hearing of the word even prior to the cognition of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); therefore, there is a difference between the two. Because the Veda teaches an object to be accomplished (kārya) that is connected with the desire for its means of accomplishment, it is established that the object to be accomplished—distinguished from action (kriyā) and so forth—is denoted by the optative suffix (liṅ) and other such markers. To this, he raises an objection: "As in the world" (lokavat).

Just as in the world an object to be accomplished is apprehended as connected with the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) already established by other means of knowledge, and not that [root-meaning] alone, so too in the Veda, it is not the mere object to be accomplished [that is denoted].

The meaning is that in expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is the cognition of an effect (*kārya*) associated with an activity (*ceṣṭā*) that serves as a means (*sādhana*) consisting of a sacrifice and so forth, which is established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). || 116 ||
And therefore, it is like the instruction for one desiring health to eat wholesome food.
By entering into another means of knowledge, the consequence of dependence [upon that other] follows. || 517 ||

He states the defect that arises when it is claimed that a ritual act (*kārya*) which touches upon a thing-in-action (*bhāvārtha*) cognizable by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is nonetheless Vedic: "And therefore," etc. Just as the sentence "one desiring health should eat ghee" is dependent on other means of knowledge because it enters into the domain of those other means regarding its own meaning, so too in the Veda—in passages such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—it is logical that the *niyoga* (injunction) enters the domain of other means of knowledge, since its object is the relationship between a means and an end already established by other means of knowledge.
The meaning is that it would result in the consequence of being dependent. || 517 ||
Therefore, this [bondage] based on the connection between action and its fruit is not equal to that of Maitreya and others.
"Because of that lack of correspondence, your [notion of] *niyoga* (an injunction) is refuted in the case of paintings and the like.

(518) [The opponent objects: "Let there be dependence [on other means of knowledge]; no," he says: "For this reason. Since an *niyoga* has as its object a relationship between a means and an end already established by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), it is equivalent to an injunction such as "One should eat *harītakī*," which is directed toward something already present. Therefore, by that other means of knowledge, the accomplishment of the result—
152 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [Vol. 1, p. 173]

Because of contradiction or obstruction by that which has as its object an effect colored by the nature of being related [to an agent], the authority of the Veda as a whole is lost in cases such as "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā"; for in the world, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are observed to denote an effect delimited by being a means to a fruit, and even in the Veda, they do not denote an independent effect.

The meaning [of the Vedic injunction] is not independent; rather, it expresses an obligation (niyoga) that is dependent upon application (viniyoga). Consequently, there is a loss of independence regarding the application—which consists in being a means to a result—due to its dependence on other means of knowledge. Furthermore, in the case of the Citrā sacrifice and others, there is the perception of existing results such as cattle. For whatever is fit to come into existence immediately after an action is capable of being perceived by other means of knowledge; therefore, because its status as a means to a result depends on those [other means], the nature of the task (kāryatā) in the Citrā and similar rites is made manifest through that dependence. And this is not the case here...

The meaning is this: even though the result is capable of being perceived immediately, it is not so perceived; therefore, because the injunction has as its object a mandate delimited by an application that falls within the scope of another means of knowledge, it is dependent [on that other means].

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction in the non-perception of the result immediately [after the act] despite the presence of causal fitness (*yogyatva*), the Citrā and similar sentences do not possess authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*). || 118 ||
Do not say so; for in the world, [the word "cow"] is applied to that which is conditioned by the act of driving and so forth, due to the influence of other means of knowledge.
And it is logical that activity is for the sake of a purposeful task. || 519 ||

The proponent of the theory of action (*kāryavādī*) refutes [the objection] by demonstrating how verbal expressions function in worldly discourse, saying: "It is not so. Since worldly sentences are of human origin, their meaning is entered by other means of knowledge; therefore, the *kārya* (action/task) denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others—which is conditioned by [human] injunctions and the like—is something to be understood through other means of knowledge. It is not... [independent].

He accepts that yoga is the primary [means]. Regarding the phrase "by other means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*), he addresses the objection that in the world, verbal activity is caused by an injunction (*niyoga*) whose meaning consists of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, as delimited by being a means to a result established by other means of knowledge; to this, he replies with the words "purpose" (*prayojana*). || 119 ||
The status of being the object of the relationship between the probandum and the probans arises from the purpose of human beings.
For this very reason, the person is enjoined here as the agent of the commission (niyoga). || 520 ||

7 Furthermore, he states that the worldly injunction (*laukika-niyoga*) has as its object a *viniyoga* (application) established by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), beginning with the words "sādhye" (in what is to be accomplished).

He clarifies that very same additional reason (*hetvantara*) with the words "pumarthatve" (because it serves the purpose of man). [In cases such as] the eating of *harītakī*, the fact that it is a means to a result is [established by] another means of knowledge—

The meaning is that because [the fruit] is something to be attained (*gamya*), the *niyoga* (injunction) delimited by that [fruit] is logically appropriate to have as its object a *viniyoga* (application) that is itself to be attained. He states the reason why a worldly *niyoga* has as its object a *viniyoga* cognizable through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) means: because the *niyoga* regarding the consumption of *harītakī* has as its object a *viniyoga* cognizable through other means of knowledge. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the mention of the consumption of *harītakī*. 120.
Since it proceeds spontaneously by itself, the agency belongs solely to the agent.
And the term "desiring health" and so forth may serve as a qualification of the agent.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the sentence "one desiring purgation should eat *harītakī*," just as in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the connection with the agent must be stated only after the connection with the person entitled to the act (*adhikāra*)—which itself presupposes the connection with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the Veda, the connection with the agent would have to come first. To this, he says: "Inherently" (*svataḥ*).

In the sentence "one desiring health should eat *harītakī*," the injunction (*niyoga*) has as its object a specific application (*viniyoga*) that is capable of being known through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara-yogya*).

The meaning is as follows: in the case of worldly injunctions, since a person's engagement in eating *harītakī* occurs through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even without depending on the sentence, there is first an association with agency for that which is subordinate;

subsequently, when the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are heard, there arises the association with being the "person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) and the "qualified person" (*adhikārī*). However, in the Veda, the situation will be shown to be otherwise. Now, one might object: if the word "desirous of health" (*ārogyakāma*), like the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*), indicates the person to be enjoined, how can there be an association with agency?
1. "It is sweet," etc.
[Vol.
1, page 174] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 153

He states its primacy there with the words "And the word. Just as the word "Devadatta" in the sentence "Devadatta cooks" conveys the agent, so too does this [word] convey the agent; for, by the force of another means of knowledge, human activity is here stated to belong to the agent, and not to the one who is to be enjoined (niyojya). This is the meaning. || 121 ||
But in the Veda, [it is established] because it is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition, such as direct perception.
The knowledge that something is a means to an end arises solely from the injunction (niyoga), and not from anything else.

Having explained the status of worldly sentences, he states the status of Vedic injunctive sentences with the words "But in the Veda. Even though an injunction (*niyoga*) is understood in the impersonal Veda, it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if sacrifice and the like were not the means for achieving heaven and so forth, it would not be logical to enjoin them to one who desires that [result]. Therefore, it is solely by virtue of the injunction that the cognition of the relationship between the end and the means arises there, and not from another means of knowledge.
This is the meaning. || 122 ||
For thus, the desirer who is not an agent is designated by the term "one who desires heaven."
Through the application [of the self] to the connection with action, it subsequently attains the state of being an agent here in this world.

Having raised the objection that—even though in the Veda the cognition of the relationship between the end and the means is dependent upon an injunction (*niyoga*)—desire nonetheless functions as a qualification of the agent, as it does in worldly affairs, [the author] says: "For thus... Since the relationship of being the end and the means is not established by any other means of knowledge in the Veda, the injunction whose object it is cannot depend on such [external] means; therefore, its establishment must come from the Veda alone. Once that [injunction] is established as having the nature of a task (*kārya*), there arises the cognition of ownership: "This is mine."

Since the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is presented at the outset by the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), there is first an association with the person to be enjoined; subsequently, that person attains mastery (*aiśvarya*)—that is, entitlement (*adhikāra*)—over the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), its means, and the ritual action (*karman*). Thus, the one denoted by the word "desirer of heaven" is both the person to be enjoined and the entitled agent, but not a causal factor (*kāraka*) or a doer (*kartṛ*); the meaning is that desire is not a qualification of the doer. This [process] is preceded by the association with the person to be enjoined.

To the question, "Let there be a connection with entitlement (*adhikāra*), but how can there be a connection with agency (*kartṛ*)?", he replies: "By means of the mandate (*niyoga*). The meaning is this: through the mandate, there is a connection by way of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); by that door, there is a connection with entitlement toward the ritual action. When that [connection] exists, one connects as an agent—subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root—with the thought, "If this ritual action is the means for accomplishing my mandate, then I shall perform it. Thus, there is a connection as an agent in a subordinate capacity within the meaning of the verbal root. || 123 ||
And because desire is primary, its predominance does not cease.
Therefore, being a qualification of the person, the enjoyer and the desirer is not the agent. || 524 ||

Regarding the statement that in sentences such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), desire (*kāma*) is not a qualification of the agent, he states another reason: "of desire" (*kāmasya*). Because desire has primacy by virtue of having the fruit as its object, its status as a qualification of the person must be asserted without abandoning that primacy; for the agent is subordinate with respect to the action. If it were a qualification of the agent, it would become subordinate to the subordinate (the action), resulting in a loss of its primacy; however, if it is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), its primacy is maintained.

The meaning is that because [the desire] is primary by virtue of being the master (*svāmin*), there is no loss of the primacy of desire. He concludes that in the Veda, desire is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). "Therefore" means: enjoyment is the fruit, and the *niyoga* (injunction) is that which possesses it; the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is the qualified person, and in the Veda, he is specified by desire—that is the sense. In this regard, he concludes that desire is not a qualification of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*): "not a causal factor" (*na kāraka*).* 124*
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which has not yet begun to function to possess the status of a causal factor (*kāraka*).
The mention of the causative suffix (ṇic) would apply to one who is already engaged in action, just as one might say, "he causes him who is cooking to cook. (525)

Regarding the point that in the Veda, the connection with the agent follows the connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*), which in turn is preceded by the connection with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), he states another reason for this: "Because [the person] has not yet acted," and so forth.

Since the relationship between the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanatva*) in the case of eating *harītakī* is cognizable through other means of knowledge, the activity of one who has already engaged in it based on that [knowledge] is not dependent upon an injunction (*niyoga*).
154 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Vol. 1, Page 175]

[Regarding] the application of the suffix *ṇic* to the sense of "connection" (*saṃbandha*), there is no scope for *ṇic* in the case of an already commenced activity; for it is established that in the case of human utterances, the cognition of the speaker's intention arises as "this person knows the meaning to be thus. Therefore, from a worldly sentence that has proceeded from another means of knowledge, the knowledge of the speaker is understood.

The meaning is as follows: since the *ṇic* affix finds its scope in worldly activity through that [instrumental cause], it has no scope in the Veda; for in the case of sacrifices and the like in the Veda, there is no activity based on other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and thus activity arises from the scripture only for one who was previously inactive.

Therefore, because a person cannot initially possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the root-meaning in the Veda, the primary relationship is that of eligibility (*adhikāritva*), preceded by the connection with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Now, an objection is raised: even in the case of sacrifices and the like, isn't it desired that there be an activity of one already active, for the sake of the initial connection with the agent? To this, he replies:

Regarding the phrase "of one who has already engaged": if the engagement in sacrifice and so forth were to arise from the word for one who has already engaged, then there would be an expression using the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—such as *yājayet* ("one should cause to sacrifice")—to denote the instigating injunction (*niyoga*), just as one says *pācayet* ("one should cause to cook") when instigating someone already engaged in cooking. Such [a causative] expression does not exist here; nor can the impersonal Veda be equated with a personal statement. Therefore, because it instigates one who has not yet engaged, it [specifies] the qualified person (*adhikārin*).
The meaning is that desire is not the agent in the Veda. || 125 ||
The genitive case would result [here] by virtue of the relationship between an action and its agent.
It is not so, because this genitive case occurs when two nouns are always in conjunction, as it is a possessive (śaiṣika) genitive.

He raises an objection: if one were to abandon the relationship between the injunction (*niyoga*) and the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) as that of an action and its agent, and instead posit a relationship of ownership (*svasvāmitva*), then—just as in the case of "Caitra’s property" (*caitrasya svam*)—the injunction would belong to the one desiring heaven, and thus the genitive case would apply to *svargakāma*. This is expressed by the words "akriya... (if it were not an action...). He refutes this with "naivam... (it is not so). That [genitive] prescribed by the rule "the genitive is used in the sense of a remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended to denote a general relationship; and this [relationship] pertains to two nouns.

Therefore, because the relationship is fixed, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is not in apposition with "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*); thus, when it is connected to that [verb], there is no genitive case [between them]. This is the meaning. || 126 ||
And when there is the connection between action (kriyā) and its factors (kāraka), the second case ending and so forth [are used], while the *laṭ* and other verbal suffixes [indicate the action].
There would be no confusion [of categories] because the meaning of the nominal stem is connected with the meaning of the verbal root. || 527 ||

In connection with the rule that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs when there is a relation between two nouns, [the author] states the determination of the scope of the other case-endings. Regarding "action" (*kriyā*):

in usages such as "the tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*) or "see it" (*taṃ paśya*), when the relation between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is understood, there should be specific case-endings—such as the nominative (*prathamā*) or the accusative (*dvitīyā*)—which indicate those [factors]. In that regard as well, [the factors consist of] the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the relation (*saṃbandha*).

The meaning is that specific case-endings (vibhakti) occur. Having stated the scope of the case-endings of the *kārakas*, he now states the scope of the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), beginning with "the *laṭ* etc. By the word "etc.," the nine verbal suffixes beginning with *liṭ* are included. When the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—as defined by the rule "that which is meaningful, not a root, and not a suffix is a nominal stem"—is understood in connection with the meaning of a root such as *pacati* (he cooks), the [suffixes] beginning with *laṭ* [are employed].

The meaning is that even there, because of the existence of distinctions such as present time (*vartamānatva*) and non-present time (*anadyatanatva*), specific verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) occur in connection with action (*kriyāyoga*).

Having thus established the arrangement of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) of nouns and the verbal endings (*tiṅ*), he states the result, which is their non-confusion (*asaṃkara*), saying: "Thus there is no confusion. || 127 ||
But in the case of the blue lotus, the name and the object abandon each other.
Since they have attained the nature of being distinct, the use of the genitive case is not accepted. (528)

If it is said that the sixth case ending occurs in a connection with a *nātha* (lord/master), then since the same would apply to "blue" (*nīla*) and "lotus" (*utpala*), the form "blue-lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) would be employed when they are connected with one another.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 155.
Anticipating the objection that there would be a genitive case (indicating possession) rather than grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says: "Blue" (*nīla*).

Although in the case of a "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) there are two distinct word-meanings, nevertheless, having abandoned mutual difference, they attain a single identity; thus, it is either the lotus of the blue, or the blue of the lotus.

The construction is as follows: "the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is not desired by those who know that [distinction]. The meaning is that the genitive occurs when there is a connection between two things that possess separate existence (*yutasiddhi*), such as "the blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*); however, for two things that do not possess separate existence (*ayutasiddha*), there is only grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). || 128 ||
That which is expressed by the optative suffix possesses the status of an object, but the desirer does not.
Since an injunction is not an action, if it were [the object], then the accusative case ending would likewise apply.

If it is argued that—even in the absence of the sixth case (genitive)—the second case (accusative) should occur for *svargakāmin* (one desiring heaven), because he is impelled by the injunction (*niyoga*), and since the accusative is observed in cases such as *grāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village) where the object is pervaded by the action; therefore, the sentence should be *svargakāmaṃ yajeta* (one desiring heaven should sacrifice)—[the author] says "No," because [this is so]:

"In the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). Since the one desiring heaven, who is connected to the injunction as the one being impelled, does not attain the status of an object (*karman*), the accusative does not apply to him.

This is the meaning. He states the reason why the person desiring [the fruit] (*kāmin*), when enjoined, does not function as the object (*karman*): "because it is not an action" (*akriyātvāt*). For an injunction (*niyoga*) that is a specific kind of action depends upon an object; however, it is not itself an action because it is that which brings about [the action]. Therefore, when one who desires [the fruit] is enjoined to it, there is no occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), since his connection [to the injunction] is by way of being the master (*svāmitva*). He expresses this very point through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "The second..."

Yeti: If the injunction were an action like going and so forth, then it would take the accusative case, as in "the village" in the phrase "he desires the village," because it would be that which is impelled by it; however, it is not an action, since its distinctness from action has already been stated—this is the meaning. || 129 ||
Therefore, the desirous agent, though not the actual performer of the action, acts for the sake of accomplishing his own duty.
Being engaged in this very process, one perceives the object as that which is to be accomplished.

He concludes what was stated— that the connection with the agent follows from the connection with the qualified person (niyojya), which itself is preceded by the connection with the mandate (niyoga)— with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since the one who possesses a desire (*kāmī*) connects with the mandate as the qualified person, therefore, being first connected as an owner (*svāmitva*) while devoid of the cognition of agency, he [relates] for the sake of that [mandate], because the existence of the manifestation of a mandate— which lacks both an object and an instrument— is otherwise impossible unless it is known as his own.

The meaning is that one who, depending on the object and so forth, is impelled toward the meaning of the verbal root by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, perceives that very [root-meaning] as the object by virtue of being its conceptual concomitant (*pratītyanubandhitayā*), and as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the motivator of its production; thus he regards it as his own duty to be performed. || 130 ||
Furthermore, the well-known injunction (*niyoga*) regarding kings and others has as its object that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
And since the meaning of the verbal root is that which is to be accomplished, it is also logical for that [action] to be so [designated]. || 531 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the status of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) for the object of an injunction (*niyoga*) is not fixed, since we observe injunctions even with respect to things like curd which are already established, as in the case of "for one desiring sensory power, [one should eat] with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*)? To this, he says: "In the case of kings and so forth. The point is that even in the case of curd and the like, it is observed that only that which is to be accomplished—by virtue of being permeated by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—becomes the object of the injunction. Even though the injunction has as its object that which is to be accomplished, curd and the like [are so only] in their own essential form.

Anticipating the objection that since the [apūrva] can be the object [of the injunction] by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is no need for it to enter into the action itself, he says: "Of the meaning of the verbal root" (*bhāvārthasya*). The meaning is that the action alone is directly what is to be accomplished, while substances and so forth are accomplished through its medium; this is self-evident. Now, one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) would be connected to the means for attaining his desired heaven; however, it cannot be that both the mandate (*niyoga*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*) are the means for a single heaven, because once the desired end is achieved by one [means], [the other would be redundant].

Because [the injunction] would otherwise be purposeless and because it would lead to the fallacy of optionality (*vikalpa*), he states that for one who desires heaven, there can be no connection with either the injunction alone or the sacrifice alone; thus he says: "Or rather... (1) ...or indeed... (2). [Vol.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection— ]

Thus, by that [statement]. According to the principle already stated—that agency is preceded by being an object of injunction (*niyojyatva*) and a qualified person (*adhikāritva*)—the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), having first been connected with the injunction, is also connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Indeed, the meaning of the root, which perishes very quickly, does not bring about the desired result without the injunction; nor does it come into existence without the sense of the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*); and that which is unaccomplished cannot bring about heaven. Therefore, [the connection] is in both respects.
The meaning is that this is the meeting of those possessed by desire. || 531 ||
In this way, even when gender and number are not intended to be expressed, they may nevertheless be expressed.
Subsequently, whatever has been heard regarding the factors of action and so forth for the sake of accomplishing the objects [of knowledge]— || 532 ||

Even though there is a connection with both [gender and number] for one who desires heaven, if the sentence were intent upon a *niyoga* (an injunction), then because gender and number would be unintended (*avivakṣita*) in the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), there would be no restriction regarding the performer; consequently, the performance would be unrestricted. Anticipating this objection, he says, "it is unintended," according to the principle of the section on the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*). Because the sentence is intent upon a *niyoga* by virtue of the aforementioned reasoning, although gender and [number] exist in the word "one who desires heaven,"...

The literal meaning is this: although the number is not something to be established [as a primary factor], nevertheless, because it is impossible to assume what is not heard [in the text] while abandoning what is heard [therein], it must be accepted exactly as it is heard. This is the underlying idea: it was established in the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]—"In that case, singularity is not a subordinate part of the sacrifice, because it is a subordinate quality of the object" (Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.1.11).
Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, in the passage "He who is initiated, he who sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," two oxen are yoked...

And it is heard in the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice as well: "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds for the sake of spring. Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether the singularity [of the number] and so forth are unintended (*avivakṣita*) or intended (*vivakṣita*). Since the meaning of the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) is that the animal is connected to the injunction (*niyoga*) by way of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*), and since there is no such [instrumentality] for the singularity itself, therefore—in the case of the animal, the two oxen, and the *kapiñjala* birds—the singularity and so forth are unintended because they are not constituent parts of the sacrifice (*ayajñāṅgabhūta*), as the purpose is the animal and so forth.

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it was concluded that because [number and other qualities] are subordinate elements (*guṇabhūta*), they cannot be subject to a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). However, the final established position (*rāddhānta*) states: "But it is perceived as being like the word itself;
for when that [word] is introduced, its cognition is seen, just as in the case of others" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 4.1.11).

In common usage, when an expression such as "bring the cow" (*paśum ānaya*) is employed, the bringing of the cow qualified by singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth is understood; upon the introduction of the singular suffix and so on, there arises the cognition of that singularity and the rest.

When something is perceived upon the arrival [of a word] or arises [in the mind], that is understood to be its meaning, just as is the case with other words. For instance, when it is said, "Bring the horse," the bringing of the horse appears as the meaning; and when it is said, "Bring the cow," the bringing of the cow appears as the meaning. Therefore, by the sentence "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the number is enjoined in relation to the sacrifice; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. And so, in the present case as well, the number is intended to be significant in the word *svargakāma* ("one who desires heaven").

[This is] refuted. Nor is it correct to argue that although the singularity of the animal (*paśu*) is intended because it is a qualification of the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya*), the singularity of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*)—unlike the singularity of the cup (*graha*)—is not intended because it is not a qualification of the thing to be enjoined; for in that case [the cup], its non-intentionality arises from the resulting split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). However, since the one desiring heaven is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and is thus something to be enjoined, why should its qualification, namely singularity, not be intended? Nor, even so, does the gender...

[The gender] is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitam*). Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), after raising the doubt as to whether the gender is intended or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established that it is not intended because it does not produce any difference in the performance. However, [the Siddhāntin] stated that although there is no difference in the performance, since that [gender] pertains to a specific [quality], it is impossible without determining the specific substance to be employed; therefore, because gender serves as the cause for determining that [substance], it is intended to be significant, just like number.

And likewise, regarding the *liṅga* (indicative mark) in the passage [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.1.17]: "Therefore, even the *liṅga* is intended to be significant in the word 'one desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*). Nevertheless, if the fruit and so forth are not intended to be significant, how can there be performance? For there is no such thing as a performance that excludes the action, the factors of action (*kāraka*), and the fruit; nor can both the mandate (*niyoga*) and the fruit be intended to be significant within a single sentence, as that would result in the fallacy of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Afterwards. This means that immediately after the cognition of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), that which is heard in proximity for the sake of accomplishing the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha)—namely, the agent, the fruit, and the procedure (itikartavyatā)—must also be grasped. Nor does a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) occur due to a difference in meaning; for although the primary purpose is directed toward the mandate (niyoga), it culminates in other elements such as the factors of action (kāraka) through the force of the meaning itself. || 532 ||
And therefore, he who desires heaven should accomplish his own duty.
By what means is the accomplishment of sacrifice and so forth understood? It is understood from the scripture. || 533 ||

He states the result regarding the intended significance (*vivakṣitatva*) of gender, number, agent, and fruit: "And therefore... Because the fruit is intended to be significant, the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one who desires that specific fruit, not one who desires just anything; because gender is intended to be significant, the qualified person is a man desiring that fruit, not even an independent woman desiring it; because number is intended to be significant, only one desiring that fruit is qualified, not two desiring it.

And because that [result] is intended by the agent, it is that very result which, through the medium of the action, fulfills the agent’s own obligation (*niyoga*), and nothing else; this is the meaning.

Since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and so forth are intended, one asks—by what means would that [agent] fulfill his own obligation—in order to state the result. Regarding the word "by what" (*kena*):

because the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure are intended, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) fulfills his own obligation by accomplishing the sacrifice together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*).

He says "yāga" (sacrifice). He states the proof for the fulfillment of the *niyoga* (obligation) through the performance of the sacrifice along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) by saying "it is this," [verse 133].
And there is no abandonment of the desire for heaven by one who possesses desire, without first removing that very desire.
In this world, it can somehow become the means for accomplishing one's own specific purpose.

Now, one might object: even if, in a sentence centered on *niyoga* (an injunction), something like the *liṅ* suffix—which is not itself the primary meaning—is accepted for the sake of the result, since sacrifices and the like would be the means to the *niyoga*, heaven and so forth would not be the means; and if the *niyoga* were the means to that [heaven], it would lose its primacy. To this he says: "And not...
Here, the sacrifice enjoined for one who desires heaven does not remove the desire for heaven from that person by producing heaven for him.

The sacrifice could not in any way be the means for accomplishing that *niyoga* called "one's own duty to be performed," for a sacrifice would not produce a *niyoga* unless it brings about heaven, which is desired by the person; therefore, the meaning is that the sacrifice fulfills that desire by producing heaven through the medium of the *niyoga*. || 934 ||
For one whose desire has not been rubbed away [is distinguished] by a particularity of its prior state.
Even when the duty has been accomplished, one may again be subject to further injunctions. (535)
[Objection:

But surely the sacrifice accomplishes only the *niyoga* (the mandate), since its purpose is the fulfillment of that [mandate]; for what other purpose could there be for the accomplishment of the *niyoga* in all injunctions? Thus, the author of the *Ṭīkā* [says] that the desire for heaven will remain [as the motive]. [Reply: No, he says; it is not so. [For] the unmindful...

Regarding the word *diteti*: if a person has not yet fulfilled their desire for heaven through sacrifice, then even though the *niyoga* (the mandate) has been brought about by that sacrifice, he remains fit for it again, because there is no difference in his state of desiring [heaven] after the completion of the *niyoga*, just as before. Therefore, the sacrifice, by means of the *niyoga*, produces heaven and thereby terminates the person's desire for it; however, the fulfillment of the *niyoga* is the fruit specifically of the obligatory (*nitya*) injunctions, whereas in other injunctions [it serves a different purpose].
The meaning is: because, by means of that [action], another result is attained. || 535 ||
Therefore, for the sake of achieving one's own goal, one should establish the primacy of desire as that which is to be accomplished.
Being brought about by sacrifice and reaching completion, it attains the status of the object to be accomplished.
1. From the mouth of Khaṇḍarī at some place; 2. Kha: *cettatsva*.

If it is argued that the sacrifice (*yāga*)— by means of heaven (*svarga*)— removes the desire for that [heaven], and therefore injunction (*niyoga*) is redundant, he says "adhikāra" (qualification/entitlement) to address this doubt.
Since the sacrifice perishes immediately and is thus not the cause of heaven, which arises at a later time, [injunction is required] as the cause of that [heaven].

Through acceptance [of the injunction], the mandate (*niyoga*)—which is the entitlement (*adhikāra*)—attains its own realization by establishing heaven as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), in order to find a person capable of being enjoined (*niyojya*) who is favorable to its own fulfillment.

This occurs by means of the verbal root’s meaning, which is the object of the mandate itself; and since it is realized through the performance of that object by the enjoined person, the object itself becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Consequently, the mandate attains the status of being the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) [by that instrument]. Thus, its primacy (*prādhānya*) is not lost, for even the fruit exists solely for the sake of finding a person capable of being enjoined who is favorable to it.
The meaning is: "by resorting to what is favorable. || 136 ||
In this case, no contradiction is suspected on account of the absence of an immediate result.
That [result] would be achievable through action; however, the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) is non-actional in nature.

Now, it may be objected that because no immediate result is perceived from sacrifices and the like—as is the case with eating and other such acts—the sentences concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) are suspected of being non-authoritative. For the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), namely the *niyoga* (injunction), is delimited by its status as a means to a result; therefore, since the optative suffix and so forth express an injunction whose object is a *viniyoga* (application) that depends on another means of knowledge, a sentence containing such [an injunction] is non-authoritative due to its dependence. As it has been said: "In the case of a result occurring at a later time, such as heaven, there is no other means of knowledge..."

Even so, since the injunction (*niyoga*) is understood as being dependent on the application (*viniyoga*) that relies upon that [result], he says "not" (*na*) to the doubt regarding the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Veda arising from the contradiction with the non-perception of the result despite its suitability. Regarding the phrase "not immediately" (*nānantara*): here, although there is perception of the result—such as cattle—immediately after the *citrā* sacrifice and other such rites, there is nevertheless a lack of perception of it at a later time; thus, there is a discrepancy with other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and consequently, a lack of authority. This is not the case.

He states the reason for this with the word "action" (*kriyā*). If the fruit were to be accomplished by action, then because that fruit is not perceived immediately after the action, one might suspect the sentence lacks authority due to non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*); however, such a suspicion is not appropriate here.

Since the mandate (*niyoga*) is not an action, the suspicion of lack of authority—which depends on the non-perception of the fruit immediately after it—is not applicable, and thus the dependence of the Vedic mandate is refuted.
Such is the meaning. || 537 ||
And since this word is the very object of negation, its non-existence is established through non-apprehension.
For in the absence of a means of valid cognition (māna), this [object] would not exist; therefore, the means of valid cognition is taught as being immediate (ānantarya). || 538 ||

Anticipating the objection that—even though the injunction (*niyoga*) is established through the performance of sacrifices and so forth, and thus does not depend on other means of knowledge—there can be no validity for the verbal testimony because the absence of a result is ascertained through "non-apprehension of the capable" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) due to its non-perception immediately following [the action], he says: "pratyarthinī" (the adversary). Since there exists the word which apprehends the existence of the result and which contradicts its non-existence, the absence of the result is not established by the non-apprehension of the capable; rather, it would require a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the absence of the result.

The sense is that [the positive cognition] does not arise because of its contradiction with the means of cognizing non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*). Anticipating the objection that the positive cognition itself might fail to arise due to its contradiction with the means of cognizing non-existence, he says: "The means of knowledge" (*māna*), etc. The meaning is: since there is no positive cognition, the non-apprehension of its form is the means of cognizing non-existence; however, in the case of sound—which is beginningless and thus a positive entity—there is simply no such non-apprehension. Therefore, the non-arising of the positive cognition is not due to a contradiction with it. If that is so, then regarding the result...

He says that the word "immediately" (*yatā*) does not express that sacrifice and the like, or the injunction (*niyoga*) produced by them, have an immediate fruit; this is stated in the phrase "But immediacy... The meaning of the scriptural mention of a fruit is simply that the fruit of the injunction arising from sacrifice and so forth is necessary; it does not include its immediacy. Therefore, since the attainment of the fruit is certain through the mediation of the *apūrva*, immediacy is not expressed by the words [of the scripture]. || 538 ||
Therefore, even one who has performed his duties may realize that his purpose remains unfulfilled.
Because he is ignorant of the scriptures, he has no authority here in the Vedic [tradition].

1, p. 180] For one who performs the sacrifice while contemplating the sentence regarding the fruit, even though the fruit is not perceived immediately after the mandate (niyoga) has been fulfilled—[the fruit arises later].

Anticipating the objection that "it is proper for one to have self-conceit [regarding the result] when devoid of reflection upon that [scripture], yet even though the injunction has been undertaken, one would necessarily become a doubter of the authority of the statement because of the non-perception of the immediate result—therefore, the fruit is not yet realized," he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning of the word "therefore" is that the fruit is inevitable for a person who has performed the enjoined act. Nevertheless, because of the lack of reflection upon the scripture, [one might doubt] due to the injunction...
Even one who has accomplished his duty, if he considers himself to have failed, lacks the qualification for Vedic ritual because of that [lack of conviction];
therefore, his doubt does not invalidate the authority [of the scripture]. This is the meaning. || 939 ||
And because the meanings of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and names enter into the purpose of what is to be accomplished.
Therefore, validity is not intrinsic; thus, the Veda possesses authority with respect to its purposeful action.

Although the authority of sentences such as "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice]" rests upon *niyoga* (an injunction), one might raise the objection that because mantras and the like do not have their literal meaning intended (*avivakṣitārthatva*), the entire Veda does not culminate in action (*kāryaniṣṭhatā*). Anticipating this, he says "mantra," etc., according to the principle of the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* and other sections. This is the meaning of it:

It is established in the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*): "Because of the scriptural injunctions regarding that purpose" (*tadarthaśāstrāt*, *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 1.2.31). When there is a doubt as to whether mantras—such as those capable of illuminating the meaning assigned by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means—are intended to convey their literal meaning (*vivakṣitārtha*) or are not so intended (*avivakṣitārtha*), [the sūtra provides the answer]. Since mantras such as "Spread yourself wide" (*uru prathasva*) and others are intended to convey their meaning, they are employed for the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-prathana*) and similar acts precisely because of that capacity; therefore, the scriptural injunctions regarding that purpose [are merely explanatory].

Regarding the passage beginning with "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the words *syonaḥ prathasva*," since these [words] would otherwise be purposeless, the scripture binds them to those very acts for which they are capable of expressing meaning; thus, mantras are useful merely through their utterance. Since both [the mantra and its application] would lack authority, it follows that the *prayoga-śāstra* (the manual of ritual performance) incorporating them is also unauthoritative. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct" (*aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ*, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.2.30). In every respect— [The text continues: ...all [mantras] are authoritative. Why? Because they possess the capacity for expression (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*). Just as the injunctions regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are authoritative because they possess the capacity for expression, so too are the mantras authoritative because they possess the capacity for expression. Furthermore, the fact that the mantras are recited at the time of the ritual performance is not for the sake of their own completion, but rather for the sake of the ritual act. Therefore, since the mantras are indeed expressive, the *prayoga-śāstra* which incorporates them is also authoritative. Thus, the conclusion is reached that all mantras are authoritative. This concludes the discussion on the authority of mantras. Now, the following is considered: "In the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a mantra: 'O Agni, bring the gods hither' (*agne devān vaha*). In this context, the doubt arises: should this mantra be used in all rituals, or only in the *jyotiṣṭoma*? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should be used in all rituals, because the general injunction (*codanā*) applies to all. However, the established conclusion is that it should be restricted to the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Why? Because of the specific connection. Just as the *agnihotra* is restricted to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* complex by virtue of its specific relationship, so too is this mantra restricted to the *jyotiṣṭoma* by virtue of its specific connection within that context.
