The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since words in common worldly usage are understood to be intent upon their own meanings, and since it is evident that even when employed in mantras they are inherently intent upon their meanings, the explanatory teachings (arthavādas) regarding those [mantras] are justified as restatements of the applications already established through the observation of the indicative power (liṅga) of the mantras. Because there is no difference in the sentence-meaning between the world and the Veda, and because [the Veda] possesses authority in both cases, this single syntactical unit—the manual of ritual application—is authoritative. Such, then, is the case for mantras.

In the *Arthavāda* section, it was stated that the authority of *arthavādas* consists in their being subordinate to an injunction (*kārya*), and their truthfulness lies in their being subordinate to that [injunction]; however, they do not possess authority regarding their own literal meaning in the absence of a connection to an injunction, as there would be no fruit [for such a cognition]. Likewise, names (*nāmadheya*) also have as their sole purpose an injunction (*kārya*) by virtue of being included within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*). For instance, in the case of words like *udbhid*, *abhijit*, *citrayā*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and *bahis*, which are capable of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a verb, [they function as names].

Having cited words such as *ṣpavamāna*, *agnihotra*, *ājya*, *āghāra*, and *śyena*, and having raised the doubt as to whether these are authoritative regarding *dharma* or not, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established as follows: since the Veda conveys *dharma* through its components of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras (*mantra*), and since words such as *udbhid* are not included within those categories, and because they do not have as their object any of the three factors—namely the result (*phala*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—words of this kind are not authoritative regarding *dharma*. Having thus argued the prima facie position, [the sūtra] states: "But that which is connected with the injunction is [authoritative]. (JS 1.2.7) This means that even though the word *udbhid* does not denote a substance, a quality, or an action, it is nonetheless authoritative because it is connected with the injunctive portion of the Veda. For the word *udbhid* is understood as being co-referential with the verb "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), and thus it is accepted as denoting a specific sacrifice characterized by the name *udbhid*. Since it is impossible for a single word to have multiple meanings, it is determined that it denotes a sacrifice. Furthermore, because the word *udbhid* is used in proximity to the verb "to sacrifice," it is concluded that it denotes a sacrifice. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "One desiring heaven should perform the sacrifice named *udbhid*. Consequently, the word *udbhid* is authoritative regarding *dharma* because it is connected with the injunction. The same logic applies to other words such as *citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ* ("One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*"), *vaiśvadevyāmikṣā* ("The *āmikṣā* offering belongs to the Viśvedevas"), and *vājibhyo vājinam* ("The whey is for the Vājins"). Thus, it is established that words such as *udbhid* are indeed authoritative regarding *dharma*. (JS 1.4.1–2) Furthermore, the following doubt arises: if the Veda is the sole authority for *dharma*, then how can one account for the fact that certain Smṛti texts, such as the *Manusmṛti*, are also accepted as authorities? To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the dependence upon that [Veda], the Smṛti is authoritative. (JS 1.3.1) This means that since the Smṛtis depend upon the Veda, they are authoritative. However, the doubt remains as to what constitutes the basis for the Smṛtis' dependence on the Veda. To address this, the following is stated: "But that which is not seen [in the Veda], there is inference from that. (JS 1.3.2) This means that when a rule is not found in the Veda, one may infer the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as the source for that Smṛti rule. For example, the Smṛti rule stating, "One should not eat garlic," is inferred to be based on a lost Vedic text. However, the doubt persists as to why the Smṛti rules of the Buddhists and others are not accepted as authoritative despite being Smṛtis. To resolve this, the following is stated: "But that which is contrary to the Veda is not [authoritative]. (JS 1.3.3) This means that since the Smṛtis of the Buddhists and others contradict the Veda, they are not authoritative. Furthermore, the doubt arises as to why the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not considered contradictory to the Veda. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the connection with the performers of the Vedic rites. (JS 1.3.4) This means that since the authors of the Smṛtis, such as Manu, are themselves performers of Vedic rites, their Smṛtis are not contradictory to the Veda. Moreover, the doubt arises as to why the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not considered non-authoritative simply because they are Smṛtis, like the Smṛtis of the Buddhists. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the absence of contradiction, there is the inference of the Veda. (JS 1.3.5) This means that since there is no contradiction between the Smṛtis of Manu and others and the Veda, one infers the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as their source. Furthermore, the doubt arises as to why the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not considered non-authoritative simply because they are Smṛtis, like the Smṛtis of the Buddhists. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the absence of contradiction, there is the inference of the Veda. (JS 1.3.5) This means that since there is no contradiction between the Smṛtis of Manu and others and the Veda, one infers the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as their source. Finally, the doubt arises as to why the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not considered non-authoritative simply because they are Smṛtis, like the Smṛtis of the Buddhists. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the absence of contradiction, there is the inference of the Veda. (JS 1.3.5) This means that since there is no contradiction between the Smṛtis of Manu and others and the Veda, one infers the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as their source. Thus, it is established that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are indeed authoritative regarding *dharma*. (JS 1.3.6–7) Furthermore, the following doubt arises: if the Veda is the sole authority for *dharma*, then how can one account for the fact that certain local customs (*ācāra*) are also accepted as authorities? To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the dependence upon that [Veda], the practice of good men is authoritative. (JS 1.3.7) This means that since the practices of good men depend upon the Veda, they are authoritative. However, the doubt remains as to what constitutes the basis for the practices of good men' dependence on the Veda. To address this, the following is stated: "But that which is not seen [in the Veda], there is inference from that. (JS 1.3.8) This means that when a rule is not found in the Veda, one may infer the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as the source for that local custom. For example, the local custom of performing the *Aṣṭakā* rite is inferred to be based on a lost Vedic text. However, the doubt persists as to why the practices of the Mlecchas and others are not accepted as authoritative despite being practices of good men. To resolve this, the following is stated: "But that which is contrary to the Veda is not [authoritative]. (JS 1.3.9) This means that since the practices of the Mlecchas and others contradict the Veda, they are not authoritative. Furthermore, the doubt arises as to why the practices of the Āryas are not considered contradictory to the Veda. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the connection with the performers of the Vedic rites. (JS 1.3.10) This means that since the performers of the practices of the Āryas are themselves performers of Vedic rites, their practices are not contradictory to the Veda. Moreover, the doubt arises as to why the practices of the Āryas are not considered non-authoritative simply because they are practices, like the practices of the Mlecchas. To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the absence of contradiction, there is the inference of the Veda. (JS 1.3.11) This means that since there is no contradiction between the practices of the Āryas and the Veda, one infers the existence of a corresponding Vedic text as their source. Thus, it is established that the practices of good men are indeed authoritative regarding *dharma*. (JS 1.3.12–13) Furthermore, the following doubt arises: if the Veda is the sole authority for *dharma*, then how can one account for the fact that certain *Dharmaśāstra* texts are also accepted as authorities? To resolve this, the following is stated: "And because of the dependence upon that [Veda], the Dharmaśāstra is authoritative. (JS 1.3.14) This means that since the *Dharmaśāstras* depend upon the Veda, they are authoritative. However, the doubt

It has been established as the final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) that because the study of the entire Veda is undertaken through an injunction and thus culminates in human goals, even words such as *udbhid* must be admitted to culminate in human goals; and since their inclusion within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) is directly perceived, their authority—whether as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) or as a name (*nāmadheya*)—must be determined therein in accordance with the injunction for study. Thus it was said: "The traditional text... (*uktaṃ samāmnā-*)... [and so forth].

"In that which has such a purpose" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 1.4.1). Thus, since it has been established that names (*nāmadheya*) are subordinate by virtue of being included within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), one might still doubt whether their subordination arises through the prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) or through their status as a name; yet, [the conclusion is] "or rather, it is a name.
1. ka. kha. *mbhādava*; 2. kha. *māṇye saṃ*; 3. ka. *dhāsa*.
160 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 181]

Beginning with the word *syāt*, and by refuting the status of various [passages] as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) here and there, it was established in the *Nāmadheyapāda* that the Veda, when joined with a name, is an authority regarding Dharma; therefore, the entire Veda has authority regarding what is to be done (*kārya*). || 540 ||
Therefore, it must be stated that the Vedāntas enter into the domain of things to be accomplished.
Alternatively, the validity [of cognition] that must be negated here is now being refuted. || 542 ||

Nevertheless, one might raise the objection that the Veda possesses authority only with respect to what is to be done (*kārya*), since the Upanishads (*vedānta*) have as their purport that which is not to be done; anticipating this, he says: "Of the Vedāntas. If it is not tolerated that they have authority as being subordinate to what is to be done, then he says: "Or else [their] authority," meaning that they would simply lack authority. Having restated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which has reached the status of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In this regard" (verse 141).

The pervasion of the self-awareness of the self—which is established by itself and distinct from them—over all mothers, their activities, and their births, occurs in accordance with the nature of reality. (542)

If it is argued that the Vedāntas lack authority because they do not enter into an action (*kārya*), either due to the absence of a subject matter or because the capacity of words is never observed with respect to an already established fact (*siddhārtha*), the author refutes the first alternative with the verse beginning "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). By the word "mother" (*mātṛ*), the intellects (*buddhi*) along with their appearances (*ābhāsa*) are grasped; the modifications (*vṛtti*) residing therein are attachment and so forth. Of all these mothers and their modifications, whatever births there are—[these are destroyed] by the [knowledge of] the intellect and its modifications.

That which is distinct from all phenomena (*dharma*), self-established, and of the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpa*)—namely, *saṃbodha*, the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*)—there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by it [of all things], because they conform to the nature of the Self which is unlimited (*anavacchinna*).
Indeed, there is no absence of pervasion by the Self in the body and so forth, even though they possess modifications such as birth and the like, because the Self is unlimited.

Furthermore, without that pervasion, insentient things such as the intellect (*buddhi*) cannot be established; therefore, the intellect and its modifications, which possess change, [are pervaded] by the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*).

The meaning is that because the Self—the witness of the intellect and so forth, which is the object of knowledge according to the Vedānta—is possible as being pervaded by [the Self], those [scriptures] do not lack authority due to an absence of an object. || 542 ||
This occurs solely by virtue of conforming to the intrinsic nature of the entity that is space, and not due to an agent.
Just as the fullness of space is perceived upon the arising of a jar, so too is it perceived by the vision of the intellects.

One might object that if the village were pervaded by Caitra, then because the pervader Caitra undergoes changes such as cognition, the Self—which pervades the conscious principle (cidātman)—would likewise be subject to change; thus, the Self known through the Vedāntas would not be immutable (kūṭastha). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Like space.

Just as when a jar is produced, its being filled by space occurs solely due to the conformity to the nature of space as being all-pervading, and not because space possesses action, so too [is it with] the cognitions and their functions.

The pervasion of those three and their attributes by the nature of the Seer occurs solely through the power of the complete nature of consciousness, even without any activity residing within them; therefore, the meaning is that the immutability (*kūṭasthatā*) of that which is known through the Vedāntas is logically established. || 143 ||
The nature of cognitions as being like a jar, suffering, and so forth, arises from causes such as merit (dharma) and the like.
Its nature as a real entity consists in its being self-awakened by virtue of being without cause. || 544 ||

If the self were to pervade the intellect and other faculties without undergoing modification, then the intellect and the rest would also assume the forms of external and internal objects without modification, since there is no distinction in their status as cognizers; otherwise, if the self’s pervasion of the intellect and so forth occurred only through modification, it would follow that the self is not eternal (akūṭastha),
which contradicts the established fact [of its eternity].
[Vol. 1, p.

182] [The author] says "if it be so" (*cet na*) and provides the example "the jar. The assumption by the intellect (*buddhi*) of an insentient form is caused by unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), not inherent; this applies to both the intellect and that which is to be known by it.

The meaning is this: because dharma and so forth are limited, and because they consist of modifications of the intellect (*buddhi*) accompanied by appearances, it is logical that the intellect assumes the form of objects through the medium of its own transformations. One might raise the objection: "Just as the intellect takes on the form of the object to be known, it also assumes the form of the inner self (*pratyagātman*); therefore, the inner self is not inherently distinct from the intellect and other faculties. Anticipating this, he says: "Without cause" (*nirhetu*). The intellect’s taking on the form of consciousness (*cidākāratva*) is not produced by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), for it is unconditioned (*anavacchinna*).
The meaning is that the existence of the formless [self] is established precisely by its conformity with the intellect and so forth, which are always pervaded by it. || 144 ||
This existence and non-existence of the intellect and its modifications also arises solely from the Self, which is not other than itself.
Since that object is established [by the means of knowledge], it should be known as eternally established by itself. || 545 ||

Anticipating the objection that—although the inward Self (pratīc), which is the object known by the Vedāntas, is immutable—it cannot be self-established because it requires another means of proof, just as the mother who perceives a jar or other objects requires another perceiver to establish her own existence—the author says: "Buddhi... The connection [of the verse] is as follows: That Reality, from which the existence and non-existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*), as well as the means of knowledge (*māna*) and error (*abhrāsa*), are experienced, is to be known as always self-established. This is because of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
He states the reason for its independence from anything else: "because of being non-other" (*ananyamāt*). This means that it manifests without depending on a cognition of its own object.
Alternatively, *ananyamāt* is an adjective for "from which" (*yataḥ*): one whose other cognition (*mā*) does not exist is "non-other" (*ananya*); [the meaning is] "from that. || 945 ||
Now, if it is maintained that [the self] is established by itself due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [then...]

It follows that the words [of the Vedas] would lack authority because they would merely be about what is already awakened by the Buddha. [The opponent] raises an objection: "But surely... [This means: the Vedāntas are not a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the immutable witness of the intellect and so forth, who is self-luminous; for in that case, their lack of authority is unavoidable due to their being merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*). This is the sense of the objection: "But surely... [which implies] that [the Vedāntas] lack a means of valid cognition, since [their object] shines even without them. || 546 || 146 ||
Because one has not yet entered into friendliness, it is through the direct experience of the object itself.
Prior to the acquisition of that proficiency, there is direct cognition arising from proficiency alone.

He refutes the claim that the Vedāntas are authoritative regarding the inner self (*pratīc*), which is self-luminous by virtue of being the awakening of the Buddha, saying: "Not so. For with respect to that reality, even prior to the knowledge arising from the sentence through linguistic proficiency, there is the universal experience of everyone: "I am ignorant; I do not know myself"—thus [the self] is self-luminous.

The meaning is that, because the Self is not [ordinarily] known, the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to it is established, since immediate realization arises therein through mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—what is designated as "cultivation" (*vyutpatti*), consisting of inquiry into the Vedānta and the like. || 147 ||
Because it is seen as such through one's own direct experience.
And when [the reason] is observed, on what basis is its lack of logical consistency asserted? || 548 ||

Anticipating the objection that occasional awakening (*kādācitka-bodha*) and beginningless non-awakening (*anādy-abodha*) are both untenable in that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), he says: "Awakening" (*bodha*). Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and the experience of the wise, occasional awakening is observed in the inner self (*pratīci*); and because of the experience "I am ignorant," beginningless non-awakening is also observed. Therefore, the authority of the Vedāntas is established therein. Even though such things as non-awakening are observed, they are [only] possible in that [self], for they would otherwise be untenable in what is self-luminous.

Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] should be abandoned, he says, "And when it is seen" (*dṛṣṭe ca*). When ignorance and the like are seen in the Self, one must state why their impossibility follows; it cannot be from the force of experience, because if ignorance and the like were non-existent in the Self, there would be no such experience. Rather, it is by the force of reasoning that their irrationality is accepted, for in the case of the immutable, conscious, inward-facing Self, neither knowledge nor ignorance can be established through logic alone without recourse to experience. This is the sense. || 148 ||
21 [Vol. 1, page 183] 162 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Introduction]
And that which is the perfect establishment of deep sleep and so forth, even in the absence of the [gross] elements and the rest;
That [cognition] also, by relying solely on the object of knowledge as it is internally realized here, [is valid]. || 549 ||

How can ignorance, which is opposed to knowledge, be established by relying upon experience, and how can it be established through its grace? One might object that what is opposed to something cannot be its means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) nor its substratum (*āśrayatva*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of deep sleep, etc. Even in the absence of objects and so forth, the manifestation (*sphūrti*) of sleep, fainting, and the like—which occurs here on the plane of empirical transaction—occurs by virtue of its support in the reality that consists of the experience of the inner self as the unknown (*ajñāta*).

And thus, just as the existence of sleep and so forth—which are opposed to knowledge—is established, the existence of ignorance—which is opposed to that [knowledge]—is also established through experience alone; such is the meaning. || 149 ||
Nor does that [non-existence] arise from the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa), for while the mother exists, there is only the absence [of her son].
How can the establishment of the non-existence of the sense-faculties and so forth be preceded by those very sense-faculties?

[Objection: Is it not the case that the establishment of sleep and so forth does not arise from direct experience, but rather from non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) of an object—given the presence of the senses and other factors—due to the absence of the perception of an object? To this, he says: "And not... The reason for this is stated as "satī" (while [the self] exists). For one who has awakened, the retrospective reflection (*parāmarśa*) "I did not know anything" regarding sleep and so forth is observed; and that reflection must be preceded by an experience of that which is being reflected upon. However, at the time of sleep and so forth, there was no non-apprehension of an object capable of being perceived.

The occurrence of [cognitions such as] "I obtain" and so forth is impossible at that time because of the absence of a knower; and without that [knower], the operation of the means of knowledge (*māna*) cannot proceed. Therefore, just as the existence of that [knower] is established from experience alone during sleep and other such states, so too is the establishment of ignorance [established] from that very same [experience]. Nor is it improper for the experience that acts as the sublater to be the locus of its own proof;

for the cognition arising from a [Vedic] sentence, which destroys ignorance, is a different entity from the experience under discussion. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, [regarding] the knower and so forth—

The manifestation of a state such as sleep is not caused by the mind (mātrā) or other factors, because one's own nature cannot establish itself, and because if something else were to establish it, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, just as the aforementioned states like sleep are established through experience, so too is ignorance established; thus he says: "By the mind and so forth" (mātrādīti). || 150 ||
Those things which are not being measured do not measure a manifold self.

How could a statement regarding that [Self] be invalid, given the actual nature of things? (551) Having stated that the authority of the Vedāntas is appropriate for the Self—even though it is self-luminous—because both its cognition and non-cognition are matters of experience, he states the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the "how much more so" argument) regarding that very point with the verse beginning "yam". Because perception and the other means of knowledge, as well as their objects, are insentient (*jāḍya*), they do not [cognize themselves] by themselves.
Nor is there any need for another means of proof for the Self, which is a non-inert, conscious reality that shines by its own nature; rather, it is the very proof of everything.

Accordingly, following the nature of such a reality, the Vedāntic words are in no way invalid with respect to that Self, since perception and other means of knowledge are unable to produce valid cognition regarding that Self and thereby apprehend objects such as sound and the like. For when [the Self] has been realized through the communication of the words...

The meaning is that even for the sake of that [liberation], according to the logic already stated, there must necessarily be a means of valid cognition regarding the Self; for when [cognition] such as "That Thou Art" has not yet fulfilled its purpose because its object is not otherwise known, its authority with respect to the inner self (pratīci) is inevitable. || 151 ||
"An amīmāṃsaka! An amīmāṃsaka!"—thus they cried out loudly.
That which they object to out of ignorance is answered by the subsequent statement through its pacification.

Having resolved the objection against the authority of the Vedāntas on the grounds that they lack a subject matter because they do not lead to action, [the author] introduces the Bhāṣya beginning with "sarvo'pi" in order to resolve the objection against their authority on the grounds that the capacity of words is never observed with respect to an already established fact. [This was stated by] the non-Mīmāṃsaka. 1. Māya.
[Vārtika, Vol. 1, p.

184] Thus, these proponents of the theory that the Veda has purposeful action as its purport (kāryavādins), being attacked by the Mīmāṃsaka who asserts that the authority of the Veda lies in established entities (siddha-artha)—an assertion which they claim is devoid of logic—[proceed as follows]: (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.)

They loudly accuse me, saying, "He is a non-investigator (amīmāṃsaka), one who is averse to inquiry," or they reproach me with the repetition [of the term], "He is an amīmāṃsaka. Having stated the reason for this reproach, he declares its refutation with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). Because of this—namely, the ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*) from which such an accusation arises, such as the claim that "there is no verbal power (*śabdaśakti*) regarding an already established object" and so forth—for the sake of pacifying that [ignorance], everyone...
The meaning is that loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] are to be cultivated. || 152 ||
The statement beginning with "the entire Veda" and so forth provides the aforementioned refutation.
The Guru spoke these words clearly, fortified by firm reasoning.
The statement "the subsequent word" was spoken in a general sense; [the author] now takes it up specifically with the words "even all.

He states the intended meaning regarding the resolution of the aforementioned objection: "as stated," etc. He says that it is not non-informative because it was spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*).—[Guru]...

He states that there is neither a state of producing doubtful cognition nor a state of producing erroneous cognition by saying "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*). He dispels the defect caused by the fallacious nature of the supporting arguments by saying "firm" (*dṛḍha*) || 553 ||
"Relying upon the nature of the mind, everyone [is so]," and so forth—this is what was uttered.
For the designation of the two sections is indeed in accordance with their respective objects of knowledge. || 554 ||

Now, one might ask: "How is it that these two sections (*kāṇḍa*), which have mutually distinct meanings, are taught here in this commentary as a single group? To this, he says: "Māna... (The means of knowledge). The meaning is that the very nature of the Veda as a whole is to make known objects not previously known; relying upon this, both sections are grasped as a single group. If so, how then is their distinction well-known? To this, he says: "Kāṇḍa... (The sections). [This refers to] that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

The meaning is that even when the Veda as a whole is grasped as a single collection by relying on the single condition of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) regarding its object, the well-known division into *kāṇḍas* (sections) remains logical, because there is a difference in subject matter due to the distinction between what is already established and what is yet to be accomplished. || 154 ||
For in the world, a measure is indeed a manifestor; and that is established by its own cause.
Alternatively, when [the object] is established by itself eternally, it is the mere object of cognition that is qualified. || 555 ||

Regarding the statement that "the nature of a means of knowledge (māna) consists in being a revealer," this is incorrect because the eyes and other sense organs are well known to be causal factors (kāraka) in the process of cognition; anticipating this objection, he says: "For a means of knowledge... The point is that the eyes and so forth are not themselves the means of knowledge, since the status of being such belongs only to the cognition arising from them.
Anticipating the objection that being a causal factor is simply the same as being a manifestor (vyañjaka), he says: "Established..."—whether by itself or by something else.

The meaning is that there is a distinction: when [the object] exists, [the means of knowledge] has the nature of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), whereas when it does not exist, it has the nature of a producer (*kāraka*). Anticipating the objection that the nature of being a manifestor is of one kind when [the object] exists by itself (*svataḥ*) and of another kind when it exists through something else (*parataḥ*), he says: "merely the object" (*meyamātram*). The meaning is that even if there is no distinction between *svataḥ* and *parataḥ* regarding the object, there is no distinction whatsoever in the means of knowledge’s status as a manifestor, because there is no evidence for such a distinction. || 555 ||
Therefore, this entire Veda is [authoritative], solely on account of its being a means of valid cognition.
He should be known as one intent upon the manifestation of the reality of the self, which consists of both the perfected and the to-be-perfected. || 556 ||

Stating that the conduct of worldly authority (*laukikamāna*) applies even to the Veda, he concludes the meaning of the commentary with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means that in the world, the [Vedic] authority is manifested by worldly authority.
[End of page 185, Vol. 1]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Introduction]:

Because of the rule that [words] possess the nature of being causes of cognition, even in the Veda, following worldly usage, the entire Veda—consisting of two sections—is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it makes known what was previously unknown; this applies there as well.

The section on knowledge pertains to that which is already established as an object, while another section pertains to that which is yet to be accomplished; the meaning is that [the latter] is the illuminator. || 596 ||
Alternatively, because they form a single syntactical unit, it is said: "Indeed, all [the scriptures]... and so forth.
Because the injunction for Vedic study culminates in human goals. || 557 ||

Anticipating the objection that—since the nature of the mind (*mānasa*) is equally present even in perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge, and thus there is no unique distinction between the two sections of the work—one cannot unify them by relying on that [mental nature]—the author states another meaning of the *Bhāṣya*: "Because they form a single sentence" (*ekavākyatvataḥ*). Anticipating the objection that they do not form a single sentence because of the difference between the established (*siddha*) and the goal-to-be-established (*sādhya*) meanings, he says: "The human goal" (*puruṣārtha*). [This refers to] the fact that the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), through the attainment of the syllables, leads to the comprehension of the meaning...

The meaning is that because they both culminate in a fruit, the two sections (*kāṇḍa*)—being taken up by that [single purpose] and thus terminating in a single human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), just like the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśa* sacrifice.
The sense of the word "iti" is that, given this unity of syntactical connection, it is proper to treat the two sections as a single collection (*ekarāśīkaraṇa*). || 117 ||
Because it brings about the attainment of every happiness without exception, and likewise because it destroys all misfortunes.
No other object whatsoever is perceived here prior to liberation.

If it is argued that there is no single unified purpose because the *karmakāṇḍa* has heaven and the like as its aim while the *jñānakāṇḍa* has liberation as its aim—and thus they lack a single fruit—the author says "no," providing the response beginning with "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). In the scripture, there is no human goal other than liberation, which is of two forms; for since heaven and the like have a beginning and an end, they are merely semblances of fruits. Therefore, the injunction for study and the intermediate injunctions find their ultimate fulfillment only in having liberation as their aim.
The meaning is that there is a syntactic unity between the two sections. || 558 ||
Or, for one whose purpose is unaccomplished, its accomplishment occurs solely through direct experience.
The statement "even all" is established, for everything indeed arises from the singular consciousness of the Self. || 559 ||

Having raised the objection that the two sections do not form a single unified whole because it has been stated that [injunctions] do not expect any further fruit beyond the task understood from their own words, he states another interpretation: "Of that whose object is unestablished" (*asiddhārthasya*). The meaning is this: the existence and manifestation of the insentient phenomenal world—which is itself devoid of independent existence and manifestation—come to be solely in the form of that one non-dual Experience (*anubhūti*); regarding this point, the commentary (*bhāṣya*)...

He causes [the Self] to descend. Regarding the statement "all this indeed": this is its meaning. Veda is knowledge, which is experience; and that is incapable of being measured by any other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because it is devoid of form and so forth. It is the means for the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, because it exists in those various forms themselves. And it is illumination, because it is the illumination of all things. And it is supreme, because it transcends ignorance and its products. Such is the Veda, the Chika... [text fragment].

The entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is nothing but the *rasa*, which is the inward-facing element (*pratyagdhātu*). He provides the reasoning for its being mere experience (*anubhavamātra*) with the word "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is of the nature of the Self, non-dual, and one—therefrom comes the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of all that is insentient (*jaḍa*). This is because, due to its very insentience, it cannot be established by itself, and because there is no other establisher (*sādhaka*) of it apart from consciousness. Furthermore, that accomplishment encompasses all—that is, the entire insentient world—within itself, since the object of experience is [subsumed] within the experience.

The meaning is as follows: since an insentient object is not perceived apart from consciousness, its establishment [as a separate entity] does not exist; for the establishment of a qualified object does not transcend its own nature.
Therefore, everything is merely the experience denoted by the word "Veda," according to the Śruti, "All this has that as its Self," and by the logic of the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*. || 159 ||
Or rather, since nothing other than this is perceived, nothing else can be conceived as distinct from the Self.
He spoke the words "all indeed," and so it will be explained further below. || 560 ||
[Mārtika, Vol.
1, Page 186] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 165.
Now, an objection: it is improper to abandon the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word "Veda" and provide an etymological (*yoga*) explanation, for "conventional meaning sets aside etymology."

Anticipating the objection that this is contrary to logic (*nyāya*), he states another interpretation: "Or else" (*yadvā*). The meaning is that no entity other than this Self can be conceived as being unknown, because it is impossible for anything else to be unknown since it would consist of ignorance (*ajñāna*); therefore, since the Self alone is unknown, the entire Veda is authoritative with respect to that very Self. He cites the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) regarding this point: "The whole [Veda] also... That which is desired is that which has not been apprehended through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge.

The meaning is that the commentary states this point: that Brahman, as the Self, is the means for attainment and so forth, and this entire Veda is solely intent upon revealing Him. To the question, "How is it that the innermost essence (pratyagdhatu) alone is the object of ignorance?", he says: "And thus," etc. The word "above" refers to the discussion concerning the unmanifest (avyākṛta). || 960 ||
That causal basis by which the validity of the Vedāntas is established;
For that very same reason, the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) also possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge.

Thus, although the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* may arise from many perspectives, [the author] addresses the point at issue: how the Vedāntas possess authority regarding an established reality, and how this *Bhāṣya* is intended to explain that. He says: "That for which there is a cause. The meaning is that since the ground for authority—namely, the quality of making known what was previously unknown—is the same, that [authority] is likewise equal for both. By that very same ground for which the Karmakāṇḍa possesses authority, the Vedāntas [possess it as well].
The connection is that even the name is established as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 561 ||
Or by what reason is the lack of authority of the Vedāntas asserted?
For that very same reason, the same consequence would also apply to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa). || 562 ||

Having raised the objection that the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) lacks authority because it contradicts the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), he says "Of the Vedāntas" [verse 962] to show that this is not so, as the opposite case is logically possible.
Moreover, all means of valid cognition [establish their objects] through their connection with their respective objects of cognition.
In this world, they produce valid cognition and attain the status of being authoritative; it is not otherwise.

Furthermore, he states that the Vedāntas are authoritative with respect to their own meaning because they inform what is unknown, just like perception; thus he says, "Moreover, all... All means of knowledge, beginning with perception, certainly produce valid cognition regarding an object not already known, and thereby attain the status of being a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For the status of being a means of knowledge consists precisely in generating a certain, uncontradicted cognition that is fruitful. Therefore, the Vedāntas also possess the status of being a means of knowledge insofar as they inform what is unknown, just like those other means.

Such is the meaning. He states the subverting argument against the contrary position—that if there were no validity regarding its own object, there would be a loss of the very quality of making known what was previously unknown—by saying "No" (na). || 163 ||
For it is only with the injunction that the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) form a single syntactical unit.
Consequently, it is not tenable for those two to be established through perception. || 564 ||

Now, [the opponent argues: "The Vedāntas are not authoritative with respect to their own meaning, because they consist of sentences devoid of injunctions, like mantras and so forth. To this, he replies: "Not by an injunction... Since it is established by scripture (*śruti*) and other means that mantras and the like possess a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the specific injunctions introduced in various contexts, they do not possess authority regarding their own fruitless meaning as a cause for cognition; therefore, "fruitlessness with respect to one's own meaning" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). This is the sense. || 164 ||
Even that conceptualization regarding one who desires a firm foundation, which is based on an explanatory passage (arthavāda), [is likewise rejected].
That [prohibition] is also connected only with the meaning of an injunction; it does not arise from anything other than that.

Objection: But if, because it lacks a human goal (puruṣārtha) regarding its own literal meaning, the Arthavāda and other such passages were to be considered non-authoritative as being restricted to that [literal sense], would this not contradict the *Rātrisatra-adhikaraṇa*?
[Vol. 1, page 187] 166 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Section on Connection]...

For it is stated thus in the fourth [book]: “Kārṣṇājini [holds that] the mention of a fruit in a ritual is like [the mention of] an auxiliary, as in the case of the Rātrisatra. Regarding the passage, “Those who undertake these nights certainly attain stability,” there arises a doubt: does the qualification belong only to one desiring heaven, or to one desiring the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (arthavāda)? In this doubt, because the expression “they attain stability” is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), as in the case of the [parṇa-wood] quality and so forth—

Since the result of the action is not understood from those [passages], the statement regarding the result in the form of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is merely a praise by way of being an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). Thus, when it is established that only one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) has the entitlement (*adhikāra*), the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is stated: "Ātreya [holds that] the result [is mentioned] because of the specific instruction; for where it is not heard, there would be inference" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.3.18). Even though the sentence concerning "establishment" is an explanatory eulogy, rather than abandoning what is proximate and imagining a heaven that is extremely remote—

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: since the statement in the *arthavāda*—"there is here the fruit, which is the form of stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) fashioned by the *gātu*"—indicates a result, only one who desires that result has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this [rite]. For when no fruit is explicitly heard, the qualification of one who desires it arises through the postulation of such a fruit. Thus, your assumption of a qualification for one desiring the fruit called "stability"—derived from the *arthavāda*—is contradicted; indeed, one cannot adopt a "half-old-woman" approach (accepting part of a passage while rejecting another).

To this, he says: "By way of an *arthavāda*. The assumption of an entitlement for those desiring that fruit—which was made regarding the *sattra* sacrifice by taking the fruit called "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) on the strength of the *arthavāda* stating "they become established"—is possible only if that [statement] possesses authority (*mānatva*) through its connection with an injunction (*vidhi*).
It is not from any other source, such as the authority of the *arthavāda* independently of its connection with an injunction. As they say:

The meaning is that the injunction will be established by the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance) together with the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) and so forth, or by means of praise; therefore, the mantra and other elements do not possess authority regarding their own primary meaning, just as in the case of the *pratiṣṭhā* sentence. || 965 ||
But surely, it is a subordinate element to the meaning of the injunction, and therefore it is a statement of something other [than that injunction].
And because they have a single purpose, it is impossible to conceive of them as having contradictory meanings. (566)

Because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is subordinate to the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*), and because it has its own meaning as its primary purport, it possesses authority in both respects; therefore, no separate result need be postulated for it through the medium of the injunction alone. To this he says: "Because of the subordination to the meaning of the injunction... Since a single sentence has a single purport regarding a single meaning, it is subordinate to the meaning of the injunction; its purport lies therein. Consequently, since its expression of its own meaning is a different matter from the injunction, there is a contradiction between these two meanings.

Since it is illogical to assume two distinct intentions for a single sentence, experts in the science of sentences cannot maintain that one and the same sentence has two primary referents; rather, the sense is that while the explanatory passage (arthavāda) has no primary intention toward its own literal meaning, it possesses a secondary intention toward its own meaning by way of its great primary intention toward the meaning of the injunction (vidhi). || 166 ||
In case of contradiction, it would be a figurative description (guṇavāda); once [the fact] is ascertained, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
Exegesis (arthavāda) is considered to be of three kinds, based on whether it expresses the actual fact, its opposite, or is devoid of meaning. || 567 ||

Now, one might object: "If the arthavāda has a subordinate purport (avāntaratātparya) toward its own literal meaning, then since arthavādas such as 'The sacrificer is the prastara' would possess a subordinate purport toward their own meaning, they would be authoritative; consequently, every sentence would be authoritative regarding its own meaning. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that there is a distinction regarding the subordinate purport residing within the arthavāda.

He says: "Contradiction" (*virodha*). This is its meaning: Arthavāda is of two kinds—Arthavāda of an existing fact (*bhūtārthavāda*) and Arthavāda of a non-existing fact (*abhūtārthavāda*). The first is also twofold: that which is devoid of contradiction with perception and that which is preceded by [perceptual] corroboration. Among these, "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*) and so forth are examples of Arthavāda of a non-existing fact. And that, fearing invalidity due to contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding its own literal meaning, becomes a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*). For it has been said: "Similarity..."

"the sacrificial post is the sun; the sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (Pūrvamīmāṃsā 1.4.21). Here, when there arises a doubt as to whether this is a lack of definitive determination (*anadhyavasāya*) or an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since a contradiction precludes its being taken in its primary sense, and because it is improper for it to be an explanatory praise through a connection with a mere quality (*guṇa*), the initial position reached is that of a lack of definitive determination.
[Note: The manuscript variants indicated are: 1. *kha* reads *ṃdasthaṃ ma ṃ*; 2. *kha* reads *vāpha*; 3. *ka* reads *'vanmāphalakānma*.]
[Vol.
1, Page 188] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri: 167.

Because of its brilliance and verticality, the sacrificial post (yūpa) possesses a similarity to the sun and the sacrificer; thus, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established through a figurative application (gauṇī vṛtti).

It has been established as a *rāddhānta* (conclusive conclusion) that this is a *tattvārthavāda* (an explanatory statement of fact). He says "it is a restatement (*anuvāda*)" because an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) that functions once its own literal meaning is understood becomes intent upon praise by being a restatement of that which already exists. As he said: "Praise" (*praśaṃsā*) [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.4.26].
In the case of "Other animals are indeed non-animals; cows and horses are animals," there is no uncertainty regarding the meaning.

Having doubted whether this is an injunction (*vidhi*) or something else, and since no praise (*praśaṃsā*) is perceived—rendering it impossible for it to be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—one might initially conclude that there is no definitive determination. However, because other animals also belong to the genus of "beasts" (*paśu*), the statement "beasts other than cows and horses" cannot be a prohibition of the genus itself; rather, it must culminate in a prohibition of their specific function. Thus, since the status of cows and others as "beasts" has already been established by the phrase "non-beasts," the subsequent statement "cows and horses are beasts" serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the fact that cows and horses possess the nature of beasts. Therefore, in cows and horses, the term "beast" [applies].

The meaning is that the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) has been established that it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because the fact of performing a function is not secondary, and thus praise is accomplished. However, in some cases, he says "bhūta" (an existing thing), meaning that there is a statement of an existing but unknown fact due to the absence of corroboration by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). And it has been stated: "On account of abundance" (*bhūmnā*, Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.4.27). Regarding the passage "He places the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks," when there is a doubt as to whether it is indeterminate or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*):

When many bricks are obtained—some called *sṛṣṭi* and others not—the doubt arises as to whether the word *sṛṣṭi* is intended as a descriptive reference (*anuvāda*) to all of them. Since it is impossible for the word *sṛṣṭi* to be a descriptive reference [to only a few], and since there would otherwise be no determination, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks are more numerous, they are connected with the single act of laying down (*upadhāna*); thus, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the other bricks can also be referred to descriptively, and the passage is therefore an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended for the praise of the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks. He states that these three types of explanatory statements are well-known in the section on the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*).
It is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 167 ||
Even if an explanatory passage (arthavāda) were to provide a purpose for that which is supplementary to an injunction (vidhiśeṣa).
If the Vedāntas are sublated by the method of non-duality (advaita), what then is the authority for them? || 568 ||

[Objection: Surely, even in the absence of corroboration or contradiction, the Arthavāda (explanatory passage) should be accepted as authoritative with respect to its own literal meaning, since—according to the *Devatādhikaraṇa* principle—it possesses an intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*). Even so, what does this have to do with the Vedāntas? To this he says: "By the injunction... etc. Since there is no evidence that the Vedāntas do not convey their own meaning on the grounds that they are implied by the injunction for non-duality—which is the realization of reality—they [must be authoritative] regarding an established fact.
The meaning of the second half of the verse is that "mānatā" (the state of being a means of knowledge) is established. || 168 ||
By the mention of perception and the rest, all means of valid cognition are indicated.
There is no other means of transition than scripture, since it alone brings about the realization of oneness.

Through the commentary on the *bhāṣya* beginning with "all [of them]," it was stated that the Vedāntas possess authority regarding Brahman as the Self (*ātman*). Now, however, fearing that because of the qualification "by perception and inference" in the *bhāṣya*, Brahman might fall within the scope of analogy (*upamāna*) and other means of knowledge—and thus the Vedāntas might lack authority there due to agreement or disagreement with them—the author says: "Perception, etc. [and so forth]. In that case, even for scripture (*āgama*), the word "all" [would apply]...

Having stated that non-dual unity (*aikātmya*) is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge because it is not apprehended by them, one might suspect a contradiction in asserting that the Veda has that [unity] as its subject matter and is intent upon revealing it.
Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the phrase "not known through perception and inference" with the words: "māntaram" (another means of knowledge). || 169 ||
"Because the operation of a means of knowledge occurs only when the object to be established is not yet known."
If ignorance were established through pride, there would be a mutual dependence.

Having raised the objection that since perception and other means of knowledge employ terms denoting other means of knowledge, they are themselves valid only insofar as they do not contradict it, and therefore the Veda is not a means of knowledge regarding Brahman—[the author responds: "The state of being knowledge" (jñānatā) [is the reason for its validity]. [Variant reading: "of perception and the rest, the state of being a means of knowledge"].

268. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Connection]: In order to state that the validity (*mānatva*) of perception and other means of knowledge is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and not ultimate (*tāttvika*), because there is no object unknown [in the absolute sense], the general principle (*nyāya*)— [The remainder of the sentence continues: ...is stated. For it is said: "The means of knowledge and their objects are established through mutual dependence; they do not exist by their own nature. Therefore, since the distinction between the real and the unreal depends upon the means of knowledge, and since those means of knowledge are themselves devoid of intrinsic reality, the entire world-process is established as being merely empirical. Thus, the general principle has been stated. Now, the specific application (*viśeṣa-yukti*) is set forth. It is said: "If the means of knowledge were established by another means of knowledge, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And so on. This is explained: if the means of knowledge were established by another means of knowledge, that [second] would require a third, and that a fourth, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, the means of knowledge must be self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*). But if they are self-established, then, like the Self (*ātman*), they would be eternal and unchanging. Consequently, the objects of those means of knowledge would also be eternal and unchanging. Since the objects are thus eternal, the means of knowledge would also be eternal. And since both are eternal, the relationship between them would be permanent. Therefore, the world-process would never cease. To avoid this, it must be admitted that the means of knowledge are not self-established. If they are not self-established, then, being dependent on something else, they are non-eternal. Because they are non-eternal, their objects are also non-eternal. Since the objects are non-eternal, the means of knowledge are also non-eternal. [The opponent] says: "It is established. The meaning is this: it is accepted that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs only after an object has been established as unknown; therefore, prior to the operation of perception and the other [means of knowledge], its state of being unknown must be known. If it is argued, "Let that [state of being unknown] be known beforehand," then one must choose between the alternatives: is its establishment through a means of valid cognition or through experience? He refutes the first alternative with the words, "Not from a means of valid cognition. Nor is it established through experience—

Since [the Self] does not admit of being an object, otherwise—because that which is superimposed upon it and distinct from it would be its very means of proof—it would follow that, like a rope-snake, it is insentient and characterized by ignorance; thus, there would be the contingency of further superimposition upon it. Therefore, it should be understood that perception and other means of knowledge directed toward that [Self] do not possess ultimate validity. || 170 ||
Therefore, there is no contradiction of the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi) by anything whatsoever.
Because consciousness has everything as its locus, it likewise does not operate with respect to the self. || 571 ||

He states the conclusion regarding the non-ultimate validity (*atāttvikamānatva*) of perception and the other means of knowledge: "The reality... He provides another reason for the lack of contradiction between scripture (*āgama*) and perception and so forth: "All... The point is that because experience is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all things, and because perception and the rest, along with their objects, are grounded in that [experience], there is no contradiction between scripture—which has that [experience] as its object—and those [perceptions]; for a means of knowledge regarding the substratum cannot be sublated by what is superimposed upon it. This is the reason for the lack of contradiction.

He states the subsequent point: "In that way" (*tathā*). The meaning is that since perception and other means of knowledge directed toward objects such as form do not operate with respect to the Self—which is dependent on those [means]—there is no contradiction between them and the scripture concerning that [Self], because they have different objects. || 171 ||
The attainment of all desired aims as well as the destruction of all that is harmful.
For that [cognition] cannot be conceived as being other than the nature of the self when measured by valid means of knowledge.

Now, although the sentence concerning the identity of the Self does not enter into the domain of injunction (*vidhi*) in order to remove its lack of authority caused by contradiction with other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), it must nevertheless enter into it to dispel the suspicion that it lacks authority due to the absence of a fruit in its own literal sense. Thus, regarding the objection stated—that there is an absence of human purpose (*pumartha*) in its own sense—he replies with the word "entirely" (*kṛtsna*). The reality of the Self, when known, is the supreme human goal; the Self—

The meaning is as follows: since there is no attainment of another gain after [the initial] gain, how can the scripture concerning that [gain] lack authority due to the absence of a result for its own subject matter? How much less, then, can there be a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) by the condition (*upādhi*)? If it is argued that the two-fold result—even that which consists of the nature of the Self—is dependent on injunction (*vidhi*), because it is a result, like heaven (*svarga*), [the author] says "No" (*na*).

He states: "For that... (*sā hi*). By the pronoun "that," the attainment of the result is referred to. It is not from the knowledge of the Self alone that the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired occur.

Furthermore, because they consist of the Self (*ātman*), they are not dependent on injunctions; nor is the aforementioned inference possible, because it would be fallacious with respect to the result which depends upon the knowledge of the rope.
This is the intended meaning. || 172 ||
Such is the meaning of the commentary (bhāṣya) regarding the reality of the single Self, presented in due order.
This will be explained with effort, according to logic, by means of refuting the prima facie position. || 573 ||

Now, even though the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman and the Self has been stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "nanu sarvo'pi," that validity does not attain stability until the previously mentioned reasons for invalidity have been refuted; therefore, he says: "ityevamādi. Here, the word *iti* refers to the absence of contradiction with other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), while the word *evaṃ* refers to the absence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) with them. The word *ādi* [refers to] the fruit and the purport (*phalatātparya*).

For the purpose of removing the misconception regarding non-existence: by this method, the meaning of the Bhāṣya beginning with "all this," which was explained as the fact that the Vedāntas are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for Brahman—

that [explanation] is [now further established] through the sequential support of reasoning (*nyāya*), by way of refuting the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), and through an examination of the intent of the means of valid knowledge.
1. *Kha* (the second section). The *Mānapravārtika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 169.

The meaning is that by this [verse], the apprehension of instability regarding the authoritativeness of the Veda—which has become the established subject matter of the commentary—is to be rendered firm. || 973 ||
The validity of the Vedānta statements with respect to their own meaning is not undermined.
Because the characteristic of being a means of knowledge is present, just like the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. || 574 ||

Anticipating the objection, "How then is the reason for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) refuted?", he replies with the words "Vedānta... to counter the argument that "because it is already established [as known] by other means of knowledge (māna), the Vedāntas have no authority regarding it. Since the self's amenability to other means of knowledge has been refuted and will be refuted further, the authority of the Vedāntas with respect to it is logical, because they provide knowledge of what was previously unknown; this is a well-established principle.
Such is the meaning. || 974 ||
For indeed, in worldly discourse, words do not have as their sole purpose the accomplishment of a specific effect.
Do you have any means of knowledge regarding the claim that these are employed invariably? 575.

Regarding the argument that "the restriction of the capacity of words [to denote] is derived from worldly usage alone," and that since the employment of words in such cases is directed toward an action (*kārya*), the word is established as being intent upon that [action], and therefore lacks authority regarding an already established fact (*siddha-artha*)—to this he replies: "Not at all. For in the linguistic practice of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), words being employed are invariably used only for the purpose of an action; there is no such measurement [of certainty] in this regard.
The interpretation. || 579 ||
By good fortune you prosper, O blessed one; a son has been born to you who shall bring you increase.
Thus, this statement is neither for the purpose of engaging in activity nor for the purpose of desisting from it.

He establishes the absence of valid cognition regarding an injunction by demonstrating that the employment of sentences is directed toward already established facts (*siddhārtha*), using the word "diṣṭyā" [as an example].

Then, he says "iti nedam" to show that even a sentence concerning the birth of a son does not terminate in an established fact, as it culminates in activity and so forth; the meaning is that no words capable of inciting or restraining action are heard therein. || 976 ||
Causes for the arising of pleasure and so forth are observed even when they do not possess an effect.
Just as with such statements as "Go to the village" and so forth. || 577 ||

Now, one might raise the objection that, according to the logic already stated, a statement such as "a son is born" would lack authority because it is devoid of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and thus results in no fruit; anticipating this, he says: "sukhādi" (pleasure, etc.). This means they are characterized by being the causes for the arising of those [feelings]. Just as in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*)—

The meaning is this: even sentences devoid of an injunction (*vidhi*) are seen to be fruitful when they convey a single action, such as the birth of a son and so forth; for these possess the inherent nature of being causes for the arising of pleasure and the like, and thus bear fruit. Therefore, just like an injunctive sentence, a sentence lacking an injunction is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own object. || 977 ||
Nor is activity enjoined by him with the thought, "May one be happy."
Its purpose is the attainment of happiness, not a dependence upon instruction. || 578 ||

Anticipating the objection that even in the statement regarding the birth of a son there is an injunction such as "be happy," [the author] considers whether this enjoins activity toward that means or toward the state of being happy; having raised this alternative, he states the defect in the first case with the word "sukhī" (happy). The meaning is that since the means for the birth of a son is already accomplished, there is no injunction to prompt activity toward it. He refutes the second case with the words "sukhībhavanam" (the state of becoming happy). The genitive case in "asya" refers to the father.
It censures. "Instruction" means a rule; that is to say, by the force of the meaning, namely, the power of the report of the son's birth. || 178 ||
22 [Vol. 1, page 191] 170 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection]...
If there were a distinction in the activity [of the agent] as well as in the intention of the speech,
it would not be so in the case of the production of pleasure and the like, because their purposefulness is established through the attainment of the object.

Immediately after hearing the statement regarding the birth of a son, a specific ritual activity consisting of the *jātakarman* (birth rites) and so forth is observed; since the purport of that statement lies in an unseen potency (*apūrva*) that bears fruit, one might suspect that it is solely directed toward such activity. To this, [the author] replies: "There is a distinction. Because the engagement in the *jātakarman* and other rites is dependent on other injunctions, such as "When a son is born, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara" and "Having kindled the fire," [the statement regarding the birth is not itself injunctive].

He refutes the claim that the sentence concerning the birth of a son has that [status of] being directed toward an end by stating, "Not so. Anticipating the objection, "How then is it authoritative by virtue of having a fruit?", he recalls what was stated previously regarding the causes for the arising of pleasure and so forth: "Pleasure, etc. Since the authority of the sentence is established through its meaningfulness in producing the knowledge of the birth of a son—which serves as the means for pleasure and the cessation of suffering—it does not terminate in mere activity (*pravṛtti*).
This is the meaning. || 179 ||
Precisely out of fear of meaninglessness, it is postulated elsewhere than where it is heard.
Because of the statement regarding sprinkling and so forth, it does not possess an inherent qualification [for the rite], as is the case with others.

Anticipating the objection that— even though the sentence announcing the birth of a son culminates in its own literal meaning— the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) does not culminate in its own meaning because of that example, since, like the sentence regarding the sprinkling of water (prokṣaṇa), it is possible for it to have a purport other than its own literal meaning, [the author] says: "On account of futility" (ānarthakya).

The meaning of this is as follows: Since the sentence concerning sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth lacks a fruit in its own literal sense, its purport (*tātparya*) is determined—by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—to lie elsewhere than what is heard, namely in the supreme *apūrva*. This has been stated in the ninth book: "In the case of those things employed for a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), because they are for that purpose, their application must be prompted by that [rite]" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 9.1.2). Thus: "One threshes with the mortar and pestle after they have been sprinkled; one grinds with the lower and upper millstones after they have been sprinkled."

In this regard, when a doubt arises as to whether the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed prior to the threshing (*avaghāta*) and other rites is for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) or for the sake of those acts themselves, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as follows: since sprinkling and other such acts are connected with preparatory rites like threshing, they must serve the purpose of those acts; thus, the sprinkling is prompted by that threshing and so forth, yet it is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) that it is to be performed for the sake of the *apūrva*. Since syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context, the *apūrva* is understood through the sentence. Having thus argued, it is said: "By that purpose, however, there is a connection with the sacrifice..."

"Therefore, there is a connection with the ritual properties (*dharma*); thus, it should be prompted by the sacrifice, because the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is for that purpose" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 9.1.13). Consequently, since here [in the case of threshing] there is a connection of the sacrifice with the *apūrva*, there is a connection of that [threshing] with the ritual property of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Therefore, the sprinkling, being prompted by the fruitful sacrifice and the *apūrva*, is connected with the purificatory rite; and because that [sprinkling] is for the sake of the *apūrva*, the threshing and so forth, which would otherwise be fruitless, [become meaningful].

The meaning of the sūtra is that, because there is no [independent] purpose for the self, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is indeed prompted solely by the *apūrva*. Nor does it follow that, because the self is thus fruitful in its own right and independent of another prompting, one should assume a different intentionality elsewhere, such as in the case of the Tattvamasi and other statements. An objection is raised: "Since threshing and the like have the nature of a productive action (*bhāvārtha*), they are objects prompted by the *apūrva*; likewise, since the knowledge arising from sentences such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*) also has the nature of a productive action, it too must have that as its object, and therefore the sentence is authoritative only as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the *apūrva*. To this he replies: "No."
"It is not independent" means that threshing and so forth do not indeed connect directly with the independent *apūrva* (unseen potency), but rather as acts of refinement (*saṃskārakarma*).

As it was stated in the second book: "Those [acts] are of two kinds, being either subordinate or principal" (*Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra* 2.1.6). In the case of "He threshes the rice-grains," "He husks the rice," and "He melts the clarified butter," there arises the question whether threshing and the other acts are objects of the *niyoga* (the injunction) or acts of refinement.

Since a direct relationship is possible in the case of doubt, it is illogical for [the substances] to be connected by way of being purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*); furthermore, because there is no difference in their status as denoting action (*bhāvārtha*), it follows that avaghāta (threshing) and other such acts, like the sacrifice itself, are the objects of the *niyoga* (injunction).
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhānta holds]: by the force of the accusative case-ending in "vrīhīn" and so forth, the substance is primary.
6.1 Sva. 3 Pra | [Vol. 1, page 192]
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

[Page 171] Since it is ascertained through scriptural injunction and worldly observation that acts such as threshing have the purpose of producing rice-grains and the like, and since the substance is intended to be brought into being (*cikīrṣyamāṇatva*), it is possible for the substance’s connection with the action to be for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) by way of the purification of the substance, in accordance with the capacity of the word-meanings. Thus, rather than subverting its own nature, there is a direct connection [with the result].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because they lack a previously unknown object (*apūrvaviṣayatva*), those [actions] are purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*). The meaning of the sūtra is that words such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and "one should grind" (*piṇaṣṭi*) are of two kinds: some denote primary acts (*pradhānakarman*) and some denote purificatory acts.
Furthermore, it is not the case that knowledge arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) has a connection to an action by way of being a purificatory act.

The sense is that because [the knowledge of reality] is independently the cause of the fruit, it is—as will be explained later—impossible for it to be the object of an injunction (*niyoga*), as was the case previously. Now, one might object:

since threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like, which produce visible effects upon the substance, are seen to be *karmas* whose purpose is purification (*saṃskāra*), whereas in acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) that [purification] is absent, they are objects of an injunction just like sacrifices and the like; likewise, the knowledge arising from statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) should also be an object of an injunction, even though that [knowledge] exists.

Therefore, with reference to the view of the essential nature [of knowledge], he says: "like a qualified injunction. The meaning of this is as follows: Knowledge cannot be the object of an injunction (*niyoga*) in the same way that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts are, because even those acts lack direct connection [to the injunction] since they are merely purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*). As it was stated in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa* (PMS 2.1.9): "But in the case of a mere property (*dharmamātra*), there would be an action [as the object], because it is not yet accomplished, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. [Regarding] the rice-grains...

In cases such as "he sprinkles" (*prokṣati*) or "he wipes the ladles" (*srucaḥ saṃmārṣṭi*), when there arises a doubt as to whether these acts constitute the object of an injunction (*niyoga-viṣayatva*) or are merely preparatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*),

if the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa-prayojana*) of the sprinkling and so forth is insufficient, then they would constitute the object of an injunction as mere qualities (*dharmamātra*). By that [injunction], the substance—

Since the *pakāra* (the act of cooking) is not yet accomplished, the substance that brings it about must be subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to it—just as the *prayāja* offerings are to the sacrifice—whereas this [act of sprinkling] is a primary action (*pradhānakarma*). Having raised this objection, it was stated:
“Or rather, because the scriptural expression is identical, that property [of being subordinate] would apply to the others” (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 2.1.10).

This means that it would possess the same nature as the other subordinate actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*), because the accusative case-ending is heard in relation to the substances in the acts of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth.

The meaning of the sūtra is that [the two cases] are equal in both respects. Furthermore, it is not the case that in this way knowledge has a connection to an action as an object of mental impression (*saṃskāra*); therefore, just like the injunctional statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the statement concerning reality (*tattvamasi*) also has its purport in its own literal sense. || 580 ||
Furthermore, how is it that this person, being unengaged with the means, is set into motion?
Or rather, because the means are known, or because the goal is accomplished through the prescribed method. || 581 ||

Fearing that if the sentence beginning with "That thou art" (tattvamasi), like an injunctive sentence, were to terminate in its own literal meaning, it would likewise have to terminate in an injunction, [the author] elaborates upon what was stated in the passage beginning with "sukhyeva" etc., in order to show—by means of the example of a sentence announcing the birth of a son—that this [sentence] does not terminate in an injunction.

He says: "Furthermore... There is no rule that a sentence must necessarily be an instigator to action, for there is a deviation from such a rule in the case of the sentence announcing the birth of a son.

This is the meaning. In that regard, he offers a dilemma (*vikalpayati*) to demonstrate the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of [the injunction] from being the motivator (*pravartaka*). He asks: "Is it the means (*upāya*)?
