The meaning of the dilemma is as follows: is the listener, who previously did not engage with the means for the birth of a son, motivated by an injunction such as "One should desire a son" (*putrīyed*), or rather, is he motivated toward that end because the means is already known even without an injunction, for the sake of accomplishing the goal (*upeya*)? || 581 ||
In this regard, first of all, there is no such means here characterized by the birth of a son and so forth.
Because its nature is already perfected, it is not likewise [attained] in the happiness that is the goal.

He refutes the first [objection], beginning with: "Since the birth of a son has already been accomplished, a person should not be impelled toward it by a ritual injunction. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
[the commentary notes] 1. *pūrvīyaṃ* (kha); 2. *radvā* (kha); 3. *dhītyuktaṃ* (kha).
172 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 193]

He refutes the second [position] with the words "Nor... He states the reason: "Because it has already been stated that the arising of happiness occurs precisely through the force of hearing the news of the son's birth. He says "In the same way... (verse 182).
For no other activity whatsoever is observed that has pleasure as its purpose.
Because the attainment of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha) is concluded by the mere mention of the birth of a son. || 583 ||

Fearing that one might think, "By the injunction 'be happy,' let a person be impelled toward some other activity that accomplishes happiness," he says, "No. The ellipsis is: therefore, even in that case, a person is not to be impelled by an injunction. He states the reason why there is no other authoritative activity: "putra... [etc.]. For from the sentence announcing the birth of a son, happiness arises merely through the cognition of its meaning.

The meaning is that, in the present context, there exists no other operation or means for its accomplishment that is supported by authoritative evidence; for even though things such as the birth of a beloved daughter or the ease of delivery exist, they are not fit to be enjoined as a ritual act (vidhi), just like the birth of a son. || 583 ||
Moreover, for one whose mind is pervaded by the opposite of that which is desired and superimposed [upon it].
When it is said, "This is a garland, not a serpent," the removal of poison is observed [to occur].

He states another reason for the absence of a rule that a sentence must be an instigator of action, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). Having cited sentences whose established meanings result in the production of pleasure,
he now cites similar sentences whose results are the cessation of suffering, thereby providing the additional reason promised.
He clarifies this: "Superimposed," etc. (184).
Even when it is said, "Do not fear," no injunction is perceived.
For, by the very mention of the garland, there is the attainment of the complete destruction of all fear. || 585 ||

Anticipating the objection that even the statement beginning with "strageṣa" (the garland) does not culminate in the reality of things because it is centered on an injunction such as "do not fear," he says: "And [the words] 'mā bhaiṣīḥ' (do not fear). He states the reason why an injunction is not perceived: "Because of the mention of the garland. The ellipsis is: "an injunction regarding a fruit does not appear. || 985 ||
An injunction is valid only in that case where the Buddha has indicated its necessity as a duty.
Immediately thereafter, there would be an engagement with the object for the sake of its accomplishment. || 586 ||
Furthermore, he states that there is no *niyoga* (injunction) in this sentence by saying "is proper" (*nyāyya*). The mention of the sentence is made by means of the words "yat" and "tat.

The mention of the *niyoga* is by means of the two genitive endings. "Being a task" (*kāryatām*) means "being something to be accomplished" (*sādhyatām*). The "object" (*viṣaya*) is the meaning of the verbal root. It is not [the *niyoga*].

The meaning is: since there is no activity directed toward an object of an injunction here—as there is in cases such as "bring [this]"—how could there be any occasion for such [an injunction]? || 986 ||
Therefore, in sentences concerning identity, there is the comprehension of the mere reality (tattva) alone.
Since the supreme human goal is accomplished immediately, the accomplishment of some further task is not observed.

Since it is observed that even worldly sentences whose meanings are already established possess fruitfulness, this is logical; however, in the case of the Vedāntas, which are devoid of injunctions, no conclusion regarding a fruit is perceived—as in the case of [the passage] "He wept" (so 'rodīt). Therefore, suspecting that there must be an injunction within them, he says:
"But here... (iha tu). || 987 ||
1. Desired; 2. *kha*: *sakalī*; 3. *kha*: from wealth (*dhanāt*).
[Vol.
1, page 194] *Vartika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 173.
Likewise, for those possessed of curiosity, [the goal is attained] merely through the completion of the narrative.
The complete eradication of the curiosities of men has been witnessed.
In order to demonstrate that even those Vedāntic texts which have already established meanings possess fruitfulness, he cites a scriptural and traditional narrative:

"Kutūhala," etc. By the word *kutūhala*, which denotes agitation, suffering (*duḥkha*) is indicated. He says "tadvat" (in the same way), meaning that just as in cases such as "This is a garland," suffering is removed through the mere knowledge of the object, so too it is here. [This refers to] the established meaning (*siddhārtha*) produced by the mere narration of a completed event.
Whatever narrative is either worldly or Vedic, it follows from the knowledge of the mere object therein; such is the meaning. || 188 ||
Because they determine only the mere object, those words are not [authoritative] at all.
Nor would they be sufficient for grasping or for abandoning for one who knows that [reality]. || 589 ||

An objection might be raised: "Are not even worldly and Vedic sentences, which result in the cessation of curiosity, necessarily centered on *niyoga* (an injunction), since they must have as their purpose either engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)? Anticipating this, he says: "merely the thing itself" (*vastumātra*). The meaning is that for one who possesses knowledge of the meaning of the aforementioned sentences, there is no reliance on a *niyoga* to be accomplished through engagement and so forth, because those sentences terminate fruitfully in the knowledge of their own objects. || 189 ||
And even where rejection and acceptance are understood from hearing the words, such as "this path is infested with thieves" or "this region contains treasure. (590)
Even in that case, there is no operation of the word at all, because it is the cognition of what is already established.

Since even for a person whose purpose has already been fulfilled, activity arises solely from passion (rāga), [it follows that] although sentences such as "a son is born" convey established facts (*siddhārtha*), we observe activity and so forth upon hearing sentences like "the path has an obstacle" or "the ground contains a treasure. Therefore, just as those two sentences have the nature of being objects of injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*niṣedha*), the *Tattvamasi* and other such statements must likewise be centered on injunction.

Having restated that doubt, he refutes it with the words beginning "yatra" (where). He states the reason why even in the case of the example, there is no operation of the word in regard to activity and so forth, with the word "siddha" (established). The meaning is that the two sentences are exhausted merely by making known the connection with a treasure and the like, which are not of the nature of an effect. To the question, "How then does the hearer, upon hearing the two sentences, understand activity and cessation?", he says: "nara-" (the person...).
Regarding the word "api": the particle *api* has the sense of conjoining [the cessation] from hatred. || 990 || 591 ||
Drawn by the single noose of desire, he proceeds solely according to his own will.
And because of that [cognition], a person desists from the activity of speech. || 592 ||

He elaborates on the point that engagement and withdrawal proceed solely from passion and aversion, and not from injunctions and prohibitions. [The verse begins with] "kāma" (desire). The word "tat" (that) refers to objects such as obstructors or thieves. The distinction is this: an injunction consists in the communication of a mandate (*niyoga*), while a prohibition consists in the communication of a cessation; for it is accepted that the latter culminates in indifference through the cessation of an action that had been undertaken. || 992 ||
But surely, even though this sentence was not uttered by the speaker, it was intended by him.
"You must not go by this path; likewise, take this treasure."

“By one who says ‘there is an adversary on the road,’ negation is intended; and by one who says ‘this region of earth possesses a treasure,’ affirmation is intended; therefore, that [latter] sentence also is established upon that [negation]. [The opponent] objects that it is not the case that two sentences terminate in a mere thing-in-itself.
174 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 195]
"Do not say so; the status of a word's meaning is not established based on the speaker's intention."
Because the subservience [of the action] to that purpose arises from the power of the word itself, it does not have any other cause.

He states that the intended injunction and so forth are not the meaning of the word: "Not so. He clarifies his thesis with the words beginning with "No," and provides the reason for it with the words beginning with "Because of the word. The meaning is this: since it has been stated that being the meaning of a word belongs to what is cognized through the power of the word itself and is not produced by intention (*vivakṣā*), therefore even the intended injunction and prohibition are not the meaning of the word. || 194 ||
And this must also be accepted by you with diligent effort.
For if the meaning of a word depends upon a speaker, there could be no confidence in the Veda.

Anticipating the objection that, even if in your view the meaning of a word is that which is cognized through the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), in our position it is only that which is intended (*vivakṣita*) that constitutes its meaning, he says: "By you" (*bhavadbhiḥ*). By showing the fault in the view that the meaning of a word is only what is intended—without depending on the power of the word—he causes [the opponent] to accept [our position]. He says: "The speaker" (*vaktr*). Since the meaning of a word depends upon the intention of the speaker, and because there is no speaker in the Veda, therefore [there can be no such] meaning...
The meaning is that it would not be like a dog. || 595 ||
The attainment of various kinds of human goals is also desired by the speaker.
By that same reasoning, it would follow that for her as well, the word would have the status of being the meaning [of itself]. (596)
Nevertheless, suspecting that in common worldly usage the meaning of a word follows what the speaker intends (*vivakṣita*), he says: "Not so" (*na*).

Since there is no fixed rule regarding intention, according to your own statement, the meaning of a word would likewise follow the speaker's intention; in such a system of linguistic meaning, there would be total instability.
Therefore, even in the world, since that [intention] is not the meaning of the word, only that which is cognized through the word’s own power (*śakti*) can be its meaning.
This is the meaning. || 596 ||
When, with the mind, one intends either engagement or withdrawal, [then...]
Something is sought to be known by a knower through means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
Even if it is intended, there is no activity at that time, or else there is the opposite.

It can be stated by a wise person that [the object] is a means of valid cognition (prameya) such as perception (pratyakṣa). Regarding the point that "the intended meaning of a word is not [the object]," he provides an example: "pravṛttim" (activity). Just as the intended meaning is not the object of perception and so forth, so too the meaning intended [by the speaker] is not the object of the word as a means of valid cognition; this is the meaning. 197 || 998 ||
For this reason as well, one must accept that even when the object is identical, [the cognition differs].
In that case, one person has the thought of abandoning it, while another has the desire to acquire it. (599)
For if all things were the referents of words, the intellect would function solely for the purpose of grasping them.
Nor is it considered that there is a multiplicity of meanings in [the terms] equanimity (upekṣā) or abandonment (prahāṇa). || 600 ||

He states that it must also be accepted on the basis of the reason about to be stated that the intended meaning of a word is not [the same for all]. He says, "For this reason as well" (*itaśca*). He clarifies another reason with the words, "Even though it is equal" (*tulye’pi*). When it is said, "This place contains a treasure," even though the cognition of the treasure is equal [in all], there is the thought of abandoning it in one who is dispassionate; in one who cannot endure effort, there is indifference; but in one who has passion, there is the desire to acquire it. This is because, in that case, the act of taking is what is intended to be expressed, and thus it is the meaning of the word.
1. Not so. 2. Kha. ha. Not at all.
[Vol.
1, page 196] Vārtika accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 175.

Furthermore, even for those who are dispassionate (*virakta*) and so forth, their cognition would be directed toward that [object] alone, and not toward its abandonment (*hāna*) or the like. If either abandonment or indifference (*upekṣā*) were intended (*vivakṣita*) and constituted the meaning of the word, then all listeners would understand either abandonment or indifference; therefore, even though the cognition of the word’s meaning is uniform, because there is a discrepancy in the cognition regarding what was intended—such as giving and so forth—the intended meaning is not the meaning of the word. This applies to all three, including abandonment and the rest.
Anticipating the objection that the status of a word's meaning might be intended differently depending on the distinction between listeners, he says: "And not... (na ca). || 199 || 600 ||
And even if you accept that the sentence possesses the quality of being an instigator [of action],...
The syntactical connection of other words that possess [their own] specific functions can indeed be stated. || 601 ||

Since it has been established that in an injunction and similar sentences, the injunction and so forth are not the literal meaning of the words, and thus they are established as being grounded in reality, it was stated that there is no such rule that a sentence must necessarily be inciting to action; now, even while accepting that rule, he provides the introductory context for stating the defect [in that position] with the words "And not... (na ca). || 61 ||
Is it a state of being restricted solely to one's own interest, or is it a state of being restricted solely to what is to be done?
But let it be stated: does it have as its purport the connection between mere word-meanings? (602)

In order to demonstrate the impossibility of explaining the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of words other than the verb, he presents the following alternatives. [He asks: "What? Having observed the activity of the middle-aged elder upon hearing the inciting sentence uttered by the senior elder, the child perceives that words possess a capacity for their own meanings which are not yet connected; therefore, the first alternative is that the capacity has as its object the individual meanings in isolation, according to the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (connection of what is already expressed). One—

The second [view] holds that words have their denotative power residing in that which is connected with an action (*kārya*), because the power of words is apprehended in relation to an effect connected with an action. The third holds that words reside in that [connected with action], because they possess the capacity for their own referents as being connected with an action. The fourth holds that words possess the capacity for that which is connected with what is connected to an action. [The fifth view] holds that words denote their own referents as being connected with something capable of connection—whether that be an action or a non-action—because the apprehension of their power occurs in respect to such a referent.
The phrase "the otherness of words" means the fifth [alternative], which signifies a conceptual construction (vikalpa). || 602 ||
If [the word] were to terminate in its own meaning alone, from what source could there be a cognition of the sentence-meaning?
And there would be the futility of the formal argument, because it would be incapable of practical application. || 603 ||
Having restated the first [position], he refutes it with the words "svārtha" (its own meaning).

If one were to admit that words possess capacity only for unconnected word-meanings and that they reside solely therein, then the hearer would have no cognition of the sentence-meaning, because the cause for it would be absent. Nor can the word-meanings themselves be the cause of that [cognition], for that would result in the sentence-meaning not being verbal in nature (*aśābdatva*).

Nor can its verbal nature be established by virtue of being produced by word-meanings indicated by words, for that would entail the absurdity of an inference arising from a visible mark (*liṅga*) also being visual in nature (*cākṣuṣatva*).

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). Having raised the objection that the sentence alone is the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, [the author] replies: if the sentence depends upon the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of its constituent words, it cannot have a qualified object as its scope; if it does not depend upon them, then the apprehension of such capacity is useless. Furthermore, regarding the view that the related (*anvita*) word possesses the capacity, since the specific connection is understood through the purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence, that [capacity] is not rendered useless. With this in mind, he says: "uselessness" (*vaiyarthya*).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "In linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). If words were incapable of denoting a specific object when used in a sentence whose meaning is not already connected [by prior cognition], it would be impossible to employ words that denote connected meanings; for a sentence—which consists of a collection of words in mutual connection—depends upon the power of its constituent words.

Consequently, specific linguistic usage would remain unestablished, according to the maxim: "For people employ words in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) only when prompted by a specific intended meaning."
This is the meaning. || 603 ||
Even in the case of the mere association of word-meanings, those [words] lack the purpose of conveying a specific action.
Since worldly transaction is fully established, the postulation of an effect is useless.
[Vol. 1, Page 197] 176 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Relation— ]

Having restated the final position—that the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of a word consists in its connection with a meaning that is either fit (*yogya*) or otherwise—he refutes the opponent’s view by means of a general argument.

[The text says: "padārtha... etc. By the suffix *mātra*, whether it be something to be done (*kārya*) or not to be done (*akārya*), that which is fit (*yogya*) is grasped. Since, if one accepts that the power (*śakti*) resides in what is connected with the fit, there is economy of postulation (*prayojaka-lāghava*), and because verbal usage is possible even in the absence of an action (*kārya*)—insofar as the object of the power is [the fit meaning]—our own position is established: [the power resides in] the fit...

The meaning is that in the position [of yours] that "the capacity resides in that which is endowed with the suffix," there is a flaw in your own view because you must postulate an effect [in the form of the suffix] as the counter-correlate of the capacity, due to the resulting burden of complexity (prayojaka-gaurava) and other such factors. || 604 ||
And when there is a single connection with an action, it arises from a sentence that merely restates what has already occurred.
There would be no comprehension of the sentence-meaning, and the utterance itself would also be rendered purposeless. || 605 ||

Considering that if words possess their capacity only in relation to a single effect (*kārya*), they would be synonyms, he addresses the second position with the words "kāryaiketi" (only in relation to the effect). Having restated the third position—that the capacity [of words] resides in that which is associated with a connection (*vyatiṣaṅgavati*)—he refutes it with the words "vyatiṣaṅga iti. Under the view that the capacity [of words] lies in an object associated with an effect, there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning for a listener from a sentence devoid of [words such as] the optative suffix (*liṅgādi*), and the same would apply to the speaker.

The application [of a syllogism] would be futile, for a syllogism is indeed employed to inform another; if the other does not understand that meaning from a statement of an established fact, then the application is rendered useless—this is the sense. || 605 ||
And because there is no other purpose, [the word] denotes only that which serves as its own purpose.
There would be no connection with others who express the means of proof and so forth. || 606 ||

Furthermore, does the word denoting an action (kāryapada) have its expressive power (śakti) in that which is connected with another action, or in that which is unconnected, or in that which is connected with an established fact? Regarding the first [option], he says:

"of another action" (*kāryāntarasya*). The meaning is that in sentences such as "Bring the cow," the connection of the word expressing an action with an object connected to another action would not be established, because there is no second action within a single sentence. Nor does the word denoting an action have a connection even with its own meaning when that meaning is unconnected [to anything else].

He says, "It would not exist," because he does not accept the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the relation of what has been expressed). He says, "There would be no relation," because he does not admit that the word denoting an action (*kāryapada*) has a relation even with its own meaning when that meaning is already established as being connected [with something else]. He says, "There is no relation," because it cannot be said whether that [action] is related through its connection with another action (*kāryānvaya*), since it is difficult to define such a connection either as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

By this, the fourth alternative is refuted. He states the conclusion—that if the connection of the injunctive word is not apprehended, its connection with the nominal words cannot be established—by the words beginning with "saṃbandho na" (no connection). The collective meaning is that it is necessary for the word denoting the action (kāryapada) to have its power residing in what is connected with another, and likewise for the other words. || 606 ||
And here, if all [words] were connected with the action, they would likewise be mutually [connected].
There would certainly be no relation between things because of their independence. || 607 ||

He states another defect regarding the fact that the capacity [of words] has as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) an object associated with an action (kāryānvita). [The verse begins with] "kārya... etc. The word "iha" refers to the sentence employed [in the context]. The meaning is: if all words possessed their expressive power (sāmarthya) only with respect to an object associated with an action, there would be no verbal relation (śābda-sambandha) between the words themselves; for, having fulfilled their purpose through connection with the action, they would have no mutual dependence on one another. || 607 ||
Likewise, the injunction would not be understood as having a qualified object.
And in that case, the injunction would result in the accomplishment of a single object. (608)

Anticipating the objection that even though these are not distinct from one another, the establishment of specific conventional usage is achieved solely through their connection with effects, he says:
[Vārtika, Vol. 1, p. 198; accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā, p. 177].

Regarding the term *niyoga*: the meaning is that if there were no mutual syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between word-meanings, then in the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), the *niyoga* (the injunction) would not appear as having for its object a sacrifice qualified by *soma*. He states another defect regarding the view that the potency of all words resides only in what is connected to an action (*kāryānvita*). [He says] "And then": when all words possess potency only in what is connected to an action, then [there would be no relation] between *soma* and the sacrifice individually.

The meaning is that because of its connection with the *niyoga*, each individual [element] would become the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); and in that case, its intended status as being accomplished by a qualified sacrifice (*viśiṣṭayāga*) would be lost. || 608 ||
Now, [the agent] is considered to be [the one who acts] with respect to objects such as sacrifices connected to Soma and so forth.
What then is the appointment (niyoga)? Let the cause for the prior relationship be stated. (609)

He raises an objection—beginning with "Now" (*atha*)—by accepting a mutual connection between the word-meanings as a collective whole (*pārṭiṇaka*), on the grounds that since there is no mandate (*niyoga*) to be accomplished by the *soma* alone or the sacrifice (*yāga*) alone, the mandate must have a qualified object. However, first of all, there can be no connection of each element individually with the mandate;

for in your own view, the mutual connection brought about by factors such as semantic competency (*yogyatā*) must necessarily precede the connection with the mandate, prior to the connection of the *soma* and the sacrifice.

Is there a cause for mutual concomitance (*anyonyānvaya*), or is there not? If there is, is it something else such as "fitness" (*yogyatā*) or the like, or something other than that? It cannot be the first, because if the concomitance were produced by fitness and the like, the insistence upon an injunction (*niyoga*) would be fruitless. Nor can it be the second; for is that [cause] distinct from the action (*kriyā*) or is it the action itself?

In the first case, since it must be either a causal factor (*kāraka*) or a result (*phala*), if the concomitance depends upon that, the injunction is redundant. Furthermore, it is not [the case that it is] beyond the causal factors and the results...

Thinking that something other than the action (kriyā) is empty [of causal efficiency], and that prior to the connection with the injunction (niyoga), a cause for the relationship is well-known, he raises an objection:
"What then from that? || 609 ||
When the qualified object is not established, no effect is admitted with respect to that object.
Now, it is precisely through action that our desired goal is accomplished.

He says "it is established" (*siddha*) because, in the position that there is no cause for a relationship, the relationship itself remains unestablished; thus, in the absence of that specific object of the injunction (*niyoga*) which has been established, the injunction cannot be established as it would be without an object. Alternatively, he states that prior to entering into the injunction, the action (*kriyā*) alone is the cause for the connection with *soma* and so forth; this is expressed by the word "now" (*atha*). When the connection between the action and its factors (*kāraka*) is accepted while setting aside the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished),...
He states that what we maintain—namely, that the expressive power (śakti) resides in the word as connected with its meaning—is established: "It is established. || 610 ||
Therefore, this other [means] is for that purpose; thus, this is consistent.
If the status of being an effect were to exist in an object only after the comprehension of that effect [has already occurred], [then there would be a logical fallacy].
Since there is no other effect within an effect, how could there be a cognition of an effect?
In the absence of that [cognition], even the object to be practiced would not exist for you.

He cites the *Bhāṣya* on the *Pratipadādhikaraṇa* as authority for the view that "the expressive power [of a word] resides in that which is associated with another. He says: "In that case... There, a doubt arises as to whether the *dharma* is expressed by each individual word or by all of them together. Having established the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) position that there is a distinct *dharma* for each word, the author of the *Bhāṣya* establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by stating: "When the *apūrva* [resultant merit] follows from one [word], the others will serve its purpose. This too implies that the expressive power [resides] in that which is associated with another.

The meaning is that it would be logical to accept [the injunction] as a constant factor, for words do not become subordinate to anything else unless they possess the capacity to convey a meaning connected with something else.

Even in the case of the connection between factors of action (*kāraka*) and the verb, the necessity inherent in the action itself is dependent upon the mandate (*niyoga*); therefore, the necessity [of the action] is [established] through that [mandate]. (Note: The numbers and letters refer to variant readings found in the manuscript notes:
*ka* refers to the reading "bandhe yā"; *kha* refers to the readings "yataḥ" and "yatām".)
178 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection—] [Vol. 1, p. 199]

Regarding what was stated there [in the previous section], one might suspect that the capacity [of words] resides in the related meaning (*anvita*) rather than in the task (*kārya*); anticipating this, he says: "The object" (*viṣaye*).

If the status of being a task (*kāryatva*) in the sacrifice and so forth—which are the objects of the mandate (*niyoga*)—is preceded by the cognition of the mandate, then the cognition of it [the task] in the mandate itself must also be produced by the cognition of that [mandate], as there is no distinction [between them]. And since there is no further mandate within the mandate, the cognition of its being something to be done (*kartavyatva*) is not established therein. [This is the meaning. By means of the cognition of the mandate’s being a task...

He states the fault incurred when [the action] exists: "Because of its absence," etc. The meaning is that the performance of the root-meaning (dhātvartha) is dependent upon the cognition that the mandate (niyoga) is what is to be accomplished. || 611 || 612 ||
Consequently, the purposefulness of the action would be lost if it were not performed.
Now, even in the absence of another effect, its status as an effect is still maintained. || 613 ||

He states the fault that follows if the object (*viṣaya*) also lacks the status of being something to be accomplished (*kāryatva*): "Because it would have the purpose of an effect" (*kāryārthatā*). The meaning is this: since there would then be no performance of the sacrifice and so forth, and without such performance, its status as the purpose of the mandate (*niyoga*)—which you yourself desire—would necessarily be lost. He raises an objection, suggesting that the aforementioned chain of faults does not apply, on the grounds that if the mandate has the status of being something to be accomplished in the sacrifice and so forth, then that same cause is not established for itself: "Now" (*atha*)... [693]
In the same way, the object itself would also possess the status of being an effect by its own nature.
If the object, because it consists of something that cannot be produced [by itself], requires [something else] for its own establishment; || 614 ||
Even that task should be examined as being of an unachievable nature.
And thus, even in the case of an effect, its very status as an effect would be caused by the object.

He refutes [the opponent’s view] by stating that if the status of being an action (*kāryatva*) belongs to the mandate (*niyoga*) by its own nature, then it should likewise belong to the sacrifice and so forth; thus, the mandate is redundant. [The opponent] objects with the words "of the object" (*viṣayasya*), suggesting that because the meaning of the verbal root—which is of the nature of toil—is not an action by its own nature, there is a need for the mandate to establish its status as an action. [The author replies: Even the action (the mandate) would require the meaning of the verbal root because it is not an action by its own nature; otherwise, the meaning of the verbal root would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, it depends upon that.

Thinking that there is parity between the two—since if the non-obligatory (asarvya) were to have the nature of an effect (kāryatva) by itself, why should the other (the obligatory) not likewise possess it by its own nature even while depending on an effect—he says: "That too... He states the conclusion regarding the obligation's dependence on an object: "Even in the case of an effect... (614).
Furthermore, there would be mutual dependence, and the primacy of the effect would not be established.
When it depends upon human activity for its own accomplishment, it is called an effect (kārya). || 616 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the performance of the *niyoga* (the mandate) depends on its object for its being an action, the object’s status as an action nonetheless depends on the *niyoga*, he says: "Mutually" (*anyonya*). The meaning is that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): the object’s status as an action follows from the *niyoga*’s status as an action, and the *niyoga*’s status as an action follows from that [object’s status]. He states another defect indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), beginning with "And not" (*na ca*). [The text continues: "The object..."

The meaning is that if the status of being an effect were dependent upon the mandate (*niyoga*), then even for that [mandate], there would be no primacy in its being an effect relative to its object (the sacrifice) and so forth, since there would be no distinction between it and the sacrifice itself. Having stated the equality between the mandate and the sacrifice, he states the definition of an "effect" (*kārya*) in order to express the distinction that the sacrifice alone is the effect: "In dependence on human activity... That which comes into being when there is a requirement for human activity for its own production is an effect.
Thus ends [the section]. || 616 ||
And that [act], such as sacrifice and the like, is not to be performed by us, because it is by its very nature solely of the form of the body.
The status of being an effect belongs only to that which is an effect; it is not admitted for that which is not an effect. || 617 ||

He states that because the sacrifice and other such acts exist at the moment immediately following [the injunction], they alone constitute the effect: "The sacrifice and so forth. This is accompanied by the Vārttika for the purpose of restriction, as found in the *Śāstraprakāśikā* commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
(Vol. 1, p.

He states the object to be excluded, which was indicated by the word "ca" (and) used with a displaced order [of words]: "it is not an effect. He provides the reason why there is an absence of the definition of an effect in the case of a mandate (*niyoga*):
"by itself. For those who maintain that doctrine, the status of a mandate as an effect is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*), not dependent upon human activity.

Otherwise, it would follow that [the injunction] is equivalent to a jar; therefore, the meaning is that because the injunction lacks the aforementioned definition, it does not possess the nature of being an action (*kāryatā*). He states another reason for its lack of being an action with the word "not. The meaning is: that which is called an injunction (*niyoga*) is not itself the nature of being an action, for if it were, it would result in self-dependence (*svāśraya*); nor is there another nature of being an action [within it], for that would lead to infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). To whom, then, does the nature of being an action belong? He says: "to that which is non-action" (*akārye*).
The meaning is that, although sacrifice and the like are by nature not things to be accomplished, they are rendered "to be accomplished" (kārya) by means of an injunction (vidhi). || 617 ||
It is not the case that whiteness is predicated of a cloth or the like by way of its attaining the state of being white.
The pot, the effect, the sacrifice, and so forth, exist by virtue of their own respective natures. || 618 ||
When [a word] is denoted by its own form through distinctions such as "accomplished" (siddha) or "to be accomplished" (sādhya),
then there would be no such thing as "suggestion" (dhvani) in the communication of an unknown meaning.
In this way, there would be no engagement with an injunction [merely] because of some distinction. || 619 ||

He provides an example for the impossibility of "being an effect" (kāryatva) residing in that which is the locus of being an effect: "not clay. The example for the presence of "being an effect" in what is not an effect is "cloth and so forth. Since it is impossible for an effect to possess the property of being an effect, and since that [property] belongs only to sacrifices and the like, the position that [the injunction] is due to the entry of "what-is-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) is untenable. Because the connection between action and its factors (kāraka) does not depend on a mandate (niyoga), [the word] is connected [to the agent] without regard for the effect.

Since it has been established that [the word] signifies *śakti* (potency), he states the resulting conclusion: "The jar," etc. The term "effect" (*kārya*) refers to the injunction (*niyoga*). The term "sacrifice" (*yajati*) refers to the action (*kriyā*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used to include qualities, parts, states, and the like. In that context, whether it be a jar, an injunction, an action, or a quality and so on, each exists in its own unique form—such as being made of clay, being eternally to-be-accomplished, having the nature of motion, or being dependent upon a substance—and is denoted by its own expressive word, whether that word denotes an accomplished entity (*siddha*) or a thing to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*).

Or, when it is stated that [the person] is conjoined with something else that is suitable as a remainder of that [injunction], then there would be no distinction whatsoever in making known what was previously unknown between a sentence whose meaning is an accomplished fact (*bhūtārtha*) and one whose meaning is an action to be performed (*kāryārtha*). This being the case, the meaning is that the claim "activity is dependent upon a mandate" (*niyoga*) would not hold true.
But once the meaning of the word has been understood, [the application of the injunction] follows from the pursuit of human goals.
The activity would arise from itself alone, and not from the word, nor likewise from the object.
Then, raising the objection as to how activity can follow immediately after the word, [the author] recalls what was stated in the verse beginning with "narasyāpi rāmādeḥ," namely, "avabuddhe tu...

(But when [the object] is understood...). When the object is unknown, it is only upon its being known through the word that, due to the desire for the human goal associated with it, another—[namely, activity]—[occurs].

The meaning is this: the activity of a person arises from their own expectation (rapekṣā), not from words such as the optative suffix (liṅ); for it is not observed that those who hear such words engage in activity if they lack the cognition of its meaning. Nor does that activity arise from the mandate (niyoga) which is the meaning of those words, because that very mandate is not accepted [as the cause]. || 620 ||
That which is external to the triad beginning with the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is excluded from the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
Who is the wise one that would accomplish this, or what is its form? Let it be told.

Having accepted the position that [an injunction] whose nature is something to be accomplished lacks the capacity to impel action, he now states that its very status as something to be accomplished is unestablished: "sādhanādi" (beginning with the means). The meaning is that an effect distinct from the instrument (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the end to be produced (*bhāvya*) is not pervaded by human effort (*kṛti*). He establishes its difference from the end to be produced: "puruṣārtha" (the human goal). Pleasure or the cessation of pain is the human goal; [an injunction] is other than that.
[Vol. 1, Page 201] 180 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection]

The meaning is that, because of this [definition], there can be no "bhāvya" (that which is to be brought into being) for the *niyoga*. He states the conclusion: that a *kārya* (task) distinct from the fruit (*phala*) and so forth is unfit to be produced by one who acts with prior cognition. Then, considering that even the essential nature of the *niyoga* is difficult to define, he offers alternatives: "Or what?"—is it impulsion (*preraṇā*), or the internal effort (*niyoga*), or action (*kriyā*), or the fruit (*phala*), or the causal factor (*kāraka*), or something else?
Or, O King, it may be said that [the object] is either unrelated to the three times, or it is something beyond the senses; such is the deliberation of the opponent. || 629 ||
An instigation cannot be the object to be accomplished, for it has as its object the thing to be accomplished.
Likewise, there would be no internal effort either, since [the object] is already known through another means of cognition.

Therein, he refutes the first [position] with the words "not, for... He provides the reason: "because the operation of the word is instigation (*preraṇā*), and because that [instigation] has the *niyoga* as its object, and because a distinction between the object and the subject is well-established. With the words "kārya... he addresses the second [position]: when it is said "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), an internal effort arises in the hearer consisting of a departure from his natural state; that [effort] is the *niyoga*. He rejects this with "no," [arguing] that the effort...

He states the reason: "Because it would follow that even the *niyoga* (injunction) would possess that nature [of being mental] due to its being mental; because it would then lack the quality of being *apūrva* (unprecedented); and because it would not be the meaning of the word, as it would not be something unobtainable through other means. This is expressed by the phrase "mānāntara... [verse 622].
An action [does not produce] a result through its connection with an agent, nor because it is undesirable in nature.
Nor is it an agent, because it is unestablished; nor is it anything else, because nothing else can be defined.

He states the third [objection]: "Not an action" (*na kriyā*). He provides the reason for this: because an action is related to an agent (*kartṛ*), whereas an injunction (*niyoga*) is connected to a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); thus, there is a difference between the two. He addresses the fourth [objection] with: "Not the fruit" (*na phalam*). He provides the reason why an injunction is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*): "Because it is undesired" (*aniṣṭa*). He replies to the fifth [objection]: "Not an agent" (*na kārakam*). [The reason is that] an injunction is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
He states the reason: "because the agent is established" and "because it is unestablished. He rejects the sixth [alternative] due to the absence of evidence, saying: "Nor... (623).
Furthermore, the state of being expressible without contact with the three times is not the defining characteristic of an effect.
Let there be no causality in the pot [merely] from the word "pot," due to the lack of contact with time.

He states the seventh [point]: "And not... The non-connection of the *niyoga* (injunction) with the three times may be either verbal or factual; it is not the first [case], as he says: "A jar... When "jar" is uttered, since that too would lack connection with time verbally, it would possess the nature of an injunction. To prevent this, the fact that it does not touch upon that [time] verbally is not conducive to its being an injunction; for from the word "jar," there is no [cognition of] time in the jar.

Otherwise, the residual connection (*śeṣayoga*) would appear redundant in cases such as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo'sti*), because there is tautology. Nor is it correct to say that although the mere temporal relation of the jar is already manifest from the word "jar," the word "exists" and so forth are used for the sake of expressing a specific temporal relation; for the word "jar" has the form of a wide-bellied object as its meaning, and thus lacks any function regarding a mere temporal relation. Otherwise, it would follow that a single word possesses multiple meanings. This remains true even if the meaning of a word is held to be the generic form (*ākṛti*).

The meaning is as follows: because manifestation is what is characterized, nothing other than that [manifestation] is [the object]; for there is no non-temporal time, nor is there anything insentient that is not conjoined with time; furthermore, it should also be stated that there is nothing other than the injunction (niyoga), because that very thing is not accepted [by the opponent]. || 624 ||
An injunction (niyoga) is also an activity of the person to be enjoined; how could that [activity] come to be?
Since [the object] is beyond the senses, how could there be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, and how could its establishment occur? (625)
[Vol.

1, Page 202] Together with the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri, [the author] refutes the eighth [position]: "The mandate (*niyoga*) also... Just as the agent's activity consists of the sacrifice and so forth, the mandate also [consists of] the activity of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

Being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is *pāra* (the transcendent), like a sacrifice, because it is an operation of the person (*puṃvyāpāratva*). Nor is there a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), because the Viṣṇu-steps, the offering of oblations, and so forth, are perceptible (*adhyakṣatva*)—this is the meaning. Having raised the objection as to what, then, is the referent (*ālambana*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the rest, he states: "The referent of the optative and the rest," implying that by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the referent of the optative and the rest must be accepted as something other than the mandate (*niyoga*). Having rejected the nature of the mandate (*niyoga-svarūpa*), he now rejects its proof (*sādhaka*).
"Success, indeed! || 629 ||
If it is argued that accomplishment occurs through the accomplishment of the object, it is not so; for it does not happen by means of action alone.
Attainment, arising, and so forth are possible by virtue of having a nature that does not require superimposition.

He raises an objection: "It is incorrect to say that [the *niyoga*] does not accomplish the *niyoga*, because it is the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, once accomplished, that possess such a nature. He refutes this: "Not so. For it is impossible to bring about the production, attainment, refinement, or modification of the *niyoga* through human effort, since those who maintain the doctrine of *niyoga* admit that it cannot have any excellence (*atiśaya*) imparted to it; otherwise, its status as eternally established would be contradicted.
The word "tad" (that) clarifies the very resolution [of the objection] by means of action. || 626 ||
If the effect, being established by its own nature, were to accomplish the purpose of man, then because it would always be of that same nature, the purpose of man would exist at all times. (627)

Having stated that [the Vedic injunction] lacks a means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*), he begins to argue that the injunction itself lacks the capacity to be a means of accomplishment. In this regard, one might raise the objection that since it was stated—under the principle that "it [the injunction] would exist when the fruit is to be accomplished by action"—that the injunction is the means for accomplishing heaven and so forth, it does not exclude the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Anticipating this, he considers the following alternatives: does the *kārya* (the "to-be-done") accomplish heaven and so forth while existing in its own nature, or does it do so having its existence (*sattā*) dependent upon human activity? Having thus proposed the options, he first addresses the first alternative.

[The opponent] says: "It is an effect. [The author] refutes this, saying: "In that case, heaven and so forth would always exist, because the mandate (niyoga), which is their cause, exists eternally by its very nature"—this is expressed by the word "always" (*sarvadā*). Nor can it be argued that heaven and so forth do not exist eternally because they depend on a causal complex (*sāmagrī*); for the mandate brings about the fruit in order to obtain a fit person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and it does so precisely by implying the requisite causal complex, since its power of implication depends upon that very complex. Thus it should be understood.
[This is] the end of the section. || 627 ||
Furthermore, it is considered established as accomplishing its own purpose through the establishment of human activity.
Because its nature cannot be augmented, it could never produce a result.

It takes another kalpa [to bear fruit]. Regarding "human activity" (*puṃvyāpāra*): since it was stated in the passage beginning with "for an excellence cannot be imparted to an injunction by an action" (*niyogasyānādheyātiśayatāyāḥ karmaṇā na hi*) that [the result] is not established through human activity, he says that heaven and so forth could never be dependent upon it.
"Of that," [it is said]. || 628 ||
For it is the very possibility of accomplishment that is considered the "task" (kāryatā) of sacrifices and the like.
There can be no proof for the sky and its flower, which are respectively absolutely established and absolutely unestablished.

He states another reason for the fact that no excellence can be imparted to the *niyoga*: "saṃbhāvyamāna... (in the phrase beginning with "saṃbhāvyamāna"). The meaning is that because the arising of the entity (*bhāva*) is possible through human activity, it is that entity alone which possesses the status of being the effect (*kāryatā*), and not the *niyoga*, since the *niyoga* cannot be accomplished by that [activity]. How [is this so]? He says: "puṃ... (referring to human activity).
182 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 203]

Anticipating the objection that [the object of injunction] is not something to be produced because it is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), [the author] states: "Like space" (*vyoma*). Just as that which is already established is unproduced like space, so too is the intended injunction (*niyoga*) unproduced, being absolutely non-existent, like a flower in the sky. Thus he says: "Like space. (629)
Just as the thought "the sacrifice must be performed" is seen to be distinct from the sacrifice itself.
Even that which is thought "this must be done" is transcended by this [realization]. || 630 ||

Even for a sacrifice (*yāga*) whose success is merely anticipated, there is no status as an "effect" (*kāryatā*); for there is a perception of difference between the sacrifice itself as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the effect as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the effect.

Anticipating the objection that the essential nature of that [effect] belongs only to the mandate (*niyoga*), he says: "It is to be performed. The remainder of the sense is: "The status of being an effect is distinct. (630)
The necessity of performing an action is nothing other than the action itself.
Therefore, this [notion] is not an inherent property of the object, because it arises from the word itself through its excellence.
Now,

even if the status of being an action (*kāryatā*) is not the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the mandate (*niyoga*), nevertheless, since sacrifice and the like— which are of the nature of suffering— are not its nature, the cognition of that [sacrifice] has as its object the mandate to be accomplished by it; in that case, the status of being an action must be sought for the mandate itself, which is of the nature of an action.

Having raised the alternative "or not," he refutes the first [position] with the words "kārya" (as an effect). If it is accepted that the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) of the mandate (*niyoga*) is itself an effect, then—just as in the case of a sacrifice—that status of being an effect belonging to the mandate would be distinct from the mandate itself, because of the designation of difference; and since there would be yet another effect for that [status], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the second [position], the status of being an effect of the mandate would be equivalent to something prohibited; therefore, the status of being an effect must be the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the mandate.

Or, considering that [the property] is merely conceptual because it is connected with the nature of *dharmatva*, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He clarifies the very same reason for why this is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor a property (*dharma*) of the real entity (*vastu*): "From the word" (*śabdāt*). The meaning is that by means of words such as "the sacrifice is to be performed," "it is an effect," or "it is a task," the state of being an effect is separated from the real entity itself. || 631 ||
Therefore, that very thing which is understood as the means for accomplishing the object to be proven [is the logical reason].
Because it is to be accomplished through the Veda, that alone is the "task" (kārya); nothing else exists apart from it.

Now, one might object: "How can the 'task' (kārya), understood from Vedic injunctions such as 'one desiring heaven' as something to be performed because it is the means to attain heaven and so forth, be set aside by reasoning? For reasoning is weaker than the Vedic word. Anticipating this doubt, he states that there is no task other than that [of sacrifice and the like], because there is no proof for the nature of a distinct "niyoga" (impulse) and so forth; rather, the Vedic task is precisely the sacrifice itself, since it is logically possible for it to bear fruit through the mediation of an intermediate *apūrva* (unseen potency), and thus it is the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is no task other than that.

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (hence): thinking that it is difficult to define [the self] either as having the nature of sacrifice and so forth, or as being distinct from them, the word "separately" (pṛthak) was used. || 632 ||
Since the optative suffix and others denote instigation, let it be explained why [the object] is called "that which is to be done" (kārya).
There is no implication by way of being an object; the meaning of the verbal root is considered the object. || 633 ||

The *niyoga* (injunction), which is cognizable through Vedic optatives (*liṅ*) and the like, cannot be refuted even by a hundred arguments; for the optative and other such suffixes do not lack an object, nor is the sacrifice itself their referent, since although the sacrifice is the meaning of the verbal root, it is not the meaning of the suffix. Anticipating this objection, he states [the view] according to the Bhaṭṭa school: "The optative and so forth... Now, since instigation (*preraṇā*) possesses an object, that which expresses it—the optative—...
1. Kha. Since:
[Vol. 1, p.
204] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 183.
He says "no" to the claim that the injunction (niyoga) is implied by the verbal suffix as having the [action] as its object. Regarding the phrase "as its object":
since the instigation (preraṇā) has the action as its object, it does not have the injunction as its object; this is the meaning. || 633 ||
Even instigation would not exist here as something distinct from the making known of what was unknown.
Because of the consequence of stating faults in all actions, and due to the absence of certainty. || 634 ||

Having stated, according to the opinion of the author of the *Vārttika*, that there is no evidence for an injunction (*niyoga*), and desiring to refute the view that instigation (*preraṇā*) is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers in order to state his own position—that it is rather the state of being a means to a desired end—he first refutes the initial alternative by asking whether this instigation is something other than the making known of what was previously unknown, or not. He states the reason why it cannot be something other than the making known of the unknown in the verse beginning with "instigation" (*preraṇā*). In the case of the optative suffix and so forth, just like an injunction, this [instigation] also cannot be denoted as something other than the making known of what was previously unknown. This is the reason.

He says: "All" (*samasta*). The meaning is that [impulsion] does not exist, because it would entail the necessity of stating [impulsion] even when one informs an ignorant person of all those defects already shown regarding the effect—such as being external to the triad beginning with the means (*sādhana*)—and furthermore, because there is no proof for the impulsion you yourself desire. || 634 ||
The intrinsic nature [of words] such as the optative suffix (liṅ) is not [the cause of action], because they merely inform one of the instigation.
Even though there is a difference in their respective forms, [the injunction] is so because of the persistence of the instigation (preraṇā).

Furthermore, is that [instigation] another thing, or is it the very nature of the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth, or some power (śakti), or a specific operation (vyāpāra)? It is not the first [option];
thus he says: "No. The meaning is that since the optative suffixes and so forth are indicators (jñāpaka), whereas the instigation lacks that status, it cannot be their essential nature.

He states another argument [to show] that the nature of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not the instigation (*preraṇā*): "Though there is a mutual difference in form between the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*leṭ*), and so on—such as in 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) and 'one offers' (*juhoti*)—there is no such difference in the instigation; because it is a single entity following through all of them, and because of the distinction between one and many, the nature of the *liṅ* etc. is not the instigation. He says "mutually" (*anyonyam*).
It is stated "likewise" (*tathā*) regarding the point that the nature of the *liṅ* etc. is not the instigation. (Verse 635)
Since power (śakti) is not denotable, its operation is also not admitted.
In the Veda, even the operation [of a word] is not denotative by virtue of its being an instigator (preraka).
He refutes the second [position], that "instigation (*preraṇā*) is the power (*śakti*) of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth," with the words "of the power" (*śakteḥ*).

Those who maintain that theory hold that instigation is what is expressed by the optative suffixes and the like; however, if it were their power, then—given the non-difference between power and the possessor of power—it could not be the expressed meaning, since both would reside in a single locus.

Because denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is impossible, even though there is a distinction [between the power and its locus], it cannot be the denoted object (*vācyatā*), since it is the motivator (*prayojaka*). For the power that serves as the motivator for burning is not itself denoted by the word "burning" (*dahana*); such is the sense that *preraṇā* (the impelling force) is not the power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Regarding the third [alternative] as well—whether the specific operation (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*) belongs to the optative suffixes or to the impeller—the first case is rejected; he says: "And its operation... For the operation of the optative suffixes...

The meaning is as follows: neither vibration (*spanda*) nor effort (*yatna*) can be their cause. First, vibration is impossible because, due to their omnipresence or their being qualities [of a self], they lack corporeality (*mūrtatva*), and thus cannot be followed by vibration. Nor is effort possible, since effort is a quality of a conscious being and cannot exist in those insentient things. Furthermore, there is no other operation (*vyāpārāntara*) for them, because such an operation—defined as "that which is produced by something and produces what is produced by that"—cannot be established in their case. This also applies to a prompter (*preraka*).

Whether it be a person or the Veda [that prompts action], in the first case, because the Veda is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), there would be no prompter therein; consequently, its specific activity would remain unestablished.
Thus, due to the absence of a prompter, the optative suffix (liṅ) and others would become devoid of an object; so he says: "The prompter... (636).
Therefore, by making known the reality as being the means for attaining what is desired, [the scripture acts].
The Veda is the impeller for that which is not already understood; incitement is considered to be the act of causing one to know.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the connection]: Since no other form of instigation is possible than making known what was previously unknown, it follows that the Veda is non-different from that [instigation], and thus it accepts the position that the Veda is the instigator. Therefore... || 637 ||
And thus, its status as a means of valid cognition [is established] by making known the true nature of things.
It cannot exist as an impeller, because it is not perceived through perception or other means of valid cognition. || 638 ||

One might object: "Even though it is established that the Veda is the cause [of knowledge] in the sense of being an instigation (*preraṇā*) that makes known what was previously unknown, how can your position be proven simply on the grounds that the Veda is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of being an instigator? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And so it is" (*tathā ca*). Since perception and the other means of knowledge are not seen to be instigators, their validity consists solely in making known what was previously unknown;
likewise, the validity of the Veda also does not consist in its being an instigator. This is the meaning. (638)
Just as for one who has fulfilled his duty [regarding the injunction] on the basis of the authority of the Veda.
In that same way, the fruit necessarily arises from the performance of the means. || 639 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that even if the *liṅ* suffix and others do not have "commission" (*niyoga*) or "impulsion" (*preraṇā*) as their meaning, how can "being a means to what is desired" (*samīhitasādhanatā*) be their meaning—he says:

"Having been accomplished," etc. Just as in the theory of commission (*niyogavāda*), once the commission has been produced by the performance of the root-meaning, a result necessarily follows from the sentence such as "one who desires heaven," so too, for a sacrifice and the like that have been performed, [the result follows] precisely by the force of that [commission], through the intermediate operation of the *apūrva*.

The rule regarding the fruit [of action]. Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth can be stated as the fact that sacrifice and the like are means to what is desired; this is the sense. || 639 ||
Nor should any suspicion of contradiction be raised regarding the meaning of the injunction, whether it be one way or another.
Because it is Vedic, even with respect to the means, there is no deviation from truth.

Now, if the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is that sacrifice and the like are the means to heaven and the like, then heaven and so forth ought to occur immediately after their performance; for we observe that satisfaction, which is the fruit of eating, follows immediately [after the act].

Since no immediate fruit is seen in this case, it would be impossible for the Vedic statement to have as its purpose the status of being a means to a fruit, and since no other purpose is desired, the sentence such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) would lack authority. To this, he replies: "There is also non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*)."

Just as in the case of an injunction (*niyoga*), which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, one does not suspect the futility or the lack of authority of the sentence even when the immediate result is not perceived, so too in the case of sacrifice and the like—which are the means to that [result]—discrepancy regarding the intended goal does not deserve to be suspected; for in that regard, the status of being a means is knowable solely through the Veda.

Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth is precisely the status of being a means to the result. This remains true even though the status of sacrifice and the like as a means is based on the Veda.

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be no suspicion of non-conformity? he says: "In that which is human" (*nṛtatra*). The meaning is this: although in the world there is suspicion of non-conformity because one observes discrepancies regarding results and so forth in human speech, such suspicion is not appropriate in the case of the Veda; for the Veda, being non-human (*apauruṣeya*), is free from defects. || 640 ||
For even in the world, no sacrifice is ever seen to have an immediate result.
Therefore, the argument "because it is an action" (kriyātvāt) is not a refutation of the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [type of inference]. || 641 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the immediacy of the fruit is inferred from the argument, "The action of sacrifice and so forth has an immediate fruit because it is an action, like the act of massaging"? And if that were so, how could a suspicion of non-correspondence (visaṃvāda) arise when such [immediacy] is not perceived? [Reply: He says, "No. By the word "sacrifice" (yāga), an action is meant. Even though there is immediacy of the fruit in cases such as massaging, not every action is seen in the world to have an immediate fruit; for instance, it is not seen in the case of service and the like. This is the meaning.

Nevertheless, he states what the refutation of the inference is—namely, its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*)—with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that the inference [based on the premise] "because it is an action" (*kriyātvāt*), having observed the nature of action (*kriyātva*) in sacrifices and the like, does not entail a fault, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of service and similar activities. || 641 ||
1 kha. mmādatra | [vol 1, page 206] M
[The Vārtika:
Just as, by its own power, it declares the effect to be untouched by time.
In this way, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth will express even the sacrifice; thus, there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Now, if the sacrifice and so forth—which are the means to heaven and the like—are denoted by the optative suffix and such, does it have a connection with time or not? In the first case, that which is connected to past and other times cannot be performed. In the second case, if there is no contact with time through the word itself, it would be equivalent to a jar or similar objects; if there is no contact with it through the meaning, [the same fault follows].

Since it was stated that [the sacrifice] is non-existent, he says: "By its own capacity. There is indeed an equality between the mandate (*niyoga*) and the sacrifice insofar as both are expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth through their own expressive power (*svaśakti*) as not being touched by time; for it is not the case that the sacrifice is non-existent because of its lack of connection with time. Even when there is no such connection [with time], it is connected with time in its own essential form (*svarūpa*) by way of being the means to a desired end (*iṣṭopāyatva*). However, as for the mandate, even in its own essential form, [it is not connected with time].

The distinction [of the agent] as "the sacrificer" (*yogitā*) is not intended; for a sacrifice qualified by being a means to a desired end cannot be connected with time, since that which is other than time and insentient lacks existence.

Nor is it the case that the mandate (*niyoga*) itself belongs to that [sacrifice], because it is impossible to establish a connection between the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and such a non-worldly entity.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the mandate alone is expressed by the sentence, while the qualified [sacrifice] is the object of the word’s power; for that would result in the opposite [logical] consequence, namely, that there would be no need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The meaning is this: because [the mere fact of being a means] is not undesirable, it is the state of being a desired means that is the object of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; and while this is touched upon by other meanings, it is precisely that [state], in its worldly aspect, which is understood through the intention (*tātparya*) of the sentence. || 642 ||
And in this way, there would be a direct relationship between the probandum and the probans.
There is no mockery of an intervention by the meaning of an excessive optative suffix or the like. (643)

He states another reason for the fact that the status of sacrifice and so forth as a means to the desired end is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers. [The verse begins with] "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). If the status of sacrifice and so forth as a means to the desired end is the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth, then an unmediated relationship between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is established. If, on the other hand, the mandate (*niyoga*) were its meaning, there would be the absurdity of an intervention between the sacrifice and heaven; and that is improper, for when an unmediated relationship exists, a mediated one is not [accepted].
The meaning is that he finds pleasure [in it] out of respect. || 643 ||
When a direct connection does not exist, there is a connection through a succession [of intermediaries], but never otherwise.
If [the object] were to exist, that [cognition] too would not be perceived here in this way, as it is elsewhere. || 644 ||

Anticipating the objection that—just as in the case of "He buys with a ruddy [cow]," where a connection is accepted even though it is mediated by an intervening term—the same might apply to the sentence concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). When a direct connection is untenable, mediation is accepted.

The meaning is that when a direct connection is possible, a mediated one is never accepted; furthermore, such a mediated connection cannot be admitted even in a sentence like "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice]," because it is not perceived there, just as in the case of "he buys with a red [cow]. || 644 ||
In the Vedic scripture, the connection with the purchase is established only by excluding other means.
Aruṇa is seen as a practitioner; he is not indifferent, nor is he in vain.

He elaborates upon the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) with the words "by the Vedic text" (*śrutyā*). In the passage "One purchases [Soma] with a red [cow]," it is understood through the instrumental case-ending that the quality of redness (*aruṇa-guṇa*), even while being connected to the act of purchase, is a means (*sādhana*) only by qualifying the animal; it does not accomplish the purchase of Soma independently of a substance.
Otherwise, the quality would be useless, as that quality alone cannot be a means anywhere. Therefore, how could there be a combination (*samuccaya*)?
1. *Kra.* refers to action (*kriyā*). 2. *Kha* refers to that which is bound (*baddha*).
24 [Vol. 1, page 207]

In the section concerning "substance and quality" (*dravyaguṇavat*), having introduced the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*, it was established that this [principle] does not apply in the same way to sentences such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
The meaning is that it has already been stated that the possibility of an uninterrupted relationship between the two terms exists. || 645 ||
Even though the sacrifice is connected to an action to be performed, it does not produce a fruit for you.
If one were to somehow accomplish the task, it would not exist [in that way]; therefore, it is not a means of accomplishment.

It has been stated that the connection of sacrifice and the like with heaven and the like is not through the *niyoga* (the mandate). Now, even while accepting the connection with the *niyoga*, he states the fault:
"The sacrifice," etc. Even if the sacrifice is connected to the *niyoga*, does it produce that [mandate] devoid of an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), or endowed with one?
Not the first, because an instrument devoid of operation is not admitted; in the second case, there must be either the production of the fruit or another intermediate operation.

[This refers to] the operation (*vyāpāra*). In the first case, if the sacrifice does not produce heaven, it could not in any way accomplish the *niyoga* desired by you; for an instrument devoid of operation is incapable of producing an effect, and no one has ever observed heaven immediately following the sacrifice. Therefore, the meaning is that the sacrifice would be the means (*sādhaka*) for the *niyoga*. || 646 ||
Furthermore, you maintain that his activity regarding the accomplishment of the task is distinct from [the activity of] the mantras.
Therefore, because no fruit arises, there is no connection even with an effect. || 647 ||

Anticipating a second objection, he says: "And not... The meaning is that you do not accept any other operation of the sacrifice and so forth directed toward the accomplishment of the *niyoga* apart from the accomplishment of heaven and the like; otherwise, since heaven and the like would arise from those [sacrifices] directly, the *niyoga* would be redundant. Anticipating the objection that the accomplishment of the *niyoga* might then occur through the medium of the arising of the fruit, he clarifies that this too does not exist.

"It does not bear fruit. For the result is not perceived immediately after that sacrifice or other such act; therefore, even by way of that [result], the sacrifice and so forth do not connect with the *niyoga* as its means of accomplishment—this is the meaning. || 647 ||
Now, if it is argued that [the existence of such a result] must be accepted even though it is not perceived, on the grounds that the scripture is authoritative;
In that case, the production of the fruit will occur for me as well.

He raises an objection: "Even though the production of the fruit is not perceived immediately after the sacrifice and so forth, its occurrence is accepted because of the authority of scriptural statements such as 'one who desires heaven [should sacrifice]'; therefore, it is logical that the sacrifice produces the *niyoga* (the mandate) by means of that [unseen result]. [The author replies: "Now (*atha*). By relying on the authority of the scripture, even for one who maintains that [the Veda teaches] the status of being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatā*), the production of the fruit will occur—even if it is not seen immediately—by the force of that [authority]; thus, the *niyoga* is redundant.
Thus he said: "It is mine. (648)
Since my scripture is the authoritative means of knowledge, the fruit may indeed come about even later.

But previously, it was logical for you [to hold that]; for in its absence, [the means] would not be effective. (649) Showing the distinction in his own position, he establishes the pointlessness of postulating an *niyoga* (an injunction). "Mine" (*mama*)—the meaning is that in the theory of the means to the desired end (*iṣṭopāyatāvāda*), heaven and so forth would exist even at a time remote from the sacrifice and other acts, because of the authority of sentences such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). This is also the case in the theory of *niyoga*.

Anticipating the objection that no distinction can be established because the validity [of both types of injunctions] is equal, he says: "But previously... In the theory of *niyoga* (the mandatory injunction), it is logical that the fruit follows immediately after the sacrifice and so forth, at the very moment the *niyoga* arises; for if heaven and such fruits were absent, a *niyoga* devoid of an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) could not accomplish its purpose. Furthermore, if one were to admit another intermediate operation, the futility of the *niyoga* itself has already been stated. Nor...
1. Sva. *baddho'yam* | 2. Sva. *cānyavyā* | 3. Ka. *’dhakaḥ* || 649 || 4. Ka. *svargādi* | [Vol.
1, page 208] Bāṭakam | Accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 187.
