The meaning is that even one devoid of a practitioner (*sādhaka*) attains success, because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless; furthermore, since the attainment of the fruit results from the sacrifice itself when one relies on the authority of the scripture, the postulation of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*) is useless. || 649 ||
Upon the accomplishment of the task and the attainment of the fruit, there arises the possibility of further fruits.
For you, the effect would occur only once, because there is no difference [in the cause].

Having accepted the rejected view that the fulfillment of the *niyoga* (the mandate) results from the accomplishment of the sacrifice and so forth, and that from that [fulfillment] heaven and other rewards arise, he states the defect [of that view] with the words "kārya" etc.

When the sacrifice and so forth produce the *niyoga*, and that [in turn] produces heaven, then—since the *niyoga* is accomplished by performing [the rite] once and since it is a single entity—the accomplishment of all fruits would occur simultaneously without succession; consequently, there would be no need for the performance of multiple rituals or the repetition of a single one.
The meaning is "in vain. || 650 ||
If it is argued that the fruit [of action] arises through a specific determination due to the connection with its consequences, [we reply: no.
For that very reason, it could not arise from the effect, because [the effect] exists only when that [cause] exists.

He raises an objection, suggesting that although the *niyoga* (the mandate) is identical in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), a distinction in the allocation of results (*phalavyavasthā*) is possible because it differs according to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as sacrifice and the like; thus, the aforementioned refutation does not apply. [The author replies with] the verse beginning "anubandha": Since the distinction of the *niyoga* arises precisely from the distinction of its adjuncts (*anubandha*), the result and its allocation would follow from that;
for when there is a difference in the adjuncts, the *niyoga* exists, whereas otherwise it does not. Therefore, he states that under that view, the *niyoga* is rendered useless. [Verse 611]
And that which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (aupādhika), characterized as the relationship between the probandum and the probans, would be false.
The conventional usage of the Śruti is understood as being solely expressive of the ultimate reality.

He states another fault for one who attempts to differentiate the injunction (*niyoga*) based on the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). [The text says: "And that which is conditioned by adjuncts... When it is said that the conditioned injunction is the means (*sādhana*) and by it heaven and so forth are to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then—just as the redness of a crystal is illusory—the conditioned [injunction] is false, and consequently, heaven and the rest dependent upon it are likewise [false]. Furthermore, for one who maintains that everything is ultimately real, the Vedic discourse consisting of the means and the end would itself be false.
The meaning is "it is finished. || 652 ||
Thus, even in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), such an action is not tenable.
But since there is oneness of self, it is stated specifically how [the distinction] does not exist. || 653 ||

Fearing that [the objection] might arise that even if there is no *niyoga* (injunction) in the *karmakāṇḍa*, it might exist in the *jñānakāṇḍa*, he recounts what has already occurred with the words "Thus" (*evam*). The word "also" (*api*) is intended to indicate the impossibility of a *niyoga* even there. For the sake of ease, he summarizes the matter about to be discussed with the words "But in the case of oneness" (*aikātmye tu*).
He explains, by means of the subsequent passage, the specific reason why a *niyoga* is not tenable in the *jñānakāṇḍa*.
This is the meaning. || 653 ||
First of all, the rule for practice is this: "The Self is to be seen."
Because it is grounded in the meaning of the verbal root, there is no logical possibility for it to refer to a real entity. || 654 ||

If it is argued that because of the scriptural statement "the Self is to be seen," an injunction (*niyoga*) cannot be refuted in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), [the author] refutes the first alternative—namely, that the injunction concerns either the thing itself or the knowledge of it—by stating: "In regard to the realization... This means that even this injunction, "the Self is to be seen," has realization as its object, not the thing itself. He states the reason for this: "Of that... and so forth, in that very same place.
He states another reason: "In the case of a real entity," [verse 654].

Whether the identity [of the self] is already established or not yet established, an injunction is simply not tenable.
There is no independence from human effort regarding either the sky or its flower.

[The author] establishes the impossibility [of injunction]. Regarding the word "established" (*siddha*), he provides an example for the case where, since oneness of self (*aikātmya*) is eternally established, an injunction is impossible: "No" (*na*). The word "injunction" (*vidhi*) connects with what precedes it. Even if oneness of self were unestablished, an injunction would still not apply there; regarding this, he provides an example: "Nor" (*nāpi*). He states the reason for both cases: "by human activity" (*puṃvyāpāra*). Whether [the object] exists or does not exist, [it is not dependent] upon human activity—
The meaning is that because it is appropriate [for both], there is no injunction in either case; for one accepts that [the injunction] applies only to what is suitable for it. || 655 ||
Even if [the object] were seen, there could be no injunction, due to the fault of mutual dependence.
Because the accomplishment of the injunction arises from seeing [the result], and because the seeing [of the result] is accomplished through the injunction. || 656 ||

Having raised the alternative view that even though there is no injunction regarding the object (*vastu*) because it is not something to be accomplished, there is nevertheless an injunction regarding the act of seeing (*darśana*), which has the nature of an action (*bhāvārtha*), he considers the further alternatives—whether it is an injunction regarding that [seeing] alone or regarding it as qualified by Brahman—and refutes the first with the words "There is no injunction. The meaning is that even regarding that [seeing] alone, there is no injunction, because it would then follow that there is an injunction for the cognition of jars and other such things. He then asserts with the word "also" (*api*) that there is likewise no injunction regarding that [seeing] when it is qualified by Brahman.

He states the reason: "mutually" (*anyonya*). He demonstrates that very same fault: "because of seeing" (*darśanāt*). If the vision qualified by Brahman were the object of the injunction, then Brahman must be said to be already known; for if the qualifier is not apprehended, the qualified [object] cannot be seen, and without that, the injunction regarding it cannot be established. Therefore, if Brahman is known, then there is an injunction regarding the knowledge of it, and from that comes the knowledge of it—thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there can be no injunction regarding the knowledge of the qualified [object], nor indeed [can there be].

The sense is that if one accepts injunctions in the Vedāntas, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) because it would have to convey both the nature of reality and the injunction. || 696 ||
Nor can it be established by the Veda alone, as in the case of the sacrificial post and similar things.
Because the oneness of self is established by itself, the object [of comparison], such as the sacrificial post, cannot be that which is to be proven. || 657 ||

Now, just as a worldly object such as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is presented through statements like "one should carve the post" (*yūpaṃ takṣati*) as a subordinate element to an injunction such as "one should bind the animal to the post" (*yūpe paśuṃ badhnāti*), so too Brahman is presented by the statement "Being, Consciousness, etc. (*satyajñānādi*) as a subordinate element to the injunction "Brahman is to be seen" (*brahma draṣṭavyam*). Thus, if the Vedāntas were intent on injunctions, they would not have the status of being a means of knowledge regarding the [ultimate] entity; nor would there be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), because there is an intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*) toward the entity. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca...*).

He states the reason why Brahman is not presented as a subordinate element (śeṣa) of an injunction: "Because of the oneness of self" (aikātmyasya). He states the reason for presenting the sacrificial post (yūpa) and so forth as subordinate to that [injunction]: "Because it is something to be accomplished" (sādhyatvāt). || 617 ||
If the Veda were established, then its perception would likewise be well-established.
And the sentence would be restricted to that alone, and the injunction would then be rendered purposeless. || 658 ||

It has been stated that the Veda does not present Brahman—which is immutable and eternal—as a subordinate element of an injunction; now, he states the establishment of his own position by way of a counter-argument, beginning with the words "And [if it were] established. This means that his own view is that the Veda presents even an established entity as its object of cognition. To the question, "If the aforementioned matter is established solely from a sentence whose purport is an injunction, how is your own position established? he replies with the words "And that which culminates in that. From the sixfold marks, Brahman—

The sense is that since the statement "That thou art" and others do not have injunction as their primary purport, it is rightly said that the intermediate purport (*avāntara-tātparya*) of the Vedāntas lies in the reality itself. He states the conclusion: that if the sentence were concerned with a [mere] thing, then an injunction regarding the knowledge of that would be useless; hence he says, "it would be purposeless. (658)
1 kha. kṣataḥ || 655 || 2 kha. 'diralauki' | [vol 1, page 210] Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 189
Furthermore, there is no impossibility regarding the reality of the statement "all is the Self."
Because the meaning would remain incomplete, an ellipsis (adhyāhṛti) must be supplied for the word.
Anticipating the objection that there is no pointlessness [of the sentence] because a sentence cannot convey a factual reality (*vastu*) without an injunction (*vidhi*), he says: "All...

The meaning is that it is not impossible for a sentence to convey a factual reality apart from an injunction, since a person who has mastered language understands its meaning upon hearing the sentence. If it is argued that even in that case, the word "injunction" must be supplied [to the definition], because we observe that a sentence conveys meaning only when it possesses such an injunction, he says "no."

Regarding the phrase "by which": the meaning is that if, due to a lack of capacity to cognize a real entity (*vastu*), one were to supply an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) for a word expressing an injunction (*vidhi*) because no cognition of a real entity arises from a sentence devoid of injunction, such is not the case; for there is no lack of capacity in a sentence void of injunction to cognize a real entity, since the cognition of that [entity] is observed from a sentence addressed to a qualified person (*adhikārin*). Thus, the ellipsis is not established. || 659 ||
The realization that "the Self is Brahman" does not depend upon an injunction at all.
Because that [realization] arises spontaneously for one who has heard those words. || 660 ||

Furthermore, is the knowledge of Brahman enjoined as verbal (śābda), or as a form of creative contemplation (bhāvanā), or as characterized by direct realization (sākṣātkāra)? Even regarding the first case, one must consider the following alternatives:

is the injunction for the sake of its production, or for the ascertainment of the object of the already produced [knowledge], or for the determination of the sentence-meaning (vākyatātparya), or for the fact that knowledge is a human goal (puruṣārtha), or for the fact that Brahman is not accessible through other means of knowledge (mānāntara), or for the connection between word-meanings (padārthasaṃsarga)? Having thus raised these options, he refutes the first.
"Self," [so it is said]. || 660 ||
The knowledge that "one should sacrifice" does not look toward another injunction.
There would be an infinite regress regarding another injunction, and this is not the case because [the result] resides in the action.

He provides an illustration for the following point: that for one who has studied the Veda, the knowledge that "the Self is Brahman" arises from the sentence itself without depending on an injunction, and thus an injunction is not purposeful in that regard. He says: "one should sacrifice. In the sentence concerning the seeker of heaven (*svargakāma*), the cognition that the sacrifice is a duty does not require another injunction for its own production beyond this very sentence; for if such another were required, then for the sake of knowing the meaning of that [second] injunction as well, yet another injunction would be required, and so on ad infinitum.

Nor is this injunction regarding the necessity of sacrifice (yāga-kāryatā-vidhi) required [to be inferred] because of the absence of a fixed rule (navasthā), since that [injunction] has ritual action as its object; therefore, the knowledge of the necessity of sacrifice arises from the sentence itself, and the same applies to the knowledge of Brahman—this is the meaning. || 661 ||
When the object to be accomplished has been understood, activity toward it is held to be the result.
And since activity depends on the knowledge of the injunction, there is thus a mutual dependence.

Regarding the claim that verbal knowledge of Brahman must be enjoined for its production, he states another defect: "When [the object] is already understood," and so forth. The general rule is that when the meaning of the verbal root—such as a sacrifice—is apprehended, activity toward it is the fruit of the injunction. Anticipating the objection that this might also apply to the knowledge of Brahman, he says:

"And because of [the need for] activity": when Brahman is known, and knowledge qualified by that [Brahman] is apprehended, there is an injunction; and from that injunction comes activity. Thus, since the knowledge of Brahman is the qualifier of the knowledge to be enjoined, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, there can be no injunction regarding that [Brahman], nor could there be an injunction even regarding the vision [of it]. The meaning is that while mutual dependence was stated previously in relation to its *origination* (*utpatti*), here it is stated in relation to its *cognition* (*jñapti*); this is the distinction. || 662 ||
Since awakening has already arisen for me, this sound should not be set in motion, as it would be fruitless.
And when [the object] has not arisen, there is absolutely no possibility of a cause for its manifestation. || 663 ||
Furthermore, does knowledge regarding Brahman arise from verbal testimony or not? In the first case, a person cannot be impelled toward it by an injunction (*vidhi*).
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:

He states that there is an absence of any task to be performed (*kṛtyābhāva*). Regarding the phrase "in this awakening" (*bodhe'smin*): in the second case, a person is all the more not to be impelled by an injunction (*vidhi*).

He says "due to the absence of an object. Regarding the phrase "and when [the object] has not arisen," he expresses the same intensity as was stated by the word "utterly" (*nitarām*). Regarding the phrase "of activity":
since knowledge is the cause of activity, in its absence there is no activity; for even an injunction does not impel one to act without knowledge—this is the meaning. || 663 ||
Then, for the sake of achieving certainty, one is set in motion even when [the result] has already arisen.
Tell me, is that certainty of yours derived from verbal testimony or from something else? (664)

He adopts the second [position] with the words "Now" (*atha*), thinking: "Even when knowledge of Brahman has arisen from the word, a person is impelled toward it by an injunction for the sake of ascertaining the object. He says "That" (*sa*) to state that it must be declared whether the fruit of knowledge—ascertainment—arises for you from the word alone or from another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). || 664 ||
If it is sound, then this very same refutation as before follows.
And if another [object] were desired, it would follow that there is dependence. || 665 ||

Therein, having restated the first [position], he recalls the futility of the injunction: "From the word" (*śabdāt*). He refutes the second [position] with the words "In the other" (*anyasmin*): [the objection being that] if another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) were required to produce certainty, the Veda would become dependent upon it, just like human speech; and thus its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), which is based on its independence, would be lost. || 669 ||
Alternatively, a mandatory injunction (vidhi) is intended here for the purpose of precluding what is not meant to be praised.
For when it is said, "This is the object to be known," there arises from that [statement] the cognition of what was intended to be expressed. (666)

He refutes the third [position], which holds that the purport (*tātparya*) of a sentence lies in the object (*vastu*), while the injunction (*vidhi*) resides in the knowledge produced by it, with the words "not intended" (*avivakṣita*). Even if one accepts an injunction regarding knowledge, he asks: how can there be an understanding of the sentence’s purport toward the object? To this he replies: "This [object]... When the necessity of performing the act of knowing is stated in the sense that "this object is to be known," an understanding of the sentence’s purport toward the object arises; therefore...
The meaning is that in the case of verbal cognition, an injunction exists for the sake of establishing its intended purport. || 666 ||
It is not so by way of a general rule, because of words [used] in both common worldly usage and the Veda.
The state of being restricted to a specific object does not arise from itself, nor from an injunction.

He refutes the claim that a word possesses referential intent (*arthaparatva*) by the force of an injunction (*vidhi*) with the words "Not so. He states that this does not apply either to the word (*pada*) or to the sentence (*vākya*). Regarding the first alternative, he says: "By way of a general rule" (*utsargataḥ*). The meaning is that, in the absence of a subverting factor, the natural tendency of a word alone to have as its object a related meaning is not produced by an injunction. || 667 ||
Furthermore, since the meaning of a sentence is understood to be no different in both worldly and Vedic sentences, an injunction is therefore not intended [as the primary meaning]. || 668 ||

He addresses the second [objection] by means of the logic of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the section on mantras: "And it is not distinguished" (*aviśiṣṭaśca*). The meaning is that, just as every word by its very nature has as its object that which is already connected [with others], so too every sentence, by its own nature, is directed toward a qualified meaning; therefore, its purport does not arise from an injunction. || 668 ||
Furthermore, even when there is identity with that which has a visible purpose, as in the case of ritual actions, it does not differ.
Therefore, since the study of the Vedas is already enjoined, an injunction for this [study] here would be purposeless.

Furthermore, the fact that the injunction for Vedic study has a perceptible fruit is equal in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) as it is in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*); and thus, from that [injunction], the Veda— [Vol. 1, p. 212] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 191. He says "api" (even/also) [in verse 669]: since it is possible for the *trayi* (the three Vedas) to have as its ultimate purpose the knowledge of Brahman, an injunction regarding that knowledge is not required; for even without such an injunction, the Vedāntas possess a natural intent toward their own meaning by virtue of the injunction to study them.
When one rule is intended to be superseded by another rule, the entire meaning [of the former] is not intended to be expressed.
Therefore, by the very same reasoning previously stated, no ritual injunction can be postulated from that.

Fearing that the previously stated principle— that the Veda’s inherent orientation toward its own meaning follows from the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*)— would be abandoned, he rejects that acceptance [of the opponent's view] by saying "of the injunction" (*vidheḥ*). Whether the injunction for study has its own purpose as its end follows from another injunction or from itself...

In the first case, because there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the purport (*tātparya*) of the injunction to study would not be established, and the mere recitation of the *svādhyāya* would not be directed toward its own meaning. In the second case, let the Veda itself possess intrinsic purport; the injunction to study would then be redundant. Therefore, by the logic stated in such passages as "thus, by way of general rule," since the fact that all words are directed toward their meanings is established, there is no need to postulate an injunction for the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of [establishing] purport. This is the meaning. || 670 ||
It is held that for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life, an injunction regarding knowledge is required.
Because the fruit is dependent upon an injunction, otherwise it would have indifference as its result. (671)

He formulates the fourth [point]: "It is considered [to be so]. Since the fruit [of an action] in sacrifices and the like is dependent upon an injunction (*vidhi*), and since it is accepted that the knowledge of Brahman also possesses a fruit, the meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), there must be an injunction regarding that [knowledge]; otherwise, if that were not accepted, its fruit would not be intended. || 671 ||
Apart from the pervasion of the object of knowledge, there is no other fruit than consciousness itself.
Since it is accepted that [the self] is not like karma, there is no need to postulate a rule for its sake.

Is the fruit of knowledge the ascertainment of the object or something else? It is not the first, because of the defects already stated regarding the injunction for the sake of ascertainment; nor is it the second, as he says: "In the knowable... Furthermore, is the other fruit [of knowledge] located in the knowable or in the knower? It is not the first, because—just as the fruit of an action resides in the agent—the fruit of knowledge must likewise reside in the knower. Therefore, he says that one cannot postulate an injunction for the sake of a fruit of knowledge residing in the knowable.
As in the case of karma. || 672 ||
If the fruit is obtained from the mother even then, what is the use of a ritual here?
Because that [cognition] is established even without a positive injunction in cases such as the cognizer, the means of cognition, and the object of cognition. (673)

Having restated the second [position], he states the futility of the injunction: "Even when... (yadāpi). The meaning is that even without that [injunction], the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), which is the fruit of knowledge, is always established as the means of realization (*sādhaka*) for the subject (*mātṛ*). Anticipating the objection that the injunction regarding knowledge is for the sake of connecting the fruit—which resides only in the subject—with the object of cognition (*meyādi*) and so forth, he says: "In the subject" (*mātṛ*). Just as the fruit of the means of knowledge (*māna*), namely consciousness (*saṃvedana*), exists without an injunction as the means of realization for the subject.

In the same way, it shines forth even in the case of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the agent, and the action; since that [consciousness] is established by itself even without them, the postulation of an additional category [such as "existence"] is useless—this is the meaning. || 673 ||
Moreover, because it lacks a purposeful effect, it would be a redundant restatement of what is already established.
Nor would it be a valid means of knowledge, because of its connection with another means of knowledge.

He introduces the fifth [point] with the words "Now, moreover" (*athāpi*). The meaning is that even if the fourfold method previously described is impossible, there will still be a method by another way. For, apart from an injunction (*niyoga*), a statement concerning an already existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) would merely be a restatement (*anuvādaka*) and could not function as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
192 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Relation— ] vol. 1, page 213.

The interpretation: How is it that a statement regarding an established fact (*siddhārtha*) is merely repetitive? To this he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Since an object that is an existing reality (*bhūtārtha*), untouched by what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), is not fit to be an object of knowledge other than scripture (*āgama*), a statement expressing that [reality] would be repetitive; such is the meaning. || 674 ||
But if the injunctive meaning is accepted, this [scripture] attains the status of a valid means of knowledge independently.
It is not non-existent because of its intermediate state, just like the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. || 675 ||

How, then, can a statement expressing a fact (bhūtavācin) possess authority once the status of being a mere restatement (anuvādakatā) has been set aside? To this he says: "In an injunction" (vidhau). Since there is no other means of knowledge for the mandate (niyoga)—which is the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth—if that [mandate] were accepted as a subordinate element (śeṣatva) within a sentence whose content is an established fact (siddhārtha), then even though that established fact is by its very nature fit for other means of knowledge, it would become unfit for them due to its contact with the mandate. Therefore, for that purpose, the statement [beginning with] "one who desires heaven" (svargakāmā)—

Therefore, the meaning is that since Brahman is not amenable to other means of knowledge, the scriptural statement is independent of other measures, and thus there is an injunction for the knowledge of it. || 675 ||
If an entity were capable of occupying another location, it would remain so even when a positive injunction is present.
Now, even in the absence of an injunction, that [object] is such as to be fit for the application of the suffix -man.

Having raised the dilemma as to whether Brahman, in its true nature, is capable of being known through other means of knowledge or not, he refutes the first alternative by stating "vastu" (the thing).

Since it is impossible to alter a real entity by means of an injunction (*vidhi*), even in the case of an injunction, a statement concerning a real entity would lack authority as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, the injunction must have some other purpose. Having restated the second alternative, he refutes it on the grounds of the injunction's futility, beginning with "atha. And thus:
Even a statement that expresses a thing untouched by injunction is an independent means of valid cognition; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 676 ||
Is the status of the sentence as a restatement (anuvāda) due to the fact that its object is already established, or for some other reason?
In that case, even if the former [meaning] were established, it would not be a mere restatement (anuvāda). || 677 ||

As for the claim that a statement whose object is already established is merely repetitive (anuvādaka), he offers an analysis to refute it. The meaning of the alternative [presented by the question] "What [is it]? is as follows: Is the repetitiveness of a sentence that functions to convey knowledge of an existing object due to that object being known through another means of valid cognition? Between those two options, he states regarding the first alternative:
even for a sentence that conveys knowledge of an existing object, there is no repetitiveness. This is expressed in the verse beginning with "Therein" (tatra). || 677 ||
It makes known an established object that has not been apprehended by any other means of knowledge.
Why would pride not be indifferent [to the goal], and why would the human purpose not exist by its own nature? (678)

He demonstrates the impossibility of the statement of one who speaks the truth (*sad-arthavādin*) being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) by saying "by another means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*). The meaning is that a statement which makes known an existent reality untouched by any means of knowledge other than scripture (*āgama*) must indeed be an independent authority (*anapekṣa-māna*), just like perception (*adhyakṣa*) and so forth. If it is argued that a sentence making known a pure, established fact is not a valid means of knowledge—because, as in the case of "The earth consists of seven islands," there is no human goal (*puruṣārtha*) arising from the cognition of an already established thing—he says: "and the human goal."

The meaning is that because the inward-facing reality (pratyagvastu) is unsurpassed bliss, it constitutes the supreme human goal; therefore, the scriptural statement concerning it is not invalid. || 678 ||
An object that is the domain of a cognition as a male being requires another means of valid cognition.
Because the person (puruṣa) does not exist here [in this world], the Vedic [tradition] is not established even though it exists.

Anticipating the objection that the Vedāntas are merely restatements (anuvāda) because they consist of sentences whose objects are already established—just like a sentence stating the existence of fruits on a riverbank—one says: "puṃbuddhi" (human intellect). Since the subject sentence [of the Vedānta] is of human origin, its meaning is accessible to the intellect; and because it is capable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge, it depends upon them. The point is that the capacity to convey its own meaning through dependence on another means of knowledge is the limiting condition (upādhi). [The proof of this]—
1. ‘Śeṣa’; 2. kha. ‘Devā’. [Vol.
1, page 214] [Kārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 193.

He refutes pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "because of non-existence" (*abhāvāt*). The meaning is that since there is no author for the Veda, which is not of human origin, the Vedic object—though established—is not accessible to other means of knowledge; therefore, the Vedantas do not possess the quality of making their own meaning known by depending upon such [other means]. || 679 ||
Nor is another means of knowledge suspected anywhere merely on account of [the other's] being established.
For the dependence of that which is being doubted is equal to that of pride itself. || 680 ||

If it is argued that Brahman is accessible through another means of knowledge because it is an established entity (*siddha*), like a pot—thus implying that the probans (*sādhana*) is over-pervasive (*upādhi*) due to this inference—the author says "no" (*na*). For, in the case of a pot or similar objects, another means of knowledge does not apply merely because they are established entities; rather, insentience (*jaḍatva*) is the determining factor there.

Furthermore, even under the view of equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*), there is no lack of pervasion by the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of an effect (*kārya*), since it will be stated later that another means of knowledge does indeed apply there as well.

This is the intended meaning. Although the entry of another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) into Brahman is not established by any other proof, nevertheless, it is suspected; for suspicion is unrestrained, and thus the pervasion of the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*) is doubtful. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of that which is being suspected. Just as a word, regarding its own object, requires the dependence on a mind that suspects [other means], so too does that [object] equally require dependence on the word; and thus, [there is dependence] on another means of knowledge that is being suspected.

The meaning is: why is it that sound is not invalid in relation to perception, while that very [perception] is invalid in relation to sound? For a perceived [object], even if suspected, is stronger than a mere suspicion regarding sound. || 680 ||
Nor is there any dependence for a cognition, because it possesses the nature of being a means of valid knowledge.
For that which awakens what has not yet been understood within is called "knowledge" (māna). || 681 ||

Furthermore, is the Vedic statement, which has an established meaning, authoritative with respect to its own sense or not? In the first case, there would be a loss of its independence (sāpekṣatākṣati), because for that very reason of being authoritative, it lacks such dependence [on other means] in any instance;

thus he says: "Not so" (na ca). Nor is the second [alternative] correct, because it is impossible for a statement that makes known what was previously unknown to be non-authoritative; thus he says: "By another means of knowledge" (māntara). || 681 ||
If a means of knowledge were to make known its object without depending on another means of knowledge, [then there would be no infinite regress].
At that time, it would be nothing but the means of knowledge; there is no other characteristic of a means of knowledge than this.

If it is argued that [the scripture] should not be considered a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even though it makes known what was previously unknown, he says "no," beginning with the words *mānāntara*. The meaning is that the aforementioned statement is indeed a means of valid knowledge, because it possesses the defining characteristics of one. || 682 ||
Now, that measurement which depends on another measurement is what makes the magnitude known.
Nevertheless, because two [factors] are involved in a single act of application, there is likewise independence from anything else.

Having refuted the claim that a sentence which conveys the knowledge of a real object (*sad-artha*) is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), [the author] restates the second position: that a sentence which conveys an object already known through another means of valid cognition (*māna*) is repetitive because it makes known what has already been measured by that [other means]. This is introduced with the word "Now" (*atha*). Since it has already been stated and will be further explained that no other means of valid cognition is possible regarding Brahman, a sentence cannot in any way be a conveyor of knowledge regarding Brahman as something already measured by another means of valid cognition.

He offers a rebuttal [to the objection] by stating: "Of the two," [verse 683]. Even in the case of a single act of cognizing an object, since both the word and its other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) operate toward that same objective, the word does not depend on another means of knowledge for the cognition of its own referent; for there is no mutual dependence between perception and inference when they are directed toward fire.
25. 1. Kha suspects. 2. Kha: *kṣaṃ* as the measure. 3. Kha: *medānavoṃ*. [Vol. 1, page 215]
194 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:
Now, because the subsequent [cognition] apprehends nothing not already apprehended, it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*).
But because of the existence of that [subsequent cognition], let the validity of the preceding cognition be established. (684)

Unable to tolerate the simultaneous occurrence of two [cognitions] as a single operation, he suspects [an objection], beginning with "Now" (*atha*). If it is argued that because there is no object not yet known, the subsequent word lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how can another means of knowledge operating upon that same object also be a *pramāṇa*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the existence of that" (*tatsadbhāvāt*). Since it is difficult to ascertain whether a prior cognition has an already-known object when it is preceded by a future word, [the object remains] unknown.
The meaning is that its status as a means of valid cognition is appropriate because of its existence. || 684 ||
Either the establishment of that which is to be known would come from itself, or else from something other.
Or, tell me: how is the state of being known established either intrinsically or otherwise? (685)

He offers an alternative analysis in order to state that, according to your own view, this distinction cannot be established because both "known-ness" (*jñātatva*) and "unknown-ness" (*ajñātatva*) are impossible to prove. He says: "The knower," etc. The meaning of the alternative analysis is as follows: prior to the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how is the unknown-ness of the object established—is it through a means of knowledge, or through eternal consciousness, or by virtue of self-luminosity? Does that which establishes known-ness itself establish the unknown-ness existing prior to it? What is there to say in this matter?

If it is argued that [this is established] by means of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), he says in response: "And because of the state of being known" (*jñātatā*). For even the proof of that [state of being known] is not easily understood, since, as before, conceptual constructions would apply; this is the meaning. || 685 ||
Because the state of being unknown is established prior [to the cognition itself], there is no risk of over-extension (ativyāpti).
And therefore, there is no establishment of the unknown through inference anywhere.

He refutes the proof of "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) in all three ways, beginning with the words "of unknownness. First, its proof does not arise from a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding either the Self or the non-Self, because that [means of knowledge] would have to operate only after it is already established; for it is accepted that a means of knowledge operates upon an object that is already established as unknown.

Therefore, its proof cannot come even from eternal experience (*nityānubhava*), since you do not admit this—otherwise, that [experience] would fall into the status of being merely imagined (*kalpita*).
The meaning is that because it has been stated thus, its establishment cannot occur through itself, as neither of us accepts that. || 686 ||
If [the object] were unknown like a jar or other such things, it would be capable of being pervaded by human [cognition].
then that form would be real, yet it would also be eternally unknown. || 687 ||

He states another argument for the fact that [the Self] is not established by means of knowledge (*māna*). He says "by means of knowledge" (*māna*): if that [Self] were fit to be made an object by a means of knowledge, then, like a jar, it would not be something to be set aside by that means of knowledge; and thus the true nature of the thing would remain unknown even after [knowledge], just as it was before. This is the meaning.
By this, the proof of the "knownness" (*jñātatva*) of the object is also refuted.
In the same way, this [process] as previously described applies to doubt and false cognition.
Therefore, the entire system of conventional discourse cannot be established unless logic is stated. || 688 ||

Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] might be established as unknown, like doubt and so forth, he extends the argument with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). For doubt and the like are not established by the witness (*sākṣin*) either through itself or by its own nature, because such a position is not admitted; and if they were objects of knowledge (*meyatva*), it would follow that they too could not be removed by a means of valid cognition (*māna*). If it is argued: "Let it be that ignorance and the like do not cease like a jar due to being objects of knowledge," he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*) to refute this. [The cessation occurs] through the worldly activity brought about by right knowledge (*samyagdhī*).
The meaning is that it is not possible [for such a state] to exist when objects such as ignorance and so forth are fluctuating. || 688 ||
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, Page 216] [Commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri:
Even though there is no difference in their being unknown, if the status of being a means of knowledge (*māna*) belongs to the various instruments of cognition;
Since that which is known is other than that which is unknown, why should there not be validity in that case? (689)

He raises the following objection: although there is no difference in the object’s state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) prior to and after the operation of the means of knowledge (*māna*), the status of the means of knowledge as a valid means (*mānatva*) remains uncontradicted; thus, the conventional usage of "means" and "object" (*mānameyavyavahāra*) is established precisely through the cessation of that state of being unknown. [The author replies: "If it is argued that... regarding the phrase *ajñātatva*... Since the form qualified by "knownness" (*jñātatva*) is a different entity from the form qualified by "unknownness," if a means of knowledge, even while failing to produce any further excellence (*atiśaya*) upon an object already unknown, were to attain the status of a valid means, then—[the argument continues]—it would follow that the means of knowledge...

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "of that which is already known" (jñātasya), [arguing]: "Why should there not be validity for a word even when it does not produce an excellence [in the object] once it has been known? Nor is it impossible for that which does not impart a distinction to possess validity, since this is established just as in the case of a means of knowledge [that apprehends] what was previously unknown. || 689 ||
If it is maintained that there is dependence because of the occurrence of multiple factors directed toward a single object;
And thus, it follows that all means of valid cognition would be dependent upon something else. || 690 ||

He raises an objection regarding the validity of verbal testimony when its object is already known through another means of knowledge. [The verse] says "ekārtha" (having the same object). He states that, like verbal testimony, other means of knowledge would also result in being dependent [on something else]. [The commentary] says "tathāca" (and so it is). || 690 ||
Even with respect to a single existence, all the sense organs possess the status of valid means of cognition.
In the case of a substance, however, the same lack of validity would consequently apply to both the sense of touch and the eye. (691)

Anticipating the objection—"If they do not have a single object, how can there be mutual dependence?"—and considering that their having a single object is intended by means of the word [in the definition] which has an established meaning, he states that the eye and the other senses have a single object: "In one... He states another over-extension: that because the skin and the other senses have a single substance as their object, they would possess mutual dependence just like sound: "In a substance... He states the result of this mutual dependence: "The consequence..."

The meaning is this: just as the eyes and other sense organs do not lack authority due to their dependence on one another even when they share a single object, so too, even if there is an entry of other means of knowledge regarding Brahman, the Word (Śabda) does not lack authority due to such dependence. || 691 ||
In the case of a legal injunction and even in the consumption of myrobalan and other such substances.
Because other means of cognition would be impossible, it would follow that [the Veda] is independent [of other means]. || 692 ||

The argument that a sentence resting upon Brahman is not an independent means of knowledge because Brahman is already established has been refuted. As for the claim that a sentence concerning *niyoga* (an injunction) is an independent means of knowledge because *niyoga* is incapable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), we must consider the following alternative: is its incapacity to be known through other means due to its very nature as *niyoga*, or is it due to its being a Vedic *niyoga*? Regarding the first alternative, he states the flaw: "In the case of *niyoga*... [and so on, regarding] *harītakī* and the like.

The construction is as follows: regarding the act of eating, there is a worldly injunction; and because it is an injunction, since no other means of knowledge is possible therein, the consequence would be that it is independent [of other means of knowledge]. And thus, the implication is that even a human-authored sentence concerning that subject would be an independent authority. || 692 ||
This is not a fault, for the cognition of application is preceded by the knowledge of the person.
Therefore, there is dependence [on other means of knowledge] regarding what exists in the world; however, in the case of the Veda, the reverse would be true.
Introducing the second [point], he raises the objection that human speech is not independent by saying, "Not this.

For a speaker, having understood the relationship between the end and the means—designated as *viniyoga*—composes a sentence such as, "One desiring health should eat the yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*).
Therefore, in a worldly sentence, there exists for the listener a relationship between the end and the means in the form of *viniyoga*, which is the object of the *niyoga* being understood.

Therefore, since that [verbal cognition] is preceded by the knowledge of the speaker, it possesses a different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) as its antecedent; for the worldly injunction has as its object a relationship established by other means of valid cognition.
*Sureśvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikam*, [Saṃbandha-vārtika], Vol. 1, p. 217.196.

An explanatory sentence (*arthavākya*) regarding that [injunction] certainly requires another means of knowledge (*mānāntarāpekṣā*). However, in the case of the Veda, because the injunction (*niyoga*) has as its object a relationship that is not within the scope of such other means, the explanatory sentence concerning it does not depend on another means of knowledge. Thus, the meaning is that the independence [of the Veda] is established by the fact that the Vedic injunction itself is independent. || 693 ||
This being the case, the word is not independent, because it depends upon its effect.
For it is because [the Veda] is preceded by human cognition that its dependence [on other means of knowledge] is asserted. || 694 ||

He refutes [the objection] by abandoning his own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), saying "it is not so. For if a sentence whose meaning is a worldly injunction (*laukikaniyoga*)—which has as its object an application (*viniyoga*) cognizable through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*)—were dependent, then there would be a contradiction of the initial thesis: that a word has independence because its object is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), yet it is dependent because its object is an already established fact (*siddhārtha*). Furthermore, since dependence is stated to have the cause of being preceded by human cognition, in the case of the Vedāntas, because they are not preceded by that [human cognition], there is no dependence even with respect to their objects, which are established facts (*bhūtārtha*).
The meaning is "dependence. || 694 ||
It is not so, because the Veda is based on injunction; therefore, it possesses independence.
And in the world, there would be dependence [on other factors] because the primary focus is on application. || 695 ||

Unable to tolerate the loss of his own thesis, the proponent of *niyoga* (the injunction) says: "It is not so. Because in the Veda the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such forms have *niyoga* as their object, and because that *niyoga* does not depend on any other means of knowledge (*māna*), its independence is logical. However, in the world, in human utterances, the optative suffix and others have *viniyoga* (application) as their object, and since that is capable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge, there is dependence. Therefore, in both the world and the Veda, it is precisely the fact that the object is capable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge [that constitutes the difference].
The meaning is that it is the cause of dependence. || 695 ||
There is no such identity between word and meaning in both worldly and Vedic usage.
Then it is impossible to state any distinction between those two. || 696 ||

He provides a resolution, stating that the claim that Vedic *liṅ* and other suffixes have *niyoga* (an injunction) as their object, whereas worldly ones have *viniyoga* (application), contradicts the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa*. He says, "Not so. The meaning of this is as follows: It is established in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras*] that "because there is no difference in usage and injunction, there is unity of meaning due to non-distinction" (*Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* 1.3.27). Are the words that are worldly the very same as those that are Vedic? [The answer is yes.]

When there arises the doubt as to whether the meanings of these [words] are the same or different, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because of the difference in designation—namely, "worldly" (*laukika*) and "Vedic" (*vaidika*)—there is a difference in word-meaning in both cases.

However, since the difference in designation between the world and the Veda is caused by dependence and independence [respectively], and since a word whose capacity is already known in the world is what conveys meaning even in the Veda, there is identity of word and meaning in both. This being so, the injunctions for usage are possible.

Otherwise, due to the difference in words, a single meaning would not be cognized; nor do we perceive any distinction between these two cases. Therefore, their identity is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus, since the identity of word and meaning is established in both worldly and Vedic usage, it is impossible to assert any difference between them in the manner described above. || 696 ||
If the attainment of its own nature is established, whether from itself or from another.
Because it is not useful for its own nature, there is no dependence upon a means of valid cognition.

Having refuted the claim that "because the effect is incapable of being apprehended by other means of knowledge (*māna*), its [Vedic] statement is independent (*anapekṣa*)," it is established that it is dependent (*sāpekṣa*). In this regard, one considers the options: whether the establishment of existence is achieved intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*), or whether it is such a cognition itself; of these, he adopts the first [option], beginning with the words "svarūpa... (the essential nature). First of all, a means of knowledge is not employed for the sake of the existence (*sattā*) of an already existing thing, because its existence has already been obtained; nor is it for the sake of making it known, since [in that case] it is the word alone [that performs the function].
In that case, since it is accepted as being a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is unnecessary; thus he says: "In its own nature" (*svarūpe*). || 697 ||
[Vol.
1, Page 218] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri:
"Now, is this [self] manifested, or is it established by itself, or perhaps by something else?"
For that which has already been manifested, further observation within the self is fruitless.

It resorts to a second [reason]: "because it is already manifested. First of all, there is no dependence on another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) for the sake of manifesting again what has already been manifested, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is there any other result (*phala*) to be accomplished by another means of knowledge; therefore, since there is no result, he says that dependence on such a means is not logical even for that which is already manifested. || 698 ||
Therefore, one might suppose that [the object] is established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Since no other means of knowledge is mentioned, there is no possibility of another means of knowledge existing.

He concludes by stating that the claim "an established fact is dependent" is difficult to maintain: "Therefore... If even a Vedic statement whose object is an established fact were independent, then of what could there be dependence? To this he replies: "In the case of human [speech]... Since the possibility of other means of knowledge exists regarding the meaning of a human sentence, and since a sentence is composed for the purpose of communicating that known object to others, therefore, in the case of speech composed by humans, it is dependent upon those [other means of knowledge].
This is the meaning. || 699 ||
It is further stated that there is no connection between word-meanings without an action.
In that case, let action alone be depended upon; for what is not accomplished without an injunction? (700)

Having rejected the position that there is an injunction regarding the knowledge of Brahman because Brahman is incapable of being an object of other means of knowledge, he sets forth the sixth [position] with the words "an action" (*kriyām*).

The sense is that if an action is accepted for the purpose of connecting the meanings of words, then an injunction concerning that [action] would also emerge; thus, the establishment of an injunction for comprehension (*prati-patti-vidhi*) follows. If it is argued that without an action there is no connection between word-meanings, then that [action] must be required as the motivator (*prayojaka*) thereof.

He accepts [the objection] as a constant [position]. Regarding the word "action" (*kriyā*): it clarifies that even for an injunction of performance (*pratipatti-vidhi*), dependence upon an action is indeed precluded by the suffix *-kāra*.
[The question is: "Is it not so? || 700 ||
And even though an action is required [as a correlate], it is not just any action whatsoever that is required;
rather, because of its suitability, such an action as "beginning" (ādi) certainly exists for this [word] in the Veda. (701)

He raises an objection: "If it is argued that even in the absence of an injunction for practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*), action is accepted as the cause of conjunction [with Brahman], then that very action should be accepted as the object of injunction;
for it is not that action alone is required, since requirement is determined by factors such as compatibility (*yogyatā*) and so forth. [The author replies: "And as for action...

If a compatible action is required, then such an action exists in the *Tattvamasi* and other scriptural passages in the form of "I am That" (*asmi*) and so on; therefore, it does not exist [as something distinct] in the Vedāntas.
"Let it be considered," he said. "In that case," [he replied]. || 701 ||
Since this root *ad* is intransitive, no object exists for it at present.
Furthermore, there can be no production of what has not previously existed, because the self is eternal. (702)

If it is argued that even that [act of knowing] must be enjoined, because the fruit depends upon an enjoined action, we ask: what is that fruit? Is it an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the object (*karman*), or is it the becoming of what was not previously so (*abhūtabhavana*), or is it the communication of the union between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman? It is not the first, because this act of knowing has no object (*akarmaka*); since there is no object, an excellence residing therein is impossible. Thus he says: "Because it is without an object" (*akarmakatvāt*). Indeed, there is no object for this knowledge.

The meaning is that, therefore, no excellence residing in that [jīva] is possible. He refutes the second view—that the fruit of the enjoined action is the manifestation of the jīva, who is non-existent in the form of Brahman, as being in that form—by stating "abhūt" (it has become). This is because, according to such scriptural texts as "Being indeed Brahman," the self exists as the very nature of Brahman.

[Śureśvarācārya] states the reason for its constant existence: "because it is eternal" (*nityatvāt*). The first *ca* (and) is used for conjunction; the second— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full sentence would likely conclude by explaining that the second *ca* serves to exclude other possibilities.]
In the act of holding. || 702 ||
Because it is an awareness of a self that is not mixed with others, there is no cognition of association from that [awareness].
"Because of the connection with the word 'Self' (ātman), existence is not expressed as being [the essence] of that which exists. (703)

He refutes the third [view] with the words "asaṃsṛṣṭā" (unconnected). The meaning is that because the sentence has as its purport a single flavor (*ekarasa*), there can be no cognition of a connection between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman due to the force of the enjoined action of "becoming" (*bhū*) and so forth. [Objection: By the sentence "Being alone, my dear... (*sad eva somyedam...*), Brahman is spoken of as the universal (*sattā-sāmānya*); and since that is without distinction (*nirviśeṣa*), it is not a universal. Therefore, the action of "becoming" and so forth is enjoined for the sake of a connection with the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of such a Brahman. [Response: ...this is the intention.

He said: "It is thus. The Self (ātman) is devoid of both universals (sāmānya) and particulars (viśeṣa), for otherwise it would follow that it is not the Self, since being a universal-particular is pervaded by that [nature of being the Self].
Therefore, because of its connection with that Being which is Brahman—by virtue of which it is called "the Self"—that [Brahman] too is devoid of both universals and particulars.
Consequently, existence (sattā), which is a universal, is not spoken of as "Being is Being" and so forth. And thus, there is no [universal] in Brahman, which is the Universal.
The meaning is that an injunction (vidhi) serves the purpose of [establishing] a specific connection. || 703 ||
Therefore, since the object is not within the range of words and so forth, it is [known] through the recourse to indication (lakṣaṇā) in the scripture.
By words such as "sat" (being) and so forth, the Self is directly presented to us. || 704 ||

One might raise the objection: "If the words 'Being' (sat) and so forth, situated within the sentence, do not denote both the universal and the particular, then what would they denote? Anticipating this, he says: "Sound, etc. But how could these words of the Śruti possibly succeed in making known the Self—which is devoid of universal and particular—as something immediate to us, given that in the absence of genus and the like, it cannot be a denotable object? To this, he replies:
"Therefore, the characteristic" (ato lakṣaṇeti). The word "therefore" (ataḥ) has the sense of reflecting upon [the subject's] lack of fitness. || 704 ||
Even when existence is defined as the fitness for being an object of cognition, and that [fitness] is indeed perceived;
Even then, the scripture's orientation toward the actual object is not impaired. || 705 ||

Having established that existence (*sattva*) consists in the essential nature of the object, it was stated that the Vedāntas possess independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*) with respect to Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). Now, adopting a bold position (*prauḍhivāda*), he says: "Even when... [meaning] even if one accepts that existence is the fitness for being an object of knowledge (*mānayogyatva*) and that this alone is what is to be known through the Vedāntas, their independent authority is still logically established. He asks: "When existence is the fitness for being an object of knowledge and is what is to be known through the Vedāntas, how can they have as their purport the thing-in-itself (*vastu-paratā*)?"

Anticipating this objection, he considers the alternative—whether the other means of knowledge (mānāntara) exists outside the object of knowledge (meyāt)—and refutes the first position with the words "Even then" (tadāpi).

When the other means of knowledge exists outside the object of knowledge, then, since fitness (yogyatva) is an essential nature of the thing itself, the fact that the Vedāntas have the aforementioned reality as their purport is established; for they do not depend on another means of knowledge to impart the meaning already stated, because they are themselves capable of doing so. However, that [other means of knowledge] serves merely as an incidental indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of that fitness.
This is the meaning. || 705 ||
Even without [explicit] connection, a sentence brings its meaning to light.
Just as the word of a trustworthy person in this world, it never abandons its authoritative status.

He states that even in the second case, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is indeed established: "by another means of knowledge" (*māntareṇa*). This refers to the Vedānta statement as a means of knowledge distinct from others.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 199.

It was asked how [the Veda], even when making known an object not previously known (*aprāpta*), does not lose its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To that, he states an illustration: "The world," etc. The meaning is:
just as in common worldly experience a statement from the *Āgama* (scripture) is a means of valid knowledge even while making known an already cognized object, so too is this [Veda]. || 706 ||
In the case of the statement, "That object has been known by me," the word *jñāta* (known) is not contradicted.
Because it would depend upon another means of knowledge, it would fail in its determination of the object. || 707 ||

Anticipating a dispute even regarding the illustrative example, he establishes what is accepted by the opponent—that the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) independent of the speaker’s knowledge—by stating: "known" (*jñāta*). Now, if its status as an independent means of valid cognition [is granted], why should it not be so with respect to the object (*artha*) as well, just as it is with respect to the speaker’s cognition? To this, he replies: "by another means of valid cognition" (*mānāntara*). Since the word of a reliable person depends upon the speaker’s knowledge for the ascertainment of the object, it does not possess independent validity with respect to the object itself.
As they have said: "And because it is intervened by that cognition, words for their part remain indifferent. (707)
Even when accompanied by the particle *mā*, the speech of an unreliable person is never considered a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the word *āssrava* is established as having the sense of "measure" (*māna*) in the context of *mā-yoga*. || 708 ||

Fearing that if there were an absence of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its sake, it would be no different from the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*), he says: "Even when associated with *mā*. The meaning is that even if the speech of an unreliable person is sometimes connected to a well-established means of valid cognition just like the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*), it does not possess the status of a means of valid cognition; thus, the two are mutually distinct. Having relied upon this stated distinction between the speech of an unreliable person and the speech of a reliable person, he states his own view: "By that."

Since the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) is a means of valid cognition (*māna*) with respect to the connection between the speaker’s cognition and [the object], it is therefore a means of valid cognition with respect to the object itself by way of that [cognition]. For it is not merely the speaker’s cognition that is apprehended; rather, when there is the knowledge of a qualified cognition, its status as a means of valid cognition with respect to the object is unavoidable. As they say: “The establishment of its validity occurs because of the possibility of the cause, which is the speaker’s cognition. Therefore, the meaning is that the word of a reliable person is a means of valid cognition regarding the object by way of the speaker’s cognition. (708)
And this being so, if the Vedāntas are an authority regarding that which is supramundane, [then...]
They awaken [the mind], which has destroyed the entire sphere of duality. || 709 ||
How could those [cognitions] be non-authoritative at that time, like the words of a trustworthy person?
Since the accomplishment of the object is already established when the means of accomplishment is established, it is not something that remains to be proven.

The illustrative example having been established, he elaborates upon the point to be illustrated with the words "In this way. The meaning is that if the Vedāntas produce a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) that is a means of valid cognition (*māna*), then there can be no suspicion of their being non-authoritative. Anticipating the objection that those [Vedāntas] which produce a mental modification well-known in the world would be non-authoritative—just like the statement "Fire [is] the enemy of cold"—he says: "That which is extraordinary (*alaukika*). They awaken and cause to blossom the people...

"Go" means "they proceed. He establishes its transcendental nature [by the word] "destroyed" (*vidhvasta*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: that in which all duality has been destroyed is its very object (*gocara*). When self-knowledge itself is the means of valid cognition (*māna*), then the term "awakening" (*prabodhayantī*) is easily understood.

Alternatively, it expresses the state of being free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*): that in which the entire object known as duality has been destroyed. This is what is intended to be expressed.

To demonstrate that specific portion [of the meaning], he again takes up an illustration with the words "āpta" (reliable). The meaning is as follows: just as from the words of a reliable person, at the time when the speaker’s cognition is established, there is also the establishment of the object qualified by that cognition; so too, from the Vedāntas, at the time when the Self (māna) is established, Brahman—which is its qualifier—is also established.
To the objection—"If Brahman is the object of the Vedāntas by virtue of being a qualifier of the Self, how can they possess independent authority regarding it?"—he replies:

Regarding the word "artha": when it is said that valid cognition (*māna*) arises from or is known through the Vedāntas, then the realization of Brahman (*brahmajñapti*) has also already arisen; thus, there is no [need for further] investigation into the reality of the object.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:

Furthermore, in order to illuminate Brahman, a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is sought; therefore, with respect to Brahman, the Vedas possess either the capacity to produce that [knowledge] or merely the capacity to indicate it.
The meaning is that validity is independent of other factors. || 709 || 710 ||
Furthermore, because of the relationship with what is already established, there is no inference of another means of knowledge regarding identity.

Just as [the existence of] being an effect is established by this [reasoning], why is there not likewise an inference regarding the injunction (niyoga) on account of its connection with being an effect? (711)

Having abandoned the doctrine of mere acceptance (*aṅgīkāravāda*) and relying instead on reality (*sattva*) as the actual nature of the subject at hand, he states that the independent authority of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman—defined by the aforementioned characteristics—is to be accepted even for the reasons that will be stated hereafter. He says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). Anticipating the objection that if reality were the nature of an object, then because the object would exist, it would necessarily be an object of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) like a jar, he clarifies another reason: "Because of its being established" (*siddhatve*). [This refers to] the state of being the one Self (*aikātmya*).

The meaning is as follows: even if it were possible to argue that "the mandate (niyoga) is cognizable by another means of knowledge because it is already established, like a [previously] accepted fact"—just as with inference—or that "it is cognizable by that [other means] because it is something to be accomplished (kārya), like a command (preṣa)," etc., then why would statements concerning objective reality (vastu) not likewise be independent [of other means of knowledge], given that the sentence expressing the mandate is [supposedly] independent? 711 ||
Even in the case of *niyoga*, its status as a task (*kāryatva*) is established through [the modes of] commanding, entreating, and so forth.
For its apprehension of the relationship occurs through that very same path in an identical manner. || 712 ||

He establishes the reason that *niyoga* (the mandate) is what is to be done (*kāryatva*) with the words "of the mandate" (*niyogasya*). He states another reason for that very point with the words "by its path" (*tadvartmanā*). The meaning is as follows: in the world, the connection of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is with "what is to be done" (*kārya*) in general; there is no separate apprehension of it in the Veda. Therefore, the knowledge of the power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix and so forth regarding *niyoga* occurs only through the medium of "being what is to be done"; thus, the reason is established. || 712 ||
In this context, the "task" (kāryatā) of an injunction consists in its acquisition of its own nature being dependent on something else.
She is in no way distinguished from those who are to be understood through their effects.

Furthermore, he states that an injunction (*niyoga*) is cognizable through another means of knowledge because its existence is dependent on something else, like a jar: "parāyattā" (dependent on another).

He further states that the status of being a *kārya* (an action to be accomplished) is established because an injunction is perceived as something to be produced in both worldly and Vedic contexts: "niyogasya" (of the injunction). He dispels the deficiency of the probans (*sādhana*) in the example of the jar: "kāryaiḥ" (by actions to be accomplished). He refutes the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhya*) with: "māntara" (by another means of knowledge). [The reason is... (Note: The final word "hetu-" appears to be an incomplete fragment of the original text.)

It determines that the state of being an effect, which was previously stated to be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), does not belong to the substratum (*dharmin*). It says: "That is not [the case]. || 713 ||
But that which is unique [to it] is said to be its "being an effect."
Even in worldly affairs, that [activity] is not at all prohibited. || 714 ||

He raises the objection that the example in the previously stated inference is deficient in its probans (*sādhanavikala*). [The objection is: "As for that which... [The author replies: Being the object of volition (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*) qualified by being achievable through volition (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is the unique definition of "task-to-be-done" (*kāryatva*) belonging to the *niyoga*; it does not apply to commands (*praiṣa*) and the like. However, he states that even for the *niyoga*, being the object of volition is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), and that being achievable through volition is common even to commands and so forth. Thus he says: "In worldly [matters]... (verse 714).
Now, if it is maintained that [the self] is to be determined by uncommon knowledge;
And that [nature] of all things cannot be warded off even by sticks. (715)

He raises an objection: "But [the object of] the *niyoga* (injunction) is its status as an effect (*kāryatā*), and that [status] does not belong to commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, which are of the nature of exertion.

To this he replies: "But that... Since it is accepted that the very thing to be accomplished (*kārya*) is designated by terms such as "command," the status of being an object of the cognition of "being an effect" is equally present for those [commands] as well. || 715 ||
