[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"The manifestation of its own object of cognition is dependent solely upon the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."
Whether something is an effect or a non-effect depends upon the object of cognition, not upon the means of cognition itself.

Furthermore, he states that if the mandate (*niyoga*) were the object of the cognition of "being an effect" (*kāryatā*), it would be cognizable through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). He says: "By means of a means of knowledge... The locative case in *pratipanne viṣaye* signifies the locus. This means: "it is not [cognized] from a means of knowledge," that is to say, not dependent on scripture. Only this much is dependent on scripture: the manifestation that "this is a means to achieve what is desired for its own object" or "this is a means to achieve what is undesired"; however, the two cognitions that "this is to be done" (*kāryam*) and "this is not to be done" are not so.

However, regarding those objects dependent upon scripture, which consist of the cognition that something is a means to a desired end or the opposite thereof, they are mental [cognitions]: "If it is a means to what is beneficial, it is to be done;

if it is the reverse, it is not to be done. Therefore, since the cognitions of "to-be-done-ness" and "not-to-be-done-ness" do not possess scriptural status, the sense is that if the niyoga were the object of a mental cognition of "to-be-done-ness," it would follow that it is cognizable by another means of knowledge (mānāntara). || 716 ||
Furthermore, whatever fault is alleged against monism on the grounds of its being unestablished, [it does not apply].
Even if the commission (niyoga) were successfully accomplished, that fault would not be removed. || 717 ||

It has been stated that for one who asserts that Brahman is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) on the grounds of its being an already established entity (*siddhatva*), it is easy to likewise assert that same thing regarding the injunction (*niyoga*) on the basis of another ground. Now, he says that by the very same ground on which the cognisability of Brahman through other means of knowledge is asserted, that [cognisability] would necessarily apply to the injunction as well:

"On the grounds of its being established" (*siddhatva*). If it is argued that there is no defect based on the ground of being established in the case of an injunction, whose very nature consists solely in being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then—

Does he succeed in the performance of action, or not? If it is the former, then because his state of being already perfected would be established, there would be a fault resulting from that; thus [the author] says: "In the case of perfection... (717).
Nor is it the case that this [self] does not become established because objects such as sacrifices are unestablished.
If that [self] were not established, it would follow that the injunctions are fruitless. || 718 ||
He refutes the second [position] with the words "yāgādi" (sacrifice, etc.). He states the reason for this with the word "vidhi" (injunction). The meaning is as follows:

if the mandate (*niyoga*) were not established through the performance of sacrifices and so forth, then that performance would be purposeless, rendering the injunctive sentences meaningless. Nor can it be argued that the performance has purposefulness because it accomplishes heaven and other such results;
for its being for that purpose is not admitted without the establishment of the mandate. || 718 ||
[Salutations] to that which is most skillful in illuminating the true nature of the reality of the single Self.
Apart from verbal testimony, what means of knowledge could bear the burden of proving that? || 719 ||

It was stated that even in the case of an injunction (*niyoga*), there is a similarity [to the Veda] by relying on the entry of other means of knowledge (*māna*) into Brahman. Now, he says that in that case, the very possibility of such entry does not exist: "Aikātmya... etc. The reality of things (*vastuyāthātmya*) is precisely the oneness of the self (*aikātmya*). Regarding its manifestation, the word "Tattvamasi" and so forth is more powerful due to factors such as the uniformity of the beginning and the conclusion; beyond that, there is no other means of knowledge whatsoever.

There is no other means of knowledge capable of illuminating that [object]. The meaning is that there is an absence of any proof for the entry of another means of knowledge into this [process]. || 719 ||
Wherever knowledge arises immediately, depending upon the mother and other such factors;
In that very case, there is dependence on another means of knowledge, but not when difference has been destroyed.

Having raised the objection that "the object of dispute is cognizable by another means of knowledge because it is not an action, like a jar," he states [the following] to show that the dependence on the measure (mātra) and so forth is a limiting condition (upādhi).
[Vol. 1, Page 223] 202 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Relation— ]

Regarding the phrase "mātrādi" (the mother and so forth): having raised the doubt that [the definition] is over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*), he says "but not" (*na tu*). The meaning is that in that Brahman in which the distinction of mother and so forth has been destroyed, there is no cognition dependent upon it. || 720 ||
In Vedic utterances, the meanings of words possess a relation that is dependent upon the injunction.
In the world, through the power of composition, there are arrangements that are established by internal connection. || 721 ||

Even though other means of knowledge are excluded from bearing upon Brahman, the Vedāntas do not possess independent authority; for there is an absence of the factors that motivate worldly or Vedic syntactic relations (*saṃsarga*) within them, and consequently, the cognition of the sentence-meaning produced by them is erroneous. Thinking thus, [the author] raises an objection while demonstrating the motivator of those [factors], in order to state the absence of the motivator for Vedic syntactic relations in the Vedāntas: "vidhyartha... etc. That which has an injunction as its object is "vidhyartha" (that which has an injunction as its meaning).

The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others are employed. Among these, with the desire to express the absence of that which motivates worldly syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*), he states its motivator: "In the world" (*loke*). The word-meanings (*padārtha*) are connected as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*). || 721 ||
Furthermore, the arrangement of word-meanings is necessarily preceded by the speaker's intention.
And when an object is cognizable through another means of valid cognition, the speaker's intention is already established. (722)

He states how, through the impossibility of composition, worldly connection (*saṃsarga*) is dependent upon other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). [The text says: "Composition... [and so on]. Then, raising the objection—"In that case, let it be assumed that there is merely a desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) by virtue of that [connection]; but how can another means of knowledge be postulated?"—he replies: "By another means of knowledge... Since a desire to speak is impossible regarding what is unknown, one knows [the object] through another means of knowledge, desires to speak it, and then composes a sentence for another; thus, in the world, connection...
The meaning is that it is dependent upon another means of knowledge. || 722 ||
And this being the case, the cognition of the meaning of the Vedānta passages is an error.
In this world, one who has uprooted the ritual procedure is like the notion of water in saline soil.

It may be that these two [injunction and negation] are the factors that bring about the connection between the world and the Veda; nevertheless, what follows for the Vedāntas? To this he says: "And so" (*evam ca*).

Since it is established that in the world, injunction is the factor that brings about the connection with the Veda and is a means of knowledge distinct from other means, then in the case of the impersonal Vedāntas—where no other means of knowledge is possible and where an injunction is not admitted—the cognition of the meaning of the sentence derived from them must be an error, like the cognition of water in a mirage. This is the meaning.
"One whose ritual procedure has been uprooted" means one whose ritual procedure has been discarded; that is to say, one who does not employ it. || 723 ||
When this has been said for the sake of refutation, listen now to what is being stated.
Why is it that the connection between word-meanings is held to be dependent upon an injunction?
Why is it not postulated that [the cognition] depends on a distinct entity as its cause? || 725 ||

The objection being raised is that since the Vedāntas lack authority, their status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman is far-fetched. To this, [the author] replies: "It is said thus. The connection is: "Listen now to what is being stated. How is there a connection with the Vedic? One might raise the objection: "Does the instigator (prayojaka) exist in the Vedāntas? For there is no injunction (vidhi) in them. Anticipating this, he explains the resolution: "Regarding the meaning of words" (*padārtha*). Why is it accepted that the relationship [of words] is dependent on an injunction, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth? Why is it not preferred that the cause is another word-meaning which is compatible, required, and proximate? For an injunction is not the instigator, as is the case with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.
1. Regarding this, first:
[Vol. 1, p.
224] *Vārttika*, together with the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Because there is deviation [from the rule] in cases such as "the first portion" (*prathamabhakṣa*), therefore the triad of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other two is the determining factor; since this exists in the Vedāntas as well, the meaning derived from them is not an error—this is the sense. || 724 || 725 ||
If the conjunction of categories were to occur even without an injunction, [then injunction would be purposeless].
In this way, the injunction would be purposeless due to the absence of an object.

The proponent of injunction (vidhivādī) raises an objection: "If [the relation] were through association" (saṃsargaśced iti). If the association of word-meanings were established even without the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth, merely through proximity and the like, then injunction would be purposeless; for since the association of its own object would already be obtained from elsewhere, the injunction itself would be of no consequence.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedic association is caused by that injunction in order for the injunction to be meaningful. || 726 ||
Surely this same fault applies equally to other words as well, such as those expressing injunctions.
Other [words] are also employed for the purpose of conveying a specific meaning. (727)

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that if the relation were dependent on an injunction (*vidhi*), then the fault of redundancy would be equal in the case of nouns and words. He introduces this with "But surely" (*nanu*).

The word "also" (*api*) serves as a corroborative example, meaning that just as an injunction would be redundant if the relation had another cause, so too would it here. Anticipating the objection that nouns and words might still be purposeful by generating a cognition of the mere word-meanings even if they do not generate a cognition of the relation, he replies with the words "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*).
The meaning of "also" (api) is like that of a prescriptive word (vidhipada). || 727 ||
This being so, let it be explained why the injunction is not purposeless.
Because of the equality of acquisition and preservation [of the meaning], it is not [the case that] other words have the sense of an injunction. || 728 ||

He states the result of the employment of words other than the injunction for the purpose of establishing their mutual connection: "In this way. Since the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) [of the meaning] are equal through words other than the injunction, one must explain why the injunction alone is useless if the connection is established without it; or, conversely, why those other words are not also useless if that [connection] is established by them. Thus, the lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) is equal in both cases.
This is the meaning. || 728 ||
It is said: for an injunctive word has as its object that which is not known through other means of knowledge.
For him, there is no fulfillment of purpose other than through the engagement with sense objects. (729)

The proponent of injunction (*vidhivādī*) asserts the disparity between the word denoting an injunction and other words. He says: "It is stated. In order to clarify that very point, he states the nature of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth: "Injunction," etc. Even though it has as its object the aforementioned *niyoga* (compulsion), how is it that the relation (*saṃsarga*) is dependent upon it? To this he replies: "Not of that," etc. Without the presentation of the relation, which is the object of the *niyoga*, [the *niyoga* cannot function].

The meaning is that since an injunction (niyoga) expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth cannot find its completion in an objectless state, the connection [of the action] depends upon the injunction. || 729 ||
Because it expresses a meaning already established by another means of knowledge, it is merely reiterative.
Because, from that [statement], no implication (ākṣepa) of a word other than the one prescribed is perceived. || 730 ||

With the intention that even noun-words, like injunctive words, would have their function incomplete without implying a relation and would thus imply it [directly], he says: "By another means of knowledge," etc. The meaning is that noun-words do not imply [the relation] because they are merely reiterative (anuvādin). || 730 ||

1, page 225] 204 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]
Likewise, even when the relationship has not been fully understood, there is comprehension of the meaning of the injunction.
Furthermore, a statement whose connection [to a result] is already known would be merely informative regarding an established fact, rather than being injunctive.

If the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth have as their meaning an *niyoga* (an injunction) that is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, then even if its relationship with that [injunction] is not cognized, would it cause that [injunction] to be understood, or would it not? It is refuted by the argument: "Not the first," because if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even one who is unlearned in the linguistic convention would act preceded by a cognition of the *niyoga* upon hearing the optative suffix and so on. This is stated in the phrase: "Even for one who is unlearned. He then raises the second alternative: "Now" (*atha*), [namely] that the optative suffix and so forth are denotative only for one who has cognized the relationship [between word and meaning].

Furthermore, since a cognition of a relation is not established when the related term has not been apprehended by another means of knowledge, a word expressing an injunction—just like a noun—does not possess the power of implication; thus he says: "because its meaning is already established" (siddhārtham). || 731 ||
One should abandon one's own duty and station when the knowledge of the relationship has arisen.
Therefore, a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has been cognized is the indicator in all cases. (732)

He states another defect regarding the fact that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others convey meaning when their power is unknown: "And its own property" (*svadharma ca*). The meaning is this: the capacity to convey its own meaning by depending upon the apprehension of a relation is the property of a word; if it were to convey meaning independently of that [relation], the word would abandon its own property and instead adopt the property of a sentence, which is the capacity to convey meaning without depending on the knowledge of a power (*śakti*). Even though in common worldly usage a word conveys meaning when its relation [to the object] is known, in the Veda...

Anticipating the objection that this is not so, he states "therefore" [verse 732], saying "it is not so," because it would contradict the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning worldly and Vedic usage).
If it were conceived otherwise than this, everything would be inconsistent.
The connection between the sentence and the sentence-meaning is characterized by the relationship between the signifier and the signified. || 733 ||

He states the defect in the opposing view [beginning with] "From this": even if the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) exists in common worldly usage, its absence in the Veda would entail either the transgression of the nature of words or the resorting to the nature of sentences;

furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the established principle that "a word whose capacity is understood in the world is also expressive in the Veda. Thus, many inconsistencies would arise—this is the meaning.
Anticipating this, he raises an objection while breaking the seal of the Mīmāṃsaka school out of a desire to avoid the transgression of the nature of words.

Regarding the term "sentence" (vākya): the relationship between word and meaning, characterized as that of the signifier and the signified, which is established in the world between a sentence and its sentence-meaning, is a connection belonging to the sentence with the sentence-meaning, not to the word with the word-meaning;

for the union of those two is established in the world [only] through the sentence. However, the sentence-meaning is an injunction (niyoga) that is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply—this is the meaning. || 733 ||
Because it would be restricted solely to that particular [individual], there could be no relation for you.
A particular does not subsist in another particular, just as the universal "cowness" [does not subsist in another cow].
Since that [cognition] is established through the absence of expectancy, no relation is therefore apprehended. || 734 ||

He refutes the apprehension of the relationship of a sentence with its own meaning [in the following passage]: "tadviśeṣa... etc. The meaning is this: since that sentence is fixed upon one specific object, such as the bringing of a cow, it cannot function toward another specific object; furthermore, because the bringing of a cow is not observed in cases such as the tethering of a cow, it would follow that the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) must occur for every individual sentence. Since that is difficult to accomplish even in a hundred years, your position cannot be established.

Anticipating the objection that—just as the particular *gotva* (cowness) exists in another particular such as a specific cow (*khaṇḍa*) in relation to existence (*sattā*) and so forth, and just as the meaning of a sentence may exist in another sentence-meaning—the power (*śakti*) of a sentence with respect to its own meaning is easily grasped—he says: "No. The reason for this is given by the term "due to lack of expectancy" (*nairākāṅkṣyeṇa*).
Since the sentence-meaning of "bringing the cow" and so forth is established independently of the tethering of the cow and other such factors, it does not possess equality with *gotva*; nor...
The meaning is that while "cowness" (gotva) is independent of particulars such as the spotted cow, the "bringing of the cow" is observed to be independent of other sentence-meanings.
This concludes the *Vārttika* on the connection [of words], together with Ānandagiri’s commentary, the *Śāstraprakāśikā*. 205.

He concludes by stating "dhī" (cognition). Regarding the phrase "saṃbandha" (relation): since it must be admitted that the relation of a sentence to its own meaning is also cognizable through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), the impossibility of the sentence-meaning being *apūrva* (newly known) is equally applicable; thus, because it is impossible for a sentence to have its relation [to its meaning] known, that relation must be grasped by the word alone. Even though in common worldly usage words and their meanings are observed to be coupled together, a word whose relation is unknown does not convey its own meaning.
The meaning is that it would follow [as an undesirable consequence] even in another case. || 734 ||
Even he who considers the relation to follow from verbal cognition... (735)
Even he does not correctly understand it.
Since it is an effect residing in the hearer that serves as the logical mark (liṅga), how can [the object] have sound alone as its domain? || 736 ||

Having rejected the acquisition of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) on the basis of the sentence and asserting it instead for the individual word alone, [the opponent] argued that the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would have as their object a mandate (*niyoga*) that falls within the scope of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*); furthermore, if that [mandate] were not already known through linguistic convention (*avyutpannatva*), it would not be conveyed by them, otherwise there would be a transgression of the nature of words.

Now, however, when it is understood that there is no fault because the power of the injunctive suffix and so forth is grasped with respect to a mandate that is known from the word itself, and not otherwise—[this is the position of the Mīmāṃsaka].

Anticipating the objection stated in the *Vārttika* beginning with "dityādi," he says: "The relation. Even one who, being obsessed by the passion for *niyoga*, thinks that a child understands the denotative power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth toward a *niyoga*—which is apprehended through that [action] after seeing the activity of the middle-aged listener (the *madhyama-vṛddha*) following the cognition arising from the word uttered by the superior elder (the *uttama-vṛddha*)—does not understand correctly; for [cognition arises] only from a known relation.

The meaning is that there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): from the word arises the cognition of the injunction (*niyoga*), and from that [cognition] arises the knowledge of that [word’s] denotation. If it is argued that this is not the case because the child grasps the word’s power (*śakti*) through the sign of activity (*pravṛtti-liṅga*) observed in the middle-aged person who has understood the injunction from the word as the motivator, the author replies with the words “of the hearer” (*śrotṛ-stha*).
Since the injunction that motivates is accessible through the sign of activity residing in the middle-aged person, it does not have the word alone as its object; and thus, in some way—
The meaning is that even when mutual dependence is eliminated, its priority does not [thereby] follow. || 735 || 736 ||
If it is argued that this too is preceded by verbal testimony, we reply that it is preceded by an inferential mark (liṅga).
Why, then, is verbal cognition also not preceded by inference? (737)

He raises the objection that even for an inference whose mark is activity (*pravṛtti*), since activity occurs toward the injunction (*niyoga*) understood from the word, its status as being cognizable solely through the word will be established; this is expressed by the words "of that too" (*tasyāpi*). For the hearer’s comprehension of the injunction from the word is preceded by inference, because inference operates toward it beforehand; therefore, why should the comprehension of the injunction from the word not also be preceded by a logical mark (*liṅga*)? Thus, [the opponent argues] that the word and the inference...
He states the similarity between these two: "The mark," etc. (737).
Even that listener who proceeds after having understood [the meaning] through the word of an injunction (niyoga), [is so moved].
For him as well, the cognition of the word's meaning would arise solely from inference. || 738 ||

Now he shows the specific distinction of inference [in this context] with the words "niyogam" (the mandate). For one who has already mastered the language, at the time of engaging in activity, the cognition of the mandate arises through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth;

however, at the time of learning the meaning, there is an unavoidable dependence on the inference of activity toward the meaning of the optative suffix and other such markers—this is the sense of its being "primary. || 738 ||
Because the mandate (niyoga) is inferred from its effect, which is accessible to direct perception.
It would follow that it possesses the character of being worldly, like that which has perceptible effects. || 739 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [on the connection]:

He states the conclusion resulting from inference being primary because it has *niyoga* as its object. [The verse begins with] "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). Perception is the *liṅga* (inferential mark) that prompts activity...
The meaning is that because this so-called "effect" (kārya) is inferable from it [the niyoga], the niyoga—unlike a jar or similar objects—is not cognizable through verbal testimony alone. || 739 ||
If there were no injunction regarding an effect, what purpose would there be in the accomplishment of sacrifices and the like?
At that time, even for a positive injunction (vidhi), there would be the state of making known an already established entity. || 740 ||

It is raised as an objection that *niyoga* (the mandate) is non-worldly (*alaukika*) because, like a jar or other such things, it does not touch the three times and is therefore not something to be produced.

[The author] refutes this with the words "If not" (*na cet*): if it were not something to be produced, then the performance of sacrifices and so forth would be useless. [He asks] "What is the purpose? (*ko 'rthaḥ*). And it is not...

The sense is that for the sake of heaven, there must be a basis [for action], because without an injunction (*niyoga*), the purposefulness of that [action] cannot be established. Furthermore, if the injunction were not something to be produced, then since its non-existence would not be admitted, it would necessarily be eternally established; in that case, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth which convey it would be conveying what is already established. Thus he says "established" (*siddha*) to indicate that this is a different position. || 740 ||
And here, priority is difficult to discern, just as it is between a seed and its effect.
Therefore, verbal testimony is not accepted as being prior to inference.

"Let it be then that the *niyoga* (injunction) is something to be produced, yet it is not worldly like a jar; for while the eye and other senses do not precede [the cognition of] a jar, another means of knowledge (*māna*) does precede [the cognition of] the *niyoga*. Having raised this objection, he elaborates [on the reply] beginning with "because that too is preceded by verbal testimony," and so on. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the *niyoga*. It should be understood as referring to either verbal testimony or inference. For indeed...

The priority of either the seed or the sprout is understood [from experience]. Since the possibility of such priority also exists for inference, it follows that this is the meaning of the word [in question]. The implication is: "How then can that [priority] be cognizable by verbal testimony alone? || 741 ||
Alternatively, it is precisely inference that is appropriate here prior to the verbal testimony.
A word whose connection [with its object] is not known is not a means of cognition; therefore, it is merely reiterative. || 742 ||

Having raised the objection that when the primacy of the word is possible, then the fact that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is cognizable by the word alone is also conceivable, he elaborates on this with the words "having understood the *niyoga* from the word," and so forth. Or else [he says] "yadvā" (or rather). He states the reason why primacy belongs to inference alone regarding the *niyoga* with the words "nāvitteti" (not being known). A word whose potency has not been apprehended is not a communicator; and that [apprehension of potency] resides in the *liṅ* suffix and so forth, which refer to the *niyoga*.
There is no dependence on a word, nor can that cognition arise from the word alone due to mutual dependence, as has been stated; therefore, the meaning is that inference comes first. [Objection:

Let it be that the *niyoga* (injunction) is inferable; in that case, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would be merely reiterative (*anuvāda*) with respect to it. To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 742 ||

He who understands [an object] through inference does not know it as cognized by means of verbal testimony. Even when the object of cognition is different or the same, the cognition [of one person] is not a mere restatement for another cognizer. (743)

[Objection: Is it not the case that when a word enters into a particular application (niyoga), why should the inference entering into that same application not be a mere restatement (anuvādaka)? To this, he says:

"It is understood" (*budhyate*). The point is that a child, perceiving through inference what was unknown to him from the word, does not make the inference a restatement. Now, for a child who cognizes through a mark (liṅga) what was already known from the word by means of hearing, how can there be inference?

He does not state there that it is a mere restatement. He says, "distinct" (*bhinna*). This means that immediately after the cognition of one cognizer, [it occurs] in another cognizer; in that case, it is not known.
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 207.

A cognition regarding one object or another does not constitute a restatement (*anuvāda*). For instance, when Caitra has perceived a jar, Maitra’s cognition of it—whether in that same place or elsewhere—is not a restatement. Therefore, the meaning is that between two cognitions residing in different knowers, one is not the restatement of the other. || 743 ||
And here, by means of activity, only the cause of activity is inferred.
Since that [object] is established even by worldly means, there is no proof for the non-worldly.

Having previously accepted that *niyoga* (the mandate) is inferable from activity (*pravṛtti*) and thus equal to other word-meanings, he now states that it is not even inferable from activity at all. [The verse begins with] "pravṛtti... The locative case-ending has the sense of "in the listener. At the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), by means of the listener's activity, its cause— [...is inferred]. (The sentence continues as follows.)

Anticipating the objection that what is inferred from the suffix *liṅ* (the optative/imperative) is not something other than an injunction (*niyoga*), he says: "By worldly [usage]. The meaning is this: since in the world, within the continuum of one's own activities such as suckling at the breast, the listener’s engagement is established precisely through the known cause—that is, by the fact that it is a means to a desired end—it follows that the capacity of the *liṅ* and other suffixes is grasped with respect to that very thing characterized by its fitness for action (*kṛti-yogyatva*). Consequently, because there is no evidence for an extraordinary injunction (*alaukika-niyoga*), such an injunction is not established. || 744 ||
Nor is it understood that activity is pervaded by the very cognition of an effect.
For activity is observed even when there is a cognition of an object such as a snake. (745)

If it is argued that because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever activity is preceded by deliberation (*prekṣāpūrvikā pravṛttiḥ*) is caused by the cognition of an effect (*kāryadhīkṛtā*)," even in one's own activity, the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭopāyatādhiyaḥ*) is not the cause—[the author] says [in response]: "The effect" (*kārya*). He states the reason for the refutation of the aforementioned pervasion: "From snakes, etc. (*sarpādīti*). Nor is the refutation of the pervasion equal even in the position that "whatever activity is preceded by cognition is caused by the cognition of being a means to a beneficial end (*ahitasādhanatvadhīkṛtā*)," because [one acts] to move away from this [snake].

The point is this: activity does not arise from the cognition "this will destroy the object," nor does activity arise from the cognition "this is its effect"; rather, activity arises solely from the knowledge that it is a specific means for achieving a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), even when that [desired end] is qualified by being the cause of that [destruction]. || 745 ||
The fruit of male conduct is the effect, and the purpose of the injunction is also the cause.
You yourself have stated that the cause of engagement is not the fruit. || 746 ||

For this reason as well, he says that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is not the motivator: "Because of the person's activity. It is your view that only the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) is the motivator, and not the fruit (*phala*).

But that is contradictory; for the *kārya* is indeed the fruit of activity, since it is to be achieved as something desired. Furthermore, it is accepted that the *kārya*, being the very meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*), is the cause of activity. Even so, you yourself could not say that the fruit is not the motivator; for no one other than you [could maintain such a position].

Therefore, because you possess the quality of being a proponent of contradictory views, you lack the skill to speak of the Dharma and its meaning; thus, an injunction is not that which sets one in motion—this is the sense. ||746||
For one who retreats from a snake or similar creature, no fruit of action is recognized.
Since it is merely the absence of disadvantage, non-existence itself can never be a result anywhere.

Having accepted that the fruit is the effect of human activity (*puṃvyāpāra*), it was stated that the *niyoga* (the mandate) is not a motivator. Now, he says that it does not even have the fruit of inducing activity: "of one who is fleeing" (*apasarpyasya*). He states the reason why the effect of human activity—consisting in fleeing from a snake or the like—is not a [desirable] fruit: "because of the absence of evil" (*anartha-*) etc. The meaning is that, in that case, only the cessation of suffering is desired. How can there be a fruit for a non-entity?

Anticipating the objection that [the cessation of suffering] cannot be a fruit because it is like a sky-lotus, he says: "Not so. For the absence of suffering is not a fruit by its own nature, but rather as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of happiness; however, a sky-lotus, being absolutely non-existent, lacks such manifesting power.
The point is that the status of the cessation of suffering as such will become clear later. || 747 ||
1. Tora | Ka 'divāyo | [Vol.
1, page 229] 208 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]
Furthermore, an injunction (vidhi) manifested by the word "injunction" (niyoga) is of the nature of valid cognition.
Being independent of other means of knowledge, it is a valid cognition by virtue of its necessitating nature.

Since the possibility of the injunctive word (*vidhipada*), whose meaning is an *niyoga* (injunction) not amenable to other means of knowledge, implying a connection with its own object has been rejected, the author now raises the objection that the *niyoga* itself must imply it. He says: "The *niyoga*, moreover... Even if the *niyoga* conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is a valid means of knowledge, he asks how the optative suffix could not be a restatement (*anuvāda*) in that case; to this he replies: "By another means of knowledge... If the *niyoga* were a valid means of knowledge, it would be logical for it to be independent of other means of knowledge.

Anticipating the question "How is that so?", he says: "By way of implication. The meaning is that since an injunction (niyoga) is untenable without a connection to an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, it serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) in that regard by virtue of implying them. || 748 ||
The capacity to prompt [action] does not arise from the word itself, nor does it likewise arise from another means of valid cognition.
Because it would entail the previously mentioned faults, such as being unevolved or lacking activity. || 749 ||
Whether that capacity to imply [the injunction] is established by the word itself or by something else, it is not the first case; thus he says: "The capacity to imply.

For this is not understood by virtue of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, because those are exhausted by conveying the *niyoga* (the mandate); such is the meaning. Nor is it the second case, because no evidence is seen to establish that the word implies a connection with a *niyoga* residing in another means of knowledge; otherwise, it would follow that the *niyoga* itself would also fall within the scope of that other means of knowledge. Thus he says.

"Nor [is it so]"—the word "thus" (*tathā*) refers to the fact that the *niyoga* (injunction) implies [other factors]. As for the claim that [the injunction] is independent of other means of knowledge (*māna*), he says that since the *niyoga* cannot be known through other means of knowledge, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would not be grasped therein; thus, even a person who has not grasped that power would proceed to act upon hearing the optative suffix and so on. [He uses the term] "unlearned" (*avyutpanna*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the inclusion of the transgression of the properties of words and so forth is intended. This summarizes the aforementioned defects.

If the injunction [of the Veda] regarding the desire to act were dependent on another means of knowledge, its status as *apūrva* (something not previously known) would be lost; thus he says: "It being so stated" (verse 749).
It follows that one would incur the undesirable consequence of abandoning the very method one has accepted for oneself.
And as for its authority, let that reside where it is desired for the Veda; what is the use of this [Smṛti] there?

Regarding the objection that there would be no loss if one were to accept the activity of those who have not yet attained proficiency (*avyutpanna*), he replies: "By what one has accepted for oneself" (*svābhyupeta*). The meaning is that if one resorts to the activity of only those who have already attained proficiency—such as those who have heard the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—then it contradicts the established doctrine (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*) that verbal linguistic usage belongs only to those who are proficient. Having accepted the validity of the mandate (*niyoga*) while discarding its capacity for implication (*ākṣepakatva*) and so on, he now rejects its very status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). Validity...
And so it is said. || 790 ||
And how could its status as a means of knowledge be established through inference, since it is not explicitly stated by its own word in the case of sacrifices and the like?
For even worldly association does not exist as something dependent upon an injunction.
For even in the absence of an injunction, a connection exists for the listener, even where there is no injunction.

Furthermore, he reflects upon whether its status as a means of valid cognition (mānatva) resides in the sacrifice and so forth, or in their relation, or in the fact that the sacrifice and so forth are the means to the desired end. He says "and" (*ca*). He rejects the first [option] by saying "no. He provides the reason: "because it is understood from the word 'sacrifice' and so forth itself. This means: in that case where the word itself—which denotes the sacrifice and so forth—is the means of knowledge (*mā*). He refutes the second [option].

"Even worldly" means that even the connection between the meanings of words such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*) and so forth is not dependent upon an injunction (*niyoga*), because that [connection] is worldly.

[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 209] It establishes that relation (*saṃsarga*) is worldly (*laukika*). Regarding the phrase "since" (*yataḥ*): because even in a sentence devoid of an injunction, such as "the man of the king," a relation is observed by the hearer; therefore, even in the absence of a mandate (*niyoga*), since the relation is perceived, its worldly nature is established—and it is not merely a specific relation.
The meaning is that its being worldly would result in the futility of the injunction (*niyoga*), since it would already be established by the word itself. || 711 ||
If the capacity to accomplish the fruit were dependent upon an injunction, [then it would follow that the Veda is not eternal].
In that case as well, who can prevent the capacity of the word from functioning in this way? (752)

He takes up the third [point]: "phala" (the fruit). The capacity of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to be a means toward the fruit is its "means-ness" (*sādhanatā*); that is produced by the injunction (*niyoga*).

If the sacrifice and so forth did not accomplish heaven, then there would be no injunction for one desiring it with respect to that [sacrifice]. Therefore, the meaning is that the injunction is the proof (*māna*) for the sacrifice and so forth being the accomplishers of heaven and the like. He says that even in that case, it is not a proof: "not at all..."
"In that regard" refers to the statement concerning its being a means to the fruit. The word "also" (api) is used to provide the *niyoga* as a corroborative example. || 752 ||
Therefore, because it is equal to the other [cases], it is not based on the meaning of an injunction.
There would be a conjunction of word-meanings; thus, [the desired result] is well-established even without an injunction. (753)

Having stated that because the suffix is understood to have its power (śakti) in the sense that the meaning of the verbal root is a means to a desired end, neither an injunction (niyoga) revealed by the word "vidhi" exists, nor is it a valid cognition (pramā) due to the absence of an object, he concludes what was said regarding the question "From what [source] does the connection between word-meanings arise? with the words "Therefore... (tasmāt).

Since even the sixfold [means of knowledge] are not devoid of scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) regarding verbal cognition, he states the conclusion: that the verbal cognition "the Self is Brahman" is established even without an injunction—thus, it is well-established. || 793 ||
Therefore, because all word-meanings possess expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity, [the sentence meaning arises].
Through mutual connection, there arises the comprehension of a specific meaning. || 754 ||

Anticipating the objection that since connection (*saṃsarga*) is not dependent on an injunction (*vidhi*), it cannot be established without a cause, and therefore words cannot be the cause of a cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭadhī*), he concludes what was stated in the verse beginning with "because [the word-meaning] is dependent on other word-meanings" (*padārthāntaratantratvāt*): "Therefore, all... Since an injunction is not the cause of connection, it is logical that words [convey their meaning] through the mutual relation of all word-meanings—whether they be things to be done (*kārya*) or not to be done (*akārya*)—by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth.
The meaning is that it is the cause of a distinguished cognition. || 714 ||
But surely, just as the injunction of origination is established for the purpose of making known the ritual action, [so too is the injunction of application].
Let this rule for the knowledge of the Self remain established for the sake of awakening to that Self. || 755 ||
And here, activity will also be established, just like the authority over karma.
Non-occurrence and the cessation of occurrence, as well as the awakening to the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings. || 756 ||

Having stated that [the teaching] is well-established even without an injunction (*vidhi*), the author, unable to tolerate this, raises the objection that there are two types of injunctions in the Vedāntas, beginning with "But...

(*nanu*). Therein, first, he establishes the existence of an origin-injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) among them by means of an illustration, beginning with "Origin... (*utpatti*). An origin-injunction is an injunction such as "One should offer the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*); an injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-vidhi*) is an injunction such as "The Self is to be seen" (*ātmā draṣṭavyaḥ*). Now, [he discusses] the qualification-injunction (*adhikāra-vidhi*) among them—

He said: "Action. Just as when an action has arisen, there is engagement due to an injunction whose fruit is the head [of the matter], so too for one desiring liberation, there is the application of wisdom.

The meaning is that once knowledge has been enjoined by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), one engages in it; "one should act" is the sense. He demonstrates the nature of the injunction of qualification and the injunction of origination (*utpattividhi*) in sequence: "not yet engaged," etc. (vv. 755–716).
Thus they desire a ritual procedure even regarding an object that is unfit for such a procedure.
Now, this is stated with respect to those who [act] under the influence of passion for ritual injunctions. || 757 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, how injunctions could apply to ritual action, which is fit for engagement, but not to the knowledge of the Self, which is unfit for such engagement—he says: "In this way. The meaning is that if one does not accept an injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self, the engagement of those seeking liberation would be untenable; therefore, the two injunctions serve as the proof for it. Regarding that, he states another reason for accepting the injunctions: "Injunctions," etc. For origination and qualification are inseparable from application and performance.

The sense is that those two [the injunctions] are also possible within the Vedāntas. He resolves the objection—that there must be two types of injunctions in the Vedāntas because otherwise their application would be untenable—with the words: "tān prati" (with respect to them). || 757 ||
For it is not accepted that the injunction has an operation regarding the cognition of the essential nature of the action.
But rather, there is a connection with the authoritative injunction because of its dependence on that which has already arisen. || 758 ||

He refutes [the opponent's view] beginning with the words "that which is the injunction of origin" (*yattatpattividhi*) and so forth, by stating "the action" (*karma*). The meaning is that the operation of the injunction of origin does not rest in merely making known the essential nature of the action, because such mere cognition is fruitless. He asks, "How then does its operation come to rest? and answers with "but rather" (*kiṃ tu*). Since the essential nature of the action, once understood through the injunction of origin, stands in need of a result, [the injunction of origin] culminates in a result.
He states that through the application of the connection with yoga, there is the completion of its operation: "Of that which has arisen," etc. (758).
It is not logical for the knowledge of the Self to be something that enters into a sphere of ritual authority.
That which has a connection with the qualification [of the agent] is not enjoined as the self. || 759 ||

Anticipating the objection that even the knowledge of the Self, arising from an injunction to "behold," might be connected with an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra*), he says: "Qualification" (*adhikāra*). The meaning is this: the knowledge of the Self, which is desired as something to be enjoined, does not enter into the sphere of an injunction regarding qualification; for it depends upon valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the like, and being independent of the person (*apuruṣatantra*), it is unfit for connection with qualification. [On the other hand,] the Self has a connection with qualification by virtue of being the owner (*svāmin*).

If it is argued that through that [object], the knowledge of it would also have a connection with the injunction, he says "no," beginning with the words "of which" (*yasya*). Whether the self in question is the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) or the supreme Self (*para*), in that regard, even if the transmigrating soul has a connection to the qualification (*adhikāra*), it cannot be the object of the injunction because it is already established; nor is it the object of the cognition produced by the injunction, since the sentences such as "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) do not have that as their subject matter. As for the supreme Self, however, it is not connected to any qualification; how then could there be a connection with the injunction through the cognition of it?
This is the meaning. || 759 ||
Just as that which has rice and other grains as its object, even when investigated with great effort, [remains as it is].
Perception does not admit entry into the domain of [scriptural] authority. 760 ||

He clarifies, by means of an illustration, that the knowledge of the Supreme Self—which is intended as the object of an injunction for production (*utpatti-vidhi*)—is not connected with an injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*). [The text says:

"Just as rice, etc. Just as direct perception regarding rice and the like, even when thoroughly examined, does not gain entry into the qualification for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) by way of the rice and so forth, so too the knowledge of the Self does not enter into the qualification by way of the Self.

Thus, even though injunctive rules regarding origination (*utpatti-vidhi*) are possible within the Vedantas, there is no possibility of injunctions regarding qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth; for the purpose of human fulfillment is accomplished solely by making known what was previously unknown, and thus [the Vedanta] culminates in that alone, as there is no recognized invariable concomitance [with other types of injunction]. This is the intended meaning. || 76 || 0 ||

Page 232] • Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 211
There is also another means of direct experience, characterized by reflection and meditation.
The means has indeed been prescribed, even without a formal rule for practice. || 761 ||

Intending to show that even though there is no injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) engages in it by following the injunctions regarding its means, the author has refuted an injunction for verbal knowledge (*śābda-jñāna*). Now, he raises the position that there is an injunction for repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), stating: "There is another as well. This means that even without the injunction concerning the object of verbal comprehension—which was previously refuted—there is some other means for direct experience (*anubhava*).

The connection is that [it] is "prescribed. "Experience" (anubhava) means direct realization (sākṣātkāra). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should see with a concentrated mind," and so forth, as prescribed in such passages. He states the nature of the means: "by reflection" (manana), which means consisting of the repetition of the words and logical reasoning. Anticipating the objection that there would be futility even if the instrument [of knowledge] were prescribed without its procedure (itikartavyatā), he says: "with its means" (sopāya), [referring to] tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), and so forth.

The meaning is that it is enjoined that one should perceive *prasaṃkhyāna*—designated by such terms as "reflection" (*manana*) and so forth—which is endowed with various skillful means and is the instrument for the direct realization of the Self. || 761 ||
Since the act of seeing is what is to be enjoined, [the agent] is characterized by its connection with that [act].
In this case as well, the effort directed toward experience consists of discernment (prasaṃkhyāna). 762.

One might object: "Is it not the case that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is enjoined by the word 'one should see' (*paśyet*), since seeing is connected to an injunction as its object? Therefore, *prasaṃkhyāna* [is not what is enjoined], because there is no word expressive of it. Anticipating this doubt, the author sets forth the third alternative through the mouth of the proponent of *prasaṃkhyāna*, saying: "Of seeing... [The meaning is: First of all, seeing as the very nature of the Self cannot be enjoined, because it is eternal; nor can seeing consisting of a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) having that [Self] as its form, because it is [already established]. Nor is it the face... [and so on].

Because direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) is the fruit by virtue of being a direct perception, it cannot be something to be enjoined; therefore, the effort called "contemplation" (*prasaṃkhyāna*), which is characterized by the relationship of means and end with that [intuition], is understood as the means toward direct intuition even in the phrase "one should see," just as in the expression "one should produce discernment. The connection is that [contemplation] is enjoined with respect to experience (*anubhava*). || 762 ||
Endowed with the limbs of tranquility and the like, he is adorned by the praise that "all is the Self."
The injunction "one should see" is prescribed so that reflection and the other [preliminary stages] may have purpose. || 763 ||
He clarifies what was stated as "with means" by saying "śamādi" (tranquility, etc.). The word "effort" (*prayatna*) is to be connected as the subject (*viśeṣya*).

He indicates the maxim that "whatever is enjoined is praised. Regarding the phrase "all this": this [statement] "All this is indeed this Self" is not primary, because it contradicts direct perception and other means of knowledge; therefore, since it possesses such praise, the aforementioned effort deserves to be an injunction, like the *darśa* sacrifice and others. This applies to the passage concerning "it should be reflected upon" (*mantavya*), etc.

Anticipating the objection—"Since reflection (*manana*) and so forth are enjoined elsewhere, what is the purpose of enjoining them here?"—the author says: "Reflection and so forth. For there is no injunction for them in the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa*, because that section has as its primary purport the reality (*vastu*) itself; nor can there be an injunction through a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), since an injunction is improper when syntactical unity (*vākyaikya*) is possible; and furthermore, reflection and the rest do not bear fruit unless they are enjoined. Therefore, the meaning is that an injunction is provided here so that these may possess fruit. Or, even if an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) were present there, nevertheless—

Thinking that there is an injunction for the practice of meditation here, he concludes that by the word "paśyet" (one should see), the *prasaṃkhyāna*—characterized by the act of seeing which is the meaning of the verbal root—is enjoined by the suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus: "paśyediti. || 763 ||
If the effort were "one should see," then the result would be the act of seeing itself.
If it is not the characteristic of effort, how can it be the result? (764)
212 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 233]

The proponent (siddhāntin) raises an objection, stating that it is not possible to enjoin *prasaṃkhyāna* by this [passage]: "If it is an effort [expressed by] 'one should see'... If here an effort consisting of *prasaṃkhyāna* were enjoined with the purpose of seeing (*darśana*), then seeing would be the result of that enjoined effort; it could not be its qualifier, because it would be a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of something unestablished, whereas only that which is already established can serve as such a qualifier.

If direct perception were characterized by effort, its status as a result [of that effort] would be unestablished because it is already established; therefore, it is improper for it to be both the result of an enjoined effort and the characteristic of that effort.
Thus, the meaning is that there is no room here for an injunction regarding *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative cultivation). || 764 ||
In the world, discriminative discernment is regarded as being connected with vision.
Does that [result] also exist in the Veda in such a way, or not? Therefore, it is prescribed. (765)

The proponent of *prasaṃkhyāna* says: "In the world. In the world, in the study of scriptures and so forth, *prasaṃkhyāna* is observed to be connected as a means to the fruit that is [direct] perception (*darśana*). Similarly, regarding the Veda as well, there is a doubt as to whether that *prasaṃkhyāna* is likewise a means to perception or not. Because it is perceived from this [Vedic context], *prasaṃkhyāna* is enjoined by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, since the connection between those two is established in the world, it is an indication.

The meaning is that because there is no fixed rule as to whether it exists at that time or not, the injunction applies to this [act] as characterized by that [result], since it has the nature of being the fruit of the vision. || 769 ||
Just as a medicine in general is characterized by its capacity to destroy fever.
This has been observed even in the case of severe fever; it is taught specifically [for this purpose]. 766.

He clarifies the stated point by means of an illustration: "In general" (*sāmānyena*). Just as in the world it is observed that a medicine such as the drinking of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) generally cures fever, there arises a doubt as to whether that very same medicine will also remove a severe fever of the *saṃnipāta* type and so forth.

In response to this doubt, that which is established as the cause for the removal of the intended [ordinary] fever is enjoined as the cause for destroying irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*), being characterized by the removal of the fever in question.
For it is said:
"One should administer a thin decoction that is either digestive or palliative to the fever patient after six days have passed, provided they can tolerate a light meal."
They do not settle, they do not undergo digestion, and they produce irregular fever;
therefore, one who considers the strength of equilibrium should feed the patient once the *tarpaṇa* has been fully digested.
"If the fever does not subside through these procedures,
one should pacify it with purgatives for a patient whose strength and flesh have not yet diminished."

Similarly, since in the world *prasaṃkhyāna* is observed in works such as the *Dīrghaprapāṭhaka* to be a means for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), there arises a doubt as to whether it might be so in the Veda as well. To this, it is specifically ordained that "it must indeed be so"—this is the meaning of the term *prasaṃkhyāna*. || 766 ||
Even that whose fruit is not directly known [is known] through other means of knowledge by virtue of its dependence on an injunction.
Because there is no certainty regarding non-existence, meditative discernment leads to our desired result.

Now, [the opponent argues that] contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) does not have direct realization as its fruit because it is a form of contemplation, like worldly contemplation; to this he replies: "Even though... Although even in the world, contemplation does not have the fruit of direct realization of what is unknown through other means of knowledge distinct from scripture, [nevertheless...]
1. Regarding that,
[Volume 1,
Page 234] the Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Although that fruit—direct realization—is observed [in the world], nevertheless, because the fruit is postulated in the Veda by the force of injunction (*vidhi*), realization does not arise from *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) alone; this is because there is no certainty regarding its absence [otherwise]. Therefore, for us practitioners, that [realization] is produced by that [Vedic injunction]. Consequently, inference—which contradicts the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* as its fruit—is sublated, because the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*, being non-human (*apauruṣeya*) in origin, is more authoritative than an inference conceived by a person; thus, the reverse is not the case.
This is the intended meaning. || 767 ||
The same would apply even to animals and the like; thus, there is certainty even regarding what is doubtful.
But regarding a sky-flower, because it is not an object [to be attained] through means, there is certainty regarding its opposite [non-existence]. (768)

[Objection: But surely *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is held to have a visible result; thus, as in the case of agriculture and the like, since no immediate result is seen, there is no certainty regarding its non-existence—so [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Reply: No, he says: "In the case of cattle and so forth. Even though cattle and other results of the *Citrā* sacrifice and the like are not seen immediately, when one considers whether they occur in another birth or not, there is no certainty of their non-existence; and because of the scriptural injunction, it is indeed assumed that they do occur. In the same way, *prasaṃkhyāna*...

Regarding the doubt as to whether that result arises from the realization of the fruit of manifestation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) in the immediate future or at some later time—even though it is not perceived immediately—since its non-existence cannot be determined (as is the case with the results of agriculture and the like), and because the injunction (*vidhi*) determines a result in a subsequent time, *prasaṃkhyāna* is not equal to [actions] such as ritual performance (*kārya*), but rather is similar to [sacrifices] such as the *Citrā*. This is the meaning. Even if the result is doubtful, it is established in accordance with the injunction; and if it is... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on a philosophical discussion regarding the efficacy of meditative realization versus ritual action.)

Fearing that existence (*sattva*) might be attributed even to things like sky-flowers by following that same logic, he says: "But as for the sky-flower... The meaning is this: because it is a mere nothingness (*tucchatva*), it cannot be accomplished by any means and thus simply does not exist; therefore, there is a certainty regarding the negation of its existence. Consequently, the existence of a sky-lotus and the like does not arise through the force of an injunction (*vidhi*), nor is there any injunction directed toward its existence. || 768 ||
Having thus established the method of discernment, some further [proceed].
They also maintain, through logical arguments, that its ultimate purport is the knowledge of the oneness of the Self. || 769 ||

[Objection: But surely, by one who accepts the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation), it is intended that the Vedāntas have that [contemplation] as their primary purport; therefore, since the reality [of Brahman] is not established due to the absence of a means of knowledge, there can be no injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*. For when a thing is not established, there can be no repetition of verbal cognition regarding it. To this, he replies: "In this way. Because the scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) have the reality as their purport, and because the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* is subordinate to that [reality] according to the arguments to be stated later, the reality—

The meaning is that through the establishment [of the object], there is the non-establishment of the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*. Having established the injunction regarding the subject matter of *prasaṃkhyāna* by the method stated, when there is again a doubt as to the non-establishment of the reality (*vastu*), some maintain—on the grounds of the following arguments—that since the scriptural word (*abhidhāśruti*) has the reality as its primary purport, its intention (*tātparya*) lies in the knowledge of the reality produced thereby; this applies even to the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*. Such is the construction of the verse. || 769 ||
For indeed, under the view that the Creator is independent, oneness of self is not established.
That treatise, because it is centered on injunctions, does not [establish] its own nature through explanatory passages (arthavāda).

[Objection: But surely, since it is an established principle that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the subordinate (*śeṣin*) and the scriptural statement of denotation (*abhidhāśruti*) is the subordinate (*śeṣa*), how can there be a reversal of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇapradhānatva*) in this case? [Response: To this, he says:

"In the case of the injunction," and so on. Although elsewhere than in the Vedāntas, it is indeed the rule that the injunction is the subordinate and the scriptural statement of denotation is the subordinate; yet...

The meaning is that even so, in this context, that [negation] alone is primary while that [positive injunction] is secondary; otherwise, the reality of the thing would not be established. Thinking that you yourself have stated that the reality of a thing is not established when the positive injunction is primary, he says "kila" (it is said). The sense of the word "hi" (for) is that a sentence whose primary focus is an injunction does not convey the reality of a thing, because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). To the question, "How is it that the reality of a thing is not established when the injunction is independent? he replies:

Regarding the phrase "that scripture": if the emphasis were on injunction (*vidhi*), the statement beginning with "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) would not culminate in non-duality; for, being subordinate to an injunction, it would be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
The meaning is as follows:

since an injunction would lack the capacity to be authoritative regarding its own object in the face of contradiction by perception and other means of knowledge, one who desires the establishment of reality must consider that in the Vedāntas, the injunction is subordinate while the expressive power of the words (*abhidhāśruti*) is primary. || 770 ||
Furthermore, even when this [Self] has been reached through scripture, its indirectness is not removed.
For the very purpose of realizing that [truth], meditative discernment (prasaṃkhyāna) is enjoined. || 771 ||
[Objection: "If the identity [of the Self] is established from a sentence possessing *tātparya*, what is the use of an injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*? To this, he says: "Even" (*api*).

The meaning is that even though identity is perceived from sentences such as "That thou art," because the remoteness (*pārokṣya*) inherent in it is not destroyed without direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* exists for the sake of achieving the direct intuition that destroys that [remoteness]. || 771 ||
When objects are not established through pride, there is an absence of the desire to see them.
The rule of higher discernment would not exist, even together with reflection and the other stages.

Anticipating the objection—“If the direct realization of reality (*vastu-sākṣātkāra*) were dependent on the injunction for contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna-vidhi*), what would be the use of the scripture?”—the author says: “By means of valid cognition” (*mānena*).

If the reality were not established by the scripture, there could be no desire for its direct realization; yet, once it is understood [through scripture], there is a restriction [to that specific means] because it cannot be established otherwise. Therefore, since the injunction for contemplation along with its means would not be possible if directed toward a direct realization [of something unknown], the reality must be known through the scripture.
This is the meaning. || 772 ||
One who has learned the nature of the self from scripture [knows] even that which is not personally experienced.
For one who desires a stable state, the practice of self-investigation according to the scriptures is prescribed. (773)

[Objection: But if that knowledge is indeed experienced through the scripture, then because knowledge and experience are one, otherwise it would simply not be known; thus, there can be no injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) with a view toward direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). To this, he says: "From the Śruti. For although a person who is learned, having engaged in the inquiry into the subject matter of the true nature [of the Self] based on such sentences as "That thou art," might not have experienced the state which is his very own nature, nevertheless...

The meaning is that, because of the authority of the scriptures and the certainty that the experience of reality will arise through *prasaṃkhyāna*, the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* is taught by the words "one who desires that [should see]," and so forth. || 773 ||
A treatise brings about the understanding of its own subject matter solely by means of its own specific function.
But it is not because of the absence of an operation that the scripture lacks a twofold purpose. || 774 ||

Fearing that if the scripture were both the means of awakening one to the reality (*vastu*) and the prescriber of *prasaṃkhyāna*, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to having two distinct purposes, he says: "By its own operation" (*sva-vyāpāra*). The meaning is that since *prasaṃkhyāna* is the operation of the scripture, and through that [operation] it brings about the awakening to its own subject matter, there is no split in the sentence because there is not actually a duality of objects. Without the operation called *prasaṃkhyāna*, it does not bring about the awakening to its own subject matter.

He establishes that the treatise possesses the function of stating [its meaning] by means of the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*). With the words "But not," he states the conclusion: that for a sentence which makes known a reality through a positive injunction (*vidhi*), there is no duality of purpose. With the words "Not therefore," he explains that duality of purpose consists in the communication of two distinct meanings, each of which is primary. || 774 ||
Nor is it established that causal factors conceal their own respective operations.
Therefore, when the intended purport is the unity of the self, practices such as *prasaṃkhyāna* are well-established.

[Vol. 1, p. 236] Anticipating the objection that if *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative realization) constitutes the operation of the scripture, then the scripture—being mediated by it—would not convey its own meaning, there is the following *vārttika*, accompanied by the commentary (*ṭīkā*) titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 215. [The *vārttika*: "But this is not so; for the scripture is not dependent on anything else. [The *ṭīkā*: This is not so; for the scripture does not depend on anything else. Why? Because the scripture is established as authoritative by itself alone, through the very fact of its being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*). It is not the case that the scripture, having first produced a cognition of its own meaning, subsequently depends upon another means of valid knowledge to establish that meaning. Therefore, since the scripture is established as authoritative by itself alone, it is not dependent on anything else. Consequently, even if *prasaṃkhyāna* is the operation of the scripture, the scripture does not fail to convey its own meaning. For the scripture, having first produced a cognition of its own meaning, establishes that very meaning through the subsequent operation of *prasaṃkhyāna*. Thus, the scripture is indeed dependent on something else, but this dependence does not contradict its status as a means of valid knowledge. Just as the eye, though dependent on light and so forth, remains a means of valid knowledge, so too the scripture, though dependent on *prasaṃkhyāna*, remains a means of valid knowledge. Therefore, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the scripture is not dependent on anything else because it is established as authoritative by itself alone. He says "its own operation" (*svavyāpāra*) according to the maxim that "one's own limb does not act as an obstruction.

Since the direct realization of reality (*vastu-sākṣātkāra*) is not established without the injunction for contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna-vidhi*), and since such an injunction is impossible apart from the scriptural cognition of reality, he concludes: "Therefore," [it is logical] that even though the *Tattvamasi* and other such texts have reality as their primary purport, there exists the injunction for contemplation, and that this [injunction] stands in a subordinate relationship (*śeṣatva*) to that [realization]. || 775 ||
Nor does the state of identity with the Supreme persist in the interval.
Until the attainment of the goals of human existence, the scripture is clearly [authoritative], out of fear of invalidity. (776)

Having raised the objection that since the human goal is accomplished through the knowledge of identity derived from the scripture, direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is of no use, and therefore what is the point of *prasaṃkhyāna* for that purpose, he says: "Having made known" (*bodhayitvā*). Having made known the oneness through sentences such as "That Thou Art," the [scripture] does not venture to stop midway without reaching the culmination in the direct realization that is the means to liberation; for the human goal cannot be fully accomplished by the mere indirect cognition arising from the sentence alone.

Since validity is impossible in the absence of a substratum (*dharmin*) and the consequent lack of determination regarding the human goal, and since it is not possible to deny validity clearly without a reason, the meaning is that for this purpose the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* is prescribed, because the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) which is the cause of liberation is required. || 776 ||
For a word, by its very nature, expresses its own meaning through an indirect mode of operation.
Accepting reasoning as a means of valid cognition, he proceeds by honoring it. || 777 ||

In that case, one might suspect that the scripture, having been introduced with reference to *niyoga* (an injunction), will produce direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) and not through reasoning; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Indirect" (*parokṣa*). It is the nature of words to convey a mixed and indirect cognition, as seen in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). By virtue of that [nature], this word also functions toward an object that is mixed and indirect. And while expressing its own object in such a manner through that function, [the scripture]—insofar as it is of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*)—[does not require human reasoning].

The meaning is that, by not suspecting any defects in himself and by considering his own [cognition] to be valid, he employs even reasoning as an auxiliary for the sake of reaching the final result, thereby directly perceiving the reality; for reasoning is also a constituent part of valid cognition. || 777 ||
And she too is incapable of realizing the true nature [of things], just as smoke is [incapable] regarding fire.
The analytical investigation regarding the object proceeds precisely by means of the feminine grammatical gender. || 778 ||

One might object: "In that case, let reason alone be the auxiliary to the scripture, since the awakening of the knowledge of reality occurs through reason assisted by scripture; what is the use of injunction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "yāthātmya... (regarding the true nature). Even when accompanied by scripture, that reason is not capable of bringing about the direct perception of the reality, because both [scripture and reason] are equally characterized by being indirect (parokṣa) in their operation—just as smoke, even when assisted by a verbal statement, cannot directly [perceive] fire.

In the same way, even when supported by the aforementioned reasoning, logic alone cannot bring about the direct realization of reality; rather, it brings about the understanding of the reality only by taking up the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna* as its auxiliary. This is the meaning. || 778 ||
In this manner, through such a path, the scripture directly establishes the reality.
Having accepted its primacy with respect to the ritual procedure, it attains the status of a means of valid cognition. || 779 ||

Intending to show that even in the other "foot" (pāda) called the Self (*ātman*), there is dependence upon reasoning (*yukti*) and contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) as taught in the scripture (*śāstra*), he concludes that the means of knowledge (*māna*) consists of four parts. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): by the word "scripture" (*śāstra*), reasoning and contemplation are denoted; and together with the "Self," which is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), these three directly make known the reality. Thus, taking primacy with respect to injunction (*vidhi*) and the rest, the means of knowledge is four-footed.
The meaning is that you attain it. || 779 ||
216 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 237]
It awakens the unity that is devoid even of the conceptualization of association.
In this very manner, a treatise, even when expressing a composite meaning, [is to be understood]. (780)

Anticipating the objection that "the scripture does not directly cause one to know the reality, because its very nature is to convey a mediated (parokṣa) and associated (saṃsṛṣṭa) understanding, and it is impossible for it to abandon its own nature even through the influence of auxiliary factors," he says: "Through association... Although the scripture expresses an associated and mediated object, nevertheless, by means of the distinction of auxiliaries such as *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation), it brings about the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that reality which is free from such conceptual constructions, unassociated, and immediate.
