The meaning is that there is no contradiction in its initiating another effect through the attainment of auxiliary causes (sahakāri), just as in the cases of curd or poison. ||780||
This has been shown by the scripture itself in the passage: "from which words turn back."
Brahman is fearless, with all conceptualization of association completely cast aside.

He states the proof for the fact that oneness is devoid of the conceptualization of association: "Since... The mention of the apprehension of a relation is intended to indicate indirectness (*pārokṣya*). He states that the knowledge of Brahman as described is the cause of the human goal: "Fearless... (781).
But if it is not expressed by the scripture, then it is not tenable even in the case of an injunction.
Since entry [into cognition] occurs by way of being an object, the objection is equal for both. || 782 ||

[Objection: Surely, when the true nature of reality (*vastu-yāthātmya*) is established by this scripture, that reality cannot enter into the injunction for meditative cultivation (*prasaṃkhyāna-vidhi*), because those who know it have accomplished their purpose without an injunction; therefore, he says: "By the scripture," etc. [He explains: Since, as shown by the words "because" (*yataḥ*) and so forth, if the reality were not denoted by the scripture, its entry into the injunction would be improper, as it would become an object of the verbal cognition whose scope is the enjoined meditative cultivation; for [the reality] is not known through the word...

Because that would contradict its status as an object of verbal cognition, the objection is equal in both cases—whether the reality is expressed or not expressed by the scripture—since it is impossible for it to enter into the injunction (*vidhi*). For a reality revealed by scripture does not enter into an injunction insofar as it is of the nature of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), nor does that which is not revealed by it enter into it, because what is unknown cannot be known to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to an injunction; and there is nothing other than scripture that can convey the reality.
The meaning is "whom. The word "api" (also/even) is to be joined after the word "dvayoḥ" (of the two). || 782 ||
Without ritual procedure, one who has heard of the oneness [of all things] lacks the experience of that reality.
Out of ignorance regarding the skillful means, one might treat that scripture as being merely of the nature of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). || 783 ||

In that case, let it be granted that the reality (vastu) does not enter into the scope of an injunction; for even without that, the attainment of the fruit results from the knowledge of the reality derived from the sacred scripture (śruti). With this intention, he says: "The injunction... [vidhim]. If the injunction for contemplation (prasaṃkhyāna) is not accepted, one who has heard the truth would render the scripture teaching the reality invalid, because of the non-acceptance of the means to experience called contemplation, and because the scripture [would appear] ignorant of other means for that [experience].

Furthermore, because there is an absence of the experience of that object [of knowledge] as it truly is, one must therefore accept this as an injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative realization), since without it the fruit is not accomplished and the scripture would lose its authority.
Thus, the sense is that the object known through the scripture in a superficial manner enters into the scope of the injunction. || 783 ||
Even in a scripture based on injunction, there would be a cognition of a real entity because it is not unestablished.
The fruit, which is the realization of identity, should be understood as being like the meditation on a deity. || 784 ||

Having raised the objection—given that the fruit depends on the injunction as previously described, how can it be said that the verbal testimony (*abhidhā-śruti*) is subordinate to that [injunction] because of its primacy?—the author elaborates on the statement "for under the view of the independence of the injunction" (*vidhi-svātantrya-pakṣe hi*). He says: "The injunction... If the injunction were primary, then in the scripture concerning the knowledge of reality (*tattva*), such as the *Prasaṃkhyāna-vidhi*, [it would follow that...]. "Tastadu. [End of fragment].

And since that [injunction] is subsidiary to it (the Upanishad), its purport lies elsewhere; therefore, when there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, the cognition of the reality [of Brahman] cannot be established through that injunction, as the knowledge of oneness is [attained otherwise].
[Vol. 1, Page 238] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

217. And because that [injunction] is subsidiary to it, its purport lies elsewhere; therefore, when there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, the cognition of the reality [of Brahman] cannot be established through that injunction, as the knowledge of oneness is [attained otherwise].

The fruit must be postulated. Just as the attainment of that state [of the deity] is postulated as the fruit of the worship of a deity—since the scriptural passage beginning with "having become that very deity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.4.1) understands that state because that passage primarily concerns its worship, and thus, by the force of that very [worship], it merely restates the attainment of that state—therefore, in the case of a scripture concerning reality, the injunction is subordinate while the reality is primary. Even though the injunction holds primacy as the cause of the fruit, nevertheless, regarding that fruit, which is the knowledge of reality...

The meaning is this: because of the principle of "that which one intends" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), the scripture whose subject matter is the reality (*vastu*) has primacy; however, meditation on the deity (*devatādhyāna*) has its own primacy [as a means]. Furthermore, even though *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is enjoined, it lacks authoritative status (*apramāṇa*) and cannot be the cause for the realization of reality. Therefore, the scripture concerning reality is not merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*). || 784 ||
One who has realized the true nature of the self no longer perceives through discursive meditation and the like.
But the ignorant person, even if made to hear this, does not obtain that fruit without [the teacher]. || 785 ||

Fearing the charge of infinite regress—that even one who has understood the identity of Brahman and the Self through the scriptures might still require *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation) and so forth, and thus, despite knowing the reality, would depend on that [contemplation]—he says: "Having realized... (*pratipanna*). If it is argued that one who has known the reality through *prasaṃkhyāna* and the like does not require it again, then one who has known the reality from the scriptures should likewise not require it, since there is no difference between the two cases; anticipating this, he says: "But the ignorant one... (*ajñas tu*). [This refers to one who is] not direct...

The meaning is this: even one for whom the reality has been established and who has been made to hear the truth nine times through the mantra "That thou art," does not attain direct realization—the fruit of hearing—without *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment); for even one who has heard the scriptural statement lacks that [realization] if he is devoid of it. || 785 ||
Even though this treatise is grounded in objective reality, [it would be incomplete] without the injunction for contemplative realization (prasaṃkhyāna).
"The human goal is certainly not attained"—this [objection] too has been addressed. || 786 ||
The experience of oneness cannot arise through positive and negative concomitance.
Only upon the establishment of those two would that [relation] exist, and that [relation] would [in turn] establish them; thus it is a circular dependency.

He concludes the discussion regarding the requirement for the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) in the Vedāntas with the words "In this scripture. Raising the objection—namely, that since the direct realization of reality is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone, what is the use of *prasaṃkhyāna* and the like?—he explains what was stated there [in the previous verse] regarding the inability [of those means] to bring about the comprehension of the true nature of things, beginning with the words "Not by positive and negative concomitance. Positive and negative concomitance, consisting of the discrimination between the seer and the seen and so forth, are independent and do not depend upon the scripture.

He states the reason for the claim that reasoning (*yukti*) does not bring about the direct experience (*anubhava*) of a thing (*vastu*) with the words, "In the establishment of that" (*tatsiddhau*). For those two [reasoning and the experience] occur when [the thing] is already known; yet there is no knowledge of the thing from anything else, because independent reasoning lacks the status of being its cause. Therefore, since the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exist when there is the experience of the thing, and that [experience] exists by means of them, the meaning is that a clear circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) is evident. || 786 || 787 ||
Just as in the case of the term "Viśvajit sacrifice," there is the preservation of its own primary meaning.
Acting thus, she displayed her pride along with those who desired heaven as they departed. || 788 ||

In that case, one might suspect that since reality is experienced through scripture (*śāstra*) and reasoning (*yukti*) alone, *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) is useless; anticipating this, [the author] provides an example to show that those two [scripture and reasoning] convey their own meaning in dependence upon it. He says "as follows" (*yathā*). The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," there arises a doubt as to whether the word "Viśvajit" is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or the name of a rite (*karmanāman*). If it were an injunction of the rite, the mention of the accessory would be purposeless; therefore, in the injunction of that [accessory], that...

Because the action [of recitation] possesses purposefulness through its capacity to impart a specific qualification to the locus of expectation (*apekṣā*), and because the necessity of performing it does not depend on other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), there is no invalidity of the sentence; nor is there [any contradiction], for it is characterized [as such]. 28. kha. lakṣyate.
[Vol. 1, Page 239] 218 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection]

It is established in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* that when an injunction (*vidhi*) is encountered, because its object is the efficient force (*bhāvārtha*), it is understood as enjoining that very force by its own nature; furthermore, since the word "Viśvajit" is the name of that [sacrifice], the sentence possesses independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*). Thus, these two words, following their own respective meanings as objects, when connected with the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), convey the authoritative status of the injunction (*niyoga*). For what [else] could there be here, since an injunction without an eligible person (*niradhikāra*) is heard?

When there is doubt as to whether an agent (*niyojya*) should be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or not—given that the expression of the connection between the object and the action reaches its completion [without it]—if no such supply is made, the action must be defined by the effort (*kṛti*) required to accomplish it; and just as that effort is defined by the verbal root-meaning which is its own effect, it is unavoidable that it is also defined by the person who is its locus. Consequently, through that medium, the agent also becomes connected to the action, and it is precisely the cognizer of that [action] who [is the agent] in relation to himself.

Since it is established that an agent (*niyojya*) must be supplied to complete the sense of the subject matter through its connection [with the injunction], a doubt arises as to whether all [words] or only one should be supplied. Upon reaching the initial conclusion that all should be supplied due to the lack of distinction, it is settled that only one should be supplied because the expectancy is satisfied by a single element. Then, when the question remains as to which one—anyone at random or specifically "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—it is determined that it must be "one who desires heaven," for otherwise there would be no restriction due to the lack of distinction; thus, that heaven would belong to everyone without qualification.

In the passage beginning with "because it is established," it is determined in the fourth [book] that only one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is to be supplied; thus, the authority for these two and their connection [to the result] is established. || 788 ||
In the same way, the preservation of its own subject matter is achieved through scripture and reasoning.
While they were acting thus, he attained the state of being honored; it could not have been otherwise through mere enumeration.

He applies the meaning established in the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). The word "thus" (*tathā*) means that, by means of the aforementioned illustration, scripture (*śāstra*) and reasoning (*yukti*), when conjoined with contemplative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), attain the status of valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) regarding the reality. It is only together with contemplative discernment that scripture and reasoning possess validity regarding the reality; in the absence of such association, words and reasoning merely convey an object indirectly and, being incomplete, do not [attain full validity].
He says that in the case of wind there is a state of being measured; it is not otherwise. || 789 ||
Thus, even though the purport of the scripture is established through reasoning as being solely oneness, [the following objection arises].
Some also maintain that it is an effect; for that reason, it is not tenable. || 790 ||

He concludes the discourse on *prasaṃkhyāna* with the word "thus" (*evam*). The construction is as follows: even though it has been accepted that the purport of the scripture lies in the ultimate reality (*vastu*), some still maintain that within the Vedāntas there is also a task consisting of the object of *prasaṃkhyāna*, by means of the methods previously described for liberation.

The phrase "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) means "for the sake of the experience of the identity of the Self. He anticipates a defect in the doctrine of *prasaṃkhyāna* with the words "that is not so" (*tan na*). || 790 ||
"Since the triad beginning with the knower possesses a body consisting solely of pure consciousness,"
That which was previously unestablished becomes established; once it is established, what further dependence does it have? || 791 ||

If it is asked how this is improper, [the answer is: the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* is for the purpose of establishing that reality, or for the purpose of removing the remoteness associated with it, or for the purpose of concluding its non-establishment,
or for the purpose of dispelling the darkness regarding it, or for the purpose of making it directly manifest, or for the purpose of liberation from that very [reality].

Having thus conceptualized [the opponent's view], he refutes it with the words "pramātrādi" (the knower, etc.). He states the reason for its independence from anything else in establishing itself with the word "saṃvit" (consciousness).

By the phrase "siddhyaty eva" (it is established), he indicates that the existence and manifestation of the knower and so forth are merely appearances within consciousness. He provides the reason for its insentience (*jāḍya*) in the absence of self-luminosity and the like, with the words "aprasiddham" (unestablished). || 791 ||

Even that real entity which is otherwise remote [from direct perception], because it is of the nature of the witness-self, [is directly known]. [Vol. 1, Page 240] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 219.
Since it appears directly as if it were the Self itself, how can there be a notion of its being remote? (792)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "parokṣam" (indirect). The meaning is this: since the non-self entity such as the ego (ahaṃkāra) is experienced by [the witness-consciousness], and because that [consciousness] is its very self, it manifests as if directly present and like the Self itself; therefore, it is improper to conceive of it as indirect. Consequently, there can be no injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* even for the purpose of destroying the notion of indirectness regarding that [entity]. || 792 ||
“Even ignorance and the like, which cause the obstruction of all objects of knowledge without exception...”
Since it would be established by that which is self-established, how could there be a lack of establishment for it? || 793 ||

He states the third [point] with the word "api" (also). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), doubt and false knowledge are meant. Since even the entire veil over the object of knowledge, such as ignorance and the like, is established solely by virtue of the self-luminous reality, it is impossible for the proving reality itself to remain unestablished; therefore, the meaning is that *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) need not be enjoined even for the purpose of removing those [veils]. || 793 ||
He who is established by his own majesty alone, and who is the innermost self of all.
For one who has transcended passion and delusion, what other effect could there be that is produced from such valid cognition? (794)

The fourth [verse] replies: "By its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*). One might object that, just as the body and so forth are established as being dependent upon their respective internal selves (*pratyagātman*), so too the Self must have its establishment dependent on something else within itself; therefore, it does not possess establishment by its own majesty. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "All... (*sarva-*) and so on. In that regard, the fruit produced by the functioning of a means of knowledge (*māna*) is simply the destruction of the ignorance residing therein; thus, since the destruction of the darkness (*tamas*) inherent in the reality is the effect of the means of knowledge, there is no need for further effort for that purpose either.
He states the method of manifestation: "That is darkness" (794).
Even when the triad beginning with the mother is lost, it is perceived as the witness of that loss.
Since his sense organs are not impaired, how could there be such remoteness from that [object]? (795)

He states the fifth [reason]: "mātrādi" (the mother, etc.). The meaning is that since the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the eternal light of consciousness, is understood from scripture and other sources as the witness of the existence and non-existence of the mother and so forth—that is, of the enjoyer, the agent, and the rest—it cannot be something remote; because immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is its very nature, there is no injunction even for the sake of that [immediacy]. || 795 ||
Just as the meaning of an injunction is impossible when there is identity with the path of cultivation (bhāvanā).
This has been explained previously in the *Adhikāraparīkṣā*. || 796 ||

"Now, beginning with the words 'Is liberation like worldly prosperity?', an examination of the qualification for the path of injunction (*vidhi-mārga*) proceeds; and it has been stated in the *Adhikāra-vārtikas* that the examiners do not accept a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) here that is devoid of the three factors. Therefore, having raised the objection that the practice occurring subsequent to verbal cognition is what is enjoined, a resolution was given. Consequently, since that injunction is also refuted here, [the author] says 'meditative cultivation' (*bhāvanā*) to avoid redundancy. [End of quote from Vārtika]

The meaning is that, having raised the objection regarding injunctions in the Vedāntas according to the opinion of the author of the *Kakāra*, I have already stated in the *Adhikāravārtika*—in passages such as "Therefore, an injunction is useless"—that there is an absence of any function for such an injunction. || 796 ||
How the meaning of an injunction is impossible when relying on the theory of *niyoga*.
Just as it was established with effort in the *Aikātmyasiddhi*, so too is it demonstrated here. || 797 ||
1. Not so; it is not directly its own nature. 2. Ba.
states: [Vol. 1, page 241] 220.

In this context, however, having raised the objection regarding an injunction for the practice of knowledge according to the view of Brahmadatta and others, it is refuted; thus he says, "niyoga... (verse 797), [to show] that there is no tautology therein.
The self is by its very nature liberated; its state of bondage arises from ignorance of that [nature].
There is a dependence on a means of proof regarding an object to be proven; once it is established, one does not depend upon such a means. || 798 ||

He refutes the sixth [position] with the words "of the single self" (*aikātmyasya*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "there is no requirement for an injunction. Then, how can the notion that the self is bound exist there? [The answer is] "due to ignorance" (*ajñānāt*). He states the conclusion regarding the first quarter-verse with the word "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). || 798 ||
Because it is obscured by the constituent of darkness (tamas), the reality known as the single self (aikātmya) [is not perceived].
Since that [means] accomplishes what is unaccomplishable, what need is there for cultivation? (799)

Raising the objection that if liberation is self-established and thus independent of any means of accomplishment, then knowledge too would be useless, [the author] states the intended meaning regarding the passage beginning with "from ignorance" (ajñānāt) and so forth: "merely darkness" (tamomātra). The sense is this: although there is no requirement for the practice of an injunction regarding a reality that is devoid of the distinction between the goal and the means, knowledge exists in order to obscure the opposing darkness. || 799 ||
When that which is to be accomplished is perceived as an effect for one who desires experience.
How can it be said that the purpose of that [state] is identity with *prasaṃkhyāna*? || 800 ||

If it is argued that even though there is no injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) as a direct means to liberation, it is nevertheless a means to it by virtue of being a supplement to knowledge (*jñānaśeṣatva*), and thus its prescription for the sake of liberation is logical— the author says "no," beginning with the words "yadā" (when). When an injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* is established for one who desires immediate realization (*sākṣātkāra*), then the Upanishads (*vedānta*) would have no purport regarding non-dual identity (*aikātmya*), because they would be devoted solely to the aforementioned injunction.
This is the meaning. || 800 ||
That it is both an effect and something other than its cause—these two [claims] are contradictory.
For that which is to be accomplished must always be performed as something distinct for the sake of its establishment.

Having raised the objection that because the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation) is a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) dependent on an existing entity, the Vedāntas—which form a single syntactical unit with it—must also terminate in unity, he says: "And [if] the effect... He establishes the contradiction by means of the principle of the "already existent and what is to be brought into being" (*bhūtabhavyanyāya*). For that which is to be accomplished... || 801 ||
Experience, being a qualification of the person to be enjoined, constitutes the fruit.
The object is real; the enumeration [of its parts] is not a means for the apprehension [of the whole]. (802)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)—known as *prasaṃkhyāna*—is also enjoined as a means for attaining experience? And thus, because of that injunction, its status as the primary purport (*tatparatva*) is necessary? Anticipating this objection, the author concedes the point and then refutes it with the words "the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇam*). Experience, being the differentiator for the person to be exhorted (*niyojya*)—who understands the task as his own duty in the form "one desiring experience should perform *prasaṃkhyāna*"—is [merely] enjoined.

The meaning is as follows: you state that "contemplation" (*prasaṃkhyāna*) is the fruit [of practice]; however, contemplation—which is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*) by virtue of being its conceptual correlate—does not directly cause the realization of the reality, because realization is the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*māna*), whereas contemplation is not itself a means of valid cognition. || 802 ||
1 ka. ga. viṣayaṃ | 2 kha. 'dhairvastuparaṃ | [Vol.
1, page 242] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 221
How could the duty, which has as its object the meaning of the verbal root, exist in the state of higher discernment?
For it is established that *prasaṃkhyāna* (thorough examination) is indeed a repeated application of both verbal testimony and logical reasoning. (803)

Having accepted that *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), its status as a means to direct experience has been set aside; now [the author] states that it does not even have that as its object. He says: "Because it consists of the meaning of a verbal root" (*bhāvārtha*). If it is argued that, because it too consists of the meaning of a verbal root, it must have that as its object just like a sacrifice, he says: "Repetition" (*āvṛtti*). Since you accept that *prasaṃkhyāna* is the repetition of hearing and reflection, it cannot be so, because it is merely the repetition of an action.
The meaning is "the state of being an action. || 803 ||
Now, if it is maintained that the duty has as its object the meaning of the state of hearing;
In that case, there would be only hearing; the object [of cognition] would be distinct from you.

"In that case, let there be no injunction regarding *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative realization) in the Vedāntas; nevertheless, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) have the nature of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha*), the injunction will concern them. And thus, how could they transgress the injunction?"—with this he raises an objection. [The author] replies with "But then" (*tathā ca... atha*), stating that in that case the initial proposition would be destroyed. For you have desired the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of hearing and reflection as something to be enjoined; by abandoning that, [you are left with] hearing and so forth alone.

If it is held that the injunction has a specific scope [limited to ritual action], then you would be abandoning your own thesis; moreover, we ourselves accept that there is an injunction regarding hearing and so forth, whether in the context of an object or within a [philosophical] treatise, because of the syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
The underlying sense is that hearing and so forth must be enjoined in order for the engagement of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) to be based upon the scripture. || 804 ||
Even where a fruit is mentioned, it refers to the repetition [of the rite] performed by one who is capable.
The fruit [accrues] from the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice and others when accompanied by their accessories; even there, it does not arise from the accessory alone.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice and others, a fruit is desired from a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), as they say: "In the context of the established *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, a fruit is stated to result from a subordinate quality; no separate sacrifice is enjoined"? And so, in the present case as well, since the attainment of direct realization occurs through the door of injunction based on the subordinate quality of the repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, there is no loss of the initial proposition. To this, he says: "In the *Dākṣāyaṇa* and others. This refers even to cases such as the *Dākṣāyaṇa-Agnihotra*.

The literal meaning is this: the fruit is desired by virtue of a prescribed repetition (*āvṛtti*); even in that case, the attainment of the desired heaven and so forth is ordained from the very ritual action (*bhāvārtha*) designated as the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice and others—which possess the quality of repetition—and not from the mere accessory (*guṇa*) alone. This is the underlying idea: according to the principle, "In the case of the *Ayana*s, there is a separate injunction because of the attachment of a distinct name" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 2.3.5), the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* is [distinct] from the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the sake of attaining heaven...

"One desiring desire should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya; one desiring progeny should sacrifice with the Saṃkramaṇa-sacrifice"—thus it is heard in scripture.

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether another action is enjoined there, or whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the very two rites previously mentioned, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that because these rites are heard of in connection with the *Ayana* sacrifices—which possess the quality of repetition—and because of the difference in their names, they must be injunctions of distinct actions, [the author] establishes the conclusion through the enthusiasm of Dakṣa...

Since these *dākṣās* belong to the sacrificer Dakṣa, and their *ayanam* (course) is a repetition (*āvṛtti*), the term *dākṣāyaṇa* applies by virtue of its connection with the quality of repetition to the very same *darśa* and other sacrifices under discussion; for the Śruti states: "He is indeed named Dakṣa; because he sacrificed with this [sacrifice] first, therefore it is called the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*.

Likewise, since the term *sākaṃprasthāyīya* applies to that very same sacrifice by virtue of its connection with the quality of proceeding together (*sahaprasthāna*), it does not denote a separate ritual action.

The term *ravidhi* (repetition-injunction) is established as the defining characteristic of differentiation (*bheda*). For it has been stated: "Or it is a modification (*vikāra*), because of the context" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 2.3.8). Thus, the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice and others are modifications of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and so forth; for in this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be upheld.

222 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [The Meaning of the Sūtra on the Connection]: Thus, it being established that the fruit arises from the qualified action under discussion, even the mere repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— [is not the cause].
It does not require an injunction for the sake of direct realization. || 805 ||
Even in cases where a quality such as curd and the like is considered the delimiting factor of the effect.
That [attainment] also occurs through the penetration of the meaning of the verbal root when this [state] has been reached, but not by itself.

[Objection: Just as in such injunctions as "He offers with curd" (*atha dadhnā juhoti*), even though the quality (*guṇa*) such as curd lacks the nature of being a verbal action (*bhāvārthatva*), it is nonetheless something to be enjoined (*vidheya*); let it be accepted that repetition (*āvṛtti*) is also enjoined even without having the nature of a verbal action. To this, he says: "The quality" (*guṇa*). Even in a sentence where a quality such as curd is enjoined—

Even in that case where [an action] is desired, it delimits the effect only through its connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); for no injunction is perceived for that which is not colored by such a root-meaning. Therefore, the meaning here is that it is not merely the non-performance of an action that is enjoined for the sake of a specific result. He states another distinction between the injunction regarding the repetition of hearing and so forth (*śravaṇādyāvṛtti*) and the injunction regarding curd and the like (*dadhyādividhi*), beginning with the words "And when [it is] already established" (*prāpte ca*). This refers to the case where the act of offering (*juhoti*) is already established by the rule, "One offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

The meaning is as follows: when the act [of offering] is being restated by the verb occurring in a sentence such as "with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the curd and so forth are enjoined as qualifiers of that act; however, since the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is already established, there can be no injunction of it in itself without its contact with a verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*). For this is established in the second book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]: "The Āghāra and Agnihotra are not [independent acts] because they lack a specific form" (*āghārāgnihotram arūpatvāt*, PuMīSū 2.2.13). Having stated "one performs the Agnihotra," the texts "one offers with curd" and so forth are heard regarding the Āghāra.

Having stated "he pours out" (*āghārayati*), [the texts] further state "he pours out continuously" (*saṃtatam āvārayati*) and so forth; therein, by means of such injunctions as "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "he pours out continuously," actions qualified by specific accessories (*guṇa*) are enjoined. Regarding these, there arises a doubt: are the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* mere restatements (*anuvāda*) of established collections [of acts], or are two entirely new (*apūrva*) actions enjoined by them, while the other [injunctions] are merely accessory prescriptions? In this regard, concerning the *agnihotra* and the *āghāra*—

Since the form of the *agnihotra* and other rites is not perceived as qualified by substance and deity in the original injunctions (*vākya*), whereas it is perceived in the subsidiary injunctions (*guṇavākya*) concerning them, the injunction of those [substances and deities] is established in those very [subsidiary] passages; thus, the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collective whole. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: the *homa* (oblation) and *āghāra* (pouring) must be performed. Since the meaning of the words "he offers" (*juhoti*) and so forth consists in the act of performance, what is intended here is the injunction of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*). Because of their proximity to that [original injunction], the [subsidiary] substances and deities are mentioned for the purpose of specifying the qualities.

Regarding the passage beginning with *juhoti*, the repeated mention of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) or for the purpose of connecting a subordinate element (*guṇa*). Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the injunctions “He performs the Agnihotra” and “He pours the Āghāra libation,” there is an original injunction of the ritual action (*karma-vidhi*), while within those very contexts, the sentences concerning curd and other substances constitute injunctions of subordinate elements (*guṇa-vidhi*).

And it has been said: “Or rather, it is an injunction (*codanā*) because the meaning of the word constitutes the performance; the repeated mention is for the sake of a subordinate element due to its proximity. (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.2.13).
Thus, the sense is: how can there be an injunction for mere repetition in the absence of the coloring (uparāga) of an already attained objective state? || 806 ||
Nor is there attainment through hearing and so forth, nor is a fruit heard from the qualities.
For the mere meaning of the verbal root "to see" (paśyet) is heard in the scripture as the object [of the injunction]. || 807 ||

"Let it be then that one should see [the Self] after becoming concentrated. To this, he replies with the words "of hearing and so forth," meaning that even here, although there is a restatement of the already established hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means, the injunction is for their repetition. He explains why: in the passage concerning "one who is tranquil" (*śānta*), there is no attainment of hearing and so forth because of the absence of words denoting them; nor is there such attainment in the passage "one should hear" (*śrotavya*), nor in the passage concerning "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*)—such as "he is a scholar" (*paṇḍitaḥ*) or "he is wise" (*medhāvī*)—nor in the passage "desire to know that" (*tadvijijñāsasva*).

The meaning is that there is no injunction for repetition qualified by those [well-known factors], because there is neither a restatement of well-known hearing and so forth at the beginning of such passages, nor is there here a word that functions as a restating term or a word expressing repetition. Furthermore, due to the non-hearing of a fruit resulting from the quality of repetition, it cannot be an object of injunction; however, this is not the case with curd and the like.
(Note: *ka* reads *yārūpāvṛ*).
[Vol.
1, Page 244] *Vārtika*, accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 223.

He states that it is established in the section concerning the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*) that that which is colored by a future result is to be enjoined, because of the scriptural mention of a specific fruit. [He says: "The qualities..."

The sense is this: nor can the result be postulated according to the *viśvajit*-rule (the principle that a result must be assumed for every action), because when an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is already accepted, that rule does not apply; furthermore, seeing (*darśana*) is not the result of the quality [of meditation], since its result is hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, nor is liberation its result, since liberation is the result of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Then, whose injunction is "one should see"? For this is not an injunction for hearing and the rest, as seeing is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with those.

Since being a means (*sādhanatva*) does not depend on an injunction, and even if it did, that [status] has already been enjoined elsewhere; furthermore, this is not an injunction for tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, because they are not seen after the verb *paśyet* (one should see), nor is it an injunction for the act of seeing itself, as you yourself do not admit that seeing is something to be enjoined. Therefore, by process of elimination, he says "for [the text says] 'one should see'" to show that there is no injunction for repetition (*āvṛtti*), since scripture clearly indicates that seeing alone is the object of the injunction. Thus, repetition is not what is enjoined here.
This is the meaning. || 807 ||
Nor can the non-occurrence of that which is characterized by it be enjoined, because that would involve abandoning what is directly heard in the scripture.
How could that effect [arise] from the repetition of a quality, since it does not even arise from the meaning of the verbal root?

As for the argument that because the act of seeing (*darśana*) itself cannot be enjoined, the repetition (*āvṛtti*) characterized by it must be enjoined—the author refutes this with the words "Nor also" (*nāpi*). The meaning is that it is not proper to abandon the injunction heard in the scripture regarding the act of seeing and instead enjoin an unmentioned repetition, for that would entail the fallacy of discarding what is heard and assuming what is not heard. An objection is raised:

"Even if unmentioned, an injunction might apply when the mentioned one is impossible; however, an injunction of 'seeing' (*dṛṣṭi*) is not appropriate here, because that [seeing] is the very nature [of the meditation] and its fruit."
Since it has already been stated that [the Self] is not a fit object for injunction, there is no fault here such as the abandonment of what is heard in scripture; therefore, he says: "The effect.

That result which is not produced from an action does not arise from a quality consisting in the repetition of that action. For one who is afraid of the cold and fails to obtain the cessation of suffering by immersing himself in extremely cold water, does not attain its destruction by repeating that immersion. Therefore, [this applies to] verbal knowledge—

The point is this: since direct realization arises from the cessation of that [misconception], and because the injunction regarding the [wrong] view is not authoritative, even if what was heard is abandoned, the cessation of what was not heard cannot be enjoined for the sake of direct realization. || 808 ||
Even when an object has been understood by oneself, if one still requires logical reasoning and the like;
In this way, the scripture would be dependent [on something else], because its own intrinsic validity is abandoned. || 809 ||

Having refuted the prescriptiveness of *prasaṃkhyāna* on the grounds that it is merely a means to direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), [the author] reiterates what was stated previously—that the scripture depends upon reasoning and so forth even regarding the matter it itself makes known—by the words "The scripture [is concerned with] the account of one who has already known the Self," and so on. [He says: "By itself. If the scripture were dependent on reasoning and so forth for its own meaning, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) would be lost; consequently, like human speech, the Vedic statement would be dependent and thus lack authority.
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "it might be" and "dependent. || 809 ||
If it is argued that reasoning and so forth are not a separate means of knowledge, we reply that they exist as constituent parts of such a means.
All the feet, having come together, make us understand the whole.

He raises an objection, suggesting that even if reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth depend [on scripture], there is no lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) for the *Tattvamasi* and other such statements, because reasoning and the like do not constitute separate means of valid knowledge (*mānāntara*). He says "reasoning and so forth. He states the reason for their not being separate means of valid knowledge with the words "because of being a means of knowledge" (*māna*). He establishes that the fourfold nature of reasoning and the like is established as constituent parts of the means of valid knowledge with the words "having come together" (*saṃbhūya*). The four parts—word (*śabda*), reasoning (*yukti*), meditative enumeration (*prasaṃkhyāna*), and the self (*ātman*)—only when combined [bring about] the desire to know (*jijñāsā*)...
They indicate the object of the slaughterhouse, as it has been said:
"From *ṭā* when that is seen" [vol.
*Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Bhūriśvarācārya. [Introduction:
"Those desiring liberation [attain it] through words, reasoning, repeated meditation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), and the Self."
"They perceive the self as liberated by means of the fourfold instrument of knowledge."
Therefore, the meaning is that they do not possess independent authority. || 810 ||
For the parts do not come together, just as in the case of oil, a wick, and fire.
This is for the sake of the cognition's own acquisition of its nature, and not for the apprehension of the object of cognition. || 811 ||

This refutes the idea that the four factors (*pāda*) together constitute the means of cognizing an object. [The verse says: "Not together. Just as oil and other ingredients combine to become the cause of a lamp, which then illuminates objects, so too the four factors combined provide the essential nature of the means of knowledge (*māna*);

and since that [means] is the cause for the apprehension of the object of knowledge (*meyopalabdhi*), the meaning is that the individual factors are not the causes for the apprehension of the object. || 811 ||
If all these, having come together, produce a single fruit;
If it were the case that there is an increase in each individual cognition, then this [position] would be false.

One might object: "Do these [feet] not merely bring about the apprehension of the object? Since they are the cause of their own nature, there is an absence of a [separate] cause [for the cognition]. To this, he raises the doubt with the words "saṃbhūya" (having come together).

Does this mean that these [feet] merely produce the apprehension of the object, or do they also constitute the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? It is not the first case; thus he says: "pratyekam" (individually).
When the feet possess only the capacity for apprehending the object, then the increase of the means of valid knowledge occurs from each individual foot.

The statement of the proponent of *prasaṃkhyāna* would thus be false; therefore, the meaning is that your own words alone are the reason for the feet being the cause of the nature of valid cognition. || 812 ||
The capacity to produce an effect through combination arises from the conjunction of action and its factors.
Apart from the acquisition of its own nature, it requires nothing else for its manifestation. || 813 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "by means of a collective" (*saṃbhūya*). Action is the means of cognition; because the factors of action (*kārakas*) intended for that [action] are capable of mutual conjunction, it is logical that they act as the agents of cognition collectively. And thus, if the feet were the agents of cognition, they would not be the perceivers of the object, because two operations cannot occur simultaneously (*aparyāyeṇa*), and a succession of operations is not admitted in the case of sound and so forth—this is the sense. Now, [an objection]: "But..."
Although the parts (pādas) perform the act of measurement, nevertheless, that [cognition] which has arisen from them would not manifest the object in the absence of auxiliary causes;
therefore, even in the cognition of the object of knowledge (*meyabuddhi*), the parts are auxiliary causes. Thus he says: "In its own nature" (*svarūpa*).

A means of knowledge (*māna*) does not require any other assistance for the manifestation of its own object beyond its own birth, because it is inherently capable; nor is there a dual operation of the parts through either succession or simultaneity.
This is the meaning of what was stated. || 813 ||
For it is because the tip of the oil-soaked wick is the cause for the arising of the lamp.
A lamp that has attained its own existence illuminates the object by itself. || 814 ||

Regarding the meaning of the first half-verse beginning with "saṃbhūya" (having come together), he states a reason containing an illustration: "In oil... etc. The meaning is that since those causes of light are seen to be mutually joined, by that same logic, the means of knowledge—sound and the rest—which are capable of mutual conjunction, produce valid cognition only when combined. Regarding the second half-verse beginning with "svarūpalābhato nānyat" (nothing other than the acquisition of their own nature), he provides an illustration: "labdha... etc. Just as...
They perform [it].
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

[Page 225] Just as a lamp, having acquired its own nature through its own cause, illuminates an object while being independent of anything else, so too a means of knowledge (*māna*), having obtained its own self from sound and other factors, should illuminate its own object by itself; such is the meaning. || 814 ||
If it were indeed established by logical arguments in exactly the same manner that it is made known by words, [then it would be real].
If, on the other hand, there is a distinction [between the two], then the fallacy of futility (vyarthatā) follows, and a difference in their means of cognition is established. || 815 ||

If it is argued that because words and so forth are themselves the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are not the cause for the arising [of that cognition], then is their functioning as a means of cognition collective or individual?
Regarding the first case—that the object manifested by the word is exactly the same as that manifested by reasoning and so forth, or whether it is something else—the first is not tenable;
thus he says: "By the word. The meaning is that reasoning and so forth contribute nothing to the object known through verbal testimony (*śābda*). Having raised another alternative, he replies:

By the words "atha" and so forth: if the object [of cognition] for reasoning (*yukti*) and the others were different from that of verbal testimony (*śābda*), then because there would be a distinction in the objects of knowledge (*meyabheda*), it would follow that those [means of knowledge] possess distinct instruments of knowledge (*māna*); thus, their functioning in combination (*saṃbhūya*) would be unestablished. This is the meaning. || 815 ||
If this is established by means of arguments such as "self-existence" (svabhāva) and so forth that are based on worldly convention;
The subject matter would be non-Vedic, and there would be the status of a mere restatement of the scriptures.

Even if each of these [means of knowledge] possesses validity, [the opponent might argue that] Brahman is revealed either by reasonings known in the world—such as those concerning dreams and so forth, which consist of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—or by those accessible solely through the Vedas. To the first alternative, he says: "In dreams, etc. If Brahman were revealed by worldly reasonings such as "the three states are false due to their variability, while the Self is not false because of its non-variability," then [it would follow that it is not the ultimate reality].

The meaning is that its status as a direction [of authority] is thus established; however, if it were merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of Brahman, then the independent authority (*anapekṣa-prāmāṇya*) of the *Tattvamasi* and other such passages would not be established. || 816 ||
Even though the arguments are Vedic, they serve to bring about the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures.
It would merely be a restatement, and it would be non-different from the treatise itself.

He states the second [objection]: "Even though they are Vedic" (*vaidikatve’pi*). The meaning is that although the arguments intended to illuminate the reality are understood solely through the Veda, because they concern matters derived from scripture (*āgamika*) and are thus restatements (*anuvāda*), they do not constitute a portion of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāṃśa*). He states another defect: "And it would be... (*syāc ca*). For if those arguments were Vedic, their distinctness from the *Śāstra* (the primary scripture) would be unestablished, which would result in the means of valid knowledge having three parts instead of four, thereby destroying the position that it has four parts.
For it has been said:
"The reasoning known as Mīmāṃsā is entirely born from the Veda; therefore, it is like the Veda itself, just as water reaching the ocean attains the state of salt. || 817 ||
And how could repetition and meditative discernment produce anything that possesses excellence?
For there is no excellence in the object of knowledge resulting from the repetition of the means of valid cognition.

Having refuted the claim that reasoning (*yukti*) requires the assistance of words (*śabda*), he first states the nature of *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated meditative realization) which excludes such assistance:
"And repetition... He explains that this [repetition], when said to be an aid to the word, either produces an excellence regarding its object or it does not;
it is not the former case, as he says: "It would produce... He provides the reason why the repetition of a word is not a cause for excellence regarding the verbal meaning.

"Not indeed," [he says]. The ellipsis is "because it is not observed in jars and the like. He states "since" because, since there would otherwise result the futility of repeated meditation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), the second [alternative] is not tenable. Furthermore, repetition does not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the case of sound; for an excellence produced therein—[the rest of the argument follows].
1. Primarily from Ka and Ga.
The meaning is as follows:

since the apprehension of clarity regarding that [object] does not exceed [the object itself], and since that [clarity] can sometimes occur even without repetition, repetition is purposeless with respect to the object of knowledge (*meyaviṣaya*), even though it may have a purpose in that regard [otherwise]. || 818 ||
And even where there is no determination of sequence due to defects such as darkness, [the sequence remains].
Even in that case, because the objects of cognition (*meyatva*) are distinct, there can be no such thing as acting in combination (*saṃbhūyamānatā*).

Anticipating the objection that—since objects situated in dim light or at a great distance are determined sequentially through the repetition of the means of knowledge (*māna*), such repetition is purposeful—the author says: "Where... Even if that [repetition] is fruitful, there is no acting in combination on the part of the means of knowledge, because the objects of cognition are distinct for each [instance].
And if it were a means of valid cognition (*māna*), it would not have that status because there is no recurrence of a single means of valid cognition; this is the meaning. || 819 ||
The cognition "this is a former object," as well as "this is a man" and "this is a Māṇava."
"‘This person is dark-complexioned’ and ‘He is Ḍittha’—therein lies a difference in meaning. (820)
He illustrates the state of having distinct objects of cognition with the words "Previously," etc. (820).
For the nature of a means of valid cognition consists in having delimitation as its fruit, and that [delimitation] differs.
But in their absence, however, only the subsequent among the preceding [authorities] possesses authority. || 821 ||

If it is argued that even though there is a difference in the objects, because the means of knowledge (*māna*) remains the same, that single [means] being repeated is what brings about certainty, and thus the repetition is purposeful—the author says "no," citing the term *pariccheda*. The meaning is that since there is a difference in the delimitation (*pariccheda*) for each respective object, the status of being a means of knowledge (*mānatva*), which is the cause of that [delimitation], also differs; therefore, the production of a complete and certain cognition does not occur through the repetition of a single means of knowledge. It is only the final cognition of "Dittha" that has the result of delimitation.

Fearing the objection that there might be no difference between the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and their results, he says: "But in the absence of that [result]" (tadabhāve tu). Since prior cognitions are not valid means of knowledge because they lack the result of definitive determination (pariccheda), whereas the final cognition possesses that result, there is neither a need for repetition nor a collective operation (saṃbhūyakāritva) of the means of knowledge;
this is the meaning. || 821 ||
Now, even though there is a distinction between the objects of knowledge, if it is maintained that the means of knowledge is one;
Because the sense organs and so forth apprehend the actual object, they possess a single purpose and thus have an identical measure.

He raises an objection, saying "Now" (*atha*), [arguing] that even though there is a difference in intermediate objects within the cognition of an object and so forth, because the undifferentiated object-in-itself (*vastumātra*) is consistently apprehended (*anusaṃdhāna*) everywhere, there is no difference in the means of knowledge (*māna*); therefore, it is incorrect to say that it [the means of knowledge] differs. Thus, the meaning is that the ascertainment of the object is established through the repetition of a single [cognition] itself. He refutes this by way of an over-extension (*atiprasakti*), saying "The object" (*vastu*). The phrase "by virtue of grasping the object" (*vastugrāhitayā*) is to be construed with both sides [of the argument].

The meaning is that since even the five means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, have real entities as their objects, they would constitute a single means of knowledge if they were directed toward a single object. || 822 ||
The practice being cultivated should bring about its fruit, just as a sacrifice does.
The treatise is either a producer or an indicator; how could there be identity between these two? || 823 ||

Having stated that the verbal testimony (śabda) does not assist [the means of knowledge] because it does not impart any excellence (*atiśaya*) to the thorough enumeration (*prasaṃkhyāna*) or its object, he states another reason for that very point: "That which is being accomplished" (*sādhyamānam*). He says, "Of those two," meaning that there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the teaching on thorough enumeration and the scripture, as they stand as either a producer (*kāraka*) or a communicator (*jñāpaka*). || 823 ||
1 kha. 'venaikaṃ | .2 ka. ga. hi | 3 ka. ma. 'natā matā | [vol 1, page 248] Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 227
If this empirical self were not a part of the [true] self, it would not be the mother.
If that [cognition] were an object of knowledge (prameya), how could it be the result (phala) of experience?

By one who rejects the dependence of reasoning (*yukti*) and contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) upon verbal testimony (*śabda*), the status of [the self] as a constituent part of the means of knowledge (*mānāṃśatva*) has already been refuted. As for the further claim that "the self is also a constituent part of the means of knowledge," one must consider whether this self is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) or a non-transmigrating being (*asaṃsārī*). Having raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the words "as a knower" (*pramātā*). If the self, following worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is intended as a transmigrating being that constitutes a part of the means of knowledge, then for that transmigrating being—

The meaning is that the object of cognition cannot be a part of that [cognition] itself, because the relationship between locus and located requires absolute difference, whereas such a difference does not exist between a part and its whole.

Having restated another alternative, he refutes it with the words "If it were other... The meaning is that the object of cognition cannot be a part of the means of cognition, because the relationship of object and subject is impossible in a single entity. Having removed the fourfold nature [of cognition], he removes its result: "How?"
And so [it is said]. || 824 ||
If its own nature were unachievable, it would be because it is established independently.
If that knowledge is a valid means of cognition, then that [scripture] is also [a valid means] by virtue of its function.

What, then, is the impossibility here? Is it that experience (*anubhava*) is the very nature of Brahman, or is it a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having that [Brahman] as its form? It is not the first; thus he says: "The nature" (*svarūpam*). The ellipsis is: "Therefore, it is not the fruit of a means of knowledge (*māna*). Regarding the second [option], he says: "That knowledge" (*tajjñānam*). If it is argued that even the knowledge of Brahman, which is itself a means of knowledge, is the fruit of a fourfold means of knowledge, he says: "And that" (*tacceti*). For that [knowledge] arises from words such as "Thou" (*tat tvam asi*).
The meaning is: from what does it arise? It does not arise from the practice of discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) or other such means; this is the sense. || 82 ||
For a treatise, when being repeated, does not indeed abandon its own nature.
How can inference and reasoning function regarding that which is beyond perception to increase your understanding? (826)

Regarding the claim that each quarter-verse (*pāda*) is a cause for the increase of valid cognition (*pramiti*), he says: "The scripture" (*śāstram*). While the scripture and reasoning are being repeated, they remain as means of producing knowledge regarding an object that was previously indirect (*parokṣa*); they do not abandon their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the meaning is that there is no transition from indirect to immediate (*aparokṣa*) cognition through the repetition of words and so forth. || 826 ||
Indeed, there is no increase in the object of knowledge from its own side when there is an increase in the knower.
Its increase occurs when its measure increases; thus, there is a mutual dependence.

He states another defect in the position that there is an increase in cognition through repetition (*āvṛtti*). [The verse says: "And because of the cognized object" (*pramiteśca*). The meaning is as follows: if an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the object of knowledge (*meyastha*) is established, an excellence in the means of knowledge (*mānastha*) is established, according to the maxim, "For the distinction of cognitions is by the object itself. And if an excellence in the means of knowledge is established, an excellence in the object of knowledge is established, because without that [excellence in the object], it would not be a means of knowledge. Thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there is no increase in cognition through repetition. || 827 ||
Even if it has produced a cognition, if the treatise still depends upon reasoning, [then it is not authoritative].
It would be exactly the same regarding heaven and so forth; and in that case, it would be dependent upon something else.

The fact that each individual word is a cause for the increase of valid cognition has been refuted. Now, what was stated—that the scripture depends upon reasoning and so forth—is answered again by another method. In this regard, one must choose between two alternatives: does the scripture depend on something else for the sake of accomplishing the result after having made the object known, or for the sake of making that object known itself?
Refuting the first alternative, [the author says]: "Even if it were produced... For in the first case, even a sentence such as "one who desires heaven" would be connected...

Having induced a person's engagement with the meaning of the verbal root by means of making [the result] known, it would depend upon reasoning and so forth for the sake of heaven and the like; however, that is neither observed nor desired.
This is the meaning: "Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter 228.

Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "And if it is dependent" (*sāpekṣaṃ ceti*). This means that when a sentence depends upon reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth for the comprehension of its own meaning, then...

The meaning is this: [the objection that] it would be non-authoritative due to its dependence [on other means] is not valid; for there is no fault because reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth are themselves authoritative, and because the establishment of reality arises from a portion of that authority.
Furthermore, since the sentence possesses the capacity to convey its own meaning by itself, there is no cause for dependence on anything else. || 828 ||
For one who realizes the Self as being free from the web of misfortune, [there is no further rebirth].
What further object is there to be attained through scripture and the like, such that one would depend upon reasoning and so forth? || 829 ||

Having previously stated that there is no need for reasoning and the like because the scripture accepts a fruit greater than the knowledge of the object [of the self], he now says, "vyapāsta... (devoid of...), to show that it has no such greater fruit at all; how then could there be a need for it? The connection is as follows: for one who understands the Self as characterized by the attributes taught in the scripture, there is nothing further to be attained—how, therefore, could there be a need for reasoning and the like? || 829 ||
Or what is the reasoning [behind] a lamp's dispelling of fear regarding snakes and the like?
For one who brings about the realization of the true nature of the rope and so forth by means of their own brilliance.
He establishes, by means of an illustration, that the scripture requires no reasoning or other means for the communication of its own meaning. The phrase "What indeed... [means]:

just as the knowledge of a rope or similar object—which destroys a snake or the like, as well as the trembling caused by it—requires no reasoning whatsoever when it produces its effect through the power of its own light, so too the scripture is independent when communicating its own meaning. || 830 ||
For the relationship of subordinate and principal cannot exist at all without syntactic unity.
Nor would it exist here due to the differences in substance, function, object, and intentionality. || 831 ||

Having established the independence of the scripture (*śāstra*), it was stated that its primacy [is established] while the injunction for meditative cultivation (*prasaṃkhyāna-vidhi*) is subordinate; this is now refuted by means of another method. [The author says: "Subordinate... etc. Let it be then that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and the injunction for meditative cultivation—no, he says:

"The thing... etc. Because statements such as "That thou art" have the real entity (*vastu*) as their primary purport, whereas the injunction for meditative cultivation has the mandate (*niyoga*) as its primary purport, there is no syntactic unity; nor is there [unity] through the power of denotation (*abhidhā*).

The meaning is as follows: because it would entail the impossibility of establishing a real entity, an injunction cannot have a real entity as its primary object; nor can an injunction have a real entity as its primary object because that would contradict its own nature as a mandate. Furthermore, even if there were no such restriction, it would contradict logical principle (*nyāya*). Therefore, when there is a difference in meaning, a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is inevitable. || 831 ||
Nor is there here a unity of sentence characterized by a single purpose.
In this case, syntactic unity may be established through the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, as in the case of the limbs and the body. || 832 ||

Having raised the objection that, although the treatises on *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) and the [ritual] injunctions have multiple purposes, they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) due to the unity of their result—just as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśa* sacrifice—one must consider the alternatives: do these two have a single result in the form of heaven, or a single result in the form of liberation? Refuting the first alternative:

[The author] says: "Not so. Regarding the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated meditation) and the scriptural mention of the verbal expression (*abhidhā*), he states a counter-example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) to show that there is no single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) based on the fact that they share the same fruit of heaven. He says: "The subsidiary... The meaning of this is as follows: by such passages as "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni [is offered] on the new moon day," the rites such as the Āgneya are connected with specific times;
whereas by such passages as "He pours the Āghāra libations," the Āghāra and other rites are not connected with specific times.

Having raised the doubt as to whether all those [rites] heard in the texts are equally primary, or whether the Āgneya and others are primary while the others are subsidiary, it is concluded that because two sentences containing the term *vidvat* enjoin distinct rites, and because the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote time and thus cannot be established as names [of rites],

the word [denoting the time] in the injunctional sentence must be assumed to be a name through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); therefore, [the rites] are dependent upon that [name].

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that because terms such as *gryādi* and *yajeta* denote sacrifice (*yāga*) in general— just like their basic forms— all [the constituent acts] possess primary status, [the author] states the Vārtika on the second [topic],
accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śāstramakāśikā*. 229.

In the second [section], the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) was established as follows: because the two *yajati* verbs in the two sentences are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the previously mentioned *Āgneya* and other offerings, and because the words "Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "New Moon" (*amāvāsyā*) are well-known to denote two specific collections [of rites], the qualifying term (*upapada*) pertaining to the entitlement (*adhikārika*) applies precisely there. Consequently, since the verb *yajati* also serves that same purpose, the *Āgneya* and other primary offerings alone are connected to the entitlement and thus possess primacy, while all others are subordinate (*aṅga*). This was concluded in the section concerning the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅgeṣu*)...

Since it has been established in the *parṇamayītvādhikaraṇa* that the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), the principle that the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*) share a single fruit—namely, "that which lacks a fruit in proximity to that which possesses a fruit is its subsidiary"—is well-established by logic. However, this is not the case here; therefore, the reason why one should not assume a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the *tattvamasi* passage and the injunction for contemplation (*prasaṃkhyānavidhi*) on the grounds of sharing a single fruit (as is the case with the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which share the single fruit of heaven) is as follows:

The author says: "By which... The meaning is that it is by virtue of having the same fruit as heaven (*svarga*) that a single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatva*) could be postulated for the scripture and so forth; however, this [work] does not have heaven as its sole fruit, since you yourself have denied that. || 832 ||
For liberation, which is established by its own nature, there is no need for a goal to be accomplished that would serve as a benefit.
And the status of being an auxiliary is not observed for that which does not assist the primary. || 833 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "of that which is established by itself" (*svataḥsiddhasya*). The remainder of the sense is: "Therefore, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) because [the means such as] *prasaṃkhyāna* have liberation as their sole fruit. Furthermore, if the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* were a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the scripture, it would be either an auxiliary contributing to the result (*phalopakāryaṅga*) or an auxiliary contributing to the essential nature (*svarūpopakāryaṅga*).

It is not the first, because it has already been stated that the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* provides no assistance regarding liberation, which is the fruit of the scripture; thus he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

He explains otherwise [as follows]: "The primary," etc. For that *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplation) which does not assist in liberation—the fruit of the scripture which is the primary goal—cannot be considered an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the scripture by way of assisting its fruit; for such a status as an auxiliary to something else is never observed in the case of that which does not assist toward the fruit.
This is the meaning. || 833 ||
In the attainment of its own nature, the scripture does not regard itself as something to be produced, because of its eternity.
Nor [is it capable] of conveying identity, because it possesses the power of denotation inherently.

Regarding the second case as well—whether the injunction for meditative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) is helpful for the attainment of the scripture's own nature or for the comprehension of its meaning—he says that it is not the first:
"In the attainment of itself. He says it is not the second: "By itself" (svataḥ). || 834 ||
And once the meaning of the scripture has been fully comprehended through contemplation, it becomes established.
If there were no experience of the identity [of all things], it would lack validity due to contradiction.

Furthermore, as for the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation) being either a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) or a principal element (*śeṣin*) of the scripture—it must serve either an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) or a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). The first case is not accepted by us. As for the second, does it produce its result when performed once or repeatedly? Regarding the first of these, he says: "And if [the result were produced] from *prasaṃkhyāna*... If, in the case of *prasaṃkhyāna* which is the object of injunctions such as "one should see with a concentrated mind," the result were produced even when it is performed only once—

The meaning is that realization bears fruit [only when practiced repeatedly]; otherwise, the cultivation (bhāvanā) desired by you—which must possess long duration, earnestness, and continuity—would not exist. He rejects the position that it is only when performed once that it yields the fruit, with the words "If not. If the practice of higher discernment (prasaṃkhyāna), when performed once, does not cause one to experience identity with the One Self (aikātmya), then even when performed repeatedly, it would not cause such experience; for if the fruit is absent when performed once, [it will likewise be absent when repeated].
The meaning is that because there is the possibility of contradiction regarding the nature of non-apprehension, the scripture that establishes that [nature] lacks authority. || 835 ||
1. māsyadhi | 2. ka. ga. mīkṣya | [vol 1, page 251]
Furthermore, neither time nor number has been specified here by which a definitive conclusion could be reached.
Nor could there be activity toward that which is doubtful by means of such [an inference]. (836)

Anticipating the objection that—just as in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites—the defects of optionality (*vikalpa*) do not apply here because one obtains the experience through enumeration (*prasaṃkhyāna*) by the force of the enjoined time and so forth, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). First of all, unlike the times of evening and morning in the *agnihotra*, no specific time is enjoined for the enumeration; nor is there even in the *agnihotra* a rule such as "they perform the *agnihotra* for a month," or "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni is offered at the new moon. [End of fragment]

Just as time cannot be enjoined because it is not something to be performed, so too it is not subject to injunction; for in that case, since the action is enjoined with respect to the time, its non-subjectivity to injunction is logical.

However, in passages such as "he offers in the evening," since the oblation is already enjoined by the rule "he performs the Agnihotra," it is the time that is being enjoined as a restatement (anuvāda).
Even there, if the action were being enjoined with respect to the time, your very example would fail to be established. Nor [is it the case] regarding the seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati...

In this context, the number is prescribed as in the expression "he obtains" (*labhate*). For in that case, since the animals—which serve as qualifiers for the sacrifices whose sequence is regulated by the performance—are things to be acquired (*upādeya*), their number is prescribed; this was established in the *Paśvekatvādhikaraṇa* (the section on the singularity of the animal) regarding the statement "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where the singularity of the animal is what is to be enjoined.
However, such a prescription of number does not exist in the case of the *prasaṃkhyāna* (the recitation of the *prapada* formula). Therefore, by means of that [number],...

The meaning is that, consequently, there is no establishment of the certainty of experience. Nevertheless, one might object: "Even though it remains doubtful whether experience arises from that [practice] or not, those seeking experience will still engage in it, just as they do with agriculture and the like. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Nor even... In the case of agriculture and so forth, engagement is appropriate even amidst doubt because the presence or absence of the fruit is observed; however, in the case of *prasaṃkhyāna*, it is not so, because experience resulting from it is never observed anywhere, even after a long recitation.

The meaning is that even if meditation (*bhāvanā*)—possessing the three aforementioned qualifications—is successful regarding the letter *ka* and so forth, a valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the object to be known (*prameya*) has not been observed to arise from it. || 836 ||
Or else, having ascended even to a great height, he remains averse to all contradiction.
Whatever one might do out of desire, if one's purpose remains unfulfilled, one would fall from the path.

He says that even if one engages in that [practice] while it remains doubtful, there is no cessation of defects: "Having ascended," etc. The word "or" (*athavā*) is used to refute the restriction that there must be an absence of engagement when *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is doubtful. Even after practicing *prasaṃkhyāna* repeatedly, one may turn away from it due to a discrepancy characterized by the non-perception of reality; having desisted midway, or if one has not desisted, one may act according to some desire.

The meaning is this: unless one has turned away from the unseen [world], one would not attain the desired success through mere wishful thinking; otherwise, one would encounter misfortune because nothing else has been done and because no such result is observed from this experience. || 837 ||
