Alternatively, its having an unseen result (adṛṣṭaphalatā) should be postulated, just as it is accepted [in the case of other rituals].
Or else, its status as an auxiliary to ritual action (karmāṅgatā) would have to be postulated, just like the injunction regarding the udgītha. || 838 ||

Now, one might object: for one who practices *prasaṃkhyāna* throughout their entire life, it is not logical to speak of a fall from grace, given such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as "No one who performs good deeds... and so forth. To this, he replies with the words "not seen" (*adṛṣṭa*). If the non-falling from grace for one who always practices *prasaṃkhyāna* were intended by the *smṛti*, then that injunction would have to be assumed to serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, or like the injunction regarding the *Udgītha* chant which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that same sacrifice. Thus it stands.
The meaning is that even that [recitation] would have to be considered a constituent part of the ritual action (karmāṅga). || 838 ||
And therefore, the procedure should be performed in reverse order, because of the contradiction with the scriptures.
Furthermore, lack of faith exists among those seeking liberation, and there also persists the sublation of what is to be done. || 839 ||
[Vārtika, Vol. 1, p.

252] If the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative enumeration) were intended as a subsidiary part of ritual action, like the injunction for the *udgītha*, then it could not be established as a subsidiary part of the scripture whose goal is sought; for one thing cannot be a subsidiary to both simultaneously.

He says, "from yoga. And then, "therefore. Now, he addresses one who desires that the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative enumeration) has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the injunction for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, by saying, "in reverse order" (*prātilomyena*). If the aforementioned injunction were for an unseen purpose like the injunction for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, then—since that [injunction] would be the primary act (*śeṣin*) and the realization of reality (*tattvam-ādi*) would be its subsidiary (*śeṣa*)—the [injunction] imagined for the sake of the authority of that [realization] would, by being the opposite, stand as something contrary.

The meaning is that a scripture whose primary intent is something else cannot be authoritative regarding its own literal sense when it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition. Furthermore, if the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation) were for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) or as a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), then those who desire the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) as the cause of liberation would have no faith in it—just as they lack faith in the injunctions for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth. Consequently, since such realization would not be observed, the performance of that [contemplation] by seekers of liberation would be impossible, and thus the injunction itself would fail to be established.

To this he says: "Lack of faith" (aśraddhā). Nor is this an injunction for those seeking liberation, because it has been established that [such an injunction] is sublated by the fact that [liberation] lies outside the triad of means and so forth; thus he says: "The effect," etc., because even that qualified [injunction] is impossible. || 839 ||
Because it does not depend on the reality of things, there is a predominance of mere causal efficiency.
Furthermore, since the object [of negation] is not found even in the treatise, what could be the objective domain of the action? (840)

Furthermore, regarding the doctrine of *prasaṃkhyāna*, he states that neither the sentence enjoining it nor the sentence concerning reality (*tattvamasi*) etc. can convey the nature of the thing (*vastu*). This is because the former is restricted solely to the injunction (*niyoga*) and is thus incapable of conveying the nature of the thing; this is expressed by the word "vastu. Nor is the second case possible, because if the sentence concerning reality (*tattvamasi*) etc. were intent upon an injunction, its validity with respect to its own meaning would be untenable due to contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge; this is expressed by the word "śāstrāt."

And thus: since the obstruction of that [cognition] is untenable in the absence of knowledge of the object, he states the conclusion—that an injunction (niyoga) is without an object—by saying "kāryam" (the task). || 840 ||
If that scripture were not to establish the true nature of that reality, [it would be useless].
Because the object [of the injunction] is not established, and because the action is primary, it is therefore an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 841 ||

Regarding the doctrine of *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation), does the scripture concerning oneness (*ekatva*), being intended for that [contemplation], not establish it, or does it establish it?
In this regard, he restates the first position with the words "If... He says: "In that case, because oneness is not perceived from that sentence, it would lack authority;
for you yourself accept that a text whose purport is the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* cannot produce valid knowledge regarding its own subject matter when it contradicts another means of knowledge."
"Substantial entity" (vastu) refers to the statement that it is not a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). || 841 ||
Thus, the true scripture would be that which establishes and teaches the reality of the oneness of the self.
Then, because it has become directly perceived, the effort that merely effects the removal of indirect perception is rendered useless. (842)

He takes up the second [objection] with the words "Now" (*atha*). He says: "If [the object were known] through direct perception (*āparokṣya*) from the sentence itself, then the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna*—which is intended to remove the indirectness (*pārokṣya*) of the reality—would be useless. || 842 ||
And how can that be established from a treatise that does not convey reality as it truly is?
Even though the non-eternal nature [of sound] is established, the horse remains well-known as distinct from the cow. (843)

Now, one might object: "The scripture does not produce the immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) of the reality, because its nature is to remove only the mediated (*parokṣa*) cognition of the superimposed [world]; therefore, there must be an injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation) in order to realize it directly.

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "From the scripture," intending to show that since the reality is non-superimposed and immediate according to the scriptural text, "That which is direct and immediate," it cannot be established through the scripture—which does not penetrate the true nature of that reality—and thus the scripture would face the contingency of being invalid.
232 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 253]

One might object: "Surely, when a scripture reveals an object that is distinct from what is unconnected and immediate, it will also reveal its counter-correlative (pratiyogin)—that which is likewise unconnected and immediate; therefore, the scripture possesses validity. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not so" (*nānaśva*). Just as even when a cow, which is distinct from a horse, is established through perception, the horse is not thereby established, so too, even when an object is conveyed by verbal testimony as being connected and mediate (*parokṣa*), its counter-correlative is not [established].
Therefore, since the reality [of the object] is not established through verbal testimony (śāstra), the meaning is that it lacks authority altogether. || 843 ||
If there were experience [of reality] merely through hearing the scripture and through its practical application, [then what need would there be for other means?].
Even in the case of a merchant's report, discourse is seen regarding a matter that has not been ascertained. (844)

Now, one might object: even if a reality that is unmediated and non-conceptual is established by the scripture, it is established merely through hearing (*śravaṇa*) without yet having ascended to direct experience (*anubhava*). Furthermore, because of the injunction for meditation (*prasamkhyāna-niyoga*), its experience [is attained]; therefore, the injunction is not purposeless, nor is the scripture lacking in authority. This is the objection raised with the words "From the scripture" (*śāstrāt*). In this regard, is the reality ascertained from the scripture or not? It cannot be the first case, because [if it were already ascertained], it would not have ascended to direct experience.

[The author] refutes [the opponent's view] by stating: "In reality... (vastuni). Because experience is defined as a certainty that is both uncontradicted and not previously apprehended, in the second case—where it is claimed that knowledge arises from words regarding that [object]—it would be mere talk. This is because any cognition other than the aforementioned certainty is a semblance (*ābhāsa*). Furthermore, since such a semblance is devoid of an object, it could even be possible in the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); therefore, there is no distinction between an explanatory passage and [words like] "That Thou Art" (*tat tvam asi*). Thus he refutes [the position]. || 844 ||
And consequently, the state of being restricted to the effect is abandoned by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves.
A treatise would be supreme in its perfection only if it were devoid of any underlying reality or intended meaning. (845)

If the statements beginning with "That Thou Art" (tattvamasi) were identical in status to explanatory passages (arthavāda), what would be the loss? To this he says: "And therefore... If there were no distinction from an arthavāda, then just like that, the statements beginning with "That Thou Art" would also terminate in an action; consequently, the proponent of the doctrine of meditative realization (saṃkhyāna) would have abandoned it in vain. For even upon its abandonment, it would not be established as being grounded in reality, just like an arthavāda. Therefore, the scripture—being identical in status to an arthavāda regarding its grounding in reality—is necessarily grounded in an injunction for meditative realization known as "becoming one" (sampat).

Furthermore, because [the Self] has been abandoned [as an object], and because one who desires the authority of the scriptures based on their being devoted to that [Self] must accept the certainty of an immediate experience of the unconditioned object, an injunction is not purposeful; this is the meaning. || 845 ||
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the form of a narrative (ākhyāyikā) is to be adopted in the Śruti.
Because it is flawed by such defects as having a beginning, it is described as not being the ultimate goal of man.

[Objection: "But if that [the intention to communicate] is not accepted, then because they consist of a narrative, the Vedāntas would lack authority; whereas if it is accepted, they possess authority like sentences such as 'one who desires heaven [should sacrifice]'. To this, he says: "And not... By this, it is meant that even though the form of a narrative—such as "this was said by him" and "this was understood by him"—is heard in the Śruti, it is not intended to be conveyed (*avivakṣita*). For it has been stated: "Indeed, it cannot be said that this entire sequence of narratives is intended to be conveyed."

The meaning is that if [the Veda] were not accepted as such, there would be an absence of human purpose; otherwise, it would follow that the Veda has a beginning and so forth, and this is not a fault because it contradicts such scriptural and traditional texts as "by speech, which is manifold and eternal," "without beginning or end, eternal," and so on, and because it contradicts the *Autpattika-sūtra*. Why, then, is a narrative told in the scripture? To this he says: "By way of human purpose. [This refers to] the engagement of the person...
The meaning is that it is the cause of heaven and liberation by virtue of being its constituent part and by virtue of being a hymn of praise. || 846 ||
And if, out of fear of tautology, one were to imagine here a different meaning for the word "yadi" (if);
The conception of duality [is held] because the rule regarding the teaching of oneness is otherwise rendered futile. (847)
1. Also the meaning of this.
[Vol.
1, page 254] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 233.

For this reason as well, there is no injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) at the beginning of the scripture regarding reality; for if that too were dependent on an injunction like the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), then since the injunction itself would be the subject matter of both sections, the fault of tautology (*paunaruktya*) would arise. Thus he says: "Because of tautology. [The opponent might argue: "In the ritual section, the injunction is independent, whereas in the Brahma-section, the reality is the subject to be established, and the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* is subordinate to that [reality]; therefore, there is no tautology."

The proponent of *prasaṃkhyāna* says: "In this case. Alternatively, he says: "In this case" [is not a tautology], because it was stated there that the injunction (*niyoga*) has external means, whereas here it is said that it has no external means. Or alternatively: if one did not accept the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* regarding "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*) and so forth, then liberation would have to be desired as resulting from the knowledge produced by hearing the sentence only once; in that case, the instruction of "That Thou Art" nine times would be—

In order to avoid that [objection], he raises the doubt that the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative realization) constitutes the remainder of the scripture (*śāstraśeṣa*). [The opponent objects: "There would be tautology. [The author replies: The scripture of ritual action (*karma-śāstra*) is intent upon its own inherent injunction (*niyoga*), whereas the scripture of Brahman (*brahma-śāstra*) teaches the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* as subordinate to the reality (*vastu*). Thus, there is no division [of the scriptures].

Even in that case, if an injunction were admitted, its primacy would have to be accepted according to the principle of the "already existent and the yet-to-be" (*bhūta-bhavyanyāya*). Therefore, in a single unified text (*aikyavākya*), [the two] cannot in any way [be related in that manner].

He refutes the first objection—that the distinction between the two sections (kāṇḍas) is appropriately conceived as "this is the injunction in the case of ritual action"—by stating that it is not according to the manner you have described, beginning with the words "aikātmya" (the oneness of self). Even by virtue of being grounded respectively in external and non-external means and in the application of injunctions (*niyoga*), there is no difference between the two;

for such specific distinctions are established only when they belong to a single scripture, as in the case of the second and third chapters. Therefore, there is no injunction whatsoever at the beginning of the section concerning Reality (*tattva*); rather, it is the other [section]...

To the second [objection], which claims that the postulation of a division of scriptures is logical, he replies with the words "aikātmya" (oneness of self). Even for one who is wise due to the repeated practice of "That thou art," if it were argued that the injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) is still to be accomplished, then—since there can be no injunction without duality in a scripture of oneness—the phenomenal world of duality would have to be accepted as ultimately real. However, that has already been refuted and will be refuted further; nor does [the injunction] depend upon imagined duality.

The injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) follows immediately upon knowledge; however, since that injunction depends upon imagined duality, it would result in being merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*).

Consequently, for the duality that manifests after knowledge, there can be no status as a real effect of ignorance, and thus its reality is untenable, as it is merely a persistence of what has been sublated.
Furthermore, the repetition of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is for the sake of true knowledge by way of dispelling various doubts. [The author] states this to refute another objection.
"Regarding 'aikātmya' (oneness of self): || 847 ||"
And once the object has been cognized by means of a pramāṇa, there is no further investigation.
In some cases, it is observed that both the action and its release [from doubt] occur because the intrinsic validity [of the cognition] is sublated. || 848 ||

By stating that there is no injunction even in a sentence of unified meaning (*aikyavākya*), it has been shown that the application of *prasaṃkhyāna* is of no use regarding an object known through the scripture;

now, having raised the alternative as to whether there is a need for *prasaṃkhyāna* and so forth when the object is known from the scripture only superficially (*āpātataḥ*), or when it is directly ascertained (*sākṣānniścita*)— starting with the first [alternative]:

Having accepted the latter [position], he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). Regarding an object directly ascertained by the scripture, there should be no further investigation between the injunction (*niyoga*) and the reasoning (*yukti*), whether in the case of an injunction or a reason. This is because, upon the direct realization of reality, distinctions such as agency (*kartṛtva*) have been sublated.

Furthermore, if the scripture, once it has brought about valid knowledge, were to depend on anything else, its inherent validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) would be destroyed; thus, even for reasoning and the like, the fourfold [criteria]—

The meaning is that [it is] a means of valid cognition because it possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition through its entry into [the category of] means of valid cognition, just like verbal testimony. || 848 ||
When a jar is perceived through direct perception, what logic or what effect [could there be for further inference]?
Furthermore, the fact that the Veda has no defective causes is established by the absence of human agency.

He provides an illustration for the point that the scripture has no need for reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth regarding the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality (*tattva*). He says: "By perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). Now, one might object: even regarding what is seen through perception, one must investigate whether this cognition arises from a defective cause (*duṣṭahetu*) or a non-defective cause (*aduṣṭahetu*), in order to determine that it is produced by a non-defective cause. 30.
[Vol. 1,
Page 255] 234 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [Introduction]

He raises an objection: "Just as there is a dependence on proximity and so forth [for perception], it is reasonable that there should be a dependence on reasoning and the like to ascertain that even knowledge derived from the Śāstra has non-defective causes. He replies with the word "anuṣṭhe" (in practice). In the world, because defects such as jaundice (kāca) can occur, it is reasonable to depend on other means to ascertain that even regarding a perceptible object, the knowledge has non-defective causes; however, in the case of the Veda—which is not of human origin—since there is an absence of defects mediated by a person, the absence of such defects in the knowledge produced by it [is self-evident].
He provides the rebuttal that because it is innate (*sahaja*), it does not depend on anything else: "It is established" (verse 849).
Furthermore, contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition remains present even in the position that [the world] is an effect.
For how could there be the experience of the unity of the self when it is sublated by the senses and other means of knowledge? (850)

One might object: "Even if there is no need for an injunction (*niyoga*) to ascertain the absence of defects in scriptural knowledge, if one does not accept an injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated contemplation), then statements such as 'That Thou Art' (*tat tvam asi*) could not be the cause of the direct realization of non-dual reality, because that would contradict perception and other means of knowledge. However, if one does accept it, there is no such contradiction, because an injunction is stronger than all other means of knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Perception, etc. For [the injunction] does not reside in the "That Thou Art" [statement]. *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full argument would typically conclude by demonstrating that an injunction cannot be applied to the realization of the Self, which is already established by the Upanishadic texts.*
The resolution of the contradiction with other means of knowledge regarding the statement "the cow exists" is merely a formal assertion of the absolute authority of the *niyoga* (injunction).

Therefore, even if a sentence is intent upon *niyoga*, it does not produce cognition of a real entity (*vastu*)—as in the case of the sentence concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) being the sun—because that sentence is sublated by perception and other means of knowledge which contradict it;
however, when there is no such contradiction regarding *niyoga*, cognition of a real entity is established from the sentence because it is intent upon that [entity].
The meaning is "because of its strength. || 850 ||
But the proof that results from its negation does not arise through the power of an effect.
That [validity] arises from the scripture itself as a means of valid cognition, not from the object of cognition or from its result. || 851 ||

Regarding the position that [the Self] is an object to be accomplished (*kārya*), there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, because the reality of the thing is established through the injunction by way of negating that [contradiction]; to this he says: "By its negation.

The meaning is that the establishment of the reality of the thing, achieved by removing contradictions with perception and so forth, does not depend upon the injunction, because that [injunction] lacks authority (*prāmāṇya*) in that regard.

If one asks, "Then from what is the reality of the thing established by its negation? he says: "From the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāt*)," namely, from sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

The meaning is that the cognition of a real entity (*vastu-dhī*) possesses validity because it is not contradicted by the presiding deity (*devādhyakṣa*) and others. By means of the removal of contradiction, the cognition of a real entity does not depend upon a mandate (*niyoga*), because such a mandate is included within the category of objects of knowledge (*meyakoṭi*); this is the sense of the word "not" (*na*). || 811 ||
Or what reasoning is there regarding the task? If it is scripture, then that is equal for both sides.
It has been stated previously that there is nothing other than the scripture for making known what was unknown. (552)

He states another reason for the claim that there is no requirement for an injunction of *prasaṃkhyāna* regarding what is seen through the scriptures: "Or what [is it]? By the passage beginning with "That which is the cause of being a means of valid knowledge," it was stated that the Vedānta scripture is equal to you both in its status as a means of valid knowledge regarding an established entity (*siddha-artha*), and that it makes known what is unknown through the scripture, and nothing else.

Thus, when Brahman—which is unknown and seen through the scripture—is present, there is no logical justification for a requirement of an injunction, because there is nothing to be accomplished by such an injunction.
The meaning is "because of existence. || 852 ||
Even though the Veda has as its primary purpose the instruction of the goals of human life, it nevertheless [proceeds] by its very nature...
Speaking of that very [Self] along with logical arguments, one perceives one's own purpose.
(853) If the primary Śruti itself, by its own inherent power (*svārasya*), were to reveal the Self as Bliss, then the presentation of logical arguments in the Śrutis would be useless;

for the application of logic is not possible regarding an object that is unknown prior to [the knowledge arising from] those [Śrutis]. Therefore, even though there is no dependence on an injunction (*niyoga*), [the Śruti is self-sufficient].

[The *Vārttika*] accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 235.

Anticipating the objection that scripture requires reasoning (*yukti*), he says: "The goal of man" (*pumartham*). The construction is as follows: although scripture, by its very nature, teaches its own subject matter—the goal of man—it nevertheless looks to reasonings as the destroyers of obstacles, for when doubts such as impossibility (*asambhāvanā*) arise, it expresses that same meaning through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while employing those reasonings. Even the knowledge of the inner Self as Brahman, though derived from words, [remains obscured] due to human error and [the presence of] impossibility.

The meaning is as follows: Scripture, together with the reasonings that refute [the contrary], teaches that very Self—which has been seen—as its own primary object through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

It thus makes known that which is free from obstruction and non-contracted by the immediate [consciousness]. And since that knowledge arising from the sentence, by its mere production, brings about the cessation of all ignorance along with its effects, how could there be any need for reasoning and the like? || 853 ||
One is not joined with the cause for pride on account of such a transgression alone.
Because [the object] is not established from the mere word, its independence is lost. || 854 ||

Anticipating the objection that even in the case of scriptural knowledge (*śrauta-jñāna*), there must be a dependence on reasoning (*yukti*) because it destroys obstacles, [the author] says: "Not merely this much. He means that by the mere fact that scripture has a dependence on reasoning, reasoning does not become the cause for the certainty regarding its own object for the knowledge already produced; rather, reasoning is the cause for the destruction of the obstacles to that [knowledge].

This is the meaning. He establishes that since logical arguments (*yukti*) determine the meaning [of a statement] only through the sentence itself, their independence is compromised; and because, like the words of a person, they cannot possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), their function is solely to destroy the obstacles to the ascertainment of that [meaning]. This is stated in the verse beginning with "śabda" (verse 814).
Nor does the touching of white [objects] lead to the manifestation [of power], because of the wind's quality of acting with speed.
But since that [meaning] is established from the statement of the injunction itself, its brevity is stated for the sake of inciting activity. (855)

He provides an illustration for the point that there is a reliance on reasoning only when certainty is obstructed, beginning with the words "Not so" (*na*). From the Vedic statement, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," which describes the swiftness of Vāyu, it is not made known that the immolation of a white animal is the cause of prosperity;

for its status as the cause of that prosperity is established by the injunction itself: "One desiring prosperity should immolate a white animal dedicated to Vāyu. However, the swiftness of Vāyu mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) [is intended] for the person...

In the case of one desiring prosperity, the motive for engaging in the sacrifice of a white animal is that Vāyu is indeed swift in action; thus, considering that by sacrificing a goat dedicated to that deity, the fruit is attained very quickly, one becomes inclined to act out of a desire for the fruit. Similarly here as well, the presentation of reasoning is not for the sake of producing knowledge from the statement, nor for the sake of ascertaining one's own object once knowledge has arisen; rather, it is for the sake of destroying the obstacles to that [knowledge].
This is the meaning. || 855 ||
If indeed [the Self] is distinct from the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
Just as the nature of a genus (gotva) is perceived [as distinct] from individual instances, what has come of this regarding its being Brahman? (856)

For this reason as well, he states that logical arguments do not lead to the ascertainment of reality: "In the waking state," etc. Just as the universal "cowness" is distinct from individual cows because the distinction between exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and inclusion (anuvṛtti) is observed in the case of a jewel and its string, so too, if the non-deviating reality of the Self were seen through logic as being separate from the three mutually deviating states, then let it indeed be seen; however, for this [Self], which is the meaning of the word "Thou"— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning is that, regarding the ultimate reality, nothing at all arises from logical arguments without the [scriptural] statement, because of the Śruti text: "This realization is not to be attained by means of logic. || 856 ||
1 kha. "Decline," etc. 2 kha. "From sleepiness," etc.
Even that which is unestablished by means of scripture and reasoning cannot be established even by its own absence.
For non-recurrence is certainly not the cause of validity, since it is not observed in other cases. (857)

Anticipating the objection that even for one who has heard the statement, knowledge does not arise from it, and that since a statement—even when accompanied by reasoning—is not the cause of that knowledge, the repetition of both is the cause, he says: "It is unproven. The meaning is that repetition lacks authoritative status. Anticipating the further objection that because repetition is the cause of the statement's authority, it becomes determinative through that medium, he says: "By no means. For repetition is certainly not the cause of a word's authority.
The meaning is that [it] exists because, in the case of perception and so forth, repetition is observed to be the cause of validity. || 857 ||
And such a nature of being a means of valid cognition has not been observed anywhere else.
Nor is there any possibility here for another means of valid cognition. || 858 ||

He explains that very reason with the words "And not... If it is argued that because repetition is not a means of certain knowledge in worldly cognitions, it likewise lacks the power to produce certainty here [in the Upanishads] as well, then one might suspect that since worldly sentences are seen to be causes for the perception of a connected and indirect object, the same would apply to the *Tattvamasi* and other such statements; anticipating this objection, he says: "By another sense-organ... Here, regarding the Brahman-Self, which is unconnected and immediate, the worldly sentence— [The sentence continues: ...is not the cause of the perception of a connected and indirect object. Therefore, the suspicion that the *Tattvamasi* etc. would function like worldly sentences is refuted. Thus, the meaning is that the *Tattvamasi* and similar sentences are indeed the cause of the perception of the unconnected and immediate [Brahman-Self]. Therefore, there is no lack of certainty here. This is the sense. Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) implies that even in the case of the cognition of a jar and so forth, where the object is already present, repetition is not required for the production of certainty. Hence, there is no deficiency in the argument. This is the intention. Moreover, the phrase "not by another sense-organ" (*anyākṣa*) indicates that the cognition produced by the Vedic sentence is not mediated by another sense-organ, thereby establishing its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, if it were mediated by another sense-organ, it would be merely a recollection (*smṛti*) and not a valid cognition. This is the point. Furthermore, the word "immediate" (*aparokṣa*) serves to exclude the possibility that the sentence produces a cognition of an indirect (*parokṣa*) object. If it were to produce an indirect cognition, it would be like the cognition of fire derived from the statement "there is fire on the mountain," which is not a valid cognition of the immediate object. Therefore, the word "immediate" is used to show that the sentence produces a cognition of the unconnected and immediate [Self]. Thus, the conclusion is that the *Tattvamasi* and other such sentences are indeed the cause of the perception of the unconnected and immediate [Brahman-Self]. This is the meaning. And the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the context of the Upanishads. It does not mean that the sentence is the cause of the perception of the unconnected and immediate [Self] only in this specific instance. Rather, it is intended to show that the sentence is the cause of the perception of the unconnected and immediate [Self] in all cases, including the *Tattvamasi* and others. This is the sense. Therefore, the meaning is that the sentence is the cause of the perception of the unconnected and immediate [Self], and thus there is no lack of certainty. This is the final conclusion. Furthermore, the word "unconnected" (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*) is used to exclude the possibility that the sentence produces a cognition of a connected (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) object. If it were to produce a cognition of a connected object, it would be like the cognition of a pot produced by the sentence "bring the pot," which is not a valid cognition of the immediate object. Therefore, the word "unconnected" is used to show that the sentence produces a cognition of the unconnected and immediate [Self]. This is the meaning. The meaning is that it cannot be said that there is no possibility of a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) having a beginning, because a valid means of knowledge conforms to its object (*vastu*). || 898 ||
Because the designations "Self" and "Brahman" refer to a supramundane reality.
Since no relationship [between them] is apprehended, how can it be said that "the Self is Brahman"? || 859 ||

The validity of the *tattvamasi* and similar statements regarding Brahman and the Self has been stated; however, an objection is raised there: are Brahman and the Self unknown through other means of knowledge (*māna*) or already known? In the first case, since the word-potency (*śabdaśakti*) toward those two is not grasped, and a word whose potency is not grasped does not produce cognition, there would be invalidity in the form of non-origination [of knowledge].
This is expressed in the verse beginning with *alaukika*. (859)
A word whose connection with its meaning is known is capable of conveying the sense of a sentence.
And when the purpose of the self as Brahman is accomplished, people are made to enter into honor.

One might object that even if individual words lack the power to convey meaning because their specific potencies are not grasped, the sentence as a whole may still possess the power to convey meaning since it does not depend upon them. Anticipating this, he says "jñātā" (known), etc., to show that this is not so, because only words uttered in proximity constitute a sentence. Regarding the second [alternative], he says "brahma," etc., to show that if [the sentence] were merely reiterative—as in "That thou art"—it would result in its being non-authoritative; for if the meaning of Brahman and so forth is already known from common worldly usage, it lacks novelty (*apūrvatā*). ||860||
It cannot be non-worldly merely because the word "self" is used for the self alone.
Even the meaning of "Brahman" is well-known through common usage by virtue of its greatness. || 861 ||

First, the self (*ātman*) is not something beyond the world, because it is well-known as the perceiver of objects; since the word "self" is used by the elders for that [perceiver], the cognition of its denotative power resides there—thus he answers [the objection] with the words "not in the self. Furthermore, the meaning of "Brahman" is not unknown, as it is derived from the verbal root *bṛṃhati* (to grow).

He states that the word *brahman* has its primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is well-known as the Self—being established through the usage of elders in accordance with the meaning, and being renowned for its unsurpassed greatness—as follows: "Brahman. (861)
1 kha. 'ddaśapraṃ | 2 kha. 'dṛśeti | 3 kha. game kṣa | [Vol.
1, page 258] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 237
Thus, when the word-meaning has been fully understood from the word according to worldly convention, [the sentence-meaning follows].
In the Veda, by what can the fact that the meaning of a sentence is perceptible by the senses be refuted? || 862 ||

Regarding that point, he states that because the individual self (*ātman*) and Brahman enter into the scope of other means of knowledge (*māna*), [the Upanishads] are merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*) with respect to their true nature (*tattva*) and so forth. He says: "In this way.

The meaning is as follows: since the meanings of the two words are already perceived through worldly usage alone, the sentence-meaning—which is of the nature of an indivisible, uniform whole (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) and beyond the reach of other means of knowledge—is cognized from the sentence itself; therefore, it is not capable of being considered a mere reiteration. || 862 ||
Even regarding the categories of the unprecedented (apūrva), the deity, and heaven, [knowledge is derived] from the world.
Even an object beyond the reach of the senses is understood from the very words of the perfected ones (siddhas). || 863 ||

Regarding the point that, even when the word-meanings (*padārtha*) are established through worldly usage, the cognition of the unprecedented sentence-meaning (*apūrva-vākyārtha*) arises from the sentence alone, he provides an illustration with the words "Apūrva... and so forth. Here, "apūrva" refers to the *kārya* (task) which is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*) and is primarily characterized by such effort; this is understood through common observation as being cognizable even by other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, deities such as Indra and others, whose forms are [well-known], are also established through worldly usage; for indeed, people depict Indra as having a thunderbolt in his hand and Varuṇa as having a noose in his hand.

The meaning is as follows: since even heaven—which is a particular kind of happiness or a particular world—is well-known and understood from common worldly experience, just as one perceives a specific object through words whose power is established in things like heaven or the unseen potency (*apūrva*) that are already known in the world—by means of a sentence consisting of a collection of words whose powers are known—so too, even though the self and other such entities are established in the world, the meaning of the sentence, which consists in their essential unity, is established solely from the sentence itself. The two occurrences of the word "api" (even/also) serve this purpose.
The two meanings of the lips situated at the edge of the example. || 863 ||
There is no inherent presence [of the word] in its usage, because it lacks the capacity to fulfill the expectation [of the listener].
Since the extraction of sentences and so forth occurs from words together with their meanings, [it is not possible for the sentence-meaning to be produced by them]. || 864 ||

Anticipating the objection that since there is no sentence-meaning distinct from the word-meanings, and since the cognition of that [sentence-meaning] arises from the words themselves, the sentence is redundant, [the author] says: "There is no dependence. Because each individual word, independent of other words, and its respective meaning, lack the capacity to produce a cognition that incites the action of the middle-aged elder (*madhyama-vṛddha*)—a cognition which is free from expectancy (*anākāṅkṣa*)—words are not employed for that purpose alone. Therefore, a sentence must be employed for the sake of cognizing the sentence-meaning.

That is the meaning. Furthermore, since one observes the activity of the middle-aged elder after he has understood the meaning from the sentence itself, [the author] says "from the sentence" (vākyāt) to indicate that this is what is required for that understanding. || 864 ||
For a sentence is always employed solely for the sake of the sentence-meaning.
In legal proceedings, the interpretation adopted by the elders is accepted in that regard. || 865 ||

An objection is raised: "Do not words convey word-meanings? And from those [word-meanings], when they are in proximity and so forth, does the cognition of the sentence-meaning not arise from the words themselves? Anticipating this, he says: "For the sake of the sentence-meaning. It is the sentence alone that is employed for the purpose of understanding the sentence-meaning, both at the stage of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) and at the stage of proficiency; for word-meanings never convey the sentence-meaning, because they lack the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).

The meaning is that it has already been stated that there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of the sentence-meaning not being verbal. Furthermore, in the linguistic transactions of elders, when the knowledge of the sentence-meaning is intended, the capacity of this word for this specific meaning is grasped; and the apprehension of this relationship is not useful unless one has perceived the qualified object.
Therefore, he says "in linguistic transactions" (vyavahāreṣu) to show that the employment [of words] is solely for the sake of comprehending the sentence-meaning. || 861 ||

The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [is characterized] by the clear entry into other sections and the abandonment of certain parts.
When there is a distinction between the sentence and its meaning, the word-meanings serve as the cause.

He demonstrates the method for grasping the relation [between word and meaning] through insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*). Regarding the phrase "in another part" (*bhāgāntara*): although inference and other means are ways of grasping the expressive power (*śakti*), since the specific [power] is not established thereby, whereas it is established through insertion and so forth, he says "clearly" (*sphuṭam*) to indicate that the knowledge of the power is made manifest by this [method].
The connection with the preceding clause is: "the relation is grasped. Because insertion and deletion are subordinate to the grasping of the power, [the author speaks of] the sentence...

Having raised the doubt as to how there can be a distinction [between sentences] and a distinction between their respective meanings, he states that when there is a difference in the insertion (*āvāpa*) and so forth, there is a distinction of sentences due to the distinction of words, and a distinction of sentence-meanings due to the distinction of word-meanings.

He says: "In the case of a sentence... The construction is as follows: in the case of a distinction of sentences, words are the cause; and in the case of a distinction of sentence-meanings, word-meanings are the cause. || 866 ||
Whichever portion of the [astrological] division may have an excess of meaning through its arrival or other factors;
This [perception] would be a part of that part [of the object], serving as its cause, but it is not a means of valid cognition (pramā).

Objection: Is that word by whose insertion a sentence is divided authoritative with respect to its own meaning or not? In the first case, since other words would likewise be authoritative, the sentence would have no utility. In the second case, that which is non-authoritative cannot be a cause of division. To this, he says: "Of whichever part... In a certain sentence, due to the introduction of a particular word, if a certain word-meaning becomes additional, [then it is that word-meaning...].

That word is a "remembrancer" (smāraka); because there is no additional [cognitive content] beyond what is already remembered, it does not differ from a remembrancer according to the logical principle [that a source of knowledge must provide new information]. However, it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Nevertheless, it is a differentiator, just like the meaning of a word; otherwise, there would be confusion (sāṃkarya)—this is the intended sense. || 867 ||
For this very reason, it is held that there is a commonality between the sentence and the meaning of the sentence.
Even though a sentence is expressive, it denotes a meaning through the relation of its constituent parts. || 868 ||

One might raise the objection that, just as there is a relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācya-vācakabhāva*) between a word and its meaning, so too it exists between a sentence and its meaning; and since, like a word and its meaning, a sentence and its meaning cannot possibly possess parts (*sabhāgatva*), it follows that—just as a word has a capacity (*śakti*) toward its own meaning—a sentence would likewise have such a capacity toward its own meaning. Consequently, one might suspect that a sentence, like a word, is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Anticipating this, he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). He clarifies the meaning of the word "for this reason" [by stating]: "Even though it is a denoter" (*vācakatve 'pi*).

Even though a sentence is expressive, because it expresses a specific combined meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭārtha*), the sentence and its meaning possess constituent parts. Therefore, the connection of a word—which is a part of the sentence—with the word-meaning—which is a part of the sentence-meaning—is easily grasped when the limiting condition (*upādhi*) is the universal form (*ākṛti*). However, it is not logical for that [connection] to belong to the sentence as a collection of words with respect to the sentence-meaning as a collection of word-meanings; for it has been stated that such [a connection] is impossible in the case of a specific [meaning].
This is the meaning. || 868 ||
And thus, the denotative capacity of the collection is established in this way.
Therefore, the state of being a devotee (bhāgavattva) is established through both the words and the meaning of the sentences. || 869 ||

Having established that the cognition of the word’s power resides solely in its own meaning as qualified by compatibility with others, while that of the sentence resides in the whole, he states the resulting conclusion: "And therefore...

Since, according to the reasoning stated, both the sentence and its meaning possess parts, and since the power of the word alone resides in its own meaning as qualified by compatibility, it follows that the sentence—as a collection—possesses the status of an expressive agent and is authoritative; because its object is unknown [prior to its utterance], it is not non-authoritative like a single word.
This is the meaning. || 869 ||

And thus, the meaning of a sentence would be established even in the Veda by virtue of worldly convention.
For it is precisely worldly words and meanings that have been stated in the Śruti by means of logical reasoning. || 870 ||

[Objection: Even though the capacity of words is established in the world with respect to objects endowed with relational fitness (*yogyānvita*), how can the indivisible object (*akhaṇḍārtha*) desired by you be established in the Veda? To this, he says:

"And thus" (*evam ca*). When the apprehension of the word's capacity occurs through worldly usage with respect to an object endowed with relational fitness, then—by virtue of the collection of words whose capacities have been so apprehended—the sentence-meaning, whether it be a relation (*saṃsarga*) or the related (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), which is established in worldly sentences, would likewise exist in the Veda, for there is no distinction [between the two cases].

According to the principle that "the meaning of a sentence [is primary]," there is no distinction between words and their meanings in worldly usage and in the Veda; since this principle has already been set forth previously, it is not repeated here. Therefore, the meaning is that even in the Vedāntas, words—whose capacities are known to reside in the relation with a compatible [meaning]—convey the indivisible (akhaṇḍa) reality through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). || 870 ||
In the world, doubt might even arise due to the intervention of human intention.
But because the Veda is not of human origin, it possesses direct validity regarding its own subject matter.

Now, if there is no difference in the meaning of the sentences in both cases, then—just as with worldly sentences—the other [Vedic] sentence would also fall within the scope of other means of knowledge (*māna*), thereby undermining the Veda’s authority characterized by independence (*anapekṣatā*). To this he says: "The intention of a man" (*nṛvivakṣā*). In the world, because of the connection with a person's intention, and because that intention is not restricted as the cause for the meaning of a word, one might suspect that a word lacks authority regarding an object perceived through other means. In the Veda, however, which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is no intention...

The meaning is that, because there is no sublation and because there is no defect caused by such sublation, its status as a valid means of knowledge regarding its own object is established as being directly independent. || 871 ||
And even if words were directed toward an action, their collective aggregation would not be established.
Otherwise, there would be no comprehension [of the meaning], because of the absence of knowledge of the relationship. || 872 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the Veda is independent [of other means of knowledge], it cannot have an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatā*) because it is intent upon a related action (*saṃsṛṣṭakāryaparatvāt*), he says: "And not... Even if you accept that the Veda is intent upon action, a collection of words does not stand as being intent upon that [action alone], because it has been stated that words possess the power (*śakti*) to denote their meanings as connected with one another; and since there is no rule that a collection of words whose powers are known must necessarily be intent upon action, a sentence functions even toward that which is not an action, just as it does toward an action.

The point is that their status as having an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) has been demonstrated both through the fact of their being expressive and through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). If it is argued that the sentence must have "purport toward action" (*kāryaparatā*) because of a restriction on its semantic power (*śakti*)—whether that power resides in the action associated with [the other words], or in the word's own meaning as associated with that action, or in the meaning of another word which itself is associated with the action, or in that which is associated with what is associated with the action—the author says "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) to refute this. This is because, if the semantic power were restricted to an action associated [with others], then from the nominal stems (*nāmapada*), their own meanings [would not be conveyed].

There would be no cognition [of meaning] for those [words] regarding those [objects], because their capacity is not grasped when the restriction of capacity is limited to that which is connected with an action (*kāryānvita*). In a sentence such as "A son is born," there is no comprehension of the meanings of the words "son" and so forth from those words themselves, because their relationship is not grasped in respect to those objects connected with an action. Furthermore, there is no understanding of the meaning of the word "action" itself from the word denoting action, because an action lacks connection with another action; thus, its relation to it is impossible. This remains true even if the restriction of capacity is held to reside in the object denoted by a word that is itself directed toward an action.

The sense is this: since being subordinate (*tatparatva*) is not distinct from being a subordinate element (*taccheṣatva*), the aforementioned defect remains as it was. Even if there were a restriction on expressive power (*śakti*) such that it resides in that which is connected with the action to be accomplished (*kārya*), the same defect would persist because the action to be accomplished—whether alone or both together—would necessarily be the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that power. || 872 ||
And just as there is an intention toward an effect, yet that effect itself does not exist.
This has already been thoroughly established by us through logical arguments. || 873 ||
For this reason as well, he states that the Veda does not have action as its primary purport: "Just as... [873.1] Or also...
And because that [convention] is established solely through the linguistic proficiency acquired from the usage of ancient elders since time immemorial.
The relationship between a word and its meaning cannot be said to have a beginning.

When the proponent of the view that words denote actions has been refuted, some say: "Since the relationship between word and meaning is conventional (*sāṃketika*), even if a word does not have action as its primary referent, the [Vedic] word's lack of dependence [on human agency] is not established. To them, he says: "Beginningless" (*anādi*). This is because, in the *Autpattika-sūtra*, the relationship between word and meaning is established in the form of a power (*śakti*) designated as the proficiency (*vyutpatti*) that serves as the cause for the aforementioned linguistic usage; therefore, conventionality (*saṃketatva*) does not apply to it.
It should not be doubted from the perspective of ultimate reality; the meaning is that the Veda does not depend upon him by way of convention (*saṃketa*). || 874 ||
Where, upon the first hearing, there is no comprehension of the word and its meaning.
In that case, the cause is the lack of proficiency with words, not their incapacity. (875)

[Objection: If the relationship between words and their meanings were based on an inherent power (*śakti*), why would everyone who hears words such as "cow" not have a cognition of the object? For the power of the word is no different for anyone. Furthermore, those who are unlearned (*avyutpanna*) do not have a cognition of the word's meaning; therefore, the relationship between them must be one of convention (*saṅketa*). To this, he says: "The first... [and so on]. For those who are unlearned, upon hearing a word, there is no determination of the meaning because they do not know the power of the word.
The meaning is: because of the lack of knowledge regarding the relationship called "convention," which is distinct from [the object's] capacity. || 875 ||
For in the case of the eye, there is no perception of an object without external illumination.
Its capacity is not destroyed by this much, nor would that of another be so. || 876 ||

If the cognition of the word-meaning occurs only when the apprehension of the relationship exists, then the efficacy of the word would be lost; or else, that [efficacy] would belong to the apprehension of the relationship itself, because it is that alone which, through the distinction between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained, serves as its cause. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The eye. Just as the eye, although endowed with the power of vision, does not function in the perception of color and so forth without external light such as a lamp, nor does it [lose its efficacy] merely by depending on a lamp or similar source.

Nor does that [perception] arise from a lamp or the like; thus, although a word requires the apprehension of a relationship for its capacity to convey meaning, there is no loss of its cognitive power, nor does that [power] belong to the apprehension of the relationship itself.
Furthermore, the relationship between two words is not created by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
For when the relationship is already established, it is learned from the elders. || 877 ||

Furthermore, regarding the position that [the relationship] is conventional (saṃketa), is it established by someone through linguistic instruction (vyutpatti)—whether by a non-omniscient person or by the omniscient Lord? It is not the first case; thus he says: "By linguistic instruction. He provides the reason why the production of a convention does not occur without the apprehension of the relationship: "For, once established... When the relationship between word and meaning is already established, that linguistic instruction arises by virtue of the usage of elders; from that [instruction], [the convention is formed].
The meaning is that she, being turned away (*parācīnā*), would not produce a connection with one who is turned toward her (*prācīna*). || 877 ||
Because it is impossible to establish a relationship [between words and their meanings], and because there is no recollection of anyone who created that [relationship].
And because of the continuity of linguistic usage, the eternity of the relationship is established. || 878 ||

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case], stating: "Because of the connection" (*saṃbandha*). For one who is not omniscient is not capable of creating the connection between word and meaning, because that connection is infinite; thus, the convention (*saṃketa*) was not created by him—this is the meaning. He says that the third [alternative] is not [the case], stating: "Of its creator" (*tatkartuḥ*). Since the Creator God (*īśvara*), the maker of the connection, is neither perceived nor remembered, it is not tenable that even this [connection] was created by an omniscient being; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding God as the creator of the convention.
1 kha. Capability. 2 kha. 'ketaḥ saṃ. 3 kha. 'cīnaṃ saṃ. [Vol.
1, page 262] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 241.

The sense is that [the proof] pertains to an *īśvara* who is not distinct from [the world], because inference and scripture both refer to such a one. He states a defect common to all three positions with the words "without that" (*tadvinā*).

By this, he means that since verbal usage is observed even without the recollection of an agent in the form "this connection was made by him," the connection was not created by him. He states the resulting conclusion: "The subject of dispute (the connection) is eternal, because its author is not remembered, like the self (*ātman*)."
It is established. || 878 ||
Furthermore, the fact that the creator is not remembered is like [the case of] a dilapidated well and so forth.
Nor does it lead to the comprehension of non-existence; thus, it is not equal [to inference] by virtue of its relationship [with the object]. (879)

Anticipating the objection that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in cases such as dilapidated wells, he says: "In the case of the dilapidated," etc. In those instances, the non-remembrance of the agent while the agent actually exists does not prove his non-existence, because that [non-remembrance] can also be accounted for by the interruption of the tradition (*saṃpradāya-viccheda*). However, in this case, the non-remembrance of the agent does not prove his non-existence in the same way; for the non-remembrance of the agent—qualified by the absence of an interruption in the tradition—is invariably concomitant with his non-existence. Furthermore:

The relationship [between word and meaning] is comparable to an ancient well and the like, because it is difficult to establish due to its infinity, whereas other [relationships] are easier to establish due to their limited nature;
therefore, its eternity may also be inferred from the impossibility of there being an author. Thus he says: "Nor... (879).
Furthermore, in some cases, even when objects are known, doubt may arise due to causes such as distance and the like.
However, since [the object] is absolutely unperceived, its non-existence is therefore ascertained. || 880 ||

He states that the eternity of the relationship is established because the absence of an author is ascertained through the non-apprehension of what is otherwise capable of being perceived. Regarding the phrase "in some cases":

in the world, in certain places and times, when objects are generally perceived but their specific features are not grasped due to causes such as distance or darkness, doubt is observed—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—but not regarding things that are absolutely unperceived, for there is no cause for the apprehension of common characteristics. However, in this case, [there is] an absolute... of the author of the relationship.

Since there is no perception [of such a relation], there can be no doubt regarding it; how, then, could there be certainty of it? Therefore, because its non-existence is ascertained through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*), the eternity of the connection is established—this is the meaning. || 880 ||
Because it denotes its own meaning alone, which is connected with a proximate object.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of a sentence, whether in common worldly usage or in the Veda, possesses validity as a means of knowledge.

Having rejected the view that the relation [of words] is mere convention (*saṃketa*) and having established it as inherent power (*śakti*), and having accepted that this power resides in the "fittingly connected" (*yogyānvita*), he concludes the validity of the word with respect to the intended object: "In close proximity," etc. Because words denote their own respective meanings—which are already conjoined with other meanings possessing proximity and so forth, and which are indifferent as to whether they are to be performed or not—the meaning of a sentence, whether in common usage or in the Veda, is either the connection between word-meanings or the word-meanings as thus connected.

The construction is: "the established [object] is authoritative. The two ablative cases are in apposition. Thus, while this general rule stands, the meaning is that the establishment of the indivisible nature (*akhaṇḍārthatā*) [of Brahman] follows from reflecting upon the intended purport (*tātparya*) in the Vedāntas. || 881 ||
Therefore, because it brings about understanding and because it avoids defective causes, [it is valid].
And because it is uncontradicted, the scripture possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding the real entity, just like the senses and so forth. (882)

One might wonder: is the word’s incapacity regarding the reality due to its being non-cognitive, or due to its being doubtful, or due to its being a cause of error, or due to the absence of human purpose? Having thus raised these alternatives, the author refutes three of them in succession with the words beginning "ataḥ" (therefore). The connection is: "Therefore, from the Śruti.
Because this Śruti—such as "That thou art"—is cognitive for the qualified seeker, and because it is not of human origin, the cognition arising from it possesses an unimpaired cause.

The meaning is that the validity of this [scripture] is established— just like that of the eyes and other sense organs— because it is free from doubt and error, because there is no sublation due to the absence of any contradicting factor, and because it cannot be considered erroneous since no such sublation is perceived. || 882 ||
Just as there is authoritative status regarding an action because it teaches what is beneficial for human goals, [so too is there authoritative status regarding liberation].
Likewise, [this is so] either because of the distinction within the single self, or because of the excellence of the human goal. || 883 ||

He states the fourth [reason]: "puruṣārtha" (the human goal). Having accepted the identity of the two based on the equality of their effects, and having stated that there is no difference in the authority of the word in both cases, he declares the excellence [of the Upanishads] by stating that in the case of identity, the scripture’s authority consists in its revealing the ultimate reality (*tattvāvedana*). He states the reason for this distinction with the words "viśeṣāt vā" (or because of a distinction). He provides the reason for this further distinction regarding the uncontradicted human object of knowledge with the words "pumartha" (human goal), [meaning] that which makes known the as-yet-unknown unsurpassed human goal.
The meaning is that the validity of the primary [cognition] is real. || 883 ||
A person [seeks] the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired.
Desiring [the goal], one intent upon it also depends upon a suitable means.

In order to clarify that the meaning of the sentence, which constitutes the inner self (*pratīc*), possesses the status of the supreme human goal (*pumarthātiśaya*), he states its twofold nature: "The person" (*pumān*).

Since it is accepted that a result is characterized by being desired, he establishes the status of those two as results with the words "desiring" (*icchan*). He indicates the maxim that "the end to be accomplished depends upon the means" with the words "requires" (*apekṣate*). The meaning is that [the person] requires that which is suitable and capable of producing the goal to be attained; he is intent upon that result.
And it means that one who possesses intent toward its cause. || 884 ||
In this world, one desires to obtain some village or other thing that has not yet been obtained and is desired.
Hemādri forgets something even when it is right in his hand, yet he longs for it.
In that case, since both types of human goals (puruṣārtha) are impermanent because they are achieved through means, one might suspect that no excellence of human goal can be established in the Self;
anticipating this objection, [the author] distinguishes the attainment of the desired object with the words "village, etc. Here, the term "here" refers to the sphere of worldly transaction. || 885 ||
Likewise, one seeks to avoid what is undesirable, such as thorns and the like, because one wishes to abandon them.
One abandons even that which has already been discarded, such as the snake [superimposed] upon a rope. || 886 ||
He also analyzes the cessation of the undesirable: "That which is to be avoided," [as stated in verse 886].
Because that which is to be attained and that which is to be avoided are both accomplished through fixed means.
From both injunction and prohibition, there would arise a dependence upon a means of accomplishment. || 887 ||

He states the means for attaining what has not been attained and avoiding what has not been avoided: "Niyata" (certain). Since the attainment of what has not been attained and the avoidance of what has not been avoided are to be accomplished by means established through the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) found in the scriptures, one understands the distinction between the means through injunctions and prohibitions, as well as through positive and negative concomitances; and by practicing those means, one attains the desired object that was not previously attained, and avoids that which was undesired and not yet avoided.
The meaning is "he avoids. || 887 ||
Because they are separated by ignorance, those [states] that were attained and then abandoned may occur again.
Nothing other than the knowledge of reality as it truly is conduces to the goal of human existence.

He states the means for the remaining two—attainment (*āpti*) and avoidance (*parihāra*)—in the verse beginning with "ajñāna" (ignorance). [This is from] the *Vārttika*, accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā*. 243. [The text explains: Regarding that which has been attained and that which has been abandoned, [the means consists in] ignorance... [end of fragment].

The meaning is that when the desire to acquire and the desire to abandon exist by virtue of being concealed, it is only through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) that one becomes capable of attaining and avoiding those two for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). || 888 ||
For one who desires, through the sacred tradition, the complete severance of all misfortunes, [this is the means].
"You are Brahman," [he said], for you have destroyed all afflictions through the abandonment of delusion. (889)
Thus, even regarding this distinction, he explains how the status of being the supreme human goal is established for that which is to be known through the Vedāntas: "Aśeṣa... [and so on].

For one seeking liberation, when the identity of the self with Brahman—namely, "Thou art Brahman"—is known from sentences such as "That Thou Art," one becomes one who has attained the known Brahman, with all afflictions dispelled due to the absence of the delusion that causes them. Therefore, it is appropriate that the Vedāntas possess ultimate validity with respect to the self as Brahman, which is the unsurpassed and uncontradicted human goal.
The meaning is "of the Vedāntas. || 889 ||
"The authority of the Veda is established because it brings about the comprehension of an object not already known."
Just as there is validity regarding an effect, let it be accepted likewise regarding oneness. (890)

And here he states that those [sentences] possess authority in that regard: "Of the Veda," etc. The meaning is as follows: since the authority of the Veda is established on the basis of its making known an unknown object, just as sentences concerning action—which make known an unknown action—possess authority regarding their own meaning, so too sentences concerning unity, which make known that [unity] which is unknown, possess authority in that regard;
for there is no difference between them in terms of being a means of cognizing what has not been previously apprehended. This has been stated more than once. || 890 ||
If its status as a means of valid cognition depends upon the [accomplishment of] an action, then its status as a means of valid cognition depends upon that action.
In this way, there would be mutual dependence, because one [of the two] is not established without the other. (891)

[Objection: Is it not improper to say that a sentence such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is a means of valid knowledge regarding its own meaning because it awakens one who has not yet understood, just like a sentence concerning what is to be done (kārya-vākya)?

For in the case of the validity of a sentence, being grounded in what is to be done (kāryaniṣṭhatva) is the determining factor. To this, he says: "From [the requirement of] what is to be done" (kāryāt).

If the Veda’s status as a means of valid knowledge were due solely to its being grounded in what is to be done, then there would be a circular argument (anyonyāśrayatā): the Veda’s grounding in what is to be done follows from its being a means of valid knowledge, and its being a means of valid knowledge follows from that grounding. Thus, neither of the two [would be established].

The meaning is that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in some respects. The sense of the word "but" (*tu*) is that being directed toward an effect (*kāryaniṣṭhatva*) is not the determinant for the authority of the Veda, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished. || 891 ||
"In cases of indifference and prohibitions, the status of a valid means of knowledge would not be obtained."
For indifference is indeed cessation, and that has its own intrinsic nature as its support. || 892 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the following inference establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? "The subject under dispute is not a means of valid cognition regarding its own object, because it is a sentence whose terminus is not an action (*akāryaniṣṭha*), like [sentences] such as 'the sky-lotus is fragrant'.

[Reply: Because [in prohibitions] there is indifference (*audāsīnya*). In prohibitions such as "one should not kill" or "one should not drink," the meaning is indifference, which is distinct from an action (*kārya*). If the Veda’s purpose were exclusively action, these [prohibitions] would lack authority; yet their authority is indeed accepted. Therefore, [your reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

The meaning is that this is the movement of the reason (*hetu*). [The opponent] anticipates the objection that since indifference (*audāsīnya*) itself is the effect, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the negations directed toward that [indifference]. [The author] says: "Indifference. The meaning is that indifference is the cessation of an action that has been undertaken; it is not an effect. [The opponent objects: "In that case, then cessation itself is the effect. [The author] says: "Its own nature (*svarūpa*). Cessation is indeed the thing itself; for it does not exist as something other than the changeless, non-dual reality (*kūṭasthādvaya*).
The meaning is that even if it were distinct [from the self], it would not be an effect; therefore, how could prohibitions be directed toward it? || 892 ||
The authority of such passages as "He wept" (so 'rodīt) arises from their being directed toward a ritual action.
And because it teaches that which is not the goal of man, there is no reason [to accept it] here. || 891 ||
244 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 265]

It has been stated that even prohibitions—which terminate in non-action characterized by the cessation of an action already undertaken and consist in the non-deviation from one's natural state of indifference—possess authority;

likewise, sentences expressing identity (aikya-vākya) possess authority with respect to their own meaning. Now, one might object: "The sentence 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi) and others are authoritative regarding a remainder of action (kārya-śeṣe), because they are Vedic sentences devoid of an injunction (vidhi), like [prohibitions] which are accepted as such. Anticipating this doubt, it was already stated that the absence of a human goal (puruṣārtha-rāhitya) with respect to its own meaning serves as the limiting condition (upādhi). I shall now recall that very point.

He concludes: "So he wept" (*so'rodīt*). He states the pervasion of the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*) with the words "And that" (*tacca*). For the meaning is this: in the *Tattvamasi* and other such passages, there is no teaching of something that is not a human goal (*apumartha*), because the identity (*aikya*) which is their referent is declared to be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being supreme bliss (*parānanda*). He states the final conclusion—that the stated probans is non-conclusive due to its being based on a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*)—with the words: "Thus, [it is] not a cause" (*ityakāraṇam*). || 893 ||
Nor is the falsity of the means for realizing the single self suspected here.
Because one has achieved the goal upon attaining the end, one no longer looks toward the means. || 894 ||

Even though it may be argued that the cognition arising from sentences such as "That thou art" is not valid knowledge because its cause is false—just like a cognition produced by a fallacious appearance of smoke—even if the inference [of its falsity] based on the Vedic statements being devoid of injunctions is untenable, the author says "And not... to address this doubt. The falsity of the means of knowing reality, such as the Śruti, is not raised as a reason for the absence of validity in the cognition produced by it; rather, what is intended there is the absence of the fruit of valid knowledge.
The meaning is: "because it is not established as a probans. Anticipating the objection that the reason is over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*), he says: "upeya" (the goal). The meaning is:

since this [knowledge], which is the goal (*upeya*), results in liberation, the person’s purpose is fulfilled; consequently, there is no further search for the means such as the Vedas (*śruti*), etc., and thus the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). || 894 ||
Prior to the realization of the identity of the Self, [the world] is not false, because of the absence of a cause [for its falsity].
Nor does it proceed further upward without dependence [on other causes], because its purpose is fulfilled by reaching the human goal. || 895 ||

Furthermore, one must consider whether the knowledge that the means [to liberation] is false constitutes a reason for its invalidity by way of its own nature, or whether that knowledge occurs either before or after the knowledge of reality (*vastujñāna*).

Having thus formulated the alternatives, he refutes the first: "aikātmya... (The meaning is that prior to the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, the means is not false; since there is no evidence for such a cognition at that time, the reason is unestablished). He refutes the second: "puruṣārtha... (After the knowledge of reality...).

The meaning is that even if the falsity of the means is known, it does not destroy the validity of the knowledge regarding the goal, because since the fruit—liberation—is already attained, there is no need for further means of knowledge; thus, the aforementioned condition remains as it was. || 899 ||
Apart from making known that which is to be attained, there is no other truth for a means of valid cognition (mīti).
For even from a real object, fire is not inferred from a pot, because it is not a means [to that inference]. || 896 ||

Furthermore, for one who asserts that a cognition produced by a false means (*upāya*) is not valid knowledge (*pramā*), is it intended that (1) a false thing cannot function as a means, or (2) that only a true thing can function as a means? Not the first, because even false things such as reflections are accepted as being means.

As for the second, does "truth" of the means consist in its capacity to produce an effect (*kāryakaratva*), or in its freedom from sublation (*bādhavaidhurya*)? Having accepted the former, [the author] refutes the latter...

[The opponent] objects: By the word "means" (*miti*), the Vedas and other means of knowledge are indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). It is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency (*kāryakaratva*) that constitutes the essential nature of such a means as being a revealer of its object (*upeya*).
