Therefore, since the cognition under dispute is not produced by a means devoid of such truthfulness, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) with respect to its capacity for causal efficiency.

The meaning is as follows: without [the realization of] the goal, there is no truth—characterized by the absence of sublation—for the means, because sublation such as "neither here nor there" (neha nānā) is clearly evident;
thus, the stated adventitious condition (*upādhi*) exists in the reason [of being produced by a cause] which lacks such reality. Furthermore, truth does not reside in the means. [End of fragment].
[Vārtika, Vol. 1, p.
266] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri:

"For [the jar] is not the efficient cause; for even though a jar is real, fire is not inferred from it, because despite its reality, it lacks the status of being a means for the cognition of that [fire]."
Thus he said: "From truth," [verse 896].
But because smoke-like vapor and the like are not fire, fire is not cognized from them.
In that case, the reason is the lack of means, but not the lack of truth. (897)

One might raise the second position, arguing that the falsity of the means (*upāya*) by its very nature is the determinant for the invalidity of the cognition, based on the following inference: "The object of dispute is not valid knowledge because it is false, like a fallacious appearance of smoke.
To this, he says "dhūma... [verse 897], stating: "Not so; because the absence of an invariable relation (*avyabhicarita-sambandha-rāhitya*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*)."
Like smoke, its ultimate reality is not attained because it is a means.
Likewise, there would clearly be a contradiction of the Vedāntas and the scriptural texts concerning the oneness of the Self. || 898 ||
Then, raising the objection that even the Vedas and other such means must be real because they are means—just like smoke—the author says: "like smoke. He states the reason for this:
"so," meaning provided that the Vedas and so forth are real. (898)
Even tears, because they are false, are considered to be a non-means.
But the reality of the means is established by the sublation of the ignorance regarding the identity [of the self]. (899)

One might object that the reason [in the argument] "one should resort to what is doubted because it lacks an invariable relation, like a non-existent thing" is not established, since the aforementioned *upādhi* (limiting condition) pervades the probans (*sādhana*). Anticipating this, he says: "like steam. Regarding that, he states the reason for the non-establishment of the probans: "because of identity," etc.

Since the "reality" defined as the capacity to produce an effect is admitted [in the case of steam], the probans is indeed unestablished; for even in the case of smoke and the like, there is an absence of ultimate reality.
The meaning is that there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) regarding existence. || 899 ||
Because scripture has fulfilled its purpose through the realization of the identity of the Self, it is measured [as complete].
The examination of a means would be in vain, like [testing] the boat after one has already crossed over. || 900 ||

Raising the objection that there is a mutual dependence—namely, that the means is true only if the realization of the identity of the Self exists, and that realization exists only if the means is true—he replies: "Of the Śruti," etc. Since a person has achieved their purpose through the cognition of reality derived from the indifferent Śruti and other sources, the search for a means is useless; furthermore, since there is no contradiction even if that means is sublated after the cognition has arisen, there is no mutual dependence. [The phrase] "of the Śruti" [indicates that] the search for a means occurs once the cognition has been established.
Regarding the word "in vain," he provides an illustration: "of one who has crossed over. || 900 ||
Furthermore, because external objects are not the self, doubt may still arise.
In this case, since the object to be attained is of the nature of the self, what doubt can there be regarding its validity? (901)

Furthermore, he states that even if the Vedas and other means of knowledge lack ultimate reality, they are not devoid of the power to produce cognition. [He says: "Regarding external objects. Even though non-self-objects established by perception and other means may be such-and-such or not, a doubt on the part of the mother (the seeker) is possible; however, because those [external objects] are non-self while the object known through the Vedas and so forth is the Self, no suspicion whatsoever arises regarding the absence of validity for that which makes its own nature known, even if the means [of knowledge] be false.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, he states that there is not even a suspicion of falsity regarding the Vedas and other means of knowledge by saying, "In external [objects]," etc.

In the case of vomit and the like, because the means [of cognition] is not the Self, there may indeed be a suspicion of its falsity; however, in the case of the non-dual Self (ekātmya), since the means such as the Vedas are nothing but the Self itself, their lack of authority [as independent entities] does not arise.
(Note: *lavo* in manuscript *kha* is a scribal error for *bhavet*).
246 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction] [vol. 1, p. 267] Connection—

The sense is that since even the suspicion of falsity does not arise regarding the Vedas and other scriptures because they are true in their own nature, and because they serve as a means despite being [ultimately] imagined distinctions, the authority of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman as the Self is established. || 909 ||
Moreover, here, as in other cases, the meaning of the sentence does not consist in a distinction [between the parts].
Or it may be characterized by conjunction, arising from the non-difference between Brahman and the self. || 902 ||

Anticipating the objection that, in that case, it would follow that [the sentence] has the status of a sentence-meaning desired by others (i.e., a relational meaning), and thus its indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) would be lost, he says: "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*). The meaning is this:

in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the sentence-meaning is a distinction consisting of the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*); in the case of "The blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), the sentence-meaning is the connection (*saṃsarga*) between the word-meanings expressed by the words sharing the same case-ending; but this is not so in the case of "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and similar sentences, because their meaning is the identity (*aikya*) of the referents of *tat* and *tvam*. || 902 ||
Just as Brahman has the state of non-Brahmanhood consisting in its being not the Self, so too does the Self [have the state of non-Selfhood].
Knowledge arising from the scripture destroys ignorance as it emerges. (903)

One might raise the objection: "How can there be non-duality [of Brahman], given the inference that 'Brahman and the Self are not identical because they are mutually contradictory, like cold and heat'?

Anticipating this, he replies with the words "Of Brahman," etc., stating that such is not the case because the contradiction asserted by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) is unestablished, while the other kind of contradiction [found in ordinary experience] is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*), as seen in the case of an object and its reflection.
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that qualities such as non-Brahmanhood are produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*): "From the scripture," etc. (903).
In this context, the Self is not other than Brahman, nor is Brahman other than the Self.
Therefore, the identity of these two is distinct from that of a blue lotus.

If it be argued that, because difference also exists alongside the non-difference of Brahman and the Self—as in the case of a blue lotus—the meaning of the sentence here must be a "conjunction" (saṃsarga), like that between the blue and the lotus; [the author] says "No. By "Scripture" (śāstra) is meant the present context. If the inner self (pratīc) were other than Brahman, it would be non-Brahman, like a pot;

and if that [pot] were other than Brahman, it likewise would be non-Self. Therefore, there is no identity (tādātmya) between the blue and the lotus, which possess both difference and non-difference, but rather—
The meaning is "delicious. || 904 ||
Just as the notions of non-Brahman and non-Self are here based on ignorance, so it is in this case.
Selfhood and Brahmanhood are not thus [attained] from another; therefore, they are [known] intrinsically.

One might raise the objection: "Just as Brahman's non-selfhood and the self's non-Brahman-hood are due to ignorance (*avidyā*), why could it not be that the self's nature as Brahman and Brahman's nature as the self are likewise produced by ignorance? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not non-Brahman" (*abrahma*). Here, the word "here" (*atra*) refers to the self and so forth; "from another" (*anyasmāt*) expresses ignorance. Considering that difference is seen to involve mutual dependence and other such fallacies, whereas non-difference does not, [the author] states: "of the self..."
He states the conclusion—that the state of being Brahman and the state of being the Self of Brahman are innate—with the words "Therefore... (909).
Furthermore, such a connection between two atoms would not be possible without an action, because they are of a single nature.
And the genitive case does not occur without a distinction between the relation of possession and the relation of action. (906)

Anticipating the objection that since there is not even a trace of difference between Brahman and the Self, the genitive case [in "Brahman's Self"]—which depends on distinctions such as qualities or actions—cannot apply, and thus the identity of the two terms *tat* and *tvam* cannot be established, he says: "Of the two names. Since even a scent of difference is absent, he provides the reason for the application of those two terms to the effect [of the sentence] solely through the exclusion of action and so forth: "Because of the oneness of self" (*aikātmyāt*). This is because the referent of the words is of a single flavor, and within it, difference is impossible to define.

This is the meaning. Having raised the objection—“Even if [Brahman] is of a single flavor, how can there be the application of words in the absence of a [direct] cause?”—and considering that it occurs through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), he says:
“Not action” (na kriyā). || 906 ||
[Vārtika] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 247.
Just as greatness exists in space in comparison to the space within a jar.
In the same way, when compared to that which is external (parāktva), the internal nature (pratyaktā) is not perceived within the Self. || 907 ||

One might raise the objection that even though there is no difference between the inner self (*pratyak*) and Brahman, a distinction must still be asserted between the inner self and the non-self, because the nature of being "inner" (*pratyaktva*) is dependent upon the form of the "outer" (*parāgrūpa*); therefore, it cannot be partless (*akhaṇḍatā*). This is the doubt expressed by the words "mahattā" (greatness). The response is given: "Not in the Self" (*nātmāni*). The inner nature does not depend upon outerness within the Self; rather, it is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). To this, he provides the proof of the experience of the realized ones (*vidvadanubhava*) with the word "it is perceived" (*īkṣyate*).
Thus [ends the verse]. || 907 ||
"Inwardness and non-duality, like consciousness itself, are not dependent on anything else."
For indeed, there would be no understanding of that which is not for the sake of another, because of the exclusion of non-understanding. || 908 ||

Nevertheless, fearing that the non-dual reality cannot be partless because it depends upon duality, he says: "Selfhood" (*pratyaktvam*). [This refers to] the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on the statement of "awakening" (*bodha*) in Brahman with respect to the destruction of ignorance, according to the principle that "selfhood is its own innate form, and the fruit is the state of being devoid of activity. Fearing that the illustrative example might lack the property to be proven (*sādhya*), he says: "Because it does not have another purpose" (*apārārthyāt*).

Because consciousness is the very nature of Brahman—as established by such scriptural texts as "Brahman is not this, it is not that" (neti neti)—it is not described in relation to Brahman merely as the exclusion of insentience (*jaḍa*). Likewise, its non-duality (*advayatva*) is its own form, synonymous with fullness and independent of anything else; thus, the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatā*) of Brahman is established—this is the meaning. || 908 ||
"This very Self is indeed Brahman, yet it is obscured by remoteness due to delusion."
In that same way, even Brahmā perceives himself as having a second.
He concludes the systematic exposition (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman, the Self, which is the partless, single essence, with the words beginning "The Self also... (909).
"Because [the notions] of being remote and having a second are sublated by the realization that 'the Self is Brahman'."
The desired conclusion is established: "The treatise has been completed. || 910 ||

[Objection: Since Brahman is perceived as remote (parokṣa) and the Self is perceived as having duality (sadvayatva), how can there be an understanding of non-difference? To this, he says: "The Self" (ātma). Because the remoteness [of Brahman] is removed by its connection with the Self, and because the state of having duality [of the Self] is removed by its connection with Brahman, the sentence culminates in its purport being their identity, insofar as [Brahman] is supreme bliss and the supreme human goal. Thus, when the concordance (samanvaya) is established...
He states the resulting conclusion—that liberation arises from the knowledge of oneness derived from the sentence itself—by saying: "Thus it is established. || 990 ||
But surely, by means of sentences based on duality that are prescriptive or prohibitive, [this is established].
Nor is there identity with the eyes and so forth, because that is sublated, just as in the case of the self and the means of valid cognition. || 911 ||

Unable to tolerate the aforementioned *samanvaya* (systematic concordance), he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely). The meaning is that since injunctions and prohibitions, as well as perception and other means of knowledge, have difference as their object, and because non-duality (*aikya*) is sublated by them, it cannot be known through the Vedānta texts. || 911 ||
Nor can there be either option or combination with those [other doctrines] for the scripture of the doctrine of non-duality.
Nor can they be sublated in any way, even while possessing validity. (912)

Since the Vedāntas also possess authority without distinction, one does not observe either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) of them with perception and the other means of knowledge.
1. *nīkṣate* | 2. *kha. īkṣata* | *naiṣi*.
248 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection—] [Vol. 1, p. 269]

Anticipating the objection that reality might therefore be that which is known through the Vedāntas, or that which is accessible through perception and other means, or even both, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). Just as there is no option (*vikalpa*) regarding the performance or non-performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there is no such option between the authority of the scripture and that of the others. Nor is there a combination (*samuccaya*), as in the case of the six sacrifices, whereby both it and they would possess authority. [The opponent suggests: "In that case, let the others be sublated by the scripture."
"No," he says; "nor even," [he says]. || 912 ||
For even when there is a state of conflicting cognitions, the object itself is not thereby rendered indeterminate.
Furthermore, difference and non-difference could not both exist simultaneously in the same place due to their mutual contradiction. (913)

Anticipating the objection—"Why does no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise regarding a reality that possesses mutually contradictory powers?"—he says: "Contradictory" (*viruddha*). The meaning is this:

conceptual construction occurs only with respect to action (*kriyā*), not with respect to a real entity (*vastu*); and since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) pertains to a real entity, it is not subject to conceptual construction. Otherwise, by way of that [conceptualization], it would follow that even the real entity itself would be subject to it, which is impossible. Furthermore, in the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), both difference and non-difference would result; yet neither exists anywhere.

Thinking that it is not logical for existence and non-existence to occur simultaneously in a single locus—since they are contradictory, otherwise there would be no occasion for even speaking of them—he states the synthesis of the two means of valid cognition: "Difference and non-difference" (verse 993).
For you, there is no entity that is both different and non-different, by virtue of which it would not contradict valid cognition.
Since diversity is negated by the statement "not here, not manifold," how can there be a cognition of difference? (914)

He states another fault regarding the contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that arises for those who propound non-dualism (*aikātmyavādin*) if they were to admit difference. [The verse begins with] "bhinnā" (different). He says: "By the acceptance of objects as both different and non-different, the non-contradiction of all two kinds of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be asserted; yet that [non-contradiction] is refuted precisely because such [objects] do not exist. Furthermore, he says that such a thing cannot be accepted by you, because it would contradict the accepted scriptures (*śruti*).
"Not so," [he said]. || 994 ||
Nor is the sense organ or other means of apprehending color and so forth sublated here.
And that treatise which is conducive to self-knowledge is for the sake of spiritual refinement. || 915 ||

Having rejected both the alternatives and the combination [of the two] regarding the treatise (*śāstra*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, he states the reason why there is no sublation (*bādhyatva*) [of perception by the treatise] in the words "varṇādi" (phonemes, etc.).

The meaning is as follows: first of all, perception and the like are the means for grasping phonemes, words, sentences, and so on; it is not logical that these be sublated by the treatise, because if that were the case, knowledge of reality would be unestablished due to the absence of a cause, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of liberation (*mokṣa*). [This applies to the claim that] the treatise on unity [sublates] the treatise on ritual action (*karmaśāstra*).

He states the reason for this sublation: "For the sake of purification" (*saṃskārāya*). The meaning is as follows: the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) produces the knowledge of the Self through the purification of the intellect by means of the performance of its own prescribed duties; if that [ritual section] were sublated, there would be an absence of knowledge due to the absence of ritual action. Therefore, the ritual section, as well as perception and so forth, are not to be sublated. || 995 ||
Or else, one may recite the scripture with its scope remaining open, for the sake of ritual practice.
Since the sense organs and so forth have not yet achieved their purpose, how could there be sublation by them? (916)

What, then, is the status of the Vedāntas? He states it: "It is figurative" (*upacāra*). The meaning is that the scripture achieves its purpose by relying on a figurative non-duality of Brahman, just as there is a figurative designation of a village headman as being "non-dual. He states another alternative: "It is for recitation" (*japa*). Or rather, according to the maxim that between two [statements], one with scope and one without scope, the one without scope is stronger, [the Vedāntas] have no scope except for duality.
He states that [the Vedas] are not sublated by a treatise that has scope [only for the empirical world], according to the manner shown, with the words "akṣādeḥ" (of the senses, etc.). || 996 ||
It is said: "The injunction relies upon a distinction established by common worldly experience."
It has proceeded for the sake of the human goal, and not for the purpose of perceiving difference.

Since there is a contradiction with the cognition that grasps duality, it follows that the Vedāntas do not possess authority regarding Brahman, which is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*); this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is said. Therein, first, he dispels the contradiction with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*). Regarding the phrase "from common worldly experience" (*lokataḥ*): for the *karmakāṇḍa* proceeds for the sake of prosperity by taking up the worldly distinction of agent and so forth, and not for the purpose of establishing such distinction, because that [distinction] is not something previously unknown (*apūrva*) in that context.
The meaning is "due to the purport" (tātparyāt). || 917 ||
And since difference does not serve the purpose of man, it would lack authority if it were for that purpose.
And its validity as a means of knowledge is accepted by the proponents of the Veda on the grounds of its being the word of God (Martha). || 918 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the scripture does not have difference as its intended meaning, beginning with the words "of difference. Since difference is an evil according to the scriptural text, "From duality, indeed, comes fear," if the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) were intent upon that [difference], it would result in its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Furthermore, because the scripture is intent upon the unprecedented goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), which is the supreme end...

He says that if the scripture on ritual action were established upon [the reality of] difference, there would be a contradiction with that [scripture on liberation], which is accepted as authoritative; [he states this] by saying, "as the human goal. || 998 ||
It has arisen from the eyes and other sense organs through contact with the essential nature of objects.
Thus, since the cognition born of the senses does not touch upon difference, there is no sublation of its identity with that [object]. || 919 ||

Even if there is no conflict with the *karmakāṇḍa*, what is the resolution regarding the Vedāntas when they conflict with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like? One must consider the alternatives: is perception merely prescriptive, or merely prohibitive, or does it function through both prescription and prohibition? Having raised this doubt, the author adopts the first alternative, stating "the thing" (*vastu*).

The words "cognition that has arisen" (*utthitaṃ jñānam*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Since perception functions solely through prescription, and since difference is not its object, by that [perception], the thing...
He states that there is no sublation of the statement: "bhedeti" || 999 ||
The means of valid cognition has the object of knowledge as its domain, and the object of knowledge is that which possesses reality.
Nor can difference possess the nature of a real entity, because it does not depend upon the reality of the entity itself.

Anticipating the objection, "Why should perception not touch upon difference as it does the object itself? he says: "The object of knowledge" (*prameya*). To the question, "Why should difference not also possess the fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*māna-yogyatva*)?", he replies: "And of the object" (*vastunaśca*). If it is argued that difference also possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*), he says: "No. He states the reason for this: "A real entity" (*vastu*). This is because the nature of a real entity is independent, whereas difference is dependent upon attributes such as similarity and so forth.
The meaning is that, because it is imagined like a snake and so forth, it is not a real entity. || 920 ||
For when the ground has been apprehended, the pot that was [previously] apprehended therein is negated.
It is not unknown because it is cognized by another means of knowledge, since it is attained through emptiness. || 921 ||

He addresses the position that perception is exclusively negative by saying, "For when [the locus] is obtained," etc. When the locus (*dharmī*) is perceived, the negation of a non-perceived counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) takes the form "this is not it" or "this is not here. For that which is already established by valid cognition cannot be the object of negation, as that would contradict the means of knowledge;
nor can that which is unknown be so, because that would entail the negation of all unknown things. Therefore, the meaning is that perception is not exclusively negative. || 921 ||
For the manifestation of a thing occurs through the very union of one thing with another thing.
Cognition does not arise through the absence [of an object], nor through the exclusion of selflessness and so forth. || 922 ||
1. [The section on] Dharma and so forth. 800.
32 [vol 1, page 271] Is negation non-existence or difference? It is not non-existence, for perception does not operate with respect to non-existence; thus he says: "the manifestor..."

The meaning is as follows: since perception is a real entity (*vastu*), it can only be connected with a real entity and not with non-existence (*abhāva*), which is a non-entity because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and thus cannot function as a substratum;

furthermore, if that which is unconnected to perception were perceivable by it, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Regarding the second [alternative] as well, perception cannot be connected with a distinction called "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), because even that distinction is a non-entity; therefore, it too is not perceptible. Thus he says.
"Having seen," [it is said]. || 922 ||
Therefore, there is no differentiation in the object, because the object has a non-differentiated nature.
There is no object external to the means of valid cognition, nor is there a means of valid cognition external to the object.

He states the conclusion regarding how difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abhāva*), being non-entities (*avastu*), are unfit to be objects of valid cognition: "Not therefore" (*nātaḥ*). Because difference and non-difference are non-entities, they lack contact with the real entity (*vastu*); thus, for us, the entity does not become non-dual in the form of non-difference—this is the meaning. Alternatively, he states the reason why the real entity is untouched by difference: "Of the entity" (*vastunaḥ*). This means that by its very nature, it possesses the inherent character of non-difference (*abhedasvābhāvya*). Or else:

The meaning is that in that [non-dual reality], there can be no contact with difference and so forth, because it is impossible for it to possess a form characterized by such distinctions. Having raised the objection that—although difference and its absence are non-entities elsewhere—there might still be a dualistic entity due to the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyabheda*), he says: "No. The meaning is that even that distinction does not exist as a real entity within the non-dual. ||923||
There is no mutual conjunction between two non-entities, because they are both unreal and indistinguishable from one another.
Just as there is no difference between non-existence and existence, what difference could there be among things that possess the nature of existence? (924) 3116

Having refuted the absence of difference within a single entity, another reason for refuting difference is stated. In that regard, difference must consist either of the existence or non-existence of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or of two existences themselves. It is not the first case; for there is no mutual difference between two absences, because they are indistinguishable in their lack of reality. Thus he says: "Not between two absences. By the word "union" (*yoga*), difference is indicated. He refutes the second case with: "Absence... [etc.].

"It is 'sat' (Being). The meaning is that there is no mutual difference in non-existence (*abhāva*) because it lacks a substratum (*anādhāratva*). He refutes the third [position] with the words "In entities... (*bhāveṣu*). For difference does not exist in entities; since there is no differentiator (*bhedaka*), first of all, "entity-ness" (*bhāvatva*) cannot be the differentiator, because if the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) were itself an entity, it would result in the collapse of the distinction between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*). Nor can "non-entity-ness" (*abhāvatva*) be the differentiator, because being a non-entity means it is unreal (*avastutva*); if the property-bearer were unreal, it would result in the collapse of the distinction between the property-bearer and the counter-correlate. This is the intended sense. || 924 ||
Of the property of impermanence and of the substratum, such as a jar, [and] of those two.
In this context, "conjunction" (saṃgati) refers to either inherence (samavāya), conjunction (saṃyoga), or identity (tādātmya). || 925 ||

By means of the refutation of difference, he implicitly refutes non-existence; and by means of the refutation of non-existence, he implicitly refutes difference. Regarding the phrase "of impermanence": by the word "impermanence," non-existence is understood. Is there a relation between existence and non-existence, or not? If not, then existence would be beginningless and endless, and non-existence would be independent. If [a relation] does exist, it must be one of the types such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, which are recognized on the plane of conventional usage.
The meaning is: because of the absence of an intermediate state. || 925 ||
Just as there is the cognition "the jar is here" regarding the relationship between the locus and the located;
Likewise, no one possesses such a cognition regarding the conjunctions of existence and non-existence through inference.

Anticipating the objection that "let there be one of those three types of relation; what is the harm?", [the author] refutes all three types of relation by means of the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The verse begins with] "The substratum" (*ādhāra*). The meaning is that even when conjunction and other relations exist between the ground and a jar, the correct cognition "the jar is here" does not arise for anyone through any means of valid knowledge regarding those [relations]. || 926 ||
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, Page 272] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:
"Indeed, the non-existence of an entity does not possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from the existence of that entity."
Therefore, even by way of its own nature as an entity, an entity is fit for conventional usage. || 927 ||

For this reason as well, there is no connection between those two in any of the three ways; for non-existence (abhāva) is either different from existence (bhāva) or not different. It is not the first case, as he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). The meaning is that if non-existence were distinct from existence, one would have to admit another non-existence [to account for the first], leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Nor is it the second case.

Thus he says: "By way of being" (*bhāvātmanā*). The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "The non-existence of an entity is not a part of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabhāk*). The sense is this: first of all, non-existence cannot be included within existence, because that would result in the collapse of the non-duality of that [non-existence]; nor can existence be included within non-existence, because that would entail the consequence of the non-duality of non-existence. If it is difficult to describe non-existence as being either different from or non-different from existence, then how is its conventional usage possible? To this he replies: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 927 ||
"Furthermore, even non-existence is indeed a real entity, because it gives rise to the cognition that 'it does not exist.'"
Since the two possess a single nature, what excellence could there be in the measurement of those two?
He raises an objection, saying "Now" (*atha*), [suggesting] that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not imagined either, because it is an object of cognition.

He refutes this, saying "Of the two," (*dvayoḥ*): if non-existence were also a real entity (*vastu*), then because existence and non-existence would be of a single nature by virtue of both being real entities, there would be no differentiator; consequently, since the distinction between existence and non-existence could not be established through their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no connection between the two. || 928 ||
For one for whom the entire world is established as real, how could its non-existence be proven by any means of valid cognition?
And one does not perceive its establishment as something distinct from existence, just like existence itself. || 929 ||

Furthermore, is non-existence (*abhāva*) existent or non-existent? In the first case, because everything would be mere existence (*sanmātra*), the non-existence of anything else would be non-apprehended; therefore, there can be no real connection between it and existence. Thus he says: "The universe... He refutes the alternative view: "Nor... Just as existence is not established as distinct from existence due to the absence of any differentiator, so too non-existence cannot be distinct from existence, for such a distinction is impossible.
And because the cognition of such a thing is not possible for an authoritative means of knowledge, the meaning is that there is no connection with the reality of non-duality (sadadvaita). || 929 ||
If existence were to tolerate the connection with non-existence, it would be like its connection with the color blue.
Because there is no contradiction with non-existence, there can be no transition from existence to non-existence. || 930 ||

He states another defect regarding that connection as well: "abhāva... (non-existence). The sense is this: if a positive entity (*bhāva*) were to tolerate a connection with non-existence (*abhāva*), just as a blue lotus tolerates inherence (*samavāya*), then because there would be no contradiction, the positive entity could not be eliminated by non-existence; consequently, the positive entity would be without beginning or end. || 930 ||
This conjunction is observed between two entities when they are perceived as existing separately from one another.
Just as there is [no connection] between two rams or two wrestlers, so too between existence and non-existence.

Regarding the threefold lack of connection between existence and non-existence, he states another argument: "This is a conjunction. A mutual conjunction is observed between two things established through their difference, such as in the case of rams and the like; however, since these two [existence and non-existence] are not established separately, their conjunction is not established.
This is the meaning. || 931 ||
A conjunction between two non-existent things is observed, as in the case of the son of a barren woman and a sky-flower.
Thus, because of their mutual contradiction, existence and non-existence do not [coexist] in this way.

Furthermore, Sureśvarācārya, in his *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, states that there is no relationship of three kinds between non-existence (*abhāva*) and existence (*bhāva*). He says, "There is no conjunction" (*na yoga*). The meaning is that, just as there is no relationship between two non-existent things, there is likewise no mutual relationship between the existent and the non-existent, because they are mutually contradictory. || 932 ||
The absence of a jar in a location on the ground is not cognized as being like the jar itself.
Neither conjunction nor inherence exists between non-existence and the locus of its substratum. || 933 ||

Furthermore, on the ground, a jar appears due to its conjunction with the eye; however, its absence does not appear there in the same way because it lacks such conjunction, as [other relations] like being a qualifier of what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatva*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, there is no conjunction or similar relation for absence on the ground. This is elaborated upon in the passage beginning "in the relations between locus and located" (*ādhārādheya-yogeṣu*). He states: "On the earth... (*kṣitau*). The word "relation" (*yoga*) here refers to both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and identity (*tādātmya*). || 933 ||
Thus, everything has the nature of existence; there is no nature of non-existence for that which exists.
Even though existence has the nature of non-existence, it is because of its having the nature of non-existence.
Where there is no difference, how could there be room for division? And where there is no division, how could there be conjunction?

Furthermore, if there were identity between existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), would non-existence be included within existence, or would existence be included within non-existence? Regarding the first case, he says "the nature of being existent" (*sadātmatā*): this leads to the consequence of the non-duality of the Real (*sadadvaita*). Regarding the second case, he says "not [included] in non-existence": the meaning is that they are mutually contradictory. Even assuming that existence is included within non-existence, he states the fault: "even though," etc., meaning even when there is such a contradiction.

This is the meaning of the verse: even if an entity (bhāva) were of the nature of non-existence (abhāva), there would be no distinction between the two because only non-existence would remain; and in the absence of that [distinction], there could be no relation.
Therefore, the meaning is that one must not accept that an entity is of the nature of non-existence. || 934 || 935 ||
Whatever differentiated object is perceived whatsoever in this world, [it is all of that nature].
It is held that this very [reality] is devoid of beginning, middle, and end. || 936 ||

Fearing that the same [relationship] as between two positive entities—the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—might also apply to existence and non-existence, he says: "As long as...

The meaning is that this objection is invalid, because everything intended to be a differentiator is seen to be nothing but pure Being (*sanmātra*), devoid of beginning, middle, or end; thus, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished. || 936 ||
"‘All this is indeed Being’ is one clear [scriptural statement], and ‘[all beings] have Being as their root’ is another."
The Śruti has been directly cited for us so that we may realize the eternal identity of the Self.

He states the proof for the fact that everything consists of pure Being (*sanmātra*) with the words "Being alone" (*sadeva*). It should be understood that the word "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*) is spoken with the intention of referring to what is directly stated in scripture (*śruta*), whereas the word "furthermore" (*aparam*) is intended to indicate what is established through scriptural presumption (*arthāpatti*). He explains the purport of citing these two sentences with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*). || 937 ||
The absence of a means of knowledge is itself a means of knowledge; the absence of an object of knowledge is itself an object of knowledge.
How it cannot tolerate logic at all is now being explained. (938)

Having refuted the connection between non-existence and existence, the perceptibility of non-existence has been primarily rejected; now, while restating another opinion, he declares its contradiction with logic: "Māna... (verse 938).
1. It is obtained. 2. Kha: Let it be seen. || 936 ||
The Explanatory Commentary (*Vārtika*),
together with the sub-commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri;
that which brings about awakening.
"That which belongs to one who is not a Buddha is [mere] conceit"—this is indeed the established principle.
And since the non-existence of the means of valid cognition is not of such a nature, it is therefore not tenable. || 939 ||

In order to state that the absence of a means of knowledge (*mānābhāva*) cannot be a means of knowledge because it lacks the defining characteristic of a means of knowledge, he states its definition: "that which makes known" (*bodhaka*). He states that the absence of a means of knowledge is not pervaded by that [definition] with the words "nor... (*na ca*). For the non-existence of the object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*) is not "unknown" simply because of its non-existence; nor for this very reason can the absence of a means of knowledge be a "maker known. He states the consequence of the absence of such a definition with the words "therefore... (*tasmāt*). [The word] *māna*...
The word "iti" is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 939 ||
If the absence of means of valid cognition is itself cognized through an absence, [then what is the means of that cognition?]
What will there be that indicates the non-existence of the means of valid cognition?

Furthermore, does the absence of the means of knowledge (*māna*) cognize the absence of the object of knowledge (*meya*), or does the [means of knowledge] itself, once it has been cognized, [cognize it]? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that there could be no doubt regarding the absence of Devadatta once he has already departed from the house. Thinking thus, [the author] adopts the second [option], stating: "The object of knowledge... [referring to] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The phrase "measured by means of existence" (māvena mitena) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding the status of non-existence as a means of knowledge (*māna*) for that which has been measured, he presents the following alternatives: is it the fivefold set of means of knowledge that establishes it, or is it the absence of those? [This is expressed in the verse: "Of the means of knowledge... (940).
The pentad beginning with the sense organs is not its indicator, because it exists in constant concomitance with it.
Nor can there be an absence of that [object], because it exists precisely as an object of cognition (meyatva). || 941 ||

He says, "It does not exist," meaning "not from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. He says, "Not the second [alternative]," meaning "because it leads" (*nayataḥ*). The meaning is that there is an absence of the fivefold means of knowledge;
for that very leading, according to logic (*nyāyataḥ*), is not a cognizer of the state of being a means of knowledge and its object (*mānameyatva*), because that depends upon a distinction. || 941 ||
If non-existence were a qualifier of the senses and so forth, just like blue and other such qualities;
Since [the object] is reached by means of a qualifier, how could its absence be known through cognition? || 942 ||

Furthermore, is this non-existence qualified or unqualified? In the first case, is the qualification a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or an object of knowledge (*meyam*)? It restates the former: "like blue and so forth. The meaning of this restatement is that just as the blue color and so forth are seen to be the qualifications of a lotus and the like, so too would the means of knowledge be the qualification of non-existence. If that were so, then because non-existence would possess a specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) through its qualifier—the sense organ and so forth—just as a lotus possesses a specific distinction through its blue color and so forth...

He states that the remaining absence is not an object of the senses and so forth, because that would entail [the senses] having their own objects only partially; nor is the qualified absence the object of the absence of proof, because it is itself an object, and because if the senses were the qualifier, there would be a rule of connection between the qualifier and the qualified, which has already been refuted—thus, the absence of the senses and so forth would not be established by valid means of knowledge. He says: "By the qualifier... (Verse 942).
"Furthermore, you assert that non-existence is devoid of any qualification."
Otherwise, it would follow that the non-existence of the object itself possesses the status of a means of valid cognition, as there is no distinction [between them]. || 943 ||

He states another alternative with the word "atha" (now/if). In that case, he says "meyā" (the object of cognition), meaning that there would be no establishment of the distinction between the absence of a means of knowledge being a means of knowledge and the absence of an object of knowledge being an object of knowledge; this is because there is no difference, that is, because one does not admit any specific distinction within the category of non-existence. || 943 ||
It is my view that the statement "the absence of a jar and so forth" is not correct.
Because the words lack semantic competency and because two entities are mutually contradictory. || 944 ||

He refutes the position that "the object of cognition" (*meyam*) is a qualifier of non-existence (*abhāva*), stating: "A jar, etc. [In this way,] there is a mutual connection between the two terms "existence" (*bhāva*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
(Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Vol. 1, p. 275, v. 254)

1 [He states the reason: "Because of the absence of the capacity for a relationship. Regarding the phrase "of the words," he asks: "Whence does that incapacity arise? and thereupon says: "Because of the contradiction..."

"Because of... This means that since existence and non-existence, being respectively a real entity and a non-entity, are mutually contradictory in their conjunction, the words [denoting them] lack the capacity for syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*). || 944 ||
If there is a compound [of the two words] "existence" (bhāva) and "non-existence" (abhāva), it is due to their semantic capacity.
Because it does not depend on [external factors] such as a jar and so forth, the compound is not established. || 945 ||

Anticipating the objection that—despite the contradiction between existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*)—the formation of a compound is possible because of the compatibility of those two words, just as in the case of the words "darkness" (*tamas*) and "light" (*prakāśa*), and thus the statement that there is no possibility [of such a compound] is incorrect—the author says: "Existence... etc. According to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the prescription of word-formation applies to words that are semantically related" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), if a compound occurs only when there is semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*) between one word and another, such as with the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and others, then there can be no compound of the words "existence" and "non-existence," since their respective meanings are mutually contradictory.
The meaning is that [the objection] does not hold because of independence, and because it is equally inapplicable even to the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). || 949 ||
In the expression "the non-existence of an entity," what is considered the meaning of the genitive case?
There is no relation whatsoever for that which is formless and of the nature of non-existence. (946)

In that case, let there not be a compound [expressing] "the non-existence of existence" (*bhāvasyābhāvaḥ*); for he will explain the relationship between qualifier and qualified even by means of an analytical expression (*vyāsa*).

To this he says "no," beginning with "of existence. Fearing that the meaning of that [genitive] might be a relation, based on the traditional rule "the genitive is used in the sense of the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*), he says "none whatsoever. The lack of form is the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); the reason for this is "because its essence is non-existent" (*asadātmanaḥ*). || 946 ||
If non-existence were another entity, how could one thing be different from another?
If there were another [entity] distinct from it, there would be no contradiction, just as in the case of blue. || 947 ||

He raises the objection that the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) is unestablished, because of the established principle that "the non-existence of one thing is another thing. [The opponent says: "It is another thing. Just as when it is said "the jar exists," there is no difference between the jar and its existence, so too when it is said "it does not exist," oneness must be asserted between the jar and its non-existence. Consequently, if the non-existence of the jar were the cloth, then saying "the jar is the cloth" would follow; but this is not tenable, since something else [the cloth] remains present.

He says, "Or [it is] because that which has perished cannot have another nature," namely, "another. Alternatively, if the absence qualified by a jar were to be the cloth, then since the qualifier—the jar—would also be included within the cloth, the aforementioned refutation should be understood to apply. He says, "Even another [is not so]," because, as in the case of blue being the very essence of the lotus, there is no contradiction in one thing having the nature of another; thus, the consequence would be non-duality (*advaita*). || 947 ||
If that which is associated with it is not contradictory, it does not effect the cessation of the relationship.
Without the apprehension of the related terms, this relation is not established. || 948 ||

He raises the objection that although there is a contradiction regarding identity between non-existence and existence, the meaning of the genitive case is still possible because it does not contradict other types of relations; this is expressed by the words "saṃgatāv iti" (in the case of connection). He replies with "na" (no), stating that this is not so because such a relation has already been refuted. Furthermore, does that by which non-existence is related obstruct [existence] or not? If it does not, then since there would be no contradiction between existence and non-existence, contradiction would not exist anywhere.

He says that even when there is a connection, it is contradictory [to say that one thing obstructs another]. He states: "The related entity... Furthermore, is negation (abhāva) possessed of a counter-correlative (sapratyogika) or devoid of a counter-correlative (niṣpratyogika)? In the first case, does the connection with negation occur when the counter-correlative exists or when it does not exist? Not the first, because of contradiction; nor the second, because if the related entity is non-existent, it cannot be apprehended, and thus the connection of negation to it cannot be established. Thus he says: "Not the related entity... (948)
[Vol. 1,
Page 276] The Vārttika, together with the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.
When the relation is absent and unestablished, the status of being the meaning of the genitive case is not established.
Because of contradiction, there can be no simultaneous enjoining and prohibiting. (949)

Considering that, under the view that [negation] is without a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), negation would possess independence because its relation to a substratum (*dharmin*) has been rejected, he says: "The related" (*saṃbandhī*). The literal meaning is that the counter-correlate is the related; since it is absent in the case of negation, and because the relation to a substratum is unestablished, neither the sense of the genitive nor the nature of being a relation belongs to negation. He has thus refuted both the claim that perception is exclusively negative and the authority of that [perception] for the purpose of negation.

As for the claim that "this is the operation of injunction and prohibition," even there, one must consider whether injunction and prohibition occur simultaneously, or whether the prohibition is preceded by the injunction, or the injunction is preceded by the prohibition. He states that the first case is not possible: "Because of contradiction" (virodhāt). || 949 ||
Because cognitions are momentary, there can be no sequential order for a persisting entity.
Nor is there a cognition of blue by means of that which is turned away from the absence of non-blue. (950)

"No," he says regarding the second [alternative], "because of momentariness. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that even if cognitions were to persist for two or three moments, there would still be no activity distinct from their arising. He says "no" regarding the third [alternative]: "not non-shining" (*anīla*). || 950 ||
There could be no negation of the unperceived, as in the case of a water-jar on the ground;
nor would there be the qualification "distinguished by the absence of others" when there is a cognition of total non-existence. (951)

He states the reason for the claim that "there is no cognition of blue by way of the negation of yellow and so forth" with the words "For not... (na hi). A negation of a visible object, such as a jar, is observed on a surface like the ground when it is not perceived; however, this is not the case for an invisible object such as an atom. Thus, since the negation of an invisible thing is impossible, the statement "it is not non-blue" is itself not a negation. In the absence of that [first negation], there could be no second negation of it; how then could there be a positive determination of blue by way of that [negation]? Nor is it the case that...

The meaning is that there can be no injunction preceded by a prohibition, because without that [prior] procedure, there would be no negation of "non-blue," since a negation cannot be cognized without a cognition of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); thus, a circularity (*cakraka*) would result. Furthermore, is the absence of non-blue—such as yellow and so forth—the qualifier of blue, or its very nature? It is not the first, as he says: "Not other... For only when all non-blue things, such as yellow and so forth, and their respective absences are cognized, could there be the absence of others for blue.

The meaning is this: there can be no qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) otherwise than through the perception of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because a qualified entity is not perceived when its qualifier is not seen. Consequently, for one who perceives only "blue," there would follow the absurd consequence of perceiving the absence of all other entities; and since such [omniscience] is impossible for those who are not lords (*anīśvara*), there would be no such thing as the exclusion of blue (*nīlavivira*). || 999 ||
The existence of the non-existence of another would be a [mere] non-entity, like a flower in the sky.
If non-existence is merely another state of existence, then the entity is established by its own nature.

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case], stating "anyā" (other). If the absence of yellow and so forth were of the nature of blue, there would be either the inclusion of blue within its own absence, or the inclusion of that [absence] within blue. In the first case, blue would be insubstantial (*tuccha*), like a sky-lotus. In the second case, however, the absence would likewise be non-existent; such is the meaning. To avoid the charge of the insubstantiality of absence, he restates the very objection already refuted: "bhāvā-" (of existence...).

Regarding the word "immediately" (*anantaram*): is that [reality] an existent (*bhāva*) or a non-existent (*abhāva*)? Since both [alternatives] lack the distinction between existence and non-existence, he says "established" (*siddham*) to indicate that the reality untouched by those two is self-established. || 952 ||
And by what means is the exclusion of those cognitions which grasp that [object] understood?
Even when the object is variegated, it is a single, variegated entity, because it is perceived as one.
1 ka ga. Vasvabhā [vol 1, page 277] 156
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:

Now, an objection is raised: "Since both difference (*bheda*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are established by means of knowledge (*māna*), how can the reality (*vastu*) be untouched by them? To this, he replies: "Those which grasp it...

It has been stated that neither exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), nor difference, nor non-existence is an object of knowledge (*meyā*). Therefore, even the means of knowledge (*mānāni*) are not tainted by difference or non-existence.

The meaning is that they reveal only the positive entity (vastu). Now, an objection is raised: when a variegated object is perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa), its differentiation (vyāvṛtti) is also perceived by it; otherwise, the variegated nature of the variegated object would be untenable.
Therefore, the challenge—"By what is the differentiation perceived?"—is without foundation there. To this, he replies: "Even in the case of the variegated... (citre 'pi).

For in that case, exclusion from a single [perceptual instance] does not appear, because the variegated thing is a real entity (*vastu*) and it is unitary; furthermore, if its exclusion were to occur elsewhere, it would be a non-entity (*avastu*). This is the meaning. || 953 ||
If blue, yellow, and so forth were apprehended individually, how could there be variegation?
If the nature of a thing consists of differentiation, it follows that the thing itself would be non-existent. (954)

He states the reason for his lack of approval, which was indicated by the particle *api*, following the doubt raised by the maxim: "If the variegated [whole] were one, its variegatedness would be untenable; and that it is both one and variegated—this is most wonderful indeed! He says: "Each individually... [The opponent asks: Is it each one [of the parts], or is it the aggregate?

It cannot be the first, because variegatedness is not perceived when blue, yellow, and so forth are perceived individually; nor can it be the second, because the aggregate, whose nature is a collection, is not distinct from the blue, yellow, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: because difference is difficult to express and because it is not a real entity (*avastu*), if exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were grasped as residing within that [difference], then that [exclusion] too would not be a real entity. Anticipating the objection that—since exclusion is the very nature of real entities such as blue—the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends the real entity also takes that [exclusion] as its object, and therefore exclusion is neither a non-entity nor lacks a basis in valid cognition—he says: "Of the real entity" (*vastunaḥ*). Its [the real entity's] inclusion is within difference; for difference...

The meaning is as follows: either difference is included within the entity, or it is not. It cannot be the first, because difference consists of a tearing apart, and if the entity were of that nature, it would result in its becoming void.
Nor can it be the second, because if difference were not a distinct thing from the entity, it would lead to the consequence of the reality of non-duality (sadadvaita). || 994 ||
If it were non-different from another property, the entity would be established by itself as the basis for valid cognition;
however, because being both different and non-different is contradictory, it cannot be the object of a single means of knowledge. (955)

[Objection: "Surely difference may not be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but it will be a property (*dharma*). [Reply: He says "no," with the words "but in the case of another property" (*anyadharme tu*). For that [difference] must be either a property of a real entity (*vastu*) or of a non-entity (*avastu*). It cannot be the former, because if the property were itself a real entity, the difference from the substratum (*dharmī*) would remain unestablished; and if it were a non-entity, the consequence of monism (*advaita*) regarding the real entity would follow. Nor can it be the latter, because if difference were a property of a non-entity, it would have no contact with the real entity, and thus non-duality would be established as the only valid conclusion by its very nature. This is the meaning.

The word *āśraya* (substratum) denotes the object (*viṣaya*) and functions as a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending with an abstract suffix, emphasizing the state [of being the substratum]. Anticipating the objection that non-duality is not established because the entity is both different and non-different [from its attributes], he says: "different and non-different" (995).
If there is no contradiction with the nature of the thing itself, then the thing alone is the object.
How could a real entity be divided by that which is constructed through dependence on a person?
There is a distinction; however, in the case of being a son and so forth, the state of being produced is conceptually imputed upon the entity. || 956 ||

He raises the objection that [difference and non-difference] may be objects of valid cognition (*māna*), because there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference in the form of a real entity (*vastu*). He says "the entity" (*vastu*). He replies: "It is the entity alone," meaning that only that form in which the two are non-contradictory is the object of cognition, not difference and non-difference themselves.

Even though it is the entity alone that is the object of cognition, nevertheless, difference is an object of cognition because it has the nature of a real entity; yet this does not imply the non-existence of the entity, for an entity is not admitted to be different with respect to itself, but rather with respect to another.
Anticipating the objection that it possesses that nature precisely because of such dependence, he says: "True. An object whose nature is acquired from its own causes is non-erroneous and independent.
The Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.

If there were difference, then that difference, being dependent, could not produce the conventional usage of difference within a real entity (vastu) that is non-different from it; for the dependent and the independent are distinct.

Furthermore, dependence is a property of persons (puṃdharma) and is not applicable to insentient things. If difference is produced by that property of dependence, then it would not be a real entity, because that which is created by dependence is imagined (kalpita), like a snake [mistakenly perceived in a rope]. The meaning is: difference is imagined because it is relative.

Regarding the phrase "like a serpent," having raised the objection that there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the father and so forth, he says: "of the son, etc. The state of being a son is birth; the state of being a father is the material cause (*upādāna*) or the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) of that [birth]. When that [birth] exists, the body of the son functions as the object (*karman*), while the body of the father functions as the agent (*kartṛ*). Since both of these are relative, they are merely imagined (*kalpita*) with respect to the substance that is the particular body; how, then, can there be any inconsistency? As for that which...

The meaning is that the two bodies of the *vastu* (the substrate) are unconstructed (*akalpita*) and independent [of the son], because even prior to the birth of the son, the father’s body exists, and the son’s body exists in the form of the *anuśayin* (the transmigrating entity) before its connection with the father. || 996 ||
Even though there are differences in burning, cooking, illuminating, and so forth, fire remains undifferentiated;
even from the perspective of its effects, there can be no difference, because the non-difference of the entity is established.

The establishment of difference [between the world and Brahman] has been refuted by means of perception and non-apprehension (*pratyakṣābhāva*). Now, one might raise the following objection: "The world, being a subject of dispute, is distinct because its effects are distinct, like clay and other materials"—thus, either through inference (*anumāna*), or through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—since a diversity of effects is untenable without a diversity of causes, such a cause must be postulated—and thereby the distinction between the causes of the world is established. Anticipating this, he states the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the inference and the possibility of another explanation (*anyathopapatti*) regarding the presumptive testimony, beginning with the word "burning" (*dāha*). In a single [cause]...

He states the conclusion: "Even from the effect" (*kāryato 'pi*). Since it is observed that different effects can arise from a single cause, there is no difference in the cause of the world despite the difference in its effects;
this is established because the cause remains non-different, just like fire. By the word "even" (*api*), he indicates his lack of enthusiasm for the distinction between effects.
Just as there is a substratum for various powers that perform distinct functions, [so too is there a substratum for the various cognitions].
Even though fire is one and not contradictory [in its nature], why is it not likewise [non-contradictory] with respect to its effect for you? (958)

[Objection: But surely the powers of burning and so forth are distinct within the fire; since the difference in the effect arises solely from the difference in the cause, how can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason "because of having different effects," and how can there be an alternative explanation for the presumption (*arthāpatti*)? To this, he says: "Vibhinna... (distinct...). First of all, it is not the powers themselves that possess causality, because those [powers] are never observed in isolation; furthermore, since the fire also exists when they are absent, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Thus...

The meaning is as follows: even if those [causes] alone are the cause, why could there not be a single cause for a manifold effect—just as a single entity may be the locus of multiple powers? Therefore, because inference and the other means of knowledge are flawed by defects such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*), they are not capable of establishing [the conclusion]. || 998 ||
Just as a jar would be established in the absence of a cloth, so too would a cloth [be established] in the absence of a jar.
From the perception of mutual non-existence, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence for you.

Having accepted that both [existence and non-existence] are absent in the cause because there is no difference in the effect, he now states that they do not exist in the effect either, beginning with the words "ghaṭa" (pot). The non-existence of a pot is a cloth; when that cloth is established as the non-existence of a pot—namely, in the sense that "the pot is not in this"—then the pot would have to be established as the non-existence of that [cloth]. Alternatively, the non-existence of a cloth is a pot; when that pot is produced as the non-existence of a cloth—namely, in the sense that "the cloth is not in this"—[then the cloth would likewise have to be established as the non-existence of that pot].

The literal meaning is that "the cloth would be accomplished. Alternatively, the jar itself is the absence of the cloth; when that [absence] has arisen, the non-jar—the cloth—is produced from the absence of the jar.
258 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [Volume 1, Page 279]

The meaning is that the non-existence of a jar is established precisely as the cloth (by virtue of their being related); once that is established, the jar is established as "not-cloth" by way of being the absence of the cloth. He states the resulting fault in both cases: "mutually. This refers to the fact that the jar and the cloth would exist merely as the form of each other's absence.

Since that [position] is accepted as a view, if a pot were established in that context, a cloth would be established; and if a cloth were established, a pot would be established. Thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), nothing at all would be established.
Therefore, the meaning is that because of the absence of both difference and non-difference, reality would be non-dual (*advaya*). || 999 ||
The perceptibility of separateness is also accepted by those who [assert its] quality-ness and other such properties.
Even for those [qualities], there is cognition of the quality, as in the case of "blue," but not of a non-entity.

Having stated that difference and non-difference are unestablished in the systems of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he begins to state their non-establishment even in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others: "Perceptibility," etc. Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is difference; since it is a quality (*guṇa*), it is a real entity (*vastu*). Even in the view of those who accept its perceptibility, there is valid cognition of it as a quality in perception—just as in the case of blue and so forth—because it is a real entity and thus capable of sensory contact. However, difference itself is not a quality.
The meaning is that since [the means of knowledge] exists even when there is a quality, it does not have validity regarding a non-existent difference. || 960 ||
Now, if the object is understood as qualified by its distinctness, then—
Just as in the case of "the white cow," measurement is a property residing only in the object itself; it does not bring about a difference [in the object]. (961)

He raises an objection: "The distinction called 'separateness' (*pṛthaktva*) is not a non-entity, because it is a qualifier of an entity, like color (*rūpa*). [This is introduced by] "Now" (*atha*). The intention is that in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, such a distinction is perceived because it is produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*). Considering that there is also a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), he states another fault: "In that case" (*tadā*). In that position, just as the cognition "the cow is white" occurs only with respect to a white cow...

Likewise, even the cognition "the jar is broken" is a cognition directed toward a distinct entity (*vastu*) alone, not toward the difference (*bheda*); for although that difference serves as a qualifier of the entity, its status as a non-entity is established just like [the absence] itself. Therefore, the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive. Furthermore, if difference were primary, why would it be considered merely figurative?
This is the meaning. || 961 ||
If there were distinctness among things, they would exist only as non-distinct.
That [entity] is indeed a real thing; if it were other than that, then those two would not be non-distinct entities.

One might object: "The cognition 'the cow is white' is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the cow; likewise, it is also a valid means of knowledge regarding its qualifier, whiteness. Similarly, even in the case of [the cognition] 'the pot is distinct,' it is a valid means of knowledge regarding the distinction as well.

Anticipating this, [the author] analyzes whether the difference from separateness (*pṛthaktva-bheda*) is non-different or different from the object, and adopts the first alternative. He says: "By way of non-difference. To this he replies: "In that case, there would be the consequence of monism (*advaita*) regarding the object, because there would be no separateness existing apart from that [object]."

"It is only the entity itself. Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is: if separateness (*pṛthaktā*) were something other than the entity, then the entity would not be separate from it, because that [separateness] would be extracted from the entity; furthermore, a relation cannot be coherently described as being either different or non-different [from its relata]. ||962||
If even the distinctness between existence and non-existence is non-different [from them], then it is not separate.
If existence and non-existence were distinct, they would not be mutually different from one another. (963)

Is there a difference between existence and non-existence, or not? He restates the first position [with the words] "Existence" (*bhāva*). He then entertains the alternatives as to whether that [non-existence] is non-different or different from those two [existence and non-existence], [introducing this with] "also" (*api*). Therein, he adopts the first [alternative] with "If" (*yadi*).

Then, because there is no difference [between them], there would be no exclusion of existence and non-existence from anything; thus he says, "Consequently," (*tataḥ*), implying that there would be a non-duality of reality (*vastvadvaitam*).

He will cast aside another alternative through his intention; he brings it forth. Regarding the distinction of "separateness" (pṛthaktā) from both existence and non-existence, or rather, its relation to those two—this is the Vārttika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 259.

Because their relationship is difficult to establish and because there is no mutual difference between them, there would be non-duality alone; since existence and non-existence have no separate identity, the implication here is that it is precisely that [non-duality]. || 963 ||
If separateness depends on something else, then the pot itself is non-separate.
Even though it possesses two properties, this entity would be one, like a blue lotus and so forth. || 964 ||

Furthermore, regarding the separateness (*pṛthaktva*) of a jar, is it relative to itself or relative to another? Anticipating that the first case would imply the emptiness of the jar, he restates the second position: "relative to another. He then says: "In that case, the jar itself would be non-separate and non-dual, because that which is produced in dependence on another is false, like a snake [superimposed on a rope]. He continues: "The jar, by its own nature, would possess the properties of both separateness and non-separateness," as this is what is accepted [in that view].

To the question, "How then can there be non-duality (advaita) of the jar? he replies: "Even though it possesses two attributes. Even though the jar possesses the attributes of separateness and non-separateness, since it is impossible to describe those two attributes as being either different or non-different [from the jar], the jar must be considered partless (akhaṇḍa). The meaning is that just as a lotus or similar object remains partless despite possessing various attributes such as color and form, so too is this [jar] partless. By the word "even" (api), he indicates that the contradiction with the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding difference and non-difference is avoided.
And its purity is indicated. || 964 ||
Even though there is no difference in the property, a difference in the substratum of the property is nevertheless accepted.
Therefore, even though there is difference among cows and other such things, pure existence alone is apprehended. (965)

Anticipating the objection that if there is a difference between properties (*dharma*)—as in "separateness" and "non-separateness"—then the substratum (*dharmin*) must also be divided by virtue of being their locus, and thus how can it be partless (*akhaṇḍa*), he says: "Dharme... (In the verse). The sense is that although there is a difference among properties based on cognition, there is no difference in the substratum; for even when there is a difference in burning and so forth, one observes no difference in the fire itself. He states the consequence regarding the non-difference of the substratum: "Ataḥ" (Therefore). [This applies] to the mutual [distinction] of particulars such as cows and the like.

The meaning is this: even though there is deviation (vyabhicāra), pure Being (sanmātra) alone is the underlying commonality and does not differ; it is that alone which is the object of knowledge (meyam), and not the cow or other particulars, because they are subject to deviation.

Alternatively, the difference between the cow, the jar, and so forth has been refuted; even if such difference were admitted, it could not be the object of knowledge due to fallacies such as mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya). Pure Being, however, is the object of knowledge. Therefore, he states that non-duality alone is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika): "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 965 ||
Even in the case where "cowness" (gotva) is the object of cognition, there is no departure from the state of being a similar instance (sapakṣa).
The object of cognition is indeed the universal itself, such as "cowness" and so forth, which is as clearly manifest as the individual cow Śābaleya and others. (966)

Fearing the objection that "the object of cognition (*meyam*) is not merely Being (*sanmātra*), because even 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth possess that [status of being an object]," he says: "Cowness, etc. When cowness and so forth are the objects of cognition, is it that very [particular] that is the object, or is it the form of Being (*sadrūpa*)? Not the first, because there would be no reason to conceive of cowness and so forth as the objects of cognition while discarding the form of Being—which is followed everywhere in such cognitions as "the pot is Being," "the cloth is Being"—and because that [form of Being] is distinct from cowness and the like.

Because that [particular] does not exist, in the second case (the universal), only "Being" (sat) is the object of cognition; for it is accepted by both parties. Cows and the like are not the referents of words such as "cow" because they are variable—just as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and other such individuals, being variable, do not constitute the form (*ākṛti*).

Since the form exists [as the constant], and since even "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth cannot logically be the object of cognition [in the same way], the meaning is that only "Pure Being" (*sanmātra*) is thus [the object], free from doubt. || 966 ||
Because they do not abandon their nature as being (sat), they have intermediate causes.
