Conventional transactions are perceived, yet true reality is established within them.

But surely, even though it has the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), it is not an object of cognition (*meyam*), because its fallibility is equal due to its exclusion from the subsequent triad, just like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
A.
1 kha. Because it is not a means of accomplishment.
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the section on the Connection]:

otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the accepted position that universals (*jāti*) and so forth are themselves devoid of universals; nor can it be argued that even in those cases, because their own-form existence (*svarūpasattva*) is admitted, they do not deviate from the nature of "Being" (*sadrūpa*). For that which is variable, such as a specific cow (*khaṇḍa*), is not denotable by the word "existent" (*sat*). To this, he says: "Being... (*sad-rūpa...*)

The opponent [Pūrva-pakṣin] says: Those linguistic usages (vyavahāra) which are caused by subordinate categories such as pillars, jars, and so forth, are perceived without abandoning their nature as "Being" (sat). Therefore, one must admit that the nature of Being is established within pillars and the like; for if they were extracted from it, they would lack existence and thus could not serve as causes for linguistic usage regarding what is seen or unseen.
Thus, Pure Being alone is the reality; everything else is superimposed upon it, and nothing exists apart from Pure Being, which is the substratum of all conceptual constructions.

The point is this: there exists no other generality (sāmānya) besides [substancehood] that could deviate from the subsequent triad [of existence, knowability, and nameability]; nor can its existence be established through such inferences as "substancehood is not a generality residing in the genus 'space' because it is a generality distinct from that," for it is equally easy to state: "substancehood is a generality distinct from the generality that pervades its own instances. || 967 ||
There would be no distinction even from "existence" (sattā); how much less so from anything else, such as "substantiality" (dravyatva) and the like?
For consciousness is indeed of a single form; likewise, it possesses substance as well as qualities.

Now, it might be argued that nothing additional is imagined within pure Being (*sanmātra*), because some maintain that the six categories—beginning with substance (*dravya*) and ending with inherence (*samavāya*)—are mutually distinct and exist as ultimate realities (*paramārtha*). In this regard, one must consider the following alternatives: are generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) two separate entities; or are only the particulars the entities; or is there a single entity consisting of both generality and particularity; or is it generality alone? Having thus proposed these options, he states the fault in the first alternative.

"Also from existence (*sattā*)" means: although there is a distinction between the excluded [particulars] and the inclusive universal of existence (*satsāmānya*), that [distinction] is not tenable; for if the excluded [particulars] were extracted from it, they would result in being mere non-entities (*tucchatva*). Furthermore, as for the mutual distinction among the six categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, from where could it arise? Since there is no differentiator and because they are non-different from the single, undivided existence, the claim that "there are two things" is untenable. This is the meaning. The reason why there is no distinction between substance and so forth and the universal of existence is—

The author says: "Of a single form. The meaning is: "That which is under dispute does not differ from Being (sat), because it possesses a cognition of that single form, just like that [Being]. He provides an example for the single form of consciousness: "Being" (sad). That is to say, because there is a cognition of identity due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), there is no cognition of difference between substance and so forth and the universal Being (satsāmānya). || 968 ||
Furthermore, if the relation were through inherence (samavāya), there would be no uniformity between two distinct entities.
Therefore, there can be no trust in this [person], because even when born, they possess only a single cognition.

Anticipating the objection that the cognition of oneness regarding substance and so forth, as well as the universal "Being" (*sattāsāmānya*), is produced by inherence (*samavāya*) precisely because they are distinct, he says: "And from inherence. The meaning is that a cognition of oneness between two distinct things cannot be produced by a relation, since such is not observed in the case of [the cognition] "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*). To this, he raises the following doubt: "And that... [referring to] the cognition of oneness; [the opponent argues that] there is no manifestation of oneness for substance and so forth with respect to Being due to the absence of inherence therein, whereas that cognition exists because of the presence of that [inherence].

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that because of the doubt as to whether [the cognition of oneness] is produced by inherence (*samavāya*) or produced by the identity of essence (*svarūpa-ekya*), it is not possible to ascertain that cognition from inherence; thus he says "No. He states the seed of the doubt: "In the case of the universal (*jāti*)," etc. The cognition of oneness, such as "cowness is one," is observed even in the case of cowness; yet that [oneness] is not produced by inherence, because inherence is not admitted in cowness, and because that which is not a substance cannot possess qualities. Therefore...

The meaning is that [the opponent argues] that this [inherence] is what effects the identity of essential natures; thus, even in cases such as "this is a real substance," the cognition of identity would depend upon it, leading to the undesirable consequence of doubt as to whether that cognition arises from inherence or otherwise. || 969 ||
1. Ka. Bandhāmaikaṃ.
[Vol.
1, page 282] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 261.
Nor is there the nature of association, because it is not perceived as distinct.
If it is asked what the cause is for the relation by way of inherence, that is not accepted [as a valid answer]. (970)

It has already been stated that, even by admitting an inherence (*samavāya*) between existence (*sat*) and the cow and so forth, the cognition of their identity is not produced by that [inherence]. Now, it is argued that it is also not logical for those two to possess another inherence as their relation (*saṃsarga*), because no mutual difference between them is perceived, just as in the case of "existence" itself or like the cow and other such entities; thus he says: "In relation to the relation... Furthermore, is inherence independent or dependent? It cannot be the first, because the genitive case in "this [inherence] belongs to these two" would be untenable. Duality...

He states [the following], saying "by inherence" (samavāyena): the relation between two inherent entities must be expressed by inherence; however, that [relation] is neither conjunction (saṃyoga) nor inherence itself, because there is a lack of evidence for it. || 970 ||
There is both conjunction and disjunction, yet there is no further persistence in inherence.
If [the unity] is from itself, then the conceptual construction is useless; for the substance's own unity is also from itself. (971)

He establishes that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) lacks authoritative status with the words "If there were conjunction... The meaning is that if there were a conjunction between inherence (*samavāya*) and its inherent relata (*samavāyin*), then because that [conjunction] must terminate in disjunction, a disjunction between those two would also occur at some point; and consequently, it would follow that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth would possess independence (*svatantratā*). He demonstrates the untenability of the inherence of inherence and its inherent relata with the words "Inherence..."

The sense is that there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that [qualities] do not inhere in eternal substances or in inherence itself. He raises an objection, suggesting that the dependence of inherence upon its substrata is self-evident and does not require another relation; this is expressed by the words "by itself" (*svataḥ*). He replies that if this were so, then the postulation of inherence would be useless; this is expressed by the word "postulation" (*kalpanā*). The postulation of inherence is meaningful because it serves as the cause for the cognition of identity between a substance and its attributes through their common existence (*sattva*).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the substance" (*dravyasya*). The meaning is: just as the dependence upon inherence (*samavāya-pāratantrya*) is inherent [in the substance], let the cognition of oneness (*aikya-dhī*) also arise spontaneously (*svataḥ*) from the existence of the substance and so forth; what is the use of inherence? || 979 ||
For all these entities are indeed always enveloped by existence.
They are suitable for conventional usage, yet difference is always indeed an illusion.

Having rejected the position that there are two categories, namely the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), he states the position that particulars alone are the real entities, beginning with the word "existence" (*sattā*). For all particulars are invariably pervaded by existence; at the time of linguistic usage, they become fit for such usage. Therefore, because they consist of nothing but existence (*sanmātratva*), any appearing difference must always be subsumed within the category of difference from "Being," just as [all differences] are subsumed within the category of difference from the moon. Furthermore, there is no persisting existence (*anugata-sattva*) [apart from them].

There is no such thing as "pot-residence" (the property of residing in a pot), because the generality that resides in that [residence] is perceptible; nor is there a contradiction in the statement "there is no generality," for the meaning is that here the word "that" (tat) refers to pure existence (sanmātra) alone. || 972 ||
For even those for whom an object is perceived as possessing both generality and particularity;
"From where could there be a difference even among those [particulars], since the entity is one and the substratum is non-different?

He states the argument against the position that "the entity consists of both the universal and the particular": "Of those... and so forth. This is the reason for the non-establishment of difference according to that view.

[The author] says: "The entity" (*vastu*). How is it so? To this he replies: "The substratum" (*dharmī*). The meaning is that because the substratum—which consists of both the universal and the particular—is non-different [from them], and because that [substratum] is an entity (*vastu*). || 973 ||
1 kha. It will not be seen.
[vol 1, page 283] 262

Even if there were a cognition of difference between the universal and the particular, [it would still be established]. *Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction] Even if there were a cognition of difference between the universal and the particular, [it would still be established].
Moreover, because it rests solely upon those [objects], it is not admitted to touch upon difference.
Anticipating the objection that "since the universal and the particular are seen to be mutually distinct, their difference must enter into the substratum (dharmin)," he says: "api" (even).

In your view, since the universal and the particular lack substantial reality (vastutva), the cognition of difference cannot apply to them; for such a cognition is not possible regarding a non-entity. Nevertheless, as for the cognition of difference between these two that you accept, is it a cognition of the universal, or a cognition of the particular, or a cognition of both, or a distinct cognition altogether? Regarding these three alternatives:

Because it determines only the universal and so forth, that [cognition] does not rest upon difference; nor does another cognition have difference as its object, due to faults such as mutual dependence. Therefore, there is no difference even between the universal and the particular; how then could that [difference] exist in the substratum? This is the meaning. || 974 ||
If there is no difference in the one, how can there be unity in that which is divided?
Even in the case of a variegated [object], there is no status as a universal-particular because of the absence of a pervasive [common] nature. || 975 ||

Furthermore, is the universal and the particular non-different or different from that which possesses them (the substrate)? It is not the first case; thus he says: "If one... If both the universal and the particular were non-different from the substrate, then there would be no relation of universal and particular, just as there is none between [different] attributes and their substrate—this is the meaning. Having stated the second alternative, he points out the fault of the consequence of three entities: "If there is difference... When it is said that a single entity is tripartite, [the following occurs].

Anticipating the objection, "From where does this conceptual construction [arise], since the object is manifold?", he says: "Even in the case of a variegated [object]. Even if the object is accepted as having a dual nature, it would have to consist of the specific (viśeṣa) alone, not of both, because there is no co-presence (anvaya) between the broken-horned, the hornless, and others;
and because that which persists (anvayin), being a mere universal (sāmānya), lacks the status of a real entity (avastutva). This is the meaning. || 975 ||
"When it consists of both being and non-being by virtue of its own nature and the nature of another,"
When the object is a single thing within the scope of human cognition, how could there be non-existence at that time? (976)

In the statement "one entity is threefold," having refuted non-existence by means of refuting difference, he now refutes difference by means of refuting non-existence while proposing another alternative. [He says: "By its own nature... If it is maintained that one entity—which is existent by its own nature and non-existent by the nature of another—is encompassed by the domain of valid cognition (*māna*), then there is no non-existence of the entity, because there is an absence of valid cognition [for such non-existence]; and therefore, difference, which depends upon that [non-existence], does not exist either.
Such is the meaning. || 976 ||
If it is the cessation of perception and the other means of knowledge, then what is said to be its nature?
If there were indeed a state of inertia in the self, then that very thing would be what we desire. (977)

He raises the objection that "pramāṇa" (the means of knowledge) is the non-arising of the five types of cognition when an object is absent. He states "perception, etc. and then analyzes the nature of that non-arising. The meaning of the analysis in the phrase "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) is as follows: does it consist in the Self abiding in a state of inactivity, or in the cognition of another entity, or in some distinct positive state?
Having restated the first alternative, he establishes his own position by stating that there is no such thing as "non-existence" apart from the immutable reality (*kūṭastha-vastu*).
Having this in mind, he says: "Stagnation. || 977 ||
Furthermore, if it were the cognition of another object, then that [other object] would be an entity in the highest degree.
Even non-existence is a different state of being; it is not accepted as something devoid of any designation.
Therefore, because it is based on a single entity, difference is not within the range of the senses and other means of cognition.
1. ka. ga. *spṛgīkṣyate* | 2. ga. *nirupā* | [Vol.
1, page 284] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstramañjarī composed by Ānandagiri. 263.

Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words beginning with "atha" (now). He states the excellence [of this view] by saying that because it is knowledge (*jñāna*), its status as a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) is accepted. He says "nitarām" (exceedingly) [to emphasize this]. Regarding the third [position], he replies: "bhāvāntaram" (a different entity). If a different entity were itself a positive entity, the word "different" (*antara*) would be inappropriate; furthermore, since its distinctness (*anyatva*) would not be established, it is impossible for another positive entity to possess that [state of being a different entity]. And if it were a non-positive entity (*abhāva*), the word "positive entity" (*bhāva*) [could not apply to it].

The meaning is that because its production is not non-existent, and because it is impossible for its own self—which is an absence—to be so [non-existent], it must indeed be a real entity (*vastu*). Since the non-arising of the five means of knowledge (*māna*) in all three ways is a real entity, its object must also be a real entity; for a real entity does not establish the absence of a real entity, as that would entail the absurdity of establishing its own non-existence, and because the distinction between real entities remains unproven even now. This is the collective sense. By refuting non-existence, he also [refutes] difference.
Having rejected the position that the universal alone is the real entity, he concludes that difference lacks any basis in valid cognition with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since it is established that, because a thing cannot logically be of three kinds, it must by process of elimination be the universal itself—and since that universal is pure Being (*sanmātra*)—there is no difference perceived therein through any means of valid cognition; this is the meaning. || 978 ||
From the cognition "this is a jar," the jar is apprehended as the object of knowledge;
there is no exclusion of cloth and so forth, because [the cognition] does not possess that form, just as in the case of a cloth.

[Objection: Since a jar or the like, which is distinguished from everything else, is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why is it that difference (*bheda*) is not an object of the senses and so forth? To this, he says: "A jar. [The question is: does indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) grasp the jar as distinguished from everything else, or does determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) do so? It cannot be the first, because it contradicts the established principle that "indeterminate cognition has only the bare thing (*vastumātra*) as its object," and so forth. Nor can it be the second, because even there, only the jar itself is observed to be the object, and no exclusion of other things (*itaravyāvṛtti*) is perceived.

Since that specific nature [of the object] has been refuted, it was stated that as long as everything else is not grasped, the jar cannot be known as being excluded from them; therefore, the meaning is that perception does not convey its exclusion from others. He extends the logic demonstrated for the jar to the cloth and so forth with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Just like the jar, even in the case of the cloth, the exclusion is not perceptual, because in the cognition "this is a cloth," the cloth is the object of knowledge (*meyam*).
The meaning is that it can be easily asserted in all cases that "the exclusion [of others] is not perceived in the case of jars and so forth, because they do not possess that nature. || 979 ||
Because it is contradicted by perception, [the probans] does not exist in a pot, nor even in any other object.
Therefore, because it does not have the sense of the genitive case, this conceptual construction does not pertain to the real entity.
By refuting the perceptibility of difference (*bheda*), its dependence [on perception] is also refuted. Furthermore, is the absence of a jar without a locus or with a locus?
In the first case, it would follow that it is independent; in the second, does it reside in the jar or in some other object? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "The jar... and so forth.

For the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of a jar and the like cannot reside in the jar itself, because they cannot occur at the same time. Although the mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) of a jar may have the jar as its locus, since difference has already been refuted, that [non-existence] does not exist either in the form of the jar or as dependent upon it; this is the sense. He refutes the second alternative with the words "even in another object" (arthāntare 'pi). Whether that other object is a non-entity (abhāva) or an entity (bhāva), the first case is impossible because a non-entity cannot serve as the locus of a non-entity; nor is the second case possible.

He says "not the sixth" because it has already been stated that there is no relationship between existence and non-existence. To the question, "In that case, what is the status of the cognition of non-existence?

he replies with "Therefore. Anticipating the objection that even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being a cognition, must have a real object like any other accepted cognition, he says "No," because according to its definition—"conceptual construction is that which follows from verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object"—it does not have a real object.
The meaning is "he should cause to lie down. || 980 ||
For the jar, while producing cognition, [serves as] a qualifier of its own form.
In that same way, it acquires its own self-nature, but not from a cloth or other such things.
264 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 285]

Raising the objection that since the jar, its existence, and the absence of difference from it all appear in the cognition of the jar, such a cognition is not merely conceptual (vikalpamātra), he elaborates on this with the words "This is a jar" (*ghaṭo'yam iti saṃvitter*). He explains: "For the jar," etc. Just as the jar, while producing a consciousness qualified by itself, is an existent entity (*bhāva*);...

It does not happen that, through insentience (*jāḍya*), it abandons consciousness and seizes upon itself; nor does it, even while performing the concealment of cloth and so forth, obtain itself as its own [subject], because both its being the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its being a property (*dharma*) have been refuted—this is the meaning. || 981 ||
Likewise, even in the cognition of a cloth, the cloth alone is the qualifier.
"Nothing other than absence and so forth is superior to the cloth," as it is said.

Thus, he clarifies the extension [of the term] "cloth" with the word "paṭa. The two locatives are in apposition. In the cognition of a jar, just as the jar is seen as a qualifier, so too in the cognition of a cloth, that which is desired as a qualifier—namely, absence and so forth—which is additional to the cloth, is seen as merely that [cloth].

The meaning is that neither something other than the arrangement nor something non-other is established; for if it were other, it would not touch the cloth and so forth because any connection has already been refuted, and if it were non-other, it would likewise not be established. || 982 ||
Thus, by qualifying the property of cognition through such [states] as doubt and certainty;
Cognition is differentiated from the object of cognition; however, the notion of difference [between cognitions] occurs only with respect to each individual [object].
Now, [the opponent argues: "Just as in the case of internal things like cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth, the absence of difference cannot be denied even in external things like jars and the like.

To this, [the author replies]: "It is doubtful" (*saṃdigdhā*). The word *saṃdigdha* (doubtful), by virtue of its proximity to the word *niścaya* (certainty), has the sense of a state (*bhāva-pradhāna*). Thus, just as doubt and the like—derived through the instrumental analysis (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*)—are attributes of the internal organ denoted by the word "cognition," such that one speaks of "doubt-consciousness" (*saṃśaya-saṃvit*) or "false-consciousness" (*mithyā-saṃvit*), [so too is the case here].

Excluding other objects of cognition (*meyas*), consciousness (*saṃvit*) does not itself become differentiated; for no notion of difference arises with respect to it, precisely because it has been stated that the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is difficult to cognize.
Thus, the meaning is that even a jar or the like, while qualifying consciousness, would not be differentiated from anything at all. || 983 ||
Likewise, [there are those who say], "I alone know; my mother is none other"—such are their views.
The qualities of the Mother are perfected, excelling one's own self-awareness.

Anticipating the objection that "just as there is a distinction between the knower and so forth, let the distinction between jars and the like, as well as the distinction between doubt and the like, be established," he says: "In the same way.

Just as properties such as being a knower, a hearer, or a seer—which take the form of "knower-ness" and so on—by means of expressions like "the knowledge of the knower," differentiate the consciousness that serves as their own substrate, yet fail to obtain any mutual distinction from one another or from the object of consciousness (*meyam*), and are thus superimposed upon consciousness; in the same way, doubt and the rest [are superimposed] upon jars and the like.
And the meaning is that those things which are superimposed therein do not, in reality, differ from one another. || 984 ||
Consciousness alone is self-established, characterized as the innermost, immediate, and singular.
It serves as a basis for conventional discourse in the form of existence, non-existence, and so forth. || 985 ||

[Objection: Surely we do not maintain that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), since it too, being differentiated, must be considered a conceptual construction—just like the snake [superimposed] on the rope. To this, he says: "Consciousness... [The opponent continues: "In that case, because it is a substratum, it must be insentient (*jaḍa*) like the rope. To this he says: "Self-established (*svataḥ-siddhā*). [The opponent continues: "In that case, by accepting two entities—consciousness and the Self—you fall into the fallacy of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*. To this he says: "The inner self (*pratyak*)."
He states that since it is the substratum for all conceptual constructions, it follows as a consequence that it is the locus of all conventional usage: "bhāva... (verse 985).
1. *Arthāt* | 2. *ka*. *ga*. *pantaśca saṃ* | [Vol.
1, page 286] [Kārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Transcending both existence and non-existence, there is neither difference nor non-difference.
But if [the measurement] is by means of its back, on what basis would there be a contradiction? (986)

Having rejected the notions of difference and non-difference everywhere by asserting that they are the objects of perception and other means of knowledge, he concludes the present topic—the non-contradiction of the Vedāntas with other means of knowledge—with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the immutable self-experience (*kūṭasthapratyaganubhava*) is the substratum of all things, transcending it, [the world of] manifestation—

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for statements such as "That thou art," because the difference between the two [the individual self and Brahman] and so forth are unestablished, and these statements reveal such a reality. Furthermore, the validity of all means of knowledge follows from conformity with experience; therefore, how could the Vedāntas, which follow that [experience], be contradicted by other means of knowledge?
Thus he says: "By following upon that" (*tatpṛṣṭhena*). || 986 ||
The object of the means of valid cognition is held by disputants to be that which is not yet cognized.
Its establishment does not proceed from that [cognition] itself, because that [cognition] is established prior to the means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, since it is experience itself that is unknown, and since perception and the other means of knowledge have that [experience] as their object, there is no contradiction between them and the Vedāntas which operate upon it;

to state this accepted point, he says: "It is unknown" (*avijñāta*). If it is argued that because even its state of being unknown is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), the restriction to experience alone would be violated, he says: "Not of that" (*na tasya*) [referring to verse 987].
How could it be "measureless"? Let it be explained here what is meant by its being "unknown."
Or else, how could it exist without that pride, since its object would be impossible? (988)

If it is argued that because [the object] is established even prior to the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it lacks the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), then, due to the absence of a prover, there would be non-establishment itself; thus he raises the doubt: "Is it non-measurable? Here, the word "here" (*iha*) expresses the very state of the thing being unknown.

It is stated that either the non-existence of the state of being unknown, or its being accessible through a means of valid cognition, or some other prover must be asserted; of these, it is not the first.

Thus he says: "Or how? The meaning is that without the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), valid cognition (*māna*) itself would not be possible; for in its absence, there would be no object characterized by it, since there is no valid cognition without an object. || 988 ||
Cognition attains the status of valid knowledge only when it effects the destruction of the state of being unknown.
If it is argued that the state of being unknown arises from pride, that [state] is not accepted as the fruit of that [pride]. || 989 ||

He sets aside the second [alternative] with the words "ajñātatve" (if it were unperceived). The meaning is that knowledge, while removing ignorance, is not able to take that ignorance as its own object;

for a lamp does not illuminate darkness itself. He states the defect in the opposing case with the words "mānāt" (from valid cognition). The sense is: if ignorance were known through valid cognition, then the destruction of that ignorance could not be the fruit of that cognition, because that which is apprehended by a cognition cannot be removed by it. || 989 ||
Therefore, it is that which, being always known through direct experience, makes known what was previously unknown.
Valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest, would exist neither by itself nor through anything else.

He states the third [point] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning of the word "therefore" is the impossibility of both alternatives. Alternatively, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "therefore" and "from experience" (*anubhavataḥ*), the connection being that it is obtained from the constant experience. He states the established conclusion: that perception and other means of valid cognition apply only to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as characterized by the state of being unknown, which is established by an experience that neither rises nor sets. He says, "The unknown," [referring to] that which is self-luminous.
1. Not from the navel.
[Vol. 1, Page 287] 266 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection]

He clarifies that non-cognition is established by experience because it is not accepted [by the opponent] and because its status as an object of cognition has been refuted: "Not by itself" (na svataḥ). || 990 ||
"When a jar has been cognized in this way: 'I did not know it before,'"
For there is a further experience whose object is that which was previously unknown.

[Objection: Is it not the case that non-emptiness (*atucchatva*) is pervaded by being one or the other of "being an object of cognition" (*meyatva*) or "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*)? Therefore, when [non-emptiness] is excluded from this [object], it also excludes its own pervader, non-emptiness; and thus, there would be emptiness for that which is unknown. [Reply: He says "No," and so forth. When a jar has been cognized, one has the experience: "For all this time, I did not know this. Thus, with respect to the jar experienced as unknown prior to the arising of the cognition, [the following applies].

The meaning is as follows: since the experience [of an object] is observed, its state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*)—established through that very reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—does not become nullified; rather, it must be accepted that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this non-nullification (*atucchatva*) with respect to any one of the following—knowability (*meyatva*), self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), or being established by experience—is necessarily present. || 999 ||
Cognition directed toward an object is considered to have delimitation as its result.
However, it has no function regarding what is already known or unknown, because it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa). || 992 ||

[Objection: "If the cognition that an object is known through the Veda arises only when the object has already been cognized [by other means], then since its establishment is accomplished by that very [prior] cognition, the talk of it being established by experience (anubhava) is useless. Anticipating this, he says: "pravṛttam" (engaged). If the means of knowledge (māna) engaged with respect to a jar or the like terminates in the experience of that [object], then at its own time, regarding the object—

Anticipating the objection that, just as there is a production of "knownness" (*jñātatva*), so too there must be a manifestation of "knownness" at a prior time, he says: "Known" (*jhātā*). For it is not the case that the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) consists in the production of knownness, because that would result in its ceasing to be a means of knowledge by virtue of being a causal factor (*kāraka*). Nor is it logical that what produces knownness is necessarily a manifester (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, since it is untenable for that [means of knowledge] to possess both luminosity and non-luminosity with respect to the object, nor can it be [the manifester] at a prior time.

The sense is that the operation of making known [an object] as already known belongs to mental perception (*mānasa*), which consists of the apprehension of an object (*arthāvagraha*); for it is not admitted that there is an operation distinct from its birth, and because it has been stated that if [the object] were an object of measurement (*meyatva*), then the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) would result in not being removable by a means of valid cognition (*māna*). || 992 ||
Everyone, even a child, knows by their own experience that there is an ignorance of things not yet known.
993. When asked "Do you know nothing at all?", he says, "Except for me."

Furthermore, he states that the fact that "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) is established by experience is common to all people, saying: "Everyone indeed... When a child, even an ordinary one unskilled in human affairs, is asked by someone, "Do you know what a *gavaya* is?", he, from his own experience, indicates through this very method—"I do not know"—that there is unknownness; therefore, for everyone, that [unknownness] is established by experience alone, without any means of knowledge (*māna*).
It proceeds; how then could there be any misconception? This is the meaning. || 993 ||
Even upon the dissolution of the entire collection of instruments, experience remains by its own nature.
Because even in deep sleep, the vision is not lost, there is no difference from the awareness of the waking state.

Now, even if the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) is established by experience, one might object that experience itself possesses the status of a means of knowledge (*māna*) because it is produced by the instruments of knowledge (*mānakaraṇa*), and thus [the state of being unknown] would be known through that.

To this, he says: "Niḥśeṣa... (In its entirety...). Even in deep sleep, despite the absence of the causal complex for valid cognition (*pramāsāmagrī*), there exists an experience of the state of being unknown, which is of the nature of the eternally established essence of consciousness (*nityasiddhaciddhātu*).

Otherwise, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of one who has awakened—"I did not know"—would be impossible. Therefore, even in the waking state, the cognition of the state of being unknown [persists] from sleep...
The meaning is that, due to its specific nature, it is established by experience everywhere. || 994 ||
1 kha, 'tvatra ṃ | 2 kha. 'tajñā | 3 ka. ga. va nu | 4 kha tyeva pṛ | [vol 1, page 288] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary named Śāstramañjarī composed by Ānandagiri.
Regarding objects on the slopes of the Himalayas that have never been experienced before.
Even the experience of one who is awake does not differ from that of one in deep sleep. || 995 ||
In that very context, he states another reason: "Atyanteti" (regarding the absolute...). [He asks: "Have you seen the objects situated on the slopes of the Himalayas?"

When someone is asked by another whether something is known, they determine "no" and declare its state of being unknown (*ajñātatā*). In that case, it is not the case that this [state] has been cognized (*pramitā*) by them in every respect;

rather, because there is no cognition (*apramiti*) of it, that state is established in those [objects] solely through constant experience (*nityānubhava*). Even so, the objection that this is "unreasonable because there is no distinction from waking consciousness" is incorrect;

for while in deep sleep there is an absence of the causes of valid cognition (*māna*), and thus the state of being unknown remains uncognized (*ameyatva*), in the waking state such causes exist, and therefore its being cognizable (*tadgamyatva*) is established.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of one who is awake. Even though the aforementioned distinction exists, there is no difference in the experience of the unknownness [of objects] in both states;

for the experience of unknownness in the waking state does not differ from the experience of unknownness in deep sleep, since its status as an object of knowledge (*meyatā*) has been refuted—this is the meaning. || 999 ||
And in this case, experience is not lost, because there is the cognition, "I do not know."
Even though it was not seen, upon seeing it there is the cognition: "I did not know [it before]. || 996 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that in some instances the state of being unknown is established by experience itself? Since that experience is absent, there is no such state [of being unknown]. Is this absence [of experience] during waking, or during sleep? To this he says, "And not... The meaning is that during waking, because of the experience "I do not know the matter you have mentioned," its absence does not exist.
Furthermore, upon seeing an object previously unseen, there arises a cognition dependent on recollection (parāmarśa) in the form: "For all this time, I was unaware of this."
He states that there is a denial of experience during waking, saying: "The unseen," etc. (996).
In this way, even when a person has awakened from sleep, the dissolution of the subject and other factors occurs spontaneously.
It connects [the moments] through direct experience itself; therefore, there is no interruption for it in the interim. || 997 ||

He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case]: "The person" (pumān). Just as one might say upon waking, "I was unaware [of anything]," a person who has risen from sleep likewise perceives through his own experience the absence of objects such as a mother and so forth during that time. For once risen, he says, "I did not know anything at all"; the meaning is: since there was no awareness during the interval between being awake and dreaming, how could there be an absence of experience? || 997 ||
Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of the absence of cognition from the present cognition.
Sauti: Indeed, there is no differentiation in consciousness due to a difference in time. || 998 ||

Furthermore, as for the cognition of the absence of deep-sleep consciousness (*sauṣupta-bodhābhāva*), does it arise from the consciousness of the waking state or from the consciousness of deep sleep? It is not the first; thus he says, "Nor [is it from the waking state]. The reason for this is stated: "For not... Due to differences in place, time, and state, there is no distinctness in experience, because its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth are unestablished—neither by itself nor through another is that established. Therefore, experience must be accepted as non-dual, immutable, and eternal. By this, the second [alternative] is also refuted.
That which has also been explained [is so] because of contradiction; such is the meaning. || 998 ||
For it is from awakening alone that the divisions of time, states, and so forth are established.
And how could there be any modification of this [Self] due to pride toward one's mother and so forth? (999)

Now, one might object that experience (anubhava) is not immutable because it undergoes transformation due to time and other factors, like milk and the like; to this, he says: "Because of consciousness" (bodhāt).

Time and so forth do not establish themselves independently, as they are insentient (jaḍa); therefore, their existence and manifestation are dependent upon consciousness. Thus, [consciousness] must be established first.
268 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Volume 1, Page 289]

The meaning is as follows: since the experience of one's own nature is established as being [eternal], its modification cannot occur by virtue of that [experience]; for an experience of one's own nature, which was previously devoid of modification, cannot subsequently undergo modification by its own inherent force, because it is impossible for the essential nature to be lost. || 999 ||
"Among the three—the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—which arise and pass away, consciousness, which is unchanging and unarisen, shines forth as the one within. (1000)

He states another reason for the unchanging nature of the experience of the Self: "The knower," etc. Since the experiencer and so forth, which come and go, as well as their coming and going, appear as being established by an experience that is itself devoid of coming and going and whose sole nature is inward-turned, there is no modification of this [experience] due to the absence of a cause; such is the meaning. || 1000 ||
Overwhelmed by experience on all sides across the planes of the known and the unknown.
Objects do not manifest elsewhere, nor do they dissolve into that which is not the Self.

One might raise the objection: "The mother and others possess the status of a locus (*ādhāra*) because the locative case is used for them; conversely, that which is to be contained (*ādheya*) possesses the status of being located there because the nominative case is used for it.
Therefore, how can that [Self] be the one inner Self (*pratyagekatva*)? Anticipating this, he says: "On all sides" (*abhitaḥ*).

At the time of worldly discourse concerning objects pervaded by experience—whether as known or unknown—pillars and other such things attain their existence as being permeated on all sides by experience, and not merely by [the object's own] experience.

They do not exist elsewhere, nor do they dissolve into some other object; for in the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*), which transcends experience, it is impossible for inert things to undergo activities such as arising and so forth. Therefore, since objects such as the "measures" (*mātrā*) arise, persist, and dissolve only within the nature of experience itself, they lack existence apart from that; their apparent distinction and the relationship of container and contained are merely conceptual (*kālpānika*). This is the meaning. || 1001 ||
Therefore, experience alone is the object, characterized by being unknown.

Where the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge is established by themselves, [that is the case]. (1002) 8:57: He says that because there is no object other than experience, its non-duality results; thus he says "therefore. He says that this alone is the object of perception and the others, because there is no other object; thus he says "object. He states the reasoning for that: "unknown," etc. [The object of] the means of knowledge—

Anticipating the objection that this would entail the loss of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). In whatever experience the status of being a means of knowledge (*mānatā*) consists in the removal of the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), that [experience] has a nature that is self-manifesting; its manifestation is not dependent on anything else. For there is no contradiction between self-luminosity and being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*); even for that which is solely consciousness (*saṃvid-ekatāna*), there is a dependence on a means of knowledge for the purpose of removing ignorance residing within itself.
Such is the meaning. || 1002 ||
Therefore, for those things established by experience in the world, [it is] the destroyer of ignorance.
The sense organs and so forth do not proceed [to grasp objects] in any way other than by making the unknown known. 1003.

If it is argued that the sense organs and so forth do not have [pure] experience as their object, because it is well known that they have objects such as jars and the like, he says in response: "By that" (tena). Indeed, in the world, the sense organs and so forth attain their status as conventional means of knowledge by removing the state of being unknown from jars and the like—which are established as superimposed upon an experience that is itself unknown; otherwise, if there were no superimposition upon experience, they would merely be indicators of those things already established as unknown through other means of knowledge.

The meaning is that there is no validity for perception and the other means of knowledge, because of that reason—namely, the impossibility of subverting what is established by a means of knowledge through another means of knowledge. By this, even the well-known status of perception and the others as having jars and such things as their objects is to be refuted. || 1003 ||
[Vol. 1, p.
290] [Vārtika], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 269.
Pots and other objects, established through valid cognition, do not cease their state of being unknown.
Even though self-established, the Self does not abandon its nature as a real entity without valid cognition. (1004)

An objection might be raised: "In empirical experience (*vyavahāra*), since [cognition] removes the ignorance regarding jars and the like that are superimposed upon it, and because it rests upon the experience of what was previously unknown, even though perception and other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) possess validity, the ignorance regarding the conscious Self (*cidātman*)—due to its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*)—would be removed without a means of knowledge. Thus, there is no purpose for the operation of a means of knowledge therein. Anticipating this, he says: "Jars and the like," etc. Just as jars and the like are empirical...

The means of knowledge (*māna*), once established, do not abandon their own state of being unknown without depending upon that very knowledge; likewise, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), though its nature is consciousness (*cit*) and it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), is nevertheless unable to abandon its state of being unknown without a valid cognition (*pramā*), because it is only the manifestation of the fruit of knowledge (*mānaphalaprakāśa*) that is opposed to ignorance (*ajñāna*), whereas the manifestation of its own essential nature (*svarūpaprakāśa*) is not so. This is the meaning. || 1004 ||
The establishment of even a worldly object occurs prior to the arrival of a subverting cognition.
Precisely by the power of the true nature of reality, [it is perceived] despite the obstruction of darkness. || 1005 ||

If it is argued that the state of being unknown cannot cease without a means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and therefore its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) is dependent upon a means of knowledge, [the author] says "prior" (prāk) to address the doubt that this would imply its nature is adventitious (āgantuka). Before the arising of the subverting cognition "I am Brahman," all non-self (anātman) is established solely by the force of experience mediated by ignorance; thus, while illuminating the phenomenal world of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth, the Self shines by itself, independent of any means of knowledge.

The meaning is "manifestation. The word "api" (even/also) serves to indicate the pervasion of all worldly objects. This occurs by the power of the reality of things—that is to say, by the force of the manifestation of consciousness which constitutes the very nature of the Self. || 1005 ||
But the sublation of the darkness consisting of the grasping of the entire measure and so forth occurs through awakening.
[This arises] from the direct realization of the true nature of the absolute oneness, which originates from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 1006 ||

Anticipating the objection that if perception and the other means of knowledge were authoritative regarding the Self, then the ignorance of it would be removed by those very means, rendering scripture useless, he says:

"Entirely" (kṛtsna). Anticipating the further objection as to why the knowledge produced by perception and the rest might not be what dispels the ignorance which is the cause of all [limited] measures and so forth, he qualifies that awakening: "Complete" (pūrṇa). || 1006 ||
Therefore, in that case, scripture would have the power to dispel [the opponent's] ignorance regarding it.

That alone is considered by the wise to be the state of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) and the goal of human endeavor (*pumartha*). Regarding reality (*tattva*) as characterized by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), cognition produced by perception and other means is applicable there because activity (*pravṛtti*) is possible therein; however, regarding reality without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), it is [cognition] derived from scripture (*śrauta*), for only scripture is capable of engaging with that [reality]. Furthermore, cognition characterized by limiting adjuncts cannot remove ignorance (*ajñāna*), because its object depends upon ignorance, whereas [the cognition of] the reality without limiting adjuncts— *Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.*

However, that [empirical] knowledge would be uprooted by the power of its object; therefore, since the cessation of the ignorance that is the material cause of misfortune results from the knowledge arising solely from the sentence, it follows that the authority of statements such as "That thou art" is established regarding identity. He states this conclusion with the words "by that. This means: because it has been stated that the destruction of that ignorance occurs through the very knowledge of the Self derived from the Śruti.
The word "therein" (tatra) refers to Brahman as the Self, which is understood through the purport of the Śruti. It is the human goal by virtue of being supreme bliss.

And because of this, he states that the validity of the *tattvamasi* and other such [scriptural passages] resides in Brahman as the Self: "The goal of man... etc. If it is argued that while the status of being the goal of man is well-established in the case of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, it is not accepted for the Self in that way, he says in response: "For the wise... (1007).
Is it not so that [this is for] the sake of abandoning the accumulation of the unbearable sufferings of saṃsāra?
What other desired happiness could there be than this, whose status as a human goal is established by its very nature? (1008)
270 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 291]

The objection is raised according to the view of the ancient logicians (*jarattārkika*): "But [it is said] that by the word *pumartha* (the goal of man), Brahman, the Self, is called 'bliss' (*sukha*); that is incorrect, because there is no bliss other than the cessation of suffering, and because it is impossible for existence and non-existence to be one. [The author addresses this with] "But... The meaning is: the very destruction of the mass of those unavoidable sufferings of *saṃsāra* is itself bliss, since nothing other than that possesses the characteristic of being desirable. [This is so] because the definition of bliss is not [currently] under discussion...
It refutes that [position] with the words "of which" (yasya). || 1008 ||
Even in the world, one is seen to be happy when the torment of disease is dispelled.
Nor is there any activity on the part of those free from passion for the sake of a pleasure distinct [from the cessation of suffering].

(1009) He provides the empirical experience of the world as proof for the claim that "the destruction of suffering itself is happiness," with the words: "In the world also... For when worldly people perceive a man afflicted by the torment of disease, they say, "Alas, this man is exceedingly miserable"; and when he is freed from his illness through the turn of fate—

The meaning is that as they depart, they say, "By good fortune, this one has been born happy. Now, it might be argued that the activity of the dispassionate seeker of liberation (*virakta-mumukṣu*) is for the sake of happiness other than the mere destruction of suffering; since such [mere destruction] is insufficient, the existence of happiness as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is established. To this, he replies with the words "distinct" (*vyatirikta*). The activity of the seeker of liberation is for the sake of *mokṣa*, and that *mokṣa* is the dissociation from bondage. Since those who are turned away from *saṃsāra* have no suffering to be removed, [the activity cannot be for its removal]. In that regard, he says: "distinct. The activity of the seeker of liberation aims at *mokṣa*, which is the separation from bondage.

Bondage is suffering because it is undesirable; therefore, the purpose of its cessation is precisely that [liberation]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, pleasure that is not consciously experienced is neither a human goal (puruṣārtha) nor an object of action.
In its own essential nature, it is impossible for there to be the state of being both the object of knowledge and the knower, because that would entail the consequence of duality. || 1010 ||

Furthermore, is this happiness, which is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), unperceived or perceived? In the first case, it would not be the goal of human life (*apumartha*), like a treasure hidden in the depths of one's house that remains ungrasped;
thus he says: "unperceived" (*asaṃvedyam*). He refutes the second alternative with: "and not" (*na ca*). He states the reason for this: "in its own nature" (*svarūpe*).

The meaning is that in a single entity, the relationship of object and subject is impossible, because that [relationship] depends upon difference, which would contradict non-duality (*advaita*). || 1010 ||
Since pleasure and pain are not established as distinct entities in this way, how could there be [a distinction] between the two?
Why is it not conceived that the unity [of the self] is pleasure and its separation is pain? || 1011 ||
He refutes the claim that "the destruction of suffering itself is happiness" with the words, "Not so. The reason for this is stated as "by way of distinction.

For one who is tormented and has half his body submerged in a cool lake, pleasure and pain are perceived simultaneously and without confusion; therefore, how could there be an identity between the destruction of suffering and happiness?
This is because it is impossible to perceive existence and non-existence in the same place, nor is there a spatial division there between the presence and absence of pleasure and pain.

The meaning is as follows: there is no simultaneous contradiction between two states existing in different parts [of the body], because the self (*ātman*) has no spatial divisions (*apradeśatva*), and because the body and its locations are themselves insentient.

Furthermore, if the self were to exist as delimited by those parts, then even though the delimiters (the body-parts) differ, there would be no difference in that which is delimited (the self); thus, since it would reside in only one place, it is impossible for those two states to simultaneously possess both existence and non-existence.
Moreover, if the absence of pain is pleasure, then why should the absence of pleasure not be pain? Since there is no distinction [between the two cases], the opposite consequence would follow.
The ascetic [says]: "Of happiness... || 1011 ||
For even those who are not suffering are seen to act out of a desire to attain happiness.
Those who engage in the means to that [attainment] are not logically justified in its non-differentiation. || 1012 ||

He states another reason for the claim that "pleasure is not the destruction of suffering" with the words: "even those who are not suffering. Even those such as kings who are devoid of suffering are observed to engage in various forms of dancing, singing, and so forth, out of a desire for pleasure; yet, that observation does not [thereby] prove the destruction of suffering. (Note: The variants indicate that in one version it is "not desired," while in another it is "is possible.")
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, p. 292] [Commentary by Ānandagiri, titled Śāstraprakāśikā:

Since pleasure and its destruction are not distinct, it is logical that activity toward the destruction of pain—which has not yet been attained—would be impossible; therefore, the pleasure resulting from the destruction of that pain is something additional.

This is the meaning. Although there is a rule that the root *vṛt* takes the ātmanepada endings, the phrase "they proceed" (*pravartante*) is used to illustrate the maxim: "The practice of those who know [the Veda] is like that of the Vedas. Alternatively, the prefix *pra-* may account for the deviation from the rule. || 1012 || Even those who are happy, being endowed with means of pleasure such as sandalwood and the like, are [not truly satisfied].
They experience a different kind of happiness through news such as the birth of a son. || 1013 ||

If it is argued that the absence of suffering for those engaged in the means to happiness is unproven, he says in response: "Sandalwood," etc. But how can there be an engagement with that very same means by those who, having attained unsurpassed happiness through the perfection of the means, remain [in that state]—driven by the desire to obtain more of that very means?
[The answer is: "The birth of a son," etc. (1013).
And the suffering consisting in the non-attainment of sons and so forth is not postulated there.
For that which is not perceived due to a lack of awareness cannot be an object of suffering, just like the suffering of an enemy [who is unknown].
Now, one might argue that when happiness arises in a person upon hearing of the birth of a son, there is the destruction of suffering caused by the non-attainment of that son and so forth.

He says "no" to the claim that the body itself is happiness. He states "son, etc. as the reason for this; the underlying cause is "because of non-cognition. Anticipating the objection that suffering exists there even if it is not being experienced, he says "unperceivable. To provide an illustration for its lack of suffering, he says "enemy," and then "no."

Indeed, the suffering of one person belongs to another, because it is not experienced by that other; likewise, when a person has uprooted suffering and experiences pleasure resulting from the acquisition of a son and so forth, although there is no occurrence of suffering [in that moment], since pleasure is perceived, the meaning is that this [pleasure] is something entirely different from the destruction of that [suffering]. || 1014 ||
For this very reason, even animals here desire happiness in that same way.
They desire to abandon what is unpleasant, yet they do not know the means for doing so.

In that very context, he states another reason: "Even animals... Since they distinguish between the cessation of suffering and [the attainment of] happiness, even animals, birds, and the like in this world desire the attainment of happiness and the cessation of suffering through such differentiation; the meaning is that the cessation of suffering is one thing and happiness is another. If that is so, then the performance of means by both animals and ourselves—driven by the desire for happiness and the aversion to suffering—[is established].

To this he replies: "But not... The meaning is that the accomplishment of a distinction in practice arises from the fact that the scriptural means (*sādhana*) is within the scope of our own realization alone, and not that of others. || 1011 ||
The Veda also demonstrates that the pure Self is the primary happiness.
Likewise, that which is non-self and suffering is not accepted as the goal of man. || 1016 ||
Anticipating the objection that although happiness exists as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) in the world, it does not exist in the Self (*ātman*), he says: "The Veda also...

The meaning is this: since the Veda—which declares the Self to be devoid of all attributes such as hunger and so forth, and which describes the Self as consisting of extraordinary bliss (*alaukika-sukha*) untouched by suffering—is accepted as authoritative because it brings about the final determination of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), therefore, in accordance with worldly usage, happiness in the Self must also be of a positive nature. || 1016 ||
This very [Self] has been heard of in many ways from such passages as "This is dearer than that."

Likewise, for the sake of the self; therefore, there can be no other happiness.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya—[in the section on the *Saṃbandha*]:

Anticipating the objection, "What is this Veda which declares the Self to be happiness?", he cites Vedic statements regarding the happiness of the Self. Regarding the phrase "That very [Self]": the ellipsis is "the happiness of the Self has been heard [in scripture]. In that regard, he points to repetition (*abhyāsa*) as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those statements.

He explains: "In many ways. Because everything is dear as being subordinate to the self, he says that the self is the supreme bliss due to its being the most unsurpassed object of affection. "Likewise"—the remainder of the sentence is that by this statement as well, the fact that the self is bliss is shown through the principle of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Based on the stated passage, he states the conclusion: that the self alone is bliss and nothing else. Therefore—
[The opponent says:
"No;
for detachment is dependent [on something else], just as it is based on the connection with human goals. (1017)
If even the desire for supreme bliss is likewise [a form of attachment], why is it not prohibited? || 1018 ||

[Objection: But surely, if the self were of the nature of happiness, then because of the desire for that happiness, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) would engage [in worldly activity], resulting in the persistence of saṃsāra; for activity dependent on desire has that [desire] as its seed. To this, he says: "puruṣārtha" (for the sake of the human goal). The meaning of this is as follows: Just as you accept the dispassion of seekers of liberation—their aversion to saṃsāra—as arising from yoga by way of being a cause for liberation, which is the human goal, and not as arising from an activity born of aversion like any other such activity—so too [is our case].

If attachment to supreme bliss is also accepted as a human goal (puruṣārtha) like the attachment to the seed of liberation, then it is not proper to prohibit it. Therefore, even when one who seeks liberation engages in activity out of attachment to happiness, there is no engagement in saṃsāra. || 1018 ||
If it is argued that there is passion when there is a desire for ultimate happiness;
If there is a desire for resorting to secluded places and so forth, why is there no passion? (1019)

Now, in our view, activity does not arise from attachment or aversion, but rather from a sense of revulsion toward them; nor are aversion and revulsion identical, because aversion is caused by false knowledge, whereas revulsion is caused by the realization of the truth regarding the worthlessness of saṃsāra. Likewise, in this case as well, activity does not arise from passion (rāga), but rather from faith in supreme bliss; nor are these two identical, because passion is produced by false knowledge, whereas faith is not.
Thinking that [desire] is preceded by discrimination (*viveka*), he states the fault in [the opponent's] view that mere intention constitutes passion (*rāga*). He says, "absolute," etc.
The sense is that in that case, detachment (*virāgitva*) alone is well-known. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the service of the teacher (*ācāryopāsana*) and so forth are included. || 1019 ||
This has been elaborated upon by such statements as "Now, those who [number] a hundred," and so forth.
For this is indeed clearly stated even in the Taittirīya Śruti: "This alone... [1020]

Having dispelled any suspicion of contradiction regarding the self’s being happiness, he shows other scriptural passages on that very point. [The word] "Now" (atha) means, in short, that this self is unsurpassed happiness. He states that its nature is happiness because the term "bliss" (ānanda) is clearly applied to the self in such passages as "This, indeed, is the blissful one" (eṣa vā ānandayāti). Thus he says: "For this... (eṣa hi...). || 1020 ||
And for this very reason, one who is oriented toward his own bliss during sleep is awakened.
Just as one is afflicted by the interruption of pleasure resulting from contact with women and the like. || 1021 ||
He states that even the experience of deep sleep (*sauptānubhava*) is proof for the blissfulness of the Self, saying: "svānanda... (one's own bliss). He provides the reason for this, saying:

"bodhyamāna... (while being awakened). This means precisely because of being attached to the experience of bliss. He offers an example accepted by living beings who are inclined toward sense-objects—namely, the pain felt by one experiencing the bliss of deep sleep while being awakened—saying: "khyādi... (women, etc.). || 1021 ||
[Vol.
1, Page 294] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri:
"Because its essential nature is solely bliss, the state of being an object of knowledge does not exist therein."
For that [ignorance] is honored in the absence of perfect awakening, but not in that which is characterized solely by awakening.

As for the objection that if the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) were an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), there would be duality, and if it were not an object of knowledge, it would not serve the purpose of man (*apumarthatā*), we reply: "The bliss... [etc.]. Even though the Self consists solely of the essence of happiness (*sukhaikarasatva*), why is its being an object of knowledge not desired? To this he says: "It is devoid of cognition" (*niḥsaṃbodha*). For the state of being an object of knowledge is desired in the case of the insentient (*jaḍa*), because in that case the act of knowing is not already established by itself; but in the case of the Self, since it is of the very nature of consciousness (*bodhaikarūpatvāt*), [objectivity is not required]. Therefore, in the case of the Brahman-Self...
The sense is that when there is the experience of supreme bliss in a state of undivided unity, the authority of the Vedānta is unimpeded. || 1022 ||
This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the accessibility of the qualification.
That this applies to all persons has already been explained in detail previously. || 1023 ||

The meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "sarvo'pi" has been explained both concisely and in detail. Now, he states the purport of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "sarvapuruṣāṇām": "adhikārasya" (of the qualification). Since everyone, by their very nature, is observed to have the desire, "May I have happiness; may I not have suffering," and since liberation consists merely in unconditioned happiness and so forth, those who desire that [liberation] possess the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore—

The meaning is that the commentary [is written] for the purpose of making known the ease with which the qualification for knowledge is accessible—that is, the accessibility of the connection with qualified persons.

Having raised the objection, "Since liberation is either known or unknown, a desire for it is impossible; how then can one who desires it be the qualified candidate?", he says "In the same way" (tathā), explaining that it is not logical to have a desire for liberation in the manner [the opponent suggests], because of its inherent accessibility. || 1023 ||
For even one who desires heaven and the like does not desire liberation.
Desiring liberation, he does not look at anything else even with a sidelong glance. || 1024 ||

[Objection: But surely, for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), in the interim there may arise a longing for heaven and the like—just as there is for food when one desires a village—and since such a person is subject to that [desire], they lack the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*). How, then, is the availability of a qualified candidate (*adhikārin*) established here? To this, he says: "Heaven and so forth... One who longs for heaven and the like might somehow also long for liberation because of its being the unsurpassed fruit; however, one who desires liberation is not [such a person].

The sense is this: he who, having become a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), again desires heaven and the like, is the lowest among seekers of liberation, like a camel among beasts, because he obtains only a very meager fruit. || 1024 ||
And for all human beings as well, the entitlement is unrestricted.
"Therefore, [the author] said: 'for men, from all [sides']"—thus spoke the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt). || 1025 ||

He concludes the meaning of the present commentary with the words "of all" (*sarveṣām*). Nor should it be argued that this commentary is redundant because the qualification of one who desires that [result] has already been stated in the *Nāmabhāṣya* by way of declaring the fruit; for the distinction between the two meanings is established by the fact that the qualified person is indicated in both places through both the explicit statement and the context. Although the qualified person was indeed shown directly in the phrase "to those desiring to escape from the cycle of transmigratory existence,"...

Even so, because its accessibility is desired here, it is not useless. Nor should it be thought that this implies the scripture has universal eligibility (*sarvādhikāratva*), for it is stated that accessibility is intended only for those qualified for knowledge who possess the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). || 1025 ||
When it is said, "Bring a white cow," [one understands] some action having the cow as its object.
Observing one who is acting, the ignorant person forms an inference regarding the cause. || 1026 ||
