Sureśvarācārya, in his *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*,

sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to explain the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "dṛṣṭaviṣaya" and ending with "nāgamānveṣaṇā," starting with the words "śuklām."

The meaning is that when an elderly person utters the command "Bring the cow," an ignorant child, having observed the middle-aged person—the listener—engaging in activity directed toward a cow, infers that there must be some cause for that activity. || 1026 ||
It is certainly known by this that what is observed is the action of a cow.

Since the arising of what was previously unknown is never observed anywhere, [the author] states how inference functions: "It is known," etc. This is the cause for its operation; by this [inference], one who is proceeding [toward an object] necessarily—

Since it is understood by this listener that there is an activity called "bringing the cow" which has been communicated, and because nowhere in the world is an activity observed to be performed regarding something that is not already known as something to be done prior to its performance, the child infers: "The disputed engagement is preceded by a cognition that prompts it, because it is an engagement preceded by cognition, like [any] agreed-upon case. And of that prompting cognition, there is the syntactical connection with the word...

The meaning is as follows: determining that birth [of the effect] possesses a positive concomitance (*vyatireka*), and having ascertained that the word alone has the capacity for mere instigation (*pravartaka*), one—through the method of presence and absence (*āvāpodvāpa*)—concludes that a specific word has the capacity for its own meaning as conjoined with the instigator. || 1027 ||
Having observed that [the effect] is dependent upon its causes, one infers those causes from it.
In that case, it would follow that [the object] is worldly, because it is cognizable by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 1028 ||

Considering that if the instigator (*pravartaka*) were a distinct entity from the mandate (*niyoga*), or if the mandate itself were the instigator, then—since one would have to admit that the word-potency (*śakti*) of words resides in their connection with something else—the uniqueness of the mandate (*niyoga*) as the sole object of verbal cognition would be contradicted, he refutes the second alternative with the words "If... (*yadi*). If, having observed the effect consisting of the listener’s activity—which is produced by causal factors (*kāraka*) such as the agent—one were to infer the instigating mandate as its cause, then, because that [mandate] would be merely inferential, it would be equivalent to a jar.
The meaning is that the status of being Vedic is not established. || 1028 ||
If there is no purpose for an agent therein, how can there be the performance of what is known?
Neither an established entity nor a non-entity is observed to depend upon a causal agent.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which is the *niyoga* (an injunction), is it unsuitable to be accomplished by the causal factors (*kāraka*s) or suitable? Among these, he first addresses the former alternative with the words "If not" (*na cet*). He says that if the *niyoga*, even when somehow known through the optative suffix and so forth, cannot be accomplished through performance, then the performance of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) would be fruitless and have no occasion; thus he says, "of that which is known. Alternatively, if the *niyoga* were not to be accomplished by the causal factors, its object—

He says [the following], starting with "of that which is known," because even the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) would not be determined as something to be accomplished (sādhya) since its nature is affliction (kleśa), and thus its performance would remain unestablished. Regarding the second [alternative] as well—whether it be existent, non-existent, or of both natures—he refutes the first two [possibilities] with the words "not established" (na siddha).

For neither an existent nor a non-existent thing requires causal factors (kāraka), as there is no evidence for such a requirement; this lack of dependence on causal factors is evident in the case of the Self and a human horn.
The meaning is: "because of perception. || 1029 ||
If it were established as a causal factor, its authority would necessarily follow by force.
But when the effect to be indicated has been accomplished, the Veda would possess authority regarding an already established matter. || 1030 ||

Furthermore, regarding the position that [the object] exists, is the injunction (*niyoga*) produced by the word or manifested by it? In the first case, because the word would be a causal agent (*kāraka*), its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established;
thus he says: "produced. In the second case, however, since there is a rule that only what already exists can be manifested, in that— [vol 1, page 296]
[The Vārtika], together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 275. He says:

"If [the Veda] were a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its status as a means of knowledge would apply to an established fact (*siddhe 'rthe*), because the injunction (*niyoga*) exists as something manifested (*vyaṅgyatayā*). Thus he says: "But in the case of the manifested... (1030).
Furthermore, the validity of a statement does not have non-existence alone as its object.
If non-existence were not the object to be produced, then the means of cognition would have its validity established in respect of an already accomplished object. || 1031 ||

Furthermore, since the injunction (*niyoga*) is non-existent, even the suspicion that the Veda possesses authority regarding it does not arise for anyone, because it is never observed that a cognition lacking an object can be authoritative; thus he says: "Of the sentence. To refute the aforementioned objection, he recalls the defect stated in the position that [the injunction] is manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*), provided that the injunction exists: "If not... (1031).
Now, the effect consists of both natures, having the character of being both accomplished and unaccomplished.
Nor is there any real entity anywhere that is subject to these two aforementioned defects. (1032)

He restates the third [position] with the words "Now" (*atha*). He refutes it by pointing out the recurrence of the aforementioned defects: the impossibility of the Veda being dependent on an agent and the fact that the Veda’s authority would apply only to an already established object. With the words "It has been said" (*uktā*), he states that having accepted an entity consisting of both existence and non-existence, it was said; however, that very [entity] does not exist because of contradiction. He says: "And not" (*na ca*) || 1032 ||
A means of knowledge is the manifester of what is already established; it is never a producer [of that which did not exist].
If the injunction is the means of valid cognition, then let it be explained how that [injunction] is to be accomplished.
Furthermore, regarding the "task" (kārya) called *niyoga*, whether it be Vedic or worldly: in the first case, it would follow that it has the nature of an already established fact (*siddhārtha*).

Thus he says: "of the established" (*siddhasya*). Since perception and other means of knowledge are observed to indicate established facts, if *niyoga* were also Vedic, its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) would not be established;

for it would follow that, like perception and the rest, it indicates an established fact. As for the second alternative, it is extremely weak because it contradicts the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
Always disregarded. || 1033 ||
That which is established through the object is designated as "the effect" (kārya).
Since the sacrifice is unestablished prior to its accomplishment, how can it be measured by an injunction? || 1034 ||

Furthermore, does the accomplishment of the *niyoga* (the mandate) occur only after the performance of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), or even before it? Regarding this, he restates the first position. The construction is as follows:
"If it is the view (*mata*) that the effect called *niyoga* is accomplished by means of the performance of the root-meaning. Then he says:
"By the sacrifice," etc., meaning that since the *niyoga* does not exist previously, it cannot be known through the Veda. Indeed, that which is non-existent...
The meaning is that its status as Vedic is like that of a human horn. || 1034 ||
If the agent has already achieved perfection through prior practice, what fruit could there be from the accomplishment of a sacrifice?
Even if that [result] were established through the accomplishment of the sacrifice, on what basis could the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) be considered the instrument? || 1035 ||

He raises a second objection, [claiming] that even prior to the performance, the *niyoga* (the mandate) is established as the impeller of that performance; this is indicated by the word "prior" (*prāk*). He refutes this, stating that such performance would be fruitless because it would not accomplish the *niyoga*; this is indicated by the question "What is the fruit? He then raises another objection, suggesting that the performance is fruitful because even though the *niyoga* is already established, it is to be accomplished by means of the sacrifice; this is indicated by the word "sacrifice" (*yāga*). [The author replies: No, because what is already established cannot be further accomplished.

He states that performance is for the sake of accomplishment: "the state of being prompted. This means that the state of being prompted for the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) consists in its being impelled by a *niyoga* (an injunction).
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the section on the *saṃbandha*:

1] that which is to be performed does not succeed for an established *niyoga*, because an established *niyoga* does not depend upon accomplishment; thus, it lacks [the capacity] toward the performance of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
The meaning is "because of being the unifier. || 1035 ||
If it is thought that this [attainment] results from the performance of sacrifices and so forth, just as [the production of] a jar does;
How is it that the assistance of an injunction does not result in its being equivalent to a pot? || 1036 ||
Furthermore, does the performance of sacrifices and other rites provide some benefit to the *niyoga* (the mandate), or not? If it does not, then the performance would be useless;

thus, he states another alternative: "The sacrifice, etc. (*yāgādi*). The meaning is that if the performance of the meaning of the verbal root provides a benefit to the *niyoga* in the form of its attainment of existence—just as a pot and the like attain existence through the activity of a potter and others—then the *niyoga* would be equivalent to a pot or similar object.
And if there were an injunction regarding that which is not the goal of man, such being the case, [it would follow that the Veda is not authoritative].
How can that be grasped by the wise when the human goal is its adversary? || 1037 ||

If it is argued that its similarity to a jar is not undesirable, he says in response: "It would not be for the sake of man" (*apumartha*). The meaning is that if there were similarity to a jar, the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence would have to be a *niyoga* (an injunction) devoid of the attainment of pleasure, the avoidance of pain, and the means thereto. Anticipating the objection that even if such were the purport, the Veda’s status as being centered on *niyoga* would remain unimpeded, he says: "Contradictory" (*pratyarthinī*). [This refers to] the human goal (*pumartha*).

The meaning is that when an injunction (*niyoga*)—which is the intended object of the purport of an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) and serves as the means to achieve a desired end—is opposed by something that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), it is impossible for those possessed of discernment (*vivekin*) to comprehend its purport. || 1037 ||
When the optative suffix and other such markers are heard, that which is perceived by a person as a task to be accomplished [arises].
That [cognition] is established for the speaker and the agent as being dependent upon assistance and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that—in worldly usage such as "Bring the cow," where one observes that a person’s cognition of a task arises from hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers—therefore, in the Veda as well, following worldly precedent, the purport must lie in a task called *niyoga* (an injunction), he says: "The optative suffix, etc. Immediately after hearing the word of injunction...
The cognition of an action (*kāryajñāna*) arises in the listener either in the speaker or in the listener itself, depending upon the attainment of pleasure or the destruction of pain.

Therefore, when one understands from the purport of the sentence that "the bringing of the cow and so forth is the cause of what is desired by me, whether as a listener or as a speaker," a mental cognition arises that "this is an action" (*kāryam*).

Consequently, since it is impossible for the status of being an "action" called *niyoga* (an injunction) to be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, the meaning of those suffixes is simply the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*), even in the case of prohibitive sentences.
The intended meaning is that, in the absence of that [other], this is the purport. || 1038 ||
If the human goal were not possible for an agent to bring about through any injunction, [then there would be no point].
At that time, no one in the world would act at all, simply because of the command [of the Lord]. || 1039 ||
No man is independent, for he exists merely to accomplish the purposes of another's command.
By the force of the injunction, one directs the mind toward sacrifices and the like, even though they are of the nature of suffering.

He states the justification for the claim that "in all cases, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the cause of what is desired" with the words "If not... If, in instances such as "Bring the cow," the listener or the speaker does not perceive through the heard optative suffix (*liṅ*) that it is a cause for the human goal, then— since those who act intentionally would not engage in worldly activity based on a mere command— the person's engagement in positive injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*) occurs only after they have understood from that [suffix] that the meaning of the verbal root is a means to a desired end.

The meaning is that only the means toward what is desired is the referent of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; through its connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), there arises the cognition of the absence of that [means] in the case of a prohibition. This is from the *Vārttika* on the command of a king and so forth, accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā*.

Since activity is observed even in one who is devoid of a connection to a result— such as a dependent person acting for the sake of fulfilling an order— it follows that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) does not [express] the status of being a means to a desired end.

If it is argued that there is no restriction [to the meaning] being the object of an injunction (*ājñārthatva-niyati*), he says in response: "The injunction" (*ājñā*). The meaning is this: even for a servant or similar person who acts with prior deliberation, their engagement in an action is preceded by a consideration of the result, which is the destruction of suffering; thus, it is established that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth have as their meaning the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). For, in the case of sacrifices and the like—which are of the nature of affliction—a person acting with prior deliberation would not engage in them under the authority of an injunction without a consideration of the result; therefore, even in the Veda, [the optative suffix] signifies precisely the means to a desired end.
He states that [the suffix] *liṅ* and so forth have this meaning: "in the case of sacrifice and the like. (1039 || 1040 ||)
Having aimed at a human goal, one then engages in ritual sacrifice and other such activities.
In that case, the fruit would be the instigator, and the injunction would be the means of attainment. || 1041 ||

In that regard, even if one engages [in action] after ascertaining the result and knowing, "This is the means for that," he asks, "What does it produce for you? [The answer is: "The human goal" (*pumartha*). Having stated that when one accepts engagement upon knowing that sacrifices and the like are the means to a result, it follows according to my view that the motivator is "the means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhana*), whereas your position—that it is the *niyoga*—is defeated; thus he states the conclusion: "The result" (*phala*) [is the motivator]. "Its cause" (*taddhetu*)...
If it is thought that the activity [of the agent] is like that of the imperative mood (*loṭ*) and so forth, as in the case of a master;
One would certainly not be subject to penance on account of a livelihood dependent upon another. || 1042 ||
Even if the *niyoga* (the mandate) is the motivator, it must either depend on the knowledge that it is a means to a fruit or not depend on it.

In the first case, by distinguishing between what is already attained and what is not, one considers that the knowledge of being a means to a fruit alone is the motivator; thus, he adopts the second alternative. [He says: "In this view... Having seen a person possessed by a spirit (*bhūta*), a knower of mantras employs a mantra—either vernacular or refined—from the scriptures for the sake of effecting the departure of that possession, and the possessed person likewise [acts].

The meaning is: if it is accepted that a person acts under the control of that [command], such that the activity of a person who is dependent on another proceeds even without depending on the knowledge that [the act] is a means to a desired end—due to a *niyoga* (command) expressed by the imperative mood (*loṭ*) and so forth—then, just as there is no fault for a frightened person who somehow transgresses the application of a mantra, there would likewise be no fault for one acting under dependence on a *niyoga*, even upon transgressing it; consequently, since he would not be subject to penance (*prāyaścitta*), the injunction for such penance would be rendered useless.
He refutes this [notion of] "one who has performed penance" with the following verse: || 1042 ||
Just as the efficacy of a mantra does not depend on the power of that which is being acted upon, so too is its capacity to set [an effect] in motion.
In that case, the accomplishment of the effect would not arise from the sacrifice and so forth by themselves alone. || 1043 ||

He clarifies that very point with the words "the state of being an instigator" (*pravartakatvam*). Just as a mantra such as the *Prākṛta* functions as an instigator by its own power without depending on the capacity of the person to be instigated, and yet does not incur any fault for exceeding that [capacity], so too here, one who performs [the act] under the force of the *niyoga* (command) does not become liable to penance even if he transgresses it due to the conjunction of destiny; therefore, the injunction regarding that [transgression] would be purposeless. This is the meaning. [The text continues: *niyogāti-*...

In the sequence, he states another objection regarding the absence of fault: "No," etc. The meaning is that if there were no fault in the transgression of an injunction (*niyoga*), then no one would perform sacrifices and other rites which are its objects; and thus, the injunction itself would not be established. || 1043 ||
Whether it be the agent, the action, or the fruit of the action;
Since that [reason] is not established for him, it follows that it would be merely worldly (laukika). || 1044 ||
1 kha. This is not so. 2 ga. Then. 3. Activity.
Furthermore,

whether it be the causal factor (*kāraka*), the action (*kriyā*), its fruit (*tatphala*), or the injunction (*niyoga*), in every respect, because that is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*),...
He says, "Or [it would be] a causal agent," because, being similar to a jar or other such objects, it would follow that it is non-Vedic. || 1044 ||
But when one is established in the reality of the single self by way of the path of reasoning as previously described, [the following occurs].
There would not be even the slightest fault, in the least degree, in this statement.

[Objection: But surely, since an injunction (*niyoga*) is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*māna*), if the Veda were not concerned with it, then because Brahman is also already established, it too could be cognizable through other means of knowledge; why, then, would the Veda have authority there? To this, he replies: "In the case of the identity of the Self" (*aikātmya*). Since statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) are concerned with the reality (*vastu*), and because the word "Self" (*ātman*) is applied to the Self [in those contexts]—according to the reasoning stated previously, such as "because it is used for the Self"—there is no defect whatsoever regarding its authority therein.
Therefore, there is not even the slightest similarity between an injunction (niyoga) and Brahman; such is the meaning. || 1045 ||
The meaning which is reached through the statements "not this, not this" and so forth, and which consists of non-dual experience;
How can that [cognition] be worldly when it transcends all objects of knowledge? || 1046 ||

As for the claim that Brahman, being an established reality, is accessible through other means of knowledge (*māna*), that has already been refuted; now he refutes it again by another method, beginning with "No" (*na*). The meaning is this: because Brahman is devoid of attributes in accordance with the scriptural texts of negation (*niṣedha-śruti*), and because it is self-luminous in accordance with the scriptural texts concerning consciousness (*prajñāna-śruti*) and so forth, an entity distinct from sound and other sense objects cannot be apprehended by ordinary means of knowledge. || 1046 ||
Having spoken thus with this underlying intention, he uttered the words "seen" and so forth.
This is for the purpose of establishing that the injunction (niyoga) is worldly (laukika), like a jar or other such objects. || 1047 ||

He introduces the commentary on the point that "the Vedic [injunction] is indeed Brahman, but the *niyoga* (impulse) is not," by stating: "It has been said thus. Since the *niyoga*—whether as an action, an instrument, a result, or a duty—is susceptible to other means of knowledge (*māna*), scripture (*āgama*) need not be relied upon; for the comprehension of the *niyoga*, which is intended as the means to the two kinds of results acquired at the time of linguistic learning, can also occur through other means of knowledge. Therefore, it is not [dependent] on that [scripture].

It has been stated that [the means of knowledge] are Vedic; however, keeping this in mind, the commentary begins with the words "having an object within the range of perception" (*dṛṣṭaviṣaya*) and so forth, in order to establish its worldly nature (*laukikatva*), like a jar.
This is the meaning. || 1047 ||
Let alone the authority of the Vedānta; you have abandoned that out of desire.

If you say that [the Veda] is not authoritative regarding established entities because it is an injunction, then that same [lack of authority] would apply even to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa). || 1048 ||

He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "na cāsati" and preceding "sarvathā'pi": "Āstām" (let it be). Let the validity of the *Tattvamasi* and other such [scriptures] regarding reality remain; that has been relinquished by us according to your wish. Nevertheless, if the validity of the Veda regarding an established entity (*siddha*) is not desired, then its invalidity regarding its own subject matter would also apply to the *Karmakāṇḍa*, because without a cognition of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, that [Karmakāṇḍa] would lack authority. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, for one who desires that [the Veda] be a means of valid cognition, since its authority is admitted with respect to the self—which will be joined to a future body—and with respect to heaven and so forth, there is no restriction on the Veda’s authority regarding what is to be accomplished (kārya); thus, the meaning is that the validity of the Vedāntas regarding their own subject matter is established. || 1048 ||
If the Self, as connected with a future body, were not known from the scriptural statement, [then there would be no liberation].
Furthermore, what wise person would perform actions whose results are unperceived based on another means of knowledge? (1049)

Raising the objection that—since one engages in actions for unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*) even without knowledge of a self connected to a future body, such a self is not understood from the scripture—he explains the commentary beginning with "And not" (*na ca*), starting with the word "future" (*bhaviṣyat*). [Page 300, vol. 1]: "connected to another body" (*dehāntarasaṃbandhin*).
[Vārtika], accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 279.

If the Self were not cognized through scripture, nor through other means of knowledge, nor through the reasoning to be stated hereafter, then, due to ignorance regarding the enjoyer, one would not perform sacrifices and other rites intentionally for the sake of the world, since such a person does not know the existence of the Self in another birth.

The meaning is this: since one does not engage in Vedic rituals out of a desire to attain the desirable or avoid the undesirable [if such a Self did not exist], the scripture of the *karmakāṇḍa* and the commentary mentioned therein serve as authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of such a Self and other matters; furthermore, its authority is accepted because there is no difference in the reason [for its validity] as stated in the *autpattikasūtra*. ||1049||
Nor does it apply to one who understands the self as established by the Sāṃkhya means of valid cognition.
Because there is no connection with the body and so forth, there would be engagement in actions here in this world. (1050)

The Sāṃkhyas, however, establish the Self as described by them through the inference: "The reflection of consciousness in the internal organ is preceded by an object of that same nature, because it is a reflection, like [the reflection of] a face. To those who do not tolerate the authority of the Veda regarding that [Self], he says: "Nor... Even for one who knows the Self through the Sāṃkhya inference, there is no engagement in ritual actions, because that Self is unattached and indifferent.

The meaning is that [the self] is inactive due to its lack of connection with the body and so forth; otherwise, in the absence of such a connection, there would be no activity, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that even one who is liberated would likewise be inactive. || 1050 ||
In this section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), such a qualified person (adhikārī) is directly described as being possible.
And it is not said that "it does not exist" for the sake of such a comprehension. || 1051 ||

Then, raising the doubt as to whose the authority over action (karmādhikāra) might be, he introduces the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the point that it belongs to one distinct from the body and so forth, who is connected [to them] through that superimposition (*adhyāsa*). He does so with the words: "Action... (1051).
By those desiring fruit from actions, [the cause] must be either the unseen (adṛṣṭa) or the seen (dṛṣṭa).
The means of valid cognition for the self's entry into another bodily state must be stated. || 1052 ||

One might object: "Since the self—which is distinct from the body and so forth, and which undergoes connection with other bodies—is established by itself without the need for a means of knowledge (*māna*), no such means need be sought for it; how then can scripture be the authority regarding that self? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From actions" (*karmabhyaḥ*).

Even though the self is established by itself, a means of knowledge must be stated regarding its discarding of the present body and so forth and its connection with another body; otherwise, that [transition] would not be established.

The meaning is that there is no agent or enjoyer of Vedic rituals apart from [the Self] established by scripture (āgama), nor can there be activity solely through the force of the fourfold injunctions without knowledge of that [Self], because this would contradict the commentary on the section concerning permission which begins with "Even though" (*yadyapi*) regarding scriptural practice. || 1092 ||
And how can it possess agency, given its omnipresence and its lack of activity?
And there is no fruit for one who is not the agent; if it were argued that this is so through a figurative sense, then all the more so is it not [the case]. (1053)

The Vaiśeṣikas and others, however, believe that the self is established as the agent of Vedic rituals solely through the force of reasoning—such as the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of "attaining what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) if it were not known from the Vedas. To them, he says: "And how? The meaning is this: agency consists in being the prompter of those factors of action (kārakas) which are themselves not prompted;

since the self is all-pervading like space, it is illogical for it to be an agent, as it is devoid of action. [The opponent objects: "Granted that the self may not be the agent, it must nevertheless be the enjoyer."

The Sāṃkhya replies to them with the words "Not so. The meaning is that, according to the logical principle that "the fruit of a treatise belongs to its performer," [the agent must be the enjoyer]. Furthermore, as for the self's status as an enjoyer, is it secondary (gauṇa) or primary (mukhya)? Regarding this, he restates the first position: "If [it is] secondary. This means that since the activity of Pradhāna is for the sake of the Self, the Self might also be called an enjoyer by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). If that were so, then because primary enjoyment is absent, the Self would not possess even that metaphorical enjoyment.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:
"And that [connection] is not real for the Self, because it is unattached and indifferent; therefore, he says that it is indeed accepted as unreal. Furthermore—
Thus [it is said]. || 1063 ||
For even under the view that the self is the primary agent, the consequence of non-liberation follows.
Ignorance is destroyed by pride, for that which makes known is not a causal agent.

If primary agency were [the nature of the Self], then primary enjoyership would likewise follow, and from that, there would be no liberation; thus, he states another alternative [to refute this] with the word "mukhya" (primary). Anticipating the objection that even real agency and so forth might be sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "mānena" (by valid cognition). He provides the reasoning for why that [cognition] does not remove the reality [of agency]: "For [valid cognition] is a revealer... (verse 1014).
The connection with another body is not within the range of the senses because it is yet to come into being.
Because it lacks both a logical mark (liṅga) and similarity (sādṛśya), there can be neither inference nor analogy. || 1055 ||

If it is argued that, according to the views of the Sāṃkhyas and others, the self—which is capable of inhabiting another body, is a non-agent yet an enjoyer, and though unknown—is established by other means of knowledge even without the Veda, [the author asks]: "Is that [means] perception, inference, comparison, presumption, or non-existence? He says "not the first," meaning: because perception has only the present as its object. He refutes the second and third [alternatives].

Regarding the word "liṅga": the meaning is that inference arising from a mark (liṅga) that is inseparably connected [to the object] does not arise because of the absence of such a mark, and comparison, which has similarity as its instrument, does not proceed because of the absence of that [similarity]. || 1055 ||
And the self is not established by means of sound, according to the reasoning previously stated.
Even presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) does not apply here, because there is no means of valid cognition [for its existence].

(1056) First of all, presumptive testimony based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) is not possible here, because there is no observed absence that would be inexplicable without the self under discussion. Nor is there presumptive testimony based on what is heard, because it concerns a real entity (*vastu*); according to the principle beginning with "If not," [the text says]: "Others enter the womb for the sake of a body. etc.

He says "from the word" (*śabdāt*) because, once the Self has been established by the very scripture cited from the *Dīpabhāṣya*, the non-occurrence of that portion of the statement which is otherwise untenable cannot serve as a means of knowledge for that [Self]. He says "no" (*na*) to show that even the non-existence of the word—meaning the failure of a means of knowledge to arise—is not a means of knowledge regarding that existing Self. || 1056 ||
Nor can the existence of a self ever be established on the basis of the notion of "I."
For the words *bodha*, *anubhava*, *saṃvitti*, and *vitti* are indeed designations for the self. || 1057 ||

Having raised the objection that the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) regarding the self as previously described is a valid means of knowledge—since the manifestation of the body's form within the thought "I am" does not occur, and thus the existence of a self distinct from it is established by that very cognition—the author says, "And not... The word "at any time" (*kadācana*) refers to the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. He provides the reason for the self not being an object known through the notion of "I": "Because of consciousness," etc. This refers to the usage of learned people regarding words such as "consciousness" (*bodha*), which are within the scope of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

The point is that because it is well known that the word "self" (ātman) refers to the self in terms such as "the self's necklace," and because the self is self-luminous, it cannot be an object grasped by the cognition of "I" (ahaṃdhī). || 1057 ||
"For that which is established solely by the establishment of its own experience, just like the establishment of a water-pot."
Then, how can experience perceive the establishment [of the self] from the notion of "I"? (1058)
Furthermore, he states that the cognition "I am" is not a grasper of the Self because it is external, like the cognition of a pot. Regarding the phrase "of which":

just as the cognition of a pot, being of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is established only through experience because it is not self-established due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), so too is the case with the notion of "I.
[Vārtika] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Because there is no distinction in their insentience (*jaḍatva*), manifestation occurs only through the very radiance of the nature of experience; that experience does not depend on itself for its own establishment. Therefore, the meaning is that the Self, which consists solely of experience, does not have its establishment dependent upon the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). || 1058 ||
If experience were established through the ego-sense (māna), it would be insentient, like a jar, unless [it is otherwise].
If [the self] were of the nature of consciousness, there would be independence; otherwise, there would be mutual dependence. || 1059 ||

He states the defect in the opposing view—that if the cognition "I" were the grasper of the self, then the self would be insentient like a jar—by saying "mānāt" (from the means of knowledge). He raises the doubt that even the object of knowledge (*meyasya*) might lack insentiency by saying "na cet" (if not). Then he says, "nairapekṣyam" (independence), meaning: since the self's nature as consciousness is established by force of logic, it cannot be grasped by the "I"-cognition; for it is of the very nature of consciousness, just like that [consciousness itself], according to the inference [stated]. This refers to the subverting arguments against its being grasped by the "I"-cognition.
He states the subsequent [point]: "And it may be," etc. (1059).
| || [End of Section] ||
The establishment of the notion of "I" regarding the self is the establishment of the self; it is the proof of the ego-consciousness.

In this way, there would certainly be a mutual dependence between the "I-cognition" (ahaṃbuddhi) and the Self (ātman). Furthermore, the Self—being unknown, like the eyes and other sense organs—cannot be the cause of cognition, because such causality is not observed in one who is asleep. Moreover, if the Self were the agent of the "I-cognition," it would follow that it must always produce that cognition, as it does not depend on any other instrument. If the known Self were the agent of cognition, then by means of non-perception (apratyakṣeṇa)— [The sentence continues with the logical consequences of these positions.]

He clarifies the mutual dependence [of the two] by stating that there is the cognition of the self, and from that cognized [self], the arising of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). [This refers to the phrase] "of the self. || 1060 ||
The self-conceit of "I" is always attained through its own cause and effect.
How can there be pervasion of that [object] by it? If there is no pervasion, how can there be the status of being an object of cognition?

Furthermore, he says that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is not a grasper of the Self because it is its effect, just like attachment and other such states; this is expressed by the words "the notion of 'I'. Moreover, the Self is not graspable by the notion of "I" because it is the illuminator of that notion; for that which is the illuminator of something is not itself illuminated by it, just as a lamp, which illuminates a jar, is not illuminated by the jar; this is expressed by the words "by the cause. Let there be no pervasion of the Self by the notion of "I."

Nevertheless, suspecting that it might still be an object of cognition (*meyatā*), he says: "In the case of non-pervasion" (*avyāptau*). The meaning is that without such pervasion, its status as an object of cognition has never been observed. || 1061 ||
Because it becomes subordinate at the time of the action, and because it is impossible for it to exist once the action has been accomplished.
The agent could not, in any way, be an object of cognition through the notion of "I."

Furthermore, is the pure self alone the object grasped by the notion of "I," or is it the self as mounted upon action by way of being an agent? It cannot be the first, because that would entail its presence even in liberation (mokṣa) and so forth; if you argue that this is not the case because [the notion] is absent there, then [we reply] that in that state, just as it appears, so it should appear elsewhere as well. Nor can it be said that its manifestation simply does not exist there, because scripture declares that its vision is never lost. It is not the second either, as he says: "kriyā... (action).

The meaning of this is as follows: At the time of the action consisting of the notion of "I" belonging to the agent-self, or at a time prior to it, or at a time subsequent to it, that self cannot possess the status of being the object (*karman*) of that very action.

It is not the first case, because the agent is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the action; once the action is accomplished, it is impossible for the same entity to be its object with respect to that same action, since the object is primary (*pradhāna*), and it is impossible for one and the same thing to be simultaneously subordinate and primary with respect to a single action. Nor are the other two cases possible, because [the status of object] occurs neither before nor after the accomplishment of the action.

Because that [cognition] does not exist in the two times [past and future], the agent is impossible; therefore, it cannot be an object of measurement (*meyatā*) for him by means of the notion of "I. Thinking that if the notion of "I" were the object of the agent, then that [notion] itself would also become its own object—since agency belongs only to that which is qualified by it—the author stated "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcana*). || 1062 ||
In the case of the object of knowledge being of the nature of consciousness itself, there would have to be another consciousness as the fruit.
And there is neither an appearance of consciousness nor an inferable result anywhere.

Furthermore, is the state of being apprehended by the cognition "I" (ahaṃdhī) [applicable] to that which is non-conscious in nature, or to that which is conscious in nature? Having accepted the first alternative, he refutes the second with the word "saṃvit" (consciousness). Let it be granted that there is a consciousness as the fruit [of knowledge] distinct from the consciousness of the inner self (pratyagātman) which is the object of measurement; what loss is there [in this]? To this, he says: "na ca" (nor...). Even if another consciousness is not experienced within the conscious self, one might suppose it is inferable through the mark of worldly activity (vyavahāra). To this, he says: [the following].

He states that there is no inference regarding that which is self-luminous and devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "No. Because the fruit [of cognition] is self-manifesting and because there is no other fruit, it cannot be inferred, whether with respect to the Self or the non-Self; at that time, even the empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) of the Self is established by its very nature as consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatva*).
This is the meaning. || 1063 ||
Just as in the case of consciousness appearing in the form of a jar or other objects, so it is even in pure consciousness.
Cognition would have to be qualified by another cognition, yet such [a second cognition] is not observed within the self.

He clarifies the meaning of the first three quarters [of the verse] by means of an illustration: "A pot, etc. Having raised the objection that it might be acceptable for consciousness to arise in the form of consciousness within the self of consciousness, he says: "And not... (1064). Furthermore, it must be stated: if [consciousness were the object], to whom would the fruit belong—[to the] cognizer or to the object?
It cannot belong to the mother because she is an object of cognition; nor can there be any fruit in the object itself. || 1065 ||

Having stated that [the self] is not an object of knowledge because there is no other consciousness within itself, and wishing to state that it is so also because it would follow that there would be no fruit [of knowledge], he raises an objection with the words "mamātari" (in my self). To the question, "Since the mother [consciousness] alone possesses the nature of being the fruit, how can there be an absence of that [fruit] there?", he replies with "na mātuḥ" (not of the mother). Anticipating the objection, "Even if it were an object of knowledge, why should it not possess the nature of being the fruit, since that is accepted in the case of objects such as a pot?", he says "nāpi" (nor even...). [The fruit is] the manifestation...

The meaning is as follows: in the first case, it is non-luminous, and that which is non-luminous cannot be the substratum of luminosity; in the second case, since no further action has been performed by it upon objects such as a jar, the world would be in darkness. || 1065 ||
If it is held that, because the object of cognition is insentient, the fruit [of cognition] resides in the cognizer;
To this extent, even here, insentience is established by the means of valid cognition through the force of consciousness itself.

Since objects of cognition such as a jar are insentient (*jaḍa*), it is logical that there is no fruit [of cognition] therein; however, one might object that since the cognizer is also an object of cognition, there would likewise be no fruit because of that same insentience. To this he replies: "Because of being an object. One might further object that the Self is not insentient, because its nature as consciousness is desired precisely for the sake of distinguishing it from jars and the like. To this he replies: [it follows from your premise].

"Because [it] is consciousness itself. To this he says: "No," because it has been stated that no other consciousness produced by a means of knowledge (māna) can be postulated for the Self, since two distinct consciousnesses are never observed. || 1066 ||
Even as the nature of reality (dharmatā), I am not distinct from the Buddha, nor am I distinct from him as the possessor of that nature (dharmin), the Self.
Form is not other than the substance itself; it is distinguished from taste and the rest only through that [substance]. || 1067 ||

Furthermore, regarding the cognition of "I," does it have non-self as its nature or self as its nature? Not the first, because that is not accepted [by us] and because it would result in the fallacy of attributing consciousness to the material elements (*bhūta-caitanya-vāda*).

Regarding the second, [the author], considering that if there is no difference between the substrate (*dharmin*) and the attribute (*dharma*), there can be neither the state of being a substrate nor the state of being an attribute, and that reality cannot reside in one and the same thing, states the fault in the position of difference.
(Note: *ga* reads *staddhibhi*).
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 283] Regarding the phrase "as a property" (*dharmatvena*): the sense is that if there were a difference [between the self and the I-consciousness], then the relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmitva*) would be unestablished, as in the case of a cow and a horse. Even if the I-consciousness is accepted as a property, the construction [of the argument] is that there is no difference between it and its property-possessor, the Self. He provides an illustration for the absence of difference between a property and its property-possessor.

"Form" (rūpa). Otherwise, it would not be "that which possesses form" (rūpin); this is the meaning. If it is argued that form appears as being differentiated, [the author] replies, "from another property (dharma) and from another substratum (dharmin)," referring to [the verse beginning with] "from taste, etc. Thus, regarding the cognition of "I" (ahaṃjñāna), which is accepted as a property of the self—whether it be different or non-different [from the self]—the point is that it cannot grasp that [self]: because if there is non-difference, the relationship of object and subject is impossible; and if there is difference, no connection is established. || 1067 ||
And the substance and so forth, which have been declared to be the nature of the self and the object of cognition;
"Like a jar, that 'I' is not the object of the inward-turning function of the intellect (buddhi).

(1068) Some maintain that because the Self consists of both substance and consciousness, it is an object of knowledge (meyatva) in its aspect as substance and a knower (mātṛtva) in its aspect as consciousness; thus, they claim that the single entity, which possesses the nature of both the grasped and the grasper, is established by the notion of "I. To them, he replies with the words "substance, etc. Substance and consciousness belong to the Self...

In this context, that substance which has been described as the object of measurement (the body) is not the domain of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃbuddhi*). Since its occurrence in the internal locus (the Self) is accepted as being based on the state of being supported [by it], that notion does not have the internal [Self] as its object. This knowledge "I" is grounded in the Self; it does not have the Self as its object because it is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) grounded in the Self, like the direct perception of a jar. Otherwise, like a jar, it would not be the Self—this is the intended meaning. || 1068 ||
Direct perception is a cognition whose agent is inseparable from our own consciousness.
Regarding that which has been proposed concerning knowledge, no distinction is observed therein. || 1069 ||
Regarding the claim that the Self, which is both the apprehended and the apprehender, is the object of the notion of "I," he says: *asmad* (our). The meaning of this is as follows:

You reject the status of the Self for momentary cognition on the grounds of the contradiction between being both the apprehended and the apprehender; that same defect applies equally to you, since you have asserted that the cognition characterized by the form of "I" within the inner self (*pratīci*), acting as the agent of knowledge, possesses the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*māna*). In that regard, the Buddhists [object]:...

Since the specific reason—the impossibility of a single entity being both the grasped and the grasper—is equally applicable [to the Vedāntin as well], you must therefore accept that the desired Self of the Vedas differs from the Buddhist view in that it is not accessible to the notion of "I" (ahaṃdhī). || 1069 ||
The Self is not measured by the awakening of knowledge, nor even by self-consciousness.
Knowledge is not dual; for if there were duality, there would be no experience of non-duality from its own side. || 1070 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the self, which possesses two aspects, is not an object of the "I"-cognition (ahaṃdhī). [He says: "Jñāna... etc. "Jñāna" refers to the cognitive aspect; its "bodha" is its manifestation. By that very [manifestation], the substance-aspect of the self is not manifested, because there is a mutual difference between these two aspects. If the manifestation of the cognitive aspect were itself the manifestation of the other aspect, then the substance would be non-different from the cognition. Nor, by the manifestation of the substance-aspect of the self, is there a manifestation of the cognitive aspect.

The meaning is that because manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) would result in being non-different from the substance (*dravya*), there would be a difference in the means of knowledge (*māna*) due to the difference in manifestation; thus, the self, which possesses a dual nature, cannot be established by a single cognition of "I" (*ahaṃdhī*). Anticipating the objection that there is no inconsistency if one accepts that the nature of the self is indeed one—the unity of substance and consciousness—and that within that, the cognition of "I" constitutes a single manifestation, he says: "And not... For it is not the case that both substance and consciousness together constitute the nature of the self.

The meaning is that if two things mutually excluded were of the nature of the Self, then the Self itself would necessarily undergo differentiation. Anticipating the objection—"Even if the Self is of a uniform nature (*aikarūpya*), it cannot be established without the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃbuddhi*); therefore, how does your view differ from that of the Buddhists?"—he says: "Non-difference" (*abheda*). || 1070 ||
1 kha. is not accepted; 2 kha. 'yormi'.
[vol 1, page 305] 284
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]:
"Let it be stated: is the form of the 'I' the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it the Self (*ātman*) itself?"
Because it is perceptible, that [cognition] is not the means of knowledge, nor is it the self, due to its being insentient with respect to its own object. || 1071 ||
He offers an alternative argument to refute the notion that the self is accessible through the cognition of "I" (*ahaṃdhī*). He poses the question: "What [is it]?

First, that which is of the nature of "I" cannot be the means of knowledge (*māna*), because, like attachment and so forth, it is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), whereas you—who assert that the means of knowledge is inferable—do not admit that.

To this first point, he replies: "Because it is perceptible. Nor is the self itself of the nature of "I," because of the difference between dependence and independence, and between insentience and sentience.
And regarding the south, he states the second [view] by way of refuting [the notion of] division, saying: "Not the Self. || 1071 ||
Furthermore, for you, the existence of the "I-notion" (ahaṃbuddhi) cannot be established when the self is unknown;
for that notion stands as something that must itself be inferred by means of the self.

Furthermore, even if the "I-notion" (*ahaṃdhi*) were a means of valid cognition (*māna*), the Self—which constitutes both parts [of that notion]—could not be its object. For if that [Self] is not perceived, there is no perception of the "I-notion," and if the "I-notion" is not perceived, there is no cognition of the Self; thus, he says "not so," because it would result in a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayatva*) regarding their mutual cognition. If it is argued that the "I-notion," like the sense organs (*akṣa*) and so forth, establishes the Self while itself remaining unknown, he says "no," with the words "by which... (the portion of the text ending with *yenājñātāhaṃbuddherātmasādha-*). By which [means] the "I-notion," while being unknown, would establish the Self...

The sense is that the Self might be the object of that [cognition] by virtue of being its substrate, but it is not so for the unawakened intellect; for according to the principle that "the intellect is illumination," its status as a means of establishment is only possible when there is manifestation, just like a lamp. Nevertheless, one might suspect that because the Self is a means of establishing the intellect by its mere existence, there is no mutual dependence; anticipating this, he says: "to be inferred. For that intellect is indeed to be inferred.

The meaning is as follows: since we infer the intellect (*buddhi*) as having various forms based on its persistence [in the form of "I"], and since the inference of the intellect as "I" depends on the self being present, the self is the mark (*liṅga*) for that inference; then, from the knowledge of that mark, there is the cognition of the self qualified by it, and because of the necessity of that, once the self is known, the notion of "I" arises, and from that, the cognition of the self—thus, mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*) is clearly evident. Regarding the establishment of the self through the notion of "I," the self is... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the circularity of establishing the self and the "I-notion" (ahaṃdhī) through one another.)*

The mutual dependence regarding the arising of the notion of "I" from the body was stated previously; however, the distinction here is that it is stated [as mutual dependence] with respect to the cognition of both. || 1072 ||
Furthermore, even the conceptualization of parts is not tenable for that which is partless.
And with respect to an object that is independent of itself, the cognition of the means of knowledge would always occur. || 1073 ||
Having stated that it is impossible for the notion of "I" (ahaṃdhī) to apply to the Self by relying on two parts of it, he says that those very two parts are not tenable:

"niraṃśasya" (of that which is partless). By this, the impossibility of both perception and postulation [of such parts] is indicated. That is to say: first, two parts of the Self are not perceived; nor can they be postulated, because there is no basis for such a postulation and because the partlessness of the Self is known from scriptural texts such as "without parts" (niṣkala). This is the meaning.

Furthermore, is the self alone the cause of the notion of "I," or is there another cause as well? To the first alternative, he replies: "The self alone. If the self by itself were the cause of the notion of "I," then because the causal complex would always be present, its effect—the cognition known as knowledge, namely the "I-notion"—would also necessarily occur at all times; thus, states such as deep sleep would be impossible. Moreover, since other causes such as the conjunction with the mind also exist at all times, the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable.
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is [as follows]. || 1073 ||
Without the state of being unknown, there can be no valid means of cognition for the self.
Therefore, its being unknown must be asserted here, just like that of a jar or other objects.

Since the mother’s status as the Self has been accepted, let it be granted that her being grasped by the notion of "I" is refuted; or rather, let it be that she is not the object of the mother's own notion of "I.
[Vārtika]. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramañjarī* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 285] He states that the Self cannot be an object of that [cognition], because it is not unknown: "The state of being unknown. Without the knower (the Self) being unknown, the notion of "I" regarding it would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Therefore, in order for a means of knowledge to operate upon the knower, its state of being unknown must be asserted; and that [state of being unknown] is established either intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*).

Nor [is it established] by a means of knowledge (māna), nor by the mother, nor by eternal experience; for in the first case, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) and the impossibility of cessation from the means of knowledge; in the second case, the mother cannot establish [the object], as she is a cognizable entity (meyya) like a jar—this is the meaning. || 1074 ||
If it is argued that its establishment is also through experience, like that of a jar or similar objects;
If the self were established as something distinct from the body, then the mother would not be established [as its cause]. || 1075 ||

It takes up the third [alternative]. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): the particle "api" (also) has the sense of an illustration, meaning "just as in the case of cognizedness. If it is argued that—since the Self is distinct from the mother, just as a jar is distinct from her—the Self is not the object of the mother's "I-consciousness," even though the mother is the object of such consciousness for herself—[the author] replies with the words "ghaṭādivat" (like a jar, etc.). For if one does not admit the Witness (Sākṣin), who is the prover of the mother's own non-cognizedness and so forth, there would be a lack of proof regarding that [Witness].
He states the fault in the counter-position—that this would not be established through the occurrence [of the reason]—with the words "If not" (no cet). || 1079 ||
The convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-saṃplava) has also been refuted from afar.
For even elsewhere, the convergence of means of valid cognition is not at all admitted.

In the view of the author of the Vārttika, the claim that the self is accessible through the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) has been refuted; rather, every cognition of an object establishes the object—such as sound and so forth—as its content, the self's own nature as self-luminous, and the self as its substratum. Thus, every cognition of an object serves as a means of valid knowledge (māna) regarding the self.

Anticipating the objection of the Guru’s school, he says: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Even that convergence of various means of knowledge—such as the cognitions of sound and so forth—within a single self which has been asserted by the followers of the Guru's doctrine, is refuted from afar. For, when the possibility of the validity of the "I-cognition" (*ahaṃ-jñāna*) with respect to the self has already been rejected by the aforementioned reasoning, there is not even the slightest possibility of the validity of cognitions such as those of sound; therefore, [the convergence] does not exist in them.

The meaning is that the self possesses the status of being an object (*karmatva*) when it appears [to cognition], because appearing therein is precisely the definition of that [object-status]. Regarding the claim of the logicians (*tārkika*) that the self is not known solely through the Veda because perception, inference, and scripture are valid means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding the self, he says "elsewhere" (*anyatra*).
Even in the system of the logicians, it cannot be admitted that various means of knowledge converge simultaneously upon the self, as in the case of the notion of "I" (*aham-buddhi*).

Since it has been stated by the aforementioned reasoning that [the Self] is not an object [of perception], how could it be an object of inference and the like? Furthermore, there is no convergence [of means of knowledge] even with respect to sound and so forth;

this is because [the Self] is distinct in every body, and since it is devoid of sound and other qualities, it is even further removed from being an object than those. This is the meaning regarding the Brahman-Self. || 1076 ||
Just as when there is the comprehension of what was previously unknown, the fruit is deposited in the cognizer.
It was not measured by this previous means of knowledge, nor likewise by other means of knowledge.

How is there an absence of convergence (*saṃplava*) regarding sound and the other objects? Is it because the preceding and succeeding means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) function as cause and effect with respect to a single object, or because they consist of that [object] alone? It is not the first case; thus he says: "Of the unknown. When the cognition of the unknown is produced, the result is deposited by the preceding means of knowledge in the cognizer (*mātṛ*), not in the object (*meyā*), because the doctrine of the sentience of the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*) is not accepted. In the same way, by the subsequent means of knowledge as well, [the result] resides only in the cognizer.
The fruit is bestowed upon the former [of the two], because there is no distinction between them; such is the meaning. || 1077 ||
Therefore, since there is no simultaneous entry [of multiple cognitions] by anyone, how could there be a confluence of all [cognitions]?
Even when it has been understood by others, it remains unknown to another because of ignorance. || 1078 ||
286 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 307]
Even though the means of knowledge (*māna*) have as their cause a result situated in the object (*mātṛstha-phala*), what happens [to them] then? He says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Since the results of the means of knowledge regarding the object of cognition (*meyam*) are purposeless, as in the previous case, they likewise do not enter into the pure reality (*vastu*) while it remains unknown; thus, they do not enter into a single object of cognition by way of being the cause of a result.

The meaning is that there is no suspicion of *saṃplava* (convergence of means of knowledge). He states another alternative [to avoid this]: "by other means of knowledge" (*mānāntaraiḥ*). Even when an object perceived by one means of knowledge is known by other means of knowledge, a convergence (*saṃplava*) cannot be suspected; for the object of the subsequent means of knowledge is distinct from the previously known object of the prior means of knowledge, being characterized by the state of having been newly known (*jñātatva-viśiṣṭa*).
Since this distinction of objects can be easily stated for all subsequent means of knowledge as well, there is no convergence even in the second case.
Such is the meaning. || 1078 ||
Moreover, even if there were comprehension of the object of knowledge, there would still be no convergence [of means of valid cognition].
The first cognition occurs regarding what has already been attained; the subsequent one occurs regarding what is being attained.

Having stated that there is no conflation of means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding the object (*meyam*) because the fruit resides in the cognizer (*mātṛsthatvena*), he says "athāpi" [in verse 1079] to show that even when the fruit resides in the object (*meyasthatve*), there is still no conflation of them. By the two occurrences of the word "api," it is indicated that the possibility of cognition—which is of the nature of illumination—occurring with respect to the object is a mere statement of acceptance (*abhyupagamavāda*). To the question of how there is an absence of conflation in this case, he replies: "pūrvaḥ" [in verse 1079].
If [the object] were already determined by the preceding [cognition], the subsequent one would not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Likewise, from one doubt, there arises certainty regarding another. || 1080 ||

If it is argued that even though there is a difference in the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no conflation (*saṃpluti*) because the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) remains the same, even so, regarding an object already ascertained by a previous means of knowledge, another means of knowledge must be either valid or invalid. In the first case, there is no conflation, because that [conflation] is refuted precisely by the difference in the form of the object; having this in mind, he restates the second alternative with the words "by the former" (*pūrveṇa*). That being the case, from the subsequent means of knowledge, there would be what is termed a "reiteration" (*anuvāda*) characterized by doubt.

He says "tathā" (so it is) [in verse 1080], meaning that since there would be certainty regarding the object from another means of knowledge being sought, there is no convergence (*saṃplava*) [of multiple means of knowledge].
Therefore, since there are no particulars devoid of universals, a commingling [of means of knowledge] is not admitted.

"Just as it is elsewhere, so too should it be accepted here in the Vedāntas. [The author] raises the objection that even though sound and the other objects do not intermingle, such [non-distinction] might occur among the selves which are distinct in every body; anticipating this, he says: "devoid of universals" (niḥsāmānya). For, according to the method shown, since sound and the others possess both universals and particulars, even though an intermingling is possible among them, that [non-distinction]... [does not occur].

Therefore, [the objection] is refuted; for the self-existence of the Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of universals and particulars, is cast far away from those [particulars], since not even a single means of knowledge (*māna*) can enter into them—whose form is self-luminous consciousness—and because its nature as being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*) has been established immediately prior. Nor does this imply a plurality of selves, because even if such difference were merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), it would lack ultimate reality (*avastutva*). Nevertheless, [one might argue] that because of the convergence (*saṃplava*) within the Brahman-Self, its status as being known through the Upaniṣads would be lost. To this he says:

Anticipating this doubt, he states the relevance of the refutation of non-confusion (*asaṃplava*) to the present topic with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Since there is no confusion among the objects such as sound or among the selves, it must be admitted that this absence of confusion exists even regarding the Brahman-self taught in the Vedāntas; for in that case, there is not even a trace of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and its entry [into the object] has already been rejected.
Therefore, since the Vedāntas alone are the authority therein, the status of being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*) is established.
Such is the meaning. || 1081 ||

Since the measures [of knowledge] as well as the triad beginning with waking are established therein, and the distinction between existence and non-existence is resolved, one is awakened to the realization: "I am Brahman. (1082)

Having raised the objection that although the inner self (*pratīc*) is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, it is nonetheless Brahman because there is no contradiction in their identity, he says that the self does not possess those [limitations], because it is the witness of the states (*avasthāsākṣitvāt*).
