The suffix does not require another agent; therefore, the meaning is that the identity of the witness with the supreme Self is what is to be understood from the sentence. || 1083 ||
Because the triad beginning with the object of cognition (prameya) is mutually distinct from one another.
The True Self attains its own nature; let that be accepted as the presiding witness.

To the objection—"The witness (sākṣin) whose characteristics have been described does not even exist; how then can its state as Brahman be made known?"—the author replies with the words "prameya" and so forth. Since the triad of object, means, and subject (mātrādi), the triad of agent, instrument, and action (kartrādi), and the triad of enjoyer, enjoyment, and result (bhoktrādi) are mutually distinct, and since that which exists in its own being and the like does not depend on anything else—because it is of the nature of uncontradicted, immutable, and existent consciousness—that immutable consciousness is here the witness within the witnessed.
The sense is that it cannot be refuted; for if it were refuted, the existence or non-existence of the state of being a mother and so forth could not be established.

Furthermore, the following formal argument (prayoga) is valid: "This [state] is graspable by our own perception distinct from the sensory cognition grasping the subject, because it is perceptible, like a jar. 108.
One whose lotus of consciousness is uncontracted is wise, as in the case of awakening from a dream.
Likewise, he whose lotus of awakening has fully blossomed is like a wise man toward himself and his own understanding. || 1085 ||

Nevertheless, one might suspect that in deep sleep there is no witness whose nature is consciousness, because such [consciousness] is not experienced there; anticipating this, he states "uncontracted" (*asaṃkucita*) and so forth. For it must be admitted that even in that state, there is a clear experience, just as there is in the waking state and others, since the scripture beginning with "for the seer is never lost" (*na hi draṣṭuḥ*) shows that the Self possesses manifest experience there, like a lotus in the presence of the sun. Therefore, it exists in sleep just as it does in the waking state.
Fearing that there might be a remainder, he says: "In the same way. One should also consider its state of non-distinction during deep sleep to be like the existence of consciousness.
[Variant reading: *atra abhidhīya*].

The meaning is as follows: because of the Śruti text, "But for him there is no contact with the mere objects" (BṛU 4.3.15), the inner Self (pratyagātman) remains, in fact, unextended toward objects even in the two states [of waking and dreaming], just as in deep sleep; this is established by such Śruti texts as, "For it is unattached" (BṛU 4.3.15). || 1085 ||
A witness exists through a relationship with the object of testimony; the self does not possess the state of being a witness by its own nature.
Because it is perceived as a single reality within each individual moment of consciousness, it is beyond the reach of words.

Anticipating the objection that consciousness must possess attributes because it functions as a witness (*sākṣin*), just like worldly objects, [the author] considers the alternatives—whether its witness-status is intrinsic or extrinsic—and refutes the first by showing it to be unproven, stating: "As a witness... If its witness-status were due to something else, it would not follow that it possesses attributes; for one must understand that what is produced by ignorance cannot destroy its real, attributeless nature. Nevertheless, because it is the object of speech and so forth...
Anticipating the objection that [the Self] possesses specific qualities like a jar or other objects, he states its lack of proof [by saying]: "The inner [Self]," etc. (1086).
For in our position, that which is to be done is imagined solely by ignorance;
therefore, due to the absence of that [ignorance], saṃsāra has not existed, will not exist, and does not exist now. || 1087 ||

[Objection: Surely the self, whose nature is experience, possesses distinctions because it is an agent, like a king; nor is this unestablished, since those who call it a "witness" (sākṣin) admit its agency in relation to the witness-object and so forth. To this, he says: "asmad... [and so on]. He cites the scripture on liberation as proof that the connection with agency and the like is merely imagined. He states: "tadabhāvāt... [and so on], meaning that because ignorance—the cause of all imagination—is destroyed by knowledge, that which is caused by it [the connection with agency] [is likewise destroyed].
The meaning is that bondage is forever destroyed. || 1087 ||
"Even though this ignorance is innate, it is manifested through experience."
Just as darkness is dispelled by the rising of the sun, it is eradicated and destroyed by knowledge. || 1088 ||

One might object: "Surely ignorance does not cease, because it is beginningless and established solely through experience, just like the Self. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] considers that being an eternal entity (*anādibhāvatvam*) is merely a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and says: "Inherent" (*svābhāvikī*). The word "also" (*api*) from the previous verse is to be connected here as well with the word "manifested" (*avabhāsitā*). "Having extracted" means having drawn out from the Self, that is to say, having loosened it part by part. || 1088 ||
Ignorance, which is beginningless, is destroyed in an instant by knowledge, which has a beginning.
For it is seen being destroyed, and its recurrence is not observed.

He states that the inference is contrary to the experience of the learned, beginning with the word "anādi" (beginningless). The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that it is well known that there is an inconclusive instance (*anaikāntya*) in the case of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge. Anticipating the objection that some hold that even the knowledge which destroys ignorance requires an obscuration (*āvṛtti*), and thus the claim that it [destroys it] "in a moment" is improper, he says: "And not... (1089).
"Even though he has become such as this, by virtue of relying upon the direct experience of his own self,"
Even before the acquisition of linguistic proficiency, he is the witness of all ignorance and so forth, though himself unperceived.

If it is argued that although the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like destroys ignorance without requiring repetition, such is not the case for the Self, because ignorance cannot exist in that self-luminous entity and thus no means of knowledge can operate upon it—the author says "no," beginning with the word "evam" (thus). Because the Self is the witness of all cognitions and their modifications, it is self-luminous; nevertheless, prior to the arising of the knowledge of reality, it is established as being unknown through its own experience. Therefore, the operation of a means of knowledge upon it is indeed appropriate.
This is the meaning. || 1090 ||
1. Ga. Sarvajñā | [Vol.
1, page 310] Vārtika, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 289.
Therefore, the reality [of the Self] is known from scripture alone, such as "That thou art," and not from any other source.
The direct realization of the reality of the single Self is unshakable. || 1091 ||

Anticipating the objection that even when ignorance and its effects are destroyed by the knowledge arising from the realization of the Self, there might still be valid cognition (māna) such as perception and so forth, he says:

"Tattvam" (That Thou Art). Because the object was previously unknown prior to the knowledge "I am Brahman" derived from the sentence, it is only from the scripture beginning with "Tattvamasi" that there arises the immediate (aparokṣa) realization of that [Self]; for it has been stated that no other means of knowledge operates regarding this unconditioned reality, and that realization is indeed [the result].
The meaning is that it is "extremely firm" because, by destroying all bonds along with their causes, it has the fruit of non-return. || 1091 ||
Regarding this [Veda], its connection with the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is as previously stated.
The question is for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion; the reply begins with "In every way," and so forth. || 1092 ||

Having explained the purport of the commentary beginning with "na cāsati" and ending with "ātmānumeyaḥ," he states the purport of the commentary beginning with "sarvathā. Regarding the word "tasya": by means of the commentary beginning with "tasya," he first asserts the relationship between the two sections (kāṇḍas) established by their fixed sequence; then, for that very purpose, he establishes the authority of the Vedānta regarding an already established reality through the passage beginning with "sarvo 'pi," [and thus determines] the qualification for knowledge.

Having stated that the suitability [of the Veda] for all persons is due to its utility for establishing validity, and having refuted the view that the Veda’s authority applies to the effects of others by stating "in matters perceived through the senses," etc., and having established that the Vedāntas are indeed grounded in their own meaning— since even the opponents must accept the Veda’s authority regarding established facts by stating "nor is it non-existent," etc.— [the author now asks: what is the connection between the two sections (kāṇḍas) mentioned previously?

The implicit question is: how does knowledge arise for one whose intellect has been purified by actions? The conclusion to be established is that it arises through the gateway of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth;
the commentary beginning with "in every way" (*sarvathāpi*) is intended for that purpose. || 1092 ||
Now, if the matter has already been established as stated, no reason for undertaking [this work] is perceived.
Because the entire purpose has been attained through the very actions previously mentioned. || 1093 ||

One might object: "If the *Karmakāṇḍa* was commenced for the purpose of making known the specific means to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), then since those very rites described therein would accomplish the desired goals of human life, the commencement of the Vedānta would be useless; thus, the statement of the relationship [between the two] has no scope. To this he replies with the words "But surely... (*nanu*). The commencement of the *Karmakāṇḍa* was indeed as stated—for the sake of making known the specific means to the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired. However, once that purpose is accomplished, there remains the commencement of the Vedānta.

The literal meaning is that its commencement is in vain because no means (hetu) for it is perceived. Anticipating the objection that its commencement might be for the sake of attaining the full human goal (puruṣārtha), he says: "Complete" (kṛtsna).
The meaning is that since the full human goal is attained by the very rites taught in the Karma-kāṇḍa, the Jñāna-kāṇḍa need not be commenced. || 1093 ||
This is not so; for the desire for happiness and the desire to abandon suffering [arise] from [the perception of] pleasure and pain.
Because the cause was not prohibited by the previously mentioned actions in the past. (1094)

He explains the commentary beginning with "But not of the Self" as a response [to the objection], saying: "This is not so. Ignorance of the Self is the cause of the desire for the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering—expressed as "May I have happiness; may I not have suffering. Since that ignorance was not previously refuted by the ritual actions taught in the Karma-kāṇḍa, it is appropriate to commence the Vedānta for the sake of attaining knowledge in order to destroy that [ignorance]; for rituals are not opposed to ignorance, nor does ignorance [cease] through them.
They destroy [the afflictions] directly; therefore, the connection between the two sections must also be stated—this is the meaning. || 1094 ||
The attainment of all bliss without exception, as well as the destruction of all misfortunes.
This is the desired purpose for all living beings by their very nature.
1 kha. Then || Saṃ | 37 [vol 1, page 311]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Introduction]...

Now, one might ask: how can there be a desire for the attainment of happiness and so forth? For an effect cannot exist without a cause, and ignorance alone cannot be the cause there, since karma and other factors are also possible. To this, he says: "niḥśeṣa... (verse 1099).
And this reality of the self is established, because it is like consciousness.
"Now, this [Self], which is indeed the Bhūman according to the scriptural authority and personal experience... (1096)

Anticipating the objection that—even though the desire for the fruit thus shown is common to all people—the cause of that [desire] is not the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), because another [cause] might be suspected, he says: "Of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). Both kinds of desired fruits are eternally attained by the Self as its very nature, just like consciousness; and since there can be no desire for what is already attained by its own inherent nature, ignorance alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) therein, while karma and so forth are the instrumental causes (*nimitta*).

This is the intended meaning. Anticipating the objection—“Since the fruit depends upon a cause, how can it be the true nature (tattva) of the Self?”—the author considers that its status as something to be accomplished (sādhya) is merely figurative, and thus states that the fruit is the true nature of the Self. To provide the scriptural authority for this, he says: “Now” (atha). For there are such scriptural passages as: “Now this is his supreme bliss,” “This is his supreme bliss,” “For he alone causes bliss,” and “That which is the Infinite (bhūmā), that is happiness. Thus, [it is] happiness...

The meaning is that the two-fold nature of the Self—both its existence as such and its nature—is established by the inference, "The Self exists because it is the locus of supreme love, like a pot," and by the experience of deep sleep. || 1096 ||
And this human goal, which has been described as it is, is designated by the word "heaven" (svarga).
By such statements as "Heaven," it is also proclaimed in the Upanishads (the conclusions of the three Vedas). || 1097 ||
He says that the word *svarga* (heaven) is also a denoter of the Self (*ātman*), which leads one to understand its nature as the aforementioned fruit: "Svarga... The meaning is this:

the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which exists without deviating from its own appropriate form—due to its self-luminosity and non-duality—is of the nature of the fruit of both [desire and liberation], because it is denoted by the word *svarga*. This is like the use of the word *svarga* in sentences such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) to refer to something other than [the celestial realm].
Anticipating the objection that "no such application [of the word] appears, so how can it be denotable by the word 'heaven' (svarga)? he says: "Heaven.

Through such Vedic passages as, "Having departed from here upwards, liberated day after day, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world," and "They are established in the infinite, great heavenly world," the Self is intended by the word 'heaven' in the Upanishads as the unsurpassed goal of human life; this applies to the Self just as it does to anything else.
The meaning is that because application is observed [in other cases], the non-observation of application in the self is unestablished. || 1097 ||
This [dharma] is intended for all living beings who aim for heaven as their goal of human life.
Whatever activity of speech, mind, or body there may be that is conducive to its accomplishment [is also included]. 1098.

One might raise the objection: "If the human goal (pumartha) is twofold and heaven is one of them, then its accomplishment is achieved through ritual acts alone, since sacrifices and other rites are prescribed with heaven as their objective; therefore, there is no purpose in undertaking the Vedānta. [The author] addresses this with the words "svargam" (heaven). The meaning is that since all those entitled to perform rituals are observed to engage in the three types of activity directed toward the aforementioned heaven, its accomplishment follows solely from the unseen potency (apūrva) produced by such activity; thus, there is no need for the commencement of the Vedānta.

Having raised the objection that the Vedānta is commenced for the sake of liberation through the means of knowledge—namely, the activities such as hearing [the scriptures] performed by one endowed with the knowledge that is the cause of liberation—he replies: "Even that...

(verse 1098). He states that even by such means, only heaven is accomplished; since that [heaven] is not liberation, and since liberation is obtained solely through ritual actions (*karman*), the commencement of the Vedānta is not purposeful.
Of all ritual actions whatsoever, which culminate in purposes such as birth and so forth.
He has no entitlement to heaven at all, because he has already attained it by his very nature.
[Vārtika, Vol.
1, Page 312] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 291.

All ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) have as their causes one or another of the four types of results: origination, attainment, modification, or purification; they do not [lead to] that which is immutable and eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*).

He offers a rebuttal [to the objection] by stating that "their activity is directed toward the semblance of heaven (*svargābhāsa*)," because in the case of heaven—which is blissful by its very nature—there is no activity on their part, since it is self-established and thus not something to be accomplished. (1099)
For indeed, every means of accomplishment exists only as something distinct from that which is to be accomplished by itself.
It is not capable of obstructing other goals here; how much less so for the accomplishment of an unattainable purpose?

He states that the primary heaven is unattainable by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, beginning with the words "one's own self" (*svātma*). Here, the term "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of worldly activity consisting of the relationship between means and ends. For every means indeed accomplishes its own specific end, but it does not have the power to bring about the accomplishment of another end beyond that; how much less, then, can there be a means for the attainment of the primary heaven, which is by nature unattainable?
The meaning is that it must be stated. || 1100 ||
Although the human goal as previously described possesses the nature of being attained, [it is not so through mere verbal testimony].
There is no attainment by way of the self-nature of the self; nevertheless, it occurs due to the cause of ignorance. || 1101 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if it cannot be accomplished by action, since heaven—consisting of the aforementioned human goals—is attained as one's very self (ātman), there is no dependence on any means, and thus the commencement of the Vedānta is superfluous, he says: "As stated... (yathokta). || 1101 ||

For one who delights in the destruction [of karma], the existence of honey cannot be brought about by ritual acts through anything other than self-knowledge, because those [acts] lack authority [in that regard]. (1102)

If it be argued that even if the goals of man (puruṣārtha) mentioned above are not attained through ignorance, they may nevertheless be removed by ritual actions (karma) alone, and thus there is no need for the commencement of the Vedānta—[the author] says "No," with the words beginning "Ignorance" (avidyā).
He states the reason why ritual actions do not destroy that [ignorance] with the words beginning "Of them" (teṣām). || 1102 ||
Apart from the manifestor, there is no other means of accomplishment that consists of an agent.
That [means] is not capable of manifesting a reality that is established by itself. (1103)

Anticipating the objection that even though actions are not themselves knowledge, they dispel the darkness of ignorance because they reveal reality—just as light does—the author states the reason’s lack of proof (*asiddhi*) with the words "the revealer" (*vyañjakam*). The literal meaning is this: setting aside action in its capacity as a *kāraka* (an agentive factor), no other means such as the eyes or other organs is seen to be a revealer in the case of action, simply because action is a revealer [of its own result]. Alas! If the eyes and so forth, while revealing the Self, were to dispel the ignorance regarding it—
Anticipating the objection that the commencement of the *Upadeśasāhasrī* would then be useless, he says: "That" (*tad*). The meaning of the pronoun is "the senses" (*akṣa*) and so forth.
For that [pronoun] is not capable of manifesting that reality, because that reality, being self-established, does not depend upon it as its means of proof; this is the meaning. 1104.
Therefore, the delusion regarding the Self has not been removed by ritual actions, nor by invalid means of knowledge.
And as long as it is not consumed by the fire of right knowledge, [it remains].
For now, not even the slightest happiness free from suffering has been attained. (1105)

He states that if actions, the senses, and so forth were to manifest the Self, it would follow as a consequence that they do not remove ignorance regarding it. He says: "By means of actions. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the senses and so on. He explains the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ): "Because they are not a means of valid knowledge" (apramāṇataḥ). Even if they were means of valid knowledge, the meaning is that the senses and so forth do not have that [Self] as their object, according to such scriptural texts as "Not by the eye. Well then, let ignorance not be removed; even while that [ignorance] exists—
° 1 kha. Thus: one's own self.
[Vol. 1, page 313]

Having raised the doubt that liberation might be attained through ritual action (*karman*), [the author] states the purport of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with the words "as long as" (*yāvad dhi*). Regarding the phrase "as long as": it refers to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

The meaning is that liberation—characterized as the attainment of bliss and the cessation of suffering—is not established in the absence of the cessation of the ignorance of sound (*nāda*), because such liberation is not distinct from the cessation of that ignorance. || 1104 || 1101 ||
Although sensual desire is not capable of leading to liberation, nevertheless—
Because it serves as a cause for dispassion in a person, that [teaching] is indeed considered beneficial.

Anticipating the objection that—since actions do not directly cause liberation because they are destroyed by ignorance—they would be entirely useless for liberation and thus should not be performed—the author says: "Not sufficient" (*nālam*). By the word "kāmya" (desirable rites), obligatory rites (*nitya*) and others are also included, according to the Vedic scripture: "Desire (*kāma*) is indeed this much. Although actions are not direct causes of liberation, they are useful for it by way of purifying the mind (*citta-śuddhi*) and so forth.
This is the meaning. || 1106 ||
Because its fruit is unbearable suffering, it causes one to turn away from one's own purpose.
Just as action is prohibited on account of dispassion, so too [is it prohibited] otherwise. || 1107 ||
Moreover, all that is performed for the sake of desire has suffering as its essential fruit.
Up to the realm of Viriñca, there must indeed be a cessation from one's own effects. || 1108 ||

Now, one might object: "Setting aside the results mentioned in the injunctions for those respective rites, how can actions be a cause for dispassion? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As unbearable... Just as prohibited acts such as killing, because their fruits consist in attaining the state of dogs, pigs, and so forth—which are extremely difficult to endure—serve as a cause for dispassion toward them for one who knows the meaning of the prohibitive scriptures, and thus, by not being performed themselves, turn a person away from their own fruits; so too it is with optional (kāmya) and other such acts.

The meaning is that because karma results in sufferings such as dwelling in a womb, it serves as a cause for detachment from fruits up to the level of Hiraṇyagarbha; thus, by means of abandoning karma along with its instruments, it leads to right knowledge preceded by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, and culminates in liberation. || 1107 ||
To explain the meaning of what had been said, he spoke these subsequent words.
And in this way, the Veda would undoubtedly possess the quality of being a single, unified statement. || 1109 ||

He concludes by stating that the commentary beginning with "as long as [there is] knowledge" (*yāvad-dhī*) and so forth is intended to convey the point that right knowledge alone is the direct cause of liberation, whereas action is useful only indirectly. Regarding the phrase "it has been said": since the connection between the two sections—that actions are causes of knowledge through purity and other means, and that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation—has been established, and because it has been stated that this is impossible through any other way, there is no [contradiction]. Nor is there... [the text continues].

Since it is logical to abandon that [separateness] when the possibility of being a single sentence exists, the aforementioned connection must be accepted for the sake of establishing the unity of those two; regarding this stated relationship, he states another means of establishing it: "The state of being a single sentence" (ekavākyatvam). || 1109 ||
With his intellect deluded by ignorance, he moves toward the south, north, and upward, yet remains facing westward.
Driven by his karma, the miserable man wanders incessantly.

Having demonstrated how the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) leads to liberation by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), he now states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "attachment and aversion to the fruits of action," while elaborating upon the fruits of action for the sake of inducing dispassion: "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," etc. The meaning is that one who lacks discrimination due to his own ignorance performs ritual action; consequently, with a mind perpetually tormented by the threefold path [of birth], he wanders in *saṃsāra*. || 1110 ||

page 314] ‘

[Vārtika] Accompanied by the desire-driven [rites], one follows the southern path; likewise, accompanied by knowledge, one follows the northern. [Commentary: Śāstraprakāśikā by Ānandagiri] Accompanied by the rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one proceeds along the southern path; similarly, when joined with knowledge (*jñāna*), one proceeds along the northern path.
And by performing prohibited acts, one accumulates a store of karma that leads to rebirth in lower states of existence.

1.293 Explaining the very path already mentioned, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "kevalam" (only) and so forth: "By means of those [rites] performed for desire," etc. "Kevalaiḥ" (by those alone)—

"By means of [omens] such as ill fortune (riṣṭa)" and so forth; that is to say, the southern path characterized by smoke and the like is the path of the ancestors (pitṛ-yāna), while the northern path characterized by light and the like is the path of the gods (deva-yāna). The word "thus" (tathā) is used for the purpose of connecting [the two paths]. The particle "ca" has the sense of conjunction. The word "api" also serves to connect [the paths] as before. The phrase "equipped with the accumulation of karma" is to be construed with every instance. || 1111 ||
And when there is an equilibrium of merit and demerit, one attains the human state.
Thus, [the world] from Brahmā down to the stationary beings is born from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ajñāna).
The primordial [nature], variegated by name-and-form, is like a dream, an illusion, or a magical display.

He explains the commentary beginning with "In the case of equality" (*sāmye ca*) by saying "Dharma," etc. He analyzes the commentary beginning with "Thus" (*evam*), which summarizes the threefold fruit of action briefly for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*), by saying "Starting from Brahmā," etc. For this course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-gati*), when extracted according to the stated method, extends from Brahmā down to the stationary beings; and when reversed, it extends from the stationary beings up to Brahmā; and all of that is [as follows].

The meaning is that [the world] is variegated by names and so forth, being produced by one's own ignorance (svāvidyā), like something commonly accepted [as real]. "Effort" (īhana) means the Lord’s desire, which is to say, karma. Anticipating the objection that the course of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra-gati) would then perish of its own accord—since it is born of ignorance like a city of Gandharvas—the author qualifies it with the word "beginningless" (ādyā). Showing its manifold nature, he provides an illustration for its being born of ignorance: "Like one's own... (sva-...). 1112.
The state of existence, which is perishable, is established by the appropriation of merit, demerit, and so forth. || 1113 ||
Although this has been declared in the Śruti as being [constituted] by name-and-form (nāmarūpa),...
Because the reality of the self is not manifested, it is said that [the self] is not manifested. || 1114 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "that which effects merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma)" as follows: "Dharma... etc. "Adoption" means performance; the word "means" (sādhana) refers to the instrumental cause. It has been stated that the threefold fruit of action is indeed of the nature of evil because it is produced by ignorance; regarding that very point, he states another reason: "Non-eternal... etc. [Objection: But is it not improper to say that the course of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra-gati) is due to ignorance, since it is established through perception and other means of knowledge? [Reply: No, for it is manifested precisely through name and form.

Having raised the objection that since the Śruti declares the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the world in the form of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), it is not logical for that which is established by valid means of knowledge to be considered "due to ignorance" (*āvidya*), [the author] states the purport of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "That very same thing is this" (*tadevedam*). [The word] "manifested" (*vyākṛta*) refers to being perceivable through direct perception and other means, as indicated by the term "this" (*idam*). Although the word "even though" (*yadyapi*) has already been used, the word "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) must also be supplied. Regarding the world, its essential nature is the Self (*ātman*); therein—

Because it has been sublated, the true nature of the Self remains unmanifest; thus, although it appears as if manifest through perception and other means as well as through Śruti, it is in fact still unmanifest. Therefore, its status as being rooted in ignorance (avidyā) is not undermined—this is the meaning. || 1113 || 1114 || [In the destruction of the darkness of ignorance, not even an atom is manifested.]
Therefore, even darkness is not excluded from being a real entity, like cause and effect.

Having stated that nothing becomes manifest when the Self is unmanifest, he says, "Ignorance," etc., to show that when that [Self] is manifested, everything becomes manifest. One might object: even if the ignorance regarding the Self is destroyed through the knowledge of the Self, there is still no manifestation of all things, because the darkness (*tamas*) that veils them still exists. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "No," etc., to show that such is not the case, since the very ignorance of the Self is itself the darkness. Therefore, the knowledge of the Self—
The meaning of the word. || 1115 ||
294 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [Connection] [Vol. 1, p. 315]
Since this is so, therefore, for the sake of realizing the true nature of the inward Self:
This supreme Upaniṣad of the Vedānta has been undertaken with great effort. || 1116 ||

Since the scripture states, "When the Self is known, all human goals are accomplished; when it is unknown, all misfortunes are attained," and "If one has realized this here, then there is truth; if one has not realized it here, there is great ruin," the commencement of the Vedānta is possible by taking as its subject an eligible seeker endowed with the fourfold qualifications for the sake of self-knowledge. Thus he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with the words, "for one who is dispassionate."

Regarding the word "yataḥ": the "commencement" (prārambha) refers to the exertion consisting in the association with the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and so forth. "The subsequent" (*parā*) means that which is intended to be explained, namely the passage beginning with "Oṣā vai aśvasya... and so on. The qualification "Vedānta" is used for the purpose of excluding the possibility that this term *upaniṣad* refers to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). || 1116 ||
If the Upaniṣad has already been commenced for the sake of accomplishing the aforementioned result, why is it not commenced now with the passage beginning "Brahma vā idam"? (1117)

Thus, the commencement of the Upaniṣad having been established, [the author] objects to that commencement starting from the words "The dawn is indeed the head of the horse" (*uṣā vā aśvasya*). Regarding the phrase "as stated":

if the Upaniṣad were commenced solely for the sake of the aforementioned result, which is the knowledge of Brahman, then it should have begun with "Brahman indeed was this in the beginning" (*brahma vā idamagra āsīt*), since the teaching on the knowledge of Brahman proceeds from that point. However, commencing the Upaniṣad with "The dawn is indeed the head of the horse" is not appropriate.
The meaning is that this is because the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is not explicitly stated here. || 1117 ||
For those who would have no entitlement here to this horse-sacrifice rite, [they are excluded].
However, it is from this very consciousness that their proclamation of those fruits [arises]. (1118)

Beginning from this point, desiring to state the desired fruit at the commencement of the Upaniṣad, [the author] first explains the meaning of the commentary beginning with "But this" (*asya tu*), which speaks of the fruit of the meditation on the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). The phrase "of those who" (*yeṣām*) means that for Brāhmaṇas and others who are ineligible for the horse sacrifice but who seek its fruit, the Śruti teaches that meditation because it considers that the attainment of that fruit comes from this very meditation alone. || 1118 ||
If it is thought that even consciousness has as its object only the sphere of karma;
Do not think so, because of the hearing of [scriptural] conceptualizations; [liberation occurs] either through action or through knowledge. (1119)

He analyzes the objection in the Bhāṣya beginning with "the state of being an object of ritual action" (*karmaviṣayatva*) by saying "ritual action" (*karman*). The meaning is that even the meditation (*upāsanā*) performed in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, like the horse and other elements, serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) as a subsidiary part of that rite; it does not have a separate fruit because there is no independent fruit for the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). It has been stated that this knowledge is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) and not for the sake of the person; for the scripture presents an option (*vikalpa*), stating that the fruit results either from the Aśvamedha ritual itself or from its meditation.

He provides the answer by stating the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the Bhāṣya passage— "Knowledge and action are equal in their possession of fruit because they have fruits of equal value"— with the words beginning "vikalpa" (verse 1119).
He who performs the horse-sacrifice and he who knows this sacrifice—[both attain the same result].
It is logical that the fruit for both of them—the performer of ritual action and the man of knowledge—is equal.
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and he who knows it thus—crosses over all evil, he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin.

This [passage] cites the scriptural statement regarding the option (*vikalpa*) as stated in the Commentary. "He sacrifices" (*yajate*); "thus" (*evam*) refers to the sequence of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). That...
This is the statement regarding the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Having established that there is indeed an option (vikalpa) heard in the scriptures, he states the result: "The fruit," [verse 1120].
[Vol.

1, Page 316] Vārtika: Because meditation (*upāsti*) is also an action (*karman*), like the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); thus it is accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 295.
Therefore, the cognitions do not have the nature of mere explanatory praise (arthavāda), nor is there any injunction for them whatsoever.

Having raised the objection that the scriptural mention of the fruit of meditation (*upāsti*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), he refutes it with the commentary beginning "And [in the case] of knowledge" (*vidyāprakaraṇe ca*).

Regarding the phrase "of meditation": since meditation, like the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), is an action (*karman*) and is prescribed by scripture, the mention of its fruit is not an explanatory praise.

The words "of the mention of the fruit of knowledge" (*dhiyaḥ phalaśruteḥ*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis. Nor is this so even for meditation—which, though prescribed by the injunction "He who knows thus"—is like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that equality [is established] because of the perception of similarity to the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*) through the scriptural mention of the option. "Because of its injunction" means because of the prescription, namely, "He who knows thus. Thus, it is said that the certainty is "utterly" brought about by these two reasons. || 1121 ||
If this alone is what you intend to express here, [then it is so]. (1122)
That purpose is easy to state even in the statement of the injunction itself.
In the section concerning knowledge (vidyā), let it be stated why its traditional teaching (āmnāya) occurs there. || 1123 ||

It has been stated that the meditation on the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha-upāsana*) is not for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), but rather for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and that eligibility for it exists even for those who are not eligible for the horse sacrifice itself. If this much alone is what you intend to establish, then since everything you desire can be easily asserted regarding this meditation—even though it resides within the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*)—it is therefore improper to study it here in the section on knowledge (*vidyāprakaraṇa*). Thus he objects with the words: "This much alone" (*etāvat*). [1122]
That great sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice, was likewise endowed with knowledge.
It is described as being solely the fruit of saṃsāra because it serves as a factor for engagement [in worldly activity]. || 1124 ||

He provides the answer with the commentary beginning with "sarveṣāṃ ca" (and of all...). It is said: "It is said that this is declared to be the king of sacrifices among all sacrifices. The meaning is that one should understand its preeminence as a sacrifice based on scriptural statements regarding its majesty—such as its being the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), the universal medicine (*sarvabheṣaja*), and the remover of all sins—as well as the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "There is nothing superior to the killing of a Brahmin or the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) for merit and sin, respectively. [The word] *aśvamedha*...

Even if meritorious action (*puṇyakarma*) is supreme, what relevance does that have to the present context? To this he says: "That too... Having raised the objection that if the Aśvamedha sacrifice is great when conjoined with meditation (*upāsti*), then it alone must be the cause of liberation—otherwise its greatness would be untenable—he replies: "Transmigration... For hunger is indeed death; [as stated in scripture] "He was not at all delighted" and "He was afraid," since fear, lack of delight, and so forth are heard [in the texts]. Thus, regarding the sacrifice conjoined with meditation...

The meaning is that because the fruit is included within the middle of the "thread" (sūtra) of bondage, even a distinguished sacrifice is not sufficient for liberation; furthermore, its greatness is relative to other sacrifices due to the excellence of its fruit. Nevertheless, why is it stated at the beginning of the inquiry into knowledge (*vidyā*) that this has bondage as its fruit?
To this he says: "In the engagement... (1124).
They have no desire for any other means apart from the realization of the inward Self.
Those whose minds have realized the worthlessness of all fruits arising from every kind of karma.

To the question, "How does the description of this [knowledge] as having bondage as its fruit serve to engage one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) in [the pursuit of] knowledge? he says: "The inner self... etc.

Now, since desire for heaven and the like is possible, and since it is impossible to be devoid of longing even for Vedic rituals which are the causes of those [results], how can there be a lack of longing for other means? To this he replies: "The creator... etc. (1129).
1 Kha tat | [vol 1, page 317] 296
How indeed might those seeking liberation be induced to engage in the knowledge of the Self? (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika by Sureśvarācārya, Saṃbandhavārtika, verse 1126)
Granted, let the fruit of desirable action be saṃsāra.
But since eternal things cannot have a fruit, let liberation itself be their fruit. || 1127 ||
In that case, since liberation is no different from heaven and other such rewards in being a fruit of the Vedas, why would there be an inclination toward knowledge?

To this he says: "Those desiring liberation. When the discerning ones—through both inference and scripture—develop an understanding regarding the worthlessness (phalgutvam), that is, the extreme insignificance, of all those fruits of the various Vedic rites known with certainty, and when they [perceive] sacrifice...

If even the principal sacrifice, the Aśvamedha, when accompanied by meditative worship (*upāsana*), results in the fruit of transmigratory existence, then what need is there to mention that rites such as the Agnihotra— which are far inferior— result in the same? With this intention, those who have no desire for this mass of ritual actions which are the cause of bondage, being endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) and seeking knowledge, how could they engage in its means, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, preceded by the renunciation of all actions?

The Śruti, possessing such an intention, enjoined meditation at the commencement of knowledge; therefore, it is possible that the Upaniṣad begins with the words "Uṣā indeed is the horse’s [head]," because this serves to provide for a qualified candidate. Having stated that all ritual actions have bondage as their fruit, an objection is raised:

"Nitya and Naimittika rites do not have that [bondage] as their fruit, because no fruit is heard of them in the injunctions (vidhi), and because they cannot have liberation as their fruit. Thus he challenges [the position].
"In cyclic existence," [it is said]. || 1126 || 1127 ||
For it is not so, because there is a scriptural teaching that all [actions] possess fruit as a general rule.
Through ritual action, the world of the ancestors and so forth is the fruit of those very things that are eternal.

He refutes [the objection] by stating the purport of the commentary beginning with "not all actions" (*na sarvakarma*). He says: "For not so. Since it is heard that the fruit of all actions without distinction is "this much desire" (*etāvān kāmaḥ*), and since cattle and so forth are also heard to be the fruits of actions performed for the sake of desire, let the fruit heard in the text "by action, the world of the ancestors" (*karmaṇā pitṛlokaḥ*) belong to obligatory and other such rites; therefore, there is no suspicion that these have liberation as their fruit. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the world of the ancestors etc.," [it includes] that which—
The fruit well-known from the tradition of the *Āmra-smṛti* is understood [here]. || 1128 ||
If it is thought that eternal rites would become optional if they were to possess fruits;
It is not so; because it is a means of purification, there is no desire for one who is intent upon enjoyment. // 1129 //

He raises the objection that if even obligatory rites (*nitya*) were to possess a fruit, they would—like the *citrā* sacrifice and others—be optional (*kāmya*), and thus there would be no sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by their non-performance. This is expressed in the phrase "If they possessed a fruit... He replies that there is no confusion [of categories] merely on account of possessing a fruit: "It is not so. Even though they possess a fruit, the distinction is that obligatory rites and the like have the destruction of evil as their primary purpose, whereas optional rites have enjoyment as their primary purpose. Furthermore, the non-performance of obligatory rites results in the accumulation of previously gathered evil...
The meaning is that it illuminates that. || 1129 ||
Even in the case of optional rites, purity certainly exists; it serves solely for the purpose of accomplishing the enjoyment [of the results].
For the fruit of Indra is not enjoyed by means of a body such as that of a dog or a boar.

By stating "because purity is the primary factor," it is acknowledged that even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), that [purity] is incidental; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the term "primary. Thus he says: "even in the case of the optional. With the intention that this [purity] is also useful for knowledge (*vidyā*), just like the purity required by the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityādi-nimitta*), he says: "regarding experience" (*bhoga*). The particle *eva* (only) is intended to exclude the notion that it is an obstacle to experience. The fact that purity has experience as its purpose is [confirmed by] experience...
1 kha. Maitraṃ | 2 kha. ṃha | Maiva. [Vol 1, page 318]
[Vārtika] Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 297] He establishes this by means of the word "viḍ" (feces), etc. For there is no purity of intellect in the bodies of boars and the like; therefore, by that [purity], a person does not become Indra or others.

He experiences enjoyment; that is to say, by means of a divine body characterized by preeminent purity, he becomes a partaker of that enjoyment. Alternatively, one should not forget what was stated here regarding its being for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). || 1130 ||
In the case of eternal [liberated souls], because purity is predominant, even enjoyment does not constitute an obstacle.
They perceive enjoyment as fragile, in accordance with the purification of their intellect. || 1131 ||

Anticipating the objection that, since the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) results in the destruction of sin as well as the attainment of other fruits, the experience of those fruits would obstruct purification and thus not produce knowledge, he says: "In the obligatory [rites]... Even though the experience of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth occurs through them, it does not obstruct purification, because purification is predominant therein; for being the primary factor, it renders the experience conducive [to knowledge]. Now, one might object:

In the case of permanent [objects] and so forth, let there be no distinction between purity (*śuddhi*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*), since no reason is seen for the primacy of purity; therefore, purity does not obstruct enjoyment, nor does enjoyment obstruct purity. To this, he says: "Enjoyment... The meaning is that purity, by means of discrimination (*viveka*), is the cause of dispassion toward enjoyment. || 1131 ||
Regarding this very [Self], one should worship it with loud recitation of the Vedas and so forth.
Detached from all worldly existence, they seek to know the supreme state.

[Objection: But surely, for those who are dispassionate and devoid of desire even for maintaining their own bodies, knowledge (*vidyā*) would not arise because they do not engage in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;

therefore, one who seeks the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) should abandon dispassion. To this, he says: "Him" (*tam*). According to the purport of the *vividiṣā* injunction, for one whose intellect is purified by the performance of prescribed duties such as the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*), and who, through the means of discrimination (*viveka*), has become entirely dispassionate even toward his own body and so on—

The meaning is that dispassion (*vairāgya*), which brings about the practice of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth by means of turning away from external objects, must be sought by one who does not stand upon worldly support, who is endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, and who desires liberation or seeks to know Brahman. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) signifies that obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) and the like are the cause of purification. || 19132 ||
The eternal [virtues] assist from afar, by virtue of the purity of the self.
Because it is not in contradiction with the ignorance of the self, it does not [remove it] directly, unlike the knowledge of the self. || 1133 ||

If it is argued that, according to the sequence already shown, ritual actions (karma) are intended as a cause for the inquiry into Brahman by way of producing dispassion (vairāgya), then why is their status as a direct cause of liberation not also accepted? To this, he says: "ārāt" (from afar). By the word "ātman," the mind (manas) is understood. He states the reason why obligatory rites (nitya-karman) and the like do not directly assist toward liberation—characterized by the destruction of ignorance—in the same manner as knowledge does: "ātma... (verse 1133).
Therefore, having abandoned actions, those who are free from attachment direct their intellects toward the inward Self.
Those who have cast off the impurities of passion and the like perceive their own welfare within themselves.

Since actions serve as a means to liberation only through the indirect path of purifying the intellect—and not directly, as does knowledge—it follows that one whose mind is purified has the qualification for *śravaṇa* (hearing) and so forth, preceded by the renunciation of all actions along with their instruments. This is stated in the verse beginning with "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*).
By the word "detached" (*asaṅgāḥ*), he indicates that the cause for the renunciation of action is dispassion (*vairāgya*). As for those who abandon action without internal dispassion...

The meaning is that those who possess two faces—ignorance and knowledge—remain in the intermediate state without having reached [the goal], being excluded from all human aims and unfit even to be touched by the learned. He now describes the steadfastness to be applied with effort toward hearing the means of knowledge and so forth by those who are detached and have renounced: "from the cessation of attachment to enjoyment... and so on.

The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [the *Saṃbandhavārtika*. Verse]: "They have cast aside... etc. This states that those very seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who are endowed with the means for meditative absorption (*samādhi-sādhana*) possess the qualification for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the immutable inner self (*pratyaktva*) established in its own majesty; it implies that this is not the case for those whose minds are directed outward. *Īnḍa...* [fragmentary].
Thus [ends the section]. || 1134 ||
Therefore, it effects the destruction of self-ignorance, which is the cause of all great misfortunes without exception.
For the purpose of causing the rising of the sun of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self.
This work, devoted to the Upaniṣads of the Vedānta, has been undertaken with diligent effort.
One thousand, ten, one, forty, and likewise eight.
All the verses in this introductory commentary on the relationship [of the treatise] have been counted by number. (1136)
Thus ends the *Saṃbandhavārtika* in the *Śrībṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*.

Since the knowledge of reality alone is the sole cause of liberation (*kaivalya*), the commencement of the *Upaniṣad* is possible for that purpose; therefore, while about to explain the commentary beginning with "From this," he concludes [the previous section] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). To show that the meaning of the Vedānta is difficult to perceive without instruction, the term "Upaniṣad"—which is a synonym for those [Vedānta texts]—is employed. Now, one might object: "The Vedāntas have their meanings manifest and thus would not require instruction"; but this is not so.
He says "parā" because, due to their profound meaning, they require an explanation. || 1135 || 1136 ||
Having constructed a bridge of the path of the true tradition, he has crossed this great ocean of the *Saṃbandhavārttika*.
By means of the store of merit accumulated in the past, which is filled by plunging into the depths of the surging waves of the sevenfold right reasoning. || 1 ||
Thus ends the Saṃbandhavārtika in the commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika-Ṭīkā.

Now begins the commentary and sub-commentary on the Upaniṣad.
Therein, first of all, the vision concerning the horse is set forth.
And because it was marked with the name of Aśva for the sake of attaining the status of Prajāpati. || 1 ||
Since the entire web of the universe, beginning with space, has arisen from ignorance;
Therefore, I am Brahman, free from desire for name and form, and fearless. || 1 ||
Thus, the introductory section of the Upaniṣad being established, he states the intermediate purport of the first two Brāhmaṇas with the words "Therein," at the beginning.

In the Brāhmaṇa, the meditation on the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) is taught. Therein, the distinction is that by the first [section], the vision concerning the horse and the vessels (graha) is presented, while by the second, the vision concerning the fire (agni) is presented. Now, one might ask: since the Aśvamedha has many constituent parts (aṅga), why is the meditation taught only regarding the horse and other such parts? To this, he says: "Because of its being related to Prajāpati. This is because the horse has Prajāpati as its presiding deity (devatā); therefore, [the meditation pertains to] the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The meaning is that because it is distinguished by the name "dog" (śvan), and because of its predominance, the sight of the horse alone was mentioned first, while other limbs were omitted. ||1||
One should contemplate that which is the horse's head as being Uṣas herself.
In this same manner, the perspectives of time and so forth are to be applied to the limbs of Hari. || 2 ||
Having briefly stated the purport of the *Brāhmaṇa*, he explains the syllables while providing the meaning of the passage "The head of the horse, indeed, is the dawn" (*uṣā vā aśvasya śiraḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "of the horse": the meaning is that one should perform the visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) of the specific momentary period called *Uṣas* upon the head of the horse used in the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice. He expresses this visualization as non-different [from the object] by saying "the dawn is the head. He summarizes the meaning of the subsequent passage beginning with "The sun is the eye" (*sūryaś cakṣuḥ*) by saying "of Hari" (*harer iti*), [meaning] of the horse's head, [visualized as] the dawn.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the [view of] the eye, one should apply the meditative identifications (dṛṣṭi) of the year, the sun, and so forth to that very body, as in the passages beginning with "the sun is the eye. || 2 ||
Because the sacrificial animal is to be consecrated, one should thus apply the visualizations to the limbs.
Since the horse sacrifice is a constituent part of the seasonal sacrifices, the vision of the horse is not intended to be enjoined [as a separate act].

One might ask: "Why is the view of Time and so forth rejected in relation to the limbs of the horse? Why could the view of the limbs of the horse itself not apply to them? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because they are objects to be consecrated" (*saṃskāryatvāt*). By the word "thus" (*evam*), he states the sequence mentioned in the Śruti and the Bhāṣya. He indicates what is to be excluded by means of the principle: "And the notions of Āditya and so forth [apply] to the limbs, because it is logical" (*ādityādimatayaścāṅga upapatteḥ*). Thus he says: "In relation to Time and so forth. (3)
When the horse and other [components] are present, one should apply the views of time and so forth to the constituent parts.
Having imagined a self within what is non-existent, one should apply oneself [to it].

Since it has been stated that those who lack the qualification for the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) attain its fruit through this very knowledge, one might suspect that the meditation under discussion is intended only for those not qualified for the horse-sacrifice; anticipating this, he says: "When [the limbs] exist. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "one qualified for the horse-sacrifice should apply [the meditation] to the limbs—the parts of the horse—beginning with the head. The word "ātman" refers here to the body. One not qualified for the horse-sacrifice should apply [it to his own body].
The construction is: [the application] of views such as time toward one's own limbs.
The creator, the horse, and the piled fire—Agni—as Prajāpati in his entirety.
O Arka, he knows the fruit of the horse-sacrifice and understands death as it has been described. || 5 ||
1. Vanaśvāṅga [vol2, page 4] 300
In this [work], the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya,
[it is stated that] even though he was not the performer of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, the wise Brāhmaṇa here [is the one who attained the fruit].
Thinking "I am death whose self is ritual action," he attains identity with it.
Fearing that there might be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) because the meditations on the horse-seizer, the fires, and so forth are taught here as being distinct from one another, he says:

"The agent," etc. In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, one should meditate upon the sacrificer and the horse as the locus for the contemplation of Time and the rest; upon the fire-altar (citya-agni) as Prajāpati denoted by the word 'Aka'; upon [the result] denoted by the word 'Death' as the fruit of the Aśvamedha known as the Sūtra; and upon everything consisting of all the deities as Prajāpati, exactly as described.

The Brahmin, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya who knows this—that they are the makers of the body, who possess discernment regarding the meaning of the scriptures, whose nature consists of the seasons, their causes, and their fruits, and who realizes "I am indeed Death"—ascends to the state described in the Sūtra, knowing the identity with Death. Thus, the meaning is that there is no syntactical split (vākyabheda), as this is a single result and a single means of meditation. || 5 || 6 ||
Before the ritual slaughter of the horse and likewise after it, those two cups that are taken there are made of gold and silver respectively.
The view that these two are named "mahi" is expressed in the passage beginning with "This day indeed... (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.1.5).

Having stated the view concerning the horse, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "ahar" (day) and so forth, starting with the word "aśva" (horse). The instrumental case here denotes a state of being (*itthaṃbhāve*).

A "cup" (*graha*) is a specific vessel containing the substance to be offered. "Taking up those two" refers to the employment of the cup and the horse after they have been consecrated by mantras. The word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 7 ||
The seventh case should be understood as used in the sense of the first case by way of transposition. (8)
The ocean is to be known as the Lord; it is called the source and the cause.
Because the Lord alone is the cause of the entire world here. || 9 ||
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*. || 1 ||
Having raised the doubt that there is no referent for the four locative cases in the passage beginning with "In the eastern ocean," he says: "By way of transposition.

Regarding the phrase "The ocean itself is his," etc., he states the meaning of the word "ocean" as explained in the Bhāṣya: "The ocean. The meaning is that the term "ocean" (samudra) refers to the exceedingly profound Lord, based on the etymological derivation: "in whom beings arise together (samutpadya) and dissolve (dravanti). "The ocean is the source..."

In this context, he states the meaning of the word *yoni*: "The *yoni*," he says. This same meaning also applies to the word *bandhu*. Therein, the distinction is as follows: being the *yoni* (source) means being the producer; being the *bandhu* (kinsman) means being the sustainer; being the *samudra* (ocean) means being the dissolver. Having raised the objection that Pradhāna and other such causes might be intended, he refutes them by pointing out their contradiction with scripture: "Of all," he says. Here, the word "scripture" (*śāstra*) is the meaning of the term "here" (*iha*). Therefore, it is not Pradhāna [that is meant].

The word "directions" (diśaḥ) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The sense is that, because the Supreme Lord is known from scripture to be the cause of all things, one should cultivate the perception of the Lord as the cause even in the horse. || 8 || 9 ||
Thus ends the first [section], the Aśva-Brāhmaṇa, in the commentary on the Vārttika on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 1 ||
Now, the birth of the fire used for the horse sacrifice is described.
Its origin is intended for the purpose of praise, in order to create a desire to see that [truth]. || 1 ||
After the description of seeing the horse and so forth, he introduces another Brāhmaṇa in order to speak of the vision of fire, beginning with the word "atha" (now).
[This is from] the second Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. Page 5, line 301.

If it is argued that there is no mention of the sight of fire in the passage beginning with "That," [the author] replies: "True; however, a preliminary stage (*bhūmikā*) is being established there in order to speak of the birth of fire. He says: "Of fire. If it is argued that its birth is already established in such passages as "From air, fire," [the author] replies: "True; but here the birth of a specific instance of it is being stated. He says: "The horse-sacrifice (*hayamedha*). If it is asked, "When the sight is intended to be enjoined, what is the purpose of stating its birth? he replies to this: "Regarding the sight of that. [He speaks of] fire—

The meaning is that for the sake of the injunction regarding the desired vision, the production [of the fire]—which has as its fruit the praise of the fire to be meditated upon—is intended; because of his pure birth, this one to be meditated upon is superior, like a king, and so forth. || 1 ||
In this world, as long as a cause for [the perception of] name and form is observed, [so long does it persist].
It did not exist prior to its origination, because of the scriptural teaching regarding the origination of the vital breaths and so forth. || 2 ||

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he now interprets the words of the sentence beginning with "not indeed" (*naiva*) in accordance with the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Like a name" (*nāmavat*): the meaning is that whatever is seen here in this cycle of transmigratory existence—whether cause or effect, and whether consisting of the three elements—that must be accepted as having not existed prior to its origination, on the authority of the scriptural statement. He states another reason for the prior non-existence of the effect: "the vital breaths, etc. (*prāṇādi*). The vital breath...

The subtle world is [the subject]; the word "etc. refers to the gross world. Its origination is heard in such scriptural passages as, "From this, the vital breath is born," and so forth. Thus, the meaning is: the object of dispute (the world) was previously non-existent because it is something that comes into being; whatever is not thus [previously non-existent] is not thus, just like the Brahman postulated by our opponents. || 2 ||
If it is argued that the effect exists because it possesses the quality of being produced, then its existence prior to production must be denied.
But since there is no production of a cause, there is no negation [of it] in that case. (3)

The proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavādin) refutes [the opponent] on the grounds that the effect is something yet to be accomplished (siddhasādhyatva). He says: "The effect. The intended meaning is this: it is indeed accepted that the effect is non-existent prior [to its production], but the cause cannot be so; for the cause is either not non-existent because it possesses origination, or because it is not perceived prior [to the production of the effect]. It cannot be the first [reason], because the reason would be unestablished (hetvasiddhi). || 3 ||
And likewise, let the non-existence belong to the effect itself, because it is not perceived.
The non-existence of a cause has not been stated, because the two reasons [adduced] are impossible.

He states the second [point] with the words "And likewise" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is that just as an effect, by virtue of having an origin, is non-existent prior [to its production], so too is it [the cause] non-existent prior [to the effect] because of its non-perception; for the non-perception of the cause at that time is unproven, since clay and other materials are perceived even before the production of the jar and so forth. || 4 ||
But do not speak thus because of the non-apprehension of everything, for there is sacred scripture [to the contrary].
"‘There is nothing whatsoever here’—thus he spoke, negating both cause and its opposite. (5)

Since the reason (*hetu*) has been refuted on the grounds that it is either already established (*siddha*) or impossible to establish (*asādhya*), and because the cause is non-existent due to the absence of a logical mark (*hetv-abhāva*), the proponent of Emptiness (*śūnyavādī*) says: "Of everything.

[He argues: Even if the effect (*kārya*) is non-existent prior [to its production], it is illogical to claim that the cause (*kāraṇa*) exists; for like the effect, that cause as well must be non-existent prior [to its own production].

The meaning is: because there is no distinction in their non-perception, therefore everything is considered to have non-existence prior [to its production], since it is not perceived at that time despite being capable of being perceived, just like the agreed-upon example. The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of refuting the charge of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*). He states that because even clay and other materials end in non-existence, the non-existence of both cause and effect prior [to production] is also taught in the Śruti, beginning with the words "yataḥ" (from which). || 1 ||
1 kha. ‘dāderupa’ | [vol2, page 6] 302
This is not so, because the Śruti itself directly declares that existence alone [is real].
"Clearly, by death alone [is the connection between cause and effect established]; thus she spoke with respect. (6)

Since it follows that the cause, like the effect, would also be non-existent prior [to creation], he establishes the established conclusion: "Not so. The meaning is that scriptural passages such as "not so" (naiva) refer to the object whose name and form are unmanifest; they do not declare the prior non-existence of both the effect and the cause. Furthermore, regarding the scriptural passage upon which [the opponent] relies...

The non-existence of those two is stated; however, that [non-existence], together with the immediately following sentence, itself declares their existence. Furthermore, that [declaration] possesses *tātparya* (intentional meaning) because there is no reason for it not to do so.

Therefore, he says "yataḥ" (since), meaning: just as there is no lack of trust in an object directly perceived by the senses, so too the existence of the effect (*kārya*) and so forth established by scripture (*śruta*) is not subject to distrust, owing to its extreme clarity. || 6 ||
This entire effect is completely enveloped by death as its cause.
If these two had not existed previously, he would not have spoken thus.

[The author] explains the commentary on the *Śrutivivaraṇa* beginning with "2012 yadi hi" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by death": here, the first half [of the verse] explains the literal words of the scripture (*śruti*), while the second half states the intended meaning of the sentence. The scripture speaks of both that by which [the world] is concealed and that which is concealed; therefore, the ellipsis is that even prior to that, it was indeed existent. || 7 ||
The Supreme Lord is the ocean of effects such as the vital breaths and the physical body.
The self is said to be the cause and the kinsman; yet it is that very same self which is death in this world.

One might object that it is improper to say "by death" as the cause, because the word "death" (mṛtyu) is conventionally established in another sense; anticipating this, he says: "prāṇa... etc. In passages such as "The ocean alone is his kinsman," the Lord—who is the cause of the birth and so forth of the collective and individual forms of the Sūtra and Virāj, as well as other effects—is denoted by the term "ocean. It is He alone who is "death" in this sentence, and no other, because it is impossible for anything else to be the destroyer of all effects, and because [the Lord] is so conventionally established.
The meaning is: "because it is subject to being carried away. || 8 ||
That Brahman whose true nature is pure consciousness, yet whose true nature remains unknown.
Death is the direct cause of birth, because therein [in death] there is the dissolution of the effect.

Anticipating the objection that since the Lord, who is the immutable substratum of consciousness (*kūṭastha-cid-dhātu*), cannot logically be a cause, He too would be subject to death, the author says:

"By knowledge," etc. The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is to be connected with every instance; its meaning is the existence of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for each respective point. He provides the reasoning for how death is possible even for Brahman, the cause of the universe, through the power of *māyā*: "Therein," etc. (Verse 9).
It has a good seed, a good foundation, and likewise a good basis.
Existence is established as being nothing but direct perception, because existence is not established for anything other than that.

Having stated through scripture (*śruti*) that both cause and effect exist, he demonstrates direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) regarding that very point with the words "the seed is existent" (*saddhījam*). The meaning is that the entire world, being existent during its origination, maintenance, and dissolution, is internalized by everyone and is established through one's own experience. [This is so] because what is non-existent is not perceived.
He states the logical justification for the fact that effects and the like do not have prior non-existence, with the words: "of that which is other than the existent" (sadanyasya). || 10 ||
Whether by way of being distinct from the non-existent or by way of not being distinct from it.
If it were distinct [from existence], would it be existent or non-existent? Why then is it called "existent-non-existent"? || 11 ||

If it is asked, "How is there non-establishment?"—for that reason, he analyzes [the object] through the alternatives of whether it is different from or non-different from both the existent and the non-existent. Regarding "non-existent":
[Vol. 2, page 7, Brāhmaṇa 2, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri, verse 303].

He states the fault in the position of difference: "If there were distinction," and so forth. The meaning is that if there were difference, even the non-existent would become existent, because it would possess the property of being distinct, just like a pot.

Anticipating the objection that such a claim—that the non-existent is existent—is contradictory, he says, "Or the non-existent," concluding the demonstration that the non-existent does not exist under the position of difference; thus, it is not so. || 11 ||
Here, it is not established by its own power apart from negation.
Since everything depends upon existence, existence does not depend upon anything else. || 12 ||

Having stated the defect by assuming the position that difference exists, he says "not so" (neha) to show that such a position cannot even arise; for [difference] does not exist as an inherent distinction from the existent itself.

By its very nature, nothing in the world attains existence or manifestation apart from dependence upon the existence that constitutes its own essential nature; for nothing is established without such dependence. Therefore, the meaning is "the non-duality of Being" (*sadadvaita*). Anticipating the objection—"Since Being is merely the exclusion of non-being (*asadapoha*), it too is not independent; how then can there be the non-duality of Being?"—he says: "Being... The point is that Being is not the exclusion of non-being, because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). || 12 ||
Therefore,
let it be asserted that the existence of that which exists is inseparable from its non-existence.
How could that non-existence be obtained, which is eternally established within the Self? || 13 ||

[The opponent] takes up another alternative: "It is thought [that the non-existent is apprehended]. [The author] says: "If that were so, then because it is non-different from the existent, even the non-existent would be the existent itself; thus, the doctrine of the non-duality of the existent (*sadadvaita*) remains intact.
He explains this very point: "Why? Because that [non-existent] is established within the nature of the existent (*sadātman*)."
The meaning is that what is non-different from the existent does not attain the state of being non-existent, just like the existent itself. || 13 ||
Because they are mutually distinct, there is no identity between the two.
And because they are mutually contradictory, there can be no connection between them, just as between heat and cold.

Having stated the defect by assuming the position of non-difference (*abheda*), he declares that very [position] to be untenable with the words "anyonya" (mutually). For there can be no identity (*tādātmya*) between the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*asat*), because they are observed to be mutually distinct by virtue of being dependent and independent, respectively—this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that even if there is no identity between the two, the eternity of the existent might still follow from their relation, he says: "because of contradiction" (*virodhitvāt*). || 14 ||
Even when manifesting, it cannot be designated as something other than the existent, unlike a jar or similar objects.
For an unreal entity cannot be defined by means of a designation. || 15 ||

If [existence and non-existence] were unrelated and independent, then existence and non-existence would both exist; therefore, there would be no non-duality of existence (*sadadvaita*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Sphurati" (it shines forth).

Even by one who is well-trained, a jar or the like cannot be said to be other than existence, because that would entail its being a mere nothing (*tucchatva*); likewise, even non-existence cannot be said to be other than existence, because words and cognitions function only with respect to what is existent. [Objection: But is it not well-known that non-existence is something other than existence, as evidenced by the words and cognitions "is not"?

Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in objects," one must ask therein: is the non-existent (*asat*) something void (*tuccha*), or is it a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) of a real entity? It is not the first case; thus he says: "No.

For it is not said with certainty by means of the designation "non-existent" [that there is such a thing], because of its lack of essential nature (*niḥsvarūpatvāt*). Indeed, only a real entity (*vastu*) can be denoted;
for it is undesirable that even the word and the cognition of "is not" should have as their object something devoid of essential nature. This is the meaning. || 15 ||
Some excellence of the object itself is expressed by words denoting non-existence.
Because it is thoroughly permeated by that [nature], there can be no denial of it in any way whatsoever. || 16 ||

He addresses the second [objection] with the words "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*). He refutes it as follows: "In that case, the non-existence of the unreal is established [as being expressible], but not the absence of the thing itself; for the excellence is pervaded by the thing possessing it. This is stated in the words "of that" (*tasya*). || 16 ||
304 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] [vol2, page 8]
It would be either the action or its fruit; it could not be non-existence that destroys its own cause.
How can that which brings about the existence of something from its cause ever obstruct it? (17)
Having set aside [the possibility of] non-existence without qualification, he sets aside its specific form, destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), by means of the word "action" (*kriyā*).

That is to say, destruction—whether it be an action or the fruit of an action—does not, in either case, cause the cessation of its own cause. He explains how destruction does not cause the cessation of its own cause with the words "whatever [arises] from whatever. Whether destruction is an action or the fruit of an action, the jar is its cause; therefore, it [destruction] does not belong to it [the jar].
