The meaning is that it is not a remover, for the removal of clay and so forth from a jar is not observed. || 17 ||
Destruction does not destroy the destroyer, just as the act of going does not destroy the goer.
Tell me, how can one who desires success from something destroy that very thing? 18.

Furthermore, if destruction were an action (*kriyā*) and its result (*phala*), it could not bring about the cessation of its own cause, because—like motion and like the result of motion—it is an action and a result. Thus he says: "Not destruction. If it is asked, "Why should destruction not possess the property of destroying its own cause, just as fire does or as the knowledge of Brahman does? he replies: "Whatever [is different from what] from which... For destruction is indeed distinct from fire and the like; even when there is the absence of a jar...

For fire does not persist in the absence of fuel such as wood, nor does the cognition of Brahman persist in the absence of ignorance; therefore, if the pot were the material cause (upādāna) [of its own destruction], its destruction would not remove it, because the pot depends on that [destruction] as the cause of its own persistence. Nor can the pot be something to be removed by its own destruction simply by virtue of being the instrumental cause (nimitta) of its destruction, for that would entail the absurd consequence that the potter and others must also be removed by the pot. As for the claim that sound and the like remove their own causes, that is merely a conventional theory (prakriyāmātra).
The state of being. || 18 ||
And the state of being an object (caṃdabhāva) would be non-different from consciousness and possess a cause.
Even if [the destruction] were non-different from the cognition, it would follow that the cognition is eternal. || 19 ||

Having refuted destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), he restates the position of the Vijñānavādins. [The verse begins with] "vijñāna... and so on. In that regard, is non-existence (*abhāva*) included within consciousness (*vijñāna*), or is it its absence? It is not the first, because like consciousness, non-existence would also possess a cause, leading to the consequence that it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Thus he says: "abhāvaḥ" (non-existence). The word "abhāva" is connected to both [the preceding and following terms]. Having restated the second alternative, he refutes it.
"Because of destruction," [it is said]. || 19 ||
Therefore, for the sake of establishing its nature as non-existence, it must also depend upon non-existence.
The establishment of its own cause [is proven], for an effect is never seen without a cause. (20)

Lest one should suspect that, according to the views of the Logicians (Tārkika) and the Yogācāras, there is the destruction of everything through the established tenets of the Mādhyamikas, [the author] says "ataḥ" (therefore), meaning "it is not so," because this contradicts direct experience. Furthermore, is the non-existence of all things an effect or not an effect? In the first case, the establishment of its cause would entail the failure to establish the non-existence of all things; thus he says "abhāvatve" (if it were non-existence). The phrase "just as by a jar, etc. serves as the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

The word "api" (also) has this meaning. He states the reason why the existence of its own cause (*svahetu-sadbhāva*) is required for the establishment of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*) by means of non-existence itself, in the phrase "kārya" (an effect). Whatever is an effect depends upon a cause, just as a jar [depends on its causes]. Since non-existence is also an effect, it must depend on a cause; therefore, there is no universal void (*sarvaśūnyatā*), because the cause exists. Otherwise, it would not be established, since an effect cannot exist without a cause. Thus, one is caught in a double-bind (*ubhayataḥ-pāśā*).
The meaning is that it is like a rope. || 20 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 9] 2 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri: 305.
"The locus of the property would be unestablished in the proposition, and the reason would be without a substratum."
For one who maintains that everything is empty, no illustrative example exists at all.

Even the non-existence of everything, which is something that cannot be [established as] an object of action, is not proven either by perception or by inference. The first [perception] is not possible because it has all existing things as its object; the second [inference] is not possible because such [an object] cannot be specified. With this intention, he says: "The locus" (dharmī). || 21 ||
For whomsoever this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is mere consciousness.
Knowledge [established] by means of the thesis, the reason, and the example is also refuted by that very same [method]. || 22 ||

The proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) extends the argument regarding the inapplicability of inference, which was stated against the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin), by means of the term "consciousness" (*vijñāne*). The reasoning is as follows: "Whatever is manifest is non-different from manifestation, just like cognition; and this [world] is manifest. Based on this inference, the proponent of consciousness asserts that everything is nothing but consciousness (*jñānamātratva*). However, for him, the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors cannot be established as mutually distinct, because he does not accept anything that exists apart from cognition.

Furthermore, its establishment through conceptual construction (kalpanā) is not possible due to the absence of a constructor; nor can it be ignorance (avidyā), because that [ignorance] cannot exist without a substratum, as knowledge—which is by nature momentary—cannot be its substratum. Moreover, if ignorance were non-different from knowledge, it would be momentary; if it were different, it would be a non-entity and thus incapable of constructing.
Therefore, the invalidity of inference is equal [in both cases]; this is the meaning. || 22 ||
And because the object of cognition is not distinct from the means of cognition, an unknown object cannot be established.
Even if there were identity [between the object and its cognition], if it is not known through a means of valid cognition (māna), what excellence is considered to be gained? || 23 ||

He states that not only is inference unfit to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the Vijñānavāda, but even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is so, because there is no object that remains unknown. He says: "The means of knowledge... [etc.]. Nevertheless, he raises the objection that there is still an aspect of the object (*meyāṃśa*) that is unknown. He replies: "Even in the case of identity... [etc.]. Then he presents the alternatives: what excellence (*atiśaya*) does the means of knowledge produce in the thing—is it the destruction of its state of being unknown, or the production of its state of being known? He says: "From the means of knowledge... [etc.]
Thus [it is said]. || 23 ||
For all proponents of philosophical systems, there would be pride in attaining what was previously unknown.
And if that were not the case, then even the cognition of the nacre in darkness would possess the status of valid knowledge.

Thinking that "this [instrument of knowledge] does not exist [as such], because even when there is no difference from the means of knowledge, ignorance regarding the object has not been removed," he refutes the second [position] with the words "ajñāta" (unknown).
It is universally accepted that a means of knowledge (*māna*) is so called because, while the object remains unknown, it produces "known-ness" (*jñātatva*) by way of dispelling that very ignorance.

Therefore, if ignorance still persists regarding an object that is non-different from the means of knowledge, how can that means of knowledge possess the status of being a "means of knowledge" (*mānatā*), even though it is performing an act of comprehension (*adhigama*) toward that object?

And how is it the cause for its realization? This is the meaning. [The opponent] objects, "It is not a rule of our school that a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must inform what was previously unknown; there is no fault in its being an informer," provided that it is not [the case]. [The author] states the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow if something were a means of knowledge merely by virtue of being an informer: "In the case of mother-of-pearl... It is not correct to say that it lacks the quality of being an informer, because that would entail the consequence that it is never known; nor is it the case that even that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as it is both a means of knowledge and not a means of knowledge.

The sense is that, in our view, since there would otherwise result the absence of any distinction [between valid and invalid], and because while all cognitions are intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) in some cases is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). || 24 ||
Because it is not distinct from consciousness, and likewise because [the reasons] such as "unestablished" (asiddha) apply.
For you, there would certainly be the same contingency regarding invalidity as there is regarding validity. (25.1) [vol2,
page 10]

In the Vijñānavāda (Idealist) doctrine, another defect is stated: that even a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) would result in being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like a true cognition. This is expressed in the verse beginning with "vijñāna... (Vijñāna...).

The suffix *vati* has the sense of "having the same nature as. For in that system, cognition (*vijñāna*) is the means of valid knowledge (*māna*); because it is non-different from that [cognition], even unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and other such [fallacious reasons] would likewise possess the status of being valid means of knowledge.
Conversely, if there were a difference, there would be a loss of the established tenet (*siddhānta-hāni*) due to the admission of external objects—this is the meaning. || 25 ||
The unborn One, self-established, whose nature is immediate perception, is seen as non-dual.
If such an entity is what is intended here, for what purpose is anything else being established? (26)

He raises an objection that even in the Advaita doctrine, if cause and effect were to exist, it would result in the abandonment of the fundamental tenet; this is expressed by the word "unborn" (*aja*).

The meaning is that since a real entity cannot be an effect, any attempt to prove the existence of an effect is invalid. Furthermore, because it is non-dual (*advaya*), there can be no existence of effects and the like; this is stated by the word "one" (*eka*). Anticipating the objection that oneness cannot be established because it depends upon a proving agent, he says "by itself" (*svataḥ*).

The meaning is that there is no dependence on anything else for the reality [of Brahman], whether as its producer or its manifester; it is not the former because it is unborn (*aja*), nor the latter because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Furthermore, because it is the Self (*ātmatva*), there is no existence of effects such as non-self (*anātman*); thus he says, "the inward" (*pratyak*). He clarifies what was stated regarding its self-luminosity with the words "not other" (*ananya*). To the question of by whom this aforementioned reality is accepted, he says, "the reality" (*vastu*). The word "here" (*iha*) expresses the Advaita position. The word "other" (*aparam*)...
The effect and so forth are stated. To the objection "for what purpose?", the contradiction of the thing itself is the reason. || 26 ||
For the sake of establishing the self as being thus, the cause and other factors are established.
That is an expedient for making [the truth] accessible, and it has been thus set forth by those who know it.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that for one who establishes the non-triviality of the cause and so forth in order to prove the inner Brahman—which is distinct from cause, effect, and their absence—there is no abandonment of the established doctrine. He says, "In this way. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let only the desired reality be stated; what is the use of discussing the cause and so forth? he replies, "It is a means. In this regard, the cause and so forth are the means for the attainment of the knowledge of reality; here [the examples of] clay, iron, and sparks [are cited].
He cites the statement of an elder, such as Riti, and so forth: "In that way," [verse 27].
Nor is non-duality intended [by us] through the negation of causes and so forth.
Because even negation is sublated by the mere realization of the oneness of the Self. || 28 ||

Anticipating the objection that Brahman’s distinction from the absence of cause and so forth is unestablished—since it is non-dual and consists in the negation of the duality of cause and effect—the author says: "kāraṇādi... (cause, etc.). To the question, "In that case, how is there non-duality?", he replies: "aikātmya... (identity with the one Self). In both cases, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being thus. [The objection: If the negation of cause and so forth exists separately, how can there be non-duality in the form of the manifestation of oneness?

To this he replies: "Of the negation as well. The meaning is that, just like the effect and so forth, because even its negation is sublated through the knowledge of reality as being merely the underlying substance, non-duality is not contradicted by virtue of its being of the nature of pure consciousness alone. || 28 ||
Having diligently established that all this is accompanied by the true nature (tattva),...
Even for that [unmanifest], fullness is said to belong to the Existent (sat) by virtue of its mere consciousness. (29)

Anticipating the objection—"If the existence of cause and effect is what is to be proven there, how can the reality (vastu) be full as pure consciousness alone? Otherwise, the proof of their existence would be misplaced"—he states the purport of the investigation into the jar: "But of the existent, it is one," etc. [The word] "effect" is the subject; [the word] "etc. indicates the reason.
[Vol.
2, Page 11] 2 Brāhmaṇam. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 307.

Having established—by way of refuting the opposing position—that this entire universe has "Being" (*sat*) alone as its cause, [the author now proceeds] to show that even that "Being" is nothing but consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*).
By that [scriptural statement], fullness alone is investigated and determined here; thus, the non-duality of the reality is not contradictory—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
Everything exists according to scripture, and it is perceived as existing through direct perception.
And because of inference, all that exists [is established]; this is now being explained. (30)
He restates the existence of the cause and so forth, which was previously mentioned based on scripture such as "by death alone" and based on perception such as "the existent seed.

He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "the existent alone" and continuing until the end of the inquiry, starting with "and because it is inferable," as follows: "from inference. || 30 ||
And the object of inference is that which exists preceded by [the mark], namely, either the cause or the effect itself.
That [nature] of the birth of the world is demonstrated here by means of its application. || 31 ||

He states the meaning of the *Vivaraṇa-bhāṣya* beginning with "for it is inferred" (*anumīyate hi*), etc., [in the words] "and the object of inference" (*anumeyaṃ ca*). The connection is: "[it exists] prior to the emanation of the world. He explains how that is inferred [in the words] "and that" (*tac ca*) || 31 ||
This would be a subject of dispute, provided it were accompanied by valid reasons.
The mind and so forth consist of effects, because they are effects, like a bracelet or a jar. (32)

Having proposed the inference of the existence of cause and effect, he states the inference as described in the Bhāṣya beginning with "because when the cause exists... and so forth, using the words "In the dispute... (*vivāda*). The qualification "in the dispute" (*vivāde*) is intended to remove the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) regarding a portion [of the subject]; this is the explanation given by Vyākṛtanaga. Because of the supplementary scriptural passages such as "He made that mind" (*tan mano 'kuruta*), it is stated that "He spoke the mind" (*mano 'vadīt*). [The phrase] "consisting of effects" (*kāryātmakam*) removes the charge of non-establishment (*asiddhi*).
It is specified for the purpose of being maintained. || 32 ||
Everything that has an origin possesses a cause, because it is an effect, like a cloth or a jar.
And since for us the ether and so forth are effects, let that [non-existence] also be understood in the same way. (33)

Even if it were an effect, let there be no dependence on a cause, since that would lead to the possibility of the doctrine of spontaneous existence (svabhāvavāda); how then can the existence of a cause be inferred? To this, he says: "It has a cause" (hetumat). The doctrine of spontaneous existence will be refuted later. Now, one might object: "In the first inference, the reason (hetu) is suspected of being partially unestablished (bhāgāsiddhi), for [the subject] is qualified as 'consisting of an effect,' and yet that very thing is the locus (dharmin) [of the inference]; thus, according to your own view, there is no fault."

Since even ether and the rest are effects, and since under the opponent's view there arises the suspicion of a partial unestablished reason (*bhāgāsiddhi*), he says [the following] regarding that: "ether and the rest. What is the proof for their being effects? In the absence of such proof, there would be a partial unestablished reason for one of the two; to this he replies: "that too.

The meaning is that the fact of ether and the rest being effects must be ascertained through inference—such as their being divided—and through scripture. Alternatively, it is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).

Having established its being an effect through those two—namely inference and scripture—he states the conclusion: "That too," etc. The meaning is that ether and the rest, because they are effects, should be known to have a cause, just like a jar. || 33 ||
An effect would be without a cause, because its birth occurs even after that [cause] has perished.
Having uprooted its own entire cause, it arises like a sprout from a jar.
1 ka. ga. pūrva | 2 kha. pramīya | [vol2, page 12] 308

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter], having inferred the existence of a cause prior to the creation of the world, he raises a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). Regarding the objection "it is non-existent" (*asad*), he states this while anticipating the charge that the example in the argument—"the subject under dispute has a non-existent cause because it is an effect, like a sprout"—is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). He says: "without that... (*tadvinā*)...

"Śyeta" means that because a sprout is seen to arise only after the seed has been destroyed, the seed is not its cause in the sense of being non-existent [as a cause]. Even so, since in the world one does not observe birth through the destruction of its own cause, it might be argued that even if it is an effect, let there be no "having a non-existent cause"; to this he says: "All. The meaning is: "The subject of dispute (the world) is not produced by the destruction of its own cause, because it is an effect, like that which is commonly accepted. || 34 ||
If every effect were produced by destroying its own cause, then all things would be born [from nothing].
Therefore, for the sake of destroying its cause, let that [cause] be warded off prior to its production. (35)

In order to state that the example in the counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*), he restates the meaning of the opponent’s argument: "from its own cause" (*svakāraṇāt*). [The opponent argues: prior to the arising of the effect, that [cause] does not have the capacity to bring about the cessation of its own cause, because it has not yet arisen.
He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating, "Because it consists of those [elements]," and "Its cause... (verse 35).
If it were capable of destroying its own cause even while being unborn, then [it would follow that]...
Both [the agent and the action] would have to be admitted [as existing]; for that which is non-existent is not destroyed by that which is non-existent. (36)

He restates the fault in the opposing view with the words "svahetu" (by its own cause). The word "cet" (if) is used as in the expression "vedāścet pramāṇam" (if the Vedas are authoritative). Alternatively, the construction is:

"If the effect is indeed unborn, yet capable of destroying its own cause, and if that [effect] is already existent. He then says, "dvayam" (both), meaning: "In that case, both the effect and the cause must be accepted as existent prior to production, because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to be either the thing to be removed or the remover. || 36 ||
Since destruction, too, is an effect, for me it also has an existent cause.
If destruction were not something to be produced, then destruction would not be accepted as being unproduced. (37)

Furthermore, is the destruction of the cause something that must be produced or not? In the first case, since that [destruction] would likewise be subject to the same logical status as the [original] position, one must infer that the cause is indeed existent;

for even when that [destruction] exists, the cause remains existent, and thus the effect cannot have a non-existent cause. Moreover, because there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the destruction of the cause, that [destruction] itself does not come into being by destroying its own cause, as that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Thus he says: "Of destruction... [referring to] a jar or similar object.

The two words "api" (also/even) serve as examples. He takes up the second [alternative] with the words "na cet" (if not). He says "nāśaḥ" (destruction), meaning that destruction cannot be accepted as the destruction of the lump (*piṇḍa*) and so forth by way of being a non-product (*akārya*). For if destruction were not a product, it would be eternal; consequently, since the existence of the lump and so forth would never cease, the destruction preceded by them would likewise be impossible to describe. Alternatively, because one must admit that destruction is something produced (*kṛtaka*), it cannot be a non-product.
The meaning is that it cannot be produced by itself, because that would contradict its own accepted principle. || 37 ||
Is it established or indeed unestablished for the sake of the destruction of its own cause?
The effect, such as the sprout and so forth, is not tenable in either case. || 38 ||

In the passage beginning with "If [the effect] were to destroy its own cause," it was stated that the effect does not destroy its cause; now he begins to elaborate upon that very point by means of a formal analysis. Regarding the words "its own cause": he asserts that whether the effect is already established or not yet established, it cannot be the destroyer of its own cause. "No" (na). || 38 ||
If it is established by means of a reason, then it is established even without sublation.
And its destruction by that which has already arisen is useless, because it has already arisen. || 39 ||
[Vol. 2, Page 13] 2 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 309.

Having restated the position that [the world] is already established (*siddha*), he establishes therein the fact that it does not remove its own cause, beginning with the words: "If it is already established... (*siddhaṃ cet*). If...

If an effect that has already been established were to destroy its own cause, then it could not be established without that cause; therefore, the meaning is that it must be accepted as established from the cause itself, without the destruction of the cause. To the objection that the cause should be destroyed by the effect once it is established without destroying the cause, he says: "by what has arisen. You maintain that the destruction of the cause is necessary for the arising of the effect; if that [destruction] is not...
The meaning is that since [the effect] arises from obstruction, the postulation of the destruction of the cause is useless for that reason. || 39 ||
If it were to destroy its own effect, then its cause would remain unestablished.
How could that be its cause if it were not produced from it? (40)

He restates the position that [the cause] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*): "It destroys" (*upamṛdnāti*). If that which has not yet arisen were to destroy the effect, it would first not destroy the mere entity [of the cause], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor does it destroy its own cause, because without having been born from it, it could not logically be its cause. Therefore, he states that if something that has not yet arisen were to destroy [the effect], it cannot destroy its own cause: "Its cause" (*tatkāraṇam*). || 40 ||
Since destruction, too, is an effect, why should it not destroy its own cause?
In the absence of a slayer, the expression of lamentation is observed as mere child's talk.

Having established that an effect—whether already accomplished or not yet accomplished—is not subject to the destruction of its own cause, [the author] states a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) in order to clarify the point that even the destruction of a cause is not subject to the destruction of its own cause, whether that destruction itself is an effect or not an effect. He says: "Even destruction... The meaning is this: if the production of an effect were to occur through the destruction of its cause, then since that destruction itself would be an effect, it would follow that it must be subject to the destruction of its own causes, such as the lump of clay (*piṇḍa*) from which it arose.

Let it be granted that destruction has the power to destroy its own cause; however, would it destroy that cause while existing or while non-existing? If it were non-existing, [the opponent] says: "O Destroyer!
For an action cannot be accomplished without an agent, as that would involve a contradiction—this is the meaning. || 41 ||
Just as going is the state of one who goes, so too destruction is the state of one who has perished.
There is no meaning of a verbal root here which could destroy its own cause.

If [the opponent] says there [is a distinction], he replies: "naṃṣṭṛ" (the destroyer). Just as motion, though dependent on a mover, does not cause the mover to cease, so too destruction, even if it exists, being dependent on a destroyer, would not cause its own cause to cease, because there is no difference [between the two cases]. Anticipating the objection that while motion does not cause its own cause to cease, destruction does cause its own cause to cease, he says: "nāsti" (it does not exist). [The subject of dispute] is not a destroyer of its own cause, because it is a root-meaning...
The meaning is that it is like motion, because it is a real entity (vastutva). || 42 ||
Because destruction is pervaded by causelessness, there would be no production of a jar from clay.
The emergence of a sprout from a seed that has been completely pervaded by fire is not observed. || 43 ||

It has been stated that neither the effect nor its destruction can be the destroyer of its own cause. Furthermore, regarding the cause—such as clay—is it permanent or momentary? Considering that the first alternative would entail the abandonment of one's own tenet, he addresses the second [alternative] with the words "without a cause" (*nirhetu*). If clay and so forth were momentary, they would necessarily be subject to spontaneous destruction; therefore, the production of a jar or the like from them would not be logical, because that which is consumed by destruction cannot possess the functional capacity for generation.
This is the meaning. He provides an illustration for the non-arising of an effect from a cause that is pervaded by destruction: "not from a seed," etc. (43).
It is not accepted that the lump [of clay] is the cause of the jar and so forth.
Since clay alone is the cause, it is understood from the lump itself.
1 kha. Not for him. 2 kha. Also ga 1 [vol2, page 14] 110

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, the meaning of the negative particle (*na*) in the commentary passage beginning with "if its own cause" (*svakāraṇaṃ cet*) and ending with "not of clay, etc. (*na mṛdādeḥ*) has already been stated.

Now, raising the objection that clay is not the cause of the jar and so forth, but rather the lump (*piṇḍa*), he explains the commentary passage beginning with "of clay, etc. (*mṛdādeḥ*) with the words "of the jar, etc. (*ghaṭādeḥ*).
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Just as clay," etc. (44).
Whatever cause has been directly determined here by the measures (mānas), that very [cause]...
That very [cause] functions in subsequent effects; the effect is not the cause according to valid cognition. || 45 ||

He establishes that the causal status belongs to the clay and so forth alone, and not to the lump and so forth, with the words "That which indeed... (*yadeva*). The meaning is: "by means of measures" (*mānaiḥ*) refers to cognitions that follow upon the investigation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the first effect, such as the lump and so forth. In that regard, he provides perception as the proof for the causality of the clay and so forth, with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). Subsequent effects are the jar and so forth. [The point is that] the clay and so forth are the cause in the lump and so forth, while [the clay] is in the jar and so forth...

Anticipating the objection regarding the established status of the "lump" (piṇḍa) and so forth, he says: "No. For the lump and so on are not established by means of valid cognition as the cause of the jar and so forth, because there is no logical concomitance (ananvaya) and because it would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā); such is the meaning. || 45 ||

If destruction is considered to be some kind of excellence (atiśaya), like a lump of clay or similar [transformation], then it would be perceived through direct perception; if not, then let the jar be permanent. (46)

If it is argued that if the effect were not caused [by its material], then clay and the like would also not be causes because they themselves are effects due to their perishability—then, having raised the dilemma as to whether this destruction is an excellence (*atiśaya*) of the clay and so forth or something else, he adopts the first alternative. He says: "Destruction. In that case, both destruction and the destructible would have to be existent, because it is impossible for that which is perceived to be non-existent; thus he says: "Because of perception. For excellence is...

The meaning is as follows: it is not logical for that [destruction] to exist without a substratum; and since there is no destruction of what is called "destruction" itself, its substratum—the clay or other material which is the destroyer—must exist even when that [destruction] is present, for clay and the like are perceived to be non-non-existent. He states another alternative: that destruction is not an excellence (atiśaya) of the clay or the like, but rather something else distinct from it. If this were not the case, then, being untouched by destruction, the clay and so forth would be immutable (kūṭastha).

He says: "Let it be so. For its connection with clay and the like is not established, since the relation between existence and non-existence has been refuted. Furthermore, considering that even for an effect such as a jar, destruction is difficult to define—whether as a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) or as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*)—the mention of the "jar" is made. || 46 ||
It would have to be either the action itself, its fruit, or yet another distinct entity.
Alternatively, there would be neither destruction nor anything at all; thus, existence is not negated. (47)

Furthermore, he states that whether the destruction of an entity is an action, a result, another entity, or nothing at all—in any of these four ways, its existence remains unavoidable: "Action... (verse 47).
Action exists, its fruit exists, and likewise other entities exist as real.
Furthermore, even destruction does not exist; without that [destruction], this world would be eternal.

He explains how that existence [of destruction] holds even within all four positions, stating: "Even action... The meaning is as follows: If destruction is indeed an action (*kriyā*), then because both that action and its substratum exist, there is no non-existence of the entity; for it exists as a result (*phala*) and its possessor (*phalin*) exists. If, on the other hand, destruction were a distinct entity (*vastvantara*), then since clay and so forth would not have produced it, and if destruction were a mere void (*tucchatva*), its existence would be well-established. Thus, in all cases, its existence is proven. || 48 ||
If even destruction is accepted as being like existence itself, then its reality is not contradicted.
Even in the case of identity, destruction is suspected because of the presence of contradiction; and even in the case of destruction, it is likewise suspected. (49)

He raises an objection: destruction is not a mere nothingness because it is the object of the linguistic usage "it does not exist," nor does it have the nature of an action and so forth due to the aforementioned defects. [The author replies: "If that is so" (*sam iti*). Then, since it would be a mere entity (*vastumātra*), and since it has been stated that there is no difference within an entity because difference is absent, the contradiction with unity is not established; therefore, he says "existent" (*sad*) to show that its reality as an entity is not negated by that [unity]. [This is] because destruction is an entity...

One might object that because there is a contradiction with its own nature, it exists; thus he says, "Even in the case of identity. If that were so, then even in the case of destruction, destruction could not be postulated, since a thing cannot be destroyed by itself. Therefore, he says, "Destruction," [implying] that because destruction is unestablished, the entity would be immutable (kūṭastha). || 49 ||
Even without a lump of clay or other such materials, this [effect] arises from mere earth alone.
But since a product such as a jar is seen being produced, [the effect] is therefore certainly real. (50)
Therefore, only clay and the like should be accepted as the cause, for there is a persistence (anvaya) of the clay.
But the lump of clay and so forth are indeed effects, because [the universal] does not persist in its effects. || 51 ||

It was stated that because the destruction of clay and so forth is difficult to define, it cannot be a cause by virtue of being an effect. Now, one might suspect that since the destruction of a lump [of clay] and so forth is likewise difficult to define, its status as an effect is unestablished, and thus its status as a cause cannot be established either. Anticipating this, and considering that such [definable] destruction is not observed in the case of clay and so forth as it is in the case of a lump, [the author] explains the *bhāṣya* beginning with "even though non-existent" (*asatyapi*), thinking: "it is not so. [He says: "by means of the lump, etc."; therefore, "[from] clay and so forth."

[This is] the connection [of the words]. The second *api* (also/even) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The construction is as follows: it is observed that an effect such as a jar arises from clay and the like—which are merely persistent substances—even without specific states such as a lump of clay. He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "Therefore, not... by means of the words "Certainly... and so forth. By the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*), the aforementioned perception is referred to. The reason indicated by the word "for" (*hi*)—
He illustrates this with the phrase "by way of positive concomitance" (anvayāt). || 10 || 51 ||
The simultaneous production of multiple contradictory effects is not admitted.
For this one reason, in the absence of the lump, the production of the jar occurs. || 52 ||

If clay and so forth alone are the cause of the jar and other effects, why is it that the jar is not produced from them while the lump and other intermediate stages still exist? Anticipating this objection, he applies the commentary beginning with "For everything is a cause," etc., stating: "Because of contradiction," (verse 52).
Because no cause is perceived apart from the lump of clay and so forth.
If it were argued that clay and so forth lack substantial existence (asattva), we say no, because that would entail the impossibility of valid cognition (mānānupapatti). || 53 ||

He raises the objection that clay and so forth cannot be the cause because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for their existence as persisting entities; this is expressed in the verse beginning with *piṇḍādi*.

He refutes this by stating *na māna*, meaning "not [due to] a means of knowledge," arguing that since the cognition of identity—such as "the clay is the jar" or "the gold is the earring"—would otherwise be inexplicable in the absence of clay and so forth distinct from the lump and other forms, a persisting entity such as clay must be admitted.
If there were a means of valid cognition distinct from the lump of clay and so forth, then...
The cause, such as clay and so forth, cannot be apprehended without the clay itself.
1 ka. ga. omit "sattā na" | [vol2, page 16] 312 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]

Anticipating the objection—namely, that even if there is a cognition of oneness due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), how can the existence of a persisting clay or the like be established?—the author says: "The lump," and so forth. The construction is as follows: if there were a means of valid cognition (*māna*) whose object is the persisting clay and the like, setting aside the excluded [particulars] such as the lump and so on, then one would obtain the persisting cause, such as clay, which is other than the excluded [effects]; for a means of valid cognition cannot exist without an object of cognition (*meya*). || 54 ||
If my cognition were [of the same nature] as that regarding a lump of clay and so forth, [occurring] with respect to a lump of clay and the like, apart from the lump of clay itself;
In this way, the cause would be established, because it cannot exist without the object of cognition.

Anticipating the objection that—since it is difficult to describe [the relationship] between clay and the like as being either identical to or different from the lump and so forth (which are excluded from them)—it is logical that valid cognition has an excluded object, and thus a distinct cause is established—he says: "piṇḍādi" (lump, etc.). If valid cognition were thus [to apply] to clay and the like just as it does to the lump and so forth, then, as in the case of the lump, clay and the like would be established as persisting entities distinct from it; for valid cognition does not exist without an object of cognition.

Otherwise, it would follow that even the "lump" (piṇḍa) and so forth must be denied; and this is correct because that which is excluded is included within that which persists—this is the meaning. || 55 ||
In their uncommon forms, they are mutually excluded from one another.
When one appears among many, that is the cause of direct perception.

The author explains, as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the view established by Bhāṣya and the means of knowledge such as clay and so forth, which were stated in the two Vārttikas. [He says: "Asādhāraṇa...
Alternatively, having raised the doubt as to what that recurring cause is, he states its nature through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): "Asādhāraṇa... (16)
If it is argued that there is an illusion of continuity due to similarity, even when that [similarity] has ceased;
It is not so, because even jars and other such things are seen to exist as composite wholes. (27)

One might suspect that the perception of a single [universal] in many [individuals] is an error, since such a perception occurs even in the absence of a real universal due to similarity; this is expressed by the words "due to similarity" (*sādṛśyāt*). He states that the perception of a universal is not an error with the words "not so" (*naivam*). He provides the reason for this with the words "of the lump," etc.; the phrase "of the constituent parts such as clay" (*mṛdādyavayavānām*) is to be supplied. (57)
When an object is being recognized, one is certain that "this is that very same thing."
A logical mark (liṅga) becomes fallacious when it contradicts an object of direct perception. || 58 ||

[The opponent argues: "Since the momentariness of all objects is established through the inference—'Whatever exists is momentary, just like a lamp; and these entities exist'—the perception of continuity (*anvaya-dṛṣṭi*) is merely an illusion arising from similarity. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "That which is being recognized" (*pratyabhijñāyamāna*). He provides the reason why the logical mark (*liṅga*) that contradicts recognition is not a means of valid knowledge: "By perception," etc. [This refers to] the fact that the meaning of momentariness, which contradicts the enduring object established by recognition, [is not perceived].
The meaning is that *bodhi* is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as the inference of non-heat [in fire] is not a means of valid cognition. || 98 ||
And there is no state of being a non-erroneous contradictory [reason] for either perception or inferential marks.
Because it relies upon direct perception, it is not eternal and independent, just like the sense organs themselves.

Perception establishes the identity of the cause, whereas inference establishes its difference; therefore, since the contradiction between the two is non-deviant, one might suspect that inference is not sublated by perception, as the reverse could also be possible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Contradictory... He states the reason for this there.

Regarding the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*): [the author] demonstrates through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that inference is invariably dependent upon perception. [He says] "no": perception does not depend on inference, whereas inference is not independent of it, because it depends on the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, the meaning is that perception is stronger because it is that which is depended upon (*upajīvya*). || 59 ||
1 [Vol.
2, page 17] 2 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 313
For there is the state of being a non-erroneous contradiction between two [reasons] of equal strength.
Indeed, this has been observed everywhere in this world between the lion and the jackal.

Even though perception is stronger, because the perception under discussion and the inference are equal in force, there exists the state of being "non-deviating contradictories" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*).
Anticipating the objection that the inference of momentariness does not depend upon recognition, he says: "Contradictory... For in the world, [they are] equal—

The sense is this: it is only when two arguments are of equal strength that they are found to be contradictory and non-deviant (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*), as in the case of a lion and a jackal; it is not so when they are of unequal strength.

Therefore, although the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvānumāna*) does not proceed because it depends upon recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the latter is stronger due to its status as the basis (*upajīvya*).
Consequently, the aforementioned inference, being of the nature of a dependent (*upajīvaka*), is weak and must be sublated by the former. || 60 ||
Furthermore, if all things were momentary, recognition and the like would be impossible.
For an object seen by one person is never recognized by others anywhere. (61)

Having established the persistence of clay and other substances through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and other means, he states the impossibility of recognition, re-cognition, positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) if those things were momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Regarding the phrase "And if [they were] momentary": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there are included the performance of remaining rituals and so forth, as mentioned in the section beginning with "But that very [self], because of the continuity of action, memory, and the injunctions of the Veda" (*sa eva tu karmānusmṛtiśabdavidhibhyaḥ*). [This would be impossible] if entities were indeed momentary, even within their respective continuums (*saṃtāna*).

Having raised the objection that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and other such phenomena might be possible [on the basis of momentariness], he says "Not indeed" (*na hi*), considering that such is not the case because [momentariness] is not a real entity (*avastu*). "In some place or time" means at any location or moment. Therefore, the intended meaning is that all things possess permanence (*sthāyitva*), which is established by recognition and other proofs that cannot be explained otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*). || 61 ||
If all this were momentary, then recognition would be the means of valid cognition [for its existence].
It follows, then, that the cognition of that [object] would depend upon another cognition of it. || 62 ||

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not intrinsically valid with respect to its own object, because Buddhists maintain that the validity of cognitions arises only from corroboration by another cognition; and since there is no other cognition that establishes permanence, one might suspect that even that which is being recognized is momentary.
[The opponent] says: "It is momentary. [The author] states the reply: "By another," etc. This is because even the cognition of momentariness lacks intrinsic validity regarding its own object.

If there were a requirement for another such cognition, that too would likewise require another, leading to an infinite regress; therefore, the validity of cognition must be accepted as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*). And so, all recognition is established in this very way. Furthermore, if the validity of the cognitions "that" and "this" depended upon another cognition, then that [third] cognition would also depend on another, resulting in an infinite regress.
Consequently, because the cognition "this is similar to that" would lack validity, it would be impossible to even suspect that the cognition of identity could ever reach a final conclusion.
Such is the meaning. || 62 ||
The statement "this is momentary" is not established if momentariness itself is unproven.
Because these two cognitions of momentariness have different substrates. || 63 ||

Furthermore, regarding this notion of "momentariness," do the two cognitions have a single locus or different loci? In the first case, there is no momentariness; for since the two cognitions existing in two moments have a single locus, and because they cannot occur simultaneously, it follows that the locus must persist for two moments. Thus he says: "This...
This refers to the statement that these two cognitions have a single locus. In the second case, the cognition of an object qualified by momentariness would not belong even to a single [cognition].
He says "it may be" [in response], stating: "this momentariness. (63)
That by which the unknown is known, and likewise that by which the unborn is born—[this is the Brahman].
*Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter. [Vol. 2, p. 18] 314.
That by which the unknown is known, and likewise that by which the unborn is born.
Without the nectar of recognition, his intended purpose is not accomplished. || 64 ||
If it is argued that the statement of a fault based on the doubt regarding a substratum is improper because cognitions have no substratum, we say no;

for, intending to show that the unity of their substratum is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), he proves that the validity of recognition is accepted even in the opponent's system with the words: "The unknown...
(verse 64).
Furthermore, an infinite regress is unavoidable, and trust arises.
Because all cognitions are false, there would be no certainty whatsoever.
If it is argued that "the knowledge of the unknown and the birth of the unborn" is not our proposition, to that he replies: "And there would be an infinite regress.
The meaning is that if what is already known were to be known again, and what is already born were to be born again, there would necessarily be an infinite regress. Is recognition, then, invalid?

If [the validity] were from itself or from another: in the first case, even by means of the cognition of momentariness, there would be no ascertainment of its own object, because that [cognition] too lacks intrinsic validity; and if it lacks validity from another, then that very cognition leads to an infinite regress—this is what he states with the words "and lack of trust. Regarding the other alternative, he says: "because of falsity. If the validity of recognition were from another, then, since its validity would be intrinsic, the existence of a permanent object would be established.

The meaning is as follows: at that time, the self would not ascertain its own object, because all cognitions are inherently non-ascertaining and lead to an infinite regress; thus, there would be no ascertainment of any cognition whatsoever, and consequently, even the claim that "everything is momentary" would not be established. "Falsity" (mṛṣātva) here refers to the state of being inherently non-ascertaining.
Furthermore, the impossibility of a relationship between that [object] and this cognition is certain.
And when there is no creator of the relationship, it cannot [be established] by relying on similarity. || 66 ||

Is there a relationship between these two cognitions or not? Not the first [alternative], because that [relationship] is impossible apart from a persisting substrate (sthāyin), which would lead to the acceptance of that very [substrate]. Thus he says: "The relationship... Having raised the second alternative—that the cognition of that [object] arises from the similarity between two cognitions when no relationship exists—he says: "And not... (66)
Just as similarity is not admitted between two things that perish, it is likewise not admitted between two things that endure.
Since there is no apprehending subject distinct from that [object], and because cognitions possess a single form. (67)

Regarding the question, "How is similarity not established due to the absence of a [permanent] relation?", he says, "Of the two perishable things," because similarity itself depends upon a permanent perceiver; without such a perceiver, there can be no establishment of similarity.

The meaning is that if there is no perceiver of those two distinct things and of the similarity residing in them—whether they are momentary or permanent—similarity is not established; yet, if one accepts such a perceiver, the doctrine of momentariness is undermined.

Even if one adopts the reading "taddhite" (in the case of a secondary derivative), since the apprehender [the cognition] is different at every moment, there is no [single cognition] that apprehends two moments;

therefore, the meaning is that there can be no notion of similarity between them. He says, "And of cognitions," to show that the very thing upon which the similarity of cognitions is based does not exist.

Even if difference were admitted, the mere perception of unity would be the indicator of similarity; however, here, because of the oneness of luminosity, there is no knowledge of it apart from difference, and thus similarity is not tenable.
This is the meaning. || 67 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 19] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 315.
"And when the object of knowledge, which is free from the contradictions of difference and non-difference, is established..."
For when the object of negation is directly perceived, how could there be a cognition of its opposite? (68)

Having refuted the erroneous nature of the cognition of identity, he has established the momentariness of entities; now, regarding that very point, he states another reason: "nāśa... (destruction, etc.). The meaning is that while non-conceptual perception (*adhyakṣa*)—which has as its object pure existence (*sanmātra*) that is opposed to distinctions and the like, and which stands as an adversary to momentariness—is present regarding entities, it is not logical for destruction and so forth, which have a nature opposed to that perception, to arise from it, because there is a lack of proof (*mānābhāvāt*). The word should be divided as *amiteḥ*. || 68 ||
It is likewise unarisen, about to arise, and arisen; undestroyed, and the agent of destruction and so forth.

Thus, you must necessarily accept that an entity exists in eight states. Furthermore, he says "anutpanna" (unproduced) and so forth to show that entities are not momentary: being unproduced by itself, [an entity] is one about to be produced (*utpitsu*), one currently being produced (*utpadyamāna*), one already produced (*samutpanna*), one not yet destroyed (*anaṣṭa*), one about to perish (*ninaṅkṣu*), one perishing (*naṣṭa*), and one having perished (*naṣṭa*). Because it thus possesses these eight states, it cannot be momentary.
Such is the meaning. || 69 ||
But if they do not have each other as their objects, how can this cognition of similarity arise?
If it is argued that this cognition of similarity is produced even without an object that is similar; // 70 //

In the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with “na tadidambuddhyoḥ,” having explained the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), he states the meaning of the remainder of the sentence: “anyonya... (mutually). First of all, there is no other perceiver of these two [cognitions] who could perceive their similarity, because such a thing is not admitted. Furthermore, the state of being mutual objects is undermined by the fact that [cognitions] are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*). Therefore, the cognition of similarity between the two is untenable, because there is no perceiver of either those two or their similarity. This is the meaning. Where it is true—

One might object that the cognition regarding the object has its requirement for a grasper (grāhaka) in that very [object] itself and not elsewhere; [the author] anticipates this with the words "similar" (*sadṛśa*). // 70 //
In this way, there would indeed be a false cognition regarding the deer and the ocean, as well as regarding those two cognitions themselves.
In this world, all sense-perceptions indeed have non-existent objects as their domain. (71)

He addresses the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) with the words "like a deer," etc. The meaning is that if the cognition of similarity were without an objective basis (nirālambana), then like the cognition of water in a mirage, the cognitions of "that" and "this" would also be without an objective basis and thus invalid. The Proponent of Consciousness-only (vijñānavādin) says: "non-existent," etc. (verse 71).
In this way, even for cognition, there would not be such a state of having a real object.
If it is thought that all cognitions are thus false, [let it be so]. (72)

Thus, since even this cognition that "consciousness is momentary and without an object" has a non-existent object, the Vijñānavāda is not established; so he says: "Not so. The proponent of Śūnyavāda objects: "Let it be so. || 72 ||
This cannot be so, because if all cognitions were false, the notion of "this" would be impossible.
Therefore, the existence of the cause prior to the arising of the effect is established. (73)

[The opponent argues: "All cognition has a non-existent object; therefore, this [cognition] would have a non-existent object, and consequently, the non-existence of the object of all cognition remains unestablished.

To this he says: "It cannot be so. Alternatively, he says: "It cannot be so," meaning that since all cognitions are non-existent, the cognition that perceives them is likewise non-existent; thus, because its non-existence is not established, there is no doctrine of universal emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Because the opposing position is impossible, the persistence of the cause is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); thus it is established.

Since it was stated that the counter-inference (pratyanumāna) suffers from the fallacy of the example being devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikalatā), he now concludes the inference for the existence of a cause with the words: "Of the cause" (kāraṇasya). || 73 ||
316 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter]—[Vol. 2, p. 20]—'
Now, the existence of the effect as well is being demonstrated in the same manner.
This effect is preceded by the quality of goodness (sattva), like a jar situated within darkness.
Because it has the nature of being manifested; otherwise, it would be like a hare's horn. || 74 ||

Having asserted that the existence of both cause and effect prior to their production is to be inferred, the inference for the existence of the cause was elaborated; now, the intent of the commentary beginning with "And of the effect" (*kāryasya ca*) is stated in order to infer the existence of the effect. Regarding the phrase "of the effect": raising the doubt as to how the effect can exist prior to its production, he formulates an inference. [The word] "existence" (*sattva*)... [this is] manifested as "this" (*idam*).

It is said to be "being manifested" (*jyāmāna*); that is to say, because its nature is to be manifested, or because it is in the process of being manifested. Alternatively, the fact that manifestation is preceded by existence (*sattva*) is to be inferred from the fact that it is manifested, just like a commonly accepted manifestation. One might suspect that this reason is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), since something could be manifested even without existence; therefore, he states that the impossibility of immediate manifestation (*aparokṣavyakti*) serves as a sublation (*bādhika*) against non-existence. He says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).

The meaning is that if a jar or the like were non-existent, then even in its conceptual manifestation, there would be no immediate (aparokṣa) manifestation, just as there is none for a human horn; yet such an immediate manifestation of it does exist, therefore its non-existence is untenable. || 74 ||
And even when the causal complex is present, [an effect does not arise] because of the non-existence of things such as the son of a barren woman.
The state of being an object of consciousness is never attained by it. || 75 ||

Anticipating the objection that the absence of direct manifestation (*aparokṣavyakti*) regarding a human horn is due to the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagryabhāva*) and not due to its non-existence (*asattva*), [the author] says "satyām" (when it exists), intending to show that the absence of a causal complex is equally applicable even to an effect that is a mere void (*tuccha*). For indeed, even when the causal complex for making known [an object] such as light exists, the son of a barren woman and so forth never becomes directly manifest to us because of his absolute non-existence; however, as for an effect, [its] direct cognition— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.)
The meaning is that because it possesses substantiality, it is not non-existent. || 75 ||
If everything were always existent, then it would always be perceived by you.

"When the causal conditions are present, as in the case of a jar, everything is certainly existent for one who maintains the doctrine that 'all exists. In the present inference, he raises an objection against the thesis (*pakṣabādhaka*)— namely, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effect would be perceived at all times— by saying 'everything,' referring to the present."

If you claim that the past and future pot and so forth are indeed existent, then they should be perceived by people just as they are now, provided the causal complex for perception is present—both before their production and after their destruction. But this is not the case. Nor is it the case that the causal complex for perceiving the effect is ever absent, because the cause itself constitutes that causal complex, and it has already been established that the cause exists even prior to the arising of the effect. Therefore, it is illogical for the effect to be non-existent at all times.
The meaning is "sentient being" (sattva). || 76 ||
For manifestation is not admitted merely by virtue of something's existence.
An entity that exists is perceived as both manifest and unmanifest.

[The opponent argues that] either mere existence (*vidyamānatvamātra*) or the presence of the causal complex (*sāmagrīsattva*) would entail the constant perception of the effect; [the author] says "no" (*na*) and so forth to refute the first [alternative]. The word "and" (*api*) in the phrase "like purposeful activity" (*arthakriyāvat*) has the sense of "also. Therein, the particle *hi* is used to indicate universal consensus. He states his own experience as the reason for the non-acceptance of manifestation through mere existence: "It is indeed existent" (*sadeva*). || 77 ||
And this must be accepted by you without any hesitation.
If not, your entire system of tenets would perish like a well dug in the sand. (78)

The existence of the causal complex for manifestation is what establishes manifestation; however, there is no necessity that such a complex must exist for that which already exists. This refutes the claim that the existence of a cause is itself the existence of the effect, because it is not observed in the case of a present jar or similar objects, even though the manifesting agent exists within that present jar.

Therefore, he states that those who maintain the doctrine of the *sthāyin* (the permanent underlying emotion) must accept that even an existing entity may remain unmanifest; this is expressed by the words "must be admitted.

He further argues that if one were to insist on the rule that "if something exists, it must necessarily be manifest," then because cognition—which consists of the apprehension of an object—lasts for only a single moment, the object itself, being simultaneous with that cognition, would also have to be momentary.

Consequently, for those who maintain the doctrine of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika-vādin*), there would be a loss of their established tenet that "everything is permanent" (*sarvaṃ sthāyi*). Thus he says: "No."
"If" (ced) [means] || 78 ||
If the object of cognition were to exist apart from the means of cognition, it would [exist independently].
"For if there were no distinction from the means of knowledge (*māna*), then both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge (*meyya*) would not be established.

(79) Anticipating the objection that in the Yogācāra view—where existence is accepted as being merely momentary cognition (*jñānamātra*)—the momentariness of an entity is not undesirable, [the author] raises the dilemma of whether the cognition is included within the object of knowledge or the object of knowledge is included within the cognition, and states the fault in the first case: "The means of knowledge... and so forth.

The meaning is this: if the means of knowledge (*māna*) were to exist as distinct from the object of knowledge (*meyā*), then the object of knowledge would be established; otherwise, due to the absence of the subject (*viṣayin*), there would also be an absence of the object (*viṣaya*) which depends upon it.

By the word "becoming" (*bhavan*), the state of attaining fitness for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) is expressed. He refutes the second [position] with the words "from the means of knowledge" (*mānāt*).

If the object of knowledge were non-different from the means of knowledge, then the distinction between the means and the object of knowledge would not be established, because the object of knowledge would be exhausted within the nature of the means of knowledge; thus, the object of knowledge would remain unestablished.
And the meaning is that emptiness results from the fact that [the object] is not established in dependence upon that. || 79 ||
If the effect does not exist, it follows that the cause also does not exist.
For indeed, no cause is observed in the world that does not depend upon an effect. (80)

One might suspect that even if the Vijñānavāda is untenable, the doctrine of a permanent entity (sthāyivāda) could not be established either, because there is doubt as to whether the non-perception of the effect prior to its production is due to its non-existence or to the absence of the causal complex (sāmagrī). Anticipating this, he states "of the cause," meaning that the non-perception of the effect prior [to its production] is solely due to the absence of the causal complex; otherwise, it would follow that the cause itself does not exist prior [to the effect], whereas the existence of that [cause] has already been proven.

To the question of why the non-existence of the effect implies the non-existence of the cause, he says: "Not so" (na hi). The meaning is that since the mutual relationship between cause and effect is established by common worldly experience, the absence of one would entail the absence of the other. || 80 ||
What function does an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) or other type of cause perform by its mere existence?
Even if one should accomplish the Veda while remaining detached, even so, the desired goal is not attained.

Even when the effect of clay is absent, the triad of causes—the inherent (samavāyi), the non-inherent (asamavāyi), and the instrumental (nimitta)—remains; for it is not the case that because a jar does not exist, its constituent parts, their mutual conjunction, or the potter and so forth do not exist. Anticipating this objection regarding the theory of origination (ārambhavāda), he says:

Regarding the word "sattā" (existence): the meaning is that a cause, whether unoccupied or occupied [with another effect], cannot produce an effect; thus, in neither case is the relationship of cause and effect established. || 81 ||
If the triad of causes were to produce [the effect] by their mere existence, then—
The arising, subsistence, and dissolution of effects generally occur simultaneously at all times.

In order to establish that very point, he restates the first [position]: "by its mere existence" (*sattāmātreṇa*). In that case, at the time of the production of the effect, both its persistence (*sthiti*) and dissolution (*laya*) would occur, because all three are present at that time and it produces the effect by their mere existence alone.
Likewise, at the time of persistence, [production occurs].

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya]: He states the lack of systematic order by saying that at the time of dissolution (*laya*), both persistence (*sthiti*) and origination (*janman*) would follow as logical consequences. He says "then" (*tadā*): when the triad...
Then he states another lack of systematic order, namely that there would be a perpetual occurrence of birth and so forth, with the words "sadaiva" (always). || 82 ||
Furthermore, because existence is without distinction, everything would arise from everything.
Indeed, all worldly transactions would fail to be established. (83)

He states another defect: "Because of the lack of distinction. [The opponent might argue: "Let everything be the cause of everything; nevertheless, the relationship of cause and effect is still established. To this he says: "Everything," etc. Furthermore, for one desiring a jar, the restriction to taking up clay and so forth would be untenable, as would the Vedic injunctions.
The meaning is that worldly transaction would not exist for one who does not rely upon established order. || 83 ||
The determination that there are only three causes would be fruitless.
Just as there are three, why is it that everything is not a cause by virtue of its existence? (84)

He states another defect regarding the fact that the triad produces the effect by its mere existence: "The three," etc. He demonstrates the futility of the restriction [implied in the opponent's view] with: "Just as," etc. (84).
Then, having come together, the triad of causes should perform their function.
Since even the act of meeting is an effect, how could it occur without those three? (85)

He restates another [opponent's] position: "Having come into being" (*saṃbhūya*). The meaning is: "having become engaged in activity. Is that engagement of his something uncaused (*akārya*) or caused (*kārya*)? In the first case, because it would exist eternally, the effect (*kārya*) would also exist eternally. In the second case, since that [engagement] itself is an effect, does it possess a triad [of causes] or not? If it does not, then even in the absence of that [triad], there would be the birth of the effect; having considered this, he says: "Then" (*tadā*). || 85 ||
O Lord, each one of these is established through a triad of causes.
"for each of those [subsequent cognitions], it would be exactly the same; thus, that infinite regress (anavasthā) follows. || 86 ||
He states another alternative, beginning with "kāraṇa," because the state of being engaged in an operation for each individual cause is not established in the triad.
He considers that the intended conjunction (saṃdhi) indeed occurs. Furthermore, if the reading is "atho," there is nothing further to be said, as the meaning is already obtained.

Since the state of being engaged in an operation for each of those three [causes] would involve a third triad endowed with activity, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā); thus, the proponent of the beginning [of the process]— [End of excerpt]

Considering that the effect must exist even prior to its production because it is impossible for it to arise from nothing, he says: "Of that. He refers back to that [infinite regress] with the word "it" (sā) in order to address the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvavādin). || 86 ||
For the existence or non-existence of an object follows from its having manifestation as its sole cause.
For the existence of a means of valid cognition is not due to its sovereign power, but rather from the force of the objective reality itself. || 87 ||

One might suspect that because of the rule that "only that which is perceived is existent," what is not perceived prior to its production cannot be existent; however, [the author] says "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*) to show that this is not so, since it has already been stated that non-perception is established otherwise. For that means of knowledge (*māna*) which lacks the capacity to establish either the existence or non-existence of something, [that object's] existence and so forth are due merely to the cause of its manifestation. Indeed, the existence of a thing is self-established by virtue of its own nature.

The meaning is that it is possible to restrict the definition such that "only that which is perceived is existent," because even things like buried treasure, though not currently perceived, are accepted as being existent;
therefore, there is no suspicion of the effect being non-existent prior to its production due to its unmanifest state. || 87 ||
Because obscuration is of two kinds, the effect is not [perceived]; therefore, it is concealed by that.
For that which has already attained its own nature, there is no dependence on causes such as walls prior to its production. (88)

In the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "na dvividhatvāt," I have explained the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and stated that there are two kinds of causes for the non-perception of an existing thing prior [to its manifestation].
He demonstrates what was stated in the commentary beginning with "Āditya" by means of the phrase "due to its twofold nature. This refers, that is to say, to the two kinds of obscuration.

He states the twofold nature of obscuration: that which is an obscuration for something already arisen, such as a wall, and that which is a cause for something not yet arisen. [The word] "labdha" [is used]. || 88 ||
The effect, closely joined with the nature of clay, is designated as the cause.
For since it exists by virtue of being a cause, how could that which resides therein be a cause without those [effects]? (89)
If one objects that if the cause covers the effect prior to its production, then there must be a distinction between the two like that between a jar and a water-pot, [the author] says:
"In the form of clay," etc. The effect, such as a jar, is pervaded by the nature of its cause, such as clay; thus, prior to its production, it exists with its own name and form concealed.
The meaning is that because [the effect] has gone into [the cause], the cause is the concealment of the effect, and not like a wall or similar objects; thus, there is no difference between the two.

If it is argued that since the effect resides in its own cause, there is pervasion by it, yet the effect does not reside in the cause—because it is impossible for those existing in prior and subsequent moments to stand in the relation of container and contained—the author says "no," adding: "Because of being the cause. Precisely because of being the cause, the jar and other effects [reside] in clay and so forth.

Regarding the word "niṣṭham" (resting upon), he states the reason indicated by the particle *hi*: "tadṛtaḥ" (because it depends on that). The meaning is that since causality is impossible without an effect, the cause must depend upon it. Even though the cause exists in the preceding moment, the effect existing in the immediately subsequent moment rests precisely upon that [cause];
for it is accepted that both the cause and the effect are enduring, otherwise, if they were unrelated to one another, their status as cause and effect would be impossible.
The meaning is that it bestows [this]. || 89 ||
If existence resides in the cause, and that cause is the sign (nimitta).
Since there is no intervening obstruction, for what reason is it not perceived? || 90 ||

If the effect resides within the cause and both are already existent, such that the cause is the instrument for the manifestation of the effect, then the effect should be perceived even prior [to its production], because it is not separated from the cause and the cause is its manifestor; otherwise, it would follow that the effect is non-existent, which contradicts what was stated previously.
He raises the objection that [the world] must be real, saying: "If... (verse 90).
Because it is occupied with another function, the clay and so forth are not perceived [as such].
But the perception of the self as real is never lost at any time. || 99 ||

Is it being argued that the jar and so forth are perceived with their own specific form (*svākāraviśeṣa*), or rather as having the nature of existence (*sadātman*)? Having thus raised the alternatives, he refutes the first by saying, "by another effect" (*kāryāntareṇa*). Because the cause, such as clay, exists in a prior state in the form of a lump and so on, the effect—the jar and so forth—is not perceived with its specific form due to being concealed by that [prior state]. This is because multiple contradictory effects cannot arise from a single [cause] simultaneously.

The meaning is that [the first case] is refuted by the aforementioned reasoning. Regarding the second [case], he states that there is the acceptance of the desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*): "By the self that exists" (verse 91).
