320. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
The cognition of the distinction between words and concepts regarding existence, non-existence, destruction, and production.
But it is precisely with regard to the duality of manifestation and concealment [that this is said]. || 92 ||

Having refuted the objection against his position—that if the effect existed prior [to its production], it would necessarily be perceived at all times—he now raises another objection regarding the impossibility of the distinction between linguistic usage and cognition, such as "the jar is destroyed" and "the jar does not exist," and says: "It is destroyed," etc. [This refers to] the lump [of clay], etc.

The distinction is as follows: when [an object] is manifested through the cessation of its obstruction, there is the conventional usage of "arising"; when it is manifested through the removal of darkness by means of a lamp or the like, there is the conventional usage of "existence"; when it is concealed by means of a potsherd or the like, there is the conventional usage of "perished"; and when it is concealed by means of a lump of clay or the like, there is the conventional usage of "non-existence. ||92||
A wall is seen as an obstruction that always conceals objects located in a different place.
How can the obstruction consisting of the lump of clay and so forth reside in the same location as the jar and so forth?

[The opponent] objects: "The lump of clay and so forth are not the obstruction of the jar and so forth, because they occupy the same location; for whatever is an obstruction of something does not occupy the same location as it—for example, a wall and so forth are an obstruction of a jar and so forth, yet they do not occupy the same location as it. Thus he raises the objection with the words "kuḍyādi" (wall, etc.). 93.
It is not so, because milk, ghee, and the like are observed to occupy the same location. (94)
If there were non-obstruction [of the pot's nature] by the shards and so forth within the essence of the pot, [then it would not be destroyed].
This is not correct because it would entail the inclusion of those things that have already been divided. || 95 ||
Furthermore, if it were thought that this is its true nature, it would follow as a logical consequence that it is subject to destruction.
But effort is not for the production of a jar; even so, this [position] is not tenable. || 96 ||
For there is no rule in the world that the manifestation of a jar is caused by [the action of] a lamp.
For it is observed here that manifestation occurs through manifold means. || 97 ||
What is this "occupying the same location"? Is it having a single substratum, or is it having a single cause? The first [option] is refuted because it is contradictory.

[The opponent] objects: "It is not so. The meaning is that because we observe mutual concealment only between milk and water, or between ghee and oil, when they have entered into the same substratum, the inference does not arise due to the contradictory nature of the reason (*hetu*). [The proponent] raises the second alternative: "Because there is no concealment. The self of the jar is its cause, which is called clay; its inclusion therein refers to the persistence of the potsherds and so forth within that [clay].

The meaning is that, because they occupy the same location, the potsherd and so forth cannot be an obstruction to that [pot], just as [the potsherd] is not [an obstruction] to the pot. Since it is already accepted that the potsherd and so forth—which exist in the state of mere clay during the condition of the pot—are not obstructions to the pot, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Furthermore, in the attempt to prove that the potsherd and so forth existing in the state of unmanifest clay are not obstructions, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because the pot and the potsherd possess distinct constituent parts (*avayava-bheda*) which serve as their own substrates. He resolves this [objection] as follows: "No."

"Excellent! [The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that there is non-perception because that which already exists is merely concealed, then effort would be directed toward removing the concealment, rather than toward the production of a jar or the like;
yet people do strive for its production. Therefore, for the proponent of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavādin*), this contradicts experience.

To this, he replies: "Now (*atha*). He states that in the world there is no such rule that a specific jar is produced solely by the removal of its concealment, making that very jar the intended object of the causal operation.

Rāmakaṇṭha says: "Not so. Regarding the reading *ghaṭābhivyaktihetutaḥ*, the meaning is that there is no fixed rule [that the cause of the manifestation of a jar must consist] in the destruction of its covering.
He states the reason for this lack of a fixed rule: "aneka... (in the verse). The word *iha* is a common worldly expression. || 94 ||
One [is known] by means of a lamp, another by means of a churning-stick, and likewise another by means of a wheel and so forth.
The object always proceeds toward manifestation, being exactly as it was before.

He illustrates that manifestation has multiple means with the words "by a lamp," etc. A jar or similar object covered by darkness is manifested by a lamp; butter and the like covered by curds and so forth are manifested by churning; while a bowl or similar object covered by a lump of clay and so forth is manifested by a wheel and other tools—such is the distinction. Anticipating the objection that there might be a difference in the underlying reality (sattva) just as there is a difference in the manifestations, he says "previously," etc. Even though there is a difference in manifestations due to the difference in means, [the reality] remains prior relative to the manifestation.
The meaning is that the very same object is manifested; there is no difference in its existence. || 98 ||
If it is thought that even a lamp exists solely for the purpose of destroying darkness;
When the darkness has vanished, even a jar is perceived by itself.

Regarding the claim that "another [object] becomes manifest by means of a lamp," he raises an objection with the words "darkness" (*tamaḥ*). The meaning of the particle *api* is that even butter and the like serve only to remove the obstruction to curds and so forth. He says "destroyed" (*naṣṭa*) because if the lamp merely conceals the darkness, how could there be the perception of the jar?
The word *api* is used to state that even in the case of butter and the like, they are perceived by themselves once the curds and so forth have perished. || 99 ||
What is established for you in this way, even if there is indeed the removal of darkness?
Everything is manifested as that very [Brahman]; thus, it is not at all negated. || 100 ||

If it is argued that darkness is destroyed by the effort of producing a lamp, let that be so; however, this does not establish your desired point—that non-existence precedes manifestation. To this he says: "What is it thus? [meaning: what follows from this? He says "No," because even for you there would be a failure of your own tenet. He then says: "Only the existent... (verse 100).
Out of pride, those who consider themselves wise desire to acquire that which is unknown and devoid of value.
The various forms of pride, as well as the state of ignorance resulting from the connection with pride, perish. || 101 ||

Furthermore, the operation of a manifestor is not for the purpose of destroying an obscuration, but rather for the purpose of illuminating the object; the destruction of that obscuration, however, follows as a matter of course.

To state this, he first sets forth the general principle: "ajñātatve" (in the state of being unknown), etc. The word "māninaḥ" means those who accept valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The particle "ca" is used to indicate that it occurs by way of the removal of ignorance. || 101 ||
For when there is a difference in actions, the inquiry arises as to which comes first.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the destruction of darkness should be the fruit of an action when there is a difference in the actions themselves. (102)

One might object: "If there is ignorance (*ajñāna*), then the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) occurs; or if it has ceased? In the first case, since there is no contradiction, that means of knowledge cannot destroy the ignorance. In the second case, the means of knowledge would be useless. Therefore, whether the means of knowledge comes first and the destruction of ignorance later, or vice versa, certainty is unestablished. Anticipating this doubt, he states the common point [of the argument] with the words "yataḥ" (since). When there is a difference between two actions, there is an investigation into their sequence; however, for those two actions performed by a single agent, simultaneity [is possible].

The meaning is this: since there is no difference in the action due to the unity of the process (*dyāyogāt*), that [objection] has no scope; for the sequence between the action and its fruit is fixed. Therefore, one should not urge a sequence between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the destruction of ignorance. In this regard, he provides an example: "dhvānta... (darkness, etc.). The destruction of darkness is the fruit of light such as a lamp; in that case, a sequence is accepted by everyone, and it is established in the present case as well.
Such is the meaning. || 102 ||

The object of knowledge, once produced by the cognition of the knower, reaches its completion when it has been known.
And that which was conjoined with the object of cognition attains the state of being the non-existence of the object of cognition. || 103 ||

15th [Verse]: [The author] establishes the sequence of priority and posteriority in the case of the illustrandum (*dārṣṭāntika*). Regarding the phrase "of the knower": knowledge arises depending upon a cognition accompanied by its semblance (*sābhāsa-buddhi*);
having contacted the object, it assumes the form of that object; and it is precisely this cognition possessing that form which destroys the obscuration of that [object].
This is the meaning. || 103 ||
Since darkness constitutes the obstruction for the cognition "this is a gourd tree," [it is not the cause of the perception].
If the jar were like light, how could there be its destruction by darkness? (104)

Anticipating the objection that since the cognition of "this" and so forth arises from the very transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) described above, what is the use of the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*), he says: "Because of the intervention. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "When ignorance, which is darkness, exists, there is no cognition of the jar.

Anticipating the further objection, "In that case, why could it not be the cessation of that [ignorance] itself that precedes knowledge? he provides an illustration: "Like light. [The jar] is pervaded by light...

The meaning is that, since the destruction of the darkness covering the jar is not observed in the absence of the jar, it is seen that the manifestation [of the jar] occurs first and the destruction of the darkness follows afterwards. || 104 ||
When the means of valid cognition operates, whether [the object] is known or unknown, it effects the removal of its state of being unknown.
From that, the result arises in the form: "The jar has been cognized. || 105 ||

He states the application of the principle (*dārṣṭāntika*): "By means of the instrument of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), etc. First, the jar, previously unknown, is pervaded by a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) through the medium of the external sense organs;

and once pervaded, it becomes characterized by the destruction of its own inherent ignorance and partakes in manifestness (*prākaṭya*). Consequently, there is the accomplishment of practical activity (*vyavahāra*) such as taking it up. This is the meaning. || 105 ||
If there were an effort for the sake of breaking through obscurations, it would be for the purpose of knowing the banyan tree.
There would be another effect resulting from destruction; by that [destruction], the state of being unproduced would also exist in the jar.

Since it is established that the operation of a manifestor (vyañjaka) is for the purpose of revealing an object, the removal of concealment (āvṛti) follows as a matter of course; and since it is thus proven that no effort is required for the manifestation of the object itself, he states another reason [for this] with the words "If... If the removal of concealment were for the sake of cognizing the jar, and effort were directed toward that end, then because other effects such as fragments or powder could also result from the removal of the concealment of the lump of clay and so forth, there would be no manifestation of the jar even when it is covered by those [fragments].
This is the meaning. || 106 ||
If there were another intervention [between the two], then something else besides that would also follow.
Therefore, in this case, the operation must necessarily be productive of a result. || 107 ||

If it is argued that its manifestation occurs even upon the breaking of a split bamboo stalk (*vidala*) and the like, he says "no," [introducing the phrase] "another intervention" (*vyavadhānāntara*). This means: from the split bamboo stalk onwards;
at that time, during the state of its breaking. By the preceding [term], there is an interval—whether of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*).

The meaning is as follows: when there is an effort toward the removal of the veil (*āvṛtibhaṅga*), then, as long as that [pot] is empty [of manifestation], because of its existence [in that state], there would be a requirement for its devotee; thus, the intention is that there would be only the non-manifestation of the pot.
Since the non-perception of the pot was shown to occur during the effort for the sake of removing the veil, it is not for the sake of perceiving it [as an object].

He concludes that effort directed toward the certain [goal] shall be fruitful: "Therefore" (ataḥ). Here, "effort" (prayatita) is what is being discussed. || 107 ||
Knowledge of a past or future jar would have an existing jar as its objective support.
Because it possesses the nature of the cognition of a jar, like the direct awareness of a jar present here. || 108 ||

Having set aside the objection that arose incidentally—namely, that an effect exists even prior to its production but is not perceived because it is concealed—he now states the inference based on manifestation (*abhivyakti*) as the logical mark (*liṅga*), which was the subject under discussion, and then presents the inference intended by the commentary beginning with the words "atītānāgatapratyayabhedācca. He says: "atīta... [The meaning is: "The object of dispute has an existent entity as its objective support, because it is a cognition of a jar, like a present cognition of a jar. What [is the reason]?

In the world, activity is observed to proceed for the sake of attaining something; moreover, such activity is not possible toward that which is absolutely non-existent. For yogis and for the Lord, direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) regarding objects such as the past and so forth is accepted, and that [knowledge] is the apprehension of what is currently existing. Therefore, he says "directly" (*sākṣāt*) to establish that the *vaṭa* tree exists at all times.
If it is accepted that past and future objects do not exist, [then...]
It would follow that the Lord possesses false knowledge regarding the past and the future. || 109 ||

Having stated the inference and restated the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) beginning with the words "atīta" (past), etc. The meaning is as follows: first, there is the omniscient Lord's cognition which is perceptual; if that were to have the past and so forth as its object and thus have the non-existent as its objective support (*ālambana*), then one would have to deny its validity (*prāmāṇya*) in that respect, because it would be non-correspondent (*ayathārthatva*). || 109 ||
Nor is the direct perception of the Lord ever contradicted by anything.
That knowledge, which has cast off extreme cold, by what could it be destroyed? || 110 ||

Anticipating the objection that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) might be acceptable, he says: "It is perceived" (*pratyakṣam*). He establishes its non-obstructed nature by saying: "cast aside" (*apaviddha*). For that which is more powerful indeed sublates; however, no cognition more powerful than the knowledge of an omniscient being (*aiśvara-jñāna*) has ever been observed. Therefore, due to the absence of a sublater, [the conclusion does not follow].
The meaning is that it is false. || 110 ||
And the inference [proving] the existence of the jar prior to its production has also been demonstrated.
Therefore, the effect must certainly exist even prior to its production. || 111 ||
Raising the objection, "Even if that [past object] exists, why could it not have been an object of cognition previously non-existent?", he says: "The pot...

The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the aforementioned reasoning. He states the result of the aforementioned proof: "Therefore... By the word "api" (also), the present effect is adduced as an illustrative example. || 111 ||
Furthermore, in the case of such a negation, a contradiction would also ensue.
The future will not have an object to be produced, just like the negation of the present.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the non-existence of a past or future jar at the time of the operation of its causes?

Does it mean that its "pastness" and so forth do not exist then, or that its existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction; thus he says: "the future" (*eṣyat*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the negation of the past jar. [This is said] because otherwise the perception of God and others would result in being invalid.
It has been stated that even a contradiction can be combined; for the future jar and the one that has passed away possess the reality of their respective natures, such as futurity and so forth.

Having stated that there would be a contradiction if the negation were at the time of the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*), Sureśvarācārya clarifies that very point with the words "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*).
The existence of a jar in its future form, such as "it will be" or "it was," is expressed as its being in the present time; if that were the case [at that very moment]...
The meaning is that if it were negated, there would be a contradiction such as "it will be," "it will not be," "it was," or "it was not. || 112 ||
Just as it is contradictory to say that a pot being perceived is non-existent.
The negation of a limited jar regarding the past and the future is likewise of that same nature. || 113 ||

He clarifies the example mentioned as being "like the negation of the present" with the words "being perceived," etc. The construction is: "Just as it is contradictory to say 'this does not exist, but rather it is non-existent'. In the reading "not existent" (*no san*), the construction is even more evident. The meaning is that if one says, "the presently existing jar does not exist," there is indeed a manifest contradiction. He explains the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "past," etc.

The meaning is that if a pot, which is currently being measured as past or future by way of its pastness and so forth, were negated in that very same place and by that very same form, such a negation would be contradictory—just like the negation of a present pot; however, in the second case, one should look to what is stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "prior to its production" (*prāgutpatteḥ*). || 113 ||
Non-existences such as prior non-existence and the rest would have to be real entities distinct [from their counter-correlates].
Because they are designated by the term "pot," their mutual non-existence is certainly established.

Furthermore, he states two inferences: "Prior absence and the others differ from the jar, because they are designated by it, just like its mutual absence; and they are real, because they are distinct, just like a cloth. Regarding the first syllogism, there is no deficiency in the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) of the example; for if the mutual absence of the jar—which is of the nature of a cloth and so forth—were not different from the jar, it would follow that the jar is of the nature of a cloth and so forth.

The point is this: there is no infinite regress even if mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is distinct [from the thing itself], because we accept that it consists in a difference of essential nature (*svarūpabheda*). Furthermore, in the second inference, there is no contradiction due to the mention of "existence as essential nature" (*svarūpasattva*), and the reason is established precisely through this difference of essential nature. He states the result of the inference regarding distinctness—that since those [entities] are other than the jar, it follows that [the jar] is infinite, non-dual, and the self of all—by saying "certainly" (*dhruvam*). || 114 ||
And this being the case, there can be no mutual relationship between existence and non-existence.
Just as there is no contradiction between two existents because they are one, so too there is none between two non-existents. || 115 ||

Anticipating the objection—"Even if they are distinct, how can this [non-existence] possess the aforementioned nature simply through its relation to the jar?"—the author states the result of the second inference:
"And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). The meaning is that if non-existences were existent, then because it would be a non-existence itself, there could be no mutual connection between existence and non-existence.

"Because of contradiction" (*virodhāt*) means, in effect, because non-existence itself is non-existent. Regarding the absence of a relation, the example is "between two existences" (*bhāvayoḥ*). For instance—
Because there is identity between existence and existence, there is no mutual conjunction; for there is no distinguishing form whatsoever in either existence or non-existence.
Likewise, because existence and non-existence are identical according to the logic already stated, that [conjunction] does not exist—this is the meaning. || 115 ||
And there can be no relation for that which is non-existent, because it lacks agency toward anything whatsoever.
Furthermore, because its nature is action, that relationship cannot be established without a causal factor (kāraka).

He states another reason for the absence of a relation in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words "and of that which is non-existent" (*asataśca*). The meaning is that because non-existence is non-existent, it is incapable of being a cause;
therefore, not even one of the relations—conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth—is established for it with an existent entity (*bhāva*). Now, [one might object] that non-existence is...

In the first case, its non-existence would not be established; thus he says, "And not... (*na ca*). "In this way" (*evam*) means: while the non-existence is included within the pot and so forth. Regarding the second case, he says, "Prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*). Here too, the mention of "prior non-existence" is as before. The ellipsis is "the pot is not its own nature" (*svarūpa*); the reason for both cases is as follows:

He said: "It has a limit. A pot is the limit (avadhi), and non-existence is that which possesses the limit (avadhimān). By the word "api" (also/even), destruction (dhvaṃsa) and so forth are included. || 118 ||
Now, having postulated a relationship, it is expressed as "of the jar."
For it would follow that there is a verbal designation of a non-existence that has already been established. || 119 ||

He raises the objection that even though antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like are not the jar itself, the expression "that [non-existence] belongs to the jar" is justified by postulating a relation, just as one says "consciousness belongs to the person" (*caitanyaṃ puruṣasya*). He introduces this with the word "atha" (now). He replies: "If the relation is merely imagined, then the relata themselves must also be imagined. He explains: "Where an expression occurs based on the postulation of a relation, there no real distinction exists."

Just as in the case of Rāhu and his head, so too here, if a relationship were imagined despite the existence of difference, then one of the two related entities would have to be real; yet there is no such reality because [the relationship] is dependent. Therefore, the meaning is that the jar is real. || 119 ||
If you claim that non-existence is a different entity, you should remember what has already been said.
That [existence] is not tenable for a jar that is conceptualized as being like a hare's horn and so forth. || 120 ||

He states another alternative: "a different object" (*arthāntaram*). He says that this has been refuted by the passage beginning with "whether it be existent or non-existent, what would that be? (*vyatireke sadevāsadasadvā tatkim...*) and so forth.

He says "it has been stated" (*uktam*). Having rejected non-existence through the alternatives of difference (*vyatireka*) and so on, he states another fault in the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*): "the horn... (*śaśa...*) || 120 ||
The connection [of a thing] with its own cause and existence [is established], because that connection always has [the thing itself] as its substratum.
Now, let it be that inseparable establishment belongs to things already established; there is no such thing as inseparable establishment for what is non-existent.

Logicians maintain that "birth" (janman) is either a connection with its own cause or a connection with existence (*sattā*). However, there can be no connection for that which is non-existent prior to its production, because such a connection occurs only between two existing things.
Furthermore, since the effect does not possess absolute non-existence, it does not resemble the horn of a hare; for that which was previously non-existent— [vol2, page 30]

The meaning is that no distinction can be established for that which is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsataḥ*). He raises the objection regarding the relation of the non-existent (*asat*)—which is not established as separate—to its cause with the words "Now" (*atha*).
He refutes this with the words beginning "No" (*na*). || 121 ||

There is no conjunction between existence and non-existence, nor even between two non-existences; since conjunction occurs only between two existents, the effect is therefore always established as existent. || 122 ||

Explaining the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "of two things that have become existent" (*bhāvabhūtayoḥ*), he clarifies what was stated [in the previous verse] with the words "not of an existent... (*na bhāva...*).

The meaning is that since a relation is observed only between two existing things (*satoḥ*) by virtue of their being inseparably established (*ayutasiddhatvena*), a relation preceded by inseparable establishment cannot be established between an existent and a non-existent, or between two non-existents.

He concludes the proof for the existence of the effect with the word "established" (*siddham*). For when the effect exists, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is present, whereas in its non-existence there is a logical flaw (*doṣa*).

The meaning of the word "iti" (thus) is "because it has been stated. The word "always" (sadā) means that [the state] exists not only in the present time, but also in the past and future times. ||122||
The form of the Vairāja, which consists of both duality and unity, is the effect of the Self.
"Samudra eva yasya"— with these words, Virāj spoke the warding-off spell.

In this context, having dispelled the doubt that everything might be non-existent prior to its origination by explaining the passage beginning with "by death," it was stated that in the phrase "the ocean indeed of this," the term *samudra* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Now, fearing that because the word *samudra* is conventionally established in other meanings, it does not have the Supreme as its object, he says: "dvaita... [The Supreme is] the form of Vairāja, which possesses manifold flavors.

The meaning is that it is well known from the Śruti and Smṛti that "the work belongs to the Self," and in such Śruti passages as "Agni is the head" and in Smṛti passages such as "He alone created [the world]," it is extremely clear that the Supreme Lord Himself is the creator of the Virāṭ-self through the medium of the Sūtra. Nevertheless, how can the word "ocean" (samudra) have the Supreme as its referent? To this he says: "In the passage beginning 'The ocean indeed is his...'," by the word "ocean," the Virāṭ-self is meant.

The Śruti has declared the ocean to be the cause; therefore, because of this indicative mark of being the cause, and because it is a different entity from the well-known ocean, its status as the Supreme Self is established by the word "samudra"—this is the meaning. || 123 ||
Having come together, they constitute the effects, from which [arises] the all-pervading source of beings.
Birth, maintenance, and dissolution go unto him; therefore, he is the creator of the universe.

Furthermore, one might object: "The word 'samudra' has a conventional meaning (rūḍhi) for something other than [Brahman] because that [conventional sense] exists elsewhere; nor does it have an etymological meaning (yoga), as that is not understood, and because conventional meaning is stronger than etymological meaning. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "saṃbhūya" (having come together). Since the elements such as ether and the rest, existing as effects, having come together, flow toward their origin—the Lord who is the unconditioned source of beings and possesses qualities such as invisibility—therefore...

The meaning is as follows: by means of that [ocean], other beings go; it is joined with the source of beings (bhūtayoni); and having come together there, beings emerge from it and run back into it—this is the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). However, the principle that "conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymology (*yoga*)" must be set aside in this context, because conventional usage is impossible here. || 124 ||
That ocean is the supreme Brahman, whose true nature is pure consciousness alone.
The failure to realize the true nature of the self is stated here as the cause.

Anticipating the objection—“Even though it is an ocean for others, how can the word ‘death’ (mṛtyu), which denotes a cause, be applied to that which is of the single flavor of immutable consciousness?”—he says: “That ocean. The meaning of the word “here” (iha) refers to the statement “by death alone” (mṛtyunaiva). The sense is that even Brahman, which is pure immutable consciousness, deserves the designation ‘death’ because it is the cause of the world through the medium of ignorance (ajñāna). || 125 ||
1. Dhātmya | He [vol2, page 31]
This world has as its material cause that which is omnipotent, unborn, and imperishable.
Through the operation of its own singular ignorance, it is both the devourer and the progenitor.

Some postulate that Brahman itself, without the aid of ignorance (*ajñāna*), transforms into the form of the world, just as milk transforms into the form of curd; to them, he says: "This [world]. The meaning is that Brahman, at the beginning of the origin of all things, being endowed with the power of its own inherent ignorance (*avidyā*), is the cause of the world; for it is not possible for that which is partless and inactive to undergo transformation either in its entirety or in part.
Even though the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is untenable, he states that the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) follows as a consequence: "Its own self" (*svātma*), etc.

The meaning is this: within its own self, there is a single, staff-like ignorance; through its "functioning," which is its capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), even this Brahman is at times disposed to swallow the world, and at other times disposed to manifest in the form of that world. || 126 ||
This occurs solely through the path of its own manifestation upon the grounds born of ignorance regarding its own self.
Just as the single reality of space appears as multiplicity within jars and other objects, so too is this [the case here]. || 127 ||

Anticipating the objection that the causality of Brahman toward individual souls (jīvas) might be as real as their mutual difference from it—and thus not merely illusory—he says: "svābhāsa... etc. That ignorance (ajñāna) in which there is the manifestation (ābhāsa) of Brahman itself, and in accordance with that very [ignorance], within the body and so forth—which are produced by the ignorance whose locus and object is itself—that single reality (vastu), though in fact one, comes to possess multiplicity through such designations as "Sūtra" and "Virāṭ."

Just as the sky appears to possess multiplicity due to limiting adjuncts such as jars and the like, so too, because this distinction is rooted in ignorance (avidyā), its causality is likewise of that same nature;
such is the meaning. || 127 ||
Just as that which is unborn attains the status of being a cause through the ignorance of its true nature, so too does the non-cause [attain it] through the lack of knowledge of reality.
In this way, [the Lord] is indeed the agent of all things, as well as the action and its fruit. || 128 ||

Based on the intention that, just as Brahman’s being the self of all is real according to the Śruti text "All this, indeed, is Brahman," its being the cause of all is likewise real, [the author] says: "It is not a cause. Brahman, which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), is not a cause in reality; for there are such Śruti texts as "This Brahman is without prior" (*apūrva*). Nevertheless, through *māyā*, it is perceived as having that nature, as in [the text]: "From this very Self, space was produced" (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*).

Since the Śruti, in such passages as "But Māyā is the material cause," declares that [Brahman's] causality is sustained by Māyā, the meaning is that just as Brahman’s status as the cause is [dependent on Māyā], its being the Self of all—which is produced by that [Māyā]—is likewise merely māyic. || 128 ||
Therefore, the relationship between that which is to be proven and the means of proof rests solely upon ignorance.
Having proclaimed that reality loudly, the Vedāntas have established it.

Having raised the objection that the causal relationship between the world and Brahman must be real—just like Brahman itself—because it is observed in scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth, he says: "sādhyā... [By the aforementioned reasoning, the Upanishadic texts such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), which teach that the nature of the imagined effects and so forth is the inner Self-Brahman who is both within and without, first restate through sentences on creation and the like the relation of cause and effect—which is caused solely by beginningless ignorance—and then establish that [nature] as their primary purport.]

They proceeded to explain [the nature of Brahman], but the elaboration of creation and so forth was not intended for them; the meaning is that such elaboration is fruitless because it lacks novelty (apūrvatva) for them. || 129 ||
That which is neither a cause nor an effect has attained the status of being both a cause and an effect through the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda).
Therefore, it is solely from delusion that the scripture proceeds toward their eradication.
1 ka. To the one who follows [the path].
[vol2, page 32]
328 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter]— 1

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Not this, not this" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*) regarding the matter already mentioned: "Without cause. The meaning is that the fact that Brahman—which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*)—is the self of the world and its cause, by means of its own ignorance (*avidyā*), is what is expressed by the passage "Not this, not this," and so forth. Nor is there any contradiction with the statement that [the world's] origination is for the sake of praise; for the distinction is made that while that [origination] is the intermediate purport (*avāntara-tātparya*), this [negation of plurality] is the great purport (*mahā-tātparya*). [The text continues: "effect and cause..."

When it is stated that the commencement of the treatise is established because knowledge—which serves as the cause for the destruction of bondage along with its causes—is the means for the removal of this [bondage] which has delusion as its cause, he states an *arthāpatti* (presumption) regarding that point: "From that... (verse 130).
Having drunk up the entirety of saṃsāra, it rests upon pure mental formations.
This Brahman is called "unmanifest" and is also called the "Inner Controller. || 131 ||

An objection is raised: "In such passages as 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existence' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), the cause of the world is heard to be the Indeterminate (avyākṛta) and so forth; how then can Brahman be its cause? To this, he says: "Because it has withdrawn [into itself]" (apīti). This means that the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) has been withdrawn into itself. He distinguishes this from the Brahman that is the support for liberation (muktyālambana). He says: "By the latent impression" (saṃskāra). The word "resort" (saṃśraya) here emphasizes the state of being; it refers to the resorting to, the taking refuge in, oneself by the latent impression.

Or rather, he states the distinction from the state of saṃsāra by saying "pure" (śuddha). The first qualification is employed to establish that [the Self] is the substratum of pure latent impressions (saṃskāra) alone;

the distinction is that the unmanifest (avyākṛta) has the limiting adjunct (upādhi) as its primary element, whereas the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) has the conditioned entity (upahita) as its primary element. || 131 ||
"That designation which arises for this [self] without the destruction of ignorance,"
This [world], being non-existent apart from its own ignorance, has for its support the real object of cognition.

(132) [Objection: But surely, it is not logical that the world lacks reality simply because it is an effect of Brahman whose nature is unknown, since it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To this, he says: "By ignorance," etc. *Vyākṛtiḥ* means manifestation. The word "this" (*asya*) refers to the world. While the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyag-ajñāna*) persists, [the world appears] through perception and other means...

The manifestation of the world is not an object consisting of real entities; for even during true sleep, the active dream-cognition does not take real objects as its domain. Likewise, even in the waking state, while knowledge persists, there occurs an appearance of manifestation through perception and other means—this is the meaning. || 132 ||
It indeed attains the status of being the cause for the arising of right knowledge.
Having fallen asleep, he awakens from that state due to his own ignorance. || 133 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the world, like a dream, is false, then the Vedas and other means of knowledge must also be false, and how then can the knowledge of Brahman arise from them, he says: "Perfectly" (*samyak*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "even though the Vedas and so forth are unreal, they lead [to the goal]. He provides an illustration for the fact that even the unreal Vedas and such can be a cause for attaining reality: "Sleep," etc. The sense of the particle *api* ("even") is: "even from what is unreal. Nor is its own nature...

The validity [of knowledge] is known through the unreality of its object, because such validity would be impossible otherwise; for the etymological derivation is "that by which an object is known. Therefore, just as a correct awakening occurs upon the cessation of sleep following an unreal cognition of a tiger or similar object in a dream, so too, even when produced by the unreal Vedas and other scriptures, there arises right knowledge—this is the meaning. || 133 ||
The validity of the means of knowledge consists in their reaching the object of cognition.
I have previously stated that, according to the actual state of things, there is no reality.

[The author] recalls what was stated [in the previous section], beginning with the words "except for the communication of the goal" (*upeyabodhanam muktvā*), in response to the objection that it might be suspected that even the validity of scripture and other means of knowledge—like smoke [as an indicator of fire]—is merely probable. He says: "The goal" (*upeya*), etc. This refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is to say, the scriptures which are the instruments of right knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*).
[The reading] *teṣām* is found in manuscripts *kha* and *ca*; [the variant] *hinlā* is in manuscript *ga*.
[Vol.
2, Page 33] 2 Brāhmaṇam, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 329.

Furthermore, even if the object is real, it does not possess reality as its own essential nature (*svarūpa-satyatva*), nor can that [reality] be inferred from that very [object], because it would contradict the scripture (*āgama*) which reveals the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
He says: "The thing. || 134 ||
This ignorance, though non-existent, manifests itself through name-and-form and the like.
Its supreme subtlety is called "māyā" by Death himself. || 135 ||

Having set aside the objection that arose in the course of explaining the meaning of the word "death," [the author] now analyzes the very meaning of that term "death. He says: "Name" (*nāma*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), action (*karman*) and the rest are included. He states: "This" (*iyam*), meaning that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not only known through inference based on its effects, but is also established by direct experience. To the objection that it must therefore be a real entity because it is validated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he replies: "Non-existent" (*asatī*). From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), it is not an object of knowledge...
The meaning is "because it is cognizable. To refute those who assert a distinction between *avidyā* and *māyā*, the term *māyā* is used; for their difference is indeed unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*).

He states that the form of *māyā*—which is designated by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), whose name and form are unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is imperceptible to the senses and so forth, and which is distinct from the state of the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) great elements—is that of which [he speaks] with the words "of her" (*tasyāḥ*). || 131 ||
"Death is indeed darkness," and likewise, "The waters alone were this."
Ignorance, as the fundamental root, constantly manifests in both manifest and unmanifest forms.

[Objection: But surely, in the passage "Death is indeed darkness; immortality is light," knowledge and action in their natural state are denoted by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*). Moreover, those two possess no causality because they are effects, whereas the causality of water will be stated in the seventh [chapter]. Therefore, how can the ignorance of the inner self, accompanied by its reflection, be denoted by the word "death," which denotes a cause? To this, he says: "Death... For it is clear in the section concerning the *udgītha*...

That very root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), which manifests as the nature of verbalized innate knowledge and action, is denoted by the word "darkness" (*tamas*) through the explanation of the term "death" (*mṛtyu*). And in the seventh [verse], that same ignorance, manifesting as the nature of *prakṛti* denoted by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), is intended by the word "water" (*ap*).

Therefore, because it exists always in the form of the perceived duality, there is no contradiction in its being designated by the term "death," since it is accompanied by the appearance of light (*sābhāsā*).
This is the meaning. || 136 ||
Having arisen from these, it [the mind] proceeds by means of its own manifestation through the birth of what is not-self.
The Lord, though immutable, attains the state of the Knower of the Field through knowledge.

One might object: "Let it be that the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta) are nothing but consciousness (pratyamātratva), since they are transformations (vivarta) of ignorance (avidyā); however, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) cannot be merely that [consciousness], because he is not a transformation of that ignorance. Therefore, non-duality (advaita) is lost. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "From these... [The Supreme Self], though changeless, having experienced manifestation in a state of equilibrium from these elements which have evolved in the form of cause and effect and are becoming manifest, [remains] His own...

The reflection, when perceived as non-self, attains the state of being a living soul (jīva) by way of birth. Furthermore, the reflection is not in reality a different entity from the original (bimba), because it appears as having the same form; therefore, since the supreme Self alone, remaining unmodified, becomes the living soul through ignorance, there is no departure from non-duality (advaita)—this is the meaning. || 137 ||
For the Śruti declares: "The waters, being more subtle, created Truth."
That supreme one, whose self consists of the powers of action and consciousness, also created Brahmā.

Now, one might object: "In both the Śruti and the Bhāṣya, the creation is said to have been performed by the author of the Sūtras, since it is stated that Death possessed a cord and other attributes; how then do you say that this creation proceeds from the Root Cause? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] speaks the following passage (verse 42) to state that the creation intended here is from that [Root Cause] alone, and not from the Sūtra-author.

The meaning is that Rbhu, being himself supreme as a transformation of the Supreme Brahman, created the Virāṭ-ātman, which is Brahman. || 138 ||
Then Virāj Brahmā created the divine Manu, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
Manu [created] the gods and human beings, as well as everything stationary and everything moving. || 139 ||

1. [The author] states that Manu is the creator of the Virāj. Regarding the word "Virāj": the meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate succession to the manifestation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of knowledge and action which constitute the cause of Manu's creation. This indicates his power to perceive and effect the creation about to be described. Regarding the word "divine" (*devam*): [it refers to him who is] not...
Having created a new creation consisting of humans, he addressed Manu, saying "Manu. || 139 ||
This is due to the intention to express the nature of the entire effect as possessing both the probandum and the probans.
This very Śruti proceeded with great effort, saying, "Not here, indeed, not here."

He states that the present scriptural passage forms a single syntactical unit with the seventh [chapter’s] scriptural passage, which refers to the fundamental cause: "sādhyā... etc. The word "here" (iha) refers to the context.
"Effort" (yatnaḥ) means the purport of the scripture regarding the fundamental cause; for it is not the case that the entire effect is joined with intermediate causes.
Therefore, the meaning is that the fundamental cause alone is denoted here by the word "death" (mṛtyu). || 140 ||
They declare that hunger and thirst are the form of death.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa) is the absorber (saṃvarga) therein, it [is the same] for speech and so forth, both with respect to the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adaiva). || 141 ||

Regarding the doubt that the supplementary passage beginning with "How [could there be] hunger? cannot apply to the root cause, since it is established that the root cause does not possess hunger and thirst—[the author], considering that the Supreme Self, having attained the state of the *sūtra* (the subtle body), possesses death due to its nature as the destroyer of all, and thus the supplementary passage is appropriate, says: "For hunger. The connection is "of the breath, which is death. How?

Anticipating the objection that this [Prāṇa] must therefore be death, he states the justification: "In that regard" (tatra). The meaning is that because the internal [senses] such as speech and the external [deities] such as fire are withdrawn into that Prāṇa, which is Vāyu, it possesses the nature of death. || 141 ||
From this, the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind (manas), and all the sense organs are born.
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth, the sustainer of the universe. || 142 ||

If it is held that creation here proceeds from the primary cause, then that [creation] beginning with space must be described; however, in that case, the supplementary statement, "It thought, 'May I be many,'" would be inconsistent. Anticipating this objection, he first sets forth the creation according to the *Atharvaṇa*: "From this," meaning from the Supreme Self whose nature consists of omniscience and other such qualities. || 142 ||
With reference to this creation, it was said: "He made that mind."
The supreme Śruti has proceeded to describe that which is unmanifest.

He now dispels the contradiction with the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*) by means of the verse beginning with "creation" (*sṛṣṭim*). That supreme Śruti, which begins with "It made that its mind" (*tan mano 'kuruta*) and ends with "Therefore this was undifferentiated" (*tad dha idaṃ tarhy avyākṛtam*), establishes the creation of the entire effect from its primal cause, as is well-known from other scriptural passages.
2 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 331.

The meaning is that even here [in this context], having aimed at that very same [cause] and determined it, the text proceeds to speak; thus, the statement "He made that mind" refers to the activity of the observation (*īkṣaṇa*) of that root cause, and therefore there is no contradiction with the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). || 143 ||
Or rather, the mind formed a resolution directed toward Virāj.
"May I possess a self," thus thought the purposeful cause of creation.

Having stated the meaning of the sentence—that he performed the mental activity denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*) as its fundamental cause—the commentary states, "That [is the mind]," and so forth. Following this, he offers an alternative interpretation: that Mṛtyu, whose nature is the fundamental cause, having attained the state of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread), made the resolve denoted by the word "mind" with a view toward the creation of the Virāj-self. With what intention did he create the mind? It is asked: "With what purpose?"—and so on.

In response to that expectation, he says: "ātmanvī" (endowed with a self). When the mind, which is of the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*), has been created, the creator Hiraṇyagarbha, with intent—that is, with a specific purpose—became one who thinks, "By means of this [mind], may I be possessed of a self. He is called the Sūtrātman because he is the cause of creation, or because his essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the cause of this [universe]. || 144 ||
The vision of one's own manifestation during creation is called the worship of the All-pervading Lord.
And the statement "the waters were born" is an indicative mark for all the elements.

Anticipating the objection that even one who possesses intention cannot be a creator if he lacks power, the author states the meaning of the passage "He, worshipping" (*so 'rcan*). He explains: "His own manifestations" (*svavibhūtīti*). The meaning is that "worship" (*arcana*) is the contemplation of one's own capacity, thinking, "I am capable in the matter of creating the subtle body" (*sūtrātman*). Now, an objection is raised: the beholder (*īkṣitṛ*) is not the creator of water alone, but rather of ether (*viyat*) and the other elements as well; why then, in the passage beginning with "of that," is there a mention of water alone? To this, [the author] replies:

"Kyāsse" means "you. The sandhi (euphonic combination) is not intended here, as the intention is to take the preceding words exactly as they were heard. By the word "all" (*sarva*), the triad beginning with space (*ākāśa*) is included; thus, the commentary states that one must say "after the origin of the three beginning with space. Here, by the word "elements" (*bhūta*), the five gross elements (*pañcīkṛta-bhūta*) are understood. || 145 ||
Because the primary purpose is the arising of knowledge, the creation [of the world] is not intended to be expressed here.
And thus, in each Vedānta text, a manifold creation is observed. (146)
Immediately following the description of Virāj’s creation, it was stated that the mention of water (*ap*)—intended as a reference to the entire process of creation—is merely an illustration.

Now, however, he says that this [creation] is not intended to be taught, because the Upaniṣads are devoted to knowledge (*vidyā*). He states "Knowledge" [in the verse]. Furthermore, he provides another reason for why the creation is not intended to be taught: "And likewise," etc. In the *Taittirīyaka*, the creation is described as beginning with ether (*ākāśa*), whereas in the *Chāndogya*, it begins with fire (*tejas*).

The creation beginning with *prāṇa* is found in the *Atharvaṇa*, while that in the *Aitareyaka* is devoid of sequential order; thus, there is disagreement among all the Vedāntas regarding the manner of creation, and the meaning is that such [specific] creation is not what is intended to be taught. || 146 ||
Since he was born from me while I was performing worship, therefore he is called Kamaṃbhaḥ, the maker of happiness.
Then Arka, Abhiṣu, Saṃvṛta, Prāṇa, Mṛtyu, and Prajāpati. || 147 ||

He explains the meaning of "Arcata" and so forth: "Arcata" means that because he is worshipped (*arcana*) and because of his connection with the water that is the cause of happiness (*sukha-hetu*), the Lord of Creatures (*Prajāpati*) is named Arka.
He states: "Then," meaning that just as Mṛtyu became the Lord Sūtrātman, so too did he become denoted by the word *Arka* in that form. || 147 ||
1 ka. 'tathā | a | [vol2, page 36] 332
Therefore, it is certain that even for this [fire-altar], the meditation belongs to the name alone. *Suresvarācārya-kṛta Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter.
For there can be no connection with the name of the sun without meditation. || 148 ||

Anticipating the question, "For what purpose is there an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) for the name 'Sūtra'?", he says: "It is meditation" (*upāsana*). Since a new designation (*saṃjñā*) joined [to a thing] lacks any other fruit, the meaning is that meditation upon the Sūtra by means of its name is intended here. He explains the stated point by way of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
He causes it to expand; [he says] "arketi" || 148 ||
Or if it is called "water-giver" (vārida) because of its function as a cause.
But the statement "the waters indeed are the *arka*" is intended solely for the purpose of providing a name for the fire-altar (*citi*).

He states another alternative for the purpose of emphasizing the primacy of fire: "Or rather" (*yadi vā*). Since it is heard in scripture that "the waters indeed are the *arka*," one might ask how fire can have the nature of the *arka*; therefore, he says: "The waters. This scriptural statement regarding the *arkatva* of the waters—which exist in the form of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread) accompanied by the other elements—is for the sake of understanding the meaning of the name *arka* applied to the piled fire-altar (*cityāgni*). For that [fire-altar] is the *virāj*, which, as will be explained later, is established within the aforementioned waters.
Therefore, because of his abiding there and his connection with worship, the meaning is that he is the fire known as Arkaśvitya. || 149 ||
By the expression "there was an arrow," the state of the spear is intended to be expressed.
"She became the earth"—this is the statement regarding the birth of Virāj.

In the passage beginning with "tadyadapām" (then that which was of water), he explains the meaning of the word *śara*. Regarding the phrase "śara āsīt" (there was a reed), the meaning is that by the term *śara*, the swelling state of the causal Sūtra, which possesses power (*śaktimat*), is intended. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "tatsamahanyata" (that was condensed). The meaning is that here the production of Virāj—who consists of the gross universe—from the Sūtra—which consists of the subtle universe—is intended. || 150 ||
While the waters were performing austerity, a golden egg was indeed born.
Thus the Śruti has declared the meaning, just as it is elaborated here.
Regarding the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya—"From those waters, the egg was produced"—he cites another scriptural passage: "Tapaḥ" (Heat).

While the waters, accompanied by the other elements, were performing austerity (*tapas*) in their form as the *sūtra* (the subtle thread), forming a volition (*saṃkalpa*), [there arose] the Vairāja body consisting of light.

He says that this [world] is not produced from those [waters] in a merely speculative sense, because it is based on scripture (*śrautatvāt*). Thus he says: "So says the Śruti. The Śatapatha Śruti states: "In the beginning, indeed, this was water, nothing but a watery expanse. It desired: 'How might I be reproduced? It exerted itself; it performed austerity. While it was performing austerity, within it a golden egg came into being. By this [scriptural passage], the *prakṛti*...

He states that [this] Śruti passage forms a single syntactical unit [with the present context]: "Just as... The construction is as follows: just as the meaning consisting of the origin of the Virāj from the Sūtra is explained in this current section (prakaraṇa), in that very same way the Śatapatha-Śruti also declared this matter. || 111 ||
Thus, the body of the Self, consisting of both the individual and the collective, is the Vairāja body.
Having thus prepared [the ground], his creation is now about to be described.

He restates the previously taught creation of the gross body with the words "Thus" (*evam*). The meaning is that the Sūtrātman, possessing manifold flavors (*nānā-rasa*), created its own gross body in the manner described.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "In that [creation] he became weary" (*tasyām aśrāmyat*) with the word "Now" (*atha*). Following the creation of the gross body, the subsequent sentence intends to express the limitation (*pariccheda*) of the creator, the Sūtrātman, by means of that which was created—namely, his connection to that creation.
Such is the meaning. || 152 ||
The phrase "of the weary one," however, expresses the body's unfitness for action.
Therefore, the heat of one who is already scorched is designated as the cause of exhaustion. || 153 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tasya" (of him), he explains the non-redundant meaning of the two words with the verse beginning "śrāntasya" (of the weary). Since heat is the cause of fatigue, the word "taptasya" (of the heated) is used separately from "tāpa" (heat); such is the construction. || 153 ||
The radiant knowledge is its brilliance; the vital breath is intended to be its essence.
[This is] of Prajāpati, whose nature consists of the power of action and consciousness, and who has performed [this]. || 154 ||
He explains the meaning of the two words *tejas* and *rasa* with the word *bhāsvat*. The luminosity (*bhāsvattva*) of knowledge consists in its unimpeded manifestation.
He provides the reasoning for why those two have the stated meanings with the word *kriyā*. For Prajāpati, who is the subject under discussion as the cause, is the Sūtrātman;
since he possesses the nature of these two powers, it is logical that his effect, Virāj, has the aforementioned form. || 114 ||
[The Self], whose body is unlimited, [appears limited] due to the cause of limitation by the physical body.
From his mouth, there issued forth a sound like that from a jar being blown.
He states the meaning of the word "niravartata" (it emerged) with the phrase "anavacchinna" (unlimited). The connection is with the words "of Him whose body is unlimited.

Just as space is delimited by a jar or similar object, so too it is said that [the power] "emerged" for the sake of delimiting the gross body of the Sūtra, whose nature consists of knowledge and action; such is the meaning. || 155 ||
Due to its connection with the body consisting of name-and-form and so forth, it appears as if possessing those qualities, though it is actually devoid of them.
For even though the thread-soul is formless, it is perceived as if it possessed form.

He states the result of delimiting [the Self] by means of the gross body in the verse beginning with "nāma. He explains its possession of contrary attributes in the phrase "though formless" (*arūpo 'pi*).
By the word "also" (*api*), the meaning is "though nameless" (*anāmā 'pi*). In the expression "as if possessing form," it should also be understood as "as if possessing a name. || 156 ||
By means of ignorance, through the two bodies— the subtle and the gross— which are reflections of consciousness.
Even the Supreme Lord, though restrained, is called the Self of the three worlds. || 157 ||

He states the meaning of the word "Agni" [as follows]: "Subtle... The particle *api* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is that the Supreme Self alone, though veiled by the two bodies produced by ignorance, becomes as it were the recipient of the designation "Agni" while existing as the body of the three worlds. [The verse continues:
"Without a body, yet abiding within bodies that are themselves unstable."
Having realized the Self as great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.

He states the proof for the claim that the Supreme alone is delimited by the two bodies: "without body" (*aśarīram*). He refutes a greatness that is relative by stating "all-pervading" (*vibhum*). Alternatively, through the etymology "that which becomes manifold by itself," all-pervasiveness is the state of being the Self of all.
You,
O Hero, are bound by the body of Virāṭ for the sake of the enemy, having attained the state of the inner self (adhyātma) and other [realms] like the sky.
Deprived of that [consciousness], it attains individuality (vyaṣṭitā), yet it remains as a totality (samaṣṭitva). || 159 ||

Anticipating the objection that—even though the other [the individual soul] is delimited by the two bodies—the thread [the *sūtra*] may possess its own inherent state of being a *vyāṣṭi* (individual manifestation), just as it possesses the nature of the *virāj* (cosmic manifestation), and therefore there is no distinction between the two, he says: "The *virāj*. For just as space, when delimited by wells, jars, and so forth, becomes distinct—[page 38, vol. 2]—so too is the case here.
Just as that which experiences the state of being a body by its very nature remains inherently undivided, so too does the Sūtrātman, denoted by the word *asu*, [enter] the Vairāja body.

Having been manifested and delimited by that [intellect], it enters into the various limiting adjuncts—namely the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva)—and thus assumes the state of individuality (vyaṣṭi).

However, when free from the connection with the limiting adjuncts of the internal and so forth, it exists as a collective totality (samaṣṭi) by way of the Virāj. Therefore, the meaning is that the Sūtra is the subtle totality, while the Virāj is the gross totality. || 159 ||
But when the earth had been produced, the Prajāpati became exhausted from toil and heat.
Or rather, his self ceases to exist due to the conceit of limitation.
The creation of Virāj was described previously; now [the author] restates the meaning of the passage beginning with "he toiled upon her" (tasyām aśrāmyat). Regarding the word *urvyām*:

after performing the great task of producing Virāj, the Self (*ātman*) of Prajāpati—characterized by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being delimited by the body of Virāj—became exhausted from toil, just like an ordinary person. This is the meaning. || 160 ||
That very same Prājāpati, though limited by the gross body, is this fire; therefore, he should be worshipped with diligent effort.

Stating the purport of the commentary beginning with "Teja eva rasaḥ" (Fire indeed is the essence), he speaks of the fruit of the restatement: "sthūla... etc. Since this very first Sūtrātman, Prajāpati himself, when delimited by the body of the Virāj, is accepted as this cit-agni (fire of consciousness), therefore this fire is to be meditated upon with care, continuously, and for a long time; such is the meaning. || 169 ||
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called Puruṣa.
He was the first creator of all beings; Brahmā appeared at the very beginning.

He cites a Purāṇic statement as proof for the claim that the Sūtrātman itself is delimited by the gross body: "He, indeed... Here, the Sūtrātman is referred to by various pronouns; he alone, having attained the state of Virāj, is spoken of by such terms as "the embodied one" (śarīrī) and so forth. Of the elements...
"At the head of the individual manifestations" means prior to the creation of individual manifestations. || 162 ||
Though his body is indefinable, he exists for the sake of establishing conventional discourse.
He divided himself into three gross forms: Wind, Fire, and Sun.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "He [became] threefold," as explained in the Bhāṣya: "Anupākhyā" (indefinable). Because Prajāpati’s body consists of the unevolved great elements (*apañcīkṛta-mahābhūta*), it is unfit for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); this is what is meant by his having an "indefinable body. Worldly transaction refers to activities such as ritual worship (*upāsti*). || 163 ||
Without destroying its own essential nature, it [is identified] with the deities of the Virāj through their self-natures.
For the sake of accomplishing worship and other such acts, he himself divided his own self.

In response to the inquiry as to who is the agent of this threefold manifestation—whether it be Prajāpati, Virāṭ, or Hiraṇyagarbha—the author states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view: "Svarūpa... etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the designation [of the object] and the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) resulting from that designation are included. || 164 ||
That Prajāpati, who is the very self of the root, divided himself threefold.
To provide a means of understanding this, it is said: "This very [is it]. (165)

In response to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Virāj is the agent who effects the threefold division, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The Root-Self" (*mūlātman*). He asks what the proof for this is and says: "Of this [it is said]. The meaning is that if the Virāj were the agent of the threefold division, the remainder of the passage would be rendered purposeless. || 111 ||

Of that Agni, the first-born of Virāj, who is like the sun and possesses the vigor of a steed—[vol2, page 39] 2 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 335. Just as [the horse] is for Vāja...
For the purpose of enjoining the act of seeing, it is proclaimed as "eastern" (prācī). || 166 ||

He states the meaning of "his eastern [direction]" and so forth with the words "of him" (*tasya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "By this statement, it is proclaimed that fire possesses the nature of time, the world, and the deity. (166)
For this reason, an effect does not exist apart from its cause.
Since the waters are the cause, fire is therefore established within them. || 167 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "this very [Self] is established in water" with the words "because... This means that it exists in the form of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread), within the waters which, accompanied by the other elements, constitute the causal state. By the word "fire," the terrestrial *virāj* is meant. || 167 ||
The man who constantly worships the deity Apratiṣṭhāguṇa.
Wherever he goes, there he obtains auspicious stability. || 168 ||

He explains the statement regarding the fruit beginning with "wherever" (*yatra kvacit*) as follows: "Without a fixed basis" (*apratiṣṭha*) means that which is auspicious, blameless, and not opposed to the world beyond. || 168 ||
He who, having thus purified himself through speech, created Virāj by his own power.
It is now stated with what kind of activity he was endowed when he emitted [the world]. || 169 ||

He states the connection between the passage beginning with "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*) and the preceding text, as explained in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "He who spoke," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the earth is included. In response to the inquiry—"By what activity was he endowed when he created Virāj, who consists of that [unmanifested world], through the sequence of creating the fivefold elements and their effects?"—it is said: "He who... and so forth. Here, "Death" (*mṛtyu*) refers to the Self of the unevolved phenomenal world (*apancīkṛta-prapañca*). He created Virāj, whose nature is that of the five gross elements and their products, according to the order of creation. It is now stated by which operation he performed that creation.
The meaning is: "by means of the internal text. || 169 ||
The creation of the Atṛs has been described previously; now the creation of the Anas is being told.
For one who is hungry, there is no subsistence due to the lack of food. || 170 ||

He states another connection that should be brought to light: "Aniti. The meaning is that while the creation of the eater was previously mentioned in the passage, "From the essence of heat, fire was produced," the creation of food is now being described; thus, the connection is more excellent. Having raised the doubt as to the purpose of describing the creation of food, he says, "Of one possessed of hunger," indicating that it is for the sake of the sustenance of the eater. For here, the creation of Virāj is made explicit. Aṃ...
This is because of the Vedic revelation, "He is Virāj," and because it will later be stated, "He will make food smaller. Therefore, the sense is that this connection as well is appropriate. || 170 ||
This is indeed demonstrated by the statement: "He divided himself threefold."
Agni and Māṇu have been described previously; now follows the origin of Saṃvatsara.

1. He states another connection: "In three ways. Now, one might object: since Prajāpati’s threefold nature was already stated previously by the passage beginning with "The sun as the third," why is there a subsequent statement for that purpose? To this he replies: "Fire... [He says] "Fire came forth," thus Fire is mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "and Vāyu as the third," it refers to Vāyu. Although Āditya is also mentioned in the passage "Āditya as the third," the meaning is that the subsequent scriptural text is intended to explain the birth of him whose self is the year (saṃvatsara). || 171 ||
336 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, Page 40]
The instruction of knowledge through the mind is called the triple Veda.
The Lord, through his wisdom, contemplated the sequence of creation as declared in the Vedas.

Having stated the connection in various ways, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "with the mind" (*manasā*). Regarding "with the mind": the construction is that "mind" (*manas*) is a designation for knowledge (*jñāna*), while "speech" (*vāk*) refers to the three Vedas (*trayī*). Having explained the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "at the time of creation," etc. "That Lord" (*sa prabhuḥ*) is a statement regarding the Sūtrātman. "By means of unimpeded knowledge" means by means of consciousness manifested through the transformation of the *sattva* quality. || 172 ||
By means of unimpeded knowledge, he [perceives] the sequence of creation as declared in the Vedas.
Śambhu, desiring to emit the manifold universe, gazed intently.

Now, one might object: "The Lord is not capable of perceiving the Vedic creation through his knowledge, because he is a person (puruṣa), just like ourselves. Anticipating this, [the author] states that "having obstructed knowledge" is the limiting adjunct (upādhi). Regarding the phrase "through knowledge": one might further object, "Is his desire to create for his own sake or for the sake of others? It cannot be the first, because he has all his desires fulfilled; nor can it be the second, because there are no other beings. Anticipating this, [the author] says that [the creation exists] for the sake of the enjoyment of the fruits of karma by the imagined living beings. Thus, its [creation's] existence is established.
Thinking thus, he said: "Śambhu. || 173 ||
For the union of the perceived object and the perceiver is called a pair.
A well-known couple can never, under any circumstances, be joined together. || 174 ||

Regarding the phrase "they became a couple" (*mithunaṃ samabhavat*), he explains the meaning of the word *mithuna*: "Having reflected," etc. The meaning is as follows: that which is to be reflected upon is the sequence of creation taught in the Vedas, while the reflector is the knowledge denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*); the union of these two—the state of being object and subject—is what is here called "the couple" (*mithuna*) as established in the Śruti. Anticipating the objection, "Why not take 'couple' here in its ordinary sense? he notes that [in the case of] a man and woman, it is irrelevant to the context.
He says "not so" [to that], stating "it is well-known. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the section concerning the internal self (*adhyātma*). || 174 ||
In order to prevent the undesirable consequence of an immediate connection.
For the author of the root text has indeed stated that [the suffix] -īya- expresses connection with the primary cause. (175)
He states the intended meaning of the mention of "hunger" (*aśanāyā*) in the phrase "death is hunger" (*aśanāyo mṛtyuḥ*) with the words "immediately following," etc.

The form *aśanīya* is a Vedic usage (chāndasa) serving as an adjective for death; it indicates that death is characterized by hunger. This repetition [of the idea] points toward the connection with the root aphorism (*mūlasūtra*).

Furthermore, in the passage "with that mind" (*sa manasā*), the pronoun (*sarvanāma*) indicates the connection with the fire (*agni*) and the sovereign (*virāj*) that were introduced immediately prior. Thus, [it refers] to that...
The meaning is that the cessation of the continuity of the relationship is the manner of the fruit. || 175 ||
That which the Householder [the Creator] produced of old as the seed for the process of the world.
Knowledge consists of duality and unity, and action is that which is accumulated through knowledge.
And the cultivation of those two—this triad is designated as "semen. (176)

Regarding the phrase "What was that seed (retas)? [the text] states the meaning of the word *retas*: "Of the world. *Prakriyā* means creation (*sṛṣṭi*). By the word "before" (*pura*), the state of the seeker (*sādhaka*) is indicated. He explains what that seed of the world's creation is which was accumulated by the sacrificer: "Duality... [and so on]. Upā... [text continues].

Since fame is the sole cause of vigor, let fame be regarded here as one's very life-breath.
Fame is of the nature of radiance, and vigor arises from the cause of that power.

In the passage, "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed glory (*yaśas*) and vigor (*vīryam*)," the fact that the vital breaths constitute glory and vigor has been stated; therein he states the reason [for this] with the word "glory. The second occurrence of the word "glory" is also an indicator for "vigor. By the word "here," either the sentence or the body is understood. He explains the specific meaning of the words "glory" and "vigor": "Glory," namely, renown (*khyāti*); it is so called by virtue of being the cause thereof.

The meaning is as follows: you are the glory of the vital breaths (prāṇas), for a man is not glorious when his vital breaths are non-existent; moreover, they possess the quality of being the cause of strength within the body, for no strength is observed in the body once they have departed; therefore, it is logical that they possess glory and vigor. || 203 ||
Fame and vigor departed from Virājas, who was emaciated by exhaustion.
In this context, the "mark" (liṅga) refers to fame and vigor, for both of these arise from it. || 204 ||
He analyzes the commentary beginning with "Thus, in this way" (*tadevam*) as follows: [The text says] "It departed. How can many vital breaths (*prāṇas*) possess fame and vigor (*yaśovīryatva*)?
For that state does not belong to each of them individually; even if one exists while others are absent, neither renown nor strength is perceived in the body.

Nor do they possess such a nature when combined, because if even one were absent, it would follow that those qualities would cease to exist. This is the intended meaning there, according to both the scripture (*śruti*) and the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

[The author] says: "The subtle body (liṅgātman). Here, "here" refers to the gross body. Anticipating the objection that this is not so because there is no usage of the words "glory" (yaśas) and "prowess" (vīrya) in reference to the subtle body by the elders, he says: "For both. Both glory and prowess arise from the subtle body;
since they are impossible in its absence, it is therefore correct that the subtle body possesses such a nature. This is the meaning. || 204 ||
Even though his body had been cast away, he still possessed attachment to his former life.
The abandonment of attachment is conceivable only through the realization of non-duality.

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "tasya" (of him) as follows: "pūrva... (the former...). [Objection: Even though he had emerged from the body of Prajāpati, why was there still attachment to that very same [body]?
For one who acts with deliberation does not long for a body which is a locus of suffering. To this, he replies: "saṅga... (attachment...).
The word "hi" (for) is used to indicate that the Smṛti passage beginning with "rasavarjam" (except for the sapid) is concordant with this point. || 205 ||
