Having incurred attachment to the body at birth, he remains there with a desire to realize identity with it.
Desiring [to create], he desired that which begins with "medhya" as his task.

He applies the commentary beginning with "In that" (*sa tasmin*) and so forth. Regarding the word "born" (*jāta*): the phrase "one who desires" (*kāmuka*) is used to state that attachment to that very body is the cause for the aforementioned longing. || 206 ||
His body, having cast aside its fame and vigor due to separation from the Sage, [remained].
Because he swelled (*aśvayat*), he became the horse (*aśva*); that vital breath (*asu*) was enclosed, and he became Prajāpati.

Now, one might object: "Since this was begun for the purpose of etymologically explaining the names of Prajāpati’s horse and so forth, why has something else been undertaken instead? To this, he says: "Apaviddhā" (cast off). Because of the separation of which vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the body, this body became devoid of fame and vigor, and *aśvayat*—that is, it became emaciated or fell into a state of decay.
Since it is a horse that goes, Prajāpati entered into that which is the horse; this is the meaning. Although the body is the horse, Prajāpati does not possess the nature of a horse.

Anticipating this doubt, he says, "The horse is Asura," because it possesses identity with that [Prajāpati]. The sense is that since the horse has been praised as Prajāpati, its status as an object of meditation is established. || 207 ||
Having lost its present glory and vigor, the impure attained purity.
Because he entered that [state], this Lord became the Aśvamedha. || 208 ||
Anticipating the objection as to how the etymology of the name *Aśvamedha* follows from the etymology of the word *aśva*, he says: "vyapete" and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is: "that from which glory (*yaśas*) and vigor (*vīrya*) have departed. For the body indeed becomes fit for sacrifice (*medhya*) through the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and upon their re-entry.
He deserves the name Aśvamedha; the meaning is that Prajāpati possesses the nature of the Aśvamedha sacrifice due to his identity with the body [of the horse]. || 208 ||
In this way, both the horse and the horse-sacrifice are directly [attained] through the nature of Prajāpati.
It is said: "How indeed might the two of them be praised? (209)
He states the result of that designation of "horseness" and so forth according to the method already described: "Aśva... (verse 209).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "The state of being a horse and the state of being the Aśvamedha sacrifice are declared [to belong] to Prajāpati."
Now, you are the horse and the mare, whose bodies are time, the world, and so forth.
The subsequent text has the meaning that the worship of the *samasyā* must be described. || 210 ||

[Objection: But since the horse, as a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), has been praised as being the Aśvamedha itself, and since the fire has been praised in the manner stated, and since the meditation (*upāsti*) upon them has already been mentioned, for what purpose is the passage beginning with "This indeed is the Aśvamedha" [repeated]? To this he replies: "Time," etc. The word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include the deity. And this qualification is connected to both [the horse and the fire]. The meditation on the horse was stated in the passage beginning with "The dawn indeed," etc., and the meditation on the fire has also been stated.
The meaning is that the subsequent sentence, beginning with "naiva" (not at all), is intended to state that those two are not mutually distinct, but rather are one and the same. || 210 ||
Due to the absence of an injunctive word, there is no mutual connection between them.
This subsequent scriptural statement, "of the words," is intended to prevent [the application of the rule] to those [words]. || 211 ||

He states [the answer] regarding how there is oneness between the two aforementioned meditations: "vidhāyaka... (by the injunctive word). Since in the preceding passage there was an absence of an injunctive word, it followed that the words were not mutually connected; so that this might not be the case, the subsequent sentence is set forth together with an injunctive word.

Although in the preceding part the injunction "he knows him as the beginning" (*āditi*) was heard, nevertheless, that was an injunction for meditation upon the qualified [Brahman] and not the primary injunction; whereas here, [the injunction concerns] the Aśvamedha.
The sense is that the primary injunction is what causes one to experience [the result]. || 219 ||
He alone truly understood the horse sacrifice according to its essential reality.
Therefore, one should know the Veda in the manner that will be described hereafter.

Having stated the purport of the subsequent statement, he connects its words [beginning with] "This" (*eṣa*). Since the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) suggests a well-known fact, one might ask: "How can there be an injunction? Anticipating this doubt, he states the intended injunction: "One should know" (*vidyāt*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that [the knower] is indeed a knower of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to the manner that is about to be described. || 212 ||
1 ka. ga. eva | [vol2, page 48] 344
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: Having conceived of the Self as possessing attributes such as time, worlds, and so forth...
Possessing such a body, he is the grandfather of all the worlds.

He provides the introductory context for this injunction with the words "the self" (*ātmānam*). The word "self" refers here to the body. He qualifies the horse-sacrifice with the word "time" (*kāla*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the deity is included. To determine the meaning of the word "self," he qualifies Prajāpati with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). It is appropriate that the horse, which is perceived through its association with time, world, and deity, should be regarded as the body of Prajāpati.
He says "all" because, as the cause of everything, there is the possibility of identity with all things. || 213 ||
"I shall perform the horse sacrifice once again," he thought.
He [beheld] himself as the horse, consisting of the worlds beginning with Bhūrloka, free from all restraint.
I released him from his bonds at will, setting him free as far as the end of the world.
Then, after a year has passed, he should also sacrifice that [animal] for himself.

In response to the inquiry as to why Prajāpati imagined his own body to be a horse-skin, he says: "I shall sacrifice. The meaning is that he imagined his own body to be a horse in accordance with his own resolve. Now, [one might object]: since he is himself a deity, there is no other deity [for him to offer to]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

Thinking that the aspiration "How might I sacrifice again? cannot arise because one lacks the qualification for ritual action (*karman*), [the author] considers that this is not so, as it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding meditation (*upāsti*). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "him" (*tam*) as follows: "Bhūḥ. "Unrestrainedness" (*niravagrahatva*) means being without restriction (*niraṅkuśatva*), that is, being unimpeded. The reason for this is "liberated" (*mukta*). "Independence" (*svacchandātva*) means acting according to one's own will, which is the fruit of being unimpeded. The word "horse" (*aśva*) occurs twice to indicate its attainment.

Dhānyadyotin. When it is asked what he did immediately after that, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Having passed that year" (taṃ saṃvatsaramyetya), etc., by saying "Then" (tataḥ).
By means of the two deities who have become the constituent parts of his own self, according to their respective roles.
That Prajāpati gave the domestic and wild animals to the other [goddesses]. || 216 ||

He explains the passage beginning with "the animal" (*paśu*) and so forth. Regarding the word "his own self" (*svātman*): for that Prajāpati, from those very deities who constitute the limbs of his own self—namely Agni and the others—in whatever manner each is described in the scripture, by that very manner [he offers].
The construction of the sentence is: "He gave domestic animals such as cows and so forth, and wild animals such as the gavaya and so forth. || 216 ||
Since Virāj acted in this manner, therefore here in this world, those who perform sacrifices act likewise.
The horse, dedicated to all the gods and to Prajāpati, was set free.
Therefore, one who knows the reality as it has been explained should perform the ritual slaughter.
One should perform this rite with the desire for the attainment of immortality. || 218 ||

Having introduced the ancient tradition (*purākalpa*) and considering that the injunction regarding meditation (*upāsti-vidhi*) is equal to the injunction regarding the sacrifice (*kratu-vidhi*), he explains the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

[He says] "Since" (*yataḥ*); "sprinkled" (*prokṣitam*) means consecrated by water purified through mantras. "Here" (*iha*) refers to the sacrificial ground. He states the reason for the phrase "belonging to all the gods" (*sarvadevatyam*) by saying "belonging to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyam*). Having thus prepared the preliminary stage (*bhūmikā*) for the injunction of meditation, he concludes that injunction.

"Yataḥ" means: because Prajāpati meditated in this manner, therefore anyone else should also meditate in this way; such is the construction of the sentence. As for "yathā," [in the manuscripts *kra* and *ga*, it is read as *svapavana*].
[Vol. 2, page 49]

[This section] excludes anyone who lacks the qualification for meditation [on the breath]. The word "yathā" (as) indicates that even such a person is qualified here only if they are dispassionate and desirous of liberation (*mumukṣu*).

The phrase "mṛtyutve" (in the state of death) implies that one who is dispassionate toward the breath cannot have the qualification for meditating on it as the Self, because of that [breath's] nature.
If one desires the status of being a master of recitation (jāpati), one should worship in this manner; such is the meaning. || 217 || 218 ||
Having thus explained ritual action and worship, [the author] now speaks with the desire to instruct on their fruits.
For it was with this very effort that the later Vedic revelation arrived, saying "This indeed. || 219 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the meditation on the horse itself is intended to be enjoined here, and since the injunction for that has already passed, what is the purpose of the subsequent sentence? To this he says: "Karma" (Action). He clarifies the occasion for the instruction regarding the goal (*upeya*) immediately following the instruction regarding the means (*upāya*), as indicated by the context. The word "atha" (now) serves this purpose. The particle "hi" (for) is used to indicate the reason: because the expectancy [of the listener] is not pacified without an instruction regarding the fruit (*phala*). Regarding the statement of the fruit—
The word "with effort" is stated for the purpose of precluding the view that [the Buddha's words] are merely discourses on things as they actually are (*yathārthavāda*). || 219 ||
But that which is thus accomplished by means of the horse, having been brought forth through vision and so forth—
It is shown that this very [Self] is directly perceived in the form of the fruit. || 220 ||

Having stated the purport that the subsequent passage is intended to declare the fruit of the meditation on the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), he explains the words: "From seeing," and so forth. That two-fold sacrifice—the horse-sacrifice which was previously described as being accomplished mentally through vision with the mind and having the fire-altar as its means, and the ritual performed physically with external horses and other materials—both of these, existing in the form of their fruit, are indeed Savitṛ; and he is this very one.
The meaning is that direct perception is thus demonstrated. || 220 ||
By means of the single path that is the final transformation of the performance of the horse sacrifice.
The horse-sacrifice is the Sun himself, declared by such passages as "the dawn," and so forth. || 221 ||

How is it that the Sun possesses both forms of the Aśvamedha? For he is not a ritual action performed by mind or body; to this, he says: "He is the horse. Indeed, the Aśvamedha rite is twofold: mental and physical. Through the attainment of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) resulting from its performance, the Sun himself is the mental Aśvamedha, which was previously set forth in the passage beginning with "The dawn is indeed the sacrificial horse" (*uṣā vā aśvamedhaḥ*). And [he is] the physical one as well.

This very [sacrificial essence] is what he directly accomplishes by means of horses and other such offerings; the meaning is that this is based on the traditional teaching (smṛti): "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun. || 221 ||
Who is he? His self is the year, because the sun is its sole cause.
Of that [sacrifice], which is of the nature of the Rite (ṛtu), that which was previously mentioned as its constituent part is the Citiya.
This very fire of the earth is now shown in its state as the fruit.
These three worlds, as previously described, are his very self.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the Sun is the essence of the fruit of ritual action (*kratu*), or the solar orb, or the deity, he accepts the second alternative and explains the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). As for "of that": how is the year the self of the Sun? For it [the year] is encompassed by time.

To the objection that what is cut cannot be non-different from that [from which it was cut], he replies with the words "of that" (*tasya*). By means of the rising and setting of the sun, through the mediation of day and night and so forth, there is the establishment of the year; therefore, it is appropriate for that [year] to have identity (*tādātmya*) with its creator—this is the meaning. Having stated that the sacrifice (*kratu*) is the sun, he now states the meaning of the passage "Agni is the sun" (*agniḥ arkaḥ*), in order to declare that Agni, who is a constituent part of that [sacrifice], is likewise [the sun]. He says "of that" (*tasya*): "This which..."
• [vol2, page 50] 346
The meaning is that by means of the present passage,

it is demonstrated that the very fire which was mentioned in the statement, "From the essence of light, Agni was produced— the fire to be piled up from earth, consisting of parts"— is indeed the fruit-bearing *arka*, namely Savitṛ himself. Alternatively, by the word *arka*, Agni himself is meant, and he is Savitṛ alone.

This is the meaning of the sentence. Now, one might object: "Why is it restricted that the fire previously mentioned is itself the sun? Why could it not be that the fire to be piled (*cit*) is one thing and the fire that is the sun is another? Anticipating this doubt, he connects the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). Regarding the phrase "the selves" (*ātmānaḥ*): the fact that it was previously described as having the form of the fire to be piled has been stated; furthermore, by means of the passage beginning with "its eastern [quarter]," its nature as the self of the world (*lokātmatva*) was attributed to that fire to be piled. That—
Moreover, it is said that its very nature as the sun (ādityatva) is intended here; this is the meaning. || 222 || 223 ||
The sacrifice and its means, which constitute the self, have been explained as being like the Ādityas.
Those two, whose natures are established as subjects, would become one and the same vital breath.

Now, one might object: "The Sun has been called the *kratu* (the sacrifice), and Fire is its cause; how then can there be an identity between these two, the means and the end? Anticipating this doubt, the author explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "those two" (*tau*). Regarding the verse beginning with *ṛtu*: The Sun is the self of the *kratu*, because he is its fruit; and the Fire to be piled up (*cityo 'gniḥ*) is the self of the means of the *kratu*. These two, having performed their respective functions—such as meditation—as previously divided, are in truth one single deity named Prāṇa. Thus, between those two...
The meaning is that this is a figurative expression (khyokti). || 224 ||
Hunger is yoked as death, which devours all beings without exception.
The very self of the wise man who practices service shall become the manifest Self, undecaying and immortal.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "What is the death beyond death? by saying, "possessing hunger and thirst. For hunger is indeed death; thus, that deity called *prāṇa*, who possesses hunger and thirst and is the destroyer of the entire gross phenomenal world, is said to be the object of meditation. The meaning is that by the principle of "as is one's resolve (*tatkratu*"), that very deity is the self (*ātman*) of the meditator. [Objection: If the deity possessing hunger and so forth is the self of the meditator, then [the meditator] would suffer from hunger.
Fearing that one afflicted by scabies might suffer great misery and thus there would be no benefit from worshipping such a [limited] entity which causes harm, he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*).
For the Self of Death is indeed direct—the unconditioned, devoid of old age and so forth. If that is the Self of the worshipper, how could it not be free from all afflictions?
And by the mention of "hunger and so forth," the sense is that its nature as a destroyer is intended. || 225 ||
No internal death can reach him, for that [internal death] is itself his death.
Having died but once with this physical body, one is liberated from all bonds.
Although for the knower death is the Self, one might still suspect that because of his connection with the body, he would be subject to the death pertaining to the body;

anticipating this doubt, the author explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "not him" (*nainam*). [He says: "Not him. Then, one might suspect that if so, the body of the knower would remain indestructible, and thus his status as a body would be contradicted; anticipating this doubt, the author explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "death also" (*mṛtyurapyeti*). [He says: "Once," [by means of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇātmanā*)].

The wise one, remaining established [in that state], abandons the present body at the conclusion of the karma already set in motion; thereafter, he attains liberation from all bonds, meaning he does not take up a body again for the purpose of birth. || 226 ||
Of all the deities, without exception, who are distinguished by differences such as Agni and others.
This wise one, through the aforementioned meditation, becomes non-different from the Self.
Thus ends the second [chapter], the Aśvamedha Brāhmaṇa, in the *Vārttika* on the commentary to the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*.
[Vol. 2, Page 51] 3 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

347. Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not improper for the man of knowledge (vidvān) to be entirely liberated from all connections, since he remains subject to the command of deities such as Agni? Anticipating this doubt, [the text says]: these—
He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "sāmityādi" as follows: "agnyādi," etc. || 227 ||
Thus ends the second Aśvamedha Brāhmaṇa in the commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārtika-Ṭīkā. || 2 ||
Now begins the third Brāhmaṇa.
[It concerns] actions endowed with the knowledge prescribed in the scriptures, as well as through knowledge itself.
In this entire Vedic scripture, it is heard that the state of death is the result.

Anticipating the objection that since "victory over death" is spoken of through the power of action combined with knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation must therefore be rendered purposeless by right cognition (*samyagdhi*), he recounts the preceding context: "In the scripture," etc. This refers to those meditations (*upāsanā*) taught here and there in the scripture, as well as the actions combined with them; and [it refers] to the mere [actions] in this immediately explained work consisting of the Veda, which is devoted to the instruction of what is beneficial.

Furthermore, in all other contexts concerning meditative worship (*upāsti*), the result is stated to be [merely] freedom from death; for that liberation is secondary (*gauṇī*) because of the continued connection with hunger and so forth.
However, absolute liberation (*ātyantikī muktiḥ*) arises only from perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); such is the meaning of its purposefulness. || 1 ||
That upon which the cessation of internal conceptual differentiation depends.
That death is here designated by the word "death" as the resulting fruit.

In order to exclude the death that will be described later, the author of the *Bhāṣya* explains the meaning of the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) in the phrase "the nature of death" (*mṛtyvātmabhāva*). [He does so] by saying "ādhyātmika... and so forth. For one who meditates constantly on the Sūtra as the Self, there arises the cessation of the conceit of limitation dependent upon connection with the body; for one who meditates through identification with that Self, death exists as the fruit that destroys the conceit of limitation, as stated in the passage beginning with "death belongs to him," etc.

And in the present commentary, it is stated that by the word "death" (mṛtyu), that death which is about to be described is meant; the meaning is that there is no occasion here for the [other] death. || 2 ||
That statement regarding the attainment of the horse-sacrifice is for the purpose of establishing it as an illustration.
For those between ritual action and knowledge, there would be no attainment of the horse sacrifice.

Anticipating the objection that the attainment of death is stated as the fruit of the meditation on the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha)—whether accompanied by the sacrifice itself or performed alone—and not as the fruit of other meditations or other ritual acts, he says: "But that which... The statement regarding the fruit of the meditation on the Horse Sacrifice is intended as an illustration of the fruits of other meditations, whether performed individually or in combination; it is not meant to restrict the fruit solely to the meditation on the Horse Sacrifice, for [the fruit] arises from all [meditations].
The meaning is that dispassion (*vairāgya*) is desired because it is the aggregate of all means [to liberation]. || 3 ||
The attainment of a lesser fruit results from limited knowledge and action.
The smallness of these two [the individual soul and the intellect] is due to their being overwhelmed by the evils of the asuras.

If actions conjoined with knowledge have as their fruit the attainment of the *sūtra* (the subtle body), how can there be the attainment of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth? For a single means does not lead to both the world of Brahmā and the world of the ancestors; otherwise, it would contradict such scriptural statements as, "By action one attains the world of the ancestors, by knowledge the world of the gods. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The smaller [is attained]... By the greater [means], namely knowledge and action combined, or by either alone, [the respective results are attained]. Thus...

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the Śruti in establishing the rule that through knowledge one attains the world of Brahmā, while through those same two [knowledge and action] in their lesser degree one attains the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) and so forth.
Now, one might object: what constitutes the "lesserness" of knowledge and action? Is it the yielding of inferior results, or is it having a limited scope?

It cannot be the first, because that would involve mutual dependence; nor can it be the second, because [limited scope] is seen even in the case of sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) and the like, just as one might experience a cold sensation when striking one's own foot.
1 [vol2, page 52] 348

Regarding the phrase "insignificance" (*alpatvam*): the insignificance of those two—knowledge and ritual action—would arise from their being overwhelmed by the evil of the Asuras; thus, the construction is that their very state of being overwhelmed constitutes their insignificance. (4)
How could there be [freedom] for one who is overwhelmed by the demonic evils of passion and the like?
Let the manifestation of action and, moreover, of knowledge be described.

The *sūtrānta* (the conclusion of the aphorism) concerns the excellence of the fruit of knowledge and action; however, it is objected that it is improper to say that when those two are impaired by passion and so forth, the result is the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and the like, because even in meditations on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so on, there is the possibility of such impairment, and thus unimpaired knowledge and action would be absent. [The author] asks: "Why?

The sense is that since the cause for the emergence of those two is difficult to state, the attainment of the *sūtra* (the subtle body) through them when they have emerged is difficult to obtain. || 1 ||
"One attains death directly through action joined with knowledge"—
this very point has been proclaimed in the ancient scriptures and the traditional teachings.
To state that the deity of breath (prāṇa) is the object of worship and the cause for the emergence of those two [day and night], he summarizes what has been stated at length: "Mṛtyum" and so forth.

The meaning is that it has been heard repeatedly in earlier passages—such as "Death is his self"—and in other statements within the context of meditations (upāsti), that one attains the thread (sūtra) as one's self either through ritual action combined with meditation or through meditation alone. ||6||
For the sake of destroying obstacles to the arising of that knowledge and for the attainment of knowledge that brings about its destruction.
The subsequent scriptural passage begins for the sake of attaining the deity of the *udgītha*.

Now, he states the connection between the preceding and the subsequent Brāhmaṇas with the words "tajjñāna" (knowledge of that). Knowledge and action are the means for accomplishing that state of being a Sūtra;

passion and the like are the obstacles to their arising. For the purpose of attaining that knowledge and so forth which serve as the cause for the destruction of those obstacles, the deity of the Udgītha known as Prāṇa must be grasped. To that end, the Śruti beginning with "dvayā ha" is commenced in this Upaniṣad.
For the meaning is that the vital breath (prāṇa), when manifested by the mantra and sustained, is the cause for the destruction of the aforementioned obstacles. || 7 ||
Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that [liberation] results from the knowledge and ritual action concerning the Udgītha, which transcend death?"
Because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit, death does not result from this; that is the fruit for those two.

Having stated the commencement of the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of defining the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which brings forth both knowledge and action, [the author] raises an objection regarding the aforementioned connection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). For, on the one hand, there is the hearing of the result of the knowledge and action of the Udgītha—which is yet to be described—as "he shines, having transcended death," while on the other hand, in the preceding section, the state of being the Self of death was stated as its result; therefore, between these two [results], there is no... death.

The meaning is as follows: "Attainment is the fruit of the two preceding [meditations], but that [attainment] belongs to them"—thus, because there is a difference in their fruits, and because these two (the preceding and succeeding ones) differ in their objects, they are not included among those already mentioned or those yet to be described; therefore, this Brāhmaṇa is intended to reveal the nature of the knowledge and action of the former [meditation]. || 8 ||
Because the scripture reveals that [the sacrificer] has the nature of deities such as Agni and so forth, and [attains] their fruits.
The transcendence of natural, unimpeded death is a distinct fruit.

He offers a rebuttal, stating: "Not [the case] regarding Agni and the others. Since the nature of the deities beginning with Agni—which is the fruit of the knowledge and ritual action concerning the *udgītha*—is about to be explained, and since it was already stated previously in the passage "of these deities," there is no difference between the fruits of the knowledge and ritual action in the preceding and succeeding sections. Because they share a single subject matter, the Brāhmaṇa is stated for the purpose of explaining them both together. Thus: "He becomes one of these deities"; he is that Agni...
The subsequent Śruti passage beginning with "He becomes" (*bhavati*) and so forth is what is understood by the term "Śruti. How, then, does he shine having transcended death?

Thus the Śruti says there: "Inherently" (*svābhāvikā*). Regarding the word "separate" (*pṛthak*), the phrase "from the state of death" (*mṛtyubhāvāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The sense is that this statement concerns the intermediate fruit, whereas the supreme fruit is the state of being the Sūtra. || 9 ||
What is this innate evil, and from where does its manifestation arise?
Therefore, it is said: "By what means would there be a cessation [of this], and how? (10)

Having stated that knowledge and action are death and that their supreme fruit consists in being unobstructed, and having explained the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of teaching meditation on the vital deities (*prāṇadevatā*) and so forth—which destroys such obstructions—the author restates the question found in the commentary in order to explain the scriptural meaning of the narrative: "Who is this? Therein, the nature of innate evil (*svābhāvikapāpman*) is addressed regarding the first question.

One should distinguish that the object is for the second [question], that which produces it is for the third, that which removes it is for the fourth, and the instrument for its removal is for the fifth.
Having restated the four questions, he announces the answer: "This, namely... (10).
The scripture, consisting of narratives, exists for the purpose of establishing the meaning as it has been stated.
"Is it two? and so forth—she proceeded in this manner to examine him. || 11 ||

For this scripture, beginning with "These two," which takes the form of a narrative, has commenced in order to determine the true nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the knowledge of the fourfold set—natural evil and so forth—as it was previously described and sought to be understood; thus it indicates the subsequent [result]. As stated:
Whosoever is the qualified seeker who desires to attain the station of Prajāpati.
Having been determined by this scripture, one attains the state through meditation.

In response to the question—whether this definition benefits only the meditation on the *udgītha* or all meditations on the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the author adopts the second alternative by stating, "Belonging to Prajāpati. Whoever desires to attain the position described in the Sūtra, seeking the means thereto, determines through this scripture that the vital breath possesses qualities such as purity; and [he then applies this] to the various qualities mentioned in each respective context.

The meaning is that through its meditation one attains that state; therefore, this inquiry is beneficial for all meditations upon the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is stated that "the qualified person" [is required] in order to exclude others. || 12 ||
Whatever was performed by the current Prajāpati in his previous birth.
The particle *ha* is employed here as an indicator (*dyotaka*) of that [meaning].

Having stated the meaning of the Brahmana and the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), he explains the meaning of the particle while analyzing the syllables, beginning with "pūrva" (before). This refers to Hiraṇyagarbha—the current Prajāpati—who was manifested in the form of the fruit at the beginning of this Kalpa. It is precisely the indicative function (*dyotakatva*) of particles [that is intended], and not [their denotative function].
The phrase "vācakatvam" (the state of being expressive) is a word used as an indicator; it is the meaning of the locative case in the first sentence. || 13 ||
Relying on his future state, the sacrificer is Prajāpati.
But here, no other [entity] whatsoever is declared to be purposeful. || 14 ||

Regarding the term *prājāpatyāḥ*, he states the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*): "bhaviṣyat" (future). The word "iha" (here) refers to the mention of the word ending in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*).
[Vol. 2, p. 54] 1. ka. ga. [variant: 'caye]
350. One might raise the objection: "Why should it not be that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is intended here by the term *prajāpati*? Anticipating this, he says: "Another..."
"Let it be so. || 14 ||
For the instruction regarding knowledge and action is in every respect intended for human beings alone.
Since everything is based on what is heard from scripture, that alone is what is designated here.

Although it exists in identity with the purpose (*prayojana*), nevertheless, as for the question "What is the status of that very thing which has become the fruit?", [the author] states: "Knowledge," etc. For here, by means of the narrative of the battle between the Prajāpati-born gods and demons, the duties of knowledge and action are declared for Prajāpati; and all instruction regarding knowledge and so forth is presented equally in terms of subordinate and primary status.

Or rather, in every respect, it is appropriate that the scripture—whether based on Śruti or Smṛti—applies only to one who possesses the conceit of being human and so forth, because its authority is restricted to such a person; therefore, the meaning here is that Prajāpati is the sacrificer. || 15 ||
And because they are born from that karma and knowledge, those vital breaths (*prāṇas*) arise from purity and impurity.
In this context, they are called "belonging to Prajāpati" (prājāpatya) because of their connection with speech and the indicative mark of the yoke-pole.

He explains [the term] for the sake of indicating the meaning of the suffix and to prevent its application elsewhere: "that action" (*tatkarma*). The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is connected with the word *prāṇa* that follows. Because they are produced by both the scriptural and the natural knowledge and action of that sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is precisely speech (*vāk*) and the other [organs], which have those as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that are intended in this present passage as belonging to Prajāpati; and they are pure—

The meaning is that the gods are born from scriptural knowledge and action denoted by the term "pure," while the asuras are born from innate knowledge and action denoted by the term "impure"; however, this does not imply that Indra and the like, or Virocana and the like, are actually involved here. Now, one might object: since there exist many channels (nāḍīs) and other structures within the body belonging to the sacrificer, why are only speech and the other [organs] mentioned here? Anticipating this doubt, he states [the answer]: "Because of the remainder of the sentence."
Regarding the phrase "speech and so forth": the word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. || 16 ||
And because of its connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, as well as [the mention] of "fear" (*bhaya*) and so forth.
Therefore, this narrative has been set forth for the purpose of purifying the object of worship.

Having explained the purport regarding the status of a Brāhmaṇa and the meaning of the scriptural narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), the words "Two [groups], indeed, [were] of Prajāpati" have been interpreted. Now, suspecting that the narrative might be restricted to its own literal meaning, he states its true purport: "In the Udgītha," etc.

The meaning is that because the passage beginning with "Two, indeed," is connected to the meditation on the Udgītha, it is not restricted to its own literal meaning. Since it is not so restricted, [the following] is the object of meditation.
Having distinguished [the two], he states the resulting conclusion that it is a narrative (ākhyāyikā): "The object of meditation," etc. || 17 ||
In this case, for the recitation performed while ascending, let the vital breath (prāṇa) itself be the deity.
Why, then, are speech and the other [organs] not [the self]? To examine this, the following investigation is undertaken. (18)

How is that purification [attained]? To this he says: "He ascends. Here, when it is asked—"Let the deity of both the recitation named 'Abhyārohaṇa' which will be described in the Brāhmaṇa and of the meditation on the Udgītha be Prāṇa alone, and not Speech and the others; why so?"—the meaning is that the examination of that deity is carried out by means of the narrative under discussion. The subject matter of the narrative under discussion is—
Therefore, it is sound. || 18 ||
1 Kha.
tu | [vol2, page 55] Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 351
By means of positive and negative concomitance, for the purpose of establishing the primacy of the vital breath.
These narratives have been set forth with effort through the censure of the organs of speech and the rest. (19)

He states the result of the investigation: "By positive and negative concomitance," etc. Since the activity of speech and the other organs occurs only when breath exists and not otherwise, it is established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—as well as by the censure of speech and the others for being pierced by the evil of Asura—that breath is superior. This is for the purpose of establishing that breath, which is free from such piercing and sustains the aggregate of the body, is the object of meditation by way of its preeminence. Therefore, breath is the one to be meditated upon.
The knowledge that speech and the other [organs] are not [the Self] is the fruit of investigation; this indeed is the purity of the object of meditation—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
This is due to the causes consisting of the knowledge and karmic impressions born from the intrinsic nature of the scriptures.
The state of being a god or an asura arises from the cause of the vital breaths when their limiting adjuncts are restrained.

Having stated the ultimate purport of the narrative, the author addresses the doubt as to how the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the sacrificer can possess the nature of both gods and demons, and says: "By the scripture... Because speech and the other organs are refined by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge and action—which arise from both the scripture and one's own innate nature—their state consists of being refined by scriptural knowledge and the like, as well as being refined by other [non-scriptural] knowledge and the like.

The meaning is that, due to the cause consisting of a connection with contradictory attributes, the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the sacrificer possess both the nature of a deity and the nature of an asura. || 20 ||
Just as the single vital breath (prāṇa) is designated by various divisions such as "thousandfold" and so forth.
Or rather, there is a division of speech and the other [organs] according to the distinction of their respective functions. (21)

He states the twofold nature of speech and the other organs by means of a scriptural illustration: "A thousand, etc. Due to the specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of their various offices and locations, the single Sūtra-self is said to have a division into a number of three thousand, three hundred, and six in passages such as, "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? Similarly, speech and the others possess a twofold nature based on the limiting adjuncts of being either natural or refined by knowledge and so forth.
The meaning is that there is a twofold nature. || 21 ||
The innate conduct of all beings is considered to be demonic.
Where the deity is to be established, from there the Asuras were more powerful. || 22 ||

He states the purport of the verses beginning with "tataḥ" as follows: "Innate" (*sahaja*). For, through the medium of identification with the body, the demonic conduct consists of violence, falsehood, and so forth, whereas the divine conduct consists of non-violence, truthful speech, and so forth; this is the distinction. It should be understood that the gods (*devas*) are indeed few in number. || 22 ||
In this context, words such as "speech" (vāk) and others denote deities.
But because they are mortal, those things situated in the senses and within the range of perception are not grasped.

Having denoted the sense organs by means of words such as "speech" (*vāk*) and so forth, he states that they have the deities as their objects. Regarding the word "here" (*iha*), it refers to the Brāhmaṇa passage.
Anticipating the objection—"Why are the well-known sense organs themselves not mentioned by those very words?"—he says: "Because of their mortality," etc. [The text continues: "The hand..."

The locations of the [senses] are called "golaka"; it is the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) residing therein that are meant, not the words such as "speech" (*vāc*) and so forth, because their nature is perishability—this is the intended meaning. || 23 ||
1ka. It is cherished; 2 ka. ga. from that;
[vol2, page 56] 352.

In this [work], the identity with the deity alone is the fruit of the knowledge and ritual actions concerning the gods, as composed by Sureśvarācārya in his *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, in the first chapter.
The section concerning the internal [self] and so forth is not accepted because it pertains to the demonic nature.

Anticipating the objection, "Even though they are subject to destruction, why should there not be an acceptance of those very things? he says: "The deity. In this Brāhmaṇa, it will be stated that the fruit of ritual action accompanied by meditations on speech and the other organs is the state of having the nature of deities such as Agni. Therefore, that which exists within the body in the context of the internal self—

The limitation of speech and the other organs, which is designated by the term "instrument" (karaṇa), is not what is intended here, because that belongs to the asuras. Rather, the meaning is that through the internal (ādhyātmika) speech and other organs, those terms ultimately refer to the divine (ādhidaivika) fire and so forth. || 24 ||
For even among those who seek the highest good, the mind generally inclines toward violence.
Therefore, the Asuras are more numerous than the gods; the Atiyavrajās are fewer still.

Having identified the sense organs, beginning with speech, by those very terms, he explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "for [it is] natural" (*svābhāvikī hi*). He says "violence" (*hiṃsā*). The word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is used in order to set aside the restrictive rule (*niyama*). The word "also" (*api*) is used in order to state what further [actions] lead to misfortune (*aśreyas*). For violence of the mind—

Regarding the state of being inclined [toward the senses], because there is an abundance of the functioning of innate knowledge (*svābhāvikajñāna*) and so forth, there follows an abundance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) characterized by those qualities; this results in the statement that the Asuras are numerous.

He says, "The many" (*bhūyāṃsaḥ*). Regarding the state of being few, because scriptural knowledge (*śāstrīyajñāna*) and so forth are scant, the vital breaths characterized by them are likewise few; this results in the further conclusion that the Devas are few. He says, "The Devas. The phrase "born of excessive effort" (*atiyatnajāḥ*) refers to knowledge and action that are accomplished through extreme exertion.
The meaning is that they are obtainable. || 25 ||
Because everything from Brahmā down to the stationary objects is produced solely by merit and demerit.
Then the Daityas contended with one another and with the gods.

He explains the meaning of "tad-tyādi" (beginning with 'ta') as "dharma" and so forth. Since every place of enjoyment is produced by dharma, adharma, and both of these, it follows that for that reason—in that causal context—the Asuras and Devas, through their own natural and otherwise [acquired] knowledge and karma, engaged in mutual conflict; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
Having raised Prajāpati up from his Asura offices, [he established him] here.
"By leading him to the divine realms," such was the intention of the gods.

He states the intention of the gods as they compete with the asuras: "To the asuras... The meaning is that the gods' intended purpose is: "Having turned the sacrificer—who stands upon the path of worldly conduct—away from innate knowledge and action, we shall lead him to scriptural knowledge and action. || 27 ||
Having wrested him away from the gods, those whose means are desire, anger, and so forth—
"Bring the lands of the Asuras," was the resolve of the Daityas.

He states the intention of the Asuras with the words "from the gods. The meaning is that the Daityas intended: "Having separated the sacrificer from scriptural knowledge and the like, we shall bring him under the power of desire and so forth, such as ignorance and the rest. || 28 ||
Wherein the gods and the dānavas [subsist] by means of the two modes of life arising from the two solstices.
The divine and the asuric beings contended with one another in mutual opposition.

He states the intended meaning of the commentary beginning with "of the gods" (*devānām*) as follows: "When... (*yadā*). At no time does the goddess—the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of scriptural knowledge and so forth—[arise].
[End of Brāhmaṇa 3, Volume 2, page 57] accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 353.
The divine nature sometimes overcomes the demoniac, while at other times the demoniac—consisting of natural tendencies such as ignorance and so forth—arises and overcomes the divine;

this is the meaning of "the rivalry between the gods and the demons. Because of the mutual opposition between these two types of tendencies, which serve as the cause for the rivalry between the gods and the demons, their conflict cannot be reconciled; thus he says: "due to opposition" (virodhataḥ). || 29 ||
Furthermore, those gods, deprived of support, were overcome by the power of the Asuras.
Wealth and honor did not find refuge because of their insignificance.

[The author] states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "ta evam" (those very ones thus): "bhūyaḥ" (furthermore). He states the reason for being oppressed: "nirāśrayāḥ" (without support). "Śaraṇam" means happiness or a place of refuge. He states another reason for being tormented: "alpatva" (insignificance). || 30 ||
Not seeing him, they gathered together and spoke to one another:
"Let it be done without hesitation!"—the word "hanta" is used here in the sense of assent. (31)

He states the meaning of "te tyādi" (those words beginning with "te") as "anīkṣamāṇāḥ" (not looking). The word "hanta" expresses consent; he states the nature of that consent as "kriyatām" (let it be done). || 31 ||
Having conquered the Asuras who sought to defeat us by taking refuge in the Udgātṛ priest himself.
Transcending the demonic nature, we recognize him as being of the very essence of the gods.
In response to the inquiry "What is that which is to be done?", he says: "Asmad... He explains the meaning of "by means of the Udgītha" with the words "udgātriti.

The meaning is: by means of the Prāṇa, which is the self (ātman) of the Udgātṛ, serving as its support. Demonstrating this very point through the phrase "having conquered the Asuras," he explains the sense of the prefix with the word "atilayeti. He explains the meaning of "ayāma" with the word "devateti. || 32 ||
The attainment of the deity of the Udgītha results from the combination of knowledge and ritual action.
The ritual of the Abhyāroha-japa has been performed; now, knowledge is being examined here.

Anticipating the question by what means one may take recourse to the Udgātṛ as the Self and the vital breath (prāṇa), he says: "The Udgītha," etc. To specify whether that is an action or a form of knowledge, he says: "By superimposition" (abhyāroha). || 33 ||
Because it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to an injunction, this is not a definitive description of knowledge.
If it is argued that this would be so because of the two-fold [nature] expressed as "it is thus" and "one should know it thus," [we reply: no.

The opponent objects: "The passage beginning with 'dvayā ha' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1) is not intended to define knowledge, because it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) subordinate to an injunction; therefore, how can there be an examination of knowledge here? [The author] replies: "vidhi... etc. Since the injunction for meditation (*upāsti*) is heard, he counters that the sentence is indeed intended to convey that [meditation]. [The opponent says: "Not so... (verse 34).
And [the meditation] is a subordinate element of the rule for the *udgītha*, because it is heard in the context of the *udgītha* archetype.
It is not logical that this [scripture] should have no specific subject matter, because such a thing is seen elsewhere as well. // 35 //

As for the claim that this is an *arthavāda* because it is supplementary to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatvāt*), one must consider whether it is supplementary to the injunction regarding the *udgītha* or supplementary to the injunction regarding the *japa*. Having raised this alternative, he restates the first position: "The *udgītha*... The meaning is: since a mythological narrative (*purākalpa*) beginning with "dvayā ha" is heard in proximity to the *prastāva* within the context of the primary ritual (*prakṛti*) of the *audgātra* rite, how can this be considered a determination of knowledge, given that this *arthavāda* is merely supplementary to that [ritual] injunction? It is not [supplementary] to the *udgītha*...
45 1 ka. ga. its procedure; 2 ka. ga. its procedure.
[vol2, page 58]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter One, Verse 354:

He provides the following resolution: "It is logical that [the Upaniṣadic teachings] are subordinate to injunctions (*vidhiśeṣatvam nyāyyam*), because they do not belong to the context of those [injunctions], and because what is to be known is enjoined within the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇe*)."
"No," and so forth. || 39 ||
And because this is a section concerning knowledge (vidyā), the udgītha is not being enjoined here.
And because the recitation (japa) is also non-obligatory, it may indeed be employed by one who possesses such knowledge. || 36 ||

[Objection: But why should the injunction regarding the *udgītha* not apply right here, given that we see such [injunctions] as "one should chant the *udgītha" (*udgāyet*)? To this he says: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*). This is a statement regarding the context (*prakaraṇa*). The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that the injunction "one should chant the *udgītha*" is not an injunction for the *udgītha* itself; rather, it serves the purpose of accepting the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) by means of deprecating speech and the other [organs], following upon that [mention of the *udgītha*]. He states that [the passage] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) because it is subordinate to the injunction for recitation (*japa*), saying: "Of the recitation" (*japasya*). It is not mandatory.

The meaning is this: since the recitation (*japa*) is not something that must be performed by one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*), even in the absence of such recitation, the attainment of the fruit occurs for the knower through knowledge alone; however, meditation (*upāsana*) is indispensable, because without it the superior fruit cannot be achieved through mere recitation. Therefore, since the non-obligatory recitation cannot necessitate the obligatory meditation enjoined by scripture—due to the impossibility of joining the obligatory with the non-obligatory—the sentence in question cannot be subordinate to an injunction regarding recitation. Alternatively, [the argument concerns] the vital breath...

The recitation (japa) is to be connected with one who possesses knowledge; it does not exist prior to that knowledge, nor does it occur subsequently [to it], for it employs a knowledge that is already established beforehand.

Indeed, the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth do not cause the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), precisely because they are themselves employed by them. Likewise, the recitation employed by the knower of the vital breath (*prāṇavid*) does not cause that knowledge, since it is already established as being employed by it. Thus, the meaning is that this [recitation] is not a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of that [knowledge]. || 36 ||
For it is heard here that knowledge possesses a noble fruit.
Therefore, because it possesses a fruit, this knowledge is intended to be enjoined. (37)

Furthermore, since in this context the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by a superior fruit, is heard from the passage beginning with "This indeed" (*taddhaitat*), and because it possesses such a fruit, it is intended that the knowledge concerning it be enjoined; thus he says, "Two [classes of gods]... and so forth, meaning that this refers only to that [knowledge of the *prāṇa*] and not to another injunction. (37)
In this context, meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) is intended according to the principle of purity and impurity.
If the meditation on the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) were not intended here by means of the censure of speech and the other [senses], [verse 38].
Furthermore, what would be the result of praising or censuring that which is intended to be destroyed?
Therefore, an explanatory passage (arthavāda) and so forth are inferred here from the indicative mark of an injunction (vidhi-liṅga). || 39 ||
1.1 He states another reason for the intended subject being the meditation on Prāṇa: "Purity," etc. The purity and impurity of Prāṇa [are dependent] on speech and so forth—

The meaning is that, by virtue of the statement "the miserable," meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is intended in this section; otherwise, the mention of purity and impurity would be useless. Making this very point explicit, he explains the commentary beginning with "for" (*hi*). "Speech and so forth" (*vāgādi*): "here" (*iha*) is as before. The word "then" (*atha*) means "in that case. "Censure of that" (*tannindā*) is the censure of speech and the other senses. The word "this" (*ana*) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For... [yaddhi]...

Relying on the maxim that "that which is praised is thereby enjoined," he states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that, based on this *arthavāda*—which functions as a metaphorical praise of Prāṇa due to its purity by contrast with the impurity of speech and the other [senses]—an injunction for the meditation on Prāṇa is inferred.

The word "for" (*hi*) is used to indicate that the inference of an injunction from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of an *arthavāda* is well-known in other instances as well. Indeed, the context itself...
The meaning is that of the locative case. || 38 || 39 ||
1. Smārta | [vol2, page 59] 3 Brāhmaṇa | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 355
And because it is heard in scripture that the fruit of meditation is the attainment of the very nature of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore, let it be observed that the worship of the Unmanifest (Anas) is what is intended to be enjoined. || 40 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the meditation on *prāṇa* is what is intended to be taught, by saying "prāṇa... Since it ought to have been said, "because it is the fruit of meditation," the alternative phrasing is used to indicate its Vedic (chāndasa) character; hence the sandhi [elision] is like that in the word *soṣām*. According to such scriptural passages as "having transcended death, he shines," the fruit of meditating on speech and the other organs is the attainment of the nature of fire and so forth, which is caused by the attainment of the true nature of *prāṇa*; therefore, it is what is intended to be taught.

The meaning is that it is the meditation upon that [Prāṇa]. Regarding the phrase "possessing noble fruit," in the previous instance the fruit of the meditation on Prāṇa was stated to be the state of being the *sūtra* (the thread-like cosmic self); here, however, the distinction is that the state of being Agni and so forth—produced by that [meditation on Prāṇa]—is declared for the speech and other organs of the meditator. Thus, since the meditation on Prāṇa is intended to be enjoined, he concludes that the passage beginning with "Two kinds indeed... is a supplementary portion (*śeṣa*) to that injunction, stating: "Meditation. || 40 ||
Let there be the worship of the Sun as desired, according to the justification provided by the hymns.
However, the possession of qualities such as purity and so forth is not established by means of valid cognition. || 41 ||
He concedes, saying "let it be so," that there may indeed be meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by virtue of the occurrence of unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) as taught [in scripture].

However, there is no deity of the vital breath (*prāṇadevatā*) possessing qualities such as purity and the like, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). This is because the scripture, being intent upon the injunction for meditation, has no underlying purport (*atātparya*) regarding such a deity. For it has been said: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act would be primary..."
He states this [in the verse] beginning with "purity" (*śuddhi*), [meaning]: "In reality, there is no scriptural mention of a deity. (41)
Let there also be possession of qualities for these two; let it be just as their meditation is.
For it is observed that, according to the authoritative sources, the attainment [of the result] occurs in both cases as well. || 42 ||

He resolves this by means of the principle of the section concerning deities (*devatādhikaraṇanyāya*): "The possession of qualities as well. Just as the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is accepted because it is seen in the scripture, so too its connection with qualities must be accepted because it is heard in the sacred texts. Since there is no difference in the authoritative attainment of the vital breath—both as the object of meditation and as possessing qualities—from the mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), histories, Purāṇas, and worldly renown, [it follows that] the fivefold [form] beginning with the physical body (*vigraha*)...

The sense is that since the seers, poets, and deities have perceived [these things], their denial is not possible. Here, "scripture" (śruti) is mentioned; and even though it is primarily concerned with injunctions, in the absence of contradiction with or disagreement from [other means of knowledge], it possesses authority regarding the nature of the means [to liberation]. || 42 ||
But surely, it is understood that this [mention of] purity and so forth is intended solely for the purpose of praise.
Therefore, let it be regarded as an explanatory passage (arthavāda), because it is supplementary to the procedure for worship. || 43 ||

Having explained the Bhāṣya passage, "But it might be so because it is stated in scripture," he analyzes the prima facie argument beginning with "It would not be so. He introduces this with "But" (nanu).
He states the resulting conclusion—that the doctrine of purification and so forth is merely for the purpose of praise—with the words "It is an arthavāda" (arthavāda iti). || 43 ||
For an authoritative connection of the vital breath is thus understood.
Relying on what basis is it asserted that [the injunctions for] purification and so forth are merely explanatory passages (arthavāda)? (44)

He offers a rebuttal, stating that even though the doctrine of purification and so forth is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is not an explanatory passage concerning non-existent matters: "It is authoritative.
Regarding this, it is said: "Embodiment, the enjoyment of oblations, sovereignty, graciousness, and the bestowing of fruits—this pentad constitutes the [qualities] beginning with embodiment."
1. Therefore, this is it.
[vol2, page 60] 356. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]

Since the connection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with purification and so forth, though established as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), does not become non-existent [even if the literal sense is absent], therefore the status of that statement as an *abhūtārthavāda* (an eulogy of what is not fact) is without foundation; such is the meaning. || 44 ||
For indeed, without abandoning conceit, one cannot achieve certainty regarding what is to be proven and the means of proof.
We perceive another eye, by the power of which, O Noble One, [this] might be false. (45)

One might raise the objection that even the connection with purity and so forth is merely figurative (*ārthavādika*), because the relationship between a quality and its possessor (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) is not established by any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*); therefore, such a statement would be a non-factual explanatory passage (*abhūtārthavāda*). Anticipating this, he says: "For not... In the context of scriptural practice, once the relationship of quality and possessor is determined, there is no other means of knowledge apart from the scripture; for it is on the strength of the absence of any other possible [means of proof] that this connection with purity and so forth belongs to it.
It might be argued that it is false; however, no other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) can be conceived here, for since such a means is absent, the scripture cannot have an unreal subject matter.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga); this is the intended meaning. || 45 ||
Furthermore, qualities such as being seated and so forth do not belong to another [the Self], nor can they be attributed to it as one does to a woman.
Because these are established through direct perception, they possess purity and other qualities.

Furthermore, he states that the disputed qualities such as purity and so forth are not false, because they are qualities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), just like its being "situated in the mouth" (*āsanya*) and so on: "The state of being situated in the mouth, etc. The construction is as follows: since the qualities of the vital breath, such as being situated in the mouth, are not false—just as the nature of fire attributed to a woman [in the ritual context] is not false—its qualities such as purity and so forth must likewise not be false. Nor is the nature of fire in the woman [merely figurative], according to the scripture...

It is logical that [the object] is not unreal because it is cognizable, since one accepts superimposition for the sake of meditation. He avoids the fallacy of the probandum being unestablished with the words "of those" (*teṣām*).
He states the result of the inference with the words "hence" (*ataḥ*); the word "since" (*yataḥ*) is also connected here. || 46 ||
However, those qualities which are considered to be beyond the scope of the senses and so forth are known through scripture.
Because they do not contradict valid cognition (māna), how can these [notions] such as purity and so forth be false? // 47 //

Suspecting that "non-contradiction by other means of knowledge" (*mānāntarāvisaṃvāditva*) might be a limiting condition (*upādhi*), he states that it pervades the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*) with the words "akṣādi" and so forth. The meaning is this: those qualities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), such as purity and the like, if they are heard [in scripture], are not false; for there is no contradiction by other means of knowledge, since such contradiction is impossible regarding things accessible through scripture alone, and there is no other reason for their falsity. Alternatively, the statement that a woman is fire is [false] because it contradicts perception (*adhyakṣa*).
It is ordained: as for those qualities such as purity and so forth of the vital breath (prāṇa) which are understood from scripture (āgama), they are not objects of perception and the like;
since there is no scope for them regarding a matter established by Śruti, they do not contradict it, and thus their unreality does not follow—this is the meaning. || 47 ||
Just like the sense of hearing and the other senses, the means of valid cognition have their own unique objects of comprehension.
In the crushing of that object of knowledge, there is no means of valid cognition other than direct experience. || 48 ||

An objection is raised: "Since qualities such as purity (śuddhatva) are no different from the quality of being the vital breath (prāṇa) in that they are attributes of the Self—just like the qualities of being the seat (āsanya) and so forth—it may be inferred that they are accessible through other means of knowledge. Thus, because of agreement or disagreement with those [other means], the Śruti has no authority regarding them. Anticipating this, he says: "Like the ear and the other senses" (śrotrādivat).
Just as there is a fixed determination of objects for the senses, such as sound for the ear, so too must the unique objectivity of all means of knowledge be accepted.

The meaning is that since another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is of no avail regarding what has already been established by another means of knowledge, there is no possibility for the eye or other senses to apply to the purity of the Vedic word and so forth; therefore, one need not fear their contradiction. Now, does a relationship exist between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, or not? If it does not exist, then the status of being an object of knowledge would be impossible, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it does exist, is it apprehended or not? If it is not apprehended, its existence would be without a basis; if it is apprehended, is it by that very same means of knowledge or by another?
[Vol.
2, Page 61] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 357.

Because the object of the word would not be established even partially due to the fault of grasping its own form, and because in the second case, since the relata are also grasped by that which grasps the relation, it is not uncommon.

To this, he says: "That which is to be measured" (*tanmeyam*). The meaning of the word *tat* (that) is the relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. That very [relationship] is the object to be measured;
its manifestation (*prathanam*) is its appearance (*sphūrti*). The point is that there is no means of knowledge other than the direct experience of that witness. || 48 ||
Whether by way of being distinct from the ultimate reality or by way of non-difference from it, [it exists] in the ultimate sense.
Even in this way, it is not logically tenable that an entity could possess a false nature. || 49 ||

Furthermore, since the opponent has failed to define the meaning of the term "false" (*mithyā*), [the author] refutes [his position] by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*) in order to show that the purity and so forth residing in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) cannot be false. [He says: "In ultimate reality... That falsity which is intended for an entity must be either different from ultimate reality or non-different; it is not possible in either case. For there is no evidence for the existence of something other than ultimate reality if it were different from it; nor [is it possible] through falsity—

The sense is that [the object] cannot be non-different from that which is perceived, because it would involve a contradiction. Now, he states that even if both alternatives are accepted, the falsity [of the world] remains unestablished:
"Not so," etc. Alternatively, having shown the two possibilities, he demonstrates that a fault applies to both: "Not so," etc. (49)
If it attains distinction from the ultimate reality, then it is something other than that.
Since that [result] is established by its own inherent power alone, how could it possibly have a false meaning? || 50 ||

He restates [the opponent's position] in order to demonstrate the untenability of the theory of difference: "It obtains," etc. That is to say, the other [entity] is accepted as being false (*mṛṣātvena*). Now, does that [false entity] manifest or not? If it does not, its existence cannot be established due to the absence of any means of certain cognition. If it does manifest, is it by itself or from another? It cannot be from another, because no relation can be defined. If it manifests by itself, then it would not be false, like the Self (*ātman*); thus he says: "By its own power" (*svamahimnā*). || 10 ||
But if [all things] were of the nature of ultimate reality, nothing anywhere would be false.
Even that which is unreal possesses unreality by virtue of its being of the nature of the ultimate reality.

Having restated another alternative view, he refutes it with the words "paramārtha" (in reality). He states that the very emergence of the position of difference is impossible with the words "asatya" (unreal).

Since there would be the consequence of unreality if [the unreal] were distinct from the ultimate reality which is of the nature of Being, even the unreal must be described as having Being as its essence; therefore, because the position of difference is untenable, there is non-dualism of Being—this is the meaning. || 51 ||
This distinction between the real and the unreal exists within the reality that is itself undivided.
Arising from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self, it ceases only through the realization of that [self]. || 52 ||

Anticipating the objection that even for one who says "having coupled truth and untruth," the defects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are excluded by the very distinction between truth and untruth—which would thus render the [original] argument irrelevant—the author says: "Truth... (verse 12). He states the resulting conclusion: since the distinction within the inner self (*pratyak*) is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*), when that ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of the inner self, the distinction produced by it is likewise destroyed; this is expressed by the words "from the realization of That" (*tadbodhāt*). || 12 ||
Mounted upon the board of his own manifestation, he [moves] through the stages born of that ignorance.
Though situated therein, he is unconnected with it; having attained the nature of the Self through the grace of the Lord. || 53 ||
Now, does this Lord exist for you or not? If He does not exist, then you fall into the position of a nihilist (*nāstika*), and there is a contradiction with inference and other means of knowledge.

If He does exist, then because He is a Vedic entity and thus a real thing, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is His object of governance must likewise be real; [in that case], how can ignorance be destroyed by the knowledge of the inner Self (*pratyag-jñāna*)?
1. *mṛ* | 2. *kha. smādbhina* | 3. *kha. pattimaṃ* |
358 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 62]

Regarding the destruction of duality therein, he says: "Self-manifestation" (*svābhāsa*). Upon those transformations of ignorance—which take the form of all duality—within the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), the Self, having mounted that very board of its own manifestation, assumes the forms of being the Witness (*sākṣitva*), the Lord (*īśvaratva*), the Cause (*kāraṇatva*), and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmitva*).

And although it stands within this phenomenal world (*prapañca*), in reality it is not connected with it, because that would contradict the scriptural teaching of its non-attachment (*asaṅga*); therefore, [it is] as if...
This is merely a conceptual construction. For it has been stated: "The Lord becomes such by conforming to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form created by ignorance.
Thus, the meaning is that it is not contradictory to say that its manifestation arises from that very [ignorance]. || 53 ||
That is ignorance, and the entire world arising from it has that as its essence.
Therefore, following that [fact], the Śruti clearly declares, "The Self alone. (54)
He cites scripture as the authority for the fact that the world, together with its Lord, has ignorance as its body. Regarding the phrase "that ignorance":

since all duality—both effect and cause—is superimposed upon the Inner Self (pratyak) and is therefore nothing but That, the Scripture, by restating it as "all this," declares without doubt that the non-dual Reality is the Self alone; thus, the meaning is that the world, including the Lord, is encompassed by this [ignorance]. || 94 ||
The single self-nature alone is held to be the object of measure for all means of valid cognition.
We shall explain it accordingly, even further on, with supporting arguments. || 55 ||

Having raised the objection that if duality is merely avidyā (ignorance), then because there would be no objective referent, perception and the other means of knowledge would be non-existent, he offers another solution, considering that even in the absence of ultimate validity, empirical validity is possible; thus he says, "Aikātmyam" (The oneness of the Self). Fearing that this [oneness] might be unacceptable, he states that it is indeed accepted based on the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated; thus he says, "Yathā" (Just as...). The word *udarka* refers to the section concerning the manifest.
This is the scope of the [particle] *na*. The word *api*, however, serves to indicate that the aforementioned meaning has already been stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha*. || 55 ||
Likewise, the arising of a false cognition occurs due to defects in its causes.
It would be the cause of the sublated cognition; there is no other cause for its sublation. || 56 ||

Now, is the cognition of oneness (aikātmya) a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? In the first case, there would be the reality of duality consisting of its cause and so forth; in the second case as well, since there is no sublater (*bādhaka*), that [cognition] would indeed be real.
Thus, in both ways, perception and other means of knowledge would have duality as their object. To this, he says: "It is false.

For that [cognition] is the cause for the manifestation of a sublatable cognition, and the defect in its cause is what produces it, as in the case of the cognition of silver and the like—both of these [are present].

Since it is seen even in dreams, the meaning is that for this reason, there is nothing other than these two [the object and the cognition] that can either inform or produce the sublated cognition. || 56 ||
And since neither of these two exists here, how can it be called "false"?
Since falsity is established by means of cognition, falsity cannot belong to that very cognition. || 57 ||

Having stated the general principle, he says "And not... [in the verse], asserting that the validity [of the cognition of oneness] is established because there is no arising of the notion of falsity regarding the knowledge of oneness (*ekātmya-jñāna*), and thus its falsity cannot be proven. Furthermore, is the falsity of the cognition of oneness due to its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) or due to its object (*viṣayataḥ*)? It cannot be the first, because that is accepted [by us]; nor does it follow from this that it lacks validity, since that is established by the truth of its object. Nor can it be the latter, because the cognition of oneness is supreme with respect to the object of knowledge (*meyam*).

He says that [the knowledge of non-duality] culminates in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Regarding the phrase "from valid cognition" (*miteḥ*): for this reason as well, the knowledge of non-duality has no falsity by virtue of its object; for there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) of that cognition, nor is there any powerful sublater present here. Thus he says: "Falsity... (verse 17).
1. Sovereignty and so forth.
[Vol.
2, page 63] [Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 359
Therefore, the highest good is attained through knowledge of the object as it truly is, free from error.
Furthermore, no cause for the world's having a contrary nature is observed.

Since it is difficult to maintain that the objects of others' desires are false while asserting that the connection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with purity and so forth is not false, it has been stated that everything other than the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is born of ignorance regarding that [Self]. Now, relying on that, he introduces the commentary beginning with "not contrary" (*nāviparīta*) concerning this point: that the inner self alone is real, bondage arises from ignorance of it, and liberation arises from knowledge of it. He does so with the words "Therefore... (*tasmāt*). [The text continues: "perfectly bound... (*samyambaddho*)...

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that it is well known from the *Sthāṇv-ādi* [section of the Mahābhārata] that the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) depends upon [the teacher]. As for the lack of sandhi in the reading, it has been disregarded because it yields no fruit. Having raised the doubt as to how knowledge of the inner self (*pratyag-jñāna*) can have a non-perverted object, he says "viparīta... [verse 58], considering that although [knowledge] may be false in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), the absence of such falsity regarding its object has already been stated.
For that [cognition] is grounded solely in the object itself; it does not have its basis in the ignorance of that object.
Therefore, upon the destruction of that delusion, there shall be the destruction of that which is born of pride.

[Objection: But surely even the cognition of the inner self (*pratyagdhi*) may have a contrary object, because verbal knowledge has as its object a composite and mediate thing, and according to your own position, both are admitted to be produced by the play of ignorance regarding the inner self. To this, he says: "resting on reality" (*vastuniṣṭhā*).
