There is only one non-composite, immediate reality, which is non-dual, as stated in such scriptural passages as "That which is directly," etc.; it is only with respect to that [reality] that valid knowledge arises from the sentence, because knowledge arises in accordance with its object, and not because it is born of ignorance regarding the reality.

Since that which consists of ignorance is incapable of being an object of valid cognition regarding objects such as the "emitted" (raṃsṛṣṭa) and so forth, it follows that the knowledge of the inner self arising from the sentence has an object that is not contrary [to reality].

This is the meaning. Since that which is produced by ignorance—such as the remote (parokṣa) and so on—is not an object of knowledge, when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, that which is born of it is also destroyed;
thus, the immediate, single-flavored reality is established, and in that regard, there is not even a suspicion of the knowledge arising from the sentence having a contrary object.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. || 19 ||
And this being so, the means of valid cognition (māna) would not be rendered useless in any way;
for it is precisely in this manner that a means of valid cognition comes to have the character of making known an object as it truly is. (60)
Now, does that means of knowledge which destroys ignorance along with its effects (the world) reveal the inner self (pratyak), or not? In the first case, it would follow that it has a dual nature;

in the second, there is an impossibility of its being a remover [of ignorance], for a means of knowledge cannot remove ignorance and its products without making them its object. To this, he says: "Not so" (na ca). If one accepts that the operation of a means of knowledge occurs within that whose essence is pure consciousness, then both the capacity to inform (bodhakatva) and the capacity to remove (nivartakatva) [are established].

And thus, there is no duality of modification; for consciousness is natural (*svārasika*) with respect to the real object (*vastu*), whereas cessation alone is something superimposed upon it. However, in the case of the insentient (*jaḍa*), if a means of knowledge (*māna*) were to operate, it would indeed be futile, because that [insentient object] is not established by itself. Therefore, the meaning is that the operation of all means of knowledge occurs only within the self of consciousness (*saṃvidātman*). For this reason as well, those means of knowledge have that [consciousness] as their object; for when that is the case, one obtains the status of having as its object a thing as it truly is (*yathābhūtārtha*), while anything else is merely imagined (*kalpita*). Thus he says:
He recites: || 60 ||
The inner reality is free from conceptual constructions such as those of Īśvara and the like.
The object is not a false cognition, because [falsehood] does not exist apart from the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 61 ||

Now, if the world and the individual soul (*jīva*) are merely imagined (*kalpita*), does this not result in the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) due to the absence of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for that error? To this he replies: "The Lord and so forth. The object is the substratum; he states its fitness to be a substratum by saying "unimagined" (*avikalpita*). Regarding the point already stated:

Sureśvarācārya provides the reasoning in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* (First Chapter), beginning with the words "Not" (*na*) and so forth: "Nor is it the case that emptiness alone is the ultimate reality, serving as the superimposed substrate for that which is superimposed."
Therefore, because there is an absence of penetration by that [unreality], the meaning is that reality itself is thus. || 61 ||
Whatever has been apprehended by the limited [means of knowledge] is not false, because it is limited.

"A scripture that causes one to grasp [things] as false would be for the sake of what is not beneficial. By means of this statement from the Bhāṣya—"not having a non-perverted meaning," etc.—which contains within it an explanation of the meaning related to the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*), the author has stated that the falsity of the qualities such as purity associated with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as desired by others, is not established. He now states another meaning of that very same Bhāṣya which does not contradict the context.

"Up to this point": the meaning is that the purity and other qualities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) established by the scriptures are not false, because there is no reason [to consider them so]. He states another reason why the purity and other qualities of the vital breath are indeed real: "If it were false... If the scripture were to teach that the purity and other qualities of the vital breath are determined to be false, then there would be a disadvantage regarding the existence of the object and the cognition of it as qualified by that [quality], just as in the world there is harm from a cognition of a contrary object.

The meaning is as follows: A scripture that teaches useless things, such as false notions of purity and so forth, would have a useless purpose; however, this is not accepted [of our scripture]. Therefore, the purity and other qualities prescribed by the scripture are indeed real.

Nor is it proper to claim that these are false merely because they are metaphorical—like the case of "woman as fire"—for, in that instance, it was stated that there is no contradiction regarding the intended secondary sense (*dvārārtha*). || 62 ||
If it is argued that Brahman resides in the name, that is not so, because of the perception of difference.
For, just as in the case of an image, this cognition "This is Brahman" arises once the name and so forth have been known. (63)

He raises an objection regarding the deviation [from the rule] that the attainment of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) results only from the correct understanding of the scriptures and so forth, by stating: "Not so. For, according to the scriptural passage, "One should meditate on the Name as Brahman," one perceives Brahman in the Name itself—which is not Brahman; since this cognition is false, being a perception of something as what it is not, yet the fruit described in scripture (such as "as far as the Name extends") is seen to be realized, it is incorrect to say that the fruit results only from the correct understanding of the scriptures and so forth.

Such is the meaning. He states that this is not false knowledge with the word "No. He provides the reason for the perception of Brahman there through the distinction of the name of Brahman with the words "through distinction. He applies the commentary beginning with "not like an image" to the point already stated, using the phrase "like an image. || 63 ||
Just as in the case of the division of the navel, [it occurs] within the self that possesses the form of Viṣṇu and Vīra.
In that same way, the cognition of Brahman is enjoined with respect to these [non-Brahman objects]. || 64 ||

He explains the illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). The phrase "from Viṣṇu" is to be supplied as the source from which the distinction among those devoid of knowledge is known. He states the application to the case at hand with the word "tathā" (so too). That is to say, when a distinction among the Brahmins is perceived within the name [itself]. || 64 ||
For one who does not know that it is a rope indeed perceives the rope as a snake.
But since this is not the case with names and so forth, therefore this statement is false. || 65 ||

Anticipating the objection that the vision of Brahman in the name (nāman) is a false vision because it is preceded by the cognition of difference—just as [the vision of] fire in what is not fire—he says:

"By one who does not know" (*ajñāta*). For one who does not know a rope as a rope perceives it as a snake; however, there is no such non-cognition regarding the name and so forth as being identical with Brahman, because [the name] manifests as distinct from that Brahman. Since this is so, therefore, it is preceded by non-discrimination (*aviveka*).

He states that the claim of falsity regarding the perception of Brahman in the name is untenable, because that perception is preceded by discrimination, whereas the cognition of non-difference [in the case of the rope-snake] is false;
thus he says: "Therefore... (61).
If it is held that Brahman does not exist as a reality here at all, but is merely a vision;
Because among those who possess [the sense organs] such as the nose, the possession of visual perception is observed only when those [objects] exist. || 66 ||

Now, surely the subject (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of discrimination must be stated; yet that which is non-existent cannot possess such a status. Nor does Brahman exist as something that could have the status of a subject or a counter-correlate, because there is a lack of evidence, and because the Upaniṣads, being like "oyster-shells" for the Vedas, are not authoritative [on this point]. Therefore, since [discrimination] is preceded by [such] discernment—

Thinking that [the view] is false—just as the perception of a snake in a rope is false because it is a meditative superimposition (*yoga*) upon the name and so forth—one objects with the word “Brahman. The literal meaning is this: let the perception of Brahman indeed be superimposed here upon the name and so forth, but Brahman does not exist as a real entity, because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*māna*). [The objector continues: “Brahman does not exist—that which is known through hundreds of scriptural passages such as ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite,’ ‘Brahman is consciousness and bliss,’ and ‘Brahman is pure intelligence.’”

It is impossible to say [that it does not exist], because its status as a valid means of knowledge has been established in the *Saṃbandha-grantha* (the section on the relationship between scripture and reality). Therefore, Brahman certainly exists, as shown by such passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1); "He is to be apprehended only as 'it is'" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 6.13); "He becomes non-existent indeed" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6.1); and "If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent; but if one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6.1). [The opponent] objects: "No. [The proponent asks: Is the meditation upon Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) based on a real object, or is it scriptural—?
He says that this very [meditation] is "the Ṛk is fire, the Sāman is fire," and so forth, by way of viewing [them as such]. Regarding the phrase "in the Ṛk and so forth":

since the superimposition of existing things such as the earth is seen upon the Ṛk and so forth, the meaning is that even in the case of names and the like, the superimposition of the vision of the existing Brahman must likewise be performed. || 66 ||
Since the secondary depends on the primary, there can be no "existent" without the primary Brahman.
The secondary Brahman is like a secondary fire, which is preceded by the primary fire. || 67 ||

He explains the commentary beginning with "Because of the dependence on other reasons for the existence of Brahman, and because of its being primary," according to the logic of the section concerning the secondary and the primary (*gauṇamukhyādhikaraṇanyāya*), [with the words] "Of the secondary" (*gauṇasya*). || 67 ||
Furthermore, no cognition whatsoever is observed in the world that has a non-existent object.
Even when all objects are erroneous, consciousness itself is non-erroneous.

He states that Brahman exists based on the following inference: "The intellect under dispute has an object of support, because it is an intellect, like the cognition of a jar. Furthermore, he asks: "Moreover, even though all objects such as the knower and so forth are subject to deviation, there exists an unchanging conscious reality (cidvastu) which establishes both existence and non-existence; how then can it be said that Brahman—which is immutable and of the single essence of consciousness—does not exist? He says: "sarvārtha... (verse 68).
Nor is there any semblance of scripture here, because it does not possess the characteristic of being an injunction (*codanā*).
Because the statement regarding the purpose of knowledge concerning the Supreme Self is not distinct from those [statements] whose purpose is ritual action. (69)

[The author] refutes the objection of one who reflects upon the *Saṃbandha-grantha*: "Is it not the case that there is no valid cognition of Brahman from the Vedāntas? Because they lack an injunction (*vidhi*), they are not authoritative; for no sentence whatsoever can be a means of knowledge (*māna*) unless it is touched by an injunction. Therefore, Brahman does not exist. [The author replies: "Not so" (*na ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). It is also not the case that the scripture (*āgama*) is a fallacy and thus not a means of knowledge, on the grounds that it is devoid of an injunction such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) regarding the Self which is Brahman.

He states the reason for why it is not at all logical [to claim that the Upanishads are injunctive], as set forth in the Bhāṣya beginning with "if [they were] for the sake of action" (kriyārthaiḥ), in the verse: "By those for the sake of action... (69).
Just as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices possess numerous specific means of accomplishment, so too [is this case].
Likewise, an action that lacks its constituent parts in the proper sequence is fruitless. || 70 ||
362 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya] [vol2, page 66]

Fearing that the lack of distinction [between the two] might be undesirable due to the disparity arising from the fact that one has an accomplished object (*siddha-artha*) while the other has an object to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*), he states the intended lack of distinction:

"The Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth... The word "action" (*kriyā*) is to be connected [to this]. By "action," the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is intended. The phrase "just as" (*yadvat*) is to be connected with "and likewise" (*tathā ca*). Distinction consists in being an auxiliary to the essential nature (*svarūpa-upakāritva*) and being an auxiliary to the fruit (*phala-upakāritva*). He refutes the mode mentioned in the fifth [chapter]...

"It has been thus commanded to be performed," and so forth. This refers back to the qualification [for the rite], which is established through the injunctive statement and by means of the Viśvajit-nyāya and other such principles. Thus ends the section on the fruit. || 70 ||
Or rather, it is understood from the sentence alone as being beyond the scope of any other means of valid cognition.
Just so, here too, it is understood precisely from the mention of entities such as the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth. || 71 ||

It indicates the logic of the *apūrvādhikaraṇa* [of the Brahma-sūtras] by the word "other" (*anya*). Having restated the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it states the point to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "just as" (*yathā*).

Here, the word "here" (*iha*), signifying the context of liberation (*mokṣa-prakaraṇa*), is connected with the word "because of the statement" (*ukteḥ*). It is qualified by such descriptions as "without what precedes," "without what follows," and "without anything in between."
The term "vastu" (the real) means Brahman. || 71 ||
Nor is it [the cognition] that is either perverted or of the nature of doubt regarding the sentence.
The understanding arises in us who perceive the object as it truly is. || 72 ||

[Objection: "But surely, since there is no distinction in the arising of cognition, let it be that the non-arising [of cognition] constitutes the invalidity of the *Tattvamasi* and other such [Vedic statements]; however, let it not be that they take the form of error or doubt. [Reply: He says "No" and so forth. He states the reason: "because for those qualified [disciples], a single uniform, uncontradicted cognition arises," as expressed by the words "for us" (*asmākam*). || 72 ||

If it is argued that [the statement] is improper because there is no object to be accomplished, we reply: no, for the statement is made according to the nature of the intellect and its corresponding object.
In this context, the object of cultivation does not possess that nature simply because it is an object to be cultivated;
rather, it is accepted as being "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) because it has been presented by a valid means of knowledge.
Furthermore,
regarding the point that this is not a semblance of scripture (*āgamābhāsa*), the reality within the sentences beginning with "Tattvamasi" is indeed stated here through both objection and resolution.

He raises an objection: "Since there is no *niyoga* (injunction), validity is untenable," [expressed by] the word "kārya" (action/task). He refutes this by pointing out the dissimilarity between sentences whose purpose is knowledge (*vidyārtha*) and those whose purpose is ritual action (*kriyārtha*), [using the phrase] "not stated" (*nokta*). Because the cognition arising from the sentence is true to reality, the authority of the sentence remains unopposed even in the absence of a *niyoga*; for being directed toward that [action] is not the determinant of its [validity], as it is contradicted in cases such as "one desiring heaven should eat sand. What then? [It is the correspondence with reality.]

The meaning is that its status as a revealer of what was previously unknown is due to its non-deviation in all cases. Having raised the objection—“How can word and cognition have such an object with respect to an existing entity (vastu) without depending on something to be performed?”—the author considers the options: does their dependence [on performance] exist for the sake of the reality of their object, or for the sake of their own validity? He refutes the first [option] with the words “bhāvanā” (productive activity). Here, the term “iha” (here) refers to the *Karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section of the Veda). [This concerns] that which is the object of the cognition of performance...

The meaning is that the "being such" (tathārthatva) of an object to be performed does not depend upon its being something to be performed; rather, it depends on its being cognizable through a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), for otherwise, the same status would result even for the words of a deceiver. || 73 ||
Nor,
because it is an effect of that cognition, could it have such an object.
The cognition's correspondence with reality arises precisely from its origin in a valid means of knowledge. (74)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "nor indeed" (*nāpi*). The particle *ca* has the sense of adding what has been stated. [The phrase] "because it is an effect" and "because it has that as its object" refers to the doubt.
[Vol.
2, Page 67] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 363.

Up to this point: "correspondence with reality" (*tathārthatā*) means being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*). "Being such as it is" (*tathābhūtārthatā*) is likewise [the same]. The mention of "cognition" (*dhī*) is an elliptical indication for liberation (*ukti*) as well. The application (*prayoga*) and so forth regarding an object that is a duty (*kartavyārtha*) do not possess the status of a means of knowledge because their object is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*); rather, they have that status because they are instruments of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*) and because they produce it. Otherwise, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasakti*) would remain as it was. Thus, the meaning is that "being already accomplished" (*bhūta*) is irrelevant to the status of being a means of knowledge insofar as it is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheyatva*). || 74 ||
For one who maintains that the validity of cognition is established by its effect, there is the fault of mutual dependence:
[validity] would exist only when there is the apprehension of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by persons in accordance with the object to be known (meyānurodhataḥ).
Later, the thought may arise that what was to be performed is not to be performed. (76)

If validity were based on being grounded in an action (*kāryaniṣṭhatva*), then there would be a circularity: validity would depend on being grounded in that [action], and being grounded in that [action] would depend on validity. Therefore, validity consists solely in making known what was previously unknown. Since the fact that sacrifices and the like are means to a desired end cannot be apprehended by any other means of knowledge, it is precisely this that is to be measured by the section on injunctions (*vidhikāṇḍa*). Thinking thus, he says: "mutually" (*anyonya*). If one asks, "From where, then, does the cognition of what is to be done and what is not to be done arise?"—anticipating this doubt, he states that it is mental (*mānasī*).
With the words "pramāṇa," he recalls what was stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha*. || 79 || || 76 ||
For pride is of a single form, whereas those [objects] are contradictory and possess many forms.
The sun is seen as an illuminator, but from it no cognition arises regarding what is to be practiced. || 77 ||

Furthermore, perception is observed to be a means of knowledge that makes known jars and other objects possessing multiple contradictory forms; likewise, a Vedic statement is also seen to have a single form with respect to both what is already established and what is yet to be accomplished. Since there is no difference between these two cases in terms of making known what was previously unknown, its validity is equally established in both. Thus he says: "of a single form. Now, one might object: desire to obtain and desire to avoid arise from the scripture; therefore, because it is a causal agent (*kāraka*), it cannot [be valid] anywhere...

To the objection that [the means of knowledge] might be invalid, he says: "Like the sun. Furthermore, intending to state that the subject under dispute is a valid means of knowledge only with respect to something other than the effect desired by opponents—because it possesses the nature of a means of knowledge, like the eye and so forth—he says: "Not from this. (77)
Surely, because it lacks the status of a scriptural authority, it would result in a lack of practical application.
For a collection of words is not observed here in this world to exist without an action.

In this regard, the proponent of the theory of action (kāryavādī) refutes [the opponent's position] by proposing the alternatives of whether Brahman is cognizable through a sentence (vākya) or through a word (pada), beginning with "But surely... He states that the first alternative is not tenable: "Not [so], because it is not [cognizable] through a sentence. The meaning is that since only an action is cognizable through a sentence, and Brahman is not an action, it is therefore not cognizable [by a sentence].

To the objection—"Even if Brahman is not an action, why could it not still be the meaning of a sentence?"—he replies: "Of words... [meaning that words have no syntactic relation to one another unless they denote an action].

If Brahman were not something to be produced (akāryatva), then, because there is an absence of verbs (kriyāpada) in the Vedāntas concerning it, and because the formation of sentences would be impossible due to the lack of a combination of words, Brahman could not be their subject matter;
this is the meaning. Since in both worldly and Vedic usage the mutual combination of words is never observed without a verb, the construction is as follows:
in the Vedāntas, which are devoid of verbs, there is no combination of words. || 78 ||
And its establishment as a category [of existence] results from reliance upon inference and perception.
Because it has scripture alone as its authority, it is not accepted as being a [conventional] category (padārtha). || 79 ||
And because one has accepted [the view] that "I am this," it is likewise logically consistent.
It exists like Mount Meru, distinguished by four colors.
For even regarding an object that is not currently present, such as Mount Meru, the cognition "Meru exists" arises from hearing the report of it.
Just as right cognition arises [from that], so it is from the statement "Thou art That. (81)
[vol2, page 68] 364 1

He replies to the second [objection] with the words, "And if it were a word-meaning" (*padārthatve ca*). Furthermore, for one who asserts that Brahman is a word-meaning, there would be a loss of the established tenet (*siddhāntahāni*).
To this he replies: "It is scripture. Since the proponent of Brahman (brahmavādī) accepts that the Vedic statement is [authoritative], there is no fault arising from its being a mere word-meaning.

He refutes [the objection] by stating "asīti" (it is so), showing that even in the Vedāntas, there is no lack of a collection of words due to the absence of a verb, because a verb is present that is consistent with what is being propounded. Alternatively, having accepted that [the Self] is the meaning of a sentence, he rejects the claim that it is not the meaning of a word.

By stating "āgameti" (by scripture), he also refutes the notion that [the Self] is cognizable through a sentence, since a sentence cannot be established in the absence of a collection of words, which in turn requires a verb.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "It exists" (*asti*). He clarifies with an illustration the fact that a sentence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object untouched by [human] action, as stated in the Commentary.

By the words "It exists," etc., he means to say that just as a sentence is a means of valid cognition regarding a real entity even without a connection to action, so it is explained by way of an illustration. The four colors—white, black, red, and mixed—which exist in a single direction on Mount Meru...

This should be understood as follows: Just as in the statement "there exists Mount Meru, distinguished by four forms," a correct cognition arises from the word "Meru" even though Meru is not the object [of that specific action], and just as in the statement "there exists a bird in another continent, a *suparṇa* whose flight is characterized by golden and silver wings and which is seen very swiftly," a cognition arises from the word "bird" (*pakṣin*) even though the bird is not the object [of that specific action].
The meaning is that, just so, from the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi), there arises perfect knowledge regarding Brahman, even though it is devoid of any connection with action.
If it were like the knowledge of Mount Meru and so forth, it would lack authority due to its fruitlessness.
It is not so, because that fruit is directly realized immediately following the arising of knowledge.

One might raise the objection that the *tattvamasi* and similar statements are not valid means of knowledge because they lack fruitfulness, on the grounds of the following inference: "That which has a known object as its content is fruitless, like a [statement] such as 'Meru exists' (*saṃmata*). To this, he replies with the words "Not so" (*naivam*). He refutes the inference by contradicting it with the experience of the wise:

since immediately after the dawning of the knowledge arising from the sentence, its fruit—the liberation from sorrow and so forth—is directly perceived, an inference contrary to that perception cannot arise.
Such is the meaning. || 82 ||
"The knot of the heart is severed and one attains Brahman," according to the Śruti.
Nor is it a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because there is a declaration of a fruit for this [action], just as in the case of the *juhū* ladle. || 83 ||

In this regard, he states the contradiction with Śruti concerning one who disputes [the point]. He says, "It is split," etc. Anticipating the objection that the scriptural mention of the fruit (phalaśruti) is not an authoritative means of knowledge because it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and thus cannot sublate inference, he says, "And not... Here, "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmadhī*) is the meaning of the locative case. However, in the reading with the genitive case, it is the scriptural mention of the fruit of that [knowledge] which is being stated. According to the principle of the *parṇamayī* section, it is appropriate for the scriptural mention of the fruit in relation to the *juhū* ladle to be an *arthavāda*; but in the case of Brahman—

The meaning is that, since there is no factor establishing that the intellect (dhi) is subordinate to anything else, the scriptural mention of its fruit is not a mere figurative statement; otherwise, it would follow that the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras] need not be commenced. || 83 ||
The connection between the prohibited and the undesirable is understood from the sentence itself.
And its being something to be practiced does not arise even in the slightest degree. || 84 ||

It has been stated that it is logical for statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) to possess authority regarding their own meaning—which is untouched by anything to be accomplished—because it is observed through both scripture and experience that the knowledge arising from such sentences is fruitful. Now, he states another reason why the scripture is not necessarily restricted to having *kārya* (that which is to be done) as its primary purport: "niṣiddha...
[etc.]. 1. *vākyamā* 2. *ka. ga. tasthā ju*
[Vol.
2, Page 69] 3 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 365.

That the connection between killing and other such acts with undesirable results is known from the Veda itself through injunctions such as "one should not kill," and that such an act cannot even be suspected of being something to be performed (kāryatā).

It is possible [to understand it thus]: for one who has been consecrated by that [initiation] does not perform what is prohibited or what is connected with the undesirable as understood through a prohibition; therefore, since prohibitive sentences possess authority even without reference to a [positive] action to be performed, the meaning is that there is no fixed rule that scripture must have a positive action as its ultimate purport. || 84 ||
Nor [is there any cognition] for one whose intellect is refined by negation regarding an object that has been negated.
From the scriptural injunction against eating onions and such things, another kind of wisdom arises. || 85 ||

One might ask: "Why should even prohibitive statements not have the same status as injunctions, since their effect consists in the non-performance [of an action]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Prohibitive... The word *palāṇḍu* denotes a specific type of garlic. If even prohibitive statements were intended to convey a positive action (*kārya*), the distinction between injunction and prohibition would collapse. Furthermore, since the negative particle (*nañ*) primarily conveys the absence of its correlate, to apply it to another meaning would result in the fallacy of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, [prohibitions do not denote an action].

The meaning is this: for one who has been inclined toward an object of addiction by passion and the like, but whose mind has been refined by the understanding of the purpose of the prohibitory scripture, no cognition regarding an object to be performed arises—distinct from mere indifference—which is characterized by the cessation of the activity that had been prompted by the hearing of the prohibition. || 81 ||

"Just as there is no cognition other than non-performance [of an action] arising from prohibitive sentences, so too it is certain that [no such cognition arises] from sentences such as 'That thou art' (tattvamasi).
(86) Having restated the intended example, he states the point of application (dārṣṭāntika): "Just as" (yathā), etc., referring to sentences such as "One should not kill" or "One should not drink."

From those [Vedic injunctions], only the non-performance of what is not to be done is cognized, but no cognition regarding an object that is to be performed arises from them; likewise, since valid knowledge of Brahman—which is not something to be accomplished—can arise from the Vedāntas, the meaning is that they do not touch upon what is to be performed. || 86 ||
Because of the neglect of one afflicted by thirst who has set out toward a mirage.
Just as there would be cessation when [the senses] are overwhelmed by darkness, so too, for us, it occurs through the knowledge of the Self. (87)

He states a worldly example to show that knowledge arising from a sentence such as "That Thou Art" destroys ignorance and consists in the cessation of all worldly transactional activity. [The verse begins with] "A deer... When one who is overcome by thirst superimposes a flood of water upon the rays of the sun reflected in a desert and proceeds toward it, the realization of the truth—"This is a desert"—brings about the cessation of that ignorance; when that [ignorance] ceases, there is the cessation of the superimposition, and when that has ceased, there is the cessation of the activity [toward the water].

The meaning is that peace is attained. Based on the aforementioned analogy, he states "so it is" (tathā), asserting that for us this is a matter of direct perception: for one who has been engaged in actions through the conceit of agency and so forth arising from ignorance of the Self, there occurs the cessation of all such activity upon the removal of that ignorance through the knowledge of the Self arising from the [great] statement.
Therefore, the prohibitive scripture is based upon the nature of things as they truly are.
It is certain that not even a trace of human agency exists therein. || 88 ||
In the same way, let steadfastness in the knowledge of the true nature of the Self be observed.
There is not even the slightest performance of ritual practice in sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi).

He concludes the illustration with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He concludes the application to the subject of the illustration with the word "Self" (*ātma*). The meaning of the two *vārtikas* is as follows: just as a prohibitive statement possesses authority by being intent on cessation through the removal of delusion, theft, and so forth, so too the [scriptures] beginning with "That Thou Art" (*tat tvam asi*) possess the validity of being authoritative by virtue of removing all specific attributes such as agency, which arise from ignorance regarding the inner Self (*pratyagajñāna*). || 88 || 89 ||
[Vol. 2, Page 70] 366 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
"But surely, unlike the eating of *kalañja*, there is no [prohibition] for Vedic ritual action."
The fact that [the agent] acts for what is harmful due to ignorance is understood through valid cognition.

He raises the objection regarding the disparity between the illustration and the subject of the illustration with the words "kalañja," etc. Just as, because the eating of *kalañja* and similar acts are performed out of ignorance and result in undesirable consequences, it is appropriate that prohibitive injunctions such as "one should not eat *kalañja*" possess authority by being intent upon cessation—mediated through the cognition that these acts are means to an undesirable end—so too, Vedic ritual action is neither performed out of ignorance nor intended for an undesirable purpose; for that [action] is based on the scripture...

The meaning is that although the knowledge of reality arising from the *āgama* (scriptural authority) generates the realization of truth, it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) as a liberator, because it does not bring about the cessation of ritual actions enjoined by the scriptures. || 90 ||
It is not so; for there is no equality [between the two], because one has ignorance as its cause while the other has the purpose of achieving a harmful end.
Therefore, through the consumption of *kalañja*, [the sin] arises; upon its cessation, that [sin] ceases. || 91 ||

Just as the eating of *kalañja* and similar acts produce harmful results due to ignorance, so too ritual action prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta-karma*) arises from the sense of agency and other factors born of ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*). Furthermore, the assumption of a body produced by that [action] is itself an evil. Therefore, when ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge arising from the [great] statement, the destruction of the actions produced by that [ignorance] follows;

thus, because it functions as a remover [of evil], the validity of statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is established just like prohibitions. This is the answer given: "Not so," and so forth.
The phrase "of the Śrauta rite" is also connected here [with the following]. || 91 ||
Because eternal things have the scripture alone as their cause, it is not accepted that they are [produced] in this manner.
If it is argued that [the Vedic injunctions] have false knowledge and so forth as their cause, just like those rites performed for desired ends (kāmya), [then the following applies]. || 92 ||

One might raise an objection regarding the distinction [between obligatory and optional rites]: although optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) result in harm because they are caused by ignorance, obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—since their performance is mandated solely by scripture—do not arise from ignorance nor result in harm, as they destroy sin (*pratyavāya*). To this, he replies with the word "scripture" (*śāstra*). The meaning of the word "thus" (*evam*) is that [obligatory rites] result in harmful fruits just like those performed out of ignorance; the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes passion (*rāga*) and other such factors. This is because optional rites are indeed produced by ignorance.
He accepts [the opponent's position] under the guise of a scriptural illustration: "Of those rites performed for specific desires" (kāmyānām). || 92 ||
Not for one who is defiled by such faults as ignorance, passion, hatred, and the like.
Just as the injunction for the *agnihotra* is for one who desires heaven and the like, so too [is this]. || 93 ||
Action is prescribed for one who is constantly defiled by delusion, desire, and the like.
2.1 There is no distinction here between optional and obligatory action based on its own nature. (94)

He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating, "It is not ignorance," because it is unproven that the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) rites is based solely on scriptural injunction. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the subject matter of obligatory rites. Explaining the commentary beginning with "Just as... he elaborates upon what was previously stated: "Heaven, etc. By asserting the defectiveness of optional (*kāmya*) rites, does he also intend that for obligatory rites—which consist of the injunctions of origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), performance (*prayoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*)—the same applies?
He says, "Because there is no distinction," [and] "not from itself. Here, the word "here" refers to the scripture. || 93 || 94 ||
For the quality of being desirable [in rites] arises from the fault of desiring heaven and so forth, which resides in the agent.
Therefore, the quality of being desirable for an action cannot arise in any other way.

How, then, is the distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites established there? He says: "By the dependence on the agent" (*kartṛsya*). The word "and obligatoriness" (*nityatā ca*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
1. *kha*: *tulyataḥ*. 2. *ka*: *mityame*.
[Vol.
2, Page 71] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary known as *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 367.

The distinction is as follows: for one who seeks a specific goal, such as "one desiring heaven" or "one desiring cattle," there is the *kāmya-vidhi* (optional injunction); whereas for a person whose activity is prompted by a general desire—thinking "may what is desired be mine" and "may suffering not be"—there is the *nitya-vidhi* (obligatory injunction). That which is impelled by desire is *kāmya*, while that which sustains life...

Anticipating the objection that there is no distinction between what is not prescribed (*aprayukta*) and what is obligatory (*nitya*), he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). It is incorrect to claim that there is a division between the optional (*kāmyatva*) and the obligatory (*nityatva*). For, by means other than the manner already stated, the distinction between the optional and the obligatory is not established; for even that which is obligatory is equally dependent upon desire. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "Whatever a living being does, all that is the movement of desire. Nor is it [the case that] life...

The meaning is that even though the [auxiliary] is always present in the case of a compulsory (nitya) rite, because that [result] is sometimes absent despite its presence, the fact that the result exists only when it is present is equally true for an optional (kāmya) rite as well. || 95 ||
For one who is detached from all that is manifest and desires the Self as distinct from it.
A person has the qualification for liberation only when their mind is not carried away by desires.

Anticipating the objection that—just as one who is tainted by passion and other defects is qualified for ritual action (karman), so too is such a person qualified for knowledge (jñāna) if they desire liberation (mumukṣu)—there is thus no distinction between knowledge and action, he says: "From Viriñca down to... The phrase "down to" implies "down to the stump," meaning down to the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). The word "that" (tat) refers to the realm of impermanent saṃsāra. The word "liberation" (mokṣa) refers to the knowledge that is the means to it. [The seeker] is distinguished by the fourfold qualification (sādhanacatuṣṭaya).

The meaning is that only one who is free from passion and other such defects is qualified for the knowledge that is the means to liberation, because one possessed of passion and so forth contradicts the principle expressed by the word "unworthy" (a-yaśabda). || 96 ||
"Higher desires," "desires for these [worlds]," and likewise "he who is without desire"—in this way, the Śruti prohibits desire. (97)
He states the authoritative basis for the eligibility of one who is dispassionate for knowledge: "The fools pursue outward desires;

they go to the snare of widespread death. Such is the statement. Furthermore, another statement—"He who, thinking [of them], desires desires, is born through those very desires in this or that place"—likewise prohibits desire by means of censure, just like the previously mentioned statement. He who—

The meaning is that the Vedic scripture, by directly prohibiting desire through the word "kāma," establishes the qualification for the path to the highest good—namely, right knowledge—for one who is not afflicted by desire and the like. || 97 ||
And for the eradication of ignorance, nothing other than knowledge is required.
Furthermore, for the arising of knowledge, nothing else whatsoever is required apart from the eyes and so forth. || 98 ||
For the arising of tranquility, nothing other than the purification of the intellect is required.
And for the purification of the intellect, nothing other than the performance of obligatory and other such duties is prescribed. || 99 ||

One might raise the objection: "How can one who is detached from the fruits of action have the qualification for liberation, since that [detachment] is itself a fruit [of action]? Otherwise, there would be no connection between actions and their supreme fruit. Anticipating this, he sets forth the sequence [of means], beginning with the words "Of ignorance... The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that it is well-known from the Śruti that tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are the instruments for the arising of knowledge. || 98 || 99 ||
Because actions of speech, mind, and body have exclusively the ignorance of the self as their cause.
Since that [ignorance] is sublated by the knowledge of the Self, how could there be any dependence on ritual action? || 100 ||
If it is argued that actions are useful for liberation even through a traditional succession (paraṃparā), why then is this not accepted directly? To this, he says: "The Self," etc.
[Vol.
2, page 72]. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Chapter.

The meaning is that since all three types of karma are produced by ignorance, when ignorance is removed through knowledge, the karma arising from it is also removed; therefore, for one who possesses knowledge, dependence upon that [karma] for liberation is not logical. || 100 ||
That activity which proceeds from ignorance—how could it arise from the knowledge of that [reality]?
Therefore, upon the arising of the knowledge of the inner self, there is the completion of all ritual actions.

Anticipating the objection that even for a knower whose ignorance has been destroyed, there is still a dependence on action for liberation because of the persistence of the view of action (*karmadṛṣṭi*), [the author] says, "That which [occurs] from ignorance," with the intention that such a view exists as a residual impression (*bādhitānuvṛtti*). The word "after that knowledge" (*tajjñānādūrdhvam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Considering that the cessation of action is the cause for the ripening of knowledge—based on the statement, "For one who has ascended to yoga, tranquility (*śama*) alone is the means"—and that action itself is not the cause, [the result] is stated: *phalitam*... [resulting...]
The author says: "Pratyak" (the inward-facing). The meaning of that word is the impossibility of action after the arising of knowledge. || 101 ||
And for one whose delusion regarding the self has been severed and whose cognition of the Self remains ever-present, there is here no occasion for the activity of speech, mind, or body. (102)

Anticipating the objection that "even for one whose intellect has arisen, there will still be future karma after the destruction of that [intellect]," he says: "Not so. The word "of its persistence" (sthiteḥ) is to be understood as "in the form of a continuous flow" (pravāharūpeṇa). The connection is: "because here, in the case of the knowledge of the inner Self, there is always persistence. || 102 ||
If there should be an occasion for action, it shall be like the occasion for your alms-round.
Because right knowledge always abides, having the reality of the Self as its cause. || 103 ||

He raises the objection that for the knower (*vidvān*), there may be an occasion for ritual action (*karman*) just as there is for wandering for alms and so forth; this is expressed by the words "of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*). The underlying thought is that even for the knower, such an occasion does not cease to exist, because we observe the maintenance of the body and because of the scriptures concerning liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). He refutes this by rejecting the validity of the example with the word "no" (*na*). The reason for this is given as "the Self" (*ātma*); for the reality of the Self is the cause for the constant and perfect abiding of the intellect in its flow.

The construction [of the verse] is "tvāt" (because of that). For indeed, when the knowledge of Brahman as the Self—which is neither an agent nor an enjoyer—is truly established, there is no room for activities such as wandering for alms;
nevertheless, because that [activity] appears through the persistence of what is sublated, like a burnt cloth, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is not contradictory—this is the sense. || 103 ||
An entity does not depend on an occasion [for its existence], because it is established by its own nature.
Action alone depends upon the occasion, for it is dependent upon its causal factors (kārakas).

Now, an objection is raised: since Brahman is a real entity (*vastu*) distinct from time, it must have a connection with time—just like a jar—and therefore, for the knower who has that as his very self (*tadātman*), there would also be a connection with it;
and consequently, there would likewise be a connection with karma. To this, he replies: "Not a real entity" (*na vastu*).

For a real entity, dependence on time—whether regarding its origination (*janman*) or its manifestation (*jñapti*)—is not tenable, because [Brahman] is eternal and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*); such is the meaning. Then, to whom [does time apply]?
Regarding that, he says "action" (kriyā) to address the expectation concerning time; by the word "action," every effect whatsoever is understood. || 104 ||
When the flame of right knowledge is present, how could ignorance arise again?
Furthermore, because it arises from pure defects, karma is not accepted as being like this. || 105 ||

It has been stated that for one whose ignorance has been burnt by knowledge, there is no possibility for karma. Now, fearing that even for a knower there might be scope for karma because ignorance—though destroyed by knowledge—might arise again, he says: "Perfectly... For ignorance that has been destroyed does not come into being again, due to contradiction; nor does something of the same kind [as the previous ignorance] arise, due to the absence of a cause; nor is ignorance itself the cause, because it has been destroyed; nor is that which is not destroyed its cause.
The battle is established.
[vol2, page 73]
3 Brāhmaṇa] With the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri: 369.

[If it were] otherwise, the arising of that [knowledge] would be purposeless, and there would follow the consequence of no liberation. Nor is the Self itself the cause of that [knowledge], because the aforementioned defects remain as they are. Nor is the distinction of ignorance [the cause], because there is a lack of evidence; for even though [ignorance] is perceived as one, such a distinction is possible. Therefore, for the knower in whom ignorance has been destroyed, there is no karma.

[This is] the state of being. As for the argument that for such a person, rites like the *agnihotra* should continue just as begging for alms (*bhikṣāṭana*) and so forth do, [we ask: does this apply to one who possesses direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), or to one who possesses indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)? It cannot be the first, because we do not admit it; for in his case, begging for alms and so forth are held to be merely the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*). He refutes the second [possibility] with the words "śuddha" (pure), etc. For one who possesses indirect knowledge, due to the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), hunger and thirst—[which arise] independently of the scriptures—...

The meaning is that because it is caused by mere defects, the activity of wandering for alms and so forth does indeed occur. However, he states the distinction that the *agnihotra* and other such rites are not caused by mere defects, as they are prompted by the scriptures: "But not... (verse 105).
However, we do not maintain that our eating and so forth are caused solely by defects such as hunger.
Because there is a fixed multiplicity of causes, the action is therefore not equal to eating. || 106 ||

He elaborates on what has already been stated: "Hunger and so forth. He explains the commentary beginning with "Because it depends on the scripture, its cause, time, and so on," as follows: "Niyata... (Verse 106).
Likewise, even in the case of a fault, there is a restriction of time and so forth.
If it is argued that [this] might occur during begging for alms and so forth, this is certainly not the case.

One might object: "Even though begging for alms and the like are causes of fault, just as there are restrictive rules such as 'one should beg from the four castes,' 'one should beg at one time,' and 'for ascetics [the rule is] fourfold,' so too should there be restrictive rules for the knower regarding the Agnihotra and other rites. To this he replies with the word "fault" (*doṣa*).

Just as there are rules regarding time, caste, and number even in your own case concerning the purity of begging and so forth—which are themselves causes of fault—so too must there be rules regarding the Agnihotra and other rites.

The construction is: "It may be so. He says, "This is not so," [meaning]: for the learned person, even the wandering for alms and such is unestablished; therefore, the restriction of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites—which would entail such rules—is cast far away. || 107 ||
This is not a restrictive rule for us, because it is actually an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā).
Nor does this [consciousness] instigate action; therefore, it is said that [the opponent's position] is inconsistent. || 108 ||

To the objection—"How can there be a lack of accomplishment for the wise when there is a rule of injunction?"—he replies: "Not at all. Rules such as "one should move about at one time" and so forth are not applicable as injunctions for us, the knowers of Brahman, because they have transcended the domain of rules. Yet, this does not imply acting according to one's whims; for such behavior is caused by a lack of discrimination rooted in unrighteousness (*adharma*), and those two do not exist for the wise. Even in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), they were non-existent [for the knower].

How could activities belonging to the path [of worldly life] possibly exist during the state of knowledge (*vidyā*), given that even residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) are absent? Furthermore, because rites such as the *agnihotra* are sublated, there is no persistence of what has been sublated; this is the intended meaning, since they are merely semblances (*ābhāsa*). Moreover, the injunction applies only to the ignorant who desire to know (*vividiṣu*);
even for them, this is not a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because it is accepted as being a well-known injunction of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*). He says: "Exclusion. And that too—

He says "action" (kriyā) with the intention that, otherwise, the knowledge of Brahman—which negates what is to be acquired—would likewise negate ritual actions such as the Agnihotra. Indeed, since that [knowledge] brings about the cessation of other things, it does not impel action;

therefore, how could there be any contradiction with knowledge? And for what reason would there be any application of the Agnihotra and so forth for one who possesses such knowledge? This is because there is a rule that an injunction must have a positive entity as its object.

370. Having raised the objection that there exists a capacity to imply action, Sureśvarācārya, intending to show the absence of such implication because it would be contrary to knowledge (*vidyā*), says: "Therefore—"
Diti: The meaning is that there is an inequality because alms-giving and the like produce both purity and fault, whereas ritual action does not. || 108 ||
Therefore, there can be no detractor of one who has given birth to the knowledge of the identity of the Self.
The arising of the cognition of the Self is for the purpose of negating all entitlements to ritual actions.
Therefore, like a prohibition or an injunction, there is an injunction regarding the knowledge of the true nature of the Self.
For verbal, mental, and bodily actions have a single cause, namely, the intention (pratyaya). || 110 ||

Fearing that if a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) were prescribed for those desiring to know (*vividiṣu*), it would be untenable because it would be impossible for them—who are intent on performing those very acts for the sake of knowledge—to engage in the pursuit of knowledge, he says: "Not from this" (*nātaḥ*). Since a restrictive injunction, whose fruit is the exclusion of other [acts], does not impel one toward a contradictory action, it therefore does not sublate the cognitions of the Self; rather, it is indeed supportive, just as [the restriction] of one who is devoid of eating and so forth [is supportive].

The meaning is that for one who delights in the cessation of all activity, those [works] do not arise; for one possessed of passion and other such qualities has the qualification for ritual acts (*karma*), whereas one who is dispassionate has the qualification for knowledge (*jñāna*).

Since for the knower there is an absence of the very cause [for action], ritual acts are impossible, and because such a person’s state is equivalent to that of a mendicant and the like, the author—having established the authority of the *Tattvamasi* and other such texts as being sublaters by causing the cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—concludes the intermediate subject matter (*avāntara-prameya*) with the words "all ritual acts," etc. Adhi...

Are they the ritual acts (*kārāḥ*), or their performances (*pravṛttayaḥ*), or the pride of being a Brahmin and so forth which is their cause, or the relationship between the injunction and the person, or the fruits? He refers to what was stated in the first half [of the verse] by the word "that" (*tat*). The injunction is the sentence that is the cause of right knowledge; the remainder is that it is the means of knowledge (*mānam*) by virtue of its being the remover of that [ignorance]. He states the reason why the Self is to be known as the cessation of all karma: "the inner" (*pratyak*)—[verse 109, 110].
Therefore, the validity of a statement is certainly established when it is based on a single, real entity.
For there is no distinction between the two regarding the rule of prohibition. || 111 ||

He concludes the primary subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states that there is no difference between a prohibitive statement and a statement such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), because in both cases the erroneous activity [of the world] is eliminated, leaving no remainder of what is to be done (*akāryaśeṣa*). Thus he says: "In both. By this, the reason indicated by the word "that" (*tat*) is established.
It has been made clear. || 111 ||

In this world, worldly conduct arising from a single natural defect is demonic, while that which has the scripture as its sole cause is divine; between these two, there is conflict due to their opposition. (112)

Thus, by this investigation, once the purity of the Brahman-Self is established, the authority of the Vedāntas is established; and it is established that other [passages], such as those concerning the meters (chandasya) and so forth, possess authority regarding the meaning heard in scripture when there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge. Consequently, since the purity and other qualities of the deity Prāṇa are established and the meditation upon him has been proven, it is understood that the passage beginning with "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) has that very [deity] as its primary subject. This is the knowledge [to be gained].

Having concluded this incidental investigation concerning "that which is being examined," they [the commentators] proceed to explain the passage beginning with "They, indeed, [spoke] to Speech. They restate the meaning of the sentence beginning with "The gods and the Asuras," exactly as it was previously stated, along with its supplementary elements, through the textual sequence starting from "natural" (*svābhāvika*) and ending with "agency and so forth" (*kartṛtvādi*). Here, within the speech and other organs of the sacrificer's body, that which is designated by the term "nature" (*svabhāva*)— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
Nature (*prakṛti*) is that activity consisting of knowledge and action which arises from defects such as passion and the like, independent of the scriptures that teach its cessation.

Among those very [beings], that which is primarily scriptural—the worldly activity consisting of knowledge and so forth—is the divine (*daiva*); because of the mutual opposition between these two, there is a rivalry between the gods (*deva*) and the asuras—this is the meaning. || 112 ||

If the capacity for the activity of consciousness arises spontaneously from attachment to the natural state, it belongs to the enemies of the gods; but for the gods, it is illuminated by the knowledge arising from the scriptures.
There would be an authority over both action and knowledge; therefore, there is conflict between them. (113)

Anticipating the objection—“If both groups can be designated by the same term, how can there be rivalry between them due to their opposition?”—he says: “Prākṛta,” etc. *Prakṛti* is ignorance (*avidyā*); from that arises attachment to sense objects, and thence knowledge and action. In this regard, for the Asuras, there is naturally established what is called "qualification" (*adhikṛti*), which signifies active engagement; whereas for others, there is qualification in ritual action and so forth as illuminated by the light of scriptural discernment. Therefore, because of the opposition between these two, for them...
The meaning is that there was a conflict. || 113 ||
Elevation above the human state for a person occurs through pure dharma alone;
degradation results from adharma, while birth as a human arises from both. (114)

He says "utkarṣa" (exaltation) for the purpose of instructing the disciples that those appointed [to officiate] must strive for the victory of the gods and the defeat of the asuras. When there is victory for the gods and defeat for the asuras, then for the sacrificer—who is conditioned by speech and the other [senses] denoted by the word "deva"—there arises exaltation from the human level up to Prajāpati, due to the predominance of dharma; whereas in the case of victory for the asuras and defeat for the gods, [there is degradation] through the asura-speech and the other [senses].

Due to the power of unrighteousness (*adharma*), there may be a fall from the state of a human down to that of a stationary object (*sthāṇu*); likewise, when there is an equality between gods and asuras, for one who has been so established, there may be a fall due to the equality of dharma and adharma, resulting in human status. Therefore, the meaning is that those authorized [to govern] must strive for victory over the gods and not for defeat. || 114 ||
Because of the assumption of bodies beginning from the first-born [Brahmā] up to a stationary pillar.
The Veda declares [the world] to be beyond the worlds; contradiction is based upon that. || 115 ||

He cites scriptural corroboration for the stated point, beginning with the words "āpraja" (from Prajāpati). Since the previously mentioned fruits such as *dharma* and so forth are intended by the Śruti, therefore, in the phrase "in the worlds" (*lokeṣu*), the nominal stem of the Śruti refers to the assumption of bodies—from Prajāpati down to an inanimate post—which are births resulting from the fruits of karma.
Furthermore, the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) declares that there is mutual conflict among the gods and others caused by those aforementioned fruits; it speaks of their rivalry therein.
This is the meaning. || 115 ||
Only toward the fruits of the lower worlds, which consist of ordinary knowledge and action.
"This father is to be served as long as he lives"—such was the conviction of the Asuras. || 116 ||
Having freed this father from attachment to the mundane world by means of divine practices, [he departed].
One should fulfill the desire of the gods to the best of one's ability. || 117 ||

He states the intention of the Asuras who were vying with the Devas: "In the lower worlds... [etc.]. Even though their father was facing toward the Devas, the fact that he was turned away from them by the sins of his own attachments is where [the text] states the disposition of the Devas who were competing with the Asuras: "By means of natural... [etc.]. That is to say, having brought about a separation from attachment to sense-objects created by ignorance (*avidyā*). The divine means are tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth.

[The practices] beginning with celibacy (*abrahmacarya*) and so forth. "One should rise" means from the state of humanity up to the attainment of the status of Prajāpati; this is the remainder [of the sense]. "According to one's capacity" means without exceeding the capacity for knowledge and action. 116–117.
* Here, the absence of qualities (guṇa) is to be considered.

Thus did the gods and asuras contend with one another, each regarding himself as a lord of men and a sovereign of subjects.
In accordance with their own natures, they vied with one another through their respective functions.
He concludes the account of the rivalry between the gods and the asuras with the word "nara" (man). The qualification [“man”] is intended to exclude Prajāpati in his state of fruition.

The word “evam” (thus) refers back to the intention already described. According to the nature of the sāttvika and tāmasa [types], there is [the attainment of] tranquility and so forth, or desire—[the latter being] for the tāmasa.
The meaning is that, due to the emergence and suppression of their respective functions, the rivalry between the gods and the asuras proceeded, causing distress. || 118 ||
Whenever the conduct arising from the scriptures manifests as a goddess, at that time it is demonic.
Because he passes beyond everything without exception, he is remembered as the one to be conquered by the gods.

How then is it that there is victory for the gods and defeat for the asuras? To this he says: "When... Since, at the stage when scriptural knowledge and action arise, there occurs a complete suppression of innate knowledge and action, therefore the arising of scriptural knowledge and so forth is the victory of the gods, and the suppression of non-scriptural knowledge and so forth is the defeat of the asuras—this is the meaning. || 119 ||
But when the demonic army, led by desire and anger, advances;
For the birth of those asuras is indeed the victory of the Unborn One.

How then is there defeat for the gods and victory for the asuras? To this he says: "But the asuric... Here, the group of instruments (the senses) dominated by innate knowledge and so forth is called the "asuric army. "Of those gods" means of them [the senses]. The expansion of desire and so forth through the medium of innate knowledge and so forth is the meaning of the pronoun "their. This refers to the distinction between the previously mentioned victory and the victory to be described hereafter.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "and"; the second "tu," however, is used for emphasis. || 120 ||
Because it is their inherent nature, they are afflicted by a vast army belonging to the asuras.
The gods found no peace, because they did not perceive a means for their own protection.
Having restated the meaning of the sentence ending with "aspardhanta," he prepares the ground to explain the purport of the subsequent sentence beginning with "te ha... by stating:
"Because it was natural. This "naturalness" regarding their numerical superiority is the reason why the gods, being fewer in number, were oppressed.
He states another reason for their lack of happiness: "Their own self... (121).
Then, the gods of their own realm were being oppressed by the asuras.
A virtuous thought appeared, which destroys the fear of the Daityas.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "te ha" [they, indeed] as follows: "From their own ground," etc. The meaning is that, while the speech and other faculties associated with *tamas* were being suppressed by the sattvic speech and other faculties—which are the cause of scriptural knowledge and the like—in that state of calamity, there arose an intellect (*buddhi*) that was the cause of their welfare; therefore, they spoke to one another. The reason for their goodness is given as "by the Daityas"; the meaning is that it was the cause for destroying the fear produced by the Asuras. || 122 ||
Having resorted to the Udgītha here in this Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [one attains the goal].
Having cast aside the demonic state, we now proceed toward the divine state.

Explaining that very same thought, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "Hanta" as follows: "The Udgītha. The word "now" (adhuna) is used to express that the recourse to the deity of the Udgītha is the immediate cause for both the removal of the state of being a mortal and the attainment of the divine state. || 123 ||
1. ‘Tamo’śe; 2. jayastataḥ; 3. kha. ‘te’paja’.

Whatever agency and so forth is established here is seen to have speech and the other [senses] as its medium.
For one who is free from ignorance, that [notion] which arises from ignorance regarding the self is negated.

Having restated what has been said, he explains the purport of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "They [said] to Speech," which speaks of all worldly transaction as residing in Speech and the other organs.

He says: "Agency and so forth. Whatever agency and so forth is observed here in the Self (*ātman*), that belongs to it [the Self] only by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as Speech; for such [agency], which follows and ceases with ignorance (*avidyā*), cannot possibly exist in the Supreme, who is free from ignorance, eternally liberated, and described by such passages as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Thus [the text concludes].

Therefore, because all specific attributes are negated, the meaning is that it [the Self] is superimposed upon the Inner One (Pratīc) through the medium of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as speech and so forth, which are the effects of ignorance (avidyā). || 124 ||
All worldly and Vedic conventional usage will now be explained.
For, in the context of non-refuge, [the notion of] "I" and so forth occurs with respect to the mind and other things that are not the self. (125)

He states that even from the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), agency and so forth do not exist in the supreme Self, using the words "Laukika... and so on. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to indicate the consensus among the wise (*vidvatprasiddhi*) regarding the fact that there is no real agency and so forth in the Self. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), speech and breath are included. (125)

Because the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), when enveloped in darkness, conforms to the tendencies of primordial matter (bhūti), no form other than that [of matter] is perceived apart from the immutable self (kūṭasthātman). || 126 ||

In this regard, having raised the objection that "even though that [agency] is absent in the Lord (Īśvara), it is observed in the individual soul (jīva); therefore, it must belong to him," he says: "bhūta... (the passage beginning with *bhūta*). The meaning is that since the Supreme Self—remaining unmodified, yet having attained the state of a *jīva* by being delimited by ignorance (*māyā*)—is described in scripture as "as if meditating" and "as if moving" (*dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva*), it is logical that the notion of agency and so forth applies to Him, as He conforms to the activities of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties. If that is so, then there would be duality: one who possesses agency and so forth, and another who is devoid of it.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The immutable" (kūṭastha). The sense is that it has been stated that agency and so forth, superimposed by one's own ignorance, belong to the supreme inner self (pratīc) alone, by means of its specific limiting adjuncts. || 126 ||
Having deliberated thus, they said: "The udgītha is the supreme means."
Then the deities, having assembled together, performed an examination of it with great effort. 127.
Having stated the purport of the narrative in the form of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), he explains the meaning of the section beginning with "They said" (*te hocuḥ*) as follows: "Thus.

The meaning is that, having determined through the sequence described in the passage "Come, let us overcome the Asuras" (*hantāsurān*) that the *Udgītha* is the cause of excellence, the deities such as Speech (*vāk*) and the others held a mutual discussion.

To the question "What is this so-called *Udgītha*?", he replies: "The investigation of that," which is an effort other than [the mere understanding of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Activity. || 127 ||
They honored Speech, for it was indeed employed in the ritual of the Udgītha.
Seeing them exceedingly busy, the gods then spoke these words.

Regarding the phrase "they spoke these words," the author explains its meaning by showing the very manner of their examination. He states "these words" (*vācam*) and provides the reason for the possibility of that [examination] by way of the *udgītha*:
"For this... He then states the result of that possibility: "they spoke these words. (128)
Sing the Udgītha for us; let this chanting have you as its primary agent.
In this context, the word *udgītha* denotes the very action of yoga. || 129 ||
1. He observes.

In response to the expectation of what they said, Sureśvarācārya introduces the subsequent passage and states its meaning: "Thou" (*tvam*). No sandhi has been applied here due to the preoccupation with citing the *pratīka* (key word). Having commenced the examination of the *udgītha*, how is speech (*vāk*) employed in the ritual act of the *udgātṛ*? [It is employed] in the *udgītha*.

Anticipating the objection that she (the syllable) should be employed for a specific kind of devotion, he says: "The Udgītha. By the word "here" (iha), the statement of the passage beginning with "Hanta" is referred to. || 129 ||
Because it is connected with this hymn, there is merely devotion, but not [the attainment of] anything else whatsoever.
And here, by the word "speech," Agni is meant, as he is the one who presides over speech.

He states the reason for the aforementioned point: "by means of the *stotra*. Its meaning is as follows: because the *udgītha* enjoined in passages such as "By means of the *udgītha* let us pass over [evil]; do thou sing for us" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.2.7) is the subject of the context (*prakaraṇin*), and because its connection with the *pavamāna* chants is perceived in the passage "Now, therefore, of the *pavamānas*" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.2.1), there is no room for the *udgītha* sub-division (*bhakti*) therein; thus, the injunction "Whenever he should begin the *prastāva*, then he should mutter these [mantras]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.2.3) transcends the *udgītha* sub-division.

Since the injunction for the act of recitation (*japa*)—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—is connected solely with the mere act of chanting (*udgāna*), it follows that here too the word *udgītha* does not intend to denote the mere musical part (*bhakti*).

Furthermore, in this context, the word *udgītha* is never used in any sentence to denote the mere musical part alone, because that alone is not to be meditated upon, whereas the meditation on the *udgītha* as a whole is what is intended here; nor, however, is the act of chanting itself not to be meditated upon.

He states that there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya because the intention is to enjoin the meditation on that deity by way of restating the *udgītha*—which is a specific part (*bhakti*) of the Sāman known as the *udgītha*, not merely the act of singing (*udgāna*)—since it is desired that the meditation on that deity follow such a restatement; for in that context, the status of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha* is enjoined through a restatement of a meaning that does not conflict with the subject matter. [The opponent objects: "But we observe that only a conscious being, such as a servant, is directed by another conscious being, such as a king..."

One might raise the objection: "How can there be an injunction of speech, which is insentient, by means of the eye and other organs, which are also insentient? To this, he recalls what was stated in the passage, "Speech and so forth are words," using the word "speech" (*vāk*). Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sentence beginning with "They said to Speech.

Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), the fact that the words "breath" (*prāṇa*) and so forth in the subsequent sections—such as "Then they said to Breath"—also denote deities (*devatā*) is likewise included.

He specifies that very [deity] with the words "Agni. According to the Vedic scripture, "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth," Agni alone is the deity presiding over speech; and it is she who is to be understood here, because—as will be stated later—the impossibility of any other [well-known meaning] will be demonstrated. || 130 ||
For this object of entreaty is indeed considered to be sentient.
In this context, the union with the deity is intended through the practice of the female devotee (upāsikā). || 131 ||

But to those who assert that the deity is insentient, he says: "The object. In common worldly usage, it is observed that one who is the object of a request is sentient, as in the case of the statement, "O Chaitra, chant the udgītha! Since she is the object of such a request, the sentience of the deity of speech (vāg-devatā) is established. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to express the consensus of both ordinary people and investigators regarding the fact that a sentient being is the object of a request. This concerns the deityhood of speech.
He states another reason: "upāsi" (one should meditate). Here, the meaning of the word "iha" (here) is the context of meditation (*upāsti*). || 131 ||
For this reason as well, it is the deity alone that is denoted here by the word "speech."
Because that [state] arises from human effort, the deity is indeed the supreme Lord.
He states the aforementioned cause and effect with the words "for this reason also" (*ato 'pi*). The particle *api* has the sense of adding [the fact] that [the Self] is the object of entreaty.

The word *iha*, as before, refers to the subject matter of the present statement. Furthermore, because the state of being fire is the fruit of the meditation on speech, it is understood by the word "speech.
