He says "nam" (indeed) because that [state] arises from it. Having raised the doubt as to how the state of being that [deity] can constitute the human goal (*pumartha*), he says "devatā" (the deity), because the deity possesses unsurpassed sovereignty. || 132 ||
Therefore, that very [nature] is to be understood as present in all stages of meditative concentration.
But here, they are not to be understood as having the instruments, locations, and objects [of the senses]. || 133 ||

By the logic of the sequence stated in the passage beginning with "They [said] to Speech," he says "That very [one]" to show that even in the subsequent sections beginning with "Then to Breath," it is the Deity itself that is denoted by the words "Breath" and so forth.

Anticipating the objection—why should the words "Speech" and so on not refer to the sense organs themselves by virtue of their conventional usage—he says "But not... Here, the "contexts" (iha) refers to the stages of meditation under discussion. || 133 ||
Because of being for the sake of another, because of insentience, and also because of mortality. || 134 ||
In this way, words such as "speech" (vāk) and so forth denote deities.
It is to be understood everywhere wherever meditation is intended to be expressed. || 135 ||

Regarding this, he states the reason: "pārārthyeti" (because of being for the sake of another). The word "api" (also) is intended to include [attributes] such as "not being the Lord" (anīśvaratva). Having stated in this section that words such as "speech" (vāk) refer to deities, he extends the principle—that this is the same even in other sections with the same meaning—by saying "evam" (thus). He prevents over-extension [of the principle] by saying "yatra" (where...). 134 || 135 ||
Those who have reached this certainty [hold that] speech is denotable by the mere act of recitation.
The gods performed worship; she indeed is the deity of the Udgītha.

The view of the author of the Bhāṣya—who employs the word *devatā* (deity) in reference to Speech (*vāk*) in the statement that "the function of the Udgātṛ consists of the work to be accomplished by the deity of Speech"—has been stated. Anticipating the objection that the deity of Speech cannot be an object of meditation because she is not revealed by the *japa-mantras*, he says: "By the *japa*...
etc. The gods were certain that this very Speech is the referent of the mantras beginning with "Lead me from non-existence to existence," and that she alone is the deity of the Udgītha.
The meaning is that they worshipped speech with the notion that it was the Udgātṛ priest. || 136 ||
This speech is for the sake of the gods; it is a song of praise for the exaltation of the gods.
One should sing the *udgītha* according to one's ability; whatever enjoyment is free from attachment [is to be offered]. || 137 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "tathā" (so be it) as follows: "O God" (deva). When the prosperity of the gods is intended, the means for that is indeed *udgāna* (chanting); therefore, this Speech, out of a desire to conceal her own power, performed the *udgāna* for the sake of the gods who were seeking wealth. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yo vāci" (he who [is] in speech) as follows: "him" (tam). || 137 ||
By means of which enjoyment one [satisfies] the deities of speech, sight, and so forth, day and night.
He directly experienced that enjoyment and sang it forth in its entirety.
Anticipating the question, "What is this enjoyment based on speech that is common to all living beings? he says:
"By which... Enjoyment is benefit (*upakāra*). [He describes] the benefit produced by the act of speaking through the deity of speech (*vāg-devatā*), which is common to all causes and effects.

The meaning is "singing. This indicates that the constant life of the aggregate is dependent upon the deity of the *udgītha*. By saying "day and night," it is stated that the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) was used to express that the dependence of that life upon it is perceptible. || 138 ||

During the Pavamāna hymns, the Udgātṛ priest should perform the duties of the sacrificer according to the prescribed rule.
He sang for the *bubhukṣā-phala-mudrā* and for the remaining [mudrās], and then he sang for himself. || 139 ||

What is this *udgāna*? Is it exclusively the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), or is it also the duty of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*)? Not the first, because that would contradict the statement, "He should sing for himself food and nourishment. As for the second [alternative], in order to determine which *stotras* involve the sacrificer’s *udgāna* and which involve the priest’s *ārtvijya*, he says: "In the *pavamānas*," meaning according to the rule, without transgressing the defining scripture. *Jyoti-*...

In the *Ṣoḍaśī-stoma*, there are twelve chants (*stotra*); among these, in the three known as the *pavamāna*, the chanting (*udgāna*) belongs exclusively to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because the fruit of the ritual action generally accrues to the sacrificer.

As for the remaining nine chants, the chanting also belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because the connection of the singer (*udgātṛ*) with the fruit in those cases is based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*) stating, "he should chant food for himself. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate the aforementioned reason. Just as it is for the sake of the sacrificer—
Thus, the meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) is that [the author] has likewise attained his own purpose. || 139 ||
In the remaining hymns, Speech sang for herself.
Whatever auspiciousness she spoke, she indeed bestowed that upon herself.

What was stated as "in the remaining [stotras]," and so forth, is now clarified. Regarding the phrase "in the stotras": the meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that the *udgāna* (chanting) for the sacrificer has already been performed in three of the stotras. The word *atha* (now/then) is used to show the occasion for the chanting for one's own sake (*svārthagāna*) in the remaining stotras. Having thus explained the division, in response to the inquiry "What is that which is chanted for one's own sake?", he says: "That which... and so on. Not here...

The meaning is that in the hymns (*stotra*), the one with the auspicious face (*kalyāṇavadana*) is to be employed for the sake of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); this is what has been chanted. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to establish that the aforementioned task cannot be accomplished by other means. || 140 ||
In accordance with the scriptures and as is appropriate, it is free from defects of phonemes.
"May such power of articulating phonemes belong to me alone. (141)

He describes what that "auspicious mouth" (kalyāṇavadana) is like: "Just as" (yathā). The meaning is that the capacity for the pronunciation of phonemes—being free from defects such as excessive rapidity and so forth, and in accordance with the sequence prescribed in treatises characterized by grammar and the like, as well as the requirements regarding the points of articulation such as the palate—is itself what is meant by "the auspicious mouth," which is to be cultivated. || 141 ||
Whatever arises from a beautiful countenance belongs entirely to the gods alone.
The fruit is merely a matter of speech; it is not dependent on fate.

How then is it that, regarding the *pavamāna* [stotras], the singing (*udgāna*) is said to belong exclusively to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), since it enters into the aforementioned form of speech? Anticipating this objection, he states: "The singing belonging to the sacrificer manifests [itself] as 'auspicious' (*kalyāṇa*)," etc. Thus, the effect arising from the aforementioned speech belongs indeed to the sacrificer in the *pavamāna* stotras.

The meaning is that there is no priestly function (*ārtvijya*) here because there is no scriptural statement to that effect. He concludes that the priestly function consists of singing. By saying "mere recitation," the meaning is as follows: just as it was stated that the task produced by mere recitation and its specific variations in the *pavamāna* chants is, by default, for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), so too all tasks consisting of recitation in other hymns (*stotra*) are exclusively priestly (*ārtvijya*) and not for the sacrificer. Alternatively, [the word] *yāja*...

By this *vārtika*, it is concluded that the office of the *māna* priest is not divided [among the other priests], nor is the singing of the *uttama* (final) verses [performed by them]. For whatever effect is produced by speaking auspicious or inauspicious words—that entire result belongs to the deity and is indeed for the sake of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), and not for the sake of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). As for that which is called "the auspicious [sacrificial] butter" (*kalyāṇājya*), it is not [for the priest].

The phrase "having a beautiful face" should be construed as applying specifically to the office of the officiating priest (*ārvtijya*) and not to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Even if one adheres strictly to the literal reading, there is no contradiction; therefore, one need not exert oneself excessively [to resolve it otherwise]. || 142 ||
But as the darkness was being dispelled by the Udgātṛ priest with his voice, [the darkness] of the enemies of the gods...
Not being diverted from their own offices, they know the Divine.

He states the meaning of this: "In darkness" (*tamasīti*). When the voice sang the *udgītha*, while the voice was being meditated upon in its form as the *udgātṛ*, the enemies of the gods—the Asuras—perceived the intention of the gods; that is to say, when the power of the Asuras, consisting of desire, anger, and so forth, which is rooted in non-discrimination, was being cast out by the *udgātṛ* in the form of the voice, the enemies of the gods, being driven away from their own natural knowledge and action regarding their respective objects by the sign of that [power's] diminution, understood the purpose of the gods. This is the perception of the intention of others.
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of an introduction. || 143 ||
"By this word, O deities, let strength be ours and darkness [be removed] by the Udgātṛ."
Having conquered by means of their own light, they shall attain the form of fire and the other elements.

He states what that was which resided in the heart of the gods and was understood by the asuras: "By this," etc. "Darkness" refers to desire and so forth preceded by that [darkness]; "light" refers to knowledge and so forth pertaining to the science of the self (śāstra). || 144 ||
"The great danger has arrived," thus the asuras realized.
At that time, those whose minds were abandoned [of worldly attachment] were engaged in improper actions.
Attachment to speech and other faculties arose from self-conceit.

(145) [The commentary] reveals the intention of the Asuras: "If, through the destruction of the Asura forces, the deities of speech and so forth were to assume the forms of Agni and the others, then the Asuras—being of inferior strength—would suffer a loss of their own essential nature; therefore, one must strive to defeat the gods. [This is expressed by the words] "mahat" and "asurāḥ," where "asurāḥ" is the word division.

Having demonstrated that the Asuras possessed the notion that the gods were their food by means of the sign of the diminution of passion and other qualities, [the author] now provides an introductory transition (*pātanikā*) to show that they also held that notion by means of a sign stated in the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "in the ritual action" (*karmaṇi*): when Vāk and the others, who had been appointed to the office of the Udgātṛ priest by the gods other than themselves, were in the presence of the Asuras—an unsuitable occasion—due to the force of their own self-conceit and their lack of skill in discerning positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they failed to perform auspicious speech and so forth.
The meaning is that attachment has arisen for him, and its unsuitability consists in its being related to himself alone. || 145 ||
The wise understand that what is called "auspicious" is intended by the gods as a means to find a flaw.
"Indeed, by this Udgātṛ priest, they shall transcend their own form through speech. (146)
Now, he states the sign by which it is known that the Asuras understood the intention of the Devas, as declared in the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "that which [the Udgātṛ] speaks auspiciously":

the meaning is that the Asuras knew the intention of the Devas because of a lapse on the part of the Devas—namely, their attachment to speaking what was auspicious—which provided an opening for the Asuras. He demonstrates the very same knowledge of the Asuras regarding the object intended by the Devas with the words "by this," referring to the Udgātṛ’s speech.
The connection is that [the elements], having transcended us, will attain their own form consisting of fire and the other [elements]. || 146 ||
Having understood this, he rushed forward with waves of arrows released from his own bow.
Then the Udgātṛ priests pierced them and abandoned their ritual duties.

Having restated the demonic knowledge (*āsuraṃ jñāna*), he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "attacking him" (*tam abhidrutya*) as follows: "Knowing thus. This refers to the approach (*abhigamana*) of that knowledge.

Thus it has been stated. The phrase "then" (*atha*) indicates that the cause for abandoning Vedic performance is the destruction of attachment and evil. He states the resulting consequence—that those whose speech and other faculties are seized by demonic attachment turn away from Vedic knowledge and action—by saying, "They are pierced. (147)
No other power exists for anyone else in the destruction of the asuras.
By this improper speech, which lies at the heart of the matter.
The contact with defects such as sin is inferred as residing in the cause. || 149 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since the deities of speech and the other senses are objects of meditation, it is possible for them to destroy the Asuras, how can they be said to be pierced by evil (pāpman) and thus averse to scriptural rites such as sacrifice—he replies with the words beginning "No" (na hi). The meaning is that no one other than the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), such as speech and the rest, possesses the capacity to repel the Asuras, because they belong to the side of the Asuras due to their identification with limited individuality. Nevertheless...

Anticipating the objection that "since there is no affliction by evil among the offspring of Prajāpati, it is not logical [to attribute the world's defects] to the cause, because such [evil] is absent there; otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of being accidental," he says: "By this. By the sign—namely, the untruthful speech and so forth experienced by the class of Prajāpati’s offspring—and by the sin and so forth inferred from that sign residing in them, the connection with sin and so forth residing even in Prajāpati, who is the causal self, is likewise inferred.

The subject of dispute (the world) is preceded by sin and so forth, because it is the object of an adverse cognition, just like suffering; and that [suffering] is preceded by a cause, because it is an effect, just like a pot.
The meaning is that the misfortune pertaining to living beings cannot arise from some other cause alone without [prior] sin, since an effect conforms to its cause.
Having emerged from the form of the narrative, the Śruti now speaks in its own person.
He explains what occurred in the cause by means of the effect, through his asuric nature.

Having raised the doubt that there might be a lack of confidence even regarding a matter established through inference due to the absence of corroboration by direct revelation (*śruti*), he introduces the passage beginning with "He who... (*sa yaḥ*). Regarding the word *vyutthāya* ("having risen"): the *Śruti*, having determined that the deity of speech is not to be meditated upon, and having turned away from it because of its lack of commendatory statements (*arthavāda*), rises up in opposition;
yet, because she herself speaks what is true, she [speaks of] the sin and its effects as described in the Sūtra, which are inferred from the untruth and other vices observed among her offspring.

The meaning is that he did not say so because of the mark of sin associated with the Asuras. This has been stated excessively [as an exaggeration] with the intention of generating confidence in those who follow the Śruti regarding the matter thus explained. || 110 ||
It is inferred from an effect that is forced and improper.
Before the creation of Prajāpati, that which was known as evil existed in the cause and in speech. || 151 ||

[Objection: Surely, because falsehood and other such effects are perceived among living beings, the piercing by evil (pāpavedha) is postulated [for the soul]. However, in the case of urine, since there is no basis for such a postulation, it is not so postulated. Furthermore, the inference from the nature of being an effect cannot serve as the basis for postulation, because an effect is established merely through its cause; and since an effect conforms to its cause, the establishment of evil and the like would follow even there [in the case of urine], leading to the undesirable consequence that it would apply to the Supreme Being, who is the cause of that [universe]. To this, he says: "Because it is seen... (dṛṣṭe).

No. That which was the piercing by evil in the speech of Prajāpati while he was in the state of a sacrificer in a previous kalpa is inferred there by the mark of the evil residing in its effect; nor does this entail [the presence of evil] in the Supreme Cause as well, because of the scriptural text "unpierced by evil," and because of the scriptural text "evil does not reach him here"; nor is there piercing by evil even in the Sūtra, since for him who is in the state of fruition, although he is free from evil, [the piercing occurred] when—

The meaning is that because that state belongs to one who is in the condition of the ego (māna), and because for one who is embodied there is no removal of pleasure and pain, according to the Śruti. || 151 ||
That evil which was cast out by the Asuras is seen in the effect.
A statement that contradicts valid cognition must rely upon its respective [intended] effect. || 152 ||

Having prepared the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to explain the passage beginning with "He who," he explains it: "He who. The meaning is that the evil (*pāpman*) which was previously cast upon Prajāpati’s speech by the Asuras is understood through its effects—such as falsehood and the like—in the class of living beings (*prajāvarga*).
While explaining the passage beginning with "Whatever this," he clarifies the very evil perceived within the class of living beings: "Falsehood. One should not speak untruth.

The meaning is that whatever—such as speaking untruths—is contrary to the scriptural injunctions prohibiting [actions like] *diti* and so forth, and is observed to reside in the subjects who are the effects of that Prajāpati, by that [observation] he is inferred to be "evil" (*pāpman*). || 152 ||
The reasoning that "it is that very same thing" applies to the relationship between cause and effect.
That which is manifest evil among living beings, and that which resides in its cause; || 153 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "that very same evil" with the words "sa eva" (that very same). The particle *hi* is used to indicate that those two are well-known in both worldly experience and the Vedas. He further distinguishes those two evils with the words "among progeny" (*prajāsu*). That evil which is clearly seen among progeny through such things as falsehood, and that which resides in the *sūtra-vāk* (the causal speech) that serves as their source—that is precisely this [evil]. And thus, by means of the letters *ā* and *ya*...

Having referred to evil residing in the cause, its very presence in the effect is stated. However, the intention of the two subsequent verses is that, having referred to evil residing in the effect, its very presence in the cause is intended to be expressed. || 153 ||
The nose, the eye, the ear, and likewise the mind, in this sequence.
Just as the gods had spoken their words, so too were all the asuras pierced by them.

Having determined that the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatā) is neither the object revealed by the mantra of recitation nor the object of worship, he now states the purport of the four sections beginning with "Then [they approached] Prāṇa" (atha ha prāṇam).
He says: "The sense of smell," meaning in sequence according to the order of the text; thus, up to the section concerning the goddess of speech. || 154 ||
Among all the organs of action, speech alone is the representative indicator here.

"The eye and the ear [are the organs] of the sense-faculties (*dhīndriya*), and likewise the mind (*manas*) of the intellect (*buddhi*). (155) He says "karma" [in the following verse] to indicate that the unmentioned sense-faculties are to be understood by implication. Here, the context under discussion is the subject matter. The eye and the ear are included along with the nose because there is no difference in their having been mentioned [previously]. As for the phrase "of the sense-faculties," it refers specifically to the skin and the tongue.

The multiplicity of expressions arises from their various distinctions. The phrase "in the same way" was stated in order to provide speech and so forth as examples. The word "and" (ca) serves to include the unmentioned mind (citta) and ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 155 ||
Without taking up the entire world, the action of even a single individual is not admitted.
What more need be said regarding the vital breath (prāṇa), which encompasses the entire internal self and the senses? || 156 ||
Why is it said that by mentioning the mentioned sense organs, the unmentioned ones are implied; why is there not simply a literal grasping of those that have been mentioned?
For that [literal approach] would be flawed.
To this, he replies with the word "entire" (*kṛtsnam*). It is not authoritative that even a single cause can perform its own function without encompassing the entire world;
for in the Śruti passage, "This earth is honey for all beings," the causality of everything toward everything is established everywhere.
Since this will be explained later, it follows that when one sense organ acts as the agent of its own function, there is a grasping of all internal organs; otherwise, agency would not be possible.
What more need be said? For that [agent] which depends on everything for its own effect, dependence on all internal organs is unavoidable;
therefore, the term used is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is the meaning. || 156 ||
Although this entire world is perceived as a composite aggregate, [it is nevertheless empty].
Nevertheless, although this matter has been urged here, it has not been established in its true sense.

One might raise the objection: "If, by virtue of being the cause of its activity, the entire world were included [in the meditation], then everything here would be an object of worship, just as speech and the other organs are;
otherwise, even speech and the rest would not be objects of worship, as there would be no distinction. Anticipating this, he says: "Even though...

Because it is connected as a cooperative factor in the activity of speech and the rest, that which is mentioned here in this context as speech and so forth for the purpose of worship—even though it pertains to the entire world—[is intended].

The meaning is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is established through the impossibility of the production of effects [if it were not real], cannot be an object of worship; for according to the maxim, "that which is obtained as a matter of course is not the purpose of the Vedic injunction" (*yaścārthādartho na sa codanārthaḥ*). || 157 ||
It is observed even among the remaining [beings] in both auspicious and inauspicious forms.
Their division is that of the Asuras; by that, their piercing [of the heart] is inferred in them. || 158 ||

By what has been stated, the indication of what has not been stated has been established. Now, an objection is raised: "In the case of speech and the others that have been mentioned, the piercing by evil (pāpman) is known;

however, it does not exist in the remaining ones, such as the skin and so forth, because there is no evidence for its existence. Therefore, how can the unmentioned be indicated by those that have been mentioned? To this, he says: "The auspicious," etc.
Because even in the unmentioned skin and other organs, there is the "touching of the auspicious" and the resulting effect, and so forth—in this manner, the effect [serves as the evidence].

Since a distinction is observed, it is inferred that even in those [other cases], there is the piercing by the demonic evil as in the previously mentioned instances; because the logic is the same, the [previous] indication is appropriate—this is the meaning. || 158 ||
Therefore, for that purpose, there is this further scriptural statement: "Thus, indeed."
Just as speech and the other [organs] were pierced, so too should the skin and the other [organs] be understood. || 159 ||

The statement beginning with "evam" (thus) introduces the subject matter already stated. The word "ataḥ" (therefore) means: since there is penetration by evil (*pāpman*) even in the skin and other [organs], this scripture (*śruti*)—referring to that very object, namely the penetration by evil—speaks regarding the skin and so forth by relying on the principle established in the case of speech and the others. This intention is that the statement of a matter already established by logic through scripture is for the purpose of establishing that the logic itself has a foundation.
He explains the Śruti passage cited again with the words "yathā" (just as). || 159 ||
Therefore, placing forward the examples of the perfected ones (siddhas) and the like, it is said as follows:
Having spoken thus, [this was said] for the purpose of establishing that the remaining [entities] are likewise pierced by evil. || 160 ||

Having raised the doubt as to what establishes that the skin and other [senses] are pierced by evil (pāpman) just like speech and the others, he recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "in the form of the auspicious and its opposite. The phrase "of the established" means: because inference is possible when there are existing examples.
"Of the remaining" means: of those not mentioned, such as the skin and so forth, which remain after speech and the others have been mentioned. [The subject] under dispute is permeated by evil.
The meaning is that [the self] possesses that activity, just like speech and the other [organs]. || 160 ||

An effort is made here to explain the meaning of this [verse], namely, "I pierced through."
Each of them afflicted those [beings] with their respective attachments to the senses and with evils. || 161 ||

Fearing that there may be tautology in the two phrases "they assailed with evils" (*pāpmabhir upāsṛjan*) and "they pierced with evil" (*pāpmanā avidhyan*), he says: "They pierced. The meaning is that there is no tautology because they stand in the relation of explanation and that which is to be explained. He states the meaning of the explanatory sentence:
"By their respective [means]," meaning by such modes as "the touch of auspiciousness belongs to me alone," and so forth. The word "them" refers to the deities of the skin and the other senses.
It should be distinguished that the mention of the asuras' status as objects is expressed by the first case ending, whereas their status as agents is expressed by the verbal suffix. || 169 ||
That which they formerly performed in conjunction with it is here called "piercing" (vidhyam).
The separate process of the emanation and withdrawal of those deities who have been pierced [by the rays]. 162.

He states the meaning of the passage to be explained with the word "yad" (that which). The construction is as follows: that very thing which the Asuras attributed to speech and the other organs as a connection with evil in the preceding sentence is here expressed by the phrase "they pierced them with evil" in the subsequent sentence. Anticipating the objection that the phrase "evam etā devatāḥ" is redundant because its meaning is already conveyed by the phrase "evam u khalv etāḥ," he says "yāḥ" (which). This refers to those deities, speech and the rest.

According to the logic demonstrated, those [entities] pierced by evil (pāpman) are distinct from the context of the vital breaths (prāṇa); thus, the conclusion of that section is made with the words "Thus" (evam) and so forth, meaning that this [conclusion] is not redundant. || 162 ||
For speech and the other [senses] were pierced by the Asuras with arrows consisting of attachment and evil.
Therefore, those [women] should be avoided and not cultivated by those who desire their own welfare. || 163 ||

He states the purport of the section thus concluded: "With regard to attachment," etc. The sense is that speech and the other [organs] are not to be meditated upon as being primary in themselves. || 163 ||
Thus she was despondent regarding the former deities, because they had failed to destroy the Asuras.
Then, by process of elimination, they approached the middle vital breath with reverence.

Having restated what has been said above, he introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "atha hemam" by means of the word "evam. The reason for this is that, according to the logic already stated, there is a lack of expectation regarding their being manifested by the mantra of recitation or being the objects of meditation, because it has been determined that they are subordinate due to their destruction of the Asuras. Stating the reason for his lack of recourse—namely, that the previously relevant deities have been excluded and no other deity is relevant—he sets aside what was expected and introduces the word "atha" (now). [The text continues with] "pāri..."
It would remain, [as stated in verse] 164.
The word "atha" (now/then) serves to indicate immediate succession and likewise for the purpose of dramatic representation.

Because it is not well-known, [the word] "this" (*imam*) refers here to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), just as it does for the skin and other [senses]. [The commentary] states the meaning of the word "then" (*atha*) as the exclusion of [the possibility of the sense organs] speech and so forth; this is expressed by the word "now" (*atha*). It states the meaning of "this" (*imam*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). A gesture (*abhinaya*) is a specific activity of the body or its parts that indicates the intended meaning. Because there is no such gesture in relation to the other vital breaths—
Fearing that this too might be useless, he says: "Because it is not well-known. Here, the word "here" (iha) refers to the body.
For [the Self] is not well-known in the body as being located in a specific abode like the collection of organs; therefore, the purpose of the gesture is established. This is the meaning. || 165 ||
Because this breath is always present in the mouth, it is therefore considered to be *asura*.
This qualification [of the breath] is for the sake of distinguishing it from speech and the other [organs]. (166)
He states the fruit [of the practice], preceded by an explanation of the meaning of the term *śrāsanya*: "It exists," etc. (verse 166).
382 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, Page 86]
By the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), it should be understood here that the term refers exclusively to recitation (japa).
"The deity of the Udgītha is Prāṇa"—this became the firm conviction of the gods. || 167 ||

In response to the inquiry as to with what intention the speech and other organs approached the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), he says: "Japa," etc. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The construction is as follows: among the vital breaths, let it be understood that the principal breath is the one revealed by the *japa-mantra*, because that [revelation] is not possible for any other; thus the gods reached the certainty that this very breath is the deity of the *udgītha*. It is revealed by that...

The gods determined that the defeat of the Asuras was due to the power of the deity of the *udgītha*. Since neither of those two [qualities] exists among any of the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the gods reached the conclusion—by the method of elimination—that the principal breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is both that which is revealed by the mantra and the deity of the *udgītha*;
thus, the meaning is that they approached him. || 167 ||
In the application of mantras, it has been revealed for the presence of all.
We shall resort to that refuge who is capable of bearing our burden and to whom we may go.

Anticipating the objection as to how the status of the *udgītha* deity as being revealed by the mantra is established for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he says "In the mantra," because the meaning of the mantra is complete therein. The word "ana" is to be split [as *an-a*]. || 168 ||
Examining for a refuge by means of the path of the narrative as it has been told, they...
In due order, they sat down around the Āsandi throne, having overcome all evil.

Having raised the doubt that speech and the other organs, like the vital breath (prāṇa), do not depend on a physical substrate, he says: "While they were examining. He describes the manner of their examination: "As stated. He states the reason for the examination of the protector: "By evil" (pāpman). He states the conclusion of the examination: "They reached" (āseduḥ). || 169 ||
For the sake of providing a means of worship for those humans who seek the highest good.
This is a narrative; the eye is not to be meditated upon in any other way. || 170 ||

The objection that it is improper to follow the path of the narrative as it was told—on the grounds that the Śruti lacks intent regarding the narrative and thus its composition would be unjustified—is raised; in response, [the author] states, "For those seeking the highest good," to show that the narrative was composed by the Śruti in order to determine the object of worship. The mention of "human beings" is intended to state that the qualification for the worship of deities belongs to humans alone. He demonstrates the aforementioned point by way of contrast: "Not others..."
Thus [it is said]. || 170 ||
Why is it not stated here, as it was previously, that "enjoyment [occurs] in the vital breath"?
For, as in the case of speech and the other [organs], no distinct experience of the self is perceived. || 171 ||

One might object that, as in the previous case regarding speech and so forth—where it was said, "the enjoyment in speech"—here too one should say, "the enjoyment in breath," on account of the context.

[The author] raises this doubt with the words, "That which is breath. Considering that the context is set aside by an indicative mark (*liṅga*), he provides the resolution with the words, "Of speech and the rest. For there is no specific enjoyment belonging to breath; therefore, since it is impossible to qualify it, even though [breath] exists...
The meaning is that the context, being sublated by the impossibility [of its own premise], is rendered ineffective. || 171 ||

The qualification [of "not-omnipresent"] applied to speech and the other [faculties] is appropriate because their enjoyment is not complete.
Since everything is indeed of the nature of unsubstantial enjoyment, what is distinguished here, and by what? || 172 ||
Anticipating the objection that even in those cases, the qualification "as if living" (prāṇavat) would be inappropriate, he clarifies the illustration with the words "not in its entirety" (akṛtsna).
For speech has only speaking as its enjoyment, not seeing and so forth; and the eye has only seeing as its enjoyment, not speaking and so forth.

Thus, since there is no enjoyment belonging to the entirety of speech and the other organs, the statement "of speech" and so on refers to the specific enjoyment of each individual organ. Let it be so, then.

Anticipating the objection that, like speech and the other organs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) also lacks a specific qualification because there is no difference in its not experiencing the full range of objects, the author clarifies the point of comparison by stating "of all. This means "of seeing, hearing," and so forth. Why is the effect questioned, and why is the cause questioned?

The word "prāṇa" functions here as the locative case. And it has been said: "Because the vital breath is not well-known here [in common experience], it is treated like the skin and other organs. (172)
The intention of the enemies of the gods was that [the sacrifice] would not be completed.
One who has begun an action that is not yet completed is said to be "about to pierce. || 173 ||
He explains the verbal form in the passage beginning with "having rushed toward him" (*tamabhidrutya*). Regarding the term "intention" (*abhisaṃdhi*):

the meaning is that by the word "wishing to pierce" (*avivyatsan*), it is stated that a desire to strike the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the Asuras arose. He clarifies this very point with the word "unaccomplished" (*aniṣṭhita*).
An unaccomplished action, which consists in the cause for contact with evil, is its undertaking; that is the desire, and it is here expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
This is the meaning. || 173 ||
By merely pointing out the region, Prāṇa became the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
Such an example is stated for the purpose of understanding this meaning. || 174 ||

In the passage beginning with "not as" (na yathā), he explains the meaning of the word "sa" (he). Regarding the phrase "he would pierce" (vivyatsyet): the meaning is that an illustration is stated in the manner about to be described, in order to convey the sense of the statement "the vital breath (prāṇa) is the slayer of the life-forces (asu)," [a sense understood] merely by the arising of the desire to strike the vital breath. || 174 ||
Just as a clod of earth thrown from near a rock with great force is intended for the purpose of shattering it.
It would indeed shatter into a hundred pieces by its own momentum upon contact with a whetstone. || 175 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "yathā" [as follows]: "of the desire to split. This means that when there is a desire to split a stone, for that purpose one stands near it;
then, regarding the cause of the powder-ball being destroyed in many ways by virtue of its own momentum once it has been hurled with great force at that stone, he says:
"ākhaṇa-. The meaning is: "due to contact with a stone that is difficult to split. The word "hi" is used to indicate that the stated matter is a common worldly observation. || 175 ||
Thus, having reached the invincible Prāṇa, they perished by the thousands.
Through the destruction of those Daityas, the gods became truly gods forever. || 176 ||

In this way, he explains the illustrative application (*dāṣṭantika*) beginning with the word "cause" (*hetu*). Regarding the term "invincible" (*apradhṛṣya*), it means "unassailable," "extremely profound," and "beyond the reach of the Asuras. He then states the meaning of the phrase "thereupon the gods became [so]" as follows: "They attained him. This means that the gods—namely, the deities such as Speech (*vāk*) and the rest—having abandoned their conceit of limitation due to the destruction of the obstructive Asuras by the Chief Breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), became truly gods.
It means "the gods indeed became [so]," up to that point. || 176 ||
For this very reason, even the asuras, who share the same causes for their human nature, are equal [to them].
They perished, their movements scattered in all directions, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone.
1. ka. ga. read *bhitsayā yauṃ*. 2. kha. reads *necchayā*.
[vol2, page 88] 384.

Showing the meaning of the word *viṣvañcaḥ*, Sureśvarācārya explains the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*) along with the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). He says, "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Precisely because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unassailable, by the mere desire to strike it, the Asuras became the causes of humanhood, stationary existence, and so forth, as well as the causes for the loss of their divinity.
The meaning is that all bonds, simultaneously, have perished in both the present and the future, like a clod of dust thrown against an indestructible stone. || 177 ||
Because they possess the same nature as the vital breath, the deities are also like the vital breath.
The gods indeed became [victorious] through the destruction of all the sins committed by the Daityas. || 178 ||

He explains the very meaning already stated in the passage beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*). [The verse begins with] "Prāṇa... etc. Because the sacrificer, who is conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of speech and so forth, attains their true nature through the meditation on the "I-grasping" (*ahaṃgraha-upāsanā*) in Prāṇa, and because all evil consisting of the conceit of limitation is destroyed, speech and the other organs—being always of the nature of deities like Prāṇa—attain the state of being deities such as Agni once the obstruction of the conceit of internal (psychophysical) limitation has ceased.
The meaning is "they worship. || 178 ||
The sacrificer is the aggregate of the sense organs, such as speech and the rest, just as in the past.
Having destroyed the sin arising from the nature of his vital breaths, he attained the form of Virāj.

He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) in order to explain the meaning of the phrase "becomes the Self" (*bhavaty ātmanā*). [The commentary says] "Speech, etc. (*vāgādi*).

What is intended here is the portion of evil known as the conceit of being the Self, which is limited merely to the internal physical body (*piṇḍa*). The word "in the city" (*pure*) describes the stage of the maturation of meditation (*upāsanā*). || 179 ||
Likewise, one should worship Him by means of the path of narration as it has been described.
Having destroyed evil by means of his own self through the Virāj, he becomes pure without delay.

Explaining the commentary beginning with "In that manner" (*tathā*), he connects the sentence: "In that manner. The meaning is that, just like the previous sacrificers, having set aside speech and the other [senses] and taken hold of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having abandoned the limited identification resulting from the meditation upon it, the practitioner becomes one who meditates upon the *virāj* as the Self.
With the intention of stating that there is no delay in attaining the state of *virāj* once obstructing sins have departed, he says "without delay" (*acirāt*). || 180 ||
In this context, the form of the deity is always to be worshipped as being infused with the individual soul (jīva).
The vital breath (prāṇa) is the self of Hiraṇyagarbha; as long as there is absorption in that, it is silence (mauna).

[Objection: But surely Virāj cannot be an object of meditation because he is insentient; therefore, becoming that [Virāj] cannot be the fruit [of meditation]. To this, he says: "The individual soul," etc. In this context, it has been stated that the fruit is not merely the limiting adjunct (upādhi), but rather the deity’s body—the Virāj-self—which, through the predominance of the power of action, is Prāṇa, and through the predominance of the power of knowledge, is Hiraṇyagarbha, being characterized by the reflection of consciousness (caitanyābhāsa) and meditated upon through continuity and other means. This is the fruit.

The meaning is that this is logical. He states the limit of the meditation with the word "as long as": the meaning is that the meditation lasts for as long as there exists the state of the conceit of "I-ness" (abhimāna) toward that divine Self, just as one thinks, "I am a human being. || 181 ||
Having destroyed one's own asuric limitation through the accumulation of meditative cultivation.
Constantly permeated by that state of being, he quickly attains the very self of the deity. || 182 ||

Anticipating the objection that the attainment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) might also occur through mere knowledge, just like the attainment of other faculties, he says: "By cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). Having ascertained the object of worship from the scriptures, one accumulates cultivation toward it; then, having swiftly destroyed the conceit of identification with the body—which is bound to oneself—one [attains it] always.

"Purified by his disposition toward that very Self of the deity, he goes to that very one"—this is according to the Smṛti beginning with "He goes to each and every one of them, O son of Kuntī."
Such is the meaning. || 182 ||
Only the destruction of the constituent of darkness (tamas) occurs; however, the vital breath (prāṇa) and the other [elements] are not thereby attained.
For, being an effect, that effect cannot possibly exist apart from its cause. || 183 ||

"Because it is an effect" (*kāryatvāt*). The meaning is that attainment does not result from mere knowledge alone. || 183 ||
Having been a god here in this world, he becomes a god through the accumulation of meditative cultivation.
That [the Veda] originates from human activity has been established by us even through scripture. || 184 ||

He states that even scripture (*śruti*) is an authority for the fact that the state of being the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth does not depend on mere knowledge. He says: "The deity" (*deva*). The meaning is that by this scripture—[which says] "having experienced the state of a deity in this very body through the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one shall become the deity to be worshipped after the fall of the body"—it is declared to us that the state of being the vital breath and so forth is to be accomplished through human effort (*puṃvyāpāra*). The word "also" (*api*) refers to the aforementioned Smṛti.
He flows forth. || 184 ||
"He attains Brahman alone; for he was indeed Brahman even before, since he is non-dual."
"By the mere destruction of that delusion"—thus also is the instruction of the Śruti. (185)

Anticipating the objection that, just as the state of being the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth [is not attained] through mere knowledge, so too the state of being the Supreme Self (parātman) is not, he says: "Brahman alone.

Even prior to the state of oneness with Brahman, the individual soul (jīva), though in reality Brahman itself, was perceived as non-Brahman due to delusion (moha). Through the knowledge arising from the [great] sentence, by the removal of that [delusion], one attains nothing other than non-dual Brahman; thus, according to the Śruti, the attainment of Brahman is established as dependent solely upon cognition. Regarding the soul's [identity] with Brahman—

The term "non-dual" (advaya) is stated in order to refute the notion that [the Self] is a different entity. By the word "also" (api), other scriptural passages such as "and he is liberated" are included. || 185 ||
If [the self] were established by itself, it would follow that there is a contradiction with the Śruti regarding all other things.
Therefore, the Śruti declares: "Everything else is miserable," and likewise, "It is indeed one alone. (186)

Anticipating the objection that, just like the state of Brahman, the state of being the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is also established by itself and thus logically dependent on mere cognition, he says:

"By itself" (*svataḥ*). By the word "that" (*tat*), Brahman is denoted; by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), there is a reference either to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) or to the Imperishable (*akṣara*).

He states the contradiction with the previously cited statement, just as the statement "not here, manifoldness" (*neha nānā*) negates the duality of the vital breath and so forth: "In the same way" (*tadvat*).

By means of the word "ca" (and), he combines the inconsistency of censuring dualistic views such as "He is the death of death. The word "api" (also) indicates that [the view] would also contradict the meaning of such Śrutis and Smṛtis as "The one God in all beings" and "But the Self of beings is indeed one. He states the contradiction with other Śrutis: "One... (verse 186).

386. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
There is no establishment of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) and so forth as something distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
If there were a measurement here as there is for Brahman, then likewise the absence of liberation would follow.

1.1 Having stated the contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the eternal establishment of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), he states the absence of valid cognition [for its existence] with the words beginning "not" (*na*). [The text continues: "it exists"— *Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

The meaning is that while there is seen to be evidence for the independent establishment of Brahman in passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam*), there is no such evidence for the independent establishment of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the thread (*sūtra*), and so forth, by virtue of their being self-sufficient. The word "here" (*iha*) is connected with the preceding locative case.

Furthermore, regarding whether the unmanifest and so forth are unreal or real: in the first case, he says that if they were real, there would always be transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus [ends verse 187].
Then, when the Self manifests in the form of ignorance, the unmanifest, and so forth;
Upon the cessation of that [ignorance], there is cessation; this cessation is the state of pure selfhood.

He raises the second [objection] with the word "atha" (now). Therein, he states the establishment of his own position—that upon the destruction of ignorance through knowledge, there remains the existence of the unmanifested and so forth, which are its manifestations—with the word "tadā" (then). Nevertheless, one might object: "Is that cessation [of ignorance] different from the Self or non-different? In the first case, there is the consequence of duality; in the second, the coexistence of existence and non-existence is untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "nivṛttiḥ" (cessation).

The meaning is that, apart from consciousness as characterized by the mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) arising from the sentence, there is no existence for the imagined states of being and non-being, such as the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and so forth; for it is observed that the imagined serpent has neither existence nor non-existence apart from the rope. || 188 ||
The entire demonic evil, being hostile, was utterly defeated like the life-breath itself.
For one who attends upon that Prāṇa, the entire demonic [nature] perishes.
Furthermore, an enemy is desired to be one who hates, as well as one who does not hate, such as an Asura or someone other than that. || 189 ||

Having established the disparity between the state of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the state of the Supreme Self (*parātman*), he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "he goes to the other" (*parām eti*). [He begins with] "of the vital breath.

In order to explain the significance of the qualifying term "hating" (*dviṣan*), he states the twofold nature of the enemy—the Asura and the non-sinful—saying "the hating. The word "enemy" (*śatru*) refers to one who possesses a rival (*sāpatna*). || 189 ||
This Asura is considered to be a constant creator of obstacles for the attainment of vital breath.
Therefore, he is specifically distinguished by the Vedic revelation through the form of the hating enemy.

But regarding the demonic enemy (*āsura*), there is no such twofold division; thus he says: "eternal," etc. Since the demonic enemy is indeed always hating, therefore, by the scriptural statement (*śruti*) "the hating rival (*bhrātṛvya*) is the enemy," the term "hating" is used as a qualifier for the "enemy" who has attained the state of a rival; the meaning is that this [hating] is its specific attribute. || 190 ||
Once the Asuras have been defeated, no other enemy remains.
"He who knows thus"—this is an injunction, because the statement of the fruit is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). || 191 ||

Anticipating the objection that even in the case of the removal of enemies, there might be another obstacle [to liberation] and thus it would not follow from the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇātman*), he says:

"It has been stated. Just as in the case of "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*yad āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), a sentence is intended to be injunctive (*vidhipara*) even when connected with a well-known fact by the phrase "whoever knows thus" (*ya evaṃ veda*);
therefore, he says that what is intended is "one should know thus" (*evaṃ vidyāt*). He states the reason why the injunction is indeed intended:

"Because of the mention of the fruit": since the fruit is being stated by virtue of the previously mentioned explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and since that statement is a praise which would be inappropriate without an injunction, the meditation upon it is enjoined here as having the attainment of the Sūtra as its fruit; this is the meaning. || 199 ||
Or, by means of the statement regarding the incidental fruit, that meditation leads to liberation.
In this section on the knowledge of the Self, [this is stated] because of the injunction for its worship. || 192 ||

Alternatively, its worship is enjoined here as having liberation as its fruit. Regarding the intent of the Sūtra, he says that for the sake of the primary fruit, there is an incidental fruit—just like shade and fragrance when seeds are sown. He uses the word "incidental" (ānuṣaṅgī) to this effect. He states the authority for the claim that the worship of the Sūtra results in gradual liberation by way of attaining it, using the word "Self" (ātman). 192.
Therefore, it is understood from those very statements that [the Veda] is beneficial for the knowledge of the Self. || 193 ||
Then Āyāsya Aṅgiras, distinguished by his pure deeds and free from evil actions, [proceeded].
"This subsequent scriptural passage has been commenced with the intention: 'I shall prescribe the method of worship. (194)

Fearing that, since the meditation on the Sūtra is enjoined in the section concerning the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā), its fruit would be liberation, and thus the restrictive rule that "knowledge of the Self alone is the cause of liberation" would be unestablished, he says: "Knowledge of the Self," etc. That [knowledge] alone is the cause of liberation, because [the meditation on the Sūtra] is an auxiliary to its arising.

The meaning is that this is because of the context concerning Pāśadyumna. Furthermore, from the statement, "O you who possess the aforementioned secret doctrine (upaniṣad), when released from here, where will you go?", it is understood that the meditation on the Sūtra has gradual liberation as its fruit. Therefore, he says, "And because of the [subsequent] statement," indicating that the meditation under discussion culminates in liberation by means of the knowledge of Brahman. Since the primary meditation, which possesses its own fruit, has already been described, the subsequent passage beginning with "They said" refers to the meditation on the qualities.

Anticipating the doubt that [the teaching] might be limited to three methods, he states its intended meaning with the word "atha" (now). The meaning of the word "atha" is the immediate succession following the statement regarding the meditation on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) along with their fruits.
The passage beginning with "They said... and ending before "Now, for oneself, food-eating... is referred to by the subsequent scripture as the "later portion.
An injunction is superior to a restatement; in a mere restatement, there is fruitless effort.
Therefore, because it is connected with human goals, an injunction is relied upon here. 195.

You may raise the objection that since the fact of Prāṇa being Āṅgirasa and so forth is already established in common worldly experience, it is merely restated (anūdyate) and thus cannot be an object of injunction (vidheya) as part of the sphere of meditation. [The author replies: "Because it is a restatement" (anuvādāt). He states the reason why such a restatement would be improper: "A restatement," etc. The meaning is that in that view, a restatement is not tenable because a figurative statement (guṇavāda) would be fruitless. He states the reason why an injunction is superior: "Because it serves the human goal" (puruṣārtha), etc.

Because a mere restatement would be improper, because the distinction [between the fires] is logically established, and because the meditation on the vital breath—which possesses qualities such as being of the nature of Aṅgiras—is what is to be enjoined, it follows that these qualities also fall within the scope of the object of meditation. Thus he states the conclusion: "Therefore... (195).
In this context, it is heard that a connection with fruits exists in those meditations (upāsās) wherein such a connection is mentioned.
The procedure based on the qualities [of the mantra] should be understood as being like that of the staff, the senses, and so forth. || 196 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the qualities are to be enjoined by virtue of being objects of meditation (*upāsya*), why should this not simply be an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), he says: "It is heard" (*śrūyate*). In the case of the text, "One desiring sensory power should offer oblation with curd," it was explained in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* that because a different result—namely, the clarity of the senses—is heard as distinct from the result of heaven belonging to the primary Agnihotra, this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by way of referring back to the primary rite; and so it is here in the context of meditation (*upāsti*).
In those meditations on qualities (*guṇopāsti*) where a different fruit is heard of than the primary fruit, there is an injunction based on the qualities, as in: "The husband is the best" [vol2,

In passages such as "one who goes before" and so forth, as well as in those concerning Āyāsya and others, no result other than the primary fruit is heard; therefore, the meaning is that there is no injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) here. || 196 ||
But where there is a connection with the primary fruit directly from the Vedic text, [that alone is to be accepted].
That specific procedure is to be understood as it is for the [mantras] beginning with "yathāsyāt. || 197 ||

In that case, what kind of injunction applies to [the rites] beginning with the *Ayāsya-Āṅgirasa*? To this he says: "The principal," and so forth. Just as in passages such as, "One offers the cake on eight potsherds to Agni; one offers the cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma; one performs the *Upāṃśu-yāja* in between," since a distinct result is intended for each individual instance other than the result of the principal [sacrifices] like the *Darśa*, the *Āgneya* and others are accepted as being enjoined by a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*). Likewise [in the present case].

In those meditations (*upāsā*) where a connection with another fruit—distinct from the primary fruit—is not perceived through the words of the scripture, there is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*); and since no other fruit is heard in the case of the *ayās* and so forth, the meaning is that there is an injunction for a meditation on the action of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as qualified by that [absence of another fruit]. || 197 ||
Having attained the form of fire and the other elements, they do so by resorting to the embrace of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Then the vital breaths, speech, and the others, remembering the benefit they had received, said:

Although it is accepted that even for something connected to the primary fruit, there may be an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) without a connection to another fruit, nevertheless, with the intention that the aforementioned division is possible within the context of meditation (*upāsanā*), he explains the purport of the subsequent section by way of that division,
and then applies the words "They said" (*te hocuḥ*). [The word] "attained" (*avāpta*) refers to the cause for their attainment of the nature of Agni and the others.

The text says: "māha" (he said). "Prāṇeti" means the embracing of the primary vital breath—that is, its reliance upon it as the principal support; from that very dependence, meaning from that firm foundation. He states that having remembered Prāṇa, by whom the service consisting of the attainment of divinity had been performed, they spoke to one another at the stage of the result: "kṛta" etc. || 198 ||
He who, by becoming the infinite fire and other elements, has generated our vital breaths.
Where indeed does that Self abide, which is the destroyer of our enemies? (199)

In response to the expectation of what they say, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "where" (kvā). He says "Ananta... and so forth. He explains that its recollection is appropriate because it is their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and because it destroys the conceit of limitation which obstructs the divinity of speech and the other senses. He uses the word "ātman" and so forth;
the particle "hi" indicates the aforementioned reasons. || 199 ||
Reflecting thus upon their own selves, those young men spoke as follows.
They beheld him performing that service with the same devotion as before.

He explains the meaning of the words *nu*, *iti*, and *ayam*. Regarding "they reflect" (*vitarkayantaḥ*): "previously" (*prāk*) means prior to the state of fruition (*phalāvasthā*). Furthermore, "reverence" (*ādara*) should be understood as being directed toward the benefactor, the teaching, or both. || 200 ||
For even in the world, people understand that an object of investigation consists of meaning.
Just as speech and the other [senses] did, so too did the vital breath (prāṇa) depart into the Self.
Recalling the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the benefactor, speech and the other senses, while abiding in their respective fruits, deliberated within themselves and beheld him;

having said this, he shows that very point in accordance with worldly usage. "In the world too" (*loke 'pi*): the word "too" (*api*) is for the purpose of including the Veda. [Note: *dvividha* in the manuscript is likely a corruption.]

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the practice of the wise is not contradicted. The word "atha" (now/then) is stated in order to clarify the realization of the object, which is the fruit of inquiry. It has been said...
Having used the illustration as a basis, he states the point to be illustrated with the word "yathā" (just as). The self (*ātman*) is the aggregate of the body and the organs. || 201 ||
When it is stated in general terms as "of this," its specific qualification is then expressed.
Otherwise, O Prāṇaniścita, let there be no attachment to anything else in the interval.

He states the purport of the qualification "within" (*antar*) in the phrase "within the mouth" (*āsye'ntar*). [The verse says: "In general," etc. The meaning is as follows: if one intends to express a definitive determination and were to state without qualification that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) resides in the mouth," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [calling] the skin and other such things "vital breath" as well, since its presence there is no different. To prevent this, the qualification "within" is appropriate for the vital breath located in the mouth. || 202 ||
Since skin and other [elements] also exist in the mouth, this is therefore a qualification of that [tongue].
Then he distinguishes the vital breath (prāṇa) that moves within the cavity of the mouth. || 203 ||

When it is said that "breath is in the mouth," one might ask how there could be a possibility of its being in the skin and so forth in the absence of a qualification; to this he says: "The skin and so forth also.

Since these too exist in the mouth, when there is a general statement, they too would be included; therefore, the qualification "within that" (tad-antara) serves to distinguish the breath located in the space within the mouth from those [other things]. This is the meaning. || 203 ||
The skin and other [tissues] extend only as far as the mouth, not into the middle [of the body].
But the vital breath (prāṇa) is in the middle of the mouth; therefore, it is distinguished by the internal [prefix]. || 204 ||

How is it that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is distinguished from those [organs] by the aforementioned specifications, given that they too were said to be included within the mouth? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Within the mouth" (*āsye*). The point is that while the fact that the skin extends up to the mouth is established by experience, although speech and the tongue are located therein, they do not occupy the middle position by way of pervading the entire space. He explains how the vital breath occupies the middle position with the words: "But the vital breath... (*prāṇastu*).

The vital breath (prāṇa) exists within the space of the mouth and nose, whereas the skin and other [senses] do not; therefore, the qualification "internal" serves to distinguish it from them—this is the meaning. || 204 ||
Or rather, the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be the self (ātman) of all the sense faculties.
"This [is] within the mouth," thus it is shown by the illustration of the navel at the time of death. || 205 ||

He states another meaning for the word "antaḥ" (end/within) with the words "sarva... and so on. By the word "antaḥ" occurring in the aforementioned sentence, which signifies "conclusion," it is said that Prāṇa is the self of speech and the other organs; for it is there that they reach their conclusion, as they lack any nature other than that [of Prāṇa], according to such scriptural passages as, "Speech indeed merges into Prāṇa. To the question, "How do they reach their conclusion therein by virtue of lacking any nature other than that? he replies:

"Thus" means that, by the illustration of the spokes supported by the rim being fixed to the nave of a chariot, the scripture demonstrates—following the stated meaning—that the entire expansion of the elements and elemental products is fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa). || 205 ||
Having previously perceived the vital breath (prāṇa) thus, as being "within the mouth."
The immortals uttered [this], and from that [the deity] named Prāṇa arrived. || 206 ||

He states the meaning of the term "Ayāsya" with the words "This one. He indicates the connection of this utterance with the sacrificer of the previous kalpa by using the word "formerly. He states that the agency of speech and the other [organs] belongs to them in the state of fruition with the words "the immortals. || 206 ||
