390. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
Since it is the essence and the vital sap of the limbs and the organs, therefore...
Prāṇa is declared by those who know it to be Āṅgirasa, because he is the locus of those qualities.

He first explains the reason for [the name] "Rasa" among the limbs (*aṅga*). Regarding the phrase "of the limbs," he explains the proposition "Āṅgirasa. Regarding the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*), he provides the authority of the experience of those who know the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in that very context. By the phrase "by those who know it," he summarizes the meaning of the reason itself: that its status as *Āṅgirasa* is based on the quality of the vital breath being the essence of the limbs and their functioning.
"By its own quality," [it is said]. || 207 ||
How is it that the vital breath (prāṇa) is [called] Āṅgirasa? This is for the sake of understanding this point.
This will be explained later by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 208 ||

He says that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not possess the nature of being the essence of the limbs (*aṅgarasa*), because it is not established that the vital breath is the essence of the limbs, since it is possible for any one of the others—such as speech and so forth—to be that essence. He asks: "How so? To establish the meaning of the proposition—that it is indeed the essence of the limbs—he states: "Of this [breath]," indicating that the reason (*hetu*) consisting in its being the essence of the limbs will be made clear later through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). || 208 ||
In the same way, another quality of the wind is also established as being "far."
For the sake of accomplishing the noble fruit, the Śruti says: "That indeed is this. (209)

Now, one might object: "Granted that the Prāṇa is established as an object of meditation (*upāsya*), its qualities must be stated; yet that is not established, because its purity is unestablished. For one who is connected with impure speech and so forth, purity is not established—just as it is not established for one who has touched a corpse or someone who has touched that corpse. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the purport of the passage beginning with "That indeed is this" (*sā vā eṣā*) by saying "tathā" (so it is). This means: "possessing the previously mentioned qualities such as being the 'āyāsya' (the one to be approached) and so forth. Indeed, when these qualities are stated, the Prāṇa—

The sense is that its status as an object of worship is established because it is described as being free from attachment and evil, due to the firmness of its purity. Furthermore, since the superior fruit of meditating on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as qualified by this aforementioned quality—namely, the destruction of sin—will be established, he says that this quality is now set forth. He states: "It is noble" (*udāra*). Having indicated with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) that the quality is the subject to be expressed, he introduces the scriptural passage (*śruti*) regarding it: "That indeed... (*sā vā...*)
Thus [ends the verse]. || 209 ||
This breaking of the sequence is intended for the sake of accomplishing the method of worship.
Having abandoned satisfaction, it is indeed called "difficult" (duri). || 210 ||

[Objection: But surely, the state of being Āṅgirasa is first attributed to Prāṇa [in the passage beginning with "That which is this..."], and immediately thereafter, its quality of being *durguṇa* (difficult to attain) is introduced by the passage beginning with "That indeed is this... In that case, since the scripture will explain what is heard first later on, whereas the scripture beginning with "For it is far away" explains what is heard last right at the beginning—what is the reason for this reversal of the sequence? To this, he says: "Upāsti" (meditation). First, the quality of being *durguṇa* is to be meditated upon; immediately after, the state of being Āṅgirasa...

The sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) has been accepted as being set aside for the sake of establishing the sequence of meditation (*upāstikrama*), because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of the text; for if the [quality of] "goodness" were not mentioned first, the purification of *prāṇa* would not be established, nor would its status as an object of meditation be secured. Therefore, the meaning is that there is a transgression of the textual sequence, just as in the case of the sequence between the *agnihotra* oblation and the cooking of the rice-gruel (*yavāgū*). He states the result of adopting the sequence of meaning by setting aside the sequence of the sacred text (*śrautakrama*): since...
Thus [ends the section]. || 210 ||
This is indeed a distinguished form of meditation, because of the proclamation of its primary fruit.
This should not be understood as an injunction regarding qualities, because no fruit for such a fruit is mentioned. || 211 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 95] 3 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 391 1

Nevertheless, anticipating the objection that—just as in the case of curd and other substances—this must be an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) rather than an injunction regarding a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) because of its connection with a specific result, he says: "The qualified... There are two kinds of results for the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇopāsti*): the destruction of sin and the attainment of the state of the deity.

Regarding these, he provides the reason: "Because of the hearing of only that result, namely the destruction of sin, here. He says "This is not [the case]" because it is not an injunction regarding a subordinate quality.
He states the reason preceded by a proposition: "of that result," meaning that because no other result is heard of apart from the primary result, it is unlike the case of curd and so forth. || 211 ||
An object that has become subordinate to the ritual action is taught as a deity.
Because there is a connection with the practice of worship, it is therefore called a deity.

Having established that the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) as characterized by specific qualities is what is intended here, the author raises the objection: "Since the word 'deity' (devatā) is applied to the vital breath in the phrase 'this deity,' how can its status as a deity be justified? Anticipating this, he says: "In ritual action," etc. The meaning is that in sacrifices and the like, the deity is a conscious entity such as Agni, who exists as a quality distinct from the agent. Nevertheless, he asks how the vital breath possesses that status, and answers: "It exists," etc.

Nor is it correct to say that [the vital breath] is not a quality because it is an object (*karman*); for by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), what is intended is a factor of action (*kāraka*). Thus, since the vital breath is a conscious agent distinct from the [individual soul] and is a factor of action in the performance of an act, its status as a deity is appropriate; so he says: "As a deity. (212)
For one who knows thus, evil is far away; how could it possibly take hold?
Because it is not opposed to such knowledge, evil becomes far removed from him. (213)

[Objection: "The destruction of sin results from the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth, because scripture declares that through *dharma* there is the exhaustion of evil; however, this meditation (*upāsana*) is neither obligatory nor occasional, since it is enjoined for one who desires to become the very self of the deity. Therefore, it is objected that 'sin does not depart from one who knows thus'. [Reply: He refutes this by explaining the statement regarding the result, namely the word "far" (*dūram*). [He says] "Thus": for the destruction of sin is not necessarily restricted to the performance of obligatory rites alone, as [the removal of impurity occurs even] through bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).

Because that [distance] is well-known; therefore, since he is an adversary to evil by virtue of possessing such knowledge, the meaning is that this [evil] indeed remains far away from one who possesses such knowledge. || 213 ||
For the evil born from the connection between the sense objects and the senses is indeed demonic.
That which is limited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arising from the infinite [Self] taught in the Śruti is contradicted. || 214 ||

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "viṣaye" and so on. From the connection of the senses with their objects, a limited ego-inflation (*abhimāna*) arises; since this [limited ego] manifests as something natural that does not depend upon scripture, it is in contradiction with the unlimited ego-sense (*gaṇātman*) arising from scripture, because the contradiction between limited and unlimited ego-inflation is well known.
The meaning is as follows: || 214 ||
The discernment of the eye and so forth arises from the cause of ordinary cognition.
For one whose nature is solely focused on the inner self, sublation occurs through pride in the scriptures. || 215 ||

Now, since there is no distinction in the mutual opposition between the two types of conceit (*abhimāna*), it would follow that neither could function as the sublated nor the sublator, and thus both would mutually cancel each other out;
to this, he replies: "The eye, etc. This refers to the limitation and conceit regarding the eyes and so forth, which arises from ordinary knowledge and action.
(Note: *ka*, *ga* read *tukaḥ*; *yu* reads *yaḥ*).

192 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: A specific function has occurred for that [Self], which is of a single form internally (*adhyātma*) and situated merely in the body, [namely] the identification with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arising from the scripture, which is otherwise undivided.
The construction is that it is not logical for there to be no lower limit. || 215 ||
The mental modification consisting of vibration is present even in the ears and other sense organs.
Furthermore, it is the devourer of the objects such as sound by means of the vital breath and the sense organs. || 216 ||
The mental modification that perceives sound and other objects [is characterized] by its own attachments and the evils inherent in them.

"Corrupted, there is no movement; therefore, death is far away. [This means: Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has no connection with sin, it is established that its presiding deity (*abhimānin*), who is of the same nature as it, also has no connection with sin. Now, one might object: "The vital breath’s lack of connection with that [sin] is unproven, because, being a vital breath, it must be connected to it—just like other vital breaths—by inference. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Movement... and so forth.

The meaning is that the function (*vṛtti*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of movement, is unlimited and pervades the entire body; therefore, it is not defiled by sin. One might raise the doubt that the functions of the other vital breaths are likewise [unlimited]. He addresses this with the word "now" (*atha*) and dispels the doubt with the word "but" (*tu*). As for the phrase "of the senses, however":

the function of speech and the other senses, which perceives sound and so forth, has as its object only those respective [sensory data]. For there is no seeing by means of speech, nor hearing by means of the eye.

The meaning is that the function of the face is likewise limited. Nevertheless, suspecting that the contact with evil (pāpman) and its absence might be equal in both cases, [the author] states "by their own [powers]" to show that the limited functions of speech and so forth are defiled by that [evil], because limitation is the fruit of evil.
He then states that the function of the vital breath (prāṇa) is unlimited and not defiled by sin, because non-limitation is the fruit of merit (dharma).
"No. Thus, since inference is impossible in this way, he states the resulting conclusion that there is no connection of the vital breath (prāṇa) with evil: "Far...
Just as death is the gateway for the vital breaths, so too is the demoniacal nature the gateway for the self because of its identity with it.
And death would come to one who knows that; therefore, it is taught that "better" is the superior choice. || 218 ||

Having bowed and spoken of the non-connection with evil, he concludes that very point even for one who knows it, saying "Death. Just as death, in the form of attachment to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, becomes distant according to the logic previously stated, so too shall it be distant for one who knows it; because the knower is always of that nature through constant contemplation of it, the statement regarding the fruit—"it is far away," etc.—is not contradictory. This is the meaning. || 218 ||
The end of the quarters here is characterized as the middle of the village.
Because space is infinite, there is no direct end to the directions.

Having observed the clarity of the passage from "mā vā eṣā" up to "apa hatyai," [the author] explains the meaning of the phrase "yatrā'sām" and so forth, ending with "diśām antaḥ. Regarding the word "diśām": in this sentence, the term "dik" (direction) refers to the central region (madhyadeśa). The meaning is that the region situated beyond what is delimited by that [central region], being distinct from it, is the "end of the directions" (diganta). The very limit of the directions, such as the East and so on, is what is expressed by the term "diganta."
To the question "Why is this not accepted? he replies: "Infinite. Therefore, the fault remains that the end of the directions is exactly as previously stated. || 219 ||
People whose minds are refined by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.
Since it is stated here that [the self] has the intellect as its limit, there is not even the slightest fault.

2, page 97] 3. *Brāhmaṇam*, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

391. Fearing that if one were to take the term "Madhyadeśa" (the Middle Country) to refer to the well-known Central Region—defined as the holy land of Āryāvarta situated between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains—it would contradict authoritative consensus to claim that all other regions are inherently more sinful, he says: "Śruti... and so forth.

The Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*) consists of those whose minds are refined by conduct that is irreproachable and renowned in the scriptures; for even though it is already well-known, it is designated as the "Middle Country" precisely because it is presided over by such people, and since it is accepted that a region presided over by outcastes is more sinful, one takes those people and the land they inhabit as the limit.
Consequently, other regions and their inhabitants are called "extremities" (*anta*) in contrast to them; thus, any country other than the Middle Country is a direction (*diś*).
The meaning is: when it is said "it is so," how can there be any contradiction? || 220 ||
Therefore, the "limit of the directions" is understood as the boundary of the Middle Country.
The designation of "borderland people" results from their association with wicked persons.
Therefore, those who know this avoid it with great effort even nowadays. || 221 ||

Then, fearing that the word "Madhyadeśa" might have multiple meanings, he says: "Madhye... Since the aforementioned distinguished people constitute the Madhyadeśa, and the region inhabited by them is so called by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), therefore, in this sentence, the term "limit of the directions" (*diganta*) should be understood as referring to both the people other than those [distinguished ones] and the regions where they reside. Having raised the doubt, "Even if what has been described constitutes the limit of the directions, what follows from that? he states its distinction—

He states that it must be abandoned by saying, "prātyantika" (borderland). A "pratyanta" is a border region distinct from the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), specifically a land of barbarians (*mleccha*); the region inhabited by people dwelling there is occupied as their own home. Because such a place is a refuge for wicked people who abound in sin, it is abandoned in every respect even by cultured (*śiṣṭa*) persons who possess discernment while living there—how much more so by those of former times? This is the meaning.
Therefore, the word "ataḥ" is connected with the fifth case (ablative) of the preceding [term]. || 239 ||
In those border regions and among their inhabitants, [he saw] those belonging to the Asuras.
Since the vital breath deposited [the seed] therein, we should therefore avoid that.
He connects the passage beginning with "tadāsām" and so forth as the reason for the matter already stated. Regarding the word "teṣu," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the demonic evils. || 222 ||
A region is distinguished by its people, and people are distinguished by their region.
The learned, avoiding both of these as they are touched by evil, [do not accept them]. || 223 ||

He clarifies the meaning of this very "pair" with the word "people. He recalls the previously stated reason for its being something to be abandoned with the word "sinful" (*pāpman*). Since the learned (*śiṣṭas*) avoid both of those because they are touched by sin, he says that they should therefore be abandoned with effort by others as well: "the learned. || 223 ||
Or else, this word "ned" would signify either a combination or a distinction.
If the collective sense were not intended to be expressed, there would be no cessation of the undesired [individual meanings]. // 224 //
In order to explain the meaning of the passage beginning with "na id," he states the division: "samāhāra" (the aggregate). Regarding the view that there are two words, he states the intended meaning:

"anīpsita" (the undesired). When it is intended that there are two words—the indivisible word "nañ" and the word "it"—then the meaning of the sentence would be the non-cessation of that which is undesired or unwelcome. || 224 ||
1. ga. It is explained.
[vol2, page 98]
"If I were not to act in this manner, as enjoined by the prohibitive scriptures— "
One should ward off inherited evil by means of prohibitions and transgressions. || 225 ||

In this regard, he applies the statement: "Thus," etc. The meaning is that if one were not to observe what is stated in the prohibitive statements—such as "Therefore, [one should] not kill a living being"—in accordance with the scriptural injunctions of prohibition, then, due to the transgression of the prohibition, one would incur sin; and since that is undesirable, the observance of the meaning of the prohibitive statements must be performed. || 225 ||
Thus, when a distinction is intended to be expressed, the explanation should be applied to both words.
But the meaning of the word "mātra" (only) should be explained as performing a negation when there is non-difference.
He concludes by stating that this sentence is explained through its connection with the prohibitive statement only when both words [mā and na] are intended to be expressed:
"Thus, regarding difference... However, in the view that [the sentence] is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), the word *na* is not to be explained as a negator;
rather, he says that one should preserve the meaning of the prohibitive statement, thinking, "May I not be followed by evil. This refers to the sense of the particle *mā*.
Let it be so. || 226 ||
And this negation has a general scope; it does not apply to one who is unlearned.
For a sentence, due to its powerful grammatical derivation, apprehends only the general [meaning]. (227)
Fearing that, because the prohibition is heard within the context of the meditation on *prāṇa*, this prohibition might apply only to that [meditator] and not to all, he says:

"In general... That is to say, it applies to one who knows the *prāṇa*—that is, its meditator. An objection is raised: since the prohibition is understood from the context to concern specifically the knower of *prāṇa*, how can the statement "therefore, no person... and so forth have a general scope? To this, [the author replies] by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so on...

He says that [the sentence] is stronger because of its power over the context (*prakaraṇa*) in the Sūtra: "It is stronger. The meaning of this is: "In the case of a conflict among direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding due to the remoteness of its meaning. Here, an example of the conflict between syntactical connection and context is found in the *sūktavāka* recitation at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, where there are words denoting the deities of both the full moon and the new moon.

[The mantras] such as "May Agni and Soma enjoy this oblation," "May Indra and Agni enjoy this oblation," and so forth—regarding these, there arises a doubt: should this wording of the mantra be employed twice, both at the Full Moon sacrifice and the New Moon sacrifice, or should it be used where it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with a particular [rite]? Since *vākya* (syntactic connection) and *prakaraṇa* (contextual application) possess equal force, [the conclusion is that] by virtue of *vākya*, its own [mantra] is employed [wherever it fits syntactically], while by virtue of *prakaraṇa*, the other [mantras] are employed [in their respective contexts]. Thus, the entire [set of mantras is used according to these principles].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this very mantra is to be employed in both places. However, it is established in the third [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] that because the syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) based on the word (*śabda*) occurs more rapidly, whereas the application (*viniyoga*) based on context (*prakaraṇa*) is remote due to its being merely conceptual, the sentence (*vākya*) is stronger; thus, there is no application in both places by virtue of context. And so, in the present case as well, since the sentence is stronger than the context, from that...
Therefore, it is logical that [the principle of] non-proximity (asannidhi) applies only to those subjects who are commonly qualified. || 227 ||
He [then] restrained those [organs], speech and the rest, which had their evil removed by the Asura.
It is now explained how the vital breath (prāṇa) brings about the attainment of divinity. || 228 ||

Having accepted that the fruit of the meditation on *prāṇa* is the destruction of sin as previously stated, [the author] challenges the fruit of attaining deities such as Agni and others with the words "by the Asura-like" (*āsureṇa*).

The sense is that it is impossible for *prāṇa* to cause Speech and the other organs, whether they remain in their places or have perished, to attain their divine nature. [The reading] "sthite" is complete in manuscript *ka*.
[Vol.
2, Page 99] 1 Brāhmaṇam] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 395.

It is only through the destruction of the obstruction caused by the conceit of limitation that the attainment of divinity occurs for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within those very beings who are, in reality, the self of the deities.
He says, "This is stated," meaning that this [point] that "it arises" is expressed by the immediately following passage. || 228 ||
Through knowledge, ignorance is destroyed; through the power of meditative cultivation, divinity is attained.
Because there is a duality of action in the immediate [sequence], the word "atha" (then) would certainly [be used]. || 229 ||

He explains the sentence introduced by "atha" and so forth with the words "jñānataḥ" (from knowledge). From the knowledge of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), there is the destruction of ignorance regarding it;

from that, through the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward it, the state of being the deity arises. Thus, because there is a distinction between the acts of knowledge and cultivation, the word "atha" is employed in the sense of immediate succession to knowledge. Then, by the power of cultivation, the meditator transcends death—the deities such as Speech who constitute his limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—and [attains] Agni...

The meaning is that the vital breath (prāṇa), becoming the self of the lay follower (upāsaka), led him to a divine state. Regarding the stated point, "certainly" (dhruvam) is used to express certainty. ||229||
The vital breath (prāṇa) carries death away, because of the general statement and specifically because of the particular context.
The attainment of distinguished deities for speech and the other [senses] is brought about. || 230 ||

Anticipating the objection that the subsequent statement is redundant because the transformation of speech and the other organs into fire and the other elements has already been stated by the preceding sentence, he states the difference in meaning:

"Mṛtyum" (death). Since it was stated in general terms that the Prāṇa causes those deities—speech and the rest—to transcend Mṛtyu, which is evil, and attain the state of fire and the others, [the subsequent passage specifies] the particular nature of each, such as the fire-nature of speech and the wind-nature of the breath.
The meaning is that the nature of the deity as distinguished by the six [attributes] is explained by the subsequent passage. || 230 ||
Because speech alone [is superior] to the others here in the rite of the udgītha.
Therefore, it is said that the first [syllable] belongs to the breath (prāṇa) and to the udgātṛ priest. || 231 ||

Regarding the statement "Speech indeed is the first," one might ask how speech possesses primacy—that is, preeminence—and in response to this doubt, he says, "It is the nearest. The meaning is that because the breath (prāṇa) is the most effective agent in the ritual of the Udgātṛ priest, and because the Udgātṛ is extremely close to it, speech holds preeminence over the other instruments [of action]. || 239 ||
Thus, by attaining speech and the rest, as well as the fires and the rest, one casts off evil from every side.
Thus, the well-cultivated sacrificer attains the state of Vairāja. || 232 ||

One might ask: "Even if speech and the other organs attain Agni and the other deities, what does that have to do with the worshiper? For that [attainment] is not itself his fruit. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Speech and the others... By casting off all sins that obstruct their status as deities, through the aforementioned path, speech and the other organs—which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the worshiper—attain Agni and the others; and by that very attainment, the worshiper too, constantly meditating on Prāṇa as his Self, [becomes one with it] through the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
The meaning is that one attains the state known as Prāṇa, which belongs to two kings, just like the previous sacrificer. || 232 ||
Due to its connection with attachment to the auspicious, speech and so forth become causes of unwholesome action.
Having abandoned food, one should take refuge in the primary Self, which is free from death.
He summarizes the meaning of the section with the words "Kalyāṇa," etc. That which is the cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*), or that for which unrighteousness is the cause, is described as such.

Taking refuge in the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), one should meditate upon it as qualified by these three attributes; he states the reason for this: [it is] "devoid of death" (*mṛtyuvarji*).
"Regarding that," [it is said]. || 233 ||
I [present] the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya. [In the first chapter:
Virāj, endowed with the five [organs] beginning with speech, together with the physical realm (*sādhibhautika*).
Having abandoned the internal limitation, he then attains that [state]. || 234 ||

Since it has been stated that one should abandon speech and the other [organs] and take refuge in the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), there arises the possibility that they are not to be meditated upon at all; therefore, it is said, "by speech and the others. The phrase "by the five" is stated with reference to their enumeration [in the text], but it should also be understood as referring to the skin and so forth. He qualifies [the breath] with the words "the Virāj," etc., in order to show that the principal breath is free from death. It should also be understood as being "pertaining to the self" (*sādhyātmika*).

[It is] "all-pervading," meaning it has the entire world as its self; this is to be connected with the word "one should take refuge in. He states the fruit of meditating on the unlimited vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is established by such scriptural passages as "in whatever way... and so forth, beginning with the word "from that" (*tataḥ*). || 234 ||
Together with the elemental and the divine, it consists of name, form, and action.
The Sūtra is said to be Prāṇa, Aṅgiras, Satya, Ṛk, and Sāman. || 235 ||

Raising the objection that since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is likewise limited like speech and the other organs, how can its worshipper attain an unlimited fruit, [the author] establishes the unlimited nature of the *prāṇa*, which was indicated in the passage beginning with "Virāj" and so forth. [The term] "sādhibhūta" [is explained as follows]: the neuter form [of the compound] is connected with the masculine [subject] through the sūtra and the expanded context supplied by it. The world, consisting of three aspects—namely, the internal self (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*)—
The meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is thus designated in the Śruti. In that context, he states its nature as action by means of two words: "the thread" (*sūtra*).

He states its nature as form by means of two words: "Aṅgiras. He states its nature as name by means of [the word] "Ṛk. The mention of the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* is indicative of the *Yajus* as well. || 235 ||
One should know that single Self within all beings, which is the locus of knowledge, action, and their fruits.
He who worships through the consciousness of a self that lacks intrinsic nature shall go to Him.

Having stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indivisible, he states the resulting conclusion—that it is logical for the worshipper of that breath to attain its own indivisibility—with the words "That one" (*tamekam*). The word "substratum" (*āśraya*) refers either to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or to the ultimate ground where the intended meaning culminates. He specifies the limit of the meditation with the phrase "until its own nature": namely, until the manifestation of the knowledge of self-identification (*abhimāna-jñāna*) in the form "I am the vital breath. || 236 ||
That which was stated for the sake of worldly prosperity regarding speech and the other [faculties] has now been addressed.
The *āgāna* is prescribed for the *udgātṛ* in the remaining stotras. || 237 ||

Now, having restated the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then [he sings] for himself food," he states its purport with the words "It has been said," and so forth. The sense of the restatement is that the singing performed by the sacrificer—who is conditioned by the limiting adjunct of speech—for the sake of prosperity has already been described in connection with the three *pavamāna* chants. The word "now" (*atha*) signifies "at this point. He states that among the nine chants, the fruit to be accomplished through singing is indeed the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijyam*), because of the scriptural injunction; thus he says: "For oneself..."
Thus [it is said]. || 237 ||
However, since the word "food" (anna) refers to food in general, therefore—
It is called "the first" because it serves as a qualifier for that [word]. (238)

Fearing that the terms *annādya* (food) and *anna* (edible) might be redundant because they share the same meaning, he states the distinction between their referents: "The general... [and so on]. By means of the qualifier, it is intended to express the state of being consecrated (*saṃskṛtatva*) of that very [food] itself. || 238 ||

Since, from the very beginning, this conduct of eating food occurred in what is not the Self. Therefore, even today it is observed among the subjects who have come into being as its effects. || 239 ||

It is not only in the case of Prajāpati’s acceptance of food that scripture alone is the authority; rather, having observed the acceptance of food among living beings, who are its effects, one may infer it for the cause as well, because the effect conforms to its cause. Thus he says: "Since... The meaning is: "in the non-Self," that is, in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the acceptance of food for one's own sake is seen. (239)
The phrase "whatever it may be" is a restriction meaning that it refers to everything.
Indeed, by means of the vital breath alone, this entire world always sustains itself.

He explains the words contained in the passage beginning with "yaddhi" (for that which...). Regarding "yaddhi," he states the meaning of the sentence: "by means of breath. The sense of the word "hi" (for) is that the world's status as an eater of food is established through the medium of breath alone, as proven by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 240 ||
The lack of benefit is observed to be indistinguishable for all. || 241 ||
Now, it is asked: why is it stated that the restriction is by this alone?
Their assistance is mediated solely through the vital breath (prāṇa), and not by themselves.

He raises a doubt regarding the statement "it finds its support here" with the words "Now [he says]... He refutes the objection that the restriction—"all food is eaten by the vital breath alone"—is improper because speech and the other organs are also seen to receive assistance caused by food, with the words "It is said... (249).
How is it that their assistance is mediated by that [consciousness]? This is now explained.
But surely, how is it that the vital breath (prāṇa) is called "dūr" (far), just like speech and the other organs?
Because he does not sing for his own sake or for anything else, he is not pierced by the evils of the asuras. || 243 ||

One might raise the objection that the benefit to speech and the other organs provided by food does not operate through the medium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because there is no restrictive rule to that effect. [The text asks: "How so? In response, the immediately following passage is cited as the restrictive rule: "It is said thus. Then, another doubt regarding that very point is raised: "But surely... Just as speech and the others are pierced by the evil of attachment due to their grasping at their own objects, so too the vital breath [is pierced] by its own object, food—
The meaning is: how could the evil of the Asuras not be established from that [source], and yet there be no piercing of it for him as well, since it has been stated that "it is far away"? || 243 ||
This fault is not accepted because it is connected merely with the state of abiding. || 244 ||
Because it remains as long as the body exists, it protects the vital breaths.
Therefore, the Śruti declares with effort that one becomes firmly established here in the Self.

In this context, the fault of the "piercing by evil" (*pāpmavedha*) regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) need not be raised, because it applies universally to all [organs] for the sake of their maintenance. Since the maintenance of speech and the other organs depends upon the maintenance of the vital breath through the acceptance of food, [the author] considers this to be a qualification of the Self (*ātman*) and offers a rebuttal with the word "maintenance" (*sthiti*). Because the assistance of speech and the others, which is caused by food, occurs through the medium of the vital breath, the restriction [implied in the text] is justified; thus, in the first position, the sentence is to be construed accordingly.

[The author] explains: "Asau" (that). Here, the word "asau" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Food, being established in that breath, protects the gross body and the other vital breaths. Therefore, the scriptural passage beginning with "iha" (here) states, with the intended meaning that food is established in the breath, that it alone [protects]. The sense is that there is an emphasis because the existence of speech and the other senses is dependent upon the food associated with their group. || 244 || 241 ||
I [present] the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya;
[herein is the section on] Virāj, endowed with the five [senses] beginning with speech, together with the physical elements (*sādhibhautika*).
Having abandoned the internal limitation, he then attains that [state]. || 234 ||

Since it was stated that one should abandon speech and the other [senses] and take refuge in the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), it might follow that they are not to be worshipped at all; therefore, it is said, "by speech and the others. The word "five" is used with reference to their enumeration in the text, but it should also be understood as including the skin and so forth. The principal—
He qualifies [the breath] with the words "Virāj," etc., in order to show that the vital breath (prāṇa) is exempt from death. It should also be understood as "consisting of the self" (sādhyātmika);

that is to say, it has the entire universe as its essence. The connection is with the word "should resort to" (āśrayet). He states the fruit of meditating on the unlimited breath, as established by such scriptural passages as "In whatever way... and so forth, with the words "From that" (tataḥ). || 234 ||
Together with the elemental and the divine, it consists of name, form, and action.
In this context, it is said that the Sūtra is Prāṇa, Aṅgiras, Truth, Ṛk, and Sāman. || 235 ||
Raising the objection that since the vital breath (prāṇa) is likewise limited— just like speech and the other senses— how can its worshiper attain an unlimited fruit,

[the author] establishes the unlimited nature of the prāṇa, which was indicated in the passage beginning with "Virāj," by stating "sādhibhūta" etc. [The word *sādhibhūtam* is used in the neuter gender].

The Person is connected with the *sūtra* and its elaborated manifestations (*prapañca*). The meaning is that in the Śruti, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is designated as the threefold world, accompanied by the internal self (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*). In this context, he states its nature as action (*kriyātmatva*) by means of two words: "the *sūtra*. He states its nature as form (*rūpātmatva*) by means of two words: "Aṅgiras. He states its nature as name (*nāmātmatva*) by means of "the *ṛc*. The mention of both *ṛc* and *sāman* [is intended to include all mantras].
This is an indicative mark for the *yajuṣ* formulas. || 235 ||
One should know that single [Self] which, among all beings, is the substratum of knowledge, action, and their fruits.
He who worships through the consciousness of a self that lacks intrinsic nature shall go to him.

Having stated the indivisibility of the vital breath (prāṇa), he states the logical conclusion—that it is fitting for the worshiper of that breath to attain its own indivisibility—by saying, "That one... The word "āśraya" (support) refers either to the essential nature (svarūpa) or to the ultimate ground where the intended meaning culminates. He specifies the limit of the meditation by saying, "until [the realization] of one's own nature," meaning until the manifestation of the knowledge of the conceit "I am [that] Prāṇa-self. || 236 ||
That which was stated for the sake of worldly prosperity regarding speech and the other [senses] has now been addressed.
The *āgāna* is prescribed for the Udgātṛ in the remaining stotras. || 237 ||

Now, having restated the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then [he sings] for himself food," he states its purport with the words "It has been said," and so forth. The sense of the restatement is that the singing performed by the sacrificer—who is qualified by the limiting adjuncts of speech and the other organs—for the sake of his own prosperity, has already been described in the context of the three *pavamāna* chants. The word "now" (*atha*) signifies the present moment. He states that the fruit to be accomplished through singing in the nine *stotras* is indeed the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), on account of the scriptural injunction, with the words "the office... (*āmāna-*).
Thus [it is said]. || 237 ||
Since the word "food" (anna) refers to food in general, therefore—
It is called "the first" because it serves as a qualifier for that [word]. (238)

Fearing that the words *annādya* and *anna* might be redundant because they have the same meaning, he states the difference in their meanings: "sāmānya... etc. By means of the qualification, it is intended to express that very [food] as being consecrated (*saṃskṛta*). || 238 ||
Since,
from the very beginning,
this occurred among those devoid of portions [of merit], due to their lack of self-knowledge.
Therefore, even today it is observed among the subjects who have come into being as its effects. || 239 ||

It is not only scripture that is the authority for the acceptance of food by Prajāpati; rather, having observed the acceptance of food among living beings, who are its effects, one may infer it for the cause as well, since the effect conforms to the cause. Thus he says: "Since... The meaning is: "in the non-self, which is the nature of the vital breath (prāṇātman). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the acceptance of food for one's own sake is seen. || 239 ||
The phrase "whatever it may be" (yaddhi kiṃcit) serves as a restriction (avadhāraṇa) meaning "only all things."
Indeed, by means of the vital breath alone, the world always eats all that food.

He explains the words found in the passage beginning with "yaddhi" (for that which...). Regarding "yaddhi," he states the meaning of the sentence: "by means of breath. The sense of the word "hi" (for) is that the world's status as an eater of food is established through the medium of breath alone, as proven by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 240 ||
The absence of benefit is observed to be indistinguishable for all. || 241 ||
Now, it is asked: why is this restriction stated by means of this very [word]?
The benefit for these [senses] occurs solely through the gateway of the vital breath (prāṇa), and not by themselves. || 242 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the statement "it establishes itself here" with the words "Now [he says]... He refutes the objection that the restriction—"all food is eaten by breath alone"—is improper because speech and the other organs are also seen to receive assistance caused by food, by saying: "It is said... (249).
How is it that their assistance is mediated by that [door]? This is now explained.
But surely, how is it that the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be "far" (dū), just like speech and the other [senses]?
Pierced by the melody of the essence of the goal of the Self, he is not struck by the evils of the asuras. || 243 ||

One might raise the objection that the benefit to speech and the other organs provided by food does not occur through the medium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because there is no restrictive rule to that effect. [The author asks: "How so? In response, he cites the immediately following passage as the restrictive rule: "Thus it is said. He then states another objection to that very point: "But surely... Just as speech and the others are pierced by the evil of attachment due to their grasping at objects for their own sake, so too is the vital breath pierced by the evil of its own object—food.

The meaning is: how could he not be pierced by the evil of the Asuras from that place? And yet, for him too, there is no such piercing, because it has been stated that [the piercing] is far away. ||243||
Because it is connected merely with its own persistence, this fault is not admitted for the Noble One. || 244 ||
Because this food, being present, protects the body and the vital breaths, it is called *anna*.
Therefore, the Śruti declares with effort that one who is devoted to this [practice] becomes firmly established here. || 245 ||

In this context, the fault of the "piercing by evil" (*pāpmavedha*) regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) need not be raised, because it applies universally to all [organs] for the sake of their maintenance. Since the maintenance of speech and the other organs depends upon the maintenance of the vital breath through the intake of food, one considers this to be a qualification of the Self and offers a rebuttal with the word "maintenance" (*sthiti*). Because the benefit of speech and the others caused by food is mediated through the vital breath, the restriction [of the term "Self"] is appropriate; thus, the sentence should be construed according to the first position.

[The author] explains: "Asau" (this). Here, the word "asau" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The "dwelling" (*sadana*) situated within this [breath] is the gross body; it protects that [body] and the other vital breaths. Therefore, the scriptural passage beginning with "here" (*iha*) declares, with the intended meaning (*tātparya*), that "food is established in the vital breath. The sense is that there is an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) because the existence of speech and the other [organs] is dependent upon their connection with the vital breath. || 244 || 245 ||
For the non-existence of the two [the self and the world] is merely their persistence; thus, no attachment is to be suspected.
He is the supporter, the most excellent, the one who goes before, the consumer of wealth, and likewise the sovereign lord.
The subsequent section is introduced for the purpose of prescribing such qualities as these. || 246 ||

In this second position—that there is no piercing by evil for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) because of its connection with food for the sake of common subsistence—the text analyzes the sentence, beginning with the word "subsistence" (*sthitau*). Here, the vital breath subsists in food that has been transformed into the form of the body, and speech and the other organs, which follow it, likewise subsist therein;
therefore, since food is for the subsistence of the vital breath, there is no piercing by evil upon it. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But as for the injunction..."

Anticipating the objection, "Since the distinction has already been stated, what is the purpose of the subsequent text?", he says: "The Lord" (*bhartā*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the sake of establishing that the aforementioned qualities reside in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the object of meditation, even on the basis of scriptural authority (*śruti*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one's own gold and so forth are included. The "subsequent text" (*paro granthaḥ*) refers to the portion beginning with "Those gods said" (*te devā abruvan*) and ending before "Now, therefore, of the Pavamānas" (*athātaḥ pavamānānām*). || 246 ||
This should be understood as an injunction of qualities (guṇavidhi), because the respective fruit of each is heard [in the scripture]. || 247 ||
For the food we have consumed passes into us by way of becoming the body and the liṅga.
Therefore, that which undergoes transformation is said to be "just this much. || 248 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "There those gods... and ending before "That is Ayāsya. He says: "This [is the meaning]. The reason for this is given as "in each one," which means that in each individual quality, there is heard a result—consistent with the injunction and distinct from the primary result—just as in the case of the curd and other substances; such is the meaning of the reason. While explaining the syllables, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "as much as... as follows: "consumed."

For the food we have eaten, as it undergoes digestion through time and other factors, remains by way of sustaining the two bodies. Therefore, the meaning is that food is solely the sustainer of the two bodies, and nothing else. || 247 || 248 ||
Since you have sung of the path of remembrance (smṛti), all food therefore belongs to you alone.
And we, O Lord, are not able to remain even for a moment without food. (249)

He states the meaning of the verse "Then you sang for yourself" with the words "By you. The sense is that if you had sung for your own sake alone, then all that [the world] would have remained only within you; consequently, there would be no attainment of food as its cause for us.
Anticipating the objection—"Let there be no food for you, yet may your sustenance be like that of the Self"—he says "And we," thereby warding off the logic of "stretching out the feet."

The word *yati* [is used]; *kṣaṇamapi* [means] "even for a moment. By this, he indicates the worldly maxim that a servant should report his own calamity to his master. [The word is] *īśvare*. || 249 ||
O Lord, by means of this, may you satisfy yourself and us as well.
"Grant food to those who are hungry; because you are a follower of the Vedic style (chandasa), the causal suffix (ṇic) has not been applied. || 250 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "anu no 'smin" (may you favor us in this): "He satisfies. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is that it is impossible to remain without food. Anticipating the objection that "you yourselves should take a portion of the food," he says "īśvara" (the Lord), because we are dependent upon Him; thus, it is not so for us. He indicates our state of being objects of grace by saying "kṣudhitān" (hungry). This is [the sense] when the word "ābhajasva" (partake) is heard.
To the question, "How can there be a statement of a different meaning? he replies therein: "Because it is Vedic (chāndasa). || 250 ||
I 1 ka. ga. It is possible.
[vol2, page 105]

"Without me, food is not capable of nourishing you even for a moment anywhere. Therefore, all of you, being seekers of that [food], quickly enter into me indeed. (3.3.251) [End of Brāhmaṇa 3] — accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 399.
He states the meaning of the phrase "May they indeed enter into me" with the word "me. To express the logical principle of what ought to be said, he says "even for a moment.
The word "somewhere" (*kvacit*) refers to the body. Since it is impossible for food to nourish speech and the other organs independently, this is the literal sense of the words.
The word "quickly" (*āśu*) expresses that the act of entering does not require deliberation. The particle "vai" is used for emphasis. [This applies to] one whose vital breaths have departed...
The meaning is that because speech and the other organs cannot remain by force [without it], they stay surrounding the vital breath (prāṇa), even though they seek food;
thus, by this [breath], all these deities are satisfied in every way.
If it is asked, "How is this meaning established?", it is said: because... [252]

Since the passage beginning with "tathā" (so it is) is clear, he raises an objection regarding the word "tena" (by that). He says: "By that. It is incorrect to say that all deities, such as speech and the rest, are always satisfied by that food which is eaten by the world through the medium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For it is not the case that when one person has eaten, another is satisfied. He provides the resolution outside of both the scripture and the commentary, saying: "It is said. That manner by which the stated meaning is established—[that manner is as follows:]...
The construction is: "it is called the cause. || 252 ||
Food, through the process of transformation, becomes threefold when consumed.
Thus, in terms of time and fire, [the elements] are respectively the grossest, the middling, and the subtlest. || 253 ||

Following another scriptural passage beginning with "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold," he clarifies the manner of expression [in the verse]. He states that it is "threefold" (tridhā). He explains the reason for this threefold nature as being due to "transformation" (pariṇāma). He illustrates this threefold nature by saying "the grossest" (sthavīyān). He states the cause of the cooking [or digestion] as being "due to time" (kālataḥ). || 253 ||
The lower portion is the grossest, while the other [upper portion] follows the sequence of rasa and the rest.
It constantly builds up this gross body, just as clay builds a wall.

Stating the specific application of the aforementioned portions of consumed food as it pertains to the subject at hand, [the author] first describes the downward movement of the grossest portion in the form of feces, beginning with the words "The grossest... The middle portion [becomes] the gross body through the sequence starting with the skin.

He says, "he makes nourishment" (*pacayaṃ karoti*), meaning "from the essence" (*rasāt*) and so forth. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to provide authoritative proof for the well-known fact that the gross body is built up by food.

In response to the inquiry as to what the gross body is, he states its easy-to-know nature through direct perception with the words "this" (*imam*). This [word] is connected with the verb "knows" (*videt*). He provides an illustration for this process of building up with the words "a wall" (*kuḍyam*). It is excellent and refined.
It is called "mṛtsnā. || 254 ||
That which is subtler than an atom, more subtle than the subtle, is called vigor and immortality.
Then, having entered the subtle channels (nāḍīs), he gratifies the deities. || 255 ||
He states the form of the third portion of food with the words "But he who... He speaks of the subtle portion designated by terms such as *amṛta* (nectar) in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
With the word "deities," speech and the other senses are understood. Not only [the two]—[the text continues with] "always."
400 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on Śaṅkara’s Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārtika [First Chapter]

The word *atha* should be explained as having the sense of the particle *api*, meaning: "It is not merely the entry into the three thousand channels, but having entered, it also brings about the gratification of the deity. || 255 ||
Furthermore, the support for the sake of the master alone is called satisfaction and fulfillment.
Therefore, that arising of happiness belongs to the conscious self alone.

It has been stated that the subtlest essence (*aṇiṣṭha-rasa*), having entered the channels, nourishes the aggregate of the instruments (the body). Now, fearing that—since the Self also experiences satisfaction through the essence of food—the Self might likewise be subject to materiality (*bhautikatva*) just like that [body], he says: "The Master" (*svāmī*).

Here, the "Master" is the aggregate of the body and the instruments; its purpose is indeed the maintenance of life (*utsambha*) caused by food, as well as its non-falling away, its satisfaction, and its growth.

The meaning is this: those two [the body and the organs] have that [food] as their cause and serve that purpose alone; there is no effect for the Self caused by the transformation of the essence of food. Therefore, how could it (the Self) possess the nature of being composed of material elements (*bhautikatva*)? Anticipating the objection—that if the strengthening of the aggregate of the body and organs is caused by food, then pleasure must also belong to that [aggregate] alone, since pleasure is a quality of a conscious being and thus would entail the consciousness of pleasure belonging to the aggregate itself—the author says: "But from that... [referring to the passage beginning with *tatastu*]. The consumption of food...

Alternatively, the meaning of that word [“food”] refers to the strengthening [of the body] and so forth resulting from its consumption; the point is that because food is insentient, it cannot logically be the abode of happiness. || 256 ||
Those respective deities are seventeen in number, consisting of the nature of knowledge and action.
This very seventeen-fold village is characterized as the instrument of the enjoyer. || 257 ||
He states the form of those deities to whom the most excellent essence, having entered the channels, brings satisfaction: "Those...
He says "This very [self]" to dispel the suspicion that the collection of seventeen instruments might possess independence like a conscious being.
There are exactly five organs of perception, and likewise five organs of action.
The five vital airs, the intellect, and the mind—they know these to be seventeen. || 258 ||
He enumerates that very group of seventeen instruments (*karaṇa-grāma*) as being subordinate to the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). [The verse begins with] "Intellect" (*buddhi*):
the skin, tongue, ear, palate, and nose are the five organs of cognition; the voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the five organs of action;
the vital airs—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—and the mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*) constitute the two internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, there is a group of seventeen.
It is called the *liṅgaśarīra*. And he says that this *liṅgaśarīra* can be known only by those who possess discernment (*vivekin*), using the word "the wise" (*viduḥ*). || 258 ||
It is the common refuge of the deities whose individual forms have been cast aside.
This would always be merely the five elements due to their commonality. || 259 ||

If it is argued that by the word "deities" (*devatā*) one refers to the collection of organs (*karaṇagrāma*), then since these reside in the gross body (*sthūladeha*), upon the destruction of that body they would remain without a support; thus liberation would follow. Anticipating this objection, he says: "apāsta... (rejected). When the gross body is destroyed, for speech and the other organs whose bodily support has been cast off, the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*) alone—which have been set aside—would be their locus. Since those [elements] are common to all effects and serve as the support for everything at all times, [the organs would not attain liberation].
This is the meaning. || 259 ||

This Liṅga is like water, endowed with various forms.
It exists within the causal self through manifestations and disappearances.

Raising the objection that since even the five elements are perishable by virtue of being effects, how can they serve as the substratum for the aggregate of the organs, the author states "like milk and water" to show that the primal cause itself is their support. Just as milk and water assume various forms through curds and so forth, or through frost and so forth, so too this seventeen-fold subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of both the collective and the individual, is endowed with manifold configurations.
The meaning is that, through the distinction of time and by way of manifestation and non-manifestation, it abides in the primal cause. || 260 ||
By means of that which consists solely of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the delusion of the immutable conscious principle (kūṭasthabodha).
Having drunk this essence of waking and dreaming, the Lord indeed remains in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).

Even though the *liṅga* (the subtle body) resides in its primary cause (*mūlakāraṇa*), it does not have the Self as its substratum, because that status belongs to the *pradhāna* and so forth; for it is not fitting for the immutable Self. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The immutable," etc. That [ignorance] is such in which there is a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) due to that indescribable delusion (*moha*) belonging to the changeless conscious Self (*cidātman*). That [ignorance], designated by the term "delusion" (*avidyā*), is one and rod-like.

Unconditioned by the state of being an object of knowledge (*mānatva*), and being identical with that [knowledge] because it is the primary cause of the objects of knowledge such as sound and so forth, this Lord—having withdrawn the two states and their respective effects—exists during sleep in the form of the causal substrate. Therefore, due to the influence of *avidyā* accompanied by its appearance (*sābhāsā*), even though he is immutable (*kūṭastha*), he possesses the status of being the substratum for the instruments of cognition; for such a status is not possible for the *pradhāna* and so forth, since that which is insentient is equal to wood and other such inert things.
The sense is that, if it were not dependent on that [object], one would simply be accepting ignorance itself under a different name. || 269 ||
All external objects have been cast aside, and [the mind] is purified of the latent impressions arising from them.
One whose ignorance regarding the inner self has been destroyed is called the Supreme Viriñca. || 262 ||

Anticipating the objection that non-duality is not established because the Sūtra has a different meaning even though the other [the individual soul] remains in the state of having ignorance as its cause, he says:

"apāsta... (cast off). Anticipating the objection as to how there could be a further creation of the non-self for one who has withdrawn the entire category of non-self, he says: "tajja... (born from that). He argues that being endowed with the impressions produced by effects is not tenable even for one who is liberated and for whom external states have been discarded.
Śaṅkha says: "Undestroyed. He states that the Supreme is of the nature of the *mūtra* (the seminal essence) in the form described above: "Viriñca.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is so stated in the Śruti and Smṛti. || 262 ||
Having especially remained in the abode of the heart during the time of waking.
It remains pervading the seventy-two thousand channels. || 263 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the *virāj* exists in the form of the *sūtra*, non-duality remains unestablished because the *virāj* is distinct from that [individual soul], he says: "In the waking state," etc. Although Viśva, who identifies with the waking state, pervades the body everywhere, nevertheless, due to its manifestation specifically in the chamber of the heart, it abides there and [traverses] the principal channels within the body, numbering seventy-two thousand.

The meaning is that the *sakala* (the one with parts), pervading all during the waking state, remains experiencing gross objects; thereafter, being the very Supreme Self designated as Viśva and so forth through the conceit of grossness, it abides in the form of Virāṭ. Thus, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). || 263 ||
51. 1. Kha: *yāñjitaḥ*; 2. Ga: *abhyasta*.
[Vol. 2, page 108]
This very same Supreme Self, accompanied by the delusion regarding its own nature— Śureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Chapter.
By means of the self as vital breath (prāṇa), he acts; likewise, by means of the self as fire (agni), he sees.
Nevertheless, one might raise the objection: "Since the agent and the knower are distinct from the Supreme, how can there be non-duality (advaita)? Anticipating this, he says: "He is this very one.

The meaning is that the Supreme Self alone—who was introduced as the cause and as the thread (sūtra), who is present here as the Virāj, and who exists in the form of Prāṇa—is the agent in the form of fire and the knower in the form of Agni. One might then ask: "How can the one Supreme Being possess manifold forms, given the contradiction between oneness and multiplicity? Anticipating this...
He specifies: "one's own self" (svātman). || 264 ||
These two are said to be Indra and Agni; among them, Prāṇa is considered to be Indra.
Because it is illuminating, speech is indeed fire; thus, Prajāpati is one. || 265 ||

Since it is accepted that whatever form of power exists is indeed the work of Indra, one might object: "If it should be said that he acts through the self of Indra, then it is improper to say 'through the self of Prāṇa'; and it is inconsistent to say 'he sees through the self of Agni,' for the capacity for vision is well-known to proceed through the doors of speech and the other senses. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Indra... The construction is as follows: those two who were mentioned as Prāṇa and Agni are to be understood here as Indra and Agni. Here, Agni—

How is it that when the term "prāṇāgni" (the fire of breath) is used, there is the inclusion of both Indra and the collection of organs (*karaṇagrāma*)? For one does not understand a cloth from the word "pot. To this, he says: "Prāṇa. Between prāṇa and agni, "prāṇa" here refers to Indra;
he is the aspect characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), because of the strength of prāṇa, because its presiding deity is Indra, and because it will be stated later that "he is Indra."

The meaning is that the group of instruments, such as speech and so forth, constitutes the aspect characterized by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), because there is no difference between fire and speech in their capacity to illuminate.

According to the stated principle, the single Supreme Self alone—having assumed the body of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread)—abides in the form of the agent and so forth through its aspect characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) and its aspect characterized by the power of knowledge; thus, there is no possibility of duality. He says: "In this way. (265)
It is said to be either four *āra*s or one and a half [circumferences].
Whether it be thirty-three, or even seventy-two.

Nevertheless, fearing that non-duality (*advaita*) is not established here because of the existence of distinctions such as "the first" (*ādya*) and so forth, he states that it is the Supreme alone who exists in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body. He says, "Here, the first... and so on. Furthermore, raising the objection as to how there can be non-duality when distinctions such as "one and a half" (*adhyardha*) are well-known from the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, he says, "Or else... He will explain "one and a half" later; [as for] "thirty-three," there are eight Vasus, one...

The meaning is that the ten Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, Indra, and Prajāpati constitute the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is said that there are seventy-two [channels] by following the number of the channels under discussion, through the internal subdivisions of those very thirty-three deities. || 266 ||
Or rather, though divided into infinite distinctions, it is said to be indeed one.
Moreover, each and every one of these conceptual constructions is likewise [to be understood] individually. || 267 ||

He asks: what is the point of specifying intermediate numbers when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses innumerable divisions? He says: "infinite. However, he states that in reality it is one: "it is one. There is no concern for the ocean [of divisions]. He extends the principle demonstrated regarding the vital breath to all its subdivisions: "all of them too. This division of the vital breath that has been described is, moreover, each one of them again and again infinitely divided.
The meaning is that [the self] would be divided like the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The word "not" (*na*) is used to indicate the repetition of the word "again" (*punaḥ*). || 267 ||
1. And not; 2. nor in the three; [vol2, page 109] 3. Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 403.
By way of the divisions of gods, asuras, and so forth, through birth, form, action, and qualities.
Each one attains the state of being infinite, and from that, again returns to the state of oneness.

To the question of how each [individual] is divided into infinite varieties, he says: "O Deva," etc. The word "etc. (ādi) is for the purpose of including other classes [of beings]. Then, as to how the vital breath (prāṇa) is one, he says: "Again," etc. The connection is that it "attains a single nature" (ekātmatā).
He concludes that its non-duality is not contradictory because the Supreme itself exists in that form: "Therefore," etc. || 268 ||
In this context, the state of ignorance regarding the inner self consists precisely of both the collective and the individual.
But it does not exist in the Supreme Self, which has cast off all darkness and is defined as "not this, not this."

Some maintain that Brahman consists of both the aggregate (samasta) and the individual (vyasta); anticipating the objection as to how there can be such unity (*ekarasya*) in that case, he says: "The aggregate... The literal meaning is that the state of being both aggregate and individual—the state of possessing manifold aspects—is based solely upon the ignorance (*ajñāna*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within the self of the vital breath (*prāṇātman*). Now, one might ask: why could this aggregate-individual nature not be real (*vāstavī*) in the Supreme Self itself? To this he replies: "But not... For it is not [the case] in the Supreme Self. Nor is it...

The meaning is this: since ignorance and its effects have been negated by such scriptural passages as "Not this," "Not coarse," and so forth, neither their totality nor their individuality exists; moreover, that [totality] does not exist in reality, because it would contradict the definitive determination that Brahman is a mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). || 269 ||
He abides by means of every conceptual construction exactly as it has been described.
In every way and everywhere in the world, he is supreme according to his respective authority.
Then, fearing that because both the Sūtra and the Supreme [Self] are the Self of all (*sarvātman*), there might be two "Selves of all," he says: "By the whole" (*sarveṇa*).

The meaning is as follows: throughout the entire universe, without overstepping their respective spheres of authority, the Supreme Self alone abides as the Self of all particularities—both those mentioned and those unmentioned; therefore, since He alone exists in every manner, how could there be two "Selves of all"? || 270 ||
For indeed, without taking up this entire world, even in the slightest degree, [it cannot be known].
Therefore, no agent whatsoever acts for the sake of an action with its entire being.

He states the reason for the Supreme Being’s existence in every form: "Indeed not," and so forth. Among the factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and others, not even a single *kāraka* can accomplish its own function here without taking this entire world as its auxiliary support. For it is impossible for a thing to produce its own operation when another entity stands as an obstacle; therefore, since everything is the cause of everything everywhere, [this applies] to the Supreme Being, the root cause.

In comparison with everything else, the Supreme must be accepted as the creator of all its own effects; nor is it logical for the effect to be something other than its material cause, because that would contradict the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* (the section on "mere naming"). Therefore, the meaning is that the Supreme exerts itself in every respect toward the production of its own effects. || 271 ||
The causal self is the entire universe, the means for attaining the vision taught in the Vedas.
Since he performed an action previously, therefore he acts in the same way toward its effect as well. (272)

Regarding the point that everything is both the effect and the cause of everything, he states another reason: "Because it is the nature of the cause. Since the Sūtrātman—accompanied by the scriptural vision, meditation, and action, which serve as the foundation for all categories of objects—performed at the beginning of creation the entire world as its activity, therefore, within the range of his effects and the range of his progeny, [he acts] likewise with respect to all his own effects.
The meaning is that emanation is logical because an effect conforms to its cause. || 272 ||

The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya:
[In the first chapter—] "Because they are impelled by a single unseen potency (*apūrva*), whether in their collective or individual forms..."
Therefore, everyone proceeds everywhere by depending upon everything. || 273 ||

Regarding the point that "everything is both the effect and the cause of everything," he states the inference here: "Of one... and so forth. The literal meaning is as follows: because it was produced by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) acquired during the state of being a sacrificer—which is the prior [cause] of the single Thread (*sūtra*)—the Thread is the cause of all modifications, whether they are of a recurring or distinct nature. Having accepted everything other than itself as its auxiliary causes, it proceeds toward every effect everywhere by virtue of the aforementioned reason. [The subject of the inference is: the object under dispute...
The meaning is that [the atoms] perform their own function only by combining together, because they are impelled by a single *apūrva*, just like the hands and other [limbs]. || 273 ||
The internal, the elemental, and the divine—everything in its entirety at all times.
One should perform all ritual actions by means of the application of a single apūrva.

He clarifies that very point with the words "adhyātma" (pertaining to the self). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of the sub-divisions of the internal is intended. Alternatively, it means that which has the internal as its beginning, namely the objective (adhibhūta) and the divine (adhidaivata). The phrase "taking everything" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "All" is the designation of the agent.
The word "always" (sarvadā) is connected both with the taking up [of the vow] and with the instrument [of its maintenance]. || 274 ||
For Prajāpati formerly stood upon this very view.
By means of sacrifice and ritual action, he brought forth this world of moving and unmoving beings.

Anticipating the objection that the reason—being produced by a single unprecedented [potency] (ekāpūrvaprayuktatva)—is unestablished, he states "yataḥ" (since), intending that it is established by scripture. The word "pūrvam" (previously) refers to the state of being half-formed; therefore, the reason is established—this is the implied conclusion. || 275 ||
His infinite channels are the rays, and his heart is the orb of the sun.
And for those whose lifespan is one hundred years, there are that many days and nights.
In former times, by means of this perfection, the sacrificer who was knowledgeable in that [rite] [performed it].
The sacrificial fires, piled like suns, numbered thirty-six thousand.
What was that vision? He says: "The channels," etc.; for this sacrificer, the channels and rays were infinite.

In those [bricks], the visualization of rays should be performed because of the commonality of infinity; in that very [central brick], the visualization of the solar orb should be performed because of the commonality of oneness.

Regarding the lifespan of that sacrificer, measured as one hundred years—which consists of thirty-six thousand days and nights—there are as many bricks. By this correspondence (*saṃpat*), through the connection with the commonality of number, the sacrificer who knows that commonality [attains the goal].

In this manner, in the previous *kalpa* designated as Fire and Sun, thirty-six thousand bricks were seen piled up during an equal number of days and nights. Therefore, there is a perception of the bricks within the days and nights of the sacrificer. Thus it is said: by practicing meditation, the sacrificer, following his own actions and the actions of living beings, created the world which is the fruit of those actions—this is the meaning. (276–277)
In this way, every single deity is indeed present within each and every vibration.
It is both one and manifold, according to its internal and other divisions. || 278 ||

Having established that the other exists in every form, he concludes that this very one, whose self is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is the self of all, with the words "in each and every one. Since it has been established by the aforementioned reasoning that everything is both the cause and the effect of everything, the supreme deity called Prāṇa [is the cause] because of its non-obstructive nature.
