2, Page 111] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 401.
Being the self of all, she is present in every single activity everywhere; this is the meaning. This also applies to the deities who constitute the limbs of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In the same way, the meaning of the word "api" (also) is that there is a presence [of the deity] in each individual function. He states the oneness of the vital-force deity (*prāṇadevatā*) in its essential nature with the words "and one.

He states its multiplicity through distinctions such as the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth with the words "and of manifold forms. The two *ca*s (ands) serve to conjoin the two aforementioned points mutually.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that a multiplicity conditioned by external adjuncts (*upādhi*) is well-known in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and other such things. || 278 ||
It is pervasive, omnipresent, infinite, and yet it reaches its completion in every single action.
The entire fruit resides in each individual substance, just as the universal "cowness" (gotva) resides in each part of a cow.
He says that she herself exists in the form of various effects: "Vibhvī" (the all-pervading). He states her presence everywhere among her own effects: "Sarvagatā" (all-reaching).

He says she is "Anantā" (infinite) because there is no destruction of her in her specific aspect without the knowledge of Brahman, and because there is no such [destruction] in her as characterized by Brahmanhood. He speaks of her function as being complete within each individual instance of action, instrument, and fruit: "Samā—"
Thus [it is said]. To the question, "How can one [entity] exist simultaneously and in its entirety in many places?", he replies: "In the case of a fragment [of a gem] and so forth. || 279 ||
Thus has been described the greatness of Prajāpati; it is exactly like that.
The sacrificer also certainly becomes exactly like that through identification with it. || 280 ||

When it is asked, "Why is this glory of the Sūtra mentioned? he replies, "For the sake of praise. Even so, what follows for the worshipper? To that he says, "In the same way. The meaning is: by worshipping Prāṇa as endowed with the aforementioned majesty, one necessarily becomes possessed of such glory just like Prāṇa, because of the scriptural text beginning with "As that [is]... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1). || 280 ||
The subsequent Śruti text, beginning with "Thus," is for the purpose of declaring the fruit of the meditation on qualities.
Now it proceeds toward one who meditates upon the meaning as it has been explained. || 281 ||

Having thus explained that "by this these deities are satisfied," the scripture introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "In this way" (evaṃ ha) at the occasion of stating the fruit, in order to declare the fruit of meditating on the qualities such as being a supporter for one who meditates by taking recourse to speech and the other organs; thus he introduces the following scripture with the word "guṇa. || 289 ||
Speech and the other [senses] have entered [into it], just as food is for the sake of life.
In this way, kinsmen who seek their own livelihood enter into one who knows that [truth]. (282)

He explains the words contained therein with the passage beginning "speech and so forth. The meaning is that one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes a refuge for kinsmen who seek speech and the other [senses], just as they do for the vital breath itself. || 282 ||
And he shall be the husband of those who have settled there, and the most excellent in terms of his qualities.
Otherwise, the aforementioned qualities would be rendered fruitless before they even come into being. (283)

One might suspect that even if kinsmen take refuge with one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he may still not be capable of protecting them due to a lack of means; anticipating this, the author says, "And [he is] a supporter. The meaning is that by the power of knowledge, his capacity to support those who ought to be supported becomes present. Fearing that "supporter" and "superior" might be identical, he states the distinction: "And [he is] superior. [This applies] to a Kṣatriya and a learned Śrotriya.

The meaning is that the perception of difference between the two is extremely clear; for when [the status of] being a master and so forth exists, the act of going before [them] is of no consequence, hence [the term] *puraetā*.

If it is argued that [the statement] "it comes to be" is meaningless, he says "no," providing the example: "Just as... The meaning is this: in the absence of being foremost among kinsmen, his status as a protector and so forth bears no fruit;
for even if he is superior in virtue, a weak and good man does not find happiness when there are powerful wicked men acting as his masters. ||283||
All this would indeed be exactly so, were it not that he possesses a blazing fire.
Therefore, he says "it is beginningless" in order to establish its purposefulness. || 284 ||

If it is argued that even so, since he possesses the quality of being a leader and so forth, the mention of his being an "eater of food" (annāda) is redundant, [the author] says "no," stating: "All of this. Even if qualities such as being a sustainer exist, they would be useless in the absence of a blazing digestive fire; for one who is diseased and has weak digestion does not find satisfaction despite possessing the aforementioned qualities. This is the meaning. || 284 ||
Even if one possesses sovereignty over both enemies and one's own people, it is nevertheless [the same].
Anticipating that what has been stated might be fruitless, [he] proclaimed the result of being the sovereign lord.

Nevertheless, one might ask: why is sovereignty (ādhipatya) mentioned, since it is already established by his very role as a leader? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Among those who hate... The point is that the role of sovereignty is not redundant with the role of being a leader;

for even though the domestic priest (purohita) acts as a leader, it is the king alone who attains sovereignty. [This is stated] because [the qualities such as] possessing a blazing fire would not follow in the absence of presiding over and protecting [the kingdom].
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that futility is well-known. || 285 ||
One who meditates upon the Self as "I am" attains the aforementioned fruit;
even his kinsmen become partakers of that fruit, just as speech and the other [organs] do.

In response to the inquiry, "Whose is this fruit?", he says: "Prāṇa. He states another fruit obtained through the power of the knowledge of Prāṇa: "His kinsmen also... The ellipsis to be supplied is: "shall become possessors of the fruit. || 286 ||
Just as the Asuras perished when they vied with Prāṇa, so did they perish.
All those who hate the knower of the vital breath (prāṇa) are not even capable of [protecting] their own wives.
1.1 He states the purport of the passage beginning with "ya u haivaṃvidam" as follows: "Prāṇa... and so on. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "all perish. Why?

And he who desires that [wealth] is unable to support those who are dependent upon him. For one whose mind is afflicted by hatred toward the learned, being devoid of prosperity, is not capable of providing protection for those who ought to be protected; thus he says, "is not able" (nālam). Therefore it has been said: "Day after day, one should pay homage to Brāhmaṇas who are conversant with the Vedas, and one should not utter vulgar speech toward them. (287)
He who, out of hatred, reviles one who knows the vital breath among his own people.
A rival would not be able to sustain it in any way whatsoever. || 288 ||

Clarifying that very point, he explains the words: "He desires to rise up. Among his kinsmen, whoever, out of malice, desires to rise up against the one who meditates upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that rival shall in no way be able to cause the death of those who are to be supported;
for the meaning is that one who harbors hatred toward the great does not find peace. || 288 ||
He shall not be a preeminent leader, nor shall he be an eater of the first fruits among the followers of the Asuras.
Nor should one be a dominant authority among kinsmen, acting with rivalry and without discernment.

The statement regarding the absence of lordship (*bhartṛtva*) is an indicative mark for the absence of excellence (*śraiṣ�ṭhya*) and so forth; for since excellence and the like have been attributed to the knower of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is logical that these should be absent in one who hates him. Thus he says: "Not he... (289).
Thus, the nature of Ayāsya Āṅgirasa has been explained there; as was the case with Ayāsya, it has been determined previously, and now the determination of his being Āṅgirasa follows. (290)

Having raised the objection that there is a lack of connection with the immediately following scriptural passage beginning with "He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa," he states the connection with a non-adjacent [passage]: "He is Ayāsya... (290).
This is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, beginning with the words "He is this Āyāsya," and so forth.
This is stated according to reason in order to establish, through scripture, the status of being an Āṅgirasa.

Raising the objection that "only that which needs to be determined should be stated; why then is there a repetition of what has already been said?", he replies with the words "of what was previously stated.

The construction is as follows: this restatement by the Śruti—beginning with "This is that Āsyā" and ending with "for [he] is the essence of the limbs"—is made according to reason for the purpose of establishing that Prāṇa is indeed Āṅgirasa. || 299 ||
The vital breath is established as the essence of the limbs; how is it that the vital breath is the essence of the limbs?
He said "hi" for that much, and the other spoke further in order to explain it. || 292 ||

In order to demonstrate that very principle, he asks—after first stating the meaning of the passage "Prāṇa, indeed, is the essence (rasa) of the limbs"—whether [the status of] Prāṇa as the "son of Aṅgiras" (Āṅgirasa) is established or not. The intention of the questioner is that the well-known status of Prāṇa as Āṅgirasa is unestablished. He refutes this with the word "hi" in the sentence beginning with "For Prāṇa... (prāṇo hi). The word "hi" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). The meaning of the word "for" (*yataḥ*) here is that the well-known status of being Āṅgirasa is what is to be proven. He provides that very reason by means of the word "hi."

In order to clarify that which establishes conventional reality for the sake of the ultimate meaning, he states the passage beginning with "Therefore," etc.; this is for the purpose of its explanation. || 292 ||
For from whichever limb the vital breath departs from a person here in this world, [from that very limb does he fall].
Thereupon, the body of that deity, being devoid of moisture, quickly withers away.
He explains the subsequent passage [beginning with] "because" (*yasmāt*). Here, "here" (*iha*) refers either to the state of worldly convention (*vyavahāra-daśā*) or to the body (*deha*).

"Man" (*nuḥ*) means the person (*puruṣa*), that is to say, the agent of worldly convention consisting of the aggregate of cause and effect. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in that state of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkramaṇa*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is connected with the word "quickly" (*āśu*). The particle *hi* indicates that the stated meaning is in accordance with experience.
The meaning of the word is as follows: || 293 ||
1.1 Since this has been thus observed through positive and negative concomitance, [it follows...]
Therefore, the wise should know that the vital breath (prāṇa) of the descendant of Aṅgiras is the Self (ātman). || 294 ||

The passage beginning with "For this" (*eṣa hi*) and so forth, together with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) found in the preceding sentence, is divided here for the purpose of providing a conclusion. [The commentary continues: "Since... (*yataḥ*).

This explains why the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called *Āṅgirasa*. When the vital breath is present as the presiding agent, the limbs such as the hands and so forth become flavorful (*rasavat*); otherwise, they would be sapless.

He shows that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the means for realization by saying, "by means of positive and negative concomitance. He states the result of this by saying, "therefore. In response to the question, "What is the extent of his [knowledge]? he says, "the nature of being the effect and the instrument. "The knowable" refers to this. Expertise in the aforementioned positive and negative concomitance is what constitutes scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is primary as the very nature of the effect and the instrument, one should set aside speech and the other organs.
The sense is that it is to be worshipped by means of that. || 294 ||
1 [vol2, page 114] 408 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Adhyāya— ]
Of the effect, which is of the nature of form, and of the action and the instrument.
Not only is the vital breath the self, but even the name is said to be the self. || 295 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "This indeed is Bṛhaspati" as follows: "Of the effect," etc. For, having stated that the body—which is directly perceived—is essentially form, and that the collection of organs is the object of action possessing the powers of knowledge and action, and that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self (*ātman*) of those two;
the meaning is that the subsequent four sections [of the text] are intended to state that the same applies to the aggregate of names (*nāmarāśi*). || 295 ||
Thus, one should diligently praise the letter *m* as being the nature of all things.
The scripture shows respect so that it may be venerated by embodied beings. || 296 ||
Anticipating the objection—"Why is the universal selfhood of the vital breath (prāṇa) proclaimed by identifying it with the Self?"—he says: "In this way.
He states the intended result of praise and respect, which have the same object, as follows: "For the sake of being meditated upon" (upāsyatvāya). || 296 ||
The worship of the other [deity] is performed through attributes such as Bṛhaspati and others.
Desiring to state the distinction, he says that the scripture is exactly as before. (297)

Having stated that the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of form and action, one might raise the objection that if the subsequent section were intended to state its nature as name (*nāma*), then the specific mention of "Bṛhaspati" and so forth would be purposeless. Anticipating this, he states another underlying intention: "By Bṛhaspati and others. Just as previously meditation on the activity of the vital breath was taught as qualified by attributes such as being the "unfailing" (*ayāsyatva*), so too is there meditation upon it characterized by the qualities of Bṛhaspati and the rest.
Desiring to enjoin the scripture, [the author] states a specific quality; yet this is not an injunction of a quality, because no fruit for it is heard.
Rather, it must be an injunction of a qualified whole, since the principal fruit is stated as "union with the Sāman" (sāmnah sāyujyam). This is the meaning. || 297 ||
For speech is seen to be most intensely active in the act of chanting the Udgītha.
One might suspect that the deity itself is not the vital breath; therefore, this is stated [in response]. || 298 ||

Now, an objection might be raised: "The connection with the primary fruit is indeed heard for one who meditates on *sāman*, but nothing at all has been said regarding one who meditates on Bṛhaspati and the others; how then can this be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)? Anticipating this doubt and considering—according to the maxim of the lamp in the middle—that the fruit mentioned in the third section is connected to both sides, the author introduces the subsequent text by way of another method of exposition, beginning with the word "Speech" (*vāk*). Since speech is included within breath (*prāṇa*), [the fruit belongs to the meditation on breath].
The meaning is that this sentence is intended to state that [the breath] is the deity of the udgītha. || 298 ||
The wind, impelled by the digestive fire within the abdomen and struck against various locations, [produces sound].
Because it attains color (varṇatā) through this, the vital breath (prāṇa) itself is Bṛhaspati. || 299 ||

Or how is speech included within that? For one thing cannot be included in another; anticipating this objection, and intending to offer the solution that will be stated later regarding the fact that the sense organ or its presiding deity has that [Prāṇa] as its self, he explains the sentence "This indeed is Bṛhaspati" by refuting the objection that sound has that as its self, saying: "By the fire residing in the chest... [The air situated there, impelled by the fire residing in the chest, moves upward...]

As it moves, being struck by the throat and other articulatory organs, it is manifested as the phonemes *ka*, *kha*, and so forth. Furthermore, since the author of the Bhāṣya has determined this in such a manner—stating that speech, consisting of phonemes, is accepted as the instrument for the invocation of deities, and asking "with what essence, then, does one intend the word? and so on—it is correct [to hold this view].

The meaning is that she is included within the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since speech (*vāk*) is *bṛhatī* (the Great), and the vital breath is its producer and protector, he is *Bṛhaspati*. Furthermore, because the Ṛg-veda is of the nature of speech, it is therefore called *sarpati* (the gliding one). Thus he says: "The vital breath. [299]
Because of the scriptural statement, "The Yajus is Brahman," and because of the mention of the *sāman* at the end of the *graha*.
It is understood that the designation of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman [Vedas] occurs in their respective order. || 300 ||

To the question, "Why is Bṛhaspati not referred to as the priest of the gods, given the Vedic text: 'Bṛhaspati was the priest of the gods'?", he replies with the word "Yajus. In the subsequent sentence, "Brahmaṇaspati," the term "brahman" is heard to signify the *yajus* (the sacrificial formula). Since it is understood there that "Prāṇa is the lord of the *yajus*," the meaning is that in the preceding passage as well, that same Lord is designated by the name Bṛhaspati. This is so because in the subsequent sentence...

Anticipating the objection that the application of the word *brahman* to the *yajus* is doubtful, he says "at the end," according to the maxim: "But when there is doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence. Since the remainder of the sentence describes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as having the nature of *sāman*, it is intended that its nature as *yajus* and so forth is also meant in the opening; for the opening of a sentence, which requires a specific detail, is determined by the conclusion.

The meaning is "according to logic. Furthermore, since the sequence of the words *ṛc* and so forth is observed thus in the Śrutis, he states that the *ṛk* and *yajus* are grasped by the two words *bṛhatī* and *brahman*. He says: "The *ṛk*... Therefore, it appears that Bṛhaspati is the lord of the *ṛks* and Brahmanaspati is the lord of the *yajus*;
thus it is understood. || 300 ||
The word "sa" is a designation for speech, and likewise, "ama" is a designation for the vital breaths.
That [state] is both combined, by way of the predominance of either quality. || 301 ||
Because they function with a single meaning, the singular number has been employed.
Therefore, because of the similarity between the two sounds, the vital breath (prāṇa) is designated as Sāman. || 302 ||

In the passage "This indeed is Sāman," he explains the word *sāman* as "She" (*sā*). The meaning is that, according to other scriptural passages such as "By what [do you know] my masculine powers?", the words *sāman* denote speech (*vāk*) and breath (*prāṇa*). Nevertheless, he states for which [entity] there is the status of being denoted by the entire term *sāman*: "Sāman. Both speech and breath, when combined, are what is denoted by the entire term *sāman*; therefore, speech—[and so forth].

The meaning is that *sāman* refers to the creator, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and not to the well-known musical chant (*sāman*). Having raised the objection as to how the singular number in the word *sāma* is used when there are two things (speech and breath) in the state of being *sāman*—since their referents are distinct—the author states that the reason for employing the singular is the relationship of subordinate and principal between speech and breath. Because of this relationship of subordinate and principal between those two, both words denoting *sāman* function as a single term referring to the vital breath with speech as its subordinate; therefore, it is so formed.
The singular number is not contradictory; therefore, the meaning of the word "Sāman" in its entirety is the vital breath (prāṇa) with speech as its subordinate element—this is the sense. || 309 ||
The status of being a *sāman* is also attributed to the other [the *ṛc*], because it is accomplished by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, the Sāman is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), joined with speech as its subordinate element. || 303 ||

Now, one might object: according to the maxim that "the name *sāman* applies to songs," a particular song is called *sāman*; for the word *sāman* is accepted by the learned as referring to a mantra-text when it is sung. Therefore, since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) cannot be a *sāman* merely by having speech as its subordinate attribute, the status of being a *sāman* must belong only to the well-known musical melody (*sāman*). Anticipating this objection, he states the meaning of the phrase "that [is] the *sāman*-ness of the *sāman*" with the words "of the other. Now, regarding the word *sāman*:

It has been stated that there are two types of objects, consisting of words and their meanings; however, since it is not logical for a single word to have multiple meanings when it is possible for it to have only one, he says:
*Sureśvarācāryakṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtikam*, First Chapter, [page 116].

Regarding the term "prāṇa": the meaning of the word is that the well-known existence of the *sāman* depends upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since there is no difference in the primary sense of the word *sāman*, and because any other sense would be secondary—given that a distinction between primary and secondary meanings is observed in words such as "platform" (*mañca*) and the like—there is nothing objectionable here; this is the intended sense. || 303 ||
Alternatively, the vital breath (prāṇa) is designated as "sāman" because it is equal to all beings without exception.
Because it is caused by ignorance regarding the inner self, the infinity of that which is born from it is declared. || 304 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "yadveva" as follows: "niḥśeṣeti" (without remainder). It is true that the infinity of the *prāṇa* was established through its equality with all things; however, since the *Brahman* is infinite according to such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and since two things cannot both possess primary infinity, [the author] anticipates this objection with "pratyagiti. The infinity of the *prāṇa*, which is born of ignorance (*ajñāna*), is merely relative (*āpekṣika*), just like the property-bearer (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*) itself is also relative.
The meaning is that because it is produced from that, its non-occurrence [as a separate entity] is not tenable. || 304 ||
For the extremely subtle body is indeed called the "pusi" (the hollow or pore).
The vital breath (prāṇa) is equal to the body, such as that of an insect and so forth, because it has that [body] as its support.

Having first explained the meaning of the word *plaṣi*, he states the literal sense of the sentence concerning the *laṣi* along with the subsequent sentences, beginning with "atisūkṣma" (extremely subtle).

The particle *hi* is used to indicate that this is well-known in the world at a particular time. He explains how it can be equal in size to various bodies with the words "tadāśrayāt" (because of its dependence on those [bodies]). This means: because it functions by completing itself within each respective [body]. || 305 ||
Just as it has been taught, the vital breath (prāṇa) is equal to the bodies of mosquitoes and even to those of great beings.
Likewise, according to the Hiranyagarbha school, the self consisting of the subtle body (liṅgātman) is indeed identical [to Brahman].

He restates the meaning of the three statements beginning with "equal to a mosquito" as an illustration: "A mosquito," etc. The construction is: "Just as the risen vital breath (prāṇa) is equal to the bodies of mosquitoes and so forth. He states the application to the subject of the illustration (*dāṣṭantika*)—that it is "equal to all this"—with the word "so.
Having raised the doubt as to how the vital breath, known as the *sūtrātman*, can have equality with that [universe], he states the qualification: "the subtle body (*liṅgātman*)."
The sense is that there is an equality between one who possesses the power of action and one who possesses the power of knowledge. || 306 ||
Because all the sense organs are completely dissolved within the self of the wind.
There would be equality for all bodies in accordance with the karma of living beings. || 307 ||

He states another meaning of the phrase "equal to all this" with the words "in the nature of air. Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is delimited by every body according to the karma performed by living beings, is equal to all bodies—whether they be collective (*samastadeha*) or individual (*vyasta*)—as defined by those respective delimiters, it is said to be "equal to all this. Nor should it be argued that the limitation of the body by the karma of living beings applies only to the aggregate of the organs (*karaṇagrāma*) and not to the vital breath; for [this applies] to all...
The meaning is that because of the cessation [of activity] within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is an absence of the rest of the collection of organs (*karaṇagrāma*). || 307 ||
The differentiation for each individual living being occurs in accordance with their knowledge and karma.
Being independent of merit and demerit, it remains infinite. || 308 ||

He accepts the objection that the mere karma of living beings is not the sole cause for the limitation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to each individual body, since the scripture states, "according to their karma, according to their knowledge" (*yathākarma yathāśrutam*), and thus knowledge (*jñāna*) is also a cause; he does so by saying, "it is measured" (*pratimāṇīti*). This is because the subtle body (*liṅgātman*) [is limited] due to the influence of these two [karma and knowledge].
[Vol.
2, Page 117] 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 411.
Since even that which is unlimited (the Self) has a body as its effect produced by karma, this [Self] possesses no form whatsoever that is innate.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Dharma... The meaning is that its infinity is relative, insofar as it persists as long as the substance exists. || 308 ||
Through the Sāman, one attains union, identity, and the nature of Prāṇa.
Sharing the same world with him is designated by the term *sālokya*. || 309 ||

He explains the statement regarding the fruits, beginning with "wonderful" (*adbhuta*). Regarding the phrase "with that" (*sāmnā*), he states the meaning of the term *sāyujya* as "identity" (*aikātmya*). He uses the term "identity" to exclude the well-known identity with the *sāman* [as a musical chant]; rather, he explains it as "the state of having the nature of breath" (*prāṇarūpatā*). Regarding the meaning of "sharing the same world" (*salokatā*), he says "common" (*samāna*). By this, the meaning is "together with this breath, which is the *sūtrātman*. It is accompanied by the eightfold [attainment].
The practitioner of meditation attains these fruits: sālokya and sāyujya. || 309 ||
Because there is no influx of conceptual constructions, the wise one therefore obtains the twofold fruit in the state of non-hearing.
The threefold fruit is said to arise either from variety or from cultivation and so forth. || 310 ||

One might raise the objection: "Even though the meditation (*upāsti*) is of a single form, it is the cause of three types of fruits because the authority of the scriptures establishes this, and because no option (*vikalpa*) is mentioned. [The author] addresses this with the word "option" (*vikalpa*). It has been stated that by unifying [the goals], there are two fruits—*sārṣṭi* and *sālokya*—exactly as heard in scripture. However, stating his own position—that the threefold fruit arises precisely from the gradations in meditation and so forth, and not from that single form—he dispels the doubt with the word "but" (*vā*). [The text continues with: "variety... (*vaicitrya-*)...
If it is argued that there is a difference in the magnitude of the fruit for two [practices] with equal means, that is not so.
Through the sovereignty of yoga, there is equal accomplishment [of time and so forth], because the Lord is the master of time and other such factors. || 311 ||
To clarify that very point, he first restates the objection with the word "bhūyaḥ" (furthermore). The dual number [in the compound] refers to taking both knowledge and action.

He proposes the refutation of that with "na tat" (not that). The reason for this is given by "yoga-" (yoga, etc.). Yoga consists of knowledge and action; its excellence or preeminence is the Lord (Īśvara); or it is Time and so forth, the Sūtrātman; or it is that which has Time as its beginning (kālādi); or it is Time itself which is the beginning (kālaścāsāvādiḥ).

Because that [result] depends upon him, the fruit is equal; through the excellence of knowledge and action, there is *sāyujya* (union); through inferior knowledge and action, *sālokya* (residing in the same world); and through middling ones, *sāmīpya* (proximity). Thus, the meaning is that due to the diversity of causes, there is a diversity of fruits. || 311 ||
The seed of the world is indeed one, due to the cause of the Lord’s intention.
It establishes itself within each individual through the differentiation of numerous names. || 312 ||
Anticipating the objection that this is not tenable from the standpoint of Advaita because, in reality, there is no distinction between causes and so forth, he says: "One.

Although the cause of the world—which is beginningless, indeterminable, and designated by such terms as the *avyākṛta*—is indeed one, nevertheless, due to the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the Lord's intention regarding that [cause], it appears to each individual soul through various distinctions of causes and various distinctions of fruits, in accordance with that [intention]. Thus...

The meaning is that, in reality, even though there is no difference between entities, the diversity of causes and so forth is established within the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda) due to imagined difference. || 312 ||
One might conceive the idea of Mount Meru in an atom, and likewise the idea of an atom in Mount Meru.
The Great Lord is indeed unimpeded everywhere, facing toward everything. || 313 ||

Anticipating the objection, "How can the ignorance residing within the inner self (pratyagajñāna), even though it is self-luminous, manifest a distinction that does not exist?", he says: "It would create.
Ignorance, designated by the term *māyā*, is renowned for its power to effect the impossible; yet, even for that ignorance which possesses a semblance of light (*sābhāsa*), there is nowhere...
[vol2, page 118]
The meaning is "obstruction. To indicate its lack of independence, there is a designation that subordinates ignorance and emphasizes the primacy of the conscious Self (cidātman).
—The meaning is "for the sake of [that] object. || 313 || 77 * —In the contact, there is no non-apprehension of the syllables. Page 138.
For one who does not know reality, darkness [is like] a snake and so forth arising from ignorance of a rope.
Through the differentiation of the eight stages, false knowledge arises. || 314 ||

However, some maintain that duality is not ignorance, arguing that because it possesses eight states—namely, the individual (piṇḍa), the genus (jāti), the cosmic body (virāṭ), the subtle thread (sūtra), the divine (daiva), the undifferentiated (avyākṛta), the inner controller (antaryāmī), and the witness (sākṣin)—it is a real entity. To them, he replies with the words "atattva" (not reality). Just as the error of a snake arises from the ignorance of a rope, so too for one ignorant of the Self, there occurs the delusion of these eight distinct states due to their own ignorance, according to such scriptural passages as, "where there is [the appearance] of another, as it were."
The meaning is that this world is born solely from ignorance. || 314 ||
When the ignorance regarding the inner Self is destroyed, it is like the destruction of the ignorance concerning a rope.
The cessation of that which was thus imagined occurs through the awakening to the eight states. || 315 ||

In this regard, he states another proof: "The inner self," etc. When there is ignorance regarding a rope, a snake or the like is imagined; when that ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge that "it is only a rope," the destruction of the snake and so forth is observed. Likewise, while there is ignorance regarding the inner self, the world consisting of eight states is imagined;

when that ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), that [world] also perishes. Indeed, one who is liberated from the ignorance of the Real does not perceive duality, for otherwise there would be the consequence of non-liberation.

Therefore, the meaning is that the world is produced from ignorance, as established by the method of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka) through the following inference: "The subject under dispute is produced from ignorance, because it possesses the presence and absence [of its cause] corresponding to that [ignorance], just like a rope-snake. || 315 ||
The entire category of non-self entities arises from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self.
Just as it is here, so it will also be explained further on by means of logical arguments. || 316 ||
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* through both scripture and reasoning that everything known as "not-self" arises from ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*);
he states [in the verse] "anātma... that this same point will be explained by those very same means in passages such as "tad dha idam... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). || 316 ||
Either the body itself, or some particular part of it, may be intended as the *udgītha* chant.
If it is argued that this is because of common usage, it is not so; for the *udgītha* belongs indeed to the Asuras. (317)

Even in the Advaita system, having established that the diversity of fruits arises from the diversity of causes, [the author] presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the passage "This very one is the Udgītha" with the words "The office of the Udgātṛ. This is because, in the phrase "Come, let us slay the Asuras," the word *udgītha* is used to denote the action of the Udgātṛ priest, as is the case with the words *prastāva* and so forth.

He says "because of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *bhakti* in the sense of a specific liturgical portion" by the phrase "because of its well-known meaning. Regarding the statement that the *udgītha*—which is a specific portion (*bhakti*) of the *sāman*—is not "singing" (*udgāna*), he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by considering that the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected to both terms. He says, "Not so," because the reason intended in the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—"on account of the context of the *sāman*"—refers to the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), denoted by the word *sāman*, is the subject under discussion; and this is the meaning of the word "for" (*hi*). || 317 ||
This prefix *ud* is based upon an action that has reached its ultimate limit.
Therefore, having connected it with action, the Śruti explains it directly.

How can the word *udgītha* have its application (*vṛtti*) in the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? It cannot be through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), because no such usage by the elders is observed; nor can it be through etymological derivation (*yoga*), because the meaning of the constituent parts is not perceived.
Having raised this doubt, the author states the nature of the components of the word *udgītha* in order to accept the position of etymological derivation. [The prefix...
[Thus ends] Brāhmaṇa 3, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page] 413. He states that this [root *ud*] denotes an elevated action (*utkṛṣṭakriyā*) with the words "And he" (*sa ca*). He states the result of the word *ud* denoting that [action] with the words "Having joined" (*saṃyojya*). Since this [root] denotes an action, therefore one should join it with the action denoted by the prefix (*upasarga*) as its expressive element.
The meaning is that the Śruti directly declares that the vital breath (prāṇa), which possesses the power of action (kriyāśakti), is [designated] by the word "ut. || 318 ||
For it is by the vital breath that this fleeting world is upheld and sustained.
Therefore, the *utprāṇa* is well-known; however, the two qualities (*guṇau*) are called the *udgītha*. || 319 ||

How can this word, which denotes an action, have its application to the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? To this he says: "Supported" (*uttabdham*). This indicates the world's dependence upon that which sustains it. "Ephemeral" (*itvaram*); the meaning is "transient" or "subject to destruction. It has been stated that the *udgītha* is a liturgical division (*bhakti*) based on common usage. Thus, raising the objection—given that conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*), how can the word *udgītha* refer to the vital breath through etymology—he says:

"But it is well-known," [he says]. The meaning is that since the designation "Udgītha" applies to the breath by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) because the act of devotion (*bhakti*) is accomplished through it, there is no need to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for that [breath] as well, due to the principle of parsimony (*kalpanā-gaurava*). || 319 ||
Because it is sung by this [breath], it is called *gīthā*; and by that [speech] it is spoken.
And because it is connected with that [high pitch], it is designated by the term *udgītha*. || 320 ||

Raising the objection that even though *prāṇa* possesses the meaning of the word *ut*, it lacks the nature of being *gītha*, and thus how it can be called *udgītha*, [the author] states the meaning of the word *gītha*: "By this... Even so, he explains how *prāṇa* is the *udgītha*: "Ut...". *Udgītha* is that which is the *gītha* of the high (*ut*);
for *prāṇa* is the support (*uttambhakatva*) of the meaning of the word *ut*, and speech (*vāk*), as the meaning of the word *gītha*, is subordinate to it. Thus, [it is connected].
The meaning is that it is not [the case] because of the absence of smoke. || 320 ||
The Udgātṛ priest of the Naimiṣīyas became so through his meditation upon Ayāsya.
He, named Ayāsya, sang with speech that was dominated by the vital breath (prāṇa). || 321 ||

In order to provide support for the stated point—that the deity of the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and not speech (*vāk*) and so forth—the text begins with "And that also," etc.; its intended meaning is as follows:

Regarding the word "Udgātṛ": among the ancient seers known as the Viśvasṛjs who dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest, there was one who served as the Udgātṛ priest in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) involving many sacrificers.
Because he meditated upon the vital breath (*trāyāsyaprāṇa*) as his own Self, he became identical in form and name with it; he [the Udgātṛ] had speech as a subordinate [to that breath].

Having accepted *prāṇa* as the deity of the *udgītha*, he performed the act of chanting (*augātra*) by means of speech which is subordinate to *prāṇa*; therefore, the meaning that "the deity of the *audgātra* is *prāṇa*" is determined after deliberation by the immediately following sentence—this is the sense. || 321 ||
By means of the dharmas beginning with Bṛhaspati, one becomes worthy of worship.
Therefore, because of the excellence of cultivation, this investigation is accepted with respect to that. || 322 ||

Anticipating the objection that "let whatever deity there may be be the one for the Udgātṛ; what is the use of this preliminary deliberation and determination thereof?", he says: "By Bṛhaspati and others. Since the scriptural meaning is that one becomes that [deity] through the direct realization of identity with it—brought about by the excellence of meditation upon the Prāṇa endowed with the aforementioned qualities—therefore, an inquiry is conducted regarding that Prāṇa which is to be meditated upon, for the sake of strengthening the scriptural meaning.
This is the meaning. || 322 ||
Because of the connection with the heart, the deity here is Prajāpati.
Having raised the doubt as to what the basis of this inquiry might be, [Sureśvarācārya] states the conflicting views that serve as its basis, beginning with the words "By the heart.

Here, regarding the office of the Udgātṛ, let Prajāpati be the presiding deity; for, since he is of the nature of the Moon, he is connected to the heart through the mind (manas), and thus the Moon is the mind.

Having become [the breath], it entered the heart; thus, according to the Śruti, since it has been stated for the office of the Udgātṛ, "Thou art our Udgātṛ," there is a connection with the mind (manas). Therefore, Prajāpati is the deity—this is one position. He states another position: "The Udgītha... The mind, the eye presided over by it, and its support, the Sun—"Becoming the eye, the Āditya entered the eyes"—so says the Śruti; and the office of the Udgātṛ exists therein.

Because of the statement, "Do not sing the Udgītha for us," the meaning here is that Savitṛ alone is the deity of the Udgītha in this sacrifice. Alternatively, the literal meaning [of the mantra] applies because Brahmā and Āditya are connected with the intellect (*buddhi*), since they are deities presiding over it; and because of the Vedic text, "He who shall impel our intellects" (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*);

and because singing (*udgāna*) is connected with the heart, whereas it would be impossible for one without a heart [to perform it]. Thus, the Moon is supported by the mind, according to the text: "The Moon was born from the mind."

"Because of the Vedic revelation" is an alternative interpretation; or rather, since the connection between Savitṛ and the mind will be stated later in this very section, it is merely the presentation of a single position. || 323 ||
Whether it be Indra, the lord of speech, or the deity of the phonemes.
Or it may also have as its objects the words, sentences, accents, places of articulation, resonance, and so forth.
He states another alternative interpretation: "Because of being the lord of speech" (*vāgīśvaratvāt*). Indra is the deity of strength (*bala*), and speech (*vāk*) is produced from that;

thus, by way of strength, Indra is the controller of speech. Since the *udgītha* chant has speech as its essence, the meaning is that Indra is the deity therein. Alternatively, because of the connection with the syllables, he says that the deity presiding over it—or the deity of the *udgītha* itself—is the deity of speech. Or else, [it is] the deity presiding over the words and so forth.
He states further divergent views, beginning with "the deity," on the grounds that [the deity] is connected to the words and so forth of the *udgītha*: "The word (*pada*)," etc.

Accent (*svara*) such as the acute (*udātta*), the place of articulation (*sthāna*) such as the throat, and resonance (*nāda*) or sound (*dhvani*)—by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), the hymn (*sūkta*), context (*prakaraṇa*), section (*kāṇḍa*), and so on are included; and by this, effort (*prayatna*) is also grasped. Brahmadatta pronounced a loud oath against the disputants.

(325) Having concluded the discussion on conflicting views, he describes the method of reaching a decision regarding their cause with the words "Thus" (*evam*). A certain sage named Brahmadatta was the *udgātṛ* priest at a particular ritual; when many people had arrived there—either out of a desire to see or a desire to refute him—[the following occurred].

Since the former Udgātṛ had performed the office of the Udgātṛ for previous performers of sacrificial sessions (*satrin*) by means of speech subordinated to breath (*prāṇa*), even while the disputants maintained contrary views according to the manner previously shown, he— having ascertained this— placed the former Udgātṛ forward as an authoritative witness against the conflicting disputants and took an oath right there in the assembly. And by means of that act of swearing, the deity of the Udgītha was established as breath (*prāṇa*) with speech as its subordinate.

The meaning is that he has thus established [his claim]. The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to establish the well-known reliability of the previous singer. The word "loudly" (uccaiḥ) expresses the clarity of the oath. || 325 ||
When, by some fortunate person, even insignificant speech from here [is uttered]...
That Ayāsya, whose body was breath, sang between the gods.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the firmness of his own conviction. || 326 ||
Was it not the case that in former times the Udgātṛ of those performing the sacrificial session was one who had become the embodiment of all means of valid cognition?

"Why is this person made a witness? Why could not someone else here be made a witness?

Fearing that this might lead to an over-extension (*atiprasakti*), he recalls the relevant context by stating: "But there is a contradiction. At that time, as the Soma was being consumed, my head began to throb.
May he swiftly cause those who speak falsely to fall down before his very eyes. || 329 ||

He says "the Udgātṛ," thereby precluding the possibility that the previous Udgātṛ was not an examiner. He says "diligent" (*prayatnavān*). Anticipating this objection, he says, "The form (*ākṛti*)," following the logic of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*: "But the form [is denoted], because it serves the purpose of action" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.33).

In this [passage], it is established that words such as *śyena* (hawk) denote the generic form (*ākṛti*). As they say: "One should pile the *śyenacit*"; the act of piling (*cayana*) is possible with respect to the form, provided that the word *śyena* has the form as its meaning. And it is stated there in the *Ṭīkā*: "By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the meaning of the sentence is that one should effect the altar-site of fire, piled like a hawk, by means of piling. Since it is impossible for me to perceive similarity with every individual instance of a hawk, because similarity with all individuals cannot exist, and because similarity with past and future individuals is untenable, it is determined that the word's meaning is the *ākṛti* (form), as similarity with the form of a hawk can be achieved;
likewise here, since words such as "Brahmadatta" denote the *ākṛti*, the Veda does not incur the fault of impermanence resulting from denoting individual instances (*vyakti*).
The meaning is: how is there a contradiction with the *Autpattikasūtra*? || 332 ||

The external quality is a melodious voice, while the internal wealth is a golden complexion.

What is that external wealth? He says: "that which belongs to this [person] is external. What then is that internal? He says: "the quality of being well-sounded (*sauvarṇya*). Sweetness residing in the throat is external wealth; it is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), as its utterance is preceded by the knowledge of phonemes (*varṇa*). In this context, speech has eight locations, beginning with the root of the tongue.

[Objection: But surely the body is not the foundation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for it is not seen that the breath has that as its foundation. To this, he says: "Of food" (*annasya*).

According to the scriptural sequence beginning with "Food, when eaten," the body is a modification of food; the vital breath resides therein and attains the state of being sung (as the *gīti*). Therefore, it is called the foundation of the vital breath. The meaning is that this is another alternative view according to the Śruti. || 343 ||
The worship of the two foundations known as Vāgīśvarī and Anākhya is performed optionally.
One should worship that which is established in speech, or that which is established in breath.

He states the fruit of the declaration of the installation: "Worship," etc. He clarifies the very same alternative: "Speech," etc. (344)
For which purpose his greatness has been celebrated by this intelligent man.
That recitation for ascending [the altar] is now stated as it has reached its proper occasion. || 345 ||

Now he introduces the context of the passage beginning with "Then, therefore, [the verses] of the Pavamānas," by asking "For what purpose? The meaning is as follows: for the sake of the injunction regarding the recitation (*japa*) as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to that principal meditation (*upāsana*) on Prāṇa—the greatness of Prāṇa, which is distinct from its meditative visualization, has been described through the mention of its various qualities and fruits;
that recitation, which is subordinate to it and is named "The Ascent" (*abhyāroha*), is now stated in the subsequent text. In this regard, the word "first" (*atha*)—
Having taken it up, he explains it: "Now," [it says]. || 345 ||
This ritual action is intended to be performed by one who possesses the knowledge as previously described.
Because it has been explained in its entirety, it is therefore stated here as follows: || 346 ||
Therefore, he states the meaning of the word: "as has been said" (yathokta). || 346 ||
Thus, because it is to be employed by the learned, for this very reason it has not been set forth as a formal aphorism.
Therefore, as it is with obligatory rites (nityakarman) in the Sūtras, they are to be performed by the learned.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*) does not constitute a ritual action (*karman*), since it was not codified as such by Baudhāyana and others who composed the Sūtras? To this, he replies with the word "evam" (thus). By the aforementioned method, the very fact that the act of recitation is to be performed by one possessing the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vijñāna*) is what is referred to by the word "ataḥ" (therefore). Furthermore, suspecting that the act of recitation might be merely occasional, he says "tena" (by that); for by that [knowledge], it is employed by the wise.
Its impermanence is as follows. || 347 ||
Because of its connection with the characteristic marks of the *udgītha*, it has the power to denote singing in general.
The restriction of this very [term] is stated by means of the particle *eva* in the case of the Pavamāna [stotras]. || 348 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "of the *pavamāna*s alone" with the words "by the *udgītha*," etc. Because of the context—"May we pass beyond by means of the *udgītha*;

you [O Pavamāna] sing for us"—and because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) connecting the act of recitation (*japa-karman*) with the *udgītha*, it follows that this [recitation] would apply at all times of singing; therefore, the meaning is that the restriction is established specifically for the time of the *pavamāna* chants. || 348 ||
Furthermore, he stated that there is a contraction of time with the words "sa vā" and so forth:
"Where the Prastotṛ should chant the Prastāva, at that time one should mutter these [mantras]. (349)
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "He indeed [thinks] 'in the ether'" as follows: "Even from that," etc. He clarifies the very contraction of time with the words:
"The Prastotṛ," etc. (349).
And from the designation "these," it is understood that they are *yajus* verses.
And because it is seen in the Śruti itself, the Śatapatha accentuation is used in the recitation (japa).

Because the *yajus* mantras do not have a fixed number of feet or syllables, there might be the suspicion that they consist of only one or two mantras, beginning with "Lead me from non-existence to existence" (*asato mā sad gamaya*). Anticipating this, he says: "And these... (*etāni ca iti*). This is to show that these [verses] constitute *yajus* mantras, and for the purpose of guiding [the recitation] according to the mantra-syllable (*māntra*) accent as found in the Vaibhāṣika texts. [Note: 1. For the purpose of leading; ga: for the purpose of obtaining. 2. ga: will be explained in three ways. 3. *sphoṭayauṃ*.]
[Vol. 2, Page 126] 420 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Adhyāya]—

Anticipating the objection that [the accent] must necessarily be observed, he says: "In the Śruti. Because it originates from the *Śatapatha*, the accent prescribed in its own defining treatise (*lakṣaṇagrantha*) should be employed for the mantras, and not the accent of the Mānava school, since the latter is intended as a mere indicator (*avivakṣitatvāt*). This is because, in cases such as "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*) or "softly" (*sāmnā*), when the accent is intended to be significant, the instrumental case is seen; however, here, because of the use of the accusative in "these" (*etāni*), the accent of the Mānava school is not intended to be significant. Nor is there [a conflict with the rule] regarding the subordinate and the primary...

According to the principle stated in *Jaiminīya-sūtra* 1.3.9, "In the case of *vikrama*, because it is for that purpose, there is a primary connection with the Veda," even the mantras of the *Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa* lack their own specific accents; for their application (*viniyoga*) is observed in that very same place, and thus there is no discrepancy.

However, in the section concerning the conflict between the subordinate and the primary (*guṇamukhya-vyatikrama-adhikaraṇa*), it is held that when the origin (*utpatti*) is in one place and the application (*viniyoga*) is in another, the origin is set aside by the application. Application—
Because origination (utpatti) is subordinate to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) as its primary motivator, it is subsidiary to that [performance]. As it has been said:
"In the case of a quality (*guṇa*), one property [arises] from its own nature, while the other arises through the medium of the principal."
"Wherever [the latter] might exist, there the sublation of the quality-dharma is to be understood."

And it has been said: "A quality dependent on a primary injunction (pradhānavidhi) overrides a quality dependent on a subsidiary injunction (guṇavidhi). Therefore, the meaning is that the mantras produced for the Brāhmaṇa, being employed in that very [context], partake of its specific accent, and not the accent belonging to the [Sāman] itself. || 350 ||
And this designation of the act of recitation is intended as "ascent" (abhyāroha).
And the denotation should be understood as etymological (yaugikī), because of the possibility of connection with action. || 351 ||
Fearing that the performance of the recitation (*japa*) enjoined after mounting the *amyā* would be inconsistent with the sequence of the ritual, he says: "Recitation...

Anticipating the objection that the word *amyāroha* lacks conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) there due to the absence of its employment by the elders, he says: "And it is etymological (*yaugikī*). || 351 ||
Having abandoned the internal limitation, one should thereafter [abandon] the divine seed.
Because one ascends by means of this, it is therefore remembered as *abhyāroha*, which is recitation (*jepa*). || 352 ||

In the context of ritual action (*kriyā*) and the practice of recitation (*japa-karma*), he establishes the very possibility of yoga. By the word "having abandoned" (*hitvā*), he states the cause for attaining the form of the Divine.
By the word "seed" (*bīja*), he means "from this delimitation of the inner self" (*adhyātma-paricchedāt*). The word "hence" (*ataḥ*) refers to the possibility of yoga.

"Marśī. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the act of recitation conforms to its proper sequence; the remainder of the sense is that, therefore, this designation is not merely conventional. || 352 ||
Because the forms of the noble ones are concealed, there is no perception of them by ordinary people.
Therefore, the Teacher himself directly explains this through the Śruti.
He states the intended meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "When he says... as follows: "Tirohita... (Verse 353).
Having first explained the meanings of the individual words, he subsequently stated the meaning of the sentence.
"The fruit follows that which was previously stated"—this is the sequence of interpretation according to the scripture (śruti). || 354 ||

He addresses the objection regarding the repetition seen in the *Brāhmaṇa* with the words "Previously," etc. Whether it be the fruit, the intended meaning (*tātparya*), or that which is heard literally, they indeed explain [the text] without transgressing this very scriptural sequence (*śrauta-krama*). || 394 ||

Whatever knowledge may be innate, and whatever action is born of one's own nature—[these are not to be abandoned]. 3 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Āmanda Giri. 421. Whatever knowledge may be innate, and whatever action is born of one's own nature—[these are not to be abandoned].
Because it is the cause of falling downward, it is called "non-existent" (asat) in the mantra.
Therefore, he explains the meaning of the word *asat* found in the mantra beginning with "lead me from non-existence" (*ato mā sad gamaya*) as follows: "that which might be" (*yatsyāt*). || 359 ||
Because they are the causes of the state of being a *saha* (companion), knowledge and action [are to be practiced] according to the scripture.
These two are denoted by the six syllables in this mantra as previously described.

In that very mantra, he states the meaning of the word *sat*: "The real" (*sat*). The meaning is that the ritual actions such as the Agnihotra mentioned in the Karma-kāṇḍa, and the knowledge mentioned in passages such as "The dawn is indeed [the sacrificial ladle]," are the causes for attaining the state of divinity which is the "Real"; therefore, they are designated here by the word *sat*. || 356 ||
Unnatural death is to be known for those two [types of persons] due to the causes of death mentioned previously.
The immortal [state] consists of knowledge and action according to the scriptures, because they destroy death. (357)

He states the meaning of "death is indeed the unreal" (*asad*): "the unreal. Between those two—namely, knowledge and action, both scriptural (*śāstrīya*) and non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*)—since the previously mentioned non-scriptural knowledge and action are causes of death, the meaning is that death consists of non-scriptural action and so forth, which are denoted by the word "unreal" (*asat*). He states the meaning of "immortality is the real" (*sat*): "immortality. For by means of those two [scriptural knowledge and action], one abandons mortality and becomes a god.
Through you, the person is liberated; therefore, the meaning is that immortality belongs to those two [the teacher and the disciple]. || 357 ||
Having raised me up from demonic knowledge and action, and then having conquered them;
Therefore, quickly cause the scriptural knowledge and action pertaining to the divine to proceed. || 358 ||

He states the meaning of the sentence "May he lead me from death to immortality" with the words beginning "āsurī. The word "atha" (then) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*), meaning "only through the destruction of natural karma and so forth, which are obstacles to the Divine. The word "tataḥ" (from that) is connected with the ablative case. || 358 ||
Then the scripture declares: "Make an effort regarding the meaning of the mantra; I am dead."
The second [part] here is the recitation: "O darkness, do not come to me. (359)

He states the purport of the statement beginning with "It is nectar for me" (*amṛtaṃ me*). [The phrase] "the meaning of the mantra" [is explained as follows]: the word *atha* (then) has the sense of immediate succession (*anantarya*) by way of the logical connection of the word-meanings (*padārtha-yukti*). The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used to reveal that the meaning of the first mantra is well-known according to the method already shown. Anticipating the objection that stating what has already been said would be redundant, he says: "[Regarding] the second... Since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of explanation (*vyākhyāna*), it is not [redundant].
This is the intended meaning. || 359 ||
Since they are relative, death would occur even in the case of scriptural knowledge and action.
These two are considered darkness because they depend on their own benefit and are for the sake of another.

Regarding the statement "Death is indeed darkness," he explains the meaning of the word "death" [in that context] with the phrase "because of its relativity. This means because it possesses excellence and is subject to destruction. He states that these two possess the nature of darkness with the words "for its own sake. The meaning is that because they are subordinate (śeṣa) in relation to their own primary object—the fruit of scriptural rites and the like—they lack independent luminosity, and thus they possess the nature of darkness. || 360 ||
"By means of spiritual practice (*sādhana*), lead me from darkness to the light that is the goal, the nectar (*amṛta*).
Because the destruction of darkness occurs precisely through the attainment of the fruit, he said, "Lead me to the nectar [of liberation] hereafter. (361)

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya]:

He analyzes the meaning of the sentence "May he lead me from death to immortality" (*mṛtyormā'mṛtaṃ gamayet*). From the phrase "from the means" (*sādhanāt*), he states the meaning of the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "may he lead me to immortality" (*amṛtaṃ mā*). From the word "fruit" (*phala*), he explains that by means of the state of being a deity, through the destruction of its causes—such as ignorance and the like—he establishes me in the very nature of the fruit itself.
The meaning is that [the author] states the intended purport (tātparya). The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is connected with the phrase "from the destruction of darkness" (tamodhvaṃsāt). || 361 ||
The meaning which was previously explained at length in the two preceding tantras is [here] stated once again.
It is briefly described with the mother as the third. || 362 ||

He avoids the charge of redundancy regarding the third mantra by means of the two preceding ones, stating: "Of the two preceding [mantras]. For this very reason, the authors of treatises compose their works in the form of a summary followed by an exposition. || 362 ||
For you should observe that the consequence for the latter two cases is not the same as it was for the former two.
The scripture states the words beginning with "Not here," etc., to express that the meaning is concealed.

He states the intention of the passage beginning with "not here" (*nātra*) as follows: "the contingency" (*prasaṅgam*). The meaning is that, having observed that the two preceding mantras have their meanings obscured, the Śruti utters the sentence "not here" after suspecting that the same contingency might apply here as well. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to state that the clarity of the context of the mantra-exposition is a subverting factor. For this very reason, commentators [have stated that] the meanings are clear.
They speak of the reality of some ineffable thing. || 363 ||
Having sung according to the prayer, [he brings] the supreme fruit for the sacrificer.
Just as in the past by means of speech and the other [senses], it was done during the three Pavamāna [stotras]. || 364 ||

Now, introducing the passage beginning with "atha" (then), he recounts what has occurred: "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that just as in the past, not disregarding the request made by the sacrificer through speech and the other senses, they performed singing for his sake in three stotras, while in the remaining ones they sang for their own sake, so too did the Udgātṛ. || 364 ||
Then, as for "the others," the *udgātṛ* takes the middle portion for himself.
From the statement "one should sing," it is understood that there is also a connection with desire on the part of the agent.

Now, he explains the passage beginning with "Then those which... The word "then" (*atha*) indicates that immediately after the singing for the sake of the fruit of the sacrifice during the *pavamāna* chants, there are other hymns (*stotra*s); from the scriptural statement, "In those [other hymns], one should sing for oneself food and nourishment," it is understood that the performer also has a connection with the fruit, just like the patron (*yajamāna*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the *yājamāna* (the duties of the sacrificer) consist in the singing (*udgāna*) during the *pavamāna* [stotras], while the *ārtvijya* (the duties of the officiating priest) belong elsewhere. The word "hi" is used for the purpose of establishing the well-known twofold nature of the *āgāna*. || 369 ||
"For what reason should he sing for the sake of the Self?"—this is the reason stated here.
Since he who possesses such knowledge is indeed this very one, therefore he is that.

By the principle that "the praise consisting of the cognition of qualities accomplished by means of chanted mantras follows from the sense [of the context]," one disregards the order of recitation; thus, in order to demonstrate the principle supporting the connection with the agent's desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), the sentence beginning with *sa eṣa* is raised through the door of expectancy. [The question] "Why? expresses the doubt that it is improper for one engaged in another's ritual action to chant for his own sake. [The answer is: Chanting for one's own sake is possible for the Udgātṛ.
Regarding the phrase "it exists," he states that the subsequent sentence is intended to provide the reason. He says, "the reason. He explains that [reason] as follows: "because... (116).

Therefore, it is sufficient for oneself as well as for one's master to refrain from pursuing desires. [Vol. 2, Page 129] 3 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śākhaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 423.
Since Īśvara is the singer, there is therefore auspiciousness in the attainment of desires. || 367 ||
Therefore, among those [desires], the sacrificer may choose whatever he wishes according to his own inclination.
While the nine [verses] are being sung, he should choose him without hesitation.

Having raised the doubt—“Even though one who knows thus is the vital breath (prāṇa) by the very power of knowledge, how can there be singing for his own sake?”—the author states the meaning of the passage beginning with “for himself” (ātmane vai).
[He says: “Therefore” (ataḥ); that is to say, because he is the self of the vital breath. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with “therefore among them” (tasmādu teṣu).
[He says: “Because” (yasmāt); the connection is that there is no stability among them. Therefore, the meaning is “from this Udgātṛ. “Auspicious” (śubham) means blameless.

By this very fact, the suitability of the bridegroom for the journey to the next world is stated. Since it has been declared that the Udgātṛ priest possesses the power to sing of the fruits resulting from his own and others' welfare, there is no occasion for deliberation regarding the request for the bridegroom; thus he says: "without deliberating" (avicārayan). || 367 || 368 ||
And this vision is urged upon one who follows the application [of the path]. (369)
Therefore, the attainment of the deity arises from the combination of knowledge and action.
Therefore, no doubt whatsoever exists regarding the person who performs ritual action. || 370 ||

He states the purport of the explanatory commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "Thus, first... as follows: "In application," etc. The meaning is that because the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is enjoined by taking up the *udgītha* occurring in the context of the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there arises an identification [of the self] through the combination of that [vision] and the act of recitation (*japa*).
He states the result when action exists as an auxiliary to knowledge: "Therefore," etc. This is the doubt.
The word "heated" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. || 369 || 370 ||
It is highly doubted whether [the result] would occur even for a learned person who is devoid of action.
To dispel that apprehension, the Śruti says: "Therefore, this [is so]" (taddhaitat).

[The author] states "Karma" [in verse 371], anticipating the doubt: "Since the fruit is attained through the combination [of knowledge and action], there is no doubt regarding its attainment even from knowledge alone.
This means that a doubt is being raised by overstepping the power of knowledge. For it is observed that a seed and the like, when deprived of auxiliary factors, is of no avail.
The sense is that it would be a mere cry. He introduces the subsequent statement as a reply to this: "tadāśaṅkā" (the suspicion regarding that). || 371 ||
Since he has already become a god right here, what could possibly be the basis for such a doubt?
For indeed, there is apprehension regarding the attainment of the world through both the performance of recitation and its lack of understanding.
"Only from knowledge does it arise"—for such indeed is the Śruti: "That is this. || 372 ||
He clarifies the intended method for dispelling doubt, which is indicated by the word *hi* (for), with the words "right here" (*ihaiva*). The meaning is the state of being alive.

Thinking that the word *kim* (what) has the sense of an inquiry, he raises an objection: "recitation" (*japa*), etc. When it is stated that the attainment of the world occurs through the combination of the ritual act known as *abhyāroha-japa* and the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇopāsanā*), [the opponent asks] regarding a knower who is devoid of ritual action—[in the case of] mere knowledge alone...

The doubt arises as to whether the attainment of the world of the gods might or might not occur, because the combination [of knowledge and action] is the cause of the fruit; the meaning is that this [attainment] does not exist in a person who possesses exclusive knowledge. He cites the scripture to refute the cause of this doubt: "Because of that" (taddhā). || 372 ||
1 ka. ga. as follows | 2 kha. 'neta triṃ | 3 ka. in the attainment of the world | [vol2, page 130] 124
[In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, in the first chapter:
How could there be [the state of] one who has become a god through the accumulation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
Then that [cognition] would be a perception for the god, just like the perception of a human being. || 373 ||
He clarifies the refutation indicated by the word *hi*: "Of one who lives," etc. A doubt regarding a human attaining divinity is appropriate;

it is not so for a god attaining that [human state]. For just as a human attaining another human is not doubted, likewise a god attaining that [human state] is not doubted, because of his very nature (*asattvāt*). This is the meaning. || 373 ||
For even the attainment of divinity for those engaged in ritual action comes from knowledge alone, not from action.
But regarding the attainment of that through a combination [of means], certainty arises from scripture alone. || 374 ||

1.1 He divides the very portion concerning doubt: "Even for the performer of ritual acts" (*karmiṇo'pi*). This means that even for a wise person who possesses ritual action, [liberation] does not arise from ritual action alone.

The meaning is that divinity is not attained through name alone, but rather through the combination [of name and action]; thus, the doubt regarding one who possesses *kevalajñāna* (omniscience) is difficult to ward off. He offers a rebuttal in another manner by relying on scripture itself, starting with the words "tatprāptau" (in the attainment of that). For there is no means of knowledge other than scripture (*āgama*) that definitively establishes divinity through a combination; therefore, by virtue of the authority of that scripture, the attainment of it even through *kevalajñāna* alone must be accepted. || 374 ||
This very knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses the form as it has been explained through the series of metaphors.
In this world, it would certainly be a conqueror of the world, even though it is devoid of action. || 375 ||

He applies the literal words of the scripture (*śruti*) to the meaning already stated: "That, indeed, this... The meanings of the words *tat* (that) and *etat* (this) are expressed by the two qualifiers.
The word *iha* (here) means even in one who is devoid of ritual action—that is, the knower. He states the sense of the particle *eva* (indeed): "permanently" (*dhruvam*). || 375 ||
Indeed, even the hope for this world does not exist here for one who lacks vision.
For, because it is like the world, doubt arises regarding an object that has not been attained. || 376 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "na haiva" (not indeed) as follows: "na ha" means that for a person who possesses knowledge, there is not even a desire for the absence of results in authoritative worldly activity. Anticipating the objection that even a knower might be without fruit due to the absence of auxiliary factors, he says: "iha... (in this world...).

Or rather: having raised the doubt as to why there might not be a similar apprehension even regarding the state of being a god while still in the condition of being alive due to the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā), he says:
"Because it has not been attained. || 376 ||
Right here, due to the demoniacal state consisting of the conceit "I am the vital breath," [the self is bound].
Since [the self] has been utterly destroyed, how could there be doubt, given the impossibility of its being rooted in that? || 377 ||

Now, one might object that the state of being an undivided deity cannot be attained while the present body exists, because it is obstructed by the conceit of limitation; to this, he says: "Here" (iha). This means that the conceit of limitation, which is the root of doubt, is impossible [in that state]. || 377 ||
In this regard, it should be reflected upon that [liberation] results from the combination of knowledge and action.
Is the state of divinity that of the Udgātṛ priest or rather of the sacrificer? (378)

It has been stated that the attainment of the gods results both from worship combined with ritual action and from worship alone; considering it improper for both to bear fruit in those two cases respectively, [the author] deliberates to determine which one actually bears fruit. "This," etc. Therein, first, he shows the deliberation regarding that which bears fruit through combination (samuccaya).
