[The opponent] objects:

"From knowledge," etc. Because the attainment of a fruit for the Udgātṛ results from the knowledge of one's own gold and so forth; because the acceptance of a fruit for the sacrificer results from the knowledge of the Prāṇa possessing qualities such as being the *ayāsya* [breath]; and because of scriptural texts such as "for himself" (*ātmane*) or "for the sacrificer" (*yajamānāya*), [the fruit arises] from the combined meditation on the Prāṇa. For whom [then would there be a conflict]?

The meaning is that the thought "this is the fruit" enters [the mind]. He indicates another inquiry with the word "atha" (now). He asks "what? (kimiti) regarding whether the state of divinity belongs to the one who performs mere meditation, or to the Udgātṛ priest, or to the sacrificer, or to someone else. || 378 ||
A combination [of duties] is not accepted for the Udgātṛ, because of the absence of [multiple] functions.
Because he has entered into another's duty, he would be an udgātṛ, not in his own duty. || 379 ||

By the words beginning with "No" (na), he refutes the position that the state of being a god results from the combination [of ritual action and meditation] on the part of the Udgātṛ. Here, the word "here" (iha) refers both to the context of the Udgītha and to its fruit. Now, one might object: how can there be an absence of ritual action for one who has entered into ritual action, and how can he be the agent of meditation? It is not logical that the fruit belongs to the Udgātṛ through such a combination; for in that case, does his meditation combine with his own ritual action, or with that of the sacrificer (the Yajamāna)?
He says "not the first" [and] "the other. 379.
And because of that attachment to ritual action, even the practice of knowledge is difficult to attain.
There is neither direct realization nor a continuity [of it], and that continuity does not exist. || 380 ||

Having established that there is an absence of ritual action for the Udgātṛ by means of his knowledge, [the author] states that he also lacks knowledge itself: "Kriyā" (action). The meaning is that because the Udgātṛ priest—so named due to his connection with the act of chanting—is unable to perform his own specific ritual duties at that time, the practice of knowledge regarding what must be done is not accomplished; consequently, the direct realization of the deity dependent upon that knowledge would not occur. Now, one might object: even without the practice of knowledge, if the Udgāna is performed according to the scriptures...

He says "no" to the claim that there will be a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the deity through the *nāda*. He states: "direct realization. The meaning is that while a direct realization of a real entity through the performance of ritual action is not observed, a direct realization of that which is being practiced through repeated practice is observed in some cases. If it be argued that there is then a direct realization of the deity through a continuity of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃtati*), he says: "Not so," because at that time the Udgātṛ lacks his own ritual duty, and thus a continuity of knowledge regarding what is to be performed is impossible.
He says "because it has been stated in the *Pattrikā*": "And the continuum... (380).
Nor [is liberation attained] merely by the birth of knowledge, as is the case with the awakening to the Supreme Self.
His divine nature is to be expected, for it is heard in scripture that "having become a god, he becomes [a god]. (381)

One might object: "If the state of being a god were to arise from mere knowledge alone, just like the state of being Brahman, what is the use of practice? Anticipating this doubt, he recalls what has been said: "Not so" (na ca). Having stated that the state of being a god does not arise from mere knowledge without practice because there is no evidence for it, he says "Thus [it is]" (iti) because it would also contradict authoritative testimony, stating: "The god... (devaḥ) || 381 ||
Nor does it accrue to a learned Udgātṛ through the ritual act of another.
There would be an establishment of a composite [whole], because those two have different substrata. || 382 ||

It has been stated that because the Udgātṛ lacks his own ritual action when knowledge is either present or absent, there can be no combination of that knowledge with such action. Now, having raised a second objection, he says: "Of the Udgātṛ. Even if the Udgātṛ is a knower, nevertheless, a combination of his own knowledge with the ritual action—which belongs to the sacrificer—is not established, because the action belongs to the sacrificer and the knowledge belongs to the Udgātṛ.
The meaning is that because they reside in three [locations] and have different substrata, it is impossible to state their conjunction. || 382 ||
It would be a product because of its continuity; it is a continuum.
In the first chapter, Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* states:
"The sacrificer possesses ritual action (*karman*), whereas knowledge (*jñāna*) resides in the exalted knower."
Therefore, there is no conjunction for that [cognition] either, because its substrata are distinct.

Having rejected the position that the attainment of divinity belongs to the *udgātṛ* priest due to the combination [of knowledge and action], he now rejects the position that it belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) through that same combination.

Regarding the phrase "of the sacrificer": he clarifies the reason taught in the first half of the verse—which is referred to by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*)—namely, that even for the sacrificer there is no combination of knowledge and action to be performed as a cause for attaining the state of divinity. He does so by stating: "Because [the two] are distinct. (383)
That knowledge which was previously described should be understood as pertaining to the sacrificer.
Since he has himself achieved his purpose, what need has he for a sacrificial priest?

When the opponent has refuted the possibility of [the Udgātṛ] becoming a deity through the combination of both [the Prāṇa and the sacrifice], the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) establishes that the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) attains that state [of divinity] by means of the sacrifice alone. Regarding the word "mata" (view): the meaning is that the previously mentioned meditation on the Prāṇa is intended to belong to the sacrificer because the Udgātṛ was purchased by the sacrificer;

and since the ritual action (*karman*) is agreed upon by both parties as belonging to the sacrificer, it is logical that his divinity results from the combination [of the two]. Thus speaks the opponent who maintains that there is no such combination.

He raises an objection with the words "svayam" (himself). If knowledge, like ritual action, were to be performed by the sacrificer himself, then he would have no need for the Udgātṛ priest, since his own power would suffice in both cases;

yet such dependence on him is not observed. Therefore, the meditation belongs exclusively to the Udgātṛ; thus, the sacrificer does not attain divinity through the combination [of knowledge and action]. This is the meaning. || 384 ||

If it is held that there is a dependence on the Udgātṛ priest even in the case of knowledge, just as there is in the case of ritual action, then that [dependence] applies equally to the Udgātṛ as well; for there is no activity apart from the Udgātṛ. (385)

The proponent establishes the combination [of duties]. Regarding the phrase "in the ritual action": if it is held that, when the ritual action belongs to the sacrificer, he requires the Udgātṛ for its accomplishment, then likewise, even in the case of knowledge belonging to the sacrificer, there is a requirement for another for the sake of birth; and thus, because of this combination, the sacrificer possesses divinity—this is the meaning. Now, he establishes the divinity of the Udgātṛ as well through combination. Regarding the phrase "of the Udgātṛ": just as...

Without a donor, rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma do not succeed; likewise, without that [donation], the Udgātṛ priest would also not succeed, because he exists only when engaged in the ritual action. Therefore, just like the sacrificer (yajamāna), the ritual duty of the Udgātṛ must also be postulated. However, knowledge is common [to both], since even though it is purchased [from the teacher], its locus is the Udgātṛ.
Thus, the meaning is that it is logical for him [the Udgātṛ] also to attain divinity through the combination [of ritual action and knowledge]. || 389 ||
For the ritual act becomes fruitful only by depending upon the officiant who performs it.
The singing of the *annādya* chant belongs to the Udgātṛ; that knowledge is dependent upon it. || 386 ||

As for the claim that there can be no combination of knowledge and action because they have different substrates, he says in response: "Belonging to the sacrificer. Just as the singing of the *sāman* by the chanter, being combined with the ritual action belonging to the sacrificer as its master, accomplishes the fruit of obtaining food; so too, the other action, being combined with the knowledge belonging to that same sacrificer, accomplishes the fruit, since it is dependent upon the sacrificer's action.

The meaning is that even knowledge other than [the specific one] would accomplish its own fruit; therefore, through the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action, even though they have different substrates, the state of divinity for both is possible. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish the connection between his knowledge and action, just as there is a connection between the *udgātṛ* priest and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). || 386 ||
If it is a combination, then for both the Udgātṛ and the sacrificer.
"What is the purpose of this divine state?"—for such indeed is the Vedic revelation.

Thinking that the attainment of divinity [occurs] through perfect knowledge (kevalajñāna) either for the Udgātṛ and the Yajamāna or for someone else—and that it is not the former case because those two have the qualification for the combined performance (samuccaya), nor the latter because such a person is not under discussion—he says: "For what purpose? (387).
This is stated here as being common to all stages of life (āśramas).
For this very reason, because it is already established, [the rule applies] to both the Udgātṛ and the sacrificer. || 388 ||

He provides the answer that the attainment of divinity comes from absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) for all members of the three castes who are devoid of ritual action (*karmaśūnya*), beginning with the word "all" (*sarva*). The meaning is: if the fruit is desired through absolute knowledge based on the authority of the present statement, then this knowledge is said to be fruitful without distinction for all those entitled to [Vedic] rites (*adhikṛta*) who perform actions (*karmin*). Anticipating the objection, "Why should this knowledge not belong only to these two [castes] under discussion? he says:

"Because it is established": the meaning is that since their eligibility for the combined practice (samuccaya) is firmly established, there is no eligibility for isolated knowledge (kevalajñāna). || 388 ||
Indeed, through its divine nature, consciousness conditions that very intellect.
Why, then, does that which exists for the sake of another not succeed without dependence?
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika. 3.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper for *kevalajñāna* (isolated knowledge) alone to be the cause for attaining divinity—since such attainment is seen only when [knowledge and action] are combined—the author states the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"): "The deity... etc. Even the knowledge of the *Udgītha*, which is performed by the *udgātṛ* priest but owned by the patron (*yajamāna*), unites the performer with the state of divinity;

how much more so, then, does meditation—which is independent and owned solely by the performer—bring about the state of divinity for the performer? Therefore, knowledge, even when isolated, [is the cause].
Why would it not lead to the attainment of that state? The meaning is that it is logically established that even knowledge alone has the attainment of divinity as its fruit. || 389 ||
Thus ends the third Udgītha Brāhmaṇa in the commentary on the Vārttika of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth Brāhmaṇa:
And this fruit of knowledge and action is impelled by the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa).
By such scriptural passages as "the Self alone," agency at the beginning of creation and so forth is declared. (1)

In order to state the connection between the two preceding Brāhmaṇas, he restates the subject matter already discussed: "Jñāna... etc. The meaning is that in the preceding Brāhmaṇa, the fruit of both combined and independent knowledge—consisting in the attainment of the status of Prajāpati—has been elucidated regarding the topics of knowledge and action.

Now, he states the superficial purport of the passage beginning with "The Self alone this [was]... (ātmaivedam...): "Ātma... etc. [This refers to] Prajāpati, who is the fruit resulting from the combination [of knowledge and action].

The meaning is that this is stated by the preceding section of the text, beginning with "In the beginning of the creation of the world, the Self alone is sovereignty," and ending with "the differentiation thereof. || 1 ||
In the creation, destruction, maintenance, and so forth of the world, [He acts] as the Self of the world.
The independence of that which has become the fruit of action and intellect is described.
1 kha. Tikanyā [vol2, page 134] 428

In order to state the fruit of describing [the Lord's] sovereignty, [Sureśvarācārya] restates the meaning of the second half of the verse: "The world... and so forth. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the acts of governing and so on are included.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "is described by the present treatise. (2)
And by this praise, there shall be praise for the ritual action and knowledge declared in the Vedas.
However, all of this that has been stated here is intended for a specific purpose.
The Vedic means of accomplishment is to be known as consisting of knowledge and action from of old.
It is certain that this leads only to the fruit of great misfortune, and not to liberation. || 4 ||

He states the result of the declaration of Prajāpati’s independence with the words "by way of praise" (*stutyā*). The meaning is this: an excellence of the fruit depends upon an excellence of the cause; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of its being accidental (*ākasmikatva*). Therefore, the manifestation of the *sūtra* (the thread), which is the fruit of knowledge and action, as it is being described, illuminates the greatness of those two causes. Having stated the incidental intention (*āpātika-tātparya*), he states the ultimate intention (*parama-tātparya*) with the words "but what is intended" (*vivakṣitaṃ tu*).

The construction is as follows: that which was stated in the preceding context—the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*)—namely, that knowledge and action are the means of attainment (*sādhana*) based upon the authority of the Veda, all of that is determined to be solely for the sake of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), such as dwelling in the womb, and not for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*); this is what is intended to be known here in the passage beginning with "the Self alone" (*ātmaiva*). The qualification "great" (*mahat*) is used with the intention of expressing that there is no misfortune greater than transmigratory existence. (3.4)
Every Vedic means of accomplishment [is invalid], because its cause is the arising from ignorance.
"For the sake of [avoiding] the fruit of intense misfortune" is stated from the perspective of the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
The intended meaning [is explained] with effort, out of a desire to produce detachment from that.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that knowledge and action do not have saṃsāra as their fruit? For neither Vedic meditation nor Vedic action has an undesirable result; otherwise, that consequence would apply even to the knowledge of Brahman. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Vedic... The purport is this: although everything prescribed by the Vedas—consisting of both knowledge and action—is for the sake of an undesirable end, because the means are born of false knowledge such as "I am the agent," and because the enjoyment of their fruits depends upon the body and other such factors.

The intended meaning here is not that [ignorance] is the primary subject, because this is a section concerning the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and meditation (*upāsti*) and the like are not intended to be discussed here as the principal focus. Although the knowledge of Brahman arises from ignorance, its status as the cause of the supreme human goal is established by scripture and other authorities; the meaning is that the other [ignorance] is merely the cause of a semblance of that goal. The qualification "intense" (*tīvra*) is used with the intention of emphasizing that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is the most difficult to cure among all evils. [This refers to the fact that] Vedic meditation and the like do not result in evil consequences...

Fearing that the statement regarding "loathing" might be irrelevant in a context dealing with the knowledge of Brahman—the cause of the supreme human goal—the author says: "tadvairāgya... (for the sake of detachment from that).

The meaning is that, because of the scriptural injunction "one should loathe that," the statement regarding its being an undesirable result is made within the context of knowledge with the intent of prescribing detachment for one qualified for knowledge from the fruits of ritual action and the like—which, along with their means, are of the nature of misfortune. || 5 ||
For one who is not detached from worldly existence is not fit for the knowledge of the Self.
For this very reality of the Self is indeed to be reached through such instruction. (6)

In the section concerning knowledge (vidyā), one might raise the objection: "Let knowledge alone be expounded; what is the use of speaking of dispassion (vairāgya)? Anticipating this, he says: "yataḥ" (since). The word should be split as "aviraktaḥ" (one who is not dispassionate). Therefore, the remainder of the sense is that dispassion must be stated as a qualification of the qualified seeker (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa). [This is because one who is not dispassionate does not seek] from the fruit of ritual action or knowledge...
Fearing that there might be no distinction even from the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman for one who possesses passion, he says: "This very [is it]," etc. [It is] other than the Self.

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that there is an absence of fitness for attaining the state of the Supreme Person, which is a human goal. The sense is that because it contradicts scripture (*āgama*), inference (*anumāna*) does not arise; therefore, there is no dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman. || 6 ||
He will respectfully say that [the Self] is even more beloved than sons and other such things. || 7 ||
It is taught that everything declared in the Vedas has the purification of the individual's being as its fruit.
Karma, such as meditative absorption and the like, is practiced with effort by those seeking the highest good.

[Objection: How can the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), which is not itself a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), be something to be sought? To this he says: "from [the attainment of] sons and so forth. The word "thus" (*tathā*) means in accordance with the fact that the reality of the self is what is to be sought. And so, since it is the supreme human goal by virtue of being the highest bliss (*paramānanda*), how could there be detachment from the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman? Otherwise, even knowledge and ritual action would not have undesirable results, just like the knowledge of Brahman.

Fearing that the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) might be rendered invalid because it culminates in what is not the ultimate goal (*anartha*), he says "The Veda... to show that this is not so, since it leads to liberation through an indirect path (*praṇāḍyā*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are included. "Diligence" (*yatna*) means conformity to the scriptures.

"By those seeking the highest good" (*śreyorthibhiḥ*) means by those who desire only the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) without a specific longing for particular fruits. [This refers to action] performed as an offering to the Lord (*īśvarārpaṇa*).

The word "by means of" (*buddhyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is: "whether remembered or heard. This is heard in such passages as "one should sacrifice with whatever [is available]," and so forth; and it is also recorded in the Smṛti, such as "he for whom these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) have been performed," and so on. *Sattva* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); its purification (*śuddhi*) is the departure of passion (*rāga*) and other such qualities belonging to it. (Verses 7–8)
Possessing perfectly purified intellect, he understands cyclic existence according to reality.
And having perceived the true nature of saṃsāra, one should cultivate detachment.

For what purpose is the purification of the intellect for one seeking liberation? To this he says: "Properly," etc. The qualification "again" (*punaḥ*) by means of the word *sam* is for the sake of establishing the extreme firmness of that purity. He states that purity is the cause of discrimination (*viveka*), and its fruit is dispassion (*vairāgya*): "Seen," etc. (Verse 9).
For one who desires to turn away from cyclic existence must be weary of it;
yet that turning away is not established unless one is weary of the actions [that cause it]. (10)

He states that the fruit of that [knowledge] is the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) through the medium of tranquility (śama), by saying "from the beginningless... The word "ā" implies "up to the Avīci hell. Anticipating the objection that all this is fruitless because the destruction of saṃsāra occurs through karma and other means alone—rendering knowledge useless—he says "not so," on the basis of such scriptural texts as "There is no other path" and "The uncreated is not attained by the created. || 10 ||
Because of the suffering to be accomplished through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
Having emerged, he pursues the means for liberation from that which is harmful. || 11 ||

Anticipating the question, "What then is the means to liberation? he states that it is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) born from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

Regarding the verse beginning with "Speech" (*vāk*): because the fruits of the three types of action possess defects such as impermanence and are therefore insubstantial, one should rise above them. Having renounced actions for the sake of right knowledge—which is the cause of liberation—into this worthless and essence-less cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the qualified seeker should repeatedly engage in hearing and the other practices.
Therefore, the meaning is that liberation arises from right knowledge. || 11 ||
1. Sāre mā | [vol2, page 136] 130 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter— ]
And even eternal actions [are so called] because they depend upon the fruits of their own formative impressions (saṃskāra).
One who perceives all the defects of the entire cycle of existence renounces them all.

Anticipating the objection—"Even when optional and prohibited rites are avoided, why should the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) abandon the obligatory (nitya) rites? There is no reason for such abandonment"—the author says: "The obligatory ones also... The meaning is that the abandonment of the obligatory and other such rites is established for one who perceives the defects of saṃsāra, by virtue of relying on the fruit in the form of purification (saṃskāra) produced by the performance of the obligatory rites and so forth. || 12 ||
One does not experience suffering greater than that born from the fire of saṃsāra.
What other greater suffering could there be than the abandonment of constant practice? (13)

Anticipating the objection that the abandonment of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is improper because of the sin incurred by failing to perform what is prescribed—according to such Smṛti texts as "By not performing the ordained action..."—he says: "Saṃsāra... [and so on]. It is stated that the qualified seeker is one whose intellect is purified and who is dispassionate; he does not consider the suffering caused by the grasping of the body and so forth resulting from the performance of obligatory rites and the like to be anything other than absolute suffering, equal to the hell of Kumbhīpāka. Thus, rather than the suffering already mentioned arising from the non-performance of obligatory rites and the like, [he considers the former to be the true suffering].

There is no suffering whatsoever that does not exist; therefore, since suffering is equal whether one performs or does not perform [worldly actions], one who desires to uproot all suffering and wishes to engage in hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is declared to be the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*). Consequently, like optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) and the like, he abandons even the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and so forth. The meaning is that the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) concerns one who is dispassionate and seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). || 13 ||
"Those who fear liberation," and so forth; such also is the teaching of the Śruti.
And the Smṛti, such as "the Vedas are eternal" and so forth, is clearly rooted in that [Veda]. (14)

He cites the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as authorities for the renunciation of action by one who is dispassionate. Regarding the phrase "of liberation," it is stated that they are "rooted therein" (*tanmūla*) for the sake of establishing their authority.

He declares their authority here to be like that of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they bring about the understanding of the intended meaning. Regarding the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*), it refers to the state of bringing about an unambiguous understanding.
Nor does he say that; [it is] "clearly" (sphuṭa). || 14 ||
The supreme reality, which is the cause of all that is born, is not known through the Veda.
From the final effect, that very thing would be the qualifier of all effects.

Since Vedic rituals and the like result in the fruits of saṃsāra, one who is detached from them is the qualified seeker for the knowledge about to be described. To demonstrate this—just as it was shown in the section on the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) by means of the teaching on creation occurring after the intermediate dissolution—the passage preceding the statement regarding the unmanifest (*avyākṛta-vākya*) is intended to explain the meaning of "The Self alone... (*ātmaiva...*) and so forth; having thus stated the intended meaning, [the text proceeds] from Prajāpati’s presence immediately following the intermediate dissolution.

To state that even while undergoing emanation, creation has Brahman alone as its agent, [the author] says, "The Unknown," asserting that Brahman itself, though unknown, is the cause of the entire universe. The construction of the verse is as follows: that which is heard in the Śruti as the cause of the world consisting of born beings is the Supreme Reality itself, variegated by ignorance (*avidyā*). Although pure Brahman is the root cause of the world, nevertheless, ignorance serves as the medium therein; otherwise, it would be like a stone statue.

The sense is that [the Sūtra] is not possible for that which is non-dual and free from attachment. Anticipating the objection that even if the Supreme is the root cause, the Sūtra and so forth might be intermediate causes, he says: "Until the end" (*āntyāt*). The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman itself, in the form of the Sūtra and so forth, is the cause that distinguishes all effects up to the final effect, which is earth (*pṛthivī*). || 11 ||
1. And *smṛti*. 2. *ka*: and *śruti*. 3. *ka*: ‘dānvityā’. [vol2, page 137] 4.
*Brāhmaṇa*], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 431.
By each respective action of the self, the limit of darkness is the appearance of one's own self.
Viṣṇu, being distinguished, created fire, water, and so forth through his *māyā*.
Anticipating the objection as to how the supreme, which is changeless, can be the cause, he clarifies what was indicated by the word "unknown" (*avijñāta*) with the words "by that" (*tena*).

That is to say, the Supreme, conditioned by that *tamas*—designated here as the "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*)—which consists in the appearance of his own conscious essence (*cid-dhātu*), [manifests] in the form of the *sūtra* (the subtle thread) and so forth.

The meaning is that, distinguished by his own function, he produced the world consisting of the elements and their derivatives. To avoid the distinction in meaning where Brahmā is the creator, Viṣṇu is the protector, and Īśa is the destroyer, the term "Viṣṇu" is used. By the word "māyayā," he indicates that the darkness (tamas) serving as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is the instrumental cause for the birth of the world. || 16 ||
Through ignorance, this [Self], though eternally immutable, possesses the state of being a creator at all times.
Because it constantly produces cognitions that correspond to the actual state of things, it is for that reason considered eternal.

It has been stated that even the Supreme Being, though changeless, possesses causality dependent upon *māyā*. Now, raising the objection that because He is a cause, His changelessness—like that of clay and other materials—is not established, [the author] replies that this is not so, because the reason is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) and because it is contradicted by scripture (*āgama*). He says: "By ignorance" (*avidyayā*). Raising the further objection that since causality, like immutability (*kauṭasthya*), exists eternally, what is the use of ignorance? He says: "Just as... (*yathā*). [This refers to] positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

From the scriptural authority stating, "But Māyā is Prakṛti," the meaning is that the power of creation is dependent upon ignorance (avidyā). Anticipating the objection that if the cause of the world were eternal, it could not be dependent on ignorance, whereas if it were non-eternal, there would be an infinite regress and a contradiction with established doctrine, he says: "eternal" (nityam). By virtue of being beginningless (anāditva), the cause is intended to be eternal, but not by virtue of being endless; otherwise, knowledge (vidyā) would be rendered futile. This is the meaning. || 17 ||
From that, the Satsūtra, which is the foundation of knowledge, action, and so forth, was born from the All-pervading Lord.
That which possesses the powers of knowledge and action, wherein this entire world is established.

He shows the sequence regarding the statement that "the unknown Brahman is the cause" with the words beginning with "jñāna. The word "ādi" (and so forth) is intended to include latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Then, from the "all-pervading one"—that is, from Brahman in its unmanifest state (*avyākṛta*)—[arises] what? He states what that *sūtra* is: "jñānakriyā" (knowledge and action). The *sūtra* is the subtle body (*liṅga*) consisting of the five great elements in their unevolved state and their effects; and that [subtle body], possessing the power of action, is called *prāṇa*, while [it also possesses] the power of knowledge.

The meaning is that "mortal" refers to that which is called Hiraṇyagarbha. In that regard, the Sūtra states an inference based on the mark of an effect, beginning with the words "yatreti. For this [world] cannot be established as being without a support, nor can its support be anything other than the Sūtra, because of such scriptural texts as, "By the Sūtra of Vāyu, O Gautama," and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Sūtra is the substratum for the visible, gross effects. || 18 ||
From that, Virāṭ was also born, possessing a body consisting of the three worlds.
From the aforementioned knowledge and action, the birth of Manu occurred, and from that as well [the subsequent births]. (19)
He describes the emergence of Virāṭ from the Supreme, who is not [directly] known, by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Sūtra, stating: "Virāṭ also...

In response to the inquiry as to what this Virāṭ is, he states that it consists of the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) and their effects once they have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*), saying: "The three worlds... He states the cause for its arising, saying: "As previously described... He describes the emergence of Manu from the Supreme who resides within Virāṭ, saying: "From Manu... From him, the Supreme Manu—

The author [Patañjali] states that this entire human creation belongs to Prajāpati. He says "from that too" (tato 'pi) to indicate that the causality of knowledge and action is common to all creation;
the word "and" (ca) is used for this purpose. || 19 ||
The creation that occurs after the great dissolution shall be described as belonging to Viriñca.
But that which begins with the intermediate dissolution (āntarapralaya) is said to be [the dissolution] pertaining to Virāj. || 20 ||
432 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 138]

He says: "By whom," etc., to explain where the creation of the Sūtra is said to proceed from the primary cause, in passages such as "From that, indeed, this [was born]" (*tad dha idam*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "immediately after the great dissolution. This refers to the Sūtra belonging to Viriñca, who possesses two powers. Although the creation of Virāj from the Sūtra is explained in the Aśvamedhika-parvan Brāhmaṇa, he says "up to the end" to address the question of where the creation of Manu and others from Virāj is described.

The meaning is this: after the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*), that creation of Virāj, Manu, and the rest which follows, is described here as "she caused this very Self to fall into two parts. || 20 ||
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
He was the first creator of all beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning.

He states the consensus of the Paurāṇikas regarding Virāj, the creator of the mantras and so forth, with the words "sa vā" (he indeed). By the word "bhūta," the gross individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*) are understood. "Agra" means prior to the creation of the gross bodies that have become individual manifestations. || 21 ||
That which has become inwardly turned, in relation to objects other than itself, with respect to the non-dual experience;
"He is proclaimed here in this world as the 'Self' (ātman).

Having thus stated the purport of the passage beginning with "the Self" according to the *Bhāṣya*, the author of the *Udbhaṭabhāṣya* explains the meaning of the word "Self" by interpreting that very sentence as referring to the Supreme Self. He says: "The inward-facing one... In this world, [He] is the inward-facing one (*pratyagbhūta*) relative to all effects and causes which are other than Himself.

That which manifests as every individual appearance, depending solely upon the experience of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and which is devoid of cause and effect, is here designated by the word "Self" (ātman); this is because of the principle [found in the scriptures]: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," where the term "Self" is understood in the same manner as in other [Vedic] passages. || 22 ||
Because it is established solely as a reflection of the self, it arises from ignorance regarding that [self].
Out of delusion, the self itself is cultivated [as the object], because it is not distinct from that [subject].

One might raise the objection: "Since the word 'Self' (ātman) is applied even to the elements and the senses in such passages as 'the elemental self' (bhūtātmā) and 'the sensory self' (indriyātmā), why should that [elemental self] not be understood here as well? Anticipating this, he says: "The appearance of the Self" (ātmābhāsa). The elements and so forth, which arise from ignorance regarding the Self, do not establish themselves by their own nature; rather, since they are established solely through the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), that reflection is figuratively called the "Self" when it is superimposed upon the Self. For a conceptualized entity cannot have existence or manifestation (sattāsphūrti) without its substrate (adhiṣṭhāna).

The meaning is that because those two [cause and effect] do not exist, and because they are merely appearances of the self (ātman), the word "self" is not used here; for when a primary sense is possible, a figurative meaning should not be accepted. Now, one might object that if the referent of the word "self" were distinct from cause and effect, there would be limitation (pariccheda); to this he says: "Due to delusion.
Because the effect and so forth are merely superimposed upon the Self through delusion, in reality the Self alone is that [effect]; thus, there is no limitation.
This is the meaning. || 23 ||
The word "eva" (only) is used for emphasis; it serves to negate the sense of "belonging to that" (ātmiya).
Prior to the birth of Manu and the others, this world was indeed only the Self.

Explaining the meaning of the word *eva*, he states the nature of its restrictive function (*avadhṛti*) with the words "It is *eva*. Explaining the meaning of the remaining three words, he states the meaning of the sentence with the words "Manu and so forth. The connection is:
"This world, beginning with Manu, etc. By the word "etc.," space and the other elements are included. (24)
[Vol.
2, Page 139] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
In the division into internal and so forth, there would arise the cognition of distinctions such as "self" and "belonging to self."
In its absence, that [dependence] would not exist, because the Lord is devoid of dependence. (25)

One might raise the objection that even in the prior state, when the knowable world was merely unmanifested as the Self, there was no absence of knowledge regarding it on the part of Brahman because of its omniscience; therefore, the restrictive emphasis [in the text] would be untenable. Anticipating this, he says: "The internal self, etc. The word "etc. (ādi) is intended to include the objective realm (adhibhūta) and the divine realm (adhidaiva), while the second instance of the word is intended to include the notion of duality such as "this belongs to another. Knowledge exists only when the object exists; [thus, it is not non-existent]. Nirā-...

The meaning is that because there is no connection with an object (*ālambana*) for knowledge, prior to [creation], knowledge itself does not exist as something other than the knowable (*jñeya*). If so, how then is Brahman omniscient at that time? For it is not by assuming some particular state that it is called such. To this, he says: "In dependence" (*apekṣā*). Since there is no requirement for knowledge of an object when the object is non-existent, the Lord’s omniscience consists in His unobstructed knowledge of all existing things. || 25 ||
For this world, consisting of name, form, and so forth, is indeed dependent upon mutual worship.
If it were a means of valid cognition only when facing toward itself, it would turn its back on external variety. || 26 ||
Fearing the charge of Nihilism— that in the prior state, due to the absence of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the world would necessarily be non-existent—
the author says, "Mutually" (*mithaḥ*). This world, consisting of name, form, and action, is not devoid of mutual dependence in such ways as "this is knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge."

The meaning is that, because it consists solely of the nature of the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), prior to its production, its dimension must reside only in that [Self] and cannot reside in non-existence (*abhāva*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that the world, as apprehended through its persistence in Being (*sat*), does not reside in non-existence. Having raised the objection that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were identical with the Self alone, then because of the Self's uniformity, the world would also possess that same nature—since it is impossible for a single entity to have multiple forms—the text continues by stating that at the time of creation, [the world appears] as distinct from the inner Self...
Having attained multiplicity, he says "the other" (parāṅ). || 26 ||
This worldly existence yields contrary fruits, like the apāmārga creeper.
For those who perceive within, it leads to liberation; for those who perceive without, it leads to worldly existence.

He states the resulting meaning—namely, that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is of a single nature as mere Self (*ātman-mātra*), yet appears manifold through its differentiation—by means of an illustration: "Like the *apāmārga* [plant]," and so forth. The meaning is this: just as that very plant, when grasped in the natural direction (*ānulomyena*), is a cause for the absence of pain due to its softness, but when touched in the reverse direction (*pratilomyena*), it is indeed a cause of pain due to its roughness; even so, this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is the basis for contradictory results.

He clarifies precisely the contrary nature of the fruit of saṃsāra: "The inner self," etc. For those who perceive saṃsāra as being merely this [world] and, by way of distinction from that, consider it to be non-existent, for them there would be the destruction of misfortune; for saṃsāra, when seen as mere consciousness, does not [lead to such a result].

Failing to perceive any distinction from that [Self], it is incapable of causing harm. However, for those who view the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as something external to the Inner Self (*pratīc*), possessing an existence attained through its own independence, that world leads to their misfortune; for it will be stated later that "from duality, indeed, fear arises" (Brhadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2).
This is the meaning. || 27 ||
The universe, whether determined or undetermined, is nothing but the immediate internal cognition.
From the knowledge "I am the cause of delusion," there arises fear, aversion, and so forth.

Having stated this, he says "vyākṛta... (manifested) to explain what the means of knowledge is regarding that [Self], which is the cause of bondage and liberation according to the aforementioned method: namely, *sākṣipratyakṣam* (the direct perception of the witness).

The world, whose name and form are manifested through distinction from the inner self (*pratīc*), is seen as the cause of misfortune; that which is perceived as being of the nature of that [world] when its name and form are unmanifested—[that is the witness].
1. ga. *dātmīyātmādi* | 2ka. *hātprabhoḥ* | 55 [vol2, page 140]

That very [Self] is the remover of misfortune; the meaning is that it is self-evident (*svasākṣika*). He establishes that the world, when perceived as external (*parāktvena*), is the cause of misfortune.

Regarding the word "delusion" (*moha*): when duality arises from that [ignorance], through the cognitions "I" or "mine," that very [Self], which is accessible through those two cognitions, becomes the cause of fear and so forth.
This is the meaning. || 28 ||
When the consciousness of "I" and "mine" has been destroyed by knowledge, [then one is liberated].
Then, when the two visions are seen as non-dual, fear and the like do not arise, because darkness has been destroyed.

He establishes that what is seen as mere condition (*pratyayatva*) is the cause of liberation. [The verse begins with] "I" (*aham*). When the two kinds of false cognition regarding everything have been removed by the direct, immediate knowledge (*aparokṣavidyā*) of one's own inner self (*pratyaktva*)—brought about through scripture and other means—then, once the non-dual Self which is pure consciousness (*dṛgātman*) has been directly realized, the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is destroyed, and thus there is no room for fear, aversion, or the like; this is the meaning. || 29 ||
This is that which is beyond the reach of the intellect, wondrous, and yet manifests distinctly as reality.
Prior to the creation by Manu and others, this entire world was nothing but the Self alone.
Having concluded the digression concerning the explanation of the passage beginning with "the Self alone," he concludes the explanation of the present passage with the words "this" (*idam*).
The word *hiruk* means "separately" or "distinct from the Self. The connection of the word "Manu" and so forth is as before. || 30 ||
This much is the actual occurrence; now that which arises from delusion is being described.
The author of the *Kośapañcaka* has departed because of his ignorance regarding the inner self. || 31 ||
This very Self, though supreme, [appears otherwise] due to the affliction of desire, ignorance, and so forth.
Having assumed this human form, he seems to feel compassion for us. || 32 ||

He restates what was said [previously] for the sake of distinguishing it from what is about to be said: "This much" (*etāvat*). How, then, can that which is partless and of a single flavor (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) have the form of a person (*puruṣavidhatva*)? To this he says: "Through delusion" (*moha*). He clarifies how the Supreme Being is described as having the mode of a person due to the power of delusion. "The sheaths" (*kośa*): the Supreme Self, who is free from cause and effect and self-luminous, [is obscured] by ignorance (*avidyā*) which has as its locus and object the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

Because he has attained the state of the five sheaths—beginning with that consisting of food (*annamaya*)—due to those afflictions, he has become shaped like a person (*puruṣākāra*). For this reason, when the *Śruti* sees those seeking liberation, it seems to express compassion, wondering, "How can this [self] have such a condition? Thus, the meaning is that his being shaped like a person is not real. || 31 || 32 ||
Beginning with bliss and ending with the supreme, they possess the nature of both cause and effect.
He did not perceive them as having abandoned their various forms, such as that of a man and so forth.
By the statement "in the form of a person," and previously as well, this will be explained. || 33 ||

Raising the objection—how can the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) be understood from the word *puruṣavidha*, which merely indicates a human-like form—he states [the answer] by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*):

"Ānanda, etc. The distinction is that the *ānandamaya* is of the nature of the cause (*kāraṇarūpa*), while the other four are of the nature of effects (*kāryarūpa*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "puruṣa, etc. is intended to include female and neuter forms. [The text continues: "The self of each of the *ānandamaya* and the others..."

Lest it be suspected that [the Self] is merely human and does not possess that [human] form, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). This means that the inner self is the reality of these sheaths (*kośa*) which are superimposed thereon. To state the suitability for the description of the "human form" (*puruṣavidha*) in view of its characterizing the five sheaths, [he says]:
"He was indeed... (1).
[Vol.
2, Page 141] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

435. Indeed, this is the word "hi" (for/indeed). Now, one might object: "The five sheaths (*kośapañcaka*) are not heard here, nor are they indicated here as being present in another Vedic text, due to the absence of proximity."
Regarding this, he says: "And above. The word "and" (ca) is used to cite another scriptural passage as an illustration. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the five sheaths will be explained. || 33 ||
The Virāj, consisting of the self, [becomes] the three sheaths of speech, mind, and vital breath.
And it is said: "This is indeed that," and likewise, "Bliss is not thus. (34)
How is it that the statement regarding the five sheaths (*kośa*) occurs later? For there is no word denoting them here as there is in the *Taittirīyaka*. To this he says: "Speech" (*vāk*).
The three sheaths—mind, speech, and breath—will be mentioned in the section on food (*anna*). By the word "speech," the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is grasped;
the ellipsis is "he will declare the three. He states that the term "person-shaped" (*puruṣavidha*) refers to the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya*): "Virāj."

Alternatively, he says "Virāj" to indicate that the one who exists as the Virāj-self by being the creator of Manu and others is the one consisting of food (annamaya), which will be described in the passage beginning with "He, having reflected.

He says "tad ha" to indicate that the description of the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa) is intended both in the subsequent passage "tad dha idam" and in the preceding one "naiveha kiṃcana. || 34 ||
And likewise, he is revealed by the mantra beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā."
"And the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) [of the terms] 'That' and 'This' is logical.

(35) Having introduced the Virāj consisting of food (annamaya), the creation [of the other sheaths] is to be described immediately thereafter; therefore, he specifically shows the corroboration by means of a mantra regarding that.
[The word] "Agni" [is used]. The word "ca" (and) serves to include another statement concerning the nature of the Virāj. This conforms to the aforementioned form of the Virāj.

The meaning of the word *thā* [is "like"]. The word *api* (even/also) has the sense of "just as by the word 'puruṣavidha' (man-like)," etc. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the Virāṭ is revealed. He states the consistency with the remainder of the passage regarding how the Supreme [Self] itself, through its own ignorance, possesses the state of being "man-like" (*puruṣavidhatva*) by pervading the five sheaths (*kośa*) consisting of the cause and its effects: "And there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)," etc. [This refers to] the word *tat*, which denotes the unknown Supreme, and the word *idam*, which denotes the world consisting of the five sheaths.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "mine" (*mama*) indicates that the five sheaths (*kośapañcaka*) belong exclusively to the Supreme [Self]. This is because it is an established principle that coreferentiality consists in the application of words with distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single referent; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
Likewise, the question of Vācaknavī concerns everything from the earth up to the Imperishable (akṣara).
It has as its sole means of valid cognition the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), which is permeated by the inward-looking vision (pratyagdṛṣṭi).
Having thus perceived the form arising from ignorance through a vision born of self-delusion, [he reflected]. (37)

If the Supreme alone constitutes the five sheaths (*kośapañcaka*), then the question in the fifth chapter—which concerns the ultimate dissolution of the entire world within the Imperishable (*akṣara*)—becomes consistent. [The phrase] "earth and so forth" refers to Gārgī Vācaknavī; that which was asked by her is "Vācaknava. Thus, it is in accordance with the fact that the Supreme constitutes the five sheaths. For if the Supreme Imperishable did not possess the nature of the world consisting of the five sheaths, [the question regarding its dissolution] in that [Imperishable] would not be appropriate.

The sense is that [the creation] is appropriately new. Having explained the passage from "the Self alone" up to "of human form" according to his own view, he now adopts the subsequent explanation by taking the *virāj* mentioned in the Bhāṣya as the referent of the word "Self.

He accepts the meaning of the sentence as follows: prior to the production of another body, the entire collection of differentiated things existed as mere subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and that [Self], being of the nature of a person (*puruṣa*), possessed a head, hands, and so forth. Thus he introduces the next section with the words "the inner self" (*pratyak*).

The meaning is that the Virāj-Ātman—who is accessible only to the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃdhī) pervaded by his own self-luminous consciousness—having observed the phenomenal world created by the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagavidyā) through a vision arising from delusion, saw nothing other than himself. || 36 || 37 ||
That which was previously practiced by him— the notion "I alone am this"— is this very thing.
With reference to that vision, this word "anu" (after/along) is employed. || 38 ||

Now, as for this word "anu" (after/along), it denotes either proximity or posteriority; however, it is not appropriate in either sense because we do not observe its application in connection with a proximate subject. To this, he says: "That which... Since the vision "I am this Vairāja form consisting of the three worlds" was practiced by him while in the state of a sacrificer, the word "anu" is employed in reference to that; therefore, it is not redundant, nor does it denote posteriority.
This is the meaning. || 38 ||
The vision that "I alone am this" when well-cultivated—
Having investigated that fruit, he saw nothing other than the Self.

Now, one might object: "Since the aforementioned 'seeing' (darśana) is established as being in the state of the sacrificer, the word 'anv' (after/along) is not appropriate, because that very same [state] is expressed by the word 'īkṣaṇa' (looking/inspecting) as well; therefore, it cannot depend on that. To this, he says: "I myself... The meaning is that the word 'īkṣaṇa' in the phrase "having looked after" (anvīkṣya) refers to the fruit of that seeing. He takes up the passage beginning with "not another," etc., and says: "No. (39)
Therefore, because it does not produce a different object, [the cognition arises] merely from the nature of a single lump.
Not seeing anything else at all, he then declared, "I am that. (40)
He explains this with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since no other body arises from the body of Virāj, he saw only his own physical form;

the meaning is that there was nothing else—neither independent nor dependent. In response to the inquiry, "Not seeing anything else, what did the self of Virāj do?", he says: "I am he" (*so'ham*). The word "then" (*atha*) signifies the immediate sequence following the non-perception of anything distinct from himself. || 40 ||
The self whose body consists of the three worlds did not perceive anything else as separate.
Because his connection with the noble ones was severed, his intellect became as if turned back toward the West.
He restates the meaning of the preceding statement in order to explain it: "trailokya... (the three worlds). The meaning is: whether independent (*svatantra*) or dependent (*paratantra*).

He states the reason for this: "bhinnena" (by that which is distinct). Since there is no contact with anything other than one's own body, the intellect of Virāj does not reside therein; where then does his intellect reside? To this he replies: "pratīci" (in the inner self). || 41 ||
His perception, along with its verbal expression, is exactly as it was previously practiced.

He uttered the word "I," which denotes the self, while in the state of fruition (phalāvastha). Anticipating the doubt—how could he have such a notion regarding the Self within his own body—he explains [the passage] beginning with "He [said] 'I am that'" and so forth. The word "sa" (that) refers to the previous state as the sacrificer (yajamāna); that is to say, it refers to Prajāpati in both his state as the sacrificer and his state of fruition.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish singularity as the reason. || 42 ||
Therefore, its name is "Upaniṣad" because it serves as the means for meditative worship (upāsana).
Therefore, by means of this very self, he designated the self as "I. || 43 ||
"Why is the name 'I am Prajāpati' stated, since this [name] is common to all? To this he replies:

Making known the designation of the cause by means of the mark consisting of its effect.

Of men who desire to conquer one another by means of knowledge, action, and other such instruments.

He summarizes its meaning with the word "mutually" (*mithas*). Among those desiring to attain the status of Prajāpati through a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*) for primacy, he who first attained that state by virtue of an excellence in causes such as knowledge, by him the others were surpassed as if burnt;
therefore, because he was "first" (*pūrva*), he is the Person (*puruṣa*), the Virāj—this is the meaning. || 47 ||
From the great multitude of sacrificers who desire to attain the state of Vairāja.

He burned away those inherent evils with the fire of his previously acquired excellence in knowledge and other virtues.
Therefore, he is designated as "Puruṣa" by those who desire the state of Virāj.

Stating the cause for the burning away of sins that obstruct the state of Prajāpati, he concludes by affirming that the status of Virāj as a "person" (puruṣa) is etymological: "He burned them away" (auṣat). || 49 ||

"I shall state the fruit of the aforementioned meditation"—this is the subsequent statement.

Desiring to state the meaning of the passage—that the meditator on Virāj, characterized by the qualities of Puruṣa, having conquered those who desire fruits through inferior meditation, becomes Prajāpati right at the outset due to the excellence of his meditation and so forth—he says "veda" (he knows). || 10 ||
He who is beyond the senses, unapproachable, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable—he himself has manifested. 51.

The fruit of knowledge and action is that which has been extolled with great effort.

"And why would it have been otherwise?"—this is the corroboration of the meaning previously stated.

From whence did this vision of oneness manifest for Prajāpati?
Because causes such as scriptures and teachers are non-existent, that [liberation] is impossible.

The destruction of fear through Prajāpati’s knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self has been stated. Since he is not a human being, he lacks the qualification for the scriptures; for the scripture has humans as its qualified audience, according to the principle that "it concerns humans because it considers the heart," and furthermore, because he is attached to the sovereignty of powers such as tranquility (*śama*) and the like. Therefore, since the causes for knowledge—such as the well-known scriptures and other means—are absent in him, it is illogical for Prajāpati to possess the realization of oneness. || 71 ||

If this opinion arises from the latent impressions produced by practice in previous births;

In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, [First Chapter]:

Since Prajāpati exists in the state of a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and as a teacher (*ācārya*), through the repetition of hearing and so forth, the knowledge of unity arises; from that, [the result] produced by its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) [occurs].

He raises the objection that such knowledge remains independent even in the state of fruition, using the words "it is held" (*matam*). He refutes this by way of an over-extension (*atiprasakti*), stating "pointlessness" (*nairarthakya*). This means that [such knowledge would be useless] for everyone, including ourselves and others. || 73 ||
Even for Virāja, whose every internal obstacle has been burnt away, there remains the Great Darkness.
Self-knowledge has not yet burnt away our ignorance; what hope, then, is there for the removal of that ignorance?

Anticipating the objection that it (the scripture) must be purposeless because its purpose is the destruction of ignorance, he says: "Burnt," etc. Even though there is birth in another life for one who is free from the obstacles to knowledge (*vidyā*)—that is, for a *virāj*—if knowledge does not burn away ignorance, which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), then...

For us, who possess many obstacles, even the mere hope for that [knowledge] to arise for the sake of burning away those [impurities] is not appropriate due to their power; therefore, the meaning is that the knowledge of its oneness did not arise in another birth. || 74 ||

If it is held that only the final cognition is the destroyer of darkness, then the reason [adduced] would be inconclusive, because other final cognitions are not observed [to possess such power]. For it is not the case that the cognition of identity regarding that [self] arises independently within this very life; for there is the traditional teaching (smṛti): "He whose knowledge is unimpeded... and so forth. It is not [so].

And immediately after its arising, it suppresses bondage along with its cause; however, because it is obstructed by the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma which has fear, dissatisfaction, and so forth as its fruit, [the opponent] objects that knowledge at the time of death is what destroys ignorance. Regarding the word "final" (*antya*): the particle *eva* reiterates the meaning of the word "if" (*cet*). Even though the power of knowledge—which destroys the subtle residue of ignorance that produced that very [karma]—is obstructed by the karma whose fruit has already begun to operate, [knowledge still destroys ignorance].

Since there is no evidence that knowledge—which destroys ignorance, the cause of all saṃsāra such as rebirth—can have its power obstructed, it is impossible to claim that knowledge arising in the interim does not effect cessation. Furthermore, regarding the final knowledge’s capacity to bring about cessation, one must consider the alternatives: is its "finality" (*antyatva*) the cause, or is it simply "knowledge-ness" (*jñānatva*), or perhaps "the state of being a single, unified knowledge"? Having raised these options, he states the flaw in the first alternative with the words "It might be... (*syāt*). [The text continues: ...of Prajāpati...

Regarding the statement that "the final unitary knowledge destroys ignorance," the quality of being "final" (*antyatva*) is not invariably concomitant (*aniyata*) with the destruction of ignorance; for we observe that such destruction does not occur in the final cognitions of other sacrificers or of people like ourselves. This is the meaning. || 75 ||
It should be understood everywhere that the final [awakening] is the knowledge that dispels ignorance.
Because it brings about the realization of the reality of the single self, it is like the penultimate cognition. || 76 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "not the last" (*nāntya*). The meaning is that the final knowledge in us and in Prajāpati is not the destroyer of ignorance, because it possesses the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*); for the reason of "possessing the nature of knowledge" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it is not observed to destroy the ignorance that is the cause of bondage in previous cognitions. He answers the third [position] with the words "the unity of the self" (*aikātmya*). It is incorrect to say that the final knowledge of unity in Prajāpati destroys ignorance because of its being such [a knowledge], due to the state of being penultimate (*upāntyatā*).
The meaning is that even at the end, because that [reason] is not applicable, the penultimate reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika). || 76 ||
Or rather, knowledge of the self may arise from a valid means of proof, just as it occurs in the world.
Just as here, by means of bodies and organs manifested through meritorious deeds of men, [the results are experienced]. (77)
Majesty, wisdom, mindfulness, and steadfastness are determined through knowledge and the like.
In the same way, O one of great intelligence, it would also be so for Virāj. || 78 ||
