In response to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that Prajāpati’s cognition of unity is untenable, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "Or rather" (*syād vā*). The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the previous position.

Since Prajāpati possesses causes and effects arising from superior unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), much like one who has awakened from sleep, and since he possesses the recollection of the words, meanings, and sentences belonging to the preceding *kalpa*, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) would arise for him from sentences revolving in his memory—when those sentences are being reflected upon and aided by unseen merit—just as it occurs in the world.

The sense is this: since those who perform distinguished and superior actions are seen to possess an excellence of wisdom and other qualities, even when ignorance—the cause of future births and so forth—is destroyed by that knowledge, karma already commenced and its resulting fear, dissatisfaction, and so on, will still persist due to a residue of ignorance. He explains the phrase "worldly convention" (*lokavāda*) with the word "as follows" (*yathā*). The term "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of worldly transaction; the words "of those endowed with body and organs" (*kāryakaraṇairyuktānām*) are to be supplied as the subject.

He dispels the doubt that there do not exist humans who possess the performance of actions as previously described by stating "of men" (*nṛṇām*). He states the application of the example (*dāṣṭantika*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "it may be" (*syād vā*) by saying "in knowledge and so forth" (*jñānādau*). From the aforementioned example, it is understood that even Prajāpati—who possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of unsurpassed knowledge and action, and is endowed with the organs of action produced thereby—possesses proficiency (*vaiśāradya*) in knowledge, dispassion, and the like; therefore, his...
The meaning is that even the knowledge "I am Brahman" may arise from the remembered statement alone, without depending on a teacher or others. || 77 ||
Whose knowledge is unimpeded and whose dispassion belongs to the Lord of the World.
"Both sovereignty and righteousness are attained together as a matter of course," so says the Smṛti. || 79 ||

Regarding his mastery in knowledge and the other [perfections], he cites an ancient tradition: "Knowledge," etc. Each term—unimpeded (*apratigha*), unobstructed (*apratibaddha*), and unrestrained (*niraṅkaśa*)—is connected individually. The syntactical connection is: "He for whom these four are innate emerged [as such]. (79)
If knowledge were established simultaneously [with its object], there would be no possibility for fear to arise.
Darkness does not arise together with the sun, which destroys the calamity of gloom. || 80 ||

He raises an objection based on the principle of the section concerning contradictions (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), arguing that [the opponent's view] lacks authority because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "he was afraid" (*so'bibhet*) which imply fear despite the recollection of being eternally perfected (*sahasiddhatva*).
[The author replies: "Together indeed" (*sahaiva*). If it is argued that even fear and the like could arise from their own causes while innate knowledge (*sahaja-jñāna*) still exists, he says:
"By darkness" (*dhvānta*). || 80 ||
It is not so, because [the passage] is intent upon prohibiting the purpose of another's instruction.
Therefore, because his words are accompanied by supernatural powers (siddhi), this fault does not apply.

He resolves the contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti with the words, "Not so. For the teachers maintain that when there is a contradiction, there is a lack of authority due to mutual conflict and the like;
however, he states that in this case, there is no contradiction such as exists between the Smṛti regarding the complete wrapping [of the post] and the Śruti regarding singing after touching it.

"Others say": The meaning is that there is no contradiction because the instruction given by another teacher is intended to negate that [previous] matter; thus, before he attained that knowledge, Prajāpati’s experience of fear was appropriate, and after [the realization], it was due to a mere trace of ignorance. Therefore, there is no conflict. || 81 ||
Faith, earnest intent, desire to hear, prostration, and so forth are the means of accomplishment.
If it is argued that there is no fruitlessness for those things which have the single cause of the birth of knowledge, it is not so; because: || 82 ||

If the arising of knowledge were independent of teachers and other such factors, then the injunctions regarding the means such as faith would be rendered purposeless, which would contradict numerous Śrutis and Smṛtis.

One might raise the objection: "It could be so. [The author] replies with the word "śraddhā" (faith). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) and the rest are included. Furthermore, the purposefulness [of these means] varies according to the distinction between individuals, as is heard in the specific scriptural texts.

The sense is that [the opponent's position] is contradictory to such [scriptural statements]. He dispels the objection regarding this contradiction with the words "not that" (na tat). He states the reason why there is no pointlessness in the injunctions concerning faith and so forth with the words "since" (yataḥ). || 82 ||
It is the conceptualized aggregate of that which possesses qualities and that which possesses defects.
Because it is the sole cause for the birth of knowledge, it would be consistent, as in the case of the world. || 83 ||

He clarifies this very point with the words "possessing qualities" (*guṇavat*). The meaning is as follows: since faith (*śraddhā*) and the other factors—whether taken individually (*vikalpita*) or collectively (*samuccita*)—are suitable for the single arising of knowledge in the form of being "endowed with qualities" or "endowed with defects," there must be an injunction regarding their relative emphasis (*tātparya*) and so forth;

for in the world, one observes the variation of causes and so on in the cognition of forms and the like according to their respective purposes. Among faith and the others, "possession of qualities" refers to excellence (*utkarṣa*).
The distinction is that being possessed of defects constitutes inferiority. || 83 ||
In the arising of the cognition of form and so forth, there are manifold causes for those [cognitions].
Conceptual construction is observed in the world; likewise here too, such is the certainty. || 84 ||

He explains what was stated as "like the world" with the words "rūpādi" (form, etc.). This refers to the causes of that [perception], namely light and so forth, which are the causes for the cognition of form and the like.
The word "iha" (here) is a statement regarding the knowledge of the single self. || 84 ||
Likewise, there is the state of possessing qualities and possessing defects, as well as their conjunction.
It is observed that [the sun] performs the function of awakening and so forth, which are the causes for the arising of enlightenment.

He states that it is not only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is seen as the cause of those [qualities], but also such things as possessing qualities (*guṇavat*). He says "possessing qualities.

And he says "cognition of color-form and so forth" (*rūpādidhī*), because it conforms to its effects, such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). || 85 ||
Owls and other such creatures perceive form at night through the mere contact of their eyes with the object; they do not require anything beyond that. || 86 ||

In this regard, he cites an example of an option (*vikalpa*) that is determined according to the rule of the "offering at sunrise or before sunrise" (*uditānuditahoma*): "The cat and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other nocturnal animals such as the mongoose are also included; for otherwise, how could they catch mice and the like while situated in the midst of darkness?
This is the meaning. (86)
And [it serves] as the cause for the arising of knowledge regarding objects that are past, future, and so forth.
For yogins, it may be only the mind; but for us, it is indeed everything.

He states another alternative for the sake of providing an option: "past," etc. The words "has become a cause" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. For they, by virtue of the preeminent unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced through yoga, perceive everything—even that which is beyond the senses—like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand by means of the mind alone during the state of union (*yukta-avasthā*); this is the meaning. To the question, "How then is there a conjunction [of the two views]? he replies: "For us," etc. (87).
Furthermore, conceptual construction is manifold, according to whether its object is a fault, a virtue, or a neutral thing.
Therefore, among the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, there exists the reality of both qualities and defects.
1. ga.
– vi | [vol2, page 151] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 445
The two types of alternatives (*vikalpa*) have been stated; now he elaborates upon the alternative by way of another classification, beginning with the words "as defective" (*doṣavat*).

He explains how there is a manifold variety of causal alternatives based on the defects or virtues of the causes of cognition, such as the mother and so forth, in the passage beginning with "the mother" (*mātṛ*).

The "mother" is that which undergoes transformation into knowledge, known as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) together with its objective appearance (*sābhāsa*); her possession of virtue consists in having superior wisdom and the like, while the opposite constitutes defect.

The means of knowledge (māna) consists of the eyes and so forth, which possess defects (doṣavat); their defect is such as cataracts (timira) and the like, while their excellence (guṇa) is the absence of that defect. The object of knowledge (meyadoṣa) consists of distance and so forth, whereas its excellence is proximity (saṃnikarṣa) and the like. Thus, because there is the possibility of both alternative and cumulative application (vikalpa-samuccaya) among these causal factors, even though knowledge may arise for Prajāpati through faith (śraddhā) and other means alone, this [other means] is not useless, as it serves as a cause for knowledge. For us, the knowledge of the purport of the Vedāntas and so forth is indeed a means of knowledge for everyone.

The sense is that in the case of the sages (cāryas) and others, there is both optionality and combination [regarding the source of their knowledge], and there is no lack of a restrictive rule here; for in the Śruti, "He who creates Brahmā," it is stated that through the grace of the Lord, Prajāpati’s intellect manifests the Vedas from birth. || 88 ||
But for Prajāpati, the knowledge of Brahman did not exist prior to his transcendence of worldly existence;
this is understood from the fact that he possessed ignorance, fear, discontent, and so forth. (89.1)

As for the claim that knowledge had not arisen in him while he was in the state of a sacrificer, that he accepts with the words "No," etc. He states the reason for this acceptance with the words "This [is] so," etc. (89).
If liberation did not occur through knowledge, whose hope would not become futile?
Since there is no hearing of fear regarding liberation, what delusion could there be therein? Therefore, [there is none]. (90)

Furthermore, that which was previously challenged and refuted—the claim that the final knowledge destroys ignorance—is here approved. Regarding the phrase "in knowledge": according to such scriptural texts as "He knows Brahman," liberation occurs at the very time of knowledge. If, for Prajāpati, even when knowledge was present, that [liberation] did not occur, then our own desire for it would be in vain; thus, from such statements as "What delusion is there? and so forth, [it follows that liberation arises] through the power of knowledge, [freeing one] from fear.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement regarding the absence of duality, the goal would not be attained; therefore, it must be accepted as stated in the passage: "Or rather, [liberation] occurs from the arising of the means for attaining the Real.

Alternatively, if Prajāpati did not attain liberation while knowledge was already present in him, then whose desire for liberation could not be in vain? For one cannot have faith that Prajāpati’s own knowledge was insufficient for liberation, yet it is the very same knowledge that serves as our cause for it.
"It is possible" is the meaning of the first half-verse; the meaning of the second half-verse is exactly as before. || 90 ||
Or [the state] of one who is solitary, devoid of splendor, and whose mind is enveloped by ignorance.
Fear arose here due to the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced in a previous birth.

It was stated that the destruction of fear for Virāj results from the knowledge of oneness—whether independent of means such as prostration or dependent on means such as the knowledge, reflection, and meditation upon the purport of the Vedānta acquired in another birth. Now, raising the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the destruction of fear results from the mere knowledge of oneness with Virāj, [the author] first states the purport of the passage "he was afraid" (*so 'bibhet*), beginning with the words "being alone" (*ekākinaḥ*). The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning is as follows. Now, one might object: "Singularity is the cause for the destruction of fear, for fear arises from a second entity; so how can there be fear for Virāj while he is alone? To this, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). One might further suspect that ignorance alone is not the cause of fear, since it is not perceived during deep sleep; anticipating this, he says: "Preceding" (pūrva). This means: by following the assistance of the latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by fear at the time of being a sacrificer. "Here" (iha) refers to the result—
This is a statement regarding the state [of the subject]. || 91 ||
1 1 b. This is the meaning. || 88 ||
Then, having become afraid, he looked for a cause that would destroy his fear. [Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Adhyāya, [Vol. 2, p. 152], Verse 446]
Since there is nothing other than Me, why then do I fear? || 92 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "This [world]... as follows: "Fear...". He asks for the cause of this perception: "Now...". Thinking that, according to the Smṛti which says "the distressed person is a seeker of knowledge," distress (*ārati*) can also sometimes be a cause for reflection, he says: "one who has become afraid. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That which other than me...": "That which other than me...". Since there is nothing else other than me that could be a cause of fear for me, therefore...
The construction is: "For what reason should I fear? The word *iti* serves to mark the conclusion of the investigation. The word *atha* has the sense of "therefore. || 92 ||
I am indeed alone here; for fear arises from a second.
There is no second one other than myself; for what reason, then, should I have fear? (93)

He explains the passage beginning with "For from what... as follows: "One" refers to the body, which is the self of the three worlds denoted by the word "I" and is permeated by the individual soul (*jīva*). "Here" is an expression for the sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-maṇḍala*). Even so, he asks how there can be freedom from fear, and answers: "From a second.
The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that it is well known that the arising of fear occurs upon seeing a thief or similar object. If that is so, then that cause—the second—must also exist.

He says "no" to the suggestion that it should be so imagined, stating "the second. For cognition is the means of knowledge regarding that which is to be cognized; and since a second [entity] does not appear, he concludes that there is no fear due to the absence of a cause. Why? || 93 ||
From that very knowledge of the identity with Virāṭ, that fear [ceases].
Because it is not recognized by others, lack of joy (arati) is also admitted [as a result]. || 94 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tata eva" (from that very [knowledge]). Regarding the word "tataḥ": in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the knowledge of the identity of the supreme Self is referred to by the word "tat"; he explains that [knowledge] as follows: "not so. The reason for this is given: "for this reason. Even when fear has vanished, dissatisfaction, desire, and so forth are observed in Prajāpati; furthermore, since such [defects] are incompatible with the knowledge of the Supreme due to the absence of their causes, it follows that his fear was not destroyed by that knowledge.
Such is the meaning. || 94 ||
From the cognition "I am alone," which has as its object the oneness of the self with the three worlds.
"Since fear arose from that [state], the lover felt a lack of delight.

Anticipating the objection—"How could there be a lack of delight for one whose fear has been destroyed?"—the author restates the verse beginning with "ekākī" (alone). The phrase "advaitajñānam" (knowledge of non-duality) is excluded by the term "trailokyam" (the three worlds). Because fear had departed due to the realization of his solitude, he consequently experienced this lack of delight.
To this he says: "Because... [The opponent objects]: "Surely the knowledge of identity, which removes fear, would also remove discontent (*arati*), rather than producing it.

To this he replies: "Of those who possess desire (*kāmin*). Knowledge of being alone is destructive of fear when it is without accompaniment; however, when accompanied by desire, it becomes a cause of discontent.
The state of being. || 95 ||
When ignorance has been utterly destroyed by perfect knowledge, how could there be any dissatisfaction?
If that [consciousness] were to exist even for one whose blindness has been destroyed, it would follow that there is no liberation. || 96 ||
1. It is observed. 2. However. [Vol.
2, page 153] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 447.

Anticipating the objection that even when fear has been destroyed by the knowledge of the Supreme (parajñāna), a seeker might still experience dissatisfaction, he says "samyak" (properly). The meaning is:
for a knower whose ignorance has been destroyed, even desire is not possible due to the absence of its cause; so how could there be dissatisfaction? [He states] the fault in the contrary case:

He says: "Dhvasta" (destroyed). The meaning is that even for one whose ignorance has ceased, liberation would be impossible because pleasure still exists, which constitutes a lack of ultimate purpose. || 96 ||
For the Lord, the destruction of fear did not arise from a consciousness that had merely struck down ignorance.
For this meaning is determined by the sign of the arising of dissatisfaction. || 97 ||

He concludes by summarizing the result: that the destruction of the fear of Prajāpati does not arise from the knowledge of oneness with anything other [than Brahman]. He does so with the words "Not through ignorance" (nāvidyā). To support this stated point, he recalls the very same scriptural indication mentioned previously with the word "aratim. The meaning of the particle *hi* is that the absence of delight in the vision of others is well known among living beings who possess such a lack of delight. || 97 ||
And there is no occasion whatsoever here for this right knowledge.
When the creation of the body has commenced, auspicious knowledge does not arise without a cause. (98)

For this reason as well, he states that the destruction of Virāj’s fear does not arise from the knowledge of the Supreme (parajñāna). He says: "And not... He clarifies the lack of scope for the knowledge of the Supreme within Virāj’s authority over the creation of Manu and others by means of the word "piṇḍa. By the word "piṇḍa," the body of Manu and others is understood. The meaning is: "not abruptly," that is, without a break in the context. || 98 ||
A subject matter that is inappropriate to the context, even if it is well-spoken, [is flawed].
Like flowers out of season, it brings no joy to the virtuous. || 99 ||

Even in the section concerning the *virāj*, one might suspect that the knowledge of the Supreme (*parajñāna*) should be taught because it yields a distinguished fruit; anticipating this, he says: "The procedure" (*makriyā*). Now, as for the fact that the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) stated here that the knowledge of identity with the Supreme destroys fear—how is it that you do not accept that? To this he replies: "It has been stated. Even the knowledge of identity with the Supreme, though possessing a distinguished fruit as stated by the author of the Commentary, is out of place and untenable for the learned.
Regarding the phrase "heart-piercing," he provides an illustration: "Not [limited by] time. || 99 ||
For one who knows the true nature of the inner self, there is no delusion regarding the pleasure of sexual union and the like.
Since it has been prohibited by the scriptures, how could it possibly exist here? || 100 ||

Since it was stated that the cognition of the Supreme is not possible [in the case of the Virāj] due to the signs of the arising of dissatisfaction (*arati*) and because of the context of the Virāj, he states another sign in that very same place:

"The couple," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the desire for a second [being] and so forth are included. "Here" refers to the context of the creation by Prajāpati. "Of him" refers to the aforementioned person of knowledge (*vidvat*). || 100 ||
And the scripture states: "He sports with himself; his delight consists in the activity of the self."
Likewise, there is "union with the Self" (ātmamithuna), as well as "delighting in the Self" (ātmarati). || 101 ||

He cites scriptural and traditional authorities (āgama) in the form of *śruti* and *smṛti* which prohibit improper activities such as sexual intercourse for one who possesses supreme knowledge. "In the Self" (*ātman*) means that his play (*krīḍā*) is directed toward the Self alone, and not toward non-Self objects such as sons and so forth; thus he is so described. "In the Self, delight itself is his activity" (*kriyā*);
by this, other activities are excluded. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to include the passage beginning with "Desiring what? For whose sake? (*kim icchan kasya kāmāya*).
"Thus" (tathā) means according to the traditional scripture (āgama) as stated; that is to say, the couple exists within the Self alone and not in a second entity, as has been explained.
The meaning of the Smṛti, however, will be stated later. 101.
The relationship between cause and effect is logical only for one who possesses ignorance (avidyā).
Because it is taught as being neither prior nor posterior, it is not appropriate for one whose blindness has been destroyed [to require further instruction].
Regarding the point that it is the knowledge of Virāj alone—and not the knowledge of the Supreme (Parajñāna)—that destroys fear here, he states another supporting reason: "kārya... etc. 102.
Even for those who have attained the realization of the self, [this remains necessary] until their qualification is fully completed.
Just as dissatisfaction and the rest were seen [in others], so it would be for Prajāpati. || 103 ||

Having thus presented the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Even for one who has attained [knowledge]," and so forth. For even in the case of Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and others who have attained perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), we observe traits such as discontent due to a residue of ignorance (*avidyāleśa*) until the completion of their respective offices. Likewise, although Prajāpati had indeed attained perfect awakening, it was possible for him to experience discontent and the like through a trace of non-awakening as long as his office lasted; therefore, the cessation of his fear occurred only upon the realization of the Supreme.
The meaning is that it is according to the principle that "the state of remaining established in one's office belongs to those holding an office. || 103 ||
Because that which has an unentered intrinsic nature is encompassed by the word "saṃ" (together).
In this sentence, "sa eṣa," there is certainly no mention of anything being accidental.

Regarding the objection that this is inconsistent with the context (*prakriyā*), he says: "Not having entered" (*apraviṣṭa*). In the sentence, "This very one has entered here," the word "this" (*sa*) refers back to the Brahman described in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever but It," which is by nature unentered.

For it is not possible for a pronoun to refer to something that has not been introduced as the subject matter (*aprakṛta*); nor has Brahman been introduced elsewhere [in this context]. That [Brahman] he—

And the word "this" (eṣa) draws near the proximate [subject], namely the "minium" (mini). Furthermore, even in the sentence concerning the unmanifest (avyākṛta), there can be no reference to Brahman as the cause by means of the pronoun "that" (tat) without the subject being previously established; therefore, in passages such as "other than me," there is no mention of a supreme being that is inconsistent with the context.
Nor is it the case that the status of being the creator and so forth is more appropriately applied to Virāj while excluding the Supreme; this is the intended meaning. || 104 ||
It is that instability of the mind which arises from lack of contentment and lack of equanimity.
Even though her own delusion had been destroyed, she nevertheless experienced a sense of dissatisfaction.

Having shown that Virāj, though sharing in fear, was like one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) by demonstrating that the destruction of fear occurs through supreme knowledge alone, [the text] now explains his lack of delight (*arati*) in the passage "he did not at all rejoice," stating another cause for his state of being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). [This is the first section.]

"No. The word *ha* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Alternatively, its meaning is that even among those who are recently liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), a lack of delight (*arati*) may still be perceived due to the influence of the seed of ignorance (*avidyā*). Mental despondency caused by the failure to obtain what is desired is dissatisfaction (*asaṃtoṣa*). From that arises intolerance and timidity, which is the instability of the internal mind.

This lack of delight, characterized by a lack of joy (*anullāsa*), is established by one's own experience; it is that very [instability] which is destroyed by the previously mentioned supreme knowledge that dispels delusion (*moha*).
The meaning is that even for this Virāj, [this state] has indeed arisen from a mere trace of delusion. || 105 ||
Since Prajāpati’s intellect had been seized by the demon of discontent, he became [distraught].
Being alone, he created that [woman], for a man does not delight in being solitary. || 106 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt) as follows: "He who" (yaḥ). By the word "man" (nara), one who is ignorant and possesses the conceit of being a human being and so forth is denoted. || 106 ||
Through this well-known affection and by means of the effects as logical marks, the cause is established.
The Sāṃkhyas as well as other disputants always infer in this manner. || 107 ||

By relying on the scriptural statement—"The delight residing in the effect is the mark (liṅga) of the delight residing in the cause"—which indicates the process of inference, [the author] incidentally makes known that the delusion of certain disputants—that the cause is cognizable solely through inference based on the mark of the effect—is rooted in that very delusion.

The word "śrautyā" (based on scripture) [is used]; the particle "ca" (and) serves to include other marks such as "being limited" and so forth. The word "sadā" (always) indicates that [the cause] is eternally inferable.

And thinking that the mention of the Sāṃkhya is not for the purpose of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), he says: "And likewise" (*tathā ca*). The word "also" (*api*) is intended to include all proponents other than those who maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*). || 107 ||
Desiring to dispel discontent, he should practice a second [meditation] according to his preference.
Virāj desired; desire for the Lord is not possible without ignorance (avidyā). || 108 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "he desired a second" with the word "aratīti" (he was not pleased). Anticipating the question of what kind of object his desire for a second had, he says "yathārutrīti" (as it was heard). Anticipating the objection—how can there be desire in Virāj, who possesses supreme knowledge and is thus devoid of ignorance—he says "ṛtaḥ" (from the Real). Since ignorance existed prior to the arising of knowledge, and since a trace of it remains thereafter, desire is appropriate for him.
The state of being. || 108 ||
I,
possessed by the grasp of passion, am the Virāj for the sake of casting that [grasp] aside.
Indeed, he became as large as the extent of his wife's body when she was joined with him. || 109 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "He became this much" as follows: "He became desirous. For that Virāj, possessed by extremely fierce planetary influences in the form of desire, in order to destroy them, fashioned his own body into the form of a female body; the meaning is that he became a female through his own mere volition, possessing a body of the same dimensions as the mass formed by the perfect union of a couple who have become one. [The text continues: "mutually joined..."
The word "ha" is used for the purpose of indicating that the measure of the *piṇḍa* for a married couple is well-known in the world. || 109 ||
The woman and the man remained embraced for as long as they had been measured.
By means of yoga, that Supreme Lord became of such a magnitude.
He explains the sentence beginning with "yathā" (as) as follows: "a woman and a man. He states the reason for their being of such a size: "by yoga.
This means by the power of volition accompanied by meditation, action, and their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 110 ||
In a man who has not yet found a stable footing, it is merely a desire arising from discontent toward a woman.
Because of her fitness, she employs [her means]; yet, O Lord, having not obtained that, there is no pleasure for him.

Since the scripture states, "He desired a second," indicating that he merely desired a second [being] in general, one might ask: how can that second be female? Or, how is it that in the illustrative example [the phrase] "a woman" (*strī-hūṇam*) is used? Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "He desired. Due to his loneliness, there was dissatisfaction; consequently, there arose a desire for a second. That desire, being devoid of any specific qualification of "female," had as its object a second being in general. Since such a desire would not be capable of removing that dissatisfaction if directed toward a male—who is not fixed [as a solution] by virtue of being a "second"—it presents the female as the "second."

Because one does not obtain that [pleasure] from Prajāpati, there is dissatisfaction; therefore, for the sake of removing that dissatisfaction, women alone are suitable for that purpose due to their fitness for such desire and action.
For this very reason, women are mentioned even in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). This is the meaning. || 111 ||
1. Existence (bhāva) is that which...
And when the mind had become present, there arose for that one the sacrificial intention (*kratu*) directed toward a woman.
On account of his resolve being true, he appeared as if attached to women.
If it is argued that the destruction of discontent arises simply from the auspicious connection [with a woman], then why is the birth of such a woman not mentioned?

To this he says: "And when she was present... Since Virāj possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), a woman appeared in his mind from his *kratu* (volition). The meaning is that she was not a woman present externally who is capable of performing worldly functions (*arthakriyā-samartha*). Having created a woman by means of his mind, he [approached] her... in the worldly manner.

The phrase "he became attached to morsel-food" states the result of the manifestation of womanhood. The word "ca" (and) is used to indicate that this state of being [womanhood] culminates in that very result. || 112 ||
That creation of his which proceeds through the gateway of the couple is now being described.
For this reason, he then divided himself into two parts.

Fearing that the creation of humans and other beings, which is about to be described, might also be like the mental creation of women, and thus suspecting that the creation of women is not useful for the subsequent creation, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "He [Brahmā] created this... as follows: "By means of pairs... The meaning of the word *atha* (then) is that after the physical creation, the two types of creation—mental and vocal—will become clear; or else, the word *atha* is a synonym for the word *ataḥ* (therefore). || 113 ||
Because of the restrictive emphasis "this very [world]," there is no dual designation of Virāj.
He who existed as the measure of woman and man was himself divided in two from this point on.

Now, is this twofold division of Virāj, or of the physical body (piṇḍa) consisting of a man and woman joined together? In the first case, there is a contradiction with the word "him" (tam), because Virāj is the object [of the action]. In the second case, the use of the word "Self" (ātman) would be inappropriate. To this, he says: "Him" (imam). The implication is that, therefore, it is not contradictory to understand Virāj as the agent by means of the word "him. Then, for whose sake is the twofold division? To this, he says: "He who... (yaḥ).
Thus, the *piṇḍa* (the physical body) is qualified. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the absence of a twofold division of the *virāj*.
Nor is there an incompatibility with the term "Self" (*ātman*) in that context, because that [body] also possesses the form of the *virāj*; such is the intended sense. || 114 ||
For by the mere act of falling down, husband and wife attain liberation even in this world.
A woman appears as a man, just like the appearance of mother-of-pearl and similar objects.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore" (tataḥ) as "because of causing to fall" (pātanāt). By the scriptural authority, "The wife is indeed half of one's own self," he also indicates this. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore this" (tasmādidam) as "the woman" (yoṣit). "Vidala" means a part or portion. From the word "etc. (ādi), bamboo and other such items are included. || 119 ||
For this portion indeed desires form; therefore, it is male space [pums-ākāśa] compared to the female.
The sky is certainly filled completely, like a pair of oyster shells. 116.

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "nammādayam" (this is the mother, etc. as follows: "For [it is] the resonance," and so on. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish the well-known mutual dependence between the male and female portions. The term "vyoma" (space) is a designation for the male space (*pumākāśa*). He says that because of the joining together of the two "mother-of-pearl" portions, there is completeness; thus, the activity of the male is always complete, being never interrupted. This he expresses by the words "śukti" (mother-of-pearl), etc. || 116 ||
Rama created Viraj; that Viraj created Purusha.
Know that Manu to be the Puruṣa, of whom this progeny is the offspring of Manu.
[Vol.
2, Page 157] 4 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā*.
451. Now, it may be objected: the creation of humans and other beings will be described through Manu and Śatarūpā; yet, without first teaching their own creation, how can one speak of others?

To the objection that it is not logical to speak of creation [in this context], he replies with the words "the Virāj. Fearing the doubt that the Creator, being the Puruṣa, would not enter into the category of the created, he says "the Puruṣa. The sense is that under the pretext of the twofold division mentioned in the phrase "he cast him down in two ways," the creation of Manu and Śatarūpā is described. || 117 ||
Then Manu united with that woman through sexual intercourse; being impelled by his own past actions, he procreated offspring through those very acts.
He states the meaning of the phrase "he united with her" as follows: "With her. The sense of the word *atha* is: when Manu was Śatarūpā.
But how could Prajāpati, whose self was Manu, venture confidently upon approaching his own daughter—an act censured even by common folk—being himself the foremost among those who know the Dharma?
Regarding this, he said: "By their own respective actions. (118)
Through the power of the karma produced by her, she has been repeatedly connected with many births.
And thus, from his own mind, he created this world, down to the smallest ant.

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "That [is] the cow" (*sā gauḥ*) by means of the word "bhūri. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "In this way" (*evam*) by means of the word "evam. || 119 ||
Whatever is observed in this world is joined with pairs of opposites.
Then Manu emitted them all through the application of pairs of male and female.

He explains that very point: "The pair," etc. The meaning is that the statement beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) is intended to show that it is not only the aforementioned cows and so forth whose creation is intended here, but rather the creation of every pair consisting of female and male. || 120 ||
Herein has been described the creation of the physical bodies of Manu together with Śatarūpā.
Even that [deity] such as Soma, Agni, Indra, and so forth, depends upon Him, just as previously stated. (121)

He recounts the preceding narrative in order to explain the passage beginning with "so 'vet" (he knew). Regarding the phrase "of Manu": the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the context of the previous section on creation.

The meaning of the restatement is that the creation of humans and others was described as proceeding from the *piṇḍa* (body) of Manu and others, which itself originated from Virāj. Anticipating the objection—how can the creator determine "I am the creator" without having brought about a complete creation—the subsequent sentence [is introduced].

He causes [the world] to descend. Regarding the word "Soma": that which is the creation of the auxiliary (anugrāhaka) to be described hereafter is also considered to have been described in the same manner as the previously mentioned creation of the objects of assistance (anugrāhya);
therefore, with reference to that, the meaning is that he resolved, "I am the creation. || 121 ||
Having directly created the world from himself, he is the means for knowledge, action, and so forth.
"Know that I am the creator who has emitted the universe; indeed, I alone am this entire world. (122)

Anticipating the objection that the determination "I am the creation" is impossible because of the lack of identity between the agent and the action, he clarifies the meaning of the passage beginning with "He knew" (so 'ved):
"The world," etc. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies that the created world is a specific internal manifestation of the Creator. || 122 ||
I alone am the created world, for whatever I have created, that is indeed myself.
For this very reason, the Manu named Sṛṣṭi was born.

He explains the reason beginning with "I indeed" (*ahaṃ hi*), etc., by saying "I. For that which is created does not become something other than its creator; it belongs to that very [creator] alone. 1. *pīlaka* (variant *ga*). 2. *nvādeḥ pra* (variant).
452 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] — [Vol. 2, Page 158]
The meaning is: "because it exists in the form of this or that. He states the meaning of the phrase "from that, creation came to be" as follows: "creation," etc.
The meaning of the word "this" (etat) is that the creator is expressed by the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi). || 123 ||
Just as Manu, having created this world, perceived, "I am this."
In this same way, whoever else knows [this] shall also be a creator of the world.

Anticipating the question, "For what purpose is the manifestation of the Creator described in this way?", he explains the passage beginning with "In creation," etc., using the word "Just as" (yathā). || 124 ||
Then, for the beings that have been created, these [energies] beginning with Agni are their mouths.
"I shall now describe those who bestow grace"; thus the Śruti proceeded.

"Then he churned," and so forth; this [passage] awakens [the understanding]. Regarding the phrase "of those created": the meaning is that the subsequent sentence is intended to state the creation of the supporting elements, such as fire, following the creation of the supported beings, such as the Brāhmaṇas. || 125 ||
Because these [deities], beginning with Agni, are subject to differentiation in many ways.
The distinction among all castes, characterized as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and so forth, [is based on this]. || 126 ||

Now, since it will be stated that the deities such as Agni exist in the form of the castes (varṇas) beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, how can there be both the state of being the recipient of grace and the state of being the bestower of grace for one and the same entity? To this, he says: "Because of division" (bhedāt). This is because, due to the distinction between the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva), the office of Agni and the others is manifoldly divided;
and because it will be stated in the Śākalya-brāhmaṇa that each individual deity exists in many forms, [this applies] even to the castes.

The meaning is that [the Lord] appears in the form of Brahmins and others; thus, this distinction among them is merely imagined, and from this imagined distinction, the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary is established for the One alone. || 126 ||
This great creation of the benevolent deities has now been set forth.
In that regard, the arising of Indra and others is not spoken of here as being produced without prior impulsion (apreraṇa).

[The author] asks, "Regarding the *anugrāhaka* creation," in order to understand the intention of the Śruti which speaks of only a portion of it when the *anugrāhaka* creation is under discussion. Its greatness is due to its having unconditioned deities as its object and because it is superior to the *anugrāhya* creation; thus, he [created] Agni—

By the statement "He created [it]," the creation of Agni alone is declared; by the statement "He created that [tejas]," the creation of Soma—the moon, whose nature is fluid—is declared, and not that of Indra and others according to the initial context. Thus he says: "In that case... (verse 127).
When ignorance has been established, their creation will be described hereafter.
But it is solely for the purpose of establishing the connection with the authority over ritual action. || 128 ||

Anticipating the objection that the creation of Indra and the other gods is not mentioned here because they are not among those to be created [in this context], [the author] states "ignorance" (*avidyā*) to explain what is intended: that their creation will indeed be described in the section on ignorance (*avidyā-prakaraṇa*), in proximity to the discussion of karma. Regarding the fact that the creation of Indra and others is not mentioned here but is mentioned there, he states "karma" to express the intention of the Śruti: that within the section on ignorance, just as there is an inclusion of karma, the creation of the gods occurs in proximity to karma.

The meaning is that it is intended to state that bathing is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only to those [rites] belonging to non-knowledge (*avidyā*), for those who are authorized as recipients (*saṃpradāna*) therein, and not to knowledge (*vidyā*). || 128 ||
1. Prakṛta | [vol2, page 159] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 45.
Having described that entire creation as it was told, the conclusion is now presented here in relation to it.
Now, [this is] for the purpose of refuting the notion of a deity held by the ignorant. || 129 ||

One might raise the objection: "If the creation of Indra and the others is to be described later, then this concluding statement—'For he alone is indeed all the gods'—is improper, because the creation of the gods has not been stated in its entirety. Anticipating this, the author says: "Him" (*tam*). Although the creation is yet to be described, the conclusion is made here by intending to speak of that future creation as if it were already spoken; otherwise, the word "all" would be inappropriate. And there is no contradiction in using what is yet to be said as a figurative indication of what has already been said.
This is the meaning. He introduces the passage beginning with "tadyadidam" (Now, as for this...). Regarding "avidvat" (the ignorant):
the construction is that the passage beginning with "tadyadidam" is now set forth to negate that notion of difference which exists among the ignorant regarding the one supreme deity alone. || 129 ||
By means of limiting adjuncts such as qualities, origination, action, form, praise, name, and so forth.
Those of deluded vision split apart the deity who is non-different from themselves. || 130 ||

Furthermore, raising the objection that "how can there be a recognition of a distinction between deities, for a deity whose nature is the Self cannot logically be divided," the author presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "guṇa" (quality) and so forth. Just as a distinction is appropriate in the case of Agni, Indra, and others who possess various qualities— as in the instances "the *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas" and "the *vājina* belongs to the Vājins"—

so too is there a distinction based on the difference in origin (*utpatti-bheda*), such as the installation (*ādhāna*) prescribed in the Yajurveda, the installation prescribed in the Sāmaveda, and the *vāravantīya* chant belonging to the Sāmaveda.

Even among those [Vedic texts], there is a distinction due to differences in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), as in the case of a cloth, a jar, or a cart; here, there is also a distinction due to differences in form, such as "the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice on eleven potsherds" versus "on twelve potsherds," or "having a thunderbolt in hand" and so forth; and there is a distinction of the existent (*sat*) due to differences in name, as in the cases of the *Kāṭhaka* and the *Kālāpaka*;

furthermore, praise differentiates that which is praised, for otherwise the distinction between praises would be useless; and thus, due to the difference in praise within the sacrificial rites (*ṛtu*), there is a distinction between them.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [faults] such as the repetition of specific attributes of the Dharma are included. Therefore, the meaning is that just as there is a distinction between ritual actions, there is likewise a distinction between the deities contained within them. He states the reason for the desire to differentiate the supreme deity, which is itself devoid of intrinsic distinction: "The deluded," etc. (130).
This is what those of dull intellect who perform ritual actions say regarding the land of action.
"Offer this oblation to Agni, offer this to Soma"—from such an audible proclamation of the sacrifice [the deity is determined]. || 131 ||

He connects the words of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the stated meaning: "As for this... Ignorance (*amedhasvam*) consists in the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the deity. Now, the verb "they say" (*āhuḥ*) requires only an agent; since this occurs within the context of that [esoteric] knowledge, one might think that only the knowers (*vidvāṃsaḥ*) are the agents there, not the ritualists (*karmiṇaḥ*). To this he says: "Because of the mention of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). (131)
Because of the indicative mark "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), this [knowledge] is understood as pertaining only to those engaged in ritual action.
But not for those whose delusion has been destroyed and who rest solely within the individual self. || 132 ||

Now, in this passage, it is understood that there is merely a restatement of the difference between deities, not a censure of ritualists; nor can they be censured, because they are engaged in the path to the highest good. As they say: "He who performs a sacrifice is indeed called a righteous person."

Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, there would be censure even of those who possess knowledge; therefore, this is not the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). To that he says: "yajeta" (one should sacrifice). Although dharma is that which, when engaged in the path to the highest good through ritual action, unites men with supreme bliss (niḥśreyasa), nevertheless, this very censure of them is indicated under the guise of restating distinctions, saying: "Sacrifice to this Agni, sacrifice to that Indra," thus addressing the deity.
They are seen as being thus shattered; and according to the principle beginning with "he who [represents] himself as being otherwise," this is a mark of erroneous cognition.
The meaning is that they become worthy of censure. As for the objection that there might be censure even of those who possess knowledge, he says in response: "But not... (na tu).
The ellipsis is "the state of being worthy of censure. He states the cause for the destruction of delusion: "pratyak... (verse 132).
But that person who should find delight only in the Self and be satisfied with the Self—
And for one who is content in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed.

Fearing that there might be censure [of the wise] because even knowers of the Self are performers of action—as suggested by such Smṛti texts as "For no one, even for a moment..."—he cites the very words of the Lord as authority for their state of non-action: "But he who... (133). The distinctions between these internal states are as follows: *ullāsa* is mental delight; *rati* is the pleasure arising immediately thereafter; *sukha* is contentment (*tṛpti*), which is itself the highest form of satisfaction (*saṃtuṣṭi*).
For those whose dense darkness of ignorance has been incinerated by the sun of luminous consciousness that has arisen as the true nature of the single self, there is the destruction of karma. (134)

Now, having raised the doubt as to how there can be an absence of karma for the knower when its absence is described here for one who is liberated, he states the purport of the cited passage: "Having arisen," etc. The connection is that [the text] established the negation of karma even for the liberated one. || 134 ||
He established the prohibition of all offices for ritual action.
The ancient and eternal Viṣṇu [spoke] to the diadem-wearing Arjuna who had sought refuge in him.

He explains that very point with the words "all," etc. By the term "qualification" (*adhikāra*), activity and so forth are understood. Nor is there a lack of faith regarding the reality spoken by the Blessed One, because it has been taught for one who possesses the characteristics of qualification; thus he says, "to the surrendered one" (*prapannāya*). It is without beginning and without end.
To state the distinction that the Blessed One is also of a nature to pervade, he says: "The Ancient One" (purāṇa). || 135 ||
When each individual deity was present separately at the sacrifice.
That is to be understood as unreal, because the deity is indeed non-existent. 136.

By the passage beginning with "tadyadidam" (that which is this), it was stated that the censure of ritualists is effected through the restatement of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas such censure does not apply to the knowers; now, while explaining the commentary beginning with "tanna" (that is not so), he shows the prohibition which is the fruit of that censure. Regarding the word "mithas" (mutually): the entire universe (*viśva bhūta*)—the world (*bhuvana*) that is manifold, already born and being born—is indeed the Self alone, according to the Śruti text, "For all this is Rudra," and thus "all deities are the Self alone."

He states the reason—namely, the identity of the deity through their nature as the Self—based on the reasoning that "there is one [deity] for Smṛti, because there is no distinction in their conjunction, form, injunction, or name," and so forth.
This is indicated by the word "yataḥ" (since). || 136 ||
Our cognition does not apprehend difference even in the case of things such as jars.
How much more so in me, who am that very Self pervading all objects without exception? || 137 ||

Anticipating the objection—“Since there is a distinction within the self (ātman) as well, according to each body, how can there be oneness of the deity through that non-distinction?”—the author says: “The grasper of difference,” etc. The meaning is: if no means of knowledge grasps difference even in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha—who is the very nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the innermost self (pratyagātman) of all—then what need is there to mention it for others? || 137 ||
The universe is not like non-existence, nor like space and so forth, for it possesses divisions such as the internal self and the rest.
He remained with his very self woven through and through within the substances of feces, urine, and so forth, which constitute the Virāṭ.
1 ga. Nirodha | [vol2, page 161] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary named Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 455

He establishes the non-difference of the deities even by relying on another scriptural passage: "Not as spokes... Just as the spokes of a chariot wheel are fixed in the nave, and the rim is fixed upon them, so too the entire universe—divided into the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva)—rests upon the Virāj, the Sūtra, and the Unmanifest (avyākṛta), like long threads and crosswise threads respectively. For everything composed of elements does not exist apart from the elements.

Even those [elements] do not exist apart from the fivefold-composed (*pañcīkṛta*) and the non-fivefold-composed (*apañcīkṛta*); nor do they exist as distinct from the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*); and even that [unmanifest] does not exist apart from the inner self (*pratyak*). Therefore, the meaning is that difference is not established anywhere. || 138 ||
"Various indeed is this very creation"—this is the impelling cause.
In this world, an effect does not exist elsewhere once it has abandoned its cause.

Having refuted the distinction between deities through scripture (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*), he states the meaning of the passage "this indeed is its emission" with the words "various," etc. The construction is as follows:

that various creation consisting of Agni and the others which was introduced is [in fact] that of the Creator under discussion. He explains the intended sense by stating that the subsequent sentence, "for this one indeed," expresses the reason for this; thus he says, "thus, for this reason. Here, the fact that the Creator is the cause of all deities is observed.
Anticipating the question, "What is the reason for his being the essence of all the deities? he says: "The reason. (139)
Since this is so, therefore all the gods would also be Prajāpati.
In each respective office, he assumes that particular form.

Having stated the meaning of the logical reason (*hetu*), he takes up the proposition (*pratijñā*) with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Because the entire world, consisting of gods and so forth, is the effect of Prajāpati, and because it cannot exist apart from its cause, the meaning is that the entire world is nothing but that [Prajāpati]. He analyzes the proposition as follows:
"In that [state]"—thus [it is said]. || 140 ||
But the Self of the universe is indeed one alone, deluding the world through his illusory power (māyā).
Unity attains multiplicity, as in the case of a jar through its reliance on various jewels. || 141 ||

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for a single entity to possess manifold forms, he says: "The One. The *viśvātmā* (the Self of the universe) is called *virāj*; according to the etymology (*nirukti*), he is the Self of the universe, or rather, his Self is the universe. Although in reality his nature is the non-dual reality (*advayavastu*), through *māyā*, while deluding the world, he assumes the state of both the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual parts (*vyaṣṭi*). Just as a jar appears to take on various colors through contact with gems such as blue or red, so does he appear.
The meaning is "so it is. || 141 ||
The elemental self (bhūtātman) is indeed non-different [from the individual soul], up until the completion of each respective element.
It is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon reflected in water. || 142 ||

He supports the stated point by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "Abhinna" (undivided). Although the Self of beings is in reality one, it is seen as manifold because it exists completely pervading all beings—just as, for example, "cowness" (*gotva*) exists in its entirety in every individual cow such as Khaṇḍa and others;
or just as the single moon, reflected in various separate vessels of water, is perceived as many. This is the meaning of the *smṛti*. || 142 ||
Here, those who deny anything other than that [self] disagree.
Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the Self, who is celebrated as the Supreme Self.

It has been stated that all the gods, beginning with Agni, are indeed Prajāpati himself. Now, with the desire to determine his true nature, [the text proceeds]. (Variants: 1. *lābha kāra*; 2. *tadyogā*).
[Vol. 2, Page 162] 456 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]

In this regard, he shows the disagreement [among opponents]. Regarding the word "here": one might ask, "Since even in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) both the transmigratory nature and the non-transmigratory nature of Prajāpati are accepted, how can there be a disagreement? Anticipating this, he states the distinction: those who hold the disagreement assert his transmigratory nature while denying his non-transmigratory nature; whereas those who assert his non-transmigratory nature deny his transmigratory nature. Thus he explains the specific point of contention.
"Other than that" refers to the nature of the misconception, which he states as "Hiraṇyagarbha. || 143 ||
"He is indeed the transmigrating being here," so others also declare.
It is now considered which of these two positions is the superior one. || 144 ||
Having stated that the self called "Sūtra," which is celebrated in the Śruti and Smṛti, is indeed the Supreme Self (parātman), he states another alternative: "The transmigrating soul" (saṃsārī).

The word "here" (iha) refers to the statements of Śruti and Smṛti. Anticipating the question, "Which of these two positions, then, should be accepted?", he says, after deliberation and determination: "Of the two positions... (pakṣayoḥ). || 144 ||
But the Supreme is indeed like Viriñca, according to the statements of the Mātṛkā and Brāhmaṇa texts.
The statement of the mantra beginning with "Indra," and the Śruti text "This is Brahman," [are the evidence]. || 145 ||

He takes up the prima facie view: "Viriñca. The connection is that he is indeed the Supreme (para). The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of excluding his being subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva).
He states the authority for the claim that the Sūtrātman is indeed the Supreme Self: "And because of [my] statement" (maca). || 145 ||
Some declare this very one to be Agni, according to the traditional teaching that "he who is yonder [is Agni]."
He should be known as one who is still transmigrating, because he has merely heard the scriptures and remembered them.

In that very context, he cites two Smṛtis, beginning with "etam" and so forth. The sense is that in the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and Smṛtis, the Supreme is seen as being all the gods; and since He is perceived here in this Sūtra as well, His status as the Supreme is established. He states another prima facie argument: "saṃsāryeva" (only the transmigrating soul). He provides the authority for that: "śruti" and so forth. || 146 ||

Because of the scriptural declarations regarding the burning away of evil, the cessation of hunger and thirst, freedom from fear, and the transcendence of mortality, as well as because of valid cognition [to that effect].
And for us, there are also Smṛti passages such as "Hiraṇyagarbha. (147)
He shows the scriptural authority for this very point with the words "pāpmā" (sin) and so forth. By the word "etcetera," the second desire and the rest are included.

The meaning is that through the aforementioned scriptural testimony, the transmigratory nature of Prajāpati is perceived as distinct [from the Self], because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of burning away sin and so on in one who is non-transmigratory.
He also cites a mantra to demonstrate his transmigratory state: "Hiraṇyagarbha... and so on, including "for he does not see one being born."
The sense is that [liberation] arises in one who is not a transmigrator. He states that even the Smṛti texts demonstrate his state of being a transmigrator to us, saying:
"Smārtāni" (the Smṛti passages). || 147 ||
Brahmā is the Dharma of the creators of the universe; thus, he is the embodiment of the fruits of action.
Even by Smṛti it has been stated many times: "To whom does the state of being a transmigrating soul belong? (148)

It does not grasp anything else. "Brahman" refers to Virāj; "the creators of the universe" refers to Manu and others; "Dharma" is the deity presiding over it, Yama; "Mahat" is the first transformation of Prakṛti; and "Sūtra" is the Unmanifest (Avyakta)—the distinction being that this is the Prakṛti which will be described later as consisting of ignorance, karma, and latent impressions (saṃskāras). He clarifies the meaning of the phrase "having the nature of the fruit of karma" by stating "in the form of the transmigrating soul" (saṃsārin).
1 Kha. Pataḥ || 148 ||

The meaning is: of which Prajāpati? Of the Sūtra, having become the Virāj and having attained the state of Manu and others, there is the condition of being a transmigrating soul (saṃsāritva). It has been stated that the *Smṛti* does not speak of one who is outside the cycle of transmigration (*asaṃsārin*), for the *Smṛti* is established on the process of the ripening of karma. Therefore, he says "repeatedly" (*bahuśaḥ*) to indicate that the *Smṛti*'s intended meaning concerns Prajāpati’s state of being within transmigration (*saṃsāritva*). || 148 ||
Because both of these two traditions also propound mutually contradictory doctrines.
If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of invalidity, we say no, because it relies on a different established theory.

Having thus presented the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states the relevant context (prasaṅga) in order to establish the final conclusion (siddhānta). Regarding the word "mutually" (mithaḥ): although the Self (sūtra) is by its own nature free from transmigratory existence (asaṃsāritva), its state of being a transmigrant (saṃsāritva) is due to limiting adjuncts (aupādhika); since this alternative view is established, there is no contradiction with the two kinds of scripture.
Thus he states the final conclusion: "No" (na). || 149 ||
Due to its association with numerous and diverse limiting adjuncts (upādhis) born of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-ātman).
Statements whose meanings are contradictory may even be possible in a single instance. || 150 ||

Having raised the objection—namely, "How can statements with contradictory meanings, such as 'being subject to transmigratory existence' (saṃsāritva) and 'not being subject to transmigratory existence' (asaṃsāritva), have authority regarding a single entity?"—the author explains the summary statement beginning with "pratyak" (the inner self). The word "saṃsāritā" (being subject to transmigratory existence) is to be supplied [to the first part]. Having accepted that [the self] is by its own nature "asaṃsāritā" (not subject to transmigratory existence), he states the resulting conclusion:
"Contradictory" (viruddha) means, that is to say, those cited sentences which are perceived as having contradictory meanings. || 110 ||
Because it is free from ignorance and its products, it is the object of such scriptural descriptions as "not gross" and so forth.
Being conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance consisting of its own reflection, it attains the state of being the witness and the inner controller.

Establishing that these [attributes] can indeed coexist within a single Self, he first states the justification for the statements regarding its non-transmigratory nature with the words "apāsta" (dispelled). Then, he explains the possibility of even the qualified (saviśeṣa) statements in that very same context with the words "svābhāsa" (self-manifestation).

The distinction is this: the witnesshood belongs to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance as qualified by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), while its status as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) arises from its being the director of Māyā and its effects. || 151 ||
Likewise, that very same [Self], having the intellect as its limiting adjunct, is the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Through association with darkness, goodness, and passion, the Unborn attains the state of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

He describes the state of Hiraṇyagarbha as belonging to the one endowed with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), by virtue of having the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*)—composed of the five unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*) consisting of *māyā*—as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) connects with the preceding [phrase] "should go. Of that very same being, when it has the collective vital breath (*samaṣṭiprāṇa*) as its adjunct and is endowed with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), there is the state of being the Thread (*sūtratva*). Of that very same being, when it has the collective adjunct composed of the five evolved elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*), there is the state of being Virāj. Of that very same being, [when it has] the primordial elements...

Intending to show that the state of being various individual souls (jīva) arises from the connection with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the intellect (buddhi)—whether it be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—he says:
"But [it is] of that very [Self]. (152)
It possesses non-difference for those with non-different cognitions, and difference for those with different cognitions.
Thus, due to one's own delusion, nothing at all is truly unstable. || 153 ||
He concludes the possibility of contradictory meanings occurring in a single instance with the verse beginning "abhīti" (153).
All living beings that have come into existence arise from hunger alone.
Therefore, being pithless and lacking stability, even when joined together, they are not sufficient for remaining firm.

Having established that Prajāpati, who is the self of all deities, is by nature non-transmigratory (*asaṃsārī*) yet appears to be transmigratory through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), [the author] now—[proceeding with the word] "atha" (now)— [The text continues: Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter.
He states the reason for the creation of food immediately after the creation of the world: "Possessing hunger, the Eater... (aśanāyāvān attā).

Since Prajāpati was possessed of hunger, all living beings born from him are likewise possessors of hunger and eaters, following that same cause; because they appear as such, they are unable to exist without food. Thus, the statement regarding the creation of food immediately after the creation [of the world] is logical. || 114 ||
Therefore, the subsequent section is introduced for the purpose of explaining the creation of Soma and food.
Whatever object whatsoever is perceived here in this world, [it is all composed of the five elements].
The Lord emitted that seed for the sustenance of what had been produced.

Having stated the reason for the mention of food in the context of the path (*arga*), he introduces the scriptural passage concerning its creation with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). He joins those syllables [of the text] with the words "yat kiñca" (whatever...).
To the question, "Having begun with the creation of food, why is the creation of other things mentioned?", he says: "utpa... (for the sake of production...).
He causes fear. || 155 ||
In this context, the waters, which constitute the cause of the world, are designated as "semen."
The restriction that "Soma alone" [is food] establishes the distinction between Agni and Soma.
[The author] says "the world," etc., having raised the objection that the creation of food from semen is illogical based on the Vedic text, "They created food.

Here, the meaning of the word "here" (*iha*) is the statement, "He creates that semen. The intended meaning of the restriction in the passage, "Soma alone is food, and Agni is the eater of food," is as follows:

He states the meaning: "Soma. That which is eaten is food (*anna*), and that which eats is the consumer of food (*annāda*); since it is determined that these are Soma and Agni respectively, the meaning is that the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma; this is certain. || 116 ||
Let it be understood that Agni and Soma are [distinguished] due to their connection with various distinct functions. || 157 ||
One should know that it is indeed Soma, even when clarified butter is offered.
Soma also should be known as fire, if an oblation is offered therein. (158)

Anticipating the objection that there is no fixed rule for food being of the nature of *soma*—since even fire (*agni*) can be extinguished by water and the like—and that there is likewise no fixed rule for *soma* being of the nature of fire—since *soma* is also sometimes offered as a sacrifice and thus acts as an eater—the author says: "Not manifold... Fire, too, [is the locus] of offering...

The meaning is that while *soma* is connected to the action as the object (*karman*), it is also connected to the act of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-kriyā*) as the agent (*kartṛ*); thus, the restriction [of identity] is established. Anticipating the objection—"Why disregard the restriction as it is heard in the text and explain it in another way?"—the author analyzes the commentary beginning with "for by the force of the meaning" (*arthabalāt hi*). He says: "*Soma*"—if *agni* is also that which is to be withdrawn, then he too is indeed *soma*, and he too is the withdrawer.
The meaning is that the restriction "only fire" would be appropriate. || 157 || 158 ||
The entire world is divided into two parts: those who eat food and that which is the eater of food.
The entire world of moving and non-moving beings is called the breath (prāṇa), which is without hunger. || 159 ||

He concludes the statement that the world exists in the form of Agni and Soma with the words "dvedhā" (in two ways). Having begun by establishing Prajāpati as the self of all, one might ask how there can be a conclusion regarding the world divided into two parts; in response, he says "anam" (the eater), intending here the fruit consisting of freedom from all defects for the meditator who, through the intellect of the Self, finds his final rest in that [Prajāpati] as the thread (sūtra) of the universe. || 119 ||
