Now, the Śruti, which knows the creation of the gods, intends to describe the results [of that creation].

"Now it proceeds as such"—this is what is called its praise. [The author] states the purport of the passage beginning with "This very... by saying "the fruit. The sentence beginning with "In the further creation" (*atisṛṣṭau*) and so forth is for the purpose of stating the fruit for the worshiper of the divine creation who is the recipient of grace;
whereas the preceding passage beginning with "This very... is for the purpose of praising the divine creation—such is the distinction. Now, at this point—

The connection is as follows: immediately after the desire to state the fruit [of the meditation], and at the occasion for praise, the scripture begins with "In the over-creation" (*atisṛṣṭau*) and so forth, with the intention of declaring the fruit for those who know the creation of the gods. Now, the construction is that the praise of the creation of the gods is intended by the scripture beginning with "This very [creation]" (*saiṣā*) and so forth. || 160 ||
The creation of the benevolent deities that was described previously—
This would be the granting of permission for the creation by Prajāpati of those beings who are to be favored. || 161 ||
He explains the syllables of the passage beginning with "saiṣā" as follows: "anugrāhaka... (161).
From those unworthy ones who were to be favored, he created the more excellent gods.
For this very reason, that which is here described as beginning with fire and so forth is called "the emission" (atisṛṣṭi).

He explains the causal statement beginning with "those [beings] from the gods who are superior" with the words "from what is not superior. It should be understood that the connection is not with the ablative case (*pañcamī*)—which would imply separation through action—but rather with the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the preceding context. The phrase "Agni and so forth" indicates the creation of those [beings]. || 162 ||
Or rather, being a mortal sacrificer, he has created these immortal gods.
Therefore, this is declared to be a supreme gift; it is certain that it is most excellent. || 163 ||

Now, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "But being mortal... with the words "Or, a mortal... The word *vā* (or) serves to indicate another reason for the fact that the creation of the gods is a "super-creation" (*atisṛṣṭi*). By this, the word *atha* has been explained. He concludes by stating that the description of the creation of the gods as a super-creation is a form of praise, using the word *sā*. || 163 ||
In this creation, a man may become like Prajāpati, the creator of beings.
For one who possesses the knowledge of creation as it has been described, this fruit is declared.

He explains the passage beginning with "atīsṛṣṭyām" (in the act of emission) as follows: "Prajāpati. The meaning is that for one who meditates—thinking "I am indeed Prajāpati, the self of the gods and others"—the fruit is the attainment of his creative power through the realization of that identity. || 164 ||
But for those whose eyes are shrouded by the veil of ignorance, this alone [is perceived].
The Vedic means of accomplishment should be known as having the nature of both knowledge and action. || 165 ||

He states the preceding narrative for the purpose of establishing the connection between the preceding and following sections, beginning with the words "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). For those whose consciousness is veiled by ignorance, the means such as knowledge prescribed in the Vedas—which arise due to the influence of the agent and other factors, and which result in fruits ranging from the human state up to the state of *sūtra*—have been explained in the *Karmakāṇḍa* by such Vedic passages as "For the sake of desire" (*yad iṣe tvā*) and have been previously elucidated in the section on manifestation by such passages as "The dawn is indeed the horse's... (*uṣā vā aśvasya*). That [is what follows].

The meaning is that the remainder is to be known as exactly that which has been described as the world consisting of saṃsāra; it is the means for accomplishing the human goal for those who are ignorant.
[Vol. 2, p.

When it is said [in verse 459], "liberation," the means of liberation appears before one's mind; he refutes that with the word "jñāna" (knowledge). For liberation, which is of a single uniform nature, [cannot be attained through] a manifold nature...
The meaning is that it does not constitute a means of proof (*sādhana*). He dispels the doubt that such [a means] might be unacceptable by stating "Vedic" (*vaidika*). || 165 ||
It depends upon the causal factors such as the agent and bestows fruits culminating in the state of Viriñca.
That which was previously explained by Śruti has now been expounded in its entirety.

He says that this knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which depends on the human agent as the means for attaining liberation, is not the cause of that [liberation] because it is accomplished by an agent (*kāraka*). He states this with the words "by the agent" (*kartrā*) and so forth. Furthermore, its fruit extends only up to Viriñca (Brahmā), and that itself is not absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), according to scriptural texts such as those mentioning fear and aversion; therefore, he says this is not the means to that [liberation] with the words "Viriñca" and so forth. Moreover, liberation is something entirely different from the manifested object.

He says "this is differentiated" to show that this name-and-form is indeed differentiated; therefore, it is the cause of only that which is differentiated, not of liberation. He establishes its Vedic nature by saying "by the Śruti. || 166 ||
Now, concerning this aforementioned [system] which consists of the nature of the goal and the means;
The indestructible state of the seed of the manifested world came into being.
With the desire to point that out, this supreme Śruti has exerted itself through its own manifestations. || 167 ||
Now, introducing the section on the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), he states the purport of the passage beginning with "its division" (*tadbhedam*) prior to the introductory sentence: "Now" (*atha*).

The meaning of the word *atha* is immediate succession to the statement regarding the fruits of knowledge and action. He refers back to the fruit already mentioned with the words "of this" (*etasya*).

He explains that it exists without transcending the form described as being of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), using the phrase "as it is" (*yathā*). Of that [form], which consists of the means to the fruit...

He states that the subsequent scripture beginning with "Tad dha idam" (That indeed was this) is directed toward that very purpose, as it is introduced for the sake of explaining that state of the seed of this world—which, prior to its differentiation by name and form, is the appearance-aspect of the inner self (pratyag-avidyā) and is indestructible without knowledge—that he wishes to describe. [The commentary continues: "sādhyā... etc. Alternatively, there is a word-break as "vinaśvarī" (perishable). For she (avidyā) indeed exists...

"Character is to be destroyed by knowledge. The phrase "with the desire to indicate" (*nirdidikṣayā*) is stated to mean that it is intended to be indicated only in its state as a seed (*bījāvasthā*), rather than being directly indicated, because it is inexpressible (*anirvācyatvāt*). Through the mention of the state of the seed known as objective-appearance-bearing ignorance (*sābhāsa-pratyag-avidyā*), one is to ascertain that the Supreme Self alone—whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—is the individual self (*pratyagbhūta*), the knower, and knowledge itself; this is prior to the sentences concerning the entry [into the body].
Thinking that this refers to the statement, he says: "With effort" (yatnāt). || 167 ||
Since that alone, and nothing else, is the primary cause of the miseries of cyclic existence.
For in this world, ignorance of the Self is the very root of all misfortunes.

Regarding the question, "Why is it that only that knowledge in which the human goal is attained is spoken of as 'ignorance of the inner self' (pratyagavidyā)? he says: "In saṃsṛti... The meaning is this: ignorance of the inner self alone is the root of the evils such as agency (mātṛtva) and so forth known as saṃsāra; it is not something like Pradhāna, for which there is no means of valid cognition (apramāṇaka). Therefore, since the human goal is accomplished upon the destruction of that [ignorance], its mention is appropriate. To the question, "How is it established that ignorance of the Self is the root of evil? he says: "Since..."

Thus, it is observed that one who, failing to recognize the Self as being of such a nature—thinking "I am this"—proceeds toward the wives of others and so forth due to an excess of delusion, incurs misfortune; therefore, the meaning is that ignorance regarding the inner Self (pratyagajñāna) is determined to be the root of all evil in the world. The word "api" is used to include scriptural passages such as "Remaining within ignorance, [they wander about like blind men led by the blind]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.8), which establish this through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). 168.

From the destruction of that [ignorance] alone, the attainment of all human goals without remainder would thus occur.
Embodiment would be the cause of that misfortune which one seeks to abandon.

He states the consequence regarding the fact that one's own ignorance (*svājñāna*) is the root of all misfortune: "Because it stands above that" (*tadūrdhvasāt*). The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that [ignorance] is established as the root of misfortune by both worldly experience and the Vedas. Now, one might raise the objection: "If that [ignorance] is the root of misfortune, then even in deep sleep and cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), there would be misfortune such as being a subject (*mātṛtva*) due to its influence. Anticipating this, he says: "Of that which is to be abandoned" (*jihāsitasya*). It is the delusion of the individual self (*pratyamoha*), acting through the identification with the body, that is the cause of misfortune, not [the mere absence of knowledge].
The meaning is "directly. || 169 ||
It is determined from the scriptural text, "Not indeed for one who possesses a body," that [liberation does not occur while embodied].
And dharma and adharma are the source of the body, according to the authority of the scriptures. (170)

He states the proof for the fact that the conceit of being the body (*dehābhimāna*) is the cause of misfortune, beginning with the words "Not [so]," etc. [Objection: In that case, the conceit of being the body would also occur during sleep and so forth, simply due to the delusion regarding the self; to this he says, "Dharma," etc. The connection is: "It is determined that [the body] is the source (*yoni*). [The reason is] because of dharma and so forth, of those two...

He provides scriptural authority for the statement "according to their deeds and according to their learning" regarding the state of being an individual soul (jīvatva), by citing the word "āgama. || 170 ||
Action—both that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited—is the root of those two as well.
But surely, for that which has no connection with either dharma or anything else, [how can there be such a relation]? (171)
Anticipating the objection that since dharma and so forth also exist during sleep and other such states, the state of possessing a body caused by them would likewise persist, he says:

"That which is enjoined. He provides the reason for the claim that the performance of what is unprecedented (apūrva) is the cause: "For not... If dharma and the like were joined with one who is inactive, it would follow that even a liberated soul would possess a body during sleep and so on; however, even though dharma and the like exist then, they are ineffective because of the absence of ego (ahaṃkāra), due to its non-manifestation—otherwise, it would not be so.
The meaning is that there is no occasion for raising objections regarding the absence of sleep and so forth. || 171 ||
Likewise, in this world, there is no connection with action for one who is not an agent. || 172 ||
Because the status of being an agent is caused by the existence of that [action], it is the cause.
Apart from passion and hatred, there is nothing else that impels action in the world.
Then, what is the cause of action? To this he says: "Not for that which is without a causal factor. Likewise, for that which is without action, there is no connection with dharma and so forth.

This is the meaning: [the author] states the reason why being a *kāraka* (an agentive factor) is the cause of action. He says "tadbhāve" etc. The meaning is that because action exists when that [being a *kāraka*] exists, and does not exist otherwise, it is certain that being a *kāraka* is its cause. He states the reason for this: "kārakatvasya" etc.
Therein, he establishes the proof through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), saying "na tāvat" etc. || 172 || 173 ||
Having stated "according to his desire," the Śruti [speaks] of the production of the seasons and so forth.
And he stated that in the absence of desire, there is the cessation of that [suffering], as in the verse beginning "He who is without desire. (174)

He states that scripture (*śruti*) is also an authority for [the fact] that passion (*rāga*) and so forth are the motivators [of action], saying: "As it is" (*sa yathā*). The scripture beginning with "Whatever his desire becomes, that he becomes" (*sa yathākāmo bhavati tatkraturbhavati*) declares that volition (*saṃkalpa*), action (*kriyā*), and so forth arise by virtue of passion and the like; and the scripture beginning with "He who is without desire, whose desires are fulfilled" (*yo'kāma āptakāmaḥ*) declares that in the absence of those [passions], volition and the rest do not exist. By the two uses of the word "and" (*ca*), [it is shown that] this bondage of desire is indeed the play of the self (*ātmakrīḍā*).

The meaning is that, based on such scriptural and traditional texts as "He who possesses the activity of self-delight would be one whose delight is indeed in the Self," it is intended that the presence or absence of worldly activity depends upon the presence or absence of desire and other such states. || 974 ||
The superimpositions of "good" and "bad" are themselves rooted in ignorance; that ignorance is the foundation for both of them as well.
Since attachment and aversion are observed [to be the causes], good and evil do not exist otherwise.
He states the cause of attachment and aversion: "Excellent! In this regard, he indicates the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) with the words: "Attachment and aversion... (175).
Furthermore, without an object of cognition, neither the valid nor the invalid [cognition] exists.
The cognition "this is good" or "this is bad" arises with respect to the object of knowledge that has been known.
Stating that the known object is the cause for the mental dispositions (*adhyāsa*) of the beautiful and the ugly, he first expresses the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Without...
He then states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "It is good... (176)
The relation of being a knower and so forth does not exist in an entity whose nature is non-existent.
The cognition of objects such as a jar is not admitted [to exist] while the world itself is unreal.

[The author] states the reason for its being known: "By the state of being a knower," etc. For the state of being known is indeed a relation to the status of being a knower (mātṛtva) and so forth; that [state] is impossible if [the world] is unreal.

The meaning is that since existence is not observed in cases such as a "human horn," existence is therefore the reason [for its cognition]. He establishes this very point through experience with the words "not a jar" (*naghaṭa*).

In the world, the cognition of both existence and non-existence is seen only when [an object] exists, not when it does not exist; for a cognition of something utterly non-existent (*tuccha*) is not possible. Therefore, the meaning is that existence is the reason for being known (*jñātatva*). || 177 ||
Existence is found nowhere except in the delusion regarding the true nature of the inner self.
When there is perfect awakening to the true nature of the inward Self, neither "being" nor "non-being" is predicated.
He states the reason for existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*): "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc. The word division is *sattvam asattvaṃ ca*.
The meaning is: in some place, time, or object. Anticipating the objection that because the inner self (*pratyak*) exists, its [the world's] existence is not caused by ignorance, he says:

although it exists in reality, after the knowledge of the inner reality, it is no longer designated as either "existent" or "non-existent"; therefore, its existence is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and rooted in nescience (*avidyā*).
He says "no" [to that], stating: "the true nature of the inward Self. || 178 ||
For uncommon ignorance resides only in the inner self.
Therefore, only this object of cognition is accepted as the means of valid cognition, and nothing else. || 179 ||

The fact that ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*) is the cause of evil was stated in the *Praśna Upaniṣad*; however, one might object that by omitting the qualifier "inner" (*pratyak*), it should simply be said that "ignorance" is the cause, and thus it would follow that ignorance common to both the Self and the non-Self is established as the cause of evil. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Regarding the term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇam*): the meaning is that ignorance is not common to both the Self (*ātman*) and the non-Self (*anātman*), but rather it belongs exclusively to the Self; for it resides in the internal witness (*pratyak*) as both its locus (*āśraya*) and its object (*viṣaya*), as evidenced by the experience, "I am ignorant," "I do not know myself. Furthermore, since ignorance is of the nature of non-knowledge, it is impossible for it to exist in the non-Self. Moreover, since the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs elsewhere than the internal witness, the state of being unknown must be admitted there as well, because those means operate upon that which is characterized by ignorance.

Anticipating the objection, "How can it be that the Self alone is unknown?", he says: "This" (etad). For the state of being unknown does not belong to the non-Self, which is of the nature of ignorance; for it is impossible for the relationship of subject and object to exist in one and the same thing. Therefore, the meaning is that while this internal Self (pratyak) remains unknown as the object of knowledge, there exists no means of knowledge (māna) that can reveal the non-Self. || 179 ||
Thus,
this subsequent portion of the Śruti has commenced for the purpose of establishing the objects of knowledge.
In this worldly transaction, which consists of action and agent, [the self appears] due to its association with darkness (ignorance).
An object that is neither an action nor an agent is apprehended solely through mediacy. || 180 ||

Fearing that the proposition "the Self alone, when unknown, is the object of knowledge" might be a mere assertion, he says: "Thus. Fearing further that if the Self alone is the unknown [object], then since perception and other means of knowledge also operate upon it, the Self would be cognizable by them and thus the hearing of the Vedāntas would be redundant, he says: "Action. This is because, in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the cause—namely *tamas* (ignorance)—pervades the world being transacted, which consists of action and so forth; [therefore, the Self] is distinct from that.
Because the reality is concealed by that [ignorance], it is beyond perception; thus, it is not apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge.

According to such scriptural texts as "The senses are directed outward," the subject matter of those [means] is only the qualified [Brahman], whereas the unqualified [Brahman] is accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*). This is the meaning. || 180 ||
That which is unseen, being the effect of ignorance, is like a serpent upon a garland.
"He sustains everything without attachment," according to the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "it is both attached and unattached. || 181 ||

Fearing that if the inner self (pratyak) were not seen even when the world is seen, it would result in the loss of non-duality (advaita), he says: "That indeed... The inner reality, though unseen by perception and other means—that is, unknown—bears all ignorance and its effects like a garland bears a snake. Therefore, regarding the second [entity]...

The meaning is that because it is unreal by virtue of being imagined (*kalpita*), there is no loss of the non-duality of reality (*vastvadvaita*). Having raised the objection—“If the inner self (*pratīc*) is the locus of duality, how can it be unattached?”—he says, “Being unattached,” because the relation itself, like the related entities, is imagined. Having raised the objection—“If the reality is devoid of attachment, how can it be a substratum?”—he says, “And [it is] unattached. It is unattached, yet it sustains all, and it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).

The meaning is that by the Blessed One stating "and the enjoyer of qualities," it is shown that the inner self (pratīc) possesses the nature of being the substratum of all things even in the absence of any real connection. || 181 ||
That in which a reality consisting of the unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth is directly established.
In that case, it is obtained in its entirety; therefore, conventional usage there is not born of delusion.

Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say "the world has the unknown Self as its substratum" because agency and other attributes are still perceived even when the Self is known, he says: "apūrvādi" (beginning with the unprecedented). In that state of knowledge (*vidyā*) where the reality—devoid of cause and effect, of one essence—shines forth as immediate and non-differentiated, transcending all doubts and impossibilities, there no worldly transaction such as agency can be found through ignorance; for at that time, that [ignorance] is absent.

Because it is filled by the supreme bond, that which appears as agency and so forth is merely a persistence of what has been sublated; therefore, the meaning is that the world has its locus in the Self that is not known. || 182 ||
As it was said:
"By restating what has already been established as proven, he did not previously state [the conclusion] clearly. (183)
In this context, both the words and their meanings are indeed well-established through common worldly usage.
Having taken up the treatise on ritual action, he composed it as an exposition of both prohibitions and injunctions.
Anticipating the objection—"What is the purpose of the subsequent text, since it has already been stated in passages such as 'The dawn is the head of the horse'?"—he says, "Just as...

The meaning is this: by restating worldly objects, the Śruti, in the preceding text, declared the reality of the Self (ātma-vastu) as the object of meditation in the form of the Sūtra; however, the true nature (tattva) was not clearly taught there. Therefore, the subsequent text is meaningful. [Objection: Even so, in the Karma-kāṇḍa, regarding the aforementioned Self...

He says that the subsequent statement is not useless because its meaning has already been established; he states, "the words. Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the stage of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*).
*Sureśvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter, [page 170].

The meaning is: "from the world," that is, by virtue of the linguistic usage of the elders. The meaning is that the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is engaged in merely to the extent of establishing, by accepting words and word-meanings as they are established in the world, that "this is a means to the desired end" and "that is otherwise"; it does not have ultimate reality as its object. || 183 || 184 ||
Henceforth, let there be an opportunity for the investigation of the reality of things.
First, the object of knowledge derived from the Veda (śruti) is considered here.

He states the point already established regarding the absence of any other reality for that [knowledge]: "From this" (*itaḥ*). Beyond the scriptures of ritual action (*karma-śāstra*), the Upaniṣads—which are essentially the Self—have obtained their opportunity and proceed for the purpose of defining the nature of Reality (*vastu-svarūpa*). For one whose intellect has been purified by the multitude of rites performed according to the *Karmakāṇḍa* becomes inclined toward the Inner Self (*pratyak-pravaṇa*) and takes up the desire to know That (*tad-vividiṣā*); and with reference to such a person, the Upaniṣads approach. Since...

Thus begins the subsequent section of the text; therefore, in the passage beginning with "tad dha idam," the meaning that has not yet been known is first examined, because the authority of the Upaniṣads depends upon it—this is the sense. || 185 ||
One reflects: what is the root of this great disease called saṃsāra?
And for its destruction, this medical treatment would then become fruitful. || 186 ||

Now, while the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) ought to be defined, why is ignorance (*ajñāna*) defined instead? For that [ignorance] alone is not such [a goal], since the human goal is always accomplished [without it], which would render knowledge useless. To this, he says: "Saṃsāra... (referring to the verse). The qualification "greatness" (*mahattva*) is for the sake of distinguishing [this] from the fever and so forth that affect only a few people, as [this] transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) pervades all without exception. He states the fruit of this reflection: "taddhvastaye" (for its destruction). That is, for the purpose of eliminating the disease of transmigratory existence.

The medical treatment consisting of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, when performed by those seeking liberation, becomes fruitful once the diagnosis is determined, because it is possible to eliminate that [suffering] along with its cause; for indeed, it is not proper to treat without knowing the cause. As it has been said:
"One who possesses memory, who knows the reasons for the arguments, who possesses intelligence, and who possesses practical application..."
"A physician ought to perform medical treatment through the combination of medicines."
And Suśruta also said: "He who understands the accumulation, the provocation, the spreading, the localization, and the specific differentiation of the doṣas— he shall be a physician."
Therefore, the meaning is that medical treatment preceded by knowledge of the cause is fruitful. || 286 ||
Likewise, there exists a scriptural passage in the Mantra [Upaniṣad] stating, "With roots above."
In the Gītās as well, this is likewise stated in the passage beginning with "upward-rooted" (Gītā 15.1).

Now, one might object: "Surely the very root of saṃsāra does not exist, because according to the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda), the root is merely primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth, and not the unknown Brahman. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of both Śruti and Smṛti with the words, "With its root above" (ūrdhvamūla). For there indeed exists a root of saṃsāra; it is not this [world] alone.

The meaning is that, according to the scriptural statement "it shall be the root," and just as Brahman itself is ignorance, so it is according to the *Kaṭhaka* scripture; this is precisely what is meant by "in accordance with the wording of the mantra. || 187 ||
Of that which is the root of all misfortune without exception, and whose nature is the ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna).
When these two are destroyed, there is the destruction of all misfortunes, and the goal of human life is fully accomplished. || 188 ||

Raising the objection that Brahman, when unknown, is not the cause of bondage because it continues to be perceived even after ignorance has ceased, [the author] states: "After knowledge, for those of dull intellect...
[Vol.
2, page 171] (Brāhmaṇa 4), accompanied by the commentary *Śāstramakaranda* by Ānandagiri.

He says "not so" because it has been stated that [liberation] is the persistence of those [remedies]; [he explains this with the words] "without remainder. Not only is there the destruction of what is harmful, but [this occurs] through the destruction of ignorance.
He says that the fruit of knowledge is not only [liberation], but also the attainment of bliss: "And the goal of man... (verse 188).
The nature of the inner self is a bliss from which all excellence has been cast away.
Now, this very [Self] is established by the scripture itself in the passage beginning with "That which is the Plenum" (bhūman). || 189 ||

Fearing that one might object—“By the destruction of ignorance through knowledge, when all misfortune is destroyed, the Self merely attains a state of being free from affliction, but not happiness”—the author says: “Nirasta... (verse 189). He provides scriptural authority for this point with such passages as: “Now this is the highest bliss,” “This is his highest bliss,” and “That which is the Infinite (bhūmā), that is happiness. Thus [ends the commentary on] verse 189.
Since its true nature is inherently blissful, how could there be any association with suffering?
Nevertheless, because it is stated that even when [the truth] is concealed, the scripture is not defiled. || 190 ||

Anticipating the objection that if the Self were of the nature of happiness, suffering would also exist therein because of its invariable concomitance with it, [the author] states "by itself" (*svataḥ*), meaning that although sense-based pleasure is invariably accompanied by suffering, this is not the case for the happiness of the essential nature (*svarūpa-sukha*). Then, anticipating the objection as to what the purpose of the scriptural statement negating suffering in the Self might be— since such a negation is not appropriate in the absence of a possibility of its occurrence— he says:

"Even so," [it is said]. This means that although in reality there is no connection with suffering, the scripture negates the notion that one is "not smeared by worldly suffering" by taking up that [suffering] as it has been acquired through delusion; for what is already established cannot be negated, because that would contradict the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 190 ||
This world exists in the state of a seed, perfectly established as the single, unknown Self.
This was expressed by the word "tat" (that), which denotes an object that is not present to the senses. || 191 ||

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "tad dhi" and having shown the incidental succession of objections and answers, [the author], desiring to explain the literal words of the Śruti, states the meaning of the word *tat*: "ajñātā... (Verse 199). The meaning is this: that state of being a seed which is one with that Self (*ātman*), consisting of the non-apparent ignorance (*avidyā*) of the inner witness (*pratyag-avidyā*) accompanied by its reflection (*sābhāsa*), is the world; it is remote (*parokṣa*), and is expressed by the pronoun *tat*, which refers to it. || 199 ||
Because the indeterminate world is connected with past time.
The particle *ha* is employed here for the sake of easy comprehension. || 192 ||

To explain how the aforementioned world is beyond direct perception, he says: "of the unmanifest. The word "beyond direct perception" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He states the purpose of the particle [ha]: "happily. The meaning is that since the world beyond direct perception is known through tradition (aitihya), the particle *ha* is used here in that sense. || 192 ||
Transformed by name-and-form and so forth, it has as its sole sphere of activity the supreme non-cognition.
This world is said to be directly [manifest] as possessing a thousand divisions. || 193 ||

He states the meaning of the word "this" (idam): "name," etc. The word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to action. He states the ground for the application of the word "this" with respect to that [name]: "outwardly," etc. The word "single" (eka) means independence from scripture. He qualifies it with "directly" (sākṣāt) to indicate that the word "this" does not apply even to such things as inferable objects. || 193 ||
1. ka. ga. siddhibī; 2. kha. rāṅiti;
[Vol. 2, Page 172] 466 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
"Because of the hearing of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words 'that' (*tat*) and 'this' (*idam*)."
The non-difference between cause and effect is always determined. || 194 ||

He states the fruit of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words: "of the coreferentiality... The meaning is that by hearing this coreferentiality of the words "that" (*tat*) and "this" (*idam*), the difference between cause and effect is refuted. || 194 ||
In the absence of action and its effect, a cause is never established anywhere.
If the cause were inactive, then the arising of the fruit would likewise be eternal.
Some say that these two possess substantial reality; that is not so, because both are merely conceptualized. For a cause—whether inactive or active—is not [itself] of the nature of action.

Since there is no effect in the absence of an action, the cause cannot be established in any effect whatsoever; thus he says: "not an action. He states the fault in the case of it being inactive: "inactive" means "like that," i.e., like the cause [in the previous argument]. || 195 ||
And if those two were to exist simultaneously, there could be no determination of the cause.
Furthermore, because it would entail the necessity of another action, there would be an infinite regress if that [action] were itself an effect. || 196 ||

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because there can be neither simultaneity nor sequence between the action and its possessor. In the first case, their existence cannot be established—like that of two horns—due to the absence of any certain means of knowledge; thus he says: "Of those two. If it is argued that there is a sequence where the cause exists first and the action follows, he replies: "By another action," etc. For when an effect arises from a cause, it requires an action; and if that [action] were to arise from that [cause] which is already established as prior, [it would require] another action...

There would be an infinite regress due to the dependence on another [action]. Nor can there be a sequence where action comes first and the cause afterwards; for if that [action] were also an effect, it would depend on another cause, leading to an infinite regress. If it were not an effect, then because it would exist even at the time of the [initial] action, a sequence would be impossible. Furthermore, it cannot be without a substratum, like a movement [without a mover]; and even if it were the first [action], if it were an effect, another action would necessarily follow, resulting in an infinite regress. An action does not produce another action.
And the sense is that it is not something that does not have an effect. || 196 ||
And a task that is not being performed attains the status of a non-task within the assembly.
If an effect were to be without an agent, then the cause would itself become the effect.

Even if an effect requires an action, that action does not require it, because the action is self-established; having raised this objection, he states—beginning with "And if [it were] an effect"—that whether the action is an effect or not an effect, if it were an effect, there would be a contradiction in its not being pervaded by an action, and if it were not an effect, it would exist eternally. Having thus refuted the causality of that which possesses action, he points out another fault in the first [position].

He said: "It is without an agent. The meaning is that if the effect were not pervaded by an action residing in an agent, then the cause itself would become the effect, because it alone would lack that state of being pervaded by such an action. || 197 ||
Because that which is other than the existent is a cause, and likewise, because the existent is an effect.
And since they are not mutually distinct, how could there be the possibility of destruction and so forth? || 198 ||
If it is suspected that, upon investigation, there is no connection between cause and effect because both are insubstantial (*tuccha*) and thus merely imagined, he says:

"Because of being a cause" (*kāraṇatvāt*). The meaning is this: the cause is excluded from what is insubstantial because being a cause is impossible for the insubstantial; and the effect is likewise excluded from what is insubstantial because being an effect belongs only to what is not insubstantial, as it is untenable for the insubstantial to be an effect. By saying "of another," he refers to the effect—

Anticipating the objection that one might desire a real distinction between the two causes, he says: "anyānyeti" (as different from each other). For there is no difference between those two like that of a cow and a horse.
[Vol. 2, page 173, Brāhmaṇa 4, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 467.

Nor is their non-difference real, because that [non-difference] would entail it [the distinction] in the very same thing; therefore, the meaning is that both are imagined. Furthermore, since the modifications such as birth and destruction cannot be described as either different or non-different from the reality, he states that these two are merely imagined within that immutable reality. Why? [Verse 198]
It would be either the action, or its fruit, or the agent; it would be nothing at all.
This destruction would be without continuity; not even one of these [other types] could it be. (199)
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the destruction of an effect is without any residue (niranvaya). To the question of how that [destruction] is impossible, he says:

"Or it is an action," and so forth. The phrase "not anything" is a statement indicating its insubstantiality (tucchatā). He then points out the defect in all four positions with the word "of these" (eṣām). || 199 ||
The destruction of an action, in the form of its fruit, cannot occur while it still persists.
By each such particularity, the Cause is always manifested.

He clarifies the fault in the position that destruction without residue (*niranvaya-nāśa*) is an action (*kriyā*). [The phrase] "of the action" [is explained as follows]: the construction is that its destruction would not be desired, because it persists in the form of its fruit. He clarifies the possible fault even in other positions with the word "therefore" (*tena*): the very root cause manifests as the action, the agent, and the fruit, and as the undifferentiated, eternal form. Thus.
The meaning is that the proof of absolute destruction without residue (niranvaya-nāśa) never occurs at any time. || 200 ||
Just as a seed does not perish because it is the agent of birth and so forth.
Even upon its destruction, because it is the destroyer, the destroyer cannot itself be subject to destruction. || 201 ||

He clarifies that absence [of the seed] by means of an illustration: "Just as" (yathā). The word "etc. (ādi) signifies persistence. Even upon the destruction of the seed, because there is agency—as in the case of birth and so forth—it does not follow that it is destroyed without leaving a trace; otherwise, due to the absence of an agent, the destruction itself would be unestablished. He states the point of comparison: "Even upon destruction" (nāśe 'pi). || 201 ||
If this were so, there would be no destruction of the existent, nor likewise the arising of the non-existent.
And because the effect is designated as indeterminate, it might [arise] at some time.

Having stated that the intention of this scriptural teaching regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of these two terms is to show that [the world] is imagined (*kalpita*) by negating the distinction between cause and effect, he states the result of that imagined nature: "In this way," etc. If it is difficult to define the arising and destruction of both cause and effect, then there is no destruction of the existent (*sat*), because such [destruction] is impossible whether existence is abandoned or not abandoned; nor does it differ from the existent—neither...

The sense is that [the effect] does not differ [from the cause] because it would result in the loss of its inherent nature, as this would entail the consequence of it being mere existence; by this, the birth and so forth of the non-existent are also refuted.

Regarding that very point, he states another reason: "the unmanifest," etc. If it is said that this very effect is the unmanifest, there is no destruction of that existent even at dissolution, because it remains in an unmanifest state; nor is there ever the birth of that which was non-existent, because its reality consists precisely in the manifestation of the unmanifest.
This is the meaning. || 202 ||
Just as there is no destruction other than the realization of reality, so it is in this case.
It will be proclaimed even at the time of the new moon with great effort. || 203 ||
1. Affliction (tāpa).
1. [vol2, page 174]
468 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

Now, it may be objected that even you accept total destruction without residue (*niranvaya-nāśa*), since through the knowledge of Brahman there is a complete annihilation of bondage along with its cause.

Regarding how that [bondage] is sublated by taking refuge [in the Self], he says: "But the reality... The very realization of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñapti*) is the destruction of bondage along with its root;

it is not something additional to that. This has been stated with great effort previously, and will be stated further on as well. Therefore, in our view, there is no annihilation (*nāśa*) that is distinct from the reality itself or that leaves no trace (*niranvaya*); this is the meaning. || 203 ||
The time prior to the manifestation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth is called [the causal state].
In that case, it is said that the unmanifest is expressed by the term "unspecified. || 204 ||
Having explained the words "tat" (that) and "idam" (this), he now explains the word "avyākṛtam" (undifferentiated). He says: "nāma" (by name).
The particle "hi" is used for the purpose of establishing that the aforementioned time is well-known in both worldly usage and the Veda. || 204 ||
Ignorance, karma, and the formative predispositions depend upon the fiery eyelashes and the thread.
Dissolved in the void, they exist as mere existence, called the unmanifest, together with the Self.

What is that which is unmanifest? It is not, first of all, the mere absence of manifestation, because such an absence cannot function as a cause; nor is it something other than that, or its opposite, because as an effect, those options would entail the aforementioned defects. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning of this is as follows:

ignorance is false knowledge and the grasping of the ego (ahaṃkāra); action consists of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma); latent impressions (saṃskāras) are the tendencies toward various forms of effects; and the thread is the wind (sūtraṃ vāyuḥ).

"O Gautama, Vāyu is indeed that thread," according to the Śruti; and those [factors] beginning with ignorance (avidyā) have the four elements as their support, yet they further take space (ākāśa) as their support.

They rest upon the five great elements in their unquintuplicated state and find their stability in the form of the primal cause. And they, being of the nature of objective ignorance (avidyā) associated with the internal witness (pratyagātman), become designated by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) together with the enjoyer. || 205 ||
The manifold world that was previously described through the distinction between cause and effect—
And that which will be stated above, beyond that, this is now declared. || 206 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "by name and form" (tannāmarūpābhyām) as follows: "The effect," etc. Relying on that which stands above the expansion (prapañca) already mentioned and yet to be described, the words "that" (tat) and so forth are used. In this context, by the two words "name and form" (nāmarūpa), the ether and the rest are understood; it does not refer to the well-known name and form, nor is their manifestation possible without a primal cause. Therefore, the meaning is that it is appropriate to take those [ether and the rest] here. || 206 ||
For it is indeed through ignorance alone that [the world] manifests in its universal form in every way.
Because its true nature consists solely in ignorance, therefore this is said: || 207 ||

Having stated that there is always non-difference between cause and effect, [the author] says "mathataḥ" (in reality), anticipating the objection that there would be a contradiction for one who speaks of them as distinct through the relation of cause and effect. The meaning of "vaiśvarūpeṇa" is "in manifold forms," that is, as effect and cause. "Always" means throughout all three periods of time. Since both cause and effect are of the nature of nescience (avidyā), their non-difference is established through the aforementioned grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); [otherwise], there would be a distinction.

And there is no contradiction because ignorance appears in that form, as stated in such scriptural passages as "Indra by means of his powers of illusion" (Indro māyābhiḥ); this is the meaning. ||207||
Let there not be a conceptualized cognition in men regarding the reality that consists of name and form.
Therefore, this statement—that [the effect] arises from that very [cause] and nowhere else—is due to the manifestation of their single essence.

He explains the word *eva* (only) found in the passage beginning with *tat*: "Mā bhūt" (let it not be). Because the Śruti considers that there should not be a cognition in the form of a delusion among men—that the world could be spoken of without the manifestation of the Self—it says: "by name and form alone."
469 4 [Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

Those who maintain that the world is manifested not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) but as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) hold that, although it is manifested through names and so forth, it remains unmanifest.
The meaning is that the particle *eva* is employed with the intention that [the rope] is like a rope in the form of a snake. || 208 ||
The statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is for the purpose of establishing the unmanifest through the manifest.
For there is no completeness in manifestation, since that which has been manifested is seen to be incomplete. || 209 ||

For this reason as well, he says that the world is not manifest in the same way that it appears to be manifest. The phrase "sāmānādhikaraṇya" (grammatical coreferentiality) means that the coreferentiality expressed as "this is that" reinforces the intention of the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇā*). The term "avyakta" (unmanifest) is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning. [The word] "ātma... [is to be supplied].

He states another reason for the world not being directly manifest without the individual self (vyakti): "For not... He gives the reason why the world, though manifest, is incomplete: "Of the manifest... [The meaning is: the Self alone is the reality, not the world; therefore, it is not perceived when that [Self] is perceived.
Thus, as long as Brahman is not measured within as the inner self (pratyak), so long the world remains unmanifest. || 209 ||
By means of the negation of the knower and so forth, the Unmanifest is declared by the Śruti.
Since there is no means for the cognition of that [object], how can it be known? || 210 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "taddha" (that indeed), he raises a doubt while refuting the first alternative—namely, whether there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) under discussion—by stating: "the knower and so forth. The sense is that it cannot be said that there is no means of valid cognition there, because that would contradict the scripture (*śruti*) under discussion. He rejects the second alternative by stating: "the knowledge thereof. If there were no means of valid cognition there, then that [indeterminate] would remain unestablished due to the absence of a prover.
This is the meaning. || 210 ||
With all connections shaken off, it consists of a non-dual experience.
I am Brahman, whose nature is the single, unchanging pure consciousness alone. || 211 ||

In order to state that the understanding of the unmanifest arises from constant experience and not from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he defines experience [with the verse beginning] "shaken off" (*vidhūta*).

Fearing the charge of non-establishment because it has no connection even with knowledge, he says "not other" (*ananya*). By the word "not other," which expresses its qualification, he intends to convey that duality is merely imagined (*kalpita*) within the experience. Nevertheless, if that [experience], which possesses modifications such as birth and so forth, were of the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*), [it would be untenable].

Anticipating the objection that this [consciousness] might also be subject to such [change], he says: "The immutable" (*kūṭastha*). He refutes the view that the reality consists of both substance and consciousness by saying: "Only" (*mātra*). Since difference appears within consciousness, one might think that if it were a real entity, the reality itself would also be divided; to this he says: "One" (*eka*). What was indicated here by the word "non-other" (*ananya*) is now made explicit: the cognition of difference therein is adventitious (*aupādhikī*), not real (*vāstavī*).
Such is the meaning. He states what follows for the individual soul (jīva) from the aforementioned Brahman: "I am" (asmīti). || 211 ||
Its consciousness is never obscured; it is eternally risen and never set.
It is devoid of common or specific attributes and is established solely in the inner self.

Anticipating the objection that the inner Brahman, though of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), is not self-luminous because consciousness is an object of knowledge, he says: "It is not hidden" (*atirohita*). The sense is that it is not an object of knowledge, for if it were, it would follow—like a jar—that it is not consciousness itself, which would lead to an infinite regress. He clarifies its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) by saying: "Always" (*sadā*). Anticipating the objection that since rising and setting are observed in lamps and the like, and they are real entities, those two [phenomena] might also apply here, he says: [He continues: "For there is no rising or setting of this [consciousness], because it is eternal. Rising and setting consist in the production and destruction of something previously non-existent; however, in the case of consciousness, there is no such prior non-existence, as its existence is established by its very nature as consciousness. Nor can it be said that it is produced from the mind, for the mind is itself an object of that [consciousness]. Furthermore, since the mind is momentary, if consciousness were produced from it, it would follow that consciousness is also momentary. Moreover, if it were produced from the mind, it would be insentient (*jaḍa*), like sound and other objects produced from the mind. Therefore, consciousness is eternal and self-luminous. Thus, it is established that the inner Brahman is of the nature of consciousness and is self-luminous. It is also established that it is free from the attributes of being a knower and so forth, and is devoid of all distinctions. This is the meaning. *Note: The final sentence is a summary of the philosophical conclusion drawn from the preceding argumentation.*

Regarding the phrase "without generality" (*niḥsāmānya*): with the intention that it should also be noted that this [Self] possesses the nature of being either a generality or a particular because it is an object of cognition, he says: "the innermost Self" (*pratyak*). || 212 ||
Since that [Self] is eternally free by its very nature, it has never been perceived as non-existent by us.
For one who is free from ignorance, there is no association with the impurities born of the cause of ignorance.

Fearing the objection that "this [Brahman] is not established in its own majesty because it is an entity, like a jar," he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). By [the term] "eternally awakened" (*nityabuddhatva*), he expresses eternal purity. By [the word] "since" (*yasmāt*), having made that the reason, he expresses eternal liberation. [The word] "connection" (*saṃgati*) [is used]. || 213 ||
Although this [world] has such an intrinsic nature, it is not recognized as such by its very nature.
"This is said with reference to the highest darkness (tamas), and not to that which is real by its own nature.

[The author] says "evam" (thus) out of the apprehension that an entity of the aforementioned form might manifest in exactly that way. He explains the reason for stating "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) as being "ignorance" (*ajñātatvam*). He explains "tama" (darkness) as follows: the connection is "this is unperceived" (*etad-avijñātam*). That which is the nature of the object (*vastu-rūpa*) by itself—
He says "But not... [verse 214], meaning that in relation to that [consciousness], there is no state of being unknown, because it would follow that [consciousness] is eternal.
Let the meaning as it has been stated be understood in accordance with one's own direct experience.
Because it transcends the causes of pride, there is no possibility here of [attachment to] mother and so forth. || 215 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, how there can be a manifestation (*pratīti*) of that Brahman which, as previously described, is unknown and designated by the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*)—he says: "By one's own experience" (*svānubhūti*).
The meaning is this: the undifferentiated, which was stated in such passages as "the unknown inner reality, ignorance, karma, etc.," is established through the aforementioned experience.

Having raised the doubt that if it is accessible through experience, it must be an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) like a pot, he says "not so" (*māna*), because of the absence of manifest sound and other qualities; [this applies] here.
The proof of the inner self is established. || 215 ||
Even though the darkness has been dispelled therein, ignorance persists through its own self-experience.
Whether it is one's own experience or not [is uncertain] prior to the awakening to oneness.

Anticipating the doubt that there might be a state of being unknown or a state of ignorance regarding the inward consciousness which is of a single essence, he says: "In that... As to how experience of that [consciousness] is possible when ignorance has been destroyed, he says:
"Self-experience... He precludes the unrestrained nature of experience due to ignorance by saying: "Priorly... (216)
One who has realized the true nature of the self knows that [the three times] are non-existent.
This connection with something else is established only when left unexamined.

One might object: "If ignorance exists even in the inwardly self-luminous [Self], how can it be destroyed? Nor can its destruction arise from the knowledge of unity derived from the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), because even for one who possesses such knowledge, the possibility of disregarding eternal experience and so forth remains. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Known" (*jñātā*). The meaning is that the absolute destruction of ignorance results from the knowledge arising from the Great Sentence, because that knowledge is its direct opposite, whereas innate [self-luminous] knowledge merely serves as its manifestor. [This applies to the Self] with respect to ignorance and its products.

One might raise the objection: "Does yoga exist or not? If it exists, there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning non-attachment; if it does not exist, then ignorance and so forth cannot be established. To this, he says: "From another [source]. (217)
Because darkness cannot be established through either its own nature or through exclusion [from other things].
If this [self], which is of an unmanifest nature, is not established by means of valid cognition, [then it does not exist].
And since it does not possess a nature of a single self, how could it be an object of that means of valid cognition?
[218] 1. *vayam* | 2. *vaya* | [Vol.
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 471.

He establishes that [nescience] is established without being subjected to critical inquiry (*avicāritasiddhikatva*). [He says: "By its own nature" (*svabhāva*), etc. The meaning is this: nescience and the rest are not established as real entities (*vastu*), for that would lead to the consequence of their non-sublation; nor are they established as distinct from such entities, because distinction is untenable in the case of what is non-real (*avastu*). Thus, nescience cannot be characterized as either identical to or different from reality (*tattva-anyatva*). Regarding nescience...

Anticipating the objection that "even though it is immeasurable, it is measurable by its own nature," he says: "If not" (*na cet*). The meaning is this: if there is no establishment through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of ignorance and so forth—which belong to the Self—either as distinct from or non-distinct from it, then the statement that it is "measurable" is not meaningful, because it involves a contradiction: [on the one hand] it is established by valid means (*prāmāṇika*), and [on the other] it is "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*). The phrase "of this" (*asya*) expresses its relation to the Self. [This refers to] that which has the form of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "as distinct from the self, such as knowledge and so forth. || 298 ||
By the phrase "That indeed is this," there is the statement regarding the two natures: the manifested and the unmanifested.
Only the fitness for being a means of valid cognition has been stated, not identity with the cognizer or the nature of being a cognized object.

Anticipating the objection—"How can that undifferentiated [state], which is understood from the sentence 'That thou art,' not be an object of knowledge?"—he says: "taddhā" (that indeed). By this sentence, there is first of all the mention of the world in its two forms; likewise, its state of being unknown is restated as established by experience. Therefore, the meaning is that the differentiated [world] is not an object of knowledge for the sentence, because the sentence does not have that as its purport. || 219 ||
That which is indeterminate and unknown is considered to be beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition.
To claim that something is not connected to the means of valid cognition and yet arises from the means of valid cognition is sheer audacity.
He states another reason for its immeasurability: "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*). Its explanation is "unknown" (*avijñāta*).

That is said to be that wherein there is no scope or object for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He establishes its status as not being an object of valid cognition with the words "by a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
The connection is: "and it is considered known from a means of valid cognition. The sense is: for it is not measured, because it is to be discarded by the means of valid cognition itself. || 220 ||
For those who maintain that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are those which bring about the apprehension of an object not yet known.
The meaning accepted by all is now considered: from what [source] does it arise? || 221 ||

Having stated his own position—that the Supreme Self alone, having become the inner self (*pratyag-bhūta*), is both the locus and the object of ignorance, and that the establishment of its being unknown and so forth arises from the experience of its own nature and not from a means of knowledge (*māna*)—he now states a point established for both sides in order to show that in the opponent's view, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible. He says: "Unknown... And as for that [Self], from what does it manifest? Is it from itself or from another? If from another, is it from a means of knowledge (*māna*) or from the Witness (*sākṣin*)? Thus he proceeds to investigate.
He says that it must be determined. Why? || 221 ||
An object may be known, or unknown, or both, or neither.
The object of knowledge would be [known] by means of the instruments of knowledge; all of this is now investigated.

First of all, the first [position] is not tenable, because neither of us accepts that "unknownness" is self-luminous, and because it would follow that an unknown object could never be an object of knowledge (*aprameya*).

Considering that this [unknownness] is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and thus it would amount to our own view, he proceeds to another investigation regarding the position that it is accessible through a means of valid cognition (*māna*).

He shows [the alternatives]: "Or, it is known. Having reflected that all these other possibilities brought forward by mere supposition are untenable—namely, that an object which is not known is either self-luminous like the Sāṃkhya, or insentient like the Tārkika, or consists of both knowledge and the knowable like the Yogācāra, or else is neither actually unknown nor known (being "unknown" due to lack of cognition and "known" due to cognition)—he proceeds.
Therefore, it is determined that an object unknown through a means of knowledge does not manifest; this is the meaning. || 222 ||

In the case of the establishment of the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge, we do not perceive any proof for this.
Because that which is known lacks any distinction [from itself], and because even that which is unknown is not being measured. || 223 ||

He first demonstrates the untenability of the position of the Vaiśeṣikas and others with the words "meya" (the object of knowledge). The meaning is that if the insentient were an object of knowledge by virtue of being unknown, there would be no means of knowledge (*māna*) for perceiving the difference between the two—namely, "this is the means of knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge. Anticipating the objection that a difference between the two is experienced through the relation of object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*), he replies: Is this objectivity [established] in the form of being known or in the form of being unknown? It cannot be the first, because that which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) is not [itself] such [as an object].

He states that there is no evidence for a difference from what is already known (*jñāta*). Regarding the phrase "of the known" (*jñātasya*): it is not the other [the unknown], because the operation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) upon something whose nature is unknown has never been observed;

and if its form were seen by another means of knowledge, it would be sublated by that very means of knowledge, so its form cannot be unknown due to the absence of a means of knowledge. Thus he says: "of the unknown" (*ajñātasya*). || 223 ||
For whatever object exists in the world, it is indeed known, just like the intellect itself.
"He is known through pride alone"—how could this be so, given that [pride] is immeasurable?

To the objection—how can that which has its form known be non-existent due to the breaking of its measure—he says: "The world," etc. Whatever object is being dealt with on the plane of empirical usage (*vyavahārabhūmi*), all of it is invariably concomitant with manifestation (*prakāśa*). Just as cognition (*dhī*) is invariably concomitant with its own existence, so too this [object], as long as it persists in empirical usage, is non-different from knowledge, because it is being dealt with; this is the meaning. Empirical usage [is] manifestation...

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is non-existence [of concomitance]. Now, it may be argued that cognition is known by itself; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. However, the state of being known (*jñātatā*) of an object arises from a means of knowledge (*māna*); otherwise, that [means] would be futile. To this, he says: "From a means of knowledge" (*mānāt*). || 224 ||
Since there is no proof of an excess of the means of knowledge, why is it not the case that the object of knowledge itself is likewise [established]?
For one lamp does not acquire the nature of light from another lamp. || 225 ||

Anticipating the objection that the impossibility of the object being known (*jñātatvānupapatti*) is the proof for this, he says: "Māna... etc. The meaning is: since there is no proof (*māna*) for the existence of an object distinct from the proof itself, the object remains unestablished; therefore, let the object be self-luminous (*svayaṃ-prakāśa-rūpa*) like the proof itself—how then can there be any impossibility of its being known? Now, one might argue: even the self-luminous Self is established only through a proof, as we see that a lamp is established in dependence upon the eye; to this, he replies:

"Indeed not. The remainder of the sense is that an object, which is of the nature of manifestation, is not established by depending upon a means of knowledge (māna) that is of the nature of manifestation. || 225 ||
No form other than that which exceeds the known form is perceived.
If the object of knowledge is thus known by means of the measure, what [doubt] remains for me? (226)

That "because what is known lacks any deviation [from being known]" has been elaborated upon. As for the claim that "there is no such thing as an unknown form because there is no means of knowledge (māna) for it," that is not tenable; for the very means of knowledge consisting in the "knownness" of a jar serves as proof even when that jar is otherwise unknown. Anticipating this objection, the author explains that even the unknown is not established by a means of knowledge, stating: "In the form of the known," etc. To begin with, the means of knowledge consisting in the knownness of an object does not prove its unknownness at the time [of its own occurrence].

The meaning is that because the proof of "knownness" (*jñātatva*) is dependent upon the subject (*pakṣa*), and because [the object] does not exist at another time, there is no form of the thing over and above its known form, due to the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*). He concludes the failure to establish the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyabheda*) in the position of the Vaiśeṣikas and others with the words: "If it is thus. If it is established that there is no difference of the known form from the means of knowledge, or that the unknown form is non-existent, then [from the means of knowledge]—
The meaning is that since cognition cannot be established because there is a lack of means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), there is therefore no cognition of its differentiation. || 226 ||
1. Not in the case of non-difference.
[vol2, page 179] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 473
And there is no other means for establishing the existence of the object of cognition.
Because no fruit arises from those conceits, it is like a dance in the darkness.

[Objection: "But surely, even without dependence on means of knowledge (*māna*), the establishment of the insentient (*jaḍa*) occurs because its empirical usage is observed; otherwise, that [usage] would be impossible. To this, he says: "And not... The connection is with the words "other than the means of knowledge" (*mānebhyaḥ aparaḥ*). Because it is impossible for the insentient to be established by itself—

This is the meaning. He states the conclusion regarding the non-establishment of the insentient (*jaḍa*) either through itself or through a means of knowledge (*māna*): "tatphala... etc. Therefore, since the result consisting of the determination of the insentient is not established either through a means of knowledge or by itself, all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are impossible therein—like dancing in the dark; such is the meaning. || 227 ||
Even though the object of cognition is established by itself as being white, it is nevertheless not so [in the way you claim].
Since its establishment does not depend on anything else, what could be the basis for its being an object of knowledge?

Having refuted the second [position], he restates the first: "svataḥ" (inherently). He refutes that as well by stating that the failure to establish the distinction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyya*) is equal in that case too: "tathāpi" (even so). Anticipating the objection that this might apply to his own position just as it does to yours, he says: "ananya-" (non-different). In my position, because the reality (*vastu*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it does not possess the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) by virtue of being the locus for the manifestation produced by a means of knowledge; rather, [the removal of] ignorance dependent upon that [manifestation]— [...is what constitutes its being known. (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the function of the means of knowledge in removing ignorance.)

The state of being such [as Brahman] is due to its possessing the fruit of its own function; moreover, a means of knowledge (māna) produces manifestation by destroying ignorance regarding that [Brahman], but this is not possible for you, because both ignorance and its connection are real entities (vastu).

If they were unreal, there would be no distinction from the subject (pakṣa). Nor can it be argued that ignorance and its connection are merely superimposed upon the Self while actually residing in Pradhāna, because it is difficult to explain how ignorance could belong to anything other than the Self. This is the intended meaning. || 228 ||
There is no probandum without a probans, nor is there ever a probans for that which cannot be proven.
Nor is there ever mutual indifference among those who possess equal power. (229)

Furthermore, do the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) stand in a relationship of mutual independence or mutual dependence? It is not the first case; thus he says: "without an instrument" (*niḥsādhana*).

The object of knowledge does not exist independently of the means of knowledge, because that which is pervaded by the means of knowledge is what constitutes an object of knowledge. Likewise, the means of knowledge does not exist independently of the object of knowledge, because it is impossible for it to be without a support.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no mutual independence between the two. In the second case, like the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge must either be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) or not; if it is not, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is argued that [consciousness] is self-luminous, he replies: "Equal," etc. The sense is that no mutual dependence between two lamps has ever been observed. || 229 ||
There is no dependence between two things that are not yet established in themselves, nor is it accepted between two things that are already established.
For even in the world, there is no relationship of dependence and dependent without some excellence [or distinction]. (230)

Furthermore, does the mutual dependence between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyya*) exist when both are unestablished, or when both are established, or when one is established and the other is unestablished? It is not the first case; thus he says: "No. The meaning is that there can be no mutual dependence between two things that are non-existent and non-manifesting by their own nature, just like the son of a barren woman or a sky-flower. It is not the second case either; thus he says: "And [not] when both are established. The meaning is that there is no mutual dependence between two things that are existent and manifesting by their own nature, because there is no need for such a result. As for the two remaining positions—

Those who state the common objection [beginning with] "it does not depend" [is answered as follows]: the word *hi* (for) is used for the purpose of establishing that when there is excellence (*atiśaya*), the absence of that [excellence] is well-known;
the word *api* (also), however, serves to include the treatises (*śāstra*). || 230 ||
Nor does that which is established by itself depend upon what is unestablished, such as a human horn.

Due to the absence of the connection between the object and the sense organ, that [cognition] is impossible. || 259 ||

Raising the objection, "Even if there is an absence of both self-evidentness (*svataḥ-siddhatva*) and non-self-evidentness (*asiddhatva*), how can there be a failure to perceive the means of knowledge that establish them?"—the author considers the alternatives of whether such a means is perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), and refutes the first. "Not, first of all," he says; the meaning is that perception cannot even be suspected in regard to [states such as] being unknown (*ajñātatva*). Is that [perception] produced by the external senses or produced by the mind? He states that it is not the first.
"Because that is impossible. This establishes the impossibility of an external-sense-born perception that could prove [the existence of] "unknownness" (ajñātatva) and so forth.

Regarding the word "object": the meaning is that since there is no contact between the eye and the like with unknownness and so forth, there can be no establishment of perception born from contact with those [objects]. || 259 ||
Nor would it be like the cognition of suffering and so forth, because [the object] must be experienced only when it has already been known.
This false cognition is experienced as if it were a direct perception of an object. (260)
He rejects another alternative with the words "na ca" (nor). For even suffering and so forth are established by mental experience; this is the meaning.

He addresses another position with the words "jñātasya" (of that which is known). For experience is the fruit of a means of knowledge (*māna*); therefore, only that which is already known can be an object of inference, not that which is unknown, because there is no probans (*liṅga*) pervaded by such [unknown] states. Having provisionally accepted that what is known is inferable, he abandons that concessionary argument.

Regarding the term "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*): the meaning is that, like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, false cognition, right cognition, knownness, unknownness, and the like are not inferable because they are directly perceived (*aparokṣya*), as there is no utility for inference in their case. || 260 ||
How can knowledge, which is the fruit of perception and the other means of cognition, itself be an object of cognition?
The fruit of that [knowledge] is not said to reside within the object of measurement, unlike the fruit of ritual action. || 261 ||

He states another argument for the fact that *jñātatva* (the state of being known) is not an object of cognition (*ameya*). [The verse begins with] "pratyakṣādi... Here, by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), *jñātatva* is indicated through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). Since it is the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*māna*), just as it is not itself a means of valid cognition (*amānatva*), so too would it be an object of cognition (*ameyatva*); otherwise, why would it not also be a means of valid cognition? The sense is that if it were an object of cognition, one would have to postulate another *jñātatva*, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, because the fruit of a means of valid cognition depends upon an object of cognition (*meyāśritatva*), like color and so forth—

Anticipating the objection that there is no infinite regress—since even if one does not admit a further state of "knownness" (*jñātatva*) once something is known, its status as an object of cognition (*meyatva*) is established by its being the object of the linguistic usage produced by the means of knowledge—he says: "The fruit of the means of knowledge. Just as the fruit of the act of cutting, namely the state of being split in two, resides in the wood, the state of being known, which is the fruit of the means of knowledge, does not reside in the object; for if it were not luminous (*aprakāśatva*), it would be indistinguishable from the object and thus ineffective. However, if it is luminous...

The meaning is as follows: because it is impossible for [the object] to be established as having the nature of an object (*arthaniṣṭhatva*) through its being known (*jñānavat*), there is no "knowability" (*meyatva*) when there is an absence of "unknowability" (*ajñātatva*). For knowability is not simply the state of being the object of a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) dependent upon a means of knowledge (*māna*); otherwise, since everything would be such [an object], there would be the consequence of confusion (*sāṃkarya*) in your own view. || 261 ||
Furthermore, the connection of the means of knowledge with the object of knowledge is indeed logical only when it is through the object itself.
But for one who possesses only the fruit of pride, effort elsewhere is in vain. || 262 ||

Furthermore, he states that the state of being an object for a means of knowledge belongs only to the object of cognition (*meyena*), and not to the result (*phala*), because its status as an object of cognition has already been refuted.
He says: "Even... Even if the means of knowledge is connected only with the object of cognition, the result might still stand in a relationship of being an object (*viṣayatayā*) toward it;

yet this is not so, because it would follow that the result lacks the status of being an object of cognition (*ameyatva*). For it cannot be self-established (*svataḥsiddhi*), since it is not the Self (*anātmatvāt*); nor can it be the Self, because it is occasional (*kādācitka*).
[Vol.
2, Page 187] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 481.
