He speaks out of doubt, saying "of the fruit" (*māphalasya*). The remainder of the sense is that there is a connection with the measure alone (*mātra*), and not with the object of knowledge (*meyādi*) and so forth. Of the fruit, with the object of knowledge...

The connection [of the means of knowledge] has been refuted; nor can it have a connection with that [result] by way of being its object, because [the result] is included within the object of cognition (*meyāntarbhāvāt*) and thus cannot logically be the fruit itself. Therefore, the effort expended in stating that "it has a relation to the means of knowledge and so forth" is entirely in vain; the meaning is that what depends on the cognizer is established through experience along with its own substratum. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the connection of the result with [the means of knowledge] such as being an object of cognition has already been refuted. || 262 ||
But if that fruit were itself an object of knowledge, an infinite regress would result here.
It must be stated: what is the means of knowledge for the connection between the instrument of cognition and its result? (263)

One might suspect that even the fruit [of knowledge] is connected with the object of cognition (*meyasaṃbandhin*), since it too, being a real entity, could be suspected of being an object of cognition (*meyatva*); anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the fruit of the means of knowledge" (*māphalasya*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of the means of knowledge (*mānabhūmi*). The meaning is that, according to the principle stated in such passages as "in each and every fruit there is that measure," [the fruit is not an object]. The particle *tu* is used to clarify that infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is a defect because it leads to the destruction of the root. [This concerns] the validity of the cognition and its fruit...
Fearing that, just as the relation of cause and effect might be an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), the result (*phala*) might likewise be so, he says: "Valid cognition" (*pramā*).

For the result is not an object of knowledge in the same way that the relation is, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); nor is that relation itself an object of knowledge, because there is no means of valid cognition (*māna*) to apprehend it. This is the meaning. || 263 ||
And here too there would be an infinite regress; therefore, inference is not applicable in this case.
Furthermore, no operation of a means of knowledge (māna) is observed in the establishment of passion and the like. || 264 ||
Anticipating the objection that "the connection with the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth, which constitute the cause, may be inferred from the effect known as the result (*phala*)," he says:

"In this case also. The meaning is that even if that [connection] were inferable just like the result, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow because another connection with a result would have to be established there;

therefore, it is not logical for the connection itself to be inferable in the same manner as the result. The word *api* is used for the sake of the analogy with the result, and the particle *ca* (translated here as 'also') serves to emphasize the point.

It is connected with the word "action" (*saṃskriyā*). Lest it be thought that "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*) and the like might constitute the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), just as there is a relationship between valid cognition (*pramā*) and its fruit, [the author] says "and not" (*na ca*) to show that this is not the case, as it is with passion (*rāga*) and so forth. || 264 ||
Nor is there an absence of passion and so forth, because of their existence and because they are experienced.
And there is no difference whatsoever regarding the fruit [of knowledge] among the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the cognizer.

If it is argued that because its immeasurability entails the non-acceptance of self-luminosity, it must be non-existent, he says "no," with the words "of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. The meaning of the particle *api* is "even though it is not accessible through means of knowledge (*māna*). The particle *ca* is used for emphasis and is connected with the negative *na*. The meaning is that since the existence of that passion and so forth is established solely from experience (*anubhava*), it is not non-existent. Alternatively, by the word *tat* (it) having such a sense, the eternality of experience is expressed. Now, as has been stated—

Is experience (*anubhūti*) inert (*jaḍa*) or non-inert (*ajaḍa*)? It cannot be the first, because like a jar it would lack the capacity to be a means of proof; for even a lamp does not possess the capacity to prove itself inherently. Nor can it be the second, because being differentiated, it would be an effect (*kārya*). To this he replies: "Not so. For there is no inherent difference in the result (*phala*) by itself, as in the case of space (*nabhas*), apart from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); rather, the difference produced by the subject (*mātṛ*) and so forth belongs to that [result] and not to the experience itself. Therefore, it is appropriate that experience is non-inert. This is the meaning. || 265 ||
If pride were the cause of action, then it would not exist for one who is free from pride.
And since there is no cognition in the absence of that [object], how could that [cognition] exist without itself? (266)

He raises the objection that consciousness must be insentient (*jaḍa*) because it is well-known for being an effect of a means of knowledge (*māna*). [The text says: "By the word *māna*... If cognition were an effect of that [means of knowledge], it would not be the establisher of the means of knowledge, the knower (*mātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*meya*), because it is an effect of the means of knowledge—just like the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which is its effect. Consequently, since there would be no establisher, the knower and the rest would be non-existent; this is the refutation. [Notes on variants: 1. *rasyatvaṃ* (in manuscript *kha*). 2. *'naśā'* (in manuscript *kha*). 3. *nmāphaleṃ* (in manuscript *kha*). 4. *nmātrameyayoḥ* (in manuscript *ka*).
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
"It would not exist. The proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādī*) thinks, "Let there be the non-existence of the mother and so forth," and in response to him, he says: "In the absence of that..."

And so it is said. In the absence of those three, because there would be no means of proof (*sādhaka*), even the desired emptiness (*śūnyatva*) would not be established; for that [emptiness] is not self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Anticipating the objection that by saying "due to the absence of means of knowledge" (*mānābhāvāt*), one would be admitting the non-existence of that very emptiness, he asks: "Why? [The answer is: Even the entity called the "absence of means of knowledge" is not established in your view due to the absence of a means of proof; however, for me, the absence of means of knowledge and so forth is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

The sense is that [the means of knowledge] is established. Alternatively, having raised the objection that even in the absence of the knower (*mātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*meyya*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) might occur through the means of knowledge (*māna*) alone without requiring a practitioner (*sādhaka*), he says: "And in the absence of those two. The meaning is that in the absence of those two, since there would be no means of knowledge devoid of an object and a locus, there could be no transaction produced by it. Or else, even if there were an absence of transaction caused by the means of knowledge, there might still be one caused by its result (*tatphala*).

Anticipating this objection, he asks: "Why? The meaning is that since the result cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (māna), there can be no worldly transaction (vyavahāra) brought about by such a result. || 266 ||
And even in the absence of the knower and so forth, it is not the case that non-existence itself is being cognized as an object of knowledge.
O you who sleep well, because of the priority of the mother, everything here remains unoccupied.

Raising the objection that although desire (*rāga*) and the like are not objects of knowledge because they are known through constant experience, ignorance (*ajñāta*) and so forth are objects of knowledge—just as the absence of a knower (*mātṛ*) and the like [is known]—he says:

"Of the knower, etc. In this regard, is there a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that absence, or something else? First of all, the non-arising of a cognition whose object is the knower and so forth during deep sleep is not the means of knowledge; for in the world, the operation of a means of knowledge depends upon a knower, and in the absence of that [knower], it does not occur. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, this is the meaning: the word "ca" (and) serves to include other states along with sleep. || 267 ||
Therefore, it is not [established] by perception or inference; nor even by presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
For presumptive testimony is established only when one perceives what has been seen or heard [to be otherwise inexplicable]. || 268 ||

In the second [verse], having raised the alternatives as to whether perception, inference, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of knowledge (*māna*) therein, he refutes the first two with the word "no" (*na*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the absence of the measurer (*mātṛ*) and so forth is being measured. He states that because those two [perception and inference] also presuppose a measurer, they cannot function in its absence. He refutes the third [alternative] by the aforementioned reason with the words "also not from presumptive testimony" (*arthāpattito’pi*).

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is of two kinds, distinguished by being based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*) or what is heard (*śruta*). Among these, the first depends on what is seen; for example, having seen that Maitra, who is alive, is present inside his house, one postulates his presence outside. The second requires what is heard; for example, having heard the partial statement "The fat Maitra does not eat during the day," one postulates the other part of the sentence, "He eats at night. Since presumption depends on such [evidence] as what is seen or heard, it is [independent of verbal testimony].
He says that there is no activity regarding an existent entity: "For not... (268).
And because similarity is impossible here, there is no possibility of an analogy.
And when false cognition and the like are fully established, even non-existence is not suspected [to be the case]. || 269 ||

He says, "It is not the fourth," and explains: "Because of similarity. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction, meaning that the impossibility of comparison (*upamāna*) is combined with the impossibility of other means of knowledge (*māna*). The meaning is that comparison, which has similarity as its cause, cannot function as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of [the object] such as a mother, because that [similarity] is absent. Having refuted the establishment of non-existence through a means of knowledge based on ignorance and so forth—just as in the case of the absence of a mother and so forth—he now considers the alternative: whether its establishment occurs through a means of knowledge for existence (*bhāva-māna*) or through a means of knowledge for non-existence (*abhāva-māna*).

Since the [existence of] silver has been refuted, he refutes the second [possibility] with the word "mithyā" (false). And the purpose of the example is to establish the non-existence of the "mātrā" (measure/aspect) and so forth. (Note: This refers to variant readings ka, ga, and ta.)
[Vol.
2, Page 189] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 483.

The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "just as in the case of positive entities. For indeed, non-apprehension of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is not possible in the case of false cognition and the like, apart from [the category of] non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is the meaning. || 269 ||
"Regarding this object never seen before, I have never seen this mountain before."
It is recognized directly, just as it was previously seen. || 270 ||

Since [properties] such as "being unknown" are not established by either the existence or non-existence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can they be established? With this hidden intention, he says: "Atyanta... (verse 270).

The meaning is: when an object such as a mountain, which has never been seen before, is perceived, one reflects, "I have not seen this before," and thus even that which was not previously seen is directly known; therefore, "being unknown" and so forth are established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor does the existence of its mother and so forth [apply], because it is absolutely unperceived.
It is not accepted [as established] through valid cognition, nor through non-existence, but rather through recognition. || 271 ||

If it is argued that, because it is recognized through *pratyabhijñā* (recognition), [the existence of] "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) and so forth is established by perception (*māna*), he says: "And not... The meaning is this: first of all, with respect to a mountain or similar object being seen now, a person such as a mother was not previously active toward it, because such a person was never seen at all. Therefore, since there is no prior experience (*anubhava*) of it, there is no resulting mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and thus the aforementioned recognition is impossible; consequently, "unknownness" and so forth are not objects of knowledge (*meyatā*). If that is so, then how can "unknownness" and so forth be [established] by recognition?
Suspecting that the logical argument for proof might be hollow, he states his own intention with the words "No" (na).

The meaning is that the recognition of "being unknown" and so forth does not arise from the cognition of existence or the cognition of non-existence, but rather from direct experience (anubhava) alone. In this context, since the commonly accepted [logical] recognition lacks the requisite capacity, "experience" is therefore the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence). || 271 ||
Therefore, [the definition] applies exhaustively to all means of valid cognition, as well as to fallacious cognitions and non-cognitions.
In the same way, the establishment of darkness would follow from its own object being a means of valid cognition for nothing else.
He concludes that the cognition of "being unknown" and so forth arises from experience itself, because such states are not objects of measurement (aprameyatva). He says, "Therefore":

the independent direct means of knowledge is that which is called the experience of the Witness (sākṣyanubhava); therefore, there is the establishment of valid cognition and the like, as well as its cause, ignorance (ajñāna). This is the meaning. || 272 ||
"Relying upon the internal object of knowledge, it is self-established, non-dual, and peerless."
All this universe, consisting of existence, non-existence, and so forth, is established [by this].

Anticipating the objection that there would be an infinite regress because even the means of knowledge that establishes the means of knowledge (the *māna-sādhaka-māna*) would require another means of knowledge, he says: "Internal" (*āntaram*).

The meaning is that the term "means of knowledge" (*mānatva*) is applied to the Witness (*sākṣin*) only because of his being the establisher; it is not a primary means of knowledge in that regard. If that is so, then [regarding] the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*)—

"O King, [the objection] that there is a dependence on a means of knowledge for that [Self] is not so," he says. "It is established by itself. He explains how that is so: "Because its nature is consciousness.
He clarifies the reason for stating that the Witness, characterized as described above, is a means of knowledge:

"Of existence... Existence and non-existence refer to birth and destruction; by the word "etcetera," transformation and so forth are included; and "the universe" refers to the objects of cognition and the like. (273)

Because there is no connection with a real object, this [cognition] is not a cognition of the thing as it truly is. Since the object is already known, its absence is also accepted as being perceptual; thus, it is memory. (274)

Now, in order to establish that the world is cognizable by a witness (sākṣivedyatva), he states the reason for the fact that false cognition is established through experience: "It is mine" and so forth. The meaning is: false cognition does not conform to the object because it is not a true awakening [to that object]; therefore, the establishment of the reality of the object does not follow from it. If that is so, then what is the means of proof (*sādhaka*)? [The text continues: "the means of proof. [Variants: 1. *pra*; 2. *ka. ra mānamā*; 3. *kha sādhikā*.]
184 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter] [vol2, page 190]

Lest it be suspected that [the silver] does not exist at all because of its non-existence as a real entity, he says "because it is known" (*jñātatvāt*) to show that this is not so, since it is established by experience. The connection is with the word "is not accepted" (*neṣyate*). He refutes the *ākhyāti* theory—the view that "false cognition" (*mithyādhīḥ*) is merely a memory arising from non-discrimination, and that such memory is self-evident—by stating "because it is perceptual" (*prātyakṣyāt*). Since it is an immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*), the cognition of silver is not a memory; rather, it is the perception of the jar standing before one.
This is the meaning of "he says. || 274 ||
An object of such a nature as "this is silver" does not exist anywhere.
There is no cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl; for us, the quality of "this-ness" does not exist in silver. (275)

Anticipating the objection that false cognition is merely the appearance of mother-of-pearl standing before one in the form of silver existing in another place or elsewhere—and that such a cognition is fruitless—the author says "this" (*idam*). Even though the form of "this" exists in the space before one, and the silver exists in another place or elsewhere, a specific [combined] form is not seen here; nor does it exist anywhere here, for it is contradicted by the sublation-cognition (*bādhadhī*).

If it is argued that this [appearance] is not non-existent because it is directly perceived, [we reply: no, because there is an absence of a realizer (*sādhaka*) for it elsewhere. Therefore, the perception of a qualified object is *anirvacanīya-khyāti* (the theory of indefinable appearance), and its nature is that it is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*). How is it that the qualified form is non-existent everywhere? Is it in the locus of the mother-of-pearl, in the locus of the silver, or elsewhere than those two? Not the first; for even if "this" (*idam*) exists in the mother-of-pearl, silver is absent there, as there is a lack of evidence [for its presence] and because of the cognition of sublation (*bādhadhī*).

He says "and because of contradiction" and then "not in the mother-of-pearl. Not the other [silver], because even though its form exists in the location of the silver, the "this-ness" (idantā) does not exist there.
For he says "no," meaning that for us, the "this-ness" of silver situated in another place does not appear. || 275 ||
Because that [duality] is absent elsewhere, it is not admitted even in the case of a witness and so forth.
There is no comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas, because of the cause being false knowledge.

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because in a location such as a jar, there is an absence of both the silver and the "this-ness" (idantā), and thus the qualified form is unestablished; this is what he states with the words "other than that. Some say that the qualified form resides in the witness (*sākṣin*) or the knower (*mātṛ*), since its body consists of mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*) and that appearance resides in either of those two; others say it resides in the intellect (*buddhi*). In response to them, he says "in the witness, etc."; the ellipsis is "because of the lack of evidence" (*mānābhāvāt*).

He restates the nature of false cognition as it was described under the doctrine of *anirvacanīyakhyāti* (the theory that the object of error is indeterminable), namely, "because of the lack of connection with an object of knowledge," by saying "And not... Here, "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*) is the meaning of the locative case. || 276 ||
Tell me, what are the means for the complete accomplishment of false knowledge and the rest?
Furthermore, its establishment does not arise from right cognition, because that [cognition] would involve a regressus ad infinitum regarding the object of knowledge.

Desiring to establish that this [cognition] is established by experience (*anubhavasiddhatā*), he introduces another proof, beginning with "false" (*mithyā*). Thinking it has been asked, he states the means: "correctly" (*samyak*). He says "no," because that [subsequent cognition] is not the prover of that [first cognition], since its causality as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāhetutva*) exists only in relation to its own object of measurement (*meyārtha*) through a connection therewith. || 277 ||
In the case of the immortal, the object of knowledge is the effect; no other [object] is intended for the means of knowledge.
Nor is it possible for there to be a cognition of silver and so forth based on mere similarity.

[Objection: Since even false knowledge and the like are objects of knowledge (*meyatva*), a correct cognition connected with that [false knowledge] will produce valid knowledge (*pramā*) regarding it. [Reply: To this he says, "object of knowledge" (*meya*). False knowledge and the like are not objects of knowledge, because what is an effect of ignorance cannot, like ignorance itself, be characterized as being unknown; nor can there be valid knowledge regarding that which is not an object of knowledge.
1. ‘Dermeya’ | [Vol.
2, page 191] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 485

The meaning is that, since it is other than the fruits of pride (*māna*), there is no attainment of right knowledge (*samyagdhī*) from that which is an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Now, one might object: "Ignorance is not the cause of false cognition; rather, it is the similarity [of the object] to *sattva* and so forth, for the appearance of silver is produced by the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the perception of a similar object."

To this, [the author] replies: "Or not. The meaning is that even though the ignorance regarding it (the shell) has been destroyed by the knowledge of the shell, since there is an absence of the cognition of silver despite the similarity in terms of existence and other qualities, the ignorance of the shell itself is the cause of that [cognition of silver], as established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 278 ||
Because it is the object of a cognition arising from its own uncommon nature.
Therefore, from one's own mind, which has been refined by the impressions of silver, memory arises.

Anticipating the objection that false cognitions cannot be the effects of ignorance because they correspond to reality by having existence (*sattva*) and so forth as their objects—since all cognitions are true on account of being cognitions, like those generally accepted [as true]—the author says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Because the cognition of silver and the like has as its object the same thing as a correct cognition produced by silver and the like through its specific form, mere similarity to existence and so forth is not its object; nor is it the case that all cognitions...
"If one accepts [the existence of] errors, there would be a contradiction of one's own established tenets;
if one does not accept them, the lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been raised. (Taṭa)

The meaning is "according to this logic. Some [hold] that because silver and the like are objects with respect to the cognition arising from their own specific forms (*asādhāraṇākāra*), it is not existence (*sattva*) alone that is the object of that [cognition]. However, in any case, since false cognition has an unreal object and no other cause is possible, it follows that it is an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*). He states the conclusion: "Therefore... [Silver arises] from the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*) residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of previously experienced silver.

And that error is called "memory" because it is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). The meaning is that for one who has not previously perceived silver but perceives a mother-of-pearl shell, a mental impression is not of service to the error of [mistaking it for] silver. || 279 ||
It manifests from the Supreme Self, who is perceived as eternally one and unchanging in nature. || 280 ||
Apart from knowledge and the knower, nothing exists even in darkness.
Therefore, this object of knowledge is ignorance; direct perception is accompanied by the knower.

Having stated that which produces false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), he concludes by stating that which makes it known. "It manifests" (*prathate*): the meaning is that false cognition appears as something other than its own nature—that is, from the Supreme, which is the vision (*dṛṣṭi*) that is changeless, devoid of difference, and eternally established. Anticipating the objection—"Just as ignorance has a means of proof, why should false knowledge and its effects not likewise have another means of proof?"—he provides an illustration, following what was said regarding darkness (*tamas*).

He refutes [the objection] with the words "jñāna" (knowledge), etc. Based on the etymology of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is "knowledge" (*jñāna*); its knower is the immutable experience (*kūṭasthānubhava*).

Apart from that, there is no means of knowledge (*māna*) by which a form could be pervaded, as is the case with false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and so forth; for there is no such example in the case of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Therefore, the meaning is that ignorance, together with the measures [of knowledge] and so on, is established by the immutable experience. || 280 || 281 ||
For the subject and so forth are not established unless they have ascended into consciousness.
[This is] because the non-self, such as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, has as its sole true nature nothing but pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra). || 282 ||

Having raised the objection—“Even if ignorance is established by the aforementioned experience through the experience ‘I am ignorant’ [on the part of the knower], how is it established for the instruments (mātrādi) and so forth?”—he says: “For not... Because they are insentient (jaḍatva), it is illogical for the instruments and so forth to be established independently, without depending upon consciousness (saṃvit).
(Note: *anusmṛtya* is a variant reading for *anubhūya*).
486 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 192]

This is the meaning. He states the reason why the establishment of the "measurer" (mātrādi) and so forth occurs only as something superimposed upon the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthānubhava): "Consciousness" (saṃvit). By the word "mātra," the exclusion of manifold flavors (nānārasatva) is intended. Consciousness alone, being of a single flavor (ekarasa), is the sole reality (yāthātmya), existence (sattva), and manifestation (sphūrti) of the "measurer" and so forth;
since that is impossible for the insentient non-self, the meaning is that the manifestation of that [non-self] occurs only as something imagined within consciousness. || 282 ||
Whether this object is known or unknown, this cognition resides in the agent.
Memory is not in accordance with the object as it actually exists; therefore, it is not considered a valid means of knowledge. || 283 ||

Anticipating the objection that just as the distinction between the known and the unknown is not imagined because it is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), so too the "measurer" (*mātṛ*) and other factors might not be imagined, he says: "This is known. This means that memory is an error (*bhrānti*). The measurer is the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the act of measuring; and there can be no agency without superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon that which is inactive. Therefore, since this twofold cognition is a modification of the superimposed measurer, he states that it is an error: "The agent," etc. (Verse 1).

He states another reason for its being an error: "That is not [the case]. Since the distinction between the knower and so forth lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) and is therefore merely imagined (*kalpita*), it follows that the self (*mātrādi*) and other such entities are not imagined in that same way; this is what he expresses by the word "therefore" (*tena*). The meaning of that pronoun (*tat*) is "having an imagined substrate" and "not conforming to reality. The word "this" (*asau*) refers to the aforementioned cognition of the distinction between the knower and so forth. || 283 ||
For this characteristic of being known or unknown does not conform to the nature of the object itself.
Form is that which arises from the non-cognition of the real object and depends upon a knower. || 284 ||

Anticipating the objection that because "knownness" (*jñātatva*) and so forth follow the nature of the object, the cognition of them must also follow it and thus be valid, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). He states the reason for its not following the nature of the object: "The object... (*vastu*); the meaning is that it is produced by the ignorance (*ajñāna*) of the inner self (*pratyak*). Since "knownness" and so forth follow what is not a real object, the cognition of them—though residing in the knower—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), as it does not follow a real object; thus he says: "Cognition... (*jñā-*) [and so on].
Therefore, the distinction between the known and the unknown has as its subject a self that is established by itself.
The establishment of "knownness" (jñātatā) occurs through consciousness, not even by the means of knowledge (māna) itself.

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a means of knowledge for the distinction between 'knownness' and so forth, how can there be a cognition of it?"—he says: "Known" (jhāteti). Since it is impossible for it to be accessible through a means of knowledge, the meaning is that the distinction between an object being "known" or "unknown," which resides in the object of knowledge (meyagata), has its comprehension dependent upon the self-luminous Self (svaprakāśātman). This applies also to the "knownness" and so forth residing in the object of knowledge.

Anticipating the objection that [consciousness] might be an object of knowledge (*meyatā*), like the "knownness" (*jñātatva*) residing in a cognition, he says: "By consciousness" (*saṃvidā*). For the knownness of a cognition cannot be established by another means of knowledge (*māna*), as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); therefore, just as that [knownness] is established through experience (*anubhava*), so too is the other [consciousness]. This is the meaning. || 285 ||
Aiming at an object that is unknown, those who possess the conceit of knowledge desire to know it.
Therefore, it is established either by its nature as being known, by its function, or by its result.

In order to state another reason for the fact that the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) is established by experience, he states a point accepted by authoritative persons: "The object (*vastu*), when unknown, is the object of knowledge (*meyam*). By one who asserts this, a means of proving the state of being unknown must be stated; therefore, its establishment [must come] either from the state of being known (*jñātatva*), which is the effect of knowledge, or from the practical activity (*vyavahāra*), which is its fruit. It cannot be the first, because at the time of the state of being known, [the state of being unknown] itself is absent; nor can it be the other, because that [activity] serves as the means of proving the state of being known.
Since it cannot be established by yellow color, he says [the following], considering that its establishment arises from experience alone: "jñātatve" (in the state of being known).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of indicating the refutation of the two aforementioned alternatives. || 286 ||
[Brāhmaṇa] From which the establishment of both the state of being unknown and the state of being known occurs directly. *Ānandagiri’s Commentary entitled Śāstraprakāśikā, Volume 2, Page 193.*
And for that very reason, validity does not depend on another cognition; it is not dependent on a triad.

Anticipating the objection that "the very thing which establishes cognizedness (jñātatva) must also establish non-cognizedness (ajñātatva), because the latter is preceded by the former," he says: "Where... etc. The meaning is this: since the establishment of non-cognizedness arises from that very experience, the direct establishment of cognizedness likewise arises from that same source; therefore, if one accepts that the very factor establishing cognizedness is what establishes non-cognizedness, then both would necessarily be established by experience alone. By this, the first [particle] "eva" is explained.

This has been explained by way of synonyms. Anticipating the objection—“Is it not enough to establish the status of being a means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) that [the object] is unapprehended (*ajñātatva*), and what is the need for experience (*anubhava*)?”—he says:

“*tvām iti*. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: “It is established precisely from the experience under discussion. For this very reason, there is a second *ca* (and). He concludes: “*saṃvidā*,” meaning that the state of being known (*jñātatva*), the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), and the status of being a means of knowledge (*mānatva*) cannot be established without experience. || 287 ||
The state of being unknown, which is the sixth variety of the object-sphere, is observed.
And it is not established like perception, because it relies upon one's own experience. || 288 ||

Anticipating the objection that "whatever exists is an object of knowledge" (*meyam*)—and thus, by this rule, if ignorance (*ajñātatva*) were not an object of knowledge, it would be a mere nothingness (*tucchatā*)—the author states another way [of understanding it] with the words "The sixth... He states the reason why its immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) implies the absence of non-existence: "It is perceived. If that is so, then like a jar established by perception, ignorance would not be an object of knowledge; to this he replies: "And not... If so, how then was it said that "it is perceived"?
To this, he replies: "By one's own experience," etc. (288).
Having experienced the object as distinct from the knower and so forth, one subsequently arises from that state.
"I did not know," he said, in accordance with his own experience.

Anticipating the objection that its establishment is unproven because it cannot be established through self-experience alone in the absence of a means of knowledge (*māna*), he says: "The knower, etc. (*pramātrādi*). The meaning is this: during deep sleep, one experiences the unknown [state] which is distinct from the knower and so forth, by means of self-experience; upon waking, one reflects upon that very experience, thinking, "I did not know [anything]. Therefore, it is established that [ignorance] exists in deep sleep solely on the basis of that experience. || 289 ||
Prior to the emergence of the [five] elements and so forth, there was darkness, because consciousness was not connected to anything else.
Consciousness alone, as the specific qualifier, is known through its own self-experience.

Anticipating the objection—"Why does ignorance (ajñāna), which is associated with the knower (mātṛ) and so forth in the waking state and elsewhere, not likewise appear during sleep?"—the author says "pramātrādi" (knower, etc.). Since the knower and others are absent in sleep, there is no connection of consciousness (cit) with that [ignorance] produced by them; therefore, in that state, only consciousness remains as the substrate for ignorance. Thus, the meaning is that in sleep, it is consciousness itself—untouched by the knower and others, yet qualified by ignorance—that is perceived. This is because of the absence of any cause for the manifestation of those [factors like the knower].
Anticipating the objection that "the cognition of that [dream] occurs during sleep," he says "by one's own experience" (svānubhūtyā), reminding [the reader] of what was stated previously. || 290 ||
This was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, and without defining marks.
"It is beyond reasoning and unknowable"—this is known through one's own direct experience.

Anticipating the objection that the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) is accessible only through experience (*anubhava*), whereas its indicator—the subsequent statement—is contradictory [to that], he says: "It existed" (*āsīt*).

He states the imperceptibility of the world in its prior state with "unperceived" (*aprajñātam*). He states its non-subjectivity to inference with "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇam*). He states its ungraspability by reasoning that establishes or subverts [a conclusion] with "inconceivable" (*apratarkyam*). [He states its ungraspability by] all remaining means of knowledge...
1 kha. ‘Vibhaktā’ | [vol2, page 194] 488

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: He states its excellence with the words "unintelligible" (*avijñeyam*). He says that this statement is not contradictory to the subject matter because it restates what is established by one's own experience, with the words "this very thing" (*ityetad*). || 291 ||
He who manifests himself directly in the grounds such as ignorance and the rest.
That object of knowledge is self-luminous, established prior to its being an object for the knower.

Fearing that if "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) and so forth were not objects of knowledge (*ameya*), then the means of valid cognition (*māna*) would lack an object and thus fail to be valid, he says "It manifests" (*prathate*) to show that this is not the case, because the inner self (*pratīc*), characterized by unknownness, is indeed the object. He states the reason for its being of the nature of immediate consciousness (*pratyakṣasaṃvidrūpa*)—namely, that it is self-manifesting—with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). To the question, "How can this, which is the support for liberation, be an object of perception and the other means of knowledge? he replies with "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*).

[The word] "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes doubtfulness and error. Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction with the previously stated self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) because the Self is said to be an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) regarding those [states], he says: "by itself" (*svayam*). The meaning is that even if it is an object of knowledge when its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is unknown, its self-luminosity is not contradicted. When the aforementioned nature of the thing is known, since non-knowledge is destroyed, it is not an object of [ordinary] means of knowledge (*māna*).

Anticipating this objection, he states that the non-existence of objects after the cessation of conventional usage such as "being a mother" is not a defect, because it occurs prior to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

[He says] "prior" (*prāk*). Alternatively, he provides another reason for its self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣ*), stating that it is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddhatā*) as the very means of proving that [reality], because it manifests inwardly even prior to the differentiation of the knower and so forth. [He says] "prior" (*prāk*). || 292 ||
This very [Self], though uncomprehended by others, has its true nature realized by itself.
Because [the self] was previously measured as being limited to only this much, such as ignorance and so forth. || 293 ||

Since that which is manifesting by itself cannot be unknown, it cannot be an object of knowledge; for it is not the case that only what is already known can be its object, as that would lead to an infinite regress.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "This" (eṣa). The word "only" (eva) is intended to exclude even the non-self from being like the self in terms of being unknown and so forth.
He states that being unknown is not its essential nature: "It is realized... (avagata). He dispels the contradiction with experience by saying: "By itself" (svataḥ).

He establishes that even that which is self-luminous possesses the state of being unknown due to the power of ignorance (*ajñāna*). The phrase "to this extent" means that prior to perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because ignorance pervades pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it is established as being superimposed there; thus, its state of being unknown due to ignorance is logical. || 293 ||
Just as here, in the cognition of a jar, the form of the jar is experienced.
In this way, there is neither the knower nor its witness; there is no other witness for ignorance.

Having stated that the self (*ātman*) is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) by virtue of its being unknown, he states another argument for the fact that its state of being unknown is established through experience even without it being an object of knowledge. [He says] "Just as" (*yathā*). Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "If the self is unknown and thus an object of knowledge, then ignorance (*ajñāna*) must also have it as its object, just as when a man with a staff (*daṇḍin*) is being led away, the bringing of the staff is seen to follow. Anticipating this, he says "Just as": "In the cognition 'I know the jar,' just as the jar and the knower..."

The meaning is this: [objects] are not experienced in this way while one is asleep, because in the state of ignorance, apart from the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the ignorance itself, and the witness (*sākṣin*) who is the prover, no other prover manifests. Even when the knower manifests at the beginning of waking, since ignorance along with its knower is established by the witness alone, it is to be known through that; and because it is to be removed by a means of valid cognition (*māna*), there is no possibility of its being characterized by "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*). Thus, [ignorance] is not experienced as before. || 294 ||
~ Unknowability does not arise from means of knowledge, since knowability is produced by them.
If even by them [the means of knowledge] there were non-cognition, what excellence would there be for the means of knowledge? (295)
1kha. ‘abhāne vā’ | [vol2, page 195]:
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 489.

It has been stated that ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like are not objects of knowledge (*ameya*). In this regard, one might raise the objection: "Even though the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) does not have its manifestation dependent upon the means of knowledge (*māna*), it does require the means of knowledge because its production is dependent upon them. Anticipating this, he says: "The state of being unknown... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "does not arise from the means of knowledge. He states the defect in the opposing view: "By those... [If it were so], would the means of knowledge produce only the state of being unknown, or would they also produce the state of being known (*jñātatā*)? In the first case...

The futility of the means of knowledge (māna) would follow even before its accomplishment; however, in the second case, there would be no distinction [between the object and the state of being known], because "the state of being unknown" would itself be "the state of being known," since it is an effect of the means of knowledge—this is the meaning. || 295 ||
Because it is perfectly established through one's own direct experience, it is not unknown, unlike the horn of a donkey.
Because even consciousness may lack full awakening, there must be a dependence upon that [external] means of knowledge.

Fearing that if there were no production or apprehension of "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) through a means of valid cognition (*māna*), it would be a mere nothingness; and that in the absence of an unknown object, the means of valid cognition could not function because it would lack an object, resulting in the collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), he states the very solution already mentioned repeatedly: "By one's own experience" (*svānubhūtyā*). Now, [an objection may be raised]: since everything that is insentient (*jaḍa*) is established by experience, it has no need for a means of valid cognition; nor does the experience of the Witness (*sākṣin*) require it, as it is the establisher of all.

Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, he states [the following] to show that the futility of the means of knowledge (*māna*) remains as it was: "Because of consciousness" (*saṃvitter*). The construction is as follows: even though experience (*anubhava*) is the establisher of everything, since it is itself unknown, there would be a requirement for a means of knowledge directed toward that Self in order to remove that ignorance. 296.
Like a pot directly perceived before one's eyes, [the Self] is directly manifest in deep sleep, yet it is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge.
For the Self, being devoid of agents, knows itself by itself through its own unity. || 297 ||

Anticipating the objection that experience, being an object of knowledge, cannot be its own prover due to its insentience (*jāḍya*), like a piece of mother-of-pearl, he says: "By perception," and so on.

Just as Caitra perceives a jar through direct perception, so too the Self, during deep sleep, knows itself—which abides in non-dual consciousness within its own majesty—as something immediately present; therefore, how can it be insentient? [Regarding] the Self’s status as a knower, [there may be an objection concerning] the object, the instrument, and so forth—

Fearing that the non-duality [of the Self] would be lost due to the distinction between the factors of action (*kāraka*), and that because it possesses agency (*kartṛtva*) it would lack immutability (*kauṭasthya*), he says: "The Self" (*ātmānam*). By the phrase "to be known by no other," the exclusion of any other substratum is expressed. By "the Self" (*ātma*), another agent is excluded; by "the Self" (*ātmānam*), another object (*karman*); and by "by the Self" (*ātmanā*), another instrument (*karaṇa*). The statement "it is not an agent" (*akāraka*) expresses that, in reality, the Self lacks agency and so forth; this is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self.

The mention of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is intended to clarify the absence of any distinction among causal factors (*kāraka*) for one who knows; the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish his status as a knower. The reason for the absence of distinctions among causal factors is stated as "due to oneness of self" (*aikātmyāt*). || 297 ||
With a gaze directed outward, he perceives knowledge residing within himself.
Like the blackness of the sky and so forth, that which is produced from it is conceived [as such], but not by itself.

Anticipating the objection that—since the non-inert experience, as the knower of the object through its state of being unknown, establishes that state of being unknown and so forth, the state of being unknown must itself be a real entity (vastu) because it is established by experience, just like the object—he says: "parāk" (turned away). First, the Self undergoes the superimposition of identity with beginningless, established ignorance, according to the Śruti: "The power of the Divine Self is hidden by its own qualities. Consequently, [the Self] attains identity with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is an effect of that [ignorance].

The superimposer, through an outward-turned vision, conceives of ignorance and its effects within himself (but this possibility does not exist there according to the true nature of the Self); the meaning is that it is just as children project objects and so forth onto the sky. || 298 ||
1. Vṛttamā | 62 [vol2, page 196]
Neither ignorance, nor false knowledge, nor doubt is perceived [as the cause]. *Suresvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter.

[Objection: Just as there is the possibility of ignorance and so forth regarding the external [object] through the outward-turned vision, why should there not also be the possibility of ignorance and so forth regarding the inward [Self] through the inward-turned vision during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep? [The author] says "no" with the words "not at all.

The meaning is that by means of the vision following the Self, there can never be the possibility of ignorance and so forth in That, because that would lead to the consequence of no liberation (anirmokṣa). || 299 ||
There is no recollection such as "I did not know" regarding the consciousness of deep sleep.
Because it is not separated by time and so forth, it abides within the self and partakes of the past. (300)

[Objection: Granted that through the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*) ignorance and the like do not exist there [in deep sleep], yet the knowability of ignorance must be admitted even without a [present] experience, because of the recollection (*parāmarśa*) of the ignorance of deep sleep by one who has awakened, namely, "I was not aware of anything. And this recollection is not possible without a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), nor does an experience produce such an impression [since it is eternal]; therefore, the ignorance of deep sleep is knowable only through experience. [Reply: No, he says with the words beginning with "no" (*na*). It is memory (*smṛti*).
The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—the realization upon waking that "I was not conscious"—is the indicator of an occasional experience regarding the ignorance existing during the time of sleep;

he states the reason why this is not the case [in the following]: "Because of time, etc. Since the Self is devoid of spatial and temporal separation, the ignorance residing therein is likewise not connected to them. Thus, both the ignorance expressed as "I did not know" and the prior time are superimposed upon the Witness (*sākṣin*) by that very [Witness] itself.
The meaning is that because it is not perceived as an object of sight, there is no latent impression (saṃskāra) here. || 300 ||
It does not touch the past, nor is it seen to touch the future; it is inward-looking.
The teaching for one's own benefit is the goal for oneself; the goal for others is conceptual construction; by that [distinction], it is remembered. || 301 ||

To explain how the Self has no connection with time and so forth, he says: "No. This means according to the Śruti: "Other than what has been and what is to be. Furthermore, because space and all else are its very nature as the inner self (pratyak), it has no connection with them; thus he says: "The inner self" (pratyaṅ). For without a connection between those two, their coexistence would result in the loss of non-duality; thus he says: "For its own sake" (svārtha). Every insentient thing, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope...

Therefore, since it applies to the non-insentient cow and so forth, that [conceptual content] is held by the elders to be "following upon word and cognition" yet "devoid of a real object"; what loss of non-duality (advaita) is there in this?
Such is the meaning. || 301 ||
For pastness is not perceived through direct sensory cognition.
And since the object of cognition is not in the future, there would therefore be no false knowledge.
Anticipating the objection that [the object] is fashioned as present time because it is established by perception and other means, he says: "Not indeed," etc.

Since perception grasps only what is present, it does not grasp [an object's] pastness and so forth; nor is its establishment possible through inference, for that too [grasps only] the present, not the non-present.

Since the relationship of object and subject is possible only between consciousness and its object, pastness and so forth are merely imagined; thus, the meaning is that this [imagined nature] is established even in other insentient things, as in the case of the example. || 302 ||
Whatever is the true nature of a thing, that thing does not transcend it.
A snake that has not recognized the rope does not exist beyond the rope. || 303 ||

Fearing that the imagined might be thought to be distinct from its substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), which would strike at the heart of non-duality (advaita), he says: "That which is of the nature of reality" (yattattvakam). To provide an illustration for the point that the imagined is not in reality different from that [substrate], he says: "Not as ignorance" (nājñāna). || 303 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 197] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 491.
Therefore, the unborn one remains constant throughout the three states that come and go.
For the Self perceives itself as eternally existent by means of its own unimpaired vision. || 304 ||

Fearing that if the imagined (*kalpita*) and the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were identical, then like the imagined, the other would also be false as an effect, resulting in the appearance of a void (*tuccha-khyāti*), he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that although the superimposed object lacks existence apart from the substrate, the substrate exists independently; thus, there is no appearance of a void. Since the Self (*ātman*) is by its own nature devoid of modification through the consciousness of its true essence...

The construction is as follows: because it always experiences itself, therefore it is immutable (*kūṭastha*) throughout all three states; this is the meaning of the word *hi* (for), which indicates that the coming and going of the states and the changelessness of the Self are well-established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 304 ||
The same applies even to other bodies, due to their mutual variability.
The internal cognition alone is the one that is non-deviating in all cases.
[Objection: But surely the Self is not immutable, because—like the mind—it appears to undergo modification due to its being distinct in each body; to this, he replies:
"In other bodies... Just as the Self is accepted by both disputants as one in a single body, so too must it be accepted in all bodies.

Because that [consciousness] is non-deviant everywhere, whereas the body and so forth are mutually deviant, and because there is no evidence for a plurality of selves, the meaning is that the self is non-dual and eternally unchanging (*kūṭastha*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the absence of evidence for a plurality of selves in each body. || 305 ||
Existing as the very nature of pure consciousness, ignorance manifests within the Self.
Because it is established in the directly perceived immutable [Self], that which is other than the cause is sublated by it. // 306 //

Having stated that the entire duality, along with its cause, is false—like a snake [superimposed] on a rope—by pointing out the fallibility of the body and so forth, he now states the result, preceded by another reason for that very point: "Consciousness... Ignorance and knowledge in the Self appear as devoid of any form other than consciousness; for they abide in that immutable (kūṭastha) Self, just as a snake [appears] in a rope. Therefore, from that knowledge arising from the [great] sentence, that which was imagined by it—the cause together with its effects—is [sublated].
The meaning is that it is to be sublated. || 306 ||
It could not be so in their own effects, because those [effects] have that very nature as their cause.
No form other than that which is insentient by nature is perceived in effects. (307)

Anticipating the objection that ignorance does not reside in the immutable inner self (pratyak-kuṭastha) because it resides in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, he says: "Not so. He provides the reason why ignorance cannot exist in the internal organ and so forth as it does in the inner self: "Of those," etc. He establishes through experience that the internal organ and so forth are of the nature of ignorance by stating: "Inert," etc. (307).
If this is so, then what is the difference between these two, cause and effect, as measured by cognition?
Through both positive and negative concomitance, it does not transcend insentience. || 308 ||

He states the implied meaning: that since the effects of ignorance are nothing but ignorance itself, it is established by valid means of knowledge (*māna*) that there is no difference between cause and effect.

This is expressed by the words "If this is so" (*evaṃ cet*). As for the reason for rejecting the difference between cause and effect, which was stated in the passage beginning with "because of its insentient nature" (*jaḍasvabhāvāt*), [that is as follows].
1. *kha*: *si* (corrected).
[Vol.
2, Page 198] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

He establishes that [point] with the words "anvaya" (positive concomitance), etc. Since an effect is observed only when ignorance exists, and is not observed when it does not exist, the effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*) are born [of ignorance].
The meaning is that, having transcended cognition, it does not remain independent. || 308 ||
Therefore, it is real because it does not possess the nature of either the effect or the cause.
Self-knowledge alone shines forth everywhere, realized through one's own self.
Anticipating the objection that there is no fixed rule that ignorance alone is the cause of the intellect and so forth—since there are disputes among various theorists—he says: "The effect," etc.

Ignorance, established by one's own experience, manifests everywhere in the world both as the effect and as the cause; and that [ignorance], when endowed with the supreme reality called the Self which is free from both [effect and cause], leaves behind only that non-duality (advaita). Thus, the word "therefore" [refers to] the effect and the cause.
One who reflects upon the impossibility of another form [of the object]. || 309 ||
An insentient thing does not obtain its own self by means of itself as an intrinsic nature.
Therefore, that is the locus of its own purpose, and its own purpose is established by nothing else.

Anticipating the objection—“How is it that no other form [of these two] is possible apart from ignorance?”—he says: “Not at all. For that which is insentient (jaḍa) does not obtain existence or manifestation by its own nature due to its insentiency, just like silver and the like; therefore, it is imagined within the non-dual inner self (pratīci), because of its insentiency, just as the body is imagined to be the self. [The opponent asks: “How can the non-insentient Self be for its own sake (svārthatva)? [The answer is: Even for that, there is the superimposition upon the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-āropa).
Anticipating the objection that "because it is one of the two [superimposed things], it must depend on another substratum," he says: "If for its own sake...
The meaning is that since the other [the superimposed] cannot be sublated in its own essential nature, there is no dependence on another substratum. || 310 ||
If [the Self] is awakened by itself, whence could there be ignorance? Without that, whence could there be saṃsāra?
This speech belongs to one whose nature is awakened to suchness; it does not belong to one who is enveloped in darkness.

Since ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like are contradictory to that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it cannot be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); for it is not the case that [the self] is merely so [self-luminous].

Anticipating this objection, the author considers the alternatives—whether the statement of contradiction refers to the knower of the Self (*ātmavit*) or to someone else—and accepts the first. He says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). The sense is that from the perspective of the enlightened one (*vidvat*), since ignorance and its effects do not exist in the Self, it is precisely intended that the Self lacks the status of being a substratum. He refutes the second alternative.

"No," [it is said]. Since the true nature does not manifest during the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), such a statement of contradiction does not apply to the ignorant person. Thus, from the perspective of the ignorant, because ignorance and its effects exist within the Inner Self (*pratīcī*), it remains indisputably their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This is the intended meaning. || 311 ||
Just as for one whose delusion regarding the self has been severed, there is no denial even of the destroyer.
Thus, prior to the awakening to the Self, there is the concealment of non-dual oneness.

Anticipating the objection that because [the Self] is self-luminous, the non-dual bliss shines forth even at the time of ignorance, and thus there is no room for conceptualization, he says: "Just as... Just as the concealment (*nihuti*) of the knower—one whose ignorance has been dispelled and who possesses the knowledge that destroys ignorance—or of the mother is accepted by virtue of [her] knowledge, so too, prior to the arising of that knowledge, the concealment of the non-dual blissful Self—a mere false construction—is indeed logical through the power of ignorance.
This is the meaning. || 312 ||
This cycle of existence is like the night for both the crow and the owl, who do not know their own true nature.
"Whatever is night for all beings," thus Hari himself has spoken. [1.313] [vol2,
page 199]
4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 493.

He provides an illustration for the fact that, from the perspective of the wise, the "measure" (*mātrā*) and so forth do not exist, whereas from the perspective of the ignorant, the reality (*tattva*) does not exist. [He says: "The owl...
When that night which is well-known to crows and others occurs, the owl remains awake; thus, from its perspective, that [night] is denied [as being night]. And when the crows—...

The meaning is as follows: when those who see by day are awake, then for those who see by night, it is "night"; thus, by the perspective of crows and the like, that [day] is denied. In the same way, when this worldly cycle of mother and so forth manifests for the ignorant, then from their perspective, the reality is imagined as non-existent; and when there is the realization of reality for the wise, then from their perspective, mother and so forth are non-existent. Thus he states the application of the analogy with the words "this" (*ayam*). In that regard, the Blessed One—

He cites a scriptural statement as proof: "That which is night for all beings... That state of Brahman which exists like night for all living beings—indeed, in that state no one is awake—is being denied by the ignorant; yet the man of knowledge has arrived therein. From his perspective, there is an absence of objects such as mother and so forth. Furthermore, that state of ignorance in which all those wandering in saṃsāra deny reality is "night" for the wise man whose ignorance has been dispelled.

The meaning is that the Blessed One has stated this distinction: that because cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is non-existent, the mother and so forth are non-existent from the perspective of one who knows reality (*tattva*), whereas they appear to exist from the perspective of one who does not know it. || 313 ||
Therefore, its form is not real, as it does not effect the removal of darkness and the like.
Even while that [reality] exists, delusion and so forth have not previously arisen prior to its realization.
(314) Although the true nature of reality does not manifest due to ignorance during the state of non-knowing, nevertheless, this ignorance does not exist within self-luminous consciousness.

Then, raising the objection that [ignorance] would not cease because there is no remover—since light does not remove that which is dependent upon itself—the author considers the alternative of whether it is the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) or the knowledge derived from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) that is the remover; he accepts the first [position] with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He clarifies the meaning of the word *tat* (that) itself with the words "In that" (*tasmin*). "Vyutpatti" refers to the knowledge derived from the means of valid cognition. || 314 ||
Established by valid means of knowledge, this very [wisdom] destroys ignorance and the rest without remainder.
"Therefore, those who know Brahman have diligently relied upon this as the authoritative means here.

(315) [This] refutes another alternative view. Regarding the term "authoritative" (*pramāṇa*): although the knowledge that constitutes valid cognition does not cease by itself, for the Self which is the Seer—

The meaning is that its accomplishment [is achieved] through the door [of this means]. This very reality, when mounted upon the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) arising from the sentence, removes ignorance and everything born thereof;

thus, he states the two positions that indicate this: either "knowledge ignited by the intellect" (*buddhy-eddho bodhaḥ*) or "the intellect ignited by knowledge" (*bodh-eddhā buddhiḥ*), which destroys non-knowledge and so forth.

By the phrase "by those who know Brahman," he shows that, according to the stated method, because valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) destroys ignorance, the Vedāntas [are established] with respect to Brahman.

Validity has been accepted by the learned. For it has been stated: "But [the scripture] is established as authoritative because it brings about cessation [of ignorance]. Furthermore, beginning from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra up to the end of the chapter, great effort has been exerted by the authors of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya and others on this point; the meaning is that otherwise, its validity would not be established in the case of self-luminous consciousness. || 315 ||
Likewise, the Śruti itself [states] "whether ignorant," preceded by a question.
"One discerns the manifest reality clearly by the very path already described.

(316.11) He says "Moreover" to show that it is not only presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that serves as the means of knowledge here, but that scripture (*śruti*) as well corroborates both positions.

Now, therefore, follow the further questions: "Does even one who does not know go to that world after death? and so forth. Since Brahman is common to both the knower and the non-knower, the text—beginning with "He desired" (so 'kāmayata)—first poses the question as to whether even the non-knower attains it, or whether only the knower attains it, or perhaps neither. This concludes the section [kha].
494 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 200]

The meaning is that by means of proving the existence of Brahman, the scriptural passage beginning with "When indeed he [sees] in this... clearly determines the fruit according to the two aforementioned positions through the knowledge of That. The explanation of the word "tathā" (thus) is given by the words "yathā" (just as), etc. || 396 ||
Because it relies solely on the form arising from the object that is unique to the self.
Even that [cognition] attains the status of being a means of valid cognition, and not merely [the object] alone. // 317 //

To the question, "How is it that an object mounted upon the intellect arising from a sentence destroys one's own ignorance and so forth, while that which is mounted upon knowledge produced by the eyes and other senses does not do so? he replies: "The Self. That is, the knowledge which arises regarding the Self alone from a sentence— [...is what destroys ignorance.]

The meaning is that [the cognition] attains the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) by dispelling the ignorance and other defects residing therein through its reliance on that [object] alone; however, another cognition, while grasping a different form, is not a means of valid knowledge with respect to itself, but rather with respect to the jar and so forth—thus the qualification is meaningful. The phrase "that is the means of knowledge" (*tanmānam*) is a statement regarding the cognition arising from the sentence.

The particle *api* expresses possibility. Because it has arisen with respect to that unique object (*asādhāraṇe 'rthe*), it possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge with respect to that [self].

The reason is that [consciousness] carries only that form; it is not merely [consciousness] alone, which excludes other modes of functioning (*vṛtti*). This is the distinction based on the Vedic scripture beginning with "The senses are directed outward" (*parāñci khāni*). Alternatively, one might raise the objection: why is it postulated that consciousness, when ignited by the intellect (*buddhi*), destroys ignorance, rather than consciousness alone? For consciousness, as the means of knowledge (*māna*) that establishes everything, is independent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Self" (*ātma*). Although...

The consciousness that constitutes one’s own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*), termed "awakening" (*bodha*), is indeed the means of knowledge (*māna*) by virtue of being the establisher of all things; nevertheless, it attains the status of a means of knowledge—consisting in the destruction of its own inherent ignorance and its effects—only through the assistance of that cognition which takes the form of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) arising from the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*) and assuming the aspect of the Self as the non-dual reality of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). It is not the case that consciousness alone, independent of the mental modification produced by the saying, [attains this status].

The meaning is that cognition which has already been liberated cannot attain the status of a means of knowledge (*mānatva*), because it is impossible for that [cognition] to remove what has already been accomplished by it. Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "Why should cognition ignited by [the means of] awakening dispel ignorance along with its effects? Let the cognition arising from the sentence itself dispel it, since as a means of knowledge it possesses the power to do so within its own result.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Self" (*ātma*). Although the knowledge derived from the sentence is indeed a means of knowledge, nevertheless, of the Self—

The meaning that has been explained as common [to all]—that which is manifested in its true nature (*tāttvika-rūpa*) by means of that [common object]—it is precisely through the support of that alone that this knowledge attains the status of a valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇya*), because it consists in the destruction of ignorance and so forth. However, mere functional cognition (*vṛtti-jñāna*) would not attain the aforementioned status of being a valid means of cognition; for being insentient (*jaḍa*), it is impossible for it to possess that [status] without the power of the objective reality (*vastu-bala*). This is the meaning. || 317 ||
Because of the nature of the inner self as the reality of that alone.
Just as there is no distinction in the case of what is external, so too there is no distinction here within the inner self (pratyagātman) regarding the measures (mātrā) and so forth. // 318 //

Now, at the time of the arising of knowledge from a sentence, does the distinction of the *mātrā*s and so forth exist or not? In the first case, even the knowledge arising from a sentence would grasp another form and would thus be similar to the cognition of a jar or other objects. In the second case, there would be no arising of that [knowledge] due to the absence of a cause; to this, he says: "only that much" (*tāvanmātra*).

Just as there is a distinction of *mātrā*s and so forth in the case of sounds and the like, there is no such distinction in the inner self (*pratīci*); for in that [self], it remains exactly as it was at the time of the arising of knowledge, even at other times.

The meaning is this: although that [world] exists here while knowledge has not yet arisen, it does not exist after [the dawn of knowledge]; for, since the mere world consisting of the mother and so forth is sublated by being inseparable from that birth [of knowledge], it culminates in the form of that one true nature of reality, which is the inward Self (pratyag-vastu). || 318 ||
One assumes agency solely through the back of delusion, as if possessing the appearance of speech.
Even while abiding [therein], it does not, by its own nature, turn inward in dependence upon the functions of the self. || 319 ||
It has been stated that after the arising of knowledge, the mother and others, being sublated, become nothing but the inner self (pratyak). Now, regarding that knowledge...
[Vol.
2, page 201] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 495.

Fearing that if the agent were either the inner self (*pratyagātman*) or something else, there would be a loss of immutability (*kauṭasthya*) in the first case and a loss of non-duality (*advaita*) in the second, he first dispels the second defect with the words "svacid" (by its own consciousness). He then removes the first defect with the words "kūṭastho 'pi" (even though it is immutable). The meaning is that there is no loss of real immutability for the agent, because [the agency] occurs through the medium of *moha* accompanied by the reflection of its own consciousness. If the Self were the agent, then...

"Let it be so by itself; what is the use of delusion? And let there not be immutability (kūṭasthatva)," [to this] he says "no. The meaning is: for it is impossible to even suspect agency in the inner self (pratyagātman), which is established by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts as being unattached, non-dual, and immutable, once delusion has been removed. || 319 ||
Thus, when the two eyes of perception are established as being self-evident witnesses to all modifications of the intellect, [the Self is realized].
Those who assert that experience is the effect must state the means by which that effect is accomplished.

By stating that "cognition is impelled by the intellect (*buddhi*), or the intellect is impelled by cognition, and thus [the latter] destroys ignorance," it was asserted that consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is not an effect but rather immutable (*kūṭastha*).
Now, by restating the preceding argument and repeating an alternative position, he refutes it with the words "all... and so forth.

He refers back to what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "that which possesses non-obscured consciousness" etc. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the totality of the intellect and its modifications, consisting of both the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*).

The meaning is as follows: since the seer-self (dṛgātman), which is the substrate of the flavors (rasādhaka), is established by the previously stated reasoning—beginning with "devoid of all relations" and so forth—as being naturally free from modification, those who maintain that it undergoes an effect or experience even without the association of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) must provide proof for its being an effect; yet such proof cannot be stated. || 320 ||
"It is not born, it is unborn," and so forth, as well as "the mass of consciousness."
Why is this statement, which completely excludes the activity of males, being disregarded? || 321 ||
He states that if experience were an effect, there would not only be a lack of evidence, but also a contradiction with authoritative testimony: "It is not born," etc.

He explains the intended meaning of the scriptural and traditional passages already shown: "In its entirety," etc. And because that [scriptural statement] is free from defect, he states that it is not to be disregarded:
Prior to its arising from "I" and so forth, a causal agent is difficult to find through valid cognition.
In the absence of that [agent], there is an absence of action; without that [action], how can there be the state of being an effect? || 322 ||

[Objection: "But surely the statement declaring the immutable nature (*kūṭasthatva*) of the inner self (*pratīc*) does not contradict the fact that experience is an effect; [if you say] it does, we reply: 'Not so,' because that [experience] is non-different from the Self. Thinking thus, he states another reason for its being a non-effect: "The knower (*pramātṛ*), etc. First of all, there is no causal factor (*kāraka*) for experience during deep sleep, because at that time the knower and the other factors are absent. Consequently, since there is no action to be accomplished by them, there is no resulting effect (*kārya*) pervaded by such action.
The meaning is "steadfastness. || 322 ||
And this very point is admitted by you as well, solely on the basis of experience.
Even by one who is skillful, the activity of a causal agent is not perceived therein. || 323 ||

[The opponent asks: "In deep sleep there is no experience at all; how then can its being a non-product (akāryatva) be established? To this he replies: "And this... The meaning is that deep sleep is accepted by both of us precisely on the basis of experience, since there is no other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) to establish it; therefore, there is no dispute regarding its existence. The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "like the distinction between the knower and so forth. The word "also" (api) indicates that this is a point agreed upon by both parties. [The opponent objects: "If that experience of deep sleep exists..."

Anticipating the objection that there might also be a causal agent (*kāraka*) therein because of the conceptualization of it through its effect, he says: "The causal agent... For indeed, in deep sleep...
[Suresvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Chapter, page 202].
