The meaning is that the activity of the mother and others is not perceived even by one with subtle vision; nor is its existence established through the impossibility of [otherwise] accounting for experience, since such experience can be accounted for even by [the agency of] something that is not an effect. || 323 ||
If the cause were non-performing [of its effect], then the effect would likewise exist at all times.
When these two arise simultaneously, there is no determination of which one is the effect and which is the other. || 324 ||

Anticipating the objection that its status as an effect might be established because it is perceived only at certain times—just like a jar—and that it is not perceived at all times since this would entail the non-perception of other effects—the author, wishing to refute that very status as an effect and desiring to negate the causal relationship itself, first considers the two alternatives regarding whether a cause is "non-productive" (*akurvat*) or "productive" (*kurvat*), and then refutes the first by stating: "Non-productive... That cause, moreover, must be either eternal or non-eternal.

The meaning is that in the first case, the effect would also be eternal, just like the cause, because there is no distinction between them. In the second case, there must be either simultaneity or succession between the two; regarding the first of these, he states the fault: "kārya... (the effect...). For indeed, the cognition of those two [horns] does not arise when they have been produced simultaneously. || 324 ||
From a single cause alone, there arise multiple effects that are mutually contradictory.
There would be an over-extension [of the consequence] to one who does not act, because there is no distinction in the state of not acting. || 325 ||

Even in the case of a sequential order, it is not the case that the effect comes first and the cause afterwards, because such a sequence is undesirable; rather, the cause comes first and the effect afterwards.

He states the fault in this [opposite] position as "contradictory" (*viruddha*). Now, one might object: "Since those [effects] are contradictory, it is not logical for them to arise from a single [cause].
Anticipating this, he argues that since the cause is equally non-active in all cases, its capacity to produce or its incapacity to produce would be indistinguishable.
Thus he said: "Let them not do so. || 325 ||
If that which performs its respective function is indeed the agent of that effect, then let it be called "bhavya" (the future).

"The production of what is not to be produced" is the speech of one who is asleep or insane. [The author] raises another alternative with the word "atha" (now/if). [He asks: Is it that which produces always producing, or is it the effect? In the first case, the effect would also be eternal; he rejects the second with the words "tatkāryam" (that effect). "Tatkāryam" means that for which there is an effect—that is, the cause—[is so designated]. [The word] "kārya" (effect)...
The meaning is that it must be stated [as follows]: the point is that if it were an effect (*kāryatva*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to its dependence on further causes.

Having stated the infinite regress caused by the fact that the agent (*kartṛtva*) is an effect, he says "it is not an effect" (*akāryam*), intending to show that the same [infinite regress] applies to its substratum as well because of its being an effect. This is because, according to the principle that "a causal factor (*kāraka*) is a cause performing an action (*kriyā*)," the status of being a causal factor belongs to that which is colored by action, and [action]...

The meaning is as follows: because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatvāt*), even that which is qualified by it is likewise [occasional]; thus, the causal agent is not the effect. Therefore, this is not based on prior intelligence (*abuddhipūrvaka*); and because there would otherwise be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), the relationship of cause and effect is merely imagined (*kalpita*). Regarding the statement "if the cause were devoid of action" (*niṣkriyaṃ kāraṇaṃ cet syāt*), the imagined nature of the causal relation was stated there by way of action (*kriyādvārā*); however, here the statement is made by taking the cause itself as the primary focus. Thus, there is no redundancy (*apaunaruktya*). 326.
Under my supervision, Nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving.
Thus is the perfectly coherent statement of the illustrious Sureśa. || 327 ||
In this regard, he cites the word of the Blessed One as authority: "By me. The meaning of "thus" is: when the relationship of cause and effect has been conceptually constructed. || 327 ||
In the object of cognition, in the action, in the means of cognition, and in the cognizer.
Because it has that power as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and cause, consciousness (*cit*) appears as if being born from the earth.
[Vol.
2, page 203] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramakaranda* composed by Ānandagiri. 497.

Since, according to the reasoning stated, the relationship of cause and effect is difficult to define, and since experience is not an effect, how can its status as an effect be established? To this he replies: "And with regard to the object of knowledge" (*prameye ca*). The meaning is that although experience is immutable and eternal, it appears as if it were being produced due to the cause consisting of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance regarding the objects of measurement and so forth. The word *kriyā* refers to the contact between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. The word *atha* is a synonym for *tathā* (thus).
The meaning is "conjunction" (samuccaya). || 328 ||
Just as no entity whatsoever is established apart from its own negation.
Likewise, because the non-existence of a jar and so forth is impossible without [the existence of] that [ground], || 329 ||

[Objection: "In that case, since the jar and so forth are the cause (nimitta) and consciousness is the effect (naimittika), there is a distinction between the two; thus, non-duality (advaita) is lost. Furthermore, if they were non-distinct, the relationship of cause and effect would be untenable. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Just as... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "...as was shown in the investigation of the jar. [Regarding] cause and effect...

However, it is considered that the state of being a pot and so forth arises from an imagined distinction. [The opponent objects: "If there is no distinction from consciousness (*cit*), then there would be non-distinction; since there can be no other alternative that is mutually contradictory, it follows that consciousness possesses manifoldness (*saprapañcatā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the same way" (*tadvat*). The connection is as follows: even by way of non-distinction, there is no existence of anything whatsoever as something distinct. The reason for this is that, in the case of non-difference, only pure Being (*sanmātra*) remains, and consequently, things such as a jar or its absence become impossible.
He said: "Compose it. || 329 ||
For indeed, even a non-existent entity cannot be established apart from the existent.
Since that [non-existence] also depends upon existence, what else could it be without existence? (330)

Having stated that the existent [cause], such as the material cause (*mātrādi*), cannot be both different and non-different [from its effect], he states another reason for the impossibility of difference with the words "For not" (*na hi*).

By the contradiction between the existent and the non-existent, he shows the attainment of difference of the non-existent from the existent with the word "even" (*api*). The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Regarding the reason why the non-existent is certainly not established as distinct from the existent, he provides the reason following the word *hi*: "Of that too" (*tasyāpi*). By the word *api*, the argument *a fortiori* (*kaimutika*) is indicated.

He states the logical argument: "What else could it be? The meaning is: what need is there to say that a jar or the like would not exist without Being (*sat*), since if it were distinct from Being, it would necessarily follow that it is a mere nothingness (*tucchatva*). || 330 ||
Just as he does not even entertain the possibility of being deceived by such a consciousness.
Or even if it were of the nature of non-existence, it would be the same because it is not distinct from that [object]. || 331 ||

Having refuted the mutual difference and non-difference between existence and non-existence, he now refutes those two [properties] with respect to consciousness (*saṃvit*). He says "just as" (*yathā*): just as neither existence nor non-existence is possible without consciousness—because they are insentient (*jaḍa*), for an insentient object cannot be established by transcending that [consciousness]—nor can its establishment result from a relation with it, because such a relation is difficult to define; likewise, neither an entity-form nor a non-entity-form [belongs] to consciousness.

Since nothing is found apart from its own essence—due to the fact that one of the two would necessarily remain—it follows that the reality consisting solely of pure Being (sanmātra), whose sole flavor is consciousness, is established;
this is the meaning. || 331 ||
Neither ignorance nor its effect [is real], because they are neither non-different from it nor distinct from it.
Since it is established [only] in this way, it must be "established without investigation" (avicāritasiddhika).
To the question, "What then is the status of the world that appears? he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). || 332 ||
The sky has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, and the darkness is like the interior of a bee.
In this way, let darkness and that which is born from it be regarded as established even without being investigated.
498 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter] — [Vol. 2, p. 204]

He provides an illustration for the fact that duality is established without inquiry: "Blue," etc. Furthermore, regarding those who claim that even space is possessed of color and is perceptible by the eye, he says: "The bee," etc. He states that because both space and the absence of light are devoid of color, they are merely imagined:
"Without inquiry," etc. He states the application to the subject at hand: "In this way," etc. (333)
That which is by nature unperceived cannot be established by its own power.
When existence and non-existence are rejected by their very nature as not being real entities, [then that is established]. (334)

He states another reason for the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest are established without being investigated: "by its own power" (*svamahimnā*). The meaning is that since the insentient (*jaḍa*) is not established by itself, its establishment occurs through its being superposed upon the non-insentient (*ajaḍa*). Anticipating the objection that because the non-insentient is also superposed—due to mutual superposition—it is likewise sublated like the insentient, resulting in the absence of self (*nairātmya*), he says: "being" (*bhāva*). Since the Self does not touch birth and destruction, both of those are excluded from it.

The meaning is this: because they serve as witnesses to one another even in mutual superimposition, they are not deluded by their own insentience; since there is no superimposition of their own true nature [upon themselves], there is no lack of selfhood (nairātmya). || 334 ||
Therefore, although she is indeed unborn, she appears as if being born.
"Through the birth of the self, which arises from the cause that is ignorance of that [Self], there is the experience [of it].

(335) — He concludes that birth and so forth are imagined with respect to the Reality by the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that the cognition of birth in Consciousness occurs by virtue of the birth of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) produced by the ignorance of Consciousness. (335)
Even upon its destruction, because it is witnessed by that [Self], it appears as if it were perishing.
Therefore, even the Lord could not establish its status as an effect.

He states that the cognition of destruction regarding it [the Self] arises solely from the destruction of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), by saying: "Even upon its destruction. He states the consequence regarding the absence of birth and so forth for that [Self] by its own nature, with the words: "Since... (verse 336).
Apart from being witnessed by one's own self, there is no other reality for things consisting of existence and non-existence.
Since there is no proof [of such change], therefore [the Self] is devoid of all modification, as established by the counter-argument. || 337 ||
Fearing the objection that, in the absence of birth and destruction, other modifications must exist and thus there can be no immutability (*kūṭasthatā*), he says: "One's own Self" (*svātma*).
The meaning is that for the witness of all modifications, there is no modification whatsoever. || 337 ||
For every effect is observed to be preceded by prior non-existence.
Since even that [non-existence] has consciousness as its witness, there is no prior non-existence of consciousness.

1. He states another reason for the non-existence of consciousness (*saṃvit*). [He says] "the effect" (*kāryam*). The implication is that, therefore, if consciousness were also an effect, its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would have to be asserted.
To this he replies, "Of that" (*tasya*), meaning: let it be granted then that consciousness also possesses prior non-existence; [but] it is not so.
The meaning is that consciousness is not produced because it lacks prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), just like that which is generally accepted [as eternal]. || 338 ||
Its form is not cognized apart from the subject and so forth.
This object of knowledge is not established anywhere other than from the Veda.
1 ga. sākṣādvi | [vol2, page 205] 4.
Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Nakha-prakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 499

Having stated that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is immutable (*kūṭasthā*), he speaks of its state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) in that very same context with the words "mama atrādīti. Here, the construction is as follows: in this immutable consciousness itself, there exists a state of being unknown—an unperceived form—which is to be known as the object of measurement (*meyam*), distinct from the knower (*mātṛ*) and so forth. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it has been established that the state of being unknown does not depend upon the knower and the other factors. How, then, is that [state] to be known?

He says this: "This [is so]. *Veda* means knowledge or experience; apart from that—that is, excluding it—this state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) is not established even when some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists, but rather only from experience itself. Alternatively, since it was just stated that the state of being unknown resides in consciousness (*saṃvit*) alone, he now states the meaning of the particle *eva*: "This [is so]. The meaning is that apart from experience, this state of being unknown does not exist in any other substratum whatsoever.

Alternatively, he states what the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is regarding that experience in which this "state of being unknown" resides: "Not [by anything else]. The meaning is that the Vedic statement alone is the authority (*māna*) in that regard; apart from that, if there were some other authority or reasoning (*tarka*), this reality of experience would not be established. || 339 ||
"In this regard, with respect to the actual state of things, darkness [arises] both from itself and from another."
Or rather, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) in relation to that which arises from it or to that very [state]. || 340 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "Of that whose experience is the object, its ignorance must be either a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*). If it is a real entity, then because that which is produced by it is also a real entity, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) is lost. If it is a non-entity, then because experience does not have it as its object, it would follow that it is not an object of knowledge (*ameyatva*). To this, he replies: "The state of reality" (*vastuvṛttam*). Ignorance and that which is born from it do not establish themselves—either as non-different or as different—from the non-dual, self-luminous reality (*vasturūpa*), because there can be no non-difference between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*).

The meaning is this: because difference is contradictory [to unity], and because it is difficult to define whether it is the essence (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*), ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like cannot be established through themselves; for if they were distinct from the Self (*ātman*), that would be impossible, and their non-distinctness has already been refuted. Nor can they be established through another, because a relation cannot be defined. Therefore, the point is that ignorance and so forth are "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*). [Objection: One might argue that there is no "indescribability" for the darkness (*tamas*) denoted by the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*), because being "describable" contradicts its very nature. To this, [the author] says:

Thus it is said: "That darkness" (*tattamaḥ*). It is not that there is an "inexpressibility" (*avācyatva*) or "indescribability" (*anirvācyatva*); rather, what is under discussion here is the "undefinability" (*durnirūpatva*) of the entity.
This undefinability, in relation to darkness, is expressed by the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*); for it has been stated that it cannot be defined either by itself or by another.
This is the meaning. || 340 ||
Darkness should be understood as the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), because of the perception [of it] in the form "I did not know."
The birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the world occur thus within the Supreme Self.

Since ignorance is unestablished in both ways, it is not established even in one way; for it cannot be established by any other means. How then, with respect to that [ignorance], can there be the term "unmanifest" (avyākṛta) for the other? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāsa). In that which belongs to consciousness...

The meaning is that darkness (*tamas*) must be known through its very manifestation (*ābhāsa*), because otherwise it would be impossible to know that which is inexpressible. Regarding the point that the establishment of darkness depends upon manifestation, he provides experiential evidence with the word "not" (*na*). To the question, "Why [is this so]?"—that is, why does the Supreme possess the designation "unmanifested" (*avyākṛta*) due to its association with the aforementioned darkness—he replies with the word "the world" (*jagat*). [The meaning is: in the Supreme, when qualified by ignorance or dependent upon it, the world...
The meaning is that the term "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) is used for that [Brahman] in order to state that it is Brahman, which is pure from birth, or rather, ignorance (*ajñāna*). || 341 ||
Tamas is predominant among the fields (kṣetra), which have as their essence consciousness and whose nature is consciousness.
The Supreme attains the state of being the cause through meditative cultivation, gnosis, and action.

Raising the objection as to how the distinction between the sentient and the insentient appears in the world, which is an effect if the Supreme is its cause, [the author] states that this distinction exists even in the cause. 1.
Kha-rūpa-ta! (The nature of space).
[Volume 2, Page 206] Śureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter]

He states the distinction: "Tamas," etc. Anticipating the objection—namely, if the Supreme Being is the cause, how can there be the creation of a manifold world consisting of high and low states, given His freedom from defects such as passion—he replies with the principle: "Not through partiality or cruelty, because He is dependent [on other factors]," stating: "By means of [their] dispositions," etc.
Whatever is observed, such as meditation and so forth, pertaining to the task at hand;
That which exists as a seed within darkness is manifested again through conditioned activity.

If [the Pradhāna] is a cause in dependence upon karma and so forth, does it exist during the dissolution (pralaya) or not? If it does not exist, then is it manifest or unmanifest? In the first case, the dissolution of all things would be impossible; in the second, is it an instrument by virtue of the existence of the Supreme (Parameśvara), or is it manifest? In the first sub-case, the effect would arise even during the dissolution.

If it is argued that there is no infinite regress (anavasthā) in the search for a cause for the sake of establishing the nature of the third [moment], then [the opponent] would object that that which depends on it cannot be the cause. To this, [the author] says: "As far as... This means that it pertains to the effect and has that [effect] as its object. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "it is examined by means of scripture," such as "according to karma" and "according to what was heard. [The effect arises] from ignorance, which consists of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of karma and so forth awakened by the power of the Lord’s will and other factors.
The meaning is that even previously unmanifest karma and so forth become manifest, and once manifested, they serve as the instrument for the Creator. || 343 ||
Darkness is the regulator because its own effects follow from it.
That very same [nature] is the regulator both prior to manifestation and after it. || 344 ||

If it is argued that the manifestation of karma and so forth occurs due to the aforementioned *saṃskāra* (latent impression), then why does desire and the like awaken that [impression] only at certain times? To this he says: "That" (*tam*). If all karma and so forth, consisting of ignorance (*ajñāna*) accompanied by the appearance (*sābhāsa*), exist in a state of dissolution (*laya*), how is there a manifestation of them according to the specific allotment for each individual (*pratipuruṣavyavasthā*)? To this he says: "Because. Prior to manifestation, after destruction, and in the interval between them, by that [ignorance], the effects of ignorance [persist].

Since there is no independence because of pervasion (vyāpti), the meaning is that ignorance itself is the regulator for the manifestation [of things] through the fixed order of its own effects, such as karma and so forth. || 344 ||
This destroyer of darkness is the restrainer who acts with regard to that which is to be restrained.
And within those very [states], being of the nature of consciousness (citsvabhāva), it attains the state of a witness (sākṣitā). || 345 ||
Anticipating the objection that this would contradict the acceptance of the Supreme as the controller (*niyāmaka*), he says: "That which is to be controlled" (*niyamyam*).

Anticipating the further objection—why should the Supreme's status as a controller be held to be mediated by *tamas*, rather than being natural like its status as a witness (*sākṣitva*)?—he states that even that is due to ignorance (*avidyā*): "In them," meaning in *tamas* and its effects. (349)
Just as a leech or similar creature, once swallowed, takes up residence in whatever part of the body it can find.
In the same way, meditative cultivation, knowledge, and ritual actions go toward one who is enveloped in darkness. || 246 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that even though its nature as a controller and so forth is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), why does it resort only to the ignorant one upon dissolution, abandoning the liberated one who has become Brahman through karma and the like—he says: "Swallowed" (*nigīrṇam*). For it has been stated:—
“From a mixture of impure and pure flavors, the leech takes up the impure blood;
first, the swan [takes] the milk from milk-and-water, as it were.”
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadāt), the statement regarding the division based on the presence or absence of a penultimate vowel (*aupadhika*) is intended. || 346 ||
1. Kha. Tamasvinah.
[Vol.
2, page 207] 4. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
In arising, abiding, and perishing, one does not transcend the cause.
Just as it is understood in the world regarding all effects, so too should it be determined here.

Furthermore, since actions and the like are the causes for the ignorant person, that effect [of liberation] does not depend upon him once he has transcended ignorance—that is, once he is liberated; this is observed.

In the interval [between the previous discussion and the present], he says: "Arising," etc. This is called *bhāvanā* (creative contemplation) and so forth. However, the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated is merely apparent (*prātītika*), like a dream, and not real (*vāstava*), because it would contradict the remainder of the text beginning with "Brahman indeed is this" (*brahma vā idam*). Furthermore, it should be understood that even in the passage "Whosoever among the gods... (*tadyo yo devānām...*), there is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the distinction based on ignorance (*avidya*) for the purpose of indicating the difference in qualification (*adhikāri-vailakṣaṇya*). || 347 ||
Moreover, in all activities whatsoever, that which is observed as agency—
One should know that it belongs to this very [self]; therefore, it is called the "doer of all. || 348 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if meditation and the like are the locus of ignorance, Brahman’s status as the creator of all would be lost if they were its cause—since it would then be merely an instrument rather than the cause itself—the author says: "In effects... (348).
"That fire thought" means that the Sat (Being) indeed had fire as its body.
By means of scripture, [the Self] is declared to be the creator of successive effects. || 349 ||

He states the proof for the claim that Brahman alone is the cause, existing in the form of various effects, by means of the reasoning beginning with "due to the meditation of the Supreme" (*parābhidhyānāt*). [The text says] "That [Brahman] as heat" (*tatteja*). The absence of sandhi (visandhi) is for the sake of following the Śruti. By the word "iti," [the meaning of] "by the Śruti" is indicated.
The connection. || 349 ||
Likewise, in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, that which is not breath has attained the state of breath.
He is manifested as the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu) both internally and with respect to the divine.

Just as in the section on creation, the state of being fire, water, and food belongs to the Existent (Sat) because otherwise its status as a witness would be impossible, so too in the context of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the status of being Prāṇa is intended for the Supreme Self alone, who is not [literally] Prāṇa.

For no other than that [Self] can be the bestower of fruit through being an object of meditation, according to the principle: "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (*phalamata upapatteḥ*). Thus he says: "In the same way. By stating that the one who is not Prāṇa attains the state of Prāṇa, he also indicates that air does not attain the state of air.
The ascetic [reflects] upon the internal. || 350 ||
It begins with names and extends up to the demonstration of death and its cessation.
The entire universe, woven like warp and woof, is taught to be nothing other than Prāṇa alone.
He states this according to the logic of the *Bhūmādhikaraṇa*, showing that even in the *Bhūmavidyā* (the knowledge of the Infinite), the Supreme is seen to be the Self of all.
"By name" means that it has been shown that the entire world, like spokes fixed in the hub of a wheel, is offered into the Supreme through the medium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 351 ||
In the same way, it is this very [Self] that is referred to by the word "ether" in various places.
And this very [state] is called the "Supreme with seed" (sabīja), characterized by the thought "this is the truth. || 352 ||

He states that, according to the principle "space [is Brahman] because of its characteristic marks" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.22), space was described as the goal of this world in such passages as, "What is the goal of this world? Space," and so on, just as the Supreme is said to have the nature of vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. He says, "In the same way. Then he states another point regarding the Supreme accompanied by the seed of the five elements.
[Vol.
2, page 208] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
He shows the designation by means of the word "Truth" (*satya*). "That this..."—by the passage beginning with "from this it is born," he indicates that creation proceeds from the Supreme.
The meaning is "because it is the subject under discussion. || 352 ||
For there is a statement in the Atharva Veda: "This is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa) within all beings."
"O Somya, that which is bound by breath" is said to be the cause of all.

Regarding that very point, he states another scriptural passage: "For [it is] Prāṇa... The intention is this: Prāṇa does not possess the nature of being the Self of all by its own inherent nature, because it is an effect;
rather, it is the Supreme (Para) that, having attained that state, becomes so. To show that the Supreme has the form of Prāṇa, he cites another passage: "Prāṇa...

By stating that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*sābhāsa*) and designated by the term "individual soul" (*jīva*), is merged and non-different from the supreme Prāṇa, the Veda [establishes] the nature of Prāṇa...
The meaning is that Brahman is declared to be the cause of all by truth. Thus, he concludes that because the Supreme abides in those various forms, it is the cause of all: "sarva... (verse 353).
Relying upon its own activity, this [consciousness] undergoes various distinctions.
Just as the sun manifests its universal form through the streams of water it emits and other such means. || 354 ||

Anticipating the objection that if it were the cause of everything, it would be distinct from all things because it is their material cause—just as clay [is distinct from its products]—he states: "This [is not so]," for such a distinction is not to be proven as a reality because its predicate is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); furthermore, if one were to prove it otherwise, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). He provides an example of a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) with the words: "emitted by itself," etc. According to the Smṛti, "From the Sun rain is born," the stream of rain is emitted by the Sun; "etc. refers to this.
From the foot [of the Veda], there is the apprehension of mirrors and so forth. || 354 ||
In this context, the very birth of the vital breaths, the elements, and so forth, is said to be the "birth" of the self.
Just as the birth of the unborn sky occurs through the birth of jars and other such things. (355)

Anticipating the objection that the soul’s difference [from Brahman] is real, like its birth, he states the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) by means of the maxim: "But it may reside in the moving and the unmoving" (*carācaravyapāśrayastu syāt*). He says "prāṇa... etc. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to other material adjuncts (*upādhi*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the world and the scriptures. He provides an example for birth that is merely due to an adjunct: "of the ether" (*viyataḥ*). [He adds] "of non-birth" (*ajanmanaḥ*).
Severance. || 355 ||
From this, the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind (manas), and all the sense organs are born.
Nothing other than what is taught by the scripture is understood as indeterminate.

One might object that even if difference and birth are non-inherent (aupādhika), the Supreme [Brahman] cannot be the cause because the unmanifested (avyākṛta) lacks that status; anticipating this doubt, he says:

"From this" (etasmāt). The meaning is: since it is understood from the aforementioned scripture that the Supreme is the cause, the unmanifested is not different from it; and it has already been stated that the term "unmanifested" is used in reference to that [Supreme] which is characterized by darkness (tamas). || 396 ||
Just as clay is unique [to its own effects] by depending solely upon its own specific functions.
In that same way, the cause attains a state of generality through its own effects.

Fearing the objection that Brahman, being the universal of pure existence (*sanmātra-sāmānya*), must depend on particulars (*viśeṣa*) [for its manifestation], and that the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—being a particular—would therefore be different from it, he says:
"its own effects. Just as clay, although by its very nature devoid of commonality [with specific jars], [becomes such] through its effects such as jars and the like...
[1] ka. ga. *saumyeti* | 2 ka. *raṇaṃ yaṃ* |
[Vol.

2, Page 209] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 503 Since it attains commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*) in relation to other things, its commonality is imagined (*kalpitā*) because of its dependence; likewise, Brahman also—

The meaning is: since it attains the status of a universal (*sāmānya*) in relation to its own specific effects, that [status] is merely imagined for it; how then could there be anything else that exists as a particular (*viśeṣa*), given that it is unmanifest? || 397 ||
Therefore, this ignorance is eternal, because there is no recollection of the beginning of the time produced by it.
That which persists through all times in the world is designated as "eternal. || 358 ||

Regarding that in relation to which Brahman is designated by the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta)—whether that be false knowledge (mithyājñāna) or something else—if it were the former, then by one who asserts that Brahman qualified by that [ignorance] is the cause, the effect would necessarily be admitted as such; if it were the latter, since that [other thing] is unestablished, Brahman itself could not be the cause. Anticipating this objection, he says: "This very [Brahman]... He provides the reason: because time and so forth are born from ignorance, Brahman is not delimited by them.

That is born. To the question, "Even if there is no limitation by time, how can there be eternity? he replies with the word *sarva* (all). The collective meaning is this: since beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*), which is the cause of false knowledge and so forth, is to be inferred from its effects, it is logical that Brahman, as qualified by that [ignorance], is the cause. || 358 ||
Furthermore, for that which is eternal, there can be no cessation; thus, even for the "Fierce One" (Ugra), such a state is impossible.
For authority is based upon the complete absence of eternal ignorance. || 359 ||

Fearing that beginningless Vedic knowledge might not be subject to cessation—just like the Self—and considering that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), he says:

"Of the eternal" (*nityasya*). Anticipating the objection that "being beginningless other than non-existence" is the reason, he states: "Eternal," etc., [meaning] that the reason is not probative because it is refuted by a subverting argument (*tarka*) regarding the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all means of valid cognition (*māna*) would be rendered futile. || 359 ||
An object of cognition is said to be a thing not yet known by other means of valid cognition.

That which pertains solely to that reality (tattva) is called the measure (*māna*) for the destruction of the darkness residing therein. (360) Having raised the doubt—given that the status of things as valid cognitions (*māna*) consists in their destroying beginningless ignorance—what then is that object of cognition (*meya*)? [The author] addresses this by means of conventional valid cognition (*vyāvahārika-māna*).

Since the object of this [knowledge] is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), he states that it is the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveals reality (*tattva*). He says, "by other means of valid cognition" (*pramāntaraiḥ*). Anticipating the question, "What then is the means of valid cognition?", he states that it is the means of valid cognition that reveals reality, because conventional means of valid cognition are already established. He says, "that very reality... [referring to the object residing within the means of knowledge].

Knowledge is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa), not an attribute (viśeṣaṇa) included within the object of cognition; this is the meaning of the word "only" (mātra). He recalls what was stated regarding the fruit of the means of knowledge:
"tatstha" (abiding in that). || 360 ||
If ignorance here were adventitious, it would follow that there is no liberation.
What proof is there that what has passed will not return again in the future? (361)

Having stated that the cessation of beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) is the fruit of valid cognition (*māna*), he points out the defect in the failure to establish its beginninglessness with the words "If it were adventitious" (*āgantuc cet*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the Self (*ātman*). He clarifies the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) with the words "as before" (*pura*): just as ignorance, which was non-existent prior to liberation, manifests, so too would it manifest even after that [liberation], since there is no preventer of such a doubt; thus, liberation—characterized by the absence of recurrence—would not exist.

The meaning is that the established conclusion (*siddhi*) is this: because ignorance (*ajñāna*) is beginningless, Brahman as qualified by it is indeed the cause of the world, while the world itself is indeed the effect; such is the settled rule. || 369 ||
Because the two are non-different in the form of cause and effect.
This discourse on cause and effect is presented in terms of the subordinate and the primary qualities.
504 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, Page 210]

Now, if this were the established position, non-duality would not be proven, because an established order is impossible without difference; to this he replies with the words "kārya" (effect). The meaning is that because Brahman and the world stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*), they are non-different, like clay and a jar. Anticipating the objection that since the relation of cause and effect is impossible in a single entity, there must be a difference between them—like a jar and a potter—he replies with the words "guṇa" (attribute). Like a rope and a snake, independence and dependence exist within one and the same thing.
The meaning is that the conventional usage of cause and effect is imagined by the self. || 362 ||
There is no effect without a cause, nor is there a cause without an effect.
Since their establishment is due to mutual dependence, those two do not exist without one another. (363)

He says that the cause does not possess substantial reality like Brahman because it lacks independence; "Not the cause," he says. He states the reason for this: "Mutually. He states the consequence of its dependence: "Without. The sense is that although from the perspective of worldly experience the cause appears independent—since one observes clay and so forth persisting even when jars and the like are absent—even that [cause] is, in terms of ultimate reality, dependent and thus as much a conceptual construction as the effect. || 363 ||
Cultivation, knowledge, action, and so forth are the causal factors for the production of an effect.
When that [unmanifest] exists, there is manifestation of that [effect]; when it is in a state of dormancy, there is the nature of the unmanifested.
He states another reason for the fact that, in reality, a cause lacks independence: "bhāvanā" (the creative urge), etc. By the word "etc.," effort and so forth are included.

He states the reason for its being the prompter: "tadbhūtāv iti" (because they are contained therein). Since the production of an effect occurs when there is the manifestation of the creative urge and so forth, and does not occur otherwise, these [urge, effort, etc.
are the prompters of their respective productions; therefore, the cause is dependent upon them and is not independent—this is the meaning. || 364 ||

For the sake of the experience of its own creator, karma—existing in the form of the unmanifest—employs the three means of accomplishment (sādhana), beginning with earth and ending with fire, once they have become manifest. (365)

He states [the reason] why [the Lord] generates the world through [the agency of] *bhāvanā* and so forth: "of His own agent" (*svakartuḥ*). Then, in response to the inquiry as to by what sequence He generates each [effect], He shows the sequence: "action" (*karma*). The mention of "action" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *bhāvanā* and the rest. The reason for their being unified will be stated [later]. || 365 ||
Having resorted to the syllables *arararaau*, they constitute the means for those who came before.
Therefore, for these three as well, they employ wind and space. || 366 ||

If karma and the others produce the triad beginning with earth, then what is the cause for the production of air and space? To this he says: "Air and space [arise] from those three. Since the three previously mentioned elements beginning with earth are termed "instruments" (*sādhana*) because they serve as the means for experience (*bhoga*), their acquisition of self-nature and their status as means for experience occur through the medium of air and the other elements; therefore, karma and the others must first produce air and the rest.
The meaning is that they produce earth and the other elements. || 366 ||
The relationship of instigator and instigated exists between the instrument and the object of the action.
"It is held that [the elements] are thus differentiated for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of their respective owners and lords.

He concludes the relationship between the five elements—designated as the "means" (sādhana)—and action (*karman*) and so forth. [The verse begins with] "prayojaka... He summarizes the intermediate fruit of creation, stating "for the sake of the enjoyment whose nature is one's own agency," and concludes with "svasvāmī... (367).
1. It becomes manifest.
[Vol.
2, page 211] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 505.
The manifestation of the world, which exists in an unmanifest form, is indeed restricted to a specific time.
And this [power] was made internal by the Lord; no other [agency] is conceivable for Him. || 368 ||

If the birth of the world is due to karma and so forth, then since those [causes] exist at all times, the world would be born at all times; for when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present, there can be no delay in the effect. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Manifestation" (*vyakti*). By the word "world," karma and the rest are understood.
Anticipating the question of what causes this restricted manifestation, he clarifies what was indicated in the statement "whatever pertains to the effect": "The Inner Ruler" (*antaryāmī*).

To the question, "Why does even the Lord manifest [himself] only at certain times and not always?", he says: "None other. The meaning is that there is indeed no other controller of him, for that would entail the consequence of his not being the Supreme Lord (anīśvara). || 368 ||
Its activity would be like that of the wind, and its withdrawal likewise.
In the same way, from that Lord who is signless (nirnimitta), there arise the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the world.

If it is argued that the manifestation of the world is created by God, then one might suspect that He would possess a body like an ordinary worldly lord; anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the wind. Just as there is activity and so forth from the bodiless wind—which is indeed observed in the world where even a powerless person is driven by a powerful breeze—so too the birth and other states of the world from the bodiless Lord are not contradictory, for He [possesses no such body].
The meaning is that this is based on such scriptural passages as "the effect and the cause," and so forth. || 369 ||
When the enjoyment [of the fruit] is for the sake of the owner, then it is not to be employed for the sake of the ritual act.
Having abandoned all specific actions, one attains the state of the undifferentiated Self.

One might raise the objection: "Just as the Lord Creator does not depend on a body and so forth, why should He not likewise be independent of karma and the like? Anticipating this, he says, "No," and so on. A Lord who is independent of karma and the like cannot be the cause of birth and so forth, because that would entail the consequence of His possessing passion and other such afflictions. Therefore, when the experience intended for the agent is not produced due to the force of karma and the like, then [the Lord], having abandoned all manifestation along with the world, remains in a state of causality.
Thus, there is dissolution (laya) and not creation (sṛṣṭi); this is the meaning. || 370 ||
That which is the material cause of this illusory net of duality.
Depending upon that ignorance, Brahman is called the cause.

Raising the objection that even if the Creator is dependent on karma and so forth, He might still be the cause independently of a body—such that ignorance, like the body, need not be required—the author says "of this" (*asya*). Since the perceived duality, which is delightful only so long as it is not investigated, is an effect other than [Brahman] itself, it must depend upon a material cause; and since ignorance is a suitable material cause for it, Brahman is its cause by taking that [ignorance] as its material cause, according to the Śruti and Smṛti.

This must be accepted by the followers of the *Nusāri* school; for Brahman, which is immutable, unattached, and non-dual, cannot become subject to transformation without assuming ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of the world.
Nor can it be without causality, because its status as the cause is declared in the discourses of the Śruti and Smṛti. This is the meaning. || 371 ||
The Self,
because its limiting adjunct is mere ignorance, is [mistakenly identified] by those whose selves are enveloped by nescience.
Due to its immutability, even though it is dualistic in nature, the Self is superimposed as a witness by the ignorant. (372)

It has already been stated that, like its status as a cause, its status as a witness (*sākṣitva*) is also produced by its own ignorance; this is now further clarified in the context of the discussion. Regarding the verse beginning with "ajñāna":

although [the Self] is immutable (*kūṭastha*) and thus devoid of any connection with duality in every respect, it is conceptualized as a "witness" by undiscriminating people whose selves are obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*), because witnesshood is produced solely by ignorance. By the word "solely" (*mātra*), [the author] excludes the state of being a knower (*mātṛtva*), which is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*).
Exclusion. || 372 ||
The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Chapter]:
"That is the light even of lights, because it nourishes the growth of the intellect."
It appears as if it were of the nature of darkness, like the sun to those who see only at night.

Anticipating the objection that because the Witness (sākṣin) is self-luminous and Brahman is its own property—and since that [Brahman] is also the Self, it too must be self-luminous—therefore the experience of Brahman would be constant, he says: "Of lights... This refers to the Vedic texts such as, "The gods [worship] that light of lights," and so forth, regarding the Āditya...

Although Brahman is the illuminator even of the dull-witted and is self-luminous, nevertheless, for those who are unqualified and possess impure intellects, it does not shine by itself due to the impurity of their intellect; thus, it appears as if non-existent, like the sun to owls—this is the meaning. || 373 ||
"That which has the nature of the reflection of the immutable (kūṭastha) is the nest of delusion and its effects."
Knowledge and that which is inseparable from it are called the supreme witness. || 374 ||

Anticipating the objection that the status of being a witness (*sākṣitā*) must therefore belong to something other than [the Self], since it is applied elsewhere due to the power of delusion (*moha*), he says: "Delusion... etc. The Supreme is called the Witness because it has attained identity with that knowledge which consists of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) residing in ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its effects; for there is no other conscious entity [to serve as the witness]. Therefore, the status of being a witness does not arise from ignorance alone, but must also involve the reflection (*ābhāsa*).
This is the meaning. || 374 ||
This is that [teaching] in all the Vedas for the sake of knowing the meaning as it truly is.
By means of the statements beginning with "together with the gods," Brahman is proclaimed as the cause. || 375 ||

One might object: "Even if the Supreme alone is the knower (*akṣitṛ*), how can He alone be the cause of the world through that [ignorance], given the lack of evidence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This... The construction is as follows: Brahman, who is the inner self (*pratyagbhūta*) and whose existence is inferred from the effect (*kāryaliṅgaka*), is proclaimed in all the Vedas as the cause of the universe by such statements as, "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning" (*sadeva somyedam*).
To the question, "For what purpose is the causality of Brahman stated in these scriptural passages?", he replies:
"Yathā" means "the means. || 379 ||
Therefore, according to the principle of "seeking [the cause] by means of the effect," for the sake of the direct realization of the inner Self— which is the effect of that [cause]—
there exists the Omniscient, the Omnipotent, the Universal Self, the All-pervading, and the Eternal.
This very Lord is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world. || 376 ||

[Objection: Since the activity of a discerning person is preceded by knowledge, if Brahman is the cause of everything, its knowledge must be described as unobstructed in all respects; yet that does not exist, because there is a lack of proof for it. To this, he says: "The omniscient one. This is based on the scriptural authority (*śāstra*) of the Vedic text: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.9).

The phrase "and by the logic of the *nitvādhikaraṇa*" is to be understood as a supplement [to the previous argument]. Since the Sāṅkhyas have stated that the Puruṣa, despite possessing the power of vision (*dṛkśakti*), is devoid of the power of activity (*pravṛttiśakti*), he says: "He is all-powerful" (*sarvaśakti*). This is because of the Śruti text: "His supreme power... Nor does omniscience follow merely from being all-powerful; for even though Pradhāna possesses all powers, omniscience is not admitted for it, and likewise, although a magnet possesses the power of activity, the power of vision is not observed in it.

The meaning is "and his own [self]. Regarding those who say that such a Lord is situated on the shore (taṭastha), he says: "the Self of all" (*sarvātman*). Thinking that by this [term] the notion of being connected with all material forms—that is, omnipresence—is refuted, he says: "all" (*sarva*). The meaning is that He is present everywhere as the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Alternatively, the Jains assert that the Person (*puruṣa*) has a medium size; in response to them, he says: "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*).

Regarding its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), he addresses those of his own school who maintain it, saying: "It is eternal" (*dhruva*). As for the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha, however, Hiraṇyagarbha—...

They say that the definition [of the Lord] as "one who has abandoned the *ṛbhu*" is incorrect, because scripture declares that He is situated in the midst of the world; with this intention, he says: "The world.

Alternatively, the Mīmāṃsakas do not tolerate the aforementioned Lord; therefore, he says "the world" to show that He is established through the mark of His effects (the world) and through numerous declarations in the Śrutis and Smṛtis. The word "sat" (Being/Real) is connected to each of the qualifying attributes. || 376 ||
He who is the Lord of the earth is that Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Teacher of the World.
He is praised under many names, such as Hari, Brahmā, and Pinākin. || 377 ||

How is it that the Lord’s causality is established on the basis of scripture (*śruti*), given that in the *Itihāsas* and other texts there are scriptural statements regarding the agency of the three forms (*mūrti-traya*) in creation, maintenance, and dissolution as appropriate? To this he says: "He who [is] in the earth," and so forth. For the Lord under discussion, though one in his essential nature (*svarūpa*), is spoken of in many ways as the three forms; for scripture declares that he alone exists within the earth and other elements as their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*), and there is no contradiction with the Purāṇas and other such texts in light of that.

The meaning is that authority [is lost] due to weakness caused by dependence. According to the maxim "he is the teacher of the predecessors," the explanation of the term *antaryāmī* (the inner controller) is *jagadguruḥ* (the teacher of the world). || 377 ||
The immutable Self cannot be a witness, for witness-hood arises from association with a second entity.
Even for that which is perishable, there can be no witness-status, because it is not distinct from destruction.

Even if the Supreme alone, abiding in those various forms, is the cause of everything, how can it possess the status of a witness? For is that [witness] different from the material cause (mātṛ) or non-different? Having raised this dilemma, the proponent of the first view states the defect in the first case: "Of the immutable" (kūṭasthasya). The meaning is that since the immutable is other than the transforming material cause, and because it is devoid of modification, there is no connection between it and the object of witnessing; thus, its status as a witness is not tenable. As for the material cause—

He refutes the second [objection]—that because it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), it possesses destruction and so forth, and therefore cannot be the witness (*sākṣin*) since it falls within the category of the witnessed (*sākṣya*)—with the words "even for that which perishes" (*nāśino’pi*). [The objection is: Even if there is the possibility of non-destruction and so forth despite being subject to transformation—as in the case of gold and the like—how can the Mother (the Self) possess destruction and so forth? To this he replies: "By destruction" (*nāśena*). This is because transformation is pervaded by destruction and the like, and because the example [cited by the opponent] is not admitted [as valid].
Such is the meaning. || 378 ||
But if ignorance alone is the cause, all of this is consistent.
Because it is the cause of false cognitions such as agency with respect to that which has the nature of the Self. || 379 ||
Because the counter-king's position is stable, and because it is not understood through the method of agreement (anvaya).
Even for that which is immutable, there is the status of being a witness with respect to that which undergoes appearance and disappearance.

He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, in this world of ignorance (*āvidya*), it is logically consistent for the Supreme to possess the status of witness, cause, and inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) by virtue of that [ignorance]. He states "ignorance" (*aśāna*). The word "only" (*mātra*) is used to assert that there is no material cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) in the world other than ignorance. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— [The text continues: ...the prima facie view—... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.]

The word "tu" (but) serves to indicate a distinction. [The author] states this in response to the objection that agency and so forth are not appropriate for the Supreme Self even in its capacity as a witness, because of the scriptural teaching of its actionlessness (*niṣkriyatva*). He says: "Agency and so forth... Agency and so forth belong to the non-Self—the mind—which undergoes transformation through the process of knowing and which has assumed the form of the Self due to superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self; yet this agency is falsely attributed to the Inner Self (*pratīc*), because of the false knowledge consisting in the superimposition of identity with that which undergoes transformation.

The meaning is: "because of the existence of a cause. He concludes that it is appropriate for the immutable [Self] to possess witness-hood and so forth with respect to ignorance by stating: "because of its immobility.
508. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

Because the Immutable (kūṭastha) is stationary and naturally devoid of all modification, it stands as the witness (*sākṣin*) toward the aggregate of insentient objects by means of its connection with ignorance (*moha*).
The meaning is "direction. By the word *api* ("also"), he indicates that it is impossible for that [direction] to exist inherently. || 379 || 380 ||
The relationship between the self and the ignorance of the self is considered to be that of identity and its possessor.
The lack of discernment regarding other beings is called the ignorance of the self. || 381 ||

What, then, is the relationship between delusion (*moha*) and the immutable (*kūṭastha*)? He states that it is an illusory identity (*adhyāsikatādātmya*). Regarding the phrase "the Self" (*ātma*): one might ask how ignorance (*avidyā*), which is not distinct from the absence of knowledge (*vidyābhāva*), can be the means of realization for such things as being the witness (*sākṣitva*). Anticipating this doubt, he describes the nature of ignorance with the word "supreme" (*para*). The meaning of the word "supreme" is causality. It is the cause of all objects capable of coming into existence, and it is removable by discriminative knowledge (*viveka*) and is inward-facing (*pratyag*).
The meaning is that this knowledge resides in the Self alone. || 381 ||
That which extends from Īśa down to the objects of the senses is the manifestation of ignorance.
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā.
Thus, the declaration of the Vedas' head is clearly proclaimed.

Anticipating the objection that such a restriction is untenable because [powers] like those of Īśvara and others are also possible, he says: "Īśādi" (beginning with Īśvara). By this, the absolute supremacy of Īśvara’s sovereignty is refuted; therein, he cites scripture as proof: "māyāṃ tu" (but [the Lord projects] māyā). Now, one might object: the cited scripture merely states that the material cause of the world, called māyā, is dependent on Īśvara, but it does not say that Īśvara is—like sound and other objects—[unreal].

He states the reason for its being a manifestation of delusion there with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Since it must be in accordance with the fact that the Lord is a manifestation of the aforementioned ignorance, the clear scriptural statement "the Illusive One" (*māyinam*)—by declaring His possession of *māyā*—excludes His purity; therefore, the meaning is that He, being situated within impure matter, would be merely imagined (*kalpita*). || 382 ||
For there is a Smṛti text stating: "This divine power of Mine consists of the Guṇas and is called Māyā."
Indeed, it is even sung in the world that "this is the Māyā of Viṣṇu. || 383 ||

In that very context, he cites a Smṛti passage: "The Goddess, indeed... The meaning of the word "indeed" (hi) is that the difficulty of transcending Māyā is well-established through personal experience.
Furthermore, by saying "my Māyā," the Blessed Lord demonstrates Māyā as belonging to the Īśvara, thereby showing [the world] to belong to Him as qualified by it.
The state of being imagined (*kalpitatva*) has been indicated. Seeing the universe as impossible [in its ultimate reality], worldly people say, "This is indeed the Māyā of the Lord";

therefore, he states that even worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this matter by saying, "Vaiṣṇavī" (belonging to Viṣṇu). The first *api* is for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), while the other is for conjunction (*samuccaya*).
For worldly people, by qualifying Māyā as "Vaiṣṇavī," they express the specific nature of Viṣṇu—that is, the Lord's—Māyā.

The meaning is that [the opponents] consider even the moments of that [Lord] to be conceptualized; for although He is non-conceptualized in His own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it must be admitted—just as in the case of the individual soul—that He is conceptualized in His manifested form (*saṃsṛṣṭākāra*). || 383 ||
Thus, the object of knowledge (meyam) that is not apprehended by other means of cognition has been examined.
One should personally testify to one's own state here, according to one's own direct experience. || 384 ||
Since it is precisely that which has been apprehended prior to the operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that serves as the motivator for its operation,

and since there exists nothing other than self-luminous experience (anubhava) to establish that [apprehension], and because that [experience] establishes what is superimposed upon itself, it is such an experience alone that constitutes "unknowability" (ajñātatva).
1. It is said:
[Vol.
2, page 215] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 509.

It has been established that [the Self] possesses the nature of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) and the nature of being a real entity (*vastutā*). Now, he recites what has already occurred [in the previous section]: "In another vehicle" (*yānāntara*), etc. The meaning is as follows: In each individual substrate (*pratyagātmā*), the inner reality (*vastu*) is both unknown and not known; nor is this state of being unknown, etc., accessible through other means of knowledge (*māna*), because it is to be removed by them. Its establishment follows from the experience of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-anubhava*). Furthermore, because that inner reality is something previously unknown (*apūrva*), it is to be known through the Vedāntas. This has been determined in the passage beginning with "That [is] He" (*tattvamasi*) and so forth. || 384 ||
Now, with this as the cause, false cognition is being examined.

"From that which living beings fear—the characteristic of the misfortune of saṃsāra. He explains the intended meaning, which was already stated in the passage "by means of the distinction between cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇabhedeneti*), for the purpose of clarifying the literal sense of the sentence beginning with "by name and form" (*tannāmarūpābhyām*). He says: "This... By the derivation from the root *kṛ* (to act), the word *jñāna* (knowledge) also takes the object as its referent. This...

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: that false knowledge and its object, for which ignorance is the cause, are now being defined by the words "that" and so forth. By saying "now," he indicates the logical connection (saṃgati) that the definition of the effect follows immediately after the definition of the cause. Now, having begun with the inquiry, "What is the root of this great disease called saṃsāra? and having conducted that inquiry, [the author proceeds] to define saṃsāra.
He says "no" because the description of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is not inconsistent with the context; for [the word] "since" (*yataḥ*) connects to "that false knowledge" (*tan-mithyājñānam*).
The meaning is that the subsequent sentence is intended to demonstrate that the world is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the unknown Self. || 389 ||
That which is indeed constant ignorance is precisely what constitutes false knowledge.
Because there is no deviation between those two, in the form of cause and its opposite. || 386 ||

Having established that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the cause and false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is the effect, he states the conclusion with the words "That which... (*yad iti*). By the term "eternal" (*nityam*), its beginninglessness is expressed. He states the reason for this with the words "Because of the cause... (*kāraṇeti*). Since false knowledge possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with ignorance, there exists a relationship of cause and effect between the two; and since an effect cannot be distinct from its material cause (*upādāna*), bondage—which is of the nature of ignorance—is something to be dispelled by right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
The meaning is "attainment" (siddhi). || 386 ||
That which exists independently of other causes is of an indeterminate nature.
It attains manifestation by itself; there is no uncollected cause [for this]. || 387 ||

If it is argued that an unknown object is the cause of bondage, then there must be an auxiliary factor such as a defect (*doṣa*), because we observe that when an unknown mother-of-pearl is the cause of [the perception of] silver, glass and other factors serve as auxiliaries; anticipating this objection, he says: "By another cause" (*hetvantara*). The meaning is that, being unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) by itself and independent of any cause distinct from itself, it attains the state of an effect at the time of creation, because—as in the illustrative example—no additional cause is applicable here. [This applies to] karma and so forth...

Having raised the objection—"Since a cause has already been stated, how can there be independence from any other cause?"—he replies with the words "nimittam" (the cause). The sense is that while it was stated thus from the perspective of worldly convention, in reality, since even karma and the like have been withdrawn, there is no causality apart from the unmanifested (avyākṛta). One should not forget what was stated in the passage beginning with "ignorance, karma, and latent impressions. || 387 ||
Just as a king awakens from deep sleep by himself, so it is in this case.
From the unmanifest, whose body is the entirety of the consumed universe, there is a constant manifestation of the formed world.
He provides an illustration for the creatorship of that which is independent of external causes and whose internal essence is unknown: "from deep sleep," etc.
Although [this is so], 1 ka. ga. kṣaṇam || 385 ||
510 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] — [Vol. 2, Page 216]

A sleeping king awakens upon receiving a stimulus such as praise or song; nevertheless, it is observed that sometimes he awakens by himself even without an external cause, and thus the illustration is established. By using the word "muhūrta" (for a moment), [the author] shows the repetition of manifestation and indicates the beginninglessness of saṃsāra. || 388 ||
It is like the rope that has not yet been determined [to be such], as supported by this logical principle.
The words of Gauḍapāda, which have a clear meaning, are sung here for this very purpose. || 389 ||

He cites the statement of those who know the tradition as authority for the view that the world is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of the ignorance inherent in the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), beginning with the words "aniścitā" (undetermined).
The three quarters [of the verse] are: "Just as in darkness, [the rope] is conceptualized through imagined entities such as a snake or a stream, so too is the Self conceptualized."

And this is not invalid because it possesses the logic of the instruments [of knowledge]; thus he says: "The logic" (*nyāya*). The "logic" refers to the difficulty of defining the manifold nature of existence, non-existence, and so forth. And because its subject matter is free from doubt and sublation, this is valid knowledge; thus he says: "Clear" (*sphuṭa*). And because it was seen by a distinguished person, he says: "Gauḍapāda" (*gauḍha*). The meaning of the two locatives is that the world is the modification of the Self, which is yet unknown. || 389 ||
This very [reality], though nameless and formless, is [manifested] through name and form.
Thus it is explained, by relying solely on the cause of ignorance. (390)

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "That," he explains its individual words: "This very [world]. One might object that it is illogical to say "the unmanifested entity under discussion was differentiated by name and form," because those two were already established prior to that. Anticipating this, he says: "Nameless.
The phrase "according to such Vedic texts as 'without sound'" (*aśabdam*) is to be supplied. He states that this differentiation is in accordance with experience: "Thus..."

Thus it is said. In that regard, he states the primary cause: "through ignorance" (*ajñāna*). The word "only" (*mātra*) is used for the purpose of excluding any independent cause other than the ignorance inherent in the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*). || 390 ||
In this context, the form of the designation is expressed by the word "name."
Likewise, the form of the signified object is taught as being "form" (rūpa). || 391 ||
Having stated the collective meaning, and desiring to explain the meaning of the individual parts, he states the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmaprātipadika*): "abhidhāna... and so forth.

In this sentence, the meaning of the nominal stem is the general category of name—that is to say, the commonality of names. He then states the meaning of the form-stem (*rūpaprātipadika*): "abhi-... and so forth.
Regarding "dheya": just as the denotable universal is the meaning of the word *nāman*, so too the denotable universal is the meaning of the word *rūpa*; such is the sense. || 399 ||

It is not that it is a source of harm in its literal meaning, nor is its harmfulness merely superficial; rather, it is said to be so because it manifests as such upon investigation. This is the definition [of the object of negation].
