In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter—remainder]: Anticipating the objection that since ignorance (*avidyā*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), it must have a beginning, and thus its status as the cause of beginningless superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not established—and furthermore, that false knowledge itself cannot be the cause because it is absent in some instances—he says: "By nature" (*svābhāvikyā*). [This refers to] ignorance...

Anticipating the objection that even if ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless due to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge, it cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*). The point is that since both types of superimposition consist in being other than non-existence (*abhāva-itara*), the ignorance which is their material cause also cannot be non-existence, because there is no other possible material cause.
Regarding the superimposition of the non-self upon the Self, the illustration is "in the case of mother-of-pearl and so forth. (414)
But surely [this is not so], because it relies upon the cognition of a universal and the non-cognition of a particular.
In this world, false knowledge is established through the non-recollection of gold and silver. || 415 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the disparity [between the example and the case at hand] with the words "nanu" (but). The meaning is as follows: in the example there are three causal factors, but they are not seen in the case under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*); for the Self, being devoid of both general and particular properties (*niḥsāmānya-viśeṣatva*), lacks them, and as for the non-Self, memory is impossible because it is perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣatvena*). || 415 ||
Where there is superimposition and that which is superimposed, both are false once their difference is established.
Knowledge is well-established in the world, but that [knowledge] regarding the state of oneness is exceedingly difficult to attain.

He asks: Is the non-apprehension of difference the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), such that in the absence of it there can be no superimposition of the non-self upon the Self? He says: "Where...

When there is a difference between the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*), error is observed due to the non-apprehension of that difference. Since the establishment of difference is difficult to achieve in the case of a single essence (*aikātmya*), the pervader—the non-apprehension of difference—is absent;
therefore, the pervaded—superimposition—is not established. This is the meaning. || 416 ||
And for those whose identity as a single unity—both collective and individual—is established by the removal of all distinctions.
This objection would be equally applicable to both positions as well. || 417 ||

Anticipating the objection that the occurrence of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) results from the non-apprehension of difference within the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābhedavāda*), he says: "samasta... [and so on]. For even if difference exists in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference, its non-apprehension is not possible; because when a thing is apprehended, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that its mere non-difference—as well as its difference—is also apprehended. Furthermore, the relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is difficult to maintain [in such a view]. Therefore, [this argument applies] to the doctrine of absolute non-difference and to the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference alike.
The meaning is that since the absence of the two objects is equal, the objection regarding the impossibility of error is the same for both cases. || 417 ||
There is no purpose whatsoever for us in this discourse which has been avoided.
Because it is the cause of delusion regarding the individual self, it is the source of all misfortune and false cognition.

He establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) that the objection—that there can be no delusion in the doctrine of illusion (*māyāvāda*) because the three causes [of delusion] are absent—is without foundation, and thus it need not be refuted by that doctrine. He says "no, no. To explain how the objection is without foundation in his own view, he says: "The inner self," etc. For that false cognition, which consists of all misfortune, arises solely from ignorance regarding the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) which is established in its own substrate.
The meaning is that, because [the cause] is independent, the objection based on the absence of the three types of causes does not apply to our position. || 418 ||
Therefore, in this context, it is ignorance alone that is to be sublated, not the means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the refutation of that objection is undertaken, as it is not fruitless. || 419 ||

Furthermore, is error removable by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is not, there would be no contradiction with the notion of sublation (*bādhadhī*). If it is removable by valid cognition, then [the author] says: "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

Here, the term "here" refers to the sphere of valid cognition. Therefore, because error is removable by valid cognition, it is of the nature of ignorance; thus, the theory of the existence of [the world] as having a well-established cause is established.
[Vol.
2, Page 223] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 517.
Because of the absence [of such a doubt], there is no occasion for an objection regarding that subject; therefore, no refutation is offered, since there is no purpose in refuting what has not arisen.
He says: "That. Therefore, the word "ataḥ" (hence) refers to that which has not been previously established. || 419 ||
Apart from false knowledge (mithyājñāna), no other ignorance (ajñāna) is admitted.
This [objection] may apply to those [who hold such views], but not to the proponents of the self (ātman). || 420 ||

He states this [objection] which must be refuted by the follower of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣika): "It is false. The meaning is that for those who hold that there is no beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācya-ajñāna*) beyond false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), there is room for the objection—"In the absence of the three causes, how can there be superimposition?"—and therefore it must be refuted by them. He concludes that in our own position, because there is no room for such an objection, it need not be refuted: "But not... (na tu).

The meaning is that, in our view—which maintains that the world is an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of the unknown Self—there is no room for the aforementioned objection, and thus it does not even need to be refuted. || 420 ||
Surely, since ignorance is not a real entity, how can it be the cause of saṃsāra?
Since false cognition is a real entity, let that alone be the cause here.

Since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*), and since there is no room for objection when its established cause is present, it was stated that [superimposition] is unavoidable.

Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, ignorance is not the cause of superimposition, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like a sky-lotus. To this he replies: "What then is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)?
For an effect is not possible without a cause. He states this with the words: "Of false knowledge" (*mithyājñānasya*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the transmigratory existence under discussion.
Apprehension. || 421 ||
And thus, even by the great ones, it has been stated with effort and supported by reasoning.
Furthermore, invalidity is threefold; thus, this is well-established.

Anticipating the objection that false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*)—is not established as a real entity and therefore cannot be the cause [of the world], he says: "In the same way" (*tathā*).

Ignorance is not the cause because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), whereas false knowledge is the cause because it is an entity (*vastu*). It is in accordance with this view that Bhaṭṭapāda spoke, just as we have; nor is that [view] invalid, for it is logical as it concerns a distinction well-established in the world, and it is not a statement made out of indifference.

The meaning is that because it was spoken with intentional purpose (*tātparya*), the word of the great ones cannot be considered invalid; for if it were, the same consequence would follow for the words of Manu and others as well.
That very point is stated in the *Codanāsūtra* regarding authoritative speech (*āptavākya*):
"Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is divided into three types: falsity (*mithyātva*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), and doubt (*saṃśaya*)."
Because it is a real entity, its occurrence here in two ways arises from a defective cause.
"But in the case of non-cognition, there is no operation of defects whatsoever; rather,
it is established for us just as you have stated, precisely because of the absence of a cause."

Thus he summarizes: "Invalidity" (*aprāmāṇya*) is threefold—namely, non-cognition (*ajñāna*), false cognition (*mithyādhī*), and doubtful cognition (*saṃśayadhī*). Having shown this division of invalidity, he states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since non-cognition does not produce a [subsequent] cognition, it is not the cause of *saṃsāra*, as it is not observed to be so in cases such as deep sleep; however, for the other two, being the cause of that [saṃsāra] is appropriate, as they are the causes of misfortune.

Since this [false cognition] is observed in cases such as the delusion of a snake in a rope, it is established that false cognition is the cause of saṃsāra, and that it is not true knowledge; furthermore, the meaning is that prior false cognition is the cause of the subsequent [state]. || 422 ||
518 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 224]
O friend, is even an existing object directly destroyed by pride?
When that [object] has been negated, what remains in which the validity of the means of knowledge could reside? || 423 ||

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) raises a dilemma as to whether false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and the like are sublated by a means of valid knowledge (*māna*) or not. He asks: "What [is the case]? He then restates the first alternative: "Even though it exists. If an object that is established even by perception and other means were to be sublated by a means of valid knowledge, then because of the consequence that everything would be sublated by it, and because nothing would remain once everything has been sublated, there would be no object for the means of valid knowledge at all; thus, its very status as a *māna* would not exist. He says this regarding that [object]: ...tasmi... [text fragment] ...he says.
Thus ends the verse. || 423 ||
Because the means of valid cognition are manifestors, there is nothing further than the manifestation of the object of knowledge.
No other purpose can be conceived; indeed, it is the complete removal of the object itself.
He states another reason for the fact that [mere] cognition does not remove the object: "because it is a manifestor" (*vyañjakatvāt*). The meaning is "inferior" (*apara*) or "superior" (*utkṛṣṭa*).

It should be understood, however, that the word *apara* does not refer to something else [as a synonym], because that would result in a tautology with the word *antara*. Regarding the second point—that false knowledge and the like are not removed by cognition—the futility of that [cognition] follows, because the mere cessation of non-apprehension (*agraha*) is ineffective; this is explained outside [the main argument].

[The object] is to be discarded. Since there is no effect other than the manifestation of the object of knowledge, the claim that the means of knowledge (māna) discards the real entity is utterly dismissed.
He says: "Utterly" (nitarām). The connection is with the phrase "is not even conceivable" (na saṃbhāvyate). || 424 ||
How can false cognition be a real entity? For that which is false is not a real entity.
The statement that "that object is false" is fitting only for the great. || 425 ||

It was stated [previously] by accepting that false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is a real entity (*vastu*); now, he says that this very point is unestablished. He states: "If it is false... If it is false, it is not a real entity; if it is a real entity, it is not false. He provides the reason for this: "For indeed... The meaning is that whatever is accepted as a real, existent entity does not undergo falsity, and whatever is false does not become a real, existent entity, because of the mutual contradiction between the two. Now, regarding false cognition...

Regarding the statement that "because it is a real entity (vastutva), there is the possibility here of two kinds [of cognition] arising from a defective cause," he says in response: "It is false. The intention is that it is not appropriate for the great ones to utter a self-contradictory statement. || 425 ||
If that cognition of a snake and so forth in a rope were a real entity even by its own nature, [it would not be sublated].
Nevertheless, even as the nature of a rope, this [snake] is here sublated precisely because it is a non-entity.

One might object: "Since the cognition of a snake in a rope and the like are real in their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and since they are sublated by valid knowledge (*māna*), it follows that even though they are real entities, they must be discarded.

To this, he says: "Even in themselves" (*svato’pi*). Although the cognition of the snake and the snake itself, when perceived in the rope, are real in their own nature, nevertheless, insofar as the snake and that cognition exist in the form of the rope, they are indeed unreal. Furthermore, both of these are sublated by the perception of the rope.
The meaning is that because there is no obstruction there due to non-attainment, the object is not sublated. || 426 ||
Since false knowledge is an effect, let it be stated what its cause is.
If the effect exists even without a cause, then it could be produced even by children.

Is this false cognition an effect or not an effect? If the former, then one must accept the existence of beginningless ignorance (*anādya-jñāna*) as its cause; with this in mind, he says "false" (*mithyā*). Even if it were an effect, one might suspect that unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) is its cause rather than ignorance; anticipating this, he states that [ignorance] is independent of that.
1 ka. tvadiṣṭa | [vol2, page 225] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 519
He proposes an alternative: "Or is it dependent on that? He asks, "What is that? He refutes the first position with the words "without cause.

The word "even" (*api*) has the sense of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, meaning: if even by children—that is, by infants—it is not [established], how much less so by authoritative persons? || 427 ||
If one knows that desire and the like are the cause, how could the effect exist without its cause?
And even in the case of non-existence, it is indeed a real entity, because it possesses the nature of a real entity distinct from that [existence].

Relying on the second [alternative], he raises an objection: "rāgādi" (passion, etc.). Having further analyzed whether that too is an effect or a non-effect, he addresses the first case with "kāryam" (an effect). The meaning is that its status as the root cause is unestablished. Nor is it authoritative as a non-effect; and even if the defect of the cause were merely an instrumental cause (*nimitta*), it could not be the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) because it is not a substance, or because such a thing is not admitted. Therefore, [it must be] false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

The sense is this: if ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established as the cause of that [world] which is an effect, then since that very [ignorance] exists as its state of being, it is unavoidable that primordial ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) is the material cause (*upādāna*). As for the claim that it cannot be a cause because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), he says in response: "It is a non-entity," and so forth. For that...

[The opponent argues: "Is [this ignorance] void (*tuccha*), or is it non-substantiality (*avastutva*), or is it the state of not being the locus of substantiality (*vastutvānadhikaraṇatva*)? It cannot be the first, because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Even if that ignorance is established as something other than the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*), and thus it is logically consistent for it to be non-substantial (*avastu*), nevertheless, it is indeed a real entity (*vastu*) by virtue of its immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) and its exclusion of the void (*tuccha-vyāvṛtti*). In the second case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to another real entity; in the third case, however, there is unestablishment (*asiddhi*), because the state of not being the locus of substantiality does not exceed [the meaning of] being void (*tucchatva*)."

And because it has already been stated that [ignorance] is unestablished, there is no redundancy with the first and third [arguments] regarding Caitra and others; for Brahman, which is not the locus of substantiality, is itself non-trivial (atuccha), and since its non-distinctness from that [Brahman] is asserted for the sake of the opponent, there is no redundancy even for him, as this does not contradict the refutation of a position introduced through mere possibility.

Furthermore, the lack of substantiality of ignorance is not simply its being other than Brahman, because that [otherness] is unestablished in that case, since ignorance is indefinable (anirvācya); such is the sense. || 428 ||
The truth of the means of knowledge is said to consist in their having the nature of apprehending an object that has been grasped.
By that power alone, delusion and the like residing within the object of cognition are destroyed, and not by any other means.

Now, if it is inferred that ignorance and the like are real because they are excluded from what is insubstantial (tuccha), just like the Self—there, having raised the alternatives of whether they are real as a means of knowledge (*māna*) or as an object of knowledge (*meya*), he states the nature of reality as a means of knowledge in order to refute the first [alternative]. [He says: "Upātta... [etc.]. One might suspect that being real as a means of knowledge does not consist merely in assuming the form of the object of knowledge that has been made its content; rather, it also consists in the removal of ignorance and so forth residing in the object of knowledge. Anticipating this, he says: "By the power of that... [etc.].

The meaning is this: since the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), having no self-nature established independently, destroy delusion and so forth residing within the object of cognition (prameya) only by conforming to that very object and thereby destroying it, their assuming the form of that object alone constitutes their reality. || 429 ||
By the reversal of that, everything such as delusion and so forth is called false.
The unique form of a real entity is not cognized by delusion (*moha*) and the like.

[Anticipating the objection that] even delusion and the like might possess such a kind of reality, he says: "by its opposite" (*tadviparyayataḥ*). He establishes that in delusion and the like, it is precisely the opposite of valid cognition (*māna*) that occurs. Regarding the word "entity" (*vastu*): for the unique form of a real entity is certainly not cognized by delusion and the like in the same way it is by valid cognition and the like.
Because it is not measured by that [intellect], therefore, O Mānava, its reality does not consist in being measured; such is the meaning. || 430 ||
And that object is not the reality of its appearance, according to valid cognition.
Apart from the awakening of the object of cognition, there is no other way for the validity of that cognition to exist. (431)

He refutes the position that delusion (*moha*) and so forth possess reality by saying, "And not... That delusion and so forth do not have a real essence (*satattva*) like a real entity (*vastu*); rather, it is only [the mind] that...
[text fragment]. [Vol. 2, p. 226]

The construction is as follows: "and so on. For its truth consists in its being non-sublatable; that [non-sublatability] does not exist in delusion and the like, because they are removable by valid means of knowledge (*māna*), as he says.

Regarding the phrase "because of sublation" (*bādhāt*): fearing that, like the reality of a means of knowledge (*māna*) by its own nature even without the cognition of an object of knowledge (*meyabodhana*), delusion (*moha*) and so forth might likewise exist [by their own nature], he refutes the example with the word "object of knowledge" (*meya*). || 431 ||
For the reality of causal factors is indeed accepted in relation to their own respective effects.
Otherwise, its truthfulness would be fruitless and could not be attained. || 432 ||

Having raised the objection that, even if the subject and object (meya-mātṛ) lack ultimate reality, ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth might possess reality just like the causal factors (*kāraka*), [the author] considers the alternatives—whether their reality consists in the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) or in being ultimately real—and accepts the first. He says, "of the causal factors. The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows:
"such a kind of reality is also accepted for ignorance and the rest. This is intended to ensure mutual agreement regarding the stated reality in both the example and the thing illustrated.
The word "hi" [indicates the reason]. He states the second [point] as follows: "Otherwise than this. || 432 ||
Whatever entity exists by its own nature does not exist for the sake of another, just like consciousness.
And because it exists solely for the sake of another, that [self] is not distinct from the other.

Having stated that delusion (*moha*) and the like do not possess the status of ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) due to the absence of purpose (*prayojana*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he prepares the ground to state another reason for that very point. He says: "That which... This means that whatever object exists by its own nature is not dependent on another, such as the conscious self (*cidātman*). Nevertheless, what follows from this regarding delusion and the like? To that he replies: "By being for the sake of another" (*pārārthyena*). That is, delusion and the like exist solely as dependent upon another.

The meaning is that it can be inferred by the following reasoning: "That [the world] does not exist separately from the Supreme, just like a rope-snake and so forth; and likewise, the object of dispute is false because it is insentient, like that which is commonly accepted as such. (433)
Everything, being consecrated independently of anything else, [is established] by its own measure alone.
Not even the slightest thing is perceived as having a form separate from the nature of one's own self.

He states another reason for the fact that duality, such as delusion (*moha*) and so forth, is merely imagined, beginning with the word "all" (*sarvam*). By means of consciousness (*saṃvit*), everything—such as a jar—is perceived as being of the nature of pure existence, as being nothing other than its own essential nature, and as being eternally real, in such expressions as "the jar exists," "the cloth exists," "the cloth shines," or "the cloth shines. Thus, everything like a jar becomes nothing but that very reality which is self-luminous and of the nature of manifestation; for [all things] are imagined within that pure consciousness alone—this is the meaning. Of that...

Anticipating the objection that "there is a difference [between the world and consciousness] because they are perceived separately," he says: "One's own Self" (*svātman*). There is no real entity whatsoever, even the slightest, other than the existent Consciousness (*cit*) which is one's own Self; for anything else is like a lotus in the sky. Furthermore, nothing other than Consciousness is perceived, since it is impossible to describe a relationship between the inert (*jaḍa*) and Consciousness, as the latter is not perceived by itself. Therefore, the world shines forth only as imagined within the Self, which is Existence-Consciousness (*saccidātman*).
This is the meaning. || 434 ||
An entity sustains its own self by its very nature;
there exists no dependence for an entity upon anything other than itself. (435)

Anticipating the objection that because the self (*ātman*) is also an entity (*vastu*), it must—like other things—be imagined, and thus cannot be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for that imagination, he says "of the self. The phrase "by its own nature" means by its non-imagined form. The word "for" (*hi*) signifies that the self's being established in its own majesty is indeed based on scripture (*śrauta*). Anticipating the objection that even the self, being an entity, would require a substratum like any non-self (*anātman*), he says "no. It is not.
1.1.1. Dhakkṛt | 2. kha. having gazed upward.
[Vol.
2, Page 227] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 521.

It is not logical that [the Self] be established in its own majesty while depending on another; nor is it possible for the nature of reality—which is common to both the Self and the non-Self—to be grasped as the nature of a non-Self object.
The meaning is that it does not [arise] from non-existence, because that [non-existence] is its very nature. || 435 ||
Therefore, manifoldness within the inner self is produced by ignorance.
For when one realizes "I am Brahman," there is no longer any cognition of difference, because that [ignorance] has been destroyed. || 436 ||

He states the conclusion regarding the possibility of the Self being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by virtue of its being non-imagined (*akalpita*): "Therefore," etc. The meaning is that duality exists in the Self only through ignorance (*avidyā*), as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He further states that it is imagined because it is sublatable (*bādhyatva*): "Brahman," etc. The word "iti" refers to the knowledge of oneness. The particle "hi" is used to indicate the well-known fact that such knowledge removes ignorance. From the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self—

The meaning is this: when ignorance is destroyed, its effects—the distinctions [between objects] and the cognitions thereof—are also destroyed; therefore, since no distinction remains anywhere, only the non-dual reality (advaita) is left over for us. || 436 ||
Because non-arising is sublated by arising, since the two are contradictory.
Even when that [perception] is sublated, there is no need for dependence regarding the sublation of false cognition.

One might raise the objection: "Even though ignorance (*ajñāna*) is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is not sublated, because that [false knowledge] is not admitted to be ignorance; therefore, the cognition of difference must be what is sublated here. Anticipating this, he says: "Mitī" (by means of [knowledge]). Upon the arising of the knowledge of reality, ignorance—in the form of the non-arising of that [knowledge]—is sublated due to their mutual opposition. Therefore, once that ignorance is sublated, there is no further need for a separate sublation of false knowledge.
This is the meaning. || 437 ||
Even that which possesses false cognition is subject to sublation, because it is invariably associated with ignorance alone.
If that [object] is destroyed at its root and thus annihilated, what can false cognition do to us? (438)
Fearing that if the sublation (*bādha*) of false cognition (*mithyādhiyo*) were not required, it would remain unsublated, he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*).

The meaning is that when ignorance (*ajñāna*) is sublated, false cognition is also sublated without effort, because it is its effect and is identical with it. By stating that false cognition is also destroyed when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*), its status as a real entity (*vastutva*) is refuted. Now, regarding the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "The root... and so on. That [superimposition] is called false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). It cannot be that which is real (*satī*) which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because in that case, it would be the primal ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) itself that is possible as its cause;

furthermore, in the *Nigamana-bhāṣya*, it is stated that superimposition is the cause of the activity of being an agent and an enjoyer only by means of primal ignorance, since in the absence of that [ignorance], it [superimposition] itself would not exist. Nor can that which is unreal (*asatī*) be its cause, precisely because of its unreality, as it cannot perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).
The meaning is that it is due to the absence of that [nature]. || 438 ||
If false cognition and doubt both conform to the form of the object, by what reason can their distinction from right knowledge be understood? (439)

Furthermore, as for that false knowledge and so forth which is the cause of saṃsāra, is it real or unreal? It is not the first [option], as he says: "mine-ness" (meyeti). The meaning is that if those two were real, there would be a confusion with right cognition (samyagdhī). || 439 ||
Ignorance is not [the cause], because it is a state of doubt, and likewise because it is not false cognition.
When there is a desire to speak of the reality of those two, ignorance is called the reality.
He says that it is not the second [alternative], namely: "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). For if false cognition and doubt are non-conformity with reality, they are simply ignorance itself.

522 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]: Thus, because we possess doubt regarding this subject, ignorance exists; likewise, because false knowledge exists regarding other subjects, ignorance persists. Therefore, based on worldly convention, it is certain that ignorance alone is the reality (*tattva*) of those two; hence, its true nature—

When there is a desire to speak [of the cause], that which is distinguished by the wise is said to be ignorance alone. Thus, although both are causes of saṃsāra, the meaning is that ignorance alone is the cause thereof. || 440 ||
If it were unknown here, yet once that [object] is known, it would no longer be so.
Because it is entirely unestablished in nature, this is considered false knowledge.

He states another reason for their being ignorance (*ajñāna*): "When unknown" (*ajñāte*). When a thing is known, that which arises only while it remains unknown—such as false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and the like—would not exist; therefore, because false cognition and so forth exist when the object is unknown and do not exist when it is known, they have ignorance as their very essence. Consequently, due to the contradiction between positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), this [false cognition] is not a different entity from ignorance, nor can it exist everywhere in any other manner.
The meaning is "because of reality. || 441 ||
By what nature as "existent" could false cognition possibly possess the status of a real entity?
By that very same [reasoning], who can prevent even ignorance from being real? || 442 ||

Furthermore, one might argue whether that [ignorance] exists as a real entity in the form of its substrate or in its own essential nature; to this, he replies that in the first case, such a nature is common even to false knowledge, stating: "Of false knowledge... (442).
Just as a rope-snake appears to possess a self due to the rope prior to discrimination.
For even the Venerable Ones have declared that this [self], though existing, is a non-entity (avastu). || 443 ||

He provides scriptural authority for the statement of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the reality of everything, beginning with ignorance, in its nature as the Inner Self (*pratyagātman*). [The verse begins: "Like a snake in a rope. The fourth quarter [of the verse], "so too by way of its own nature," refers to this. The word "this" (*eṣa*) is a reference to the phenomenal world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*). The phrase "prior to discrimination" (*prāgvivekataḥ*) applies to both cases.
It is connected. || 443 ||
But in reality, direct truthfulness exists in neither of the two.
Because they are established without investigation, they exist neither from themselves nor from another.

Having accepted that false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and the like possess substantiality (*vastutva*) by way of their substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) during the state of ignorance (*ajñāna*), he refutes the position that they possess substantiality by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*).

He says: "Inherently" (*svataḥ*). This means: of both false cognition and doubt. Ignorance is also included by the word "api. The particle *tu* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is placed after the verb. It means: "directly through the force of valid cognition" (*sākṣānmānavaśāt*).

He states the reason why the reality of ignorance and so forth, in their own nature, is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), beginning with the words "not investigated" (*avicārita*). He explains how that very point is so with the word "no" (*na*). Ignorance, along with doubt and false knowledge, is indicated by the second [word]. For that [trio] is not established as having the nature of the Self (*pratyagrūpa*), because of contradiction and the impossibility of identity; nor is it established as distinct [from the Self], because it is difficult to maintain [its existence] either as a property (*dharma*) or as the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, it does not manifest by itself because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), nor does it manifest from another because there is no connection; therefore, the meaning is that its existence and manifestation occur only when left unexamined (*avicāritasattāsphūrtika*). || 444 ||
"Entering into that very [reality]" refers to that which is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
And the Śruti declares that the deluded self falls into such states as "that" (sa) and "this" (tyad). || 445 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 229] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary named Śāstramakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 521.

Since ignorance and the like are distinct from the inner self (pratīc), because they are real entities in their own nature while the other [the Self] lacks that [reality], how could that [ignorance] be unexamined?

Anticipating the objection that this [world] might be established as something else, he says: "That very [Self]. The construction is as follows: the scripture—"Having created that, He entered into that; having entered it, He became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*)"—states that the ultimate reality, which is that very [Self], has—as it were—attained a foundation consisting of the manifest, the unmanifest, and so forth, due to ignorance. Thus, because the Supreme alone exists in those various forms, it appears as if separate when not investigated.
The meaning is that it is delightful to the senses. || 445 ||
Nor indeed does false cognition exist even in the world when there is the presence of reality.
Because it is prompted solely by delusion, and because it is a general recollection, that [is not valid]. || 446 ||

It has been established that beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) is the cause of *saṃsāra*. As for the claim that in the world false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) arises from general cognition, the absence of specific cognition, and the recollection of what was superimposed, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). The construction is as follows: it cannot be asserted that in every case in the world false knowledge is established only when these three factors are present; for [the delusion of *saṃsāra*] is produced by ignorance, just like the [delusion of] silver—
He says that even an error can possibly arise from that alone: "moha" (delusion), etc. The first "api" (even) indicates the aforementioned example;

the word "ca" (and), however, is explained as having the sense of restriction. To the objection—"Since false cognition is observed to arise from the perception of a universal and the recollection of the thing to be superimposed, how can it be produced by ignorance alone?"—he replies: "No. Here, the meaning of the word "tat" (that) is false cognition. || 446 ||
It is likewise devoid of other generalities as well as of particulars.
Whiteness attains its very state of non-universality because it is independent of anything else. || 447 ||

He establishes that the apprehension of a commonality (*sāmānyasāmānya*) lacks the status of being a cause for error. [The verse says: "By another universal," etc. The meaning of this is as follows: the white substance present before one is devoid of those other universals—such as existence (*sattva*), insentience (*jaḍatva*), and so forth—which, when apprehended in relation to [the specific property of] mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*), serve as causes for the error of silver; [it is also devoid] of those properties such as shimmering (*cākacakyādi*) belonging to the objects present before one, even though they are perceived at will.

Because it is not a cause of error, even though [the object] is devoid of its specific properties such as "conchness" (śuktitva) and so forth—since those too are not grasped as causes of error—the white substance present before one, being perceived, itself attains the state of a universal (sāmānya). This is because, due to its lack of dependence on anything else, it is not a non-universal (asāmānya). Furthermore, the cognition of similarity (sādṛśya) is not the cause of error, as there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as the error of a yellow conch; in some instances, it is the latent impression (saṃskāra) of the superimposed silver and so forth [that acts as the cause].

Even though similarity is useful for awakening [the latent impression], since that awakening is produced by sight and other [senses], the utility of similarity is not understood from that perspective. || 447 ||
And this [cognition] is not born from memory, nor is it produced by a universal as its cause.
Because the white [color] is being perceived as it rests in the space in front. || 448 ||

He establishes that the recollection of the superimposed object is not a cause of error by first restating what has been said: "And if [it were]," etc. The construction is as follows: just as it was stated that an erroneous cognition does not arise from a cause being apprehended through its universal (sāmānya), so too it is not produced from the recollection of the superimposed object. He states the reason for this: "Of the white," etc.; because the white substance present before one is being perceived directly through the superimposition of silver.
The meaning of "cause" (hetu). || 448 ||
1. Of the cognitions; 2. kha. ṣo; 3. ka. ga. -tukam.
[vol2, page 230] 524
Thus, in this very perceptible world existing within the womb of liberation, Sureśvarācārya composed the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika*— in the first chapter.
The cognition produced by ignorance, which appeared as silver, was contrary to that [reality]. (449)
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the apprehension of commonality (*idaṃgraha*) and the memory of silver are not causes of error: "In this way" (*evam*).

Since the apprehension of commonality and so forth are not causes of delusion, one must accept a cognition in the form of silver produced by ignorance residing in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which is the immediate consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl;
and since that [silver-cognition] is to be sublated by its opposite—namely, the [correct] cognition—it is logical that it is born from that ignorance. This is the meaning. || 449 ||
This is said with respect to those for whom knowledge is considered non-perceptual.
From where did this cognition, "this is silver," arise with respect to the mother-of-pearl? (450)

Having stated the error in his own position, he asks—in order to demonstrate its impossibility in the opponent's position—with the words "not perceived. The construction is as follows: for those who maintain that erroneous cognition is not produced by beginningless ignorance established through one's own experience, it must be explained from what this cognition—"this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl—arises: whether from the universal, or from the silver, or from both. 410.
In this case, a specific form, location, time, and action are perceived.
Without the cognition of a mother-of-pearl shell, such an object cannot be established by any other means. (451)

Therein, he refutes the first [position] with the words "viśiṣṭa" (qualified). In the erroneous cognition, silver—qualified by these factors—is what appears: the *ākṛti* (form) being the universal of silverness (*rajatatva-jāti*), the *deśa* (place) being the ground-surface present before one, the *īhā* (activity) being the movement appropriate for silver, and the *kāla* (time) being the present; and the *dharma* (attribute) being triangularity and so forth. While this [silver] appears as similar to real silver, it cannot be established through mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*) due to the ignorance of the mother-of-pearl (*śukti-ajñāna*) or from any other source; rather, that very [silver] is its cause.

The sense is that there is no tautology here: in the previous [verse], the status of the apprehension of a universal as a cause was refuted by the phrase "devoid of another universal," whereas here, the universal itself is being refuted. || 459 ||
It arises from uncommon properties and does not have common causes.
The designation "this is silver" in regard to mother-of-pearl and so forth is unestablished [as a real cognition]. || 452 ||

Raising the objection, "Even if it is being manifested in an uncommon form, why could its cause not be the universal (sāmānya) itself?", he considers the alternatives—whether its causality is by way of being the object (*viṣayatvena*) or by some other mode—and refutes the first with the words "asādhāraṇa... [etc.].
The cognition is qualified; the universal is not the cause by way of being the object of false knowledge arising in the form of a particular (*viśeṣa*). The particular...

He says "because of non-establishment" (*aprasiddhitaḥ*) because it is not established that a universal (*sāmānya*) can be the object of cognition. It is not the second [alternative], for there is no such designation as "silver is mother-of-pearl" or "the rope is a snake"; likewise, the universal cannot be the cause of the cognition of silver by way of any other mode, since it is impossible for it to possess agency and so forth due to its non-establishment—thinking thus, he says "silver."
Here too, the negative particle from the preceding half-verse is to be supplied.
And here there are no royal duties; how then could there be knowledge of that form?
Knowledge is never endowed with form without embracing the form of the object.

It refutes another alternative with the words "And not...": Since silver located in another place and its properties—such as being suitable for the form of a bracelet and so forth—do not exist in the location before one, erroneous cognition cannot have that [silver] as its form; therefore, [the objection that it must be a real object] is not tenable.

The meaning is that even this [silver] cannot be the cause of error by being an object, nor by any other mode, because it is not established [as such]. By this, the third [alternative] is also [refuted].

It has been answered: because it is impossible for either the common form present before one or the form of silver located in another place to be the object (*viṣaya*) of a qualified cognition, or to serve as its cause in any other way. Now, [the opponent objects]: "An erroneous cognition is indeed formless; it does not grasp either a universal or a particular, otherwise its status as an error would be untenable. To this, he says: "Not indeed," meaning that without apprehending a form...

In some cases, whether there is error or non-error, cognition is not tenable; for all cognition is seen to possess a form. Therefore, the meaning is that in this very instance, a specific silver must be accepted as being born of ignorance (ajñāna). || 453 ||
Because it conforms to the mother-of-pearl, this [cognition] does not depend upon a remembered object.
Since memory exists only within the intellect, it does not embrace external objects. || 454 ||

Since the cognition of silver is not perception because it is of the nature of memory, its object is not that which stands before one, but rather the silver existing elsewhere; with this intention, he says:
"The mother-of-pearl. Because the silver is perceived in the form of the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearl, that cognition conforms to what stands before one;
therefore, it does not have the remembered [silver] as its object, and thus the cognition of silver is not memory. Regarding the non-memorial nature of the cognition of silver:

He states another reason: "not embraced [by an external object]," etc. Therefore, the cognition of silver is not a memory because it possesses an external object; this is the remainder of the argument.

Having raised the objection—namely, how there can be a perception of possessing an object in a memory such as "that is my father" if there is no external object—he replies: "in the intellect," etc. Even in the absence of an external object, that [memory] exists within the intellect itself, which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the previously experienced father and so forth, because it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) thereof. || 414 ||
Even those who proclaim that transformation is caused by factors such as merit (dharma) and so forth.
Since this would apply equally even to right knowledge, there would consequently be a lack of confidence [in it]. (455)

[Objection: But surely that non-recollection (*asmṛti*) is not born of ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it is simply the shell (*śukti*) itself appearing in the form of silver due to the influence of past impressions (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth;

and because either the self or the intellect (*buddhi*) undergoes a transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the nature of that [silver] for that very same reason. To this, he says: "Due to merit (*dharma*) and so forth.

Since, according to his own view, such a transformation occurs everywhere equally, then just as in the case of error, even in the case of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), the non-silver would appear in the form of silver.
The meaning is that, due to the doubt as to whether it is silver or not, there would be no certainty regarding the object at all. || 455 ||
An object perceived in the past is considered the objective domain of memory.
The knowledge of the elements, being without support, was not known by the individual self (bhūtātman). 456.

Having refuted the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), [the author] raises an objection regarding the claim that memory does not apprehend an external object. He says, "The past," etc. The remainder of the argument is that, therefore, even if the cognition of silver possesses an external object, its status as memory is established. He refutes this by stating, "That object was not previously known in its past state, nor can there be memory without transcending [prior] experience; thus, the recollection of a past object is devoid of logical support. He says, "Not that... [and so on].
Even the time of cognition is not admitted to exist apart from its own arising.
How can true reality approach consciousness that does not go toward [external objects]? (457)

Considering that even though memory has an object that has already come into being (*bhūtārtha*), because error lacks such an object, the perception of silver and so forth occurring therein cannot be memory, he states another reason why neither memory nor error has an object that has already come into being: "At its own arising... (svotpatti...). For a momentary cognition does not exist at a moment other than the moment of its own arising, as that would contradict its momentariness; therefore, for this reason as well, a present cognition cannot have an object that has already come into being.
526 Sureśvarācārya’s Gṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika [First Adhyāya] [vol2, page 232]

This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that cognition, at the very moment of its arising, goes out and touches an object situated at another time, he says: "without going" (*agatvaram*). The sense is that, unlike sound, there is no coming of an object toward the cognition in the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*), because such a thing would contradict its existence at a different time, and because movement [of the cognition] to every place is not admitted. || 457 ||
If the self is accepted as being one whose cognition of objects is never lost;
Through the complete knowledge of all things, omniscience will certainly be attained for all. || 458 ||
Having raised the objection that the momentariness of knowledge is not established by such scriptural passages as "for there is no seer," he says: "unimpaired" (*avilupta*).

Although intrinsic knowledge (*svarūpa-jñāna*) is eternal, objective knowledge (*viṣaya-jñāna*) is not eternal, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); thus he says: "of all" (*sarveṣām*). || 498 ||
The relationship between cause and effect is traditionally understood as that of the supported and the support.
How could knowledge, which exists as a present self-nature, touch upon a past object? (459)

Now, [the opponent might argue: "Even if knowledge is eternal, it will reside in something other than the Self; how then can the Self possess omniscience? To this, he says: "Residing," etc. First of all, you do not have independent, eternal knowledge, nor does the Self serve as its substratum in a way that is distinct from itself—since the relationship of substrate and superstrate between knowledge and the Self is well-established only in cases such as that of an effect and its cause. Therefore, because of the eternity of knowledge...

The meaning is that its momentariness and so forth are unavoidable. Having established that it possesses both momentariness and subsistence in the self, he states the resulting conclusion: "The present... (verse 459).
Even in the case of the right path (samyagyāna), these three things exist that have been mentioned by you.
For, having recognized it, one indeed understands that this very object was previously unknown.
Having stated that silver located in another place cannot be the cause [of the cognition] because a cognition of silver cannot possibly be a memory, [the author] considers two alternatives:

either that the intended meaning is that a cognition produced by the triad beginning with the universal (*sāmānya*) is necessarily an error, or that it is necessarily produced by the triad beginning with the universal. Regarding the first alternative, he says: "Correctly" (*samyak*). If it is asked how so, [the answer is: where that which was unknown is known, there exists a common form (*sāmānyarūpa*) between the known and the unknown.
It is cognized, and the non-apprehension of its specific qualities is possible, for no cognition whatsoever grasps an object in its entirety. Furthermore, there is memory in that regard;

since the world understands an object through recognition in the form, "That unknown thing is now known by me," these three factors bring about correct knowledge. Thus ends the section on "recognition" (pratyabhijñāya). || 460 ||
If that were the case, false cognition would necessarily follow in every instance.
Except for the one inner self, the triad does not exist therein. || 461 ||

"Let it be so; why then [is there] this triad in the case of right knowledge? To this he says: "In the same way. The meaning is that false knowledge alone is admitted to be produced by a triad of causes. The proponent of Śūnyavāda considers that falsity is indeed desired for all cognition; in response to him, he says: "Setting aside," etc. Because the inner self (pratyagātman) is devoid of the relationship of universal and particular, and because it is eternally immediate, [therefore] in its regard, no cause—
He says that it is not so there, because the basis [of the former] has no room [to exist]. || 411 ||
1 H. V.
°W* M° | [vol2, page 233] 9 Brāhmaṇa: Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śākhaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 527
That effect which occurs only when [the cause] exists, and certainly does not occur when it is absent;
The wise declare that which is independent with respect to its own effect to be the cause. (462)

He refutes the second [position] with the words "In which... Independence means the capacity to act; for it is observed that error occurs only when ignorance exists, and is not observed when it does not exist. Therefore, that [ignorance] alone is the cause, because in the world, causality is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, he will refute later on the fact that the triad beginning with the universal (*sāmānya*) follows from delusion, and has already been refuted previously—this is the meaning. || 462 ||
Something possesses form by itself, and it is also seen [to possess form] through another.
Why is cognition [of silver] in a mother-of-pearl shell, clay, crystal, and so forth, not likewise accepted? || 463 ||

Granted that error arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*), even so, does the cognition of silver possess a form (*ākāra*) or not? In the first case, does it acquire its form intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*)? If intrinsically, there is the impossibility of assuming the form of an object; for it is contradictory to the principle stated in such passages as "the distinction [of cognitions] is indeed by the object itself," that a thing already possessing a form should require another form. If extrinsically, then it must be admitted to be formless by nature. In the second case as well, there is no assumption of the form of an object, due to the absence of form.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, because it contradicts its own nature, error cannot have an objective basis," he says: "Inherently" (*svataḥ*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is connected with the word *svataḥ*. He provides an illustration for this: "Like mother-of-pearl" (*śukti*). Just as mother-of-pearl, which inherently possesses its own form, nevertheless perceives the form of silver; or as clay, which inherently possesses its own form, assumes the form of a jar and so forth; or even as a crystal—

The meaning is that by its very nature, cognition possesses form and assumes the form of lac-dye and so forth. Having presented numerous examples for the sake of easy comprehension, he states the application to the case at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "evam" (thus). Following the aforementioned examples, the meaning is that although cognition is inherently possessed of form, it is possible for it to assume the form of an object; therefore, error does not lack a basis (*nirālambana*). || 463 ||
Nor would cognition be subject to error, if it were to follow after that which is to be remembered.
Because it is directly based on a single real object, just like this cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Anticipating the objection that, because it has an object, this [dream] cognition must be non-erroneous due to its correspondence with reality—just like the cognition of a jar or similar objects—the author says: "Nor also... [The full argument is: If erroneous knowledge were established by taking a rememberable object such as silver as its domain, just like the cognition of real silver, then its validity would not fail; for it would have as its object a thing that is uncontradicted, indubitable, and directly perceived, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl. Therefore, since error lacks validity, [the dream state cannot be established as real].
The meaning is that because it is connected with the noble path, it possesses an objective support (sālambanata) by virtue of having a conceptualized object as its domain. || 464 ||
Nor can we perceive any difference between perceptual cognition and memory.
And because that object has perished, memory does not, therefore, touch the object. || 465 ||

Fearing that the non-validity [of error] might not be established because even error is admitted to possess validity, he says: "And not... The word "smṛti" (recollection) refers here to the object of error. If that were valid, the distinction between valid cognition and error would not be established; however, the meaning is that while knowledge in general is valid by default (*utsarga*), its non-validity in certain cases is established through the division [of types of cognition], such as sublation (*bādha*) and so forth. Furthermore, he states that error is non-conformable to reality (*ayathārtha*): "pradhvaṃsa... [and so on].

"Agreed. The meaning is that since the object of error is destroyed by knowledge, that [knowledge] does not take that thing as its object; therefore, it is correct that it is non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārthatva*). || 469 ||
However, for one who desires to know "what is this?", there may be a misconception otherwise even when [the object] has been negated.
Because it would involve an intervention, that [simultaneity] is not tenable. || 466 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 234] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter:

Having established that error (*bhrānti*) is the effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*) by demonstrating its non-correspondence with reality, for that very purpose, he provides further reasons to distinguish ignorance from false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).

Rāmakaṇṭha asks: "What [is it]? Even when false cognitions such as [the perception of] silver or a snake have been negated by the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*) and so forth, the desire to know (*bubhutsā*)—"What is this?"—on the part of one who wishes to know before the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is not at all tenable if ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not admitted as the intervening factor between the object and the subject.

For it is accepted that false cognition alone constitutes the intervention of the object; since that [false cognition] has already been negated, there must therefore be an intervention of the object [by ignorance].
The meaning is that primordial ignorance must be accepted as the root cause of the desire to know. || 466 ||
For when it is said, "This is mother-of-pearl," one understands it according to the actual fact.
For even apart from the negation of erroneous cognitions such as [the perception of] silver [in place of mother-of-pearl], || 467 ||

He states that there exists here an ignorance other than false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), beginning with the words "the mother-of-pearl" (*śuktikā*). In such usages as "this is mother-of-pearl" or "this is a rope," the hearer understands the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and so forth even without the negation of erroneous cognitions such as [the perception of] silver or a snake. This is established on the plane of empirical experience (*vyavahārabhūmi*);
consequently, through the destruction of that ignorance—which is inseparable from it—the erroneous cognition ceases, and that cessation is subsequently indicated by the cognition of negation.

If there were no ignorance other than false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), then correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) arising in relation to mother-of-pearl and the like—without the prior rise of false knowledge—would be purposeless; for, in the absence of any obscuring factor, its manifestation is inseparable from its own existence. Therefore, the meaning is that beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) exists. || 467 ||
One's own [nature], possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal, is devoid of both the universal and the particular.
The three types of beings would not perceive it, for it is not within the range of the visual faculty.

One might object that even if ignorance (*ajñāna*) is distinct from false cognition (*mithyā-dhī*), it cannot be its cause, because only the triad beginning with *sāmānya* (generality) possesses that causal status based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Anticipating this, he states the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekābhāva*) with the words "nīla... [and so forth]. If the triad were the cause of error, children would not perceive the sky as resembling the petal of a blue lotus; for the sky is devoid of generality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), and thus lacks the necessary causal factors.
The construction is: "because of the absence of [that]. Anticipating the objection that the cognition "the sky is blue" would then not be an error, he says: "For not... The meaning is:
in the case of a substance that is invisible and formless, a visual cognition is necessarily an error, because it is a cognition of something as being what it is not. || 468 ||
Likewise, the division of the directions, the day, and the eastern course [of the sun] are likewise [determined] by the sun.
This manifold variety in a dream exists apart from the three [factors], namely false cognition.

Apart from these three, he states other examples for the claim that "the cause [of error] is seen through delusion" by saying "direction," etc. By the word "etc.," the mention of the surface of a floor being dirty and so forth is included. For indeed, in the sky—which is devoid of the relationship between universal and particular—the division of directions such as "east" and "west" is perceived; yet since there is no evidence for direction being a substance distinct from space (*vyoman*), it is certain that the cognition of smoke, frost, and the like occurs in that very [space].

The notion that one travels from the western direction toward the eastern direction while facing the sun exists even in a dream, where a false city accompanied by various elaborations is perceived; yet, since the three causes [of error] cannot be easily established in all such cases, the meaning is that because of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), that [dream-object] is not the cause of delusion. || 469 ||
Since this is so, therefore it must be understood that the cognition of mother-of-pearl itself [is the object].
The cause for the erroneous cognition of silver and so forth is [the non-apprehension of the difference], because of the weightiness of the logical argument. (470)

Since the three [causes] cannot possibly be the cause, he concludes that the previously stated ignorance as the cause is established: "yataḥ" (since).

The connection is: "therefore, on account of the weight of reasoning. As for the reasoning, it is not tenable [to argue] that [the world arises] from a universal or from memory, and so forth. || 470 ||
Just as you possess Śrī, who is the cause of his karma, knowledge, and so forth.
Even though there is no distinction regarding universals and so forth, let such a restriction also be accepted in this way. || 471 ||

Anticipating the objection—"If ignorance of the mother-of-pearl is the cause of error, why is it that there is only the error of silver and not an error regarding some other object, since the ignorance is the same?"—he says: "Karma" (the verse). By the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the prior experience having silver and such as its object is meant; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), its latent impression (*vāsanā*) is included. Just as, despite the lack of distinction among these three, there is the cognition of silver in the mother-of-pearl...

The restriction that there is no cognition of elephants and so forth [in a dream] is due precisely to the influence of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and other factors; likewise, for the opponent, although ignorance is non-distinct everywhere, the restriction regarding error arises by virtue of karma and other such factors—this is the meaning. || 471 ||
Does the cognition of a general property that is abundant cause whiteness to become a cloud?
Even if it exists, why does another [cause] remain indifferent toward the apprehension of its own substratum? (472)

Even regarding the opponent's position, he establishes that the restriction [of error] is caused by karma and so forth, with the word "bhūri" (plentiful). The meaning is as follows: one perceives various common properties residing in the mother-of-pearl; why then does only its whiteness produce the illusion of silver? And why is it that even though properties such as "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) are being perceived, they do not prevail in causing the perception of their own substratum? Therefore, this [karma], beginning with its specific qualities (*dharma*), is the cause for this restriction. || 472 ||
Because whiteness is related to many objects, what [distinction] is there between it and silver?
Can partiality, in the absence of a cause, produce the cognition of a crane? 473.

Anticipating the objection that—by abandoning the property of being a real entity—the whiteness itself, in its operation toward the apprehension of its own substratum, would have a natural bias toward silver due to its similarity to the silver present before one, thereby establishing the restriction even without the influence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or other factors, he says: "By many [objects].
This means that because whiteness is connected with many objects similar to silver, such as cranes and the like, there is no reason for it to be biased specifically toward silver.

Why does the very cognition of silver not produce whiteness in the mother-of-pearl? Therefore, the meaning is that even in the alternative view, there must be a restrictive factor, such as the action of another [agent] and so forth. || 473 ||
For, since it is established merely by its own form, it is indeed not capable of producing another effect.
Therefore, whether it be a universal or a particular, the Smṛti would not possess the status of being authoritative.

For this reason as well, he states that the triad is not the cause of the error regarding silver and so forth: "By its own form," etc. Since universals and the like are causes only for their own respective cognitions, they lack the capacity to produce a cognition qualified by silver and so forth; therefore, by virtue of that [lack of capacity], there is no error regarding silver and the rest—this is the meaning. ||474||
For it does not present an object that is not proximate to the intellect within the intellect itself.
In this world, knowledge possesses all forms because it is unattached to those forms. || 475 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the silver located in another place cannot be the cause [of the illusion], because the triad [of cognition, object, and agent] consists of error. He says: "For not... In the world, an object not present to the cognizer does not produce a cognition in the intellect that possesses its own form; for if it did not possess the form of that which is not present, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it possessing all forms. Therefore, the meaning is that silver situated in another place is not the cause of the illusion. || 475 ||
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
"In dependence upon the existence of another category of entity, there is the cognition of another thing..."
That whose establishment is false would be like a rope-snake or a double moon. (476)

Having established the illustration that silver and the like are the manifestation of ignorance residing in the consciousness limited by mother-of-pearl and so forth, he states the application of the illustration:

"padārtha... etc. The meaning is that since another entity is intended as both the producer and the indicator [of the world], the world too is imagined, like a snake [superimposed on a rope], because it is dependent [on something else]. || 476 ||
Whatever exists here, such as the knower and so forth, is born from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna).
Because it is established through mutual dependence, that too is false, as previously explained. (477)

How does it possess this dependence? To that he says: "The knower and so forth. Whatever exists here on the plane of worldly transaction, such as the knower and the rest, is born of ignorance and is indeed false, because it is established only through mutual dependence; for the knower, the means of knowledge, and the rest cannot be established without mutual dependence, just like the previously mentioned snake and other [illusory objects]. This is the construction of the verse. || 477 ||
This transmigratory existence has been demonstrated as being of the nature of superimposition upon the Self.
Moreover, superimposition does not occur in the world without a cause. || 478 ||

Having established that, just as false knowledge in the world is the effect of ignorance, so too is the superimposition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) upon the inner self (*pratīc*), he now reviews what has preceded: "Upon the Self," etc. He provides the introductory context to introduce another portion of the Commentary: "And superimposition," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to state both the reason—that it is an effect—and the illustrative example, just like a jar. || 478 ||
Therefore, that which is called the "cause" (kāraṇa) is for the purpose of explaining the reason (hetu).
"In that [case], by the words 'through ignorance' (avidyayā), has not the cause indeed been stated? || 479 ||

He introduces that [verse] preceded by a statement of its purpose and result: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This means: because an effect is impossible without a cause. He raises the objection of redundancy: "In which... (*yasmin*) || 479 ||
Anticipating the objection that [the world] is the primary cause (pradhāna), it is stated once again:
The unknown Self is the cause of the world, not the three qualities. || 480 ||

[The author] avoids [the charge of redundancy] by saying "as the primary cause. Even though the cause has already been stated in the phrase "in which [there is] ignorance," the Sāṃkhya doctrine—which posits a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*)—might be suspected. Therefore, the very same cause is stated again for the purpose of refuting that distinction; thus, the objection of "redundancy" does not apply. To explain how the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the *pradhāna* is refuted, he says: "unknown," etc. (Verse 480).
"Furthermore, he himself will explain it through both scripture and reasoning."
O Noble One, this alone is the consequence; there is no other cause for it than that.

Regarding how the counter-argument (*uttarapakṣa*) and the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣanirāsa*) are established by mere assertion, he says: "From scripture" (*śrutitaḥ*). The word "also" (*api*) indicates that this matter has already been stated [elsewhere]. "By himself" refers to the statement of the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*). Because that which is limited is an effect, it must have a primal cause; [this is known] from such scriptural passages as, "From Him space was produced," "From Him the vital breath is born," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

It has been stated in various places, and will be stated further in such passages as the Madhu Brāhmaṇa, that Brahman alone—unknown due to its association with *tvam* (the individual self)—is the cause, and not *pradhāna* or other such principles.

The meaning is that, because no other cause is possible, Brahman alone, when unknown, is such [the cause]; thus he concludes. Not from this... [text fragment].

6:116. Since name and form consist of that [consciousness], they lack self-nature.
Therefore, it is said that [the cognition] lacks validity, like the [perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar cases. || 482 ||
He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "yadātmake" (of whatever nature). "Yadātmake" means "of those two, name and form.

He states the result of the body of ignorance, which consists of the duality of name and form, by saying "ataḥ" (therefore). "Apramāṇatvam" means lack of authoritative status, that is to say, sublation. || 482 ||
Nowhere in the world does an effect ever transcend its cause.
If it were not distinct from its own causes, then the statement of reasons such as "water" and so forth would be [meaningless]. (483)

He states the purport of the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) beginning with "like water" and so forth, starting with the words "No" (*na*). The reason (*hetu*) and the example are not distinct in their capacity to establish the point. For in the world, an effect does not transcend its cause; thus, since this duality of name and form is in reality nothing but the unknown Brahman-Ātman, the statement of examples such as "like water" is made. Just as foam and the like arise from water and are nothing but that, so too the world, arising from the unknown Brahman, is nothing but Brahman.
This is the meaning of "tram. || 483 ||
That which is grasped as a mere object is not sufficient for the removal of that ignorance.
Having an unappropriated magnitude, it exists for the sake of cognizing the object. (484)

He states the purport of the commentary beginning with "And he who... as follows: "The reality," etc. Even though the nature of reality is characterized by eternal purity and so forth, that form of reality, if it has not ascended onto the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) arising from the sentence, is not capable of destroying the ignorance inherent within itself; for while the reality alone is the establisher of that [purity], it is only when it has ascended onto the cognition produced by the sentence that it is empowered to destroy its own ignorance. This is the meaning of the commentary beginning with "And he who... (verse 484).
Since this is awakened by itself, it is therefore pure and non-dual.
For a second conjunction is the cause of impurity in the world. || 485 ||

There, he applies the commentary [as follows]: "From itself" (*svataḥ*). Having stated that the fact of having consciousness as its sole essence (*bodhaikarasatva*) is the reason for purity, he states another reason:
"Non-existent" (*asad*). However, in the reading "therefore non-dual" (*ato'dvayam*), non-duality arises precisely from purity, because of the absence of any connection with a second thing.

The meaning is: "because it establishes purity. He establishes that the absence of a second is the cause of purity by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), starting with the words "dvitīya" (the second). The ellipsis is: "Therefore, because of the state of being without a second, the aforementioned reality is established. The underlying intention is that even though such [purity] exists in the inner self (*pratīci*), the reality of the Self—which is the remover of ignorance and so forth—is not established by mere perception; rather, it is established only when it has ascended to the intellect (*buddhi*) through the power of the scriptural statement. || 4.85 ||
In the reality as it has been described, there can be no connection with duality apart from ignorance.
Therefore, the statement regarding the prohibition of impurity is the prohibition of that ignorance. || 486 ||

[Objection: But surely, because of its connection with the second [the object], the inner self (pratyagātman) lacks purity, since the Self is connected with that [duality] by virtue of being the perceiver of duality as established through perception and other means.

To this, he says: "As stated... [The meaning is: The contingency of impurity in the Self arises from its connection with the two [subject and object], which is dependent upon the connection with ignorance (avidyā); therefore, [the Self is] pure. 1. śātātma; 2. ka, kha, ga: sadvya.
