This is the meaning of the word *tad*. In the phrase "ignorance of that" (*tad-avidyā*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the reality as previously described. Since both duality and the notion of "that" (the object) are products of ignorance, the meaning is that the purity of the Self is real. || 486 ||
The Lord, the unmanifest, the individual soul, the primordial matter, the elements, the sense organs, and so forth.
Nothing can be conceived of the inner self except by relying upon ignorance. 487.

An objection is raised: "Since some maintain that the world, consisting of the eight states beginning with the Lord (Īśvara), is ultimately real, how can duality be false? To this, the author replies: "The Lord," and so forth. By the word *īśvara*, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) and the Witness (*sākṣin*) are denoted. By the word *bhūta*, individual entities (*vyakti*) capable of coming into being are understood. By the word *indriya*, the presiding deity (*devatā*) is meant. By the word *ādi* (and so forth), the genus (*jāti*) is expressed. (Verse 487)
Even one who is skillful does not perceive it through the vision of the inner self's true nature.
And without the inward-facing intellect, there can be no cognition through an outward-facing intellect.
Having asserted the proposition that duality arises solely from ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), he states the reason for this: "The inner self...
[etc.]. Nevertheless, fearing the objection that duality might be real because it is perceived through the perspective of the external (*parāgdṛṣṭi*), he says: "And not... || 488 ||
And this statement, "The openings [of the senses] are turned away," is spoken with a display of pride.
In the Vedāntas, the reality of the Self is not an object of multiple means of valid cognition.

[Objection: In that case, even the Self would be false because it is cognizable by a cognition directed toward another (parāgbuddhi); for it is accepted [by some] that the Self is knowable through all cognitions.

[Reply: He says "no," with the words "parāñci" (turned away). This state of being knowable solely through the measure of the internal seer (pratyagdṛṣṭi) of the Self is stated in the Vedāntas with intentional meaning by such scriptural passages as "parāñci. For although that [Self] when possessed of limiting adjuncts (sopādhika) is knowable through all cognitions, [this does not apply to] the Self when devoid of limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika).
The construction is: "suchness" (tathātva). || 489 ||
From this [it follows] that the state of being contradicted belongs to that which, by its own nature, consists of the two-fold [subject and object].
It is indeed possible to describe the supreme Self as Vaiśvānara, but not by means of [ordinary] measurement.

Having set aside the notion that [the Self] is accessible through external cognition (*parābhyāna*), some assert that it is accessible through internal cognition (*pratyakṣa*); against them, he says "from this" (*itaḥ*). This means "from internal perception" (*pratyakṣāt*). He states that it is unfit for external cognition to operate upon it by describing its essential nature as being "self-evident" (*svataḥ*). [This refers to one who has] daily propitiated the deity...
He mocks the statement of Bhartṛprapañca and others, beginning with "prasādāt," by saying it is not based on authoritative means of knowledge: "It is possible" (śakyam). || 490 ||
Since the supreme Self is by its very nature eternally pure and enlightened, it must therefore be understood as always liberated by one who relies on the authoritative word of the Sage. (491)

Having established the self's eternal purity and so forth, he now establishes its state of being eternally liberated. He indicates with the word "eternal" (*nitya*) that such scriptural passages as "It is not tainted by the suffering of the world" serve as the authority here. With the word "existent" (*sat*), he means: by the proponent who accepts as authoritative the Vedic declarations of the Upanishads—which are real, free from defects, and not of human origin. (491)
Even though he has become the mountain, Maheśvara remains unawakened to the true nature of his own self.
He entered into the state of being the causal self for the purpose of creating names, forms, and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned status of the Supreme as the cause is untenable because it contradicts Śruti and Smṛti, he says: "Thus."
The term "Maheśvara" is employed with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the creator and the destroyer. || 492 ||
By saying "this very [is that]," he also expresses a state of extreme contradiction.
It declares that the conjunction of contradictory things has ignorance as its sole cause. (493)

The state of ignorance (*avidyatva*) of people due to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth has been stated; therein, two scriptural terms (*padadvaya*) serve as indicators. Thus, he states the intended meaning of the two terms mentioned by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*): "He is this" (*sa eṣa*). This supreme one is this very individual soul (*jīva*). By asserting their identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) despite their being utterly contradictory—such as non-duality versus duality—the Commentator, or the Veda, [establishes] the oneness of that which is to be realized, even while [acknowledging] creation which is contradictory to that oneness.

This indicates that duality is false because it is born of ignorance; otherwise, since the identity of those two would be impossible, there would be a contradiction with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that the fact that the creation of name, form, and so on is rooted in ignorance (*āvidyatva*) is understood from the two words [of the text]. || 493 ||
By the statement "while explaining," even one who is inherently wise [is affected] due to the persistence of ignorance.
It is said that he entered the entire range of effects, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

He states that even the commentary beginning with "making the indeterminate name-and-form determinate" (*avyākṛte nāmarūpe vyākurvan*) indicates that the creation of name-and-form and so forth is rooted in ignorance (*āvidyatva*). Regarding the phrase "making determinate": although the Self (*ātman*) is by its very nature eternally pure and so forth, it creates the effect through the support of its own ignorance and enters into it; this is what is expressed by the commentary. That commentary also serves as proof for the point already stated.
This is the meaning. || 494 ||
The meaning previously stated in accordance with one's own experience is that which remains unknown [to others].
Because it licks—that is, grasps—the meaning under discussion, it is expressed by the pronoun "that" (saḥ). || 495 ||
Having stated the purport of the introductory sentence as explained in the Bhāṣya by means of the two Vārttikas, he states the meaning of the word "sa" (that). [He says: "svānubhūti... etc.

The word "pure" (in the verse) is an expression of the sentence concerning the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). He states the reason for employing the word "sa" to denote the unknown inner self (*pratīc*): "prakṛta... etc. || 495 ||
Having thus reflected upon that which is of the nature of the unmanifest (avyākṛta), he [proceeded].

Such a one, established in his own effect, is called "this" (eṣa) by means of direct perception and so forth. Having shown the mediacy (*pārokṣya*) of the Self (*pratīc*) through the word "that" (*sa*), he explains how its immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is expressed by the word "this" (*eṣa*). To that end, he says: "having referred back. This refers to the Self as the ultimate reality (*satattva*), which is unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), absolute (*pāramārthika*), and unchanging (*avikṛta*). Thus—

"Form" (rūpa) means "unknown"; that is to say, the inner self (pratyagātman) abiding in its own effects and present in the intellect. He states the reason for denoting that [inner self] by the word "this" (eṣa): "Because of its perceptibility" (prātyakṣyāt). || 496 ||
Thus, for two things that appear contradictory, there is non-duality through their nature as being beyond duality.
How could there be this designation "this is that," as in the case of a black snake? (497)

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words implies the identity [of their referents] that has been stated. Regarding the word "contradictory" (*viruddha*): the syntactical connection is as follows—how could there be a designation of oneness through such coreferentiality as "He is this" between the two meanings of *tat* and *tvam*, which are of contradictory forms by virtue of being non-dual and dual respectively?

For just as it is not appropriate to designate Caitra as identical with a black serpent, so too it is impossible for another to assert the identity of the individual soul [with Brahman], because the contradiction is no different; thus he says: "The black... (verse 497).
From the cause, the effect is known in general; likewise, from the effect, the cause is known.
And because the logic and reasoning thus stated apply here, there is no contradiction whatsoever. (498)

He resolves the objection by stating that there is no contradiction with the identity under discussion, because the principle already mentioned—that cause and effect are conceptual constructs due to their mutual dependence—is not contradicted. [The verse says: "From the cause... The meaning is that since duality appears through ignorance (avidyā), its contradiction is not established in reality; therefore, the identity obtained through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not contradictory. || 498 ||
For one who does not know the true nature of reality, nothing is difficult to achieve; such a person might even see the sky dyed blue with their own eyes, as if wearing blue cloth. (499)

Anticipating the objection as to how, even from ignorance, there could arise a dualistic cognition consisting of cause and effect—which contradicts the authoritative unity—he recalls what was stated in the verse beginning with "One might conceive of Mount Meru as an atom. [He says: "By the unknown," etc. He provides an illustration for that: "Made blue," etc.
This consideration of what is fit and what is unfit applies to human conduct.
Since [these] arise as mere conceptual construction, there is no dependence upon the stages of knowledge.
Anticipating the objection—“Even if error is dependent on ignorance, how can there be a visual perception of the sky, which is not suitable for the eye?”—he says:

“suitable” (*yogya*). Alternatively, anticipating the objection—“A blue garment can be perceived by the eye because it is suitable, but the sky, even when made blue, cannot be seen by it because it is unsuitable”—he says: “suitable. [This refers to] that which is suitable within the empirical transactions of *avidyā*.

He states the reason for the claim that there is no dependence on the distinction between the fit and the unfit: "Conceptual construction" (kalpanā). The meaning is that the stages of ignorance are delusions;
in them, there is no dependence on the distinction between the fit and the unfit, because they are established by mere conceptual construction and consist of nothing but appearance. || 100 ||
This reason is stated for the purpose of establishing what has been thus declared.
By the word "entered" (praviṣṭa), [it is meant] here because of the continuity with its own manifestation as pure light. || 501 ||
Having stated with the two words that this [identity] is not contradictory because the form opposed to identity is merely avidyā, he explains the meaning of the word *praviṣṭa* (entered).

"Thus it has been said" (*ityukta*) means: by the particle *iti*, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words is expressed; the identity thus expressed is the reason required for its ascertainment, and that is what is denoted by the word *praviṣṭa*. If it is the Supreme Self that has entered, then since that which has entered is the individual soul (*jīva*), its identity with That is logical.

Anticipating the objection that "there can be no entry into another [the Self] because it is unattached," he says: "In this context. The meaning is that "entry" occurs through connection with that undivided darkness which is the reflection of the inner self (pratyagābhāsa) within the created effect. || 101 ||
By the phrase "beginning with Brahmā," everything that is subject to birth is also expressed.
And it is said that [it exists] within bodies for the sake of all the phenomena of saṃsāra. || 502 ||
Stating the meaning of the word *iha* as explained in the Bhāṣya, he states the meaning of the phrase "among those beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass": "among Brahmā and so forth.

The particle *api* (also/even) is to be connected with the word *sarvam api* (all). Since everything that possesses birth is intended here as the meaning of the word *iha*, it is expressed in the singular.

[Page 535] Nor can it be said that the expression "many" (bahu) is unintended because it is impossible to speak [of them all]; with this in mind, it was stated "in Brahman and so forth. Anticipating the objection—"What is the purpose of the qualification 'in those' (heṣu), since the meaning of the word 'here' (iha) is simply 'that which possesses birth'?"—he says: "Entirely," etc. [This refers to] the locus of the entire cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
The meaning is that the word "body" (deha) is used for the purpose of grasping its limiting adjunct (upādhi). || 102 ||
It is likewise said that [this] exists within bodies from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
The connection between action and its fruit occurs only in the bodies, not in the self.

He explains the meaning of the phrase "among those possessing hunger and so forth, which are the substrata for the fruits of karma" with the words "beginning with Brahmā. The construction is as follows: just as the connection with action and so forth exists only in the bodies and not in the Self, so too it is stated in the commentary beginning with "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass" that [the connection] exists in the fruits of karma and so forth. || 103 ||
[This is] the eye of the wisdom of non-delusion regarding those things that have the form of the body and so forth.

When the speech has entered into identity [with the object], it is said that there is a predominance of the qualities (guṇaprādhānya). || 504 ||

Having explained the meaning of the word *praviṣṭa* (entered) found in the introductory statement as being the cause of unity, he states another meaning for that very same word: "Pratyaṅ" [etc.]. Delusion (*moha*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Supreme; the vital breath (*marut*), which is the life-force (*prāṇa*), is the limiting adjunct of the Sūtra; the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is the limiting adjunct of Hiraṇyagarbha; by the word "eye," all the sense organs are indicated; and the gross body—all of these together—is the limiting adjunct of Virāj. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—

Truly, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those such as ourselves—namely the individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*) and karma and so forth—are what is being discussed. The meaning of the word "entered" (*praviṣṭa*) refers to the identity of those [entities] such as Īśvara, who are thus characterized by being limited, with Brahman, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts. That identity is of the nature of a primary and secondary relation, like that between a rope and a snake;
therefore, everything that is limited is, when stripped of its adjuncts, merely that [Brahman], because it is superimposed upon it. This is the meaning. || 104 ||
The Supreme, being unattached, does not turn away from that which is turned toward Him, nor does He approach it.

For here, without taking up ignorance (ajñāna), the Self does not perceive the non-Self. Now, if there is non-difference between the conditioned (upahita) and the Supreme, then through its connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi), the Self’s state of being unattached (asaṅgatva) would be lost; and if there were no such connection, there could be no non-difference of the conditioned. To this, he says: "It does not approach. Because there is an absence of difference due to [the Self] being the innermost witness (pratyak) of all, even when that [difference] is conceptually imagined, in reality there is an absence of attachment.

The meaning is that because it is based on scripture (*śruti*), its real state of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) is not contradictory. Anticipating the objection that the Supreme Self cannot be established as a witness if it has no connection with the external world, he says: "No. Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of the ignorant person. The particle "for" (*hi*) is used to state that the scriptural view—that the nature of being a witness is rooted in ignorance—is well-known among the wise. || 105 ||
Just as one cannot perceive a thief and so forth without first having the cognition of a post.
Without first abandoning ignorance of the Self, there can likewise be no perception of the non-Self.
He clarifies the state of being the witness of all through an illustration due to ignorance, [beginning with] "sthā" || 906 ||
Endowed with which this transmigrating being [remains] in deep sleep due to the exhaustion of karma.
"There would remain only its own nature, because it is its effect, like a jar or similar objects" (507).

Having established that the Supreme, though non-different from those [individual souls] conditioned by Īśvara and others, possesses both unattachedness (*asaṅgatva*) and witnesshood (*sākṣitva*), he states another reason for their non-difference with the words "By which... During deep sleep, because of the absence of karma—which is the cause of manifest experience—the transmigrating soul, being devoid of distraction, attains union with the Existent (*sati saṃpadyate*); such is the Vedic scripture.

1936 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

For one who has attained identity with the Brahman that is unknown [as such], this [universe]—beginning with the Lord (Īśa)—would become non-distinct from that causal Brahman, being of its very nature, which is the state of being devoid of phenomenal expansion (*aprapañcatva*). Because it is superimposed upon that [Brahman], it is like a jar, which is a modification of clay and consists of that [clay]. Just so [is this universe].
This is the meaning. || 907 ||
That which is the entry of the reflection of one's own self [into the object] is the cause of the delusion regarding the individual soul.
That same [cognition] would also occur even among those who know it, such as the Maruts, in the form of perceptions of Buddhas and so forth.

The meaning of the word "entered" (*praviṣṭa*) as the identity of Brahman and the Self has been established. Now, fearing the objection that its meaning is not identity because it is conventionally used in other senses, he says: "His own Self" (*svātma*). For that which causes delusion regarding the inner self (*pratyag*), the "entry" known as the reflection of the inner self (*pratyag-ābhāsa*) within that delusion is itself the entry into all adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by the ignorance of the inner self; there is no other entry into that which is undivided (*aparicchinna*).

The meaning is that because of their inseparable connection (*amminna-yoga*), the appearance does not exist apart from the illuminator; thus, the word "entered" (*praviṣṭa*) ultimately results in signifying their identity (*aikya*). || 508 ||
It has the form of a thread consisting of water and earth, possessing the powers of action and consciousness.
That which has its state residing in the agent is either stationary or mobile; that which has its state residing in the object is [also] of two kinds. || 509 ||
Having stated the substrata of entry in the form of the Maruts, Indra, and so forth, he describes their essential nature with the words beginning "payombho-vādi" (like milk and water).
The meaning is as follows: like milk and water mixed together, the causal substrate conditioned by *māyā* possesses manifold forms because it consists of all effects;

from that [cause] arises the *sūtra* (the thread), which consists of the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) elements and is endowed with a power in which action is predominant and knowledge is subordinate. This is the cause.

He states a further internal distinction [between the two types of *sūtra*]: "that which exists as the agent" (*kartṛstha*). The meaning is that the *sūtra* which exists as the cause in the form of an agent—that is, as the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is the cause for the arising [of the other];
it is stable and immovable because it is beginningless. He states a further internal distinction regarding the *sūtra* as an effect: "the moving" (*cala*).
The meaning is that the *sūtra* which exists as the effect in the form of an action—that is, as that which is produced—is moving, having a beginning and an end. || 109 ||
From that [intellect], the manifestation of the self as intellect occurs; from that, the manifestation of the self as determination.
That which they call Hiraṇyagarbha is the material cause (upādāna) for the cognitions of the world. || 510 ||
Reiterating the origin from the Supreme of Hiraṇyagarbha, whose power of knowledge is subordinate to his power of action, [the author] states his intermediate nature:

"of the nature of intellect" (*buddhyātmanaḥ*). He further qualifies that very [nature]: "of the nature of determination" (*vyavasāyātmanaḥ*). He distinguishes [Hiraṇyagarbha] from the [Supreme] by means of the word "from that" (*tataḥ*); the meaning is "from the Supreme who is not known [as such]. Even though there is an origin from that [Supreme] of one whose nature is intellect, what has happened to Hiraṇyagarbha?

He says this: "Hiraṇyagarbham. In that regard, he cites scripture and tradition as authority: "They say... He indicates an inference based on the effect as the mark regarding that very [Brahman]: "The material cause... || 110 ||
Having attained the state of Vairāja and possessing the divisions of the regions beginning with the earth,
this god, who makes the deities his instruments, is called Virāj.
He states the true nature of Virāj: "The Vairāja," etc. The Supreme Self alone—the Lord of Māyā who is the cause of the Sūtra and so forth—is subtle;

having attained the state of Virāj, which consists of the gross phenomenal world and possesses spatial divisions derived from the five elements beginning with earth, He is called Virāj; and His meaning is that He possesses limbs such as the face and so forth. || 111 ||
1 ga. svabhā | 2 ka. ga. svabhā | [vol2, page 243] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri | 537
And likewise, the wording of a mantra is seen here as "nirmūrdha."
The deities would consist of nothing more than that [perception], arising from their own self-conceit.

Having described the Virāj, [the author] recalls the very same measurement mentioned previously with the words "And so" (*tathā ca*). The particle *hi* is used to indicate that the aforementioned Smṛti—beginning with "The wise call the sky his head"—is based on the aforementioned Śruti regarding the Virāj thus shown.

By restating the origin from the Virāj, he summarizes the essential nature of the deities such as Indra and others. [He says] "Taking that as its material cause" (*tad-upādāna*), [referring to] Indra—

Because the individual soul (puruṣa) remains in the state of a practitioner through the conceit of "I" and so forth, the latent impression (vāsanā) thereof is also the cause for the deities who have become the fruit; thus he says: "born from one's own conceit. (112)
Of external beings as well as of those whose form is internal.
For the limitation of those previously mentioned is indeed caused by ignorance, desire, and karma. || 513 ||

One might raise the objection: "Let such bases for entry exist; however, when consciousness enters them, is it one or many? In the first case, the conventional distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) would be untenable; in the second, non-duality (*advaita*) would be destroyed. Anticipating this, he says: "The material" (*ādhibhautika*). The phrase "in that very way" (*tathaiva*) is intended to include the collection of elemental constituents belonging to the divine realm (*ādhidevika*). This refers to those previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the individual self, the ego, the vital breath, the intellect," and so forth—namely, their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The meaning is that although there is unity in the consciousness that has entered into the intellects (*dhi*), the conventional usage of distinct individual souls (*jīva-bheda*) occurs by virtue of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate the capacity of ignorance and the like to skillfully fashion the construction of non-existent limitations. || 113 ||
Having created the universe, from the subtle thread down to the great pillar, by means of his own māyā;
Hari entered that very [world] which has His own manifestation as His sole companion.

(514) He concludes the meaning of the statement regarding the entry with the words "sūtrādi" and so forth. The construction is as follows: "He whose sole companion is His own manifestation" (*svābhāsaikasahāya*), and who is also the "Self" (*ātman*), entered the world created by Himself. This applies both to the act of creation and to the act of entry.
He states the common reason: "The Self" (ātman). This indicates that He who has entered [into all things] acts as their protector in each respective place. "Hari" [is used]. || 114 ||
But was it not stated previously that the world itself was manifested?
Since he is liberated from karma and not subject to it, how can he be designated as an "agent" (kartṛ) without cause? || 515 ||

The objection challenges the previously stated claim that "the Supreme Self, the creator of the manifest, entered into that [creation]": namely, "But [is it not so]? This refers to the passage beginning with "In the beginning, by name and form. In that context, there is no word indicating that the manifestation of the world occurred through its own power alone.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Karma... Since the verbal suffix is seen in the sense of the agent being simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*), it would follow that the world transforms by itself;
in that case, because there would be no observer, it could not be its own enterer. Thus he says: "Suddenly... (111).
Furthermore, the entry of another self is also not logically consistent.
Since this [object] under discussion is not present here, it does not partake in the entry.

He states another reason for the impossibility of the other [the Supreme Self] entering: "of the Supreme Self. Although the Supreme Self is known from the Vedas to be the creator of the world, nevertheless, His entry does not conform to reason; this is the meaning. Why is it inconsistent with reason?
538 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 244]

He says: "No. The meaning is that since the unmanifest (avyākṛta) is the subject under discussion in this context as the cause, whereas the Supreme (para) is not introduced here either as the cause or as the non-cause, its entry [into the body] is not established. || 116 ||
This is not a fault, for even the Supreme [Self] exists in the form of the unmanifest world-soul.
Because it is intended to be expressed, that which is implied—such as necessity and so forth—is denoted. || 517 ||

Demonstrating that the Supreme Self is the subject under discussion, he resolves the contradiction between the preceding and following passages with the words beginning "No" (na). The phrase "as in the case of the unmanifested" (avyākṛtavat) refers to the subsequent [passage].
The particle "hi" (for/indeed) serves to indicate that it is well known in all the Upaniṣads that the Supreme Self is the cause of the world and its enterer.

Anticipating the objection that the agency of the creator of the world is not intended because of the use of the reflexive passive construction (*vyākriyata*)—where the object itself functions as the agent—he says: "ākṣi... (the eye...).

[The opponent] says: Since the world cannot exist apart from a controller who brings about its manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*), it is appropriate that the world is expressed by the term "unmanifested" (*avyākṛta*). The verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used in the sense of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), as in the expression "the calf releases itself"; this is stated with a view toward the facility of linguistic expression.
Therefore, since the Supreme Being (*para*) remains the subject under discussion, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. This is the meaning. || 117 ||
For by the expression of the word "this," there is the hearing of a single substratum.
Therefore, the meaning of the term "indeterminate" as previously stated is appropriate here. || 518 ||

He states another reason for the term *avyākṛta* denoting the world together with its controller and so forth, beginning with the words "idaṃśabda" (the word "this"). The word "ataḥ" (from this) is connected with the ablative case. The aforementioned meaning is the association with the controller and so forth. The word "atra" (here) refers to the mention of the unmanifested world (*avyākṛtajagat*).

The particle "hi" (for/indeed) is used to establish that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) functions by referring to non-different objects. This is because when the word "this" (*idaṃśabda*) denotes the manifested world—

The construction is as follows: because we hear the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the term "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta-pada*), which denotes the unmanifest world, it is appropriate that throughout this entire world there is an association with a controller and so forth. || 118 ||
This world possesses many diverse forms, such as the controller, the controlled, and so forth.
"Just as we determine now, so it was previously.
(519) How can the fact that the unmanifested world possesses a controller and so forth be established merely from the stated grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? To this he says:

"This" (*idam*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), instruments, auxiliaries, and the like are included. And by the pronoun "this" (*idam*), visible objects such as pots and the like are referred to.
It is observed; the meaning is that conceptual construction follows what has been perceived. || 119 ||
Even when the manifestation [of effects] prior to the manifestation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth is denied, it was not non-existent.
The unmanifest is the sole presiding witness over the manifest world, of which he is the witness.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a lack of a means of proof (*sādhaka*) for the world—which is unmanifest yet endowed with a controller and so forth—he says: "By name... The very witness by whom the world is experienced as manifest through name and form, and as being endowed with a controller and so forth, is himself the means of proving its manifestation and non-manifestation both prior to its origin and subsequent to its concealment. For he does not require another means of proof, since he is solitary and self-luminous.
This is the meaning. || 520 ||
Because he is the witness to the dance of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and because he transcends it.
Since that which remains here is to be entered, therefore the Supreme alone enters.
1. Dancing.
[vol2, page 245] 6
4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 539.
By stating that the Supreme is the subject under discussion and having described its very entry [into the world], he states another reason for that same point: "The world," etc.
Whatever remains—whether heard or seen—as distinct from the Witness, all of that is included within the scope of the entry; therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the enterer into the world.
The meaning is that, therefore, there is no suspicion of difference. || 121 ||
Furthermore, the employment of words is observed in the world to depend upon the speaker's intention.
Just as it is with words such as "village" and so forth, let it be understood here in this case as well.

In response to the objection that in the case of the term "undetermined" (*avyākṛta*), the other [meaning] is not the subject at hand because the single word "undetermined" does not possess multiple meanings, he says: "And because of the intention to speak. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to provide an example in accordance with the capacity [of the word]. He shows that "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) itself is established as the example by saying: "Just as... Just as in words such as "village-chief" (*grāmapa*) or "cloth," the word "undetermined" (*avyākṛta*) also possesses multiple meanings; thus is the analogy.
He states the proximate [cause]: "In that way" (tathā). || 122 ||
The dwelling place, the dweller, and likewise both are so described.
Just as the word "village" is used in this world, so too here is the term "world" (jagat) used for Virāj.

He explains how the word "village" (*grāma*) has multiple meanings with the words "and dwelling" (*nivāsaśca*). Examples are: "the village is empty," "the village has gone [to another place]," and "one should not enter the village. Taking up the fact that the words "world" (*jagat*) and "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) have the same meaning, he adopts the very illustrative example already stated: "so too" (*tathā*). The phrase "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement of the scripture; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the intention to express multiple meanings by the word 'world'. (123)
In some cases the self alone is to be indicated; in some cases it is said to be the non-self alone.
Likewise, the intention to express both [aspects] is also established by the statement regarding the determinate and the indeterminate.
He elaborates upon the illustrative example [dārṣṭāntika]. Regarding the phrase "in some cases": he provides an illustration when both [meanings] are intended to be expressed.
"The manifested" (vyākṛta) means that the world, though already manifested, is said to be unmanifested; such is the sense. || 124 ||
Where a thing characterized by destruction and so forth is intended to be expressed as the primary subject.
In that context, the meaning to be expressed is precisely non-self (anātman), with the inner self (pratyagātman) serving as its subordinate element. || 525 ||

To the question of where it is that the non-self alone is expressed by the word "jagat" (the world), he says: "Where... In such formulations as "that which possesses the origination, destruction, and so forth of the world," the non-self alone is primarily expressed by the word "jagat," while the inner self (pratyagātman) becomes subordinate; otherwise, [the non-self] would not be subject to birth and so on—this is the meaning. || 525 ||
It is described therein as being neither gross, nor born, nor subject to decay, and utterly pure.
In that case, it should be understood that there is merely the intention to speak of the self in relation to the object of knowledge.

To the question of where it is that the Self alone is primarily denoted by the word "world," he says: "asthūla" (not gross). The meaning is this: wherever the world, consisting of the gross and so forth, is mentioned as the object of negation, there it is the inner Self (pratyagātman) itself that is intended by that word, by way of being the basis for the negation; for it will be stated later that the negation does not terminate in mere negation. || 126 ||
In which the unmanifest and the manifest universe are also designated.
In that context, the intended meaning is understood as being precisely the duality of self and non-self. || 527 ||
1 ga. loja | 2 ka. ga. mātra | [vol2, page 246] 540 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter]

Anticipating the objection that the word "jagat" (the world) might be used here with the intention of expressing both [states], he says "avyaktam" (the unmanifest) with reference to passages such as "taddhedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtam āsīt. Thus, because the distinction between the manifested (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) has been stated, this very point is clarified here; therefore, there is no tautology. || 927 ||
Because of the statement "that which is other than this," and because the Supreme is the subject under discussion.
Therefore, in this context, the reference by means of the word "sa" (he/that) must refer to the opponent. || 528 ||

In the statement regarding the indeterminate, because the other [the opponent's position] is the subject under discussion, its reference by the word "sa" (he) in the sentence concerning entry has been stated.

Even if its status as the subject there is not accepted, nevertheless, since it is the subject in the passage "There is nothing else than Me," its reference here by the word "sa" implies that it is appropriate for that very Creator to enter the created world; this he states with the words beginning with "yat," etc., [and] "iha."

This is the statement of the introductory verse. He states the resulting conclusion—that by referring to "the other" (para) with a pronoun, its very entry into the created world is established—by saying "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 528 ||
Because the reality of the self-substance is neither excluded nor followed [by conceptual constructions], it is suchness.
But how is its entry here taught by the Śruti?
He implies its entry by means of another formulation: "not excluded. Here, "here" is a designation for the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. || 129 ||
For it is not possible for one who is limited by conceptual boundaries to enter a house that has not yet been entered.
In this manner, it is for a man alone to enter; it is not possible by means of the sky, for that would be contrary to the natural order.

He clarifies the very inconsistency indicated by the word "how" with the phrase "not having entered. Just as it is impossible for a person to enter a house through space, because space is unlimited and thus distinct from that [person], he says "thus," meaning that the entry of the Full (pūrṇa) into anything is not established. || 130 ||
Just as for all beings who possess [all] qualities, by way of transformation.
If it is thought that there might be the entry of snakes and the like into stones and such things; || 531 ||

He raises a doubt by means of an illustration: "Of those that are all-pervading. Just as the elements such as earth, though they pervade all effects, enter into stones, wood, and so forth in the form of snakes and the like—having attained the state of snakes, worms, insects, etc., through transformation—in the same way, it might be argued that the Supreme Self, although all-pervading, enters into the intellect (buddhi) by means of a transformation known as the individual soul (jīva). If this is the case...
"It is thought" (matam) means "there is a doubt" (śaṅkā). || 131 ||
The expression "inherently co-arisen" (sahaja) is used for the purpose of excluding that which is established through conjunction (yutasiddha).
Because stones undergo transformation, and because snakes and other creatures result from a process of maturation. || 532 ||

One might raise the objection that it is not logical for earth and other elements to enter into stones and such things in the form of snakes and so forth, because this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* statement: "In the stone, the snake and all else are innate and internal. Anticipating this, he explains the meaning of the word "innate" (*sahaja*). He says: "Yuta" (joined). The meaning is that the word "innate" is used to dispel the doubt that a snake or similar creature, being external to the stone and established as entirely separate from it, has entered therein. [This refers to] the snake and so forth in relation to the stone and such.

He states the reason for their being co-emergent (*sahaja*) with the words "of the stone" (*aśmanaḥ*). It refers to the transformation of the five elements— which exist in the form of stones and so forth— into the forms of snakes,
frogs,
and the like.

The meaning is that because [the serpent and so forth] exist therein [within the five elements], they possess the quality of being innate (*sahaja*). To the question, "How can there be a transformation of the five elements—consisting of stone and so on—into the form of a serpent and the like?
he replies: "Through maturation" (*paripākataḥ*). || 132 ||
Due to its ripening, that which was situated outside is seen within the waters.
The transformation of entities is characterized by such forms as worms, snakes, and so forth. || 533 ||

He establishes through experience that the five elements, beginning with earth, undergo transformations such as those of serpents due to the power of maturation over time. He says, "It is seen": within our bellies and within stones and the like, there exist elemental substances designated by the term *padārtha*, characterized by water;

by virtue of their maturation, a transformation characterized by serpents and so forth is observed externally. Therefore, in the form of those [serpents], [the potentiality exists] in the stone and so on.

The meaning is that, just as there is an entry into limited elements, the entry of the unlimited Supreme Self into the intellect and so forth in the form of the individual soul (jīva) is established. || 533 ||
It is not so, because here it is stated that no other dharma has been introduced.
Just as a creator enters his own creation, so too does the person enter the body created by that [creator]. || 534 ||

The proponent says: "Not so. Just as Devadatta, who is proficient in many arts, enters his own house after having built it, even so the Creator, while the effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*) have not yet attained their specific transformations, exists as one who has entered them.
Since this is stated in the Śruti, "Having created that, [He entered it]," therefore the doubt raised on the basis of the cited analogy does not find any room; this is the meaning. || 134 ||
Just as a person, having eaten, goes to the city, [the sequence] of the two actions—eating and going—is established.
Likewise, the agent would be non-distinct [in its nature] even with respect to two [actions] situated at different times. || 535 ||
Having created this entire universe, the all-pervading Lord subsequently entered into it.
It is a phenomenon that is not appropriated, yet it is not like a snake made of stone. // 536 //

[Objection: But surely, just as one sees the entry of another person into a house built by a carpenter, so too there will be the entry of another into a world created by [Brahman]. [Response: No; he says "just as" (yathā). Just as in the sentence "Caitra, having eaten, goes to the city," a single Caitra is accepted as the agent of both the acts of eating and going—which occur in immediate succession, the former preceding and the latter following—so too that very same [Brahman] is the agent of the entire universe without exception.

The meaning is that because of the scriptural statement, "The Creator, without undergoing modification, entered," it is not the case that the enterer is someone other than the Creator. Since scripture declares that the entry into the effect occurs precisely for the Creator without his assuming another form—just as there is no actual entry of a serpent-form entity into a stone—it is this [notion of a change of state] that he excludes by saying, "But not... (131–136).
And [this is not possible] for that whose body is undivided, for the reality of the self which is without differentiation.
The departure from a previous location and the arrival at another location. || 537 ||
"In that case, let it be that for the other [the opponent], there is an entry consisting of a conjunction with another location by abandoning the previous location, like a cat or similar creature.

To this he says: "And not so" (*na ca*). The meaning is that because the Self is unlimited (*aparicchinna*) and partless (*niravayava*), the entry well-known in common experience cannot be established. || 937 ||
