542 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, Page 248]
It may be argued that because [the Supreme] is heard of as entering [the body], the Supreme must possess parts.
If this is argued, it is not so, because it contradicts the statements of the scriptures. || 538 ||

He raises an objection, suggesting that because of the scriptural mention of "entering," the partlessness [of Brahman] must be abandoned, using the words "This is the view" (*matam*). He refutes this, stating that the Supreme Being does not possess parts because it would contradict scripture, with the words "Not so" (*naitat*). || 138 ||
The divine, embodied Person is "not this, not this" (neti neti) repeatedly.

Because all dharmas accessible to speech and mind are negated within the Self, [the author] cites scripture: "For divine... and so forth. Because its nature is luminosity and it consists solely of consciousness, it possesses immateriality (*amūrtatva*), which means being partless (*niravayavatva*).
Its "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) means fullness (*pūrṇatva*). Here, he brings the scriptural texts that negate all specific attributes into conformity: "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

In this Upaniṣad, it indicates the repeated practice of negation in many places. The word "asakṛt" (repeatedly) expresses the meaning of the repetition heard in the text. The word "giri" (mountain/rock) implies that there is no possibility of the Supreme Being possessing parts and so forth. || 139 ||
In that case, let the entry of the Supreme Self be like that of the sun’s reflection and so forth.
This is not logical, because of the non-existence of that conjunction and disjunction.

He raises a doubt regarding the possibility of entry by means of another method, beginning with the word "ravī" (the sun). He states that because there is an absence of conjunction or other relations between that supreme [self] and anything else, the occurrence of a reflection is not possible; thus he says: "This is not so. || 140 ||
He by whom union and separation are perceived here, and that with which they occur—[he is the witness].
This entry of a reflection is possible there, but it is not tenable here.

He analyzes that very point: "And conjunction" (*saṃyogaśca*). Here, the first word "here" (*iha*) refers to worldly usage, while the second refers to the self (*ātman*). The word "there" (*tatra*) denotes the correlates of conjunction and so forth, such as water and the like; it should be understood as referring to the sun and so forth. Since conjunction and other relations are possible between the sun and the like with respect to water and the like, the entry known as a reflection is established.
The meaning is that since there is an absence of conjunction and other such relations in the Self—which is unattached and unlimited—there can be no entry in the form of a reflection. || 141 ||
If it is argued that substance possesses qualities because it enters [into them], we say no, because there is no dependence [of the substance] upon them.
It is logical that qualities, being entirely dependent on a single substance, [should reside therein]. (542)

He raises an objection regarding entry by way of another alternative: "guṇa... etc. The meaning is that just as there is an entry of a quality (*guṇa*) into a substance (*dravya*), so too there is an entry of the Supreme (*para*) into its effect. He refutes this with "no" (*na*). He states the reason for the difference of the Supreme from a quality: "because of not being dependent" (*anapāśrayāt*). He makes manifest this difference: "substance... etc.; the ellipsis is "entry into a substance. (142)
Such an entry is not possible for the Lord [if He were] due to [absolute] independence.
"He is the Lord of all"—thus his sovereignty is heard repeatedly in scripture. (543)

He states the lack of logical consistency in the case of the illustrative subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "tādṛk" (such). For a cause does not become an effect, because that would involve a reversal [of their natures]; therefore, just as a quality enters into a substance, it is not logical for the Lord to enter into an effect. This is because, due to His independence, He possesses characteristics contrary to those of a quality. How is there independence? To this he says: "eṣa" (this one). Therein, he indicates the purport of the scripture (*śruti*) with the words "asakṛt" (repeatedly). || 143 ||
1. ga. The oblation. || 539 ||
The entry [of the Self] may be like that of a seed; even so, it is thus logically established.
Because the reality of the self would entail the occurrence of modifications such as birth and so forth. (544)

Having introduced an alternative way of entry, he refutes it with the words "like a seed. He states the reason why the entry of the Supreme into the effect is not tenable—unlike the entry of a seed into a fruit—with the words "birth and so forth" (janmādi). || 144 ||
And because of the scriptural denial of the sixfold modifications, such as grossness and so forth.
The entry of Brahman [into the effect] is always illogical, just as [the entry of] a seed [into its fruit] is not. || 545 ||

To the question, "What is the harm if the Self were subject to modification? he replies with the words "sthūlādi" (gross, etc.). The construction is as follows: because of the scriptural negation of the sixfold modifications—beginning with "existence" (asti) and including "grossness" (sthūla) and so forth—the Self is not subject to change. He states the result of the Self's lack of modifiability with the word "praveśa" (entrance). The word should be split as "ayukta" (improper). Furthermore, the word "sadā" (always) should be supplied here. The word "ādi" (etc.)...

This is for the purpose of including everything that has entered into the fruit beyond the seed. Alternatively, he states another reason: since it is observed in both Śruti and Smṛti that there is a prohibition against even Brahman entering into the fruit—just as the seed enters—as if it were subject to the sixfold modifications such as birth and so forth, which give rise to duality consisting of the gross and the rest, such an entry by Brahman is not logical. Thus he says: "The gross and so forth... (945).
But how is this not redundant, given the case of the stone-serpent?
It has been said that [the effect exists] like a seed in the fruit; why should this not be free from fault? (546)

He raises the objection that the example of the seed and the fruit is a mere repetition of the example of the stone and the snake, by saying "But surely" (nanu). He asserts the absence of such repetition by saying "No" (na). He challenges this by asking "Why? (kutaḥ), implying that if there were no distinction in meaning, the charge of redundancy would be unavoidable. || 946 ||
The relationship between the seed and its fruit is known as the connection between the portion and its destiny.
In that case, the relationship between the support and the supported between the stone and the serpent is clear. || 547 ||

Stating a specific point regarding the meaning, he provides the answer: "By a part," and so forth. The meaning is that there is no tautology, because the relationship between the seed and the fruit is that of part and whole (*avayava-avayavin*), whereas the relationship between the stone and the snake is that of locus and located (*ādhāra-ādheya*). In the word "there" (*tatra*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). || 147 ||
It is indeed someone other than the Supreme who, as a transmigrating being, entered this world.
Even in the world, the entry of that which is delimited is logically possible. || 548 ||

Anticipating the objection that since it is impossible for the Supreme to enter [the world] in every way, one must state the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the scriptural statement regarding entry, the author concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "from the Supreme" (*parasmāt*). The construction is as follows: that which is said in this scripture to have entered the world is other than the Supreme, namely, only a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*). Furthermore, he states that the entry of one other than the Supreme is consistent with worldly logic by saying "of that which is limited" (*paricchinnasya*).
And there is no contradiction with the Śruti, because the sense is that it is the Supreme [Self] itself, having attained the state of the individual soul (jīva), that is said to enter. || 548 ||
Because the creator and the one who is impelled are one, this [distinction] is not tenable even in that way.
Having created the world, He entered into that very creation, according to the Śruti.

Thus, having presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "His own," etc. For it is the limit of the Vedānta that the Supreme is the creator of the world; indeed, the Creator alone [is the subject].
[Vol. 2, page 250]
Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement that "having created that, He entered into it," which establishes a single agent, there is no entry by anyone other than the Supreme Self.
It is appropriate; the construction is that the word "api" (even/also) has the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa). || 149 ||
If the Supreme alone has entered [the world], then how can there be a multiplicity among those who have entered?
Because it is non-different from that, even Maheśa would attain multiplicity.

He raises the objection that if there were entry into another, it would entail the consequence of multiplicity for that [Self], which is an undesirable conclusion; this is expressed by the word "para" (the other). Anticipating the question—how could the Lord become multiple even though those who have entered are many—he states: "Because of non-difference from that," meaning because [the Lord] is non-different from those who have entered.
This is not a fault, because here the Lord's connection is not through differentiation.
For its nature is that of selfhood, since the self is connected with non-difference. || 551 ||

He refutes [the objection] with the words "No," etc., showing that when [the individual souls] have entered [into the Supreme], there is no relation such as conjunction (saṃyoga) with the Supreme through differentiation; for its nature consists in being that very Self (ātmatva).

Nor is there a connection through differentiation even if it were the Self, because the possibility of being the Self arises precisely from the connection of non-difference, namely, identity (ekātmya); therefore, there is no multiplicity of the Supreme. It is well known that what is called "Self-hood" (ātmatva) is the state of having an unqualified essential nature (svarūpa), and that this implies the connection of identity.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of stating [this]. || 551 ||
For those who have entered into non-duality, it would be difficult to speak of multiplicity.
Since many [atoms] possess a single conjunction, why is their oneness not asserted? (552)

Anticipating the objection that even though there is non-difference [of the Self] from those who have entered [into it], there is still multiplicity because of the multiplicity of those non-different entities, he says: "non-otherness" (*ananyatvam*). He addresses the further doubt: "Even if it is contradictory for that which is non-other than those who have entered to be different from them, what is the resolution if there is multiplicity due to its non-difference from many? To this he replies: "of the many" (*bahūnām*). If multiplicity results from one being non-different from many, then oneness must result from the many being non-different from one.
The meaning is: why should it not be so? || 552 ||
Furthermore, conjunction does not exist in the world as something distinct, because it is the cause of non-differentiation.
Likewise, there would be a contradiction with scripture if the supreme self were multiple.

Having stated the counter-inference—"That which possesses internal difference is manifold because it is non-different from many, just like that [example]"—he points out the contradiction with common experience regarding the fact that non-difference establishes difference: "And not...

Just as conjunction is seen to be non-differentiating, so too non-difference is not observed to be a producer of multiplicity; for precisely because it is non-differentiating, it is the very opposite of that [multiplicity].
This is the meaning. He states that, just as there is contradiction with inference and worldly consensus regarding the proof of difference, there is also contradiction with scripture; thus he says:
"In the same way" (tathā). || 553 ||
"The one God exists in many ways"—this is established through the reasoning of both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, let the Lord be accepted as being solitary like the sky. || 554 ||

He clarifies the contradiction in the proposition—that the plurality [of Brahman] cannot be established through the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas stated in the Bhāṣya, and that it is not the subject of reasoning—by means of the verse beginning with "eka" (one). He states the logical consequence regarding the impossibility of plurality in the verse beginning with "viyadvat" (like the sky).
The meaning is: "The Supreme [Brahman] is devoid of any real internal difference, because it is an object of knowledge, like space. || 154 ||
[Vol. 2, Page 251] 4.
Brāhmaṇa: Let this entry remain for now, whether it be logical or illogical, as it may. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Another fault arises here; that shall now be examined.
Having rejected the consequence of manifoldness regarding the entry of the other [the individual soul], he raises another objection: "Let it be so," etc.
The construction is as follows: let the entry be by whatever means—whether logical or illogical—in accordance with the authority of the Śruti. Relying on the Śruti—

The word "tāvat" [is used] because the entry [into the womb], which was summarized by the Blessed One, must later be elaborated upon. Even if the fault of multiplicity does not apply, another fault arises for the opponent's position of "entry"; having considered whether that can or cannot be refuted, and having determined that it cannot, he says:
"another fault. He uses "tāvat" because its refutation will also follow.
The word "ccha" || 555 ||
Because those who have entered [the path] are still subject to saṃsāra, that [state] is non-different from the Supreme.
If it be argued that the state of being subject to saṃsāra follows [from this], we say no, because of the scriptural teaching on the transcendence of hunger and other such afflictions. || 556 ||

He demonstrates that very point with the words, "because of being a transmigrator. He refutes the inference—"the Supreme is a transmigrator because it is non-different from that [individual soul], therefore it is like that"—with the words beginning with "no" (na). The meaning is: since the scripture declares that the Supreme is devoid of hunger and so forth, stating, "He who transcends hunger and thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death," how can there be any transmigratory nature for It? For that would contradict the scripture. || 156 ||
If it is thought that [the self is not the enjoyer] because of the observation of pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth;
It is not so in the case of the Vedānta texts, because of the scriptural statement: "it is not tainted. || 557 ||
He raises a doubt based on experience, saying "one who is happy," etc. The ellipsis is "the absence of hunger and so forth does not belong to another. He states the very resolution already mentioned:
"Not so," etc. || 157 ||
But surely, when suffering and so forth are perceived directly through the means of perception (pratyakṣa), [how can there be detachment]?
A succession of verbal arguments is not a valid means for establishing the sublation [of a thesis] by perception.

For you assert that scripture (*āgama*) [proves] the non-transmigratory nature of another; however, that [scripture] contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is not authoritative regarding its own subject matter.
Nor can it be argued that it possesses the opposite [authority], because of its seniority and consequent strength. Thus he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). || 198 ||
Because it does not have as its object a specific quality produced by relying on an adjunct (upādhi).
Since the status of being a fallacy of perception is established by that [reason], there is no contradiction with the statement. || 559 ||

The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); the distinction produced by its being the locus is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). Because it has as its object the suffering and so forth residing within that [adjunct], the status of being a mere reflection is established for perception. Therefore, there is no contradiction between this and the scripture concerning the non-transmigratory nature of the Self; thus, the cognition regarding its own object arises from scripture, and for the opponent, there is no transmigratoriness. He refutes [this objection] with the words: "Not through the adjunct" (*nopādhi*). || 159 ||
If the self were suffering, who could be the witness of that sufferer?
When [the witness] is born [into suffering], it is improper for one who suffers to be a witness; likewise, a witness who is himself afflicted by pain is unfit. || 560 ||
Anticipating the objection—"Why is suffering attributed to consciousness (caitanya) through the medium of reflection (ābhāsa), rather than being direct?"—he says:
[1. *kṣudhāya*; 2. *kha. kṣudhādi*; 3. *ga.
nyāyokti*] 69.
646 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 252]

Regarding the phrase "one who suffers": suspecting that someone who is indeed suffering might be a witness to suffering, he says "of one who suffers. This means that [the claim] "likewise" is untenable. || 160 ||
In this world, one who undergoes transformation becomes miserable; how, then, can there be witnesshood for that which is subject to change?

"I am changeless because I am the witness of thousands of mental modifications. (561) He states the reason why suffering and the state of being a witness cannot coexist in one and the same entity: "No," etc. The meaning is that one does not become a sufferer without undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

Having raised the doubt that one might still be a witness even while undergoing transformation, he says: "Because of being a witness," etc. The meaning is that [the self] is not a witness because of its insentience (*jāḍya*) [if it were subject to transformation].

He states the result regarding the non-witnesshood of that which is subject to modification: "The modification of the intellect... It has been stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) is changeless and the witness of the fluctuations of the intellect. || 561 ||
Just as one perceives a person with a staff through his connection with the staff, so too [one perceives the self] through its connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Just as Rādhaka perceives the intellect, so too does the Witness remain unattached.

Now, raising the objection that if there is a connection with him [the object] through his witnesshood (*sākṣya*), then his state of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) is lost; whereas if there is no connection, he would not be a witness—[the author] says "mukha... and so on.
A "rādhaka" means a practitioner or an observer (*draṣṭṛ*). Just as an observer, while looking at Maitra who is joined with a staff, does not...

Being himself unconditioned (*asaṃhata*), the Self, like one who possesses a staff, perceives the intellect as being endowed with pleasure and so forth; thus, as a witness (*sākṣī*), he is not joined with pleasure and the rest.
Therefore, the meaning is that although he is in reality unattached (*asaṅga*), he is the witness by virtue of a superimposed relationship (*kalpitasambandha*). || 162 ||
The cognition that has come to regard the aggregate of the body and the senses as the self—
Ūṣā, 1617: Pleasure and the like distinguish [the self] as being illumined by the eternal light of the self. || 563 ||

He establishes that it is cognition alone, possessing pleasure and so forth, that is not the Self. [The verse begins with] "the body" (śarīra). The meaning is this: pleasure and other states exclude from the category of the Self that cognition which, along with its reflection, resides as the Self within the body and so on; thus, perception has as its object the pleasure and other states belonging to the intellect (buddhi), and therefore the consciousness (cit) is not subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritā). If it be argued that it is improper for pleasure and other states to reside in the intellect because they are well-known to be attributes of a conscious being, he says "no," [answering with the word] "eternal" (nitya).

The meaning is that because it possesses the nature of cognition (buddhi) which is pervaded by the consciousness of the self (ātmacaitanya), its status as a property of the self (ātmadharma) is well-established. || 963 ||
But all means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, apply only to external objects, not to the Self.
That statement,
"It exists in the assembly," was directed straight toward the west.

Since perception and the other means of knowledge have the non-Self as their object, whereas scripture has the Self as its object, there is no mutual contradiction between them due to their having different objects; in this regard, he cites scripture as authority: "The [senses] are turned away" (parāñci). According to the scriptural text, "The senses are indeed turned away," perception and the others have the non-Self as their object and do not have the Self as their object, because of the qualification "not within the inner Self" (nāntarātman). However, statements such as "Thou art That" (tattvamasi) establish the state of being free from transmigratory existence.
The meaning is that since the basis (pādaka) is directed toward the self alone with full intent, there is no mutual contradiction. || 164 ||
And it is clearly stated [in scripture]: "By what, O Maitreyī, would one know the knower? and "Not by sight."
Furthermore, from the statement "it is something else entirely," it follows that perception does not have the self as its object.

He also states, by means of the scripture cited in the Bhāṣya, that perception and the other means of knowledge do not have the Self as their object, with the words "vijñātāram" (the knower). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because there is a clear negation of the Self being an object of vision. The term "perception" (pratyakṣa) is an elliptical expression for inference and the rest. || 965 ||
1. ga. Bind him!
[vol2, page 253] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 547
However, with respect to the limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi), its sole function is to cast the shadow of that Self.
Likewise, in such cases as "I am suffering," perception occurs only figuratively.

In that case, what is the object of the primary perception such as "I am," etc.? He recalls what was stated previously in the passage beginning with "there, no superimposition based on limiting adjuncts" (*nopādhyāśraya*). "But rather" (*kiṃ tu*): because the reflection of the Self arises within the limiting adjunct consisting of the two bodies, the perception fulfills its purpose by taking as its object pleasure and so forth which depend solely upon that [reflection]. He states another reason for their non-contradiction due to having different objects: "likewise" (*tathā*). That very point is clarified.

Regarding the phrase "one who suffers": just as the perceptual cognition "I am a Brahmin" and so forth has as its object a superimposed identity, so too the perception in such cases as "I am suffering" is likewise merely false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). This is because the word "metaphorical" (*upacāra*) indicates that the object [of such perceptions] is false. This is the meaning. || 966 ||
In this case as well, grammatical coreferentiality occurs through metaphorical designation in that very same manner.
"This one is suffering" and "I am [suffering]"—[these arise] because of perceiving that through the object. || 567 ||

He establishes the reason for the falsity of the perception of the primary subject (*adhyakṣa*) with the words "of the grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyasya*). Just as the perception whose object is identity—such as "I am a Brahmin"—is a false cognition because that identity is false, so too, since the identity (coreferentiality) which is the object of the perception [of the self] as "the suffering one" is false by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra*), the perception itself, as the subject of that [identity], is also a false cognition; this is the meaning.
Anticipating the doubt as to how the object itself could be false, he says: "This [is the case].

Because the subject does not appear as identical with the object, their identity is false—just as in the case of silver and the like—and it is not the case that the identity of one thing with another is not false. This is the meaning. || 167 ||
There is great suffering at the tip of the nose and likewise at the tips of the big toes.
The suffering of the self is directly perceived through the suffering of the body's parts and so forth. (568)
He states another reason for the absence of suffering in the self: "The nose," etc. By the word "etc. in the phrase "in suffering, etc.," pleasure and so forth are included. || 968 ||
If suffering were located within the inner self, it would be all-pervasive, like consciousness.
Because it resides in the seer, that which resides in the object would be seen by the seer, just like cognition. || 569 ||

Furthermore, does suffering exist as a pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*) within the self, or as an occurrence restricted to a specific location (*pradeśavṛtti*)? In the first case, the cognition of it would have to occur even outside the body; nor can it be argued that this is not so because of the absence of its causes, for if that were the case, its status as a pervasive occurrence would lack any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*), since it is invariably perceived whenever it exists. It is not the second case either, because for the all-pervading inner witness (*pratīc*), there are no real locations (*pradeśa*); [if it were located], it would have to depend upon imagined locations.

Thinking that suffering is likewise [unreal], he says: "The west. He states another fault regarding the fact that suffering and so forth are attributes of the Self: "Because it resides in the seer" (*draṣṭṛsthatvāt*). Since suffering and so forth reside in the seer, being situated as an object (*karman*), they could not be perceived by that very same seer; for if one were to perceive what belongs to oneself, even the self [would be perceived].

The meaning is that, due to the great logical consequence (*mahāprasaṅga*) of infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), consciousness is not apprehended as an object; likewise, since suffering and so forth are visible to the self, they do not possess it as their attribute. || 569 ||
It would exist for the sake of its own self alone, because of the scriptural teaching that the self exists for the sake of itself.
If you think that happiness has the self as its sole object, it is not so.

One raises the doubt based on scripture that pleasure and so forth have the self as their locus, stating: "But of one's own self... First, pleasure indeed has the self as its locus, or rather, it belongs to the self.

548. Since there is a scriptural statement that "let it be for the sake of desire," which indicates that the means of happiness have the self as their purpose, therefore, suffering— which is invariably concomitant with that [happiness]— also resides in that very place, namely, in the self.

The meaning is that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is based on scripture (*śrauta*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that scripture conforms to experience. Thinking that the passage beginning with "But for the sake of the Self's desires" (*ātmanas tu kāmāya*) teaches the state of supreme bliss by restating the transmigratory nature of the Self as conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), he says:
"Not indeed... (970).
Or rather, because of the statement "where [there is] another," that refers to the domain of ignorance.
Suffering is not to be understood as residing in the Self, because of the denial [found] in the passage "but where [one sees] this [Self]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).

He provides the evidence for the statement that this is a restatement of the ignorant cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) with the words "where. He states what is to be excluded—the fact that transmigratoriness is not being taught regarding the Self—with the words "suffering. He also provides the evidence for that with the words "but where. || 171 ||
This much, at least, occurs to my mind: that which is pleasing to you is that cyclic existence is not perceived as being within the self by a vision inclined toward the inward. (572)

Furthermore, he states that the self is not subject to transmigratory existence because this contradicts the direct perception of the wise. Regarding the verse beginning with "mama": that which consists of misfortune, such as suffering and the like—which you consider to be your own interest and do not desire—is experienced by the wise within the intellect (buddhi) accompanied by its appearance (ābhāsa). Therefore, it does not reside in the Self, for that would contradict experience. If it is argued that there is indeed an experience of it as residing in the Self, he says "no," introducing the word "pratyak" (inward-facing). || 172 ||
If it is argued that this view results in the undesirable consequence of contradicting the tenets of the logicians (tārkika), [we reply: so be it.
For the self is accepted by them as possessing desire, aversion, and so forth. || 573 ||

He raises an objection that the transmigratory nature of the Self follows from the authority of the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*), stating: "The view is... He explains how there is a contradiction with the non-transmigratory nature of the Self: "Desire, etc."—from the inference that "desire and so forth must be based on something, because they are qualities, like color," and by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), since these have the Self as their substrate, and since transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) consists precisely in the nature of manifold misfortunes belonging to those [qualities], [if the Self were non-transmigratory, then its... [...transmigratory nature would be contradicted.]
The meaning is that there would be no contradiction [with reality], for the establishment of reality does not occur when it contradicts the consensus of authoritative sources. || 973 ||
If non-contradiction were not accepted even with respect to all reasonings without exception, [it would be untenable].
Then your established doctrine will certainly become extremely unstable. || 574 ||
Regarding the non-transmigratory nature of the Self, is it required that it be free from contradiction by only a few arguments, or by all arguments?

In the first case, since there is indeed freedom from contradiction by the arguments based on scripture (*śrauta-tarka*) even in the present context, [the author] says "not so" in order to establish its non-transmigratory nature. Having restated the alternative view, he refutes it with the words "without remainder. In that regard, even the established conclusion of the logicians (*tārkika-siddhānta*) is not proven; for in that [view], there is no freedom from contradiction by all arguments.

The meaning is that because there is mutual contradiction and contradiction with Vedic reasoning, the treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) lack authority; therefore, their contradiction cannot be reconciled. || 974 ||
Nor can the nature of the inner self as consisting of happiness be established even by means of logical reasoning.
Since it is understood from this, remain seated without fear.

Now, since there is no dispute among the treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) regarding the transmigratory nature of the self, and since they possess authority on that point, its transmigratory state is established by the uncontradicted reasoning set forth therein; thus, its non-transmigratory nature cannot be accepted by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) out of fear of such reasoning.
4. Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 549] He says "no" and explains: "And not... Since it has already been stated that desire and the rest are attributes of the mind, the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) is not established; therefore, even by that reasoning, the transmigratory nature of the inner self (*pratīc*) is not understood. Thus, its non-transmigratory nature can be accepted by those seeking liberation who are free from fear—this is the meaning. || 975 ||
There may be a qualification by means of suffering that is to be understood through another's testimony.
It is not [the case] for that which consists solely of the nature of a reflection, because of contradiction, like heat and cold. || 576 ||

Fearing that, because the arguments of logicians are not fallacious, one might rely on their strength to perceive the Self as a transmigrating being (saṃsārī), and thus it would be impossible for those seeking liberation to remain fearless once they have determined the Self to be non-transmigrating, he says: "The other" (parāk). Since the "other" (the external) and the "inner" (the internal) are mutually contradictory, they cannot stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified; to illustrate this, he provides the example: "heat... (uṣṇa...). 176 ||
And I have previously stated that the inner self (pratyak) is not an object of perception.
For it is because of its reliance on the shadow [of that cognition] that even perception possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge.

Anticipating the objection that the self (ātman) might also be qualified by suffering because it is perceptible, he says: "perceptible," etc. The meaning is as stated in such passages as: "A means of knowledge (*māna*) directed toward objects such as the subtle elements (*mātrā*) cannot be applied to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the witness (*sākṣin*). Furthermore, the establishment of the reality of perception depends upon its support in the reflection of the self, since that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) is not established by itself; therefore, [it is not so].
Therefore, he says that the self is established by that [scripture]: "By that scripture" (tacchākhya). || 177 ||
He who desires something from another cannot be one who has nothing to give to the seeker; likewise, it should be understood that one who lacks self-interest is incapable of benefiting others. (578)

He states this by means of an illustration: "He who [seeks] from whom... [The connection is: "he desires alms. The reason for the beggar's inability to give alms is stated as: "for he is one who possesses nothing.
In that same context, there is another reason: "to one who does not desire [it]. For a beggar does not [succeed] with one who is wealthy and has no need.

The meaning is that he is capable of giving alms. He states the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "in the same way. By the aforementioned illustration, one should understand the nature of the non-inert (*ajaḍa*) Self, which is independent, and the inert (*jaḍa*), which is dependent. For the inert object illuminated by consciousness is not itself perceived as the illuminator of that [consciousness];
such is the meaning. || 978 ||
Even without direct perception, there may be a qualification of suffering.
Just as the quality of sound in space is not perceived when it is directly present, so too [the self] is not held to be [perceived]. || 579 ||
Because it is not possible to apprehend a single measure [of the self], the self is easily grasped as something pleasant.
There would be at least some slight apprehension of that which is of a nature eternally inferred.

By stating that [the Self] is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is argued that it is improper for the Witness (*pratyak*) to have suffering as its specific object; for one might object that, just as between sound and space—which are respectively perceptible and imperceptible—there can still be the relationship of quality and possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇitva*) between suffering and the Self. Thus he raises the objection: "The perceptible... [and so on]. Even if there were the relationship of quality and possessor of quality despite the difference in being perceived or not, it would require being grasped by the same means of knowledge (*māna*); otherwise, that relationship does not exist. Therefore, the relationship of quality and possessor of quality between suffering and the Self is not established by the cited example.
He says, "It is qualified," meaning "not so. Having raised the objection that the self might then be perceived by the same means as pleasure and so forth, [he replies:
*atyakṣagam*; ka. *tvāttadduḥ*)... [omitted].

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter], having raised the objection of either the Sāṃkhyas or the Vaiśeṣikas and others as an alternative, he refutes the first [position] with the words: "Not pleasure... (179).
And thus, because the self is one, when it is made an object [of cognition], [it follows that all would perceive it].
Because anything other than that is impossible, it follows that there would be no seer. || 581 ||
He states the second [objection]: "Because of oneness" (*ekatvāt*). Just as pleasure and so forth are perceived by you, so too is the self;

thus, when it is made an object, since there is consensus on its oneness within a single body, another self cannot exist therein. Since two experiencers in one place are undesirable, and because another person is not perceptible to someone else, there is no perceiver [of that other]; therefore, the self's being seen is unestablished—this is the meaning. || 181 ||
Furthermore, one [cognition] possesses the state of being the subject and the state of being the object simultaneously, like a lamp.
If this were your view, it would not be so, because simultaneous existence is impossible. || 582 ||
He raises the objection: "How can there be the state of being a seer for a single entity, since it possesses both natures? [The author] says: "The state of being an object.

Suspecting that the status of being both seer and seen is never observed in one and the same thing, he says: "Like a lamp. [This is] because, by dispelling the darkness inherent within itself, it serves as both the object and the subject...

The meaning is that the status of being both the seer and the seen is established for the single Self alone. Regarding the subject-object relationship of the single Self—whether by way of its totality or by way of parts—if the former is the case, is it simultaneous or successive? To the first [possibility], he says: "This is not so. Agency (*kartṛtva*) is the state of being a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*) in an action, while objecthood (*karmatva*) is the state of being the primary factor (*prādhānya*) therein; therefore, it is not possible for a single entity to simultaneously possess both subordinate and primary roles with respect to one and the same action in its entirety.
The meaning is "support. It should be understood that the second [alternative] is not tenable, because when one thing exists, the other cannot exist. || 182 ||
Even a lamp does not manifest itself, because its nature is inherently luminous.
And because it is the object of the cognition of a person, the lamp does not possess a dual nature.

Anticipating the objection that, as in the given example, there is no room for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or the like in the process of comprehension, he refutes the example with the words beginning "No" (*na*).

For a lamp does not illuminate another lamp, because its nature consists solely in luminosity; therefore, the meaning is that for that which is of a single essence, there can be no relationship of object and subject.
[The opponent might argue: "In that case, let it have self-luminosity, as you desire, just like the Self. To this he replies: "Because it is an object" (*viṣayatvāt*).

The meaning is that the cognition of "man" is the manifestation of its own nature; because the lamp is pervaded by that [cognition], it does not possess self-luminosity. He concludes the lack of a supporting example with the word "no" (na). || 183 ||
And upon examination, because it is partless, there is no commonality with a lamp.
By this very [argument] regarding the grasper of Brahman, the [grasping] of consciousness as well has been refuted. || 584 ||

He states another alternative: "And as the object" (*pratīc ca*). That the self (*ātman*) is an object by its substantial aspect (*dravyāṃśa*) and a subject by its cognitive aspect (*bodhāṃśa*) is what is intended by the word "and" (*ca*). Furthermore, he says that the self, which is non-inert light (*ajaḍaprakāśa*), is not equal to a lamp, because a lamp does not illuminate itself;
thus he says: "Not by a lamp. Now, [one might object] that for the Vijñānavādins, a single cognition simultaneously [perceives] everything in its entirety...

In that case, one might argue that even your own self would likewise undergo the state of being both the grasped and the grasper; to this he replies with the verse beginning "grāhya" (the grasped). The meaning is that this is refuted by the negation of the dual nature of a single entity. || 984 ||
Likewise, [this applies] to those two which are to be understood through their respective qualities and the substrata of those qualities.
When there is a connection between two things whose natures are suffering, there is no validity for inference as a means of knowledge. || 585 ||

551. Now, it may be argued: "Granted that there is no cognition of the relationship between quality and possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇitva*) between suffering and the self through perception; however, it might exist through inference, for suffering must reside somewhere as a quality."

Once it is established that [pleasure] has a substratum (āśraya) similar to yours, [the opponent argues] that because the self is that substratum by process of elimination, [the author] replies: "In that case" (*tathā*). The connection [of the argument] is as follows: when suffering and the self—which are known through the marks of inference (*liṅga*)—are joined as quality and possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇin*), inference does not possess validity, just as perception [does not apply here].

For it is not possible to infer a relationship of quality and possessor of quality between two mutually contradictory things; and since suffering and so forth reside in a cognition accompanied by error (*sābhāsa-buddhi*), the establishment of [the self] by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) is refuted.
This is the meaning. || 585 ||
Because suffering is always cognizable by the senses, like the blueness of a lotus.
And because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with form and other objects cognized by the senses.

(Verse 586) He states another fault regarding the position that the self is perceptible like suffering: "It is eternal," etc. The meaning is: suffering is not the self, because it is an object of cognition, like form. He states another reason for [the claim] that suffering is a property of the self: "Form and so forth," etc. Wherein form and so forth—

The meaning is that burning, cutting, and so forth are observed in the body of the intellect (*mati*), because it is precisely there that the suffering and other effects produced by them are perceived; therefore, the self does not possess those qualities. || 586 ||
And even if it is admitted that suffering arises from a conjunction with the self, [it remains untenable].
The faults of homogeneity, transformation, impermanence, and so forth would consequently follow. || 587 ||
He refutes the claim that the nine specific qualities (vaiśeṣika-guṇa), such as cognition and so forth, arise in the self due to the conjunction of the self and the mind;

this is expressed by the words "of suffering" and so on. The meaning is that, because it would possess conjunction, it would follow that the self has parts like a jar; consequently, from having parts, it would follow that it is subject to modification and thus lacks the nature of a true self. || 587 ||
For a quality that is conjoined with a substance can never exist without having first modified that substance.
In this world, that which is undergoing origination is observed through valid means of cognition.

Fearing that the basis of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) might be weak, he says "No," and so forth. The meaning is: whatever is conjoined is seen to possess parts and to possess action, as in the case of a jar; therefore, if the self were also conjoined, those two [properties] would necessarily follow for it as well. || 188 ||
Furthermore, no partless entity is ever perceived anywhere.
Even while undergoing transformation, it is eternally the substratum of perishable qualities. || 589 ||
Anticipating the objection that the Bhaṭṭas maintain the soul possesses activity because its nature undergoes modification such as suffering, he says:

"And not... The sense is that the soul is not subject to transformation (pariṇāmī) because it is partless, like space. Furthermore, in the Vaiśeṣika and other doctrines, he states another defect: "Nor is it... [the soul] is not a substratum of qualities because it is eternal, like a universal (sāmānya). Because it is not the locus of those [qualities]...
This means "instrumentality. Nor is "non-substantiality" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), because "impermanence" itself serves as the limiting adjunct;

nor does the previously mentioned limiting adjunct arise in its absence, for in that case, both would lack the definition of a limiting adjunct due to their mutual dependence as limiting adjuncts—this is the intended meaning. || 189 ||
Furthermore, the eternality of space is not accepted by those who follow the scriptures.
Furthermore, there is another example even for those who hear of that effect. || 590 ||
1 kha. this; 2 ka. seen.

Having raised the objection that there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to space (*ākāśa*), he says: "Of space... Having raised the objection that there is an inconsistency with respect to atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, he says:
"Nor... Atoms do not exist at all, because there is no evidence for the existence of anything other than the triad (*tryaṇuka*); likewise, space...

It is logical that [the other elements] are included within space because space occupies infinite regions; however, time possesses origination, as established by such scriptural passages as "All moments (nimeṣas) were born," and thus there is no deviation [from this principle] in its case—this is the intended meaning. || 990 ||
Even though a substance possesses transformation, it [remains that substance] because of its continuous association with those very conditions.
If it is argued that [the self] is indeed eternal, [we reply] no, because of the occurrence of change and excess.
Impermanence does not exist in some cases, as is held by other proponents.
Moreover, even that which consists of the absence of an assembly is accepted by the proponents of emptiness. || 592 ||
Some maintain that when something undergoes modification, yet the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not sublated, it is "transformative eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*).
To this, he raises the objection: "How can there be eternity given its possession of modification? He states: "It possesses modification. He refutes this: "Not so.

For one who asserts modification, the change in the constituent parts of the substance must be stated; and that itself constitutes impermanence, as was established in the investigation of the jar regarding absolute non-existence.

The meaning is "because it has been refuted. That is to say, [it has been refuted] by others, namely the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). Why do you not accept that for them the meaning of the word "impermanence" is absolute non-existence? Regarding this, he states a further refutation by another method: "It must indeed exist," and so forth. Is that [non-existence] established by mental cognition or not? In the first case, it would follow that it possesses existence like a jar; in the second case, is it self-luminous or not? If it is not, then since it is non-existent, it would follow that everything exists.

This is the meaning. The particle *tu* (but) highlights the aforementioned distinction. The word *api* (even/also) is used to include the jar and other such things as examples. The construction is as follows: even that object which consists of non-existence and is desired by the proponents of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavādin*) is indeed existent. || 999 || 992 ||
Without the existence of consciousness as a means of valid cognition, no worldly object exists.
That which has its establishment independent of anything else is what is perceived by those who uphold the doctrine of valid cognition.

He states that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*). [The verse says: "Consciousness" (*saṃvit*). Consciousness alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the instrument of proof; its very nature is self-effulgent (*svaprabha*). Apart from that, nothing whatsoever—whether worldly or Vedic—is seen by authoritative persons to be self-luminous. Therefore, since absolute non-existence is self-effulgent, it is non-dual with consciousness due to its identity with it; this is the intended meaning. || 993 ||
Because the substance undergoes a change in its constituent parts, its impermanence is not established in any case.
Since the present moment is partless, by what reasoning could that [past] be established? || 594 ||

Since the absolute non-existence of the transformation desired by others is difficult to establish, he concludes that for a composite entity, impermanence consists precisely in the alteration of its parts.
[The word] "part" (*bhāga*) is used; the word "other" (*anya*) is to be supplied. Anticipating the objection that such impermanence might then apply to the Self as well, he says:
"Because it is partless" (*nirbhāgatvāt*). Since impermanence in the form of an alteration of parts is impossible for that which is without parts, it does not belong to that [Self].
The meaning is "the state of being subject to modification. || 594 ||
Now, even if it possesses parts, it might still be eternal, like a diamond and so forth.
It is not so because it is preceded by conjunction and terminated by disjunction. || 595 ||

The proponent of the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects), perceiving that the absence of parts has been established, raises an objection with the words "Now" (*atha*). This objection concerns the prior conjunction of parts.
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the Ānandagiri-bhava commentary and the Śākhāprakāśikā sub-commentary. 55.

[The opponent objects: "Because a diamond and the like possess the nature of being a conjunction, and since a conjunction necessarily ends in disjunction, its perishability is inevitable; therefore, how can the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) be established? He answers this with the verse beginning "saṃyoga" (996).
The non-separation from the marketplace and so forth is for the sake of spiritual welfare, because it was preceded by non-attachment.
For that which is not to be inferred, there is no conjunction of parts whatsoever.

He raises an objection regarding the establishment of the example, arguing that since it is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) that diamonds and the like are preceded by the conjunction of parts, there is no disjunction [of their parts] and thus they are not destroyed. He states: "Like a diamond, etc."—namely, "The subject under dispute is preceded by the conjunction of parts because it possesses parts, like a jar"—and then refutes this with the words beginning with "No" (*na*). 996.
For there is nothing whatsoever that possesses parts which is not a conjunction of parts.
Because, like cloth and other such things, there is no pain for the self even when it possesses parts.

If it is asked, "Even if it has parts, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against its not being preceded by the aforementioned conjunction? [the author] says: "It is the impossibility of having parts.
He states the locus of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that whatever has parts is preceded by the aforementioned conjunction—by means of examples such as cloth.

Diti: Since it is difficult to avoid [the conclusion that] that which possesses parts is impermanent and so forth, the conceptualization of parts is untenable; consequently, the conjunction of the self with the mind is impossible, and because there is an absence of any cause for the production of suffering and the like therein, it follows that [the self] is not subject to transmigratory existence (asaṃsārī). This is what he states in the concluding summary: "Therefore" (ataḥ) || 997 ||
Since the state of being free from suffering is desired for another, and because there is no one other than that [self], [it must be desired for oneself].
The Upaniṣad was undertaken by you for the sake of the cessation of suffering.

He raises an objection, suggesting that because the commencement of the scripture would otherwise be inexplicable, one must conclude that the Self is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) for the sake of destroying its own misfortune.

[The author] says, "In order to remove suffering," having raised the doubt that the scripture is begun for the purpose of removing the suffering of the individual self (*jīvātman*). Then, following such scriptural passages as "There is none other than this" (*nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā*), he says, "Of that which is other [than the Self]," [meaning] that the scripture is for the purpose of removing the suffering residing in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Anticipating this doubt—that because it is consciousness, suffering is impossible for it—he says "Of whom? (verse 198), thinking: "It is not so."

This Upaniṣad has been composed by me for the purpose of establishing that the mere appearance of silver is the cause of the cognition of another object, which arises from the delusion of the intellect. 599.

He provides the resolution that the undertaking [of this treatise] is possible in order to dispel the delusion of misfortune residing within the Self: "The Pratyag... etc. The word "mātra" (only/merely) is used to state that the scripture does not approach any real suffering whatsoever for the purpose of its destruction. 199.
Just as one who perceives only nine items might be mistaken about the tenth.
Even while looking at those nine, he does not think, "I am the tenth," nor does he think, "I am here. (600)

Establishing by means of an illustration that the scripture exists for the purpose of destroying the delusion of transmigratory existence—which is produced solely by the ignorance (*avidyā*) of another—he first states an illustration regarding its being a function of ignorance: "Not [nine]. In reality, a tenth boy, perceiving only nine boys, has his vision of the tenth stolen away; through the delusion that "he is lost," he does not perceive his own status as the tenth.

This is the meaning. He states the attainment of the realization of being the tenth [the Self] with the words, "even while seeing. The meaning is that even though one sees those who are distinct from oneself, one does not attain [the realization of] the ignorance [of the tenth], due to the power of that ignorance. || 600 || S.Rā.

He possesses the vision of selflessness without exception, and likewise, he has realized the reality of the self as being without a creator.
Even while observing that the non-self does not possess a single identity with the self, [one should not think] "I am the courtesan. || 601 ||

He states the application [to the subject] with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). Following the aforementioned illustration, the construction is as follows: a seeker of liberation who has not yet realized the true nature of the Self, though perceiving all non-Selfs and directly experiencing the ego and so forth as distinct from himself, does not know in this manner that "I am of the nature of Brahman. || 601 ||
By the flame of the fire of perfect knowledge arising from the statement "You are the Tenth," [the seed of ignorance is consumed].
Having nourished the ignorance that takes itself as the tenth, one perceives, "I am the tenth. || 602 ||
Just as by the fire of knowledge arising from such statements as "That thou art," [the seed of ignorance is consumed].
In this way, through the destruction of the darkness of the self and that which is born from it, one attains the state of oneness with the Self.

Having stated the ignorance of another by means of an illustration, he now provides an illustration regarding its destruction through knowledge. "The tenth," etc.: the meaning is that, having burned away the ignorance of his own being the tenth by means of the fire of correct knowledge arising from the words of a reliable person, the young boy experiences his own state as the tenth, thinking, "I am the tenth," and thereby attains peace. He applies the meaning found in the illustration to the subject at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*). "Reality..."
"Thus," [it is said]. "Here" is a statement regarding the state of being alive. || 602 || 603 ||
It has as its cause the ignorance regarding the inner Self, and its means are the scriptures, the teacher, and so forth.
Through Māyā, he attained identity with that which consists of the opposite of that [state]. || 604 ||

He concludes the stated subject matter with its supplementary details: "The inner self," and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all unstated causes of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are included.

The meaning is that as soon as a person realizes through the knowledge of Brahman—produced by the power of *māyā* acting through the means of the scriptures, teachers, and so on, which are themselves products of ignorance—the unity that is opposed to those effects [of ignorance], at that very moment there is the destruction of all his misfortunes. || 104 ||
Just as teachers, scriptures, and so forth do not exist in reality because they arise from delusion.
Its entry [into the body] should likewise be such as to bring about the realization of identity. || 605 ||

Having dispelled the suspicion that [the Self] might become transmigratory upon entering another, by means of the method already stated, he now begins to clarify—through reasoning—that the entry is established by the authority of scripture on the grounds that the creator and the one who enters are one. He says "scripture," etc.; the sense is that since the entry, like scripture and so forth, is merely imagined (*kalpita*), no suspicion should arise based upon it. He states the purpose for imagining an entry created by ignorance (*avidyā*):
"Aikātmya" [means] "oneness of self. || 605 ||
In its determined and undetermined states, this world exists by its very nature.
Anūgra: "The true nature of that which is perceived in the world is thus awakened. (606)

Now, an objection may be raised: "In the relevant scriptural passages, it is the manifest and unmanifest world that is spoken of, not the identity with the Self; so how can there be a conception of 'entering' for the sake of realizing that [identity]? To this, the author replies with the word "vyākṛta" (manifest). The connection is as follows: "by nature" means without the aid of scripture, and "seen by the world" means seen by people in common worldly experience. "Its true nature" refers to the reality of that world, which is the inner consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*).
This is the meaning. || 606 ||

In this *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, while stating that very same slight application of reasoning at the outset, he first establishes the non-difference of Brahman—the substratum—from the individual soul (*jīva*), which stands in the position of a reflection.

He says, "where all diversity has been shaken off," etc. The cause of that diversity consists of the apprehension of the substrate (*dharmin*) and so forth; where all diversity and its cause have been completely shaken off.

It is thus. Anticipating the objection that even if pure difference lacks a cause, it might still exist when accompanied by non-difference, he says: "possessing no division" (*avibhāgavān*). Anticipating the objection that difference exists in the form of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator, he says: "not other" (*ananya*). Anticipating the objection that difference exists in the form of self and non-self, he says: "the inward-facing one" (*pratyaṅ*). Anticipating the objection that it exists in the form of the seer and the seen, etc., he says: [the following].

Regarding the phrase "name and so forth": before the creation of the world, its distinction from the nature of the seer and so on was non-existent; therefore, the meaning is that in that prior state, there existed only the undifferentiated, partless Self (*ātman*). Anticipating the objection that [the Self] must therefore be a real entity, he says: "Name and so forth. The meaning is that in the creation of the world, by means of reflections residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), the Self itself—experiencing the modifications of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*) in the form of color and other objects denoted by words such as "seeing" and so on through the instruments of the eyes and other senses—enters into states such as being the "seer" or the "hearer. || 111 || 612 ||
Just as a light is seen in the sky arising from the sun that has risen from the eastern mountain.
Likewise, that which abides in deep sleep [is distinguished] from that which abides in the intellect and is characterized by agency, enjoyership, and power.

It was previously stated that Brahman, which is of a single essence prior to creation, subsequently attains the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) due to its connection with the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors.

Now, in order to refute any real difference between these two, the author states the distinction of their locations by means of an illustration, beginning with "appātra" (*appātreti*). The word "anya" (*anya*), following the two words in the ablative case, [indicates...]

This has been indicated. The verb is also to be supplied in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). Alternatively, because a reflection is inseparable from and accompanied by its original (*bimba*), just as the sun situated in the sky is perceived from the sun reflected in a single vessel, so too the Supreme Self, whose limiting adjunct is the cause, residing in deep sleep, is perceived from the Self whose limiting adjunct is the effect—consisting of the agent and so forth—reflected in the intellect and belonging to the two states [of waking and dreaming].
The meaning is that it is understood because it depends upon that. || 611 ||
Just as the witness of the seer, the hearer, and so forth, is distinct from the seer, the hearer, and the rest.
The intellect and its cause are designated as the "excellent field" (kṣetravara).

Anticipating the objection that "in reality there is a difference between those two due to the difference in location and the difference in name, just like a jar and a cloth," he says: "The seer" (draṣṭṛ).

The meaning is that the distinction in location and so forth arises solely from the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) between the knower designated as the *kṣetrajña*—who is the knower qualified by the intellect (*buddhi*)—and the Lord (*īśvara*) designated as the witness of the knower (*pramātṛ-sākṣin*), who is qualified by the causal adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*). || 694 ||
The Viśva and Taijasa states are associated with their own respective sleep and dream, whereas the Prājña state is characterized by the absence of both sleep and dream.
Thus, even the distinction of locations is firmly established in the teaching of the Vedānta. || 615 ||

He cites scripture as authority for the distinction of locations, beginning with "svameti" (he goes to his own). The meaning is that Viśva and Taijasa—the former and the latter—are characterized by grasping and non-grasping due to their false and correct perceptions respectively; however, Prājña is one who is possessed solely by non-grasping, namely, the conceit of deep sleep (*svāpa*). He summarizes the meaning of the cited scripture with the words "ityādi" (and so forth). By the word "ādi" (etcetera), there is the mention of locations such as the solar orb and so on. [This applies] to those possessing different locations...
The meaning of "also" (*api*) is that the absence of a distinction between entities has also been ascertained by the Vedānta. || 155 ||

"Let me smell this fragrance"—thus thinks that which is changeless.

The meaning is that, in order to reject the entry called "reflection" by refuting the existence of a substratum for the reflection other than Brahman, the objection regarding the absence of contact with another entity has been raised.

Here too, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the cause, even when existing alone, appears as such through non-discrimination.
It is perceived through the properties of effects such as cognition, like a reflection.

[The author] analyzes the illustrative example with the words "here too" (*ihāpi*). The locative case signifies one's own position (*svapakṣa*). In reality, there is no connection between ignorance (*avidyā*) and its products.

The author of the *Dhurya* says: "Only [the Self]," and so forth. Nevertheless, he shows its association [with attributes] solely through the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). He says: "By the cause," and so forth. Consequently, due to the superimposition of identity with that [intellect] through the creation of the intellect and other faculties, it is seen as non-isolated (*akevala*), characterized by such properties as agency; thus he says: "Through lack of discrimination" (*avivekataḥ*). Just as a face, though naturally devoid of blackness and the like, appears so through the medium of a reflection due to contact with an adjunct (*upādhi*).
He says "so it is seen" regarding that which possesses an excellence of blackness; [he explains this] by saying "like a reflection. || 619 ||
Furthermore, even in the Vedas, many such statements as "having created that" (tatsṛṣṭvā) and so forth are found to be applicable.

He states that for the sake of establishing the aforementioned entry, there are many statements in the Vedānta texts accompanied by reasoning, and these have been shown in the Commentary: "yathokta... (120).

The meaning is that for the Supreme Being—who is perfect and whose limitations have been discarded—there can be no real entry into an effect, like a snake into a hole.

Just as fire, the sun, and the wind have entered their respective paths, so too has he entered the world.
Although its own nature was unentered, the Self entered the world as an effect.
He states that regarding entry into what is called the "imagined reflection" (*kalpitapratibimba*), there are other scriptural passages besides those mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*:

"As fire," and so forth. These are the scriptural illustrations: "Just as fire, though one, has entered the world; as the sun is the eye of the entire world; as wind, though one, has entered the world, assuming a form corresponding to every form"; and "In the same way, [the Self] is the inner self of all beings," and so on.
He states the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning the tamed [elephant]: "In the same way," [verse 622].
And this [scripture] would also exist because it is the cause for the realization of the vision of the inner true nature.
The purpose of the creation, maintenance, destruction, and entry into the world.

[Objection: "But why is entry and so forth, which do not exist in reality, imagined as being due to ignorance? [Reply: Anticipating this very point, he says: "The inner self" (pratyak), etc. Since entry and so forth are for the purpose of generating knowledge of reality, the meaning is that this alone is the fruit of such knowledge. || 623 ||
Because it is repeatedly heard in scripture that the vision of That is for the sake of the human goal.
Therefore, the creation and other processes are established in such passages as "He knew Brahman," and so forth.

How is it that the purpose of [passages concerning] entering and so forth culminates in that [knowledge of reality], and why should they not culminate in their own literal sense? To this he says: "Because of the vision of that" (*taddṛṣṭeḥ*).

Since the scriptural texts regarding entering and so forth do not culminate in their own literal meaning as they would be fruitless, and since the vision of reality is heard to be fruitful, it is logical that those [texts] have that [vision] as their purpose, according to the maxim: "In the proximity of what is fruitful, that which is fruitless is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of it. Regarding the fact that the knowledge of reality is fruitful, [this is established] by scripture...

He formulates the mark of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*) through repetition (*abhyāsa*) in the aphorism: "repeatedly" (*asakṛt*). He states the result when those [words] do not terminate in their own literal meaning: "established" (*klṛptāḥ*). || 124 ||
For the creation of the world and so forth are not at all established by reason.
The creation of the world and so forth proceed from that [Self] solely due to the ignorance of the inward-facing [Self].

He states another reason for their being imagined (*kalpita*) with the word "by reasoning" (*yuktyā*). For as regards creation and the rest, they cannot belong to one who possesses activity, nor to one who is changeless;

not the first, because of the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and not the other, because it would result in [creation] occurring at all times. Nor can they [proceed] from themselves, because that would entail the futility of seeking a cause. Nor yet...

The meaning is that [these agents] are merely imagined through one's own ignorance, because they cannot withstand such logical arguments as follows: if their status as the cause of that [effect] depends on something else, then due to the aforementioned fault, if they do not possess that nature inherently, it would follow that the effect would never arise; furthermore, if their agency in producing that effect depended on yet another cause, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā), and so forth. Therefore, they are nothing but constructs of one's own ignorance. || 129 ||

"There is no connection of the non-existent with birth, nor is the existence of the existent desired."

In the immutable (kūṭastha), there is no modification; therefore, birth arises from ignorance. (626) Furthermore, he states that creation is imagined (*kalpitā*) with the words "not of the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*). First of all, the non-existent is not born because of its lack of existence, like a human horn; nor is the existent born because of its existence, like the Self (*ātman*); nor is there no birth at all, because it is perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that it is imagined. [The text continues with: "destruction... (*nāśā-*).

It establishes that even [the state of] being wretched is imagined. Regarding the term "immutable" (kūṭastha): for there can be no modification in that which is changeless, because that would be a contradiction; nor can it be in that which possesses modification, because instability has already been stated. Therefore, the meaning is that just as birth occurs, so too do destruction and the rest, solely due to one's own ignorance. || 626 ||
Likewise, even the Vedic mantra "rūpaṃ rūpam" refers to the Self.
He taught the creation and so forth solely for the purpose of perceiving reality as it truly is.

He states the supporting evidence for the principle already shown—that the creation and so forth are for the purpose of attaining knowledge of the Self—by saying "tathā" (so it is). This means that it is like the principle beginning with "phalavatsaṃnidhau... (when in proximity to that which has a fruit...). Pervasion (vyāpti) is expressed by the word "entry" (praveśa) from the perspective of the causal self.
The objects of the effects such as the intellect (buddhi) are the pervader and the pervaded of these two [the Self and the intellect]. || 628 ||

Anticipating the objection that if entry and so forth were false because they have another purpose, then since a false entry is not restricted [to a specific locus], why should it not belong to something other than Brahman? He says: "Pervasion" (*vyāpti*). For pervasion of the effect by something other than the cause is not primary; moreover, it is established that causality belongs only to the Supreme (Brahman). Thus, even if the entry is imagined, it belongs to Him alone. [This refers to] Brahman's [presence] in the intellect and so forth.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is either conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or identity (*tādātmya*). It cannot be the first, because that would entail the consequence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*); nor can it be the second, because of the rejection of inherence; and it cannot be the last, because of the contradiction with such principles as the fact that identity is impossible between two things that are either different or non-different. Anticipating this objection, [the author] speaks of "pervasive" (*vyāpī*), taking recourse to an identity that is merely illusory (*āvidya*). || 628 ||
Due to its non-commonality, it would not exist between two things that are distinct by way of time, direction, or location.
There is no pervasion between them due to their mutual lack of connection, like that between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.

Furthermore, regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) elsewhere—whether between two things that are different, non-different, or both different and non-different—it is not the first case. To this he says: "Because of being uncommon" (*asādhāraṇataḥ*). The construction is as follows: because two things that are different [due to factors such as time] exist as being established through their uncommon exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no pervasion, just as there is none between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains due to their mutual lack of connection. || 629 ||
This [non-difference] does not exist between two things that are mutually distinct, nor is their identity (aikātmya) admitted.
Of two distinct universals, that which possesses them is of an uncommon nature.
Having stated that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of absolute difference, he refutes another alternative with the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*).

Just as there is no pervasion between the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains, which are absolutely distinct from one another, so too it is not logical nor is it accepted that pervasion exists between two things that are absolutely non-different;

for pervasion does not exist in a single entity, whether it be smoke or fire. By the word "also" (*api*), he addresses the third possibility; for [pervasion] does not exist between things that are both different and non-different.

The sense is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot exist in one place [between two distinct things] because of their lack of connection. Furthermore, is that [pervasion] between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), or between cause and effect, or between things different from those? It is not the first; thus he says: "By the distinct," etc. The word "distinct" refers to the individual. "Like that" means there is no pervasion, just as there is none between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. The reason for this is: "Because of its non-commonality to those two," meaning to those two, the universal and the individual.

The meaning is that since two things that are absolutely distinct exist as unique natures, there can be no pervasion (vyāpti) between them; and if they were absolutely non-distinct, then by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), they would exist as a single form through their unique natures, and thus both difference and non-difference would be untenable in one and the same thing. || 130 ||
Thus, through the conceptualization of cause and effect as both different and non-different, [the error arises].
Pervasion by means of a real entity is not logically tenable. || 631 ||

He replies to the second [position] with the words "kārya" (effect). The meaning is that, by the logic already stated, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) even between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).
He refutes the third [position] with the words "bhava" (existence). Here, the term "iha" refers to the sphere of linguistic usage (*vyavahārabhūmi*).

In reality, pervasion is untenable even for things that are distinct from both the universal and the individual, or from cause and effect—whether they are different, non-different, or both different and non-different.
Such is the meaning. || 631 ||
In which both [the self and the world] would be entirely sublated, like the rope and the snake.
Let pervasion be primary in that very case; likewise, it is so for both the self and the non-self as well.

Anticipating the objection—“If there is no pervasion (vyāpti) between things that are different, non-different, or both different and non-different, how can the pervasion of the Self over the non-Self be stated?”—he says: “Where... In the case of two things, when one exists within the other through identity (tādātmya), that existence of the latter in the former is primary pervasion; just as the serpent exists in the rope, so too does the Self [exist in the non-Self].

Let it not be that even for two selves, the occurrence of the non-self—which is imagined within the self—is primary; therefore, the meaning is that the primary pervasion between the imagined and the unimagined is called "identity" (tādātmya) with the imagined. || 632 ||
Just as one enters a snake only through darkness and not by one's own power.
In this way, the Self itself, through its own ignorance, manifests as the world by means of Māyā.

Thus, it is established that the Inner Self alone is the reality, and not the world.
Such is the meaning. || 633 ||
By what means did the illusionist enter the work through his illusion?
