Just as [threads] are separated from a razor-case, so too is the self [separated] by means of the different channels.
Therein, by the explanation of the first illustration, he clarifies the specific functioning (*viśeṣavṛtti*) of the inner self (*pratīc*). Regarding the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*):

just as razors cast into a single vessel containing hair-cutting implements, due to the contradiction of multiple material objects occupying the same space, come to possess distinct locations and specific functions, and thus differ from one another and from the razor-holders; so too the Self, through its connection with the specific channels such as the eyes, becomes the seer within the body.
The meaning is that [the Self], possessing specific pervasiveness such as being a hearer and so forth, is distinct from the body and from one another. || 637 ||
Those worlds which lie below the Imperishable (akṣara) stand woven together like warp and woof.
Through the discernment of each respective stage, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), though being the Supreme itself, [is so designated]. || 638 ||

By stating that specific functioning (*viśeṣavṛtti*) is adventitious (*aupādhika*), it was implied that general functioning (*sāmānyavṛtti*) is likewise adventitious due to its similarity [to the former].

Now, since both modes of functioning in the body are adventitious, he states that the status of being the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajñatva*) is also adventitious by implication, beginning with the word "woven" (*ota*).

From the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the unknown Brahman, downward through the stages of modification such as earth and so forth—which, like long threads, exist as the warp (*ota*)—and horizontally...

And by being woven warp and woof within that very syllable—as per the scriptural text beginning with, "In this very syllable, O Gārgī, space is woven warp and woof"—the Supreme Self itself, though remaining unlimited, becomes the individual soul (jīva) due to being delimited by those various states of existence consisting of both collective and individual forms; thus, the meaning is that the state of being a jīva is merely adventitious (aupādhika). || 638 ||
Subtlety and pervasiveness are to be known as extending from the elements, such as earth, up to the unmanifest (akṣara).

"By the successive abandonment of each preceding [element], its culmination is in the nature of space (viyadātmanā). (639) Having raised the objection that if the states such as "being a living being" (*jīvatva*) are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), then if the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) were a real entity (*vastu*), non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost; whereas if it were unreal (*avastu*), that [state] would itself become unreal because an unreal adjunct cannot logically be adventitious—[the author] says: "Subtlety" (*sūkṣmatā*). [This refers to] earth and so forth, up to the Imperishable (*akṣara*). Each preceding...

By the abandonment of each preceding [element], the subtlety and other qualities of each subsequent one are to be understood in relation to its effect, because the cause possesses the nature of that effect; and because that [series] culminates in the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara), the word "ether" (viyat) is used to include the Imperishable, since the word "space" (ākāśa)—which is a synonym for it—is seen to be employed in that sense.

Furthermore, since everything else is imagined as being dependent, the Imperishable alone is non-dependent and non-imagined; thus, the establishment of non-duality (advaita) follows, and not [the existence of] an upādhi...

The meaning is that if the self were an eternal substance, it would be impossible for qualities such as being a living soul (*jīvatva*) to be adventitious (*aupādhika*); for an imagined (*kalpita*) limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) does not contradict such [adventitious] states of being a living soul and so forth. || 639 ||
1. *nācedbhiyaṃ* | 2. *’stutvopapa* | 3. *yogāditya* | [vol2, page 268]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
Here, the one who sustains the universe is to be known as the Sustainer of the Universe (*viśvabhṛt*), because of his supporting of the entire world.
Just as fire, pervading the entire piece of wood, resides within that wood.

By explaining the first illustration, he has clarified the specific function of the Self within the body; by stating that this [function] is adventitious (*aupādhika*), he has stated that its status as the individual soul (*jīvatva*) is likewise so. Now, he explains the meaning of the word *viśvambhara* found in the second illustration. He says: "The universe. An objection may be raised: "But this word does not refer to fire, for there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for it in that sense. Anticipating this, [the author replies] that [fire is intended] either by virtue of being a great element (*mahābhūta*) or by virtue of being the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*).

He states the Lord's status as the sustainer of the universe with the words "of the universe. The word "here" refers to the sentence under discussion. He states the intended aspect of the illustration with the word "as. || 640 ||
In that same way, the Self remains pervading the entire body;
yet it also exists without pervading it, just as a razor exists within the razor-case.
The Self, situated within the channels of the ears and other senses, remains without pervading the entire body.
One attains two functions during one's own states of dreaming and waking.

1 He states the application to the subject at hand (*dāṣṭantika*): "Having pervaded" (*saṃvyāpya*). Having described the general pervasion of the Self within the body by means of an illustration, he restates its specific pervasion along with an illustration for the purpose of clarifying the previously mentioned channels (*nāḍī*): "It remained" (*tasthau*). [And] "without having pervaded" (*avyāpya*).

The word "severance" (*cchedaḥ*) [is used]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "in a specific form such as 'the hearer,' 'the seer,' and so forth. He states the internal distinction between the two aforementioned functions (*vṛtti*) based on their different states with the words "the two functions" (*vṛttī*). The meaning is that, although in reality it is devoid of the two functions because it is not followed by other functions, through its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) it attains those two in the two states. The word "atadvān" is to be severed [as a compound]. || 641 || 642 ||
In deep sleep, he attains that which functions as mere generality.
This [bondage] arises from delusion regarding the true nature of the inward Self, but it does not exist in ultimate reality.
Then, suspecting that the same two-fold function might occur even in other states, he says "sāmānya" (general) to show that in deep sleep there is only the general function.
He states the reason for the connection of the unattached Self with the three states and the two-fold function by saying "pratyak" (inner).

It is argued that such a function as described in the three states cannot be real for this [Self], because it would contradict its aforementioned lack of attachment; thus, [the function] is merely apparent.
He says "but not" [in response] to this objection. || 643 ||
The great beings are to be known as such because they have completely submerged all the lower stages.
Individuals are the ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), because they are unique to themselves.

Having described the two internal functions, [the author] analyzes the categories of objects in order to demonstrate them externally as well. He says, "The Great Being" (*mahāsattā*). Since the word *vyoman*—a synonym for *viyat* (space)—is used in the sense of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) in the passage, "Space, the Imperishable, the Ṛg-verses in the supreme ether," it should be understood that this Imperishable is the Great Being, which is mere universality (*sāmānyamātra*). Thus, the Imperishable is to be known as the Great Being.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "In its entirety" (*kṛtsna*). The meaning is that because the syllable (*akṣara*) pervades all stages of modification prior to the [final] syllable, it is merely a universal (*sāmānya*). He says, "Individuals" (*vyaktayaḥ*), because final particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) are by nature absolutely distinct and thus constitute individuality itself.
Although final particulars established by the technical terminology of the Vaiśeṣikas do not exist, nevertheless, the conventional usage of "particular" reaches its limit [there].
The sense is that, since they are to be sought after as being present on all stages (bhūmis), it is appropriate to restrict their manifestation within those [stages]. || 644 ||
The generalities, the particulars, and those that fall between them.
[Vol. 2, Page 269] 24 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 561.
The generalities, the particulars, and those that fall between them.
The state of being a particular of a universal selfhood became that further limiting adjunct (upādhi).

He states that earth and the other elements possess both natures by saying, "The universals. Let it be granted that the categories (padārthas) possess the divisions as previously described; what follows from this in the present context? To this he replies: "The nature of the universal. The meaning is: the Supreme has reached the state of being both [universal and particular]—the nature of the universal through the adjunct of the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), the nature of the particular through the adjunct of the ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣa), and the nature of both through the adjuncts of earth and the rest. || 645 ||
Residing in the channels of the ears, skin, and other senses, it functions through the perception of sound and the rest.
Its activity is perceived within this body by means of name and form.

Having described the two modes of existence [of the self] with respect to objects external to the body, he now states— proving by means of experience— the specific mode of existence of the inner self (*pratīc*) within the body, beginning with the words "The ear, etc. The nature of being a seer, a hearer, and so forth, which resides in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the senses such as the ear, is produced in the body of this person Maitra by means of name and form acting as seeds, as well as through the cognition of sound, touch, and so on, and through activities such as going and speaking.
Therefore, the meaning is that the specific functioning of the self within the body is established by experience. || 646 ||
One perceives that which is to be perceived through both its uncommon and common forms.
Because it is established by all means of valid cognition, it is therefore set forth from that [source].

Having stated the intended meaning of the two examples, he establishes the preliminary ground (*bhūmikā*) that the dual nature of the world is established by perception and other means of valid cognition, in order to introduce the sentence "they do not perceive it. [The phrase] "asādhāraṇa" [means]: the visible world itself is of a dual nature, because its existence is observed only therein.
Relying on what has been stated, he explains the purport of the sentence with the word "sarva": of the dual-natured world, [the perception is] direct...

The meaning is that because the self is not established [as such] and because it is not of that nature, the self is distinguished from that which consists of the three [qualities] by means of the statement beginning with "not this" (neti).
The word "ataḥ" (hence) means "of this. || 647 ||
"This is the object of knowledge, this is the knower, and this is the means of knowledge"— in such a perception, [these distinctions are made].
People find satisfaction in false knowledge, which is like a dream, a magical illusion, or a conjurer’s trick.

[Objection: "In that case, since the world is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), and because people are seen to find satisfaction in its cognition, non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost due to its being a real entity. To this, he says: "This... [and so on].

Since the cognition of the mother and so forth is an error, like the cognition in a dream and the like, there is no loss of non-duality; however, the fact that it is established by all means of knowledge (*māna*) pertains only to the perspective of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*). Multiple examples are cited in order to demonstrate the manifold nature of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). || 648 ||
Since this is a false understanding, therefore, for its removal:
He says that those who see him as he has been described do not see him.

He states the conclusion regarding the erroneous nature of the cognition that distinguishes between the mother and so forth, beginning with the words "yataḥ" (since). The meaning is that the Śruti speaks for the purpose of destroying false cognition: those who perceive the Self as possessing two forms—consisting of the general and the particular, and characterized by distinctions such as mother and so on—do not apprehend it, because the Self is distinct from those [forms]. || 6.49 ||
For false cognition is not directed toward a real entity, since it is solely grounded in the ignorance of the real.
Because they do not see [it], it is logical that they do not perceive that ultimate reality.
1. *veṣṭitaṃ* (ka, ga). 2. *derityaṃ* (kha). 3. *śabdasya* (ka).
[Vol.
2, page 270] 564. The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Adhyāya].

Anticipating the objection that—since both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are real entities because their nature is non-different from the Self—the cognition of them cannot be considered a false cognition, just like the cognition of the Self—he says: "The entity" (*vastu*). Since the universal and so forth reside solely within the ignorance of the Self and are therefore not real entities, the cognition of them is indeed a false cognition; it is not a correct cognition by virtue of having a real entity as its object, for in a reality that is a single expanse of consciousness, the relation of universal and particular is impossible.

The meaning is that it is indeed logical that even those who perceive the Self as having the form of fear do not perceive [the true Self]. Regarding the phrase "they do not perceive Him," it is only the visual nature of the Self that is denied; this is precisely what is intended, as per the scriptural text beginning with "not by the eye. Fearing that its knowability might be rejected due to a specific negation, he explains: "No. Even while perceiving the Self as qualified by breathing and so forth, they do not perceive Him as free from phenomenal expansion (aprapañca).
The meaning is that they do not know. || 650 ||
Even though there is here a conceit regarding the self, which is devoid of action and agency.
Because it perceives things as they are not, that cognition is considered to be merely false. || 651 ||

One might object: "How can the aforementioned negation be established based on the conceit arising from the uncontradicted perception of the self as 'I see,' 'I hear,' and so forth? To this, [the author] replies with the words "Even though... and so on. Even though there exists in the self the conceit "I see" and so forth, nevertheless it is merely false cognition because it is not in accordance with reality; furthermore, it is not accepted [as valid] with respect to the immovable (kūṭastha) witnesshood and other attributes, since it is a cognition that is non-conformable to reality.
And falsity does not [apply] here; the meaning is that when the scripture negating all specific attributes exists, the conceit of being a seer and so forth is not sublated. || 651 ||
Is this not a prohibition of what has not been previously established, when it is said, "they do not see"?
It is not so, because the passages concerning creation and so forth have as their sole purpose the realization of the inner Self.

When it is stated that the negative statement is for the purpose of destroying false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), [the opponent] raises an objection regarding that negation with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). He refutes this with "Not so" (*naivam*), on the grounds that the creation under discussion—expressed as "by name and form"—as well as the entry expressed as "this very one here," are both indeed relevant to the subject at hand, since they are supplementary to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). || 612 ||
Even a single verse states this very same meaning clearly: "Form, form."
Because by seeing that, the entirety of the goals of human existence is accomplished. || 653 ||

He reminds us of the very proof already stated regarding the fact that creation and so forth are for the purpose of knowledge: "The mantra also... Having begun with these words, the construction is as follows: "The mantra also clearly declares this very meaning in the passage, 'In order to manifest its form. It is not by its power alone that creation and so forth [serve the purpose of knowledge].

It is not that [the subordinate part] possesses its own purpose; rather, it is because of such maxims as "in the proximity of that which has a fruit," and so forth. Having stated this, he states another point: "Because that is seen.
This means "of the entire" or "of the complete. || 653 ||
Even while seeing, they do not see; how can it be said that this is contradictory?
Because their view does not touch reality, it is said that they do not see. || 354 ||

One might object that since the knowledge of the Self is already obtained through such passages as those concerning creation (*sṛṣṭi*), there can be no prohibition of what has already been attained; thus, this [prohibition] is not logical because it involves a contradiction. To this, he replies with the words "Even though they see" (*paśyanto’pi*). He resolves the contradiction with the word "mine" (*meya*). Since the perception of the Self as a universal entity (*sāmānya*) and so forth is an error because it does not conform to the reality of the thing itself, the prohibition is appropriate when intended to mean the absence of right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
This is the meaning. || 654 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 271] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 565.
Because the entire reality is non-dual, based on such statements as "Being indeed" (*sadeva*).
How could there be the arising of a partial entity that is opposed to that [complete reality]? (655)

He explains how the perception of the Self as having the nature of universality and so forth is an error because it conforms to what is unreal: "It exists" (*sad iti*). He establishes its totality by characterizing it as being defined by the absence of duality. With the words "Since" (*yataḥ*), he states the conclusion regarding the reality established by scripture, which is devoid of the three kinds of limitation. Regarding the phrase "possibility" (*saṃbhava*), [he says]: since that which is limited is unreal, the perception of it is incorrect.
The meaning is that it is indeed a view. || 655 ||
The inward reality is, by its own nature, neither excluded nor followed by cognition.
In this world, that perception which is contrary to that [reality] is false in form; it is not otherwise.

He manifests the innate fullness of the Self through both reasoning and experience by the words "not excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*). The meaning is that the inner reality (*pratyag-vastu*), which is by its very nature devoid of both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), manifests with a sense of oneness to the wise; furthermore, neither universals nor particulars are established either intrinsically or extrinsically.

He states that the cognition of universals and so forth regarding the Self is false because it is contradictory to the nature of the reality, using the phrase "contradictory to that" (*tadviruddha*). [The text continues: "the perception of universals and so forth..."
He states what is to be excluded by saying that right vision does not exist when there is a contrary view regarding the self; he says: "That is not [right vision]. (616)
Since the Self attains the non-self as its entirety through the state of being the inner witness (pratyaktā).
Otherwise, because nothing else would remain, it would be incomplete. (657)

He states another reason for the fullness of the inner self (*pratīc*): "The Self" (*ātma*). Because the Self pervades the entire non-self (*anātman*), and because it is the inner witness (*pratyaktva*) everywhere therein, therefore, since there is nothing other than the Self that is not pervaded by it, it must be full. If there were even the slightest thing not pervaded by the Self, then the Self would be incomplete; however, such a thing does not exist, because that which is not pervaded by the Self lacks its own essential nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*).
The meaning is that perfection is attained when [the mind] is joined with this. || 617 ||
That which is non-self cannot achieve establishment in the form of a self, because it is inward-facing (pratyak).
Since its true nature consists solely of the inward-facing [consciousness], how could there be anything distinct from it? (658)

Having stated the fullness of the Self through the reasoning of its being the object of veneration (*māna*), he states another argument for the fact that the limited [world] is of the nature of ignorance (*āvidyaka*). He says: "The non-self... Duality is established either as non-different from the Self or as different from it. It cannot be the first, because that would result in the consequence that only the innermost Self (*pratyag-mātra*) remains. Nor can it be the second, because there is no essential nature (*svarūpa*) other than the innermost Self. Therefore, the meaning is that duality is established only by way of being superimposed (*kalpita*) upon the innermost Self. || 658 ||
"Also by way of place, time, form, substance, and likewise state."
Its deviation is fully established, witnessed by the self that is its opposite. 659.
He states another reason for the non-self being imagined: "In terms of place," and so forth. That which exists in one place and time does not exist elsewhere;

that which is the form of one thing does not belong to another. When there is the state of birth for one, it is the state of destruction for another. Thus, by virtue of place and so on, as well as by virtue of qualities, actions, and so forth, the variability of the non-self is established; nor is there a lack of evidence for this.
The meaning is that [the existence of the transitory states] is established by the experience of witnesses who have strayed [from their usual state]. || 699 ||
It is said that they do not see [the object] for the sake of establishing the meaning of their proposition.
"For it is incomplete" is the statement of the reason, and that too is established in this way.
566 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 272]

Having explained the meaning of the phrase "they do not see him," he introduces the subsequent sentence with the word "pratijñā" (the proposition). The construction is as follows: "they do not see him" is the proposition (*pratijñā*); for the sake of establishing its meaning, the statement of the reason (*hetu*)—"for [he is] incomplete"—is intended. He further states that this statement of the reason is itself established by the passage beginning with "breathing indeed," according to the method that will be explained. Thus he says, "sā'pi" (that too). The necessity of supporting the reason is [emphasized].
The word is used to indicate [this]. || 660 ||
The proclamation "prāṇam eva" is for the sake of establishing that [the self] is not incomplete.
For it is observed that there is mutual deviation among the means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest.

He elaborates upon the meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "That" (*tad*). The meaning is that the statement beginning with "only when breathing" (*prāṇanneva*) is intended to establish that the meaning of the causal sentence is incomplete (*akṛtsnatva*). Now, an objection is raised: by that [statement], the agent of breathing and so forth is indeed expressed, but not the incompleteness, because there is no word present that introduces that [incompleteness]. To this he replies: "Mutually" (*anyonya*). For it is observed that the agents of breathing, seeing, and so forth are mutually inconsistent; indeed, it is not the case that...
The meaning is that because it deviates in some respects from being complete, it is therefore incomplete. || 661 ||
When that [object] is seen, the unseen object remains as something other than it.
Likewise, even when something is not seen, if it is seen [in part], it is called "incomplete" (*akṛtsna*).

Having thus explained the purport of the textual passage beginning with "for it is incomplete" (*akṛtsno hi*) and ending before "belonging to that" (*tadanyasya*), [the author] explains the meaning of the word *akṛtsna*.

The Master says: "In which... etc. The meaning is this: when a jar or the like is seen, that object which remains unseen exists because it possesses parts; furthermore, another object such as a cloth remains unseen.

Likewise, even when the specific qualities inherent in a cloth or the like are unseen, that jar or other object which would be seen follows the manner already shown and is thus designated by the term "incomplete" (*akṛtsna*). || 662 ||
He will reveal the meaning of the reason in order to establish the incompleteness [of the opponent's argument].
That [self], being a composite of the eye, ear, and so forth, does not attain completeness (akṛtsnatā).

Having raised the objection—"Since incompleteness has been stated, how can it be established in the agent of breathing and other functions? And in the absence of that [completeness], how can there be perception of the Self even when there is the perception of the seer and so forth?"—he restates what was said here in order to establish that incompleteness, saying: "Intending to reveal... and so on.

The meaning is that the Veda proceeds by means of the passage beginning with "prāṇanneva" (while breathing indeed) to reveal the sense of the causal statement "for he is incomplete" (akṛtsno hi), for the purpose of establishing the incompleteness of the Self who performs the functions of breathing and so forth. Anticipating the objection that even the agent of seeing and other such functions must be complete because he is the Self—otherwise, his agency would be impossible—the text says, "na hi" (not indeed). The agent of seeing and so forth does not at all attain fullness, [as he is limited] by the eye and other organs.
The meaning is: because it is composed of [the elements] beginning with ether (dibhiḥ). || 663 ||
Because name, form, and action, whose natures are mutually non-pervasive, do not encompass one another.
Because of their deviation [from the nature of the Self], there would be incompleteness for those things whose sole form is non-self. (664)

It establishes the form of that which is a composite. The phrase "mutually" (*paraspara*) is to be construed as follows: because there would be a deviation [from the rule] due to the lack of mutual pervasion among the individual selves—consisting of name and so forth—which are merely non-self, and which perform functions such as vitalization, the aforementioned incompleteness (*akṛtsnatva*) would result. || 664 ||
Though previously unaggregated, it is now aggregated due to the cause of delusion regarding the self.
Performing the functions of breathing and so forth, it is designated as "prāṇa."
1. *Ve-dṛṣṭādi* [vol2, page 273] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 567.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper for the commentary to state, "While performing the very act of breathing, he is called 'prāṇa' (breath)," etc.— on the grounds that it is impossible for the inward, changeless Self to be the agent of breathing and so forth, and that it only acquires the designations of "prāṇa" and so on by virtue of being their agent— the author says: "asaṃhataḥ" (uncompounded).

The internal Self (pratyagātmā), although in reality uncomposite, becomes designated by the term "prāṇa" and so forth when, under the influence of delusion, it appears composite with the vital breaths and performs activities such as breathing; this is the construction [of the sentence]. In the word "prāṇa," the term "and so forth" (ādi) is to be understood. || 669 ||
And in that vital breath, the activity of the wind functions through the nature of the instrument.
Being cast off, that [self] attains the state of being an object for the conscious self (vijñānātman).

Anticipating the objection that, even though [the Self] is the agent by virtue of delusion, who could possess the status of instrument or object in the act of breathing—since it is not possible for the agent himself to have those states because their distinction is well-established—he says: "And in that... (666).
Directly relinquishing his own self into that wind during the act of breathing out.
Devoid of the collection of causal agents, it is experienced through direct perception alone.

If it be argued that, in the act of breathing, the internal air alone possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), and the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being pervaded by the action, then why should it not also possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the substratum of the action? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Directly" (*sākṣāt*). In that action called breathing, the Self is directly experienced as the innermost self (*pratyañc*) while emitting the air.

The connection [is as follows]: therefore, it is the Self alone that experiences agency therein, and not the wind, because the latter is merely another instrumental factor (kāraka); this is the meaning. To the objection that agency and so forth must then be real, he says: "apeta... (667).
In this witness of arrival and departure, which is devoid of their attributes, the causal factors such as the agent appear as having unique forms that do not belong to it. (668)

[The author] establishes the unreality of agency and so forth [with the verse beginning] "kartrādi" (agency, etc.). The meaning is that all *kārakas* (factors of action) appear like a snake in a rope within the inner self (*pratīc*), the witness of all, which is devoid of distinctions such as action and its factors; and this appearance is an illusion because it is mutually exclusive and subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*). Since the *kārakas* are insentient (*jaḍa*), they cannot manifest by themselves without depending upon the witness.
This is the meaning of the word "hi. || 668 ||
It is self-established in the form of a witness, because of its non-deviation from these [objects].
But the forms beginning with the agent and ending with darkness exist in dependence upon their respective attributes (dharma). || 669 ||

Anticipating the objection that even the Witness (sākṣin) cannot be conceived as the agent and so forth because it is imagined as being characterized by various attributes and is thus subject to change (vyabhicārin), he says: "The Witness. Since the Witness, which is pure consciousness (cinmātra), is immutable (kauṭasthya), it has no similarity to the agent and the like; therefore, because that pure essence alone is not imagined (akalpita) despite the changing attributes, it is logical for it to be the substratum (adhiṣṭhānatā). [This refers to] the agent and the like.

He states the result regarding the superimposition upon the Witness (sākṣin): "The agent, etc. The word "tu" (but) has the sense of a distinction from the nature of the Witness. The meaning is that the nature of the inner self (pratyag-vastu), as conditioned by ignorance and its effects—the intellect (buddhi)—is the agent and so forth. Anticipating the objection that since the aforementioned inner self is eternal, the agent and so forth would also be eternal if they were of that nature, he says: "Dharma, etc. (Verse 669).
Because it arises from an impermanent cause, it is impermanent; by this, the agent and so forth are characterized.
Therefore, innate ignorance is characterized as if it were eternal, even though it is without cause.
Regarding how the nature of the agent and so forth can be produced by karma, he says in response: "Impermanent," etc. By that witness (sākṣin),...

The nature of the agent and so forth is perceived as impermanent; and that impermanence is experienced because it is produced by impermanent attributes and the like, for otherwise there would be a contradiction with the experience of non-agency and so forth in the Inner Self (pratyagātman), which is indeed experienced by the wise—this is the meaning. An objection might be raised: "If the agent and so forth are impermanent, then their material cause, ignorance (ajñāna), must also be impermanent due to its non-difference from them; thus, it could not serve as a [permanent] material cause. Anticipating this, he says: "Without a cause" (nirhetu). Although...

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not eternal because it is removable by knowledge; nevertheless, it is perceived as if eternal by that very witness (*sākṣin*). This is because, while being causeless, it is other than non-existence, like the Self (*ātman*), according to inference; and furthermore, because its material cause is non-eternal, it cannot be eternal itself—such is the sense. (670)
Because it has as its sole abode the ignorance regarding the inner Self, it possesses no other form.
How can there be a notion of permanence or impermanence regarding those things whose forms consist of action and its factors? || 671 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are non-eternal, since space (*gagana*) and other such things are eternal, they cannot be effects of ignorance—and thus there would be a loss of the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*)—the author says:

"The inner self" (*pratyag*). Since all objects consisting of action, factors of action (*kāraka*), and so on, are established solely upon the substrate of the ignorance of the Self, which requires no other support, there is no form [for them] other than ignorance; therefore, the distinction between the eternity of space and the like versus the non-eternity of the agent and so forth does not constitute a valid object of knowledge (*prameya*).
This is the meaning. || 671 ||
Therefore, due to its deviation from that [nature], there is no [distinction] among name, form, action, and self.
By means of the designation "incomplete," the nature of false knowledge is expressed. || 672 ||

Since permanence and other such qualities are difficult to establish for that which is differentiated, and since there is deviation regarding the triadic nature of the agent and so forth within the inner self—as well as regarding space and the like—it follows that the statement "not in its entirety" declares that [differentiated reality] is the object of false cognition; this is the conclusion he states with the words "Therefore...
Just as in the case of an unperceived rope, [the notions] of those things that have the single form superimposed upon it [arise].
Just as there is deviation of birds and other [beings] toward the west, so too is there deviation for those things that are not the Self.

He clarifies, by means of an illustration, the deviation of the agent and other factors from the inner self (pratīci) for the sake of establishing their falsity: "In the case of the unknown," and so forth.

For just as in the case of a rope that is not known to be a rope, there is experienced a deviation—due to that ignorance of it and what is produced by it, which are habitually superimposed upon it—of such things as a snake and the like, whose nature is identical to that [ignorance], so too is there [deviation] in the case of the Self when it is unknown, due to that ignorance of it.
The meaning is that because the agent and so forth produced by that [consciousness] are subject to deviation, they are false. || 673 ||
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are the leaders; they remain awake before the awakening of the intellect while the others are asleep.
Therefore, the agency of the Lord with respect to that [object] is first stated.

Thus, the meaning of the reason has been established through such statements as "merely breathing" (*prāṇanneva*). Now, one might raise the objection: why does the Śruti first state that the inner self (*pratyak*) is the agent of breathing, rather than stating at the outset that it is the agent of any one of the other functions, such as speaking? Anticipating this doubt, he explains the purport of the statement that begins with "merely breathing," which was introduced first: "The vital breaths are fires. This refers to the fact that the Śruti declares the vital breaths to be fires, serving as the locus for the oblation.

And its status as the substratum [of the soul] due to its being the locus of delight is to be understood from the section on the *prāṇāgnihotra*. "Before the intellect" means during deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
1. Ga. ti | ya | [vol2, page 275]
4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 569.

"In this world" (*iha*) refers to the statement of the cited passage. "Of the Lord" (*prabhoḥ*) means of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the master of the instruments. Even though the entire collection of instruments, such as speech and so forth, is withdrawn during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not withdrawn and its activity persists—since that activity pervades all three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]—[the soul does not perish].
The meaning is that, in this sentence, the agency regarding two objects is first shown to belong to the Self. || 174 ||
Both by name and by form, in the activities such as breathing and so forth.
It is perceived through ignorance, just as a rope is [perceived] as a snake and so forth. || 675 ||

If it is argued that because the agency of breathing and so forth is described in scripture (*śruti*) regarding the inner self (*pratīc*), then by virtue of being scriptural, that [agency] must be real like Brahman—anticipating this doubt, he says: "By name" (*nāmataḥ*). Just as a rope is perceived through ignorance (*avidyā*) as possessing a snake, a stream, and so on, so too the Self, due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the vital breaths and other factors through its own ignorance, appears—as if possessing those [attributes]—as though it were identical with them, even though it is not so, despite the existence of breathing and the rest within the sphere of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
This is the meaning. || 675 ||
Because of the restriction "only as conceit," it is because [the object] has the nature of something other than that [conceit].
A deviation is demonstrated in order to establish that [the breath] and so forth are not complete [in themselves]. (676)

Anticipating the objection—namely, what purpose is served by the particle *eva* (only) in the passage beginning with "breathing, [it is] called breath" (*prāṇan prāṇo nāma*)—the author says: "breathing" (*prāṇan*). Thus, the exclusion of this [breath] from the agent of breathing—who is distinct in nature from the agents of seeing and so forth—is stated by means of the restrictive determination (*avadhṛti*). And so, for the sake of establishing that [the breath] is not the whole (*akṛtsnatva*), a mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is demonstrated between such statements as "the breath is the seer" and "the breath is the hearer. This is the meaning. ||676||
Performing this very action at this very time is what is described here.
And in this very context of the application of ritual action, he is accepted as being of that nature. || 677 ||

Anticipating the objection that although there is mutual deviation (vyabhicāra) among the vital functions such as breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest, they are nonetheless non-imagined (*akalpita*) like consciousness because they do not exist in the inner self (*pratīc*), he says:

"Action" (*karman*). While performing the activity of breathing and so forth, the Self is designated by that name and takes on that form only at the very moment those activities arise, provided that the cause for its connection with them exists; likewise, while performing other activities at another time, it is connected with other [names and forms].

Or rather, it is intended that [the self] possesses those respective names and forms. As they say: "Indeed, while performing this very function of breathing, at this very time, through its connection with this very function, it becomes known by the name 'Prāṇa'. Therefore, the meaning is that there is deviation even regarding the reality of Prāṇa and the rest. || 677 ||
But at the very same time as possessing that [knowledge], there arises the activity of measuring and so forth.
And because of the impossibility of vital breaths in other [beings] before and after [birth].
It does not possess that name, nor that form, nor does it exist in any other action.

He clarifies through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) exactly what has been stated: "tadvān" (that which possesses it). What was said as "simultaneous with that which possesses it" is now being made explicit. Regarding "trāṇanādi" (protection and so forth): [this refers to] prior to the manifestation of the aforementioned activities such as breathing, or after their destruction.

The inner self (pratyagātman) does not possess the name "vital breath" (prāṇa) nor its form; therefore, among other agents of seeing and so forth who are distinct from the agent of breathing, they do not possess those names and forms prior to the manifestation of the activities of breathing and the rest. Furthermore, in other operations, [the principle] is the same.
1 ka. ga. "siddhī vya".
The meaning is as follows:

since it is impossible for the seer to be perceived elsewhere, the seer cannot possess name and form; this same logic should be applied to the hearer and so forth. Therefore, because the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other faculties deviate from the reality and are not exhaustive of it, they are merely imagined. || 678 ||
Because the emergence of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) occurs immediately after [the emergence of] vital breath (prāṇa).
Speaking thus, he said "Speech" (vāk) from this point on, in accordance with the sequence of the method.

"Why is the agency of the activities of the organs of action (karmendriya) stated immediately after the agency of breathing (prāṇana), and why is the agency of the activities of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya) not introduced instead? To this, he says: "By 'breathing'... "Arising" (samudbhava) refers to the activity of speaking and so forth. "The connection of the sequence" means its possibility. The ellipsis is: "he states the agency of the activities of the organs of action. Although [this occurs] immediately after breathing...

The point is that although the same sequence is observed for seeing and so forth, nevertheless, because actions such as speaking depend upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of movement, their immediate succession is logical. || 679 ||
That which speaks is speech; the Self becomes speech, and sound is called speech.
Because it is said "by this," speech is therefore designated as the instrument (karaṇa). || 680 ||

Although in the Śruti the self is distinguished solely by its being the agent of breathing and so forth, nevertheless, for each respective operation of the senses, it should be understood that it is distinguished as the object and as the instrument, just as it is the agent; thus he says with the words beginning "it speaks" (vakti).
The word "hi" indicates the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word "vāk" (speech) in relation to sound. That is to say, it is derived from this [root]. (680)
Seeing, it is the eye; likewise, the seer is the same; and hearing, it is the ear.
One should thus observe that [the definition] is excluded in three ways and in all cases.

By saying "speaking is speech," he extends the reasoning already stated here to other sentences as well. Regarding the word "seeing": for there, by the word *cakṣus* (eye), the act of seeing (*caṣṭe*) is expressed; that which is seen is the object (*karman*); and likewise, that by which something is seen is the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is the distinction. In the phrase "hearing is the ear" (*śrotra*), by the word *śrotra*, the hearer (*śrotṛ*)—who hears (*śṛṇoti*)—is expressed; that which is heard is the object (*karman*); and that by which it is heard [is the instrument].
One must discern that [the body] is the instrument (*karaṇa*). One applies the aforementioned reasoning to the skin and the other [senses] as well. Thus [it is said]. (681)
The eye is for seeing alone; it is the mind that creates doubt.
The intellect is for the purpose of determination; the witness is called the field.

Having stated that the self possesses a manifold nature due to its connection with the sense organs and so forth, he describes the specific functions of the sense organs and the rest. Regarding the word "cakṣuḥ" (the eye):

by the term "cakṣuḥ," all ten sense organs are included. By the term "ālocana" (perception), the ten functions—such as seeing and the like, as well as speaking and the like—are meant. "Doubt" is also an indication for "volition. He now states the specific function of the individual soul (jīva).
"Regarding 'the witness' (sākṣī): the sense is that, in reality, the self possesses no agency or other such qualities. || 682 ||
That which is the witness-nature within the expansions of knowledge is itself, and not otherwise.
For among the various manifestations of the power of action, there is indeed mutual deviation.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a difference in witnesses corresponding to the operation of each respective sense organ, he says: "yaiva" (that very [witness]). The two locative endings (*saptamī*) are connected with the two words denoting mutual deviation (*anyonyavyabhicāri*). By the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), its power (*śakti*) is meant. In both cases, the word "expansion" (*vikāśa*) refers to a modification (*vikāra*). The meaning is that it does not otherwise become possessed of a variety of modes. Even the witness of difference is itself without difference.
1 [vol2,
page 277] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

The sense is that there is no real distinction because of the absence [of such a cause]. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to show that since the activity prompted by that [cause] is established by the witness-consciousness alone, it would be an unnecessary complication (gaurava) to postulate a distinction between them. || 683 ||
In the ether, which is devoid of constituent parts, there are regions that are mutually distinct.
Just as spiritual perfection is not possible for those in the West who are shrouded in darkness, so it is not possible here.

The passage beginning with "prāṇanneva" concludes the purport of that very argument. [The verse] states: "Nirasta... (dispelled). The meaning is that just as it is impossible for smoke, frost, and the like—which occupy distinct, mutually exclusive locations—to exist in the partless ether (ākāśa), so too there can be no possibility of ignorance or its products in the Self, which is non-attached and indifferent. || 684 ||
But those names and forms which have been declared as being endowed with breath—
These [faculties] of his arise solely from karma, and not spontaneously like consciousness itself. || 685 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tānyasya" (these belong to him) as follows: "prāṇan... (breathing...). The word "tu" (but) is used to state that being devoid of name and form is his very nature. He explains the sense of the particle "eva" (only/just): "na tu... (but not...). || 685 ||
Because their establishment is mutually dependent and because they are mutually deviant.
When perfection is not dependent on anything else, it would be like darkness in the presence of the sun. || 686 ||

If it is argued that although the names and forms such as "prāṇa" and so forth have been described as being based on the grounds of "breathing" and so on, they nonetheless exist as real entities in the inner self (pratīc) just like the "cook" and other designations,
[the author] says "no," beginning with the words "anyonya" (mutually). Since a name depends upon form and that form depends upon another [name],

and since form lacks the nature of a name while a name lacks the nature of form— due to this mutual deviation (vyabhicāra)— names and forms are impossible in the inner self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, just as darkness is impossible in the sun.
The meaning is that it is "imagined" because of its lack of reality. || 686 ||
Since, in this way, the vital breaths and so forth arise from ignorance for that which is not of the nature of those [breaths], etc.
Therefore, although one sees name-and-form through those two, one does not truly see it.

He states the result of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) being imagined: "Since... The meaning of the word "thus" (*evam*) is "because of dependence" and "because of deviation. "Not of that nature" means "devoid of name-and-form. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a state. The ellipsis is "the seer, seeing himself. (687)
This being so, he who is the seer of the supreme activity of breathing and so forth—
One does not know that "he worships"; worship arises from its own inherent nature. || 688 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who [sees] from here" (*sa yo'taḥ*) as follows: "In that case" (*tatra*). When that Self is full according to the reasoning already stated, and when everything else is merely imagined within it, the connection is as follows: he who, not seeing [the Self] in its true nature, dwells upon the Self as being merely distinguished by one or another of the functions such as breathing (*prāṇana*), "he does not know. He explains the meaning of the word "dwells upon" (*upāste*) as: "he knows thus" (*iti jānāti*). Thus he dwells upon.
By this, it is stated that one knows [the truth] from one's own nature; for the meaning is that meditation (upāsana) has not been enjoined, because a censure is seen later on. || 688 ||
For it is not possible [to know] all things either simultaneously or in succession.
Therefore, since each one exists individually, the subsequent mention is justified; thus, the established view is restated. || 689 ||
572 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 278]
"In that case, let this statement be an injunction for intrinsic knowledge. To this he says: "Not so, because...

No one who is not omniscient possesses knowledge of all things through either succession or simultaneity; rather, everyone possesses only a limited knowledge of individual objects occurring in succession. Since such [limited] knowledge is already attained, it cannot be the intended goal; therefore, that [attainment] which is possible is what is attained from the world, being intrinsic...
The "all-pervading view" (vikī dṛṣṭiḥ) is restated by the present sentence and is not enjoined; the meaning is that there is no portion [of it] that has not already been established. || 189 ||
Nor is there a deprecation of each individual form of worship for the purpose of prescribing multiple ways of viewing.
Even that view which says "from death to death" is thus censured.

One might suspect that by censuring the view of a single deity with the words "he does not know," the view of multiple deities is thereby permitted; thus, this statement would be an injunction for viewing [the deities] both collectively and individually.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not multiple. He provides the reason: because the view of multiple deities is also censured, as indicated by the words "from death" (mṛtyoḥ). || 690 ||
Because of the reasoning that "all is one," there is here the vision of the identity of all.
Since it is prescribed [in this way], there is therefore no perception of [the object] either as a whole or in its parts.

The failure to establish the view of the whole and the parts is not due solely to contradiction with other scriptural passages; rather, it is also because of contradiction with the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Thus he says: "All... The word "for" (*hi*) is used with the intention of indicating the abundance of other sentences enjoining the vision of the unity of the Self (*aikātmya*), which stand in opposition to the vision of the whole and the parts. [699]
Therefore, because it is measured by other means of knowledge both collectively and individually, [it is not the object of inference].
Having restated the unprecedented identity [of the self], the injunction [of that identity] is logically established. (692)

If it is argued that even the statement "for here all these become one" is intended merely to illustrate the perception of the whole and the parts, [the author] says "no," beginning with the word *samasta*. Since the state of being both whole and parts is already perceived through other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) than scriptural revelation—such as the common experience "the pot exists"—it cannot be the primary purport (*vākyagamya*) of that sentence, because it lacks the quality of being something previously unknown (*apūrvatva*). Therefore, having merely restated that [state], the sentence points toward the previously unknown reality which is a single, undifferentiated essence, supported by reasoning that establishes the falsity of duality.

The meaning is that, according to the logical principle that "that which is already well-known is restated here for reinforcement, while that which is not well-known is what is to be enjoined," it is precisely that [unestablished aspect] which is to be established in this context. || 692 ||
By means of the analogies of the ocean, the tree, and the ball of clay, [the nature] of the Supreme Self [is illustrated].
Some forcibly explain it as being seen both collectively and individually.

Bhartṛprapañca, by stating that "the non-distinction of particulars indeed constitutes unity, just as [there is unity] of the waves in the ocean," asserts that this passage has the purpose of teaching both the collective and distributive views (*samastavyastadṛṣṭi*). He raises this point with the words "In the ocean... Just as there is unity of the particulars—such as waves, branches, and fragments—within the ocean and the tree, so too, because everything beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is one within the Supreme, that [Supreme] is also like the ocean and so forth.

The meaning is that "possessing various flavors" (nānārasatva) is what is intended here in the verse beginning with "for here," and so on. The word "by force" (balāt) indicates a departure from the literal words of the scripture (śruti). ||193||
It is subject to deviation due to the separation of its various parts, like a chariot and so forth.
If it were established by some means of valid cognition, then it would be a mere restatement (anuvāda). (694)

Is the object here stated as something to be understood (*pratipādya*) as consisting of both the whole and its parts, or as something to be meditated upon (*upāsya*)? Having raised this alternative, he refutes the first: "Not [as such]. If it were seen through inference—namely, that the Supreme is characterized by various essences (*nānārasa*) due to its connection (*saṃbheda*, i.e., relation) with various components such as the vital breaths and so forth, and is thus both whole and part because He is the material cause, like a tree or the ocean—then, in that case:

In that case, the statement would be a mere restatement (anuvāda) and not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). If this matter were not perceived through inference and the like, then your citation of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) would be in vain.
This is the meaning. || 194 ||
Meditation consists in the non-recurrence [of thought] through the vision of the universal that is devoid of all particularity.
If such a thing were intended to be done, it would be difficult to accomplish even in ten million eons.

Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). If it is intended that this sentence enjoins a form of meditation consisting of repeated contemplation—based on the perception of all particularities (*viśeṣas*) and universals (*sāmānyas*), which possess the nature of a single entity, as being identical in essence (*tādātmya*) with the Self—then such meditation would be difficult for a person to accomplish even in a lifetime, because of the infinity of those [entities] and the impossibility of achieving a complete mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*). Therefore, [the meditation must concern] that which pertains to the self (*adhyātmaka*).
The meaning is that since it is impossible for a single entity to be expressed in two ways, the perception of it [as such] is an error. || 695 ||
For, according to experience, the Self is the object of inward vision.
Apart from the non-cognition of that [Self], how could there be the perception of the body and so forth therein? (696)

In that very context, he states another reason: "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc. The meaning [of the word "self"] would be either the nature of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) or pure consciousness (*caitanya*);
this is the object (*viṣaya*). In that regard, because it is experienced as such, the particle *hi* is used for the sake of universal consensus regarding that kind of experience.

Without ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is no perception of the body and so forth within that Self which is established by experience; since these do not exist in liberation (*mukti*), this is a matter of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
The meaning is that the perception of a body and so forth within the self—which is [in reality] non-existent—is an illusion. || 696 ||
"He has abandoned that"—thus it is perceived as imagined by ignorance regarding the west.
The Śruti declared "the Self alone" for the purpose of removing false knowledge. || 697 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the perception of the whole and the parts is erroneous, by saying "him" (*tam*). The scripture—"Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self"—condemns the view of manifoldness. Likewise, for the purpose of negating the cognition of difference based on ignorance regarding the Self, such passages as "In the beginning, this was only the Self;
the Self alone is all this" declare that everything is nothing but the Self. Therefore, how could there be a perception of the whole and the parts?

This is the meaning. Alternatively, having begun with the statement "Brahman would desert him," the Śruti declared, "All this is what this Self is," in order to sublate the perception of distinctions such as Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood which are superimposed upon the inner Self (pratyagātman). Thus, the meaning is that the view of [the world] as both identical to and distinct from [the Self] is indeed improper. || 697 ||
And because of the scriptural prohibition against "looking away," there is no looking at the rice-ball and so forth.
Because it is contradictory when viewed from the perspective of inward vision, there is no perception of external objects.

He states another reason for its not being intended [to be taught]: "parāci" (turned away). Because the scripture beginning with "parāci khāni" (the senses are turned away) censures the perception of difference, there is no perception of the specific [parts], nor is there a perception of the whole-and-parts; this is the meaning. Furthermore, because the perceptions of the Self and the non-Self are mutually contradictory and cannot coexist in one place, he says "pratyak" (inward), [implying] that there is indeed no perception of the whole-and-parts by means of a vision directed inward.

The perception of an external object is not possible through a vision directed outward, nor is the perception of the internal self possible through a vision inclined toward the external; because these two are mutually contradictory, how then can there be a perception of the whole and the parts? This is the meaning. || 698 ||
The object of knowledge, devoid of division between the means of cognition, the cognizer, and the object itself, is non-dual.
That which is immeasurable and singular is declared to be the Self. || 699 ||
574 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] [vol2, page 280]

In that very context, he states another reason: "ananya" (not other). It has no other object of measurement (*meyam*); thus it is "ananyameyam. That very essential nature (*svarūpam*) is both the means of knowledge (*mānam*) and the knower (*mātṛ*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which is the means of knowledge and the knower, and which has no other object of measurement. He declares its reality by stating that it is the substratum of mere conceptualization (*kalpanāmātra*): "vastu" (the real entity). And he states that its oneness is attained through scripture: "avi-" [meaning *avikalpita*, unconstructed].

Regarding the word "bhāgavat": by restating what has been said, he establishes the consensus of the learned (*vidvatprasiddhi*) as the authority for that [position]. Regarding "ameya": the implication is, "In that case, how can it possess both unity and diversity (*samastavyastatva*), given the contradiction with the consensus of the learned? || 699 ||
Those who declare that liberation from it comes from the practice of observing the nature of saṃsāra;
For them, nothing remains undone because they have taken refuge in the supreme Vaiśvānara.

Furthermore, he states that liberation is impossible according to the opponent's position: "The vision of the world... and so forth. For the perception of objects possessing various flavors is indeed the vision of *saṃsāra*;

thus, for those who desire liberation from that very [vision] through its repeated practice, even the power to envelop space like a piece of leather exists by the grace of the deity—this is the meaning. || 700 ||
But we, being deprived of our boon, would have to wrap the sky like a piece of leather.
We are not able [to accept it]; therefore, we do not believe it without logical reasoning. || 701 ||
Furthermore, with the intention that the performance of an impossible task does not follow from the statement "there is the grace of the deity," he says: "But we...
He states that the view [of Brahman] as both collective and individual is not to be trusted because it is devoid of authoritative means of knowledge and reasoning: "Without... (701).
And that which has been stated and that which is yet to be stated, with respect to their collective and individual aspects.
This refutation of those whose minds are corrupted is in accordance with the literal words of the scripture. (702)

He concludes the impossibility of the opponent's position with the words "And it has been said. By stating that the refutation is "well-founded," he indicates its firmness. With the word "scriptural" (*śruti*), he refers to those whose nature is refuted, whose intellects are impure, and who possess incorrect vision—so to speak. || 702 ||
For there is not even the slightest thing other than the inner self (pratyak) that has not been defiled by those whose souls are impure.
Just as an object seen in a dream can be perceived by one who possesses inward vision, [so too is this world perceived]. (703)
Now, one might object: "How can those who perceive reality by seeing both the whole and its parts have their selves corrupted? To this, he says, beginning with "No" (na).

Just as it is impossible for a dreamer to see anything other than the inward-looking vision, so too for those who possess right vision, there is not even the slightest trace of anything other than the Self.
It cannot be seen by looking at its own nature; therefore, the meaning is that the perception of it as a whole or as separate parts is an error. || 703 ||
The emergence of the power of action occurs through the two [mantras] beginning with "prāṇanvadan."
By saying "seeing" and "hearing," the emergence of the power of knowledge is thus established.

Having rejected the opponent’s view as it arose incidentally, and continuing with the explanation of the *Śruti* itself, he analyzes the commentary beginning with "by means of breathing, [he is] breath; by speaking, speech," and so forth. The meaning is that the two terms "breathing" (*prāṇan*) and "speaking" (*vadan*) serve as indicators for the unmentioned activities of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). The syntactical connection is: "the manifestation was performed. It was performed...

Up to this point: "origination" refers to activities such as going and so forth. By means of the two mentioned activities—seeing and hearing—he indicates that the activities of the other cognitive faculties (jñānendriya) not explicitly mentioned are also implied. In the phrase "while seeing," and in "while speaking" and so forth, [he implies the others] by means of the activity of speaking and so on denoted by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) portion.

He says "likewise" (tathā), [meaning] that the operation of the hand and so forth is the object of definition, just as the manifestation (udbhava)—that is, the operation of touching and so forth—is. || 704 ||

Apart from name-and-form, no object of knowledge exists.

The causes for the perception of those two, the ear and the eye, have been stated [in verse 704]. Now, since it is impossible to perceive the self’s functions such as touching without a relationship—given that its own functions have not been mentioned apart from the aforementioned operations of the cognitive faculties—it is said: "Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). This refers to the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator.

There is nothing to be known apart from the body; and since that [body] is perceived by the eyes, the ears, the skin, and so forth, it follows—due to the relationship characterized by having a single object and the possibility of such indicative marks—that the determination of the Self as a toucher and so on is established. This is the meaning. || 701 ||
And likewise, action, which consists of the means of knowledge, is that which is manifested by name-and-form.
Speech is that which effects the manifestation of names; in this same way, the application [of this principle] is to be made everywhere.

Fearing that the Self might be perceived as a mover or the like through the actions of the feet and so forth—which have not been explicitly mentioned—by means of the aforementioned activities of the organs of action and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since such indication is impossible without a connection [between the Self and those activities], he says: "Name. Every action is manifested by name and form and is supported by the vital breath; such being the case, [the Self] possesses the quality of manifesting the act of utterance, which has as its object the name supported by the vital breath.

The meaning is as follows: speech, the hands, and so forth possess the capacity to manifest actions such as grasping because they depend upon them; therefore, since there is the possibility of characterization through their connection with the manifestation of actions that have a single substratum, there arises the determination of the Self’s being a goer and so on. He says "In this way" (evam) to indicate that just as speech possesses the capacity to manifest action dependent on the vital breath (prāṇa), one must likewise apply the connection of the capacity to manifest action dependent on that [the Self] to the hands and other organs as well. || 706 ||
Whatever is manifested by the instruments such as the ear and so forth is called that [respective object].
That which is manifested as form is taught to be "name. || 707 ||

Raising the objection that because the words "name" (nāma) and "form" (rūpa) grasp well-known objects, they do not merely grasp the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator—and thus the previously stated identity of the eye and the skin is not applicable—the author says: "The ear, etc. Since it is intended here that the entire transmigratory world is superimposed upon the Inner Self (pratyagātman) by means of the statement regarding the emergence of the two powers, the grasping of well-known name and form is not appropriate here; therefore, [the text speaks of] name and form...

The meaning is that the establishment of the aforementioned relationship follows from the fact that the commentary beginning with "because it is an object" (viṣayatvāt) mentions only the illuminated and the illuminator by means of the two words "name" and "form. || 707 ||
The mind is considered the common ground for the manifestations of the power of cognition.
And it is the instrument for those things arising from the power of action, and it possesses vision of the three times.

He states the purport of the verse beginning with "manvāno manaḥ" [X.84] as follows: "jñāna... and so on. By the words "expansion" (*vikāśa*) and "arising" (*udbhava*), seeing and the like, as well as speaking and the like, are denoted. The connection is that [the mind] is the common instrument (*sādhāraṇaṃ karaṇam*). He establishes the commonality of the mind with the word "tad" [in the commentary]. And here, following the *Bhāṣya*, by resorting to three etymologies, the triad of agency and so forth belonging to the Self is to be seen—
[This is] the measure. || 708 ||
He who perceives each one individually in the midst of those things produced by the vital breaths and so forth;
Because it is incomplete, he does not know the perfect reality, since that [reality] is self-evident.
Since the passage beginning with "tāny asya" has already been explained, he restates the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa yo 'taḥ"; thus, the vital breath (prāṇa) is established.
[Note: Variant readings indicate *vyāyate* for *capyate* and *vyāyate* for *vyāyate*.]

676 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: "Not so," because the qualified [self] lacks fullness, whereas the reality (*vastu*) is by its own nature such [i.e., full], one who perceives the self as qualified is not [perceiving] the Self.
This is the meaning. || 709 ||
To this extent, he knows that "this [body] breathes," and so forth, having [the self] as its agent.
An entity that is devoid of action and causal factors cannot, for its part, be known in reality. (710)
Fearing the contradiction that "he who is perceived does not know," [the author] says: "As long as...

This person knows the Self as the agent of breathing and so forth, but he does not know it in its true nature (tattvataḥ), because the reality is devoid of action and agency—this is the construction of the sentence. The word "evam" expresses a well-known manner of speaking. || 710 ||
If it is argued that because [the self] is unmanifest in the indeterminate state, its true nature is not perceived;
And since manifestation occurs through causes and effects, how could anything further be produced? (711)

It has been stated that the reality (*vastu*) is by its own nature full and free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*); if that does not manifest, it does not exist at all. If, however, it does manifest, does it manifest during deep sleep (*svāpa*), or rather during the waking state and so forth? To this he says: "In the unmanifested" (*avyākṛte*). The word "unmanifested" refers to the state of deep sleep. The meaning is that [the reality] does not manifest because it is obstructed by ignorance (*ajñāna*). He refutes the second alternative with the words: "And if in manifestation" (*vyaktau cet*). [This refers to] the waking state—

The meaning is "in the two states of waking and dreaming. The connection is with the phrase "due to the obstruction by cause and effect. If that supreme reality is not perceived in the three states, how then can it be perceived? This is the objection; the sense is that there is no other place where it is possible to perceive this.
In the cognition of cause and effect, those two are regarded as Viśva and Taijasa.
The wise one is bound by the cause, but the two [other states] do not manifest in the fourth.
He states the proof for the claim that the Reality (tattva) is obstructed by ignorance and its products during deep sleep and waking respectively: "The effect... and so forth.

He says this considering that in the fourth state (turīya), the Reality is not below [the others], because there is an absence of the relationship between cause and effect; and since cognition does not arise without one of these two relationships, he asserts: "But the two... The two limiting adjuncts (upādhis) consisting of the effect and the cause are the objects of the dual number. || 712 ||
With eyes wide open, one perceives only sound and the like, but not that which transcends them.
For one whose collection of sense organs has not been withdrawn, one does not perceive even sound and the other objects of the senses. || 713 ||

He states another reason for the absence of knowledge of reality even during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] with the verse beginning "visphārita" (wide-open). The sense is that because in the waking state and others there is knowledge of objects contrary to reality, and in deep sleep there is the mere absence of all cognition, the realization of reality is difficult to attain. || 713 ||
When it is asked: "How does one perceive that Self directly? [the answer follows].
"He says 'it is indeed the self' in order to remove the cause of objection. (714)

He concludes the objection with the word "how" (*katham*). The meaning is: first, one who perceives the self as possessing attributes does not know it directly, because that [view] is censured; nor does one who sees the self as devoid of attributes understand it as it truly is, because it has been stated that such a vision is impossible in any of the three states. He introduces the reply by restating the objection with the words "thus objected" (*iti codite*). [This refers to] ignorance (*ajñāna*).
He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) that this statement is for the purpose of removing the cause of joy, beginning with the word "But" (*cotha*). || 714 ||
1.1 Ga. *prāṇam ity āha*.
That whose form is not concealed even in the unmanifest world is likewise [so]. [Chapter] 6, [Section] 8; compiled with the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 577.
And because it is the witness of that, it is not manifested by those parts when they are excluded. // 725 //
Refuting the argument stated previously—that "because it is unmanifested in the indeterminate," and so forth—the author states the meaning of the word *ātman*: "Not unmanifested," etc.

That which is perceived as the world is not unmanifested, because its form is not concealed; and that which is manifested by perception and other means is not manifested by them [in their own nature].

Because he is the witness (*sākṣitva*) of the world—both manifest and unmanifest—and of perception and the rest, he is the *ātman*; this is the connection with what follows. Nor is it... [the rest of the sentence follows].
The word "ca" (and) in the phrase "tathā ca" (and thus) serves the purpose of connecting with the negative particle "na. || 715 ||
He who shines forth as the inner self, whose nature is self-luminous.
It is not divided by the distinctions of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, activity, and the knower. || 716 ||

To the objection that the non-duality [of Brahman] would be lost because of the difference between the world and the Self, he says: "As the inner self" (*pratyaktayā*). By the word "itself" (*svayam*), he excludes being an object of knowledge like a jar or other such things. He states the result regarding the nature of the inner self as being merely imagined and so forth by the word "merely" (*mātra*). Alternatively, "means of knowledge" (*māna*) itself is the action; or else, by the word "action," the triad of agent, instrument, and enjoyer is indicated; or else, action is the cause for the arising of the means of knowledge.
The ellipsis is "it is not divided in reality. In that case as well, the connection is simply "that is the self. || 716 ||
He who, being changeless, perceives, "Let me smell this odor," [is the Self].
That is the Self, that is the supreme light; this is the statement found at the beginning of the Śruti.

Regarding what was stated—that one knows with eyes wide open, and so forth—it is said [in response] that the non-dual, self-luminous reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is established by scripture (*śrauta*). Thinking this, he says: "He who thinks, 'Let me smell'... Let it be that the Self is the witness of the knower (*mātṛsākṣin*); but what follows from that for Brahman? To this he replies: "That... Thus, the passage beginning with "Now, he who knows 'let me smell,' he is the Self," is the authority (*pramāṇa*) for the Self as the witness of the knower.
Having [stated] "the Self alone is Brahman," he cites the sentence beginning with "That thou art" as the authoritative source for this; thus [he says]: "In the head," etc. (717).
The word "iti" is used for the purpose of negating that [the object] is accessible through the knowledge of verbal designation.
And there is the scriptural injunction: "from which words turn back. (718)

He states the meaning of the word *iti* as "designation" (*abhidhā*). One might object that the word *iti* would refer to the mode currently under discussion, yet the Self does not have the status of being an object of a sentence in this context. Anticipating this doubt, he shows that the word refers to a mode established in another Vedic text, by saying "since" (*yataḥ*). || 718 ||
For the purpose of establishing the refutation of the nature of being either determinate or indeterminate.

He says "evam" (thus) and "anyad eva" (something else indeed), as well as "yo 'uccaiḥ śrutiḥ" (that which is heard loudly). [The author] states this for the sake of emphasis, having raised the doubt: "How can the Self, which is understood through the word and the cognition of 'Self' and so forth, be beyond speech and mind? He says "vyākṛta" (manifested): it is only that which is conditioned by either the effect or the cause that is accessible to words and cognition, not that which is without attributes (nirupādhi).

The sense is: "of some element. Regarding the statement that reality is neither effect nor cause, he provides corroboration from another scripture with the words "another [scripture]. The intended meaning is expressed clearly. || 719 ||
