The word "proximity" (sāmīpya) refers to the state of non-difference (niṣṭhā) with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman).
It is perceived as closer to oneself than both the effect and the cause.

He states the meaning to be expressed by the prefix *upa* with the words "upeti. By stating that proximity culminates in the Inner Self (*pratīci*), he expresses the actual signified meaning of the prefix with the words "tamiṣṭhe" (in that which is desired). Raising the objection—namely, that since there is proximity even between cause and effect due to the presence of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, as well as ignorance (*ajñāna*), within the Self, how can it be said that proximity culminates in the Inner Self?—he replies with the words "kārya" (effect, etc.).
He states the proof for the fact that the inward-facing [Self] is nearer—that is, extremely proximate—in the words: "It is seen. (720)
He who is distinct from both the determined and the undetermined selves due to the cause of ignorance.
Having struck those two with the intellect turned inward, one attains the state of pure selfhood.

Having raised the doubt that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) possesses duality because it is distinct from cause and effect, he concludes the meaning of the prefix by stating "the manifested" (*vyākṛta*).

For he who is distinct from cause and effect due to ignorance attains the state of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—having discarded the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of cause and effect—by means of the knowledge arising from the [great] sentence through the destruction of ignorance; this is the meaning. || 721 ||
Having emerged from both cause and effect by way of the path of knowledge of reality, one [proceeds].
Having approached the immutable and unborn, one becomes free from transformation.

Since activities such as sitting and so forth are impossible in the immutable (kūṭastha) Self which is the object of realization, he explains how it can be said that "He sat" by saying: "Having risen.

Having risen from those two—the cause and the effect—by means of the wisdom that realizes the true nature of both, and having loosened them, one should sit as the changeless Self, having attained the state of being neither cause nor effect. This very abiding in one's own nature is "sitting" (āsana); however, there is no [physical] sitting whatsoever in this Self.
The meaning is "action. || 722 ||
This distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest would be established in the Self, which is not itself such [a distinction].
This division of day and night [occurs] when the sun is present; it is as it is when he is absent.

By means of the word-by-word commentary, it has been established that the non-dual reality (tattva)—which is distinct from cause and effect, beyond speech and mind, and immutable—is thus situated. Now, raising the doubt as to how the appearance of the division between cause and effect occurs, [the author] states that it is produced by ignorance (ajñāna) through an illustration; he thereby demonstrates that, according to our own experience, the non-dual, immutable reality is there, while the collection of non-self (anātma-jāta) is superimposed upon it. [This is shown in the verse beginning with] "vyakte... [The verse: vyaktāvyaktavyaktena vyaktaṃ vyaktataraṃ bhavet | vyaktāvyaktavyaktenaiva vyaktāvyaktaṃ nirudhyate || 10 || [Commentary: By the manifestation of the manifest and unmanifest, the manifest becomes more manifest; by the very manifestation of the manifest and unmanifest, the manifest-unmanifest is suppressed. (10) [Explanation: The manifest (vyakta) is the body, the unmanifest (avyakta) is the intellect (buddhi), and the manifest-unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta) is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). By the manifestation of these three, the manifest [body] becomes even more manifest. Furthermore, by the same manifestation of the manifest and unmanifest, the manifest-unmanifest [ego-sense] is suppressed. Thus, the entire aggregate of the non-self is sublated by the realization of the Self. This is the meaning. Just as a snake is superimposed upon a rope, so too is the entire aggregate of the non-self superimposed upon the Self. Therefore, the non-dual, immutable reality remains as it is. This is the purport. [The verse: yathā rajjvāmahirjñāto jñānādajñānahānitaḥ | na bhūyo 'nugataḥ sarpa iti śāntiḥ parā bhavet || 11 || [Commentary: Just as a snake perceived in a rope, once known [to be a rope], ceases to follow after the snake due to the destruction of ignorance through knowledge, so too does supreme peace arise. (11) [Explanation: Just as a snake imagined in a rope, when the rope is known, is no longer followed because ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge, so too, when the Self is known, the entire aggregate of the non-self is sublated. (16) [Explanation: Just as in a dream the mind, imagined by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, imagined by ignorance, appears as a duality. This is the meaning. [The verse: yathā svapne dvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānavedhitam | tathaiva jāgraddvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānavedhitam || 17 || [Commentary: Just as in a dream the mind, pierced by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, pierced by ignorance, appears as a duality. (17) [Explanation: Just as in a dream the mind, pierced by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, pierced by ignorance, appears as a duality. This is the meaning. (18) [Explanation: Just as in a dream the mind, born of ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, born of ignorance, appears as a duality. This is the meaning. [The verse: yathā svapne dvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānavijṛmbhitam | tathaiva jāgraddvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānavijṛmbhitam || 19 || [Commentary: Just as in a dream the mind, manifested by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, manifested by ignorance, appears as a duality. (19) [Explanation: Just as in a dream the mind, manifested by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, manifested by ignorance, appears as a duality. This is the meaning. [The verse: yathā svapne dvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānanirmitam | tathaiva jāgraddvayābhāsaṃ cittamajñānanirmitam || 20 || [Commentary: Just as in a dream the mind, constructed by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, constructed by ignorance, appears as a duality. (20) [Explanation: Just as in a dream the mind, constructed by ignorance, appears as a duality, so too in the waking state the mind, constructed by ignorance, appears as a duality. This is the meaning. [The verse:]

By such statements as these: just as the division of day and night is conceptually attributed to the sun—which is of the single nature of light—through its being seen and not seen, even though it is devoid of such [temporal] change; so too, although the Self is a continuous flow of consciousness (cidekatāna) and is devoid of the distinction between cause and effect, that distinction is attributed to It through ignorance (avidyā).
In reality, however, the meaning is that the Self is immutable (kūṭastha) and non-dual (advaya). || 723 ||
Even this distinction between self and non-self is not observed as touching upon the Self.
Because the Self is the sole witness of that which is unknown, [this distinction] arises from ignorance and does not pertain to reality.

(724) Now, is there a division between the Self and the non-Self or not? Not the first, because it would entail the loss of non-duality; nor the other, because the identity of two contradictory things is impossible. To this, he says: "The Self... The word "also" (api) implies that it is like the division between cause and effect. The reason is the absence of any means of knowledge [to establish] contact with the Self.
1. ‘By means of two forms.

2, page 285] 4. Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 579.
[The opponent] says: No. [The author] replies: "If it is immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) that 'this is,' then how was the distinction stated there? To this he says: "By ignorance" (*ajñātā*).
[The opponent] then raises the doubt: "In that case, since touch does not exist in the Self, duality would not exist. Anticipating this, he says: "By ignorance" (*ajñāna*). || 724 ||
Just as in the *Anātmasiddhi*, there can be no establishment of a self for that which is non-self.
Furthermore, the establishment of the non-self would not be possible in the same way as the establishment of the self.

If it is argued that the non-self (*anātman*) is established in dependence upon the self (*ātman*), and thus is merely imagined, then by the same logic, the self would also be imagined since it is established in dependence upon the hearing of the word "non-self" and so forth; furthermore, for that [self] too, another witness and another substratum would have to be stated, leading to an infinite regress. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The non-self... Just as in the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the insentient non-self is established through the grace of the sentient self, so too—through the grace of the non-self—[the self is established].

The meaning is this: the self is not established [as an object] because it is self-luminous; therefore, although there is a transformation of the intellect (dhī) into a specific form that removes ignorance regarding the self-luminous principle of consciousness (cid-dhātu), which manifests by itself, there is no suspicion that this [transformation] is imagined (kalpita), even though it is produced by the Vedas and other means of knowledge. Anticipating the objection that the non-self (anātman) might also not be imagined because it is established by the self, just like the self itself, he says: "Of the self" (ātmanaḥ). Just as the self, which is the self-luminous consciousness...

Thus, the manifestation of the non-self occurs from the Self; however, there is no real manifestation of the non-self from the Self, because that [Self], being unattached, has no connection with the non-self.
Therefore, being superimposed, it manifests within the Self, like a snake in a rope—this is the meaning. || 725 ||
Because that which is not-self lacks intrinsic nature apart from the self.
In the same way, it exists without any distinction [from its substrate], like a snake in a rope or a flower in the sky.

He states another reason for its being imagined (*kalpitatva*) with the words "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). Since the non-Self (*anātman*) lacks an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) apart from the Self, and since even in terms of non-difference there would be nothing remaining but the Self alone, it would be non-existent like a sky-flower due to the absence of an independent intrinsic nature.
Yet, that which is directly perceived cannot be non-existent; therefore, the meaning is that it is imagined, just like a snake [superimposed on a rope]. || 726 ||
Therefore, there is no self for that which is non-self, nor is there a non-self for the self by its own nature.
But the self's establishment is established by itself, for the establishment of the self is not other than [the self] itself.
Now, having raised the objection that "it is not imagined because it is related to the Self, like that [Self]," he states the non-establishment of the reason: "Therefore...

The meaning of the word *tat* (that) is the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of the non-Self due to both difference and non-difference. To state that even if the relation is imagined, it does not exist in reality, he says "by itself" (*svataḥ*). One might ask: if there is no relation between the Self and the non-Self, how is the establishment of those two possible? To this [he replies]:...

He reflects upon the manner of accomplishment mentioned previously with the words "But of the Self" (*ātmanas tu*). He states that the existence and manifestation of the non-self (*anātman*) are due to the superimposition of identity upon the manifestation of the true nature of the Self; this is expressed by the phrase "because of the establishment of the Self" (*ātmasiddheḥ*). Alternatively, by this [phrase], the reason for the Self being established by itself (*svataḥ siddhatva*) is stated. The meaning of the reason is that the manifestation of the Self is nothing other than the Self itself. However, the establishment of the non-self occurs in relation to that [Self].
It has already been stated that this is because of the identity [of the two] being merely imagined (kalpita). || 727 ||
To the extent that one knows the Self within oneself, one perceives the innermost Self by means of the self.
One should perceive that [reality] within those who are not the Self, wherein ignorance and its effects have been cast out.

Now, is the Self of one and the same nature during both bondage and liberation, or not? In the first case, because there would be no distinction between the two, no one at all would strive for liberation. In the second case, because it would possess distinctions, the Self—like that which is not-self—would lack self-established existence. To this, he says: "As much as... This means "just as. Just as in liberation, one perceives the Self by itself in its own form, free from ignorance and its products, established in its own majesty and devoid of distinctions.
580 Sureśvarācārya’s *Gṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, p. 286]

Therein [in the state of liberation], no distinction such as that of an agent and so forth is perceived; likewise, even in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), one should perceive the Self as devoid of distinctions—such as being non-material—within the body and other things, because of the scriptural texts stating it is "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so on.

Nor does this imply a lack of distinction between bondage and liberation, for there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of knowledge. Furthermore, such a state of being devoid of specific attributes is not the reason for its self-established nature;
rather, the meaning is that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of non-selfhood (*anātmatva*) is the cause [of appearing otherwise]. || 728 ||
Of the self, which has been excluded from everything beginning with the intellect and ending with objects, and which exists outside [of them].
For if there were no entity that is not the self, then the internal self would indeed exist as something belonging to the self.

[Objection: But surely, since there is a statement of distinction—namely, that "one should see the Self in what is not-self"—there is a loss of non-duality (advaita). To this, he replies with the words "of the intellect, etc.
He uses the word "for" (hi) to show that it is appropriate to exclude that [Self] as being external to [the intellect], on the grounds of its being an object of perception, insentience, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "that very inward-facing Self," he states the reason: "because it belongs to the Self" (ātmīyataḥ). Because it belongs to the Self, the non-self is [distinct from] the inward-facing [Self].

The meaning is that [the world] has the nature of being possessed by the Self (ātman), just as a snake is possessed by its own self; likewise, the non-Self (anātman) is possessed by the inner Self (pratyagātman), and thus it is "possessed by the Self. || 729 ||
Thus, when there is a convergence of the object and the self, as well as the cause and the non-self, [the realization arises] from that very nature of reality.
The connection between that which is neither excluded nor included is like that of a rope and a snake.

Now, is the relationship between the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīyatva*) real or unreal? It cannot be the first, because it contradicts the scriptural teachings on the Self’s lack of attachment (*asaṅga*); nor can it be the second, because there is no means of establishing it. Therefore, he says: "The true nature of that" (*tadyāthātmya*). The Self, first of all, is the very essence of the non-self; for that which is superimposed has no essence apart from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and being conscious, it does not seek another substratum. For these two reasons, the non-self—

When the object returns to its own nature as the Self, the connection between the Self—which is devoid of both generality and particularity—and [the object] as owner and owned is merely superimposed, because such a connection is seen in the case of a rope and a snake; thus, the very fact of being a relationship proves that the relationship between the Self and what belongs to the Self is unreal. This is the meaning. || 730 ||
No other entity is established apart from the inward-facing [consciousness].
Since that [self] has been consumed by the intellect (pratīc), how can this non-self be established?
Fearing the objection that it is merely the conjunction of the two that is superimposed, and not the Self and the non-Self themselves—as if they were situated at a great distance—the author says:
"Of the Inner Self" (*pratīcaḥ*). An object that is non-Self must be established either as non-different from or different from the Inner Self.

In the first case, because it is swallowed by the Self, it cannot be established anywhere. In the second case as well, it remains unestablished due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*); therefore, [there can be] no relation—
The meaning is that it is non-self by its own nature, yet it is imagined as the self when in a state of association. || 731 ||
The Self does not tolerate non-selfhood; how could there be a non-Self in its absence?
If it were not established by way of its own nature as a real entity, how could it be established by way of a non-nature?

He states another reason for the fact that the nature of the self and the non-self, as well as their relationship, are merely imagined: "Because they coexist," etc. The meaning is that they are mutually contradictory due to being insentient and sentient respectively. If it is then asked whether their distinctness is not established by logic, he says: "The non-self," etc. Having restated the impossibility of both difference and non-difference between the non-self and the Self, he now demonstrates that very point: "Entity," etc. [The non-self...]
1. *thām* | 2. *ka 'tmasvahe* | [vol2, page 287] 4–Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 581.

The meaning is that because it is contradictory for something to be established in its own nature, if it were not established in its own nature, it would likewise not be established even in a nature other than itself; for there is no existence of that [object] apart from the self. || 732 ||
Every entity is established elsewhere only by virtue of its existence within itself.
If that which is non-existent there were to become existent, how could it be devoid of dependence elsewhere? (733)

He states the aforementioned point by means of an illustration: "In its own self," etc. Just as a jar or similar object, being already existent in the form of clay or the like, is established elsewhere—in another location and so forth—whereas that which is non-existent there could not be established anywhere due to the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because of such principles as "the effect does not exist apart from its cause," in the same way, the world is also imagined [as unreal], because it is non-existent both in Brahman and elsewhere. || 733 ||
Just as the self, though possessing the nature of a mother, perceives that which is not the self;
Because its nature consists solely of pure vision, it does not perceive itself in that manner.

Anticipating the objection that "the Self, too, must be imagined [as an object], because it is an object of knowledge, like a jar," he says: "By being the subject" (mātṛtva). For the Self, though seeing the non-Self while conditioned by the state of being a subject, does not see itself; this is because, being of the nature of eternal vision, it is not an object of sight.
The meaning is that [the reason] "being knowable" (jñeyatva) is unestablished for the subject (diti). || 734 ||
The scriptural statement "of the seer, the seeing" is for the purpose of negating agency.
But he says that vision itself is the seer; this is a qualification of vision. (735)

Anticipating the objection that the Self is not characterized by motherhood, but is itself the mother and none other than it—as per the Śruti, "There is no seer other than this"—the author says: "The agency... etc. For the Śruti passage beginning with "For there is no loss of the vision of the Seer" uses a genitive in apposition to show that the Seer is indeed the vision itself, and states that there is no destruction of it; thus, it speaks in order to negate the agency of seeing as a qualification of the Seer.

The interpretation is as follows: Since the scriptural negation intends to exclude another conscious entity, it is untenable for the Self to be the agent of seeing due to its contradiction with the aforementioned scripture; therefore, the meaning is that the Self, when conditioned by the state of being a knower (*mātṛtva*), is not the knower. || 735 ||
First, such is the actual nature of the inward object, as it has been described.
Now, the function of words is being explained correctly as follows. (736)

He restates what was said beginning with the words "This division of the manifest and the unmanifest": "Of the inward Self" (*pratīcaḥ*). The meaning is as follows: with respect to the ultimate reality of the actual state of things—the nature of the Self—it has already been explained how the inward entity is of the nature of non-dual, immutable consciousness alone, while the non-self is imagined like a snake [in a rope]. This is true both with respect to the actual mode of being of things and with respect to the linguistic usage of the word "Self," wherein the Self's non-duality and so forth are established exactly as they are.
He says that this will be stated by the following sequence of passages, beginning with "śabda... (verse 736).
Whatever one attains, whatever one acquires, and whatever sense-objects one enjoys here in this world;
And because its existence is continuous, it is therefore called the "self" (ātman). || 737 ||
In response to the inquiry, "What is the application of the word 'self' (ātman)? he cites the words of Vyāsa for that purpose: "That which... [737]
However, all instances of the word "yat" should be understood as having the sense of "because."
And one should apply the word "ca" (and) everywhere in the same way for the purpose of conjunction. || 738 ||
582 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 288]

Explaining that, he states the meaning of the four *yat* words and the three *ca* words [beginning with] "yasmāt. One should distinguish that the first *tu* word is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), while the second is intended to state the reason why no other meaning is possible there. || 738 ||
It pervades everything without exception, just as a snake [pervades] its entire coils.
Therefore, because it is the inwardness of that which is not the Self, it is called the "inward Self" (pratyagātman).
And regarding the meaning of the term "ātman" as that which "obtains" (āpnoti), he says: "it pervades" (vyāpnoti). || 739 ||
Because [the self] has not yet attained its fullness, it remains a self with a remainder due to that which is left over from the state of having a remainder.
Because one attains both the self and the non-self through it, it is therefore designated as "ātman."

Anticipating the objection that since non-selves (anātman) are also pervasive like the self (ātman), the self cannot be pervasive within them, he says: "sāvaśeṣa" (with remainder). He qualifies [the selves] as "akṛtsnān" (incomplete) in order to establish precisely that they possess a nature with remainder; the sense is that if they were complete (kṛtsna), they would not be non-selves at all. || 740 ||
Because of the delusion regarding its own manifestation as consciousness, all other things arise from that.
The wise grasp that which is not the self; therefore, they know it as the "Self. (741)

Regarding the meaning of the statement "because it takes [them], therefore it is called Ātman," he says: *svacid iti*. The construction is as follows: because it takes (*ādatte*) all non-selves (*anātmanaḥ*) produced from that very delusion (*moha*) by means of a delusion possessing its own reflection of consciousness (*svakīyacidābhāsavatā*), therefore they know it as "Ātman. "Takes" means that it withdraws [them] into its own self; that is to say, in the state of deep sleep (*prājña*) and so forth. || 741 ||
All things are established together in the one Self.
And there is a statement in the Atharva Veda: "Earth and the other elements are not the Self. (742)
In this regard, he cites another scriptural passage as corroboration: "They merge," which means they dissolve. || 742 ||
The modifications of the intellect (dhīvṛtti), which are directed toward external objects, appear as reflections of one's own self while facing outward.
Since it has returned inward, for that reason it is called "Ātman" by the wise.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "that which eats" (*yaccātti*) as follows: "one's own self" (*svātma*). The explanation of the term "turned away" (*parācīnāḥ*) is "directed toward objects" (*viṣayonmukhāḥ*).
"Eats" (*atti*) means "perceives directly" (*sākṣātkaroti*). || 743 ||
For the Viśva is always the enjoyer of the gross, while the Taijasa is the enjoyer of the subtle.
"Likewise, Ānandabhuk and Mājha," so says the scriptural teaching.

Here too, he cites the scripture: "For the Viśva... The distinction is that the grossness (*sthaulya*) of objects consists in their being presented by the external senses, while their subtlety (*praviviktatva*) consists in their being presented by mental impressions (*vāsanā*) alone. By the word "bliss" (*ānanda*), the causal sheath (*kāraṇakośa*) is understood.
He who experiences that [bliss] and perceives it is called the sleeper, the person who is the enjoyer of bliss. || 744 ||
Unuttered and unconditioned, full, he abides within his own self.
Because its existence is continuous, it is therefore designated as the "Self."
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "And that which belongs to this" as follows: "Unexcluded. Herein, each preceding term is the cause for each succeeding one. || 745 ||
1. Verṇava | 2. ‘asmādātme | [Vol. 2, page 289] 4. Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary named Śāstramakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri | 583
The mantra "sadviṣṇoḥ" also [reveals] that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indian scripts typically mark the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]
The eye, being pure, reveals the inner Self within the void. 746.

He cites the mantra as the authority here: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ | divīva cak�uṣātatam*). Regarding the phrase "that of Viṣṇu": "supreme" means that which is neither effect nor cause. Just as the eye is spread everywhere in the sky, so too the form of the Supreme is pervaded precisely within the inward-facing [Self], because there is no object that is not inward-facing; thus the mantra declares.
This is the meaning. || 746 ||
Therefore, knowledge has not arisen, nor has darkness been dispelled.
Therefore, when the aforementioned identity with the one Self is directly perceived, my own self is realized in its entirety.

Since it is established that the non-dual, immutable, and immediate reality—which is not of the nature of the "self" (ātman)—is merely imagined within that very [reality] by virtue of the usage of the word "self" and its referent, the author states the resulting conclusion: "There is no unarisen [ignorance]. Upon the correct perception of the Self as described, there is no such thing as unarisen ignorance; therefore, because everything is nothing but the Self, even ignorance, which was not dispelled, does not exist for one who possesses this knowledge whose object is the full Self.

Therefore, since everything is known when the Self is known, and because ignorance has been consumed, the state of the inner self as the fulfillment of the supreme human goal is also established; this is the meaning. || 747 ||
Therefore, the innermost reality (pratyaktattva) is that from which the seer, the seeing, and the seen arise.
Upon seeing that [reality], everything seen becomes unobstructed, like [the perception of] a snake in a rope and so forth. || 748 ||

He states the aforementioned point by means of an illustration: "The seer," etc. In the phrase "in the perception of that" (taddṛṣṭau), the meaning of the word "that" (tat) is the nature of the inner self (pratyaktva). || 748 ||
Just as the state of being known [arises] for things that have cognition as their sole cause through the cognition of a garland.
Likewise, when there is a backward comprehension of the objects that give rise to delusion. || 749 ||
He clarifies the illustration with the word "garland" (sraj). He elucidates the point of application (the subject) with the word "inner" (pratyak). || 749 ||
For when this is known, everything attains complete identity with it without exception.
Therefore, the Self alone—consisting of the vital breaths and so forth—is to be seen, because it is the seer of all. || 750 ||

He connects the statement beginning with "for here" (*atra hi*) as a reason for the meaning stated in the preceding sentence. Regarding the word "here": he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to establish that it is the Self alone, and not the non-Self, that must be known by one seeking liberation. This is because through the vision of the Self, the vision of everything becomes possible.
He states the reason: "because there is nothing else remaining to be seen," namely, "because of the vision of all. || 790 ||
Some of great intelligence explain this as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
But other wise ones [advocate] restraint (niyama), while others [advocate] exclusion (parisaṃkhyā). || 751 ||

The statement, "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self," has been explained as intended to convey its meaning even without the touch of an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, in order to refute the injunction suspected here, he states three positions, beginning with "Some" (*kecit*). The examples for these have already been mentioned.
The word *atha* is a synonym for the word *tathā*. || 791 ||
This is never understood as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
But because that [liberation] is attained at all times, there is likewise no other [means] whatsoever. (752)
584 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, p. 290]

He refutes that with the words beginning "No" (na). The connection is as follows: no injunction whatsoever—whether it be an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), or an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*)—is perceived here. The reason for this is given by the word "always" (*sarvadā*). Since the cognition of the Self is always present, its attainment is established; and because it will be stated later that there is no injunction regarding that [attainment], the three types of injunction do not apply there. For an injunction does not pertain to an already established fact, but rather to what is yet to be accomplished, since an injunction serves to restrict one toward that which is to be achieved. || 752 ||
Since it does not depend upon human activity, an injunction (vidhi) is not possible here.
For every injunction has as its sole object its own specific operation. || 753 ||

Furthermore, he states that a threefold injunction is inappropriate with respect to Brahman or the knowledge thereof, because Brahman exists eternally and the knowledge thereof depends upon the human subject (*mānavastu*). He says: "Because it depends on human activity" (*puṃvyāpāra*). To the question, "Why is there no injunction even for occasional knowledge, which is not dependent on effort? he replies: "Because it depends on one's own activity" (*svavyāpāra*). For all three types of injunction have as their sole object the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) that is to be accomplished through effort.
The meaning is that he does not exist in a cognition that depends solely upon a mere human being. || 753 ||
In this very section, the meaning of this same point is presented preceded by the statement of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
That effort which was made by the authors of the commentaries is now being revealed. || 754 ||

Since the impossibility of an injunction regarding either the object or the knowledge thereof has been established by the reasoning already stated, one might ask: "What is the use of further deliberation on injunctions?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By means of the subsequent [text]. The meaning is that the subsequent portion of the work, consisting of further deliberation, serves to strengthen the proof of the impossibility of an injunction regarding knowledge. || 754 ||
Just as the validity of a statement is clearly established independently of its practical effect.
I have stated previously that this is likewise for one who is established in the reality of the single self.

One might object: "Since it was established in the *Saṃbandhagrantha* that injunctions of every kind are impossible with respect to Brahman and the knowledge thereof, is this not a mere repetition to state the same thing here? Anticipating this, he restates what was said in the *Saṃbandhagrantha*, beginning with the words "yathā" (just as). The point of the connection (*saṃbandha*) is simply this: that the Vedānta texts, which do not touch upon any action to be performed, possess a very clear authority regarding the pure, established reality that is not an effect—just as the texts concerning ritual actions have authority regarding their respective effects.
The meaning is that it has been understood in the treatise. || 755 ||
An illusion arises here due to the hearing of the optative suffix (liṅ).
Therefore, because of the commonality with such [injunctions] as "one should sacrifice," the meaning of the injunction is now investigated. || 756 ||

The author states the meaning of the subsequent [sūtra] to avoid redundancy: "By the suffix *liṅ*," etc. Since the injunctive word is heard in the passage, "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" (*ātmetyevopāsīta*), a misconception might arise that—due to its similarity to [injunctions such as] "One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—there is an injunction here either regarding the reality itself or regarding the knowledge thereof, just as there is an injunction regarding the sacrifice and so on.
Therefore, after deliberating whether the meaning of the injunctive word is something unprecedented (*apūrva*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*), or something else, it is refuted. Thus...
The meaning is that, through the cessation of error, the factuality of the sentence must be ascertained. || 756 ||
Having first presented the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), the commencement of the established conclusion (siddhānta) is now set forth.
For one who has correctly understood the established doctrine knows the relative strength and weakness [of arguments]. || 757 ||

One might ask: "Even if there is no tautology, since a prohibition presupposes a prior attainment, one should first present the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and only afterwards state the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*); what then is the reason for the Commentator’s deviation from this stated order? [The author] replies with the words "siddhānte" (in the final conclusion), the ellipsis being "is shown afterwards. He states the intention of the Commentator regarding the reversal of the prima facie and final views: "samyak... (correctly...).
[Vol.
2, Page 291] + 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 585
Gīti: For a person who has mastered the established doctrine (siddhānta) is capable of weighing the relative strength and weakness of the prima facie and final positions;
therefore, the statement of the established doctrine at the outset is not contradictory—this is the meaning. || 797 ||
This cannot be an original injunction (apūrvavidhi), because [the action] is already established as an option.
The attainment [of the result] within the [spiritual] side will be explained at the conclusion of the investigation, based on its cause. || 758 ||

Having stated the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, he adopts the counter-argument (*uttarapakṣa*) set forth in the *Bhāṣya*: "Not [the case of] the unprecedented (*apūrva*)," etc. To the question, "How is there the possibility of the knowledge of the Self being the subject (*pakṣa*)?
For surely there is no possibility of the knowledge of the non-Self, which is its opposite, occurring there with equal force," he replies: "The subject (*pakṣa*)," etc.
Due to the influence of commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*), through the arising of defects such as hunger and thirst, there occurs the forgetting of the Self and the recollection of the non-Self.
By saying "it is well-considered," the meaning is that the author of the Commentary will state at the conclusion of the inquiry that [liberation] is attained on the side of knowledge. || 758 ||
He declares here that [the object] is eternally attained, with the desire to dispel the notion that it is something to be accomplished through injunction.
For every rule indeed follows only those portions that have not yet been attained. || 759 ||

He states the purport of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "yatsākṣāt" and ending with "prāptatvāt" as follows: "nitya... etc. The meaning is that, with the desire to refute the three types of injunctions regarding knowledge, the author of the Bhāṣya here declares its eternal attainment (*nityaprāpti*). To the question, "Even if knowledge is eternally attained, how is it incompatible with the three types of injunctions?", he replies: "aprāpta... etc. The word "sarva" is a synonym for "api"—that is, "even all."
[This is] the reason. Therefore, since knowledge is eternally attained, there is no injunction whatsoever; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 799 ||
And whether the attainment of worship is occasional or constant is determined by indicative marks (*liṅga*).
It is observed that the author of the Bhāṣya intends the attainment [of the result] to be eternal. || 760 ||
Regarding the question of how it is understood from the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "yatsākṣāt" that the constant attainment of knowledge is intended there, he says:

"pākṣikī" (it would be optional). The meaning is that in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "tiṣṭhatu tāvat," by the very force of the expression "nityā vā" (or it is constant), it appears that the constant attainment of knowledge was intended by the preceding Bhāṣya. || 760 ||
By means of the knowledge of the true nature of the inner Self, which arises from the statement "That which is immediate... and so forth.
Since darkness is burned away by knowledge, how could there be any possibility for the injunction to apply? || 761 ||

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he applies the commentary beginning with "That which [is directly]" (*yatsākṣāt*) by means of the words "That which" (*yad*) and so forth. For one who has studied the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and mastered the logic required for the verbal testimony, the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) is not established because the ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge that penetrates the inner self (*pratyagavagāhi*) arising from such sentences as "That which is directly. Even indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), by loosening ignorance, brings about engagement in the purpose of an injunction.
The meaning is that it obstructs. || 761 ||
Knowledge destroys the instruments of action, just as learning destroys the intellect in barren soil.

The status of being an agent arises from ignorance, while by its own nature there is the state of being a non-agent. (762) Now, one might raise this objection: "Even when ignorance has been destroyed, since the agents such as the 'doer' (kartṛ) and so forth still exist, there would be a [scriptural] injunction; for there is no difference in worldly activity between the knower and the ignorant, according to the maxim that [the knower] is indistinguishable from cattle and the like. Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with *tasyām* (in that [state]), starting with the words *kārakāṇi*.
Anticipating the objection that knowledge alone removes ignorance due to their mutual opposition, and not the causal factors, he says: "The state of being a causal factor...

The intention is that the notion of agency and so forth in the wise person is produced by a remnant of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*). One might argue: "Let there be an injunction based on such agency and so forth.

To this he replies: "And by itself" (*svataśca*). The intention is that an injunction does not arise from a mere persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), because an injunction must be preceded by an unsublated conceit (*abhimāna*). || 762 ||
From what ignorance does that activity arise which ceases when that [ignorance] is known?
For here, even one who has cast off sleep does not perceive a dream as if he were asleep. || 763 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the activity of the wise person is not prompted by scriptural injunction (*vaidhī pravṛtti*): "Because of ignorance of which... Activity arises from ignorance of the Inner Self (*pratyagajñāna*); since there is no cause for such activity once the Inner Self is known, it is illogical. To illustrate this point, he says: "For not... Just as in the world a sleeping person, whose mind is afflicted by sleep, perceives various high and low dreams, so it is not the case in the waking state; one who is free from sleep and possesses a healthy mind does not perceive dreams otherwise.
The meaning is that, just as he sees [the world], activity proceeds from ignorance; when knowledge exists, such activity is not tenable. || 763 ||
If something has its own inherent nature, it does not depend upon that [nature] for its attainment.
Because action has delusion as its cause, it indeed depends upon an agent.

Raising the objection that—just as for the ignorant person action is required because it serves the purpose of knowledge, so too for the knower action may be accepted as an auxiliary to that knowledge even though there is no injunction regarding knowledge itself—it is replied by analyzing whether that [action] is for the sake of attaining Brahman or for the sake of dispelling delusion; first, it refutes the former with the words "For that which... Since Brahman is the very nature of the Self, there is no dependence on action for its attainment.

The meaning is that there is an injunction regarding the action that causes the attainment of that [Brahman]. If Brahman is the innate nature of the self, how can there be the notion of its non-attainment? To this, he says: "By delusion" (*moha*). The word "of non-attainment" (*aprāpteḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Where, then, in your view, is there a dependence on action? To this, he says: "Dependence" (*apekṣā*). It is in the arising of that knowledge—which effects the sublation of agency and so forth along with their material cause—that there is a dependence on action by way of purification.
This is the meaning. || 764 ||
And there is no destruction of delusion through the awakening to things as they truly are.
We perceive another [entity] which is capable, consisting of the form of action and its factors.
He states another alternative: "And not," [verse 765].
Just as there is knowledge of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices through the rule for studying and reciting the sacred texts.
Even though the knowledge of the Self has always been attained, the injunction [to seek it] is not desired for one who already possesses it. || 766 ||

When knowledge has arisen, because ignorance is destroyed by it, activity is impossible; thus there can be no injunction [for it]. Nor is there an injunction when that knowledge has not arisen, because the object of the injunction would then be non-existent. Furthermore, it has been stated that there can be no injunction for action with respect to knowledge as its auxiliary, because such auxiliary status is impossible. Now, having raised the alternative whether the injunction applies to verbal knowledge or to some other kind of knowledge, he refutes the first view with the words "svādhyāya" (one's own Veda), etc., [meaning] "always."

The meaning is as follows: [the phrase] "without an injunction regarding its own object" means that for one who has studied the Veda according to rule and has understood the relationship between words and their meanings, knowledge of Brahman—just like knowledge of ritual action—is attained from the word itself even without an injunction; therefore, there is no injunction regarding verbal knowledge. || 766 ||
[Salutations] to the one who illumines the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and all activities.
Since it must be understood through an indicative mark (liṅga), an injunction (vidhi) is not possible therefrom. || 767 ||
1. Because of contradiction; 2. it refutes.

Furthermore, regarding whether knowledge of the self—whether it be that of a transmigrating being or one who is not—is to be enjoined: even in the first case, one must choose between the alternatives of whether that [self] is always inferable or perceptible. Refuting the first alternative, he says: "The body... [The argument is: The movement of the body and so forth is preceded by an effortful agent, because it is a specific kind of movement, like that of a chariot.

The meaning is that there is no injunction regarding the knowledge of that [Self], because the transmigrating self is ascertained through inference—such as "it is like the movement of dice"—and because such [knowledge] is impossible given the marks of bodily activity and so forth. This applies to the phrase "therefore, in that case" (tatastatra). || 767 ||
Likewise, from the conviction arising from the notion of "I," there is the direct ascertainment of the true nature of the Self.
Since it is impossible and unattainable, how can an injunction be desired? || 768 ||
He refutes the second [position] with the words "tathā" (so). "Pratyakṣatve sati" means "given that it is perceptible. "Iha" refers to the cognition of the transmigrating self.

The meaning is this: since the true nature of the transmigrating self—consisting primarily of its status as a knower and characterized by agency and so forth—is already ascertained through the "I-notion" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) under the view that it is perceptible, there can be no injunction regarding that knowledge because there is no lack of attainment (*aprāpti*). || 768 ||
In this case, however, when the self and its objects are perceived, there is no cognition that can be reached [by inference].
Because it would otherwise not apply [universally], this rule is therefore one that applies optionally (pākṣika). 769.

He raises the position that the cognition of the non-transmigrating Self (*asaṃsāryātmadhī*) is what must be cultivated, beginning with the word "But" (*nanu*). Even though the knowledge of the transmigrating Self as "I" is always present, the apprehension—through the notion of "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*)—of the non-transmigrating, non-dual Brahman, characterized by qualities such as freedom from evil (*apahatapāpman*), is only occasional;
for there is the possibility of forgetting it due to the lack of a fixed time for the arising of defects such as hunger. Therefore, one should meditate (*upāsīta*).
The meaning is that this is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) concerning the object of the cognition of the transmigrating self. || 769 ||
For now, let this [objection] rest as merely partial, for one who relishes the meaning of absolute identity.
Or let it be that the attainment of knowledge is eternal; thus, there is clearly an unprecedented injunction. || 770 ||

Having accepted that such knowledge is to be enjoined, the proponent of an unprecedented injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) says: "Optional" (*pākṣikī*). The connection is as follows: let it be for now whether the attainment of knowledge—which penetrates the oneness of the Self—is optional or obligatory; rather, let this clear injunction regarding the knowledge of oneness be an unprecedented one (*apūrva*). || 770 ||
Due to the conceit of identity with the mental states that delineate a single object.
For repetition is the meaning of the word, because the scriptural injunctions concerning meditation (upāsana) occur everywhere.

In order to establish the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of the injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self, he states the meaning of the word "meditation" (*upāsana*): "Having a single object," etc. Repetition (*āmreḍana*) means recurrence.

"Everywhere" means in all locations of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). "The meaning of the word" refers to the literal or denoted meaning. He demonstrates the limit of this repetition with the words: "Identicality," etc. Meditation (*upāsana*) consists in producing a continuous flow of cognitions of the same kind, uninterrupted by cognitions of a different kind; it is directed toward that which is to be meditated upon (*upāsya*).
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that it is accepted by practitioners (*upāsaka*) that [the practice] culminates in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). || 771 ||
Therefore, from this indicative mark, it is understood that knowledge alone is intended to be enjoined.
If it is argued that this is not meditation (*upāsana*), we say no; for there is a reason, namely their identity of purpose. (772)

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) raises an objection: "Even though there is an injunction, since knowledge (*jñāna*) is the subject under discussion and it alone is what is to be enjoined, the statement of the meaning of the word 'meditation' (*upāsana*) is useless. He begins with "No" (*na*) and so forth. [The opponent argues that] because knowledge is the subject under discussion by virtue of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) for the negation of knowledge, [the mention of meditation is redundant].
To this, he replies: "It is not so," stating that there is no such fault because the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "meditation" (*upāsana*) have the same meaning. 772.

page 294] 588. The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Adhyāya— ]
On page 132:
"In all instances, the identity of meaning between the words 'Veda' and 'meditation' (upāsana) is observed."
Why is it not determined that it is here as well, just as it is elsewhere? || 773 ||

He establishes their identity of meaning: "In all cases. Just as in passages such as, "Death indeed stays far away from him who knows thus," where it is observed that the word *veda*, which denotes knowledge, and the word *upāsana*, which denotes the repetition of that [knowledge], have the same meaning, so it is here as well.
The meaning is that, within this context, the identity of purpose between those two is established because there is no evidence to the contrary. || 773 ||
And [the mantra] "Do thou turn back the rays" consists of the act of turning back.
The ritual procedure is clearly heard in the Veda, and from that follows the connection with the fruit.
In this context, he states "the rays" (*raśmīn*) in order to show that for the sake of strengthening the injunction regarding meditation, the same injunction is seen elsewhere as well.

Regarding the phrase "paryāvartayāt," because it is Vedic (Chāndasa), it should be read as "paryāvartaya. The clarity of the injunction consists in its being explicitly stated by means of the word "tat" (that). Furthermore, he says "and therefore" (*tataśca*) to show that the injunction for meditation is not fruitless; indeed, many sons will be born from him.
For it is heard [in scripture] that they do so; such is the meaning. || 774 ||
Having become a god, he who is constantly permeated by that state [of divinity] [attains the gods].
The scripture declares that one attains the divine by relying on the power of meditative cultivation.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit [arises] from worship," he cites scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*) as authority. The word "devo" (the deity) is used; the particle *ca* (and) is employed to state that even with respect to the supreme object of worship when it is possessed of attributes (*sopādhika*), the fruit of attaining its nature occurs equally through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). By the words "always" (*sadā*) and so forth, he takes the final quarter-verse of the *smṛti*. He summarizes the meaning of those two [scriptural passages] as "attainment of the deity. The mention of *śruti* is intended to include *smṛti* by way of illustration.

Alternatively, the word "or" (vā) connected here with the preceding "and" (ca) draws in the traditional authority (smṛti). This refers to the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), which is the direct perception of the object of worship, and the support derived from that. || 775 ||
Beginning with the word "sayoṣā," however, there are indeed words concerning meditation (upāsanā).
One should meditate on the Self as being within; for such is the scriptural injunction regarding meditation. || 776 ||
Having stated that the method for worship is fruitful and that the terms "knowledge" (jñāna) and "worship" (upāsana) have the same meaning, he provides another argument for their identity: "He who...

(sa yaḥ). The meaning is this: since the passage begins with the word "worship" in the phrase "he who worships each one of these" (sa yo 'na ekaikam upāste), and concludes at the end with "one should worship [it] as the Self alone" (ātmety evopāsīta)—where the pronoun "that" (tat) is heard in accordance with the opening—the subject matter of both terms is indeed worship. This is because of the identity between the beginning and the conclusion.

The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that it is well known—in such passages as "one should sacrifice between [the two] with the upāṃśuyāja"—that there is unity of sentence due to the unity of purpose when the subject matter (*rūpya*) is one. || 776 ||
And likewise, because the scripture regarding meditation is found both at the beginning and at the conclusion.
It is accepted that this [word "veda"] also serves the purpose of meditation (upāsana). || 777 ||
Even though both [the beginning and the end] have that as their object, why is it not stated that in the middle there is something other than meditation (upāsti) because of the word "veda"?

To this he says: "And in the case of the application," etc. By the phrase "in that very way" (tathaiva), uniformity is expressed; for by means of the introduction and so forth, the word "veda" also [refers to meditation] in the middle.

The meaning is that the word "stha" serves the purpose of denoting the act of worship; otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda), and it is not proper to split a sentence when it is possible to avoid doing so. || 777 ||
1. That.
