Likewise, wherever the Śruti occurs stating "one knows all this," [it refers to that same realization].
Since that [result] is not obtained through practice, it is accepted as an apūrva-vidhi (an original injunction). || 778 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "By this," one might raise the objection: "Just as the word *veda* in such contexts refers to something other than its primary meaning, why could it not be so here in the phrase 'he did not know that' (*na sa veda*)? Anticipating this, he says: "In the same way" (*tathā*). The meaning is that wherever this entire word *veda* is heard—such as in "The Veda knew itself alone" (*vedo 'vedātmānam eva*)—in each of those instances, its meaning is likewise nothing other than meditation (*upāsti*). One might then ask: "Even if the words 'Veda' and 'meditation' have the same referent, what would follow from that? Anticipating this...

He says: "Of the practice. The meaning is that since knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditation (*upāsti*) are identical, and because the knowledge of oneness is in no way previously attained, the meditation—which is non-different from that knowledge—is likewise unattained; therefore, there must be an *apūrva-vidhi* (an injunction for what was not previously known) regarding it. || 778 ||
Furthermore, no one engages in activity based on a mere description of the essential nature of a thing.
Nor is it maintained that the human goal consists merely in the arising of that knowledge. || 779 ||

For this reason as well, he states that an injunction (vidhi) must be accepted in that case, beginning with the words "vastu" (the thing). In the mere description of the nature of a thing, such as "the earth consists of seven islands," no purposeful activity is observed on the part of one who acts with deliberation; therefore, the remainder of the argument is that an impelling injunction must be assumed.

Anticipating the objection that an injunction is useless because the passion for the fruit of knowledge itself is what impels action, he says "tajjñāna... (of that knowledge). By the word "tat" (that),...
The object untouched by injunction (*vidhi*) is what is being described here. The meaning of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is independence from injunction.

The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that independent knowledge is not possessed of a fruit, because even when such [independent knowledge] exists, no fruit is perceived. The particle "also" (*api*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). || 779 ||
Just as is the form of the injunction regarding ritual action, so too is the form of the injunction regarding meditation on the Self.
Not even the slightest distinction can be perceived here. || 780 ||

He states another reason why the meditation on the Self (ātmopāsti) must be enjoined, beginning with the words "yādṛg" (of whatever kind). The locative case-ending has the sense of a double injunction. || 780 ||
If it is asked, "From where does this lack of distinction arise?", he says: "Just as [it is]."
For the action is indeed mental, since it is not distinguished in both cases. || 781 ||
Just as it is enjoined: "One who is about to utter the vaṣaṭ-call should meditate upon that [deity]."

"Just as [the action] is mental, so too is it in the meditations for the sake of the Self. [The author] introduces the commentary beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) by way of a prior inquiry: "Why? The meaning is that the commentator states, in the commentary beginning with "Just as," that there is no distinction between the injunctions for ritual action (*karma*) and the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*) according to the [Vedic] word. [This concerns] mental action—

Following the commentary beginning with "Because of being [mental]," he states that there is no difference even in terms of meaning: "Mental" (mānasī). Since the mental activity is the common object of both the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge, the construction is as follows: just as a mental activity is enjoined in passages such as "one who will utter the vaṣaṭ-call," so too in the sentences concerning the meditation on the Self, that very same [mental activity] is what is to be enjoined. || 789 || 782 ||
For even in the injunction for meditative worship (upāsana), there are three constituent parts of cultivation (bhāvanā).
A:
Therefore, it is to be understood as an injunction (vidhi), just like [the injunctions] "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) and so forth. || 783 ||

He states that there is an injunction for the meditation on the Self based on the verbal testimony itself, saying: "The efficient force (*bhāvanā*)," etc. Just as in such cases as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is the form of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—[referring to the object of meditation and the means of meditation].
590. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

Since an injunction is accepted as consisting of three constituent parts, and since the three parts required for the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are likewise possible in the case of the instruction "one should meditate thus," the meaning is that the meditation on the Self (*ātma-upāsanā*) is something to be enjoined. || 783 ||
The injunction for Vedic study consists of the optative suffix and so forth, as well as its very nature.
Practice manly conduct through the two types of knowledge praised by the injunctions.
Anticipating the question of how the three factors [of verbal bhāvanā] are established here, he states the nature of *śabdabhāvanā* for that purpose: "Of the Veda" (*svādhyāyasya*).

This is its meaning: the injunction "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) expresses, by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the word itself which constitutes its own object, namely the Veda. By the particle "and" (*ca*), he includes the suffix *-tavya* (in "to be studied") within the optative and other such suffixes, because they possess the property of instigation (*preraṇā*).

It means: "O you who are qualified persons, through knowledge of the word's own form (*svarūpa*) and knowledge of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), perform the activity consisting of effort. Thus, for a qualified person who has mastered the language, upon hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there occurs an activity characterized by a departure from composure; the operation of the optative suffix and other such markers, called "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), which is the cause of that activity, is the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*). Indeed, because it shares the commonality of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), it is the denotation of the object-productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*).
It is not expressed specifically by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. For it has been said:
"The optative suffixes and others express a distinct *bhāvanā* called 'denotation' (*abhidhā*)."

"But another, consisting of the meaning, is understood in all verbal suffixes. Alternatively, the word itself, such as the optative (*liṅ*) and others, is the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*). As they say: "The suffix is capable of enjoining when it is complete through the requirements beginning with 'what' (*kim*)."
Therefore, in this treatise, the statement that sets [the action] in motion is called *codanā*. || 784 ||
The instrumental factor is the knowledge of the injunction; what is the objective factor? It is the engagement of the person.
And here, the manner of performance consists indeed in the praise expressed through an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
It has been stated briefly that this [efficient force] possesses three components; he now analyzes those three components. Regarding the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*):

the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such words, whose nature is to impel, constitute the injunction (*vidhi*); the knowledge of that [injunction] is the instrumental component of the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*). Thus it is said: "having its own knowledge as the instrument. Nor is there any contradiction with the statement that the cognition of the relationship [between word and meaning] is the instrument, for—as in the expression "pierced by the hand with an arrow"—there is no contradiction in both being instruments.

The *dhāt* [is the efficient force]. The objective aspect (*bhāvyāṃśa*), however, is the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*) consisting of the activity of the person. The instrumental aspect (*itikartavyatāṃśa*) of this [urge] is the knowledge derived from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as "by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one obtains all desires," and so forth. The word "for" (*hi*) is used to state that these three aspects are well-known in the earlier Mīmāṃsā. The previously mentioned verbal productive urge (*śabdabhāvanā*) is referred to by the locative case [in the verse]. (781)
Therefore, for a person who has thus engaged [in practice], sacrifice is intended as the instrument.
And heaven and so forth would be the primary fruit, while the prayāja offerings and the like would be the subsequent ones. (786)

He states the three factors of the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*) as described in the Bhāṣya beginning with "just as" (*yathā hi*). Regarding the phrase "of one who has set out": this means that for one who has set out from the verbal productive urge (*śabdabhāvanā*), having fallen away from his natural state (*svāsthya*), there is an activity consisting of effort; that is the meaning of "objective productive urge. [The objection is: Why should the activity of a person impelled by an injunction (*codanā*) abandon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) expressed in the same word and instead take another thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)?

If it is argued that this is not logical because it contradicts the scriptural statement that employs a single word, we say no; for it is impossible for that which does not serve the purpose of man (apuruṣārtha) to be worthy of veneration. Thus he says: *kara-* [vol2, page 297].
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary known as the *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

[Page 591] "The word 'fruit' (*phalam*). Now, an objection may be raised: "How can heaven and the like—which are mentioned by another word and serve as qualifiers of the person (*puruṣa*)—be understood as the goal to be attained (*bhāvya*)? To this he replies: "True; nevertheless, because that [heaven, etc. is a human end (*puruṣārtha*), its status as the goal to be attained is possible. Thus he says: "By heaven and so forth" (*svargādiva*). || 786 ||
Just as it is there, so too here it is established by the scripture alone.
Therefore, it is logical that there are three components; however, this is indeed an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).

"Let it be so regarding the injunction of ritual action; but what happens in the case of the knowledge of the Self? To this he says: 'Just as... (yatheti). Just as in the case of sacrifice and the like, when the three factors are present, it is entirely logical that the injunction here in the word "one should meditate" (upāsīta) consists in the form of an *apūrva* (unseen potency); thus he states the conclusion: "Therefore... (ata iti).
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of excluding any other type of injunction. || 787 ||
The aspect of "what" (kimaṃśa) is to be known as the Self (ātman), and likewise the aspect of the instrument (karaṇāṃśa) is the mind (manas).
The "way of acting" (itikartavyatā) consists of the means such as renunciation, celibacy, and so forth. || 788 ||

He demonstrates by analysis how the three components are presented here in this scripture. Regarding the phrase "what component": one should understand the status of being a component (*aṃśatva*) by accepting that the Self is to be accomplished in the form of liberation. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) means "like sacrifice and so forth. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is the avoidance of optional and prohibited actions. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the total avoidance of sexual intercourse in its eight forms. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to tranquility (*śama*) and the rest.
The ghee. || 788 ||
Of the entire subject matter of the section, which pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices.
Just as there is utility by way of being the subject of an injunction, so too is it here. || 789 ||
Of that which depends on the injunction for worship and which has entered into the ritual procedure.
It is employed in the threefold place of worship for one's own benefit. || 790 ||

Anticipating the objection that while Vedāntas associated with ritual injunctions (*vidhi*) may be directed toward action (*kārya*), those independent of such injunctions must be directed toward the reality (*vastu*) itself, he says: "The entire [Veda]," and so forth. The meaning is simply the context (*prakaraṇa*). That is to say, by way of being a statement of praise (*vibhyuddeśa*), they serve as subordinate elements to the primary injunctions concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. The implication is that the utility of every sentence lies in its being a subordinate element to an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*). Regarding the subject matter of the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth—

The meaning is that, just as the entire section [of the text] is applied as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the injunctions for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, so too every sentence situated within that section which is required by the injunctions for meditative worship (*upāsti*) is applied solely as a subordinate element to those injunctions for meditative worship.
The first "ca" (and) is used to state that a sentence situated within a context of injunctions cannot, by bypassing the injunction, have a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.

The second [particle *tu*], however, has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). He concludes that even a scriptural passage devoid of an injunction is employed as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) within the injunction for the meditation on the Self; thus he says: "For the sake of the Self. (789–790)
Here, regarding the presentation of the object of meditation by means of statements such as "not coarse" (asthūla) and so forth...
Application is the fruit; liberation is the non-perception of the reality of darkness. || 791 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, how sentences such as "not gross" (asthūla), which establish the non-dual reality by negating superimposed duality, can be of use as subordinate elements to injunctions for meditation—he says: "In this context" (atra). The two locative cases are connected with each other, or the nominative is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
1 ka. 'will be joined.
[Vol. 2, page 298] 592 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter—]

The meaning is "in the midst of the Vedāntas. Desiring to state that [passages] such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" serve the purpose of injunctions for meditation by way of presenting the fruit, he says: "The fruit. Liberation is the attainment of Brahman. || 791 ||
But others, who are knowers of the tradition, [know] correctly through the eye of the scriptures.
The great-souled ones explain it; that is now being stated.

Having stated the position that verbal knowledge of the Self, termed "meditation" (*upāsanā*), which has liberation as its fruit, is enjoined in the Vedāntas, he now presents the alternative position that a different kind of knowledge is what is to be enjoined. He says: "By tradition" (*saṃpradāya*). This refers to those other than the proponents of the injunction of verbal knowledge—those who possess the correct traditional lineage (*yathāvat-saṃpradāyavidaḥ*)—and who, following the perspective of scriptures such as "having known that Great Soul from that very [tradition]," explain the injunction in the Vedāntas accordingly.
The construction is: "In that case, the explanation of that [objection] is stated. Furthermore, the phrase "the great-souled ones who know the tradition" is intended as a sarcasm;

for those who seek injunctions (*vidhi*) in the Vedāntas do not know the tradition, nor are they of great spiritual power, because their acceptance of such [injunctions] would result in the invalidity of those [Vedānta texts]. Thus it should be understood. || 792 ||
Indeed, it is held that a statement devoid of an injunction possesses no authority.
For it is through the entry into the application [of the means] that the object is understood. || 793 ||

Elucidating that very commentary, [the author] first states that injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted in the Vedāntas: "Injunction," etc. Therein, he indicates the lack of consensus among the knowers of Brahman by using the particle "kila" (it is said). Now, one might object: why is a statement not authoritative even if it is devoid of an injunction, provided it makes known an unknown reality? To this he replies: "Because of the connection with an injunction," etc.; for an existent reality [is established] only as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to an injunction.
According to the principle that "what is already known is taught for the sake of what is yet to be known," it follows that there is no validity for speech regarding an object untouched by injunction;
this is the meaning. || 793 ||
For it is not [the case] for that which is of the nature of a restatement and from which injunction has been removed.
In this context, the validity of a statement that is dependent [on something else] is established. || 794 ||

One might object: "Are not the Vedāntas authoritative, like injunctive sentences, by making known an established fact (*siddhārtha*) without entering into the sphere of a mandate (*niyoga*"? To this he replies with the words beginning "No" (*na*). The meaning is that because a statement devoid of an injunction and referring to an established fact has as its object a thing accessible through other means of knowledge, it is dependent [on them] and resembles a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, since it cannot possess authority regarding the reality (*vastu*), an injunction must be admitted within the Vedāntas. [For example: "There are [trees] on the bank of the celestial river."
The word "hi" is used to indicate that the dependency of a statement whose meaning is already established—such as "fruits," and so forth—is indeed observed. || 794 ||
In every case, here and there, it is action alone that is prescribed.
For it is possible to enjoin one [to act] by means of an injunction only with respect to one's own activity. || 795 ||

He raises the objection that there can be no injunction regarding those [actions] because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not something to be accomplished by another; this is expressed in the word "action" (*kriyā*). The term "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers to the section on injunctions (*vidhikāṇḍa*).

The phrase "therein, therein" (*tatra tatra*) refers back to the injunctive sentences. To the question of how there can be such a restriction—since an injunction might possibly apply even to an existing entity—he replies:

"For in its own operation... Since it is possible for an injunction to enjoin a person toward the meaning of the verbal root which is to be accomplished through the person's own activity, [an injunction does not apply] where the person is not the primary agent (*apuṃstantra*).

The meaning is that there is no positive injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the entity itself. Even though an injunction is well-known in the case of curd and the like, it applies when that [entity] is entered by an operation (*vyāpāra*), not when it is in its pure state; this is why the word "for" (*hi*) was used. || 799 ||
Since the nature of a substance is not something to be accomplished, how can an injunction be accepted here?
For that which is already established can never be understood as something to be proven, even by one who is most skillful. (796)

Having raised the objection that the Self is something to be enjoined—based on the scriptural injunction "the Self is to be seen," just as one says "a mat is to be made"—he says: "Substance... etc. He establishes the non-achievable nature of the reality [of the Self] with the words: "For not... etc. The sense is that [the injunction] does not culminate in the status of being an object to be accomplished. || 796 ||
Furthermore, knowledge concerning the Self is not enjoined as a ritual act in the Vedānta texts.
Since that [knowledge] is established through another means of valid cognition, the Vedānta would be a mere restatement (anuvāda). (797)

Even though the Self is not something that can be brought under control [by an injunction], one might argue that knowledge of it is to be enjoined like the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*); to this he says "no. The reason for this is given by the words "of that" (*tasya*). Furthermore, since knowledge of the Self is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those [Vedānta texts] do not have the function of establishing it, as that would result in their being mere restatements (*anuvāda*).
Therefore, because there is no "newness" (*apūrvatva*) in that regard, there is no injunction there; thus he says, "of the Vedānta. (797)
Just as there is knowledge of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices through the rule for reciting and studying the Veda.
Even the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedānta was completed by him alone in this world. || 798 ||

What is that other injunction? He states it: "By means of one's own study" (*svādhyāya*). Here, the term "here" (*iha*) refers to the seeker of liberation who is under discussion. "Completed" (*samāpita*) means "dedicated" (*arpita*). || 798 ||
It might be argued that there would be no connection with the fruit if there were an absence of a mandate (niyoga).
The knowledge of the inner self might be attained, but it is not attained in that manner. || 799 ||

When it is argued that there is no injunction regarding either the reality (*vastu*) or the knowledge thereof (*tajjñāna*) in the Vedāntas, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*), harboring a hidden intention, says: "It might be so. If the connection of knowledge with its fruit could be obtained even without an injunction (*niyoga*), then it would be correct to say that the Vedāntas lack an injunction; however, since the connection of knowledge with that fruit cannot be obtained without it, an injunction must be accepted in respect to knowledge.
This is the meaning. || 799 ||
The capacity of the intellect to accomplish the goals of man is obtained solely through the mandate (niyoga).
Therefore, the validity of a statement would not exist for one who is independent of that [external object].

One might raise the objection: "Why should there not be a connection with the fruit for knowledge even without an injunction (*niyoga*), since such is observed in the case of [the statement] 'this is a rope, not a snake'? Anticipating this, he says: "pumartha" (for the sake of the human goal). The meaning is that in cases such as "the king is going," no human goal is seen to arise from the mere cognition of the object; therefore, even in the case of "this is a rope, not a snake," one must accept an injunction such as "do not be afraid. [This is said] because, in the absence of a connection with an injunction, [knowledge] would not be a cause for the human goal.

"Let it be that knowledge itself is not a human goal; what loss is there? To this, he says: "Not from that" (*nātaḥ*). The meaning of the word "from that" (*ataḥ*) is that knowledge is not a human goal in itself. The word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "independent of that" (*tannirapekṣasya*) refers to the injunction (*niyoga*). The sense is that no statement whatsoever can be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) if it is devoid of a fruit. || 800 ||
There is nothing whatsoever apart from the pervasive pervasion of the reality of non-dual selfhood.
The fruit of the realization of the self would be just like the fruit of [worldly] action.

Even though the fruit of the cognition of the self (*ātmadhiyo*) is dependent upon an injunction (*niyogādhīnaphalabhāve*), it is argued that the authority of the Vedāntas with respect to the self is established because the fruit known as the "knownness of the object" (*vastujñātatā*) is possible; thus, one who has not grasped the opponent's intention raises an objection. [The author replies: "Not so, regarding the non-dual Self" (*naikātmya*). In this regard, he provides a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*). 75.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:

"Just as..."—the meaning is that while the fruit of action is accepted as being one of the [four results] beginning with origination (*utpatti*), which is distinct from the mere manifestation of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-abhivyāpti*), such is not the case for knowledge. || 801 ||
To this it is replied: this other cognition residing in the self is indeed distinct [from the previous one].
It is prescribed along with its means for one who lacks understanding of the statements of the Vedānta. || 802 ||

Regarding the question of whether the injunction applies to verbal knowledge (*śābda-jñāna*) or to another kind of knowledge, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*), relying on the second alternative, states his own intention: "In this case," etc. The connection is as follows: [the injunction applies] to something other than the awakening produced by the statements of the Vedānta. By the word "another" (*antara*) in the phrase "another kind of knowledge" (*vijñānāntara*), the author intends to express that this [knowledge] is of a different genus (*vaijātya*) from verbal knowledge. As for the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of the knownness (*jñātatā*) of the object: if it is manifest, there is no difference from [verbal] knowledge; if it is not manifest, [then...]

Since that which is produced by knowledge but remains unmanifested is ineffective, there must therefore exist a result called liberation (*mokṣa*)—distinct from the knownness of the object—which is dependent upon an injunction (*niyoga*).

The meaning is that the Vedāntas enjoin another form of knowledge directed toward the Self, accompanied by reflection (*manana*) and so forth, as that which possesses this [liberating] result. ||802||
For Brahman, which is not of the nature of a sentence-meaning, cannot be [grasped] by that which arises from a sentence.
In some cases, it can be determined by consciousness, just like an action. || 803 ||

Anticipating the objection that since Brahman is established by verbal knowledge alone, what is the use of another form of knowledge based on injunctions (vaidhajñāna), he says: "For not... In this context, he provides an example of dissimilarity: "like ritual action" (karmavat). This means [it is not established] in any particular place, time, or person. || 803 ||
A form composed of various word-meanings arises as the essence of sound.
Therefore, consciousness does not at all comprehend that which has the nature of the meaning of a sentence. || 804 ||
He states the reason why Brahman is not limited by the knowledge arising from the sentence: "Not manifold," etc. (Verse 804).
This very nature of words is the comprehension of a combined meaning.
Because its nature is not mixed with Brahman, it is therefore not apprehended by that [cognition]. || 805 ||

[Objection: "Since verbal testimony is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it must be admitted that it produces a non-conceptual, immediate cognition corresponding to its object; otherwise, it would result in its invalidity. To this, he says: "The word... The intention is that it is appropriate to follow the internal nature [of the word] rather than conforming to the external object.
He states the consequence of verbal testimony producing a conceptual and mediate cognition: "Brahman..."—that is, by that verbal knowledge.
And it is certain that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition regarding objects beyond the reach of the senses.
Since that [object] is also not its own object, it must be within the range of another cognition of it. || 806 ||

Anticipating the objection that Brahman is accessible through verbal knowledge because it is beyond the senses, like Dharma, [the author] says: "And the sentence... Although the sentence is the means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous things such as Dharma, and Brahman is likewise supersensuous, nevertheless, since Brahman—which is unconditioned and immediate—is not an object of the sentence, it falls within the scope of another kind of knowledge; and by that [knowledge], there is the cessation of ignorance, not by verbal knowledge. Thus, "that" refers to the unconditioned...
Brahman is said to be beyond direct perception.
If it is not accepted that this [object] is delimited by the cognition arising from the sentence.
Now, there would be no purpose for the Āgama; for it is not the case that the meaning of the Veda alone [is the goal]. (807)
1. Not at all.
[Vol.
2, page 301] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstramakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

599. He raises the objection: "If Brahman were accessible through the Vedas, it would be impossible for Him to be their object; therefore, the qualification 'known through the Upaniṣads' (aupaniṣadatva) would have no scope. No.

Regarding the word "if": he says that it is not contradictory for [the Self] to be "known from the Upanishads" (aupaniṣada), because it is accessible through knowledge produced by the means prescribed in the Vedas, and thus it is the subject matter of the Veda. "Not so," [he replies]. || 807 ||
Moreover, in this regard, many Vedic passages are studied repeatedly.
One should apply oneself with effort to such [injunctions] as "one should cultivate wisdom after having understood," and so forth. || 808 ||

He states the proof for the claim that another form of knowledge is to be enjoined in the Vedāntas with the words "Moreover" (api ca). He demonstrates repetition, which is an indicator of the intended meaning (tātparya), with the word "repeatedly" (anekaśaḥ). He dispels the students' lack of faith in injunctive sentences with the word "diligently" (yatnataḥ).
Since the goal of the person seeking liberation is obstructed by nothing other than delusion alone.
Because there is no other effect [to be produced] from knowledge, this which is stated is not correct. || 809 ||

In the Vedānta texts, it might be argued that verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) or some other form of knowledge is to be enjoined as having liberation as its fruit; to this, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "For one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣu*). Liberation (*kaivalya*), which is the desired human goal, is Brahman itself. Since it is separated from us only by ignorance, it is removed by knowledge alone. Furthermore, because that [liberation] arises from the [Vedic] sentence, it is not dependent on an injunction; and since there is nothing further to be performed, an injunction is impossible.
The meaning is that the statement made in the Upaniṣads is untenable. || 809 ||
Bring about success in that [matter] where, through the cognition arising from the sentence, [the goal is achieved].
On the contrary, some ritual act is intended to be performed through exclusion. || 810 ||

Anticipating the objection that even though no other action results from knowledge, that very knowledge itself must be what is enjoined, he says: "Of the injunction" (vidheḥ). The meaning is that only something distinct from the knowledge arising from the sentence—such as a sacrifice—is to be enjoined, not that [knowledge] itself. In this regard, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the sake of agreement with those who maintain the necessity of injunctions. || 810 ||
Just as [there is no attainment] apart from the knowledge of the true nature of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
No such thing as the nature of application is observed here as being distinct [from the object]. || 811 ||

He establishes the stated point by means of an illustration with the word "just as" (yathā). He states the negative concomitance (vyatireka) regarding the subject of the illustration with the word "separately" (pṛthak).

The term "of that kind" (tādṛk) expresses similarity in the application of the practice. Here, the word "here" (iha) refers to the knowledge arising from such scriptural passages as "not coarse" (asthūla). || 811 ||
For when the object to be accomplished is first produced, human activity is required.
Because liberation is opposed to arising and so forth, it has no dependence on anything else. (812)

Anticipating the objection that "that very [cognition] must serve as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for difference, and since human activity in the form of practice and so forth is observed without it, the injunction would have that [activity] as its object," he says: "In the case of *utpatti* (origination) and so forth. The meaning is that since liberation—which is distinct from the fourfold fruits of action—is not dependent on human activity other than knowledge, such [activity] has no purpose in the Vedāntas. [This refers to] eternal, unsurpassed, and immutable...
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that it is extremely evident that liberation, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), is distinct from the fourfold fruits of action. ||812||

If origination and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature, then what would be the fruit of karma in liberation?
If birth and so forth were to occur by themselves, tell me, what would be the use of karma for liberation? (813)

Anticipating the objection that liberation, like heaven, requires action because it is to be accomplished by action (*karmasādhyatva*), the author raises the dilemma of whether liberation arises *ex nihilo* or not, and refutes each alternative in turn: "Arising, etc. (Verse 813).
But at the beginning of its arising, it depends upon a mere cause.
It must depend upon karma; otherwise, it does not depend on that.

If it is argued that, by the reasoning already shown, even heaven and the like would not require karma—just as liberation does not—[the author] says "no," beginning with the words "utpattyādau" (in arising, etc.). In that regard, the example of heaven and so forth is given; he states that there is no requirement for karma when [the soul] is incapable [of attaining them], because such [requirement] is not observed in the case of the eternal [liberation].
He says "nānyathā" (not otherwise). The sense is that since liberation is incapable of arising and so forth, there is no requirement for karma. || 814 ||
For the sake of establishing its own self through activity, it requires a causal agent.
The factors of action require an action; they do not both depend upon the self.
Furthermore, there is mutual dependence only between an action and its factors; the Self does not depend on both, because it is distinct from both. Thus he says: "By activity... (819).
One who considers oneself an agent and possesses the qualification for [the status of] a Brahmin and so forth.
One should proceed according to the hearing of the injunction, but not by following one's own established tradition. || 816 ||

Having stated that there is no injunction in the Vedāntas because there is nothing to be enjoined, he says that there is also no injunction in them because of the absence of a qualified person (*adhikārī*), beginning with the words "saṃbhāvita" (one who is considered). The meaning is this: an ignorant person, who has superimposed agency and so forth upon the Self and partakes in the conceit of being a Brāhmaṇa and so on, is impelled by an injunction; however, a knower—who has cast off agency and the like, and whose all conceits have been removed—does not become subject to being enjoined. || 816 ||
For one who realizes "I am Brahman," which is neither prior nor posterior and beyond speech.

"No one is capable of being an agent [of action] because of the absence of that delusion. Anticipating the objection that even for a wise person there might be activity prescribed by scripture (*vaidhī pravṛtti*) through the medium of agency and so forth—just as in the case of wandering for alms—he says: "Not prior," etc. "Delusion" (*tanmoha*) refers to the delusion that serves as the cause for being an agent; that is to say, in some action. [This is] like wandering for alms, etc.
The meaning is that activity, whether spontaneous or even regulated, is not contradictory [to liberation] because it arises from a mere trace of delusion. || 817 ||
"Wherein the state of Brahman belongs to the self, and the state of the self belongs to Brahman by its very nature."
If [liberation arises] from the knowledge produced by such statements as "That thou art," why then does one strive here? (818)

It has been stated that for the wise man there is no agency whatsoever because of the absence of a cause. For this reason as well, he says that the activity of the wise man is not prompted by scriptural injunction (*vaidhī*). [He says: "Of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). The word *cet* signifies certainty. The phrase "wherein" (*yatra*) means "in which state of knowledge" (*vidyāvasthāyām*). Before the word *kim*, the word *tat* (that) should be supplied. For one who perceives the mutual identity of Brahman and the Self, there is no engagement [with action].
The meaning is: because there is an absence of a persisting fruit. || 818 ||

Because it is the cause for the total destruction of the delusion consisting in the cognition of the non-Brahman as the Self.
How could one who is not deluded engage in activity toward that which consists of the realization of the true nature of the inward Self? || 819 ||
He states another reason for the absence of activity in the wise person: "Not Brahman," etc. The word should be divided as "amūḍha" (not deluded).

The meaning is that the very cognition of the Self and Brahman as "not the Self"—which arises from delusion—is destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), since such knowledge is the cause of that destruction; thus, for one who possesses this knowledge, there is an absence of the cause [for activity]. || 819 ||
In that regard, even the words of the Mantra did not declare, "What is delusion? in this manner.
For one who directly perceives the non-existence of saṃsāra and its identity [with nirvāṇa], || 820 ||
Regarding the destruction of ignorance and the like through knowledge, he states the means of valid cognition [for that]: "In that regard" (tatra). || 820 ||
And because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in the cases of the delusion and the awakening of direct perception.
Because there is no state of coexistence, the activity [of the two] would be impossible. || 821 ||

He states another reason for the impossibility of activity in the case of the knower: "bādhyeti" (sublated, etc.). For there is no activity without delusion (*moha*), and delusion cannot coexist with knowledge because it is that which is to be removed by it; therefore, for the wise one, there is likewise no activity.
The sense is that begging for alms and so forth are merely the persistence of what has been sublated, as has been stated more than once. || 821 ||
If it is argued that there is no refutation [of the opponent's view] merely through the cognition arising from their statement, [we reply: no.
Because delusion regarding the non-Brahman self is its object, it is not so [as you claim]. || 822 ||
For sentences such as "That thou art" bring about realization through that much alone.
One who understands the sentence and the meaning of the sentence cannot conceive of any other meaning [than that which follows from the words]. (823)

He restates the objection set forth in the Bhāṣya beginning with "produced by a sentence" (*vākyajanitā*), using the words "is held" (*matam*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, it must be brought about by an injunction. He refutes this with "No" (*na*). The meaning is that since the Vedāntas have as their purport the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, and since the knowledge arising from them is established as the destroyer of that ignorance along with its effects, there is no dependence on an injunction. || 822 || 823 ||
If [it is argued that] the passages proclaiming meanings such as "not gross" (asthūla) are intended for the injunction to "behold" (draṣṭavya) and so forth;
Nor is it accepted that they would hand over the realm. || 824 ||
He raises the objection found in the commentary beginning with "draṣṭavyavidheḥ" (of the injunction to see): "asthūla" (not coarse), etc. The statements [of the Upaniṣads] are qualified [by this].

By the word "vidhi" (injunction), knowledge regarding that [object] is expressed. The implication is that they do not possess independence [from other injunctions]. He answers the suspicion that the Vedāntas are subordinate to [other injunctions] because they provide the objects required by those injunctions, saying: "ityetat" (this very thing). || 824 ||
Through the awakening to the identity [of all things], which destroys the delusion that constitutes an obstacle to liberation.
I have previously stated that this is not so, because there is no other entity [corresponding to it]. (825)

To the question "From where is this [conclusion] derived?", he says: "Mukti" (liberation). Since there is no other duty to be performed than the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which removes the darkness (*tamas*) that constitutes the obstacle to liberation, it was shown at the beginning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no injunction regarding that [knowledge] in the Vedāntas;
therefore, the meaning is that they do not have that [injunction] as their primary purport. || 825 ||
1 kha. ‘ṣayajñā’ | [vol2, page 304] 598
The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Chapter:
The Explanation of the True Nature of the Inner Self alone, without [relying on] injunction].
If it is thought that [the word] would not function for the sake of bringing about the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence...

Having heard that these [scriptures] lack a focus on injunction (*vidhi*), the proponent of injunction (*vidhivādin*) objects: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is that since a discerning person does not engage in activity merely through the statement of a fact (*vastu-kathana*) without an injunction, an impelling injunction must be accepted for the sake of producing the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. || 826 ||
Not merely by hearing the words that bring about the realization of the true nature of the Self.
What else does the injunction require beyond the production of the cognition of the inner reality? || 827 ||

Considering the alternatives— that the injunction (vidhi) desired for the sake of producing the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence might pertain to that knowledge itself, or to the hearing of the sentence, or to the continuous stream of memory regarding its meaning, or to the cessation of mental fluctuations— one refutes the first alternative with the words "Not [to the knowledge] of the Self" (nātmā). Since knowledge arises from the mere hearing of the sentence for an eligible person who has performed the required means and whose obstacles have been removed, an injunction is not purposeful in that regard.

This is the meaning. Since the very arising of knowledge is the fruit of the injunction, and that is accomplished simply by hearing the sentence, the injunction would be rendered useless; thus he says, "What else [could it be]? (verse 827).
Without the proper ritual procedure, one does not even strive to hear the sacred words.
To one who speaks thus, one should say: "How can such an undesirable thing be heard? (828)

He raises a second objection with the words "antareṇa" (without). The meaning is that, just as one does not engage in the performance of sacrifices and so forth without an injunction, one likewise does not engage in hearing a sentence without it; therefore, there must be an injunction regarding the hearing of sentences, just as there is for sacrifices and the like. To the one who asserts that "hearing of sentences is dependent upon an injunction," he replies with the words "iti bruvāṇam" (to him who speaks thus), [referring to] a sentence that expresses an undesirable object and is untrue.

The meaning is that, just as there is no injunction for the hearing of the *lakṣaṇa*, so too there is no contradiction in hearing the *tattvamasi* and other such statements even without that [injunction]. || 828 ||
And there would be the consequence of an infinite regress in each respective case.
"Of another injunction"—from this, let the aforementioned meaning be understood. || 829 ||

He states another defect in the position that there must be an injunction for the hearing of every sentence: "It would lead to an infinite regress" (*anavasthā*). If the hearing of a Vedic sentence requires an injunction, then the hearing of that injunction itself would require another injunction, and so on; thus, due to that consequence, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results. Nor does the injunction that prompts the hearing of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) also prompt the hearing of the Self itself. For that [injunction] is either the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or some other one; in the first case...

In comparison to that [second view], the fact that the texts concerning the hearing of reality (*śruta-tattva*) and so forth cause one to understand their own meaning—just like ritual injunctions (*karma-vākya*)—means there is no difference between those two types of statements regarding their being established in their own respective meanings. In the second case, since that [text] would lack authority (*apramāṇatva*), its capacity to establish both itself and others is cast far away. There is no distinction between the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) and the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) regarding the object to be understood; therefore, the sense is that hearing is not dependent on another injunction, because it is not dependent on another injunction.
He states that, for this reason, the cognition of oneness arises from the heard sentence alone, independently [of other means], with the words "iti tataḥ" (829).
Just as one does not proceed to listen to the meaning of the words of a proponent of a self.
Likewise, even when the purpose of an injunction is heard, there is no [cognition] without an injunctive sentence.
He explains the aforementioned infinite regress with the words "Just as... (yathā). In both cases, the word "artha" refers to the sentence. || 830 ||
1. The Exposition of Essential Nature (*Tattvānvākhyā*). 2ka. *Svāsvadī*. [Vol. 2, p.
305] 4. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 599.
Or if it is your view that [the self] is the continuity of the stream of memory arising from the cognition produced by words;
From the knowledge arising upon hearing the statement of "only," another distinct object clearly emerges. (831)

He sets forth the third view: "It is held" (*matam iti*). The construction is as follows: if it is held that a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-saṃtati*) arising from the knowledge produced by the sentence is what is to be enjoined.

He states the reason for this: "merely" (*kevala*). The meaning is that since the stream of recollection is distinct from both the mere hearing of the sentence and the mere knowledge arising therefrom, the aforementioned defects do not apply; therefore, its status as an object of injunction is clear. || 831 ||
It is not so, because here it is precisely the direct realization of things as they truly are that is possible.
Since He is eternally present, what is the purpose of recollecting Him?

He refutes that [position] with the words "not so. The meaning is this: in that case, since Brahman—which is the inner self (pratyagbhūta), immediate (sākṣāt), of the nature of non-dual immediacy (aparokṣaikarasa), and always present as one's own self—is such that direct realization is possible by following the actual state of reality even when the knowledge derived from the [Vedic] sentence has ceased, there is no fruit for a memory directed toward the Self; therefore, a continuous stream of that [memory] cannot be enjoined. || 832 ||
Even one who was pierced by the Pāśupata weapon did not die at my hands.
That one whose body is pierced by fruitless arrows should perish is exceedingly difficult to accomplish.

If it is argued that—whether through the knowledge of the essential nature (svarūpa-jñāna) as subordinate to the knowledge arising from the sentence, or through the knowledge expressed by the sentence as subordinate to that [essential nature]—there is the destruction of ignorance and its products, and therefore a continuous stream of recollection (smṛti-saṃtati) must be enjoined for that purpose—the author says "no," beginning with the word *api*. The word *cet* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and is connected with the verb following it.
The fruitlessness of an arrow consists in its being devoid of feathers, which results in a lack of velocity, or a lack of sharpness, or an absence of iron.

The state of being "pierced" (*vitunna*) refers to the affliction of a limb. For when a battle has intensified and one perceives an opponent who has entered it to be invincible, even if he is pierced by the *pāśupata* weapon, he does not abandon his life; yet, being struck again by the mere appearance of an arrow, it is impossible that he would then give up his life. Likewise, the destruction of ignorance does not arise from the knowledge of the means (*pramāṇa*), but rather from the continuous stream of its recollection (*smṛtisantāna*).
The meaning is that [it is] difficult to attain because of pride. || 833 ||
Moreover, it is eternally the most inward, and it is radiant, being reflected within consciousness.
In this way, the intellect and its modifications are like sparks from heated iron.

Furthermore, is it the continuous stream of the memory of the knowledge of the non-transmigrating Self that is to be enjoined, or the continuous stream of the memory of the knowledge of the transmigrating Self? Thinking that the first [alternative] is not tenable because it contradicts the injunction, he establishes the pervasion of consciousness by all [beings] in order to refute the second. [He says: "Even... The word "even" (api) indicates the aforementioned alternative. Ignorance, which has the inner self as its locus and object, is beginningless, indeterminable, and the root of the world.

The meaning is that the cause is always pervaded by immediate consciousness (*aparokṣacaitanya*). He states that, like the cause, the effects—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—are also pervaded by it.
Regarding the pervasion of those two by consciousness, he provides examples in sequence, beginning with "tapteti" (like heated...). 834.
Even prior to the occurrence of the realization of non-self, the object of knowledge was already attained by the cognizer himself.
Since all knowledge is fruitful by its very birth, what else does it require?
He states that when consciousness (caitanya) pervades the intellect and its functions, the consequence is independence from memory: "Even though... etc.

All knowledge, even in the form of mental modifications such as growth, possesses an object and is directly perceived by the inner self (pratyagātman) through mere birth—that is, even prior to assuming the form of a non-self.
1. By Vinuṇā; 2. kha. Vākyārthajñā; 3. ka. Saṃvāda.
[vol2, page 306] 600

The meaning is that even after one has abandoned the form of the non-self, the mind—which depends on the recollection of the Self—remains pervaded by the consciousness of the witness-self (pratyak-caitanya) as it possesses an object; it does not depend on anything else. || 831 ||
Just as elsewhere the fruit of a cognition occurs through the intervention of the mother and so forth.
Consequently, it is through comprehension alone [that certainty arises]; it is not so here in the case of the vision of the Self. (836)

He states the distinction regarding the knowledge of the Self: "mātrādi" (mother, etc.). Elsewhere—in the case of non-self objects such as a pillar—the result of the means of knowledge (*māna*), which is manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), is established through the mediation of the knower (*mātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and so forth; however, in the knowledge of the Self, its establishment does not occur through such mediation, because the very apprehension of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) is itself the fruit. This is the meaning. || 836 ||
A jar full of space indeed attains union with various kinds of substances.
Or how they might undergo separation—thus are the intellects kindled by consciousness.

Anticipating the objection that—although the intellect (*buddhi*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*) are pervaded by consciousness (*caitanya*) prior to their connection with an object, they are not so pervaded afterward because there is no further need for such pervasion once the connection with the object has occurred—the author says: "As... Just as a jar, while already pervaded by space, experiences conjunction and disjunction through its contact with curds and the like—for it is never possible for a jar to exist without being pervaded by space—the same applies to that [intellect] as well.

Because it would otherwise follow that they are insentient, the intellects and their modifications, being always pervaded by one's own consciousness, undergo conjunction and disjunction with objects at all times;
for there is nothing whatsoever anywhere that is not pervaded by consciousness—this is the meaning. || 837 ||
Therefore, even in the case of repetition, since that [result] is established by itself, there is no injunction here that is unprecedented; for this very reason, there is also no other [injunction].
Even though everything is at all times pervaded by immediate consciousness (*aparokṣacaitanya*), he states what happens in the present case: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

According to the reasoning stated, since everything is pervaded by immediate [consciousness], even in the position that a continuous stream of recollection of the knowledge of reality (*vastujñāna-smṛti-saṃtati*) is to be enjoined, there can be no injunction of something previously unestablished (*apūrva-vidhi*) because it is already established even without an injunction; likewise, there can be no injunction of restriction (*niyama-vidhi*) or the like, because every such injunction—
The meaning is that this has already been demonstrated at the commencement of the investigation into the principle of following one's acquired lot (prāptāṃśānupātitā). || 838 ||
Having directly perceived the Self as solitary and consisting of that which is beyond sound and the other objects of the senses;

"The wise man is liberated from death"—this is the scriptural (naigamika) statement. Furthermore, he states that the continuity of memory (*smṛti-saṃtati*) is not something to be cultivated, by saying "aśabda" and so forth. Having ascertained through direct perception the Self, which is without attributes and of a single essence, the wise man turns away from the mass of evil along with its cause by the power of that [realization]; thus, liberation results precisely from the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] sentence.

The meaning is: since perfection is understood from such scriptural passages as "soundless" and "touchless," why then should a continuous stream of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃtati) be prescribed? || 839 ||
When the Self is directly realized, the purpose of the means of valid knowledge is fully accomplished.
What else that lacks any means of valid cognition could possibly be desired other than the continuum of memory? (840)

Having raised the objection that—even though the destruction of ignorance and other defects, which is the fruit of valid knowledge, is established once the Self has been directly realized—one might still enjoin a continuous stream of remembrance out of a desire for some further result—the author refutes the first alternative (that the result is perceptible) by showing it lacks scriptural authority. [Verse 840] "In the Self... etc.
The fruit connected with the future time in this context is not like that of the world of Nāka.
Because it occurs at the time of the arising of that knowledge, like an effect produced from the arising of fire. || 84 ||

Anticipating the second objection—that because knowledge has an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*) like sacrifice and other rituals, a continuous stream of its recollection must be enjoined—he says: "The future... Here, "here" refers to knowledge. The example of dissimilarity is "like heaven. The meaning is that while in the case of the *agnihotra* and so forth, a fruit called heaven is understood to be connected with a future time, such is not possible in the case of self-knowledge. Of that [knowledge], the fruit called liberation...
He states the reason—"because of the simultaneity of the birth of knowledge with the destruction of those things born of ignorance"—based on such scriptural passages as "The knower fears not.

He provides an illustration for this: "as fire," etc. The meaning is that just as the reduction of fuel to ashes occurs simultaneously with the birth of fire, so too does liberation (kaivalya) occur at the very moment the rise of knowledge takes place. || 841 ||
And because the knowledge, recollection, and continuity of that [knowledge] are already attained by their very nature, there is no need for a formal injunction.
And because delusion has been destroyed by awakening, one no longer requires mindfulness at all. || 842 ||

He states another reason for the fact that the continuum [of mental states] is not something to be regulated: "If it were not a regulation," and so forth. The meaning is that since the knower of Brahman has no other object, the continuum of the memory of self-knowledge arises spontaneously; therefore, there is no regulation (vidhi) regarding it. He states yet another reason for that very point: "And because of awakening. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, that [continuum] is not something to be regulated. || 842 ||
When the fuel of the ego along with its kinsmen has been utterly consumed by the fire of right knowledge, [the Self remains].
Apart from mindfulness of things as they truly are, no other mindfulness remains. || 843 ||

Anticipating the objection that even when ignorance and its effects have been burnt away by knowledge, the knower of Brahman still requires a continuous stream of remembrance (*smṛti-santati*) for the purpose of excluding the memory of the non-self (*anātma-smṛti*), and thus that [remembrance] must be enjoined, he says: "Perfectly... When the ignorance of the Self, along with its effects, has been burnt without remainder by the fire of self-knowledge, one abandons the memory that conforms to reality; since there is no longer any residue of the memory of the non-self, there is no injunction for a continuous stream of remembrance for the sake of its cessation.
Such is the meaning. || 843 ||
Furthermore, because it conforms to the means of valid cognition, memory is not a subsequent sublater.
The cognition of the non-self was established as being precisely sublated by the cognition of the Self. || 844 ||

He says that even if the knower of Brahman accepts the recollection of the non-Self (*anātmasmṛti*), the recollection of Brahman is not sublated by it: "Valid knowledge" (*pramā*). This means the recollection of the non-Self, which is inferior (*aparā*). There is an alternative reading, *parāṅ* (turned away). To the question, "How can the recollection of the Self conform to valid knowledge? he replies: "By way of being sublated. The cognition of duality exists precisely as something to be sublated by the cognition of non-duality; therefore, that which is born from its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)— [The text continues: ...is not able to obstruct the flow of the recollection of Brahman. For example, even when one who has attained the knowledge of a rope sees a snake, the impression of the snake does not obstruct the subsequent perception of the rope. Therefore, the recollection of Brahman, which is produced by the latent impression of the knowledge of reality, is not obstructed by the recollection of the non-Self, which arises from the latent impression of the cognition of duality. Thus, it is established that the recollection of Brahman is not sublated by the recollection of the non-Self. Furthermore, since the recollection of Brahman is the very nature of the Self, it is not dependent on external instruments of knowledge; rather, it is self-evident. Therefore, it is not subject to obstruction. Moreover, because the recollection of Brahman is the supreme goal, it cannot be obstructed by anything else. Thus, the conclusion is that the recollection of Brahman remains unobstructed. (Note: The provided source text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the analogy of the rope and the snake.)
The meaning is that memory conforms to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 844 ||
All darkness is sublated by valid cognition, and that which arises from it is also extremely weak.
Pride alone was their obstacle, and their memory was likewise impaired.

Raising the objection, "Could not the cognition of duality itself be the sublater of the cognition of non-duality? [the author] replies, "It is that which is to be sublated," etc. Since both duality and its cognition are products of ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas the cognition of non-duality is stronger by virtue of its object, it cannot be so; thus he says: "It is that which is to be sublated. All ignorance and its effects are weaker than valid knowledge (*pramiti*), and therefore they are to be sublated; conversely, valid knowledge, being stronger, is indeed the sublater. This has been established in the case of the cognition of a rope and so forth.
76 1 ka. kha. ga.
What is the supreme? [vol2, page 308]
The memory of duality is indeed to be sublated;
this is from the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [First Chapter].

For darkness is dispelled by light alone, and not by its opposite; likewise, duality is dispelled by the cognition of non-duality alone, and that cognition must be eliminated along with its cause—this is the meaning. Nevertheless, one might suspect that the memory of duality is more powerful than the memory of non-duality; anticipating this, he states that the memory of non-duality is indeed sublated because it arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the sublating cognition, whereas the other arises from the impressions of the cognition to be sublated. Thus: "Memory... (verse 845).
Neither memory nor forgetfulness could possibly be conceived here by anyone.
For this [Self] is indeed once and for all manifest, just as day and night are manifest in the sun.

Having established that there is memory regarding the self and having stated the defect [in the opponent's view], he says "it is not memory" to show that it is not merely memory in that case. The word "api" (even/also) is used to state that certainty is far removed when there is an absence of possibility. The reason for this is: "once," etc. The inner self is always...

The meaning is that it is of the nature of immediate consciousness (*aparokṣa-cid-rūpa*). He provides an illustration for the fact that even the possibility of remembering or forgetting does not exist with respect to the Self, saying:
"In the sun. The illustration is established by such scriptural passages as, "It neither rises nor sets. || 846 ||
Because it is the cause of producing what is harmful, as stated above, [it is the opposite] of the mindfulness of self.
The self-recollection [of the cognition] is obtained by itself, whereas that of the other [the object] is subject to sublation. || 847 ||

Having established that the knower must indeed attain mindfulness (*smṛti*), he states another reason for the fact that the continuity of that [mindfulness] cannot be brought under control: "Anartha... etc.

Since, upon the realization of the Self arising from the [great] sentence, no other entity is perceived as a cause of misfortune (*anartha*), and since the Self is of a nature entirely distinct from that, it constitutes the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*); therefore, because mindfulness directed toward that [Self] would result in the burning away of misfortune and its causes, there is an absence of mindfulness—whether arising from the cognition of the non-Self or from its latent impressions—immediately following the realization of the Self. Thus, by elimination...

The sense is that because the recollection of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self follows from the meaning [of the scripture] even without an injunction, its non-self-recollection is sublated by it; therefore, a continuous stream of such recollection is not something to be enjoined. || 847 ||

If, then, cessation is a different entity from the previously mentioned [causes], in that case it too must be an effect, because it is heard [in scripture] as such among those intermediate entities. (848)

He formulates the fourth [alternative]: "Cessation" (*nirodha*). The meaning is: if the knowledge of the meaning of sentences and so forth is not something that can be enjoined, then let the cessation of the mind and its fluctuations (*citta-tad-vṛtti-nirodha*) be enjoined as the means to liberation, since it is distinct from the aforementioned knowledge and other factors. He corroborates this with the *Yogaśāstra* regarding the injunction of cessation as the cause of liberation: "In that regard" (*tatra*). The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of that also" (*tasyāpi*) is used in connection with the locative case.

It is connected [to the previous context]. Now, with the words "Now follows the instruction on Yoga," the concentration (*samādhi*) which is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has been enunciated; its definition was stated as "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ*). Furthermore, the state of that cessation is declared to be the soul's establishment in its own nature, which is called isolation (*kaivalya*), according to the rule:
"Then the seer abides in its own nature. And the author of the Commentary, having said at the end of the chapter, "These [fluctuations] must, moreover, be ceased,"...

He declared: "Since those latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) of the mind are contrary to its function and are the cause of its instability, therefore, once its function has ceased, the mind—along with the latent impressions conducive to isolation (*kaivalya*)—ceases to exist. When that [mind] has ceased, the Person (*puruṣa*), established in his own nature alone, is called pure, isolated, and liberated. Thus, *nirodha* (cessation) is intended in the Yoga Śāstra as the cause of liberation.
The meaning is that it is a rule concerning the root *dhā*. || 848 ||
No, because scripture teaches that it is understood as a means to liberation.
There is no means for liberation here other than the realization of the inner Self.

Relying upon the Śruti, which is more authoritative even than the Yoga-śāstra, he states the answer: "Not in liberation. He elaborates on that very point: [Brāhmaṇa 1] accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 603.

"Pratyak" means "the supreme" (param), that is to say, the most excellent. "Iha" refers to the statement of the scripture. The meaning is that, according to such scriptural passages as "Only by knowing Him," knowledge alone is the sole means to liberation (kaivalya), not the cessation [of mental activity]; for since there is a contradiction with the Śruti, the Yogaśāstra has no scope [to override it]. || 849 ||
Because it is not of the nature of something to be performed, its accomplishment arises from the realization of the Self.
For it is in the knowledge of the inward Self that the mind and its fluctuations are brought to rest. || 850 ||

He states that although the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*) is the cause of liberation, it is not something to be enjoined: "It is not to be performed" (*ananuṣṭheya*). First of all, the cessation of the mind and its fluctuations cannot be performed in an arbitrary manner, because such a cessation occurs for everyone [spontaneously] and thus cannot be enjoined by scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). Nor can a cessation of them in their entirety be enjoined, because that is accomplished through knowledge (*jñāna*) alone; therefore, there is no injunction regarding cessation. As for knowledge—

It establishes that [the Self] is the means for attaining ultimate cessation. Regarding the word "pratyak" (innermost): therefore, even though its status as the cause of liberation is accepted, it does not possess the nature of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), because it is established even without an injunction; this is the remainder of the argument. || 850 ||
Having accepted this, we say it is because of its possibility.
There is no other means for liberation besides perfect knowledge.
Whatever is possible within Śruti or Smṛti has its authority derived from those two; nothing else possesses such authority.
In the determination of the true nature of the inward Self, it is like the reality of the Self as described by the logicians.

Following such scriptures as, "There is no other path; liberation comes from knowledge alone," he prepares the introductory stage (*bhūmikā*) to abandon the position of *upetyavāda* (conditional admission). Regarding the phrase "having admitted" (*abhyupetya*): the meaning is that, having admitted that cessation (*nirodha*) is the cause of liberation, it was stated that because [liberation] can arise from knowledge alone even without an injunction, it is not something to be enjoined. Why is this a conditional admission? Why is this alone not the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*)?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Properly" (*samyak*). If it is argued that the fact that cessation (*nirodha*) is the cause of liberation and that the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) abides in its own nature are well-known in the Yoga scriptures, he says "no," adding: "By those two. In that regard, he provides a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):

"By the logicians" (*tārkika*). Just as by the logicians God and so forth are accepted as independent authorities based on inference and other means, such is not accepted by the followers of the Veda; therefore...
The meaning is that even the Yoga-śāstra is not an authoritative source when it contradicts the Śrutis and other scriptures, according to the logical principle: "By this, Yoga is refuted.
And because of the abandonment of inward consciousness, which is the sole cause of the desire for all forms.
Cultivation is not possible here, because it occurs only when delusion exists. || 853 ||

In the Vedāntas, the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) regarding cessation (*nirodha*) and so forth has been refuted. As for the claim that there exists in them a creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) possessing the three factors [of object, agent, and means], he refutes that with the word "all" (*sarva*). When there are the expectations of "what," "by what," and "how," ignorance is the independent cause; since that is removed by the knowledge of the inner Self (*pratyag-jñāna*) arising from the sentences, a *bhāvanā* possessing the three factors is not possible in the Vedāntas. For such expectations arise only as long as delusion (*moha*) persists.
The meaning is that because such a cultivation is possible [in those cases], there is no injunction regarding them. || 853 ||
For us, there is indeed the apprehension of the meaning of the statement which has not been apprehended by any other means of knowledge.
For this reason, even the injunction would not be one whose vow is false.

Even in the absence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there certainly exists an injunction (*niyoga*) in the Vedāntas; for in its absence, activity toward the knowledge arising from the sentence would be untenable.
(Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika by Sureśvarācārya, First Chapter, page 310, verse 604)

Anticipating this objection, he says: "By another means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*). For us, injunction (*vidhi*) consists solely in making known the meaning of a sentence that was previously unknown; it is not the instigation of one who has not yet acted, because there is a deviation [from this definition] in cases such as "Eat poison. Therefore, the meaning is that in the Upaniṣadic sentences which awaken the enlightened, there is no mandatory application (*niyoga*), just as there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, there is no mandatory application regarding the knowledge of the Self, because that knowledge is not dependent on the person, whereas a mandatory application has as its object that which is dependent on the person.
"O you who are of untruthful vows," he said. || 894 ||
Where a distinction is perceived between the person to be enjoined and the object of that injunction.
That [duality] is the object of an injunction, but not in the case of the knowledge of the Self, because of its non-differentiation. || 855 ||

He states another reason for the impossibility of an injunction (*niyoga*) regarding the knowledge of the Self: "niyojya... etc. Where there is the cognition of distinction—namely, the agent, the means, and the goal—an injunction is appropriate, as in the case of sacrifice and the like; however, it is not applicable to the knowledge of the Self, because by the mere arising of that [knowledge], all distinctions are destroyed. This is the meaning. || 855 ||
For even a word devoid of the optative suffix and the like can convey a meaning that was previously unknown.
It becomes an injunction by virtue of its capacity; for when a matter is already known, [the statement] is merely a restatement (anuvāda). || 856 ||

Anticipating the objection that since only a sentence containing an injunctive word constitutes an injunction because it brings about the understanding of what was previously unknown, the Vedāntas—which inform one of the as-yet-unknown Brahman—would also necessarily involve an injunction (*niyoga*) due to their association with such words, he says: "The word.

The meaning is that even a word devoid of an injunction, by virtue of its own power, may itself be an injunction insofar as it makes known what was unknown, just like any other word. [The text continues: "the unknown..."

One must accept that there are two types of injunctions (*vidhi*): that which makes known and that which impels one to act who has not yet acted. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that this [distinction] is accepted as intended. An objection is raised: "If it is to be stated that an injunction is 'informative' (*jñāpaka*), what is the purpose of the qualification 'unknown'? Anticipating this, he says: "For when [it is] known...
The meaning is that the qualification is purposeful in order to refute the suspicion that [the injunction] might be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). || 856 ||
From which all words and designations are employed for the purpose of apprehension.
Having brought about awakening, they all cease without having expressed anything at all.

One might raise the objection that although the purpose [of scripture] is to awaken one who is unawakened, this is not applicable to Brahman, because of the scriptural statement that "from whence words return," which establishes that Brahman is beyond the scope of speech;

therefore, Brahman cannot be known through the Upaniṣads. Anticipating this, the author says: "From whence... The word "abhidhānāni" (denotations) is an explanation of the word "vācaḥ" (words). The syntactical connection is: "The wise one does not fear that Brahman from whence [words] return, which is of the nature of bliss."

If the statements intended for the realization of Brahman were to cease their operation without having produced any activity toward that end, how then could it be called "Upaniṣadic"? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "Having made [Brahman] known. Since this has been established in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, here the injunction consists in the awakening of one who has not yet awakened.
This is the intended meaning of the word "vatī. || 897 ||
And from those sounds, there arose for him knowledge whose intellect was bound to their forms.
Not having attained that which is awakened by itself, it ceases together with the name. || 858 ||
Anticipating the objection—"Just as Brahman is the object of a cognition arising from words, why should it not also be the direct object of words?"—the author says: "uda pādī" (It has arisen).

That knowledge which is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), having the form of the identity of Brahman and the Self, is produced by words such as "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*). || 856 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 311] 8 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 605.
That [mind], having failed to reach that Brahman as its object, turns back from it along with the word that is its cause; for it is said, "not having reached it with the mind."

It is heard that because Brahman, which is by its very nature of the single flavor of awakening, is unfit to be an object, it therefore manifests to the word and the cognition arising from it precisely through its non-objectivity; this is the meaning. || 858 ||
This is the majesty of the Word: that it dispels ignorance.
And because of the weakness of sleep, it does not cause affliction, as if one were in deep slumber. || 859 ||

Now, is the word’s relationship [of denotation] grasped with respect to Brahman or not? Not the first, because it would be impossible for it to be its object; nor the other, because it would be impossible for it to have the word as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is another means of valid cognition admitted in that case. Therefore, since knowledge of it is impossible, the destruction of ignorance—which consists in the non-knowledge of it—is not possible there. To this he says: "The majesty" (*māhātmyam*). Just as a person in deep sleep, upon hearing a sound, [awakens] from sleep even without a simultaneous understanding of the relationship [between the sound and its meaning].

Just as a sound that awakens someone from sleep dispels that sleep by producing cognition therein—without depending on knowledge of any relationship existing at that time—so too, the word "Tattvamasi" (That Thou Art), whose power is already known, produces knowledge through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding its intended object without depending on a primary denotative power (*śakti*). This is its greatness: that it dispels ignorance, which is the cause of all evil. Therefore, it is logical that Brahman, though not an [ordinary] object of sense, has the scripture as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
