The meaning is: "the state of being that [very thing]. One might raise the objection: "Even when Brahman is known through the sentence, how does that [knowledge] remove ignorance regarding it, since the possibility of the opposite [misconception] also exists?
Anticipating this, he says, "And because of its weakness," in order to clarify what was already stated in the verse beginning with *tama miteḥ* (the sublation of darkness by cognition). ||859||
Because ignorance is weak, and because the nature of consciousness is the Self.
Because the power of words is inconceivable, we know that [reality] through the destruction of delusion. || 860 ||

To the question of how ignorance (*avidyā*) is weaker than knowledge (*vidyā*), he says: "Because of its weakness. Since the weakness of ignorance is established in cases such as mother-of-pearl, the powerful knowledge necessarily sublates the weak ignorance which is its opposite. Furthermore, because the non-inert luminosity is the Self, ignorance cannot remain there even due to a mere cause; how much less so when knowledge is present?

To this he says: "Because it is the Self" (*ātmatvāt*). Furthermore, there is no rule that a word imparts knowledge of an object to be known only when its power [to denote it] has been previously ascertained; for the power of a word, like the power of mantras and the like, is difficult to discern. To this he says: "The word... (*śabda...*). How, then, does the cognition of the inward Brahman arise from the word? To that he says: "In the case of knowledge" (*vidye*). That supreme inward Self [is realized] by means of the removal of the contrary elements designated as "delusion" (*moha*).
The meaning is that we understand [Brahman] from the word through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); therefore, Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 860 ||
Without even grasping the relationship between the signifier and the signified.
Having abandoned sleep, they awaken in the state of deep sleep (suṣupta) when awakened by others. 861.

He elaborates upon the illustration with the words "without having grasped. The meaning is that when sleeping people are awakened by those standing nearby saying, "Maitra, get up," they abandon their sleep and become conscious even without knowing the relationship between the word and its meaning at that time. || 861 ||
For no one perceives sound during deep sleep as they do while awake.
Therefore, when false cognition has been destroyed by knowledge, the result is the realization: "I am Brahman. (662)

He states the reason for the phrase "without having grasped" with the words "as in the waking state. Just as in the waking state a person who has mastered linguistic usage understands a word whose expressive power (*śakti*) is already known, it is not so in deep sleep; there, a word whose power is unknown cannot be a communicator of meaning. He concludes the application of the example with the words "destroyed" (dhvasta).
[Note: The variants indicate that in some versions the word is *bādhyate* or *ktidhīrana*.]
606 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] [vol2, page 312]

Thus, by virtue of this analogy, when ignorance is destroyed through the knowledge produced by the word via *lakṣaṇā*—without depending on a cognition of a relationship regarding the object to be established—the fruit, which is the unity of Brahman and the Self, is accomplished due to the absence of any obstruction. This is the meaning. || 862 ||
For one who has destroyed ignorance through such words and means, the realization "I am Brahman" arises.

It perishes along with ignorance, just as medicine destroys disease. (863) Now, does the knowledge that removes ignorance itself perish or not? In the first case, if there exists another remover, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not exist, it follows that destruction occurs without a cause.
In the second case, since its cause—ignorance—would persist, there would be no liberation. Therefore, he says: "Ignorance. Indeed, that is ignorance.

The meaning is that while destroying [the fault], it perishes by itself because of its opposition to both itself and others. He provides an illustration for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in a single instance: "Just as," etc. It is well known that medicine such as the drinking of decoctions, when administered for the sake of removing diseases like indigestion, removes the disease and then perishes by itself; likewise, milk digests milk and is itself digested. Similarly...
The meaning is that knowledge, while dispelling ignorance, itself also comes to an end. || 863 ||
What remains is self-awakened; therefore, it is pure and liberated.
Therefore, there would be no dependence on mental cultivation (bhāvanā), nor upon another means of valid cognition (mānāntara). 864 ||

Now, upon the cessation of ignorance and its effects, is something left over or not? In the first case, the means of knowing that must be stated. In the second case, there would be the consequence of falling into nihilism (śūnyavāda). Therefore, he says: "something remains. The connection is as follows: because of the destruction of saṃsāra along with its cause, such a reality (tattva) remains. He states the result of that remainder: "not from this," etc. The word *bhāvanā* refers to an injunction (*niyoga*).

This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). He states another consequence resulting from its being self-evidently enlightened (*svato-buddhatva*): "Nor... [and so forth]. The meaning is that since the reality as described remains [as it is], it has no need for an injunction; and because it is self-evidently enlightened, it is not reasonable for it to depend on another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), since neither an injunction nor another means of knowledge can effect anything regarding that [reality]. || 864 ||
Either knowledge is devoid of the differentiation of action, or else all of it is darkness.
No other oblation to darkness destroys it merely by its own acquisition [of form]. || 865 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the object already described does not depend on meditation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, the knowledge of it might still depend on them to destroy ignorance, he says: "Action" (*kriyā*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of emphasis. Since all distinctions between actions, factors of action, and their results perish by the mere arising of knowledge, it is impossible for knowledge to depend on meditation and the like; thus, the meaning is that knowledge alone, without dependence, removes all ignorance. Now, one might ask: is the destruction of that [ignorance] something different from the Self?

Regarding this, he says "na tadanyā" (not other than that), [anticipating the objection]: "In the first case, there would be its eternality; in the second, there would be its having a second. By the word "tat" (that), the Self characterized by the knowledge arising from the sentence is denoted. || 861 ||
Since there is no difference between the action and its fruit, there is therefore no difference between the two actions.
Therefore, knowledge, which is inward-turned, destroys that darkness of ignorance simply by attaining its own self-nature.

If it is argued that the destruction of ignorance occurs through knowledge, then a temporal sequence between those two must be stated, just as there is between staying and moving; anticipating this objection, he recalls what was said in the examination of the jar: "Action... Knowledge is an action, and its fruit is the destruction of ignorance. Since the distinction between the action and its result—such as cutting and the resulting division—is well-established, and since it is not desired that both be considered actions, this [sequence] is prior...
The meaning is that since the distinction "this is after" cannot be stated, the objection "then what is before? has no basis. In the absence of such an objection—[vol2, page 313]
[The Brāhmaṇa] concludes with the result: "The inward" (*pratyak*). By stating that knowledge has the form of the inward, its capacity to destroy ignorance is thereby illuminated. || 866 ||
Just as an axe or similar tool, even when fully prepared, [is ineffective] due to the absence of application.
In that way, neither the cognition of the means of knowledge nor the cognition of the object is capable of producing a state of doubt.

He establishes, by means of a heterogeneous example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), that knowledge destroys ignorance merely by the acquisition of its own nature. [The verse says: "Even though accomplished," etc. The meaning is this:

even though an axe or similar tool exists, it is not sufficient for the accomplishment of splitting wood and so forth without being employed; however, knowledge produced by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not like that, because it removes ignorance by the mere fact of its arising. || 867 ||
Because that which is to be realized is supramundane, and because it is self-evident by its very nature.
For there is indeed dependence upon the worldly regarding awakening, and likewise regarding understanding from another.

Having stated that there can be no dependence on *bhāvanā* (productive activity) in this case—meaning that the cognition arising from the sentence is independent of *bhāvanā* and so forth, or of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*)—and having thus established its independence from *bhāvanā* and the like, he establishes its independence from other means of knowledge by stating: "Because it is beyond the world of ordinary experience" (*alaukikatvāt*). This refers to Brahman.

The meaning is that because it is not amenable to other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because it manifests independently, the cognition produced by the sentence—bearing that [Brahman’s] form—dispels ignorance without depending on anything else. If Brahman does not depend on other means of knowledge, then where is such dependence required? To this he says: "For regarding the object of knowledge...

The sense of the word "for" (*hi*) is that there is no absence of the cultivation of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) without depending on a means of knowledge regarding an insentient object well-known in the world. If there were dependence on it regarding the insentient... [text fragment ends]

Fearing the objection that even for the *nāda* (the primordial sound), there would be a loss of its own established tenet (*siddhānta-hāni*) due to its dependence on that [other means of knowledge], he says: "From another" (*parataḥ*). This means that while dependence on another means of knowledge is appropriate for things like form (*rūpa*), which are capable of being apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*māna*), such capability does not exist in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, despite their insentience (*jāḍya*). Therefore, there is no practical usage (*vyavahāra*) involving dependence on such a means in their case; hence, even though there is dependence on it regarding its effects, since ignorance is easily dispelled by itself, there is no requirement for a means of valid cognition (*māna*) with respect to it.

This is the meaning: or rather, that which is to be known as worldly is not self-luminous because its comprehension depends on something else; thus, there is a dependence on other means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding it.
The word *tathā* is used in the sense of conjunction. || 868 ||
Like fruits on the bank of a river, they exist independently of perception and the other means of valid cognition.
What need have you for another [means of cognition] here, given that the verbal testimony itself is being cited? (869)
He clarifies the self’s independence from other means of knowledge by means of a negative example: "Of the river," etc.

Just as the statement "There are fruits on the bank of the river" requires a primary source of knowledge—since it is accepted that human speech depends upon such a source—it is not so with the Upaniṣadic texts such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) which operate here regarding the Self; for even for you, they do not depend on other means of knowledge.

It is logical that the Self, being self-luminous, has no dependence on perception or other means of knowledge; therefore, the statement regarding its reality (tat-tvam-ādi) does not depend on another means of knowledge because it has an already established object as its meaning, like the sentence "There are fruits on the riverbank. Thus, it is not to be inferred [as having a future object], because the probans is vitiated by the condition (upādhi) of having an object suitable for another means of knowledge. This is the meaning. ||869||

The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise the ascertainment—all these are established by the mere presence of that [Self]; once it is established, what else does it require? (870)

Anticipating the objection that there might be an over-extension of the proof (*sādhanavyāpti*), he says "it is not so," because the Self, which is the prover of everything, is incapable of being apprehended by any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). [Page 314] 1. *pramā-*; 2. *ga.* reads *apekṣyate*.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter One: [The opponent says: "It is so. [The author replies:

The subject under dispute (the Self) does not depend upon means of knowledge (*māna*) and the like, because it is the establisher of those very means; for whatever is an establisher of something does not depend upon that thing, just as a lamp, which establishes a jar, does not depend upon it.
The meaning is that it does not depend upon that. || 870 ||
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is the cognition, "This is a jar."
If there were no intervention [between them], it would be because of the witnessing of both their presence and absence. (871)

Now, one might object: "The Supreme Self must depend upon another means of knowledge because it is concealed, just like fire and other such things. Anticipating this doubt, he states the [objection's] lack of proof:

"In the waking state," etc. Just as for consciousness qualified by a jar or the like, there is a spatial or other concealment because the qualifier is non-self and subject to appearance and disappearance, such concealment does not exist here—in the three states—within the Supreme, which is the inner witness; for that [concealment] exists only when that [qualifier] is present or absent.
The meaning is: because it is always manifest as the witness. || 871 ||
The intellect that distinguishes "this is thus" and "this is not thus" possesses differentiation.
Since that which is selfless here possesses a self, what does it require?

Furthermore, he says that the Self is not an object of perception and the like, because its nature is like that [of the intellect itself], in the passage beginning with "idam" (this). Here, the meaning is "in the sphere of empirical usage. The cognition that, during the state of empirical usage, distinguishes between things such as a jar—which possesses a broad base, a belly, and so on—and things such as a cloth, which does not possess those features, is itself devoid of an intrinsic nature; yet, by means of that Self, it [the cognition] acquires a nature...
The meaning is that since the Self is characterized by the nature of pride and so forth, there is no dependence upon that [external authority]. || 872 ||
Prior to the activity of the agent and so forth, it is unmixed with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Experiencing that which is undistracted and not asleep, what indeed does one require? || 873 ||

Furthermore, the Self is not the object of that [knowledge], because it is established prior to it; for whatever is established prior to something else cannot be its object, just as a pillar perceived before the perception of a jar is not the object of that [perception]. Thus he says: "The agent, etc. Knowledge is the wandering through the knower, the known, and so forth; "prior to that" means in deep sleep. This is because the Self, like a Yakṣa or similar entity, does not depend on an external instrument for its own perception.

Anticipating the objection that there might still be association [with limiting adjuncts], he says: "unmixed" (*asaṃkīrṇam*). To the question, "How is its lack of connection with limiting adjuncts ascertained during deep sleep?

he replies: "undisturbed" (*avikṣiptam*). The meaning is that the cognition of its lack of connection therein arises from the non-perception of distraction. If it is argued that even in the absence of connection with the limiting adjuncts of the effect, there is still connection with the limiting adjuncts of the cause, he replies: "not fast asleep" (*asaṃsuptam*). For indeed, [the Self is not connected] to the cause...

The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is joined with the navel in its true nature; for there is the scriptural text, "It is indeed other than the known," and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning is that even though a connection with ignorance exists therein, it does not produce an effect. He states the proof for such a Self: "Experiencing.

The sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the existence of the aforementioned experience is established by the subsequent reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of one who has arisen [from sleep]. He states the resulting conclusion regarding its independence from perception and other means of knowledge.
"What is it? || 873 ||
Valid cognition, invalid cognition, and likewise the semblance of valid cognition.
Since they indeed produce valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding that [cause], how could there be any doubt about its impossibility?

(874) Even though the self is established solely through experience, one might suspect its impossibility on the grounds that such a self lacks any means of knowledge (*māna*); in response to this, he says:

"The means of knowledge. Because these [effects] produce valid cognition regarding that cause which perceives them—due to their being effects and being objects of perception—the cause resides in the effect.

The meaning is that because the object of perception depends upon a cause, and because it is impossible for that object to exist without a perceiver, there can be no non-existence of that self-luminous perceiver. || 874 ||

Why is it that the authority of this [scripture] does not exist by virtue of its being a subsequent [statement], given the scriptural text of the designation? [Brāhmaṇa 4, with the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā by Ānandagiri, page 609].
Even an injunction possesses authority only by depending upon this means of valid cognition.

Fearing that if the supreme Self were not an object of perception and other means of knowledge, it would likewise not be an object of [scriptural statements] such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) because there would be no distinction, he says: "Validity... The meaning is this: the validity of [statements] such as "That thou art" consists in their being a means of knowledge regarding the Self described as pure experience, by way of destroying ignorance and its products; however, other means of knowledge do not possess validity with respect to that [Self], because they do not destroy that ignorance and so forth. Now, [the opponent]—who maintains the doctrine of injunction (*niyoga*)—[objects]: [The text continues: ...by the proponent of injunction... [and so on].

The validity of the Vedic statement is intended to reside in its sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); however, the experience [of Brahman] has not been stated as its object, and therefore, because that [Brahman] is not the sentence-meaning, it is not an object of another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and because it is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*), one might think it does not exist there. To this he says: "Of the *niyoga* (injunction). Even if it were a means of knowledge, since the *niyoga* is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is impossible for it to establish the reality [of Brahman] without depending on non-insentient consciousness; thus, although the stated experience is not the object of the *niyoga*, it must be accepted as its means of accomplishment. That...

The meaning is "even that [is to be granted]. Alternatively, he says "of the *niyoga*" (verse 875) to show that for the proponent of *niyoga*, who maintains that *niyoga* is the meaning of the sentence and seeks its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no room for dispute regarding it; for it is certain that one must accept the aforementioned experience as the proof (*sādhaka*) [for the existence of *niyoga*].
The statement beginning with "one should see the Self" and so forth would be injunctive.
Regarding the duty of knowledge, with respect to the person who is enjoined therein. || 876 ||

[The opponent objects: "Let it be granted that experience is not amenable to other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); nevertheless, there is an injunction regarding knowledge, as per the scriptural text, 'One should know the Self by the Self. Thus, the dependence of the object upon that [injunction] is unavoidable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "One should see" (*paśyet*). If this were solely for the purpose of an injunction, then, having enjoined the person to the performance of knowledge, the sentence would become complete; yet, with respect to the person who is thus enjoined, [the question remains: toward what [end] is he enjoined?
The meaning is that, having fulfilled its purpose by making known the relation (niyoga), it does not make known the real entity (vastu); therefore, the entity is not established. || 876 ||
Since speech, in its own function, does not depend at all upon the actual state of things;
Therefore, when a person is so appointed, the true nature of things is extremely difficult to perceive.

Anticipating the objection that even a sentence primarily concerned with an injunction (*niyoga*) might convey [the nature of reality]—on the grounds that it is possible for a single sentence to have two purposes according to the logic of the "channel-conducting" (*kulyā-praṇayana*) maxim—the author says: "In its own operation" (*svavyāpāre*). This means: in the sense-object (*bhāvārtha*) which is fit for human effort. The meaning is that, as in the case of sentences concerning women and so forth, a sentence whose focus is an injunction does not depend upon an existing entity (*vastu*); therefore, the realization of that [entity] cannot arise from it. || 877 ||
If an action is not in accordance with one's own capacity, it cannot be accomplished even by hundreds of words.
Even when commanded, he is not able to perform it; for he is indeed the Lord.

Having previously stated that the object cannot be established even by resorting to an injunction regarding knowledge, he now says that there is no such injunction at all: "By its own power" (*sva-śakti*). If some task were said to be unsuitable for a person's capacity, then even if he were enjoined toward it by numerous injunctions, he would not be able to perform it due to his incapacity. However, in the case of a suitable object, because of a person's capability—and since that knowledge is not dependent on the person—an [injunction] is not required.
The meaning is that this is an engagement based on scriptural injunction (*vaidhī pravṛtti*). || 878 ||
One should strive with diligent effort for the understanding of the expression, its hearing, and the establishment of that [meaning].
Because it follows the path of injunctions, that [cognition] does not touch upon the object, owing to its lack of independence.
If it is argued that there is an injunction regarding knowledge, then the reality of the object is not established; nor is there an injunction in that case, as has already been stated.

To this, he removes the objection regarding the non-establishment of the object with the word "bhidhā" (denotation). Even if the reality of the object is not established from an injunctive sentence concerning knowledge because its focus lies on the mandate (*niyoga*), the sentence concerning the true nature [of Brahman] establishes it.
7io.

The meaning is that one should apply oneself with focused intent (*tātparya*). The direct statement of the words (*abhidhā-śruti*) does not establish the actual reality, because it lacks independence, serving only to provide what is required by the injunction (*vidhi*).
Diti refutes this: "The injunction," etc. (879).
They even eat their own flesh, never transgressing their commands.
They even abandon their dear lives for no other reason than sheer impossibility.

Having established that there is no proof for the existence of a real entity (*vastu*) if one accepts an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding knowledge, he clarifies the impossibility of an injunction in that case by stating the reason of "impossibility" (*aśakyatva*):

"I shall attain my own [nature]" (*svam asāni*). For those who are devoted to an injunction (*niyoga*), activity even toward such things as the abandonment of life is possible due to the force of that injunction;
the meaning is that because it is possible, there is activity even toward an object that is otherwise impossible. || 880 ||
"Even when enjoined to perform what is impossible, one should offer kṛṣṇala-berries."
Even if he were to do it with his whole soul, he would act like a thief in a pit.

He states by way of an illustration that there is no engagement [in action] due to the injunction of what is impossible, saying: "In the case of the impossible. [For example, one might be told: "One should cook *kṛṣṇalas*—be they gold *māṣas* or small black stones—which are by nature black. Since it is entirely impossible to cook a vessel of *kṛṣṇalas*, one who is enjoined to do so would not perform it because of its impossibility. For it has been said: "In the case of *kṛṣṇalas*, there is no cooking because the purpose [of the act] is lost."

It might be so. Regarding the injunction, "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* oblation of clarified butter consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* seeds to Prajāpati," there arises a doubt as to whether cooking should be performed on the *kṛṣṇala* seeds or not. Since the verbal root *pac* (to cook) is observed in usage to have as its object the result of softening (*viklitti*), and since that [softening] is impossible in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, the injunction would be untenable—just as in the case of the statement "he sprinkles with fire"—and thus it is concluded that cooking should not be performed. However, this is refuted by the fact that in the expression "Caitra cooks," the term refers to the operation of the agent (*hetṛvyāpāra*).

Because the act of application (*prayoga*) itself constitutes the meaning of "cooking" (*pacati*), and because that [application] is present even in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, the fruit [of the action] has that [application] as its object by way of the agent's activity; thus, it is logical that the word denotes the operation perceived first. Therefore, based on the scriptural injunction, cooking must be performed for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). This was established as the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) in the tenth book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*], under the sūtra: "Or rather, it should be so, because it is directly enjoined, like the offering" (*syādvā pratyakṣaśiṣṭatvāt pradānavat*, PMS 10.2.2). In that regard, although...

Even in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, it is possible to produce mere heating; nevertheless, according to the maxim that "the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) consists primarily in softening," one who produces only that [softening] in them by means of heating would be a participant in mere exertion. Just as in the world, a thief who enters among those cooking cakes and the like and performs that work himself becomes a participant in mere exertion due to the impossibility of accomplishing the task, so too [is it here] because of its impossibility.
The meaning is that even when there is such knowledge, there is no activity prompted by scriptural injunction (*vaidhī pravṛtti*). || 881 ||
Since knowledge depends upon the reality of the object, it does not arise from meditative practice (*upāsana*).
Nor do the means of valid cognition produce a valid cognition through repetition. (882)

If it is argued that even though there is no application of an injunction (*vidhi*) with respect to knowledge, let there be such an injunction for meditation (*upāsti*) in the form of the repetition of that [knowledge]; and therefore, since meditation is enjoined, another cognition in the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*) must be produced—[the author] says "no," stating: "Of knowledge... Because it is not observed in perception and other means of knowledge, he states:
"Nor is it the case... (882), meaning that by meditation in the form of repeating knowledge, another cognition consisting of valid knowledge is not produced.
If the cultivation [of the mind] were not directed toward the desire for the goal, it would not give rise to the knowledge of Brahman.
Even though it has been repeatedly practiced, the cognition of silver does not arise from the cognition of mother-of-pearl. (883)

Furthermore, does meditation (upāsti) touch upon the actual object or not? In the first case, since the object would be established by that [meditation] alone, another means of knowledge would be useless; thinking thus, [the author] considers the following alternative. [Note: The text fragment provided contains a portion of a philosophical argument regarding the efficacy of meditation (*upāsti*) in establishing the reality of an object. It contrasts this with other means of knowledge (*jñāna*).]

[He] refutes [the objection] immediately following [it]. [The phrase] "not the object" [means]: although that [knowledge] does not touch upon the object, nevertheless, through repeated practice, it will produce the cognition of Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that "because it has such an inherent nature, it indeed produces an excellence (atiśaya) regarding its own object," he says: "In the case of mother-of-pearl. The meaning is: even if the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl is practiced with diligence, continuously, and for a long time, it does not become a cause for the arising of right knowledge regarding the mother-of-pearl; likewise, meditation on the Self is also not capable of producing right knowledge. || 883 ||
If the self were something to be seen, then there would be an application of effort toward the self.
Because of the prohibition of [further] seeing here, there is no injunction regarding what follows this.

Having raised the objection that "even in the absence of an injunction, it [the knowledge] will occur regarding its object, because of the scriptural statement 'it is to be seen' (*draṣṭavya*)," and keeping in mind what was stated previously—that "because the nature of a substance is not something to be accomplished" (*dravyasvarūpe 'sādhyatvāt*)—he states another defect: "If it were to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaśced iti*). The sense is this: if the Self were the object of seeing, it would be possible to claim it is the object of an injunction, because only that which is already seen can be the object of an injunction. [Regarding] the Self...

Anticipating the objection that "being an object of vision" (draṣṭavyatva) is based on scripture (śrauta), he says: "Because of the prohibition. The meaning is: since both seeing and meditative worship (upāsti) are prohibited here with respect to the Self, there can be no injunction regarding that Supreme Being who transcends both; furthermore, the scriptural statement "it is to be seen" (draṣṭavya), while declaring its fitness for being seen, does not state that the Self is the object of that action. || 884 ||
That by which the mind always thinks that which is thought by the mind.
Know that alone to be Brahman, and not that which people worship here.
He cites scripture as proof for its not being an object of that [intellect]: "It thinks" (manute). || 885 ||
The status of being Brahman has been clearly negated by the scripture through a direct, pinpointing reference.
Therefore, an injunction (niyoga) is not accepted here on account of the single defect of being an object of worship.

He states the purport of the scripture with the words "śṛṅga" (the horn), etc. Just as one might take hold of a cow standing in a herd by its horn to specifically point it out, saying, "This is the one that gives much milk," so too, by means of the scripture—which is intent on clearly demonstrating the reality—the nature of Brahman is attributed to the object of meditation; such is the meaning.

He states the reason for the denial of the status of Brahman to the object of meditation with the words "upāsyatva" (the state of being an object of meditation), etc. [The result follows] from the fact that the Self is not an object of sight and so forth.
He said: "The term 'niyoga' (application) refers here to the Self. || 886 ||
By setting aside both the known and the unknown, [one realizes] the witness of the state of the knower and so forth.
"Know that very thing to be Brahman," and thus the state of being Brahman was imparted. || 887 ||

Having stated that the object of knowledge and worship is not Brahman, and having established that its opposite is indeed Brahman, he says [in the verse] "jñāta... (known) etc., that there is no injunction therein. By such passages as "That is indeed other than the known," etc., having set aside the superimposed world consisting of cause and effect, which is of the nature of the known and the unknown, [one realizes] by that very means the non-dual reality—the witness of both the existence and non-existence of the knower—which is the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou). "That alone is you, O Brahman."
The meaning is that since the state of being Brahman has been shown by the word "know" (viddhi), there is no room for an injunction [to know it]. || 887 ||
At the time of the cognition of the sentence-meaning, that word-meaning which does not exist at all—
It must be performed with regard for the agent; it is to be enjoined, without a doubt. || 888 ||

Since neither cognition nor the object of cognition is something to be enjoined, he states whose nature it is that is to be enjoined: "The meaning of the sentence," etc. This is for the purpose of excluding what is non-existent (*tuccha*).
[Note: *ka* and *kha* manuscripts read *pe cāsā*; *kha* and *ga* manuscripts read *marthitā*.

612 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]—he distinguishes [the object] as "that which is to be done" (*kartavya*). He establishes its fitness for action (*kṛti-yogyatvam*). Regarding the term "kāraka" (instrumental factor): if it were the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), then...
This indicates the absence of any binding [condition]: "There is no doubt. || 888 ||
But that which is contrary to this is understood from the sentence itself.
Being eternal and not dependent on action, it can never be something to be enjoined.

Anticipating the objection that, like sacrifices and the like, there must be an injunction regarding Brahman as well because it is understood through scriptural statements (*vākya*), he says: "On the contrary" (*viparīta*). He states its authoritative status with the words: "From the statement" (*vākyāt*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used to clarify the meaning of the particle "only" (*eva*), namely, that [Brahman] is not accessible through other means of knowledge. He establishes this contrariety by saying: "Eternal" (*nitya*). He provides the reason for its eternality by saying: "Not an action" (*akarma*).
He states that it [the Self] possesses no status as an object of injunction, whether in its own essential nature or as something associated with that nature, in the words: "That is not... (889).
For that cognition which corresponds to the object as it actually exists is, for us, precisely what constitutes right knowledge.
Ignorance arises merely from human effort, like [the perception of] silver and so forth. (890)

Having refuted the injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditation (*upāsti*) with respect to the Self, he provides the introductory context to state another defect in the position that knowledge is an injunction.

He says, "Just as... The meaning is that valid cognition (*pramā*) is knowledge that conforms to reality. This is stated in order to show that conformity to reality is the cause for the correctness of knowledge.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) [is used]. He says that, without following that [scripture], if knowledge were produced by an injunction, it would be invalid; thus he says "pauruṣa" etc. The meaning is: knowledge produced from an injunction based solely on human effort (*yatna*)—that is, exertion related to a person—is false cognition, like the cognition of silver [in a mother-of-pearl shell]. || 890 ||
Because right knowledge conforms only to the thing-in-itself, it is difficult [to attain].
The realization of the true nature of reality occurs through the entry into the application [of the means]. || 891 ||

He states the conclusion: since a statement that conforms to reality without the mediation of a correct cognition is difficult to establish—because it would be impossible for that statement to cause the knowledge of reality through the medium of an injunction—it follows that [the former view] is untenable. Thus he says: "The reality... (verse 891).
That which is not a denotable object and for which no cognition arises;

"Even when enjoined by an injunction, one is not capable of perceiving it in such a manner. (892) Furthermore, he says "abhidheyam" [the denotable] to show that Brahman cannot be made an object of an injunction. The meaning is that in Brahman, which is inaccessible to verbal knowledge, there is also no status as an object of cognition dependent upon an injunction. (892)
Could it possibly set aside the cognition of a thing already established by another means of knowledge?
If a real entity is understood in accordance with the meaning of an injunction, [then it is not perceived by the senses]. (893)

Furthermore, he states that if one holds the position that the existence of a thing is established through a cognition dependent on an injunction (*vidhi*), then the injunction would be enjoining what has already been presented [by other means], which results in the collapse of that position.

He says "api" (even/furthermore). The literal meaning is: if the cognition of a thing follows from a mandate (*niyoga*), then the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth would be enjoining that cognition of the thing which is already obtained through a means of knowledge other than the injunction; such a mandate would thus be rendered superfluous. || 893 ||
It is employed precisely for the attainment of a cognition produced by another means of knowledge.
For it is precisely because of the injunction that the nature of being an injunction would exist in the cognition thereof. || 894 ||
1 ka. kadāca | [vol2, page 319] ‘4 Brāhmaṇa’ accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 611

He states another defect in the position that the establishment of the reality [of Brahman] results from knowledge dependent on an injunction (*niyoga*). [The verse begins with] "By another means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*): if a person is enjoined by an injunction only when the meaning of the verbal root has already been attained through knowledge produced by a means other than an injunction, and if the establishment of that object characterized as the identity of Brahman and the Self results from the injunction itself, then once that [identity] is established and the nature of the injunction is known, activity toward it [would follow]; and therefore—

The meaning is as follows: since that cognition [of the object] arises only from the injunction (*niyoga*)—because that cognition is desired [as the means to fulfill the injunction]—there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, the view that the perceptible object is the domain of the injunction is refuted. One should distinguish this point: having first stated the failure of the position by assuming that the reality of the object is established through the injunction, it is now stated here that the reality of the object is not established at all. || 894 ||
Even though this object does not exist here, it is meditated upon because it is well-known elsewhere.
However, because Brahman is not [an object] established [by the senses], a cloth without a thread is produced.

Even though the knowledge of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) is not something to be enjoined, there is the meditation (*bhāvana*) whose object is the immediate Brahman, which is not conjoined with that [empirical] object, just as [the meditation on] a woman as fire— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an incomplete commentary on a verse regarding the nature of Brahman and the role of meditation.]

Anticipating the objection that, because it is something to be accomplished (*vidheya*), knowledge must enter into the sphere of injunction (*niyoga*) within the Vedāntas—just as in the case of meditation—the author, considering that this has already been refuted by the statement "because knowledge depends on the nature of the object" (*jñānasya vastutantratvāt*), states another defect: "That which is non-existent is meditated upon. Just as fire, though non-existent in a woman, is meditated upon by being superimposed upon her, because its nature is perceived elsewhere; so too, in your view, Brahman—which is unconditioned and immediate—is not established through the Word (*śabda*), since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And because that [state] is impossible there, the meaning is that such meditation is untenable—like a cloth woven from the threads of a non-existent loom—and thus it cannot be practiced. || 891 ||
Even a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning is established by way of the syntactic connection between word-meanings.
Brahman is of the nature of non-duality; therefore, that [realization] is considered difficult to achieve.

With the intention that the meditation on Brahman—though it is non-worldly (*alaukika*) like heaven and other such things—is nevertheless scriptural (*śāstrīya*) because its characteristics have been stated, [the author] says: "It is performed. Even though it is non-worldly, [Brahman], like ritual injunction (*niyoga*) and so forth, can be both performed and known. Its...

Since Brahman does not possess a composite form—because it is devoid of association with anything else—it is not perceived through the scriptures; therefore, meditation upon it is not something to be enjoined, because it is difficult to perform. This is the meaning. || 896 ||
Tell me, how can Brahman, whose nature is beyond the meaning of words, be known?
Nothing other than pure existence (sanmātra), which transcends verbal expression, is admitted by you. || 897 ||

Furthermore, does Brahman, which consists of a meaning not expressible by words (*avākyārtha*), exist for you or not? If it does not exist, how can there be meditation upon it? If it does exist, is it known or unknown? If it is unknown, meditation upon it is impossible; if it is known, meditation is possible because of that knowledge. [The opponent] asks: "Is it known from a sentence (*vākya*) or from something else? [The author] rejects the position that it is from "something else" by not accepting it, stating: "From a sentence... [He continues: "...by you."

It should also be understood that [the word] "by me" refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, he says "likewise" regarding the position that it is known. He says "another" [in verse 897]. The construction is as follows: you do not accept any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) than the sentence for that Brahman which is the meaning of the sentence; nor is even another sentence accepted as its means of knowledge. || 897 ||
Furthermore, you may accept that other measure as well.
Since the goal is accomplished by that alone, the practice of meditation and so forth is useless.
1 kha. Is enjoined.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: He raises the objection regarding the failure to accept [the opponent's position] with the word "atha" (now). By the particle "api," the sentence is drawn forward. He refutes it with the word "tāvatā" (by that much alone). Since the knowledge of Brahman is established either by means of the sentence itself or by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the performance of meditation, reflection, and so forth through an injunction would be rendered useless.
This is the meaning. || 898 ||
By the term *nididhyāsana*, perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is intended.
Because it has been determined that [the self] is conscious of what was previously stated. || 899 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that, having restated the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) in the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), its means—the phrase "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*)—is being enjoined? Therefore, how can the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*) be rendered useless? To this, he says: "By meditation" (*nididhyāsana*). He states the reason for this: "Because it has been stated" (*ukta*). In the restating sentence concerning the vision and so forth mentioned in the passage beginning with "it is to be seen"—in the sequence beginning with "by vision" (*darśanena*) and "by knowledge" (*vijñānena*)—meditation occupies the place [of the means].

The meaning is: because of the praise [of him], because of the ascertainment of his state as possessing right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and because this matter will be explained in detail in the fourth [chapter]. || 899 ||
If Brahman, in the form of association, is determined from the sentence;
Since its measure is precisely that much, let it be exactly so according to that measurement.

Furthermore, one must consider the alternative: is Brahman understood from the sentence as having a related form (*saṃsṛṣṭarūpa*) or an unrelated form (*asaṃsṛṣṭarūpa*)? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "Brahman. Since the sentence alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, if it is understood as related through that [sentence], then its related form alone must be accepted based on that authority;
how then can there be meditation on an unrelated Brahman? This is the meaning. || 900 ||
Since that [object] is understood through a means of valid cognition to be exactly as it is, how could there be a statement that "it is otherwise"?
To assume that whatever is postulated from non-perception is exactly as it is, is mere recklessness. (901)

Even if there is a perception of Brahman as associated [with attributes] due to the verbal testimony, one might think that by following the requirements of meditation (*dhyāna*), it will become dissociated; anticipating this, he says:

"Of whatever kind... Although Brahman is understood from the sentence as associated and mediate (*parokṣa*), it is improper to say it remains so, because that would contradict the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is improper to claim that Brahman—which is actually dissociated and immediate—is conceptualized through meditation and thus becomes exactly so, for that would lack a basis in valid knowledge.
The meaning is that it is impossible for that which is excellent to be a substantial entity. || 909 ||
For us, this is also established by such scriptural statements as "the space within a jar is indeed the great space."
Therefore, there would be a cognition of an unmixed object, just as in the case of the word "sadasī" (in the assembly). || 902 ||

He accepts the second point by means of an illustration: "A jar," etc. The word "also" (api) is to be applied to the case under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*). Therefore, there is no room for the injunction regarding meditation; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 902 ||
The meaning "having understood wisdom" is not what is intended here.
In whatever manner, this will be explained with great effort in that very place. || 903 ||

Having raised the objection—namely, that since the meditation on the Self as unconditioned is enjoined in the passage "having realized wisdom" (vijñāya prajñām), how can that [meditation] be without scope—he says:

"vijñāya" (having realized). The word "this" (ayam) refers to the injunction for meditation mentioned there; specifically, it refers to the state of explaining that very [passage] in the sixth chapter.
Since an injunction is impossible [in this context], he refers to this collection of required logical principles. || 903 ||
1 ka. ga. it is appropriate.

If it is argued that the sentences such as "That thou art" lack authoritative validity because they merely restate an already existing nature (svarūpa),
like the sentence "He wept" (so 'rodīt), [then the following is said]. || 904 ||

In the Vedāntas, it has been stated that by the elimination of injunctions, they result solely in the determination of the nature of the Self. Now, he raises an objection through the following inference: "They are not authoritative with respect to their own meaning because they are sentences whose subject matter is already established (siddhārtha), like the passage 'He wept' (sa ārodaīt) and so forth. [This is expressed in the verse: "svarūpa... (Verse 904).
Because the cause for validity exists here, invalidity is not accepted.
The arising of a cognition that is certain regarding its result is the cause of validity.

Thinking that "the state of not producing a certain knowledge of a result" (*phalavanniścita-jñānājanakatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*), he provides the following resolution: "Regarding validity," etc. Here, the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the statement made by taking the subject (*dharmin*). He states what the cause of that validity is: "having a result," etc. He uses the term "having a result" (*phalavat*) in order to assert that [statements] such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) lack validity because they are fruitless with respect to their own literal meaning. This applies to [the statement] "Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire" (*yoṣā vāva gautamāgniḥ*).

He indicates that [the cognition] is invalid with respect to that [woman], because it does not establish her as being fire. He says "ascertained" (niścita); he states that words such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ* have no validity regarding their own referents because they do not produce knowledge (*jñāna*). || 905 ||
That wherein such [a quality] exists is the means of knowledge; that wherein it does not exist is not a means of knowledge.
After hearing the meaning of such statements as "That thou art," what [remains] not [to be attained]? (906)
The arising of a cognition that is certain regarding its result is directly observed.
Since that [valid cognition] exists, why is it said by you here that there is no means of valid cognition? (907)

Having stated the grounds for validity, he declares the established conclusion with the word "tādṛk" (such). Applying the general principle to the present case, he proceeds with the word "tattva" (the reality). The meaning of the question is: "Is it perceived, or is it not? Thinking that if such an arising of knowledge were not observed regarding the reality and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the experience of the wise and the scriptural testimony concerning its fruit, he states another position: "tasmin... (in that...).
Thus [ends the section on] ethics. || 906 || 907 ||
What is determined from such statements as "He wept," and what is it that possesses a fruit?
If cognition arises, by what can its validity be prevented? (908)
Anticipating the objection—“What is the example being asked for? That has already been shown in the passage beginning with ‘He wept’ (so’rodīt)’”—he says:

“‘He wept’ (so’rodīt). The meaning of the alternative is: does knowledge arise, or does it not? Therein, having restated the first position, he refutes it with the words “it arises. The sense is that, in that case, the example would be fruitless regarding the point to be proven (sādhya). || 908 ||
Now, if this non-authoritativeness is not [due to sublation], let it be as you wish; it is not being prevented.
What has come of that which produces a certain knowledge of the fruit? || 909 ||

Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "Now" (*atha*). The sense is that there is no inference because the previously mentioned condition (*upādhi*) exists. Anticipating the objection that [the reason] is too wide (*sādhanavyāpta*), he says "fruitful" (*phalavat*). The sense is: "The subject under dispute (*vimata*) is a means of valid cognition regarding its own object, because it generates a certain knowledge that possesses a fruit, like sentences concerning the *darśa* sacrifice. || 909 ||
Now, let it be considered: what is the lack of authority for this [scripture], and what is its authoritative status?
Even where validity is desired, there too, invalidity follows.

Having restated the opposing view, he points out the over-extension [of that argument] with the word "atha" (now). He clarifies what was stated—that there is no validity whatsoever—by saying: "mānatvaṃ na kvāpi" (there is no validity anywhere).

"But even there" means that if the statement concerning reality (*tattvamasi*), which produces the aforementioned knowledge, were non-authoritative, then the injunctive sentence would also be non-authoritative. || 990 ||
Its status as a means of valid cognition exists in accordance with the actual state of human activity.
The sentence concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites [is not applicable] here, however, to the realization "I am Brahman. || 911 ||

He raises the objection that the stated reason does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*mānatva*), but rather that it is due to its being a generator of an impelling cognition (*pravartakadhījanakatva*); this is the suggested *upādhi*. [The author replies: "Not so" (*na*).

The meaning is that, given the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) and being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*), the generator of an impelling cognition is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*). He refutes the pervasion of the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*) with the words: "Brahman... (999).
Because the grounds for validity exist, this which has been stated is not correct.
We have stated the cause (hetu), but not the efficient cause (kāraṇa). || 912 ||

He refutes the intended negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, that "the subject under dispute is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because, while being a sentence, it does not produce a motivating cognition, like the sentence 'an old ox' (*jaradgava*)"—by stating "prāmāṇya... [etc.]. He states "hetuśca... [etc. anticipating the objection that there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) in the argument: "The subject under dispute is a means of valid cognition, because it possesses its causes, like that which is generally accepted. It has thus been shown that the production of a certain cognition accompanied by a result is the defining condition (*prayojaka*) of validity.

Up to this point... The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). It rejects the notion that the capacity to generate a motivating cognition (*pravartaka-dhī*) is the determinant (*prayojaka*) of validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Regarding the term "activity" (*pravṛtti*): because it would follow that prohibitive statements (*niṣedha-vākya*) lack validity, the capacity to generate a dissuading cognition (*nivartaka-dhī*) is also not a determinant. This is because neither cause exists in each individual case, and thus there would be invalidity; furthermore, there can be no fixed rule regarding the determinant in the absence of a corresponding pervasion (*anugama*) with the determinandum (*prayojya*).
The meaning is: "because of non-pervasion. || 992 ||
"This is our ornament: that the fruit of knowledge, which effects the destruction of the seeds for the continued operation of all [phenomena], brings about rebirth.
Regarding the statement that the cognition "I am Brahman" does not generate an impelling thought, he says: "This is our ornament."
The word "of the Vedāntas" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For those who accept the authority of the Vedāntas, this is their ornament:

that the fruitfulness of knowledge consists precisely in its being the destroyer of false cognition, attachment, and so forth, which serve as the causes for all worldly activity; and that it produces such knowledge.
Otherwise, if it were merely a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatayā*), its authority regarding the reality of things would not be established. This is the meaning. || 993 ||
By means of the analysis as described above, there is the negation of the three modes of existence.
That has been accomplished in its entirety by stating the cause for its perpetual attainment.

Having stated that because they produce the seed as previously described, their status as a means (*mānatā*) is like that of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), and thus it is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), he restates what was said through the investigation of injunctions such as "never at any time" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by what has been stated": the connection is that by describing the cause for the certain attainment of that knowledge, the negation of the three types of injunctions—original, restrictive, and exclusive—in their entirety has been accomplished through the investigation of injunctions. || 994 ||
And I have stated that the injunction "tameva" (that very one) is impossible.
Because [liberation] is attained by its own inherent nature alone, as is the case with the meditation on the Self. || 915 ||
1 kha. *tatrāpi* | 2 ka. ga. *’rtanam* | śrī | kha. *’rtanā* | bī’ | [vol2, page 323] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 617

He restates what was said in the passage "Having known [it] through wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñām*) with the words "not [as] an object" (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "the wise man, having known that very [Self], should practice wisdom" (*tam eva dhīro vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*), he says: "I shall explain at the occasion of commenting on that sentence why it is impossible for this to have the meaning of an injunction regarding another form of knowledge. The meaning of this [injunction] is either the verbal knowledge concerning Brahman or the meditation (*upāsanā*) consisting in the repetition of that [knowledge].

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By its own nature" (*svarasena*). Since verbal knowledge regarding the Self and the meditation upon it are attained even without an injunction, an injunction is impossible for them, just as it is for other types of knowledge. This was stated by the phrases beginning with "not related to the true nature of the Self" (*naivātmayāthātmyasaṃbandhī*) and "not thus a direct awakening to reality as it is" (*naivaṃ sākṣādyathāvastubodhasya*).
Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "vijñāyate" (is known) is that there is no injunction for meditation and the like either. || 999 ||
For even an ordinary person here does not worship the non-self as the self.
It is stated that through such worship, the attainment of that [state] is eternal. || 916 ||

Having restated the established doctrine (*vṛtta*) by means of two explanatory verses (*vārtika*) with the intention of stating something further, he declares that which is intended to be stated: "The Self" (*ātmānam*).
Both the world and the class of disputants who follow it do not, failing to perceive the Self as "I," perceive the non-Self on the plane of empirical activity.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because"; the word *tat* has the sense of "therefore. Therefore, because the attainment of the worship of the Self is eternal, there is no injunction (*vidhi*) regarding it.
This is the meaning. || 916 ||
For even if it were admitted that the Self is cognizable through the notion of "I," [the following would still apply].
The arising of the cognition of "not-self" is preceded by the cognition of "I. || 917 ||

Furthermore, for one who desires that the meditation on the Self (*ātma-upāsti*) be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), one must consider whether it is intended as an object of knowledge (*jñāna-karma*) or as the locus (*āśraya*) of that [knowledge]. Having raised this dilemma, he states the failure of the injunction regarding the first alternative: "I" (*aham*). In this context, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate conformity with the common consensus of both ordinary people and investigators. He uses the phrase "also" (*api ca*) to bring together the contradiction between the object and the agent when the Self is grasped by the notion of "I. And thus—

The implication is that, according to the Bhaṭṭa school and other systems, there is no injunction [regarding the meditation on the Self], because such meditation is already established as eternal. || 917 ||
The self always worships the self through the continuous association with the cognition thereof.
For those whose cognitions of a self have been entirely eliminated, worship is attained as a constant state.

To the question, "Even if the cognition of 'I' (ahaṃdhī) is preceded by the cognition of non-self (anātmadhi), how can the worship of the Self (ātmopāsti) be eternally attained?", he says: "The Self" (ātma).

Because all cognitions of non-self are connected with the cognition of the Self, the Self always attends to itself; thus, the construction is that the worship of the Self is eternally attained. || 918 ||
For even if it is admitted that the internal self is the cause of consciousness, [the following applies].
The attainment of constant worship results from the knowledge of that [reality], because of its connection with it. || 919 ||

It refutes another alternative with the words "vijñāna" (consciousness). The word "hi" is used to state that the view of the self as the substratum of the cognition of objects is the position accepted by those who follow the system of the Guru (Prabhākara). He says "tajjñānānām" (of the cognitions of those [objects]) because non-self-cognitions are preceded by the cognition of the self.
Even though non-self-cognitions manifest the self as their substratum, nevertheless, they are preceded by the manifestation of that [self].

This must be accepted by them: Is the cognition "I" (aham) with an object or without an object? In the first case, since the Self would be perceived through its power, the subsequent cognitions of non-self would not reveal it;

for if those [subsequent cognitions] were themselves self-revealing, it would be impossible for them to be cognitions of non-self. In the second case, the rule that the verb "to know" (*jānāti*) is necessarily transitive would be violated. Therefore, the meaning is that even in the Guru's system (Prabhākara), the meditation on the Self (*ātmopāsti*) cannot be something to be enjoined. || 999 ||
610 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter— Volume 2, Page 324]
Moreover, even when an injunction has been accepted, no engagement [with the action] is desired.
When everything is perceived as the Self, there is no further activity, because it would lack a cause.

He states another defect regarding the position that there is an injunction for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*). [The phrase] "Even if admitted" (*abhyupete’pi*) refers here to the statement concerning the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. The meaning is that even if an injunction is accepted in that regard, the resulting activity (*pravṛtti*) is not established. The reason for this is stated as "all" (*sarvam*).

Since ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, and because of the destruction of passion and so forth born from that [ignorance], when the realization occurs that "everything is indeed the Self," there is no activity.
Such is the meaning. || 920 ||
"This injunction is for the purpose of restriction"—such is the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya.
Even granting [the opponent's position], I shall explain it; thus, this is consistent.

Regarding the question of how the Commentator accepts a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) in the passage "having known" (*vijñāya*), given that there is no injunction for either the worship of the Self or the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, he says: "Restrictive... Even while accepting an injunction, he intends to demonstrate that the Vedāntas have the real entity as their primary purport; with this in mind, the statement in the Commentary—"it serves the purpose of a restrictive injunction regarding what might [otherwise] occur in certain cases"—is appropriate. Therefore, this is an argument based on a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*).
The meaning is "fame. || 921 ||
Not even one [such case] is possible, due to the weight of the reasoning already stated.
Since this is a formal procedure, this statement is made as a commitment.
"Why is it not accepted that the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) was intended by the Commentator himself? To this he replies: "Not at all. He states the reason:
because the logic establishing the eternal attainment of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmadhiyaḥ*) is more powerful. This is expressed in the verse beginning with "yathokta" (as stated). || 922 ||
For perception, when it is being performed, succeeds by depending upon an object.
The self and the non-self, as well as their activity, [are established] because anything other than that is not proven. || 923 ||

He provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to explain the manner of the injunctions regarding observances (*niyamavidhi*) as set forth in the commentary. He says, "Perception" (*darśanam*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that it is because knowledge without an object of support (*nirālambana-jñāna*) is impossible. He analyzes what that action (*karman*) is by saying, "The self" (*ātma*). He states the reason for the restriction to the twofold nature of action by saying, "Of that which is other than that" (*tadanyasya*). || 923 ||
Just as the production of rice depends upon threshing.
Just so, the accomplishment of the vision [of reality] is achieved in dependence upon the self and other factors. || 924 ||
He states the aforementioned point by means of an illustration: "Just as... (924).
Just as threshing is restricted when it is only optionally obtained;
Thus, it is prescribed that one should meditate upon the Self as being "to be struck. (925)
Having established the foundation, he states the manner of the rule regarding the primary injunction by means of an illustration: "Of the threshing," etc.
Since rice can be produced even by splitting it with the fingernails and so forth, the performance of threshing is only optional;

in that context, the rule "one should thresh" serves as a restriction (*niyama*). Those actions which, when performed in a particular instance, serve a purpose, must be performed there—such as threshing and the like.

Since there is no benefit in performing them upon the *jyā* (bowstring), they are not to be performed there; therefore, those acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) pertain to the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth by way of their result.
[End of Brāhmaṇa 4] — accompanied by the commentary named *Svapnaprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 619.

The relationship is fixed. For it has been stated by you that "their relationship with the meaning [is fixed]"; the meaning here is that there is likewise a fixed arrangement in this case as well. The word *hi* (for) is used to indicate that restrictive rules (*niyamavidhi*) are accepted in many other instances. || 925 ||
Therefore, for the attainment of the worship of the non-self, one should meditate upon the Self.
The cessation [of the notion of self] occurs through the power of meditating on non-self, but not from the words themselves. || 926 ||

He illustrates the nature of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) with the words "not the non-self" (*anātma*). He states its result with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*); that is to say, by the force of this restriction, there is a cessation of the meditation on the non-self. Now, one might ask: how is it appropriate for a single word to have two meanings—both the injunction to meditate on the Self and the cessation of meditation on the non-self? To this he replies: "But not... (*na tu*). [The first meaning is] the meditation on the Self.

The meaning is that it is stated as something to be accomplished (*kārya*), and by implication, the meditation on the non-Self (*anātma-upāsti*) is excluded; for that [meditation] is not based on the direct word (*śābdī*), according to the maxim: "That which is a meaning derived by implication (*arthāt*) is not the intended meaning of the injunction (*codanārtha*). The word *tu* (but/however) is used to reflect upon the aforementioned maxim. || 926 ||
If the attainment of the worship of the Self were possible anywhere directly;
If that were the case, let there be a restriction at will by means of scripture, just as in the case of threshing and so forth. (927)

In order to show that the injunction of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is merely a concessive statement (*upetyavāda*), he refutes the charge of non-attainment by demonstrating the constant attainment of the meditation on the Self. [He says] "If," meaning "in some place" and so forth; "directly" means "by means of a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). || 927 ||
Without embracing the inward-facing reality, nothing that exists externally can be attained.
Since consciousness arises from that, the worship of the Self is therefore always [to be performed] from it. || 928 ||

That being the case, a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) is appropriate, because there is the possibility of an unobtained portion regarding that which brings it about; for the meditation on the Self is indeed sometimes unobtained, as it does not always persist. To this, he says: "The inner [Self]," etc. (928).
Furthermore, because it lacks connection with a self, this birth does not have the self as its agent.
Since consciousness is entirely [present], therefore there would be constant attainment. || 929 ||

He states another reason for its being eternally attained: "even before" (prāgapi). The meaning is that since every cognition of the non-self is necessarily preceded by the cognition of "I," the cognition of the Self is eternally attained. It should be understood that although this was already stated previously, it is recalled here as an incidental point. ||929||
"And it has not been stated that the agent of meditation exists apart from the object of meditation."
Therefore, a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) is possible here, because there is no difference [of the Self] within the Self.

And because there is no distinction between the object of meditation (*upāsya*) and the meditator (*upāsaka*), there is no restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the meditation on the Self; thus he says: "The object of meditation... He states the reason for the absence of distinctions such as the object of meditation by saying: "In the Self..."—since once the Self is known, even mere duality is impossible. By this, the impossibility of other types of injunctions should also be understood through the same logic. || 930 ||
And it has been said: "With respect to the nature of logical reasoning, a fixed rule is extremely difficult to establish."
Therefore, for the purpose of establishing the weakness of the injunction, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated this.

Not only is the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) not established due to the absence of a distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper, but furthermore, because [the Self] is "the innermost, eternal" and so forth, it is beyond action.

He says "and because it has been stated" on the grounds of the reasoning already set forth. Thus, since a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is impossible, the author of the Commentary’s statement of it is a concessionary argument (*upetyavāda*).

He concludes with the word "mātram" (only). Regarding the phrase "of the injunction": the author of the Bhāṣya indeed stated that it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) for the purpose of establishing the weakness of the original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
Since he began by stating that it is not an original injunction, the meaning is that even a restrictive injunction is untenable according to the reasoning already set forth. || 939 ||
Whatever has been stated, such as "like a released arrow" and so forth, [is now addressed].
The impossibility of that as well will be clearly explained further below.

Surely, just as a released arrow initiates its effect until the exhaustion of its momentum when there is an absence of obstacles such as stones, so too karma whose fruit has already begun must necessarily project passion and the like, because it is not contradicted by knowledge; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures concerning liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) if liberation were attained immediately.

Since even for the wise there is the possibility of forgetting the Self, the author of the Bhāṣya has supported the view that this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). To the question of how this could then be considered a "hypothetical argument" (*upetyavāda*), he says: "Mukta... Just as passion and the like are impossible for the wise, so it will be stated later in the Brahmakaṇḍikā through scripture, beginning with the words, "If one knows Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself," and so forth; nor is there a persistence of what has been sublated.

The mere [mention of] "mātra" (only) serves as the motivator for the injunction (*vidhi*), because that [injunction] is preceded by an adherence to such things as agency; therefore, he says that the statement of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is merely an acceptance-based discourse (*aṅgīkāravādamātra*). [He uses the word] "tasya" (of that). || 932 ||
This is the meditation on the non-self, because of the employment of the word "this."
Because it is observed in passages such as "the dear," the meditation on the "unpleasant" arises from a [specific] quality. (933)

Since it is not a rule that a word must produce a cognition of a composite object or one that is mediate (*parokṣa*), it is possible for a non-composite, immediate (*aparokṣa*) cognition to be verbal (*śābda*). Since the human goal is accomplished through verbal knowledge alone—whether by that very knowledge, by its repetition, or by a third cognition—there is no need for anything else to be enjoined; thus it has been stated that the Vedāntas are the means of valid knowledge (*māna*) regarding the pure, established Self. Now, the meaning of the word *iti* in the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'This is the Self'" is intended [by the author] as explained by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakṛt*).

He urges [the opponent] to speak by saying "anātmeti" (as non-self). For in passages such as "one should meditate on it as dear," it is observed that there is meditation upon Prāṇa and so forth—which are not dear—by means of qualities such as being dear; therefore, here too, because the word "ātman" follows the word "iti," the intention is to teach meditation upon the Pradhāna, which is under discussion as the unmanifested state and possesses the quality of being the non-self, rather than upon the meaning of the word "ātman."

The meaning is that [the word "speech"] is not intended to be the object of meditation (*pāsyatvena avivakṣitatvāt*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the following sentences are included: "One should meditate on this as wisdom," "One should meditate on this as truth," "One should meditate on this as the infinite," "One should meditate on this as bliss," and "One should meditate on this as stability.

For in those [passages], speech, sight, hearing, mind, and heart—which are [ordinarily] of the nature of non-wisdom, untruth, and so forth—are presented as objects of meditation characterized by their respective qualities such as wisdom and the rest.
Just as it was desired there, so shall it be here as well.
However, it is not the self itself that is contemplated here as an entity possessing the single quality of the self.
And from the statement that the Self is to be meditated upon, there arises a distinction from the Śruti. || 934 ||

One might ask: why could it not be that the very reality of the Self, possessing the attributes of the Self, is what is to be meditated upon? To this he says: "The Self. The current sentence is referred to by the locative case. The meaning is that because the relationship of attribute and substrate cannot exist in one and the same thing, that which possesses the attributes of the Self—which is a non-Self entity—is what must be meditated upon; thus, the meditation on the non-Self alone is intended here as the injunction. He provides another reason for this, stating: "The Self. [If it were] meditation on the Self...
The remainder [of the sentence] is that this alone is intended to be expressed here. || 934 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 327] ✓ 8 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 621.
The distinction [of the self] is clearly evident from the statement that it is the object of the cognition "this is I."
And because of the prohibition of the worship of a self, as stated in the passage, "They do not see. (935)

He clarifies the distinction [between the two cases] with the words "the self" (*ātmānam*). In the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), because the accusative case is not heard, the self is mentioned as the object (*karman*);
but here, due to the absence of the hearing of the accusative and because the word "self" (*ātma*) functions as the agent (*kartṛ*), the distinction between these two is quite evident.

Thus, the meaning is that the non-self itself, possessing the qualities of the self, is the object of meditation. For this reason as well, he states that this is indeed the meditation on the non-self.

Regarding the phrase "meditation on the Self": since meditation on the Self is prohibited by the statement "they do not see him," the meaning is that what is intended here is meditation on that which is not the Self, so as to avoid contradiction with the preceding and following passages. || 935 ||
This [objection] cannot hold on the grounds that the Self is understood as the object of meditation in the supplementary portion of the passage.
"Desirable, beyond the other shore, dear," and so forth, as the remainder. || 936 ||

He refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that by considering the introduction and conclusion, the meditation on the non-Self (*anātma-upāsti*) is intended here—with the words "Not the Self" (*nātmeti*). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows:

this cannot be a meditation on the non-Self, because the fact that the Self is the object of meditation is understood from the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).
