To the question, "How is the status of the Self as the object of meditation established from the remainder of the passage? he replies with the words "to be reached" (*padanīya*). "This very [Self] is to be reached at the end of all this..."

The meaning is that the status of the Self as the object of worship is established by the remainder of the sentence: "This Self is indeed the most excellent; one should worship the Self alone as dear," and "One should know the Self alone. (936)
That "the self is dear" is understood from the remainder of the sentence.
Therefore, the Self alone should be the object of worship; the non-Self is not intended as an object of worship. || 937 ||
He states that in the sentence concerning the fruit—"he who meditates on the Self as dear, for him [there is no fear]"—the fact that the Self is to be meditated upon is understood.

He says, "the Self. Having established the understanding that the Self is to be meditated upon from the remainder of the passage, he states the resulting conclusion: "Therefore. Based on the implied cessation of other [meditations], he says, "not the non-Self. || 937 ||
And that [objection] is not a refutation of the incompleteness of the meditation on the Self;
rather, the word "iti" is used for the purpose of making known its transcendence of verbal cognition. (938)

Regarding the objection that because the worship of the Self is prohibited, it cannot be the object of worship, he says: "Because it is not the Whole" (*akṛtsnatvāt*). The meaning is that the prohibition of viewing [the Self] as qualified by functions such as breathing is due to its being limited and therefore perishable; thus, it is not the object of the worship of the Self, as this would contradict the supplementary portion of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to combine the contradiction with the context of the current passage regarding the prohibition of the worship of the Self. As for the word "yat" (*yattu*)...

Because the referent of the word "Self" is a quality of that which is to be meditated upon through yoga, this sentence does not have the purpose of enjoining meditation on the Self; thus [it says] "the word," etc. (Sūtra 9.3.8).
From which words turn back, as well as [the description] "not this, not this," and so forth.
This being so, everything is meaningful; otherwise, it would be meaningless. (939)

He states the conformity with other passages regarding its having the meaning already explained: "Since... If, however, the word *iti* were not present, the sequence would not be as clear. [Note: Variants from manuscripts *ka* and *ga* are indicated in the source.]

If the meaning were already stated [by the preceding], then the [injunction] "one should meditate upon the Self" would be redundant; consequently, it would follow that the Self is accessible through verbal cognition.
He states that the statement would otherwise be purposeless: "Otherwise... (939).
For the purpose of removing the misconception that there is no self, it is designated by the word "self."
Therefore, this cannot be a separate statement, because it is a restatement of the meaning already expressed. || 940 ||

He refutes the argument beginning with "and because of the statement that the Self is to be meditated upon," etc., by saying "anātma" (non-Self). The meaning is that the sentence "the Self alone," etc., forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the preceding sentence, insofar as it serves the purpose of precluding meditation on what is not the Self. He states the reason why this sentence does not constitute a separate sentence from the former by saying "yathokta" (as stated): the meaning is that it merely restates the sense of that previous sentence. || 940 ||
"The instruction 'one should meditate on it as the Self' provides the reason for this."
This [definition] is stated for the sake of removing the fault of incompleteness regarding the inner self (pratīc). || 941 ||

Regarding the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'," the meaning established there is that one should contemplate the Self as being accessible through both word and cognition.

Having introduced the causal statement—"for here... and so forth—to state the reason when a reason was required, and having already explained it, the author introduces it again for further elaboration:
"As 'I am the Self'. He explains that: "Because of incompleteness... For limitation indeed...

The meaning is that since there is the defect [of limiting adjuncts] because of the scriptural statement that "whatever is water is mortal," and thus the mortality of what is small [is heard], the non-duality of the Self is stated by means of a logical sentence (*hetuvākya*) for the purpose of refuting that [mortality]. || 941 ||
The relationship of the self with non-self entities is without remainder.
Like a rope-snake and so forth, the subsequent [perception] remains as a negation of the prior [error]. 942.

He states the justification for non-duality (*advayatva*) therein with the words "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). Because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the Self and the non-Self—just as there is an identity between a rope and a snake—and because of the absence of any non-Self other than the inner witness (*pratyak*), just as there is no snake apart from the rope, that non-duality exists; for the rope, while experiencing identity with the snake, does not tolerate the existence of the snake as something separate from itself. In the same way, the connection of the Self with the non-Self is intended to be without any remainder whatsoever.
And thus, because there is no "other" (parāc) remaining apart from this "inner" (pratyañc), its non-duality is established; such is the meaning. || 942 ||
In that Self, everything would indeed remain unknown.
And when one thing is known, everything is known, because this entire world consists of all things [subsumed] within that [single reality]. || 943 ||

Furthermore, he states that the non-duality of the Self is established through the authority of such scriptural passages as "That by which the unheard becomes heard," etc., using the word *sarvam* (all). He provides the reasoning for this with the phrase *tāvat-tvāt* (because it is of that same extent). Since the Self is the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything, everything is of the same extent as the Self; thus, the meaning is that the knowledge of all things is established through the knowledge of the Self. || 943 ||
When examined through reasoning, the self-nature of that which is non-self is found to be like space.
If he is rejected by him, let this non-self be established.

Furthermore, he states that when the non-self (anātman)—such as a snake—is analyzed through reasonings such as having a beginning and an end and being visible, it is established that the Self is the reality (tattva) of everything, just as a rope is the reality of a snake; therefore, its non-duality (advayatva) is logical. He says: "By reasoning" (yuktyā). [The superimposed] is [dependent upon] the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna)...
1. ka. parākū.
[Vol.
2, Page 329] 4 Brāhmaṇam], accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 623.
The word "hi" (for) establishes as a reason the absence of an empty nature. He states the defect in the opposing view: "pratyākhyāta" (rejected), etc. Anā—
If the self were not itself its own reality, then, being devoid of its own nature (niḥsvarūpa), it could not be established anywhere; this is the meaning. || 944 ||
For the Self, which is unattached, devoid of qualities, and non-dual, follows the reality of non-self.
If it were not established by itself, what other remedy could there be than that? || 945 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the Self is the reality of the knower because of its connection with the non-Self? In that case, there would be a loss of its quality of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*). To this, he says: "Not the non-Self" (*anātmeti*). The meaning is that it is well known that the substrate is not actually touched by the qualities or defects produced through superimposition. Since the Self is unattached, it is impossible for it to be the establisher of the non-Self; likewise, the non-Self could not be established by itself. Thus [he speaks].

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). The word *cet* (if) is used for emphasis. The meaning is that if the non-self were established by itself, it would follow that it is nothing other than the Self; thus, what is called "the non-self" would not be established at all. Anticipating the objection that because the Self is unattached (*asaṅga*), there must be something else entirely distinct from the non-self to establish it, he asks: "What else? Since there is no object other than the Self and the non-self, [there is nothing else].
The meaning is "another practitioner. || 945 ||
Just as there is a sense of oneness regarding the various objects imagined through delusion in a recognized garland.
In this way, for those things constructed by that ignorance, unity is indeed accepted as being like the west. || 946 ||

One might object: "Since there is no other means of realization, let everything superimposed upon the inward-facing self shine forth within the nature of experience; nevertheless, what does this have to do with the present topic?
Anticipating this doubt, he states—with an illustration—that through the knowledge of the Self, the result is that everything becomes nothing but That. He says: "When [the snake] is known...

Just as when a garland is recognized as being a *sruc* (ladle) [or rather, as a garland], such that one understands, "This is a garland," then for the snake and so forth produced by delusion regarding it, there is identity with that [garland], and nothing remains separate.

The meaning is that when the Inner Self (*pratīc*) is known, since the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which arise from ignorance of That—are admitted to be nothing but That, the establishment of knowledge occurs upon the knowledge of That. Alternatively, having established the non-duality of the Self through scripture and reasoning, he concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "For here" (*atra hi*) along with its illustration, [stating]: "When [the Self] is known," etc. (Verse 946).
In the object denoted by the word "self," which consists of both the particular and the universal forms.
"Some maintain that all particulars are included within [the universal].

Having stated the meaning of the statement regarding the cause according to his own view, and having raised the position of Bhartṛprapañca as mentioned previously, he raises it once more to elaborate on the response already employed, beginning with the word "Self" (ātman). In this aforementioned non-duality denoted by the term "Self," [regarding] the vital breaths...
All the functions of the channels become one. || 947 ||
That [object] is presented collectively in its generality, and also individually through its particularities.
In this manner, one should always worship the entire supreme Brahman with diligent effort. || 948 ||

How then, in the absence of both generality and particularity, can Brahman possess totality? Or, in the absence of those, how does the previously mentioned objection not apply? To this he says: "By means of the general. Just as when a particularity is internally contained within it, the cognition directed toward that [object] becomes a grasper of the whole precisely because it includes that internalized particularity. Here, the generality is the state of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*), and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*).

There are specific distinctions [to be made]. Since Brahman is "entire" (kṛtsna) in the manner shown, he states the resulting consequence: the absence of the previously mentioned exceptions. He says, "entire" (kṛtsnam). The word "always" (sadā) expresses its long duration. The word "with effort" (yatnataḥ) invokes the remaining two qualifying attributes. || 948 ||
The Remainder Portion (śeṣabhāga).
In some cases, the whole is described by means of its states, as if it possessed those states. *Sureśvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter.
In that manner, some explain it as having the nature of cause and effect. || 949 ||
Likewise, it is like a nave, a rim, and spokes, through the division of parts and possessors of parts.
The great-souled ones indeed explain [it] by the power of the traditional transmission.

Having shown the completeness (*kṛtsnatva*) of Brahman by way of its nature as both the universal and the particular, [the author] states that others have described this completeness in another manner—namely, that the world is a state (*avasthā*) belonging to Brahman, just like the state of being Brahman itself. He says: "like a state. He further states: "as effect," meaning that completeness has also been expressed in such a manner that Brahman is the cause and the world is the effect, or that Brahman is the whole (*aṃśin*) and the world is a part (*aṃśa*). The word "somewhere" (*kvacit*) applies to both cases.

This is a citation from his own work. He provides an illustration for the relationship of part and whole between the world and Brahman with the word "navel" (*nābhi*). Just as the navel, the rim, and the spokes are the constituent parts of a chariot wheel as a whole, so too the world and Brahman stand in the relation of part and possessor of parts. Thinking that the system of Bhartṛprapañca is unauthoritative because it involves mutual contradictions, he concludes his refutation of that view with a touch of derision: "They explain... (*vyācakṣate*).
Thus; in order to indicate the disagreement of the learned regarding his commentary, the word "kila" (allegedly) was used. || 949 || 950 ||
Because the syllables lack intended meaning and because it is impossible according to logical reasoning.
We do not possess such power to immediately practice that supreme [path] directly. 951.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that because the syllables of the Veda lack conformity with an object that is both composite and unitary, and because such [an interpretation] is impossible due to the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated, authoritative persons (prāmāṇikāḥ) are not able to understand the Supreme Brahman—which in reality does not possess such manifold flavors—as being possessed of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). This is expressed in the verse beginning with "akṣarāṇām. || 999 ||
That wherein the world is unknown when it is unknown, and known when it is known.
That Brahman, being of such a nature, is considered to be all-encompassing, unlike things such as cows or trees.

To the question of how Brahman can be "entire" (kṛtsna) in the absence of both totality and partiality, he says: "When it is unknown... This means that when this [Brahman] is unknown, everything is unknown; and when it is known, that alone is known. Thus, Brahman is indeed non-dual, of a single essence, and undivided. As for the claim that Brahman is "entire" through the relationship of universal and particular as illustrated by examples such as cows and so forth, he says: "No. Just as...

The entirety [of Brahman] is not like that of a cow through the relation of universal and particular, nor of a tree through the relation of part and whole, nor of the ocean through the relation of state and its possessor, nor of clay through the relation of cause and effect; rather, Brahman is known from the scripture as a whole through both its collective and distributive aspects. Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is entirely without distinctions, and not in any other manner. || 952 ||
Universals and particulars exclude one another.
Therefore, for one who speaks of [the self] as being the vital breaths and so forth, it would not be logical for those [attributes] to exist in their entirety [in every individual]. || 953 ||

To the question of how Brahman, by virtue of the relationship between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), does not become something limited (*kṛtsna*), he says: "The universals... Universals such as cowness, horseness, selfhood, and so forth; particulars such as the humpbacked, the hornless, the red, Devadatta, and so forth—just as in the case of that which is qualified by the functions of breathing and so on mentioned in the passage beginning with "breathing" (*prāṇan*); thus he provides an example for their mutual exclusion, saying: "like breathing and so on. Mutual...

He states the result of the exclusion: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "therefore, for them, there is no singularity as one Brahman. The view that "all that" (*sāmān*) is "the whole" (*samastaṃ tat*), and so forth, has been refuted. Furthermore, that which exists as having states (*avasthāvat*)—by way of being a state (*avasthātva*), by way of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatva*), and by way of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*)—[is also refuted].

The state of being "complete" (kārtsyam) has been mentioned; however, the sense is that even there, because these states and so forth are mutually exclusive, they cannot logically constitute a single Brahman, and thus their incompleteness is equal. || 993 ||
Furthermore, because of its infinity, its cognition cannot be brought about even by God through effort.
It can never be performed either gradually or all at once.

Furthermore, as for the multiplicity of Brahman, is it for the purpose of perception (*dṛṣṭi*) or for the purpose of meditation (*upāsti*)? It is not the first [option], as he says: "Because of its infinity" (*tadānantyāt*).
Since universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are innumerable, and the lifespan of a person is limited, the realization of Brahman—which consists of universals and the like—is not possible.
The meaning is that it cannot be produced at any time, even by some means, in its entirety, whether successively or simultaneously. || 954 ||
But regarding the cultivation of identity [with the deity], there is not even the possibility for men.
How could that activity be performed even by one who is most skillful? || 955 ||

He refutes the second [position] with the words "tādātmya" (identity). Among those under discussion, even for someone with extremely subtle vision, it is impossible to entertain even the possibility of meditating on such a Brahman as the reality of the Self; for meditation must be preceded by cognition, and a cognition of the infinite number of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth is impossible. The word "api" (even) indicates that if there is no possibility of meditation, its performance is all the more remote.
He states the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so") with the words: "And the contact with that... (955).
Nor does it have the status of being the object of many worshippers, like the descent of the Gaṅgā.
Since there would be no accumulation through cultivation in each individual [moment] were that the case, [it follows that... || 956 ||

Now, it may be argued that although the meditation on Brahman possessing manifold flavors cannot be performed by a single person, it could nevertheless be performed by many— just as, for instance, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara, who were reduced to ashes by the Lord named Vāsudeva due to a particular circumstance,
were purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā and, relying on the power of austerity with great effort, achieved success in the world beyond.

He says "Gaṅgā" [in the verse] to show that, unlike the descent of the Gaṅgā upon earth—which was accomplished by many agents such as Bhagīratha—this is not so here. The meaning is that although the meditation on Brahman may have many practitioners, because the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) does not accumulate in each individual person, no one at all attains direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the object of worship in its entirety. || 996 ||
Having become a god through the accumulation of meditative cultivation, a person goes to the gods.
Thus, among all things, that which a person intends to accomplish is impossible [to achieve]. (957)

He says "The Lord" (*deva*) to show that there should be no realization [of this] because it would contradict the Śruti and Smṛti. Since meditation (*upāsti*) cannot have many agents, and since it must be stated that it has a single agent, he concludes what was previously mentioned with "Thus, by all... (*iti sarva...*). The word "thus" (*iti*) expresses the statement of meditation.

For which man indeed could meditation—which is impossible to perform regarding all objects such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, as well as Brahman whose nature consists of them—be performed by you?
The meaning is that it is desired by the piercer (the creator). || 957 ||
Even that which is known in its entirety, as well as other things, is not directly [perceived].
How can it be said here that such a totality is known by means of knowledge? 958.

Furthermore, when that [object] is seen, its own nature and everything else is not seen at all; therefore, its totality (*kārtsnya*) is contradictory—this is the meaning. || 953 || [Note: *kha* reads *dā* as well.
Sureśvarācārya says in his *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, first chapter, verse 626:
"That which is known... That which is known is also, by its own nature, other than that [object], and by means of that knowledge, it is not coextensive with it.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is not known by means of inference (*liṅgena*) to be exactly like that, nor is it entirely so; "here" refers to the statement of the scripture (*śāstra*). || 958 ||
Because it is opposed [to the nature of reality], the external object is not apprehended by the cognition of the individual self.
Since the word "supremacy" (parāśrī) is also stated as a reason, there is no cognition of the whole, such as the body and so forth, from this [word]. (959)

Furthermore, it must be stated by one who maintains that [the Self] is both identical and distinct that the external object (*parāgvastu*) is grasped through the cognition of the "not-Self" (*parāgbuddhi*), and the internal object (*pratyagvastu*) is grasped through the cognition of the "Self" (*pratyagbuddhi*).
In this regard, he first states that the cognition of the "not-Self" does not have the internal as its object, saying: "The external...

The meaning of the reason is that there is a mutual contradiction between the external (*parāk*) and the internal (*pratyak*). Nor does the cognition of the "not-Self" grasp the internal; thus he says: "...the cognition of the not-Self."

The meaning is that by stating the reason for the non-objectivity of the Self—namely, "the senses are directed outward" (parāñci khāni)—it follows that even the inner Self (pratyak) is not apprehended through the cognition of the non-Self (anātma-buddhi).

By the logic already stated, since the opponent does not possess the knowledge of everything, such as the universal (sāmānya), when a single thing is known, the establishment of the complete reality for him is not achieved; this is the conclusion expressed by the words "not from this" (nātaḥ). || 959 ||
Likewise, when the Self is known, everything becomes known.
"By which the unheard becomes heard"—in what [does this occur]? Likewise for the others. (960)

Furthermore, just as there is a single flavor (*ekarasya*) of the Self, so too are statements such as "By which all this is known, through which the unheard becomes heard" and others heard in the Vedāntas; these would be contradicted if the Self possessed multiple flavors (*nānārasatva*). Thus he says: "In that way" (verse 960).
Even when there is the apprehension of identity with the self, it is due to the apprehension of only the difference between selves.
There would be no apprehension of the self, objects, universals, or particulars. || 961 ||

[Objection: Surely, when the universal (sāmānya) is grasped, all particulars are grasped by virtue of being included within it; thus, even for the opponent, scriptural passages concerning the "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" are not contradicted. To this, he replies: "The Self" (ātman). It should be understood that even if the universal of non-self is grasped, because only its particulars would be grasped, the universals and particulars of the Self would not be grasped. || 969 ||
In the perception of things both collectively and individually, such [arguments] and others are extremely difficult to establish.
And the assertion that [the self] is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior is untenable. (962)

Furthermore, if there were absolute difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), their coexistence would be impossible; likewise, even in the case of absolute non-difference, their coexistence would be untenable because one or the other would remain alone.

Considering that difference and non-difference are contradictory, and that if they were not contradictory, all contradiction would be abolished everywhere, he says: "All... By the word "thus" (*evam*), he refers back to the defects already stated regarding the alternatives of difference, non-difference, and so forth. [The text continues: "of the universal..."

Furthermore, since particularities (viśeṣa) abide in their own individual forms, they cannot be subsumed within a single [universal] due to that contradiction; and if they do not so abide, they lack existence in themselves, so of what could there be subsumption within one? Moreover, without that [subsumption], the realization of all through a single cognition is not established—such is the meaning of the word "etc. Furthermore, he states that the view of the whole and the parts is untenable because it contradicts the scriptures (śruti) which teach the absence of distinctions (nirviśeṣatva), saying: "apūrva... (962).
The cognition of the inner self arises from objects of knowledge and means of knowledge that are external.
Raisa has spoken well regarding the state of being both collective and individual.

And for this reason as well, that [position] is not tenable; he says "the other" (*parām*). For there is the sublation of non-self-objects and their cognitions by the cognition of the inner self (*pratyagdhiyā*)—this being the meaning of "in this" (*asmin*).

Regarding what you have said concerning the "entirety and partiality" (samastavyastatā) of the Self—namely, that [the Self] is the object denoted by the word "Self" and so forth—that is incorrect; the meaning is that because the Self is of a single essence (ekarasa), such a state [of being both whole and part] is impossible for it. || 963 ||
Likewise, when the Brahman-nature of that which is to be meditated upon has been directly declared by Śruti, [it follows that the meditation is on Brahman].
Since this is not "this," how can there be such a thing as being both collective and individual? (964)

Furthermore, if Brahman were both as a whole and in its parts, it would follow that it is both an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and an object of meditation (*upāsyatva*); since this contradicts the scriptures, the view of Brahman as both whole and parts is not tenable. He states this with the word "tathā" (likewise). The word "tathā" serves to include an additional reason. The term "of the object of meditation" (*upāsyasya*) is an elliptical expression;
it should be understood to mean "and of the object of knowledge" (*vedyasya*) as well. || 964 ||
By the total negation of everything beginning with the gross, [one realizes] the imperishable inner self.
Likewise, because the entire world is described as being woven warp and woof upon that ultimate cause. || 965 ||

For this reason as well, he states that [the Self] is neither the whole nor the parts: "sthūlādi" (beginning with the gross). The meaning is that since the Imperishable (akṣara) is designated as being devoid of distinctions through the negation of all specific attributes, it does not possess the nature of the whole or its parts. Furthermore, in that very same [passage], there is the statement regarding the inclusion of the world along with its cause within it.

He says that this syllable does not have a form consisting of a combination [of parts] and so forth, by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*). That is to say, it does not possess the state of being both combined and separate. || 961 ||
And an object directed outward cannot be perceived here by an inward-directed intellect.
And thus, neither the state of being both collective and individual is established through any means of valid cognition.

And because there is an absence of a means of knowledge (māna), he says that the reality is neither as a whole nor in its parts. Regarding the word "not": here, the path of empirical usage (vyavahāra) is understood. First of all, the means of knowledge regarding the self does not touch upon what is other than it, due to contradiction; even if another means of knowledge has that [other thing] as its object, the state of being both as a whole and in parts is not established for the self from that, because that [other means] does not touch the self. Nor will that [means of knowledge] touch the self itself.

And since this has already been refuted in the passage beginning with "parāñci" and "hetūkteḥ," the sense is that the manifold nature of a single entity does not follow from valid means of knowledge. || 966 ||
And having raised them up from the stage of pride, as well as from the stage of one who has [merely] understood [the teachings].
Since Brahman is taught as being solely the inner self (pratyagātman), how can there be both identity and difference? || 967 ||

And because it would contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he states that the Self is neither identical with nor different from [the aggregate of causes and effects]. He says "māna... etc. The meaning of such scriptural passages as "That by which one knows all this is itself beyond what is known" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.14) is stated here.
The sense is that this is said because it is Brahman, and because it is spoken of as Brahman. (967)
Neither collectively, nor individually, nor both together do these exist in the inner self (pratyagātman).
Let it be examined with an intellect inclined toward direct perception, if it is possible. || 968 ||
Furthermore, because it contradicts the experience of the wise, he states with the words beginning "no" that the Self is neither as a whole nor as parts.

The entire form of the inward-facing [Self] is perceived through the vision of the inward-facing; it is not perceived as separate, nor as both whole and parts. If a manifold form could be seen there, then let it be so perceived; but it is not so perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that there is only absolute homogeneity (aikarasya). || 968 ||
1 kha. "Immediately upon being spoken"; 2 kha. "Therefore, it is of a single form.
[Vol. 2, page 334] 628 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]
Why, moreover, should one abandon this [Vedic path], which accomplishes both seen and unseen goals?
"One should worship [the Self] as the Self"—this is the great injunction of the Śruti for us here. (969)
It was stated that by the sentence beginning with "For here" (*atra hi*), the self's state of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*) is taught through the refutation of other doctrines;

now, he introduces the objection to be set aside by the sentence beginning with "That which is to be reached by this path" (*tad etat padanīyam*). He asks: "Why? The word "this" (*idam*) refers to ritual action such as the *agnihotra*. The word "here" (*iha*) denotes the knowledge of the Self. The "greatness of effort" refers to the [effort] toward the knowledge of the Self that has been promised.

The proof is by means of a reason: since it is proper to undertake what is possible among the possible and the impossible, the sense is that actions obtainable without effort—such as those prescribed by the scriptures for lifelong performance—are not to be abandoned. || 969 ||
For this is the state to be reached, the supreme state beyond all that is non-self.
Because all objects of knowledge and all human goals are fully realized within the knowledge of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna). || 970 ||

He introduces the subsequent [verse]: "That which is to be reached" (*padanīyam*). Since non-selves lack both the states of being unknown and being known, this very reality of the Self (*ātmatattvam*)—which is the supreme goal (*param padam*)—must be known as something previously unknown; therefore, the meaning is that effort toward its knowledge is required by the Śruti.

As for the objection that it is not proper to exert excessive effort toward self-knowledge after abandoning ritual action (*karma*), which is established by such Śruti injunctions as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), [the response follows].

Regarding this, he says: "All," etc. The ellipsis is: "Even though the knowledge of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna) is obtainable through effort, there is an exceeding of effort [required] according to the Śruti. ||970||
For when the Inner Self is known, nothing whatsoever remains.
Whatever object or human goal may thus be the thing to be attained, || 971 ||
He says "na hi" (not indeed) to explain how, when there is knowledge of the Self, there is the completion of all objects of knowledge and all human goals.

The sense is that there is no reality other than the Self, which consists of unsurpassed bliss. Since this is the majesty of the knowledge of the Self, he says "padanīyam" (to be reached) to show that one should abandon the Agnihotra and other such rites and devote oneself to that alone. || 979 ||
But when the meaning of "non-self" is understood, it is like the awakening from the superimposed perception of snow.
Nothing would be fully known; therefore, the non-self is not what one desires to know.

Anticipating the objection that—since it is possible for all objects of knowledge and all human goals to be accomplished once the non-self (anātman), which is the essence of the universe, is known as described in the Sūtras and other texts—one should therefore seek to know that [non-self] just as one knows the Self—the author says: "The non-self," etc. Just as a snake superimposed upon its substrate, the rope denoted by the word "self," is not known either as the rope or as the snake, so too, even when the non-self object such as the thread (sūtra) superimposed upon the conscious Self is known, neither that form nor anything else [is truly known].
Therefore, it follows that a non-self is not intended to be the knower, because knowledge of such a thing would be fruitless; this is the meaning. || 972 ||
The genitive case here is possessive (śaiṣikī), used in view of the complete coherence [of the entire work].
For the self, being distinct from the body, does not enter into association with it. || 973 ||

Having explained that "this is the path to be traversed," he states the meaning of the two genitive cases in apposition in the phrase "of this entire [world]" (*asya sarvasya*). Regarding the word "of this" (*asya*):

the genitive case is employed in the sense of a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) with respect to the relationship between the Self and the aggregate of non-Self. By the term "remainder," a general relationship is expressed.

The meaning is that the reality of the Self is the related correlate (*saṃbandhin*) of the world, which is presented through perception and other means of knowledge, and it is this reality that is to be traversed. If the genitive is used in the sense of a specific relationship...

Fearing that there might be a distinction between the Self and the non-Self because a relationship depends upon those two—and thus fearing the loss of non-duality (advaita)—he says: "Of the inner self," etc.
[vol2, page 335] n.

Therefore, being distinct, the non-Self is not joined with That; the meaning is that because distinction involves mutual dependence and other such fallacies, it lacks any basis in valid cognition. || 973 ||
For there can be no relationship with the Self without a distinction from the non-Self.
The inner self is an indivisible essence; therefore, duality is not applicable to it.

"Let it be then that there is a conjunction of those two without division. [The author] says "no," because the genitive case is accepted only when there is a relation [of difference]. He states: "Not so" (*narte*). The meaning is that since a relation resides in two things, it cannot reside in one alone. This very point is suggested by the particle *hi*. How then is the genitive used as a residual (*śaiṣika*)? To this he says: "The inward... (*pratyag...*). The word should be divided as "the nature of non-division" (*avibhāgātmā*). The subject under discussion is non-division...

He refers [to it] by the word "of the going. Although, in reality, the non-dual does not touch upon duality, nevertheless, the genitive case is used by relying on an imagined relationship; this is the meaning. || 974 ||
Therefore, it is established that this [consciousness] is not situated in another external object that stands apart from it.
Because the intellect and so forth have as their sole reality only that [consciousness], like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope. || 975 ||
1.1 But surely duality is perceived; and that [duality] is not independent because it has a beginning and an end, nor is there any substratum for it other than the Self.

Anticipating the objection—“How can there be a non-connection with duality for the Self if that [duality] is imagined independently of any substratum?”—the author establishes the previously mentioned imagined relationship by saying “ataḥ” (therefore). Since a relationship between the Self and the non-Self is difficult to explain whether they are distinct or identical, it is only through the identity of superimposition (*adhyāsika-tādātmya*) that duality is perceived in the Self; however, in reality, such [duality] is unattainable in the Self, which is the meaning of its being "non-connected" (*asaṃgati*).

Since the non-self (*anātman*) is established as being dependent upon the self (*ātman*), one might suspect that it possesses either independence like the self or else utter unreality; anticipating this objection, he says "only that much" (*tāvanmātra*) to show that this is not so, because [the non-self] is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*). "Only the self" means its own nature is independent; therein, the category of the non-self—consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth superimposed [upon the self]—possesses neither independence nor utter unreality, just as a snake superimposed on a rope is perceived through direct experience.
The meaning is that, by virtue of having the nature of a rope, it lacks independence and so forth. || 975 ||
Although this [Self] is known as something external, it is [in fact] the innermost reality by virtue of its true nature.
The self would remain truly unknown, just like the cognition of the form of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. || 976 ||

Anticipating the objection that the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is untenable because it is established by perception and other means of knowledge, he says: "by way of externality" (*parāktayā*).

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for that which is known to be unknown, he says: "as in the case of mother-of-pearl" (*śuktikā*). For when there is ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl, the cognition of silver does not negate that [underlying] cognition, since its nature is that of mother-of-pearl; and upon the cognition of that [mother-of-pearl], both the silver and the cognition of it perish, so that no knowable object in the form of silver remains—likewise [in this case].

The meaning is this: through the knowledge of the non-self, the Self is not apprehended because of the absence of any nature other than the Self; and when there is knowledge of the Self, the non-self and the cognition thereof perish, resulting in the absence of any knowable non-self. || 976 ||
Alternatively, this genitive case is to be understood as expressing selection, because it serves to specify the object of knowledge.
For there is nothing other than the Self that is attained which has not already been attained. || 977 ||

Thus, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*) has been explained. Now, he states the meaning of the genitive as mentioned in the Bhāṣya: "or in the sense of selection" (*nirdhāraṇe*). Why was that [genitive] accepted there? Why would it not apply to other meanings such as the object (*karman*) and so forth? To this he replies: "to be known" (*jñeya*). This is the essence of all things. (Note: *kha* reads *vā tajjñāne*).

The meaning is that because it has been determined that in this world only the *pratyak* (the inward Self) is the object of knowledge and nothing else, the genitive case used with respect to that subject is appropriate.

He states the reason why the knowability belongs to the *pratyak* alone and not to anything else: "For of the *pratyak*... The word "for" (*hi*) indicates the reason, namely, "because... [of the following].
The reason has been made clear; or rather, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used because this matter has already been established previously. || 977 ||
In the same way, for us, there exists a supreme Self that is distinct from the body.
Because nothing else in this world has ignorance as its cause except for the inner self. || 978 ||

Anticipating the objection that, just as there is "knownness" (jñātatva) for something other [than the Self], there must likewise be "unknownness" (ajñātatva) for it, he says: "Even though known" (*jñāto'pi*). The phrase "in the same way" (*tadvat*) means "as if unknown. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "there is no other [entity]. Furthermore, because there is no other than the Self, that [duality] does not belong to it; thus he says: "From this" (*asmāt*). Anticipating the objection that this contradicts experience, he states the perception of an object distinct from ignorance: "The innermost" (*pratyak*).
The ellipsis is that "in this case, cognition is not contradictory. || 978 ||
Of this entire [world], which is without self and consists of both the determinate and the indeterminate.
Because the self is the supreme reality to be attained, it should therefore be so. || 979 ||

Relying precisely on a derivative genitive (*śaiṣikī* ṣaṣṭhī), he explains the statement "this is the Self" as the reason for the fact that *ātmatva* (selfhood) alone is what is to be reached [by the word]. [He says: "of the non-self" (*anātmanaḥ*). || 979 ||
Because, like the universal "cowness" perceived in a broken piece [of pottery] and so forth, it is seen by inward vision within the inner self.
For even by that [means], it is perceived as having the nature of the self.

How can the Self be the reality of everything? For one thing cannot be the reality of another. Anticipating this objection, he says "In the case of a fragment [of sugar] and so forth," relying on a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta): Just as a universal manifests separately from individuals due to the difference between exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and inclusion (anuvṛtti), it is not so [with the Self].

For that [non-self] is perceived as distinct from the Self by means of the cognition of it; yet it is not perceived as being identical with the Self's own nature, because there is no other nature for it, nor is it perceived merely as the inner subject (pratyaktva), since the identity of two contradictory things is impossible. Therefore, the meaning is that it must be accepted as being superimposed upon the Self, having that [Self] alone as its true essence. || 980 ||
The object of knowledge is the Self alone, not a manifold self, because it is that which is to be reached.
Indeed, when there is cognition of one thing, there is no apprehension of another whatsoever.

Since the Self is the reality (*tattva*) of everything and everything is known through the knowledge of it, therefore the Self alone is that which is to be known; for it is established as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), whereas the non-Self (*anātman*) is not an object of knowledge because of its absence—this is the conclusion stated [by the author] in the words "the object of knowledge" (*jñeya*). An objection is raised: "But surely... [The opponent argues: Since it has been said that the Self is the object of knowledge and not the non-Self, there is a distinction between the two; therefore, the remainder of the sentence, "for by this [Self]...", would be untenable.
The meaning is that nowhere—in any place or otherwise—is a cloth or the like ever observed to be known by means of the cognition of a jar or the like. || 989 ||
This would indeed be true, if the self were also held to be something other [than the body].
The statement that "this self is other" is not the speech of one who is not insane.

He accepts that one thing is not known by means of knowledge of another. [Objection: "True. [Reply: If there were a difference between the Self and the non-Self, then the non-Self would not be known through the knowledge of the Self; nor is that difference real. Therefore, the non-Self can be known through the knowledge of that [Self]. [The opponent] observes: "sva. ga. mīkṣate."
[Vol.
2, Page 337] *Brāhmaṇam* | Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

631 He says: "If... Since the Self (ātman) is also a real entity (*vastu*), one might suspect it is distinct like a jar or other objects; however, because it is impossible for it to be non-Self, [it is not so].
He said, "Vam," meaning "the Self. || 982 ||
The word "by this" (anena) is in the instrumental case and is characterized by the sense of "being in such a state."
This [reality] is accessible through the word "intellect" (dhī), because its true essence is solely the inward-facing self (pratyaṅmātra).

Having removed the contradiction in the meaning of the sentence beginning with "by this" (*anena hi*), and having observed that its syllables possess a clear meaning, [the author] states that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) has the sense of "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhāva*) in order to exclude its application to instruments and the like. Regarding the phrase "by this": it is so called because it indicates—that is, makes known—an object in such a state. He states the reason for this: "This... (verse 983).
What object, indeed, is understood from this means of knowledge [other than the absence] in the form "the jar does not exist"?
First of all, consciousness is determined from all means of valid cognition without exception. || 984 ||

Since this entire object has the nature of being solely the internal subject whose essence is experience (*anubhava*), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is appropriate in this sense [of "by means of"]; thus, for the sake of establishing the aforementioned reason, he first reflects [on it]. He says: "The jar. Having reflected on what object appears through the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding existence and non-existence, he shows that experience is universally acknowledged as the valid means of knowledge (*māna*) among all means of knowledge by virtue of being the fruit (*phala*). He says: "Consciousness" (*saṃvit*). || 984 ||
Neither as something separate from consciousness, nor by means of a cognition directed toward it within consciousness.
Just as this consciousness [appears] by itself, so too would a non-self entity be imagined. (985)
[Objection: But surely, just as consciousness appears as a fruit, the world also appears as its object; for there can be no cognition without an object. [Reply:

He says "no," and so forth. Just as consciousness is not obtained by itself through either difference or non-difference—because in a single entity, the states of being a substratum (*dharmitva*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) [are contradictory]—...

Because of [the impossibility of] conjunction and because of the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the non-self (*anātman*) is likewise unestablished through either difference or non-difference from consciousness (*saṃvit*). It is merely imagined within the Self as having that [non-self] form; for it is not possible to conceive of the non-self entity as distinct from consciousness due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), and since its connection [to consciousness] has been repeatedly refuted, nor is it established as non-different from consciousness—whether by a cognition whose nature is consciousness or by a cognition of the non-self—for otherwise one of the two would remain [as the sole reality]. Therefore, the world...
The meaning is "merely the self. || 985 ||
A pot with its lid has been found, along with a long-lipped man who knows the place and the time.
The object of the subsequent [cognition] is not experienced as being distinct from each preceding one. || 986 ||

For this reason as well, he says that it is merely the nature of consciousness: "It exists as perceived. The meaning is that because there is no object apart from non-conceptual experience, it has been firmly established in the context of all relations that everything is nothing but that very nature of consciousness. || 986 ||
Prior to the activity of the agent and so forth, consciousness abides within its own self.
Indivisible and inexpressible, it bears fruit through its own manifestation.

Anticipating the objection that everything cannot be mere experience—because that [experience], being a result, is an effect, and because, like a rope-snake, it is imagined and thus lacks the status of being the substratum—he establishes its immutability with the words "agent, etc. Since consciousness remains in its own nature during sleep and the like prior to the knowledge of the operations of the subject and so forth, and since there is then no distinction between cause and effect, this consciousness must be understood as being devoid of the designation "result"; and that [consciousness] belongs to that [Self].

The meaning is that because the arising of the knowledge called "divine activity" functions as if it were fruitful, and because that [arising] is in reality not something to be produced, it is "unconstructed" (akalpita). || 987 ||
1 ka. ga. svakaḥ || 983 ||
Just as in the case of the actionless ether, there is [the appearance of] arising, persistence, and destruction;
[so it is here]. *Suresvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtikaṃ*, First Chapter. [Vol. 2, p. 338] 632.
Just as in the case of the actionless ether, there is [the appearance of] arising, persistence, and destruction.
Thus the world, bearing the manifold forms of both the existent and the non-existent, is deluded within me alone.

One might object that although consciousness (saṃvid) can be the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) because it is non-imagined (akalpita), it cannot be the substratum because it is inactive (akriya); for it is only things like mother-of-pearl that are seen to be active in such cases. Anticipating this, the author states through an illustration that the world is imagined within the one-tasted (ekarasa) and changeless inner self (pratīc): "Even though inactive," etc. The word "hi" is used to indicate that the inactivity of space (vyoman) is accepted by [other] disputants. || 988 ||
Having cast aside the objects such as the jar, consciousness remains as pure being alone.
Through its nature as pure consciousness, the all-seeing one remains changeless while possessing existence. || 989 ||

Regarding the argument that "the inner self (pratyagātman) is active because it is a substratum, like mother-of-pearl," having pointed out the deviation [of the reason] in the case of space (*ākāśa*), and intending to show that this is not so because of the qualification of being corporeal (*mūrtatva*), he says:

"Not so" (*naivam*). Since the existence of duality manifests only in the form of its cognition due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one should negate both existence and non-existence as being merely the reality of the nature of consciousness; thus, the inner self, whose nature is that [consciousness], is everything.

The meaning is: one who perceives is changeless and poised in yoga; for a witness of action cannot be an agent, because the witness must remain capable of being situated within the scope of the witness itself. || 989 ||
Just as the division of directions is conceptually constructed even within the undivided sky.
Even though all distinctions have been utterly destroyed, those whose intellects are divided by Māyā perceive them as such.

If that is so, then because it is the agent of seeing, its state of being active remains unchanged; for there is no agency without being the agent of that [seeing], nor is there agency apart from action. Not so; for apart from the vision of its own nature, the distinction between that [nature] and its agency is merely imagined in the Self.
He states this by means of an illustration: "the division of directions. In both cases, the state of being non-active is conjoined by the two words "api" (also/even). || 990 ||
But how, then, by means of the expedient devised from the state of non-awakening, does one reach that which is beyond it?
The subsequent statement is intended to refute the claim that "it is being understood as real. || 999 ||

Having thus established that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the phrase "by this" (*anena hi*) signifies the state of being [the means], he now introduces the sentence beginning with "just as" (*yathā hi*), after restating the objection to be set aside. "How so? [The objection is: Since the teacher and other such means are merely imagined because they are produced by ignorance of the Self (*ātmājñāna*), it is impossible to know the true Brahman—which is untouched by that ignorance and its products—through them, due to their mutual contradiction. This objection is [now] resolved...
The meaning is that it is like the statement beginning with "to take away" (hartum) and so forth. || 999 ||
Although that word is unreal from the perspective of ultimate reality, it nevertheless serves as a means of awakening.
Thus, let it be seen that even that which is unreal serves as a means for one's own purpose regarding the Self. (992)

He explains that [point] with the words "paramārtha" (in the ultimate sense). A word (*pada*), consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) such as those for "cow" or "horse," even if it is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) by the turn of fate, is the signifier of its own meaning, such as "cowness" (*gotva*); for it is not unconstructed. This is because sequential phonemes possess that [word-nature], and sequence cannot exist among them without being superimposed (*āropa*). Indeed, phonemes are eternal and all-pervading; they do not inherently possess sequence. Thus, the teachers [have stated] through scripture and reasoning regarding the nature of the self and ignorance.
The meaning is that the state of having two means should be understood. || 992 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 339] — The Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 633.
Apart from the truth of skillful means, no other kind is applicable.
What is desired from the means, which possess reality, in relation to the goal?

Furthermore, apart from the efficacy in producing purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), which constitutes their reality, ultimate reality (*paramārthasatyatā*) is not a means for making the goal known;
therefore, they do not possess such a reality. Thus he says: "The means... The locative case in *upeyabodhane* signifies the locus. When the means are real—

The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that [ultimate reality] is not perceived as a means because it lacks the fault of being devoid of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatyatva*) regarding those things that perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*).
It clarifies that ultimate truth is useless for the production of an effect. [This is stated in the verse: "In the goal... (993).
Or, the hoof-print of a cow and so forth is taught as a "footprint."
If that were the case, this example would fail to establish the intended meaning. || 994 ||

One might object: "It is unestablished that words such as 'cow' are superimposed when they convey their own meaning; for since they convey that meaning, there exists a connection between them and it. Likewise, since the Vedas and other scriptures convey Brahman, they too must have a connection [with it]; therefore, the claim that Brahman is devoid of connection is lost. Anticipating this objection, he states another meaning for the word *pada* (foot/word): "gavādi" and so on. By the phrase "the reflection of its hooves," the place marked by them is understood.
Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how Brahman—which is understood through means such as the Vedas—can be accepted as being unattached (asaṅga), he says:

"ananvita" (unconnected). The meaning is that just as when a place marked by the hoofprints of cows and so forth is designated by the word "track" (pada), [one infers] the object of the inner self which is unrelated to cause and effect; this is the sense of the illustration beginning with the word "hetau" (in the case of the cause) and so on. || 994 ||
The accomplishment of the cognition of cows and so forth arises from words and the cognition thereof.
It culminates in the single cognition of a cow-individual, even though the knowledge of the words [composing the sentence] has not been integrated [into that cognition]. || 995 ||
Just so, by means of the cause that is the proliferation of name-and-form and so forth, [the world arises].
Within the ground whose nature is free from conceptual proliferation, inward awareness arises.

He explains the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sake of establishing the intended meaning, beginning with "gavādi" (cow, etc.). The meaning is as follows: just as when a cow or similar object has been lost, a cognition arises—caused either by the place marked by its hooves or by the cause [of its disappearance]—and that cognition has as its object merely the cow and so forth, untouched by those two [the place or the cause]. It does not reside in the word or its cognition as connected [with the object], such that it would terminate in a specific individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*). This is the point. As for the example...

Takamāha says: "Thus" (*evam*). The word "beginning" (*ādi*) is for the sake of indicating action. "Pratyak-pratīcī" means "toward the west. Through the two forms of "pratyak," the cognition is qualified as "pratyak" [inward]. || 999 || 996 ||
On the level of valid cognition, oneness is not perceived because of contradiction.
Because it follows from darkness and is unapprehendable, it is not perceived even when that [darkness] is absent. || 997 ||

In order to establish that the imagined [world] is a means to knowledge and to show that Brahman has no connection with duality, and furthermore, in order to introduce the sūtra "One should meditate upon it as the Self alone" (*ātmaivety upāsīta*), and to explain this by way of answering the objections raised in the context, the objection is now set forth: "By means of valid cognition... [and so on]. In the two states [of waking and dreaming], there is no cognition of a real entity because of the contradiction between ignorance and its effects; therefore, the absence of such [real entities] is established by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that even there, the cognition of that [object] does not exist because it is obstructed by ignorance; thus, its status as an object of knowledge (*tanmeyatva*) is not established. || 997 ||
80 1. guṇa | 2. kha. pārtha | 3.
kha. sya taṃ [vol2, page 340]
For indeed, nowhere does one destroy the delusion regarding the Self and so forth by means of the Self alone.
Being independent of means of valid cognition, it is itself sufficient for its own establishment.

Lest it be argued that the cognition of the Self (*ātmadhī*) would cease by itself—since it is of the nature of pure consciousness—and that therefore valid knowledge (*pramā*) regarding it would always exist without obstruction, the author states the general principle to address this doubt: "For not... [etc.]. For the true nature of an object, such as mother-of-pearl, does not, independent of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), anywhere—in any place or at any time—bring about the cessation of its own ignorance and its products, nor does it bring about its own manifestation.

It has been observed that [the cause] is capable; however, the meaning is that it is sufficient for the aforementioned effect only by depending upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 998 ||
There would be no entering into saṃsāra, and pride would indeed be rendered fruitless.
This is the answer for the purpose of refuting this objection here. || 999 ||

One might raise the objection that while there is a requirement for a means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding insentient objects such as mother-of-pearl, in the case of the Self—which is self-luminous—there is no need for such a means, since the realization of its own nature destroys ignorance and the like;
anticipating this, he says: "saṃsāra... (beginning with the word *saṃsāra*). He takes up the passage beginning with "yathā" as a response to this. Regarding the phrase "of this":

the meaning is that the subsequent sentence serves as the refutation here of the aforementioned objection, which has been restated along with its supplementary elements. Of that [objection], what was said...
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the meaning that is about to be stated. || 999 ||
Just as one who follows the tracks of a dropa finds the cow directly by means of its own nature.
By following the path of immediate consciousness in this way, one should attain that supreme state.

To clarify the resolution, he explains the statement with the words "Just as... (yathā). Just as one who, having seen a place marked by the hoofprints of cows and other animals, goes along in accordance with them and, while searching for a cow, perceives it directly in its true form; so too, through the word "Thou" (tvam), the inner consciousness which is the referent of "Thou" [is perceived].
The meaning is that purification consists in the seeker of liberation knowing Brahman in its true form. || 1000 ||
For when it shines as the inner self (pratyak), by virtue of being the witness to that which comes and goes.
In the body, senses, mind, and intellect, it takes the form of the manifestation of consciousness.

Having analyzed the meaning of "Thou," he says: "By way of being the inner self" (*pratyaktayā*). The connection is as follows: that which shines through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the inner self and as the witness (*sākṣin*) amidst the external things such as the body, which are subject to coming and going—that very thing is "this Pure One. He qualifies it with the term "consciousness" (*caitanya*) in order to indicate that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) serves as the medium for its status as a witness. || 1001 ||
The one among many insentient things, the immutable amidst those subject to momentary destruction.
Likewise, the Self exists within those things that are non-self, and though it resides in aggregates, it remains unaggregated.

To the question, "How can there be witnesshood if there is no distinction from the objects witnessed? he says: "In the insentient," etc. The word "non-insentient" (*ajaḍam*) is to be supplied [as the subject].
Even so, one might suspect that if it were distinct [from the objects], it would lack witnesshood, like the body and so forth; anticipating this, he says: "One" (*ekam*).

Anticipating the suspicion that it lacks witnesshood due to being active, he says: "Unchanging" (*kūṭastham*). He clarifies the nature of "selfhood" (*pratyaktva*) which was mentioned in the phrase "that which appears as the inner self."
"In non-selfs," thus [it is said]. || 1002 ||
Fearing that it might be considered non-introspective (apratyakṣa) like the body and so forth because it is composite, he says:
"This is declared to be the word for that which consists of the meaning of the sentence."
Because one goes by means of this, therefore it is called "pada" (the foot/goal). || 1003 ||
Having explained the meaning of "Thou" (*tvaṃ*) as purified, he declares its status as a term leading toward its identity with Brahman, saying: "Of that," i.e., of Brahman.

The meaning is that the pure consciousness (pratyak-caitanya), which is the "thou" (tvam-artha) purified as the "that" (tat-artha), is the cause. Having raised the doubt, "How can the 'thou' be the word for the 'that'?", he says, "It is reached," based on the etymological derivation from the root *pad* (to reach).

For it is by means of the purified "thou" that the "that" is known as one's own essential nature (svarūpa), since the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence depends upon the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words. || 1003 ||
If the means were established by its own inherent power alone, like the ultimate reality, [then it would be useless].
Because it is established by itself, its falsity cannot exist, just like the ultimate reality.
If it were non-different from the ultimate reality, then its nature would be all the more non-illusory.
Thus, that which was previously stated and is to be kept in mind here has been set forth. || 1005 ||

One might object: "Since the knowledge of Brahman arises from the internal self (*pratyagātman*), and since the teacher and others who cause that knowledge are themselves real, it is not logical to claim their falsity. Anticipating this, the author considers the alternatives—whether the teacher and so forth are established by themselves or by another—and restates the first position with the words, "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*).
He then refutes it: "If it were always established by itself, then like consciousness (*caitanya*), it would not be insentient (*jaḍa*). [The text continues: "In the ultimate sense..."

[The author] replies to the second [objection] with the words "falsity" (*mithyātva*). If [the world] were established through something else (*parataḥ siddhau*), it would be false, because it could not be established by the Seer (the Self) except through a superimposed relationship (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*). Furthermore, is the means [of knowledge] non-different from ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) or different? Not the first.

Thus he says: "as if it were the ultimate reality" (*paramārthavat*). Since you accept that the means (*upāya*) is real by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), and since you admit its non-difference from that [ultimate reality], there is this excellence: because of the absence of any false object and the absence of any other entity, it is non-dual (*advaya*); such is the sense. It is not the second [alternative], because difference (*bheda*) lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇikatva*). Furthermore, there is no status as a means for one who acts or one who does not act; therefore, the fact that every means is imagined within the non-dual conscious self (*cidātman*) is unavoidable.

It is said that what was stated at the beginning of the *Kṛtavicāra* and other works should be understood here as the reason for the unreality of the means; thus he says: "and so forth" (ityādi). || 1004 ||
Neither the universal nor the particular is apprehended in the same way as they are when there is identity.
Although this has already been stated above, it will be explained again below due to a lack of complete satisfaction.

One might suspect that because Brahman consists of both the universal and the particular, the world is not a mental construction (*kalpita*); anticipating this, he says "No" and so forth, stating that such is not the case due to contradiction with the logic already stated and to be stated hereafter. The phrase "even though it has been stated thus" (*tathoktam api*) is to be construed by supplying the word *tathā*. The meaning is that because of dissatisfaction [with the previous argument], and because of the contradiction between scripture and reasoning regarding that matter, the fault is stated once again. || 1006 ||
When the inner self is realized, nothing remains unknown.
For by the statement "for by this [is] this," that which was previously described is [established]. || 1007 ||

Having stated that the passage beginning with "yathā" (as) restates the aforementioned knowledge by way of another meaning, he restates what was said in the verse beginning with "anena hi" in order to explain the purport (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "kīrtim" (fame). [The commentary begins with] "pratyak" (the inner self). One should introduce and connect the word "iti" after the verb, as well as the word "yat. || 1007 ||
The attainment of all human goals without exception and the destruction of suffering are its fruits.
Just as it is stated by the Śruti that the means of knowledge is non-different from the Self. (1008)

He introduces the statement regarding the fruit of that knowledge with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). Human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is happiness; its state of being "without remainder" [is as follows].
The *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya. [In the first chapter:

"Fullness" (*pūrṇatvam*) is the fruit of that knowledge—that is to say, the fruit of that knowledge belongs to the knower, the Self. It is non-different from the means; the meaning is that it is non-different from the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), because that very [knowledge], when accompanied by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), serves as the means. This has been stated in the passage beginning with "By this indeed," and so forth.

The sense is that, having restated the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) through such scriptural passages as "as [it is]," its fruit—liberation in the form of the Self—is then described by the passage beginning with "fame. || 1008 ||
Is it not the case that when the inner Self is known, everything other than that becomes known?
Since the subject under discussion is knowledge, why is the conclusion drawn regarding the acquisition of gain? || 1009 ||

Regarding the phrase "by this," [the opponent] raises an objection: having begun with the verb *vid* meaning "to know" and stated the attainment with the verb *anuvid* meaning "to find," the scripture concludes again with the verb *vid* in the sense of "knowledge" in the passage beginning "fame" (*kīrtim*). Therefore, there is a contradiction between the introduction and the conclusion of the scriptural statement "one should find" (*anuvindet*). [The author replies: "But surely... (*nanu*). The word *iti* should be understood as following the word for action; that is, within the word whose primary sense is knowledge, there is an intermediate sense of attainment.
Having spoken by means of words, he concludes again by means of words for the sake of knowledge; the meaning of the question "Why? is as follows. || 1009 ||
Because it is intended that "knowledge" (jñāna) and "attainment" (lābha) have the same meaning.
Since it consists merely in the destruction of ignorance, let there be no contradiction here. || 1010 ||

He says that there is no contradiction in concluding with the fruit of knowledge after beginning with knowledge and describing its attainment, because the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "attainment" (*lābha*) have the same meaning. [The verse begins with] "Knowledge... The word "because" (*yasmāt*) is connected with the word "therefore" (*tena*). He states the reason for the identity of knowledge and attainment: "Ignorance... Since the attainment of the Brahman that is the inner self is merely the destruction of ignorance—just like the finding of gold that was already in one's hand but forgotten—[the two are identical].

The meaning is that because this [consciousness] does not exceed knowledge, there is oneness between the two here. By making their identity the reason, he states the lack of contradiction through the introduction and conclusion in the passage beginning with "one should obtain" (anuvindeyāt). This is indicated by the word "tena" (by that). || 1010 ||
For that which has eternally attained a single nature, there is no non-attainment other than through ignorance.
Just as it is thus, even its attainment arises from that knowledge and not from anything else. || 1011 ||
He establishes, by means of an illustration, that gain with respect to the self is nothing more than knowledge. [The verse begins with] "eternal" (nitya).
The meaning is that since non-gain with respect to the self does not exceed ignorance, gain in that regard is simply knowledge itself. || 1011 ||
The attainment of the self is Brahman, and the state of Brahman is also the fruit of the self.
Due to the difference in what is excluded and the resulting distinction, a single entity is spoken of in two ways.

Raising the objection that since a distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and attainment (*lābha*) is observed in cases such as a village, how can they be identical in the present context as well?—in order to establish that identity, he states the meaning of the word "attainment" (*lābha*) here: "The nature of the Self" (*ātmatā*). The word "fruit" (*phala*) has the sense of "attainment. Since it is impossible for Brahman to be Brahman if it were not the Self, and since it is logically untenable for the Self to be the Self if it were not Brahman, their identity is established. How then could there be the dual expression "Brahman is the Self," given the tautology? [This is answered by the following:]...

He says: "By excluding" (*vyāvartya*). Although there is a distinction between the qualified referents due to the difference in what is excluded—namely, having been transmigrated (*saṃsāritva*) and being remote (*pārokṣya*), etc.—in reality the entity is one and the same;
it is designated twice. Thus, the meaning is that because the denoted meanings of the qualified [terms] differ according to the difference in what is excluded, there is no tautology. || 1012 ||
