Brahmanhood does not exist apart from the Self, nor does selfhood exist apart from Brahman.
Since this is so, there is therefore no difference here between knowledge and the attainment of its object. (1013)

Having restated that non-difference which was previously mentioned, and making that the reason, he concludes that knowledge and attainment are one in the inner self (*pratyak*). [The verse says: "Brahman.
For when there is non-difference between the inner self and Brahman, there is no attainment other than knowledge; this is the meaning. || 1013 ||
Wherever there is a distinction between the attainer and the attained on the planes illuminated by ignorance, [that is the realm of duality].
Due to the difference in action, there is a difference in the result; thus, those two have different purposes.

Anticipating the question, "In what case, then, is there a difference in meaning between those two words [‘knowledge’ and ‘attainment’]? he says: "Attainment... etc. Where Maitra, having attained a village or the like, is the knower (*jñātṛ*) and the pot or the like is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), there is a distinction between the functions of knowing and attaining; consequently, there is a distinction between the fruits of knowledge and attainment. Therefore, the meaning of those two words is different with respect to objects that arise from ignorance (*avidyā*). || 1014 ||
Even though he has attained all human goals, [he remains bound] due to delusion regarding the true nature of the inner self.
"The self would then be non-omniscient, and likewise not truly a trustworthy authority (āpta) or noble one (ārya).

(1015) It was stated that because of the distinction between the attainer and the object to be attained, and between the knower and the object to be known, during the state of ignorance (avidyā), the words "knowledge" (jñāna) and "attainment" (lābha) have different referents.

Now, anticipating the objection that for the element of consciousness (ciddhātu)—which has attained all human goals—there can be no such thing as being an attainer and so forth, he provides support for what was already stated.
Regarding the word "āpta" (reliable): in reality, there is neither non-omniscience nor the state of having an unreliable meaning; such is the sense of the word "ca" (and). || 1015 ||
In that regard, the ignorant one is the self who has attained [the world], and the fruit of action is that which is to be attained.
Obstructing its arising and so forth, preceded by the acceptance of honors and anger. || 1016 ||

Having shown the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), he speaks of the possibility of [the self] being the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth therein. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is stated that the ignorant self is the knower (*jñātṛ*) and the pot and so forth are the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). He qualifies the fruit of the action (*kriyāphala*) with the words "arising and so forth" (*utpattyādi*). An "obstacle" (*antarāya*) is an intervention; thus it is said to be "intervened by the action to be produced. "Appropriation" (*upādāna*) is the taking up of the causal factors (*kāraka*); the fruit of the action is preceded by that.
He says: "Because of the absence of that [effect] when there is an absence of the causal factors," namely, "the causal factors" (kāraka). || 1016 ||
Even that which has been thus attained would be as if unattained, due solely to the cause of ignorance.
And because of the absence of a beginning and an end, it is like the acquisition of a son or other things in a dream. || 1017 ||

He states that the acquisition of the non-self is a mere appearance because it is produced by false knowledge arising from ignorance. The word "such" (*tādṛk*) is used; the particle "mere" (*mātra*) serves to exclude any other real cause. He says that the acquisition of the non-self is imagined through ignorance because it is adventitious, like a consensus (*saṃmata*). [This is shown by the verse: "In the beginning and at the end... (1017).
Therefore, its nature being contrary [to that], its acquisition of self-existence is always from itself.
And that [state], which is otherwise due to the cause of ignorance, is overturned by knowledge. || 1018 ||

Anticipating the objection that "even the acquisition of selfhood is imagined through ignorance, because it is an acquisition, like the acquisition of what is not-self," he says: "contrary" (*viparīta*). This means "therefore, [it is] from the acquisition of what is not-self. He states the very contrariety: "by itself" (*svataḥ*). The point is that insentience (*jaḍatva*) and occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) are the limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Since even that [acquisition of what is not-self] is observed to be occasional and so forth, there is the fear of the reason being over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpti*).
The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Chapter— ]

He says: "By ignorance" (*ajñāna*). Anticipating the objection that the purity of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-śuddhi*) is not established because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) in the case of ignorance, he says: "And that" (*sa ca*). The cause called ignorance departs upon the knowledge that is its opposite; therefore, its acquisition of self-nature (*ātma-lābha*) is natural and eternal, as there is no cause for its manifestation as otherwise. And thus, the subject under dispute is unconstructed (*akalpita*), beginningless and endless.
The meaning is that "like yourself" constitutes the purity of the negative concomitance (vyatireka). || 1098 ||
Having begun [the discussion], he concludes with the sense of "knowing" that "all [beings] know."
Therefore, he says "one should obtain" (anuvindeyāt) with the sense of acquisition regarding that fruit. || 1019 ||

He concludes the non-contradiction [between the two uses of the root *vid*] with the words "beginning with" (*ārabhya*). Since, according to the logic already shown, there is an identity between knowledge (*jñāna*) and attainment (*lābha*), the construction is as follows:

having begun with the root *vid* in the sense of knowledge (in the phrase "one should know"), and having stated the attainment in the middle by means of the root *vid* in the sense of attainment (in the phrase "one should find again"), the Śruti then concludes with the very word *vid* in the sense of knowledge when the fruit of knowledge is to be expressed. Thus it says, "by this [root *vid*]. 1019.
Just as the Self, though unmanifest, attains manifestation within the manifested world,
so too, through the realization of that [Self], it attains an imperishable manifestation.
Having stated the non-contradiction of the beginning, middle, and end, he explains the passage beginning with "fame" (*kīrti*) in accordance with the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding the word "unmanifested" (*aprakhyāta*): although it is unmanifested by name and form in the undifferentiated state (*avyākṛta*), it is manifested by those two in the differentiated world (*vyākṛta*); thus, the person who is qualified through the aforementioned knowledge of the Self attains eternally established fame. (Verse 1020)
The collection of the eye and the other [senses] is designated by the word "world" (loka).
Just as the self, being unconditioned, brings about a composite state through the instruments and other factors.
Knowing this, one obtains a collection of sons, ministers, and so forth.
This is intended as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) for the purpose of engaging in the aforementioned meditative absorption (dhyāna). || 1022 ||

He states the meaning of the word *śloka*: "The collection" (*saṃhatiḥ*). Having explained the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Just as... (*yathā*). Now, one might object:
"The stated result is not conducive to the knowledge of the Self, because that [knowledge] is the means to a result that is unsurpassed. To this, he replies: "It has been stated" (*uktā*). || 1021 ||
For those who are free from attachment and do not desire to abandon such a cycle of existence as this.
Therefore, the fruit [of the action] is logically connected as a constituent part of the activity; hence, it must be an explanatory statement (arthavāda).

One might ask: why could this not be intended as a statement of a result, just as in the case of "He knows Brahman" and so forth? To this he says: "Of those free from desire. The meaning is that for those who are liberated from the pursuit of desires—that is, those wishing to abandon transmigratory existence which resides therein—it is not appropriate to have results such as fame and the like included within it. He states that if the intention to express a result is untenable, the conclusion follows that the purpose of the sentence is the praise of knowledge: "In [the case of] activity... (v. 9023).
Fame, the knowledge of the unity of the self, and renown, the realization of the union with the one self.
By perceiving the object as it has been described, one attains this desired fruit. || 1024 ||

By means of the two words "ca" (and), he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "fame" (*kīrtim*). Indeed, when the statement of a fruit is possible, it is not proper to assume a mere eulogy (*stuti*). Thus, there is no difference in meaning here between the attainment of knowledge and [the attainment of] Brahman, because of the non-difference between Brahman and the Self; as it has been said:
"The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not [the cause]."

The meaning is that the passage beginning with "fame" (*kīrti*) is intended for one who knows the reality (*vastu*), so that he may attain the knowledge of unity— which is required by those seeking liberation— and its fruit, which is liberation. || 1024 ||
The explanation of the indeterminate is for the sake of establishing the vision of the inner self.
An obstacle to that [is] attachment to it; regarding its cessation, there is a supreme scriptural authority. || 1025 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "That this... as follows: "The undifferentiated... Creation is described for the sake of self-knowledge, according to such scriptural texts as "This is its form. An obstacle to that [knowledge] is attachment to the created world; therefore, the subsequent statement is intended to remove that. For one's perception is indeed attached to names and forms, since attachment to external objects is perceived through the pleasure [derived from them]. Desiring to turn [the mind] away from that, he [the text] leads it inward toward the Self.
The meaning is that this is because it has been stated by Bhartṛprapañca that "one who desires to act brings [it] about. || 102 ||
For those whose minds are dragged away by the hook of sound and other sense objects, there can be no perception of the inner self.
Since they lack the capacity [to exclude others], there is no need for a further scriptural statement for the purpose of excluding them.
Anticipating the objection that attachment to those [objects] cannot simultaneously exist with the realization of the Self because they are mutually contradictory, he says: "Sound, etc.

For when these are perceived, they appear like a fishhook because they attract the mind; for one whose consciousness is inclined toward them, the realization of the inner Self (pratyagartha) is not possible, due to the contradiction between the outward-looking vision and the inward-looking vision. Therefore, the subsequent scriptural passage is intended to turn the mind away from sense objects and cause it to enter into the inner Self.
This is the meaning. || 1026 ||
Or else, it is the teaching of another reason for the self's being subject to transmigration.
This very point is stated by the scripture for one who desires to know it.

The purport stated in the Bhāṣya—that while the self's being an object [of knowledge] was mentioned as the reason for the possibility of its being unknown, its being the unsurpassed beloved is now stated as another reason—is explained by the phrase "hetvantareti" (by another reason). The meaning is: "to one who desires to know that [Brahman] or the Self, which is the reason for the desire to know it. || 1027 ||
Alternatively, let the subsequent scriptural passage be for the purpose of refuting the liberation [proposed] by the Sāṃkhya.
For it is by means of the preliminary practice (prayoga) that the culmination of one's own bliss is described. || 1028 ||

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that liberation is merely the destruction of bondage caused by the non-discrimination between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), and not the manifestation of a superlative pleasure.
As they say: "Just as the flow of the milk of the insentient [cow] is for the sake of the growth of the calf..."
"The activity of the Pradhāna proceeds in such a manner for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa."

And: "When the dissolution of the body has occurred, because its purpose has been fulfilled and the primary cause (pradhāna) has ceased its activity, one attains both the absolute and the final state of liberation (kaivalya)."

He states another intended meaning [of the scripture] with the words "tannivṛttyartham idam" (this is for the purpose of its cessation), namely, "sāṃkhya... (the Sāṃkhya...). How does this scripture, by declaring the Self to be the dearest of all, bring about the cessation of the liberation taught by the Sāṃkhyas? To this he replies: "preyo 'grya... (dearer than even the highest...). [This refers to] the dearness of the Self.

The meaning is that because this Śruti declares the cessation of bliss in that state by means of the expression "the end of that" (*tamatva*), the Śruti does not accept the Sāṃkhya conception of liberation as merely the destruction of the threefold suffering. || 1028 ||
640 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya]:
This reality is dearer to you than a son, and likewise dearer than wealth.
In this world, both a son and wealth are renowned for their quality of being beloved. || 1029 ||

Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*) according to the two commentaries and by his own opinion, he explains the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*). Regarding the phrase "than a son" (*putrāt*): since those who are free from passion and desirous of liberation do not perceive love for a son and so forth, how can it be said that the self is dearer than that? To this he replies: "A son. The particle *api* is used in the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). The word "form" (*rūpa*) is used to indicate that this dearness is not real, but rather a matter of perception.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of worldly convention, the statement [that the Self] is dearer than that [the body] is made. || 1029 ||
There would be the superlative suffix *īyasun* in that undesirable case because of the plurality of sons and so forth.
Furthermore, due to its Vedic nature, the Self likewise becomes most beloved. (1030)

He states the meaning of the suffix *īyasun* with the words "the suffix *īyasun*. He provides the reason for this by stating that since the suffix *tamap* is prescribed for the selection of one from among many (*bahūnām ekasya nirdhāraṇe*), and because he intends to express the superiority of the self over many things such as sons when it comes to being dear, [he uses *īyasun*]. He says "of sons and so forth" to address the following objection: "But surely, since there is a traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) stating that *tarap* and *īyasun* are used when a comparative term (*vibhajya*) or a dual number (*dvivacana*) is present, its having the sense of *tamap* is improper. To this, he replies:

"Because it is Vedic" means that although there is a traditional rule stating that the suffix *īyasun* has the same meaning as *tarap*, since this [usage] occurs in the Vedas (*chandas*), one must accept that it does not intend [to express a comparative degree] and instead functions in its own sense as having the meaning of *tamap*. Anticipating the objection: "Even if it is Vedic, why should it be accepted as having the meaning of *tamap* by taking merely the sense of 'excessiveness,' when a primary sense is possible, for a metaphorical sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is improper where a primary sense exists?"—[the author replies: because the state of being most dear (*priyatamatva*) is indeed possible in relation to the Self.

Because no other thing possesses such [quality], he states that the suffix *īyasun* in that context has the sense of "the most" (*tamap*). He says: "The dearest. The particle *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The construction is as follows: the Self alone is the dearest, not so the non-Self; therefore, the status of being the dearest is possible only in reference to it, because it is dearer than many others such as sons and so forth. (1030)
A son is dearer than wealth; the funeral cake is dearer than a son; and likewise, the sense organs are dearer than the funeral cake.
The vital breath is dearer than the senses, and the Self is dearer than that.

He states that this [mind] is the most beloved through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and through direct experience (*anubhava*), beginning with the words "than wealth" (*vittāt*). || 1031 ||
In this context, both types of wealth are included by the term "vitta."
Since even for a god, the world of the gods is merely a fruit and not that ultimate state.

He states what is intended by the word *vitta* (wealth): "Wealth" (*vittam*). It is twofold: human and divine. The locative sense refers to the scriptural passage under discussion (*prakṛtā śrutiḥ*). One might object: "Let human wealth, such as money and the like, be understood here by the word *vitta*, because it has bondage as its fruit; however, divine wealth—namely meditation—has liberation as its fruit, so one should not strive for that. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Divine... Just as [in the case of] sons and ritual actions...

The world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and the world of the gods (*devaloka*) are likewise fruits; for even that which is called divine knowledge (*daivavitta*), known as the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), has the world of the gods as its fruit, according to the scriptural statement, "By knowledge, the world of the gods.
Liberation is not its fruit, because of the scriptural prohibitions [against it]. Therefore, the meaning is that this [world of the gods] also should be included here. || 1032 ||
Because it is the cause for accomplishing joy, joy is attributed to the vital breath and so forth.
Like the passion of a harlot, it is not at all appropriate for the primary [self] toward those things that are not the self. || 1033 ||

To the question, "Since affection is equal toward oneself and toward vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, how can it be said that the self is the dearest of all? he replies with the verse beginning with *prīti*. [Page 347] *Prīti...* [Fragmentary text] *...kṣaya...* [Fragmentary text] [Vol.

"The mental efflorescence" refers to joy; its "means" is its production—that is to say, because it is the cause thereof. A "bandhakī" is a harlot.
*Nitā*. In the reading "like the carpenter's wife" (*vardhakīmītivat*), the term *vardhakī* refers to a well-known harlot (*prasiddha*). || 1033 ||
Because one who is overwhelmed by disease and other afflictions speaks with a despondent mind.
Death this very day is better for me, whose soul is tormented by suffering.

He states the worldly consensus regarding the fact that affection for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is not primary: "Due to disease, etc. By the word "etc.," poverty, oppression by kings, and the like are included. Therefore, the conclusion is that affection for the vital breaths and so forth is secondary. || 1034 ||
The inward [Self] is held to be entirely signless even in all states.
Just as fire is inseparable from its heat, therefore the self is dearer than the non-self. (1035)
Lest one should suspect that pleasure in the internal organ (*pratīci*) might likewise be non-primary, he states the contradiction with experience: "In the internal organ" (*pratīci*).

Regarding the statement that pleasure therein is natural, he provides an illustration: "As fire" (*agni*). He states the consequence of the fact that pleasure toward the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and toward the Self (*ātman*), is not of a uniform nature: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 1035 ||
Because all things consist of the three guṇas, they have the nature of delusion, suffering, and pleasure.
However, some indeed declare that [the self] is not superimposed at all, being so by its very nature. || 1036 ||

Having stated that love for the self is primary while love for what is not-self is secondary, he states the Sāṃkhya position regarding the opposite case with the words "Because of the three qualities" (*traiguṇyāt*).

The explanation of "by itself" (*svataḥ*) is "because it is unconditioned" (*anabhyasta*). The word "for" (*hi*) is used to indicate that this point is well-known in the Sāṃkhya treatises. Because the self is devoid of the qualities such as *sattva*, there is an absence of pleasure and so forth by its very nature. As it has been said: "The one possessing qualities... [and so on].

"Though possessing such qualities, he acts for their sake in a way that is ultimately purposeless. Thus, due to the lack of discrimination by the natural intellect (*prākṛtabuddhi*), there is a secondary attachment to him as being "pleasure" and so forth—
"In that state, the conscious person (*cetanaḥ puruṣaḥ*) undergoes suffering caused by old age and death."
The meaning is that this is because of the statement: "Therefore, suffering exists by its very nature, since the gender-mark has not ceased. || 1036 ||
But that is not so, because sattva produces the three [qualities], beginning with delusion, for the intellect.
We behold the rising of the sun for those whose eyes have been robbed by thieves.

He refutes the notion that the nature of delusion and the like in entities is produced by the three *guṇas*. Regarding the word "tat" (that), he provides an illustration for the claim that a single *sattva* alone causes delusion and so forth in the intellect: "the rising of the sun. For that [sun] consists solely of *sattva*. As it has been said: "*Sattva* is held to be light and illuminating. Here, *rajas* and *tamas* are absent because of the lack of movement and obscuration; nevertheless, even so, for thieves— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

We perceive that for those who wish to observe the divisions of the directions, as well as for those experiencing delusion, suffering, and pleasure in succession, these are the causes; therefore, the meaning is that for cows, the nature of delusion and so forth does not arise from the three *guṇas*. || 1037 ||
If the three qualities (triguṇya) are considered to exist equally in the three states of being, as they do in the sun;
Nor is the addition of another quality admitted upon the rising of the sun. || 1038 ||

[Vol. 2, Page 348] 642 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

Having raised the objection that the rising of the sun also consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and, being non-self (*anātman*), is like something already accomplished, [the author] states that regarding thieves and others, the sun—

He says "equally" (*samam*) to show that there would be an equality of delusion (*moha*) and the other qualities among those who see the day. The sense is that there is no reason why the rising of the sun—which consists of the three *guṇas*—should produce different effects for different persons. Furthermore, [this applies] to one who asserts the absence of the three *guṇas* in the sun.

He states [the following] because that which is of the nature of pure light (*prakāśaikarasa*) would suffer a loss of its fundamental tenet (*siddhāntahāni*), since it is said that "sattva is light and illuminating" due to its being the very form of existence (*sattvamūrti*).

He says: "By the other qualities... Here, the word *adhikāra* refers to the sphere of entry. For indeed, rajas and tamas do not exist there, as their effects are absent. For they recite: "Rajas is stimulating and mobile, while tamas is heavy and obscuring. Nor is there any effect...

The meaning is that, through the perception of difference, the three qualities (traiguṇya) are postulated therein because their lack of fixed order has been stated; however, by contrast, it is established through uncontradicted experience that sattva performs its function through a state of fixed order. || 1038 ||
Affection for those who are not the self is grasped by the means of valid cognition as something subject to deviation.
Just as [the notion of] a snake [is superimposed] upon a rope, it will not be perceived in this way in the inner self (pratyagātman). || 1039 ||

As for the argument that because pleasure and so forth are absent from the Self due to the absence of qualities such as existence (*sattva*), the joy experienced therein is not primary, he replies with the words "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaiḥ*). This means that such joy is inconstant; the sense is that there is the perception of an unsurpassed joy toward it even in all states. || 1039 ||
The reason why the self alone is dear is now clearly stated.
By means of the scriptural statement that [the Self] is "nearer than the near," it is here declared that the Self is the cause of that [bliss].

Anticipating the objection that although affection for one's son and others may vary, it does not waver toward the self as it does toward the vital breaths and so forth—and thus the self is not the most beloved—the author takes up another word: "The self alone" (*ātmaiva*). Its clarity is established by its being accepted by both parties. Whether it be in a third [case] used in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or even in a different case (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the sentence under discussion. Regarding its being the innermost, it constitutes the state of being the most beloved.
He says that the statement "this is the Self" is for the purpose of stating the reason regarding wealth; thus: "And that is the reason. || 1040 ||
Just as the innermost [Self] is the inward-facing one, so it will be explained later.
By means of this textual passage ending with the word "vācaknavyakṣara," [the identity] of the inner self [is established]. || 1041 ||

He states that the innermost nature of the *pratyak* (the inward-facing Self) is not only established here, but also later on, by saying "Just as... Gārgya’s question regarding the syllable (*akṣara*) concerning his daughter’s husband was answered by the Sage with a subsequent passage intended to determine it through the yoga of the *pratyagātman*. For the *akṣara* is indeed more internal than everything else, and since that is the *pratyak*, its status as the innermost is thereby demonstrated.
This is the meaning. || 1041 ||
For inwardness is indeed independent of anything else, whereas otherness depends upon that [inwardness].
For that which is the most proximate [to the object] is understood from direct perception itself. || 1042 ||

Furthermore, since the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) does not depend on anything other than the Self, whereas the non-Self (*anātman*) depends upon the Self, He is the "innermost" (*antaratama*). Thus, he states the reasoning for His being the innermost with the words "by its inwardness" (*pratyaktā*). The meaning of the particle *hi* (for/indeed) is that there is no possible object to be depended upon [other than the Self].
[Note: Regarding the variants *guru varaṇame* and *guru varṇa*, the former likely refers to a covering or concealment by the Guru, while the latter refers to the Guru's instruction or description.]
[Vol.
2, Page 349] 4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 643.

It is not that independence is impossible simply because of being the Self (*ātmatva*). He states the conclusion regarding the fact that self-awareness (*pratyaktva*) is inherent in the Self: "Since..."
Thus [ends the verse]. 1042.
He whose inwardness is held to be equal across all eight states.
For him, the statement "the most internal one" would be difficult to establish. || 1043 ||

Having established the statement regarding the internal and the external according to his own view, he says "yasya" (of whom), showing that it is not tenable according to the view of Bhartṛprapañca. Regarding the eight states—the individual body (*piṇḍa*), the genus (*jāti*), Virāṭ, the subtle thread (*sūtra*), the divine (*daiva*), the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), and the witness (*sākṣin*)—there is no relation of external and internal between them.

Just as clay alone is the reality (*tattva*) of modifications such as jars and bowls, so too the commonality is selfhood (*ātmatva*); therefore, in those [states], there is the state of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*).
The meaning is that, in the view [of the opponent], the status of being the innermost self (*ātman*) is not established. || 1043 ||
In these eight states of the self here, which are neither deficient nor excessive in form—
Based on what specific distinction is the Self considered the "innermost"? 1044.
Anticipating the objection—“Even though the inner witness (pratīc) is equal across all states, why should it not be the most internal?”—the author says: “not inferior” (*anyūna*).

The word “here” (*iha*) means while the superimposed states exist within the Self, which is devoid of any internal-external division. Therefore, the meaning is that one must posit an external-internal distinction for the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth as distinct from the Self; otherwise, the status of the inner witness as the most internal would remain unestablished.
The word "hi" is used to clarify that it is impossible for any specific [quality] to be projected [onto the universal]. || 1044 ||
Since attachment to non-selves is merely figurative, therefore [one should abandon] non-selves.
Having withdrawn all affection, one should establish it in the West alone. || 1045 ||
Having stated the reason for the Self being the dearest by means of refuting the opposing view—that it is the innermost—[the author] concludes his own position:
"It is merely figurative" (bhāktaiva). || 1045 ||
This being the established position, a brief summary of the reasoning is now set forth.
When two people are disputing over whether a son or other such [beloved object] is the self, [the answer is as follows].
He who, overwhelmed by delusion, says that what belongs to another is his own;
To him who speaks thus, one should reply; such is the instruction of the Śruti. || 1047 ||

Since it is established that the Self alone is dear and not the non-Self, the text states the passage beginning with "He who [thinks another... for the purpose of summarizing the reasoning regarding that state of being most dear. Thus [it is said]. He applies that [explanation] as follows: "Son, etc. He states the reason for speaking of things other than the Self as dear:
He deludes [them]. || 1046 || 1047 ||
He who is cherished by you as beloved will soon become a source of suffering.
For he will quickly perish; and perishing, he will be a source of unhappiness even to those who are dear to him.
Having explained the words of the sacred scripture (*śruti*) beginning with "he will obstruct what is dear," he explains the words of the opponent beginning with "he who...
He states the reason for its being a cause of suffering with the words "since...". He explains how it causes suffering even though it is perishable with the words "perishing...
The word "and" (*ca*) is used to state that it is well known that a beloved object, when perishing, causes suffering. || 1048 ||
1. 1. Kha. Sons and so forth; 2. Ga. ...ti vedānuṃ; 3. Ka. Ma. ...trādir iti.
[Vol. 2, page 350]
The Śruti also declares that there is no contradiction with what has been stated, saying, "It is indeed so."— Śureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika, First Adhyāya, Verse 644.
He replied with this proposition: "The self alone is dear. || 1049 ||

He states the meaning of the Śruti, "It should be exactly so," as follows: "Of that which has been stated. The construction is as follows: having first made the proposition that "the Self alone is dear," the Śruti then replied, "It should be exactly so," in order to demonstrate the non-contradiction of what was subsequently stated regarding the non-dearness of the non-Self due to its causing suffering, as a corollary to that initial proposition. Alternatively, the Śruti [reaffirms] that very proposition—"The Self alone is dear"—by saying, "Whatever has been stated by you, that is exactly so."

The connection is that he spoke in accordance with what was previously stated regarding the selflessness and lack of dearness [of other things]. He restates what was said in the passage beginning with "This Self is dearer than a son," namely: "The Self alone... (1049).
Therefore, since this is so, one should abandon life and other things that are dear to oneself.
One should always worship the innermost Self as the Beloved.

Having established the proposition that the self alone is dear because things such as sons—which are beloved—are impermanent, and that the self is of the nature of bliss, the text explains the meaning of the injunction "one should meditate upon the self alone as dear" by stating "because... This means: that self which exists as the innermost of all; or rather, the letter *m* should be understood as elided here, so it refers to the self which is the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratama*).
Or rather, it means "that. It is stated as "constantly" (*sada*) for the purpose of ensuring there is no interruption by heterogeneous cognitions. || 1050 ||
By the statement "He who [knows] the Self," the fault that has arisen is refuted.
The fact that [the vital breaths] have a limited lifespan is not denied, because they are mortal like the life-force (prāṇa) and so forth. || 1051 ||

He states the intended meaning of the declaration of the fruit beginning with "sa ya ātmānam... as follows: "sa ya iti. Regarding the phrase "na hāsya priyam...," "priyam" refers to the bliss of the Self (*ātmasukha*). Since that too, like worldly pleasure, would naturally be subject to destruction because it is a form of happiness, this statement of the fruit serves to eliminate that defect. The meaning is that by using the word "priya" to refer to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, [the text indicates] that for the knower, through the power of knowledge—

Anticipating the objection that there is no loss if that [ignorance] does not perish—asking what harm there would be in the sense of the sentence regarding the fruit—he says: "shortness of life" (pramāyukatva).
For one who desires liberation from that [samsara], there is delight in turning away from all objects of the foolish.
Because of the words "not for him," there is no mention of a fruit for one who seeks liberation.

Therefore, based on the scriptural statement "everything else is perishable" (*ato'nyad ārtam*), it is established that the non-destruction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is not mentioned as the fruit of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*), because they are perishable. He states this conclusion with the words "having ceased" (*vyāvṛta*). The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) refers to bondage, which is rooted in external attachment. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the inevitability of the destruction of the non-self, such as the vital breaths. [This applies to] the knower who is dispassionate, desiring to abandon transmigratory existence, and seeking liberation.

The fruit [of knowledge] is not stated by this [text] to be the non-destruction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; for it is not the case that the statement of non-destruction regarding that which is subject to destruction constitutes the fruit of knowledge, because [such a claim] would be rooted in false cognition—this is the meaning. || 1052 ||
If one here were to become dispassionate toward the Kumbhīpāka and other hells as if they were visible before one's eyes;
Having completed all remaining duties, he is then employed in liberation.

He states that for the qualified persons mentioned, since there is no dependence on the non-destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, their non-destruction is not spoken of here as a fruit of knowledge;

thus he says: "up to Brahmā" (*ābrahmabhuvanāt*). This means up to the world of Brahmā, that is to say, from the entirety of *saṃsāra*. The word "if" (*cet*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends with "cet," which is likely part of a conditional clause or a citation marker.]

The word "rarely" (virakte) is intended to indicate the difficulty of attainment. "In this world" (iha) means, in the midst of those who are qualified for the path. The result of ritual action (kriyākārya) is the purification of the mind (citta-śuddhi). || 1013 ||
"Having examined the worlds," and so forth—such is the scriptural statement from the Vedas.
"Abandon both dharma and adharma," and so forth—this is also from the Smṛti.

He provides scriptural authority (*śruti*) and traditional authority (*smṛti*) for the fact that those possessing dispassion (*vairāgya*) and other qualities are entitled to liberation (*mukti*). [The verse] says "having examined," and the connection is with the words "also from the statement of the *Smṛti*. || 1054 ||
This supreme Upaniṣad has been commenced for the purpose of dispelling ignorance regarding the Self.
And that sūtra previously cited, which begins with "The Self," [is as follows]. || 1055 ||

To explain the connection of the passage beginning with "Then they said" (*tadāhuḥ*) with what has preceded, he recounts the context: "The Self" (*ātmeti*). The meaning is that the Upaniṣad concerning the Supreme, beginning with "By the dawn [of knowledge]" (*uṣā vai*), has proceeded for the sake of one's own knowledge which destroys ignorance. In that Upaniṣad, the aphorism regarding the knowledge of the Self—"One should meditate upon the Self alone" (*ātmetyevopāsīta*)—has been described; thus he says, "having begun with 'The Self'" (*ātmetyupakramam*). That in which there is a commencement with "The Self"—that...
Thus, up to this point. || 1055 ||
By the phrase "for that is this," its object of cognition has been defined.
In the same way, by means of incomplete speech, even a semblance of valid cognition (pramābhāsa) is excluded. || 1056 ||

He restates what was said in the *avyākṛta-vākya* (the statement concerning the unmanifest): "That [is] because... This means that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of this *upaniṣad* is the self (*pratyagātman*), which has not yet been realized. He repeats what was stated in the *akṛtsna-vākya* (the statement concerning the incomplete): "Incomplete... Just as the statement regarding the object of knowledge in the *avyākṛta-vākya* concerns the meaning of the self that is unknown, so too, by the *akṛtsna-vākya*, there is merely a semblance of valid cognition (*pramābhāsa*) with respect to the non-self, and not valid cognition; such is its status as an object of knowledge.
The meaning is that it has been refuted. || 1096 ||
The Self alone is to be seen here, because of its all-encompassing nature; there is nothing other than the Self.
As long as something other than that is perceived, it would necessarily be incomplete. (1057)

Now he states the meaning of the sūtra under discussion: "The Self" (ātmeti). Here, "herein" (atra) means when both the Self and the non-Self have become objects to be seen. The reason why the Self alone is to be seen—through the exclusion of any other connection—is "because it is the Whole" (kṛtsnatvāt). This means that when That is seen, nothing remains of that which is to be seen. He states the meaning of the particle "only" (eva): "not" (na). This is the reason why the non-Self is not to be seen: because it is "not the Whole" (akṛtsna).

Thus, as long as that which is other than the Self—the non-Self—is perceived, it is necessarily experienced as limited. As long as that [non-Self] exists, because of its limited nature, and because its own form does not manifest through the cognition of it, it cannot be the object of true vision; this is the meaning. Alternatively, as long as that which is other than the Self is perceived, the Self itself would become limited, due to the perception of its counter-correlate (the non-Self); therefore, [if one were to perceive it], the consequence would be that it becomes a non-Self. Thus, [it must be abandoned].
The meaning is that, having discarded the limited self, one should contemplate the unlimited Self alone. || 1057 ||
"Who am I? To whom do I belong? From where have I come? Who shall I be, and how?"
This meaning of the injunction is understood as being the motivating cognition (prayojakamati). Thus it is said.
[Vol. 2, page 352]
The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya, Chapter One, Section 1.

If it is argued that the Self alone must be seen, then an injunction (vidhi) regarding that seeing would have to be stated; however, all three types of injunctions have already been refuted in the discussion on seeing.

Furthermore, one might object: "Since the Self is already established as such, where is there any room for an injunction? Anticipating this, the author demonstrates that injunction applies to the operation of the means—both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—for attaining that [Self], by asking:
"Who am I? This means: among the body and so forth, which are perceived as the Self, am I each of them individually, or their aggregate, or something other than these?

He reflects: "I am related to each one of these, such as the body, or to their combination, or to something else. To the question "To what? he says: "I am born from another, from the five elements, or from something else. To the question "Or from where?"—the word *iti* (thus) is connected with the phrase "of the motivating cognition" (*prayojaka-mateḥ*). He says: "Even though there is something other than the cognition, is it existent or non-existent? To the question "What? he says: "And how am I [related] to existence, non-existence, difference, or non-difference?"

He says, "May [the knowledge] arise. How so? For this is an imitation of the words of the Purāṇas. He states that in the Sūtra, a mandate (*niyoga*) is accepted regarding the purification of the object—namely, the activity consisting of the application of the causes of knowledge for the seeker of liberation who has been impelled by such inquiry.
Thus [ends the section on] the instigator. || 1098 ||
From what, indeed, could the arising, the subsistence, and the destruction of effects possibly proceed?
In this context, the operation known as positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is prescribed.

However, one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) must effect the purification of both the "thou" (tvam-artha) and the "that" (tat-artha), because the realization of the sentence-meaning—the identity of those two—is established only for one who has already understood the two referents. Thus he says: "In its origin," etc. From what [source] does the meaning of the word [arise]—from Brahman or from something else? Here, by the word "iti," the previous commentary...

The word "wood" (*kāṣṭham*) is drawn back [from the previous verse] as the object of the cognition that prompts [the inquiry]. Thus, for one who has become inquisitive but whose Brahman is unknown, the origination of the world and so forth cannot be explained otherwise;
for the body and other such things are non-self because they possess the properties of being objects of sight and so on, whereas "I" am of the nature of the seer and so forth.

He states that when the realization of the meanings of *tat* and *tvam* is desired, the operation of synthesis and so forth—consisting of the thought "I am of the nature of the seer"—is enjoined in the scriptural injunctions such as "one should hear" (*śrotavya*). (Verse 1099) "Synthesis... etc.
Therefore, from the statement, "Know that supreme Brahman through austerity," [it follows].
In this context, the operation known as positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is considered to be austerity (tapas).

He states that even in the Taittirīya Śruti, the operation consisting of *anvaya* (positive concomitance) and so forth is enjoined as a means for the knowledge of the inward Brahman (*pratyagbrahmadhīhetutvena*). He says: "By austerity... The ellipsis is to be supplied thus:

"Therefore, by this statement, the aforementioned operation is enjoined. Anticipating the objection that, based on the statement "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (*tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva*), it is austerity—well-known as a means to knowledge—that is enjoined, and not *anvaya* and so forth, he says: "Anvaya... [The word] "in the present context" (*prakṛtā*) [is understood].
The term *śruti* signifies the meaning of the locative case. || 1060 ||
Or from this sentence, "From whence [it arises]," there can be no austerity other than that.
Because of the statement of its characteristics, according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is the Self is what one must seek. (1061)

Having set aside what is well-known, he states an unfamiliar reason, beginning with "yataḥ" (from which). The meaning is that the definition of Brahman—which is to be known—has been stated in such passages as "From which indeed these [beings arise]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1); and thus, the austerity prescribed for the sake of knowing that Brahman to be defined is indeed the pursuit of it (*anvaya*), not the *kṛcchra* penance and the like, because the latter would be irrelevant to the subject at hand. This is stated starting from the passage: "That Self which is free from evil... and continuing with "He is to be sought."
He establishes the injunction by relying on the Chāndogya Śruti, stating that "the connection and so forth [of words] are prescribed as the cause of cognition.
The word "yaḥ" (which) implies that the operation of the Śruti has been prescribed and demonstrated. || 1061 ||
1. By the words beginning with "kha"; 2. "kha" refers to the letter *ya* and so forth.
[Vol. 2, page 353]
[The Brāhmaṇa] having abandoned what is unpleasant and what is supreme [to others], possessing the means such as being humble, and so forth.
One who practices celibacy should worship his own beloved self like Śakra.

The incidental [commentary] summarizes the intended meaning of Prajāpati’s words: "Having renounced," etc. Just as Indra, having observed the vow of celibacy for one hundred and one years according to the Śruti, reflected upon the Self through methods such as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too another person—having renounced the non-Self which is of the nature of suffering and being endowed with the means taught in the scriptures, such as freedom from pride (*amānitva*) and freedom from ostentation (*adambhitva*)—[realizes] the Self which is of the nature of bliss by means of that [reflection].

The meaning is that one should know [this]. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the well-known status of the qualifications such as humility (amānitva) and so forth as established in the Smṛti. || 1062 ||
By this sentence, "The Self," the knowledge of Brahman is introduced.
The entire Upaniṣad will serve as the commentary for that purpose. || 1063 ||

Having stated, under the guise of a restatement (*anuvāda*), that the operation consisting of the means of knowledge, their connection, and so forth, is what is to be enjoined, he states the purpose for which that restatement is made:

"By the word 'Self'... Because of its proximity to the aphorism on knowledge (*vidyā-sūtra*), the prefix *upa-* indicates that the Upaniṣads are subsidiary to that [knowledge] by virtue of being the generators of the knowledge thus aphorized. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of which": if it were the case that the meaning of all Upaniṣads is established merely through the explanation of the aphorism, then [the author] says "they say," and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that [the knowledge] might be useless, he says: "The conduct" (vṛtti). The construction is as follows: the text beginning with "They say this" and so forth will constitute the conduct (*vṛtti*) for the knowledge that has been set forth in the aphorism (*sūtra*). || 1063 ||
This single sūtra, "The Self," consists of only two verses.
Either this entire chapter, or just these two chapters [should be studied]. (1064)

He restates what was said—that the entire subsequent portion is a commentary on this very aphorism (*sūtra*), "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'"—with the words, "The word 'Self' is one. He states that the first section (*kāṇḍikā*) beginning with "Therefore, verily" and the second beginning with "This, indeed, is that" constitute the aphorism and its further commentary respectively, using the term "section" (*kaṇḍikā*). He further states that the entire third chapter is a single aphorism, while the subsequent elaboration belongs to it, using the term "chapter" (*adhyāya*).
He states that the third chapter and the fourth chapter are the Sūtra and the subsequent Vivaraṇa (Exposition), saying "adhyāya" [chapter]. || 1064 ||
Others understand [the categories] beginning with the "unexplained" (avyākṛta) and the "explanation" (vyākaraṇa).
"Indeed, even with only five sūtras, one's own desired [interpretation] is not contradicted.

(1065) Having stated his own preferred arrangement of the sūtras by way of alternative options, [the author] states the division favored by Bhartṛprapañca, beginning with "avyākṛta" (the unexplained). The word "kila" (indeed) is used to indicate that this division is understood from his own tradition. Even in this conceptualization—
The phrase "tathāpi" indicates the acceptance that there is no impairment of liberation through the knowledge of oneness, thereby suggesting a division of the Sūtra. || 1065 ||
Another [teacher] says that this very Self here is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The five categories of meaning (*padārtha*) have been thus stated in the aphorisms as that which is to be attained and that which is dear.

He now demonstrates those very aphorisms as they were spoken by others, beginning with "the unmanifest" (*avyākṛtam*). In the phrase "this indeed" (*eṣeha*), the sandhi has been disregarded according to Vedic usage. The unknown reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is the cause of the world; that very [reality], having entered into the created world, is that [same thing].

The meaning is that, having abandoned what is not the Self, it must be understood that only that [Self] is to be attained through knowledge and that it alone is the most beloved; thus, the five categories of objects are indicated here in this aphorism. || 1066 ||
1 Kha Ca | [vol2,
page 354] 648 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter— ]
And [this applies] to the aforementioned sūtras until the completion of the treatise.
The subsequent text would be the commentary (vṛtti), because it provides a systematic connection (samanvaya) among those [topics]. || 1067 ||

He states the commencement of the subsequent section (*uttaragrantha*) as being a commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtras already mentioned: "Of those as described. He provides the reason for this by stating that [the topics] such as the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*), which were set forth in the sūtras, are correctly followed up in the subsequent section. Regarding this, it has been said: "The subsequent section, which serves as the commentary (*vṛtti*) for these [topics] as they were introduced, begins from here until the completion of the treatise. (1067)
Now, desiring to explain the meaning of the Sūtras directly, the Śruti [proceeds].
The introduction proceeds from the desire to state the purpose. || 1068 ||

Having analyzed the aphorism (*sūtra*) regarding the positions of both self and other, he states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "they say" (*tadāhuḥ*) as follows: "Desiring to explain" (*vyācikhyāsuḥ*).

Immediately after the commencement of the aphorism, when the opportunity arises, the Śruti—desiring to directly explain the meaning of the aphorism "the Self" (*ātma*) and so forth, namely the knowledge of the Self, as well as the various means required for that, such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest—introduces a preliminary discussion (*upoddhāta*) in order to state the fruit of the knowledge indicated by the aphorism: "reflection" (*cintām*).

The meaning is that he provides an "introduction" (*upoddhāta*), defined as "that which is stated for the sake of establishing the subject at hand. The word *atha* expresses immediate succession by stating the division of the sūtras; the word *idānīm* is used to indicate the sequence, namely that first comes the sūtra and then the commentary (*vṛtti*). It should be observed that although there is unity in the knowledge of their meaning—whether the sūtras are divided or unified—one sees a diversity of methods of exposition in various places, and thus there is much that has been said. [The word *icchā* means] desire...
But [the suffix] *tu* is not intended to be expressed. || 1068 ||
The subject matter of the words that are about to be spoken is denoted by the word "tat" (that).
The Brahmins desiring to know Brahman spoke thus in the presence of their teacher.

Having stated the purport of the sentence, he explains the meanings of the words; he states the meaning of that word [“tat”] as follows: “That which is to be described,” etc. The meaning is that the reality revealed by the sentence beginning with “by the knowledge of Brahman” is what is denoted by the word “that. What is that revealed reality expressed by the word “that”? He says: “Brahman. In this context, seekers of liberation who desire to know—that the realization of Brahman is the cause of being the Self of all—[approach] in the presence of a teacher that which...

The meaning is that "that" (tat) refers to what is revealed by the subsequent sentence here; the qualification "brahmin" is used to show that the specific entitlement to the inquiry into Brahman belongs to brahmins alone. || 1069 ||
Having realized the entirety of the essence of all Vedānta, he abides in Brahman.
Having approached the Guru according to the prescribed rule, some who desire liberation say [the following].

By the Śruti text, "One who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman," they qualify the Guru. By the word "vijñāta" (known), they exclude one who possesses only indirect knowledge.
By the word "brahmaṇi" (in Brahman), they indicate the sequence of approaching [the Guru] as prescribed by the Śruti text, "With fuel in hand. By the phrase "according to the rule," they say—
He fulfills what is required by this [verse]. Regarding the words "some" (kecit), he states their desire for the knowledge of reality: "those seeking liberation" (mumukṣavaḥ).
Those whose latent impressions have been established by sacrifices and other rites, and who have cast aside all remaining means [to worldly ends].
Those whose intellects are purified are dispassionate toward the worldly aims of human life.
1. By means of the desire to uphold [the Dharma].
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 649.

Now, it may be objected that those [rites] are not to be adopted by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), because those who are intent on performing the causes for heaven and the like lack any longing for liberation; therefore, he says: "By sacrifice and so forth. Those whose intellects are purified by the specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced from the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the rest, being included within bondage—

The meaning is that those who are dispassionate toward the fruits of this world and the next, who have cast aside all causes for worldly human goals, and who desire only knowledge, cause [it] to arise. || 1071 ||
But surely, having abandoned actions because their purpose has been fulfilled through action, they are free from attachment.
By means of this fragment of the knowledge of Brahman, those who desire to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra [should proceed]. || 1072 ||

Those who perform various Vedic rites (*śrauta-karma*), even when abandoning them, do not seek knowledge alone because their minds are impaired by the desire for their fruits; therefore, he says: "Having abandoned... Since the fruits of actions have already been realized through the purification of the mind, there is no further need for them; thus, being detached from those fruits which are the causes [of rebirth], and having abandoned those actions along with their fruits, one should, by means of the boat called knowledge (*vidyā*)—as described in the commentary—[cross over].
The connection [of the words] is as follows: those of pure intellect, desiring to cross the ocean of saṃsāra which is established by experience, raise this objection. ||1072||
Because of defects such as incompleteness, the goals of human life [attained] up to Viriñca are not perfect.
Free from craving and desiring the supreme good that consists in the destruction of all those defects. || 1073 ||

One might object: "Even if there is no desire for the fruits of mere ritual action, such as heaven and the like, since such desire is possible regarding the fruits of meditation accompanied by such action—namely, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) and so forth—how can there be a desire for liberation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As far as Viriñca. The meaning is that from the human level up to Prajāpati, because one perceives defects in those human goals—such as their being limited and perishable—one becomes dispassionate toward them and thus develops a desire for liberation.

Then, raising the objection that there might likewise be no desire for liberation because it is a fruit—just like the world of Brahmā—the author says: "Aśeṣa... (etc.). That is to say, they are those who desire to attain that which is called liberation (*mokṣa*), the highest good (*śreyas*), wherein there is the destruction of all defects such as limitation seen even in the world of Brahmā and other [heavens]. || 1073 ||
Having found a teacher who was superior, they were free from desire and spoke with censure.
For it is only through the door of the guru that knowledge is capable of leading to the attainment of the highest good in this world.

He states that their challenge toward the teacher is not to be ignored because it contains a censure (*ākṣepa*). He says "with censure" (*sākṣepam*) to indicate the efficacy of the teacher’s resolution of that [challenge]. He says "the superior one" (*śreyāṃsam*) to show that, because he is a teacher, one must strive for the welfare of the disciples.

He says "the teacher" (*gurum*) to address the doubt that if they raise a challenge with censure, they are seekers of victory (*vijigīṣu*) rather than disciples; thus he says "without... (*nir-*) [to refute that].

Regarding the word "raṇā": one might raise the objection, "Since knowledge arises for them simply through the power of their own study, why should they approach a teacher? Anticipating this, he says "through the door of the guru," relying on such scriptural passages as "He who has a teacher" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2). Here, the word "here" refers to the Self. Therefore, the implication is that approaching a teacher is appropriate for them. || 1074 ||
In response to the inquiry, "What did they say?", this is now being stated.
By the word "they consider" (manyante) itself, the relative pronoun "that which" (yat) attains its connection.
The reality that is neither excluded nor followed by anything else is expressed by the word "Brahman."
In this way, the word "Brahman" retains its primary meaning; thus it is established. 1076. 1. Not an anomaly. 2. kha. by that very [nature].
3. kha. all. [Vol. 2, page 356]

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: Having explained the passage beginning with "They say that," he introduces the section beginning with "That which... He asks, "What? and therein, preceded by a statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), [he explains] Brahman—

He states the meaning of the word *dā* [in *brahmadā*]: "they think" (*manyante*). One might ask: why could that which is designated by the word *brahman*, such as the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) and others, not be [the referent]? To this he says: "primary" (*mukhya*).

When the word *brahman* is applied to a reality devoid of the relationship between general and particular, it has its primary meaning; however, if it were to have the Lotus-Seated One and others as its object, this would not be the case.
Furthermore, when a primary meaning is possible, a secondary meaning does not deserve to be accepted—this is the sense. || 1075 ||
That [object] is cognized by the intellect through its own specific nature.
They directly declare that [knowledge] to be the "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā), which is the very faculty of perception itself.

He states the meaning of the word "knowledge" (vidyā): "That" [refers to it]. The construction is as follows: that mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) arising from the sentence, by which Brahman—that which is one's own unique existence-consciousness-bliss—is directly known as the inner self (pratyak), is designated as "Brahma-knowledge" (brahmavidyā).
They think that through the knowledge of Brahman they will become everything, the All.
That we, who are human beings, should pursue opposition there. || 1078 ||

He connects the introductory statement— "Regarding that which humans think, 'By the knowledge of Brahman we shall become everything,' we raise an objection concerning the fruit of that knowledge"— with the word "everything. || 1078 ||
For that which is ultimately real has been declared to be the entirety of reality itself.
Those seeking liberation raise objections for the sake of purifying that means of valid cognition. || 1079 ||

Anticipating the objection that—for those seeking liberation whose pride has been stilled—it is not appropriate to raise an objection regarding the reality sought to be known, since the mere question is sufficient for the arising of knowledge, the author states the intention of those who raise the challenge: "The whole," etc. Alternatively, whatever is the real entity is indeed complete, as was stated previously in the passage beginning with "for here" (atra hi); therefore, the meaning is that the challenge is raised for the purpose of purifying the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that non-duality (*advaita*). || 1079 ||
For it is said that the knowledge of Brahman alone is the means for attaining everything in its entirety.
In attaining that [liberation], there would thus be only the veil of darkness as the obstruction.

Anticipating the objection that for one desiring mere knowledge (jñānamātra), even the purification of the means [of knowledge] is not useful, he says: "The knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā). For when the means is purified, that very knowledge arises; it is stated in both Śruti and Smṛti that this alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, the meaning is that its purification is purposeful.
He states the implied meaning of the statement that this [knowledge] is the cause of liberation: "In attaining that. The referent of the word "that" (tat) is the entire reality.
Since knowledge is merely a purifier (dhotikā), it is therefore not an agent.
Therefore, in this case, the effects of actions such as flying upward and so forth cannot be possible.
Even though knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of liberation, how is it that ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as its obstruction? To this he says: "It is illuminative" (*dyotikā*).

Since it is merely illuminative and not a productive agent (*kāraka*), there is no effect of knowledge in liberation other than the breaking of the veil of delusion (*moha*). Therefore, because it would be illogical for knowledge to be a means [to liberation] otherwise, it is established that ignorance is the obstruction; such is the meaning. [This holds true] when liberation is separated from knowledge by nothing more than ignorance.

Since the attainment of that [state] cannot be accomplished by action, and because its abiding in its own nature is distinct from the fourfold fruits of action, it follows that liberation is not achievable through ritual acts; this is the conclusion stated [in the verse].

[The author says: "Arising, etc."—that is to say, "in this liberation. And the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that if liberation were achievable through action, then according to the maxim "whatever is produced is impermanent," liberation would be non-eternal, and consequently, there would be bondage once again. || 1081 ||
Since a lamp illuminates an object already established and does not bring it into existence, [it is not a cause].
The nature of all beings is established as such even prior to awakening. || 1082 ||

Anticipating the objection that liberation, though not achievable through ritual action (*karman*), must be something produced because it is achievable through knowledge (*vidyā*), he says: "It is established" (*siddha*). Since knowledge does not produce [liberation] but rather illuminates it—like a lamp—liberation is established even prior to knowledge; therefore, it is not something to be produced. || 1082 ||
Therefore, due to delusion, we are incomplete, even though in reality we are the complete Self.
Having destroyed ignorance through knowledge, we go to that which is inherent in ourselves in its entirety.

Raising the objection, "If every entity is established by itself (*svataḥsiddhi*), how can there be a desire to attain it through knowledge? he says, "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), [meaning] because of the intervention of ignorance (*ajñāna-vyavadhāna*). Then, as to how liberation occurs, he says, "Having struck down" (*nihatya*); the meaning is that what is "inherently attained" (*svatogata*)—that is, obtained by its own nature—is merely obstructed by ignorance. || 1083 ||
This expression "human beings" is used for the sake of determining eligibility.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context function as a section break or punctuation mark. || [End of Section] ||
For human beings possess the authority over all things for the purpose of their complete welfare. || 1084 ||

Having established that the objection is for the purpose of purifying the non-dual cognition—which is the cause of liberation—produced by knowledge, he states the function of the mention of "human beings" with the words, "The qualification...

(adhikāra). The phrase "of knowledge and action" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. To the question, "How is the determination of qualification made?", he replies, "For among human beings... (manuṣyāṇāṃ hi).
The meaning of the word "for" (hi) is that it has been demonstrated in the earlier Mīmāṃsā that only they (human beings) possess the qualification for the meaning of the Vedas.
Therefore, it follows that the mention of "human beings" is appropriate; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 1084 ||
Or rather, the mention of "human" is made because the purpose of knowledge is visible [in this world].
In this case, the qualified person is merely that much [in scope], unlike the one qualified for the Agnihotra sacrifice. || 1085 ||

Having explained the purport of the human statement according to the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), he states another purport: "Seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), etc. Because knowledge has a visible fruit known as the destruction of grief and so forth, everyone who desires that fruit—and who is thus encompassed by the definition of a common qualified candidate—is eligible for this knowledge.
To express that there is no restrictive rule here as there is for those eligible for the *agnihotra* and other rites, the mention of "human" is used here.
Such is the meaning. || 1085 ||
And he will explain later on that "whosoever awakened to that."
Therefore, in this case, one qualified for ritual action is not required, because [the practice] has a visible purpose.

He states the proof for the claim that, unlike in the case of ritual action (*karman*), no specific qualification is required for knowledge (*jñāna*): "He awakened" (*pratyabudhyata*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "he will declare the lack of restriction regarding the qualification for knowledge. One might ask: "If that is so, how then is the *bhāṣya* [which mentions] the mention of 'human' (*manuṣya*) to be understood? Anticipating this, he says: "Not from this," meaning that it should not be accepted as authoritative because it contradicts the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).
