He clarifies this very point with the words "in whatever way" (yathākathaṃcit). With the words "or the whole" (kṛtsnaṃ vā), he presents an alternative in order to state that both positions are flawed: "the state of being Brahman" (brahmatvam) || 1103 ||
If that [liberation] were to exist by itself, then the knowledge of Brahman would be useless.
For the wise do not bring about the heat of fire from something else. || 1104 ||

He refutes the first [position] by restating it with the words "If... Having raised the objection—"Even if the Brahman-hood of Brahman is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddha*), why is knowledge useless?"—he considers the following: Does that [knowledge] produce Brahman-hood, or does it manifest it, or does it remove the ignorance that obstructs it?
It is not the first, because that would contradict its being self-established; nor is it the other, because manifestation too is of the very nature of the Self. With this in mind, he says:
"Indeed not," [he said]. || 1104 ||
For the embodiment of knowledge, there is no ignorance; it is neither adventitious nor innate.
Just as darkness does not exist in the sun, in this same way, Brahman cannot possibly be so [characterized]. || 1105 ||

He states the third [point] with the words "jñāna" (knowledge). Since it is impossible for Brahman, whose nature is luminosity, to be associated with ignorance, which is non-luminous by nature, he provides an illustration with the words "bhānau" (in the sun). He states the conclusion—that it is illogical for Brahman to be either inherently limited or limited [only] through knowledge, because [otherwise] knowledge would be rendered useless—with the words "tena" (therefore). || 1105 ||
Furthermore, the fault of rendering the commencement of treatises and so forth purposeless would also follow.
Even if there were a contradiction with one's own experience, if Brahman-hood were to exist by itself [independently], [then it would follow that it is not perceived]. (1106)

Furthermore, he states that Brahmanhood does not exist inherently [in the self], because if it were inherent, the commencement of the scripture and the engagement of persons in hearing and so forth would be purposeless.
He says: "From the scripture, etc. The word "also" (*api*) is used to indicate that there is no possibility whatsoever of suspecting that Brahmanhood depends on a cause if it were inherent.

Moreover, since there is no experience of the thought "I am the non-dual Brahman," and because there is contrary experience such as "I am the agent," the non-dual Brahmanhood of the inner self (*pratīc*) [is not established by itself].

He states that if [Brahman] were self-established, then the scripture concerning its meaning would lack authority due to contradiction with experience; therefore, Brahman is not established by itself [through scripture]. Thus he says: "By one's own experience... (1106).
If the scripture were like a woman or fire, it would merely be an injunction for visual perception.
In that case, there would be no contradiction with reality, because they would have different loci. || 1107 ||

An adherent of a particular school (ekadeśin) raises an objection in order to avoid contradicting experience, saying: "As for the woman... Just as the statement, "O Gautama, the woman is indeed the fire," is intended merely to instill the perception of fire in the woman and does not concern the actual reality, so too the scripture concerning non-dual Brahman—such as "I am Brahman"—is intended merely to instill the perception of Brahman in the self and does not concern the actual reality. [The opponent argues that] if the scripture were intended to enjoin meditation (upāsanā), it would have no conflict with other means of valid cognition regarding the nature of reality.
He said, "So be it. || 1107 ||
The word "sadasī" (in the assembly) refers to that which culminates in action and is established in the objects of perception and so forth.
What contradiction can there be here between these two, which exist without touching one another's objects? (1108)

He clarifies that the reason for the absence of contradiction lies in their having different objects by stating "existent" (*sat*). He concludes the thesis (*sādhya*) by stating "contradiction" (*virodha*), which here refers to [the contradiction] within the Self (*ātmani*). The conclusion regarding the reason is expressed as "mutually" (*mithaḥ*). || 1108 ||
1kha. Nor [is it] in the embodied [form]. [vol2, page 362] This is not so, because it was previously stated that a sentence is grounded in a real entity (vastu).
There would indeed be a contradiction because of their having a single substratum. || 1109 ||

The proponent refutes this, saying "Not so. He argues that while it was stated previously that passages such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) have reality (*vastu*) as their primary purport, here [in the case of ritual injunctions], one who asserts they have action (*kriyā*) as their purport contradicts that; therefore, he says that such a sentence does not enjoin meditation. Because the sentence lacks a focus on action, like other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is established in the nature of reality (*vastuniṣṭha*); thus, since a sentence established in Brahman shares the same object with other means of knowledge, its own...
He says that there would indeed be a contradiction with existence: "contradiction" (virodha). || 1109 ||
Furthermore, the vision of Brahman cannot be produced, because Brahman is not established [as an object].
But when [the world] is established, that perception of a woman is held to be easily accomplished. (1110)
Furthermore, is Brahman unknown or known? To the first case, he says that its meditation is impossible, stating "impossible.

Anticipating the objection that the meditation on Brahman within the inner self (pratyagātman) is as easy as the meditation on fire in a woman (yoṣidagnidṛṣṭi), he says "in the world" (loka). This means that the meditation on it—namely, the meditation on that fire—is [only] upon that woman. || 1110 ||
Now, if that Brahman is considered to be established through other means of knowledge, like fire;
Since its purpose is fulfilled by that alone, what else could be requested of the Śruti?

Having restated another objection, he refutes it with the words "Now" (atha). The meaning is that since the fulfillment of the human goal is achieved solely through the comprehension of Brahman derived from other means of knowledge, the scriptural knowledge of Brahman is of no use whatsoever. || 1111 ||
For upon the very perception of That, there is the complete attainment of all human goals.
Furthermore, that view would not be an obstacle to other results, just as the perception of fire [is not an obstacle to other results]. || 1112 ||

Even though the mere knowledge of Brahman accomplishes the human goal (puruṣārtha) in general, it does not accomplish the full human goal; therefore, one might suspect that meditation upon it according to the scriptures is required for that purpose. Anticipating this, he says: "In the vision of That" (*taddṛṣṭau*). The meaning is that if the vision of Brahman is obtained even through other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), then by that alone the full human goal is attained; thus, for that purpose, a scriptural vision of Brahman need not be performed again, as it would be like grinding what has already been ground (*piṣṭapeṣaṇa*). Just as the vision of fire dependent on another means of knowledge...

Just as, according to the scripture, the perception of fire is applied to a woman for the sake of accomplishing a result that has not yet been accomplished, so too [is this case]; thus, it is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). || 1112 ||
Moreover, if totality were derived from something else, then the status of Brahman would be established through an unstable means.
Whether by way of action, or by way of knowledge, or by relying on both. || 1113 ||
Having rejected the position that Brahman-hood is intrinsic and having stated another position, he refutes it with the words "even from another" (*parato’pi*).

The meaning is that if the Brahman-hood of Brahman were dependent on something else, it would be unstable and non-eternal, like heaven. The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate the aforementioned example. Anticipating the objection "How so?", he sets forth an alternative analysis to demonstrate this: "From action" (*kriyātaḥ*) || 1113 ||
Brahminhood does not arise from ritual action, because it is associated with birth and other such factors.
There would be no beginning or end, according to the scriptures such as the *Pūrvājā*.
1 kha. This is *bobha*. 2 kha. *'śvakāraḥ* | ka' | [vol2, page 363] - 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramañjarī* composed by Ānandagiri. 657

He answers the first [objection] with "No. He provides the reason: because that which is to be accomplished by action is subject to origination and so forth, and since those [characteristics] are seen in what is produced by it, it would follow that [Brahman] is non-eternal. He states this with the words "origination and so forth. Anticipating the objection that Brahman might also possess birth and so on, he says, "It could not be so.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the underlying logic: that if it possessed a beginning and an end, it would follow—like a jar—that it is not Brahman. || 1114 ||
And the sublation of the efficacy of karma is observed in many instances.
Since the desire for liberation is the cause of that [knowledge], ritual action is not its effect; therefore, it does not arise from that.

He states that Brahmanhood is not accomplished through ritual action, because it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "It is not by what is done that one attains the uncreated, nor by action, nor by progeny," and so forth. He says, "And there is a refutation. By the word "repeatedly" (*bahuśaḥ*), he indicates repetition as a sign of the scripture’s intent regarding the fact that liberation is not accomplished through action. The phrase "of the effect of action" is an expression emphasizing the abstract state; the meaning is: of the desire for liberation and of that [desire's] object, which is Brahmanhood.

Therefore, he says "taddhetoḥ" (for that reason) to show that Brahminhood is not something to be accomplished through action, because of reasons such as the aforementioned refutation. He then says "tataḥ" (therefore) to establish that the first position is untenable. || 1115 ||
Now, if it is thought that through knowledge all this becomes Brahman;
Even so, the status of being either different or non-different as objects of cognition is not established as desired. || 1116 ||

He speaks of another *kalpa*. Now, [the word] "atha" [is used]. Having known that [the world] is not other than that, Brahman became full; whether it be other, non-other, or both other and non-other—in all three ways, there is no establishment of Brahman. Thus he says: "anyā" (other). 1116.
A contradiction with action would ensue if that which is non-different were the object of cognition.
Furthermore, a contradiction with other scriptural passages would result if [the Self] were perceived as the inner self. || 1117 ||

Anticipating the objection, "If [Brahman] is not cognizable by anything other than itself, how can the desired conclusion be established?", he says: "Action" (kriyā). The meaning is that within a single action, there would be a contradiction for one and the same thing to be both the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, if a separate perception regarding Brahman as an object were intended, then [it would follow that] reality—

He states [the objection] that there would be a contradiction with scriptural passages such as "a mass of knowledge and wisdom" (*jñānaprajñānaghana*). Alternatively, the meaning is that if that vision were something other than Brahman, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "That by which one knows the known is itself other than the known. Or else, the meaning is that if the inner self (*pratīc*) were seen through a vision that takes itself as its object, there would be a contradiction with other scriptural statements such as "It is not seen by sight" (*na dṛṣṭer dṛṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ*). || 1117 ||
And thus, it would follow that Brahman is something to be accomplished through knowledge.
Even if the object of cognition were both different and non-different, this fault would be difficult to avoid. || 1118 ||

He states another defect [in the opponent's position]: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is that there would be a contradiction with action, just as there is a contradiction with scripture. He refutes the second [position] by means of the defect already stated regarding the position that Brahman is not an object of knowledge:

"Whether different or non-different" (*anyānanya*). Here too, the meaning is that non-difference exists. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the aspect of difference, then [there is a problem with] the aspect of non-difference...
The sense is that there would certainly be a contradiction with the scripture. || 1118 ||
Having perceived that, it then became something else; what else did that which was other than that perceive?
If that [cognition] too was previously unknown by another [cognition], an infinite regress would result.

He restates the third alternative with the words "having known. He raises a dilemma: did that which, having known something else, became everything, know something other [than itself], or not? He states the first alternative—"that other"—and refutes it with the words "even that. || 1119 ||
3 1 [vol2, page 364]
658. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya]:
Even if [the world] were entirely without cause, why is it not so for people like us?
Nor can partiality toward the Śruti be justified on the grounds of its authority. || 1120 ||

Anticipating another objection, he says: "of that which is without cause. This means "of one devoid of knowledge"; the connection is with the phrase "even for people like us. Thus, the implication is that knowledge would be useless in all cases.

Anticipating the objection that the scripture itself—in passages such as "Therefore, all that" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6)—declares that for people like us the attainment of everything results from knowledge alone, whereas for Brahman or its object of knowledge it occurs by its own nature, he says:
"Partisanship" means that the authority of the Veda is equal with respect to all [people]. By this, the position that "even though it was not known by him" is refuted. || 1120 ||
And the refutation of their conjunction will be clearly stated through logical arguments.
Moreover, due to their mutual contradiction, there can be no relationship of primary and subordinate between the two. || 1121 ||

Having refuted that the status of Brahman (*brahmatva*) is something to be accomplished through action or knowledge, he now refutes the position that it arises from both together, with the words "by a combination" (*samuccaya*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the negation of the combination mentioned in the context of their relationship. The phrase "it will be stated in the section concerning Bhujyu" is the ellipsis to be supplied. He indicates the impossibility of the three kinds of combinations—already mentioned and yet to be mentioned—for the sake of ease of understanding.
"Pradhāna" [means] "the primary. || 1121 ||
Because it possesses many such defects, it is difficult to establish as valid by means of authoritative cognition.
"By knowledge alone we infer completeness," and so forth, as has been extensively stated. || 1122 ||
He concludes the introduction with the words "ityādi" (and so forth). By the word "iti," there is the statement of the types of defects already mentioned.

Whether [the object] is real or unreal, in all three ways, the futility of knowledge (*vidyā-vaiyarthyam*) follows; and that [object] must be either different or non-different [from Brahman]. In the first case, there is a contradiction with its being "entirety" (*kārtsnyam*); in the second, there is an impossibility of desiring it (*prepsā-yoga*). Furthermore, that [object] must be either knowable (*vedyam*) or unknowable (*avedyam*). In the first case, due to its insentience (*jāḍyāt*), it would not be Brahman; in the second, its existence is unestablished.
The defect expressed by the words "because self-luminosity is incompatible with being both an object of knowledge and a non-object" refers to the phrase "in its entirety," etc.;

by the word "etc.," there is included [the following]: that from delusion there is non-integrity, whereas in reality there is integrity, the distinction between means of knowledge and so forth is merely conceptual, and that [distinction] is a manifestation of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyāvidyā*), and so on. || 1122 ||
There is no fault whatsoever here, insofar as this will be logically established.
1.1 If this were conceived otherwise, there would be a succession of faults as previously stated. (1123)

Having stated the objection containing the challenge of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), he indicates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "not anyone" (*na kaścit*). Here, the term "here" (*atra*) refers to the doctrine of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*). He says "as" (*yathā*) to show that the promise of its faultlessness is appropriate, because it will be explained later how the liberation from all states of being therein is possible through the knowledge of Brahman as the Self. However, in the doctrine of real transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), since liberation is not established through knowledge, a continuous stream of defects would result.
Thus he said: "Otherwise," [verse 1123].
Thus, the introductory exposition has been explained here in brief.
In this commentary by the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda), even that belonging to another is described. || 1124 ||

In order to state that there is no tautology between the preceding and following contexts, he summarizes what has occurred thus: "In this manner, first... Here, the word "here" (*atra*) refers to the aforementioned passage. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "having remained within this commentary by the venerable teacher. And it should be understood that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been summarized.
[Brāhmaṇa 4] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 659.
He says, "Even that belonging to another," in order to state how the introduction (*upodghāta*) was explained by Bhartṛprapañca so that it might be accepted. || 1124 ||
This very result is stated at the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman.
And the proclamation of that fruit is for the sake of its being a factor in the engagement [with the practice]. || 1125 ||

Regarding the phrase "they say that," he states the meaning of the word *tat* according to their opinion: "This very [is it]. The meaning is as follows: the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman begins with the passage "Brahman indeed is this," and in that undertaking, this fruit called liberation is referred to by the word *tat*. To the objection that the statement of the fruit of knowledge is irrelevant and therefore how can it be expressed by the word *tat*, he replies: "In its engagement..."—that is, in the statement of the fruit of knowledge, that [fruit] is...

The meaning is that one who is averse to sense-objects would proceed toward knowledge; therefore, it is appropriate to state the result at the outset as a prerequisite for engaging in that [knowledge].
The word "for" (śabdaḥ) is used to indicate that the utility of stating the result for inducing engagement in the means is well-known elsewhere as well. || 1125 ||
The introduction to what is about to be taught follows; thereafter comes the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, if the statement regarding the fruit occurs even after that, how could it be expressed by the word "tat" (that)? || 1126 ||

He raises an objection, suggesting that although what is stated [in the subsequent passage] is a constituent part of that [knowledge], it is difficult to specify the fruit by means of the word "that" (*tat*). This is expressed in the phrase "what is about to be stated. Following the word "that," there is an introductory section (*upoddhāta*) which will be stated in the passage beginning with "by which [knowledge] of Brahman"; after that comes the knowledge of Brahman itself in the passage "he knew himself as That" (*tad ātmānam evāveda*); and even further beyond that is the fruit, stated in the passage beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Thus, since the fruit is so separated [from the word "that"], it cannot properly be referred to by the word "that," because that word requires proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
The meaning is: because it relies upon what is beneficial. || 1126 ||
Because there is the capacity for connection with what immediately precedes it, it is established as true.
Why is it said that the word "that" has a more remote connection? (1127)

The follower of Bhartṛprapañca offers this rebuttal: "By the immediately following [word]. For when the word *tat* (that) has the capacity for connection with the fruit of the knowledge mentioned immediately before—namely, "not for him"—it cannot be connected with the remote state of being everything, as there is no evidence for such a connection;
therefore, it is logical that it expresses its own fruit. This is the meaning. || 1127 ||
Prior to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, it is directly characterized by the nature of both duality and unity.
Having fully obtained the fruit thereof, others became filled with curiosity.
Thus say some twice-born ones who have become detached from their former stage of life.
That which is sought by those desiring to know its meaning is considered possible by the knowers of Brahman.
Now, raising an objection regarding the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*) under discussion, he states what is required by the phrase "they say": "Dvaita... etc. Regarding "immediacy" (*aparokṣatve*):

prior to the arising of the knowledge of the object which is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*), even the entire fruit of ritual action and knowledge—which consists of the Sūtra-word (*sautra-pada*) and possesses manifold flavors (*nānārasa*)—exists within the present body.

The construction is as follows: because they have not experienced [the goal] to its highest degree, those who have faith in that superior fruit of knowledge—liberation (*kaivalya*)—become detached from the previous stage, the state of the *sūtra*, and speak as will be described hereafter. The word "supreme" (*para*), signifying excellence, refers to the fruit of knowledge. By the term "twice-born" (*dvija*), it indicates the maxim: "Among thousands of men... and so forth. Furthermore, by specifically mentioning the twice-born, it implies the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*).

The very mention of the name indicates eligibility for knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of the Veda; for even those who are curious about the fruit of knowledge would lack the desire for knowledge in the absence of such curiosity.
Fearing that [the teaching] might be fruitless, he says: "It is possible. When that unity is conceived by the knowers of Brahman, in that—
The meaning is that those who are curious about the results of the [ritual] actions also raise an objection regarding those results. || 1128 || 1129 ||
Not by the former cognition of duality-and-unity, which is of little consequence.
For it is from that [knowledge] that the prosperity of all beings is expected through the science of Brahman.

Fearing that the knowledge of Brahman might be rendered useless because liberation from all states of existence is attained through the very knowledge of the identity of duality and unity, he says "dvaita... etc., with the intention of dispelling the desire to know that [identity]. "Pūrvatvam" (priority) refers to having occurred prior to the knowledge of Brahman. By means of this insignificant activity, [the cycle of] saṃsāra—

The meaning is that [meditation] which is internal has very little fruit; for meditation indeed results in the fruit of saṃsāra and does not bring about its destruction, as that would contradict the principle of "as is one's resolve, so is one's reward" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).

Therefore, it is logical that liberation from all states of existence occurs through the knowledge of Brahman alone; thus he says, "Since... (verse 113), expressing the desire to know that [knowledge].
Just as the cognition of duality or unity leads to the attainment of a corresponding fruit.
In the same way, one who possesses all-encompassing intelligence is sufficient for the attainment of the fruits of all states of being.
Nevertheless, there is no such knowledge that would yield all results; regarding this, he says: "Duality-and-unity," etc.

"All-encompassing cognition" means the realization of the full Brahman as the inner self (*pratyagbrahma*). Through the meditation on the *sūtra* (the Hiraṇyagarbha), by the principle of "as is one's resolve, so is one's attainment" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), it is like the attainment of the *sūtra*.
The meaning is that the attainment of Brahman is logical. || 1131 ||
Those who know that [reality] say, "We shall become the entirety of Brahman through the realization of Brahman."
Now, that which they consider to be Brahman is asked: "What did it know? (1132).

Having explained "They say this," in response to the expectation of what they say, he explains the passage beginning with "That which... He says: "Brahman. Those who know that are the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidaḥ*). The word *atha* is used there in the sense of "then" (or "thereupon"). That Brahman, through the knowledge of which humans have attained the state of being all things—that is Brahman.
The teacher says to the disciples who ask, "What has been known, or what has not? "That is Brahman. || 1132 ||
Regarding the question "What was known?", would that [object] be the agent or the object?
Regarding knowledge, the agent is questioned, or else the action is intended to be expressed here.

Being asked, he reflects in order to determine [the meaning]: "What is it that is not known? He clarifies this very reflection by asking, "Is the agent of knowledge being questioned, or is 'action' (karman) intended here in this question? [Thus he says: "Of knowledge... (vidyāyāḥ). || 1133 ||
If knowledge were created by Brahmā, it would follow that this [knowledge] is fruitless.
Because from the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, that which was formerly Brahman came into being.
The proponent states the fault regarding the agent in the phrase "by Brahman. He provides the reason for the consequence that knowledge would be fruitless in the phrase "Brahman," etc.

The meaning is: since that [individual] was already Brahman even prior to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman—because it is impossible to abandon one's own nature—therefore, knowledge is not purposeful.
Therefore, it is karma alone that is intended to be inquired about here in relation to knowledge.
For it is precisely because of its dependence upon the object of cognition that validity is asserted. || 1135 ||

He states the result regarding the application of the question in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the statement of the question. The particle "but" (*tu*) is used to clarify that the particle "only" (*eva*) expresses the absence of any other subject for the question. He states the reason why knowledge and action are intended to be questioned:
[vol2, page 367]
“4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

661 ‘The object of knowledge (*prameya*)’—the meaning is that action (*karman*) is indeed highly esteemed in relation to knowledge (*vidyā*), because without it, there can be no possibility of its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it alone is fit to be questioned. || 1135 ||
There is no fault, because [the cognition] is based on the object, even when the agent is intended to be expressed. (1136)
Since everything became Brahman through that consciousness, it is therefore called "vijñāna" (consciousness) here.
The knowledge of Brahman is the unique cause for the attainment of everything.

The proponent (siddhāntin) answers by resorting to questions regarding both the agent and the object. Regarding the word "vastu" (the thing), the division [of the sentence] is "adoṣaḥ" (there is no fault).

When the question concerns the object, the agent is implied by the sense, because without him knowledge would not arise; and when the question concerns the agent, the object is likewise implied, since knowledge has the thing as its domain. Thus, there is no fault in the intention to inquire about both. Furthermore, there is no futility of knowledge even when the question concerns the agent, for [knowledge] is eternally [existent] by its own nature.

The meaning is that even in the state of being Brahman, [the inquiry] is fruitful because it destroys ignorance regarding Brahman. Having stated the intention of the questioners, he explains the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) with the words "sarvam" (all). The construction is as follows: that knowledge by which Brahman became all—that which is the uncommon cause for attaining everything—is designated by the term "brahmavidyā" in the introductory statement. 1136 || 1137 ||
This realization of the oneness of all is what is expressed by the term "knowledge of Brahman."
Because duality has non-duality as its true nature, it is like the reality of an imagined snake and so forth.

Having restated the proposition, he states the reason with the word "all" (*sarva*). Just as the rope is the reality of the snake and so forth imagined upon it, so too non-duality alone is the true nature of duality;
therefore, the realization of the oneness of all things is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—this is the meaning. || 1138 ||
They know that supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, as the oneness of all.
That is the reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth, of all those things born of delusion.

Now, this might be considered improper because it is contradictory for all things to be one and for one thing to be everything; having raised this doubt, he speaks in accordance with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which states that "the oneness of all" is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). He says: "The oneness of all. He explains the meaning of the *bhāṣya* passage "That is the Self" by saying:
"That. The meaning of the word "That" (*tat*) is the Supreme Self. The two words are "He" (*saḥ*) and "Reality" (*tattvam*). || 1139 ||
Because that [world] has ignorance alone as its cause, it is by that very Supreme Self [that it is perceived].
Otherwise, other things such as snakes and so forth would possess a self, just like a herd [of cattle]. || 1140 ||

Clarifying through an illustration that "the reality of everything is Brahman," he states the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—namely, "possessing the Self by means of this [Brahman] as the Self"—with the words "tadānīm" and so forth. This refers to all other non-self entities (*anātmavastūni*), that is to say, everything whatsoever apart from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
This has been stated regarding those whose views have fallen away from the self, solely because of their lack of understanding of that [self].
This entire world, from Brahmā down to a post, consists of name, form, and action.
This [notion] is produced solely by ignorance; it is not produced by a cognition that accords with reality. || 1141 ||

Raising the objection, "In that case, how is there the appearance of duality?", he analyzes the commentary beginning with: "For those who have fallen away from that [Self], the Self consisting of Hiraṇyagarbha is created by ignorance and is common to all;
through that Self, all beings possess a self," and so forth. He does this by means of the phrase "from the aforementioned Self" (uktād ātmanaḥ).

The cause for the deviation from the vision [of reality] is stated as "due to ignorance of that" (*tadabodha*). The sense is this: because of ignorance of the Self, for those whose minds are turned outward, the entire duality consisting of name and so forth appears through *avidyā* even without any means of valid cognition (*māna*). || 1141 ||
Therefore, Brahman is attained through equanimity alone by means of the knowledge of Brahman.
Just as the various forms imagined upon a rope are nothing other than the rope itself, so too is the case with the objects constructed therein.
The Sūtra, the Virāja deity, and whatever other object there may be here—1143.

Having stated that even though everything is nothing but Brahman, the perception of duality is ignorance (*avidyā*), he states the conclusion with the words "destroying darkness" (*tamoghnyā*). Anticipating the objection that everything cannot be merely Brahman because the threads and so forth are accepted by them as real entities through their distinctness, he recalls what was said in the passage "duality has non-duality as its true nature" (*advaitayāthātmya*): "as stated" (*yathokta*). Just as the rope is the true reality of the snake and other things arising from ignorance regarding it, so too are the threads and so forth [the reality of the cloth].

The meaning is as follows: because they are born from the ignorance of the Self, these [entities] consist solely of the unknown Self; thus, with reference to Brahman’s abiding in various forms, there is in some cases the statement of their existence.

The phrase "whatever there may be" serves as an illustration for both the individual object (*piṇḍa*) and the genus (*jāti*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including the manifest (*vyākṛta*).

By the word "entity" (*vastu*), both the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) and the Witness (*sākṣin*) are intended. The term "here" (*iha*) refers to the sphere of empirical transaction (*vyavahārabhūmi*). 1142.
Just as all this is indeed Brahman alone, born from the ignorance of that [Brahman] through [false] knowledge.
In the same way, through ignorance, the entirety of Brahman appears in the form of the threads and so forth. 1144.

Anticipating the objection as to how Brahman, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), can consist of the *sūtra* and so forth, he says: "Brahman alone. Just as this entire world arises from ignorance regarding Brahman and becomes that very Brahman through knowledge—according to the Śruti, "Therefore, it became all"—so too, through ignorance, that very Brahman assumes the form of the *sūtra* and other such states and appears to be limited; this is the meaning of the Śruti passages such as "Brahman alone is all this. The word is to be divided as *akṛtsnam*.
Although meditation, knowledge, and ritual action are indeed the means of accomplishment;
Since that very reality is indeed ignorance, therefore ignorance alone is the cause. || 1145 ||

One who asserts that Brahman is delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*) into forms such as the *Brahma-sūtra* and so forth has effectively stated that ignorance is the cause of the world; however, this is incorrect.

For, having raised the objection that ritual action (*karman*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and meditation (*upāsana*) are the causes of that [world], citing the Śruti passage, "By means of each thought and by means of actions he produces [the world]," [the author] says: "Meditative cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
One must establish through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that ignorance alone is the true nature of those [three]. Then, "He who [meditates on] another... [and so forth].
And there is the Vedic scripture beginning with, "One who worships a deity, remaining within the midst of ignorance," and so forth. || 1145 ||
For an entity that depends upon a means of proof cannot be ultimately real.
In the ultimate sense, there is no entity whose establishment depends upon something else.

Anticipating the objection that the *sūtras* and so forth are not the effects of ignorance because they are not sublated—just like the Self—the author states a counter-inference, considering that the reason [in the opponent's argument] is unestablished.

"Not indeed," he says. The meaning is: the subject under dispute is imagined (*kalpita*), because it is dependent, like a snake [superimposed on a rope]. He states another inference: "The subject under dispute is not real, because it is an effect, like that which is commonly accepted. [He concludes with the word] "paramārtham" (the ultimate reality). 1946.
1 Kha. Its effects.
[Vol.
2, page 369] 4 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 663.
Arising from delusion, they are separate entities whose success depends upon external means.
From the sūtras down to the blades of grass, these things are mutually inconsistent with one another. || 1147 ||

He states: "The object of dispute is imagined because it is distinct, like that which is commonly accepted. [This is] the verse beginning with "moha. Having restated the inference based on the reason of being an effect (*kāryatva*), he states another inference:
"sādhaneti. The meaning is: "The object of dispute is imagined because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*), like a snake [mistaken for a rope] and so forth.
For all these views belong indeed to each individual who is shrouded in darkness.
The Sūtras and other scriptures are experienced according to one's karma and according to what has been heard.

He states: "The object of dispute is imagined because it is visible, like silver. He says "all" [in the verse] to show that the pervasion of visibility by being imagined is made manifest in the case of the contact between a rope and a snake, etc.; thus he uses the word "hi" (for). As it has been said: "All these are experienced by each individual self according to their own perception. Thinking that the notion of duality belongs only to the ignorant and not to the knower, he says "of those in darkness" (*tamasvinām*).
He explains the phrase "as it was seen" with the word "yathā" (as). || 1148 ||
Since their prior non-existence is merely ignorance, it is not something other than that.
Their birth results from cultivation, knowledge, and action; therefore, it does not arise from anything else. || 1149 ||

Some, unable to tolerate that the universe is a mere play of ignorance (*avidyā*), declare that its cause is *pradhāna* and so forth; others say that Brahman itself, as something subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), is that cause. To them, he says: "It is only ignorance. This refers to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of these threads and other things, which serves as the designating mark for the material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, one should not suspect any other transforming cause.

This is the remainder [of the sense]. Brahman is not its material cause (*upādāna*), because it is impossible for that which is established by scripture and other means of knowledge as immutable, unattached, and non-dual, to undergo transformation; thus he says, "Not that. He states the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for the production of the thread and so forth: "The creative contemplation" (*bhāvanā*). Primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the like are not its material cause, because that which is insentient lacks independence; and if there were dependence on another, since Māyā must enter into it, such [dependence] would be impossible without her.
With this intention, he says: "By that. The connection is: "Their birth is not from anything else. By the word *bhāvanā*, meditations (*upāsanā*) are meant. || 1149 ||
Just as these are stages of vision, so too is their effect of that same nature.
That which is being produced, that which is to be refined, and that which is to be modified [arise] by virtue of action.
He demonstrates this by connecting it with the commentary: "That fruit consists of these very states of vision, and this alone is their function.
Regarding the word "yathā" (as): by the term "states of vision," *bhāvanā* (meditative cultivation) is understood. He explains its specific nature as follows: "that which is to be produced.
He states the reason for the distinction among the fruits: "by virtue of the action" (kriyāvaśāt). || 1110 ||
Perceiving "I am the physical body," one attains only the physical body.
Having died, he attains the divine Virāj and the Sūtra.
Explaining the commentary beginning with "One who perceives the self as a body attains the self as a body after death," he clarifies exactly what has been stated:
"The self as a body. It should be said that [he] "perceives" it. The word "ca" (and) is used to state that in each case there is an attainment of identity (*tādātmya*).
1 kha. ‘sthā: pratyagā | 2 kha. dānamiti śru | [vol2, page 370] 664 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]

The meaning is that whether [the object] is limited or unlimited, one who has attained its state through the meditation on identity becomes, at the end of the body, possessed of the fruit according to that meditation. || 1151 ||
Just as one becomes a deity through the accumulation of formative forces (saṃskāra) and thus attains divinity.
Through the exhaustion of formative forces (saṃskāra), their destruction likewise occurs; of this there is no doubt. (1152)

You raise the objection that although the *sūtras* and other texts depend upon meditation (*upāsti*), they must be eternal because their destruction is not heard of in scripture; this is addressed by the word "saṃskāra" (latent impression).
For the meditator, through the intensity of his contemplation (*bhāvanā*), experiences the state of the deity even while alive, and at the end, attains [that state] according to his meditation.

Abiding in the station of that respective deity and enjoying [there], he eventually falls from it when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that cause enjoyment come to an end. At that time, since the deities themselves—

The meaning is that destruction is designated by means of bondage; therefore, given its existence as a positive entity (*bhāvatva*), it is contrary to logic for the probandum to be non-perishable. || 1192 ||
The limit of Brahman is the reality; from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is Brahman alone.
Due to the non-comprehension of that, it appears as something other; due to the comprehension of that, it is in reality Brahman alone.

In that case, since the *sūtra* and other categories possess origination and so forth, whereas Brahman lacks them, they are mutually distinct; thus, it might be argued that these very categories—though appearing as such—are like a snake imagined upon a rope. To this, he says: "Of Brahman. Whatever entity is suspected to be other than Brahman is in reality Brahman alone; due to the non-comprehension of Brahman, it appears as something other than Brahman. Therefore, through the comprehension of Brahman, the *sūtra* and others are Brahman itself. In that regard, the notion of birth and so forth [is merely an appearance].
The meaning is that attributes cannot exist when the substratum (dharmin) is absent. The word "yataḥ" (from which) should be explained as having the sense of "yad" (that which).

Alternatively, since any object other than Brahman is, in ultimate reality, Brahman itself—appearing as something other than Brahman only due to the non-comprehension of Brahman—therefore, because it is not distinct from its locus (adhiṣṭhāna), all that which is imagined is realized as being nothing but Brahman; this is the meaning. || 1153 ||
Just as for those who see the sūtras and so forth, the fruit would be the sūtras and so forth themselves.
The state of being that [Brahman] would also belong to the vision of the Supreme Self, and likewise its fruit.

(1154) Having distinguished and stated the fruit of meditation—which was previously suggested as having the *sūtra* and so forth as its causal basis—it was said that the *sūtra* and so forth possess the nature of Brahman due to the realization of Brahman;

this is incorrect. For one does not become an image simply by realizing it to be an image, as in the case of Maitra. Anticipating this objection, [the author states] regarding the state of the vision of the Supreme Self: the supreme...
He states in the commentary that the body itself is the effect: "urine and so forth. || 1154 ||
In this context, the state of Brahman would be eternal, because it is independent of causes and the like.
Everything else that is manifested by ignorance is impermanent. || 1155 ||

Fearing that if the state of being Brahman were to be accomplished through knowledge, it would be non-eternal like heaven and other such rewards, [the author] states the meaning of the Bhāṣya—that in this case, the Supreme Self is eternal—beginning with the word "Brahman. Here, the phrase "in the Sūtras and so forth" is intended; the meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) is "being made manifest by the means of valid knowledge.

Anticipating the objection that the state of being the Sūtra and so forth must also be eternal because it is the fruit of knowledge, just like the state of being Brahman, he says: "it is non-eternal."
The vision of even the eternal Supreme Self should be understood as impermanent.
For perception is indeed occasional, because it is obstructed solely by ignorance.
1. ‘Enough with awakening. 2. Kha. *nityaṃ*.
[vol2, page 371] 4. Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary named *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 665.

One might raise the objection: "Is the vision of the Supreme as being of the nature of Brahman eternal or non-eternal? In the first case, since ignorance would be destroyed by that [vision], bondage could not arise; in the second case, there is a contradiction with scriptural texts such as 'consisting of pure consciousness,' and the Supreme would be no different from ourselves. Anticipating this, he states the meaning of the phrase "the vision is sometimes non-eternal" (*kadāciddarśanam anityam*), namely: "The vision is non-eternal," meaning that although the Supreme is of the nature of eternal cognition (*nityajñapti*), its knowledge derived from the [great] sentences (*vākyīya-jñāna*) is non-eternal.

And there is no contradiction with scripture regarding this sweetness, because that [scripture] has the essential nature [of Brahman] as its object; nor is there any lack of distinction between the Supreme and those such as ourselves, because [the Supreme] possesses eternal knowledge—this is the sense. Having raised the objection that if the Supreme possesses eternal knowledge, then from that [knowledge] ignorance would be destroyed, and consequently bondage would be destroyed, he states the meaning of the phrase "at times it is obscured by ignorance" to address this: "moha... Even though the Supreme is eternally perceiving, it is merely separated by ignorance...

Because it destroys that [ignorance], knowledge is indeed non-eternal; for we observe that knowledge arising from a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding mother-of-pearl and the like destroys that [superimposition]. The sense is that the innate knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) does not destroy that [ignorance] without being colored by the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) produced by the sentence. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that only adventitious knowledge born of a means of valid cognition is seen to be the destroyer of ignorance. || 1156 ||
The lack of awakening to this truth: "I alone am the Supreme Brahman."
We call that "ignorance" (avidyā) which does not exist here within the Self at any time. || 1157 ||
He then explains what kind of ignorance it is by which the other is concealed: "I alone," etc. As it has been stated:
that ignorance is the lack of comprehension regarding this fact—that "I alone am all this. (1157)
But the awakening regarding the self and others would be eternal, like the coolness of the moon.
For those whose intellects are shrouded in delusion, this [self] is impermanent and distinct from the self. || 1158 ||

Fearing that if the knowledge which acts as a concomitant cause for the realization of the nature of that *huṃsi* were impermanent, then because it too possesses the quality of being knowledge (*jñānatva*), it would likewise be impermanent, he states the meaning of the phrase "this very awakening is eternal in the Supreme Self" (*parātmani*). He says "in the Supreme Self" (*parātmani*).

Then, fearing that if that were so, everything else would also be eternal simply because it possesses the quality of being knowledge—just like that—he states the meaning of the phrase "it is impermanent in the other, which consists of obscured consciousness and pertains to transmigratory existence" (*anitya itarasmiṃs tiraskṛtavijñāne sāṃsārike*).
"Other than that" (tadanya). || 1118 ||
In that case, it being so, he who, due to a lack of awakening regarding Brahman, has not attained completeness—
Having destroyed ignorance through the knowledge of the Self of all, the person became Brahman.

Since it has been established that ignorance (*avidyā*) consists in the lack of knowledge regarding the identity "I am Brahman," he states the resulting conclusion with the word "therein" (*tatra*). The construction is as follows: when that ignorance exists in the form already shown, the person who—under its influence—having attained a state of limitation, remains [bound], becomes full by means of the knowledge "I am Brahman," having abandoned that contrary ignorance. As they say: "In that case, he who through ignorance is non-universal..."
Having vomited out [all conceptual constructs] through the science of the vision of the Self as the essence of all, he has attained the state of being the totality of all existence. || 1199 ||
Even prior to self-realization, this [individual] was indeed Brahman by its own nature.
Through the perfect awakening to the reality of the Tossat, one attains Brahman, indeed Brahman.

If the ignorance regarding "I am Brahman" were avidyā, then because [the world] is produced by that [avidyā], its non-totality would follow; and it has been stated that liberation occurs through the destruction of that [ignorance] by the exclusive knowledge "I am Brahman. This is incorrect. For if the state of being Brahman were already established for the Self prior to knowledge, then knowledge would be useless. If it were not established, then its establishment could not occur from that [knowledge] alone, since knowledge is not an agent [that produces something new]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even previously... [and] "of the Self, by itself... [etc.]
1 ka. ‘nasthāvi’ | 84 [vol2, page 372]
In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, verse 666:

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to declare that the nature of Brahman has been understood through all the Upaniṣads; it serves to dispel the ignorance that is opposed to that self-established Brahman-hood.
The meaning is that knowledge possesses an object. || 1160 ||
When, through the realization of the true nature of the inward Self, the mind is directed toward nothing other than that;

That cognition which relies upon external ritual action should be understood as being for the sake of another [the Self]. Anticipating the objection that "an act of worship is not liberation as its fruit, because it is a refinement (saṃskāra) of a subsidiary part of a ritual, like the *saṃmata* [oblation]," he states the non-establishment of the reason: "The inner... (*pratyag-iti*). The word "that" (*tat*) has the sense of "therefore" and is in grammatical apposition with "cognition" (*bodha*). "Rice and so forth" (*vrīhy-ādi*) is the meaning of the locative case. He states the reason for this: [text continues].
Regarding the word "external": external action refers to the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices and so forth. || 1161 ||
The knowledge that "I am Brahman" is intended to have only itself as its object.
Because it is the cause for the destruction of the darkness consisting of the seeds of all [defiled] applications. || 1162 ||

Anticipating the objection that "the subject under dispute is for another's sake because it is knowledge, like [knowledge] generally accepted as such," he says: "I am... He states the reason for this: "All... The meaning is that ignorance regarding the Self is the seed for mere ritual performance; since the cognition of oneness destroys that [ignorance], its being subordinate to [ritual action] is sublated by the apprehension of the substratum (the Self). || 1162 ||
Of all human goals without exception, and of all objects of knowledge in their entirety.
This is because it is brought to completion through the thorough realization of the nature of inwardness. || 1163 ||
He states another reason for its being a cause of the human goal independently: "niḥśeṣa... (etc.). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "that knowledge is indeed independent. || 1163 ||
Thus, this position of Bhartṛhari’s Pañcama-sthāna is exactly as it has been stated.
In other instances as well, one should understand that commentary in exactly this same way. || 1164 ||
This inquiry—namely, "Is that Brahman unknowable, from which all this came into being?"—concludes the introduction according to the Bhāṣya.
[The author] says, "Bhartṛprapañca," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: Is that Brahman, which humans consider to be the cause of liberation through knowledge, [unknowable]? All this...

It is not so; for if it were not [the case], there would be an impossibility of [Brahman] being Brahman. In the first case, did it become all by knowing it, or by not knowing it? In the first sub-case, did it become its own self or something else? Not the first, because if even the individual souls (jīvas) attained the state of being everything through their own knowledge, the realization of Brahman would be useless. Nor the other, because of the consequence of infinite regress. If everything became [Brahman] even without knowing Brahman, then that would be possible for the individual souls as well, rendering knowledge entirely useless. Furthermore, if Brahman were the agent, it would involve [the fault of] being an object of action (*karmatva*).

And because [the world] is like a jar bound within *saṃsāra*, it is therefore not Brahman; thus, by this sequence of reasoning, the position of Bhartṛprapañca is established—that knowledge of that [Brahman] is not the cause of all things. Anticipating the objection: "How is that commentary (*bhāṣya*), which concerns the introduction (*upodghāta*), explained as following the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), given that another commentary of his follows the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*)?"—he says: "From this [it follows]" (*itaḥ*). [This implies that] Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary exists elsewhere besides the introduction as well.
The meaning is that the statement "it should be understood according to the vivarta doctrine" is indeed consistent with our own view; such is the sense of that commentary. || 1164 ||
But those who, having heard the *Prabhāvirava*, explain it otherwise;
With reference to them, this investigation has been clearly commenced by the teachers.

If that entire commentary (*bhāṣya*) is not in contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) because it follows the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), why is it refuted after being cited?
1. ka. ga. *śrayāt* || 1161 || 2. ka. *ccheṣi* | 3. ka. *metroṃ* |

Anticipating the objection that this might be the view of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), he says: "Brahman. In the passage "Brahman indeed was this," the person who is to become Brahman is denoted by the word "Brahman."

The meaning is that, having heard the words of Bhartṛprapañca—"it is not said [to be real]"—those who are deluded into thinking that he does not accept the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda) are addressed by the Commentator; this inquiry was introduced for the purpose of destroying their delusion. He expands upon this inquiry with the word "clearly" (sphuṭa). || 1965 ||
This is for the purpose of expressing the intended meaning in the commentary on the aforementioned sūtra.
An effort is made to avoid the faults mentioned in the introduction.
Having explained the introductory statement in both commentaries and having stated that another commentary is not inconsistent with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*),

he summarizes the meaning intended by the two views regarding the sentence of the refutation. "As has been said" (*yathokta*) refers to the commencement of the exposition— either of a single sūtra, such as "One should meditate [on Brahman] as the Self alone," which was analyzed according to his own view, or of the five sūtras beginning with "Because of that" (*taddha*), according to the view of the opponent.

In this context, the meaning is that, with the desire to state the fruit of knowledge as formulated in the aphorism without any contradiction, the refutation of the aforementioned defects is stated by the immediately following sentence. || 1966 ||
The subject matter of the instruction on the knowledge of Brahman is now determined.
Whether it be Brahman directly, or Brahman, or having the form of both. || 1167 ||

Now, one might object that a *sūtra* and its commentary on the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are improper because no qualified candidate for it has been mentioned; to this, he says: "The knowledge of Brahman. He specifies that very qualified candidate, denoted by the word "subject" (*viṣaya*), with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). One view is that pure Brahman, which is eternally liberated, is the one fit for that knowledge. Another view is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth—which are entirely distinct [from Brahman]—are the qualified candidates, due to [the presence of] ignorance (*avidyā*).

Another alternative view is that the qualified Brahman is the eligible candidate because it possesses the state of being a transmigrator and the desire for liberation; for [the author] will later state that the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman is established through a twofold nature. || 1167 ||
It is clearly free from even the slightest scent of all suspected defects.
The Śruti offers a reply that effects the removal of the root of the fault.

Having stated the purport of the subsequent sentence in accordance with the two commentaries, [the author] takes up the passage beginning with "Brahman" in order to explain it as a response to the introductory objection raised by the opponent. The phrase "suspected" (samāśaṅkita) means, in effect, untouched by all the faults mentioned in the introduction.

Clarity consists in having a meaning that is free from doubt, uncontradicted, and not already known. Ignorance is the root of defects; the word’s capacity to dispel that [ignorance] arises because it is a cause of knowledge. (1168)
The word "Brahman" here, namely this term *brahma*, denotes the primary meaning of Brahman.
The state of being Brahman is to be known from the scriptural revelation of the "unprecedented" (apūrva) and so forth; it is not otherwise than that.

In order to refute misconceptions regarding the word *brahman*, he states the intended meaning: "Brahma iti" (It is Brahman). The meaning is that the reality which is undivided in three ways is *brahman*, because the root *bṛh* has this very sense, and because contraction is impossible in the absence of a limiting factor. Having stated the meaning of the word *brahman*, he provides the scriptural authority for it with the passage beginning "That is this Brahman. He then offers a logical argument for that same point with the words "Brahmahood... and so forth.

The meaning is that it is not logical for the status of Brahman to belong to a self that lacks unsurpassed greatness, because such a status is absent in limited things like jars and the like. || 1169 ||
[Vol. 2, Page 374] 668 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
Because of the ignorance regarding the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*), which is established without being investigated...
To one whose mind is shrouded by delusion, that [world] appears as if it were Brahmā.

Having raised the objection—“Even though the word ‘Brahman’ has the stated meaning according to scripture, reasoning, and the [etymological] root, how can there be a cognition of limitation?”—he says: “Unexamined,” etc. (Verse 1170).
Having destroyed all delusions through the awakening of individual discernment, [he realizes] the supreme Self.
It does not conceive of any other distinct entity apart from perfect awakening, just as [it does not conceive of anything else]. || 1171 ||

Regarding the point that for the ignorant person, the notion of limitation arises from their own inexpressible ignorance, he provides an illustration with the words "pratyak" (the inner self), etc. The two ablative cases are in apposition. "Another entity" means an independent, non-imagined reality. The meaning is that for one whose ignorance has been burnt away, there is no cognition of duality due to the absence of a cause. || 1171 ||
In this very way, a person whose intellect is enveloped by great delusion.
Even Brahman itself, due to its own delusion, does not even conceive of that possibility.

He states the application of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "In this way," meaning that for one whose ignorance has not been burnt away, there is no cognition of non-duality; rather, there is only the cognition of a delusory non-duality.

The "greatness" of delusion consists in its being the root of all misfortune. To the objection that such [delusion] would then be impossible because it is non-different from Brahman, he replies: "Brahman itself. The word "even" (*api*) indicates that even the possibility [of such delusion] is far removed from certainty.
The ascetic. || 1172 ||
To the reality of Buddhahood, this world is like one who is dull-witted, insane, or a demon.
Even the reality of Buddhahood appears to the world like something dull, insane, or demonic. || 1173 ||

In this regard, he cites an ancient verse beginning with "buddha" (the awakened one). The meaning is that for the world—which has fallen away from reality (*tattva*), is subject to contrary behavior, and is thus fit to be abandoned—there are three successive examples showing that duality is like something unreal for the wise. He states that for the ignorant, conversely, non-duality (*advaita*) is equal to something unreal, beginning with the words "even though he has realized reality" (*buddhatattvo’pi*). For even such a person, when he has risen above the worldly state, [his] contrary behavior...
Examples [of cases] where the student should be disregarded. || 1173 ||
Even if there were indeed a distinction between the [actual] rope and the imagined snake perceived directly;
Being indistinguishable from that which is feared, it is disregarded because of its lack of reality. || 1174 ||
Anticipating the objection that "duality is non-imagined because it is the cause of empirical transaction, like the Self," he says: "If...

The meaning is as follows: although there is a difference in the essential nature between an imagined snake and a non-imagined (real) snake, they are equal with respect to effects such as fear; therefore, since the non-imagined snake is not required for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to its being real, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of imagined snakes and the like. || 1174 ||
The innermost reality (pratyaktattva) is said here to be separated [from itself] only by ignorance (tamas).
"One who is to become Brahman" is said not with reference to the actual reality of the thing itself. || 1175 ||

If the word *brahman* were taken in its primary sense, it would be logical that duality is like something unreal; however, the apprehension of the primary sense is not accepted here by Bhartṛprapañca, because he states, "By the word *brahman*, a person who is to become Brahman (*brahmabhavin*) is indicated. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "The reality of the inner self" (*pratyaktattvam*).
(Note: The footnote markers *1 kha. siddheḥ pra ṃ* and *2 kha. bhāvipu ṃ* indicate manuscript variants for the preceding words.)

"Here" (iha) refers to the statement in that commentary (*bhāṣya*). In reality, with respect to that form of the individual soul (*jīva*) which is distinct from Brahman, the term "becoming Brahman" (*brahmabhāvin*) does not apply.
Thus he says: "No. || 1175 ||
This, which is accessible through the intellect and words, is distinguished from the nature of Brahman.
Brahman itself, through its limiting adjuncts, is denoted here by the word "this" (idam). || 1176 ||
By the commentary stating, "The world, differentiated by name and form, is indicated by the word 'this' (idam)," he explains the meaning of the term *idam*.
The meaning is that Brahman, conditioned by its effects (*kāryopādhi*), is denoted by the word *idam*. The word *iha* is an expression for the sentence. || 1176 ||
He who resides in the lap of primordial ignorance is said to have entered first.
Due to delusion, that [Self], which is its own manifestation within, became characterized by name and form (nāmarūpa).

Anticipating the objection—how can that which is unattached and indifferent come to be designated by the word "this" (idaṃ) by virtue of having an effect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi)—the author says "yo'sau" (he who is that), following the commentary beginning with "he became identified with this world through ignorance. This refers to the Witness (sākṣin) as qualified by ignorance.

The meaning is that he who was described as having entered into the created effect, having attained the state of phenomenal manifestation through delusion, becomes denoted by the word "this" (idam). By the term "inner self-luminous," the Witness is intended. || 1177 ||
But it is only the Supreme Self that, through ignorance, appears as everything from the indeterminate [unmanifest] up to the aggregate [the body].

It attained that nature, yet not in an ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ). [The author] says "avyākṛta" etc., because he anticipates the objection that the state of possessing manifoldness (saprapañcatva) for the Supreme is real based on scriptural texts such as "all odors," and answers that it is not so due to its contradiction with texts such as "not gross. From the primal cause down to the final effect, the Supreme attains the nature of this world through ignorance alone during the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra).

The meaning is that although one has entered into that state and there is scriptural mention of "all scents" and so forth regarding its object, in reality there is no attainment of the state of being the self of the world for that [consciousness].
Prior to the realization of the Self, the firm notion that "this is the Self" existed with respect to the body and so forth.
Having failed to attain that very reality, she [the notion of the body] becomes established like the cognition of a snake in a rope.

Anticipating the objection—"Since the cognition of the Self as the body and so forth is seen to be unsublated, how can the Supreme be of the nature of that [body], which is produced by ignorance?"—he states the meaning of the word "āsīt" (it was): "prāk" (formerly), etc. That reality—that is, the reality of the body and so forth, the underlying substratum, the true nature of the inner Self (pratyag-yāthātmya)—having failed to attain that...
Not knowing that, [one thinks] it has been accomplished through the grace born of her favor; such is the meaning. || 1179 ||
Therefore, it is imagined through ignorance by means of positive and negative concomitance.
Having shaken off all that was not the Self, he beheld that which is the nature of the immediate reality.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then [he knew] himself" as follows: "Ignorance. Since everything other than the inner Brahman is the body of ignorance, therefore, by means of the method of agreement and difference regarding the seer and the seen and so forth, he discarded that [body] consisting of the vital breaths and the rest; thus the meaning is that he realized that very nature of Brahman, whereas previously, having transcended all [objects], he had known only himself as the Self. || 1180 ||
All darkness has been utterly consumed by the fire of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self.
Through the [instruction of the] sentence, he realized that Brahman alone is indeed the Self. || 1181 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "But having known that, one becomes all; or by not knowing it," and so forth, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc.
[Vol. 2, page 376, line 670].

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter]: Brahman existing in its own state is the meaning of the first half [of the verse]. "It indeed awakened to That" means there is no defect resulting from a lack of knowledge. And "it awakened to itself alone" means there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Since the Śruti states, "Having known Brahman alone, it became all; it [knew] itself alone," and so forth, therefore there is no ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to individual souls (*jīva*).
The meaning is that because one knows the specific forms of things, there is the state of being "all-encompassing. || 1181 ||
Indeed, one whose ignorance has been burnt away does not perceive even the slightest difference from the inward-facing reality.
The internal vision depends on another because of its being caused solely by that ignorance. || 1182 ||

As for the objection that [the Self] would be a transmigrator if it were an agent, or a non-Brahman like a jar if it were an object, he replies: "Not so. For it is only in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) that the conventional usage of action, agent, and so forth exists. However, the Self—whose ignorance has been consumed by the vision of the Self—does not perceive even a trace of agency or the like within itself, because such notions belong to ignorance. Therefore, the Self, while perceiving itself as the cognizer, rests upon a superimposed agency and the rest.
The meaning is that, through the knowledge of Brahman, one remains full, having cast off ignorance along with its products. || 1182 ||
The Veda, whose subject matter is non-duality, declares that Brahman is one.
For neither in its totality nor in its parts is the inner self perceived here. || 1183 ||
Anticipating the objection that agency and so forth cannot be merely illusory (*āvidyaka*) because Brahman is accepted as being both collective and distributive in nature, he says: "Advaita...
This Brahman is indeed non-dual, beyond the reach of objects, and is described in such passages as "One only, without a second" and "It is indeed other than the known";
therefore, its meaning is that it is of a single, uniform essence. He states another reason for its uniformity: "Samasta..."—that is to say, in this [context], regarding Brahman.

For it is not possible to perceive multiplicity within Brahman by means of the vision of Brahman, because that would contradict its very nature as Brahman; therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed one and uniform. || 1183 ||
Through false pride, there is the attainment of prosperity in the stages where ignorance has not yet been destroyed.
Moreover, the Śruti has likewise proclaimed in this way: "Where there is another. (1184)

Anticipating the objection, "If [the self] has thus passed away, how can it have space and so forth as its nature?", he says, "It is false," based on the commentary stating that in the realm of duality, one thing may be completely merged with another as its own self. He cites scripture as the authority for the fact that the state of being space and so forth is unreal, using the phrase "wherein.
And the word "ca" (and) is used to state that its unreality is also established by reasons such as its insentience and perceptibility. For [this is not the case] for the inner self...

The word "also" (*api*) is used to demonstrate that their existence as such is not real because they are mutually contradictory; the meaning of the term *tadbhāva* follows from the sense already stated. || 1184 ||
In this non-dual reality, there is no formal distinction, because the cause of differentiation is impossible.
However, according to the scripture stating "wherein his [desire] is fulfilled by itself," there is accomplishment through its own nature alone. || 1185 ||

If it is then objected that the attainment of Brahmanhood by the inner self (pratīc) is also produced by ignorance because it is an attainment, like any other, the author addresses this in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by stating that here, moreover, due to the non-difference of all entities within non-duality (*advaita*), everything is directly attained as the Self; thus he says: "Free from ignorance" (*niravidya*).
Regarding the fact that the inner self’s attainment of Brahman is inherent, he cites scripture: "Where... (1185).
Therefore, "that" is said to be the fruit of knowledge, which is its fullness.
But for anything other than that, because it is incomplete, it cannot be the object of the desire to abandon. || 1186 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "therefore all that came into being" with the words "therefore. The word "therefore" provides the reason for the fact that fullness alone is the fruit. That which is indicated by these words arises solely from the single cause of ignorance.

for in the phrase "Brahman indeed is this," duality is conveyed by the word "this. Therefore, because that [duality] is destroyed by the knowledge "I am Brahman," it is figuratively said that "the full Brahman became full."
This is the meaning. || 1187 ||
This circulation of Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary has now been demonstrated.
In accordance with the literal words of the Śruti, and likewise by way of direct experience.
He concludes the opponent's position with the words "Bhartṛprapañca. "Pracāra" refers to the mode of activity according to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*).
To the question, "Why is the interpretation of his commentary stated in this way? he replies: "Because of the Śruti," etc. (Verse 1188).

Having stated that the supreme view is to be accepted, and having heard the word *brahmabhāvin* in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), the author of the commentary initiates the inquiry—introducing it for the purpose of dispelling the misconceptions of those who have such doubts—and presents the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: "Brahman... [and so on]. Regarding duality and unity...
The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman consists of many flavors. The word "kila" indicates that both commentators here express this view without personal approval. || 1189 ||
Because the state of being Brahman in another is not established in dependence on anything else.

In the proposition beginning with "not another," he elaborates on the reason beginning with "of that. Regarding the word "of another": the ellipsis is "therefore, there is independence from knowledge. Having restated the fact that its establishment does not depend on anything else, he states the consequence resulting from the necessity of independence from knowledge: "by itself.
The meaning of the word "but" (tu) is that the attainment of all states of being is here heard in scripture as something to be accomplished through knowledge. || 1190 ||
Likewise, because it is not delimited by time, there is no [application of] "it was" with respect to that.
The connection with time is logical; however, it is applicable in the case of Viriñca.

He states another reason for not designating the Supreme by the word "Brahman" with the words, "Likewise. The Supreme's non-limitation by time is established elsewhere by such scriptural passages as, "And the beings [were born]...
and so on. Where, then, is there a connection with time and a dependence on knowledge? To that he says: "In Viriñca.

For His status as Brahman is not intrinsic, because He is a different entity from that; therefore, the dependence on knowledge is logical, as in the phrase, "He came into being together... (samavartata).
The meaning is that the connection with time is established by scripture (śruti). || 1191 ||
But surely, even for that [person], cognition does not depend upon instruction.
Since that [status] is established for him by birth alone, this "Song of Brahman" is not appropriate [for him]. (1192)

Even though that Brahman is distinct from them, its state of being that [Brahman] is not produced by knowledge arising from instruction; rather, it is established as co-existent with them due to its possession of innate knowledge.
