[The opponent] objects: "But surely... (nanu). This is because [the text] teaches that "all this became that" (*tatsarvam abhavat*) based on the Smṛti rule regarding the fourfold [state], and because it is heard in scripture (*śruta*) that this [attainment] is to be accomplished by a cognition dependent upon instruction; therefore, one might suspect that the word "Brahman" here does not refer to the Supreme Brahman. || 1192 ||
And even in that case, the designation "it was" is not tenable.
Because Viriñci exists in the three periods of time, he was, he is, and he will be.

As for the connection of Viriñca with time expressed in the phrase "he evolved together" (*samavartata*), he says: "And 'it was' (*āsīt*)," etc. The meaning of the particle *api* is "as if in the Supreme," based on other scriptural passages such as "and other than being" (*anyatra bhūtāt*). Thinking that "evolution" (*saṃvartanam*) refers merely to birth and not to a connection with time—since that which is of the nature of time cannot itself have a connection with time due to the fallacy of infinite regress—he says: "of Viriñca. (1193)
Since it is thus, due to dissatisfaction, one resorts to an alternative position.
Or rather, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that [the Veda] is intended for human beings. (1194)

He introduces the commentary beginning with "Or because the qualification is for human beings" as a subsequent point, saying "Since": since it is thus, the construction is that there is dissatisfaction with the position of the lower Brahman. || 1194 ||
Human beings were created first, and they are seekers of the supreme good.
It is not [the case] for Brahman, because it has no desire for objects and because it is not the subject under discussion. || 1195 ||
He explains another alternative view: "Men," etc. The word "previously" refers to the statement concerning the Upadhāta bricks.

Therefore, the person who is destined to become Brahman is "Brahman"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Now, one might ask: why could either of the two Brahmans—the higher or the lower—not be understood here as well? For they too...

Because the application of the word "human" (manuṣya) is possible [in this context], he says: "of Brahman. The meaning is that neither the higher nor the lower Brahman is to be understood here, because there is no desire for knowledge [of them] and because they are not the subject under discussion. || 1199 ||
And also by the words of the sages and others, specifically through the knowledge of Brahman.
It is taught as being for all purposes, and not restricted to the domain of the twice-born alone.

In that very context, he states another reason: "Ṛṣyādi" (beginning with the seers). By the passage beginning with "tadyo yo devānām," the knowledge of Brahman is taught as the cause of the human goal for all [beings] without distinction, and not merely for Hiraṇyagarbha and others. Thus, by virtue of the remainder of the sentence and so forth, this word "Brahman" does not denote him; such is the meaning. The word "Agrajanman" (the first-born) denotes the lower Brahman and is also an indicator for the higher Brahman. ||1196||
But since that [knowledge] is established by birth itself, it does not depend upon instruction.
"Whose knowledge is unimpeded and whose detachment is such—so it is remembered. (1197)

Regarding the statement, "Because that [knowledge] is established for him by birth alone," it was said that "knowledge independent of instruction" is intended to refute the claim that the term *brahman* refers to Hiraṇyagarbha rather than the Supreme [Brahman]. Repeating that [point], he states the proof: "By birth. The meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is that there is no reason for his knowledge to be adventitious. The particle "and" (*ca*) serves to combine the scriptural citations regarding his knowledge being innate. (Verse 1197)
[The path] whose sole means is the knowledge of Brahman and ritual action, which consists of both duality and unity... || 1198 ||
He partakes of the splendor of the supreme Brahman, his mind no longer turning toward the objects of enjoyment.
And by attaining [this state] without remainder, the bonds of desire, karma, and so forth are utterly severed. || 1199 ||

He is supreme due to the accumulation of the cultivation of the thorough knowledge of the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, a person who is destined to become Brahman is here designated by the word "Brahman."
Having here refuted the application of the word *brahman* to both the lower and higher Brahman, he concludes the meaning of the term *brahman* with the verse beginning "dvaita... and so forth.

Having attained the state of being a *sūtra* (an embodied soul) through the performance of combined [rites], and having cast off the stream of karma and its results by attaining their entirety—since there is no fruit of action beyond that—he becomes detached even from the state of a *sūtra* upon seeing its perishability and other defects; then, knowing the Supreme Brahman from the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), he directs his contemplation toward that very reality.

The construction is as follows: because it undergoes that [evolution] through its accumulation, the individual soul (jīva) which is to become that [Brahman] is here denoted by the word "Brahman," since no other [entity] can logically be the referent of that term. 1198 || 1199 || 1200 ||
In the world as well, usage is observed according to future function, as for example:
Just as in the case of "he cooks rice" and so forth, it will be the same here as well. || 1201 ||

He provides an illustration for the statement that the individual soul (jīva) is denoted by the word "Brahman" based on its future state—that it will become Brahman—by saying "bhaviṣyat" (it will be). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples such as "he gives a village" and "he makes a mat" are included. He states the application to the subject at hand with the word "tathā" (so too). || 1201 ||
A householder should take a wife; this is also observed in the scriptures.
Thus some who propound profound principles explain it. (1202)

He explains the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) found in the commentary on the phrase "and in the Śāstra," etc., by saying "the householder. He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with "thus. The passage beginning with "profound," etc., is a derisive remark (*upahāsa*). || 1202 ||
Because all faults would entail the defect of impermanence, it is not so.
In this world, there is nothing that, having acquired its selfhood dependent upon causal means, is indestructible. || 1203 ||

He refutes that view by stating that if the word *brahman* were understood as something other than the Supreme (the Self), then because it would be produced by means (*sādhana*) and thus something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), liberation would result in being non-eternal; therefore, according to the reasoning already stated, that position is not tenable.
He says "all" (*sarva*) [in the verse], and anticipating the objection that liberation might still be eternal even if it is something to be accomplished, he says "by means" (*sādhana*).
By the word "world" (*loka*), the scriptures (*śāstra*) are also included. This is based on the logical principle: "Whatever is created is impermanent."
This is the meaning. || 1203 ||
Now, if you desire the cessation of the incompleteness arising from ignorance;
This conception that one "will become Brahman" would be entirely in vain.

Furthermore, having raised the alternative as to whether the soul's incompleteness is due to ignorance (*avidyā*) or is real, [the author] considers that in the first case, the very cessation of that [incompleteness] must be accepted as the soul’s attainment of all states; thinking thus, he says: "Now" (*atha*). He then says: "Conceptualization" (*kalpanā*), meaning that the assumption made—that the individual soul which is to become Brahman is Brahman—would be useless, since it would be possible to grasp the primary Brahman itself. || 1204 ||
For even prior to the realization of that [truth], every living being is by its very nature...
Because he has attained the state of Brahmahood, his possession of that state is eternal and not due to any means of accomplishment.

The reason for this is stated as "yataḥ" (since). The connection is that, therefore, conceptual construction is futile. This is because of the realization of That—that is, from the knowledge "I am Brahman."
Up to this point [is the section on] Diti. || 1205 ||
It is solely due to the single cause of being separated by the mere veil of darkness.
The person of deluded intellect conceives of incompleteness within the inner self (pratyagātman).
Anticipating the objection—"Since everything is Brahman by its very nature, and since Brahman-hood is eternally attained, how can there be a notion of incompleteness?"—the author says:

"Merely" (kevalam). Because it is separated from [Brahman] solely by the veil of ignorance regarding the inner self, for that single reason, the person of deluded intellect conceives of incompleteness in the Self.
The interpretation: By the word "only" (kevala), the absence of doubt regarding its authoritative status is indicated. || 1206 ||
If non-Brahminhood were caused solely by ignorance, it would not exist inherently.
Just as [an illusion vanishes] through the realization of the thing as it actually is, so it perishes through the destruction of its root. || 1207 ||

He states the consequence of non-completeness being due to ignorance: "That which... etc. The meaning is that this non-Brahmanhood, caused solely by ignorance, is not inherent; rather, it perishes through the destruction of ignorance via the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 1207 ||
If such were the intention, for what purpose would it be so devoid of utility?
Having completely abandoned the primary meaning, there is the conceptualization of "Brahman" in reference to the person (puruṣa). || 1208 ||

"What you say is indeed accepted by me as well; however, [the opponent] speaks thus out of the hope that the meaning of the word *brahman* is the individual soul (*jīva*) which is destined to become Brahman.

The sense is: if we were of one mind, then the postulation of a person who is to become Brahman would be purposeless, and it would be improper because it would involve abandoning the primary meaning of the word *brahman*. || 1208 ||
In this way, there would be the loss of what has been heard from the Noble Ones, as well as the conceptualization of what has not been heard.
In this world, an improper method would be in vain, as the human goal cannot be achieved through it.

He states another defect regarding the view that the living being who is to become Brahman is Brahman itself, beginning with the words "In the case of [the word] 'Brahman'... The meaning is that if one assumes the state of being Brahman for the living being, there would be an abandonment of the primary, unsurpassed, and great sense of the word "Brahman" as observed in its etymological power (*śakti*), and consequently, there would be the assumption of an unseen future person. To the objection that "let this assumption be so," he replies "No; it is an improper method. This is because it is an established principle that when there is a conflict between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is the proper method.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, he states that such a conceptualization of Brahman as a future state is not tenable because it lacks any fruit, saying "in vain" (*vṛthā*). This means it is improper (*ayukta*). || 1209 ||
If it is argued that [the world] exists by its own nature, apart from arising from ignorance— that is untenable.
There is no loss of that [non-Brahmanhood], because the means for its removal are nowhere possible.

It adopts another interpretation, beginning with "ignorance" (avidyā). He refutes it with the words "no," and so forth. He states that this is because, neither in common worldly usage nor in the scriptures, there is any possibility of [ignorance] being the remover of actual non-Brahmanhood. Thus he says: "by means of an expedient" (upāya). || 1210 ||
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is held to be merely a manifestor, not a producer.
Therefore, this knowledge neither removes nor produces anything at all with respect to any real entity.

Anticipating the objection that the impossibility of the knowledge of Brahman arises because it is merely a means [to something else], he states the general principle: "The manifestor," and so forth. He states the consequence regarding its necessity as a manifestor with the words beginning "No," etc. The phrase "in some cases" refers to state, place, and time.
The meaning is that if non-Brahman-hood were a real entity (*vastu*), it could not be destroyed by knowledge; for it has been stated that [knowledge] is the remover of ignorance alone. || 1211 ||
It is observed as that which destroys all ignorance regarding its own entire object of cognition.
Just as in the world, so here too, let knowledge be understood as that which destroys those [defilements]. || 1212 ||

Since knowledge possesses neither the capacity to produce an object nor the capacity to remove it, he states what its function is: "svaprameya... [verse 1212]. The word "brahman" is the sense of the locative case. The intention is that the Veda follows worldly convention. || 1212 ||
Because it consists solely of consciousness, which is like a sun that never rises nor sets.

If it is argued that delusion (*moha*), being of a nature opposed to that [Brahman], cannot exist in Brahman (verse 1213), he raises an objection regarding the point that the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*) within Brahman is the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*). He says, "Always" (*sadā*). Since Brahman consists solely of immutable, self-luminous consciousness (*jñapti*), ignorance is untenable in it; for knowledge and ignorance are contradictory when residing in a single locus—this is the meaning. (1213)
Because that [self] is established by experience alone, just like the experience of a known jar.
For the experience of consciousness is indeed self-evident to everyone.

He says that reasoning does not shine forth because it contradicts experience, stating: "Not by experience. The meaning is this: just as when a jar is known, the existence of the knowledge of that jar in the self is established through experience, so too, when that [jar] is unknown, the existence of ignorance regarding it is also established; therefore, your reasoning, being opposed to that [experience], cannot be proven.
He then illustrates the very experience of ignorance in the self with the word "No. For there is no disagreement regarding the aforementioned experience of ignorance.
The meaning of the word [is as follows]. || 1214 ||
And that which was previously stated in brief regarding the section on the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
All of that should be remembered here for the sake of attaining perfection in the knowledge of Brahman. || 1215 ||

Furthermore, is it being objected that Brahman possesses either "unknowability" (*ajñātatva*) or "ignorance" (*ajñatva*)? It is not the first case, because that would contradict the reasoning already stated in such passages as "the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are those which apprehend objects not previously known.
Thus he says: "The unevolved (*avyākṛta*)," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin this with the [preceding] section on the relationship [of the means of knowledge]. (1215)
And from the very prescription of knowledge, it should be understood that ignorance exists in Brahman.
For once [the truth] is known, the application of knowledge is like grinding what has already been ground.

He states another reason for the fact that Brahman is unknown: "Vidyā" (knowledge). Having raised the objection—how can there be ignorance regarding Brahman even when knowledge is enjoined with respect to it in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)?—he replies: "The injunction of knowledge. The ellipsis is: therefore, the injunction of knowledge implies that Brahman is unknown. || 1216 ||
Ignorance alone is false cognition, because of the failure to apprehend the object of knowledge.
Therefore, the superimposition of silver was illustrated by the Great Teacher [Śaṅkara].

For, in the commentary beginning with the words "Indeed, in the case of mother-of-pearl," the author of the Bhāṣya did not state that false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) exists in Brahman; rather, you seek to establish ignorance (*ajñāna*) therein.

Furthermore, since that very [false knowledge] stands in the relation of cause and effect, it would not be in accordance with the Bhāṣya. Anticipating this objection, he said: [Verse 1217]... [The rest of the verse follows].

He reminds us: "It is ignorance. Since false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is not distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*), the example cited by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) for the purpose of superimposing nescience (*avidyā*) upon Brahman—namely, the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl—is appropriate; this is the conclusion he states with the words "silver" (*rūpya*). The point is that the relationship of cause and effect does not entail absolute difference. || 1217 ||
Let ignorance exist in the supreme ground, according to the weight of the reasoning already stated.
But Brahman itself does not produce that [cognition] with respect to the omniscient inner self.

He accepts that Brahman is characterized by ignorance because the reasoning based on the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyā-vidhāna*) is more powerful. He says, "Let it be," thus adopting an alternative view. But he says, "Not so," because Brahman, being omniscient, does not produce ignorance either within itself or elsewhere.
This is the meaning. || 1218 ||
For one who acts with wisdom would certainly not [engage in that which] bestows every kind of misfortune.
One should cast away ignorance toward the West, which is not desired even elsewhere.
Because he is the creator of all, even that ignorance [of his] does not exist; thus [it is said]. || 1219 ||
Fearing that it might otherwise be impossible, he says:
"If ignorance were [the cause], then let this effect which has been described here exist."
Since ignorance is not something to be produced, what you have stated is merely the threshing of chaff.

Is this objection raised by taking [the text] literally, or because it is impossible for the omniscient Brahman to be ignorant—just as another [ordinary being] might be? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "If... The meaning is: if it were here taught that Brahman lacks the status of a creator with respect to ignorance (*avidyā*), that would be reasonable; however, that is not the case, because ignorance is an effect. [The opponent] then suggests that ignorance must be an effect because it is distinct from Brahman.
He says: "Because it is not an effect. For if that [ignorance] were an effect, its cause would have to be stated, since an effect cannot exist without a cause;

yet the Self is not such [a cause], because of its immutability (*kauṭasthya*). Nor is ignorance itself [the cause], because the relationship of cause and effect is impossible in a single entity, and because a distinction between them is unestablished.
Therefore, since it is not an effect, Brahman does not produce it; furthermore, there is no transcendence (*atireka*) of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) ignorance [from Brahman].
The state of being. || 1220 ||
Furthermore, its status as an effect is merely figurative, because it is the object of ignorance.
Nevertheless, there is no fault on our part here, because nothing else is possible in this case.

He says "Now" (*atha*) to show that even though it lacks the status of being a primary effect, because it is an object of cognition and possesses cessation, its status as an effect is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), like a jar. Having accepted this figurative status of being an effect, he says "Even so" (*tathāpi*). Stating the reason why there is no fault on our part—who maintain that Brahman alone is the material cause of ignorance—he refutes the second [position] with the words "Other than that" (*tadanya*). Here...
One's own position is what is intended to be expressed. || 1221 ||
For the form of the knowledge of Brahman is not held to exist apart from Brahman itself.
"For there is no other seer but He"—such indeed is the teaching of the Śruti.

He establishes the impossibility of there being another Brahman with the words "For not... He considers the alternatives of whether that [other] is conscious or unconscious, and regarding the first alternative, he says: "For not another... (1222).
Whether it be action or an agent, whatever is here considered to exist or not to exist in this world.
Let it be perceived that for one who does not know the true nature of the self, that [self] is indeed Brahman.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "action" (kriyā). By the two words "here" (iha), both the world and the treatises are understood. || 1223 ||
"The Puruṣa alone is all this; the Self alone is all this," so says the Śruti.
Neither from experience nor from any means of valid cognition is any entity other than that [consciousness] obtained.

He states the proof for the fact that everything belonging to one who has entered upon the path is nothing but the causal Brahman: "The Person" (puruṣa). Having rejected the position that there exists something else which is ignorant—on the grounds that it is impossible for Brahman, being omniscient, to be ignorant—he now rejects that same position on the ground of a lack of evidence: "No," he says.

[The author] says: "No. For no object other than Brahman is known through experience, because such an experience is not established. Nor is there knowledge of it through another means of valid cognition (*māna*), because since there is an absence of non-knowledge (*ajñātatva*) regarding anything other than Brahman, the operation of a means of valid cognition is impossible. Therefore, the meaning is that there is nothing else that is ignorant. || 1224 ||
But in that case, would not this instruction of the scripture become fruitless?
He finds fulfillment neither in Brahman nor in anything else.

He raises the objection that if there were no one other than Brahmā who is ignorant, the undertaking of the treatise would be purposeless, by saying "But surely" (nanu). Anticipating the question "How so?", he sets forth the alternatives—whether that [ignorance] bears fruit in Brahmā or elsewhere—and refutes them in succession with the words beginning "No" (na). || 1225 ||
Because the state of being Brahman, as the Supreme Self, does not depend upon instruction.
Because nothing else is possible, the teaching must indeed be fruitful. || 1226 ||

He states the reason why instruction regarding Brahman would be futile: "Upadeśa... (and so forth). The sense is that there can be no instruction for the sake of destroying evil for Him, because He is eternally liberated. He states the reason why instruction would not be fruitless regarding anything other [than Brahman]: "Asambhavāt" (due to impossibility). The word "hi" is used to state that the impossibility of anything other than Brahman is established by means of both scripture and reasoning. Therefore, at the commencement of the treatise...
He states the conclusion: "The instruction [would be] useless. || 1226 ||
Although Brahmā was not the creator, prior to his perfect awakening he was that non-transmigration.
Due to its connection with ignorance and its products, it does not incur any fault even while possessing agency. || 1227 ||

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) establishes its efficacy with respect to Brahman. Regarding the word "Brahman": although that Brahman is in reality devoid of transmigratory existence, such as agency and its causes, it was, prior to knowledge, a transmigrating being due to ignorance; therefore, instruction regarding it is purposeful—this is the meaning. Nor is there an impossibility of instruction in that regard due to the absence of a teacher, because there exists a teacher delimited by ignorance; nor is [the teacher] unreal, since he is not imagined like a snake [in a rope].

It should be understood that because it [the self] is not a real entity (*avastu*), its connection with omniscience is impossible, since that [omniscience] is merely a conceptual construction. Even though transmigratoriness is due to ignorance (*āvidya*). (Note: The footnote markers "1" and "9" indicate textual variants or corrections, such as *kha. 'tīṣyatā', which would be integrated into the critical apparatus of a formal edition.)

Anticipating the objection that non-transmigration is contradictory [to transmigratoriness], he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning is that there is no contradiction between being a real non-transmigrator and having a superimposed transmigratoriness; for the nature of a rope as a rope is not destroyed by a superimposed snake or the like. || 1227 ||
That identity, previously unknown, is exactly as it is experienced.
The realization "I am Brahman" likewise arises from its basis in direct experience.

One might then suspect that because it does not contradict the nature of the real entity (*vastu*), the non-destruction of the superimposed state of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*) follows; having considered this and concluded that such is not the case because the destruction of that [superimposition] results from the cognition produced by a contradictory statement, he establishes the subverting cognition through an illustration and personal experience. [He says: "Previously," etc.
Here, the operation of the sentence is intended as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). (1228)
If the means of valid cognition were fruitless while effecting the comprehension of the object of knowledge, [it would be useless].
What else could possess fruitfulness? There is no fruit of cognition other than this.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge arising from verbal testimony, even though established by experience, is fruitless because it cannot produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), he says: "The object of knowledge" (*prameya*). The meaning is as follows: the object of knowledge is the non-dual Self (*aikātmya*); its "comprehension" (*adhigama*) is the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its effects residing therein. If the means of knowledge (*māna*) were fruitless despite performing this [destruction], then it would not be fruitful anywhere else, because there is no other fruit for it than the destruction of ignorance along with its effects. || 1229 ||
He spoke as if with a sneer, saying "Certainly," and so forth;
[the opponent asks: "Granted that this is a fault in the case of what is already understood, what kind of merit is there in this other [position]? (1230)

Having stated that the knowledge arising from the scripture possesses fruitfulness, [the author] introduces the commentary (*bhāṣya*) while considering the alternative—that it might be objected that such knowledge is useless either in this world or elsewhere—and accepting the former position. The term "with a sneer" (*sotprāsam*) means: since we have declared that the knowledge derived from the verbal testimony regarding Brahman is fruitful, the opponent—who is thus provoked—should be ridiculed with a sneer, characterized by a laugh accompanied by the contraction of the shoulders and head and so forth.

The meaning is that the author of the *Bhāṣya* speaks with the words "bāḍham" (certainly) and so forth, as if accompanied by that very derision which causes one to mock and despise, and which is joined with the physical changes of the one who mocks—namely, a laugh characterized by the aforementioned bodily transformations, such as a *ācchuritaka*.
As he says: "There may be a *ācchuritaka*, which is a laugh accompanied by derision; it is slightly like a smile."

He states what was said by the author of the Bhāṣya, preceded by the aforementioned laughter: "Let it be so. With the word "this" (eṣa), he refers to the defect known as the "uselessness of instruction" (*upadeśānarthakya*). Anticipating the objection—"What is the harm if there is hell?"—and the possibility that one might accept its uselessness as the only recourse, he says: "From this... [referring to] the fact that once the reality is known, one has accomplished all that is to be done; for there is the Smṛti: "Having understood this, etc. (BhG 15.20).
Such is the intended meaning. || 1230 ||
Now, you raise the objection that understanding would be rendered purposeless.
And even in that case, the response would be: "There is no destruction of what was not previously apprehended. (123)

It is argued that instruction regarding an unknown object is useless, and since that [instruction] is not for the sake of knowledge, it too is useless; thus he raises the second objection with the words "Now" (*atha*). He refutes this with the word "Therein" (*tatra*). Just as when the uselessness of instruction was urged, its purposefulness was stated by way of being for the sake of knowledge, so too when the uselessness of knowledge is urged, the rebuttal is appropriate: its purpose is the destruction of ignorance.
Such is the meaning. || 1231 ||
1 ka. kha. [by means of divine [knowledge] and so forth].
[Vol.
2, page 385] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 679.
It is objected that, given the doctrine of the identity of the self, the cessation of those [defects] is impossible.
For one who has attained identity with that [Brahman], this cessation is not even desired, according to the Śruti.

[The opponent] objects: "Is that [ignorance] different from or non-different from the reality? In the first case, there is the loss of non-duality; in the second, it would not be dependent upon knowledge. [The author replies with the verse: "Aikātmya... (Oneness). It is stated that the destruction of ignorance is either illogical or non-existent. Even in the first case, whether the reality is known or unknown—

Having thus raised the alternative, he refutes the first one with the words "labdhā" (obtained). The meaning is: when the reality has been obtained through scripture, the cessation of ignorance does not need to be sought by that person who possesses the knowledge of the reality;

for the knowledge of the oneness of the Self alone is the human goal, according to the Smṛti passage, "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. Therefore, even if that [cessation] does not occur, there is no harm. || 1222 ||
But since the identity [of the self with Brahman] is not yet established, it is this cessation that is enjoined here.
Likewise, the contradiction with what is perceived that you incur is not prevented. || 1233 ||

He restates another alternative: "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*). There too, he accepts—as before—that cessation is untenable; thus [he says] "likewise. He offers a further position: "perceived" (*dṭa*). The meaning is that although the cessation of ignorance regarding an unestablished entity may be non-existent, its non-existence regarding an established entity contradicts experience. || 1233 ||
The untenability of everything is established by relying on the force of perception.
On what basis is the impossibility of what has been seen asserted? || 1234 ||
This was stated while accepting that the cessation of ignorance is untenable; however, in reality, it is not so, because the untenability is removed by the force of perception.
Thus he says: "Of all... (1234).
Thus,
many refutations have been stated in detail according to their respective divisions.
Regarding the subject of non-Brahman, it is established that the person becomes Brahman. || 1235 ||

Having refuted the conceptualization of a person who will become Brahman (*brahmabhāvipuruṣa*) and having stated the meaningfulness of the scripture according to his own position, he summarizes what has been discussed with the words "It has been said" (*uktāni*). The construction is as follows: when the word "Brahman" is applied to the individual soul (*jīva*) who is to become Brahman—thus referring to that which is not Brahman—all the defects such as the loss of permanence and the occurrence of everything have been stated without confusion. || 1235 ||
Furthermore, an effort is made toward a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) for the very purpose of refuting this [position].
One should strive diligently to sever the delusion produced by the appearance of a false meaning of a sentence. || 1236 ||

Now, having raised the objection that since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been refuted by the aforementioned method, its restatement in the commentary beginning with "The meritorious [becomes so] by merit" is fruitless, he says: "Furthermore... This means: [the objection concerns] the refutation of the position that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is destined to become Brahman, is itself Brahman.
Only that reasoning by which such a refutation is strengthened should be stated; however, the re-establishment of a position already refuted is of no consequence.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The semblance of the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*). This means that for the sake of destroying the delusion arising from the apparent difference between the individual self (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*), there is the re-raising of a position that has already been refuted. Now, one might ask: why is even the delusion regarding the semblance of the meaning of the sentence being removed by means of stating a refuted position? To this he replies: "With effort" (*prayatnataḥ*). [This refers to] the correct [understanding] derived from the sentence...
The meaning is that, for those desiring to know the truth regarding the object, it is due to the stability of their intellect and their focused intent. || 1236 ||
1 Kha. "The two are likewise.
[Vol. 2, page 386] 680 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]
One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action.
With reference to those subject to saṃsāra, the Śruti has declared this.

Having cited the scriptural passage mentioned in the Bhāṣya, he states its purport: "Puṇya" (meritorious), etc. This means, in short, the state of being joined with the fruits of this [worldly] action. || 1237 ||
Likewise, by the words "for this [is so]," it is clearly stated that the transmigrating being alone is meant.
Therefore, the Lord is likewise said to be distinct from that.
This very Self is described as "not this, not this," and so forth. (1238)

He states that there is another passage concerning the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), similar to the cited statement, by saying "likewise" (*tathā*). For, according to such scriptural passages as "This indeed is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the agent, the self of consciousness," and such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as "the overseer, the permitter, the supporter, and the enjoyer," as well as the reasoning to be stated later, the transmigrating soul is distinct from the Supreme Self; and it is clearly accessible through the cognition of "I" (*ahaṃdhī*).

The meaning is that it experiences its own differentiation [from the Lord]. Anticipating the objection that although the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from the Supreme, it does not possess a distinction from Him, he says:
"Therefore" (tasmāt). This means: like a transmigrating being who is distinct from the Lord. || 1238 ||
Likewise, one should exert effort in the treatises on logic composed by Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda.
The Lord is established by various disputants through hundreds of different arguments.

Having demonstrated that [the Lord] is distinct from another through scripture, he states the logical justification (*upapatti*) for that very point with the word "tathā" (thus). By the phrase "by hundreds of arguments," the meaning is:

by such [inferences] as "the earth and so forth have an intelligent agent as their maker because they are effects, like a pot. The words "distinct from transmigrating beings" (*pṛthaksaṃsāribhyaḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. It was stated that those who maintain the existence of God have as their intent the proof of God through diligent effort; and it is not the case that the earth and so forth [are produced] by the living beings themselves through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Their status as creators is due to their lack of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding those [materials], their instruments, and the raw materials for production; therefore, the sense is that the Creator is distinct from transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*). || 1239 ||
Also because we observe that [the Buddha] engaged in activity out of a desire to remove suffering.
Therefore, an absolute difference between the transmigrating being and the Lord is to be understood. || 1240 ||

He states another reason for the mutual difference between the two [the individual soul and the Lord] in the verse beginning with "duḥkha" (suffering). The meaning is as follows: the individual soul (*jīva*) is observed to engage in activity toward the destruction of its own inherent suffering with the desire, "May suffering not be mine"; however, such activity does not exist in the case of the Lord (*īśa*), because He lacks suffering. Therefore, there is a difference between them. The sense of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is that if there were non-difference, it would be impossible to have such a disparity (*vaidharmya*)—activity in one instance and its absence in another. || 1240 ||
Having understood that very [self] as such through the distinction between action and agent.
The statement regarding the field-knower (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara) is like the distinction between a deer and a hunter, and so forth. || 1241 ||
Having stated the reasoning for their mutual distinction, he states the scriptural indicative mark (*śrauta-liṅga*) regarding that very point: "Him," etc. "Knowing Him, one is not tainted";

"Desiring this world alone, wandering mendicants [renounce]"; "Having known this very Self"; "Leaving this world, I shall attain Him"—through these statements of the distinction between object and agent, the absolute difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is declared, like that between a deer and a hunter, within a single entity.
The meaning is that it is because of the impossibility of being both the agent and the object of the action. 1241 ||
1 kha. 'tigers and so forth'; 2 kha. 'of tigers and...'. [Vol.
2, page 387] 4 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 681.
This is for the sake of instructing on the distinctions between regions regarding the path of one desiring liberation.
If there is no distinction, what kind of movement could there be between the goer and the destination? (1242)

1. Regarding that distinction, he states another scriptural indicative mark (*śrautaliṅga*): "Of the seeker of liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*), etc. The meaning is as follows: the path of his journey is the "Path of the Gods" (*devayānaḥ panthāḥ*);

the distinction of its locations consists of the specific stages (*parva*) such as light (*arciḥ*) and so forth; the instruction regarding these begins with "He goes to the light" (*te 'rciṣam iti*). Therefore, there is the cognition of a distinction between the goer and the goal.
Anticipating the objection that "even if there is no difference between them, let their movement be explained," he says: "Difference. The word should be split as "asati" (in the absence). ||1242||
If that were so, the teaching regarding the southern and northern paths would be contradicted.
And because there is no destination to be gone to, motion itself is not tenable. || 1243 ||

Fearing that there might be no such movement [of the soul], he says: "The southern [path]. The meaning is this: if movement were not admitted, then just as the description of the southern path—characterized by smoke and so forth—is stated with respect to those who perform sacrifices and other rites, the description of the northern path—characterized by light (*arcis*) and so forth—would be contradicted with respect to the knower;
therefore, movement is impossible to deny. Let it be then that there is movement, and since it possesses an agent, let it require a mover; from that...

But how can there be the attainment of a distinct destination? To this he says: "The destination... For since that [action] requires an equality of dependence between agent and object, it cannot be established in the absence of their distinction. The word "ca" (and) serves as an illustration, meaning: just as there is no motion in the absence of a mover. || 1243 ||
Likewise, by means of the prescription of the means for attaining both worldly prosperity and absolute liberation.
For the absolute sovereignty of the Lord is not held to be dependent upon any means of accomplishment.

He states another reason for the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). [The word] "likewise" (*tathā*) connects with the phrase "according to the injunction" (*vidhānataḥ*). Now, if these [means] are enjoined for the Supreme [Lord] alone, how can there be a difference? To this he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). First of all, a means for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) cannot be enjoined for the Lord, because He, being eternally liberated, lacks any connection with prosperity such as heaven which falls within the sphere of bondage; His [state], however, is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).

Since it is eternally established and not dependent upon means, the injunction regarding the two types of means does not apply to it; nor does it apply to the individual soul (jīva), because of the distinction between those two—this is the meaning. || 1244 ||
Therefore, the one who is to become Brahman is not the Lord, but rather possesses a distinction from Him.
It would be designated as "transmigrating" alone, due to the weight of the reasoning already stated. || 1245 ||

Having raised the objection—"Even if the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), how can there be the conception of the person who will become Brahman?"—he concludes with the word "Brahman.
The connection here is through the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two ablative cases. In the passage "Brahman indeed this [was]," the term "Brahman" does not refer to the Lord;

rather, it refers to the individual soul that is to become Brahman, which is distinct from Him. This is because the aforementioned reasoning—that the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme—is firmly established by valid means of knowledge.
The meaning is "you" (tvad). || 1245 ||
It is not so, because it would follow that the scriptures intended for the instruction of Brahman would be rendered purposeless.
For by means of worldly knowledge alone, the fulfillment of human goals is achieved for him. || 1246 ||

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that for a living being (*jīva*) who is already of the nature of Brahman, the instruction regarding Brahman using the word "Brahman" would be purposeless. He says, "Not so," and explains that point as follows: "The transmigrating being... If it were held here that liberation results solely from the knowledge of that which is denoted by the word "Brahman"—based on such scriptural passages as "That one should know the Self"—then if the *jīva* were not Brahman, the instruction regarding Brahman through terms such as "Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (*satya-jñānādi*) would be in vain, since [liberation] would be accomplished simply through the knowledge of the *jīva*.
This is the meaning. || 1246 ||
Nor is there any contradiction with the teaching of Brahman, because [Brahman] transcends all states of being.
It is possible to state another result by which it (the injunction) would become purposeful. || 1247 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the instruction regarding the living self has liberation as its fruit, the instruction regarding Brahman characterized by "Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (satya-jñāna-ādi) must have some other fruit for its purposefulness, he says: "And not... Since the scripture, such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," indicates that the fruit of the instruction regarding Brahman characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss is the attainment of that very state, it is impossible to assert any other fruit in the form of worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) in addition to that, because such a claim would contradict the aforementioned scripture; therefore, [it is not so].
The meaning is that the instruction of Brahman possesses purpose through another mode [of teaching]. || 1247 ||
Nor is he employed for any other means of accomplishing the goals of man.
If it were accompanied by a measure, that scripture would indeed be purposeless.

Having raised the objection that [the Upanishads] possess purposefulness by being subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*), the author refutes the first alternative—namely, that they are subordinate to ritual injunctions (*karma-vidhi*) or subordinate to meditative injunctions (*upāsana-vidhi*)—with the words "pumartha... (for the sake of human goals). "In another" means, in other injunctions such as the Agnihotra and so forth.

"This" refers to the teaching concerning Brahman. In this context, "like a mantra" serves as an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); for instance, [the mantra] "iṣe tvā" is used in the injunction "he cuts the branch."

The meaning is that, unlike the mantra "iṣe tvā" and so forth, which is enjoined for the cutting of branches and other such acts by virtue of the *brāhmaṇa* injunctions, the instruction regarding Brahman is not enjoined for the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, because there is an absence of any enjoining *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) or other such means of proof. He states the consequence of this lack of injunction with the word "tena" ("therefore"). That scripture—the passage beginning with "satyaṃ jñānam" (Truth, Knowledge, etc.)—is intended solely for the purpose of instructing on Brahman; it does not serve as a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of ritual injunctions.

The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that, since the meaningfulness of the instruction regarding Brahman cannot be established through dependence on anything else, its meaningfulness must necessarily be established independently. || 1248 ||
It is held that this [practice] is prescribed for the sake of prosperity only for one who is suffering.
If it is not fully realized that "I am Brahman," how could that [realization] exist with respect to Brahman?

He states another interpretation: "is considered" (*matam*). Having raised the doubt that the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsti*) does not depend upon knowledge of it, he states the counter-argument (*vyatireka*):
"if not fully understood" (*avinirjñāte*). || 1249 ||
But once that has been understood from the treatise, it can be easily accomplished.
The scripture is purposeful because it has the attainment of Brahman as its goal. || 1250 ||

In that very context, he explains the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Regarding the phrase "in that": having stated the utility of the knowledge of Brahman for its meditation through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 1290 ||
Now, if Brahman is known, is not the goal accomplished by that alone?
If that perfection did not exist, what would there be for which one would strive after it? || 1251 ||

The proponent (siddhāntin) refutes the notion of "attainment" (*saṃpad*). He says, "But surely... [referring to the opponent's objection]. Anticipating the doubt that even in the case of the knowledge of Brahman there might be no fulfillment of one's purpose without meditation (*upāsanā*), he says, "If not... [meaning] if it were not so. Thus, fulfillment does not arise from the knowledge of Brahman alone; rather, it arises from meditation upon it, which is the authoritative means for that end.
The meaning is that it is a diverse form of scholarship. || 1251 ||
It is not so, because the realization of Brahman is itself the fruit, as it does not exist for the sake of anything else.
For all knowledge whatsoever is considered fruitful only when it serves the purpose of others. || 1252 ||
1. You meditate upon [it]. || 1251 ||

The opponent says: "Not so. The meaning is that the cognition of Brahman is not an independent cause for the human goal (puruṣārtha), because it is a form of knowledge, just like the knowledge of clarified butter (*ājya*) and other such things.

He supports that very point with the words "all," etc.; the phrase "is held by the authors of the Vārtikas and others" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Therefore, the inference stated previously is valid; this is the meaning. || 1252 ||
Because the refutation has already been stated, this cannot be so in this case.
Knowledge other than that [knowledge] is held to be for the sake of others, arising from the knowledge of Brahman. || 1253 ||

He states that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmādhi*) does not exist for the sake of another because it has been established through both scripture and experience that it possesses independent results.

Regarding the phrase "because it has been stated," the word "this" refers back to the aforementioned subordination (*pārārthya*), which here refers to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). Anticipating the objection as to what might invalidate the stated inference, and considering that [the reason] is "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) and that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like, he [concludes] its lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*).
He said: "Brahman. The connection is that it is the knowledge of that [Brahman]. || 1253 ||
For everywhere indeed consciousness is understood as being of the nature of a formative force (saṃskāra).
And because of the restriction that "the supreme limb" is other than the knowledge of the Self. || 1254 ||

In this context, he cites the statement of the Vārttikakāra in the *Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa* as authoritative evidence for the fact that the knowledge of the correctness of words is an auxiliary to usage by way of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) either of the word or of the person. Regarding the phrase "in all cases": one might object that it is not perceived whether this knowledge is a refinement of something already employed or a refinement of something yet to be employed; however, this is not so, for it is like the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), which is an auxiliary to the *Upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice.

He says, "Because it is logical that it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for that which is to be employed," and "And it is a subordinate part (*parāṅga*). Then, [an objection is raised]: "In that case, since it is knowledge (*jñāna*), the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) must also be a subordinate part of ritual action. To this he replies, "No, [it is] the Self. By means of the scripture stating "one whose evil has been struck away" (*apahatapāpman*), which describes that knowledge as the cause of liberation, [the author] excludes that [knowledge] and determines that only other forms of knowledge are for the sake of another; thus, the meaning is that that [knowledge of the Self] is independent and has liberation as its fruit. || 1214 ||
In the same way, the words "Brahman" and "Self" stand in grammatical apposition.
In the Śruti, it would not be accomplished by hearing; for this sequence is not established.

Having accepted the view that "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi) is for the purpose of identification (*saṃpad*), and having rejected the notion that the instruction regarding Brahman is subordinate to it, he now refutes identification itself. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves as an illustration by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as in the example "This is that. Even in the case of identification, [there is] the coreferentiality...

Anticipating the objection that there might be a relationship of grammatical apposition (adhikaraṇya) as in the case of "mind is Brahman" (mano brahma), he states [the verse] beginning with "in the case of identification" (saṃpadi), asserting that in that instance, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the words "Brahman" and "Self" is not tenable apart from a prescriptive word. || 1295 ||
In such expressions as "The self is Brahman," there is a statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
How could that perfection of one thing in another exist in the non-dual? || 1256 ||

Anticipating the question, "Which is that scripture in which the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words 'Brahman' and 'Self' is heard?", he says: "The Self. He states another reason for the absence of [the view of] identification (*saṃpat*): "Of another. The meaning is that while the identification of another [entity], namely Brahman, with other things such as the mind or space is observed, such [an identification] is not appropriate in the case of non-dual Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*aprapañca*). || 1216 ||
In the same way, the Śruti has declared the identity of the Self, which is to be seen.
Since everything beginning with Brahmā has become the Self, it is therefore appropriate here [to say so]. || 1257 ||
1 ka. ga. raṇyasya ta | 2 kha. ṇyadhīḥ | a | [vol2, page 390] 684
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter]:

Now, [an objection is raised: non-duality (*advayatva*) is unestablished, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) can be established otherwise—as in the case of the statement "the Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*). To this, he says:
"Of that which is to be seen. Just as the Self under discussion in the passage "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" is Brahman, so too is the statement "All this is what this Self is."

The meaning is that because the Śruti declares non-duality, there is no room for [the existence of] a correlate (saṃpad). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Brahmā and so forth," the Kṣatra and other categories mentioned in such scriptural passages as "He would exclude him from the Kṣatra" are included. || 1257 ||
And because of the scriptural statement regarding that attainment, this [attainment] is possible here when [the body] has been perfected.

Even with regard to such statements as "He becomes Brahman itself," which speak of attaining that [state], [the author] says "tadāpattau" (in the case of attaining that), anticipating the objection: "Let that [scripture] proceed by postulating a distinction even where there is non-distinction. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of refuting the aforementioned doubt. The term "iha" (here) refers to the non-dual Self. He cites the scriptural passage concerning attaining that state: "brahma... (Brahman...).

In the case of identity, there is no such occurrence, because it is impossible for that which is established or that which has perished to become something else; this is the meaning of "api" (also). || 1258 ||
If it is thought that there would be such an attainment [of the state] from the word [itself], because of the accomplishment [of the goal]; |||
It is not so; because [the world] is merely a causal condition, that [attainment] is not admitted as a perfection. || 1259 ||

One might raise the objection: "On account of scriptural statements such as 'As that [is], so [he becomes]' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), just as there is the state of becoming that [deity] through meditation on the *sūtra* and other such objects, so too the state of becoming Brahman would be the fruit of meditating on Brahman, because of such a statement. To this, he replies: "On account of the statement. [The answer is: Because the identification (*sampatti*) is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), another thing cannot become something else by its force; even if it were a means of valid knowledge, such a means of knowledge—[would not establish the identity].

Nor is there a difference [of the soul] from the meditation on the *sūtra* (the subtle body) and so forth, because it is already established as the agent; for it has been stated that it is untenable for that which is either existing or destroyed to become something else.

Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "as he is" (*taṃ yathā*) do not state that the meditator attains the previously established state of being the *sūtra* and so forth; rather, they speak of the state of being that [entity] figuratively through the attainment of similarity to it.
Therefore, the state of being Brahman is self-established and not merely produced by meditation. Thus he resolves [the objection]: "Not so. (1259)
Because it is obstructed by a mere trace of darkness, that [state], though already attained, is not fully realized.
And there is no glory of delusion regarding prosperity, because it consists of false knowledge. || 1260 ||

If the state of Brahman is intrinsic, why is that state not experienced by everyone? To this he says: "Only by darkness" (*tamomātra*). Because of the obscuration by that [darkness] alone—and since there is no obscuration by any material entity—though it is actually attained, it is not reached, meaning it is not experienced. Anticipating the objection that even if it is not experienced due to the obscuration of darkness, a means for its destruction must be sought through spiritual attainment (*saṃpat*), he says: "No."
And thus: since prosperity is not a means of measurement, darkness does not arise from that; rather, it arises only from right knowledge—this is the meaning. || 1260 ||
There is nothing other than the destruction of darkness for right knowledge.
Even a minute result can be expected from knowledge, because it is not a productive agent.

Raising the objection as to how the destruction of darkness (*tamas*) can be the fruit of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which has liberation as its fruit, he says: "The destruction of darkness," etc. Anticipating the further objection that liberation is not the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), but rather the self’s state of being Brahman, and that knowledge is merely the cause for the manifestation of that [state], he says: "Of knowledge," etc. This is because it has already been stated that since knowledge is a manifestor, it is impossible for one thing to become another.
The meaning is that there is no other fruit [of knowledge], because it is impossible for one who has attained the state of Brahman to fall away from it. || 1261 ||
Even a statement regarding the power of an entity is [considered] indicative, by virtue of its being a means of cognition.
For treatises are indicators; they are never producers [of their objects]. (1262)

How is it that the non-connection of one thing with the nature of another is not a problem? Because we accept that the very statement, "Brahman knows," and so forth, is what bestows that capacity. Nor...

Since the entry of mere logic into a matter established by Śruti is [inappropriate] due to the superior authority of Śruti, [the author] states that liberation arises from spiritual attainment (saṃpat); thus he says: "of the reality" (vastunaḥ). To explain how it is indicative, he says: "indicative means" (jñāpakāni). The meaning of the word "hi" is that the fact that scriptures are indicative of their meaning, like the sun, is universally accepted. The phrase "in some cases" (kutracid) expresses the scope of the subject. || 1262 ||
In this way, there would follow the subversion of the desired human goal.
The realization of Brahman brings about the attainment of all human goals without exception.

He states another defect in the view that the instruction regarding Brahman is subordinate to a meditative identification (*saṃpat*). [The verse begins with] "abhīṣṭa" (the desired). The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only is there the loss of what is desired, but there is also the occurrence of the undesired. Anticipating the objection that the desired result might follow by virtue of the meditative identification, he says "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). || 1263 ||
Such prosperity as that cannot exist, nor can there be suffering, once self-realization has been attained.
The attainment of all human goals without exception belongs to one whose cognition of that [reality] is free from falsehood.

One might ask: why should perfection (*saṃpat*) not be likewise? To this he says: "of such a kind" (*tādṛkṣam*). For a scriptural, full fruit of that nature is not established by the mere attainment of a non-authoritative perfection; therefore, the loss of the desired goal is unavoidable in the case of the position of perfection. Now, since bondage and liberation share a common locus, and because the individual soul (*jīva*) is bound, its own liberation—not the liberation of another through the knowledge of another—is what occurs; thus, [it follows that] the knowledge of one who is in saṃsāra...

It is not so, because that [liberation] is established [only through the knowledge of Brahman]; for if the transmigrating soul were grasped by the word "Brahman," there would be no loss of what is desired, nor would the instruction regarding Brahman be purposeless, since that instruction serves to praise the transmigrating soul as being Brahman. To this he says: "And not... He states the reason why liberation does not result from the knowledge of the transmigrating soul:

"Because of the cognition of that [as such]. Since the notion of the individual soul (jīva) is not dependent on another but is inherent, liberation cannot arise from it; otherwise, all would have been liberated simultaneously. Thus, the present state [of bondage] would be inexplicable.

There would be neither saṃsāra nor instruction intended for praise; since there is no sublation regarding the primary meaning, the sense is that if the individual soul (jīva) were spoken of as Brahman, the futility of the instruction and the loss of what is desired would be evident. || 1264 ||
Only a single object, such as the *apūrva* (unprecedented potency) and so forth, is intended to be expressed as the primary meaning.
In both sections as well, no meaning other than this is observed. || 1265 ||

Furthermore, he states that if a transmigrating being who is distinct from Brahman were denoted by the word "Brahman," there would be a clear loss of the intended meaning in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*.

He says, "apūrva" (unprecedented), etc. Anticipating the objection that since other entities such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are also seen here, it is impossible to establish [the exclusive reference to Brahman], he says, "by way of predominance. He provides the reason why the aforementioned reality is what is to be understood through the purport of this [text] by saying, "kāṇḍa," etc., referring to the *Madhu-kāṇḍa*.
The phrase "and in the *Munikāṇḍa*" means that even though another meaning is seen here, it is not what is intended by the underlying purport (*tātparya*). || 1265 ||
Because we see a conclusion indicated by the words "Thus far extends [the Brahman]."
Furthermore, a statement that contradicts both the introduction and the conclusion is not praised. (1266)

Anticipating the objection that, like other secondary meanings, the meaning of *apūrva* (the unseen potency) and so forth cannot be the intended object here because there is no difference in the observation [of the text], he says: "This much" (*etāvat*). This is also an elliptical reference to the concluding summary at the end of the Madhu-kāṇḍa, which begins with "That is this Brahman. Therefore, by virtue of the conclusion, the meaning is that non-duality is what is to be established even at the beginning. In the opening statement, "Brahman indeed is this," the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*)—

Anticipating the objection that there is non-difference [of the cause] in cases such as the dismantling of a stūpa, as expressed in the passage beginning "it is only this much," he says: "And not... (1266).
This being so, if the transmigrating being were something other than Brahman, [it would follow that it is not liberated].
There would be a subversion of the desired object, and there would be no dispelling of darkness. || 1267 ||
[Vol. 2, page 392] 686 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
How is it that their having different meanings is considered improper? To this, he says: "In that regard. That is, those two [meanings] are distinct according to your own wish.

If it were true that the individual soul (jīva) were other than Brahman, then the meaning of non-duality taught throughout all the Upaniṣads would be subverted, and there would be no destruction of ignorance through the knowledge of that [non-duality]; such is the meaning. || 1267 ||
At its commencement and conclusion, the scripture is characterized by mutual contradiction.
Even when [an alternative] is possible, that which is not contradictory [to the context] would not be considered improper.

[The author] states the undesirable consequence for one who accepts the sublation of a desired object: "In the beginning," etc. Since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) because the text culminates in a non-contradictory meaning, it is improper to assume a division of that [unity] based on a culmination in a contradictory meaning, as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* passage, where the defect of monotony (*jāmitā*) is introduced and then countered.

In the introduction and conclusion [of the passage], by relying on the unity of the sentence (*vākyaikya*), the statement "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" (*viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) and so forth is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), while "he sacrifices between [the two offerings]" (*antarā yajati*) is the injunction (*vidhi*). As they say: "This is indeed a single sentence; it cannot enjoin more than one thing.
Thus, here too, the sense is that there is a single purpose (*ekārthatā*) due to the necessity of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). || 1268 ||
Furthermore, the designation [of the knower] would be untenable if the knowledge were of something other than Brahman.
Nor can there be a conventional usage for it in something other than that, as in the case of [the compound] "aśvakarṇa" and so forth. || 1269 ||

He states another defect: that if the Supreme [Brahman] were not grasped by the word "Brahman" in the passage beginning with "Brahman," then the designation "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) would be inappropriate for its meditation. He says this with the words "the name" (*samākhyā*). Anticipating the objection that the term "knowledge of Brahman" might be used in a conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) for the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*), just as the word "cow" is conventionally used for an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, he says: "Nor... [The meaning is: the term "knowledge of Brahman" does not apply to the knowledge of the individual soul, which is other than the knowledge of Brahman.
The meaning is that there is no such conventional usage among the elders (vṛddha) as would establish the term through linguistic convention (rūḍhi). || 1269 ||
Or rather, because of the scriptural statement "I am Brahman," one should know [the Self] as the Self by means of another [cognition].
The term "inner" (pratyak) is a qualifier for Brahman, just as it is for the inner self (pratyagātman). || 1270 ||

Here, one might object: "Since the Supreme is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), who is the knower of the meaning of the word 'Brahman' mentioned here, the Supreme is grasped by the word 'Self' (ātman); and thus the designation 'knowledge of Brahman' (brahmavidyā) is established. [The author] anticipates this objection with the words "as the Self" (ātmeti). He replies, "No," because it contradicts the remainder of the passage. Let Brahman be the Self; however, the Self is not different from it, for even though the snake is non-different from the rope, the rope is seen to be different from the snake.
Anticipating that objection, he says: "Of the inner self" (pratīcaḥ). || 1270 ||
The state of Brahman is not found elsewhere than in me; it does not exist apart from my destruction of the crookedness [of the mind].
Because the reality of Brahman is directly perceived, it is not other than Brahman.

He clarifies that these two possess the nature of each other by virtue of being mutual qualifiers, stating: "Brahman is the Self. Because the attribute of Brahman—immovability—is perceived in the Self, the Self is Brahman; and because the attribute of Brahman—immediacy—is heard in scripture regarding Brahman in the words "that which is directly," Brahman is the Self. This is the meaning. || 1271 ||
And since there is no non-exclusion and no following along, such being the case, the primary meaning [of the word] remains intact.
The designation "knower of Brahman" (brahmavit) is established [only] in this way, and not otherwise.

When there is no mutual difference, Brahman is established as being devoid of both universals and particulars; once that is established, the statement "the knowledge of that" (*tad-vidyā*) is designated as "the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahma-vidyā*). [Vol. 2, p.
393] 1. The nature of the witness-self (*sākṣin*); the nature of the non-objective self (*anātmatva*).

If there were a mutual difference [between them], the word "Brahman" would not be primary, nor would such a designation be primary; thus he states the result: "avyāvṛtta" (unexcluded). || 1272 ||The text provided consists entirely of Unicode mathematical symbols (the number 4, the Greek letter gamma, and various punctuation marks). Even that doctrine which asserts both difference and non-difference is one whose establishment is precarious.
The connection with contradictory properties does not exist for the opponent regarding the subject (dharmin).

Anticipating the objection that even if there is an absolute difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, their identity might still be established through the application of a common designation—since one may admit both difference and non-difference, and thus identity is possible in the aspect of non-difference—the author says: "Even if they are different" (*bhinnayor api*). The meaning of this is: as in the case of the statement regarding absolute difference. The reason for this is given: "Because it is contradictory" (*viruddha*).

Where even mere attributes are discarded by such scriptural passages as "not gross" (*asthūla*), how could there be the possession of the contradictory attributes of difference and non-difference? And thus, [there can be no identity] even in the aspect of non-difference.
The meaning is that it is illogical for a name to be the means of proof. || 1273 ||
The relations between attributes and their substrata are apprehended in things that lack a self-nature.
Nor is there any apprehension of these [categories] within the self by means of direct perception or other valid cognitions. (1274)

Thinking that "the state of being a subject (dharmitva) resides only in non-selves (anātman), because it resides only in subjects, like potness (ghaṭatva)," he establishes the self's lack of being a subject. Regarding the word "dharmāḥ" [in the verse]: by means of perception and other instruments of knowledge, relations such as "attribute" (dharma) and "subject" (dharmin), "qualifier" (viśeṣaṇa) and "qualified" (viśeṣya), and so forth, are apprehended only in non-selves;
however, they are not apprehended in the self by perception and the rest, because the self is unfit for apprehension by perception and the other instruments—this is the meaning. ||1274||
Even the designation [of things] based on the causes of self and non-self would be difficult to establish.
Or else, their establishment as Brahman and as the transmigrating soul would occur through conceptual construction.

Or, even if there were both difference and non-difference between Brahman and the Self, nevertheless, the fixed designation "Brahma-vidyā" (knowledge of Brahman) would not apply to a knowledge that is both different and non-different; thus he says: "The Self. Even if knowledge is accepted as having both [Brahman and the Self] as its objects, the specific designation [would still not hold].

The meaning is that [the designation] does not hold; for if both were objects of knowledge (*vidyā*) by virtue of being both different and non-different, it would be impossible for "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) to be qualified by Brahman alone. Anticipating the objection that the designation is established because knowledge whose object is the two-fold [pair] is indeed also knowledge whose object is Brahman, he says: "Or alternatively... Since there is no distinction between the two being objects of knowledge, the term "knowledge of Brahman" might apply at one time or another...
The meaning is that the designation "the science of living beings" would be merely a conceptual construction. || 1275 ||
Furthermore, a partial mutilation is not appropriate when the knowledge of reality is intended to be expressed.
For in that case, doubt would arise in the listener from a statement that is not certain.

Anticipating the objection that because an object consists of two natures, its knowledge must also consist of two natures, he says: "No, not so. [The meaning is: In the case of a hen and the like, one part is fit for laying eggs while another part is cooked; this is a "half-destroyed" state (*ardhavaiśasa*). That is inappropriate here, for an object cannot be both Brahman and non-Brahman. This is because what is intended is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and a contradictory thing cannot be such [i.e., the true reality]. Let it be, then, that the object [is dual].

He says "no" to the claim that whether it pertains to the transmigrating or the non-transmigrating, it is merely conceptual (*vaikalpika*). He states: "For doubt... [If the object were of a dual nature through conceptualization,] in the case of the subject (*dharmin*)...
[End of fragment].

From that statement, doubt arises in the listener as to whether the reality is of the nature of both the transmigrating and the non-transmigrating; for it does not praise doubt regarding a real entity. The word "hi" (for) is used to state that it is well known that a sentence whose meaning is itself doubtful produces doubt.
According to the scriptures, he who possesses the fruit-like gnosis that is free from conceptual thought [attains success];
for it is not to be doubted, since one whose nature is characterized by doubt perishes. (1277)

Furthermore, he states that if the knowledge arising from a sentence were doubtful, its fruitfulness would not be established: "It is certain" (niścitam). He cites scripture as authority for this: "Of whom... (yasya). Anticipating the objection that even doubt might possess fruitfulness like certainty, he says:
"But not... (na tu). || 1277 ||
If the conceptualization of being a means of proof and so forth is inappropriate with respect to the supreme self, [then what follows?]
Because this is a critique of the treatise, this conceptual construction is not indeed scriptural.

Since an absolute difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is untenable, as is the case with both difference and non-difference, it has been stated that the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word "Brahman," and not the individual soul who is to attain that state. To this, the opponent objects regarding the position of absolute non-difference: "In the Supreme Self... [and so on]. In that case, the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is inappropriate even for Brahman, because its nature is pure knowledge; for this very reason, it cannot be the object of that action either. Furthermore, liberation does not result from a cognition where the Supreme is both the agent and the object.

Because it is distinct from action, its factors (kāraka), and their results, the conceptualization of being a knower and so forth is impossible therein; therefore, the meaning is that the Supreme Brahman is not denoted by the word "Brahman" [in the sense of an agent].

The scripture shows that Brahman is the accomplisher (sādhaka) and so on, yet that scripture is impersonal (apauruṣeya), faultless, and beyond the reach of empirical observation; thus, one must accept that the status of being an accomplisher and so forth belongs to it not through ignorance (avidyā). He says: "The scripture... (verse 1278).
What is this intolerance of yours regarding the postulation of its status as a prover?
"Do you not see that saṃsāra is constructed therein by ignorance alone? (1279).

Furthermore, since the entire saṃsāra is superimposed upon Brahman through avidyā, it is accepted that even its "prover" (sādhaka) and so forth are superimposed within it; thus, there is no inconsistency. He states this with the verse beginning "akṣamā... (1279).
Whatever entity is without self exists only due to the non-comprehension of that Brahman.
[The opponent argues: "Transmigration is superimposed upon Brahman alone, like silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell (śuktikā-rajata) and so forth.

[The author] anticipates this objection—namely, that transmigration is not superimposed upon Brahman because He is eternally liberated, whereas it is superimposed upon the individual soul (jīva), since that [transmigration] is perceived there—and says: "anātma" (not the Self). First of all, the transmigrating being denoted by the word *jīva* is not [the locus of the superimposition], because [transmigration] is included within the category of transmigration itself; for that term...

The indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) does not exceed Brahman; that is to say, because it is non-self, the non-self entity is superimposed upon that very Brahman due to one's own ignorance, just like something commonly accepted [as real]. || 1280 ||
Since this is so, therefore the conceptualization of all the misfortunes of saṃsāra [arises].
The supreme scripture exists for the total eradication of ignorance regarding the causal origins.

By the logic already stated, the individual soul (jīva) who is to become Brahman is not the referent of the word "Brahman"; rather, it is the Supreme Brahman alone. Furthermore, in that [Supreme Brahman], there is an absolute absence of all defects; therefore, the scripture beginning with "It is called Brahman" has been commenced for the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman, which destroys one's own unconditioned ignorance—the cause of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence. He concludes this with the words "Since... (yasmāt). || 1281 ||
