2, Page 395] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.
By the word "Brahman," the entire reality is denoted.
The word "vai" (indeed) is intended for the recollection of the previously mentioned self-sufficiency.

Having set aside the Brahman favored by others, he states his own preferred view with the words "Brahman" (brahma). He explains that the word "vai" serves as a reminder of the very nature of the Self under discussion here, using the phrase "for [it is] this" (atra hi). Thus he says: "of the subject under discussion. || 1282 ||
And because it would obstruct the primary subject matter and because it would result in the attainment of the primary meaning of Brahman.
And because the aforementioned defects are absent, let Brahman therefore exist here in its entirety.

He states the reasoning for grasping the non-dual [reality] by means of the word *brahman* with the words "prakṛta" (the subject at hand). The meaning is as follows: since the non-dual inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the subject at hand in the passage "One should meditate [on it] as the Self alone," and since there is no contradiction in grasping that non-dual reality by means of the word *brahman*, therefore that very [self] is what is denoted here by the word *brahman*. He states another reason for that very point with the word "mukhya" (primary). Furthermore, he says "yathokta" (as stated) because the defects suspected in the introductory section (*upodghāta*) are absent here, and for this reason it is so.

The phrase "the subject matter here" refers to the statement [in the previous verse]. He says "therefore" (ataḥ) because the opponent's position is not tenable, as it entails the abandonment of the subject matter at hand and the introduction of an irrelevant topic, contradicts the primary meaning, and suffers from the defects already mentioned in the introduction. || 1283 ||
But surely, because of the absence of pride and the other [defilements], even that which is incomplete is not admitted [as such].
How can there be a body, since everything is established solely through the conceit of "I"? || 1284 ||

He raises an objection, saying "But surely" (*nanu*), suggesting that even if the defects mentioned against the "non-whole" (*akṛtsna*) position do not apply to the "whole" (*kṛtsna*) position, the defects stated for that [other] position have not been avoided; thus, the absence of the aforementioned defects remains unestablished. He refutes the first alternative of the dichotomy—whether means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth exist or do not exist in the "whole" position—by stating "means of knowledge and so forth. Without means of knowledge and so forth, even a worldly object that is delimited cannot be apprehended; therefore...

The meaning is: what need is there to say that the non-dual, which is beyond the world, cannot be established by mere word alone? He states the reason for the fact that nothing whatsoever can be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
"Because" (verse 1284). The meaning is that according to the logical principle that whatever is established is established only through a means of valid cognition.
And once the means of knowledge and so forth are accepted, its entirety is undermined.
For when there exists an object other than Brahman, it cannot be conceived by those who are not insentient.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "And if [they are] admitted. The genitive case in "of that" (*tasya*) has the sense of Brahman. He states the reason for the claim that "if means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth exist, there would be a loss of Brahman’s nature as Brahman" with the words "For not... The word *ajaḍaiḥ* (by those who are non-inert) is to be understood as a separate term. The construction is: "When something else exists, Brahman is not conceived by the discerning, because of the limitation of its reality (*vastu-paricchedāt*). || 1285 ||
Even in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference, [the world] exists as non-different from Brahman by way of its nature.
But through exclusion, Brahmanhood cannot exist in distinct things, just as it does not exist in jars and the like.

Anticipating the objection that there is no contradiction whatsoever in the view that Brahman is both different and non-different—wherein the worldly usage of means of knowledge and so forth arises from difference, while the state of being Brahman arises from non-difference—the author says: "If [it were] different," etc. Even if Brahman exists there as a non-different self, nevertheless, while things remain different, the state of being Brahman could not exist, because [Brahman] would be excluded [from those things], like a jar; therefore, the state of being Brahman and the state of not being Brahman are difficult to reconcile. This is the construction of the verse. (1286)
The admission of another constituent part results in the destruction of the completeness of the perception.
But there is no acceptance of a means of valid cognition (māna), because that [means] terminates in the object of knowledge (miti).
690 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

The acceptance of an object other than the Inner Self (pratīc) is opposed to non-duality (*advayatva*), but the acceptance of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth is not, because they are merely superimposed (*kalpita*) upon that non-dual reality.
He gives the answer, "because of the completion," [with the words] "of another entity" (vastvantara). || 1287 ||
The existence of another entity is contradicted once totality is established.
It is not urged by one who is not insane that a person already established [in their status] should depend upon honor and the like. (1288)

Furthermore, regarding the non-dual reality (*advaya-vastu*), does the existence of means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth contradict [the realization of that reality] when it is not seen, or when it is seen? It is not the first case; thus he says: "of another entity" (*vastvantarasya*).

For when the non-dual is seen, the existence of means of knowledge and so forth contradicts it; otherwise, since the contradictory is not seen, there would be no cognition of contradiction—this is the meaning.

He refutes the second case with: "means of knowledge and so forth" (*mānādi*). When the non-dual is known, because it is already fulfilled, there is no dependence upon means of knowledge and so forth.
The meaning is: the apprehension of contradiction. || 1288 ||
Nor is there any real establishment that contradicts the knower and so forth.
For it is only when that [ignorance] exists that the delusion of the miseries of saṃsāra occurs. || 1289 ||

It has been stated that whether the non-dual [reality] is unknown or known, its status as an object of knowledge and so forth does not involve contradiction; however, one might now raise the objection that even if a thing lacks knowledge dependent upon means of cognition (pramāṇa) and the like, it could—by its own power—sublate another thing such as a cognizer, and thus the non-dual reality would not be established. Anticipating this, he says: "And not... The word "even" (*api*) implies a point of contrast (*vaidharmya*), namely, that [the non-dual reality] is unlike the establishment produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This refers to the existence of the non-dual reality.

He states the reason for [the claim that it] "is not opposed to pride and so forth" with the words "When [it exists]. If the manifestation of the true nature of reality were its sublater, then the delusion of saṃsāra would never occur; therefore, the meaning is that a real accomplishment cannot be opposed to it. || 1289 ||
Even that which is resident [in the object] is not accepted as being established by its own power alone.
And its establishment is due to the absence of [other] means of valid cognition, as well as from one's own experience. || 1290 ||

He states another reason why the nature of an object is not in conflict with the means of valid cognition (*māna*) and so forth, beginning with the words "vāstavyā" (being real). For it is not accepted that even the manifestation of the true nature of an object occurs by its own power alone without a means of valid cognition; rather, since that [nature] which is veiled by ignorance has its covering removed only through a means of valid cognition, an object—which depends upon such means—is not in conflict with them. This is because it depends on the means of valid cognition by way of the destruction of ignorance.

From what is it established that there is the proof of an object? To this he says: "And this. Alternatively, how is it established that ignorance is an obscuration with respect to the object? To this he says: "And this. || 1290 ||
Because it does not contradict the completeness of the object of measurement, no distinction is suspected regarding that cognition.
The validity of a means of knowledge consists in nothing other than the determination of the true nature of the object to be known.

Fearing that if the reality of an object were established in dependence upon a means of knowledge (*māna*), then non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost due to the distinction between the means of knowledge and its object (*meya*), he elaborates on the point "because the means of knowledge culminates in that [reality]" with the words beginning "the object of knowledge" (*meyeti*). The meaning is as follows: the object of knowledge (*meyam*) for such means of knowledge as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is unity; because the means of knowledge conforms to that [unity], the distinction between them is not to be suspected. Just as the cognition of blue establishes its own object, so too the means of knowledge regarding non-duality is simply the establisher of its own object. Even in the observation of the nature of the means of knowledge itself...

He states that non-duality is not contradicted by means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the words "the nature of the object of cognition" (*meyasvarūpa*). For the status of a means of knowledge belongs precisely to its determination of the nature of the object of cognition;

since it is accepted that such a means of knowledge is that which delimits [its object], the meaning is that the means of knowledge regarding non-duality culminates in non-duality itself, and thus it is not in contradiction with it. || 1291 ||
1. *Sāmeyakārāmya*, etc.
[vol2, page 397]
For that means of knowledge does not rival the object of knowledge, since it is itself brought to light by the cognition of the object.
That which is established through pride and faith contends with those things sublated by valid cognition.

Is the means of knowledge (*māna*) of non-duality different from non-duality, or not? If it were different, it would be its opposite; if it were not different, there could be no relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge (*meya*), as that is impossible in a single entity. Anticipating this objection, [the author] speaks of the difference being merely *avidyic* (illusory), saying "Not indeed" (*na hi*). Alternatively, he says "Not indeed" to state the aforementioned point through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). He says "The object of knowledge" (*meya*) because, if it were in opposition to it, the cognition of it would be untenable. [He then says] "of the means of knowledge" (*mānasya*).

Anticipating the objection that if the means of knowledge (*prameya*) is non-contradictory, then since the non-dual object of knowledge (*prameya*) is likewise non-contradictory, duality remains as it was, [the author] says: "The means of knowledge...

(verse 1292). He states that cognition, when kindled by the means of knowledge, competes with the measures and so forth—which are themselves sublated by eternal consciousness—and thereby destroys them; thus, there is no possibility of duality.
For indeed, without depending upon an object, the status of being a means of valid cognition cannot be attained by a cognition.
Even for those who reside [there], there would be no attainment of perfection without me.

Then, raising the objection that if the object of knowledge (*meyavat*) possesses such a nature, the means of knowledge (*māna*) must also be opposed to the object, he replies with the words "Not indeed" (*na hi*), stating that since the means of knowledge has that [object] as its support, it is not opposed to it because its own nature would be unestablished in the absence of that object. Raising the further objection that even though the means of knowledge follows the object in the case of the insentient (*jaḍa*), this is not so in the case of self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) consciousness because there is no such activity there, he recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "Even though real" (*vāstavyā api*). He says: "The real... (*vastu-*).
The meaning is that, just like its own nature, the establishment of cognition—which consists in the destruction of ignorance—is established through valid means of knowledge alone. || 1293 ||
Apart from the presentation of its own object of cognition, there is no other cause for its status as a means of valid cognition.
If there is a contradiction with what has been established, let it be; the function is not thereby vitiated. || 1294 ||

One might object: "Does the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) possess existence in its own nature (*svarūpasattva*), or not? In the first case, there is the consequence of duality; in the second, its status as a means of knowledge is unestablished.

Anticipating this, he says: "By merely making known its own object of cognition," and so on. [He asserts that] its status as a means of knowledge is established—like a reflection and the like—even without existence in its own nature.

There is no other existence in its own nature, because there is an absence of a purely negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*). Nor is it the case that in the absence of existence in its own nature, it would simply fail to bring about its own object of cognition.

The sense is that it is logical for a reflection and the like to possess the form of a cognizer, because they lack existence in their own right (*svarūpasattva*). He raises an objection: since there is no contradiction between a reflection and the object (*bimba*) being reflected, its status as a means of valid cognition (*mānatva*) is appropriate; however, in the case of the means of valid cognition for non-duality (*advaitamāna*), there is a contradiction with the non-duality being superimposed (*arpita*), and thus it cannot be a means of valid cognition therein. [The author] says "by what is superimposed" (*arpitena*) and accepts the contradiction, saying "let it be so. [The opponent asks: "How then can it be a means of valid cognition?"
Anticipating that objection, he says "it is not faulty" because it imparts the object of cognition. || 1294 ||
And at the time of knowing through the knowledge of an object, the object of knowledge also depends upon the knower.

When the function of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been accomplished, nothing else is required. [Objection: Since the means of knowledge is in opposition to its object (*meya*), once that object is destroyed, it cannot be a means of knowledge by way of delivering [the object] to consciousness. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "prior" (*prāk*) and so on: there is no fault even if there is opposition, because before the delivery [of the object], the object is still required by the cognition, and thus there is no opposition; and after [the delivery], since it is no longer required, even if opposition exists, it is irrelevant. For the object is [known] through cognition—

The meaning is that, prior to its arising and at the very moment of its arising, a means of knowledge (*māna*) requires [another] for the sake of attaining its own nature; however, after its arising, it does not require it because there is no further purpose to be served. Therefore, it is logical that the means of knowledge establishes the object of knowledge (*meyārthaka*) without contradiction. || 1295 ||
* Here it appears that something has been omitted.
[vol2, page 398] 692 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter— ]
An object unknown would be the object of valid cognition; once it is known, what excellence does the act of measurement possess?
When [the object] is unknown, there is no contradiction; and when it is known, there is independence from anything else. 1296 ||

It is stated that the object of knowledge requires a means of knowledge (*māna*) prior to cognition, but not after; this is now established. [The verse] says, "If unknown" (*ajñāte*). If it is non-dual and unknown, there is no contradiction with the means of knowledge and so forth, because of the absence of a cause [for its existence otherwise] and because it is precisely that which is accessible through the means of knowledge. If it is already known, there is no dependence on it because there is no further excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by it. Thus, he concludes what was stated: "If unknown" (*ajñāte*). (Verse 1296)
Only the knowledge arising from one's own uncommon nature is authoritative.
Because it conforms to the object and is non-different [from it], there is no contradiction. || 1297 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if [the object] is already known, a means of knowledge (*māna*) is required because [knowledge] must consist of existence (*sattva*), which would contradict non-duality (*advaita*), he says "meyā" [in verse 1297]. This is because only the knowledge that cognizes the true nature of the object is the means of knowledge; since the means of knowledge for non-duality also cognizes that [nature], it is consistent with it, and because it lacks any difference from its own object of measurement (*svameya*), it does not constitute a contradiction.
In the injunction "one should see the Self," the person to be enjoined is distinct from the object [of the injunction].
Since [the two] are not perceived as distinct, there can be no contradiction in their being of one essence.

One might raise the objection: "Even if there is no contradiction with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth in non-duality (*advaita*), is the knower of Brahman different from Brahman or not? In the first case, duality remains as it was;

in the second, the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower is untenable. Anticipating this, he says, "He should see," because in reality there is no difference, and since any difference is merely imagined, none of this [objection] applies. For here the seeing of the Self is taught, and in reality there is no knower other than the Self.
The meaning is that, because it possesses a single flavor (*ekarasa*), one should not suspect any contradiction in non-duality (*advaita*) by taking the knower as a separate entity. || 1298 ||
Furthermore, the primary meaning of the term "Brahman" as heard in scripture is difficult to find anywhere other than in the Inner Self (pratīc).
Therefore, this notion that "it is somehow [the case]" is not accepted at all.

It has been stated that the entire [universe] is Brahman by taking up the imagined distinctions such as the "measurer" (māna) and so forth. As for the argument beginning with "yadi nāma" (even if), which suggests some kind of partiality, you have already addressed that by saying "Brahman. Since the status of being Brahman is denied to anything that is not the whole, there is the certainty that it is indeed the Whole; therefore, the position of "acceptance" (aṅgīkāra-vāda) is not tenable. The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that this is an illustration similar to the scriptural passage concerning the Self (ātma-śruti). || 1299 ||
The perfection [of knowledge] arises from the self itself through its own completeness, not from the completeness [of the object] based on the means [of cognition].
It has been stated that prior to the exertion of effort toward spiritual practice, there was only Brahman. || 1300 ||
Regarding the question, "What is this Brahman-hood of that [Self]? and so forth, he accepts the first alternative and refutes the second by saying, "By itself alone" (*svata eva*).
To support the acceptance of its being complete by itself, he cites scripture: "By means of the instruments" (*sādhanena*), etc. Its exertion is its performance;
before and after that, the inner Self is Brahman, as stated in such scriptures as "Brahman indeed is this," and so on. Therefore, the effect of the inner Self is by itself.
This is the meaning. || 1300 ||
Even the word "was" (āsīt) is used in dependence upon that delusion and so forth.
In accordance with the actual state of things, this [time] was, is, and will be.

As for the argument that if the word *brahman* refers to the Supreme [Brahman], then because it is not limited by time, its connection with time—as expressed in the phrase "it was" (*āsīt*)—is not logical; [this objection is addressed as follows]. [Note: The text fragment provided contains a partial commentary on this point. *Prajñāmabodhasyai* (kha).

Thus you maintain there [in that context]. Regarding the phrase "it was also": the meaning is that, with respect to ignorance and its effects, a word expressing a connection with time refers to the reality (vastu), but not with respect to its own essential nature (svarūpa), as stated in another scriptural passage: "other than what has been and what is to be. This [refers to] each Brahmā.
It is said: || 1301 ||
"By you [it has been stated] that [the Self] is the embodiment of a single, eternally unarisen and undiminished consciousness."
How could it be known without a means of knowledge? And [how] could there be non-cognition without [the absence of] cognition? (1302)

Regarding the argument that "there is no ignorance in the form of knowledge," etc., he replies with the word "always" (*sadā*). For such a thing cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and if there is a means of valid cognition there, it must be accompanied by ignorance, because only that which is unknown is an object of cognition (*meyatva*). Therefore, knowledge is purposeful insofar as it destroys ignorance regarding the reality (*vastu*). || 1302 ||
The one Brahman is eternally awakened, according to the experience of [one's own] measure.
Just as it was previously unknown prior to linguistic acquisition, so too [it remains unknown] due to its being based on direct experience.

Therein, he establishes through experience that ignorance (*avidyā*) is established by reason. Regarding the word "one" (*ekam*): the distinction is that the statement "Being, Consciousness, etc. (*satyajñānādi-vākya*) is the means of knowledge; "experience" (*anubhūti*) refers either to the experience of the knower (*vidvad-anubhava*) or to the understanding derived from the sentence (*vyutpatti*), which is the knowledge arising from the sentence; it is not the cognition "I do not know" (*na vedmi*). ||1303||
Based on the result of proficiency, the arising of darkness is described.
Even while being the witness of that [consciousness], its state of non-manifestation prior to linguistic acquisition is understood. || 1304 ||

Regarding the objection that ignorance cannot exist in Brahman because it has been taught that such ignorance is impossible in relation to Brahman through the connection "this ignorance [is] not [in] Brahman," [the author] explains how ignorance is nevertheless accepted there. He says: "By way of etymological derivation" (*vyutpatti*). The impossibility of ignorance in Brahman was stated there with reference to the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) characterized by the destruction of ignorance, which is the fruit of knowledge. Here, however, it is said that prior to knowledge, ignorance exists in that [Brahman], and its existence must be admitted on that account; thus, there is no contradiction.

This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that Brahman cannot be ignorant even prior to the dawn of knowledge because He is its witness, he says: "Because of [the fact of] manifestation" (*vyutpatteḥ*).
The meaning is that the ignorance of the inner self-Brahman (*pratyag-brahma*), though logically untenable, is established by experience. || 1304 ||
Since an entity does not cause delusion to itself by its own existence, alas, therefore [it is not real].
Nor does the fault of not commencing the treatise apply to us at all. || 1305 ||

In the statement "Brahman is entirely by itself," the defect of the futility of the knowledge of Brahman has been refuted. As for the objection that there would be the defect of the futility of the commencement of the scripture (*śāstra*), he says: "By its own existence. The meaning is that it was established in the *Samanvaya* section that the commencement of the scripture is purposeful because ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge arising from the scripture. || 1305 ||
"Even though it is beginningless, the sublation of darkness is not admitted."
The validity of the means of valid cognition is not established by anything whatsoever. || 1306 ||

He raises the objection that beginningless ignorance might be as indestructible as the Self itself, by the words "of that which is beginningless. He answers this by way of an over-extension [of the argument], saying "of all means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇānām*). The meaning is that the validity of all means of knowledge—both worldly and Vedic—is established precisely through their capacity to remove ignorance by means of their own respective cognitions. || 1306 ||

694 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
"Prior to cognition, that Brahman which was unknown is established through experience."
With ignorance and its effects cast aside, that [reality] is established through the means of valid cognition. || 1307 ||

Regarding the objection that there is also a contradiction with one's own experience (*svānubhūti*), he says: "Of experience" (*anubhūteḥ*). The meaning is this: Brahman, which was previously unknown prior to the knowledge arising from the [great] sentence, is established as being experienced in the form of agency and so forth; when that very same [Brahman] is established through the knowledge born of the sentence, it is then experienced in its nature as the destruction of ignorance and its products, such as agency. Thus, there is no contradiction with experience. || 1307 ||
And by the very arguments stated previously, the refutation of the subsequent faults is established.
Therefore, no other refutation should be stated, because that [objection] is already established. || 1308 ||

Having set aside the question, "What is that Brahman which is to be known?", he states that the further question, "And did it know itself?", is also refuted by the very same refutation of the previous objection. He says: "By the previous... (pūrva-). The construction is as follows: since the subsequent objection, along with defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), is refuted by the statement of the refutation of the previous objection, no other refutation need be stated here; for apart from that, the refutation is already established in this case. (Verse 1308)
Furthermore, since an object that is internal must be known, an infinite regress is not accepted.
Since that which is non-agent is immutable, there is no contradiction in the vision of the Self. (1309)

To the question of how the latter [objection] is answered by the former, he says: "Of the inward-facing one" (*pratīcaḥ*). Because the Self is non-dual and is itself the object of knowledge, there is no infinite regress; nor is its status as Brahman without a cause, for even if it were innate, it would remain unmanifest without knowledge. Therefore, the claim that it is "without a cause" and so forth is incorrect—this is the meaning. As for the objection regarding the contradiction with action and so on, he says: "Of the non-agent" (*akārakasya*).

The meaning is that since the Self—which is devoid of distinctions such as action (kriyā) and its factors (kāraka)—lacks agency and so forth when perceived by itself, there is in reality no contradiction with its being actionless; nor can Brahman be something to be accomplished through knowledge, because of its immutability (kauṭasthya). || 1309 ||
Even the negation proclaimed in the scripture is based on the similarity [of Brahman] with objects of cognition such as a pot.
However, the state of having understood as previously described is by no means precluded. || 1310 ||

Regarding the objection that there is a contradiction with other scriptural passages (*śruti*), he says: "Like a pot, etc. The meaning of the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," and "By what, O Maitreyi, should one know the Knower?"—as stated in scripture—is also a negation of Brahman being the object of the manifestation (*sphūrti*) of the mind, just as in the case of a pot and so forth; it is not a negation of its being the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). Otherwise, the status of Brahman as being known through the Upanishads (*aupaniṣadatva*) would be contradicted. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with scripture when one accepts a mental modification directed toward Brahman. If that is so, then [regarding] the modification—

Anticipating the objection that Brahman must also possess a pervasiveness of manifestation (sphūrti), just like a jar because it is all-pervasive (vyāpyatva), he states "yathokta" [in verse 1310], asserting that its status as the immutable manifestation (kūṭasthasphūrtitva)—established through both scripture and experience—is irrefutable; therefore, it does not possess that pervasiveness.
Therefore, there can be no one at all here who possesses a complete understanding.
Therefore, having [addressed] this fault, we shall now clearly explain the text of the Bhāṣya. || 1311 ||

Regarding the statement beginning with "yatpunar" (but as for... and ending with "doṣatvāt" (because of being a defect), he says: "tasmāt" (therefore). The meaning is that since desire and the operation of the means of knowledge are possible when Brahman is unknown, and since the destruction of ignorance is the fruit of valid cognition (*māna*), there is no defect whatsoever in the Vedāntas concerning Brahman, which is the full, one, and single-flavored self-luminous reality. Having thus removed the defects mentioned in the introductory section (*upodghāta*), [he continues] with the passage beginning "tasmādyatpraviṣṭam" (therefore, that which has entered...).
1. Those who know by means of sentences; 2. Those who know the substrate (dharmin).
[Vol. 2, page 401] 4.
Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 695.

He brings [the argument] down [to its conclusion]: "Therefore" (ataḥ), which means because there is no possibility of the suspected fault. Immediately after the refutation of the objection raised by another, he indicates the occasion for the explanation of the Bhāṣya with the word "Now" (sāṃpratam). || 1311 ||
That previously mentioned Brahman, the creator, [acts] by way of deluding its own self.
The effect has entered by means of the reflection of consciousness, like the moon in water. || 1312 ||

He connects those words with the passage beginning with "That" (yat) and so forth; the phrase "in the previously mentioned process of the unmanifest" (avyākṛtaprakriyāyām) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The connection is that [the Lord] creates by means of the path that deludes His own Self. He causes one to remember what was stated in the sentence concerning entry: "the effect" (kāryam).
By the word "Brahman," that very [reality] is denoted here.
The excellence of that [unmanifested nature], which has been described as consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, is as follows:
This is called Brahman, which has the nature of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
It completes what is required by the word [brahman]. "Brahman" is the sentence; the locative sense is indicated by the phrase "this which resides in the body," etc.

He states the purport of that [passage] with the words "of that": the excellence of the immutable Brahman, known as cause and effect, which consists in the process of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta-prakriyā*).
The meaning is that what was described there as being situated within the limiting adjunct consisting of the two bodies is this very Brahman denoted by the word "I" (idam). || 1313 ||
The word "vai" (verily) is used for emphasis, signifying that which is Brahman alone and not otherwise.
When the reality of the Self has not been fully realized, that very Brahman appears as the world.

Regarding the phrase "of the self's completeness as it has been introduced," the word *vai* was previously explained as having the sense of recollection (*smṛti*) for the subject matter already introduced;

now, following the Bhāṣya, he states another meaning. He says: "The word *vai*. It expresses emphasis (*avadhṛti*). He says: "Brahman. Having raised the objection—"If this entire world is Brahman, then how can there be a cognition of it as something else?"—he replies: "It is not so" (*anitam*). || 1314 ||
That is to say, that which is cognizable through verbal cognition prior to the arising of right knowledge.
Even that entire Brahman is perceived as something other than what it is due to delusion.
Having restated the meaning of the word "this" (idaṃ), he explains the Bhāṣya beginning with "previously" (prāk) and so forth: "That which is this... (yadidam). || 1315 ||
Due to the non-cognition of its true nature as a rope, it is perceived as a snake, a staff, and so forth.
Since this [world] is heard to be merely Brahman, how can it be said that "there was something before"? Thus it is asked. || 1316 ||

He provides an illustration for the point that although this entire world is Brahman alone both before and after right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), yet due to ignorance of it, it appears as non-Brahman. He says, "like a rope" (*rajjuvat*). The meaning is: just as a rope is perceived in the form of a snake and so forth due to one's own ignorance, so too, due to ignorance of Brahman, that which is Brahman is seen as something other than Brahman. He anticipates the objection regarding the word "agra" (tip/point) by saying, "Brahman. Here, whether it be Brahman, the Veda, or something else, it serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) in this context.

Therefore, the meaning is that [the opponent’s position] is incorrect: in the first case, there is a contradiction in saying "that alone existed"; in the second, because there is no subject to be restated (anuvādya), an injunction (vidhi) is impossible; and in the third, since that [word] is not heard in this sentence, there is an absence of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin). He states the reply: "It is said" (bhaṇyate). || 1316 ||
The time prior to the manifestation of the world of the Sūtras is called the past.
That which is indeed "that" will also be clearly explained further above. || 1317 ||

Since the imagined world has the unimagined Self as its essence, the manifestation of that world is the cognition of the identity of the Self; therefore, the time prior to the arising of that [cognition] is the meaning of the word "Aman" (the Unmanifest).
Thus he says: "In the Sūtra. The Sūtra is the unmanifest cause; that which has this at its end is the entire world, according to the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [type of compound].

This is what is meant by "of that. Furthermore, he provides corroboration for the remainder of the sentence, stating that the fact that everything is nothing but Brahman during the aforementioned time will also be explained later in the section on sleep, in the passage beginning with "That which is... that is not" (*yad vai tat tan na*). "That which... (verse 1317).
Ignorance does not have a connection there, because it is not its effect.
Even for an effect that is devoid of darkness, there is no cognition [of it] without a cause.

Regarding what was stated here, it is clearly explained later on that one might suspect that if the unmanifested (avyākṛta) and so forth were Brahman, then Brahman would likewise possess the nature of the unmanifested and so forth; therefore, [the author] says "No" and so on, to show that Brahman has no identity with another ignorance such as the unmanifested, because Brahman is not an effect of ignorance, whereas that [ignorance] has identity only with its own effects. This applies even to its effect known as the manifested (vyākṛta).
Since it is accepted that [the world] is nothing but Brahman, how can there be an absence of its being an effect of Brahman? To this he says: "Born of darkness" (*tamojasya*).

Even that which is born of ignorance (*ajñāna*) has no connection with Brahman through non-difference (*abheda*), because it is non-different from its own cause, and because Brahman is not its cause—since scripture teaches the difference between cause and effect—and because it is established that Brahman's causality is through ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the meaning. || 1318 ||
Due to its connection with the Self as the inner witness, delusion and the like appear as having the nature of consciousness.
Because it cuts away the remainder [of faults], this [scripture] cannot be false, just like the activity of the Dharma. || 1319 ||

If so, how is it that this [world] consisting of delusion and the like is nothing but Brahman? To this he says: "By way of being the Inner Self" (*pratyaktayā*). The meaning is that because the substrate—the Self—is connected with the superimposed forms of delusion and so forth, it is always pervaded by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). Furthermore, even though there is non-difference between delusion and the like and Brahman, only Brahman remains and nothing else; to this he says: "Because of the non-remainder of the insentient" (*āciccheṣāt*). Of all [the elements] beginning with delusion—

The meaning is that, although there is non-difference from the remainder [of reality] by virtue of being directly present as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), Brahman does not possess the nature of that [remainder]. Since it is established that Brahmanhood does not belong to delusion (*moha*) and the like, and that those [delusions] do not possess the nature of Brahman, he states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning of the word "therefore" is that if consciousness (*cit*) were also imagined (*kalpita*), there would be no locus for imagination due to the absence of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); hence, imagination without a substratum is impossible. The word "this" (*asau*) refers to consciousness. Duality, which is the effect of merit (*dharma*) and so forth—
The example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). || 1319 ||
No cause other than the realization of the true nature of the inward Self is observed.
He who is capable of bringing about the destruction, without leaving a trace, of that which takes the form of saṃsāra.
Anticipating the objection, "If the world, consisting of cause and effect, is superimposed [upon reality], from what could its cessation arise?", he says: "The inner self" (*pratyag*).
The meaning is that the absolute destruction of this misfortune occurs solely through perfect knowledge of the Self, because no other means is established by valid authority. || 1320 ||
Because it is immutable and unattached, there is no connection for this [Puruṣa] with delusion or its effects.
Because delusion and the like are incapable of existing by themselves, they must have a connection with the self.

He establishes the fitness for the destruction of duality through the knowledge of the inner reality (*pratyaktattvavidyā*). [The verse begins with] "By its immutability" (*kauṭasthyena*). Because this inner self (*pratīc*) is immutable and unattached, it has no real connection with delusion and the like; nor can that [duality] be established independently, as it is insentient (*jaḍa*).
1. *adhikaraṇe ya* | 2. *vidyayā tā* |

Because that [bondage] is untenable, it is merely a conceptual construction within the Self; therefore, through the knowledge of the Self, there is its absolute destruction. — [Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya, with Ānandagiri’s Śāstraprakāśikā Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 403, Section 4]
This is the meaning. || 1321 ||
The conjunction with space exists as if by slight warmth, yet it is non-existent in relation to the nature of the mat.
Thus, the soul's connection with darkness is not due to conformity with its own functions.

He states, by means of an illustration, that the application of delusion (*moha*) and so forth is imagined within the Self: "In its entirety," etc. By the word *tamas*, its effects are also indicated. || 1322 ||
This connection [of yours] with another is established without investigation.
This [cognition] resides only within the lap of the unknown consciousness; it does not exist in an external object.

He concludes that the conjunction of the self and the non-self is merely imagined with the words "from another" (*anyataḥ*). One might object: "If there is a connection of the self with another, namely the non-self, how can it be said that such a connection does not exist in relation to the state of the self? Anticipating this doubt, he states that the notion of being joined with "another" resides only in one who has not realized the self, and not in the pure self itself, with the words "unrealized" (*avijñātā*). The term *utsaṅga* refers to the region of the thighs. || 1323 ||
Even through the medium of ignorance, its connection is not admitted as being direct.
By virtue of the two reasons—being devoid of self-nature and being for the sake of another—it is like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. || 1324 ||

Fearing that if ignorance (ajñāna) and the like were situated in the unknown Self, there would result—partially at least—the consequence that [the Self] is both the locus and the object [of that ignorance], he says:

"Ignorance" (avidyā). Just as, in accordance with the actual nature of things, there is no connection of ignorance and so forth with the Self, so too, even from the perspective of the operation of ignorance, such a connection is not admitted; for since ignorance and its effects are devoid of self-nature (nirātmakatva) and exist for the sake of another (parārthatva), their connection with [the Self] is not established in itself. Therefore, avi-...

The meaning is that for one who asserts this connection between the ear and form—like the illusory perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—there is indeed an impossibility, just as there is in the case of the connection between the ear and form. || 1324 ||
Apart from its own immediate form, there is no other form for that which is not the self.
It can never be established by disputants through logical arguments.
Fearing that opponents might argue that what is non-self does not possess "selflessness" because they accept it as a real entity distinct from the self, he says:
"The inner self... The meaning is: "The subject of dispute is not real by its own independence, because it is non-self, like a [mirage] form.

It was stated "by means of reasonings" in order to accept another form that is merely apparent; "in some cases" means in common worldly experience or in the scriptures. "Always" refers to the three periods of time.

It is explained as follows: the subject under dispute is non-existent in its own right because it is subject to deviation [from its nature], just like that which is commonly accepted. This is the meaning. || 1325 ||
From the immutable (kūṭastha) up to the end of darkness (tamas), it is eternal because of its non-differentiation.
Therefore, this world—consisting of everything from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to its objects—is eternally [non-different] from Brahman.

Having raised the objection that the world is a different entity (*arthāntara*) from Brahman by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*)—"The subject under dispute is other than Brahman because it is inexpressible (*anirvācya*), just like that [unreal thing]"—the author states "kūṭasthāt" etc., intending to point out the mutual contradiction between the reason and the proposition. And [Brahman is] "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) because it is the root of all.

The meaning is as follows: because the world is permeated by ignorance, it has no beginning; and because it is never separate from that Self (Ātman) due to its constant non-existence apart from it, its non-existence is refuted by such scriptural texts as, "O dear one, this world is indeed Being. Therefore, since the world perceived externally is indeterminate (anirvācya), its difference from Brahman is contradicted, and because this would conflict with the scriptures, the aforementioned inference is not valid. 1326.
88 1 kha. entirely; 2 kha. entirely; 3 ka. ga. having the form of scripture.
[vol2, page 404]
Therefore, for those whose minds are enveloped by the great sleep of ignorance, this [awakening]... [Śureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika, First Chapter]... [occurs].
The delusion of seeing one's own dreams is the apprehension of transformations such as birth and so forth. || 1327 ||

Anticipating the objection that the world’s being a different entity from Brahman is established because the world is seen to have birth and so forth, [the author] states "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the reality of that [world] as non-different from Brahman is based on scripture, the cognition of birth and so forth is an error, like the cognition of a dream; this is the meaning. The construction is:
with reference to the sixfold modification consisting of birth and so forth, the world is an illusion for those lacking discrimination, just like the perception of a dream. || 1327 ||
Just as it has been explained, he is primarily concerned with external objects, unaggregated, and without a sense of "mine."
It partakes of the status of all valid means of cognition, and it also partakes of the status of fallacious means of cognition.

One might object: "If all duality is merely *māyā*, what could possibly serve as the locus or the object of valid cognition (*pramā*) and its semblance (*pramābhāsa*)? To this, he says: "Just as... The meaning is that it is logically possible for the inner self (*pratīc*), which is in reality uncomposite, non-attached, and solely of the nature of consciousness—the object of valid cognition—to become the object of both valid cognition and its semblance when it is conditioned by the manifest and unmanifest world. || 1328 ||
That which arises from that [ignorance] is established without investigation, like darkness.
Therefore, when delusion is destroyed, the entire world is destroyed; consciousness alone remains.

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for that which is non-composite to possess duality as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he says "avicārita" (unexamined), meaning that this is not so because the adjunct is unreal. He states the result regarding the falsity of duality produced by ignorance, which possesses the same nature as ignorance itself, with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, the world—which is born from it—is also destroyed, and thus [the Self] remains as pure Consciousness alone. || 1329 ||
In the case of things that stand in the relation of cause and effect, such as those with different mothers or different measures, etc.
The Self is undivided, beginningless, and indeed the one non-dual reality by its very nature.

Fearing that the internal, non-composite [Self] might incur the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) by becoming the object of either valid cognition (*māna*) or its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) through the imposition of compositeness, the author states the following while demonstrating its unobjectifiability (*aprameyatva*): "Distinct," etc. The meaning is this: while the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which possesses the distinctions of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, exists as an object of knowledge, the Self alone—being devoid of those distinctions—is independent due to its non-duality; it shines forth by itself. Therefore, it does not possess the status of being an object of knowledge. || 1330 ||
The self has no dependence whatsoever upon place, time, state, or other such factors, by its very nature.
Because [the cognition] is established independently of anything else, whereas place and so forth depend upon it. || 1331 ||

One might object: "The Self is not non-dual, because it depends upon space and other such factors, just like a jar. Anticipating this, he says: "No. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the producer and the indicator are included. He states the reason for the Self's independence: "Because it is not other" (*ananyatvāt*). This refers to the unconditioned Self by its own inherent nature.

The meaning is: because of the existence of self-existence and manifestation. Regarding that very point, he states another reason: "of place, etc. The sense is that an insentient thing cannot be established without dependence on a sentient one, nor can the reverse be the case, as that would involve the fallacy known as "the barren woman's son" (a logical impossibility). || 1331 ||
Whatever object there may be that depends upon place, time, causal conditions, and so forth;
That very [cognition] would be dependent upon that [object], but it does not establish the existence of place and so forth.

Having stated the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason "because of dependence on place and so forth," he states the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). He says "place, etc. Having raised the doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probans by [the condition] "place and time as causes," he says "but not... The construction is as follows: it is not the case that for the Self, which is the establisher of place and so forth, there is a mention of another cause by means of the word "dependence"; rather, that very jar or other object which arises in dependence on those [place and time] would itself be subject to duality through its dependence on place and so forth.
[Brāhmaṇa 4, vol. 2, p.

405] Since its being an effect has already been established from that [prior state], it is distinct; thus, in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the examples such as a jar are "effects" and "distinct," while [the unmanifest cause] is "not an effect" and "non-distinct. This is the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 699.

And if there were a distinction, the self would be something to be established [as an object]; thus, even that [self] could not possess the nature of being indivisible, because it would follow—as with a jar—that it is non-self and so forth.
This is the intended meaning. || 1332 ||
Prior to the emergence of the knower and so forth, everything was indeed Brahman, just as it has been described.
Therefore, that [state] cannot be accomplished by means such as knowledge, ritual action, and so forth.

Having established the meaning obtained through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "this" and "Brahman," he concludes the meaning of the sentence with the words "the knower, etc.

"Arising" (*utthiti*) means the manifestation of reality (*tattvavyakti*). He reflects upon the fact that consciousness, though accompanied by phenomenal expansion (*saprapañca*), is eternally Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*aprapañca*). With the word "since" (*yataḥ*), he concludes the refutation of the opposing view by stating that, for that reason, that Brahmanhood does not depend upon any means of realization (*sādhana*). Then, with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*), [he concludes]. "Etc. (*ādi-*)...
The word has the sense of cultivation (bhāvanā). || 1333 ||
Even Brahmā [attains it] directly from that itself, solely through the cause of awakening to that.
Assumed this form, just as a girdle assumes the form of a snake.
Having raised the objection as to how the world can possess a limited form when it is Brahman, he states that this is due to the power of *māyā*, as has been said more than once:
"Brahman also... Here, "that" refers to the world; "directly" expresses the purity of Brahman;

and by stating "by itself, without *māyā*," he reiterates its real state and then describes its phenomenal state caused by ignorance (*avidyā*). As for "due to the non-cognition of that": how can it be so even from non-cognition?
Regarding that, he states the nature of the contradictory form: "The girdle," etc. (1334).
Mounted upon the fruit of ignorance, that very thing is of such a nature as this, supreme.
The eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman is established through its twofold nature. || 1335 ||

Even though the world consists of nothing but Brahman, one might object that there must be another conscious entity, otherwise—due to the absence of anyone qualified for the knowledge of That—that [knowledge] would not be established. Anticipating this, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). The meaning is: "of such a form" refers to that which has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). For the Supreme Brahman itself mounts the vehicle called beginningless ignorance; that very same [Brahman] is then further conditioned by the internal organ and other factors, and that constitutes the twofold state of being a qualified candidate.
The meaning is "he goes. || 1331 ||
Since it is liberated by its very nature, therefore Brahman deserves that knowledge.
From ignorance comes the state of being in saṃsāra; from that, the desire for liberation arises.

He states that there are indeed two kinds [of persons]: "by themselves" (*svataḥ*). The meaning is this: Brahman alone, being liberated by its own nature, is the support for knowledge; yet, because it is bound by ignorance, it is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) who is the cause for the destruction of that [ignorance]. By this, the fact that those who maintain the doctrine of multiple individual souls (*anekajīvavādin*) have not heard the scriptures is demonstrated. || 1336 ||
The internal, the elemental, and likewise the divine.
But that [entity], impelled by its own conceit, is designated by that word. || 1337 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "Brahman," he states the meaning of the word *tat* (that) found in the subsequent sentence: "Adhyātmam" (within the self). That Supreme Brahman, having entered into the creation consisting of the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth, is there—through the ignorance-based conceit of "I" and "mine"—concealed; it [is that which] is the Self...
The meaning is that in which there is the state of being denoted by those words [tat and tvam]. || 1337 ||

Having led the entire form of the inner self to the state of Hiraṇyagarbha, [he remains].
To that Hiraṇyagarbha, one should speak the knowledge to the one who is devoid of darkness.

Anticipating the objection as to why the word "thou" (tvam) is stated, he says, "Hiraṇyagarbhatām," [meaning] for the sake of knowing the meaning of the sentence. Having purified the referent of the term "thou" (tvampadavācya)—which is the entire Brahman, inflamed by the conceits of the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth, and which has attained limitation—by means of its unlimited nature, the compassionate teacher would impart the knowledge to that seeker; and he, knowing the meanings of the words, understands the meaning of the sentence through that instruction.
This is the meaning. || 1338 ||
Thus, by the total renunciation of the entire cycle of existence, one attains nirvāṇa.
Having cast off all ignorance, one proceeds by means of knowledge. || 1339 ||
Anticipating the question, "For what purpose is the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence?", he states its result in brief as it will be explained: "In this way.

The meaning is that by means of that knowledge—through which ignorance, the root of all misfortune, is sublated according to the manner previously described—the wise man attains liberation through the destruction of all bonds without exception. || 1339 ||
The universe, consisting of both self and non-self, is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception and the rest.
He understood that very self to be the supreme culmination of the nature of the whole.
Having explained the meaning of the two words *tad* and *aveditam*, he joins the sentence by restating them while explaining the meaning of the word *ātman*:

"The Self" (*ātman*). The world—consisting of the sentient and the insentient, differentiated and established through perception and other means—is known as that Brahman when it is realized as being nothing but the Self, which is the nature of the supreme foundation (*prakṛṣṭapratiṣṭhā*) described as "that is the limit, that is the highest goal," by setting aside the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [with respect to the world]. Thus, that Brahman has been known.
This is the meaning. || 1340 ||
Established without critical inquiry, it is the sole cause of all misfortune.
Because it is the sole witness of the mere inner self (pratyak-mātra), darkness exists within that inner self.

Raising the objection that since Brahman possesses the knowledge of its own nature within itself at all times, what is the use of knowledge derived from instruction, [the author] establishes the existence of ignorance within the Self for the sake of explaining the meaning of that [scriptural passage]. He says: "unexamined," etc. The connection is: "that darkness, which is indefinable, exists in the inner Self. The first qualification is intended to establish its indefinability. To prove the existence of darkness in the inner Self, he states an inference based on the mark of its effects: *avicāritasiddham ātmānam ātmany adhyasya...* (Having superimposed upon the Self the Self, which is established without inquiry... [The full verse continues: *avidyām ajñānanidraupetastamaḥpravṛddhaḥ svapnam īkṣate ||* (One who is possessed by the sleep of ignorance and enveloped by darkness beholds a dream. [And further: *tad evaṃvidhaṃ svapnam ātmā paśyati yasmāt tasmād avidyānidrayā prasupto lokas tad eva svapnadṛṣṭaṃ jāgarite 'nuvartamānaṃ satyam iti manyate |* (Since the Self thus sees such a dream, therefore the world, having fallen asleep through the sleep of ignorance, considers that very thing seen in the dream to be real as it persists in the waking state. [And: *tad etad avidyāvilasitaṃ sarvaṃ prapañcajātaṃ mṛtyurūpaṃ tamomayaṃ veditavyam |* (All this collection of manifold phenomena, produced by the play of ignorance, should be known as consisting of death and composed of darkness. [And: *yad etad avidyākṛtaṃ rūpaṃ tad anirvācyam ity ucyate |* (That form which is created by ignorance is called "indefinable. [And: *tad etad anirvācyatvam avidyāyāḥ siddham |* (The indefinability of this ignorance is thus established. [And: *tad evam avidyāsadbhāve kāryaliṅgakaṃ pramāṇam upanyastam |* (Thus, the proof for the existence of ignorance has been presented through the mark of its effects. [And: *tad etad avidyātmakaṃ tamaḥ pratyagātmani vidyata iti sthitam |* (It is established that this darkness, consisting of ignorance, exists in the inner Self. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvopapādanārthaṃ śrutim udāharati—* (Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating the existence of ignorance in the Self, he cites a scriptural text: *anṛtena hi pratyūḍhāḥ |* "For they are veiled by untruth. [And: *tathā ca śrutiḥ—* "And so says the scripture: *indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate |* "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaḥ siddhaḥ |* (Thus, the existence of ignorance in the Self is established. [And: *tad etad avidyāvaraṇaṃ jñānenaiva nivartyata iti darśayati—* (He shows that this veil of ignorance is removed only by knowledge: *vidyayā tad ajñānaṃ hanti |* "It destroys that ignorance through knowledge. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ prasādhya tannivṛttyarthaṃ śravaṇādividhim upadiśati—* (Having thus established the existence of ignorance in the Self, he teaches the injunction for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth for the purpose of its removal: *tasmād brahmavijñānārthaṃ sa gurumevābhigacchet ||* "Therefore, for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, one should approach a teacher alone. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ sādhayitvā tasyāḥ svarūpaṃ nirūpayati—* (Having thus established the existence of ignorance in the Self, he defines its essential nature: *avidyā nāma kim ucyate |* "What is called ignorance? [And: *sā cāvidyā dvividhā—ekā mūlāvidyā, aparā tūlāvidyā |* "And that ignorance is of two kinds: one is root-ignorance, the other is branch-ignorance. [And: *tatra mūlāvidyā sarvajaganmūlabhūtā anirvācyā |* "Therein, root-ignorance is the cause of the entire world, indefinable. [And: *tūlāvidyā tu tatkāryabhūtā nānāvidhāḥ |* "But branch-ignorance consists of various types which are its effects. [And: *tad etad avidyādvayaṃ pratyagātmani vartate |* "These two types of ignorance exist in the inner Self. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ tatsvarūpaṃ ca nirūpya tannivṛttyarthaṃ jñānasādhanaṃ darśayati—* (Having thus defined the existence of ignorance in the Self and its nature, he shows the means for knowledge for the purpose of its removal: *tasmād ātmānaṃ jānīyāt |* "Therefore, one should know the Self. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ prasādhya tasyāḥ prapañcarūpeṇa vivartaṃ darśayati—* (Having thus established the existence of ignorance in the Self, he shows its illusory transformation into the form of the manifold world: *avidyayā hy ātmā prapañcarūpeṇa vivartate |* "For by ignorance the Self undergoes illusory transformation into the form of the manifold world. [And: *tad etad avidyākṛtaṃ sarvaṃ mithyeti vijānīyāt |* "One should understand that all this created by ignorance is false. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ tatsvarūpaṃ tatkāryaṃ ca nirūpya tannivṛttyarthaṃ paramārthajñānaṃ darśayati—* (Having thus defined the existence of ignorance in the Self, its nature, and its effects, he shows the knowledge of ultimate reality for the purpose of its removal: *brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati |* "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ prasādhya tasyāḥ parihāram upadiśati—* (Having thus established the existence of ignorance in the Self, he teaches its abandonment: *tasmād avidyāṃ parityajya vidyām evābhyaset |* "Therefore, having abandoned ignorance, one should practice knowledge alone. [And: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaṃ tatsvarūpaṃ tatkāryaṃ tannivṛttisādhanaṃ ca nirūpya upasaṃharati—* (Having thus defined the existence of ignorance in the Self, its nature, its effects, and the means for its removal, he concludes: *tad evam ātmany avidyāsadbhāvaḥ siddhaḥ |* (Thus, the existence of ignorance in the Self is established. [And: *tad etad avidyāvaraṇaṃ jñānenaiva nivartyata iti siddham |* (Thus, it is established that this veil of ignorance is removed only by knowledge. [And: *tad evam āt

"Of all"—in that very context, he states another reason: "Because of the condition," and so forth. The meaning is that since that one [Self] is the witness of ignorance and its products, it is established even without a connection to nescience (ajñāna). || 1341 ||
Since ignorance proceeds only toward the opposite direction, it is therefore removed by the knowledge of reality.
When darkness, together with its effects, has been destroyed, the Self alone remains. || 1342 ||

He states the result of the assertion that ignorance resides in the Self alone: "In the innermost" (pratīci), etc. The sense is that once ignorance is established as residing in the innermost Self, the knowledge produced by instruction directed toward that [Self] becomes purposeful, insofar as it serves to remove that ignorance. || 1342 ||
Having become dispassionate toward all of saṃsāra, he then naturally desires liberation.
Tormented by the fire of saṃsāra, he desires that which is its opposite.

Because one who has abandoned the goals of human existence such as the world of Brahmā cannot possess the desire for liberation, there is an absence of a qualified seeker; consequently, the knowledge of reality (tattvavidyā) is untenable along with its effects.
[Vol.
2, page 407] Brāhmaṇa 4, accompanied by the commentary *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 701.

If it is asked how the establishment of the self alone as a remainder occurs through the destruction of ignorance, he says: "dispassionate" (*virakta*). By the qualification beginning with "from saṃsāra," the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities is expressed; that is to say, from saṃsāra. The meaning is: by virtue of the nature of saṃsāra itself. Alternatively, the meaning is: having attained tranquility (*śama*) and so forth due to one's own inherent nature of dispassion toward the subject at hand. [He is] one who possesses the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).
He states that the qualified candidate is one who desires to attain the knowledge that is the cause of liberation, which is contrary to that [ignorance]: "That which is contrary to it," etc. (1343).
By means of that [negation], which is not a partial negation, for the sake of awakening to the complete identity with the One.
The operation known as positive and negative concomitance was established previously.
1.1 By the injunction "It is indeed the Self," the distinction between the external and the internal is established. (1345)

In response to the inquiry as to what the means for that knowledge is, he recalls what was stated previously with the words "of that" (*tasya*). The meaning is: indeed, for the qualified seeker under discussion, the operation of mantras and so forth—which consists in the removal of the perception of limited objects for the sake of perceiving the unlimited object—was already mentioned earlier in the *Vidyāsūtra*. He states the fruit of this operation of mantras and so forth with the words "the outward" (*parāk*). || 1344 || 1345 ||
By him, having abandoned all that is not the Self, the state of oneness is perceived.
For the entire object is indeed other than that [consciousness], being born from the non-cognition of it.

He states the fruit of discrimination: "The state of being the one Self" (aikātmyam). Having abandoned everything from the body up to the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which are attained [as objects] but are not the Self, why should that very "state of being the one Self," which is not commonly known, be the object of knowledge? To this he says: "The whole" (kṛtsnam). Therefore, the remainder is that the entire reality alone is the object of knowledge. || 1346 ||
Therefore, the statement "one should see it in its entirety" refers to the actual object.
Having entered [into the body], because its form is incomplete, it is impelled by the miseries of saṃsāra.
By this term "self," one is enjoined toward the vision of the entire self. || 1347 ||

Anticipating the objection that by stating that the operation of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth is enjoined by the injunction "He is indeed the Self" (*ātmaiveti*), it is intended that the sentence is centered on an injunction, he says: "The whole. The meaning is that because the enjoined operation of connection and so forth culminates in the knowledge of unity, the sentence is centered on the reality (*vastu*) by means of an injunction regarding the means [of that knowledge]. If the sentence has non-dual reality as its ultimate purport, who is qualified for the knowledge thereof?

If it is argued that this non-dual reality (*advaya*) is not the very same as the cognition of jars and so forth—because it is distinct from the object for the qualified subject (*adhikārin*)—nor is it a separate entity because of its non-existence [as such], and furthermore, a cognition without a subject is not tenable; therefore, he says: "Having entered. The Supreme Self, having created the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth through its own ignorance (*avidyā*), has entered into them.

Due to the conceit of limitation (*paricchedābhimānitva*), it wanders in saṃsāra; yet, when at some point endowed with discrimination (*viveka*) and other qualities, it becomes the qualified subject for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
The meaning is that it has been acquired according to the prescribed rule. || 1347 ||
From this statement, "The Self is entirely [of such a nature]," he desires to see it as being of that form.
Because they are mutually established in their meaning, there is no distinction here between the two word-meanings. || 1348 ||

Anticipating the objection that, since the realization "I am Brahman" is already established through the previously mentioned methods such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, the statement of the sacred text (*vākya*) would be redundant, he says: "In its entirety. The meaning is this: because that which is limited, like a jar, is not the Self, the Self is indeed unlimited;

one realizes that complete Self from the sentence itself—preceded by the inquiry of the qualified seeker—since methods such as positive concomitance lack authority [in this regard]. Thus, there is no non-difference in the sense of "I am Brahman."
1. *vīkṣate* (he beholds). 2. *paramātmā* (the Supreme Self).
[Vol. 2, page 408] 702 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]

Anticipating the objection that "the distinction between the 'I' (ahamartha) and Brahman is well-established," he says: "mutually" (*anyonya*). Here, the meaning is "in this [context of] the sentence regarding the inner self" (*pratīci vākye*).

The intended sense is that because the referent of "I" culminates in the referent of Brahman, and the referent of Brahman culminates in the referent of "I"—otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of [the "I"] not being the Self and [Brahman] not being Brahman. || 1348 ||
All non-selves that are incomplete, as well as all non-selves that are complete.
Likewise, through positive and negative concomitance, [one realizes] all non-selves. || 1349 ||
Having cast it off like a withered flower of worship, by way of the manifestation of consciousness, |||
Having composed himself by means of the self, he perceives the entire self.

One might object: "Let it be then that the cognition 'I am Brahman' arises from the sentence alone; what is the use of [the methods of] anvaya (concomitance) and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not complete" (*akṛtsnān*).

By means of the path of the reflection of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*), one must disregard—through the method of *anvaya* and so forth—all incomplete non-selves (*anātman*) consisting of the individual forms (*vyaṣṭi*) which are the reflections of consciousness divided within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), as well as all complete non-selves consisting of the collective limiting adjuncts (*samaṣṭyupādhi*) such as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), and the various material bodies and so forth which are their individual manifestations.
However, having extracted the *tvam-artha* (the "thou" aspect) as the pure Self through the discriminative knowledge that has arisen, one perceives the entire Self from the sentence "I am Brahman.

Therefore, because [the methods of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are the cause of purification, both the sentence possessing those [methods] and the knowledge of its meaning are purposeful; this is the sense. || 1349 ||
This elaborate response, however, is intended to remove the faults previously mentioned.
"Indeed, this was Brahman," and so forth; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever here. || 1351 ||

He introduces the reply in order to elaborate upon that very meaning, summarizing it from the passage beginning with "Then [he realizes] himself" (tadātmānam). Regarding the phrase "It has been said":

the construction is that the response beginning with "Brahman" (brahma), which possesses more robust reasoning, serves to dispel the defects mentioned in the introduction; therefore, there is no fault in the position that liberation results from knowledge. || 1351 ||
Regarding that object of knowledge which was previously asked about—namely, "What is that Brahman?"—it has been explained.
And because everything that is called both knowledge and the object of knowledge was [contained] therein. || 1352 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Then [he realized] himself" as follows: "The object of knowledge. In the introduction, that which was asked as the object of knowledge—namely, "What is that Brahman?"—and that which was sought as the means of knowledge—namely, "From the knowledge of what Brahman did all this become Brahman?"—both of these are stated in the immediately following sentence. However, in the word "Brahman," the qualified person (adhikārī) is primarily expressed; this is the meaning. || 1352 ||
But that Brahman perceived itself alone as both the object of knowledge and what is called the means of knowledge.
The self is the object of knowledge, and likewise the means of knowledge; indeed, the cognition of the self alone [serves as both]. (1353)

Anticipating the question, "How are the means of knowledge (māna) and the object of knowledge (meyya) expressed here?", he analyzes the passage: "That Brahman" (*tad brahma*). In this context, "that Brahman" refers back to the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*);

"the Self" (*ātmānam*) is the expression for the object of knowledge; and "he knew" (*avedīt*) is the statement regarding the means of knowledge—such is the distinction. The particle *ca* serves to include the knower (*mātṛ*). He states the meaning of the restrictive particle (*eva*): "the Self" (*ātmaiva*). He indicates that the restrictive particle is also connected with the word "Self."
The word "tu" (but/however) is used for the purpose of exclusion. || 1353 ||

Since ignorance does not exist apart from the knowledge of the Self, therefore there is no knowledge of anything other than the Self that is distinct from the realization of the true nature of the Self. (1354)
[Vol. 2,
Page 409] 703 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Anticipating the objection—"Why is there such a restriction that only the Self is the object of knowledge (*meyam*) and only the knowledge of it is the means of knowledge (*mānam*), given that non-Self and its knowledge also exist in a similar manner?"—he says: "Not the non-Self" (*nātmā*). The meaning is: the ignorance of the non-Self is itself the ignorance of the Self, and the knowledge of the Self is itself the knowledge of that [non-Self];
therefore, the non-Self does not exist apart from the Self. || 134 ||
That knowledge which manifests in some instances through the division of the knower and so forth;
The object of that [cognition] arising from birth is not directly known by it [the self].

[Objection: It is not logical to say that "knowledge of the self" is itself "knowledge of the non-self," because the non-self is perceived as distinct from the self, such as in the case of a jar and so forth. Anticipating this, he says: "The knower and so forth. The word "somewhere" refers to objects such as jars. 1355.
Because it terminates in mere darkness (ignorance), it does not accord with reality as it truly is.
Even though its nature is that of the inward-facing reality, such is the wondrous activity of ignorance.

He states the reason why the non-self (anātman) is not known in its true nature even by that [cognition] which has arisen, just as it was before the arising of the cognition of a jar and so forth: "Because it consists of mere darkness" (*tamomātra*). Since the cognition of a jar and so forth does not illuminate the true nature of reality, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, the conclusion is stated: "Therefore," the non-self such as a jar does not exist apart from the Self, because of the uniformity (*aikarasya*) of the inner witness (*pratīc*) with that [Self].

Anticipating the objection that diversity is thus unestablished, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). Alternatively, anticipating the objection that if everything is nothing but the inner self, how can duality appear, he says: "The inner self. Even though everything is that alone, this activity of ignorance is diverse;
the meaning is that by its power, the one alone appears as manifold. || 1356 ||
By whose grace the perfection of darkness was attained, even though that very self was stolen away.
Even darkness [is perceived] solely through the power of prior experience, before the birth of conceptual understanding.

Raising the objection—how can even ignorance (ajñāna) be the cause of diversity in a world that is of a single essence and consists solely of the inner self (pratyagātman)—he states, by way of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, that such a thing is impossible to establish: "By whose grace... Anticipating the objection that darkness (*tamas*) is not established by a witness (*sākṣin*), because it must be established by a means of knowledge (*māna*), he says that since the production of knowledge dependent on a means of proof occurs only after the manifestation of darkness has already taken place through direct experience (*anubhava*), the cognition of that [darkness] arises from experience itself.
Regarding the phrase "even darkness": the word "even" (api) is used to provide attachment (rāga) and so forth as a corroborative example. || 1357 ||
If it has been stated here that [the object] is unknown prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The senses and so forth are not a valid means of knowledge because they are sublated by ignorance, like the [perception of] a snake in a rope. (1358)

Having accepted that perception and the other means of knowledge possess validity, he says [the following] to show that this very point is unestablished: "Previously," etc. The word "here" refers to the process of the undifferentiated (avyākṛta).
This means that because it is sublated by that [subsequent] darkness, it does not remove the ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyagajñāna) which was previously unknown. || 1358 ||
Because they do not see [it], he therefore states its endowment with the nature of being a knower and so forth.
For an object that lacks [the nature of] that [perception] is not measured by one whose intellect is dominated by delusion. || 1359 ||

Having stated that the senses and other means of knowledge are not authoritative [with respect to the Self] by following the discourse on the "unexplained" (avyākṛta), he says with the words beginning with "no" (na) that they are likewise [not authoritative] based on the statement, "They do not see Him. The meaning is that those who perceive the Self as qualified by seeing and so forth through perception and the other means of knowledge—of them the scripture says, "They do not see Him"; thus, their lack of authority regarding the reality is established. That is to say, those who perceive the Self as qualified by perception and the rest do not truly see it.
704 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] — [vol2, page 410]
