If it is argued that [the claim] is contradicted, he says "no. He explains with "for not," meaning that it is impossible for perception and other means of knowledge, which have qualified objects, to cognize a reality devoid of distinctions. || 1359 ||
Apart from the self, nothing else is capable of realizing the self.
Because it consists of the unique [cognition] together with its mother, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. || 1360 ||

Furthermore, regarding the possibility that the Self is accessible through perception and other means of knowledge, one must consider the alternative: is the knower [of the Self] different from it or non-different?

He refutes the first position with the words "the Self" (ātmānam). The meaning is this: first of all, that which is not the Self does not know itself because it is insentient; nor is there any other sentient being [that could know it], for the scripture states, "There is no other seer but He. He addresses the second position with the words "asādhāraṇa" (uncommon). That which is non-different from the inner witness (pratīc) is uncommon...

The meaning is this: since the sustainer—the substratum of the presiding deities and so forth—is the knower (mātṛ), and likewise the senses and the rest are the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the object of knowledge (prameya), all of this is nothing but the Self alone; therefore, because there is no division within that single-flavored [reality], it is not accessible through the senses and so forth. || 1360 ||
Therefore, the inner reality is exclusively unique, beginning with its own measure.
Nor does the doctrine of *niyoga* apply here, as it involves a distinction between different agents and other such factors.

Then, one might raise the objection that just as it is inaccessible [to perception], it must also be inaccessible to scripture (*āgama*), because [scripture] is centered upon *niyoga* (an injunction). Anticipating this, he says:

"Asādhāraṇa... That which is uncommon, such as the mere differentiated [phenomenon] and so forth—just as the nature of a rope subsumes a snake and the like—it is, by virtue of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*), neither an object of *niyoga* nor does *niyoga* apply to the knowledge of that inner self; for *niyoga* depends upon distinct agents, instruments, and so on. Therefore, it is not [the case that scripture] has *niyoga* as its primary purport.

Scripture (āgama) is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in itself; rather, its status as a pramāṇa consists in its being the cause of right knowledge that destroys ignorance along with its effects within the Self, in comparison to mere conceptual constructs (kalpita).
This is not the case for perception (adhyakṣa) and other such means of knowledge—this is the meaning. || 1361 ||
Everything would indeed remain unknown within that Self which has not been known.
And that which is to be known is already known through meditation, because all things are limited in number and [their nature] is fully encompassed.

How is it that everything, including the subject (mātrādi), is merely the Self? To this, he provides the scriptural authority for the statement that "by the knowledge of one, all is known": "All. He states the reason for the claim that "when the Self is unknown, all is unknown; when it is known, all is known" with the words "because of its being just that much" (tāvatvāt).
Therefore, because the Self is non-dual, there is no distinction such as subject and so forth within it; thus he says, "because of its entirety" (tatkātsnyāt). || 1362 ||
For when the non-self is examined through reasoning, its true nature is indeed selflessness.
If he is rejected by that [means], then let the non-self be established thereby. || 1363 ||

Having stated that the mother and other such objects are nothing but the Self (ātman) based on scripture, [the author] also states it by means of reasoning (*yukti*). Regarding the word "by reasoning":

the meaning of the particle *hi* is that we observe that the superimposed object, such as silver, which possesses the quality of being visible and so forth, has the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as mother-of-pearl, as its very self. He states the consequence of the opposite case—that it would result in non-existence—by saying "if it were rejected. || 1363 ||
For the Self—which is unattached, devoid of qualities, and non-dual—pursues the reality of non-self.
If it were established by itself, what else could it possibly require for its establishment? (1364)

If the Self were the reality of the non-Self, then—because the two are non-different—the Self’s freedom from attachment (*asaṅgatva*) and other such qualities would be lost. Anticipating this objection, he says "the non-Self" (*anātma*), meaning that it is not so, because the connection with the non-Self is produced by *māyā*. The word "for" (*hi*) serves as an illustration: the connection with water and the like created by *māyā* does not obstruct the actual solidity and other properties of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as the desert land. Furthermore, in the light... always...
[Vol.
2, Page 411] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
T.

Since it does not attain existence or manifestation within itself, it will be established elsewhere through that which is non-self; for there is no other agent [of establishment] due to its lack of independence. Therefore, he says: "not being established" (*asidhyan*), meaning it would be established only as something imagined therein. || 1364 ||
Just as there is agreement regarding experience, even when there is disagreement among all disputants.
There is no contradiction for the proponents [of this view], and likewise, there is no doubt even regarding ignorance (ajñāna).

Since the ego and so forth are superimposed upon the Self, since the senses and so forth lack validity, and since ignorance cannot be grasped by them, it has been stated that [ignorance] is established solely by the Witness (sākṣin).
Now, fearing that ignorance cannot be established because there is dispute regarding the experience of the non-dual, self-luminous, and immutable witness, he says:
"All... etc. Even though all philosophical positions are mutually contradictory, experience is nevertheless accepted by everyone, for otherwise worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would cease.

Furthermore, that experience is self-luminous, because if it were an object of knowledge, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). It is immutable and non-dual, because there is no evidence for its birth or other modifications. Regarding that [witness], the disputant—

The meaning is "just as [it is] accepted. Even though such an experience exists as described, there is a disagreement regarding the ignorance (*ajñāna*) to be established by it; anticipating this objection, he says:

"Because of non-discrepancy" (*avisaṃvāda*). Since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is impossible without the admission of ignorance, and since that [ignorance], if it had a beginning, could not—by its very nature—be the cause of that [activity], and since if an unreal thing (*avastu*) were its cause, there would be an infinite regress if that too had a beginning, whereas if it is beginningless (*anādi*), it is precisely that which [we maintain].

The meaning is that because it is unreal due to being false ignorance, and because it is indeterminable (anirvācya) precisely because it is sat (existent) and immediate (aparokṣa), there is indeed agreement among the disputants on this point, just as there is regarding experience itself. || 1365 ||
If it is accepted [by you] on the basis of the awakening of the Āgamaśāstra;
This much alone is sufficient for the establishment of our own tenet. || 1366 ||

To state that a misconception regarding an experience that is unimpeded is improper, he said "without doubt. Nevertheless, one might suspect that because this [experience] is established by the witness (*sākṣin*), like the witness itself, it cannot be removed by knowledge; therefore, he says "just like that" (*tadvat*) to show that its destruction is also accepted, just as ignorance is.
The sense is that in its absence, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be subverted. Even so, what is established for you? To that he replies: "to this extent" (*etāvatā*).
This means that it is established merely by the triad of experience, ignorance, and its removal. || 1366 ||
When our own established doctrine is fully realized, there is no realization of any other established doctrine.
Once that is established, its complete perfection cannot be prevented in any way. || 1367 ||

Anticipating the objection that, just as in your own system, the other systems might also be established through that same cognition [of the threefold means], he says: "Asmāt" (from this). The sense is that when the Advaita doctrine is established as authoritative, the other systems are merely erroneous because they are rooted in ignorance.

Let it be granted for the sake of argument that the other systems are established by that cognition; nevertheless, there is no harm, since they too accept the triad beginning with direct experience (*anubhava*).
He says, "the accomplishment of what was intended," meaning "in the accomplishment of that. The word "this" (asya) refers to one's own established doctrine (svasiddhānta). || 1367 ||
Ignorance, doubtful knowledge, and false knowledge—this is the triad.
Ignorance is the cause therein; the state of being an effect belongs to the remaining two.

One might raise the objection: "Even if one's own doctrine is established, if it were established only by means of the doctrines of others, then because of their mutual contradiction, there would be an optionality (*vikalpa*) regarding the reality.
Anticipating this, [the author] states his own doctrine in order to establish that the doctrines of others are erroneous: "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*), etc. [The term *pratyag* refers to the inner self].
706 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 412]
The meaning is that all other established doctrines are merely manifestations of [limited] knowledge; because they rely on distinctions that lack valid authority, they are erroneous. || 1368 ||
Because it consists solely of immutable consciousness, darkness does not exist in its nature.
Nor is ignorance adventitious, because it is impossible for it to be established separately [from consciousness]. (1369)

He establishes the imagined nature of the ignorance of the inner self (*pratyagajñāna*) with the verse beginning "kūṭastha" (the immutable). The meaning is this: that [ignorance] of his is neither innate nor adventitious;

it cannot be the former because the self has the nature of eternal perception; nor can it be the latter, because no other cause for its production exists elsewhere than in the self, and thus its production is impossible even there. || 1369 ||
From that [ignorance] comes the conjunction of ignorance and its effects with the self.
It would consist in the nature of being a self and possessing a self, but it is not produced by the karma of both.

By means of ignorance (*avidyā*), the conceptual connection between that [ignorance] and its effects—such as doubt—and the Self is established, because those [effects] are of the nature of that [ignorance].

Thus, the author establishes the imagined nature (*kalpitatva*) of the effect of ignorance. Regarding the word "ignorance": the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) indicates the non-existence of doubt and the rest apart from ignorance. To the question, "What kind of connection is there between ignorance, its products, and the Self?", he states it: "The Self... [and so on].
It excludes conjunction and so forth; however, it is not [the case that]... || 1370 ||
For there is indeed only one existent reality, which is established by the authority of the Vedānta.
Because it is solely intent upon that much alone, the knowledge of the Self is its eternal abode.

He states another reason for the imagined nature of ignorance along with its effects: "One" (*ekam*). The meaning is that the reality which consists of *Sat* (Being), as understood from such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," is indeed one; everything other than that is imagined. In this context, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that this is also the realization of those who know Brahman. Regarding its being accessible through scripture, the knowledge arising therefrom is like the knowledge arising from the scriptural injunctions concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and other rites.

Fearing the objection that Brahman must be manifold rather than of a single flavor because its objects are mixed, he says: "only that much" (*tāvanmātra*). The meaning is that since the phenomenal world consisting of cause and effect is nothing but pure Being (*sanmātra*), the knowledge of the Self has as its support that which is of a single flavor. || 1371 ||
Even when in conflict with all other disputants, that which relies on the strength of its own established tenets [prevails].
"Neither proof nor refutation is intended to negate that [reality].

(1372) By stating his own established doctrine, he demonstrates that the doctrines of others are rooted in delusion, and concludes that his own doctrine is not to be rejected. Regarding the word "all": where there exists a strength characterized by direct experience within a doctrine, the means of proof and so forth that rely upon it—[are not to be negated].
The meaning is that there is no establishment of the refutation of the established tenet (siddhānta). || 1372 ||
All proof and refutation depend upon the support of his feet.
Since it is established for those who hold the view of [other] holy sites, how could there be any refutation of it? || 1373 ||
Fearing that for the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) there can be no establishment of anything because even experience itself is denied, he says: "The means of proof" (*sādhana*).
The meaning is that if experience is denied, the means of proof and so forth cannot be established due to the absence of a prover. || 1373 ||
That state by which non-existence is conceptualized neither exists nor does not exist.
Tell me, by what can the pride regarding that state be prevented? || 1374 ||
And because it establishes non-existence, it cannot be denied; thus he says: "Non-existence. It establishes the non-existence of experience—
And because it does not exist, there is no negation of it; thus he says: "Of that," [verse 1374].
There is no means of valid cognition for any proponent whatsoever that establishes deviation.
And how can that which is established by its own inherent power be denied? (1375)

He says "it is not a mere assertion" because, in all positions, every means of knowledge (*māna*) is invariably consistent with experience (*anubhava*). Then, raising the objection that [if it is not an assertion] it would be equivalent to a jar or other objects by virtue of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*), he says "by its own power" to show that this is not so, because it provides the existence and manifestation (*sphūrti*) of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so forth.
He concludes that it is impossible to refute the reality of experience with the word "that. || 1375 ||
Because that alone is non-deviant among all things that are deviant.
That alone is our single means of valid cognition which is not contradicted by any proponent of a philosophical system.

He establishes its proof through its own majesty. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): since that which is accepted by all disputants is itself non-deviant as the prover (*sādhaka*) amidst all deviating things such as the body and so forth, it is of a single essence; thus, for us, it is indeed the means of knowledge (*māna*) and not the object of knowledge (*meya*). This is the construction [of the verse], meaning that its proof is established through its own majesty. || 1376 ||
Our notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth is never subverted.
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, [the world appears] like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth. || 1377 ||

Fearing that the cessation of worldly activity might follow from the fact that the body and such are fallible while the nature of experience is infallible—thereby making their difference manifest and rendering the notion of a self in the body and so forth unestablished—the author says: "In the body and such... Among the three states, in both waking and dreaming, the notion of a self in the body and such is never abandoned even by the discerning, just as it is not abandoned by the undiscerning; just as the notion of silver in mother-of-pearl during a moment of delusion [is not abandoned].
The meaning is that, through that [non-apprehension], the establishment of all conventional transactions occurs. The word "etc. (ādi) is used for the purpose of indicating other examples. || 1377 ||
He who is other than the agent ending with the body, and other than the knower ending with the intellect.
And that which is perceived by inward vision is other than [the body] which causes the end of the vital breaths. || 1378 ||

Let it be then that the body and so forth alone are the Self according to how they appear; having raised this objection, he addresses the Lokāyata [materialist] by saying "dehāntāt" (from the end of the body).

The triad consisting of the body, the sense organs, and the mind is the meaning of the ablative case. For that which is perceived through direct observation—that is, through the cognition of its own nature or the notion of "I"—is other than the triad beginning with the body, because that triad is composed of the elements (*bhautika*), whereas the inner self (*pratyak*) is not so. This is the meaning.

He says to the Mīmāṃsaka: "Ending with the intellect" (buddhyantāt). The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the agent of the "I-notion," because the latter is subject to deviation and is therefore not the Self.
He says to the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha and others: "Ending with the vital breath" (prāṇāntāt). Here, the word *ekaḥ* is a synonym for the word *saḥ*. || 1378 ||
Being bodiless, he is free from old age and death; being without a mind, he is devoid of delusion and sorrow.
He is free from hunger and thirst due to the abandonment of the causes of vital breath.

Since the Self is distinct from the body and so forth, its attributes do not touch it; thus, by stating that the Self is free from the six waves, he declares the purity of the Self with the words "adehataḥ" (being bodiless). || 1379 ||
[vol2, page 414]
He who is deficient is one who has already fallen away; likewise, he who has not yet arrived is one who is still coming.
One should know that as the non-self throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Thinking that since it has been stated that "non-self phenomena do not touch the Self," the Self and the non-Self must be distinguished and described, he states the definition of the non-Self: "ahīna" (not diminished). The meaning is: that which, though in reality devoid of diminution even during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], experiences such diminution within the internal witness (pratyak), and which comes from that very source even in the absence of any external arrival—that is the non-Self. || 1380 ||
He who does not come when he is departing, nor go when he has arrived, does not diminish.
That self is the witness of coming and going, because it is the substratum of experience. (1381)

He states the definition of the Self with the words beginning with "no" (na). The meaning is that the Self is that which does not undergo arrival or departure when the body and so forth undergo arrival and departure, because it is the witness of their arrival and departure. To the question, "How are those two [the body's arrival and departure] established as stated? he replies with the word "anubhava" (experience). || 1381 ||
Without depending upon ignorance, the agent who acts does not proceed.
In this world, no one who is not an agent is seen to be capable of performing an action. || 1382 ||

Anticipating the objection—“How can non-duality be established if there is no confusion between those two [the agent and the action] and their respective attributes?”—he states that the agent is merely imagined (*kalpita*).
“Not [without an agent],” he says; the meaning is “because of its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*). He then states that the action is also imagined because it is brought about by an imagined agent:
“Not without an agent. || 1382 ||
Furthermore, by means of the seer's seeing, no non-attained or non-self-existent thing whatsoever is established.
Therefore, false knowledge is non-self, for it arises from ignorance of the self. || 1383 ||

Having stated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the agent and other factors are non-self and consist of ignorance (*avidyā*), he states another reason for that very point: "Of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*). He says, "It is false" (*mithyā*); because the establishment of the non-self is dependent on something else, it is imagined like a snake [in a rope]. Regarding its being the object of false cognition, he recalls the previously mentioned reason: "The Self" (*ātman*). That which arises from ignorance is the object of false cognition, as is the case with silver and the like.
The word "hi" is used indeed to express that [the matter] is evident. || 1383 ||
Not depending upon ignorance (avidyā) in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
One perceives it as non-self because it does not persist in the tips of its limbs. || 1384 ||

He establishes that [the perception of the non-self] arises from ignorance with the words "Not without ignorance" (nāvidyām). He states the reason for the claim that no one perceives the non-self during even the three states of consciousness without ignorance:

"Because of that" (tajja-). The meaning is that since the knower, the knowledge, and so forth—which are produced by ignorance—have no connection to the non-self in its absence, the perception [of the non-self] is indeed born of ignorance. || 1384 ||
Nor is it devoid of ignorance when viewed through the perspective that conforms to the scriptures.
The self is not capable of seeing itself, just as form cannot be seen by the auditory faculty.

Anticipating the objection that the self (ātman) must also be false because it depends solely upon the knower (mātṛ), just like non-self (anātman), he says: "And not... [referring to verse 9323]. The knower... [end of fragment].
[Vol.
2, Page 415] 4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 709.
Regarding the suitability of the pure Self—which is devoid of contact with ignorance and its products—to be an object of perception, by means of the visible perception that consists of name and form:
He states an illustration: "Form," etc. || 1385 ||
Having set aside all that is not the Self by means of positive and negative concomitance.
One should perceive the non-dual Self with a vision that has direct perception as its primary focus.

Anticipating the question, "How then does the view of self [arise]? he says: "Having cast aside," etc. This means by that which arises from the sentence, which has the inward-turned as its primary focus and takes the form of that alone. || 1386 ||
From the teacher's statement, "You are Brahman," [there arises the realization] regarding those two referents established therein.
Having attained discernment through the aforementioned methods of positive concomitance and so forth, he understood.

The meaning of the particle *eva*—that the Self alone is the object of knowledge (*meyam*) and the knowledge of that [Self] alone is the means of knowledge (*mānam*)—has now been established. He now states that the knowledge of the Self arises solely from the instruction of a teacher and not through mere speculative reasoning, beginning with the word "Thou" (*tvam*). The connection is: "[He] understood from the sentence. If that is so, why does everyone not understand it from the sentence taught by the teacher? To this he replies: "Residing therein... Even one who has heard the sentence [must understand] the meaning of the words contained within that sentence.
The meaning is that, due to a lack of purification or a lack of qualification, one does not experience the meaning of the sentence. || 1387 ||
That Brahman, which previously existed as the non-self, came to know itself as the Self.
But through ignorance and, indeed, through knowledge, Brahmā himself became the Self by his own nature.

Regarding that Brahman which has become the disciple, one might ask: what is it that is meditated upon according to the teacher's word? One might suspect that it cannot be the Self alone, because of the contradiction between the object of action (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*); nor can it be the non-Self, because [the non-Self] lacks that [nature of being meditated upon]. Anticipating this, he says: "That Brahman. The meaning is that since the Self is known as being beyond the scope of objects, there is no contradiction between the object and the agent. Anticipating the objection that for the Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness (*jñapti*), what need is there for adventitious knowledge (*āgantuka-jñāna*), he says: "That which..."
He states the conclusion—that knowledge is purposeful because it destroys ignorance, since the identity with Brahman is one's own inherent nature—by the words "by knowledge.

That which previously stood as the non-Self due to ignorance, before the arising of knowledge, is that very Brahman, one's own true nature; through the sentence taught by the Guru, it becomes the fruit of vision, just like [an object] already seen.
And because it remains in a state of perfection through the cessation of ignorance—this is the collective meaning. || 1388 ||
The word "evam" (thus) is to be understood as an emphatic particle, serving as a qualifier for the meanings of "Brahman," "Self," and "object."
The self alone is to be known as Brahman, and Brahman alone is the self, because of their possible identity. (1689)

Having stated the intended meaning of the particle *eva* through the passage beginning with "The self is the object of knowledge, as well as the means of knowledge," he now states its expressed meaning with the words "the word *eva*. He explains that this [particle] is a qualifier for each of the two meanings—Brahman and the Self—by saying "Brahman... He clarifies the manner of restriction with the words "the Self alone... The word "to be known" (*vijñeyam*) is used for the purpose of syntactic connection (*anvaya*); therein, the reason is its possibility.
Thus it is said. || 1389 ||
Brahmanhood does not exist apart from the Self, nor does selfhood exist apart from Brahman.
This error regarding those two arises from a lack of understanding of their true nature. || 1390 ||

It establishes the possibility [of the realization]: "The state of being Brahman. To the question, "How can the non-Brahmanhood in the Self and the non-Selfhood in Brahman be manifested? he says in response: "Its true nature" (tadyāthātmya). || 1390 ||
The Self, too, is directly that Brahman; it is only through lack of understanding that it appears remote.
In that same way, Brahman itself—the Self—is perceived as if it were accompanied by a second.
He demonstrates the misconception regarding Brahman with the words "even the Self. He provides an illustration of that [misconception] regarding the Self with the word "Brahman. || 1391 ||
For the ascetic whose darkness has been utterly destroyed by the perfect knowledge arising from the [scriptural] statement...
Due to the cessation of the cause of differentiation, everything remains as the Self alone. || 1392 ||

Having stated that error possesses the nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*) through its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with ignorance, he says "by the [power of] the sentence" (*vākya*) that it is likewise so because it is sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*). It has been stated that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), like tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, is a cause for the ascetic (*yati*). This refers to the fact that it is the cause for the removal of error (*viparyāsa*). He says "all" (*sarvam*) to mean that the entire, full Brahman is the Self alone—the one, continuous reality of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)—which remains as the residue.
For the Śruti says: "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the Knower?"
But is it not the case that the statement "that [self] itself" expresses a contradictory meaning? (1393)

Regarding the statement "then he knew only himself," an objection is raised: "the knower. The meaning is that since the knowability of the Self is implied in scripture, the assertion of its knowability contradicts other scriptural passages. || 1393 ||
Since it is both seen and accepted, there is no contradiction here with regard to cognitions.
The cognition of the inner self arises everywhere, even with respect to the knower and so forth. || 1394 ||

There is no contradiction [in the scripture] regarding the Self, whether by virtue of its being the object of knowledge or its being the witness. He states that the first case is not so: "Because of seeing" (*dṛṣṭeḥ*).

He states that the second case is not so: "Not here" (*nātra*). The meaning is: since the Self is known as the witness of all, and not as an object, how can there be a contradiction in this statement? He establishes its status as the witness of all: "The inward" (*pratyak*). And the intellect is indeed inward...
The meaning is that consciousness shines everywhere as the witness; otherwise, the insentient would not be perceived. "Arising" (upajāyamānatva) means appearing metaphorically. || 1394 ||
Whatever object is measured here by means of the distinction between "you" and "I," [is all this world].
By each such particularity, the inner object (pratyagartha) is cognized. || 1395 ||

Anticipating the objection that there would then be a distinction between witness and the witnessed, he says: "yuṣmad... (verse 1395). Here, the term "iha" refers to the sphere of the means of knowledge.
Without embracing the inward-facing reality, that which exists as the outward-facing does not come into being.
Therefore, by means of that consciousness, everything else prior to it is inferred. || 1396 ||

Raising the objection that there can be no status as a witness because of the absence of difference, he states that its establishment is possible through imagined difference: "the inner self" (*pratyagartham*). The meaning is that, according to the logical principle that "an object of the verb 'to know' is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the intellect which does not have a witness," [the self must be the witness]. Relying on the aforementioned reasoning, he states the conclusion: "therefore" (*tena*). || 1396 ||
N ● [vol2, page 417]
From Brahmā down to a post, [this is] directly perceived among all things that are subject to change.
The cognition is non-deviant and reflected within the single consciousness. || 1397 ||

Some argue that it is incorrect to say "the cognition of everyone is preceded by internal consciousness" (*pratyakcaitanyapūrvā*), because consciousness perishes at every moment; to them, he replies: "From Brahmā down to... That is to say, although all non-self objects from Brahmā down to a mere post are perceptible and subject to change, the experience reflected everywhere in the form of consciousness is itself unchanging. This is its nature as the witness (*sākṣitva*) in all cases.
The meaning is that because the self is manifest, experience is not subject to deviation. || 1397 ||
And the disputants do not disagree regarding the nature of experience.
And if there were non-conformity in that regard, by what else could it be corrected? (1398)

Having refuted its momentariness, he now refutes its emptiness with the words "na ca" (nor...). If it is argued that even regarding that [emptiness], there is a dispute for the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin), he says "tatra" (in that case). The meaning is that if there were disagreement even regarding experience itself, everything would remain unestablished due to the absence of any means of proof. || 1398 ||
Whatever else might be postulated here as well, that too does not differ from this [reality] at all.
Since it consists of the nature of all distinctions, what could exist without the Self? (1399)
Anticipating the objection that "even in the absence of experience, [the self] is established through its mother and others, and thus there is no total non-establishment [of everything]," he says:

"Another also. Here, the meaning is "taking the establishment of everything as the occasion. Considering whether that [other] is insentient or sentient—if it were insentient, it would be superimposed upon experience like a snake; thus, he refutes the second alternative with the words: "That also. The word "also" (api) serves the purpose of providing the example of experience.

Furthermore, since everything—whether insentient or unborn—is of the nature of the Self, nothing can be established without it; therefore, upon analysis, [the Self] cannot be associated with existence (*sattva*), and because it would be contradictory [for it] to be pervaded by a function residing in its own substrate, it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
With this intention, he says: "All... (verse 1399).
Because the universe rests within the inner self, it therefore rests within the non-self through the power of that [inner self].
Even the ignorant, women, and children trust him without hesitation.

Someone might argue that because [the self] is established as the substratum for the cognition of objects, it cannot be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). To that person, he replies with the word "pratyak" (inward). The meaning is this: having first placed trust in the Self, the entire world subsequently places its trust in the non-Self by its power; therefore, the inward conviction (*pratyag-viśvāsa*) is independent of the consciousness of objects, because, occurring prior to that [object-consciousness], it cannot possibly depend upon the cognition of external objects. || 1400 ||
The knowledge of the Self by the Self alone, devoid of the sacrificer, the sacrifice, and so forth.
Because it is itself of the nature of the fruit, the fruit does not differ from this [consciousness]. || 1401 ||

To the objection that if there were reliance on the internal (pratici), then because of the requirement for distinctions such as the mother and so forth, how could there be self-luminosity (svaprakāśatā)? He says: "By the Self alone" (ātmanaiva). He states the meaning of the word "alone" (eva): "the object of knowledge" (jñeya), etc. The word "etc. (ādi) refers to the instruments [of knowledge] and their objects. Anticipating the doubt that, like the fruit of valid cognition, the means of knowledge and so forth might also be distinct from the Self, he says: "Itself" (svayam). Because the Self is self-luminous, it does not possess such [distinctions].
The meaning is that it is therefore proper to break through the fruit. || 1401 ||
712 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
This empirical discourse based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is common to all disputants.
If we were established in self-experience, it would be like the object of the sixth sense.

Fearing that non-duality might be lost because distinctions such as "mother" and so forth exist with respect to what is not the Self—namely, sound and other objects—even though they do not exist within the Self, he says:

"By means of valid cognition... He states: "If not... (verse 1402), meaning that if knowledge and the like, like their objects, were not established in self-luminous experience, they would be nothing more than a void.
This [Self] consists solely of pure consciousness, eternally neither setting nor rising.
Not touching ignorance, he remains inactive, without an agent, and without fruit. || 1403 ||

Fearing that if the world—consisting of both the determinate (*vyākṛta*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—were of the nature of the Self alone, it would be touched by the qualities and defects inherent in that world, he says: "Consciousness... [and so forth]. Then, suspecting that in that case there might likewise be arising and passing away, he says "always" (*sadā*), indicating that even in that [consciousness] those two do not exist. Furthermore, he says "inactive" (*niṣkriya*), meaning that just as there is no contact with ignorance, there is likewise no contact with its effects.
Thus [ends the section]. || 1403 ||
Because its intrinsic nature is by itself unattached, it is like the sky, which contains birds and other things.
Neither ignorance nor its effect approaches that which stands before one's very eyes.
Anticipating the objection that the Self might be touched by ignorance and its products because they reside within it, even though the Self is untouched by them, he says: "By itself" (svataḥ).

Just as the sky, due to its non-attachment, cannot touch a bird or the like even though they are situated within it, so too ignorance and the rest, though situated within the inner Self, do not touch it because of the Self's inherent nature of non-attachment; this is the meaning. || 1404 ||
Because it is incapable of establishing itself by itself, like the wind which is always [dependent] except for space.
Even though its nature is one of negation, non-apprehension appears as if it were established in the two eyes.

Anticipating the objection that if there were no mutual connection between the Self and ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, then since the world of ignorance would not be established, bondage itself would not be established, he says: "It is established by itself. The ellipsis is "the Seer (dṛk)," meaning that even though its nature has been denied [as an object], it is the Seer. "Non-apprehension" (agraha) refers to ignorance along with its effects. The meaning of the word "iva" is that the connection of ignorance and so forth with the Seer-Self is caused by ignorance. For indeed, wind never exists apart from space.

Just as that [Self] is established through its own independence, so too the world, being inherently insentient and thus impossible to perceive even throughout the three periods of time, cannot exist within the nature of the inner Self (pratyagātman). Yet, by means of ignorance (avidyā), it attains the appearance of establishment in that very [Self], though it is there utterly inconceivable;
this is the meaning. || 1405 ||
For one whose nature is common attains union with those whose natures are uncommon.
Because it has no other mode of activity, the Self does not enter into association with non-Self entities.

He states another reason for the fact that, in reality, there is no connection with duality regarding the Seer. He says, "The union. The meaning is that while a connection between a universal and its particulars is observed, because the Seer is not a universal, there is no conjunction with anything whatsoever. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to demonstrate the well-known nature of the relationship between universals and particulars in cases such as cows and horses. || 1406 ||
For when it is analyzed, its distinction from others is also established.
[Vol.
2, Page 419] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 713.
If it is argued that because a specific nature is attained, there is a connection with the general, he says "no," [stating]: "When being divided... from another.

The meaning of the word *hi* (for) is that the status of being a particular (*viśeṣatva*) for that which is excluded [from others] is established in the case of a fragment of sugar-candy and so forth. Having stated the general rule, he declares the absence of division within the Self with the words "because of its oneness" (*ekatvāt*). This means, in short, because difference (*bheda*) is difficult to define. He proves that very point with the words "because of the absence of the two. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis. Since difference depends upon a locus (*dharmin*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and since that [difference] itself depends upon something else...

The meaning is that because their establishment would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), difference (*bheda*) is difficult to define. Alternatively, he states that because the Self’s very nature consists of selfhood (*pratyaktva*) in each respective instance, there is no difference whatsoever from anything; this is expressed by the word "on account of oneness" (*ekatvāt*). He further states that because the distinction between subject (*dharmin*) and counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is impossible therein, difference is unestablished; this is expressed by the word "of the two" (*dvaya*). (Verse 1407)
Because it is devoid of differentiation and conjunction, the Self cannot be the referent of words or sentences.
Therefore, this self, being difficult to conceive, is experienced by the self alone.

Anticipating the objection that the Self must possess both universality and particularity because it is the referent of words—just like a cow or other such things—the author says: "bhedā... (regarding difference). For neither difference, as between an action and its factors, nor relation, as between a blue lotus and its color, is possible in the case of the Self; since that Self is unattached and non-dual, both of these [properties] are difficult to establish therein. Thus, it is not reasonable to suspect that it possesses the status of a universal or the like by virtue of being the referent of words.
[The opponent says: "In that case, since the Self is not established through any means of valid cognition (māna), it remains unestablished. To this, he replies: "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 1408 ||
Whatever reality there is in this duality is experienced by oneself alone.
In that state, for one in whom all distinctions have been negated, this much alone is directly witnessed by the self. || 1409 ||

Anticipating the objection that—since the Self is devoid of common or specific qualities, free from difference and relation, lacking the status of being a word-meaning or a sentence-meaning, and although self-luminous—it cannot possibly possess unity because its nature would differ during bondage and liberation—the author says: "Of whatever kind... (yādṛg iti). The meaning is that the nature of the Self, which is immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) and of a single essence, is established by direct experience. || 1409 ||
That which is the reality of the inner self (pratyagātman), from which all darkness has been dispelled.
No cognition other than the inward awareness (pratyagbodha) is capable of cutting through that [ignorance]. (1410)

If consciousness (*caitanya*) is of the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpa*) in both states, then since it is established even in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) by perception and other means of knowledge, what is the need for the [Vedic] sentence?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "apāsta... (it is discarded). The sense is that it has been explained that perception and the other means of knowledge have qualified objects as their domain, not the pure [Self]. || 1410 ||
Because, through the direct perception of the object of negation, the delusion regarding the self and its production are dispelled.
Because a second [self] is impossible, may I be one who possesses such unprecedented qualities.

He states the fruit of the inward knowledge arising from the sentence in the verse beginning with "pratyak. The meaning of the particle "mātra" is "having set aside the perception of the non-self. || 1411 ||
[He is] the witness to the coming and going [of phenomena], free from darkness, regarding that which is neither cause nor effect; [this is] the reality.
It is apprehended directly by a cognition that conforms strictly to that [object] alone.
714 [vol2, page 420] meṃ

In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, [the commentary on] the first chapter: "That" refers to the connection with "by means of direct knowledge," or alternatively, that it is "directly perceived. This excludes the possibility that knowledge produced by the eyes and other senses has the ultimate reality (*tattva*) as its object. "Only so much" means, in effect, that which conforms solely to the attributeless Self (*nirviśeṣātman*). || 1412 ||
That Brahman which, through ignorance, became differentiated by time and other such factors;
When the darkness within the inner self has been destroyed through the awakening to that very reality of the Self.
For the scripture declares: "That Brahman is indeed the self; the self is indeed Brahman. (1413)

He concludes the meaning of the statement "then he knew himself alone" with the words "from time, etc. This means from the scripture, that is to say, from the words taught by the Guru. That Brahman which, prior to the Guru’s instruction, appeared as if divided by space, time, and so forth, and as if limited due to ignorance—that very reality of the object, its pure form, being the Self, when darkness residing within the Self is destroyed through the awakening to that [truth], [one attains] the state...

The meaning is that because the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the sentence taught by the teacher and others—which serves as the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning—one directly realizes the identity between Brahman and the Self, just as one who has already realized it does. || 1413 ||
When the darkness of the inner self, which is the cause of the perception of non-Brahman and non-Self, has been dispelled;
Because there is an absence of both exclusion and inclusion, all that consequently became non-existent.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore" (tasmāt) as follows: "abrahma... etc. In this context, the word "tataḥ" should be understood as denoting the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), as is seen in the Vārttika and other such works. || 1414 ||
Because exclusion and inclusion [occur] when there is a second entity.
Because the entities of cause and effect consist of nothing more than the nature of being perceived. || 1415 ||

He states the reason for the absence of both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*) with the words "exclusion," etc. The ellipsis is "therefore, because of the absence of a second [entity], those two do not exist. He establishes the absence of a second entity with the words "perception," etc. (1415).
There is nothing whatsoever unknown, nor is there any darkness that has not been dispelled.
For the sake of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), this word "I" (asmi) would exist. || 1416 ||

He states the result of the non-duality of the Self with the words beginning with "not" (*na*). The meaning is: "from the knowledge of that which is partless and of a single essence. This itself is the meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Desiring to explain the passage beginning with "I am," he states the meaning of the word "I am" (*asmi*) as follows: "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*). Because the expression "I am" is a statement of present existence, the eternal reality of oneness is expressed, and not the coming into being of something previously non-existent; therefore, it is distinct from [the usage of] different verbal roots.

The meaning is that, according to the logical principle that words denoting different causes [of the same object] possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) for the sake of expressing identity, this word [is used] to establish the co-referential function of the terms "I" (*ahaṃ*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*). || 1416 ||
The mutual union of those two who have arrived is [the cause].
In this context, the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is the qualificand, because it is well known that it is the primary element. || 1117 ||

Having stated the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words, he explains that there is a mutual connection between their respective meanings by way of qualifier and qualified, saying:

"Brahman. To the question of which of the two has the status of the qualified and which has the status of the qualifier, he says: "The referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*). Between these two— [vol2, page 421]

He states the reason for that very [self] being the substantive (*viśeṣya*): "That" (*tad*). The meaning is that since the referent of the word "I" (*ahaṃśabda*), which is the self (*ātman*), is well-known as the primary qualifier of everything, it is possible for it to be the subject of the proposition (*uddeśya*). || 1417 ||
The term "Brahman" is a qualification for the purpose of establishing its true nature. (1418)
The connection of qualifiers is with the qualified, and [the connection] of qualifiers is with qualifiers.
The relation of the qualificand as well [is established] through independence and dependence. || 1419 ||

He states that "the meaning of Brahman" is the qualifier of the former because it determines the true nature of the "I-sense" (ahamartha), saying: "its true reality" (*tadyāthātmya*). One might object: "Granted that the 'I-sense' is primary as the qualified object being qualified by everything else, and that the meaning of Brahman is subordinate to it as that which determines it; nevertheless, why could the relationship of qualifier and qualified not be reversed? Anticipating this doubt, he explains their essential nature, saying: "of qualifiers... (*viśeṣaṇānām*).

The mutual relationship between those two is their state of being [related], and that consists of independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*). Therefore, it is well known that independence is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the other is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is that even though Brahman possesses independence, in this usage it is not contradictory for it to be a qualifier, because it is perceived as dependent upon the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). || 1418 || 1419 ||
The connection between qualifiers and the qualified occurs only through their totality.
The relationship of qualifier and qualified belongs to those things that have mutually assumed forms. (1420)

Fearing that [the definition] would be over-extensive (*atiprasaṅga*) without a fundamental connection, he states their identity (*tādātmya*) by means of the words "viśeṣaṇa" (qualifier) and so forth. "Sākalya" (completeness) refers to mutual identity. He proves this very point with the words "upātta" (taken up) and so forth. The meaning is that only those things which possess mutual identity can stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*). || 1420 ||
Only those possessing appropriated substances distinguish the blue lotus and so forth.
The substance takes on its qualifiers, and likewise, it possesses the qualifiers as they have been apprehended.

He illustrates the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) with the words "those which have substances as their substratum" (*upāttadravyakāṇi*). The meaning is this: qualifiers such as "blue," "fragrant," or "large" appear as identical with a substance such as a blue lotus and thereby distinguish it;
likewise, that substance, having attained identity with those qualifiers, experiences a connection with them only by entering into identity with them. || 1421 ||
For those things that are like individual counting-sticks, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified.
Because they are mutually independent, like the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. || 1422 ||

Anticipating the objection that in the identity (*tādātmya*) of "I" (*aham*) and Brahman there can be no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*), because such a state—as seen in the case of a staff and so forth—depends upon difference, he says "No," and so on. Even in the case of a staff and the like, the relation of qualifier and qualified does not exist between two absolutely distinct things; for that relation is merely imagined (*kalpita*) therein, since their identity is never lost. Thus, since the qualifier and qualified are non-different from both the staff and Devadatta, by means of them, those two [the staff and Devadatta] are also [non-different].
The intended meaning is that this is because mutual non-difference is possible. || 1422 ||
Once, because of the cause of being joined with the whole in an undivided manner.
By implication, there is no possibility of its own contraries existing in the qualificand. || 1423 ||

Since the Brahman and the self-essence (*ātman*) are not non-different from each other because they are mutually contradictory like heat and cold, their identity is untenable according to this inference; how then [could it be otherwise]?

Having raised the objection regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatā*), he says: "At one time" (*ekadā*). Because there is no relation of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) between those two, due to their identity, it is never possible for qualities contradictory to that [Brahman], such as being bound, to reside in the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*), nor for qualities contradictory to that [bound self], such as remoteness (*pārokṣya*), to reside in the other [Brahman].
The meaning is that, because of this, the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*). || 1423 ||
Without mutual contradiction, they qualify that which resides within themselves.
Because of these qualifiers, that which is contrary to them does not present itself. || 1424 ||

1. He supports the statement that there is no possibility of qualities contradictory to a qualifier coexisting in the qualificand. [He says: "Mutually... When it is said, "Maitra is tall and fair," the qualifier of tallness excludes only shortness in the qualificand, not fairness; nor does it exclude even redness— [The text continues: ...so too, in the case of the statement, "This is a Brahmin who is a killer of a Brahmin," the qualifier of being a Brahmin excludes only non-Brahminhood in the qualificand, not the act of killing a Brahmin. Nor does it exclude even the act of killing a Kṣatriya, for that would be an incongruity (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Therefore, the qualifier of being a Brahmin merely excludes non-Brahminhood in the qualificand, while the qualifier of being a killer of a Brahmin excludes the absence of that very act. Thus, these two qualifiers are mutually contradictory. Consequently, when one is present, the other is excluded from the same substratum. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a case of mutual contradiction between two qualifiers, as in the example, "This is a Brahmin who is a killer of a Brahmin. Rather, it is a case of mutual contradiction between two qualifiers regarding a single object, as in the example, "This is a Brahmin who is a killer of a Brahmin. This is because the two qualifiers are applied to the same object. Otherwise, if they were applied to different objects, there would be no contradiction at all. For instance, in the case of the statement, "This Brahmin is a killer of a Brahmin, and that Kṣatriya is a killer of a Kṣatriya," there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, the point is that when two qualifiers are applied to the same object, they are mutually contradictory. Just as [the word] "short" does not possess length, so too in all cases qualifiers exclude from the qualified that which is contrary to themselves; therefore, the meaning is that transmigratoriness and the like, being contrary to Brahman, cannot belong to the Self, and remoteness and the like, being contrary to it, cannot belong to Brahman. || 1424 ||
The verbal connection of qualifiers consists in the exclusion of that which is contrary to them.
Because that [result] is obtained through mere delusion by virtue of its inherent capacity, it would not exist according to the literal word.

If it is argued that if the non-difference between Brahman and the self (*ātman*) and the destruction of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) and so forth were established by the sentence alone, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the difference in its meanings, [the author] replies "No" on the grounds that non-difference is expressed by the words (*śābda*), whereas the cessation of the other is implied by the sense (*ārtha*). He states this with the words "by the qualification," etc. He gives the reason for the destruction of transmigratory existence and so forth through the power of the cognition of the non-difference expressed by the words, with the words "delusion," etc. That which is opposed to non-difference—such as being bound—is that...
The meaning of the word (padārtha) [is as follows]. || 1429 ||
Because its intrinsic nature consists solely in the cognition of the non-association with each individual form.
The application of qualifiers does not exist in the inner self (pratyagātman).

Fearing that if "Brahman" and "I" (the self) were related as qualifier and qualified, the meaning of the sentence would possess multiple flavors like a blue lotus, he says "one" (*eka*) and so forth to show this is not so. Since the Self is of the nature of a single flavor consisting of consciousness alone, free from association with any limited form, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not intended there. The word "one" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding difference from those of the same class (*sajātīya-bheda*); the phrase "of one form" (*ekarūpa*) is for the purpose of negating difference from those of a different class (*vijātīya-bheda*).

It has been stated: the word "non-association" (*asaṃsarga*) is for the purpose of excluding distinctions inherent within [Brahman] itself; the word "only" (*mātra*) is to cast aside the dependence on a substratum and so forth. Raising the objection, "How then was it previously stated that Brahman is the qualifier and the inner self (*pratīc*) is the qualificand?"—anticipating this with the thought that it was by way of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), he says:
"Of the qualifiers... (1426).
Since there is no connection of qualifiers with the inner self (pratyagātman).
Therefore, the state of being the characterized and the characteristic is determined by the subsequent [cognition]. || 1427 ||

Anticipating the objection—how can that which is inward (*pratīci*) be accessible through a sentence if, in reality, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*) is impossible there—he says:

"Of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). In that pure [Self], there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified; however, such a relationship exists in the denotable (*vācya*). Therefore, because the pure [Self] is the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the denotable is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), the non-dual inward reality is indicated by means of two distinct qualified objects. Consequently, it is logical that this [reality] is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
The meaning is "you. || 1427 ||
The state of being the inward-facing subject, independent of anything else, is characterized by the form of "I."

2, Page 423] 4 Brāhmaṇa], accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.

He clarifies that the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) functions as a secondary indicator (*lakṣaka*). Regarding the phrase "not other than": the meaning is that its unsurpassed nature as the inner self (*pratyaktva*) is indicated by the referent "I" which is conjoined with Brahman. He elucidates that the referent "Brahman" functions as a secondary indicator. Regarding the word "likewise": the meaning is that its fullness (*pūrṇatā*) is indicated by the referent "Brahman" which is conjoined with the inner self. || 1428 ||
Just as the meaning of "non-pride" and the other qualities differs according to the difference in what is to be turned away from, so it is here.
Brahman and the self (ātman) are to be known as one, because they have the same referent. || 1429 ||

Because of the relationship of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) between the pure and the impure, the identity of the inner self (*pratyak*) and Brahman has been stated by way of the definition (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, raising the objection that since the state of oneness is established by a single word alone, there is no need for another word, he says: "That which is to be removed" (*nivartya*), etc. Just as in the case of words such as "absence of pride," "absence of arrogance," and "non-violence," although they reside solely in the essential nature characterized by negation, they possess distinct meanings due to the differences among the things being negated, such as hypocrisy and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since there is a difference in what is to be negated—namely, mediacy (*pārokṣya*) in the case of "Brahman" and duality (*sadvayatva*) in the case of "I"—there is no redundancy of the other word, because there is a difference in the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, which are synonyms for "Brahman" and "I. This refers, in effect, to the two words that denote the referents "Brahman" and "I. Anticipating the objection that their referents might therefore be entirely distinct, he says: "Of those two," referring to the two intended objects (*lakṣya*) denoted by *tat* and *tvam*.
The meaning is that because of the identity of the two [words], even though there is a difference in their expressed meanings, there is no difference in their actual referents. || 1429 ||
When the darkness of the inner self—the cause of the state of being a non-Self and non-Brahman—is dispelled.

The referent of the words "Brahman" and "I" is indeed one and the same Supreme Reality. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, what causes the difference between the two things to be negated?"—the author establishes the identity of the indicated meaning (lakṣyaikya) by stating that such difference is caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*). [He says] "anātma": regarding the non-selfhood perceived in Brahman and the lack of Brahman-hood perceived in the self, the cause is beginningless ignorance (*anādya-jñāna*) within the sentence.

The meaning is that when [the superimposed attributes] are removed through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the Supreme Self alone, having become the inner self (pratyagbhūta), becomes the referent (lakṣya-artha) of the words "Brahman" and "I," devoid of difference or association, and thus becomes an indivisible, single essence (akhaṇḍaikarasa). || 1430 ||
Therefore, the purpose of this statement here is not intended to mean separation, conjunction, or destruction.
From the scriptural statement "I am Brahman," identity is directly understood here.

Anticipating the objection that "the subject under discussion must have a composite meaning because it is a sentence, like the sentence 'Bring the cow'," he says: "Difference," etc. Here, the word "here" refers to the Self.

For in that case (the inquiry into the Self), the meaning of the sentence is neither difference, nor a composite relation, nor the exclusion of others; since all such [meanings] are products of ignorance (*avidyā*) and are sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), the reason [of being a sentence] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, even though it is a sentence, it possesses an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), just like sentences such as "the supreme light."

[The author] concludes the meaning established by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I am Brahman. [He says] "I" [etc.]. By the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*), the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) of the realization of identity is intended. By the word "here" (*iha*), the mention of Brahman and the Self is made. || 1431 ||
For the perception held by the agent and the mother is one that devours the object, having arisen from ignorance.
Having rejected that [duality] through the vision of the inward Self (pratyagātman), one experiences the non-dual.

[The opponent] raises the objection: "Is scriptural knowledge (*śrauta-jñāna*) insentient (*jaḍa*) or non-insentient (*ajaḍa*)? In the first case, if it is accessible [to that knowledge], then the Brahman-Self would also have to be accessible to perception and other means of knowledge;

in the second case, because there is no difference between them, there can be no relationship of object and subject. Anticipating this, [the author] accepts the first alternative and maintains that the intellect (*buddhi*), which undergoes transformation and possesses a semblance of consciousness (*sābhāsā*), is intended here;

thus, he states that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the eyes and other senses—which has as its objects sound and so forth arising from ignorance (*avidyā*)—does not take Brahman as its object.
"Of the agent," [vol2,

The word *hi* is used to state that the sun reveals its own form. One might raise the objection: "In that case, even the Vedic vision (*śrautī dṛṣṭi*)—being a vision like any other—would not touch Brahman.
Anticipating this, [the author] sets aside the non-Vedic vision which is the object of the non-dual realization established by the Veda, as well as ignorance and its effects.

He says "that" (tat) to show that Brahman pervades the non-dual Self as its very essence. The meaning is this: it is the vision arising from the [great] sentence that touches Brahman, because of the scriptural statement that Brahman is "to be known through the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣada); other forms of perception do not do so, according to the scripture, "The senses turn outward" (parāñci khāni). ||1432||
Because there is no designation of "I am" here, liberation occurs at the very moment of knowledge.
Therefore, that [nature] is established and not something to be proven, like the performance of the Agnihotra and other such rites. || 1433 ||

One might raise the objection that the fruit of knowledge—abiding as the full Self through the destruction of ignorance, which is liberation—is not something that exists at the same time as the knowledge itself, because it is a fruit of scripture (śrauta-phala), just like the fruit of ritual action (karma-phala). Anticipating this, [the author] states the contradiction with scripture: "I am... etc. He states the established conclusion regarding the simultaneity of liberation and knowledge: "Therefore... etc. In that regard, he provides an example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta): "The Agnihotra, etc. || 1433 ||
This is for the sake of achieving proficiency in the mere knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self.
Therefore, the Śruti declares "therefore" (tasmāt) indeed for the purpose of precluding [the notions of] origination and so forth. || 1434 ||

He states that the non-arising of inference is due not only to the contradiction with the words [of the Veda], but also because of the contradiction with the immediately following sentence beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc. The specific knowledge arising solely from the sentence regarding the true nature of the inner self is "understanding" (*vyutpatti*); from that comes "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), which is liberation (*mukti*)—the destruction of bondage consisting of birth, destruction, and so forth. The sentence beginning with "therefore" is intended to indicate the attainment of that [liberation] at the very time of knowledge.
Therefore, the meaning is that liberation does not come into being at a later time, because of this scriptural statement. || 1434 ||
When liberated from ignorance and its products, Brahman became Brahman by its own nature.
"Every," "entire," and likewise "full"—these words are synonyms. || 1435 ||

He concludes for the sake of stating the result: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The meaning is that Brahman itself, though perceived as non-Brahman due to ignorance and its effects, becomes its own innate Brahman when those are removed by knowledge (*vidyā*). It is heard in scripture that the fruit of knowledge is the state of being everything (*sarvabhāva*); it is not...

Since it has been stated that one becomes Brahman, how is it that the state of being Brahman (*brahmabhāva*) occurs? To this he says: "All" (*sarva*). Because the word "all" is a synonym for Brahman, the meaning is that the fruit of knowledge is indeed that very state of being Brahman. || 1435 ||
Those things arising from ignorance regarding the self [are destroyed] solely through the true nature of the self.
Knowledge, like ritual action, requires a qualified candidate; it does not require one who is already superior.

He states the reasoning for the word *sarva* being a synonym for Brahman: "The Self," etc. Just as the rope alone is the reality of the snake and other things produced by the ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the rope, so too, because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) born from the ignorance of Brahman is nothing but Brahman, it is logical that the word *sarva*, which refers to the phenomenal world, is a synonym for the word *Brahman*. This is the intended meaning of such passages as "Whosoever among the gods... and so forth.

The author says: "Like ritual action" (*karmavat*). The meaning is that the subsequent statement is intended to show that knowledge does not require a qualified agent characterized by human birth—unlike the *agnihotra* and other rites which require an eligible performer possessing the qualification of human birth along with specific attributes such as desire for the result—even though attributes like desire are common to all. Thus, qualifications such as human birth are not restricted [to those who possess knowledge]. || 1436 ||
Therefore, whichever [deity] among the gods and others [is to be worshipped], by the very path already described, [one should proceed].
