He joins those syllables [as follows]: "Of the gods and so forth. The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (hence) is the restriction of the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*). By the phrase "and so forth" (*matha*), it is meant that this is done through the purification of the meanings of the words, such as their syntactical connection (*anvaya*) and so on, as previously described. || 1437 ||
When other means are discarded through the realization that nothing exists apart from inward consciousness.
The word "thus" (eva) should be understood as a restriction; therefore, [liberation] arises from knowledge alone. || 1438 ||

He explains the word "eva" (only). He states the result of this restriction with the word "jñānāt" (from knowledge alone). The meaning is that because there is no other means, liberation arises from knowledge alone. || 1438 ||
Other than the knowledge of the true nature of the self, there is no other means [to liberation].
Or else, there is the certainty that the absence of knowledge, or indeed everything, is nothing but ignorance (avidyā). || 1439 ||

He establishes the absence of any other cause for liberation by the word "ātma" (the Self). The word "anyat" (other) is connected with the phrase "athavā" (or else). That in which there is an absence of knowledge is "jñānābhāvaḥ"; whether that be action (*karman*) or something else such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), all of it is ignorance (*avidyā*). By the force of the particle "eva" (only), it is certain that none of these is a cause of liberation. Although the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*) is indeed of the nature of ignorance—since it is an effect of ignorance just like the aforementioned actions and so forth—[it is still not a cause of bondage].

Nevertheless, the meaning is that its status as the cause of liberation has been determined by virtue of its power to remove ignorance through the force of the inner self (pratyagartha), which is its own object. || 1439 ||
Whatever humans have thought to be right has indeed been spoken accordingly.
Therefore, none of the previously mentioned defects apply here. || 1440 ||

Relying on the meaning of the particle *eva*, he states the resulting conclusion: "Human beings. Since knowledge alone is the liberator and nothing else, the meaning is that the statement made by human beings—"By means of the knowledge of Brahman we shall become everything"—is indeed appropriate for them.
However, raising the objection as to how their view can be correct when the defects mentioned in the introductory section (*upoddhāta*) still exist, he says: "No one..."

"Furthermore": since it has been determined that the attainment of the state of Brahman arises from knowledge, the meaning is that no defect whatsoever mentioned in the introduction applies to our position. || 1440 ||
Because of the connection of the Self with the non-self entity solely through the nature of being the inner witness (pratyaktva).
Of that which is distinguished by the undistinguished, and whose nature is not imagined by that which is already established. || 1441 ||
Therefore, it is said that for gods and others, this occurs solely through worldly cognition.
The relationship of Brahman with gods and others is equal to its relationship with mosquitoes and the like. || 1442 ||

Since it has been stated that Brahman alone transmigrates through ignorance and is liberated through knowledge, one might raise the objection that the description of bondage and liberation for gods and others by means of knowledge and ignorance is contradictory to that. Anticipating this, the author states the purport of the commentary beginning with "of gods and others" and "with reference to worldly perspective," etc., using the words "as the Inner Self" (*pratyaktayā*). Because the Self alone is the reality of everything that is not the Self, therefore, in various places, [the scripture speaks] of Him as the Inner Self.

Based on the relationship with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there arises in worldly people the notion of difference among gods and others; thus, the scriptures first describe the apparent division of the Self due to ignorance (*avidyā*). However, it is the very consciousness of Brahman (*brahma-caitanya*) abiding in those respective forms that undergoes bondage and liberation through knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance, as declared by the Śruti. Bondage and liberation are not imagined for the limited entity called the "individual soul" (*jīva*), nor for the reflected image and so forth, such as the gods, which are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*). Since a conceptual construction must have a real substrate (*vastu-niṣṭhatva*), there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

This is the meaning: when there is a connection between the Self and the non-Self by way of the inward-facing nature (pratyaktva), the inward-facing one is unimagined (akalpita) and the other is its "that-ness" (tat-tva).

720 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter— see]. Because gods and others are superior, even though Brahman is connected to them as the inner self (*pratyak*), it is not so in the case of inferior beings such as mosquitoes and the like.

Fearing that this might contradict its being the self of all, he says: "Equal. Whatever relation Brahman has with gods and others, that is equal even to mosquitoes and the like, because there is no difference in its essential nature (svarūpa) everywhere; excellence and deficiency belong only to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
The meaning is that these two are real. || 1441 || 1442 ||
If it were not for this intermediate section, the realization of the Self would not be possible.
That [knowledge] of Vāmadeva could not have arisen from the impressions of a previous birth. || 1443 ||

He raises a doubt in order to introduce the passage beginning with "taddhaitat" (Now, this...). [The phrase] "without... [is explained as follows]: The subject under discussion requires a qualified candidate, because it is a cause for a specific human goal, just like ritual action (*karman*); otherwise, its very existence would be untenable—this is the meaning. He introduces the mantra as a response to that [doubt], starting with "no... and so forth.
For a person such as Vāmadeva—or one similar to him—whose intellect has been refined by the internal and external means (*antaraṅga-bahiraṅga-sādhana*) performed in previous births...
The meaning is that since that knowledge of Brahman arises from the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), it does not depend upon human qualification (*adhikārin*). || 1443 ||
Alternatively, the citation of a mantra is intended for the stabilization of the meaning declared by the Śruti.
Because the cognition of trust in men arises from corroboration by other means of valid cognition.

Having raised the objection that "the disputed [view] does not apply to gods and others because they possess the means prescribed [for human practice], just like the accepted [view]," he says "Śruti... to show that this is not so due to the contradiction with the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. Having raised the objection that "since the meaning of the Śruti—that the knowledge of Brahman results in all states of being—is determined by the Śruti itself, what is the use of the Mantra? he says "pramāṇāntara... (by other means of knowledge). The remainder of the sense is that, therefore, the citation of the Mantra is purposeful. || 1444 ||
That very reality, which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, resides within the inner self.
Upon seeing that, the seer, perceiving it directly, attained everything.

He explains the meaning of the two words established in the mantra with the phrase "not excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*). The meaning is that this Brahman is well-known as being neither excluded from anything nor followed by anything else (*ananugata*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "seeing" (*paśyan*) with the word "inner" (*pratyak*). The construction is as follows: having become a seer (*ṛṣi*) named Vāmadeva through the vision of that Brahman, someone, seeing that Brahman directly within the inner self (*pratyagātman*), attained the complete Brahman itself. 1445 ||
The utterance "vaha mantra" is for the purpose of indicating the commencement of the hymn (sūkta) and so forth.
He indeed perceived the identity of the inner self within all beings.

He states that the statement beginning with "I am Manu" is intended to indicate the opening of the Vāmadeva-hymn (sūkta). He uses the word "hi" (for/indeed) to show that its status as the beginning of a hymn is well-known among the followers of the Ṛgveda. He explains the meaning of the hymn thus introduced as "the identity of the one Self" (aikātmya). Here, the seer (ṛṣi) is Vāmadeva, who is the referent of the pronoun "all" (sarva). This indicates that the principle that liberation arises from knowledge is what is to be accepted here.
The particle *heti* is used for the purpose of illumination. || 1446 ||
By the phrase "seeing that," the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is demonstrated here.
"I was Manu"—this is stated as the fruit of the knowledge.
Now, having divided the mantra into three parts, he explains it beginning with "That" (tat).
The word "in" (prakṛte) refers to the locative sense of the sentence.
It is determined from the usage "seeing, he attained" that [the agent is the one who sees].
The attainment of everything occurs precisely at the time of knowledge; this is due to the destruction of that delusion.

He states the reason for the absence of any interval between knowledge (*vidyā*) and its fruit: "perceiving" (*paśyan*). The sense is that otherwise, the use of the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) would be inappropriate.

If it is objected that at the time of knowledge there occurs only the cessation of ignorance, but not the attainment of the whole [Brahman], we say no; because by the cessation of the delusion that constitutes the obstacle to it, the attainment of Brahman—which consists in the attainment of the whole—occurs at the very time of knowledge. Thus he says: "by the cessation of that delusion" (*tanmoha-*) [verse 1448].
Because the obstacle to attaining Brahman consists merely in perceptible delusion.
Since that [ignorance] is destroyed by the inward knowledge [of the Self], its attainment is not through any other means. (1449)

If it is argued that the attainment of Brahman occurs through the cessation of delusion, then since that [cessation] arises from knowledge alone without any other assistance, it is logical that it should happen at that very moment; for ignorance alone cannot be the obstacle to its attainment, as distance and so forth could also be factors. Therefore, anticipating the objection that liberation does not result from knowledge alone, he says: "Brahman... The sense is that since space and so forth are also the very nature of Brahman, there is no obstruction by them. Regarding the phrase "its attainment": [The commentary continues: ...In this context, the word *tat* (it) refers to Brahman. The word *prāpti* (attainment) means the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). This is because the Self is non-different from Brahman. The word *iti* (thus) indicates the conclusion of the section. The meaning is as follows: the realization of the identity between the individual self (*jīva*) and Brahman, which is the very nature of Brahman, is what is called "attainment" (*prāpti*). Since this identity is eternal and not something to be produced, it is not dependent on anything else. Furthermore, since Brahman is omnipresent, there is no spatial distance; and since it is eternal, there is no temporal distance. Thus, the removal of the obstacle consisting of ignorance is itself the attainment of Brahman. Therefore, the statement that "liberation results from knowledge alone" is established. The word "that" has Brahman as its object. || 1449 ||
Because the goal of man is fully accomplished by the mere destruction of ignorance.
Since it concludes with that much, it is certain that knowledge has its own object as its purpose. || 1450 ||

One might object: "Since the knowledge of the Self, like the knowledge of clarified butter (*ājya*) and other ritual materials, exists for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), it cannot be an independent cause of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); how then can it have an immediate fruit? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). The meaning is that by that much—namely, by being merely the cause for the destruction of the aforementioned ignorance—the knowledge (*vidyā*) has fulfilled its purpose. || 1450 ||
By the mere single birth of the Self, one obstructs all worldly existence.
By the mere removal of darkness, there is no cognition other than that, nor is it otherwise.

One might object that even when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, the goal of human life (puruṣārtha) is not yet accomplished because passion and other afflictions still arise; therefore, there must be a dependence on repeated practice. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "At once" (sakṛt). He provides the reason for the statement that knowledge dispels ignorance along with its effects in a mere moment simply by attaining its own nature: "No" (na).
Since there is no passion or other affliction apart from ignorance, the knowledge that destroys ignorance is also the destroyer of those [afflictions]; such is the meaning. || 1451 ||
Because of the lack of connection with place, time, and so forth, and because place and the rest are effects of delusion.
Therefore, there is no cognition that is either unarisen or unburnt; hence, it is not non-cognition.

One might object that, just as ignorance regarding a jar is not entirely dispelled by the knowledge of that jar, so too the ignorance regarding Brahman is not entirely removed; therefore, another means must be sought for the destruction of the remaining ignorance. Anticipating this objection, he states the distinction between Brahman and objects such as jars: "Space," etc. The meaning is that a jar and the like are delimited by space and other factors, whereas Brahman is not so delimited; since space and the rest are effects of ignorance (*moha*), they have no connection with the pure Brahman which resides within them. [Regarding] Brahman...

He states that, due to the difference from [the case of] a jar and so forth, the difference of the cognition of that [jar] is also established by the cognition of that [jar]: "not unarisen," meaning "from this cognition. || 1452 ||
If [the cognition] is not itself sublated, it cannot impose the status of being a sublater upon an object that is to be sublated.
One attains [this] by depending solely on the cause that is the true nature of the object of cognition. || 1453 ||
The nature of the knowledge of Brahman—
722 [vol2, page 428]
In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, [in the first chapter]:

the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the Self (*ātman*). Ignorance and its effects are the objects to be sublated. Anticipating the objection that knowledge might require auxiliary aids to function as a sublater, he says: "by me" (*mayā*). Since the knowledge of the Self requires only the cause that is the very nature of the Self, it possesses its fruit without dependence on anything else.
This is the meaning. || 1453 ||
One should satisfy those who know the Vidyā by means of the realization that [the world] is sublated by the knowledge of the Self.
And because it occurs only once through its connection with me, its further impelling is not desired.
Those whose nature consists of delusion and its effects have been consumed by the fire of right knowledge.
Once that which is to be sublated has ceased, what effect remains? || 1455 ||

Since the knowledge of the Self destroys all ignorance pertaining to it along with its effects, therefore—because the mere object of sublation is destroyed all at once through the knowledge arising from the connection with that [Self]—the human goal is fully accomplished; thus he states the conclusion: "yataḥ" (since). Anticipating the objection that even after knowledge there might still be a need for other duties for the sake of liberation, he says: "samyak" (perfectly).

Alternatively, raising the objection that even when ignorance and its effects are removed through knowledge, the human goal (puruṣārtha) is not yet fully accomplished because that [accomplishment] arises only from prescribed knowledge, he says: "Not after," and provides the reason for this: "Because of perfect... (1414).
In that which devours darkness and the like, and which is firmly established solely in the nature of inward consciousness.
While an adversary stands present, how could there be truth for those who lack self-awareness? (1456)

Anticipating the objection that even when the object to be sublated has ceased through right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), there is still a requirement for action in order to destroy the superimpositions (*adhyāsa*) consisting of the notion of a non-self, he says: "Of darkness, etc. He states the reason why knowledge has the nature of destroying ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its effects: "The inner self" (*pratyak*). The state of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*), non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*), selfhood (*ātmatva*), and non-duality (*advayatva*) exist in the object to be known; when right knowledge is established in that very [object], [ignorance and its effects are destroyed].

The meaning is that when the Path (Panthinī) exists, there is no possibility of suspecting the non-sublatibility of those who possess the dualistic cognition of a self that is turned away [from reality] and inert. || 1456 ||
By one who relies solely on the reality that is either unknown, falsely known, or merely cognized.
Tell me, what has not been discerned by knowledge, or what has not been sublated by it? (1457)
Anticipating the objection that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) cannot be an adversary [to ignorance] because it is illuminative rather than sublatant, he states that both qualities exist therein:

"ajñāta" (unknown), etc. The meaning is that even though knowledge is not an agent (*akāraka*), it is accepted as being both illuminative and sublatant; moreover, there is no such distinction within the Self, which consists solely of the essence of consciousness. || 1457 ||
This entire transgression is appropriate for high-souled beings such as gods and others.
If it is argued that [the existence of such a being] is not possible because people like us are shrouded in darkness, we say: no. (1458)

Having explained the passage beginning with "tadvaitat" (That indeed is this), he raises a doubt in order to introduce the passage beginning with "tadidam" (That is this). He says "sarvāpattiḥ" (the attainment of all), raising the objection: "Let their greatness be so; however, the attainment of all [states] might also occur for people like us, depending upon the means. Anticipating this, he says "asmad" (of us). [The objection is raised] because of our state of ignorance and the absence of the causes thereof. As a response to that, he takes up the sentence: "na tat" (Not that). || 1418 ||
Even now, however, that Brahman is realized directly by whomever [realizes it].
That alone becomes that [liberation] for us; therefore, birth is not the cause.

(1459) He explains those words: "This. Intending to convey that the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) alone is the cause of liberation, and not mere indirect knowledge (*parokṣadhī*), he said "directly" (*sākṣāt*). Liberation is not produced by birth, but rather depends upon knowledge.
This is the meaning; this indeed is the meaning of the word "tu" (but/however). || 1459 ||
Even now, whoever knows the non-dual Self according to the right principle, [attains liberation].
Through the destruction of ignorance, he becomes this entire universe as his very self.

Having raised the doubt that there is a distinction between the Self and Brahman based on the relationship between that which is attained and that which is to be attained, [the author] clarifies what was stated with the words "api etaddhi" (even this indeed). The meaning of "api" (even/also) is "as before. That is to say, it refers to the sequence of connection and so forth as previously explained according to the rule. Having raised the doubt—"If the Self is the nature of all things, since it exists eternally, how can it be dependent upon knowledge?"—he says: "ajñāna... (through ignorance). || 1460 ||
For [the notion] of another self does not exist among superior beings such as the gods and so forth.
Nor is any distinction observed among those who are utterly deluded;
for there is no difference in the realization of the inner reality for one whose self is by its own nature awakened as the one Self.
Fearing that "great successes are beset by many obstacles," this is now stated: || 1462 ||
Clarifying that noble birth (*ābhijātya*) is not a cause for liberation, he analyzes the commentary beginning with "na hi.

Regarding "na hi," the word "iha" (here) refers to the scripture (*śāstra*). He states the reason why there is no distinction regarding either the reality (*vastu*) or the knowledge thereof in all cases: "svataḥ" (by itself).

The meaning is that because the reality is by its very nature of the essence of pure consciousness (*bodhaikarasatva*), there is, in fact, no distinction therein—either in the reality or in the knowledge of it. [The remainder of the sentence concerns] the statement...

Immediately following this, he takes up [the next passage] as a response to an objection: "The better things... The meaning is that, having raised the doubt regarding obstacles to the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, the passage beginning with "Of him" (*tasya ha*) is intended to remove that obstacle. The word "then" (*atha*) is used to indicate its capacity to remove that obstacle. || 1461 ||
Of that ascetic, who has realized the truth of the Self and whose darkness has been utterly destroyed—
Even Indra and the other gods are not at all capable of preventing the attainment of absolute liberation.

He explains that [verse] with the words "tasya" (of him). By the word "yateḥ" (of the ascetic), he indicates the qualified person who is fit for knowledge. The meaning of the particle "api" (also) is that the power of others to create obstacles to liberation is cast far away. || 1463 ||
Because it transcends the objects of sovereignty belonging to the gods and others.
Even those who are lords, though striving for the attainment of absolute liberation, do not possess mastery over it.
He states the reason why gods and others lack the power to create obstacles for a wise person in the attainment of the fruit of knowledge: "devādī" (gods, etc.).
The word "viduṣaḥ" (of the wise person) is to be supplied [as the subject]. The particle "api" (even/also) is to be joined with the word "udyuktāḥ" (exerting themselves). || 1464 ||
The relationship between the Lord and the one to be ruled arises from the ignorance of the inner self.
Through right knowledge, having destroyed darkness, he is the Lord even of the lords.
724 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

Having stated that the lordship of the gods and others is based on their being presiding deities (*īśvara*), he says "īś" (lord) to show that this does not apply in the case of the man of knowledge. Of the lords...
"Of the gods and so forth"—this is the meaning; "the wise one" is the ellipsis. || 1465 ||
If it is asked, "Why is there a lack of sovereignty for the lords [even] when they know Brahman?"
For he said, "The self indeed belongs to these," in order to demonstrate that [the self] is their cause.

He asks [the following] to introduce another statement: "Of the lords" (*īśvarāṇām*). The meaning is that it is not logical for them to possess non-sovereignty with respect to Him, because that would contradict their very nature as lords. To establish the reason for the absence of independence among gods and others regarding the knower of Brahman, the Śruti says, "For He is the Self," and so forth;
thus he states that it is logical they lack sovereignty over Him. And yet, by this much alone, His sovereignty [is not diminished].
The word "for" (hi) illuminates the fact that [the opponent's position] is contradicted because it has scope elsewhere. || 1466 ||
The entire world is made into food by means of such practices as ritual action and knowledge.
If one does not attain liberation after having consumed that which has been acquired, [one must consume it again]. || 1467 ||

Fearing that there might be an obstacle to the attainment of liberation— the supreme good— based on the maxim that "many kinds of obstacles arise even for the great," [the author] has introduced the passage beginning with "For him" (*tasya ha*) and explained it in accordance with the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Now, in order to explain it also according to the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca, [it is stated that] the entire world is presented as food, and so forth.

He states the doubt expressed by both [parties] with the words "by way of being an object of enjoyment" (*bhojyatvena*). The meaning is as follows: liberation is untenable for one who has acquired [the world] as an object of enjoyment through the perfection of means such as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, except through its experience; for if that were the case, it would contradict the very means by which it was acquired. Furthermore, it is not logical to say that a person attains liberation after having experienced the entire universe, because such an experience would be difficult to accomplish even within a human lifespan. || 1467 ||
To dispel such a doubt, the subsequent portion of the text is introduced.
Even the gods, though they be lords, are not capable of obstructing the attainment of absolute liberation.
In that context, he brings forward a statement as a reply: "Thus [one] might suspect. He connects that [statement] with the word "kaivalya" (isolation). || 1468 ||
For it is taught that their authority extends over the domain of ignorance.
But this [liberation] does not belong to those whose darkness consists of the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the nourished self.

He states "ignorance" (*avidyā*) as the meaning of the commentary’s phrase "for they have authority regarding the realm of duality. He states "but this one remains established in non-duality" as the meaning of the commentary’s phrase "not however" (*na tu*). Regarding that [state of non-duality], there is no authority for gods and others, because he is non-distinct from them; for it is not logical that liberation occurs for the knower after having experienced the entire world, since that [world] is accompanied by its cause, which is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
The meaning is that [the object] is impossible due to its cessation. || 1469 ||
The deities create obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman.
Regarding this, it is stated: "What is the cause for this doubt? (1470).
For it is reasonable to entertain such a doubt, since according to the Veda, mortals are debtors to the gods.
And because of the scriptural statements regarding the world of cattle, and because of the dependence of those who perform ritual actions. || 1471 ||
Having explained its cause and so forth in accordance with the non-duality of Māyā, he raises an objection: "Brahman," etc. Therein, [the result] of knowledge is produced...
by that which is performed.

This is the meaning. He refutes [the objection] with the words: "It is explained. "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, being born, is born burdened with three debts. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1] This is the sense. [End of Brāhmaṇa 4] [Included in] the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. [Page

From this scriptural statement, it is understood that human beings are debtors toward the gods; thus, just as creditors act toward debtors, the gods should exact payment from them. Furthermore, because of the scriptural declaration that "as a beast is [the property] of the gods," and because of the hearing of human beings' state of being cattle, and because of the scriptural teaching that "this self, indeed, is the world of all beings" and thus their status as objects of enjoyment for all living creatures, those who perform ritual actions exist in a state of dependence.

He says that the *vāda*s (theories) are contrary to that [truth], starting with the word "paśu" (beast). The first *ca* (and) is used to add another reason for the gods and others to practice obstacles (*vighna*) in the attainment of the fruit of knowledge. The second *ca* is used to show that being a "beast" and being "of the world" are indeed intended by humans in relation to the gods and others, because their respective functions are observed among the gods and so forth. || 1470 || 1471 ||
And even in the state of knowing Brahman, the dependence upon others for the sake of the gods and so forth ceases.
Because that [state] has ignorance as its cause regarding Brahman, it ceases upon the cessation of that [ignorance]. || 1472 ||

If human beings were to assume the state of animals and so forth with respect to the gods and others, then even though they possess the knowledge of Brahman, because that state persists and their dependence [on others] has not ceased, it might be suspected that the gods and others would likewise act as obstacles toward them; anticipating this, he says: "And even in the case of possessing the knowledge of Brahman. He provides the reason: because being-for-the-sake-of-another (*pārārthya*) is nescience (*avidyā*), and it is destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*). He states the subject of that [destruction]: "of that. Alternatively, regarding human beings with respect to the gods and others...
Fearing that even though they possess knowledge of Brahman, their dependence might not cease and thus they could create obstacles to one's knowledge of Brahman, he says:
"And [if] Brahman itself... Since dependence is caused by ignorance, he states that it ceases upon the cessation of ignorance through knowledge: "Of that... (1472).
This meaning is determined by the two expressions "unpleasant" (apriya) and "calamity" (ariṣṭi).
Therefore, the deities create obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of knowledge. || 1473 ||

Regarding the statement that "in the knowledge of Brahman there is the abandonment of dependence," he states the authority [for this] as follows: "It is not dear" (*apriya*). The meaning is that by the two scriptural passages—"Therefore, that is not dear to them"—and "All beings desire non-harm," it is indicated that the destruction of dependence occurs through knowledge. Alternatively, he states another reason why gods and others obstruct human engagement with the knowledge of Brahman: "It is not dear. This is the result.
He says: "Therefore. This means: by the force of the reasons already stated and by implication. || 1473 ||
If that is so, then there would indeed be a lack of confidence regarding the attainment of results that are not visible.
One who is engaged here in the practice of the means for attaining worldly prosperity and liberation has attained [the goal]. || 1474 ||

If it is argued that they act as obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of knowledge by virtue of their capacity, then one might suspect an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of this principle, such that they would likewise act as obstacles to the attainment of the fruit of ritual action. This is raised with the word "nanu" (but surely). The three locative endings are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). The meaning is that there is a lack of confidence (*aviśrambha*)—that is, an absence of trust—in gods and others regarding the production of obstacles in that [attainment], precisely because of their capacity. This indeed is the sense of the particle *hi*. || 1474 ||
Even if the Lord of Wealth himself were to create an obstacle, by whom could he be prevented?
The power of time, non-medicines, and so forth is held to be inconceivable.
By implication, he states another over-extension regarding the status of being an obstacle-maker: "In that way," meaning "just like the gods and so forth. Furthermore— [vol2, page 432] 726

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The meaning is: "for those engaged in ritual actions (*karman*) which are the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). The phrase "an obstacle to the attainment of their fruit" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He states another undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words "kāla... (Time...). 1475.
And [the capacity] of karma, medicinal herbs, austerity, time, and so forth, is indeed present.
In this regard, it is appropriate to suspect that there is great power in the result.

He states the result by restating what has been said: "Karma... Here, the word "atra" refers to the statement regarding the fruit caused by karma. The two locative endings are in grammatical apposition. || 1476 ||
Devas and others [have power] over the attainment of results and their obstruction, because of their independence.
They would do everything without any confidence; therefore, one attains success in ritual actions.

He concludes the objection with the words "the gods and so forth. This means that [if one holds that] all restraint or favor is dependent upon their own will, then there would be no confidence in them; the implication is that the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) of the Vedas would consequently fail to be established. || 1477 ||
It is not so, because all things have fixed causes for their apprehension.
And because the diversity of the world is observed, and that [diversity] is impossible if [things were to exist] by way of their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva). || 1478 ||

Considering the alternative— whether this objection is raised by proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*) or by proponents of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvavādin*)— he refutes the first [position] with the words "Not so.
This is because we observe that living beings take up milk and other substances with the desire to produce curds and the like, and because we observe a gradation in pleasure, pain, and so forth.

The doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda) is not tenable there, because of its fixedness and because the beginninglessness [of things] would be untenable; therefore, the meaning is that the world is the fruit of karma. || 1478 ||
When this position—that karma bestows results such as pleasure—is established;
O gods, because this is established through scripture, logic, and so forth, no obstacles can be created against it.

He states the second [point] with the words "sukhādi" (pleasure, etc.). The scriptural authority (*śruti*) consists of such passages as "One who is meritorious [is affected] by meritorious action" and "Action alone, indeed. The logical argument (*nyāya*) is the impossibility of the world's diversity [otherwise]. By the word "etc.," Smṛti texts such as "A living being is bound by action" are included. The meaning is that, since the aforementioned position is established and proven by the cited Śruti and other authorities, gods and others do not create obstacles to the attainment of results by those who perform actions.

And it is said in the *Kāmasūtra*: "Since all activities are preceded by human effort, even for a goal that is certain to occur, because it must be preceded by the application of means, there is no prosperity for one who is devoid of action. (1479)
Because they have been embraced by action itself for the sake of its own accomplishment.
Action that is independent of the Lord of Gods and others does not attain its own self.

He states the reason why the Vedas and other [scriptures] do not create obstacles regarding the fruits of action because they are in accordance with them, by means of the phrase "by action. He establishes that very reason through the method of negative concomitance (vyatireka) with the words beginning with "not" (na). || 1480 ||
Because they are favorable to the act of giving, these [qualities] do not become obstacles.
Just as action is, so too is Īśa and the like; they are established only in dependence upon action. || 1481 ||

He states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*)— namely, that because gods and others act in accordance with one's karma, they do not create obstacles to its fruit— with the word "fruit" (*phala*).
Since they are the cause for the accomplishment of the very nature of the action and are thus favorable to the attainment of its fruit, gods and others cannot act as obstacles therein.

The meaning is as follows: just as ritual action (*karman*) depends upon the gods and so forth, so too does that [knowledge] depend upon ritual action; therefore, it cannot act as an obstacle to its own fruit. He states another reason with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). || 1481 ||
Everything is established only by depending upon everything else, because it exists as a composite whole.
Furthermore, the status of being primary or secondary is accepted for one thing relative to another in certain cases. || 1482 ||

Having stated that because gods and the like depend upon one another with respect to karma, they lack independence, and therefore gods and the like cannot act as obstacles to the fruit of karma, he states the reason for their mutual dependence by saying "all. This will be made clear later. Anticipating the question, "How then is there predominance of one thing over another in certain cases? he says "predominance," meaning that in a particular effect, one factor such as karma or the like may be predominant.
The meaning is that no objection can be raised against the point accepted by all disputants. || 1482 ||
Moreover, even in the act of creating obstacles, these do not proceed without depending [on other factors].
Because its capacity cannot be set aside by anyone in any ritual actions whatsoever. || 1483 ||

He states another reason for the dependence of gods and others upon karma: "Obstacle," etc. Even in the case of an effect that takes the form of an obstacle, gods and others are not the agents independent of karma; because, among all effects being produced through all [types of] karma, the efficacy of karma cannot be set aside.
Therefore, since the power of karma is unavoidable even in the case of an effect that is an obstacle—a fruit of karma—therein, the dependence of gods and others upon karma is as [inevitable] as...
The meaning is that in all other cases as well, their dependence on that [object] must be stated. || 1483 ||
The relationship of subordinate and principal [attributes] exists in the case of the gods, time, the Lord (Īśvara), and so forth.
It is observed that [the result] is not fixed by karma, nor can it be established otherwise. || 1484 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if they depend upon karma, those [divine beings] might still act as obstacles to its fruition due to their predominance, the author elaborates on what was stated in the verse beginning with *pradhānaguṇabhāvaśca*. Regarding the phrase "guṇa... etc.: in the context of karma, the relationship of subordinate (*guṇa*) and predominant (*pradhāna*) among gods and others is not fixed.

The construction is: "it is not fixed. Alternatively, one should construe it as follows: the relationship of primary and secondary importance among the gods and so forth, as well as among ritual actions, is observed to be unfixed and not otherwise. Or else, it should be construed as: the relationship of primary and secondary importance exists among the gods and so forth when they serve as the objects of ritual actions (karmasu) or tasks (kāryeṣu). || 1484 ||
When one thing possesses primacy, then the other lacks primacy.
Thus, this world dances eternally, remaining within the Self with unceasing activity.

He establishes the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) with the words "When... The point is this: there can be no primacy (*prādhānya*) for many or even two [agents] in a single effect, because it would follow that the effect would not arise due to their having different intentions; nor can there be unanimity (*ekamati*) without a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*); nor can that which is principal in one effect be so in another, because it would follow that fire, which is principal in burning and the like, would also be so in pouring water and the like. Anā-...

Even though there is no fixed rule regarding the relative predominance or subordination of the qualities among the individual selves (*ātman*), he raises the objection that there might be a fixed rule such that the conscious self (*cidātman*) is predominant while the other is subordinate; in response, he says: "In this way. The sense is that, although in reality there is no predominance or subordination in a non-dual reality, such a distinction is not contradictory when it is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*). Alternatively, [the text means] that the independence of the aforementioned world—which exists as both quality and principal—resides within the Self as its quality...
Anticipating the objection that this is impossible because it lacks the state of being a seed, he says: "In this way" (evam). || 1485 ||
Furthermore,
the relationship between the subordinate and the primary among categories is infinite.
And because time passes so rapidly, it is difficult to discern due to the confusion of the intellect.

Anticipating the objection: "Even if there is no fixed rule [regarding which is primary], why should that which is primary or secondary for one person not be perceived as such by everyone?", he says: "guṇa... (referring to the verse beginning with *guṇapradhānabhāva*). Anticipating the objection: "Is it not possible to know the state of being primary or secondary even among innumerable entities through their successive occurrence?", he says: "kṣepīyastvāt" (due to extreme brevity). This means: because the human lifespan is short. [The phrase] "guṇapradhāna... [is thus explained].
He states another reason for its being difficult to know: "matī" (verse 1486).
Some declare that karma alone is the cause for the attainment of the fruit.
"Some [say it is] fate, others time, and still others inherent nature.
(1487) This states the contradiction caused by delusion. Regarding the word "karma": the particle *eva* is intended to exclude other causes. "Some" refers to...

The mention of the *Mīmāṃsaka*s [is for the following reason]: by the maxim, "I consider fate alone to be supreme, while human effort is useless," the doctrine of the section concerning the deities (*devatākāṇḍīya*) is stated as "fate" (*daiva*). [The author] shows the acceptance of this by the experts in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) with the words "the others. However, the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) was accepted by the Lokāyatikas and others. || 1487 ||
The Śrutis and the declarations of the Smṛtis, however, establish the primacy of ritual action alone.
For indeed, all [beings] are seen to be engaged in activity only after having accepted [their respective roles].

How, then, is there certainty in this matter? To this he says: "The Śrutis. The word *tu* (but) is used to show that other means [of knowledge] are accepted as being subordinate (*guṇatvena*) to the attainment of the fruit. The word *hi* (for) is used to state that the primacy of ritual action (*karma-prādhānya*) is to be adopted because it is established by authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa-siddhatvena*). || 1488 ||
One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action.
Thus, this is observed very frequently in the scriptures.
1.1 He cites the Śruti: "By means of the rope of merit," etc. These Smṛti statements, such as "one should travel the path by means of the rope of dharma," are in accordance with the Śruti.

Wishing to speak of the essential points, he says, "words. He says, "thus," indicating that other words similar to those already shown—both Vedic (śrauta) and traditional (smārta)—are also worthy of being examined. 1489.
Even though among these, a particular one may have predominance over its own specific object in certain instances.
Nevertheless, other factors are secondary, yet this does not apply to the karmas.
The lack of causality regarding the attainment of the fruit is established through the determination of both scripture and logic. || 1490 ||

Since time, fire, water, and so forth are well known to be predominant in cases such as the rising of the sun, burning, or sprinkling, one might suspect that action alone is not the primary factor; therefore, he says: "Even though... Even if among these causes, such as time and the rest, the predominance of some—like time—in its own domain regarding certain occurrences like sunrise, and the non-predominance of others therein, is observed, nevertheless, there is no lack of predominance for actions in the attainment of results.

This is the construction [of the sentence]. "Lack of causality" means lack of primacy. Regarding the primacy of action with respect to the attainment of its fruit, he recalls the previously stated reason: "In the scripture," etc. (1490).
[Result] from one's own action.
[vol2, page 435]
In this world, the attainment and non-attainment of the fruit of action are observed.
That [result] arises from the action itself, depending on whether it possesses merit or is devoid of merit.

Anticipating the objection that because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding effects and so forth, action does not possess the status of being the cause of its fruit—how then could it have primacy—he says: "Of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*). For whatever attainment of rain and so forth is observed in the field of action (*karmabhūmi*) from some particular act such as agriculture, that is desired [to result] from the completeness of its constituent factors (*guṇasākalya*); whereas whatever non-attainment of that is observed from some particular act, that arises from its deficiency (*vaiguṇya*). Therefore, [the result is] complete...
The meaning is that its primacy [is established] because it is non-deviant with respect to the fruit. || 1491 ||
The gods do not create obstacles for us in the attainment of the fruits arising from this knowledge.
Regarding that which was stated for the purpose of refutation, the following response is provided. || 1492 ||

Having incidentally refuted the possibility that gods and others can act as obstacles to the fruit of karma, he restates the objection regarding their power to create obstacles to the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*) in order to refute it. [The verse says: "An obstacle. He refutes this by stating that they have no power to create obstacles to the fruit of knowledge, [concluding with the phrase] "for the purpose of removal" (1492).
Because its nature consists in the attainment of liberation, which results solely from the abandonment of ignorance.
Because the attainment of that [state] occurs at the time of knowledge, the deities are not capable of creating obstacles.

He elucidates that very point with the words "Ignorance" (avidyā). Since liberation, which consists in the Self’s attainment of Brahman, is merely the destruction of ignorance, it is simultaneous with knowledge;

and since that result necessarily follows when [knowledge] exists, there is no room for gods and others to exercise their sovereign power (*vibhūti*) as a fruit of knowledge. This is the meaning. || 1493 ||
Just as it is accepted that [the cognition] occurs simultaneously with the conjunction of the eye and the visible form.
In this way, there would be the manifestation of form, as well as the destruction of ignorance regarding the self. (1494)

He supports the claim that the destruction of ignorance for the self occurs simultaneously with knowledge by means of an illustration: "The eye," etc. The remainder of the sense is that the destruction of the self's ignorance is simultaneous with knowledge. || 1494 ||
This is because it arises from nothing other than the knowledge of the true nature of the self as it actually exists.
There would be no cessation of that darkness, nor of the object produced from it. || 1495 ||

For this reason as well, he states that there is no proof of an obstacle to the fruit of knowledge: "As it truly is," etc. The meaning is: if the cognition of the reality of the Self arises, then the abandonment of ignorance and so forth—which is its fruit—is not subject to obstruction, because that [abandonment] consists merely in the birth of that [cognition]. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that its cessation is nothing other than the birth of knowledge. || 1499 ||
When a staff or similar object is grasped as being a snake, the staff is not perceived.
That which is to be grasped by a single glance toward the west is not seen in that same way as anything else.

Regarding the phrase "arising from that" (*tadutthasya*), an objection is raised: "It is incorrect to say that duality is imagined (*kalpita*) because it is born of ignorance (*ajñāna*), for that [ignorance] is not established. Anticipating this, he establishes its imagined nature with the words "as the self of a snake" (*sarpātmanā*). Just as in the case of a rope, when it is perceived in the form of a snake—thinking "this is a snake"—[the snake does not exist].

At that time, there is the delusion of a staff and so forth; yet, when that [staff] is apprehended as being of the nature of a staff, at that moment there is no such establishment of the delusion of a snake.
1. [This is] established. 2. [In manuscript *ga*, it is "tu".
[Vol. 2, page 436]
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter One, Verse 730:

When the waking world, which has a single uniform form, is being perceived as such, at that very time there is no delusion of dreams and the like; nor, when it is not perceived in that form, is there a waking delusion. Therefore, the meaning is that the object under dispute is imagined (kalpita), because it is subject to deviation (vyabhicāritva), just like a snake [mistaken for a rope] and so forth. However, if the reading is *sarvātmanā* (in its entirety), the meaning is as follows: [The text continues: ...the meaning is as follows: [omitted in source].

Just as when a garland is correctly grasped, there is no delusion regarding a staff or other objects, so too, when the inner self (pratīci) is apprehended in its singular form of consciousness (cidekarūpeṇa), no duality other than that is perceived. Therefore, the object of dispute is imagined (kalpita), because it is not apprehended when true knowledge exists, just like the [delusory] examples commonly accepted. || 1496 ||
For non-selves are indeed subject to mutual deviation even in the case of ignorance.
How much more so when the inner self has utterly destroyed all ignorance without exception? || 1497 ||

He establishes their variability (*vyabhicāritva*) by means of the *kaimutika* (how much more so) argument: "Mutually," etc. Even though there exists the cause for the non-apprehension of the body and other non-Selfs, their mutual variability is observed; but when all ignorance has been dispelled in the inner Self (*pratyak*), what need is there to mention their variability? For at that time, even their very essential nature (*svarūpa*) is difficult to define. [The meaning is: their mutual [variability] by way of their own nature...
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the state of being deviant is directly perceived even in both conditions. || 1497 ||
At the time of the cognition of silver, the cognition of mother-of-pearl does not sublate it.
But here, because that [self] does not exist, there is the cognition of the sublation of beginning, middle, and end with respect to the self. (1498)

He states another reason for the imagined nature of duality: "rūpya" (silver), etc. When a cognition in the form of silver arises, the cognition of the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) of the substrate, the mother-of-pearl, does not sublate that [silver] or the cognition of it; this is because those two do not arise from the ignorance regarding the "this-portion. However, in the case of the inner self (*pratyagbrahma*), there exists a sublation—known as the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpajñāna*)—of both duality and its cognition, prior to, after, and at the very moment of the knowledge arising from the [Vedic] statement. Therefore, where...

Regarding silver and the like, the consensus on their being imagined (kalpita) arises only when there is a subsequent cognition of sublation; however, in the case of duality, since that [sublation] exists always, their status as imagined is necessary. Alternatively, at the time of the illusion of silver, the cognition of mother-of-pearl does not sublate it because it has not yet arisen; but in the case of the Self, for one who has perceived duality, the cognition of sublation occurs at the very time of that perception due to the eternally existing consciousness itself. Thus, its status as imagined is logical; the object of dispute is indeed imagined.
The meaning is that it is so because it is subject to sublation, as is commonly accepted. || 1498 ||
The signless nature of the non-self, such as the subject and so forth, is the form of immediate presence.
The form of another, together with its signs, [is perceived] due to the cause of one's own delusion. || 1499 ||

Anticipating the objection that since the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) is itself unestablished, how could it possess the power to sublate [error], the author establishes it with the words "without cause" (*nirnimittam*).

The meaning is that because the non-self (*anātman*), such as the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, naturally assumes the form of consciousness (*caitanyākāra*), its witness (*sākṣin*) is established by eternal experience; thus, the knowledge of one's own nature is impossible to deny. Furthermore, just as the non-self assumes the form of consciousness, the self likewise [assumes the forms of] sound and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that the potter’s wheel is not a mental construction because it is natural (svābhāvika), he says: "It has a cause. He clarifies this very point with the words: "Delusion... (1499).
Even the defect regarding the cognition that "the self is one" does not act as an obstacle.
For even among those of deluded minds, this does not encounter contradiction.

Anticipating the objection that the realization of one's own true nature cannot be established due to the obstruction caused by the defect of ignorance (*avidyā*), he says: "One" (*eka*). In the knowledge of the Self as the witness of the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃdhī*) in every body—expressed as "I am one, I am [the same]"—there exists neither the defect of ignorance nor any other opposing defect.
(Variant readings: *rūpyaniśā* in Ka and Ga).
[Vol.
2, Page 437] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 731.

The meaning is that even for that [knowledge], since it depends upon that [means] for its own establishment, there is no non-existence of the knowledge of the true nature [of the Self]. Furthermore, even for those who lack discrimination... [text continues]

He says "mūḍha" (the deluded) to show that knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) is not non-existent, because it is experienced as the means of establishing the notion of "I," even though it may be a locus of contradiction.

The sense of "api" (even/also) is "as if [it were] for the wise. The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that the knowledge of one's own nature, well-known in all the Upaniṣads, is not fit to be denied.
False cognition and doubt are recognized as being non-self.
For that [duality] does not exist in the inner self (pratyagātman) due to perfect knowledge. || 1501 ||

He states another reason for the existence of the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*), beginning with the word "mithyā" (false). Ignorance is indeed false only in relation to that which is not the Self, such as doubt and so forth, because it does not establish [the truth] regarding them; however, in relation to the inner Self (*pratyak*), it is indeed right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because that [Self] always assumes the form of consciousness and because [ignorance] merely manifests that [consciousness].
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no non-existence of the knowledge of one's own nature. || 1501 ||
If ignorance has the form of consciousness, what need is there to speak of doubt and the like?
Since it has been cognized as being posterior to us, there is neither a fault nor a sublation.
He states, by way of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, that doubt and the like always partake of the form of consciousness (*caitanya*). He says: "Ignorance" (*ajñānam*).

For even that [ignorance], which is eternally insentient in nature, is perceived as being pervaded by consciousness; if this is so, then since it is extremely manifest due to that pervasion within the various forms of ignorance such as doubt, that [partaking of the form of consciousness] need not be explicitly stated—this is the meaning. Why would the sublation of duality (*dvaita-bādha*) not occur through knowledge of the aforementioned nature? Indeed, for that [knowledge]...
Fearing that duality might still arise at some point even when there is sublation, and that this would contradict worldly practice and so forth, he says: "Desired to be known.

Since the inner self is intended to be known from this sentence beginning with "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*), there is neither a defect in the cause nor any sublater, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like, because their objects are merely imagined. Therefore, due to its being produced from a flawless cause and being unsublatable, the knowledge arising from the sentence is valid.

The meaning is: since that [consciousness] is ignited by knowledge, and the knowledge of its own nature (svarūpajñāna) is the sublater of ignorance and so forth—not merely [the object-consciousness]—how could there be the consequence of the aforementioned logical inconsistency? || 1502 ||
When these manifestations belong to ignorance, they do not pertain to reality.
Time, the gods, and so forth, perish when that [nature] is destroyed, because they are dependent upon it.
Who could these lords of the gods and others be, or for whom do they create obstacles? (1504)

Having stated that "knowledge (vidyā) sublates duality (dvaita) which is ignorance (avidyā)," he states the resulting conclusion: "The greatnesses... The meaning is that when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, the gods and other entities—which are its modifications—are annihilated; since everything then consists of nothing but the Self (ātman), they do not create obstacles for the knower.
But where [the text says] "But when for him," this entire matter has been made clear by the Śruti itself.
Here too, for the sake of establishing the reason, that is clearly stated. || 1505 ||

He states the authority for the claim that "for the wise man, everything is merely the Self" with the words "Where... etc. Having explained the passage beginning with "But of him [there is no fear]"—preceded by the rejection from the perspective of the wise man of the gods and so forth presented from the perspective of the ignorant, as well as their being the agents of his destruction—he will explain the nature of the section (*khaṇḍa*) to be discussed hereafter.
(Note: The text contains references to variant readings marked as *kha.*, which have been integrated into the translation for clarity.)

He says that even in the subsequent statement, "For the Self is the self of all," this is stated for the purpose of establishing the reason why gods and others do not act as obstacles to knowledge (*vidyā*). He says "here" [to indicate the context]. He states the faultlessness of the reason, "because it is the Self," by saying "it is clear. (1105)
For by this, one becomes a knower of the true nature of the inner self, which is the creator of obstacles.
The state of transcending the range of the senses occurs at the time of knowledge, due to the destruction of darkness.

He explains the statement regarding the reason with the words "Since" (*yataḥ*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, there is no effort on the part of the gods and others to act against the Self. Another reason for the fact that they do not create obstacles to the fruit of knowledge is stated in the passage beginning with "pertaining to the sovereignty of the gods and others."

He establishes this [point] with the words "within its range. The meaning is that because darkness—the cause of attachment—is destroyed by virtue of being inseparable from knowledge (*vidyā*), the wise one remains having transcended the objects of sovereignty belonging to the gods and others; thus, since there is no contradiction, they do not act as obstacles for him. || 1106 ||
Then the Self (ātman) becomes the refuge of these—of the gods and the others—that is Brahman.
That which is separated by time and so forth, characterized by attainment, arising, and the like. || 1507 ||
In that case, the fruit would be non-self, and the gods' sovereignty over it would be established.
Moreover, even for those who have realized the true nature of the self, there is the non-existence of a continuous stream of cognition.

Anticipating the objection that the wise man cannot possess the nature of the gods and others because one thing cannot become another, he says: "The Self. When ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge, the wise man, having become Brahman and being independent, becomes the Self of these [gods and others], because there exists no entity other than Brahman; therefore, they do not act as obstacles for the wise man—this is the meaning. Since they lack independence regarding the wise man’s fruit, which is liberation (*kaivalya*), where then does their independence reside?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Time and so forth. "Lordship" (īśatā) means independence with respect to restraint and favor.
Having accepted the view of his own school—that since knowledge has an immediate fruit, these [factors] cannot act as obstacles to that fruit—he says:

"Even... Just as for those who lack knowledge, even for those who know reality, there is no continuous stream of the realization "I am Brahman," because it is accepted that knowledge has an immediate fruit; therefore, it is not [obstructed].
The meaning is that it is the remover of ignorance. || 1507 || 1508 ||
The final awakening, which dispels ignorance, arises from the cessation of the mental states of passion and the like.
If this is argued, it is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to the first case. || 1509 ||

One might object: "Is it not the case that the very first knowledge destroys ignorance; why then is it said to be the last? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that just as before, even after [the attainment of knowledge], since passion (*rāga*) and its effects are observed, the knowledge existing at the time of the body's fall is what destroys ignorance. Thus he says: "The last" (*antya*). Therefore, he says: "If it is argued thus," [implying] that the liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) would be untenable. Regarding whether the last knowledge or its continuity destroys ignorance: in the first case, because of its being the last...

Having raised the alternative that [knowledge] destroys ignorance because its object is the Self, and considering that there is no supporting instance for either case, he states another defect regarding the second [alternative]:

"This is not so," etc. Furthermore, the cognition of mother-of-pearl occurring at the time of death for one who has the delusion of silver cannot be cited as an example for the inference that [knowledge] is the destroyer of ignorance, because it does not remove the ignorance that is the cause of transmigratory existence; nor, in this way, is there a failure of the example when ignorance is removed by the knowledge of Brahman.
It should be understood that since its establishment follows from scripture, the employment [of such arguments] in certain instances conforms to worldly perspective. || 1109 ||
The final cognition that dispels ignorance does not have the self as its sole object.
The reason is seen to be inconclusive, like the initial cognition of a self. || 1510 ||
He points out another defect, namely the contradiction with inference, by saying "not the last" (*nāntyā*). This refers to the fact that the final cognition does not serve to remove ignorance.
[This is from] the Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. Page 439, verse 733.

Fearing that there might be an objection—namely, that the previously stated reason [for the Self being the object] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the first cognition because of the restriction that it does not apply to the mother (*mātr̥*)—he says:
"Of the reason" (*hetor iti*). || 1110 ||
In the same way, for one who maintains the doctrine of a continuum, the reason is inconclusive.
And those [cognitions] whose nature is based on repeated practice do not bring about the comprehension of an object through their own means of valid cognition. || 1511 ||

Anticipating another objection—that your inference is *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) because you yourself accept that the final stream of cognition destroys ignorance—he considers two alternatives: does that [final cognition] remove it because it is "final," or because its object is the Self? Considering that there is no supporting example for either case, he states another defect regarding the second alternative: "It is inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatā*). [The reason is that] in the case of the final cognition being the destroyer of ignorance, the property of having the Self as its object—

The meaning is as follows: just as there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding the first cognition, so too is there inconclusiveness of the reason "having the self as its object" with respect to the final series of cognitions which destroys that [ignorance]. This is because, if the probandum were established by that [first cognition], the final cognition and its series would be redundant. Furthermore, does that [final cognition] remove ignorance by its own nature or through the medium of right knowledge (*samyagdhī*)? It cannot be the first, because of the very reasoning already stated, it is impossible; nor can it be the second, because of [the necessity of] repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).
Thinking that ignorance is destroyed through right knowledge arising from non-reliance [on external means], he says: "And not... (1511).
Because the manifestation [of the universal] occurs through mere relations, like a lamp acting as a manifestor.
Furthermore, when food and such are present, the continuity of cognition is not desired [to be interrupted]. || 1512 ||

He states the reason why the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) do not bring about the comprehension of an object without repeated practice. He says, "Because of the connection," etc. Since a means of knowledge is a manifestor like a lamp, the manifestation of the object of knowledge occurs merely through its connection with it; therefore, there is no dependence on repeated practice in that regard. Furthermore, having raised the dilemma as to whether a continuous or an interrupted stream of cognitions is the cause of right knowledge, he refutes the first alternative with the words, "In the case of eating, etc. (1112).
And because of the abundance of obstacles to that [state], it is not admitted in deep sleep and similar conditions.
For us, all cognitions are preceded by an object of cognition that is directly present.
Therefore, it is established that the cognition of the self is always accompanied by the repetition of its own production.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of that interval" (*tadantarāya*). This means because there is an abundance of activities such as eating and drinking, which obstruct the continuity of knowledge. He states another reason for the impossibility of an uninterrupted continuity of knowledge: "Deep sleep," etc. By the word "etc.," fainting, dissolution (*pralaya*), and the non-conceptual absorption (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*) are included. [This applies] to both the second [type of knowledge], namely worldly knowledge of the self, and supramundane knowledge of the self.

Having raised the alternative that it might be a "continuity" (*saṃtati*), he refutes the first [option] with the words "the inner self" (*pratyak*). The meaning is as follows: since for all of us, the arising of every cognition is preceded by the worldly cognition of the Self in the form of "I," the continuity of this worldly knowledge of the Self is always established; nevertheless, because it is not seen to be true knowledge, it is not the cause [of liberation]. || 1113 ||
Because knowledge is dependent upon the object, it does not conform to the agent.
For him, a continuity of cognition characterized by the knowledge of cold and heat is not admitted. || 1514 ||

He states the fault in the second [alternative] with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). A continuous stream of the realization of the non-worldly, partless, non-dual, inner Brahman cannot be produced by human effort dependent on injunctions and the like, because knowledge is dependent upon the nature of the object (*vastutantra*), and because the destruction of all causal agents occurs merely through its arising.
Therefore, since such a stream of the aforementioned realization does not exist, this [effort] does not destroy ignorance by means of perfect knowledge; such is the meaning. || 1114 ||
The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya [First Chapter— Page 440]: 734.
If the continuum is sustained by the cessation of food and other such necessities, [then...]
The refutation has already been stated there; it does not require further consideration.

It has been stated that the stream of cognition regarding the non-Self—whether interrupted or uninterrupted, worldly or transcendental—is the destroyer of ignorance through the gateway of knowledge (*vidyā*).

In this regard, [the author] raises an objection while warding off the defect mentioned concerning the position of the uninterrupted stream: "Bhojanādi... He states that this has already been refuted by the argument that "knowledge is, in reality, eternal" (*jñānasya vastutaḥ śrutatvāt*): "uktā" (it has been stated). || 1115 ||
Because her mind was utterly withered by hunger and thirst, she did not [speak].

"And it will not be measured by the cessation of food and so forth" (1516). Regarding "hunger": when food and so forth exist, the continuity of knowledge is somehow established through a healthy state of mind; however, in the absence of food and so forth, the mind— [The text continues: ...is not established. The word "utterly" (*nitarām*) is used to demonstrate the excellence [of this view], showing that because there is an absence of well-being, there is not even a suspicion of a continuity of cognition. Even by way of a hypothetical argument (*upetyavādena*), he refutes the continuity of consciousness due to the lack of any means of valid cognition (*māna*). [This is stated in the verse beginning with] "food," etc. (1516).
Because there is no determination of the limit of the cognitions that initiate the continuum.
The lack of certainty regarding the meaning of the treatise is a fault, and that undesirable consequence would follow. || 1517 ||

Regarding the claim that "the continuity of knowledge (jñānasaṃtati) destroys ignorance through the medium of knowledge," he states another objection: "The continuity... Having raised the doubt as to what contradiction there would be in such a continuity destroying ignorance through the medium of knowledge if the meaning of the scripture were not certain, he says: "And that... [verse 1917], pointing out the consequence of the scripture's lack of authority.
Even so, there would be certainty [of the self] if it were merely a continuum.
The reason would be inconclusive, as in the case of a superior continuum. || 1518 ||

One might raise the objection based on the scriptural text, "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self,'" that since the mere continuity of the cognition of that [Self] exists, ignorance is destroyed through the medium of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is expressed by the word "mataṃ" (the view). However, even if the continuity of the cognition of the Self exists, it does not remove ignorance through the medium of knowledge simply because it has the Self as its object;

for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a continuity of the cognition of the Self lasting only the first, second, or third moment. Nor is being the final continuity of the cognition of the Self the determining factor (*prayojaka*).
He offers a rebuttal by stating that "the absence of an illustrative example has already been mentioned," [beginning with] "nevertheless" (tathāpi). || 1118 ||
Even though they have the same object, if [knowledge] does not destroy ignorance, then...
Regarding the claim that "our final continuum of cognition will be established," what is the proof for this? (1519)
It clarifies the deviation [of the reason] with the words "samāna... (1919).
Even at the moment of death, there is no certainty for one who is subject to gasping.
Upon the accomplishment of the continuity of knowledge, there is the complete cessation of mere darkness. || 1520 ||

Nor is it correct to say that even in the absence of a positive example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the intended probandum can be inferred by means of any one of the aforementioned reasons through negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*); for [the reason] "being a cognition whose object is the self" and "being a continuum of such a cognition" would, as before, reside in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), while "being an infinite cognition" and "being such a continuum" are unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus he says: "Even at death... [referring to] hiccupping and so forth.
1. It is expected. 2. Ga. Even in the case of *gha*, there is no "ca".
