The meaning is this: even when death is inevitable because one is submerged in dense darkness characterized by signs that do not deviate from death, there is no certainty [regarding it]; what then can be said regarding the arising of the cognition of the self and its continuity? || 1920 ||
Even those who, by force, apply right-mindedness toward the gaps in their karma.
Surely they gaze upon the solar disc with the tip of their noses. || 1521 ||

Having refuted the view that the destruction of ignorance occurs through the final study and its subsequent continuity, and having completed the discussion on daily performance, another opinion is raised: that even when there is knowledge of agency and so forth during the intervening periods, right cognition (samyag-dhī) is forcibly turned back toward its object, and consequently, there is the destruction of misfortune along with its causes.
Anticipating this, he states: "Karma... [verse 121], meaning that knowledge cannot be produced by mere will.
In reality, knowledge is not false, unlike the fire of the world.
And because the knowledge of the inner self is always known by no other knower. (1522)

He establishes that knowledge cannot be produced by will: "The object," etc. For knowledge is dependent on the object (*vastutantra*), not dependent on the person (*puruṣatantra*). Just as the visualization of fire in the sky is dependent on the person, the cognition of the Self (*ātmadhī*) is not so; this is the meaning. Furthermore, he states that there is no duty to perform regarding the cognition of the Self because it is always self-evident (*svasākṣika*) during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*): "Not other," etc. (1522).
Furthermore, it is not logical for a cognition that does not turn back [the object] to be a means of valid cognition.
Because it contradicts one's own experience, like the cognition of being burned by fire and so forth. || 1523 ||

Nevertheless, one might object: "Even so, that [knowledge] does not destroy ignorance, because it would follow that saṃsāra would never arise; therefore, knowledge is simply non-remedial. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... Just as when the proposition "fire is not burning" or "water is not cold" is put forward, it is sublated by one's own direct experience (svānubhava) that fire is indeed burning and water is indeed cold, so too the statement that "the cognition of the Self destroys its ignorance" is sublated by the experience of the learned.
The meaning is "obstructed. || 1523 ||
Because all Vedānta statements have this much alone as their final purport.
Nor can they be considered mere explanatory passages (arthavāda), because there is no other reason for their being subsidiary to something else. || 1524 ||

Therefore, because statements such as "all that became this" and "the knot of the heart is pierced" are established with certainty as referring merely to the destruction of ignorance through the knowledge of the Self, they cannot be non-effortful [in their result] due to their contradiction [with the status of ignorance]; thus he says, "All... Having raised the doubt that these might be mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and thus not intended to convey a primary meaning, he says, "And not... (1524).
If it is argued that these [passages] are merely explanatory (arthavāda) because they are objects of the notion of "I," [we reply: no.
Because no solution has been stated, and because the self is not something that can be known through the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 1525 ||

He raises an objection: since those [cognitions] function with respect to the internal self (*pratīci*) which is accessible to the notion of "I" (*aham-dhī*), they cannot possess the status of valid knowledge due to their agreement or disagreement; therefore, they must be considered merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). He says, "The notion 'I'... The mother is accessible to the notion of "I," but that is not the Self, for the Self is the witness of that [notion]. Thus, there is no possibility of agreement or disagreement regarding the Vedāntas' teaching of Brahman-hood; he states this with the words, "Not so, because it has already been stated. He recalls that very point: "Not..."
And so it is said. || 1529 ||
The notion of "I" is perceived as being both inwardly and outwardly directed.
There would be the fault of mutual dependence in the perception of the activity of the "I."
736 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
He states the reasoning for its lack of being accessible to the notion of "I" (*ahaṃdhi*) with the verse beginning "By the notion of 'I'... (1126).
Since this is so, therefore, he who effects the destruction of our manifest delusion—
This awakening—whether it be initial, final, or continuous—is traditionally held to have liberation as its fruit.

He concludes the result of the investigation with the words "yataḥ" (since). Since it is established by the reasoning already stated that the knowledge of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna) destroys its corresponding ignorance (ajñāna), therefore the meaning is that perfect knowledge—without requiring a further desire for specific details—is the liberator because it destroys ignorance regarding the inner self and its effects.
The word "vā" (or) is intended to introduce an alternative view, such as "or [it is] not continuous. || 1527 ||
As it has been said: "Because even those who have realized the truth are seen to possess passion and other such afflictions."
In this context, it is not being asserted that knowledge brings about the destruction of ignorance. || 1528 ||

Because it is impossible for the final cognition of one who is weary of transmigratory existence to destroy ignorance, it was stated that only the initial cognition is such [a destroyer]. Now, having restated what has been said by others, he announces the reply with the words "As for that which... The particle *api* (even/also) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*) in relation to those who are ignorant. || 1528 ||
Because the persistence of the body is due solely to the single cause that is the remainder of the fruit already set in motion.
The arising of passion and other [afflictions] from their conditions is like the momentum of an arrow or a wheel. || 1529 ||
He reveals the rebuttal: "That which has been commenced" (*ārabdha*). By whatever karma the body was commenced, that is "commenced fruition" (*ārabdhaphala*);
because the persistence of the body of the knower is caused solely by its remainder, the appearance of passion and so forth is not contradicted as long as that commenced fruition has not perished.

The meaning is that upon the destruction of that [ignorance], liberation occurs because of the absence of both the appearance of a body and the appearance of the world. Regarding the persistence of the body of the knower, the first qualification is stated to show the absence of any cause other than the remainder of *prārabdha* karma, which is dependent on a trace (*leśa*) of ignorance. Anticipating the objection that since even *prārabdha* karma is born of ignorance, it too must be sublated, and therefore the knower could not have a body persisting due to it, he says: "Like an arrow and a wheel. Just as in the case of one whose momentum has already been set in motion—

The meaning is that the destruction of the body and so forth occurs solely through the exhaustion of momentum (*vega*), and likewise the exhaustion of what has been commenced (*ārabdha*) occurs only through experience; for according to the principle that "one attains [liberation] after having exhausted the others by means of experience," it does not result from knowledge. || 1529 ||
Because it has already borne its fruit, that [ignorance] cannot be the cause for the cessation of knowledge.
And because it is past, the realization of the self is not sufficient for its destruction. || 1530 ||

Anticipating the objection—“Since there is no difference in their being *karman*, why should knowledge not terminate even that *karman* which has already begun, just like *karman* that has not yet begun?”—the author says:

“Of that” (*tasya*). Even *karman* that has begun is not destroyed by knowledge, because it has already set out to yield its fruit and thus is not opposed to knowledge, and because it persists due to a residue of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*). As they say: “The wheel continues to spin by the force of its momentum (*saṃskāra*)...”

Regarding the phrase "one whose body is maintained": the meaning is that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the scriptures on liberation while living (jīvanmukti). He states that because the prārabdha-karma has arisen in the form of its fruit and lacks a separate form of its own, there can be no cognition that destroys it; this is because [the karma] has already passed away. || 1530 ||
For that action which has its locus in one's own self indeed remains with its fruit as yet uncommenced.
That very [ignorance] destroys all our future knowledge as it is about to arise. 1531.

Raising the objection as to how the well-known principle that "knowledge is the destroyer of karma" can hold true if karma already set in motion cannot be revoked by knowledge, he states the scope of that [principle] with the words "But that which...
This means that it resides in one's own self—that is to say, it is based on the locus of the knowledge of reality—and is situated within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). 1. *asya pra*.

Action (*karma*) is also established in that [Self], because, since it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), it is possible for it to have that as its substratum; such is the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed). Even that which has already begun (*ārabdha*)...
He qualifies such karma by saying "unbegun" (*anārabdha*). He dispels the notion that such [karma] is already exhausted without fruit by saying "having risen" (*utpitsu*).

This means it is oriented toward birth in the form of its fruit. He states the possibility of its existence both at the time of knowledge and thereafter by saying "yet to come" (*anāgata*). He says "entire" (*kṛtsna*) because it is well-known in the scriptures that all of this is to be dispelled by knowledge; he states this with reference to that subject.
Thus it is said. || 1931 ||
If it were the case that karma whose fruit has not yet begun [is destroyed], but not that whose fruit has already begun;
If one were to obstruct self-cognition, then an undesirable consequence would follow. || 1532 ||
Having restated what was said by the proponent (*siddhāntin*), the opponent (*pūrvavādin*) declares an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*): "anārabdha... (verse 1532).
If karma whose fruit has already begun were not so, knowledge would cause its cessation.
Even in the case of the statement "it destroys that which has not yet begun to bear fruit," there would likewise be no certainty. || 1533 ||

What is that undesirable consequence? He states it: "prārabdha... (beginning with "prārabdha"). The meaning is that since there is the inference—"The subject under dispute [the karma being experienced] is not removable by knowledge, because it is karma, like *ārabdhakarman* (karma already set in motion)"—there would be a contradiction with scripture regarding the claim that other [types of karma] are also not removable by that [knowledge]. || 1533 ||
If independence of knowledge is not admitted with respect to those things for which an action has already been initiated.
If [actions] were not undertaken, even a person would have absolute freedom of will. (1534)

One might raise the objection: "Even though it is karma, why could that which has not yet begun (*anārabdha*) not be destroyed by knowledge? Anticipating this, he says, "If not," etc., pointing out that the same consequence would apply to the other [type of karma] as well; otherwise, even in the other case, there would be no destruction of it because it has not yet been reached. The word "nitarām" (thoroughly) is an expression of emphasis. Furthermore, in your view, there would be the undesirable consequence of acting according to one's own will for the knower, because you do not admit the commencement of another body upon the fall of the current body for such a person. Thus, *anārabdha*— [End of excerpt]

He states another undesirable consequence: "Also for the person," [referring to] the destruction of what has been undertaken through knowledge and what has already begun through experience. || 1534 ||
And once those [elements] have ceased, there would be no purpose for us whatsoever.
Because liberation is not accomplished prior to death, and because cyclic existence lacks a seed [for its cessation]. (1535)

Having raised the alternative—whether even commenced karma (*ārabdhakarman*) is to be discarded by knowledge, or whether the other [uncommenced karma] is devoid of that [discarding]—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) replies to the first with "No" (*na ceti*). Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say "we have no result whatsoever when commenced karmas are burnt by knowledge," since the very attainment of isolation (*kaivalya*) is the result, he says "Priorly" (*prāgiti*). For the body does not fall immediately upon the arising of knowledge; [one becomes] a liberated-while-living (*jīvanmukta*).

The meaning is that because there is no destruction of the *ārabdha* (commenced) karma through knowledge—since both the scriptures and the traditions of the wise teach that liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*) does not occur as long as the body exists—it follows that there is no liberation from bondage.
If it is argued that, in that case, since it initiates another body, there is indeed no liberation at all, he says "no," because of its being "seedless" (*abījatvāt*).

The meaning is that since it is destroyed by experiencing [its fruits], it lacks the cause for the bondage known as the initiation of another body; therefore, there is liberation. It is not otherwise, because the destruction of that [karma] by knowledge is established by scripture (*āgama*).

Nor is there "acting as one pleases" for the wise; for in a body commenced by karma that leads to that [liberation], knowledge—which has liberation as its fruit—does not arise, and there is no lack of a regulating factor.

In a body commenced by demerit (adharma) which brings about acting as one pleases, such action is characterized by impure impressions (saṃskāra); since it is impossible for one with an impure intellect to engage in tranquility (śama) and other practices that cause knowledge contrary to that [impurity], the very impossibility of that [knowledge] arising serves as the regulating factor. This is demonstrated by Śruti and Smṛti...

Furthermore, because one who possesses the two characteristics is not subject to the rivalry of acting according to their own whims, it is difficult to state anything superior to that knowledge which brings about such a state; thus, regarding its causes—

In the *Sureśvarācāryakṛta-bṛhadāraṇyakopani�ṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter One, verse 738: "If one were to assume that ritual action is a means [to knowledge], then for such a person, the status of being a knower would not be admitted; for even though he has abandoned what is enjoined, this does not constitute prohibited conduct."
The meaning of "kārā" is [the act of making]. || 1535 ||
And at the time of universal dissolution, there was a cessation of everything without exception.
Even that much cessation is not sufficient for liberation; how so? [1536]
Cessation, when practiced even for a very short time, is sufficient for liberation.
Nor can liberation result from the accumulation of cultivation, because [the mind] is subject to destruction.

Having accepted that knowledge is the cause of liberation, it was stated that it destroys even uncommenced karma (*anārabdhakarman*). However, others say that the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*) is the cause of liberation, not knowledge; regarding this, he says: "All... The word *ca* (and) is placed in the sense of *tu* (but) for the purpose of refuting the aforementioned view.

The meaning is: "The cessation under dispute is not the cause of liberation, because it is a cessation, like the cessation at the time of cosmic dissolution. Others, however, setting aside both knowledge and cessation, declare that liberation arises from the accumulation of impressions produced by the uninterrupted cognition "I am Brahman"; to them he says: "Meditation" (*bhāvanā*). For [the opponent] considers that this [meditation] is both the instrumental cause and the material cause of liberation; [the author], perceiving the lack of evidence for either case, states another defect regarding the second [position].
"Because of its perishable nature"—the ellipsis is that liberation, which is to be accomplished by that [means], would likewise be of such a nature. || 1936 || 1937 ||
If even the thought "I am suffering" has been destroyed, though it was nourished for millions of eons.
"What proof is there for the claim that 'cultivation [of the truth] is effective even when practiced for a short time'? (3/√2) 1538.

Anticipating the objection that the fragility of the contemplation "I am Brahman" (brahmāsmi) is unproven, he says: "The sufferer," etc. The meaning is this: even if the contemplation of being a sufferer, though produced by long-term practice, were to cease, there is no restrictive rule that the contemplation of being Brahman—produced by the practice shown in that [text] and occurring for only a short time—must therefore be eternal. || 1538 ||
And since the purpose of the treatise is accomplished, liberation would follow from that much alone, according to the measure [of the means].
Let passion and the like exist; it is not their presence that commits the offense. || 1539 ||

How, then, is liberation [attained] in that regard? To this he says: "Of the meaning of the scripture" (*śāstrārthasya*). Liberation arises from the cognition born of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), because of the Śruti texts such as "One who knows Brahman [becomes Brahman]" (*brahma veda*); thus, since the fruit of the Upaniṣads culminates precisely in liberation through the knowledge of non-duality, the meaning is that liberation results from knowledge alone, based on the authority of the scripture. [Objection: Even in the case of a knower (*jñānin*), since attachment and other defects are observed, knowledge is not the cause of that [liberation].

One might suspect that such a vision [of the world] does not contradict [the ultimate truth], because it is a mere appearance whose seeds have been burnt by knowledge; thus he says: "Attachment and so forth" (verse 1539).
If one knows Brahman from scripture, then indeed one becomes Brahman itself.
And for one who exists in the state of fruition, how could there be any mention of passion and the like? (1540)

One might object: "Just as in the case of people like us, passion and other afflictions continue to persist even for the wise man, since their effects are observed over a long period. To this, he says: "From scripture" (*āgamāt*).

Because the state of being Brahman is necessary through the knowledge arising from the Vedic revelation "I am Brahman," and because one who has become Brahman cannot be touched by passion and the like, it is not established that passion and so forth exist for him as they did before; for all passion and the rest have been sublated, though they may appear to persist otherwise.

The meaning is that, because knowledge is not futile, there is no longer for him that same effect as before—for one who possesses transmigratory existence as before—according to such principles [as those stated]. || 1940 ||
And not even an atom has been scorched by the fire of the thorough knowledge of Brahman.
It is possible [that this is so], because the cognition of Brahman is the sole cause of the end of all [suffering]. || 1541 ||

The cognition that contradicts right knowledge does not belong to one who perceives oneness.
It arises without an object, due to the abandonment of the latent tendency toward objects. || 1542 ||

Fearing the objection that the final cognition of Brahman might not exist beyond [the body], because cognitions of non-self continue to arise until the fall of the body, he says: "Perfectly" (*samyak*). The reason for this is: "Objectless" (*nirviṣaya*). He establishes the reason with: "Of objects" (*viṣaya*). This means:
because of the non-existence of their locus, that is, their collection. Alternatively, it refers to that in which the objects [of the external senses] reside.
The meaning is that they cease to exist because of the absence of that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), by way of the function of the door. || 1542 ||
In this world, false cognition arises for one who has not realized the true nature of reality.
For one whose darkness regarding reality has been destroyed, how could [ignorance] exist without a cause? || 1543 ||

Having stated that for the wise there is no false cognition because of the absence of both the collection of objects and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he says "In the world," etc., preceded by a general logical principle regarding the absence of a cause: "In the sphere of worldly activity, a false cognition such as 'this is silver' arises for one who does not know the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and so forth; however, for a person who has known the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and so forth, that [cognition] does not exist due to the absence of a cause."
The meaning is that for the knower of Brahman, false cognition does not exist through reasoning in that very same way as it exists [for others]. || 1943 ||
If that lack of confidence were to persist even regarding correct knowledge, it would follow that there is no certainty whatsoever.
If this were so, it would follow that even the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lack the status of being a valid means of knowledge. || 1544 ||

Having stated the absence of false knowledge in the wise person, he states the defect in the contrary case [the presence of such knowledge] with the words "samyak" (correctly). Even after the knowledge arising from the scriptures, if false cognition persists, there would be no faith in the scripture; consequently, engagement for its sake would be inconsistent. He states another defect in that situation with the words "evaṃ sati" (this being so). || 1944 ||
For no distinction is perceived between right and false resolve.
Consequently, there would undoubtedly be the abolition of all worldly transaction. || 1545 ||
He states the resulting conclusion—that if there were no pride within the mind, all worldly activity would cease—in the verse beginning with "samyak" (1945).
And immediately upon the arising of right knowledge, indeed,
As for the question of why there is no falling of the body, that too has been refuted.

Having established that for the knower there is no attachment or other such passions because ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge— and thus all its effects, including false cognition in its entirety, have been sublated—

he refutes the doctrine of immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), which holds that upon the arising of knowledge the body should fall immediately due to the absence of any cause for its continued existence, with the verse beginning "By right knowledge... (1146).

[Vol. 2, page 446] 740 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika [First Chapter—]
By the very same reasoning previously stated, there remains nothing further to be said.
Therefore, upon the arising of knowledge, there is the destruction of all karmas whatsoever. || 1547 ||

Anticipating the objection that the reason [for the body's continued existence] has been cast aside, he says "pūrva... (the previous...). The meaning is that because of the persistence of the body due to *prārabdha* karma, the wise person does not attain immediate fall [from the body]. He concludes by stating that for others, the destruction of ignorance occurs by depending on the persistence of the body through *prārabdha* karma, with the words "jñāna... (knowledge...). || 1547 ||
Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna.
In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes. || 1548 ||
In this regard, he cites the word of the Blessed One as authoritative: "Just as... (1948).
When the consequence of similarity with all possible examples arises, this [reason] serves to negate it.
The Veda declares that for him, the duration of that [state] is exactly as long. || 1549 ||

By stating that "the fire of knowledge [consumes] all actions," it is declared that the destruction of karma results from knowledge, and from that very cause liberation is said to follow; therein, he introduces the *Chāndogya* Śruti as authoritative evidence: "All... (1149).
Upon the removal of the blindfold, there is instruction regarding memory.
Then follows the grasping of that meaning, and after that, its practical application.
He would go from village to village, increasing his extensive travels. || 1551 ||

What is this illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), how is its complete similarity with the subject of the illustration (*dāṣṭantika*) established, and how is the exception (*apavāda*) that negates it stated in the Śruti? Regarding this, he states the nature of the illustration: "Not by the eyes," etc. For a man from Gandhāra, having reached another country and acquired much wealth, while returning to his own land of Gandhāra, has his eyes bound on the road by thieves and is stripped of his wealth in the forest.

Having heard his instruction on the path, a certain traveler approached him; after the binding of his eyes was removed, he was instructed regarding the recollection of the route leading to the desired destination. Then, through the sequence of the hearer’s knowledge of that object and subsequently his movement, the hearer reaches the intended place, traveling from village to village by many stages according to the instructions over a long period of time.
The meaning is that one reaches Gandhāra. || 1550 || 1551 ||
One who has correctly understood the meaning of the instructions and is himself possessed of inspired eloquence.
After a much longer period of time, he reaches Gandhāra.

Regarding the two qualifiers "wise" (*paṇḍita*) and "intelligent" (*medhāvī*), which are established as examples [of the practitioner], he states the meaning of the word "wise": "correctly" (*samyak*).
He states the meaning of "intelligent": "and by oneself" (*svayam ca*) || 1552 ||
Just as it is so in that case, even so it would be here for the man who possesses a teacher.
In order to prevent the consequence of having to state every single example without exception.
This scripture declared to us that this was indeed an exception to that rule. || 1553 ||

Having restated the example, he states the application of all the points contained therein to the subject of the illustration, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). Here, the word "here" (*iha*) contains one locative case ending (*saptamī*). [Note:
*kha* says "by the speaker"; *ka* and *kha* say "its refutation"].

The consequence would be that [liberation] depends on a specific location, because the example and the thing exemplified are identical; therefore, the meaning is that knowledge alone is not the cause of liberation.

Now he cites an exception: "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The meaning is that since the entire sense of the illustrative sentence would apply to the thing exemplified, the scriptural text "For him, there is delay only so long" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2) declares an exception to that over-extension for our sake.
For that man who knows this, however, his delay is only for so long.
As long as the cloth of delusion regarding oneness is not removed. || 1554 ||
Clarifying that very statement, he explains it with the words "of that" (*tasya*). The phrase "liberation would occur" (*bhaven muktiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 1554 ||
It does not exceed the arising of the knowledge of the true nature of the inward Self.
Furthermore, there is the destruction of the obstruction of delusion through its reversal, as well as through a contrary cognition. (1555)

He establishes the topic at hand—liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—once again by means of another method, beginning with the words "pratyak" (the inner self). "Abhinahanam" means bondage, that is to say, the covering [of ignorance]. The construction is as follows: since false cognition is an effect of delusion, its cessation occurs in exactly that same manner. || 1555 ||
Therefore, prior even to the arising of the knowledge of reality as it truly is.
Ignorance of the self, together with its effects, must be sublated, because it is that which is to be negated. || 1556 ||

He states the established conclusion regarding the point that "enlightenment is impelled by the intellect, or the intellect is impelled by enlightenment, resulting in the destruction of ignorance and so forth" with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The word "but" (*tu*) is used to cite a corroborating scripture for the fact that the perception of linguistic usage regarding that [object] has already been explained previously. He states another reason for the absence of ignorance and so forth after knowledge arises with the words "Of that" (*tasya*). When a sublater (*bādhaka*) occurs, the persistence of the sublated (*bādhyasya*) is not established.
This is the meaning. || 1556 ||
When something occurs upon the arrival of a certain condition, how could that [condition] have existed previously?
Therefore, the final cognition is the sublater of everything that is to be sublated. || 1557 ||

By stating that "ignorance (avidyā), along with its effects, did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist," [the author] implies that ignorance and the like were accepted as having existed previously, even before their removal;
thus, [an objection is raised] that its prior existence and subsequent non-existence are mutually contradictory. Anticipating this, he says: "In which...

For it is not the case that the cessation of silver and the like, occurring upon the knowledge of mother-of-pearl and the like, is something desired to come into being later; in the very same way, when the knowledge arising from the [Mahāvākya] exists, [there is the cessation of] ignorance and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: "Destruction" does not exist prior to that [knowledge]; first there is the empirical usage of ignorance and so forth, and subsequently there is the empirical usage of its absence. Thus, the empirical usage of existence and non-existence follows this observed sequence; however, the real state is that there is no such usage as "it did not exist," "it exists," or "it will exist. Therefore, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Upon the arising of knowledge, because ignorance and the like are burnt away, and because the appearance of the body and so forth persists only for the duration of experience until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, there is an absence of causes [for further manifestation].
He concludes that the finality of the cognition of non-duality is established with the words "the final. He qualifies it with "all" in order to manifest its finality. || 1597 ||
Even the gods and others have no power over this knower of Brahman, even though he may be in debt.
If it is asked for what reason this was said, the following response is given: || 1558 ||

Having established that there is an absence of obstacles to the fruit of knowledge by one who maintains that liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) is refuted by those of his own school, [the author] now restates what has been said by the proponent—that even though gods and others may be creditors, they lack the power to obstruct the fruit of knowledge—and asks for the reason: "Even though they are debtors" (*ṛṇino 'pi*). He states the cause: "In that case" (*tatra*). || 1598 ||
For the true nature of the self as consciousness would not be subject to debt.
That [cognition] would have ignorance as its object, because of its being the cause of agency. || 1559 ||

Regarding their status as creditors, whether with respect to the learned or the unlearned, he says that the first case is not so: "No. He states the reason for the absence of agency and so forth in that [Self]: "Because... The implication is that, therefore, it is appropriate that they lack mastery over that [Self]. He accepts the second alternative: "Ignorance. (1119)
Or where there is something else, and so forth; such indeed is the teaching of the Śruti.
For one whose ignorance has been destroyed, that [duality] would not exist, because of his nature as the single self (ekātmya). || 1560 ||

He states the proof for the claim that agency and so forth belong to the ignorant person with the words "wherein. He also states the proof for the claim that agency and so forth do not belong to the knower with the words "destroyed," meaning: because of the scriptural text, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). || 1960 ||
Moreover, even for one who is ignorant, there can be no state of being a debtor here, because the cause is impossible.
Nothing has been bestowed upon us by the gods, by which we might incur a state of indebtedness.

Having accepted the state of being a debtor on the part of one who is ignorant, and having stated that gods and others are creditors in that regard, he says "not even that" to show that such a thing does not exist.

The phrase "not even here" means "not even among gods and others. He establishes the impossibility of the reason with the words beginning with "no," etc. As for the bestowing of wind, rain, and so forth, that is performed according to their own specific offices and is dependent upon the command of the Lord; it is not sufficient to establish our status as debtors, otherwise [the argument would fail].

The meaning is that [the Lord is the cause] because of the scriptural passage beginning with "Out of fear of Him," for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all activity. || 1561 ||
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of a scriptural statement, it is not so; for that statement is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
For that statement is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) remaining from the injunction for the ritual offering (*avadāna*).

[The opponent] objects that even one who lacks knowledge is a debtor, based on such scriptural passages as "one is born with three debts," etc.; this is stated by the words "from the statement. That is not so.

He says, "Not so," because [the passage] lacks independent authority due to being an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), like the passage beginning "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), and therefore it does not establish the intended meaning.

He supports its status as an *arthavāda* with the words "by the offering" (*avadāna*). Just as the *arthavāda* "The *nivīta* [garment] is for men" is understood as a praise of the *upavīta* and is not accepted as an injunction—because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction "Therefore, they make that the mark of the gods"—so too is this case.

The meaning is that the statement regarding the debt-owedness of human beings is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction "one should cut out the portions (*avadāna*) [of the victim]";

this is because it is well known that an *arthavāda* serves as a supplement to an injunction, as seen in passages such as "The gods, having settled upon the place of sacrifice," and so forth. The first word "eka" (one) is used for that purpose, while the second word "eka" is intended to illustrate the aforementioned example. || 1962 ||
If gods and others are considered powerless with respect to a wise man.
The domain in which they possess sovereignty is now being stated.
Even though it is heard that one becomes part of the world of cattle (*paśuloka*), no obstruction whatsoever can be placed by gods or others against liberation, which is the fruit of that knowledge.

The first [knowledge] is capable of destroying ignorance, while the final [knowledge] is not, because it belongs to a continuous series [of ignorance]; furthermore, since the perception of passion and so forth in the knower is merely illusory, it has been stated that its fruit is inevitable. Now, if the gods and others lack independence regarding the knower, where does their independence reside?
He asks, "Whom? [The answer is] "the wise man. Then he introduces the passage beginning with "But he who [worships another]," and so forth.
The meaning is that the subsequent sentence elaborates upon the sovereignty of the gods and others in exercising restraint and grace over one who does not know Brahman. || 1563 ||
In whatever subject matter the authority of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is intended to reside, [that is its scope].
The object of ignorance is directly perceived, as well as that which is understood through another [means]. || 1564 ||

He states another point: "By that very [scripture] itself, the status of being an instrument of knowledge is also attributed to the scriptural injunction regarding action, such as the relationship between the goal and the means, within the sphere of ignorance. He says "validity" (prāmāṇyam) to indicate the analogy:

just as perception and other means of knowledge distinct from scripture possess validity regarding objects within the sphere of ignorance. The word "directly" (sākṣāt) is used for this purpose. || 1964 ||
Upon the arising of right knowledge, through the completion of the effects of karma.
There would be no need for dependence on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), since its purpose has been fulfilled by that [knowledge].

[Objection: Surely, since karma and the like are rooted in ignorance, they cannot be authoritative even for a knower; for even such a one remains dependent on karma, as the Smṛti says, "Indeed, no one [remains] even for a moment... etc. Furthermore, the Śrutis also state that liberation has its cause in knowledge combined with action. To this, he replies: "Perfectly" (samyak). Since heaven and so forth are sublated by the knowledge of unity, a knower has no dependence on the Karmakāṇḍa or its objects, because there is nothing further to be done; [this dependence exists] only prior to that knowledge.

Since the authority of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) has already been fulfilled—either because its practical validity is established, or because when knowledge arises, the purification of the intellect, which is the cause of that [liberation], has already been obtained at the very outset—it is not proper to have further reliance upon it, as there is no further fruit to be gained.

Furthermore, action is shown to be sublated for Janaka and others, as seen in such statements as "nothing of mine shall be burnt"; and the Smṛti texts concerning him refer only to those who are ignorant.

And he will say, "No duty exists," yet he also says, "The wise man should act," which is stated solely for the purpose of impelling the ignorant; this is seen from such passages as, "Whatever a great man does," and so forth. Furthermore, statements regarding the combination [of knowledge and action] are intended to mean their sequential combination; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with prohibitions such as, "There is no other path" and "Not by action. Therefore, the sense is that while action and the like pertain to the state of ignorance (*āvidya*), action is authoritative according to the Śruti. Regarding its having ignorance as its domain:

Anticipating the objection that its validity might be like that of the cognition of silver and so forth, he says "That" (tad), meaning: this is not so, because its empirical validity is established just as in the case of perception and other means of knowledge.

It should be understood that the cognition of silver and the like is not [itself] ignorance, since it is accepted that error consists in the cognition together with the objects known through it. || 1565 ||
This subsequent discourse is for the purpose of emerging from the knowledge of identity with primordial nature (prakṛti).
For knowledge and ignorance cannot coexist, due to their mutual opposition. || 1566 ||

Having stated the intended meaning—that the subsequent passage is meant to express two points, namely that for one who does not know Brahman there is independence over the gods and so forth, and that the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is authoritative regarding ignorance and ritual acts—the author explains the meaning of the word "atha" (now). He says: "prakṛta... (the subject under discussion). He states the reason for creating a break between what precedes and what follows: "na hi... (for not...). This means that there is a relationship of sublation and sublated due to contradiction. || 1566 ||
For one whose vision is veiled by ignorance, there is no other [reality] than the mental construction.
Even though he is not different from the Self, a person worships a deity as if it were distinct. || 1567 ||
1 Kha kā mānābhā.
[vol2, page 450]

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter One, verse 744, explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "he who [worships] another" (*yo 'nyām*). The term "the inward" (*pratīcī*) refers to the absence of the threefold distinction, which is the meaning of the two qualifiers. Taking as a cause the state of having one's vision obscured by one's own ignorance (*avidyā*), he speaks of the perception of difference. The phrase "by ignorance" (*avidyā*) indicates the factual distinctness of the worshiper from the deity.
It has been stated that even another [person] is unable to refute it. || 1967 ||
The phrase "He is another" serves as the explanation for the word "upāsā" (meditation).
Therefore, it is said that one meditates upon the very perception of difference. || 1568 ||

What kind of worship [is meant]? It is neither scriptural, because of the supplementary statement "he would not know that," nor is it worldly, because the notion of worship is not established in the context of perceiving difference. To this he says: "He thinks 'that one is another'. The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of excluding scriptural worship. Furthermore, the term "worship" (upāsanā) is not unapplied to worldly perception of difference, as seen in such expressions as "he worships the king."
This is the intended meaning. || 1568 ||
"What would be the root of divided vision?"— this is what is stated by the Śruti.
"He does not know"—this is ignorance, which creates the manifold expansion of names and forms. (1569)

He introduces another sentence preceded by a desire for further inquiry: "What is its root? The connection is with the phrase "he does not know," according to the scripture (*śruti*). He states its meaning: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). He provides experiential evidence (*anubhava*) as proof for that: "This [is it]. In this very context, he states an inference based on the mark of its effect (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*):
Seized by the demon of ignorance regarding the self, it is conjoined with the objects arising therefrom.
By means of his own actions, he becomes an animal for the gods and others.

He provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) in order to introduce another statement, beginning with the word "the Self" (*ātma*). The meaning is that the ignorant person—who possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being a Brahmin and so forth—attains the state of being a beast for the gods by performing sacrifices and other rites, but the wise person does not. || 1570 ||
A domestic animal, such as a goat or a cow, is one that provides great assistance.
Likewise, an ignorant person becomes a beast for the gods and others by performing services for them. (1571)
He explains the simile "just as a beast" with the words "bahūpakārā" (of great benefit). He analyzes the corresponding application of the simile ("evam" etc.
with the words "devādīnām" (of the gods and so forth). The word "avidvān" (the ignorant one) is to be understood as a separate term [at the end of the compound]. || 1571 ||
In this world, cattle and other such animals are considered to have only one owner each.
Even greater than that is the excellence of men: their being benefactors to all the world. (1572)
Setting the stage to introduce another statement, he demonstrates the dissimilarity between a human and an animal, such as a cow, with the words "Each one...
(verse 1572).
Through each individual action, every person in the world becomes a beast owned by that single master.
Thus, even when combined with many others, it may sometimes be beneficial.

He states the intended meaning of the examples, such as the "plow" (*heta*), and so forth: "Each one," etc. In the world, a cow or similar animal, presided over by a single person, sometimes benefits that single presiding agent through the act of milking; at other times, through the act of carrying and so forth, it benefits many people acting together.

The meaning is that it protects him by acting as a benefactor; the word "thus" (*evam*) is used to express that it is like the way each individual animal, when not combined with others, acts as a benefactor. Thus it was said. || 1973 ||
198. But a man who performs many actions likewise becomes a master of many [wives], yet remains powerless.
Each one of them individually sustains the entire universe day and night. || 1574 ||

With the words "evam" (thus) and so forth, he states the intended meaning of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the word "bhūri" (abundant): the meaning is that, according to the aforementioned illustration, each individual ignorant person, presided over by many gods and others, remains dependent upon them; being thus [dependent], they perform actions such as giving and sacrifice, and thereby protect the entire host of gods and others. || 1174 ||
An illustration for this very point is stated as follows: "Just as..."
Since this is so, it is therefore logical that [the cessation of suffering] is extremely unpleasant to the gods and others.

Having raised the objection that since the desired point is established by the phrase "just like an animal" (*yathā paśu*) alone, what is the purpose of the phrase "just like [the world]" (*yathā ha*) and so forth, he says "of this" (*asya*) to state the specific distinction between the worldly animal and the human animal as previously described. To introduce the sentence beginning with "in one and the same," he provides the transition: "since" (*yataḥ*). Because a person assists the gods and others through sacrifices and other rites, and because of his liberation from the state of being an animal through the knowledge of Brahman...
The meaning is that it is logical for gods and others to experience great suffering. || 1175 ||
Even for a man who possesses abundant cattle, if even a single one is stolen by thieves—
As the animal is being led away, intense suffering arises within it.
What need is there to speak of the cause of suffering when all one's possessions are taken away?
He explains the statement with the word "api" (even).
By one who steals the wisdom of Brahman, a human victim is treated as equal to all one's own possessions.
When it diminishes, there is great suffering; therefore, that [diminution] is unpleasant to them.

"If humans would know the Supreme Brahman exactly as it has been described," [the text] says "tasmādeṣām" (therefore for them) and so forth; he explains the meaning of this with the words "sarvasva" (all one's own). 1977 || 1578 ||
At the birth of the Brahma-knowledge, which is the fire that serves as the cause for all authority.
Nothing remains apart from the inner self (pratyak), which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else.
[This verse] establishes that the knowledge of Brahman is "robber-like" (parimoṣitva). In all ritual action, there is an eligibility based on a connection through ownership;
the cause for that is egoism (abhimāna). When the knowledge of Brahman arises—which is like fire to that egoism along with its cause—there is the destruction of everything.
The meaning is that because [the intellect] terminates in the state of being merely a reflection, it is clear that the cognition of Brahman is subject to theft (parimoṣitva). || 1179 ||
From this, not even an atom of that which arises from ignorance remains.
Because ignorance has been destroyed by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman as the Self. || 1580 ||

Fearing the objection that even in the absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*) when knowledge (*jñāna*) exists, there might still be some other entity, he says "no" and so forth. The connection is: "other than this inner self (*pratyak*. The meaning is that an effect is incapable of existing without a cause. || 1580 ||
For the world of the gods, O son of Kuntī, is filled with those who perform ritual actions.
And this is not desired by the gods: that mortals should exist above them. || 1581 ||
746 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 452]

Having stated that the excellence of humans—resulting from the destruction of their state as bound souls (*paśu*) through the knowledge of Brahman—is a cause for the gods and others to be pleased, [the author] cites the words of Vyāsa as proof for the fact that the gods cannot endure the excellence of humans. He does so with the verse beginning "By those who perform rituals" (*kriyāvadbhiḥ*). The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that if there were no constant presence of those who have performed meritorious deeds, there would be the possibility of that [heavenly world] occasionally becoming desolate. For it is they who maintain the stability of the gods' world for humans.
The sense is that they cannot even tolerate the attainment of nirvāṇa by those [others] through their knowledge, let alone anything else. || 1581 ||
Therefore, one who desires liberation, having properly propitiated the gods and others through ritual actions, [should proceed].
Having been released from those bonds, one should desire to know one's own self.

Fearing that the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) of gods and others would be frustrated if the knowledge of Brahman were not dear to them among humans, [the author] shows through the statement regarding what is "not dear" to gods and others that this is implied. "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): the meaning is that because it is possible for gods and others to create obstacles when humans seek to attain knowledge (*vidyā*). "Properness of worship" (*ārādhanasya samyaktvam*) means its accordance with the scriptures. "Desires to attain" (*āpitsat*) means desires to obtain.
But its opposite is the fool who seeks liberation by force alone.
Even from heaven and other such realms, he falls and enters hell. || 1583 ||

Anticipating the objection that one who desires liberation and seeks the vision of non-duality (advaita-darśana) would have no desire for the worship of gods and other deities conducive to dualistic perception, he says:

"But its opposite... For one who is averse to the worship of gods and others, who is devoid of discrimination, dispassion, and so forth, and who—being unfit for knowledge without their grace—desires liberation all of a sudden, there can be neither liberation nor worldly prosperity, due to the absence of the causes thereof.
The meaning is that, precisely because of his desire for liberation, the causes [of such conduct] are absent; therefore, he would be a fit vessel for nothing but hell. || 1583 ||
Those who are negligent have their wealth carried away by others; they are malicious and eager for quarrels.
Even renunciants are seen whose inner dispositions have been corrupted by the gods.

One might object: "Even in the absence of such worship, why would there not be freedom from fear for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*)? For the desire for liberation does not have an undesirable result, as that would contradict the scriptures on liberation; nor does one who acts with the desire to seek what is beneficial meet with misfortune. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says, "For the negligent," considering that for one whose vision is directed outward, the desire for liberation becomes fruitless due to the inevitability of engaging in prohibited actions. "Negligence" refers to the lack of concentration of the mind during hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other [spiritual practices].

That negligence is not caused by the mere perception of external objects; rather, that [negligence] is the cause for being unable to endure the excellence of others, and that is the primary cause for a fondness for quarreling.

The analysis is as follows: the cause of negligence is having one's intellect insulted by gods and others who have not been propitiated. Furthermore, the word "api" (even) is intended to establish a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument. || 1984 ||
By not undertaking actions, no person attains anything.
Nor does one attain perfection merely through renunciation. || 1585 ||

If it were argued that for a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), the occurrence of undesirable results through prohibited actions would mean that scriptural renunciation cannot be the cause of right knowledge—and thus there would be a contradiction with scripture—the author, having raised this doubt, refutes the first alternative (that mere renunciation is the cause of knowledge) by means of the Lord’s own words: "Not by action" (*na karmaṇām*). This is because even in the absence of "actionlessness" (*naiṣkarmya*) resulting from the mere abandonment of action, [knowledge does not arise].
Anticipating the objection that knowledge might arise from that alone, he says: "And not... (1989).
[Vol. 2, p.
453] 4th Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri; 747.
Having boiled the decoction, however, it should be applied at the three locations of the spinal column.
"One should go forth into the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant.

(1586) Now, anticipating the second objection—that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) might be the cause of wisdom for one whose intellect has been purified by ritual actions (*karman*)—the author accepts this and recites a statement by Vyāsa concerning the subject of renunciation, beginning with the words "kaṣāyam" [etc.]. Only one whose intellect is purified is qualified for the life of a wandering mendicant.

The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "not for anyone else. "In the stages of the ladder" means in the stages of life (*āśrama*), which are like steps on a staircase; the meaning of the first "and" (*ca*) is "having remained in those. The second "and" has the sense of a conjunction, indicating that dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the cause for wandering as a mendicant (*pārivrājya*). The connection is: one should go—that is, enter—the state of wandering as a mendicant, which is the unsurpassed means for achieving the supreme human goal. This is done with a view toward the highest station, which is liberation (*kaivalya*).
The remainder. || 1586 ||
And through these cultivated faculties, throughout many births in the cycle of existence, this [being]—
The pure-souled one indeed attains liberation in the first stage of life.

To the question, "How then [is it that] one should go forth from the very state of brahmacarya?"—referring to the scriptural injunction on immediate renunciation (akrama-saṃnyāsa)—he replies with the words "by those who have cultivated [the mind]" (bhāvitaiḥ).

The word "ca" (and) is used to show that this occurs through the gateway of dispassion (vairāgya). The particle "vai" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). "Mokṣam" means for the sake of liberation, specifically for the sake of the knowledge that is its cause; "āśramam" means to the stage of life (āśrama). || 1987 ||
But for the wise man who has attained that [state] and is liberated, having perceived the ultimate reality—
Among the three stages of life (āśramas), which one would be truly meaningful for one who desires the supreme goal?

Fearing that one who has ascended the staircase might, like one descending, desire to engage again in the practices of the previous stages of life (āśramas) even after attaining the state of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), he says: "Having reached him" (*tam āsādya*). The word *tu* (but/however) is intended to exclude the aforementioned doubt. For one who is wise (*vipaścit*), possessing discrimination, dispassion, and so forth, desiring the unsurpassed human goal, having attained the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama), and having perceived reality through hearing [the scriptures] and other means—that is, one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)— [The text continues: ...there is no possibility of returning to the prior stages of life. This is because there is no further purpose for such a person to be accomplished by those stages, and because they have transcended all worldly desires. Furthermore, since the state of liberation is the ultimate end, it is impossible to fall back from it. Therefore, the meaning is that for such a person, there is no engagement with the prior stages of life. Thus, the sense is that the state of liberation is the final goal, and once attained, there is no returning to the former stages. This is established by the fact that the scriptures declare the attainment of liberation to be the supreme end. Therefore, the conclusion is that for one who has realized the truth, there is no returning to the prior stages of life. This is the purport of the entire section. Thus ends the commentary on the verse beginning with "Having reached him. Now, the author proceeds to explain the nature of the liberated one's conduct. To show that such a person does not engage in actions prompted by desire, he says: "He does not perform any action" (*naiva kiṃcit karoti saḥ*). This means that he does not perform any action motivated by desire, nor does he perform any action that would lead to rebirth. Why? Because he has transcended all desires. This is because he has realized the Self as being devoid of agency and action. Furthermore, since he has abandoned all attachment, he does not perform any action for his own sake. Nor does he perform any action for the sake of others, because he is free from the notion of "I" and "mine. Moreover, since he has realized the non-duality of the Self, he does not perceive any object distinct from himself upon whom he could act. Therefore, he does not perform any action whatsoever. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "he does not perform any action" implies that he does not perform even those actions prescribed by the scriptures, such as bathing, eating, and so forth, when they are performed with a sense of agency or as a means to an end; rather, these are performed spontaneously as natural bodily functions, without any mental effort or intentionality. Thus, the liberated one remains established in his own nature, free from all activity. This is the purport of the verse. Now, the author provides a reason for this: "For he is without desire" (*vītarāgaḥ*). This means that he is free from all craving. Since he has realized the Self as the only reality, he has no longing for anything else. Therefore, he does not perform any action. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "without desire" indicates that he is free from the three types of desire: desire for objects, desire for progeny, and desire for heaven. Since he has transcended these, he does not perform any action. This is the sense. Moreover, the phrase "without desire" implies that he is free from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past actions. Since these have been destroyed by knowledge, he does not perform any new action. This is the meaning. Thus, the liberated one, being free from desire and action, remains established in the Self. This is the conclusion. Now, the author shows that even though he does not perform actions, he is not inactive in the sense of being a mere inert object; rather, he acts spontaneously like a child or a madman. To show this, he says: "He moves about like a child" (*bālavat*). This means that he acts without deliberation or calculation, free from the notions of right and wrong. He eats, sleeps, and plays just as a child does, without any attachment to the results. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "like a child" implies that he is free from the pride of learning and the conceit of virtue. Since he has realized the equality of all things, he does not distinguish between what is pure and what is impure. Therefore, he moves about like a child. This is the sense. Moreover, the phrase "like a child" indicates that he is free from the fear of death and the desire for life. Since he has realized the eternal nature of the Self, he is neither afraid of death nor attached to life. Therefore, he moves about like a child. This is the meaning. Thus, the liberated one, acting spontaneously like a child, remains established in the bliss of the Self. This is the purport of the verse. Now, the author concludes by showing that such a person is not subject to the laws of karma. To show this, he says: "He is not touched by evil" (*na sa pāpena lipyate*). This means that he is not affected by the results of past sins or by any new sins committed through inadvertence. Why? Because he has realized the Self as being beyond all action and its fruits. Furthermore, since he has abandoned all identification with the body and the senses, the merit or demerit of actions does not accrue to him. Therefore, he is not touched by evil. This is the meaning. Moreover, the phrase "not touched by evil" implies that he is free from the cycle of birth and death. Since he has attained liberation, he is no longer subject to transmigration. Therefore, he is not touched by evil. This is the sense. Thus, the liberated one, being untouched by evil and established in the Self, remains eternally free. This is the conclusion of the commentary on the verse beginning with "He does not perform any action. Now, the author introduces the next verse to show that the liberated one is also free from the need for ritual purification. To show this, he says: "He is purified by the water of knowledge" (*jñānāmbhasā śuddhaḥ*). This means that he is cleansed by the water of realization, which removes the stains of ignorance and false identification. Unlike ordinary people who require external baths and rituals for purification, he is inherently pure through the realization of the non-dual Self. Therefore, he is purified by the water of knowledge. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "purified by the water of knowledge" implies that he is free from the need for external observances (*niyama*) and restraints (*yama*). Since he has realized the Self as being beyond all rules, he does not depend on external means for purity. Therefore, he is purified by the water of knowledge. This is the sense. Moreover, the phrase "purified by the water of knowledge" indicates that he is free from the notion of duality. Since he perceives everything as the Self, there is no distinction between the pure and the impure. Therefore, he is purified by the water of knowledge. This is the meaning. Thus, the liberated one, being purified by the water of knowledge, remains established in the supreme peace. This is the purport of the verse. Now, the author explains that although he is thus liberated, he may still appear to act in the world for the benefit of others. To show this, he says: "He may act for the sake of others" (*parārthaṃ vā pravartate*). This means that out of compassion, he may engage in activities for the welfare of others, such as teaching the scriptures or performing works of public utility. However, he does not do so out of personal desire or attachment. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "for the sake of others" implies that his actions are spontaneous and effortless. Since he is free from egoism, his deeds do not bind him. Therefore, he may act for the sake of others. This is the sense. Moreover, the phrase "for the sake of others" indicates that he is not motivated by the fruits of action. Since he has realized the non-existence of the agent and the action, he performs whatever is necessary for the world without seeking reward. Therefore, he may act for the sake of others. This is the meaning. Thus, the liberated one, acting for the sake of others without attachment, remains established in the bliss of the Self. This is the conclusion of the commentary on the verse beginning with "He may act for the sake of others. Now, the author summarizes the entire teaching by stating that the liberated one is beyond all dualities. To show this, he says: "He is beyond all dualities" (*sarvadvaṃdvavinirmuktaḥ*). This means that he is free from the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, fame and infamy, and so forth. Since he has realized the Self as being immutable and beyond all change, he is not affected by these dualities. Therefore, he is beyond all dualities. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "beyond all dualities" implies that he is free from the fluctuations of the mind. Since he has attained equanimity, his mind is steady and und

The meaning is that for one who experiences the appearance of a body and so forth due to the remainder of previously commenced karma, there is no purpose in the former stages of life (āśramas), which leads to the doubt that such a person might "fall from what has been ascended. || 1588 ||
Thus, O Blessed One, there are thousands of such words of Vyāsa here.
They are heard to be composed according to logic; therefore, one should listen to them with respect. || 1589 ||

He concludes the proof stated here—that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the cause of the intellect’s purification—by saying, "In this way. Regarding the phrase "of actions": when actions are performed with the intent of offering them to the Lord, their fruit is the purification of the intellect; and one whose intellect is purified, being endowed with discrimination and the like, having renounced action and desiring only knowledge which is the cause of liberation, approaches a teacher...

The principle is that one performs hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth by following [the scriptures] alone, and not otherwise. Therefore, he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), meaning that one whose intellect is purified and who is intent on the propitiation of the deity and so forth, having renounced ritual actions with the aim of attaining knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) based on the authority of the words of Vyāsa and others, should repeat the practices of hearing and so forth. And it has been stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "Therefore, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), intent on the propitiation of the deity... and so on. (1589)
First, the meaning of the treatise has been set forth with effort in the aphorism: "The Self, indeed."
And the connection of that sūtra has been stated along with its purpose. || 1590 ||

In order to state the connection of the passage beginning with "Brahman indeed was this" (*brahma vā idam*) with what has preceded, [Sureśvarācārya] proclaims what has already occurred: "The meaning of the scripture" (*śāstrārtha*). This refers, in short, to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). The sense is: by means of the diligent refutation of the three types of injunctions. Now, one might ask: what is the connection of the knowledge of Brahman?

Furthermore, having raised the doubt as to what the fruit is, he restates what was said in the passage beginning with "they say" (*tadāhuḥ*). Regarding the phrase "and it has been stated": this refers to the Sūtra, that is, the knowledge contained within the Sūtra. The distinction is as follows: its relationship with the fruit is that of the means to the end (*sādhyasādhanatva*); its relationship with the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) is that of the locus and the occupant (*āśrayāśrayitva*); and its relationship [with the Sūtra] is that of identity as the subject and the object (*viṣayaviṣayitva*). Furthermore, the distinction is that "the state of being everything" (*sarvabhāva*) is the fruit thereof. || 1590 ||
Furthermore, the fact that ignorance is the cause of the misfortune of saṃsāra has been described.
By the statement beginning with "yo 'nyām," its effect has also been indicated. || 1591 ||

He recites what was stated in the *Avidyāsūtra*: "In saṃsāra... The meaning is that such misfortune and the perception of duality—by the force of the word "and" (*ca*)—ignorance (*avidyā*) is also shown by way of its effects. For here, ignorance (avidyā) has also been aphoristically stated together with its effect, namely knowledge (vidyā).

He summarizes precisely that meaning which was explained in detail—that both knowledge (*vidyā*) together with its effects, and ignorance (*avidyā*) together with its effects, have been aphorized along with their relationship and purpose—by the words "like knowledge" (*vidyāvat*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to what was stated in the preceding text. The particle "hi" is used to indicate that the two aphorisms have already been made clear. Having restated what has preceded, he states the connection of the subsequent [section] with it by the words "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*). The subsequent...

This means that the statement [in the text] is made because the power to express that [ignorance] is observed in the treatise; the meaning is "of that ignorance together with its effects," which has been indicated by the aphorism (*sūtrita*). One who does not recognize the Self as it has been described is possessed of the conceit that arises from the effects of ignorance.

How does the subsequent [text] show that ignorance, along with its effects, possesses constituent parts endowed with its own powers? To this he says: "Just as...

Therefore, until the conclusion of this chapter, these are the manifestations of ignorance.
This will be explained in detail; hereafter, the next section of the text is introduced.

Since it is observed that the meaning already stated is presented in the subsequent text, and since its constituent parts are connected with ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its effects, he concludes that its commencement is for the purpose of elaborating upon that [ignorance]. He says, "From the beginning of the chapter" (*ā'dhyāya*). Having stated the purport of the remainder of the chapter, he introduces the following sentence with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the remainder has the purpose of elaborating upon ignorance together with its effects, therefore [the text describes] the manifestation (*vivarta*) of ignorance—
The meaning is that the subsequent section is intended to manifest the creation of the Turvaṇyas. || 1994 ||

The creation of Indra and the others was not mentioned previously because it was intended to describe the effects of delusion.

Regarding the question, "What is the intention of the Śruti here, since in the passage beginning with 'Then [He] thought: Let me create other beings' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), the creation of the supporting deities was commenced and only the creation of Agni was mentioned, while that of Indra and the others was not;

whereas here, having introduced ignorance, their creation is being described?"—the author replies: "Of this... The meaning is that he is explained with the intention of showing that [the self] is characterized by ignorance (avidyā), for the purpose of understanding the point that "the agency of the self is [merely] a functional designation. || 1595 ||
Indeed, the emission of fire was previously described for the purpose of the creation of the world's completion.
Since this is so, therefore every misfortune must be the effect of ignorance. || 1596 ||

One might object: "In that case, the creation of fire should also be mentioned right here, since there is no difference in its being an effect of ignorance. The word *hi* is used to indicate that this has already been shown at the time of explaining the passage on the creation of fire; it serves to highlight that the creation of fire ought to be mentioned.

The word "tu" (but). He states the consequence of the creation of Indra and others being of the nature of ignorance: "yataḥ" (since). The creation of Indra and the other gods should be examined in that very same place, because they are subordinate to it.
However, its detailed elaboration here is for the purpose of establishing the effects of ignorance. || 1597 ||

If it is argued that since the creation of Agni was mentioned there for the sake of completing Prajāpati’s creation, then the creation of Indra and the others must also be mentioned in that very place—otherwise, that creation would remain incomplete—the author says "Indra and the others" [in response]. The reason why the creation of Indra and the others is to be seen within the process of Prajāpati’s creation is because it is supplementary to it. Then, one might ask: why is what was already stated there being stated here again, resulting in redundancy? To this, he says: "of this very same meaning... [and so on].

In this regard, he recalls what was stated [previously]: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Nor should it be argued that, for the sake of establishing its being an effect of ignorance, the creation of fire should have been mentioned right here—just as the creation of Indra and others was—so that, after concluding the account of creation there, it might be said [later]; for if the creation of fire were not mentioned there either, then because there would be no inclusive term [to subsume it], its inclusion would be unestablished, resulting in the undesirable consequence that Prajāpati’s creation remains incomplete. And it is not the case that, having created Indra and the others there, one then creates fire there...

It should be understood that it is appropriate [to say] "let stability be perceived," because fire will be declared to be predominant, and thus it is proper for it to serve as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the others. || 1597 ||
That which was previously designated as the Creator of the world is indeed the Self itself.
Therefore, that which has Agni and the others as its presiding deities is designated here as "Brahman. (1598)

Having explained the connection between the preceding and following sections, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Brahman" (brahma). [The word] "Creator" (sraṣṭṛ): that which was denoted by the word "Self" (ātman) in the statement "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self," namely the Creator-Brahman, is referred to here by the word "Brahman" after having created fire—that is, as possessing the identification with the caste of the Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is that only that much had come into being prior to the creation of the Kṣatriyas and the other castes. || 1998 ||
For it was from that [Brahman], delimited by the single genus of Brahman, that [the world] first evolved.

He states the meaning of the phrase "one alone" as follows: "Brahman. Brahman, which is designated as the creator, is distinguished solely by the genus of being a Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning is "in front," that is, prior to the creation of the *kṣatra* and the other [castes]. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That was one" (*tadekam*) as follows: "Not manifold" (*nāneka*).

The construction is: since that Brahman, devoid of the *kṣatra* and the rest, was not capable of accomplishing the ritual action (*karman*) which has as its effects the various individual beings belonging to the many classes such as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, it therefore created the *kṣatra* and the others as its auxiliaries. || 1599 ||

The implication is that even the Bṛhaspatisava cannot be performed in the absence of protectors and others; thus, there must be the creation of the Kṣatriyas and so forth. Regarding the word "Brahman": the meaning is that on the plane of worldly activity, the greater strength of the *kṣatra* is established by experience. || 1603 ||
