Even if one is weak, by contending here against a king who is more powerful, [one meets with ruin].
He dares to conquer the king by relying on the strength of his own righteousness. || 1621 ||

He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "yathā" (just as): "by the stronger," etc. Here, "in the subject of dispute" means "while it exists"; likewise, the ellipsis is that the excellence of dharma is established elsewhere as well. || 1621 ||
For this very reason, form is declared to be superior to dharma.
For that [consciousness] consists of reality, whereas all other forms are not so. || 1622 ||

In that very context, he states another reason: "This," etc. The construction is as follows: since the form designated as *dharma* (the teaching) is of the nature of truth (*satya*), it is therefore superior to the fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth. The word *hi* is used for emphasis. One instance of the word *yataḥ* is a synonym for the word *ataḥ*. || 1622 ||
The mutual relationship of cause and effect belonging to this very nature of phenomena—
Having said, "That indeed is Dharma," the Śruti proceeded to speak.

Anticipating the objection—namely, that there is a distinction between the reality of *dharma*, *dharma* as a property of a person (*puruṣadharma*), and *dharma* as the nature of speech (*vacanadharma*)—the author introduces another statement beginning with "of that" (*tasya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Therefore, like clay and a jar, there is oneness between those two. || 1623 ||
This which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti is considered to have the characteristic of practical application (prayoga).
That should be known as the Dharma; truth is the defining characteristic of the meaning of the scriptures. || 1624 ||

The commentary beginning with "yathā" analyzes the intent of the [sūtra] regarding the exclusion of both [identity and difference], stating that "neither identity nor difference [is possible] for two things that are not known [to each other]. This is explained as follows: "In usage... (prayoga iti) || 1624 ||
Even if the meaning is followed through ninety-five syllables, if it is still doubted, then—
The ascertainment of that [object] arises from the cognition produced by constant application. || 1625 ||
754 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 460]

The action being performed, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, is *dharma*; one who performs a sacrifice is called a *dhārmika*. Since this is observed in the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), it does not deserve to be rejected. Having raised the doubt—namely, that if *dharma* is understood through scripture as being "truth" (*satya*) in terms of their distinct natures, how can there be identity between the two through a relationship of cause and effect—the author states that *dharma* is the cause of truth.

Regarding the word "akṣara": the meaning is that when there is doubt concerning the meaning of a treatise, certainty is reached through the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), as in the case of words such as *yava* and *varāha*; thus, the fact that Dharma has truth as its basis is established. || 1629 ||
And even when there is doubt regarding the application [of a word], it arises from relying on the knowledge of the sentence-meaning.
The wise person should thus dispel doubt regarding this mutual causality.

He states that truth is the cause for dharma: "Even in practice," etc. This means that when there is doubt regarding dharma, a determination is reached through the force of the scriptural meaning—just as by the exclusion of practices such as bowing to a caitya, one is directed toward the Agnihotra and other rites; thus, truth is the cause of dharma. He concludes what was stated in the two Vārtikas with the word "evam" (thus). || 1626 ||
So that the wise person may be able to explain [the text] by transcending the formal application.
On the other hand, another person is able to act by transgressing the scriptures in whatever way he pleases. || 1627 ||

It has been stated that the declaration of their being mutual causes signifies the identity of purpose between the Dharma and the Truth; now, to state another result in that very context, he provides an introductory transition with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). He states the reason for his capacity to explain the meaning of the scripture by overstepping established custom: "being of keen intellect" (*sudhīḥ*). He says "likewise" (*tathā*) to indicate that he explains the scriptural meaning even while bypassing its practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*). [He proceeds] disregarding the scripture—
He states that the cause for maintaining [the practice] during movement is as follows: "Now," etc. (1627).
In this world, disputants present even what is untrue as if it were true.
People skilled in the art of painting perceive both the level and the low as equal. || 1628 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to either state the meaning of the scriptures while transgressing the conduct of the learned, or to perform a practice while disregarding the scriptures, since these two are mutually contradictory? To this, he replies: "They are untrue," and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the state of mutual dispute. He states the reason for his skill in exposition therein: "of the disputants" (*vādinām*). Elsewhere too, the representation of something as being other than what it actually is is observed.
Thus he said: "Equal," [verse 1628].
But when the meaning of the treatise and its practical application are mutually dependent upon one another, [there is a logical flaw].
Then, not even the slightest negligence occurs on the part of the agent.

How, then, is there a restriction regarding knowledge (*jñāna*) and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), since in their absence the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) would not be accomplished? To this he says: "The meaning of the scripture" (*śāstrārtha*).
The sense is that when Dharma and Truth (*satya*) act as mutual restrictors, then no possibility of fault arises for either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the knower (*jñātṛ*). || 1629 ||
This which is proclaimed here in the context of creation should be known as "not-dharma" (nādharma).
Because it is incapable of the regulations pertaining to the Kṣatriya and other castes, and because its nature is insentient. || 1630 ||

In passages such as "that is the form of the excellent" (*tacchreyorūpam*), the word *dharma* refers to the well-known insentient entity called *apūrva*; now, however, [it does not]—[the text continues with the correction:
*na* instead of *tatra ca pha*, and *śāstrārthamu* instead of *śāstrārthamu*].
[Vol.
2, Page 461] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 755.

The intention behind that word [“dharma”] is not merely a property, but rather a regulating principle (*niyāmaka*) in the process of creation; moreover, an insentient entity lacks such capacity, and therefore it is not the previously mentioned property. Thus he says: “This is not [the case]. He states the reason for this: “Because of the Kṣatriya, etc. (1630).
But the presiding deity is she who possesses the conceit, "I am Dharma."
That very [nature] is created here by the Creator for the sake of restraint and for the attainment of perfection.

What, then, is denoted here by the word "dharma"? To this he replies: "The deity. The word "tu" (but/then) is intended to highlight the distinction of the deity from the aforementioned dharma. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is for the purpose of indicating its well-known status in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and the world. "Iha" (here) means for the sake of establishing the purpose known as "niyama" (regulation) within this creation. || 1631 ||
But it is held that the deity is considered to have form precisely by way of the nature of the Dharma itself.
In this way, by means of that name, there is the application of another deity to one who possesses that very name. (1632)

Now, one might object: "How can that which is devoid of name and form be the referent of the word 'dharma'? For there is no conscious entity (cetana) distinct from sound [i.e., the word], as there is no evidence for such; moreover, mantras and the like do not have their own literal meaning as their primary purport. To this, he says: "Of dharma" (dharmasya). Indeed, the nature of the deity was established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*;
and as for the "name and form" of the dharma you favor, they either exist or they do not—if they do not exist, then they must likewise exist in the deity who presides over it.
Let them be so; however, the point is that just as that [Self], which is devoid of name and so forth, is denoted by the word "dharma," it might likewise be so in the case of the deity.

Just as the word "dharma" denotes the deity, so too the words "Agni" and others may be applied to another deity, since the creation of the favoring [deities] is the subject under discussion here; thus he says: "In this way. 1632.
Therefore, there is only one deity, [though it appears diverse] due to limiting adjuncts such as name and form.
It appears as if multiform to those whose minds are dependent upon it. || 1633 ||

Is there unity or plurality among the deities that have been created? If the first [option], there would be no distinction in creation; if the second, there would be a loss of non-duality (advaita). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Only one. This means, according to such scriptural authority as "Being alone, my dear," and so forth. He states the resolution for the notion of difference: "By name. Furthermore, he says: "That," meaning that the cognition of difference belongs only to those who do not know reality, and not to others—namely, to that which is of the nature of Being (sadrūpa), the non-dual.
The third Brahman is the meaning of that word. || 1633 ||
6.1 The summary of the meaning as previously stated is intended for the purpose of explaining what follows.
Since it was not previously stated that [the result belongs] to the Brahmin, the subsequent Vedic scripture is for the purpose of stating that.

Having stated the intended meaning of the word *dharma*, he explains the purport of the passage beginning with "This is that Brahman" (*tadetad brahma*) by saying "as has been stated. If the conclusion regarding the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) is made here with the intention of stating a subsequent subject matter, then what is that subsequent subject matter intended?

To this he says: "Of the Brāhmaṇa. Since among the gods only the Kṣatriyas and others have been mentioned, [the author uses] the word "now" (*atha*) in the sense of "something else," as in the case of Agni...

The meaning is that although [the status of] being a Brāhmaṇa is mentioned in relation to him (the Śūdra) in those [passages], it is not explicitly stated regarding them (the sons of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya fathers); therefore, the scriptural passage beginning with "by that very fire" (*tadagninaiva*) exists for the purpose of declaring that [Brāhmaṇahood]. || 1634 ||
The distinction of the divine castes is also recognized among human beings.
This application of the phonemes has been stated according to their respective divisions. || 1635 ||
1 kha. *tasmād dha* | 2 kha. *bhāvaḥ* | [vol2, page 462] 766
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
He states another meaning of that Śruti passage with the words "Among the gods" (*daiva*). By the very mention of being born from Agni, the Brāhmaṇa is indicated among the gods;

among them, the Kṣatriya and others are stated as Indra and so forth. Thus, just as there is a distribution and connection of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others among the gods according to their respective divisions...

The meaning is that, having thus described the distribution of the colors associated with the gods, the connection of those [colors] to humans individually through that fire and so forth is now being stated. || 1635 ||
Because the Kṣatriyas and others have been mentioned previously, and because the Brāhmaṇa has not been mentioned.
When it is asked, "Who among these is a Brahmin?", there would be a supreme scriptural authority [to answer]. || 1636 ||

He elaborates on the first position—that it was not previously stated for the Brāhmaṇa—with the words "of the Kṣatriyas and others. The phrase "among these gods" is to be connected with both [the preceding and following clauses]. || 1636 ||
The classification of the deity based on the [four] castes has thus been fully explained.
The classification among humans based on that [distinction] is now being stated. || 1637 ||

He explains the second position [with the words] "of the deity," meaning that it is preceded by that [deity] and endowed with the divine classification of castes; the word "classification" refers to the castes—this is the ellipsis. || 1637 ||
That Brahman which existed unmodified among the gods and among men through Agni.
By the Brahmin, that very same [state] was [attained], which is indeed Brahman itself, by means of an unmodified self. || 1638 ||

He explains the sentence according to two alternative views: "That which [was] by means of Agni," etc. That Brahman, the creator, which remained unmodified in the form of the *kṣatra* and so forth, having created Agni among the gods, became identical with that; and that very same [Brahman], which, although modified in the form of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, remained unmodified in the form of the *kṣatra* and so forth, existed among humans as the *brāhmaṇa*, because it exists in its unmodified form alone as the state of Agni and Brahman among both gods and humans.

And it entered that very [state] in a dual form with a modified nature; the meaning is that, just as among the gods, so too among humans it became manifest in the form of the Kṣatriyas and others. || 1638 ||
The certainty is that whatever birth is designated as "Brahminhood" is indeed fire itself.
Abiding in the form of birth, it brings about birth itself. || 1639 ||

Is there a difference between fire and the Brāhmaṇa, or not? In the first case, it would be incorrect to say that Brahman, which is of the nature of fire, became the Brāhmaṇa-self. In the second case, the relationship of controller and controlled would be unestablished. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which is the genus... Anticipating the further question of how there can be a relationship of controller and controlled if there is non-difference, he explains that the state of being the controller exists in the form of the presiding deity (adhidevatā), while the state of being the controlled exists in the form of the individual self (adhyātma).
Having reflected, he said: "Born," etc. (1639).
The Brāhmaṇa is of the nature of Agni; therefore, due to that connection, he is mentioned in the Śruti.
Because the Brāhmaṇa possesses the power to bestow grace and to exercise control over the sacrificial fire. || 1640 ||

He states the evidence for the relationship between fire and the Brāhmaṇa as that of the controller and the controlled by saying, "The Āgneya. The word "and" (ca) is used to indicate that it is not merely a matter of fire and the Brāhmaṇa being the controller and the controlled, but also that they stand in the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary. Since the Brāhmaṇa possesses the power to bestow grace upon fire, it follows that, by virtue of this relationship of controller and controlled, and of benefactor and beneficiary, [the latter is superior] to the former.
The construction is: "Because of the connection, the Brāhmaṇa is indeed [connected] to Agni," as it is heard in the Śruti; thus it is so heard. || 1640 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 463] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.
Being constrained by destiny, he who has entered the human state is controlled by a kṣatriya.
Just as Ikṣvāku was formerly a Kṣatriya, so too was Uttara.

The scripture, through the statement "The Rājanya is [the son] of Indra," demonstrates that the relationship of controller and controlled exists between Indra and the Rājanya, just as it does between Agni and the Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding the phrase "being controlled": by the word "etcetera" (ādi), those who likewise initiated the other two lineages are included.
This indicates the birth of the human Vaiśyas and Śūdras who are controlled by the divine Vaiśyas and Śūdras, just as the human Kṣatriyas are controlled by the divine Kṣatriyas.
"Similarly," [it is said]. || 1641 ||
Because Brahman alone is unmodified, whereas the two preceding [states] are modifications.
Because he resorted to a Brahmin fire from among the Kṣatriyas and others,
there is here the complete attainment of desired goals for those performers of ritual action who possess longing.
Abiding here in the state of a Brahmin, those engaged in ritual action desire the world.

The abiding of the unmodified Brahman as Agni and others, and the modified Brahman as Indra and others, has been stated; now, he explains the fruit of the unmodified Brahman’s abiding in the form of Agni and others by stating the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore, in Agni... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.4]: "Brahman alone... Since Brahman, although modified in the form of space (ākāśa), remains unmodified in the form of the Kṣatriyas and so forth while abiding in Agni and the rest, it is likewise elsewhere.

The meaning is this: since [the elements] are indeed modified into the form of fire and so forth, therefore, while remaining here in the body under consideration, for those who possess desire regarding the results here—those who partake in actions impelled by that [desire] with respect to the conditions of fire and the Brāhmaṇa—the attainment of the desired object occurs through the power of the actions connected to them. Even in the world, having performed an action such as agriculture, one seeks its fruit; thus he says "here" (iha), meaning that the attainment of the desired object occurs through the medium of actions connected to fire and the like.
And the world here should be understood as the effect of karma, because it depends upon fire and other such elements.
The attainment of the other world is held to result solely from the cognition of the true nature of the inward self. || 1644 ||

1.1 Regarding the statement "the world," Bhartṛprapañca maintains that it is the primary designation for the Supreme Self; the author replies to him with the word "karma" (action), referring to what is under discussion.

It was stated [in the previous verse] that this applies to the mere statement. He states the reason for that: "agnyādi" (beginning with fire). The meaning is: because of the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) that [the attainment of Brahman] is to be accomplished through rites related to the fire-altar (*agni*) and the Brāhmaṇas. Even if the word "world" (*loka*) refers to the Supreme [Brahman], why could it not be accomplished by those [rites]? To this he says: "pratyak" (the inward-facing).
The word "mere" (*mātra*) is used to exclude [the attainment of] ritual results (*karman*) and so forth. || 1644 ||
This is evident from the examples of Ajātaśatru, Janaka, Sulabhā, and others.
Furthermore, because it arises from the domain of ignorance, worldly speech does not apply to the Supreme Self.

He states a scriptural indication (*liṅga*) for the fact that knowledge alone is the cause for attaining the Supreme: "Ajātā... (The unborn...). The meaning is that since liberation is heard in scripture to result from knowledge even for those such as Sulabha who were not performers of ritual action (*akarmin*), knowledge itself is the cause thereof. Alternatively, there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*) that liberation occurs only after performing rituals connected with the status of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth;
for it is observed among non-Brāhmaṇas and among those like Janaka who were knowers of reality despite being non-performers of ritual action. He says "Ajātā..."; the word "loka" [is used here].
Regarding the phrase "not here by another's word," he states another reason: "ignorance" (avidyā). This section concerns the cause of ignorance; therein, Indra... [text fragment].
[Vol. 2, page 464]
In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Chapter:
The meaning is that the word refers only to its specific [limited] object and cannot apply to the Supreme Self; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the context. (1645)
Because of the explanation of the indeterminate and because of his own intended meaning, [the view] is not accepted.
The other is concealed by the two forms of the indeterminate and the explanatory. || 1646 ||
Fearing that this word "world" (*loka*) might, according to your own view, refer only to the domain of the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*) and not according to the view of others, he says:

"The undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*). According to the intention of Bhartṛprapañca—who [interprets] the sūtra on ignorance beginning with "For this, indeed... (*taddhā*) and its explanation beginning with "Now, he who [worships another... (*atha yo 'nyām*)—this word "world" refers to the domain of the effects of ignorance even according to his view, not merely according to our own view. Thus it is established.

The meaning is "the goal. Anticipating the objection that even if the term *loka* refers to the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and its effects because it manifests them for another, this does not contradict the context concerning the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*), he says: "The unmanifest... (1646).
And because of the scriptural statement that [the self] is something entirely other than the manifested body and its negation. || 1647 ||
Because later on there is a qualification by its own term and by the word "world."
In this context, the word "world" (loka) refers precisely to the fruit of karmas.

How, then, is that manifestation [of the Supreme] established there? He says: "manifestation" (*āviṣkṛti*). He states the proof for the manifestation of the Supreme through the negation of cause and effect: "something else" (*anyat*). He provides another reason why the word "world" (*loka*) here refers to the fruit of karma:

"in the subsequent [passage]" (*uttaratra*). This means: "without having seen his own world," that is, without having realized it. This refers to the "world" known as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Here...
Therefore, the meaning is "in the passage beginning with 'tasmād agnau' (therefore, in the fire)," and so forth. || 1647 || 1148 ||
For [the term] "world" (loka) refers to that which is obtained in dependence upon the effects of karma.
By his own speech, he distinguishes his true self-nature from the world of non-self.

Anticipating the objection that "why should there not be a qualification even in the alternative view," he says: "By the word 'loka'. The meaning of the particle *hi* is that, as in one's own position, in the opponent's position as well, the qualification would be purposeless because there is no relevant object to be excluded. || 1649 ||
Because the non-self is not invariably associated with the nature of "mine," it is therefore not the self.
The qualifier would be purposeful for the sake of excluding the activity of karma. (1650)

Anticipating the objection as to how this [teaching] is meaningful by way of turning back the results of karma, he says: "By way of selfhood" (*svatvena*). Selfhood is the state of being the inner witness (*pratyaktva*); by that, the Self possesses non-deviation, because it is the inner witness of all things, whereas the non-Self is turned away from the effects of karma.
The meaning is that it is appropriate for a qualifier to be extremely clear in its non-deviation [from the subject] and to exclude the infinite [other instances]. || 1650 ||
Because renunciation is seen in the Veda for all three social classes as well.
This contradicts the Vedic scripture which states that renunciation belongs only to the Brāhmaṇa. || 1651 ||

By the author of the Bhāṣya, who asserts that the word *loka* occurring in the present passage denotes the fruit of action (*karmaphala*), it is stated that the fulfillment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is achieved for a Brāhmaṇa through the mere attainment of his caste. Now, one might object: "Even if prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is obtained from that alone based on such Smṛti texts as 'He shall indeed attain perfection through recitation alone,' how is the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) established from it? To this, the Bhāṣya replies: "Because renunciation (*pāritrājya*) is seen [to be prescribed] therein."
[Vol. 2, Page 465] 4 Brāhmaṇa. Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 759.

Is the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" unintended (*avivakṣita*) or intended (*vivakṣita*)? In the first case, if the human goal were accomplished by that alone, this [reasoning] would not be a valid cause; if it is the second case—
He says: "Of three. This means, as it occurs in the Śruti, in passages such as "having completed the period of studentship" (brahmacaryaṃ samāpya), and so forth. || 1651 ||
And a mark that is devoid of logical justification is not fit for establishing validity.
Therefore, by the power of what was spoken by the Brahmin, the desired object is not accomplished.

— [Objection: Is it not the case that, by the force of the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" in the statement "Brāhmaṇas go forth," the general scriptural injunction is restricted to that specific subject? [Reply: He says "no," adding "and because of the indicative mark (liṅga). The meaning of this is: although the indicative mark is stronger than the general scriptural injunction, nevertheless, since it is subordinate to another...

The semantic power of the words within the sentence is not an authority in the absence of that reasoning, because it would contradict the general injunction, "One should go forth from the stage of studentship itself.

Furthermore, it is illogical for the nature of the subject (*prakṛti*) to undergo a change; for although a Kṣatriya is by nature active due to his *rājasa* quality, while renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) consists of tranquility, nevertheless, one does not possess *rājasa* quality merely by virtue of being a Kṣatriya, as this is absent in Janaka and others, and is even found in some Brāhmaṇas.

And because that [state] does not exist, such practices are not seen among the cultured (*śiṣṭa*), for your view leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to know the non-perception of all [practices]. Furthermore, even a Kṣatriya’s determination to take up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is seen in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Therefore, for one day at a time, under each individual tree..."
Wandering for alms, shaven-headed, I, a sage, shall traverse this earth.
Covered with dust, dwelling in an empty house or having his abode at the foot of a tree, he has abandoned all that is pleasant and unpleasant.
"And all those elders of the city who dwell there and depend upon us must be propitiated and told: 'Pāṇḍu has gone forth as a wanderer in the forest.'"

Therefore, the commentary [which claims] that because every member of the three higher castes who is dispassionate has the qualification for renunciation and because the state of wandering mendicancy is observed [in the scriptures], is meaningless. || 1652 ||
Or rather, that mention of "Brahmins" in the Veda should be understood as an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
Because the Brahmin is the primary subject, it is appropriate that he serves as the defining characteristic.

Having stated that a sign (liṅga) devoid of logical justification is sublated by a general scriptural statement (sāmānya-śruti), he says that in the passage "Brāhmaṇas wander for alms," the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), just as in the case of "Brāhmaṇas desire to know.
He states the reason for this with the words "of the Brāhmaṇa. [Objection: In that case, since even a Śūdra would be indicated by the mention of "Brāhmaṇa," just like a Kṣatriya or others...

It might be argued that renunciation (pārivrājya) is possible for a Śūdra, on the grounds that he should perform a tonsure including the top-knot (saśikha-vapana) and then discard the sacred thread (bahiḥ-sūtra). However, this is untenable because he lacks the qualification to discard the sacred thread preceded by the discarding of the top-knot; furthermore, since it is impossible to discard what does not yet exist, the top-knot and so forth cannot be discarded at the outset. Moreover, in the section concerning the Śūdra, those who refute his eligibility for knowledge through the medium of the Vedas also refute his eligibility for Vedic renunciation (vaidika-saṃnyāsa).

It should be understood from the word "darśanāt" (from the observation). By one who refutes the commentary concerning renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), the primacy of the Brāhmaṇas was asserted; relying on that alone [it is said]:

"This dharma, which is the wearing of the insignia of Viṣṇu, belongs to those born from the mouth. This is not the dharma for those born from the arms or those born from the thighs. [Kūrma Purāṇa 1.30.1]

It is said, "therefore"; and because of the qualification "eternal" (*sanātana*) applied to the Brahmin, it is understood that his state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is permitted as non-eternal. || 1653 ||
Even the attainment of the self-nature of a Brahmin that might occur for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—
By its own power, that [fire] does not [burn], due to its reliance on the Brahmin. || 1654 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the Brāhmaṇa does not have primacy, since the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood is heard of [as occurring] for the other two as well in the sacrifice? To this, he says: "brāhmaṇatve" (regarding Brāhmaṇahood). The connection is: even the attainment of that [status] by those two would not occur through their own power. If so, how is that attained by them? To this, he says: "agnī" (the fires), etc. 1654.
For indeed, without relying upon a Brahmin, one cannot be the cause for the Rājasūya and other such sacrifices.
The connection with Brahminhood is primary; therefore, it [is mentioned] first in the two preceding cases. (1655)

If it is argued that, even without depending on a Brāhmaṇa or others, the king and so forth would obtain that [result] through the very power of the Rājasūya and other sacrifices, he says "no," stating:
"The Brāhmaṇa. The mention of him is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for Agni as well; this refers to the two preceding cases of Agni and the Brāhmaṇa. || 1655 ||
There is a dependence on another color in the case of fire and a Brahmin, but not so in their actual nature.
The Brahmin attains the goals of human existence by his own greatness alone.

If it is argued that because the Kṣatriya and others depend upon him, they lack primacy, and since the Brāhmaṇa and others likewise depend upon them, their lack of primacy is equal—[the author] says "no," [introducing the verse] with the words "varṇāntara... (in other castes). The meaning is that while the Kṣatriya and others require others for the sake of attaining Brāhmaṇahood, the Brāhmaṇas do not require others for that purpose. He states the fruit of declaring his primacy in the words "brāhmaṇaḥ" (the Brāhmaṇa). || 1656 ||
The reason for the preeminence of the foremost Brahmin is clearly stated.
For from these two very forms, Brahmā himself came into being.
With these two [verses], he takes up [the topic] with the words "Agni... and so forth. The qualification "clearly" (*sphuṭa*) is used in order to state that there is no fault in the reason (*hetu*).

He explains the reason with the words "with these two. The meaning is that since Brahman itself, remaining unmodified, became [manifest] through these two forms—namely, Agni and the Brāhmaṇa—therefore they possess preeminence. || 1657 ||
Because in ancient times, Brahman itself directly manifested as both fire and the Brāhmaṇa.
The predominance of the latter two [types of] *vikṣepa* (distraction) is mediated; by that [fact], it applies to the former two as well. (1658)
Having raised the doubt as to how the Kṣatriya and other orders can have that [Brahman] as their primary essence even though the unmodified Brahman exists in both, he says:

"Agni," etc. The meaning is: without undergoing a direct transformation into a modification. For it has been stated that for Brahman, which is devoid of transformation into a modification, there [in those cases]—

"Vasthānam" means previously, that is to say, prior to the creation of the Kṣatriyas and others; the ellipsis is "interrupted by Agni and the Brāhmaṇas," meaning [prior to] the two preceding ones, Agni and the Brāhmaṇas. || 1698 ||
In this context, the word "Brahman" should be understood as referring to the genus (jāti) alone, and not to the supreme syllable (parākṣara).
Because it is the cause of everything, the assertion of a [further] cause for it is difficult to establish. (1659)

Regarding the phrase "by these two," he refutes the view of Bhartṛprapañca, who asserts that "Brahman is indeed supreme. He does so by stating "Brahman" [is not the Supreme]. The reason why the word "Brahman" in this passage does not refer to the Supreme Brahman is as follows: after creating fire, the being who has entered it—the Brahman known as the *sūtra* (the thread) characterized by the ego-consciousness (*abhimāna*) of a Brāhmaṇa—is what is denoted here by the word "Brahman. Thus, it is not the Supreme.

He says: "Because it is the cause of that. If the word *brahman* were here intended to refer to the Supreme (Brahman), then the statement beginning with "by these two," which provides the reason for the predominance of the Brāhmaṇa and others, would be untenable; for since the Supreme is the cause of all and the self of all, there would be no distinction in its remaining as the very self of the fire and the Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is: "because of the absence of a logical reason" (hetvabhāvāt). || 1659 ||
Because [the Self] is the inner self of all, even partiality is not admitted.
Because [the worship] of Agni, the Brāhmaṇa, and Viṣṇu is completed by that much alone. || 1660 ||

Nevertheless, suspecting that it might be considered primary due to its partiality toward that [one side], he says: "Of all. Since partiality is impossible, he states another reason for its presence as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) everywhere: "Of Viṣṇu. He clarifies the meaning of the first quarter-verse: "Only that much. Alternatively, because everything is fully contained within the Supreme Self alone at the time of dissolution, there is no [need for] His...
He states that there is no establishment of partiality in any case whatsoever: "only that much" (tāvanmātra). || 1660 ||
"Brahman alone is this universe"—this is the direct teaching of the Veda.
And the teaching of the Smṛti states: "One who is endowed with learning and humility. || 1661 ||

He states the authority for the fact that everything is nothing but Brahman: "Brahman... He uses the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) to state that the validity of scripture is independent, like perception. Anticipating the objection that if everything is Brahman, then Brahman would be subject to inequality just as everything else is, he says: "Knowledge... For the wise, the reality of the Self is equal and indeed devoid of distinctions among all limiting adjuncts—whether superior, inferior, or middling.
The meaning is "they see. || 1661 ||
Just as in the case of a Kṣatriya and others, a transformation of the visual perception [of fire] is observed equally in the case of fire and a Brahmin.
The nature of being the true cause is equal for the elements, such as fire, water, and food.

Now, you might object: "Is it not the case that a distinction is intended by you, such that fire and the Brāhmaṇa are unmodified [in their respective origins], while they are modified elsewhere? How then can there be an absence of partiality? To this, he says: "In the Kṣatriya and so forth. The attainment of the state of fire and the Brāhmaṇa by the Supreme is held to occur precisely through the medium of modifications such as ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest;

thus, the modification is equal there as well, just as in the case of the Kṣatriya and others. For, although He exists in the form of the Kṣatriya and so forth after having been modified into that form, He does not exist *as* that [limited] self.

The meaning is that by the phrase "of the modified [form] in fire and so forth," there is a statement of the distinction between being modified and unmodified. Since all things are Brahman, the Śruti and Smṛti have been cited previously; now he states the logical justification for this: "Fire... Because the elements and their derivatives are effects of Being (sat), they share the same nature as it, according to such Śruti passages as, "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root. Furthermore, the effect does not originate from anything other than its cause, as established in the section on "Origin" (Ārambhaṇa-adhikaraṇa).
Because of the contradiction with the instruments of cognition, the meaning is that therefore everything is merely the existent Brahman. || 1662 ||
Brahman is directly established in the form of fire and the Brāhmaṇa.
"The causality of fire and so forth in the attainment of that [result]"—this is the speech of one devoid of shame. (1663)

By examining the statement regarding the cause, it was said that Brahman is not "supreme" (para). Furthermore, if one were to grasp [the term] as "Brahman is right here," then that very [Brahman] exists without any intervention in the form of the Brāhmaṇa and so forth; and for the attainment of that, ritual action connected with fire and the like is not the cause. This is because, since it has already been attained in the nature of the fire and the Brāhmaṇa, there can be no destruction of an intervention if it is a real entity, and if it is not a real entity, its destruction occurs through knowledge alone. With this in mind, he says: "Agni... etc.
A shameless disputant is one who, being devoid of modesty, speaks in contradiction to himself. || 1663 ||
1. ga. satattvataḥ | 2. ka. cātra brauṃ | 96 [vol2, page 468]
This creation of the castes, stages of life, and so forth, is traditionally held to be for the sake of ritual action (*karman*) by Brahmā.
And the action known as *dharma* should be understood as that which governs its own specific domain.

(1664) He states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument to be refuted by the subsequent passage beginning with "atha" and so forth, starting with the word "varṇa. By the word "ādi," his duty (*dharma*), as well as other effects consisting of the elements and elemental products, are denoted. "From Brahman" indicates the source (*apādāna*) of the creation; [the phrase] "of Brahman" refers to the Brāhmaṇa.

Or rather, the agent of the action is pointed out; the meaning is that it is remembered by those learned in the scriptures as being connected [to the action] through the absence of other causes, such as the performance of ritual acts. Anticipating the objection that this [agent] might be insentient and thus ineffective, he says: "Dharma... [etc. Because of its role as a regulator for those persons who possess an entitlement (*adhikāra*)—that is, a connection to their own action by way of ownership—it is indeed a conscious deity that acts as the regulator.
The meaning is that what is called "dharma" is designated by the term "action. || 1664 ||
By that very same action, we shall attain eternal liberation.
Even without knowing the supreme reality, when [this state] has been attained, there is the supreme Vedic revelation.

Having established that the aforementioned action is a means to the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), he states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). He excludes secondary liberation by saying "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*). Now, one might ask: why is this limit set, given that knowledge (*jñāna*) could also be a cause for it? To this he replies:

He qualifies [the statement] with "without knowing" (*ajñātvā*) in order to refute the possibility of a combination (*samuccaya*). The meaning is that in such Smṛti passages as "By action alone, indeed, is perfection attained," it is understood that action by itself is the means for attaining liberation, which is designated by the term "perfection. He introduces the subsequent sentence as a refutation of the position that action endowed with the qualities of the deity is the cause of liberation: "In this way... (1665).
O bearer of oblations, you are the controller and the conceited one regarding the state of being a Brahmin.
Karma alone would be indeterminate, as would the deity of karma. || 1666 ||

He states the position set forth by Bhartṛprapañca, which is to be refuted by the passage beginning with "Now," etc.: "The controller," etc. The term "the conceiving one" (abhimantṛ) is stated as the favoring agent. The two *ca*s have the sense of mutual conjunction between those two. He states that even for that [conceiving one], there is a controller, namely action presided over by a deity: "Action," etc. The word "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of excluding other controllers of the same class. What, then, is the controller of action?
Thus he says: "Of action" (karmaṇaḥ). || 1666 ||
It might be argued that Agni alone will lead him to the state of Brahman.
Moreover, that [cognition] is not at all possible if the reality of the self has not been perceived. || 1667 ||
"Let it be that there is a relationship of the regulated and the regulator between those two; nevertheless, what is established by this? To this he says: "This might be so," etc.
He states the conclusion reached by the commentary: "By fire alone as the deity, one attains Brahman; He Himself will lead him to Brahman. This means:
"He will lead"—that is, cause to reach—"this performer of ritual action. Just like the deity, knowledge also is a cause for attaining Brahman.

Anticipating this objection, he qualifies the performer of ritual action by saying "adṛṣṭa" (unseen). The meaning is: if a deity endowed with the qualities of ritual action can be the cause of liberation, what is the need for knowledge? He indicates the opponent's established position by saying "tacceti" (and that). The meaning is: the subsequent statement is intended to refute the view that a deity possessing the qualities of ritual action is the cause of liberation. This is done in order to provide an illustrative example for the opinion that ritual action characterized by the qualities of a deity is the cause of liberation.
The word "ca" (and) [is used]. || 1667 ||
They explain the subsequent portion of the text preceded by such a connection.
There is no difference in the result here; therefore, it exists in both ways.

He concludes the connection stated previously with the words "they explain. Anticipating the doubt, "Which one then is better?", he says, "Neither. The meaning is that since there is no difference between the two positions regarding the fruit of knowledge—liberation—and regarding the objections and their resolutions, both positions are logically sound. || 1668 ||
Liberation does not come through ritual action, nor even by taking refuge in fire.
"But liberation comes from knowledge alone; it does not exist through ignorance alone.
(1669) By means of the words beginning with "na," he demonstrates the intended meaning of the statement as introduced according to both systems, showing the consistency of both.
He asks: "If liberation is not attained through ritual action or through a deity, then how is it accomplished? To this, he replies: "From knowledge."

He states the reason for this restriction, which was indicated by the word "tu" (but): "from ignorance" (*ajñānāt*). Liberation is abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpasthiti*); that [abiding] appears as something unreal due to ignorance, and it is removed solely by knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that liberation is dependent upon knowledge alone. || 1669 ||
The word "atha" (now/then) is employed here in order to dispel any apprehension.
The word "havā" is used for the sake of common renown; liberation does not arise from anything other than knowledge.

Raising the objection that since meanings such as "immediacy following" (*ānantarya*) and so forth—which are the conventional senses of the word *atha*—have no place here, what is the purpose of the word *atha*, [the author] states the meaning of *atha* by resorting to the fact that particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings. He says: "The suspected... Having stated the well-known meanings of the two particles, he clarifies them with: "Indeed (*ha vai*). It is well-established in scripture that liberation comes from knowledge alone, not from ritual action.
This is the meaning. || 1670 ||
Even after completing all his ritual actions, he remains excluded from the knowledge of reality.
One does not attain liberation at all from knowledge alone, for that [liberation] arises from that very [source]. || 1671 ||

Although each individual action is not a cause for liberation, one might suspect that all actions are likewise so; anticipating this, the author says "action" with the intention that such [a collective performance] is difficult to carry out.
The reason for this is given as "from knowledge. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate what is well-known from scripture. || 1671 ||
The union with ignorance, through missiles, funeral cakes, and so forth, extends as far as Viriñca.
To exclude that [opposite view], it is stated: "one's own world. || 1672 ||

Regarding the phrase "one's own world" (*svaṃ lokaṃ*), he explains the function of the word *sva* (own) with the words "by means of the weapons" (*astraiḥ*). It refers to the cessation of that connection characterized by the notions of "I" and "mine" which exists between the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the non-self entities— beginning from Hiraṇyagarbha down to the trees— consisting of the body, senses, and so forth.

He states the means of attainment for the sake of [establishing] fitness: "by ignorance" (avidyayā). He says that the qualification is for the purpose of excluding the worlds that are the fruits of karma:
For the ignorant, death occurs as a merging into the causal self.
But for the wise, the cessation of darkness through knowledge constitutes death.
1 kha. By means of sound, *mūṃ*.
[vol2, page 470] 764

In order to introduce the passage beginning with "asmāt" (from this), Sureśvarācārya states the distinction between the death of the wise and the death of the ignorant. Regarding the word "ajñāninaḥ" (the ignorant): the word "tu" (but) serves to indicate the specific difference between the death of the wise and the death of the ignorant. || 1673 ||
For one who does not fully understand death, death after death is a state of darkness.
It is taught that [the soul] departs from this world for the sake of attaining death for one who is ignorant. || 1674 ||

He explains the death of the ignorant person with the words "of death" (*mṛtyoḥ*). The meaning is that death is ignorance; the Self, which has ascended to the state of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is the witness (*dṛk*). Due to ignorance of that [Self], there is contact with darkness; this is what is meant by "the death of the ignorant. He states that the sentence beginning with "from this world" (*asmāl lokāt*) is intended to illustrate the aforementioned death of the ignorant person.
Thus he says: "The ignorant... (verse 1674).
Without knowing the Supreme God, [they perceive] things as having the nature of coming and going.
That man who dies helplessly from this body and world, which are devoid of intrinsic nature; || 1675 ||

Having explained the words, he now explains the sentence: "Not having known," etc. For one who, without knowing the Supreme Self as the ultimate Self, has instead grasped as the Self that world which is in reality non-Self because it is subject to birth and destruction—
He dies while still possessed of human pride; the meaning is that, being under the sway of ignorance, he would remain subject to it. || 1675 ||
That supreme [state], whose true nature is unknown, does not benefit one who knows it.
By bestowing the fruit of isolation (kaivalya), even though he is the inner self (pratyagātman), he is yet the Supreme (para). || 1676 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the Supreme Self alone will protect the person by granting liberation, why would this person who has cast off the body remain subject to the power of ignorance?

Anticipating this doubt, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa enam" (He [the Lord] protects him) as follows: "ajñāteti" (because it is unknown). For it is only when the Supreme is known that He becomes the cause of liberation.

It has been stated that [the Self] is well-known from the Śruti and Smṛti. Anticipating the objection that "the Supreme does not protect it because it is not the Self and because it is unknown," he says: "The innermost... (1676).
Since it is established merely by seeing that, it is not obtained through anything else.
Because it is merely an obstacle consisting of delusion, that action is not sufficient for liberation.

How can one who does not know [this] protect himself quickly? For it is not a fixed rule that knowledge of that [Self] is the means to liberation; therefore, he says: "taddṛṣṭi" (the vision of That). The second word "tat" (That) refers to liberation through knowledge (*vidyā*). He states the reason why liberation is established merely by the cognition of the Supreme Self: "moha" (delusion). [Objection: Since the destruction of that [delusion] could also occur through ritual action (*karman*), how is it not obtained from something else? To this he replies: "tat" (that). For ritual action is not [the cause of the destruction of delusion].
The meaning is that it does not destroy [the cognition], because there is no contradiction between them. || 1677 ||
Just as there can be no grasping of the Veda without its formal study, [so too there is no realization of Brahman without the grace of the Guru].
Furthermore, other actions such as agriculture, if not performed, are not capable of yielding fruit. (1678)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) by saying "of the Veda" (*vedasya*). For it was established in the *Dharmajijñāsā* Sūtra that "without study, the acquisition of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic text) would not be purposeful. He explains the passage beginning with "or something else" (*anyad vā*) by saying "agriculture and so forth" (*kṛṣyādi*). The connection is: "that which is unperformed would not lead to a fruit. He states the application to the subject at hand (*dāṣṭantika*) by saying "action" (*karman*). Regarding the point "it does not protect when unknown," the first [case]...
The meaning here is that the second example serves to distinguish [the case] wherein karma is not the cause of liberation. || 1678 ||
I shall perform abundant ritual action for the sake of attaining the infinity of its fruit.
Because the power of karma is inconceivable, even this [objection] is not tenable. || 1679 ||

He states the objection to be refuted by the passage beginning with "yadiha" (if here). [The word] "bhūri" (abundant) refers to this. He states the reason for the imperishability of the fruit of great rites such as the Aśvamedha:
"of action" (karmaṇaḥ). He introduces the passage beginning with "yadiha" as a response: "not so" (naivam). || 1679 ||
If, indeed, one whose true nature of the self is unknown [remains so] day and night...
One might perform great auspicious karma for thousands of millions of eons.
That too, being of such a nature, perishes moment by moment because it is finite.
It inevitably undergoes destruction through decay, like a storehouse and the like. || 1681 ||

He explains that [state] as "not being known" (*aprajñātā*). Even if one who is ignorant performs great auspicious acts such as the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice for an infinite duration of time—day and night—one might indeed perform them according to the maxim: "Who indeed would prevent an ignorant person? However, because that karma, despite its greatness and specific qualities, is subject to exhaustion through the enjoyment of its fruits at every moment, it is finite and thus comes to an end. Therefore, if liberation were achievable through karma— [The text continues: ...it would be perishable. Hence, it is said: "That which is not known. Since liberation is imperishable, it cannot be accomplished by karma. Furthermore, the word "known" (*prajñātā*) refers to the realization of Brahman; therefore, it is stated that liberation is attained through knowledge alone. Thus, the meaning is that liberation is not something to be produced, but rather something already existing that is merely revealed. This is further explained by the statement: "By what means can one know that which is unborn, undecaying, eternal, and unchanging? For that which is unborn, undecaying, eternal, and unchanging cannot be produced by any means whatsoever. Moreover, since liberation is of the nature of the Self, it is not something to be produced. If it were produced, it would be non-eternal, like a jar. But liberation is eternal; therefore, it is not produced. Consequently, it is established that liberation is not something to be produced. Furthermore, if liberation were produced, it would be dependent on causes and conditions, and thus it would be impermanent. But liberation is eternal; therefore, it is not produced. Hence, it is concluded that liberation is not something to be produced. Moreover, if liberation were produced, it would be subject to destruction, like a jar. But liberation is indestructible; therefore, it is not produced. Thus, it is established that liberation is not something to be produced. Furthermore, if liberation were produced, it would be a created entity, like a jar. But liberation is not a created entity; therefore, it is not produced. Consequently, it is established that liberation is not something to be produced. Moreover, if liberation were produced, it would be a result of action, like a jar. Following the dissolution of the two bodies, for one who has attained the state of the individual soul (jīva) within the Supreme Self, having transcended all that is to be experienced (*bhojya*)— [The text continues: ...having transcended even all that is to be experienced... Since the obscuration [of the Self] arises merely from ignorance regarding the Pure One (Sita), the state situated between the supreme goal to be attained and [the removal of that obscuration], by means of the destruction of desire and so forth, is the fruit of the initial combination; such is the meaning. || 1712 || 1713 ||
1. ka. ga. *uktastatrātmā* | 2. ka. ga. *babhuktabhogatvāt* | 3. ka. ga. *karaṇam* | [vol2, page 477] 4. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 771.
But here, you have stated that immortality itself results from knowledge and action.
For it is stated: "His karma is not exhausted," and also, "Precisely because of this. || 1714 ||

Nevertheless, raising the objection as to how there can be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he states the opponent's argument regarding the passage "the Self" in the words "But here... (1714).
A contradiction between your preceding and subsequent statements would follow for you.
Now, even if the second [alternative] is accepted, it is not tenable in that way either. || 1715 ||

In passages such as "What indeed is this? (*kimenam*), it is stated that the fruit of the first collective practice (*samuccaya*) is the state of abiding in the intermediate stage through the destruction of desire and the like. However, in the passage "himself alone" (*ātmānam eva*), the fruit is said to be the non-destruction of desire and so forth, because his karma is not exhausted and from this very Self he creates whatever he desires. Therefore, in your interpretation, what is the connection between the previously mentioned [passage] beginning with "himself alone" and the subsequently mentioned [passage] beginning with "what indeed is this"?

He states the conclusion: "There would be a contradiction with [the word] *tyādi*," etc., namely, with the word *pūrva*. Having stated the contradiction regarding the first sense of *ātmanam* (in the phrase *ātmānam*), he repeats it in order to state that same contradiction regarding the second sense as well: "Now (*atha*)," etc. He says: "No," because even by the second method, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) in this sentence is not established due to the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. || 1715 ||
But you yourself have explained the fruit of the second [type of] conjunction.
Through the cognition of both duality and unity, one transcends death, which is characterized by desire and action.
Having crossed over by means of the knowledge of the Self, the wise one attains immortality.

In order to state that very point, he declares the result of the second conjunction mentioned by others, beginning with "the result. He demonstrates the explanation itself with the words "duality," etc. Through the meditation on the Sūtra, the destruction of desire and so forth is the result; however, through the knowledge of the Self—that is, through the meditation on the state of non-duality—the result is immortality.
The meaning is that this has been stated in such passages as "Thou art knowledge and ignorance" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1). || 1716 || 1717 ||
His karma is never exhausted; whatever he desires from the Imperishable, that he attains.
There is a contradiction between the preceding and following statements regarding "he created this and that. (1718)

Regarding the phrase "the self," however, he says "not so" (*na ha*) and so forth, stating that through these two sentences, the result of the second conjunction is the non-destruction of desire and the like. Therefore, in your position, there is a contradiction between the statement of the result of the second conjunction and the [simultaneous] destruction and non-destruction of desire and the like.
He states the resulting conclusion—that there is mutual contradiction between the two opposing statements—by saying: "Of the two utterances" (uktyoḥ). || 1718 ||
For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of the exhaustion of desire and action is immortality.
"When all are completely liberated"—thus it is heard many times in the Śruti.
He states that for one who asserts that desire and karma do not perish, there is not only an internal contradiction between earlier and later statements, but also a contradiction with the Śruti.

He says: "Desire... and so on. The implication is that for one who claims that desire and the rest do not perish in liberation (mokṣa), there would be a contradiction with numerous scriptures (āgama). The phrase "in many ways" was used to show that the purport of the Śrutis is that liberation occurs through the destruction of desire and the like. || 1719 ||
How does he attain absolute liberation when desire and action have not been exhausted?
And when isolation (kaivalya) has been attained, how can the preservation of those two be asserted? || 1720 ||
772 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter— ] [vol2, page 478]

Having stated the contradiction with common sense (*māna-virodha*), he states the contradiction with logic (*nyāya-virodha*) regarding the second type of conjunction (*samuccaya-phala*). He asks: "How? The meaning is that desire and action lead to *saṃsāra*, while its cessation leads to liberation (*mokṣa*); thus, the two are mutually contradictory. || 1720 ||
Moreover, from this [point of view], there is a clear contradiction; the knowledge of Brahman is contradicted.
It has been stated that [this occurs] by virtue of making a vow, through the act of carrying out the commands of the deities. || 1721 ||

He states another defect regarding the combination of rites such as the recitation of the Sūtras with knowledge. [The phrase] "for this reason also" (itaśca) introduces this. To clarify that very point, he recalls what was stated by the opponent—which others have accepted as the final conclusion—beginning with "Brahman. This means that because it functions as a command to the deity, it refers to the performance of ritual action. He says that if there were a combination of these two, there would be a contradiction because of its being deposited with excellence and remaining exactly so; thus, [the word] "praṇi-"...
"By means of holding," [it is said]. || 1721 ||
For one who perceives this action, along with its means, as being of the nature of Brahman.
How is it that this very knowledge of Brahman is not contradicted here? || 1722 ||

As for the statement beginning with "that which is manifest is accompanied by its means," it follows this: "accompanied by its means. Here, as long as karma remains unexhausted, knowledge is indeed opposed; therefore, he says that their coexistence is impossible, like that of cold and heat: "That very [knowledge]," etc. (1722).
Having first performed that action, one subsequently beholds it as the Brahman-self.
If it is thought that, having emerged from all ritual action, there is a hope for liberation; || 1723 ||

He raises an objection regarding the reconciliation of these two [views] with the words "pūrvam" (previously). The connection is as follows: if one first performs action and later perceives that very action as the Self, then, having desisted from all action, one is liberated by knowledge alone; such is the view that hopes for liberation. || 1723 ||
Even when it is argued in this manner, there can be no liberation from karma.
Because liberation from karmas is accepted as occurring only for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption]. || 1724 ||
Having accepted the absence of contradiction, he refutes [the opponent's position] with the word "thus" (*evam*). By the locative case, the conjunction is qualified;

that is to say, from knowledge conjoined with that [action]. He states the reason for this: "of one who has emerged" (*vyutthitasya*). This means because of the acceptance of liberation—that is, because of the existence of the acceptance of liberation. || 1724 ||
Now, this very person, while in the state of a householder and at the time of performing ritual action, possesses a divided mind.
Then, having performed an action, one will understand that the action for its pacification is Brahman.
Establishing that action (*karman*) is the cause for that [purification], he raises an objection with the word "Now" (*atha*). The meaning is as follows:

this person entitled to perform action, while possessing the cognition of agency and so forth at the time of performing action, performs it; then, through the power of that [action], once his intellect is purified, he remains in the householder stage and perceives action as Brahman; therefore, action possesses the quality of being a cause for liberation together with knowledge. || 1725 ||
For one who concentrates in this manner, the desired object is not accomplished.
Since for a living being whose death is dependent on another, liberation would be merely occasional. || 1726 ||
He refutes the claim that action is the cause of liberation by stating, "In this way," for if it were so, that very liberation would not exist. How?

Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* by Ānandagiri. 773.

Regarding the non-attainment of liberation for one who has perished, he says: "Dependent on another. Therefore, the remainder is that there is no attainment of the fixed fruit of knowledge. || 1726 ||
If, perceiving duality, a man dies, he will certainly remain bound.
Perceiving that action is Brahman, one becomes one with the immortal Brahman.
Anticipating the objection that if liberation were uncertain due to the lack of a fixed time for death, the same would apply to your own position as well, he says:

"The difference," etc. At the time of ritual action, there is the notion of an agent and so forth; if one dies while in such a state, one would remain a transmigrator simply because of the absence of knowledge. On the other hand, if one dies while perceiving that "Brahman is the ritual action along with its means," one would become Brahman. Thus, the contingency [of the result] remains. However, this fault is not equal [in our view], because liberation is necessarily determined by knowledge alone.

And because liberation results from their combination, the sense is that even for the opponent there is a restriction [regarding the means], since that [liberation] is not possible otherwise. || 1727 ||
Because the perception of difference is more powerful, and because it is innate.
Moreover, because it would still have to be brought about by desire, even then there would be no final liberation (nirvṛti).
The possibility of liberation for a householder has been stated; now, [the author] determines its absence for him. Regarding the verse beginning with *bhedā* (difference):

because the vision of Brahman is more powerful by virtue of the natural tendency toward the perception of difference such as "I am the agent," and because it is easier to achieve through will, whereas the other [vision of difference] lacks that [power], the meaning is that liberation would certainly not occur during the stage of a householder. The particle *api* is used for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). || 1728 ||
If, while performing action itself, one perceives that action is Brahman;
By acting as an executor of the gods' commands, the knowledge of Brahman is obstructed. || 1729 ||
Thus, your statement would be contradicted by the inconsistency between what precedes and what follows.
Even ritual action, when performed with knowledge that has discarded the deity and abandoned the sacrificial substance, is difficult to accomplish.

He raises the objection that liberation is easily attained because, like action, knowledge also belongs to him, by the words "performing" (*kurvāṇa*). He refutes this with the defect already stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), using the words "deity" (*devatā*). The meaning is that the statement made by the proponent of the previous view brings contradiction even to your own position; for, since it was not previously rejected, it establishes a subsequent conjunction (*samuccaya*) [of action and knowledge]. Thus, it was stated that there is no liberation for the agent of ritual action due to the absence of knowledge.

If it is argued that liberation does not result from the mere absence of action because that [absence] alone is not desired, he says: "apāsta... (it is discarded). The literal meaning is as follows: even when there is knowledge, action remains for the ritualist; however, for the knower, action is difficult to accomplish, since knowledge destroys [the notions of] deities and so forth. || 1729 || 1730 ||
Because it is necessarily determined by the very vision that abandons the distinctions of substances and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that ritual acts such as sacrifices are improper.
The contemplation that "this action, together with its means, is indeed Brahman."
In some cases, action (karma) is well-known in both the world and in the Veda. || 1732 ||

He states the reason why there is no action in the absence of an agent and so forth: "Abandoned," etc. He states the conclusion regarding the impossibility of the coexistence of knowledge and action: "Therefore," etc. Anticipating the objection that some kind of action might coexist with knowledge even without depending on an agent and so forth, he says: "Of such a kind," etc. The phrase "somewhere" refers to a difference in location in both cases. (1731, 1732)
1. By her. [Vol. 2, page 480] 774 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]
If it is argued that the self will be established as the object [of knowledge] from this very sentence, "the self";
This is not tenable even in this way, because it would result in a split in the sentence. || 1733 ||

In this regard, he raises an objection based on Vedic renown with the words "the Self. He refutes that by stating, "In that case, this is not a means of valid knowledge," because it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to the perception of that [Self] from that [text]. || 1733 ||
Such is the nature of action, and likewise the worship of the Self.
A statement that establishes both [of these] would certainly be split; of this there is no doubt. (1734)
Anticipating the objection that this is not so because there is no difference in meaning, he says: "Thus" (*evam*). This means [of that which is] devoid of distinctions such as agent and so forth.
He states that a difference in sentence is necessary when there is a difference in meaning: "Not" (*na*) || 1734 ||
The statement "the offering is Brahman" is [to be understood] according to the very path already described.
One should understand the determined meaning by relying on clear reasoning. || 1735 ||

If it is argued that the passage beginning with "one should [offer] oneself" (*ātmānam*) regarding the aforementioned action is not an authoritative means of knowledge, while the passage beginning with "the ladle is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman" (*brahmārpaṇam brahma haviḥ*) might be, the author says: "Brahman... He states the reason why this [latter passage] also—like the passage beginning with "oneself"—is determined to have as its purport the mere reality (*vastumātra*) and does not refer to the aforementioned action: "Because of the aforementioned... This means: because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). The meaning of the second quarter [of the verse] is made clear.
The ascetic [says]: "It is clear. || 1739 ||
If this third [type] is indeed different from the two preceding ones, it is a conjunction (samuccaya).
One who has mastered the Vedas is established in the Śruti, the Smṛti, or in the world; it cannot be otherwise.

In the case of non-difference (*ananyatva*), there would be one combination of the meditation on the Sūtra and obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) etc., and another of that meditation and knowledge (*vidyā*). When both of these possibilities—which are inherent in the subject matter of the passage under discussion—have been refuted, the author raises an objection by adopting the position of difference (*anyatva*), beginning with the words "From the two preceding... He replies, "It is not so, because there is no evidence," citing the Śruti. || 1736 ||
Therefore, this statement that "the self exists" is sung as something false.
And for the purpose of establishing their conjunction, this has been stated according to the aforementioned reasoning. || 1737 ||

He concludes the result regarding the impossibility of a threefold conjunction with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states the reason indicated by the pronoun "that" (*tat*) with the words "And this" (*etacca*). The meaning is that, due to the logical reasoning based on the division of sentences and so forth, there is no such thing as a threefold conjunction. || 1737 ||
The complete cessation of the causal sign is the fruit, not the complete cessation of the first [sign].
It cannot be established through reasoning because it contradicts the statements of the Vedas.

Having stated the fault of internal contradiction and so forth by accepting that the fruit of the first combination is merely the destruction of the body and such, he considers the alternative— whether that destruction is the fruit directly or through an indirect means— and refutes the first position with the words "kārya" etc. It cannot be logically maintained that the absolute destruction of both the "kārya" (the gross body) and the "liṅga" (the subtle body) is the direct fruit of the first combination.
The meaning is that it cannot be so conceived because there is an absence of such reasoning and because it contradicts the sacred scriptures (Śruti). || 1738 ||
1 kha. It perishes, but not [the continuum]... 2 kha.
...on account of that, it is not so.
[Vol.
2, Page 481] 4 Brāhmaṇa: Concerning the father who was a practitioner of rituals and possessed the realization of the Self as both dual and non-dual.
For one who has entrusted the burden of his own self to his son, the fruit [of this act] occurs after death. || 1739 ||
The passage beginning with "pṛthivyai cainam" and so forth, has as its characteristic the attainment of the nature of the threefold food.
It is heard as a clear statement: "How could there be the destruction of the body and so forth? (1740)

He establishes that very point [in verse] 776: "Dvaita... etc. With reference to the fruit consisting in the attainment of the *tryannātman* (the self of the three foods) after death for the individual soul (*jīva*) who has performed the initial combined practice and has transferred his duties upon his son once his commenced karma (*ārabdhakarman*) is exhausted, [the text states]: "From the earth and from the fire, divine speech entered him," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since speech with a clear meaning has been heard, the attainment of the Sūtra is the fruit of the initial synthesis; it is not the destruction of the two bodies, because that would contradict the Śruti and so forth. || 1739 || 1740 ||
Nor is it logical that the word "jayya" (to be conquered) has the sense of "transcending."
Because of the contradiction with the statement "it enters into that," for that very reason. || 1741 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that because the word *jayya* (to be conquered) in the passage "this world is to be conquered by the son alone" has the sense of "transcending," the destruction of the two bodies would also be a result—just as the transcendence of the three worlds is for one who performs [the rites] from the beginning in combination? [Response: To this, he says: "And not so.

The particle *api* serves as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to the phrase "like the meaning of attainment. Since it is possible for that [word] to have the sense of "attainment," it does not have the sense of "transcending."
He states the reason for this: "Of that," [verse 1741].
I consider that after the attainment of the nature of the three foods, there is enjoyment through the act of eating.
By implication, it is inferred that the effect of this is the destruction of the father's vital breaths.

He raises a second objection with the words "The view is... (*matam iti*). The logical impossibility of the body's continued existence after experience is the [intended] capacity [of the argument]. By the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*liṅga*)—in which that [breath] predominates—is denoted. The subsistence of the body is for the sake of experience; however, for one who has reached the *sūtra* (the subtle body), since all experiences have been exhausted and there is an absence of fruit, its continued existence is untenable, and thus its destruction follows. For the practitioner of the combined path (*samuccaya-anuṣṭhātṛ*), the fruit will be accomplished by way of attaining the *sūtra*.
Such is the meaning. || 1742 ||
It cannot be so, for it would entail the consequence that the realization of Brahman is fruitless.
Even prior to the attainment of the fruit of knowledge through the awakening to Brahman. || 1743 ||

He refutes the position that the destruction of the two bodies through an indirect means (*praṇāḍyā*) is the fruit of the first combination [of knowledge and action], saying: "Not so. To the objection—"How can it be fruitless? For one obtains the fruit of the destruction of the two bodies"—he replies: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*). || 1743 ||
For the desired fruit of knowledge is indeed the destruction of the miseries of saṃsāra.
If that [liberation] were to exist even without the nectar of knowledge, then knowledge would certainly be useless. || 1744 ||

Anticipating the objection that even if the two bodies are destroyed prior to knowledge (*jñāna*), knowledge is not useless because its purpose is the destruction of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), he says: "Transmigratory... The word "for" (*hi*) is used to state that the desire for such a result is established by the individual experience of every person. Even if the two bodies were destroyed prior to knowledge, since one who is bodiless (*aśarīra*) does not transmigrate according to scriptural texts such as "Verily, being bodiless... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1], there would be a destruction of bondage even without knowledge. Therefore—
The meaning is that the futility of giving is unavoidable; by the word "that" (tat), the fruit is understood. || 1744 ||
1 ga. By way of reasoning.
[vol2, page 482] 776 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter—]
If it is further asserted that the effect of knowledge is the destruction of darkness;
Since every misfortune has been destroyed, what else could there be for one who has cast out the darkness?

He raises the objection that knowledge is purposeful because it destroys ignorance, using the verse beginning with *dhvānta*. He says: "If the destruction of ignorance is intended for the sake of destroying misfortune (*anartha*), and if that [misfortune] is already accomplished by the cessation of the body, what is the use of the destruction of ignorance? This is stated in the verse beginning with *sarva*. (1745)
What will ignorance do, which is like a serpent whose fangs have been pulled out?
Even while existing, the succession of intense calamities has been utterly destroyed.
Anticipating the objection that "avidyā, being present, will bring about saṃsāra; therefore, its destruction must be achieved," he says:
"Uprooted" (utkhātā). || 1746 ||
When desire, action, and the rest have been destroyed, ignorance does not lead to the experience of misfortune.
For that which is internal is sufficient; indeed, there is no effect apart from the cause, nor is there any cause [apart from the effect]. || 1747 ||
He states the reason why ignorance (*avidyā*), though present when all harmful objects have been cast aside, is incapable of producing an effect—being like a snake whose fangs have been pulled out:

"Desire," etc. He says that without desire and the like, which are the effects of ignorance, the cause called ignorance does not produce an effect in the form of experience (*bhoga*). Thus [ends verse] 1747.
Furthermore, when it exists, desire and action may indeed proceed.
If it is held that this is ignorance (avidyā), even so, it is not tenable. || 1748 ||

One might raise the objection that ignorance, even when it has perished, continues to exist and thus gives rise to desire and the like; therefore, its destruction must be brought about. [The author] addresses this with the words "vidyamāna" (while existing). He refutes it with "naivam" (not so). The meaning is that if a thing that has already perished were to arise again, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*). || 1748 ||
If ignorance were already present, it would forcibly produce its effects by its own power.
Since you were unable to protect [them] from destruction, how could desire and action [be yours]?
