Anticipating the objection that she possesses the power to produce the destruction of desire and so forth, he says: "Ignorance" (avidyā). This means disregarding the capacity to produce [effects] by force.

Just as the power of ignorance to maintain [desire] once its destruction has been attained is not accepted, so too its power to produce destroyed desire and so forth is without scriptural authority; this is the meaning. || 1749 ||
Now, if the conjunction of causes is what is expressed by the word "destruction," [then...]
Because it is non-distinct with respect to all [beings], that fruit does not result from a combination [of causes]. || 1750 ||

Furthermore, regarding the destruction of desire and so forth, which was mentioned as the fruit of the initial combination [of knowledge and action], is it primary or secondary? If it is primary, is it with remainder or without remainder? Of these, he adopts the first [option] with the word "atha" (now). The implication is that since desire and the like arise while ignorance persists, there must be a destruction of them. Since such a destruction is established without distinction for all people during states such as deep sleep, it does not constitute a combination [with action].
He says "it bears fruit," [referring to] "all. || 1750 ||
Therefore, the destruction of the composite whole is stated here to be devoid of logical justification.
Now, even though there is delusion, the composite aggregate falls apart. || 1751 ||
1 ga, tadaṃṣṭrora | 2 kha. ga. kārya | [vol2, page 483] 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 777.

Furthermore, he states "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) [in the verse], explaining that as long as the destruction of desire and so forth is incomplete, the destruction of the two bodies cannot be the fruit of the combined practice (*samuccaya*); for since desire and the rest, which are conjoined with their causes, can arise again, it is logical that they remain the cause of the body. This means that because there is the possibility of the re-emergence of desire and so forth, which serve as the cause, the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) of desire and the rest remains. The locative sense is "in the case of an incomplete destruction. He states another interpretation:
"Now," [it is said]. || 1711 ||
Since there is no other cause for a body, further intellectual effort is indeed fruitless.
Furthermore, it is by no means logical that the cognition of Brahman should be purposeless.
Because it would follow that the entire section on the Upaniṣads would be rendered purposeless. || 1752 ||

If there were a total destruction of desire and so forth, then because of the absence of the cause for the body, there would be the cessation of misfortune and the effortless attainment [of liberation]; thus, the futility of knowledge (*vidyā*) would remain as it was, since even existing delusion (*moha*) would be ineffective and its destruction would not be desired. To this he says: "The body... Anticipating the objection that the futility of knowledge is not undesirable for those who do not maintain the doctrine of Brahman, he says: "Futility... Nor is that [futility] logical, even for one situated in the section on injunctions (*vidhi-kāṇḍa*).
The meaning is that this follows from the consequence [of such a view] and because it contradicts the definition of its own validity. || 1752 ||
Moreover, [the opponent] has utterly destroyed all means of proof, such as effects, vital breaths, and so forth.
How should one perform hearing and the other [means] for the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman? || 1753 ||

Having stated that knowledge would be rendered useless if desire and the rest were destroyed entirely by means of their collective [destruction], he points out another defect with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). You claim that one whose two bodies—the instruments for bondage such as desire and the like—are all destroyed, having not yet reached the Supreme, remains in an intermediate state and performs hearing and other acts for the sake of knowledge; but that is incorrect. For hearing and the rest are not possible for one who is devoid of the body and its organs (*kāryakaraṇa*).

The meaning is that, according to such scriptural passages as "My body is most excellent," it is illogical for knowledge to arise merely through the destruction of all desires and the like. || 1713 ||
If it is argued that destruction is considered figurative because its purpose is to signify an excellence of dispassion, we say no.
This is not tenable even in this way, because it contradicts one's own explanation. || 1754 ||

He states another interpretation, namely that for one who practices the [first] aggregate from the beginning, the destruction of desire and so forth occurs due to an excellence of dispassion (*vairāgya*); since that [destruction] has that [aggregate] as its purpose, the latter is figuratively called the destroyer of those [desires]. He says "vairāgya... and so on. He states "svavyākhyāna... because this [interpretation] contradicts the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca. || 1794 ||
Right here all the vital breaths (prāṇas) dissolve into their own cause.
The dead man lies swollen; this contradicts the state of being alive.
And you yourself have stated that this is the fruit of the first conjunction.
Therefore, you must not speak of "dissolution" as being figurative with respect to one who is living.

To explain that very point, he states his own commentary on the fifth chapter [of the *Brahmasūtra*]: "In this context," etc. Even so, how can there be the cognition of the destruction of the two bodies and of desire and the rest? To that he says: "While living," etc. The absorption of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) into the Self and the bloating of the gross body after the breath has been abandoned are both incompatible with the presence of the two bodies; and in their absence, desire and the rest do not exist. Therefore, their destruction is not [merely] apparent.
SE 1 kha. *kāra* | 2 ga. *caivaṃ tvayai* | [vol2, page 484]

The meaning is that the fruit is the combination [of knowledge and action]. For one possessing the two bodies, the destruction of the body and so forth is merely secondary; it is not accepted by the proponent of the combination as being the primary fruit.
He states the conclusion: "Because it would contradict its own explanation," beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 1751 || 1796 ||
Having stated the fruit of the first conjunction right here, [the author says: "And having stated the fruit... [etc.]
For one who has emerged from all [meditative states] and whose food is such that only its name remains, || 1757 ||
Merely through the non-recognition of the supreme self, one fails to attain the state beyond duality.
This Brahmavidyā has been commenced for the purpose of bringing about the cessation of [ignorance regarding] Brahmavidyā. || 1758 ||
This explanation of yours is contradicted by this statement.
The disintegration of the composite occurs even while it is living; thus, its state is unstable.

One might raise the objection: "Even when the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) merge into the wise Self, does that [Self] possess the connection with duality, or not? If it does, then the destruction of the body is merely secondary; if it does not, then since it is nothing other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), knowledge (*vidyā*) need not even be commenced. Anticipating this doubt, the author says, "In this very place," and so forth. By stating through the first collection of passages beginning with "in this very place they are completely dissolved," he declares the fruit to be the absolute destruction of the body for one who possesses that [knowledge]. For one who lacks it—

Because duality is impossible for one who has turned away from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth, and who—like Śuka and others—bears only the name [of a body] due to the ignorance consisting of the mere non-recognition of the Supreme, Brahman remains as if unattained; therefore, the explanation by others that "knowledge is commenced for the sake of destroying the ignorance of that ignorant one" is contradicted by what occurred in the fifth [chapter], namely, that for one possessing the two bodies, the dissolution of the aggregate of the body and so forth is merely figurative. Thus, this statement is ill-founded.
The meaning is that the destruction of the body and so forth is secondary (gauṇa). || 1757 || 1758 || 1759 ||
Of the Supreme Self, whose modifications have been prohibited by the Śruti itself.
Ignorance and its transformation are not tenable, like [the appearance of water in] a mirage. || 1760 ||
Furthermore, because the Śruti establishes that the Self is changeless, it is impossible for ignorance (*avidyā*) and the desires (*kāma*) produced by it to be truly connected to it;

and since through knowledge (*vidyā*) the destruction of ignorance and the like can occur entirely and primarily, the secondary (figurative) position is untenable—this he states with the words "niṣiddhā" etc. The particle *tu* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). He provides an illustration for the fact that the Self is not truly joined with ignorance or its products.

Regarding the word "ūpara" (barren soil): just as barren soil and the like, which are the objects of superimposition for water and so forth, do not in reality possess water and the like, so too the Self does not in reality have any connection with ignorance and the rest, because its changelessness has been determined by such scriptural texts as "not gross" (asthūla). This is the meaning. || 1760 ||
As for the statement that liberation occurs only through Hiraṇyagarbha as the gateway—
The refutation of that [position] as well should be understood by way of the method of reasoning already stated. (1761)

It has been stated that the fruit of the initial collection is not the cessation of the two bodies, as expressed in the Sūtra. As for the claim that liberation occurs through knowledge only for one who has reached the final stage of the Sūtras, he refutes that with the words "Hiraṇyagarbha," etc., intending to refer to what was said in passages such as "He who [is the first] among the gods.
Thus it is said: "As stated. (1761)
Because, as in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha, there is a connection even with worms and the like.
This conception was formed by that unvirtuous one, who [mistakes] Brahman for the characteristic of the self.

He reminds us of the path of reasoning already stated regarding the relationship [between the individual soul and Brahman], saying: "like Hiraṇyagarbha. From the cosmic thread (*sūtra*) down to the smallest worm, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on the *Tattva* and other scriptures is that all things are united with Brahman in the form of the Self.

Since liberation occurs through knowledge for every other living being—even for one who has become like a thread—this conceptualization [of a specific hierarchy] is improper; such is the meaning. The word should be split as *asādhvī* (it is not right). 1762.
In the stages prior to liberation, the state of being a transmigrator remains entirely undifferentiated.
This is because of statements such as "Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma," and so forth, [found] in the *Manu* [Smṛti].

Furthermore, the state of bondage for the multitude of living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is dependent upon their own ignorance, as established by the Śruti, Smṛti, and one's own experience.

Therefore, because bondage and liberation share a common substratum, liberation is established even elsewhere than in the Sūtra; thus he says, "The transmigrating being... The human statement [of the Sūtra] has already been shown to have a specific, restricted meaning. (1763)
Even the mantra beginning with "vidyāṃ ca" does not indicate a conjunction [of knowledge and action].
Because they are mutually contradictory, there can be no coexistence of the two. || 1764 ||

Starting from the discussion on their relationship, it has been refuted—by means of the logic applicable in each respective case—that liberation belongs only to one who has reached the final stage of the Sūtras.

As for the claim that the fruit [of liberation] is established because the mantra beginning with "vidyāṃ ca" (and knowledge) teaches a twofold combination [of knowledge and action], he says "no" to that as well:

"vidyāṃ cetyādi" (the passage beginning with "vidyāṃ ca"). He provides the reason: "because of the impossibility of the combination of knowledge and action," stating "paraspara... (mutually...). 1764 ||
From the connection with the suffix *ktvā*, the priority in time of ignorance (*avidyā*) is understood.
Natural action is called death; knowledge is said to be that which is taught in the scriptures. || 1765 ||

One might object that it is improper to reject the meaning of the Śruti by the reasoning that "two things possessing contradictory attributes, such as darkness and light, cannot be combined," because the Śruti is more authoritative [than reasoning]. Anticipating this, he says "it is not so," because upon examining the mantra, their combination is untenable due to the use of the suffix -ktvā.

[The author] replies: Because of the use of the suffix *-ktvā* (having done), which prescribes that [suffix] for two actions performed by the same agent when one occurs prior to the other, and because ignorance is observed to be prior to knowledge, there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of the two; this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that such a combination might still exist between knowledge and action despite their lack of simultaneity, he explains the mantra: "Inherent... and so on. Regarding the phrase "through ignorance, death... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the commentary up to that point.]

The non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is prohibited lead to death; because they are the causes of that [death], scriptural rites such as the *agnihotra* and "knowledge" (*vidyā*)—as mentioned in the phrase "knowledge and [rites]"—are required here.

By this, the expression "by means of ignorance" (*avidyayā*) is also explained, since ignorance is a cause of that [death] by way of defiling the intellect. [This refers to] that which is not prescribed by scripture.

The meaning is that "intrinsic action" is what is expressed by the word "death," and it is "ignorance"; thus, these two are mentioned together because the former is the effect of the latter, and because they stand in the relationship of the sublated and the sublator. || 1765 ||
Death, innate knowledge, scriptural knowledge, and likewise birth.
Having crossed over the other [world] by means of the scriptural [path], one attains immortality through knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "having crossed over death by means of destruction" (*vināśena mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā*), he states the meaning of the word "death" (*mṛtyu*): "Death," that is to say, the sight of naked women and so forth;
the meaning is that these are the causes of death. Regarding the phrase "both origination and destruction" (*saṃbhūtiṃ ca vināśaṃ ca*), he states the meaning of the word "origination" (*saṃbhūti*).

"Śāstrīyam" (scriptural) refers to the "vision of the Udgītha and so forth"—this is the ellipsis. The meaning is that it is the cause for the possibility of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). In the same way, the phrase "by destruction" (*vināśena*) is also to be explained. In that context, "destruction" (*vināśa*) is the knowledge denoted by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), because that [knowledge] is its cause. And the coexistence of those two is as before; thus he says, "tathā" (so). In both mantras, from the first quarter [of the verse], through the third quarter's [mention of] ignorance (*avidyā*) and destruction...

The scriptural action and knowledge denoted by the "arising of knowledge" (*vidyā-sambhūti*) located in the first quarter have been explained. The "higher knowledge" (*paravidyā*) is expressed by the two [terms] "knowledge" and "arising" located in the fourth quarter. Thus, having explained the word-meanings and the knowledge in both mantras, he summarizes the meaning of the sentence.

Regarding the phrase "by means of scriptural [action]" (*śāstrīyeṇa*): and regarding the phrase "and knowledge" (*vidyāṃ ca*), that which is denoted by the word "knowledge" is drawn in by the term "ignorance" (*avidyayā*), namely the Agnihotra and other such rites.
780 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 486]

The meaning of the first mantra is as follows: having crossed over death—which consists of ritual action (*śāstrīyaṃ karma*) and its opposite, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), both denoted by the word "ignorance" (*avidyāśabda*)—and having transcended natural action (*svābhāvikaṃ karma*) which is denoted by the word "death" (*mṛtyuśabda*), one attains Brahman through the knowledge of Brahman alone. And regarding the phrase "and origination" (*saṃbhūtiṃ ca*): meditation on the *sūtra*-breath and so forth, denoted by the word "origination," is drawn together with "destruction" (*vināśena*). Ritual action is [implied] by that, and its opposite, "destruction," is what is denoted by the phrase "having crossed over death."
The meaning of the second mantra is that one attains Brahman through *saṃbhūti*, which is pure knowledge (*vidyā*), having transcended innate knowledge (*svābhāvika-jñāna*).
The underlying intention is: "Why, then, is there a combination [of both]? || 1766 ||
And there is the scriptural statement: "Not for one who has not desisted from evil conduct."
Through austerity one destroys impurity; through knowledge one attains immortality.

Furthermore, since scripture declares that knowledge arises in the renunciant whose actions have been discarded and whose intellect is purified, there can be no combination [of action and knowledge]; this he states with the words beginning "no" (na). Moreover, he says "thus" (evam) because of the difference in the fruits of action and knowledge, and because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding their distinct application, as in the verse beginning "by austerity" (tapasā). || 1767 ||
Therefore, the ascent of the combination should be performed, not by relying on the individual syllables.
"But we do not prevent one who speaks what is invalid.

(1768) [The author] concludes the impossibility of a conjunction in the phrase "the self" (*ātmānam*). This means that, according to the reasoning previously stated, a conjunction of either two or three [entities] is impossible. Thus, disregarding the literal words of the scripture, [one would be] without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the conjunction—
He replies to one who says this: "It is not a means of valid cognition" (apramāṇa). The meaning is that the very absence of a means of valid cognition serves as its refuter. || 1768 ||
Therefore, having emerged from their karmic activities, those whose intellects are inclined toward the inner self [should proceed].
They attain extinction through the realization of the true nature of the inward Self; this is the certain conclusion. || 1769 ||

Having concluded the refutation of the opposing view, he now summarizes his own position—that liberation for distinguished renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*) alone arises from knowledge—by means of the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This means that the combination [of action and knowledge] is not what is being propounded in the present passage.

The meaning is: "They become extinguished" (*nirvānti*); that is, by becoming free from activity through renunciation (*nyāsa*), they become Brahman, which is the unsurpassed goal of human existence. || 1769 ||
When both demerit and merit have ceased, those who are fearless of rebirth [attain that state].
The peaceful renunciants go [to him]; homage to that one whose nature is liberation.
In that very context, he states the consensus of the Purāṇas: "Not meritorious," etc. (verse 1770).
And here, by the word "world" (loka), nothing else whatsoever is denoted.
Because the other self is connected as a qualifier by means of its own word. || 1771 ||
He refutes the claim that in the passage "he who [sees] only himself," the word *loka* refers to the *sūtra* (the subtle body) which is the fruit of karma, by saying "and not so.

The reason for this is given as "by the word 'own' (*sva*). Because the meaning of the word *loka* is connected with the qualifying attribute conveyed by the word "own" in the phrase "not having seen his own world" (*svaṃ lokamadṛṣṭvā*), it has been observed [therein]; therefore, here too, it is appropriate that the word *loka* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of abandoning the subject under discussion (*prakṛtahāna*) and introducing something not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*).
This is the meaning. || 1771 ||
"Only the self," and thus the word "self" is a qualifier.
Therefore, the perception of the world does not arise from that which is inherent in karma. || 1772 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 487] 4 Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 781.
He states another reason for the inclusion of the Supreme Being alone here by means of the word "world" (*loka*), namely: "the Self. Just as in the case of the world...

In the phrase "the meaning of the word *sva* is a qualifier, likewise [it qualifies] the self (*ātmānam*)," the meaning of the word *ātman*—which is a synonym for *sva*—is seen to be its qualifier. Furthermore, the status of being the self (*ātmatva*) is not primary for the fruit of action; therefore, the meaning is that the word *loka* refers to the Supreme Self alone. Since the meaning of the word *loka* is established as the Supreme Self by these two reasons, he says "of the world" (*lokasya*) to show that the desired conclusion for [the opponent's view of] the Supreme Self is not achieved. || 1772 ||
And because, in the section concerning knowledge, [the soul] is qualified by itself as being "above."
For those [who hold] "this is our self" in order to bring about the cessation of the world of effects. || 1773 ||

He states another reason for taking the word "world" (*loka*) here as referring specifically to the Supreme Self: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*). In the sixth [chapter], in the section on knowledge beginning with "Now, this great... and so forth, the word "world" is qualified by the meaning of the word "Self" in the passage, "This Self of ours is this world," for the purpose of negating the world that consists of the fruits of karma. Therefore, the meaning is that even here, the "world" is the Supreme Self; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. [The principle is: "That which is doubtful [is determined] by the remainder of the sentence."
The word "hi" is used to illuminate the logical principle that a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya) comes about. || 1773 ||
If it be argued that on account of the indicative mark "from this very [Self]" (asmād eva), the world must be something other than the Supreme Self;
Because one's own world is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), this [position] is not tenable even in that way. || 1774 ||

He raises an objection based on the context: "The Supreme is not [the cause] for the world, because it contradicts the indicative marks," using the words "from this" (*asmāt*). Here, if by the word "world" (*loka*) one intends to grasp the Supreme, then the expression "from this very [world]" would be improper. For in that case, the arising of the fruit is heard in scripture to proceed from the desiring person denoted by the word "world," and the Supreme cannot be the cause because of scriptural texts concerning the *apūrva* (unseen merit) and so forth; nor can it be so through ignorance (*avidyā*), since in your view, that [ignorance] does not exist within the sphere of knowledge (*vidyā-adhikāra*).
And because it is accepted that Gāda’s [text] forms a single syntactical unit with the *vidyāsūtra*, the sense is that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Anticipating the objection that an indicative mark situated within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not stronger than the context, he provides the resolution: "Of his own world... (1774).
[This refers to the fact that] as long as a result is possible through other means, it is so conceived.
It is proclaimed that for him, all this world is established as his very self.

He supports the fact that this passage beginning with "asmāt" is indeed an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). [The phrase] "by another means" (*sādhanāntara*) uses the word "other" (*antara*) in relation to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). The words "from the world" and "from knowledge" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. The word "his" (*asya*) refers to the statement of the wise man. "Is celebrated" (*nūyate*) means it is praised; the words "his own world" (*svaloka*) are to be supplied as the remainder. || 1779 ||
The very same meaning that is expressed by the sentence "risara" is [here stated].
The auspicious statement from the Smṛti, "All action without exception," is also [to this effect]. || 1776 ||

He shows the Śruti and Smṛti regarding the attainment of all human goals through the knowledge of the Supreme as one's own Self (pratyak), beginning with the words "He who is free from desire" (*yo 'kāmaḥ*). The meaning of the word *hi* is that there are many other passages similar to the stated sentence.
The word *akhila* means "not small," that is, "great. He indicates the authority [of this teaching] by showing that the word is rooted in the Śruti. *Śubha-*...
Thus [it is said]. || 1776 ||
If, due to incomplete thorough knowledge, one attains [the end] of the body through knowledge;
In that case, the employment of the word "self" (ātman) in common worldly usage would be entirely appropriate. || 1777 ||

Even though the explanatory passage beginning with "Let it not be from this very one" is an *arthavāda*, it is nevertheless appropriate here because its purpose is to demonstrate that [the Self] is the self of all.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]: He states that the Supreme Self is grasped by means of the word "Self" (*ātman*). Regarding the phrase "If...": if it is intended that limitation results from ignorance of the meaning of the word "world" (*loka*) and non-limitation results from knowledge of it, then in that case the word "Self" is appropriate, as it denotes an entity devoid of the three kinds of limitation.

By the logic stated in the passage beginning with "that which one attains through that," it is established that the word *loka*, being in grammatical apposition with that [Brahman], also has that same meaning; thus, the sense is that Brahman alone possesses the nature of the world (*lokatva*) here.
Otherwise, the Śruti would have spoken of the world as being from its unmanifest state (*avyākṛtāvasthā*). || 1777 ||
The statement would include a qualification for the purpose of excluding the world of Brahmā.

If, setting aside the "Supreme" (para), another were understood by the word "world" (loka), then the sentence would possess a qualification; however, that is not seen [in the text]. Therefore, for this reason as well, he states that the "own world" (svaṃ lokam) mentioned in the context is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman) here as well. Regarding the phrase "otherwise," the scripture has been cited as "asmāllokāt. To the question, "Why would the scripture state the qualification 'from the world in its undifferentiated state' (avyākṛtāvasthā-lokāt)? he replies:

"Regarding the term *brahma*: in order to exclude both one's own world (*svaṃ lokaṃ*)—which refers to the world called 'the Beyond' (*parākhya*) under discussion—and the manifest world of Brahmā (*vyakta-brahma-loka*) mentioned immediately prior, a qualification must be stated. For you do not accept that the creation of objects proceeds from the Supreme [Self], since that is established by scriptural texts such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*);
nor does its creation proceed from the world of Brahmā, because it is an effect (*kāryatvāt*). Therefore, the qualification is meaningful. || 1778 ||
When one thing is the subject under discussion, another thing cannot be its qualifier, such as "separation."
It can be grasped by one of wise intellect only through the grace of Vaiśvānara.
Fearing that, even without a qualification, something other than the higher and the lower might be intended by the word "from this," he says:
"Not in another. Fearing that the wise might, by overstepping the subject at hand, apply their intellect to what is irrelevant, [he states:

except through the grace of the Deity, the Sūtra is not easily grasped here by the word "world" (loka); for without the favor of the Deity, there can be no resolution of contradictions between preceding and succeeding passages.
He concludes: "In Vaiśvānara," [verse 1779].
By the speech thus spoken, he declared self-sovereignty for the knower.
How can it be said that an ignorant person performs [the worship of] gods and others? || 1780 ||

Having stated that, by considering the preceding and following contexts, the word "world" (*loka*) in the phrase "himself as his world" (*ātmānam eva lokam*) refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, the author now recounts what has been said: "By what was said. This means that the Śruti, by the sentence beginning with "of one who knows the self-world thus spoken of," has declared that liberation indeed comes from this very [knowledge]. He then asks in order to explain the purport of the passage beginning with "Now, this... (*atho ayam*).
How so? He says that the subsequent section is intended to demonstrate how the Self benefits the gods and others; thus it is said: "It is explained as follows. (1780)
One who possesses pride in the [system of] castes and stages of life, who knows the truth of the elements, and whose intellect is supreme.
By what actions does this one always protect the earless, like an animal? (1781)

Here, he elaborates upon the question: "The castes," etc. For the purpose of resolving the question—"To whom does this man, who, not knowing himself and being inclined toward the non-self, participates in the conceit of 'I' and 'mine' regarding the castes and stages of life, constantly serve like a beast, and by what actions?"—[the author says:]...
The meaning is: "it is not the word of Nanna. || 1781 ||
1 Kha. Thaṃ Tūpa | [vol2, page 489] 4 Brāhmaṇam | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstradīpikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 783
The status of being the Lord of all lords has already been described by the preceding scriptural passage.
However, its being for the sake of another is now demonstrated as follows. || 1782 ||

Anticipating the objection that this has already been determined in passages such as "like a beast" (*yathā paśu*), [the author]—intending to show that in those instances only the dependence of the ignorant upon them was stated, like that of a beast, and not this specific point which is sought to be understood—expounds upon this with the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*). The meaning is that even among Brahmā, Indra, and others, the independence of the Knower is stated precisely by this [text], and so forth. He clarifies what was indicated there by the word "is said" (*bhaṇyate*).
"But as for how... || 1782 ||
For one who does not know the Self is possessed of a body and subtle body (liṅga) due to the agitation arising from ignorance;
here, by the designations "Self" and "world," that which ends with the body is intended. (1783)

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to use two words—*ātman* and *loka*—in this context? For by the principle of 'that which one obtains' (*yaccāpnoti*) and so forth, the word *ātman* refers to the Reality that is entirely unconditioned; and by the principle stated in passages such as 'not having seen his own world' (*svaṃ lokaṃ adṛṣṭvā*), the word *loka* refers to the Supreme. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the meaning of the words *ātman* and *loka* as they appear in the sentence containing the intended purport, in a way that is appropriate to the context: "Ajñāta... (The ignorant...). [He says: "The ignorant... (*avidvān*).

The meaning is that one who possesses the two bodies of ignorance is not denoted here by the two words [“I” and “this”]. The word “hi” (for/indeed) signifies that the qualification by ignorance is the cause for the qualification by its effects. The phrase “ending with the body” means being situated within the interval between the two bodies, characterized by the superimposition of non-difference upon them. This refers to the present sentence [beginning with] “atra” (here). || 1783 ||
Ritual acts such as sacrifice and the like [are performed] by the gods and others, apart from the two, namely the body and the *liṅga*.

Since it is not otherwise logical, therefore that possessor [of the two bodies] is spoken of here. He states the reasoning for this: "sacrifice and so forth. For indeed, without the conceit of possessing two bodies, action cannot be conceived as being beneficial to the gods and others; therefore, in this sentence, the referent of words such as "world" (*loka*) and so on is precisely one who possesses the two bodies.
For no one can be a benefactor unless they have been won over by one's own past actions.
Therefore, the householder was earned by the gods and others through his own actions.

Having raised the objection that—just as in passages such as "the Self [is] itself the other"—the meaning of words like "worlds" (*loka*) here must be understood according to the direct statement of the Śruti and its inherent power (which is stronger), [the author] replies by accepting the indicative mark (*liṅga*) supported by the context: since that [Self] cannot be an agent, the meaning of the word "worlds" is simply the two-fold body acquired through the karma of all living beings, existing as the object of enjoyment for everyone. He says: "By karma. That which is under dispute is acquired through that karma.
The meaning is that because it is an agent, it is like that body. || 1785 ||
Even the gods and others, as householders, [attain their status] in that very same way through their own karmas.
They should be understood as indeed acquired, because of the observation of their causes and effects. || 1786 ||

Anticipating the objection that there might be an inconsistency—namely, that even though gods and others are beneficial to the householder, they are not acquired through his karma, and likewise, the householder who is beneficial to gods and others might not be acquired through their karma—the author says: "The gods and others also...
This means that just as the gods and others are acquired by the householder through the power of his own karma, so it is with them. By this, [it is shown that] they are indeed acquired.
1. mu | 2 ka. ghāte liṅgadehavā | [vol2, page 490] 784

"Caused by that" (tan-nimittā): the meaning is that for a householder, because he perceives benefits such as rain caused by the gods and others, there is no deviation [from the rule] on the grounds of their being benefactors, since the probandum [of being an object of worship] also exists in those cases. || 1786 ||
Whatever action has been performed through debt is sufficient for its enjoyment [in the form of repayment].
For neither the arrival of what was not done nor the destruction of what was done is accepted. || 1787 ||

One might object that there is no universal rule (*vyāpti*) stating that whatever is beneficial to a being must have been earned through its karma, because this is contradicted in the case of God (*īśvara*). Anticipating this, he says "The agent... and so forth. Here, "here" refers to the plane of experience (*bhogabhūmi*). He provides the reasoning for why [the self] is not benefited by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*): "Not unearned... and so forth. That...

If [the cognition] were to assist [the object] independently, there would be the consequence of the destruction of what has been done and so forth; and that is not desired, because it would result in the invalidity of the ritual section (vidhikāṇḍa). Therefore, since it does not assist by its own nature, there is no deviation [in the logical reason]; such is the meaning. || 1787 ||
And its agency arises from ignorance; the Self has no agency by its own nature.
O dear one, the enjoyer would likewise be like the agent; in true knowledge, both [agent and enjoyer] are non-existent.

If one objects: "By saying 'that which [is done] here by the agent' (*kartreha yat*), agency is accepted for the Self; if so, there is a contradiction with the scriptures on identity (*tādātmya-śruti*), because the unity of the agent and the non-agent is impossible.

Otherwise, the restatement that 'it is done by the agent and so forth' would be unestablished," [the author] replies, "It is not so, because agency is merely imagined (*kalpita*)," stating: "And agency... Having raised the doubt that agency, like the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), is intrinsic (*svatastva*), he states the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*).

Regarding the word "kartā" (the agent): he states the reason why both [the agent and the object] are sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*) despite being rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), saying "in knowledge" (*vidyāyām*). || 1788 ||
For even that which has been acquired but not yet experienced belongs to those whose self is veiled by ignorance.
Therefore, through the realization of the true nature of the self, the destruction of karma occurs. || 1789 ||

Anticipating the objection that—based on the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "action is not exhausted without being experienced"—the status of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) remains unavoidable even when knowledge exists because the accumulated karma cannot perish without fruition—he says: "Of that which has not been experienced. Since the cessation of even unexperienced karma acquired through ignorance is established by scripture as resulting from knowledge, there is no state of being an enjoyer after the dawn of knowledge; however, the notion of such enjoyment persists due to the momentum of what has already begun (prārabdha), though it is sublated.
This is the meaning. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to demonstrate that the burning away of karma through knowledge is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti. || 1789 ||
Everything would be the effect of everything, and everything would be the cause of everything.
An insentient entity, being uncombined with another, is incapable of acting. (1790)

Since agency and so forth are products of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning identity; and since it is established that "whatever is done by an agent is for the sake of [the agent's] experience," it has been stated that the action performed by the beneficiary is what provides the benefit. One might then object: "If that is so, since everything is a benefactor to everything else—either directly or indirectly—there would be no fixed order of cause and effect. Anticipating this doubt and while conceding the lack of fixed order, he says: "Everything... [referring to the cited verses]. These [scriptural passages]...

He states the reasoning for accepting [the existence of] a substrate (avasthā): "not composite" (asaṃhatam). For an insentient object is not capable of acting while remaining mutually non-composite, as this is never observed in cases such as a cart; nor does activity exist inherently in that which is non-insentient, because of its immutability (kauṭasthya)—this is the meaning. || 1790 ||
Everyone is indeed the enjoyer of everything, when one intends to emphasize the primacy of consciousness.
For those whose intellects are colored by external objects, experience culminates in consciousness.
1. Of the Self.
Ā. [vol2, page 491] 4.
Brāhmaṇa] Together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 785.

Anticipating the objection that "surely, just as there is a determination of the non-inert self as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), there should also be a determination of it as the agent (*kartṛ*)," he says: "All. Anticipating the further objection that "in that case, even a jar or the like would be an enjoyer," he says: "Consciousness" (*cit*). This is because, since that [status of being an enjoyer] is accepted only by virtue of the predominance of consciousness, it does not belong to the jar. What, then, is this enjoyment of the enjoyer? It is not the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure and so forth, for that is impossible in the conscious self (*cidātman*).

Anticipating the objection that there is no self because it is not admitted [by the opponent], and that there is no other experiencer because such a one is not desired, he says: "External," etc. The meaning is that experience (*bhoga*) is the pervasion of the cognition of the forms of sound and so forth by the mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*); for according to the established principle, a modification of *sattva* that lacks a witness (*sākṣin*) is not denoted by the verb "to know" (*jānāti*). || 1791 ||
This very point will be explained in the Madhubrāhmaṇa-vidyā.
For the purpose of establishing the single-naturedness of the object, [this is taught] primarily and with great effort. || 1792 ||

He cites the Madhu Brāhmaṇa as the authority for the statement that "everything is the cause of everything" and "everyone is the enjoyer of everything. Regarding the word "Madhu," he anticipates the objection—"Why should agency and enjoyment of everything by everything be stated even there?"—and replies with the phrase "the oneness of reality. Anticipating the objection that "duality also appears there," he states that the Śruti does not intend to convey that [duality], using the phrase "primarily."
Excessive effort refers to the repeated practice of hearing [the teachings] and so forth. || 1792 ||
This being so, this [body], as a composite whole, is the self of the world.
The world is to be known as food and as a sacrificial animal, providing benefit for the gods and others. || 1793 ||

Anticipating the objection that since everything is mutually bound to everything else by way of being both cause and effect, what relevance does this have to the present context— even though gods and householders are not conquered by each other's karma— the author states "Thus" (evam) to show that the term "householder" (gṛhin), as well as "world" (loka) and so forth, is established here as qualified by the two bodies. || 1793 ||
From what source is it understood that this [body] has been assumed by the gods and others?
In order to establish this point, the passage beginning with "sa yat" and so forth is stated. || 1794 ||
Having thus explained the passage beginning with "Now this," he asks [the question] in order to introduce another statement: "By the gods and others.

Although both the Madhu Brāhmaṇa and inference have been established here as means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, when asked about another means of valid knowledge, he says: "Of this. || 1794 ||
That which consists of the relinquishment of material goods for the sake of a deity is called [sacrifice].
That very same [rite], due to the predominance of pouring [libations], is called a *homa*. (1795)

Fearing that there might be a redundancy because *yajati* (he sacrifices) and *juhoti* (he offers oblations) are not distinguished in their common meaning of "renunciation," he states the division of their meanings as established in the fourth book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]:

"He who [offers] to the deity... *Āsecanam* means pouring in. [The sūtra states: "The injunction for *yajati* applies to the aggregate of substance, deity, and action, because it achieves its purpose therein" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 4.2.27).
Thus, there is a distinction between the sacrifices and other rites mentioned in the scriptures, such as "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations."

When the doubt arises as to whether [the acts] are distinct or not, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is no distinction because they are indistinguishable in their nature as renunciations (*tyāga*). However, it is established that they are distinct: for a sacrifice (*yajña*) is the renunciation of a substance with a deity in mind; a libation (*homa*) is that same act when augmented by the addition of casting [the substance] into the fire; and a gift (*dāna*) is that which extends to the point of acceptance by another. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the word *yajati* denotes the aggregate of the substance and the other factors, since it has no further expectancy regarding them.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

And it has been stated—“The root *hu* (to sacrifice) would be [the same as] *ās* (to pour out), with the addition of pouring. The word *tu* (but/however) serves to indicate that the aforementioned distinction belongs to the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]. || 1795 ||
Since being a "world" (lokatva) is that which is to be enjoined, the phrase "he offers" (yaj juhoti) is restated as a reference.
Some do not accept repetition [of mantras], for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (siddhi) through the worship of gods and others.

[Objection: But since the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth are to be enjoined here, how can they be mentioned as already established? Nor [can it be argued that] because the state of being a householder (*gṛhitva*) is what is to be enjoined, the fire-oblation and so forth—which are established from elsewhere—are merely restated; for it is possible to restate even that state of being a householder, which is itself established through common worldly experience (*lokataḥ*). To this, he says: "of the state of being a householder" (*lokatvasya*). Nor is it the case that even for a householder, the quality of being a benefactor to the gods and others is known solely from the means of knowledge that apprehend the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*); for that too...

Since it is established by the *śruti* and *smṛti* injunctions for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) that [the householder's duties] provide no assistance [to the gods], the acts such as the *homa* sacrifice mentioned in passages like "he offers the oblation" (*yaj juhoti*) are merely restated here as already established elsewhere; however, their status as a "world" (*lokātva*), though established in common worldly usage, is enjoined here in its specific form.

For the fact that a householder assists the gods and others through the *homa* and other rites is not established elsewhere, nor is the connection between the gods and the *homa* etc. unestablished elsewhere.

The meaning is that [the existence of the deity] is established by the very means of knowledge (māna) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). However, Bhartṛprapañca and others do not accept that statements such as "he who offers the oblation" (*yaj juhoti*) are mere restatements (*anuvāda*);

thus [the author] says: "No. The reason for this is given: "Because of the gods and so forth. Since the householder has acquired [wealth] from the gods and others, he must perform the oblations and other rites for their sake; for even his dispassion (*vairāgya*) is obstructed by them. Thus, the necessity of performing the oblations and so forth is what is being stated here.
The meaning is that, because it is not subject to negation, that alone should be accepted here. || 1796 ||
And their necessity is not established by any means of valid cognition other than this [scripture].
"Because [the Veda] is eternal, the statement of a reason is not logical; therefore, it is understood [that the Veda is not authored].
(1797) He refutes that with "No. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis and is placed in a different position. [The text continues: "Of the oblations and so forth, here..."

The necessity of performing the mental acts (mānas) is already established and known from other scriptural injunctions such as "he offers" (*yaj juhoti*) and others that enjoin them for as long as one lives; since they are thus established as obligatory (*nitya*), they cannot be the object of an injunction here, but are merely restated (*anuvādya*). Therefore, the reason—that [the fruit] is produced by those [acts]—is untenable. This is the meaning. || 1797 ||
And furthermore, he who diligently recites the Veda day after day;
Therefore, this world of householders is said to be the sustenance for the sages.
Now, he states the meaning of the phrase "by that [which one recites], [one satisfies] the sages" with the words beginning "yac ca. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The word *api* (also) has the sense of providing an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). The daily recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The rule regarding having the sacred grass in hand (*pavitrapāṇitva*), facing east (*prāṅmukhatva*), and so forth, constitutes *vattva*, which means being endowed with effort (*prayatnavattva*). The word *loka* is explained as "that which is to be enjoyed" (*bhojya*). || 1798 ||
Let it be observed that the same application applies to the subsequent statements as well.
Among these syllables, there is no object whatsoever that remains concealed.

He extends the aforementioned reasoning to the subsequent [passages] such as "yat pitṛbhyaḥ" with the words "in the following. If it is argued that even when the literal meaning is consistent, a distinct intended meaning (tātparya) must be stated, he says "no" in response: "not there" (na tatra). || 1799 ||
Because this [person] always benefits all living beings.
Therefore, they maintain that these [qualities] are indestructible, just like his own body.

For a householder who benefits the gods and others through the aforementioned oblations and other rites, there exists the possibility of an obstruction to knowledge; therefore, [the following] Brāhmaṇa is intended to remove that obstacle.
(Vol.
2, page 493) 4 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstramañjarī* by Ānandagiri. 787.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a cessation [of activity] on your part, he explains the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*), etc., starting with "Because" (*yasmāt*). "All beings" means all entities from the gods down to the ants. "At all times" refers to the state of being fit for the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*). "Non-destruction" (*avināśa*) means the absence of cessation from the state of being bound by the fetters of ignorance regarding Brahman-knowledge (*brahmavidyā*). || 1800 ||
There is no one at all who bestows the enjoyment acquired by one's own karma.
In this context, the distinction lies between the gods and others, and between the householder and one's own self-body.

He states another reason for the protection of the body of the agent (karmideha) by all beings, just as they protect their own bodies: "By one's own karma" (svakarma), which means because it is acquired through one's own karma and because it provides for one's own enjoyment; the meaning is that there is no difference in the enjoyment provided to gods and others, as it is prompted by both [the self and the other beings]. || 1801 ||
Through the fire of the knowledge of Brahman, there is the destruction of this [ego] as well, resulting in its state of non-agency.
This destruction of his is great; indeed, another [destruction] can be remedied.

Regarding the statement that "the gods and others protect the one entitled to perform ritual action," when the question arises as to what this "protection" consists of, the author speaks of the two-fold nature of its destruction in order to state that it is the preservation of his agency and so forth. [The verse begins: "Brahma-knowledge... If this person entitled to ritual action possesses knowledge (*vidyā*), then there is the impossibility of agency and so forth; this constitutes a form of destruction, whether through the lack of materials and other requisites for sacrifice, or through the attainment of the status of an immobile being (*sthāvara*) and so on, which results in the cessation of agency in rites such as sacrifice.

The meaning is that even death (cyuti) is its destruction. Regarding that, because the first kind of destruction is difficult to remedy, he says "this one" (*ayam*), thinking that the gods and others certainly protect the performer of ritual action (*karmī*) from it. He uses the word "for" (*hi*) with the intention of stating that its greatness is the reason for its being difficult to remedy. Regarding the second kind of destruction, he states the distinction: "the other" (*anya*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of the acquisition of wealth and so forth. Likewise...
And the meaning is that those [deities] do not protect the performer of ritual action from such kinds of destructions. || 1802 ||
Therefore, the word of the Śruti is logical; for this reason, it has been stated that they [belong] to these.
"Let there not be a loss of all our possessions through the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman.

(1803) He states that the agitation of gods and others regarding this [knowledge] in relation to humans is a sign of its being difficult to remedy once the agency and other attributes produced by ignorance have been destroyed. He says "let there not be," expressing the intention of those ritualists who hate such knowledge.
Because those who perform rituals such as sacrifices are like animals (*paśu*) due to their subservience to the gods and others, they are equal to "all one's own property" (*sarvasva*). || 1803 ||
This duty must necessarily be performed like a debt, according to scriptural injunctions such as "as long as one lives" and so forth.
As it has been stated, this is known in the Vedas as well as in the words of the Smṛtis.

Raising the objection that although one performing the prescribed rites benefits the gods and others, such agency is not necessarily required because there is a lack of evidence, he states the meaning of the phrase "tad vā etat" (that indeed is this): "Necessarily. This refers to the aforementioned action known as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), namely the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*), the sacrifice to ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*)— [The sentence continues: ...refers to [the other sacrifices].
"One should give daily to the beings; one should give milk daily; one should offer the *svadhā* daily; one should offer the *svāhā* daily;
therefore, the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) must be studied"—this is a compendium of such scriptural passages (*śruti*).

“By not commencing actions, a person does not attain freedom from action; therefore, perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction. (Gītā 3.4) [Note: 1 kha. refers to a variant reading.]
— 788 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya] [Vol. 2, Page 494]

"This world is bound by action. "Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action, free from attachment. "Therefore, you should perform action alone. "But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action."
"He who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action—
he is both a renunciant and a yogi, not he who merely maintains no sacred fire nor performs no ritual act.
"Having understood what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scriptures, you ought to perform action here."

"Acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. "He who, according to his ability, does not neglect these five great sacrifices, even while constantly living in his own home, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse."
"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five—the gods, guests, beings, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, even though he breathes.
Such are the declarations of the Smṛtis. This means that it must necessarily be performed as a rule; for him, it is like a debt.
The meaning is: "just as [something] must necessarily be counteracted. || 1804 ||
And that has been specifically examined in the section on the ritual of cutting.
In the explanatory passages (arthavāda) concerning the debt, it is said "he kills"; therefore, one should act as prescribed. 1805.

One might object: "Is it not the case that even what is heard in scripture (*śruta*) cannot be practiced without investigation? For surely, the weeping of Rudra and such things are not practiced merely because they are heard in scripture? Anticipating this doubt, he states the meaning of the phrase "it has been investigated" (*mīmāṃsita*). He says: "The portioning-off," etc. The meaning of this is as follows: "That which one offers when one sacrifices—whether it be that which one pours into the fire or that which one sets aside for the ancestors—that is the portioning-off (*avadāna*); therefore, whatever one offers into the fire is called 'the portioning-off'. Thus [ends the discussion on] the portioning-off.

In the section concerning injunctions (*navidhiprakaraṇa*), it is stated in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that for a householder, sacrifices and other duties toward the gods and others must be performed as an obligation, like a debt: "Verily, one is born with a debt; he who exists is born with a debt to the gods, the seers (*ṛṣis*), the ancestors (*pitṛs*), and men. When he performs sacrifice, he is no longer born with a debt to the gods; for in that he sacrifices to the gods and offers oblations to the gods, he discharges that debt to them. Then, when he studies the Vedas...

When he recites [the Veda] for the sages (*ṛṣi*), a debt toward them arises, for by what he recites he performs [their purpose]; thus they call one who has studied the Mantras "one who has paid his debt to the sages" (*ṛṣīṇām ṛṇīyaḥ*). Furthermore, when he desires offspring, a debt toward the ancestors (*pitṛ*) arises, for by desiring offspring he performs [their purpose]. Since this is observed in such cases, it is established that sacrifices and other rites must necessarily be performed in order to discharge that debt.

Therefore, as stated, an action that yields a distinguished fruit must necessarily be performed by a householder; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of causing injury to living beings. || 1805 ||
And regarding both engagement and withdrawal, for the qualified person as previously described:
If [the self] possesses autonomy, why does it proceed toward the creation of saṃsāra? || 1806 ||

He provides the introductory transition for the subsequent passage beginning with "The Self alone this [was]" by stating, "And in regard to active life. By the passage beginning with "Now he who [worships another]," the path of active life (*pravṛtti-mārga*) is indicated, and by "The Self alone," the path of cessation (*nivṛtti-mārga*) is suggested; in both cases, the member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) is the subject.
— [vol2, page 495] —

The meaning is as follows: since the capacity [of the two paths] is equal, one must state the reason why this person abandons the path of cessation (*nivṛttimārga*) and proceeds along the path of activity (*pravṛttimārga*). || 1806 ||
But not on the path where all the evils of saṃsāra have been utterly destroyed.
Or, regarding that which is characterized by cessation, it must be stated: by what means does this one attain mastery over the deceased? (1807)

He clarifies the very question by way of its contrapositive: "But not... The meaning is that even though the path of cessation (nivṛttimārga) is distinguished [as superior], one must state the reason why this person does not engage in it like one who is dependent on another. || 1807 ||
Do not the gods indeed protect him who is a distinguished authority?
They also protect him with great effort, and not as they would an ordinary human being. || 1808 ||

He raises an objection, suggesting that the protection afforded by gods and others to the aforementioned qualified person acts as a mandatory impetus toward the path of ritual activity (*pravṛttimārga*), stating:
"They protect. [The response is: They indeed protect even those such as householders who have attained mastery over their respective spheres of action, but not the religious student (*brahmacārin*).

Since [the protection of gods and others] is common to all stages of life (āśrama), such as that of the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), and thus serves no purpose for any human being’s engagement in the path of ritual action (karma-mārga), the author states—beginning with "No" (na)—that a reason must be given for the student’s abandonment of renunciation (nivṛtti) and his partiality toward active engagement (pravṛtti). In this context, the effort consists in turning one away from knowledge (vidyā) by means of inciting passion and the like. || 1808 ||
Otherwise, there would be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done.
Therefore, this is unsurpassed for the protection of ordinary people. || 1809 ||
Fearing the objection that "they (the gods) compel even a mere human being to engage in action by force because of their inconceivable power," he says:

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*). Its explanation begins with "sāmānya... and so on. For a man who is a *brahmacārin* common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), there would be the arrival of unearned results (*akṛtāgama*) and so forth in the protection provided by the gods and others—which consists of the restraint [of others] from actions—even though they are capable in that regard as well. His [protection]...

Furthermore, since this is undesirable to those who maintain the authority of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), the answer—that protection by the gods and others serves as the cause for the necessary inclination toward action when the instigator is questioned—is not a valid response. This is the meaning. || 1809 ||
Nor should it be called "ignorance" (avidyā), because that consists solely of darkness.
Because it is merely the cause of false cognition, its status as an instigator is not logical.

Anticipating the objection that innate ignorance (*pratyagavidyā*) is the cause for the inclination toward activity in the qualified seeker as previously described, he says: "Nor even... Ignorance consists merely in the veiling of the reality; therefore, its function is simply the production of false cognition regarding the reality, not [the production of activity] by its own nature.
The meaning is that [the mind] does not possess the quality of being an initiator, because such a quality is not observed during states like deep sleep. || 1810 ||
Even knowing that it is the ripening of what is disadvantageous, he still engages in it.
Nowhere is such activity observed except as dependent upon another. (1811)

He states another reason for its not being a motivator by its own nature: "Anartha... (It is not a motivator). Even one who ascertains through the prohibitive scripture that killing and the like result in hell, is seen to engage in them due to anger and other passions; therefore, it does not motivate independently.
790 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter]— [Vol. 2, Page 496]
This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that, in the absence of a cause, there would then be no engagement in action by the person, he says: "Dependence" (pāratantryam).
This means it results in such a [state] culminating in a fruit. The word "kvacit" refers to the person who performs the action.
Therefore, for a person seeking the highest good, there is an impeller toward undesirable action.
For the purpose of refuting that [objection], another scriptural passage must be stated; such is the meaning. || 1812 ||

The supplement says: "Therefore," etc. Since activity is impossible without a motivator, and since [the Veda] is the cause for entering the womb and so forth, it must be stated that there is an impeller toward the Agnihotra and other such acts which are undesirable; and having learned of that statement, one who seeks the highest good (śreyaḥ) should avoid it. This applies specifically to ritual action (karman).

He says that the subsequent scriptural passage is intended to demonstrate that [the person] has desire as its essence, because that which impels [to action] must necessarily be expressed. Thus is the meaning. (1812)
In this world, this human being has already attained all goals of man by his very own nature.
And though all misfortunes have been cast off, one possesses a perverted intellect due to delusion regarding that [Self]. || 1813 ||
The commentary, stating that "desire is seeking," raises an objection: "When [it is] attained. This means, in the context of examining this scripture.

For desire arises toward an unattained human goal that revolves in the mind through memory; however, the Self has already attained its human goal because it is unsurpassed bliss and because all that is non-beneficial has been eliminated.
Therefore, the meaning is that no desire for it can possibly exist. Even for one who possesses the aforementioned nature, [desire might arise] due to ignorance of oneself.
He provides the resolution, stating: "Because of that delusion. (1893)
This [world] has not attained the goal of human endeavor and is crowded with every kind of misfortune.
Thus, the dull-witted one desired human goals that were not yet attained by means of [external] instruments.
It reveals a perverted intellect. By the word "untrustworthy," it describes the arising of desire in one who is ignorant. Thus [it says], "falling from desirelessness. || 1814 ||
In the same way, the ignorant man desires to abandon the evils that have taken refuge within himself.
And indeed, there is a Vedic scripture stating: "One who is afflicted by desire arising from ignorance [is not truly free]. (1815)

Having stated the desire to obtain [objects] out of ignorance, he then speaks of the desire to abandon them, saying "desiring to abandon. This means those things which are based upon the Self, yet imagined as having the Self as their support. He states that ignorance, being of the nature of nescience (*avidyā*), is the motivator of desire, saying "ignorance.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it impels one toward action alone. Since ignorance itself, as the cause of desire, will bring about activity, what is the use of an intermediate desire?
Anticipating the objection that this is not so, he cites scripture regarding its being the motivator: "And thus" (*atho*). The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.
The meaning is that the scripture beginning with "And thus they say: this person consists of desire alone" (*kāmamaya evāyaṃ puruṣaḥ*) declares its primacy in [the person's] activity. || 1815 ||
No action whatsoever is seen here belonging to anyone that occurs without desire.
For whatever one does, that is all the activity of desire.

In this regard, he states that the word of Manu is also an authority, beginning with "unintentionally. Here, the term "here" refers to the sphere of action. He explains the teaching of Manu with the words "whatever [sin] indeed... (1816).
In that regard—
[vol2, page 497]
The statement from the Smṛti, "This is desire, this is anger," and so forth, [is authoritative]. [Brāhmaṇa 4] accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri.
Therefore, it is concluded that there is no other instigator than desire. || 1817 ||
In that very context, he cites the words of the Blessed One: "Desire," etc. He concludes that its status as an instigator is authoritative: "The instigator," etc. (1817).
Before entering into relations such as marriage, the man existed entirely alone.
Above [this state], through connection with a wife and so forth, and through union with sons, grandsons, and so on; || 1818 ||

Having established that desire is the motivator, he explains the passage beginning with "the Self" (ātma) and so forth. Regarding the word "previously" (prāk): he states the reason why everything, including sons and others, existed previously as nothing more than a celibate student (brahmacārin) before the connection with a wife and so on. Regarding the word "afterwards" (ūrdhvam): [he explains that after such connection, the various stages of life arise]. || 1818 ||
Someone [gave] that expanded family to someone else in their presence.
He explains the extensive lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth, which has arisen from desire.

He demonstrates the meaning of "only one" by means of what is well-known in the world: "vistārita" (spread out), etc. The construction is as follows: having seen that student, who possesses the aforementioned qualifications, nearby after his marriage, someone says something to another. He clarifies the first qualification: "kāma," etc. (verse 1819).
The entire family that you behold before the performance of the marriage ceremony—
The Self alone was the single person; there was no son or anything else at all.
This was previously non-existent, to be grasped solely through one's own realization.
The family which you perceive as being composed of sons, grandsons, and others—|| 1821 ||

He clarifies the manner of explanation with the words "Previously," etc. The literal meaning is: that family which you now see belonging to him was previously, before his marriage, entirely alone as a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); nothing such as sons or others existed separately from him. He confirms this very point through authoritative testimony with the words "The Self," etc. From the self-experience of the celibate student who thinks, "I am alone," the visible family [is seen to be absent].
The meaning is that prior to the marriage, there was only that alone. He states the meaning of the word "this" [in the verse]: "O son," etc. ||1820||1821||
The self whose nature consists of the seeds of all things beginning with desire, yet whose true essence is the single reality that is not known as a separate self.
Thus, possessed by the obsession of over-grasping, he arrives at a determination of contrary meaning.

Regarding the phrase "He desired," he explains the meaning of the word "he" (*sa*): "From desire, etc. Ignorance is the seed of the entirety of desire, anger, and so forth; due to the superimposition of identity with that [ignorance], one is devoid of the knowledge of the Self whose nature is unsurpassed bliss and the like. Precisely because of that, desiring the various objects of desire imagined by him, he is seized by that "grasper" known as the form of desire, his intellect settled upon sense-objects such as sound; this is the meaning of the word "he."
This is the meaning. || 1822 ||
Although complete in itself, it is incomplete due to lack of awakening; thus, one possesses perverted cognition.
Afflicted by thirst, that foolish man desired [something].

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:

It reveals a contrary determination. Regarding the word "svataḥ" (by itself): having restated the meaning of the word "sa" (he), he states the meaning of "akāmayata" (he desired) as "tṛṣṇayā" (by thirst). The distinction between those two lies in their being hidden and unhidden respectively. He states the lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) as the cause for being impelled by that [desire].

Regarding the term "fool" (*bāla*): he states that possessing perverted cognition (*viparīta-jñāna*) is also a cause for possessing craving (*tṛṣṇā*), by using the term "human being" (*mānava*). || 1823 ||
Born for the sake of authority over karma, one becomes an instrument for the accomplishment of karma.
The fact that each preceding [factor] serves as the cause for the subsequent one is expressed here by the word "atha" (then/therefore). || 1824 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "May there be a wife for me" as "action. Regarding how a wife is the cause when a man’s connection [to her] is through ownership of the action, he says: "the means of accomplishing action. He states the meaning of the three occurrences of the word "atha" (then/therefore) found in the subsequent sentences as "prior... [1824].
Then, through my nature as the individual soul, may I be born from her for the sake of performing stationary action.
And thus it is clearly heard in the statement: "By means of a son alone. (1825)

Now, stating that the wife is the cause with respect to the son, he explains the meaning of the phrase "may I procreate" (*prajāyeya*). Regarding the word "now" (*atha*): the meaning is that in order to perform his remaining duties even after his own death through the medium of the son, the father himself is born in the form of that son. He states that the scriptural passage, "He is established in this world by means of the son alone," is the authority for this. (1825)
Endowed with both divine and human wealth, I shall now proceed further.
One should perform actions as they arise for the sake of accomplishing both visible and invisible goals.

Now, he explains the passage beginning with "Then, wealth" (*atha vittam*). He says "Deva" [the Lord]. In order to state that the attainment of wealth is an auxiliary factor for the performance [of rites], he says "then subsequently" (*athottaram*). This means without transgressing the form as it is obtained and as seen in the scriptures. He states the fruit of the performance: "perceived," etc. (*dṛṣṭa*)... [and so on].
This alone is his desire; no other purpose remains beyond this.
For here there are only two aspects, namely the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
[Verse 1827] He states the meaning of the phrase "all this is desire" as follows: "All this" refers to only these two for the ignorant person: the means and the goal.

The meaning is that there is no other object to be desired. He states the reason for this: "They accomplish" (*sādhayanti*). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that the act of seeking (*eṣaṇā*) is included within that very [accomplishment]. By the word "here" (*atra*), the sphere of worldly convention (*vyavahārabhūmi*) is referred to. || 1827 ||
Moreover, these two are indeed conceived as the seeker and the means of seeking.
Because the human goal has not been accomplished and because the identity [of the self with Brahman] is not established. (1828)

Now, [the opponent might argue] that these two [son and wealth] are not objects of seeking (*eṣaṇā*) because they serve as causes for the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*), since they are their objects. To this, he says: "The two seekings. By the word *ca*, which is a synonym for *vai*, there is a restriction in both ways; thus, the status of those [two] as human goals is unauthoritative—this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that it is improper to regard them as non-objects because they are well-known as human goals—as in the case of sons and heaven—and that otherwise the introductory statement "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*) would be contradicted:

He states that, because the human goal is not accomplished without knowledge, the two subjects—the appearance and the object—are introduced for the sake of establishing [the truth]: "Of the human goal... (1828).
1. Or otherwise.
