Because wife and other such things are merely means for the performance of ritual action (*karma*), they do not constitute the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Since it is not contained within the three worlds, it is difficult to maintain that it is merely this much.

He states another reason why sons and the like are not the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and why they serve as causes for action (*karman*) which is of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*). He says: "Action" (*karma*). For it is not the case that something which is a means to a human goal is itself a human goal, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Since the means have already been mentioned, when it is said "this much [is the world]," the use of the word "desire" (*kāma*) implies that the three worlds are undesirable (*anartha*); otherwise, since the three worlds were not previously included [in the list of means], saying "this much" would not be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them, and thus their being designated by the word "desire" would not imply their undesirability.
He raises the objection that it is impossible to accomplish [this], stating: "In the world... (verse 1829).
For that which is to be accomplished by the three worlds does not depend on a single means of accomplishment.
That which has its probandum implied is [the subject], because it is the probandum; the other is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

Precisely because that [subject] is the probandum, and because it is bound to the means of proof, it cannot exist apart from it; thus, for the time being, it implies the means of proof. Furthermore, since the means of proof is also bound to the probandum, it implies the probandum. Therefore, when the means of proof is stated, the probandum is stated by implication. Having thus restated both of these points, [it is said]: || 1830 ||
He states that it is appropriate to declare its lack of benefit by means of the word "kāma" with the words beginning with "na," etc. (1830).
For it is held that the fruit of the three worlds consists of origination and so forth.
Without projecting karma, it does not project itself, nor does it obtain that [result] by its own nature.
He states by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that the goal known as the three worlds necessitates a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). [The verse begins with] "The world...

The ellipsis is: "Therefore, it possesses dependence upon a means of accomplishment. Furthermore, he states that because that [goal], being independent of anything else, lacks the attainment of its own nature, it necessitates a means of accomplishment: "Action... (1831).
Nor is there completion of the ritual action without the fruit of the three worlds.
"Therefore, the means (*sādhana*) is said here to have its fruit (*phala*) internalized.

This also expresses, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), that "the means implies the goal (*sādhya*). He states the reason for this—that the means does not reach its conclusion without the fruit—in the words "completion" (*samāpti*). He explains [this] with the phrase "internalized," and the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the conventional usage of the relationship between the goal and the means.
Therefore, even such a scriptural statement implies the result; this is the sense. || 1832 ||
Since this seeking is indeed one and the same, it will be discussed later on.
By implication, there would be a statement of the probandum (sādhya) when the probans (sādhana) has been stated, just as [in the case of the example].
For when "food" is mentioned, satisfaction is understood by implication for a person. || 1834 ||

He states the operation of the remainder of the sentence by making the mutual connection between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) the reason: "The desire" (*eṣaṇā*). This refers to the subsequent passage where it is said, "for both these are indeed desires. He states that the goal is implied in the stated means by way of an illustration: "Arthāt" (from the sense).
In the illustration, the word "hi" (for) is used for the sake of what is well-known in the world. || 1833 || 1834 ||
These two types of seeking, consisting of the goal to be attained and the means of attainment, are called desire.
Because they do not possess the nature of things as they truly are, [these two] have the single cause of ignorance regarding the self.

Since the probandum is stated by implication when the means of proof is stated, even though both are restated as being of such a magnitude, how is it that there is no desire for this [probandum] therein?
794 Sureśvarācārya’s Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika [First Chapter] [vol2, page 500]

The sense is that because there is no difference in their *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for their application), the words "iṣaṇā" and "kāma" are intended to be synonyms. He states the intention of the scriptural revelation (*śruti*) which prescribes desire (*kāmatva*) for both, with the phrase "ayathā" (unreal). The meaning is that the probandum and the means of proof are caused solely by one's own ignorance. || 1835 ||
Therefore, a wise person should not place trust in this, just as one would not trust in one's own impurity.
Therefore, having emerged from the searches for the means of knowledge, one should take refuge in the knowledge of the inner self. || 1836 ||

Even though these two [desire and action] are produced by ignorance, what would follow from that? To this he says: "Trust. Where, then, should that trust be placed by the wise person? To this he says: "Having risen above. Since desire is a source of harm and both the goal and its means are nothing but that [desire], one should abandon trust in one's own views and renounce—through *saṃnyāsa*—these three types of longing which are equivalent to gains in a dream.

The meaning is that, having made [the mind] thus composed, one should repeat the hearing [of the teachings] and so forth, directed toward the knowledge that is the cause for the desired liberation. || 1836 ||
For even if one should desire more than this, one would not find anything superior to it.
Therefore, by this much alone, one who stands upon the stages of ignorance would be complete. || 1837 ||

One might ask: "How can it be determined that there are only these many [objects of desire], given the infinity of desires? Anticipating this objection, the author states the meaning of the passage beginning with "icchan" (desiring). The meaning is as follows: even if one were to desire more than these two, the ignorant person would not obtain anything other than this, because there is no acquisition of any means or results—whether seen or unseen—that exceed them. Therefore, the restriction [that there are only these] is appropriate. Since there is nothing else to be desired beyond the means and so forth, therefore... [the text continues].
He states the resulting conclusion—that in the state of *dyāvas*, there is fullness merely through the attainment of that [state]—with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 1837 ||
Even a single one among wife and the others, as long as a man does not obtain it—
"This dull-witted person conceives [the thought], 'I am not yet complete.

Having thus stated the purport of the passage beginning with "therefore even from that," he explains the section beginning with "as long as" (*sa yāvat*) and states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding the idea that the ignorant person's fullness is due to his son and so forth. He says, "one by one. By this, he indicates that the cause of a person's ignorance lies in such incomplete conceptualization.
"Insentient," [it is said]. || 1838 ||
Until these aforementioned trustworthy persons have become motivated by desire.
Then the human being considers himself, "I am the whole. || 1839 ||

In that very context, he presents the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The word "as long as" (*yāvat*) means "when. The fact that the wife and others are preceded by desire follows from the opening statement, "He desired," which implies a state of ignorance and the conceit of being human. He provides the reason for this: "he is a human being" (*mānavaḥ*). || 1839 ||
That which is produced by the five—self, wife, progeny, wealth, and knowledge.
The *karmapada* would indeed be thus measured by the *pāla* meter. || 1840 ||
He states the introductory transition (*pātanikā*) in order to introduce [the section] beginning with "to be saluted by all," starting with the word "Self" (*ātman*).

Relying on the application of the number five and for the sake of its utility in the meditation (*upāsana*), he says "thus," following the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which states that the *paṅkti* meter consists of five syllables. || 184 || 0 ||
First, the descent of external action is brought about by the Self and other [principles].
When those [elements] are absent, then the state of being "cooked" (pākta) is said to belong to the internal action (adhyātmakarma).
[Vol.
2, Page 501] 4 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Having stated that the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) belongs to action (*karman*) alone, the passage beginning with "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*) is intended to establish the remaining subject matter for the sentence beginning with "Of that" (*tasya*).

He restates what has been established by means of the word "dinā" (by day). Regarding the phrase "of the external": in response to the inquiry as to how the internal meditation-act (*dhyānakarman*) possesses the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) when [external factors] such as the wife are absent, he takes up the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that). The word "atha" (now) is intended to indicate the doubt previously mentioned. || 1841 ||
This action, through the distinction between external and internal, consists of both these natures.
Just as that [drinking] occurs, so too is this described. || 1842 ||

In order to elaborate upon that very point, he states the twofold nature of action with the words "external" (*bāhya*), etc. Since that external action is composed of five parts, it is fivefold; likewise, this internal meditative action is said to be fivefold. He explains this by saying "of that," etc., concluding with the word "fivefold" (*pāṅkam*). || 1842 ||
Internally, the mind alone is the self, because [the body] is dependent upon it.
The same applies to the activities of speech, wife, and so forth, just as it does for the sacrificer.

He states the meaning of "the mind alone is its self" with the word "internal" (adhyātmam). The sense is that regarding the sacrifice performed with reference to the body, one should apply the perception of the sacrificer to the mind. He states the reason for this superimposition with the phrase "because it is dependent on that. Therefore, since the mind shares the characteristics of the sacrificer, he says that the perception of it [as the sacrificer] there is appropriate, using the expression "like the sacrificer. || 1843 ||
This is to be understood as "born from that," because it is dependent upon that.
For whatever one contemplates here with the mind, that very thing one speaks with speech.
He states the meaning of the phrase "Speech is the wife" with the words "Speech. He gives the reason for superimposing the nature of a wife upon speech with the word "That.

Just as the wife is dependent on the sacrificer, he provides the proof for speech being dependent on the mind with the words "When... Here, the term "here" refers to purposeful worldly activity. As it is said, "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech," thus the mind is prior and speech is subsequent.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of including another scriptural passage. || 1844 ||
Having deliberated with mind and speech in a manner that conforms to worldly convention.
Now, that which vibrates excessively is called the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 1845 ||

Regarding the statement "life-breath is progeny," he explains the meaning of the term *prāṇa* with the words "having deliberated. Having determined an object by means of the mind (*manas*), the mind itself exerts itself intensely through speech (*vāk*) which possesses two forms; that activity produced by both is the meaning of *prāṇa*.
The word "now" (*atha*) is used to establish the well-known fact that speech and mind are the mother and father respectively with respect to the life-breath. || 1849 ||
Having ascertained the meaning of the scripture with the mind, one then proceeds to act.
Those who know the Veda declare that vital breath (prāṇa) is progeny; they call that [breath] activity.

Having restated that [the king], he states the meaning of the sentence—that the vision of the subjects should be directed toward him—beginning with "āgama" (scriptural authority). The word "atha" (then) is employed to express "together with speech. The qualification "vedavidām" (of those who know the Vedas) is used to corroborate the stated point through Vedic tradition. || 1846 ||
1. Or speech; 2. Or that which is the mental cognition (manodhī).
[vol2, page 502]
—796 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
They declare that internal wealth (*ādhyātmika-vitta*) is indeed twofold, according to the difference in its functions.
Its status as both divine and human is also due to the figurative application of its being a means of accomplishment. || 1847 ||

In order to explain the meaning of the passage beginning with "the eye" (*cakṣus*), he states that there is a twofold division within internal wealth (*vitta*). He says, "twofold. He provides the reason for this twofold division of internal wealth—namely, the eye and the ear—in the words, "because of their effects" (*kārya*): [that is,] because form is perceived by the eye and sound is perceived by the ear.

The meaning is that it is due to the difference in their functions. In this context, the term "they declare" (*pracakṣate*) is used for the sake of establishing consensus among the learned. Having raised the doubt as to how the humanity of the eye and the divinity of the ear are stated in the Śruti, he says: "Divine... The meaning is that since the eye and the ear are the means for acquiring the two types of wealth (sensual and spiritual), they are metaphorically designated as divine and human respectively. || 1847 ||
For by examining with the eye, one obtains wealth such as cattle and other possessions.
The eye is human wealth, just as life-span is said to be the clarified butter.

Having explained the internal division of wealth and established its divine and human aspects, he now applies the passage beginning with "The eye is human" (*cakṣur mānuṣam*). [He says] "having examined. The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) should be placed before the word "eye. He provides an illustration for the point that the perception of human wealth is metaphorically attributed to the eye, saying "just as" (*yathā*). || 1848 ||
O Lord, the attainment of the divine state is here called knowledge and wealth.
Because it is the means for attaining that [hearing], the internal wealth is the ear of the ear. || 1849 ||

Having established the view of human wealth upon the eye and the view of divine wealth upon the ear, he states their essential nature [in the verse beginning with] "daiva" (divine). The word "iha" (here) is in the locative case for the purpose of distinguishing between the two types of wealth. He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "the ear is divine": "because it is the means for that.
Since the ear is the cause of knowledge through the act of hearing, the meaning is that the view of divine wealth is to be applied to it within the context of the adhyātma (inner self). || 1849 ||
And the activity of speech, limbs, and so forth, which is based upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Since the self is manifested in the body, action therefore arises from it.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "the self alone" (*ātmaiva*) as follows: "External," etc. The meaning is that the "self" is the body; therein lies the perception of action (*karmadṛṣṭi*), which refers to the manifestation of the two kinds of karma. || 1850 ||
It is so called because it is measured by number and by feet, and because it is derived from the *pāka* meter.
Therefore, sacrifice has always been proclaimed by the virtuous as being protected [by the officiant]. || 1851 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That very one" (sa eṣa): "Measured" (saṃmita). Because the external and internal sacrifice is measured by the feet of the *pāṅkta* metre—which is heard in scripture as "the five-footed *paṅkti*" due to its connection with the number five—it is therefore called *pāṅkta*.
This is the meaning. || 1891 ||
Because it is the effect of that [Supreme Cause], the individual soul (paśu) is "the cooked" (pāka), as are all things, moving and unmoving.
And one should know that this digestion as well arises entirely from the five elements.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "The animal is fivefold" (pāṅkaḥ paśuḥ) as "because it is its effect" (tatkāryatvāt). Now, one might object: since the world of moving and non-moving beings is not produced by the five [factors] beginning with the Self (ātman), how can this [world] possess the quality of being fivefold (pāṅkatva)? To this, he replies: "Five... (pañca). || 1852 ||

That which consists of the fivefold sacrificial acts is this world, the work of sacrifice.
Having known this according to its true nature, one attains that very state in its entirety.
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the first Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣyavārtika.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "All this" [tadidam sarvam] as follows: "The fivefold," etc. Having known both the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana) as being fivefold through the nature of the Sūtra, and having meditated upon that fivefold Sūtra as one's own self, the attainment of that very Sūtra is the fruit, according to the principle of "as is the intention, so is the result" (tatkratu-nyāya); such is the meaning. || 1853 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Puruṣavidha-Brāhmaṇa, of the first book in the Commentary on the Vārtika of the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Now begins the fifth Brāhmaṇa;
it starts from the passage "atha yo'nyām" and continues with great effort until the end of the section.
The manifestations of ignorance have been enumerated up to this conclusion. || 1 ||

And here, in this chapter, the ignorant person—who possesses the conceit of identifying the self with caste and so forth—being self-restrained by dharma, offers oblations and performs his own duties. (2)
He sustains the perishable world, from the gods down to the smallest insect.
In this very way, every single person in the world is a source of action.

He recounts the narrative to explain the connection [of the text]: "Now" (*atha*). The meaning is that it was stated that from the thread of ignorance (*avidyā-sūtra*) up until the conclusion of the third chapter, the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of ignorance are being elaborated.

Although other matters have been mentioned here and there as incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), he says "with great effort" (*uru-prayatnataḥ*) to state that the supreme intention (*parama-tātparya*) lies in the exposition of the manifestations of ignorance. This follows what was stated in the passage beginning with "Now this" (*atho ayam*).

He says: "In this regard," meaning in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*). The sense is that [the Self], characterized by ignorance and its effects, dependent on merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), sustains the entire universe through its own actions. The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is an adverbial modifier. Anticipating the objection that the status of being the creator of the universe belongs only to the *Sūtra* (the individual soul) as qualified by specific knowledge and action, and not to others due to the absence of such excellence in knowledge and so forth, he says: "Thus..."

The meaning is that, like the thread [of a garland], the status of being the creator of the world can also belong to others through their knowledge and actions, whether prescribed or not prescribed. ||1||
Just as it has been fully acquired by the entire world through its own actions.
In that same way, the world was acquired by him through the aforementioned actions.

By means of an illustration, he establishes that each [deity] is the creator of the entire world, as if it were a single thread. "With the whole" means by means of the aforementioned rites such as the *juhūti* (oblation) and so forth; that is to say, by performing those rites. || 4 ||
Since each one enjoys it entirely, as if it were his own body.
Common objects as well as those that are uncommon. || 5 ||

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, regarding the statement that "the entire world is acquired by each [individual]," he provides the regulating principle: "as one's own body. The meaning is that since it is impossible for something not acquired through one's own karma to be an object of experience (*bhogya*), the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) has acquired everything that is to be enjoyed. This is divided into external and internal categories, as well as common and uncommon.
The classification of battle. || 5 ||
Furthermore, the enjoyment of that which has not been acquired through one's own karma is not observed here.
Because each one acts as a benefactor, the world has therefore been acquired [by them]. || 6 ||
Anticipating the objection, "Could it not be that even what has not been acquired through one's own karma is to be enjoyed? he says: "By one's own karma.

The meaning is that in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), a house, field, or the like belonging to another is never seen to be the object of enjoyment for that other person. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that what is acquired through one's own karma is what is to be enjoyed: "By each one... The connection is: "Therefore, the world was acquired by each one [individually]. [This refers to] the benefactor...
The meaning is that [it exists] because it is the cause of enjoyment for each and every enjoyer in the world. || 6 ||
By its very nature, all action characterized as dharma, adharma, and so forth, [is devoid of intrinsic existence].
It initiates a twofold fruit consisting of both the common and the specific.

If it is argued that only that which is earned by one's own karma is to be enjoyed—since karma is determined for each individual—and therefore that which initiates a non-common result cannot be the cause of a common result, and thus [the world] would not be fit for enjoyment, he says "by nature" (svabhāvataḥ) to address this doubt. The word "etc.
(ādi) has the sense of "mixed" (miśra). || 7 ||
By way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, and through the distinction between the common and the specific.
From the action of the Sūtra and so forth, there arises the effect ending with the worm. || 8 ||

He clarifies the statement that action initiates manifold results with the verse beginning "guṇa... (Verse 8). The meaning is that the threefold karma of the entire range of living beings, from those like silkworms up to insects, produces its fruit in every way—both as elevation and degradation, and as both general and specific states—since the objects of experience are seen to be of both kinds. || 8 ||
The fruit of every action is dependent upon the perception of substance and so forth.
Therefore, the fruit of action is distinguished by the various combinations of common [and other] factors.
He states another reason for the claim that action initiates various fruits: "dravyādi" (beginning with substance), etc. The word "ādi" (etcetera) is intended to include action and so forth.

The phrase "sādhāraṇādi" (common, etc. refers to the uncommon (asādhāraṇa). Thus, the meaning is: by virtue of being a vow consisting in the perception of substances and so forth as the instrumental causes of the fruits of action. || 9 ||
In some cases it is indeed common, while in others it is uncommon.
And both [the agent and the object] must be established as such, because of the diversity observed in substances and other categories. || 10 ||
He confirms that very point by means of an illustration with the words "In some cases," etc. "In some cases" refers to such things as watching a dance;
"in some cases uncommonly" refers to such things as seeing one's own son; and "in some cases in both ways" means such things as seeing a beautiful garden.
He states the reason for the aforementioned diversity of causes for the variety in the fruits of action: "Substance, etc. (Verse 10).

Therefore, by means of the aforementioned knowledge and action, both in brief and in detail.
"By each one [of them], the entire world was seized for the sake of attaining enjoyment. || 11 ||

He concludes the demonstration that karma initiates all undertakings with the verse beginning "samāsa-". The meaning is that the entire world has been acquired by each individual enjoyer through karma and other factors, both in their general and specific forms, for the sake of experience. The referent of the word "tat" (that) is the possibility of karma initiating various kinds of fruits. || 11 ||
Just as everyone is the agent of everything and also the effect of everything, so it is.
This will be clearly explained in the context of the Madhu-vidyā. || 12 ||
Anticipating the objection that it is unproven that everything stands in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, he says: "All... (verse 12).
The agent, whose means are his own action and knowledge, produced that fruit.
Having divided it into seven parts, it is now demonstrated by means of that division. || 13 ||

Under the guise of restating what has already occurred, he states the purport of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa by supplying the required ellipsis with the word *yad* ("that which"). The phrase "for the sake of meditation" (*dhyānārtham*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

The meaning is that the subsequent Brāhmaṇa is intended to enjoin meditation upon the world—which was created by one's own karma and so forth, divided into seven parts, and consisting of the *sūtra*-self—as being identical with one's own Self, with the result of attaining that very state. || 13 ||
Of the four types of food, three are the fruit for the agent; however, those which are directly involved in the performance [of the action] serve as the means for accomplishing the ritual act.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, one person dwells having abandoned both internal and external clinging; he does not cling to anything in the world, and being unclinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned internal clinging, but not external clinging; he clings to something in the world, and being clinging, he is agitated. Being agitated, he does not personally attain Nibbāna. Yet, through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned external clinging, but not internal clinging; he clings to something in the world, and being clinging, he is agitated. Being agitated, he does not personally attain Nibbāna. Yet, through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned neither internal nor external clinging; he clings to something in the world, and being clinging, he is agitated. Being agitated, he does not personally attain Nibbāna. However, he possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

He states a further distinction among those [elements]: "Three," etc. The meaning is that because they are inherent in the performance (*prayoga-samavāyitva*), they are included within the status of being causal factors (*kārakatva*) in the execution of the ritual action. || 14 ||
The father, whose nature is consciousness, is neither the mind nor Prajāpati.
Because the qualification is non-distinct, there is no one other than the cognitional self (vijñānātman). || 15 ||

Having raised the doubt that the mind (*manas*) might be the father—either because of the Vedic text "The mind alone is the father," or because the mind is the creator of the entire world, or because the word "father" in the mantra refers to Prajāpati—he says:

"The self of consciousness (*vijñānātman*). The meaning is that since the individual soul (*jīva*) is the common cause of the entire world by means of its karma and so forth, this [soul] alone is the father here; it is not the mind, etc., as he concludes with "No. || 15 ||
Because the mind, as well as the Lord consisting of the three foods, desired to create.
Therefore, there is no creator other than the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), whose nature is common [to all]. || 16 ||

Anticipating the objection, "Why could the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and Prajāpati not also be causes?", he says: "Because they desire to create" (*sisṛkṣitatvāt*). The meaning is that since both [the mind and Prajāpati] are involved in the act of creation, they fall within the category of effects and thus cannot be causes. The connection is as follows: the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), who is the common self of the entire universe, is distinct from those others and is the creator. || 16 ||
Although it is said that *medhā* is the capacity for retaining the meaning of a text, [it is actually the power to retain both the words and their meaning].
Nevertheless, it is knowledge alone that is intended here as the means. (17)

In the verse "The Father generated [him] through *medhā*," he explains *medhā*. [He says] "of the book" (*grantha*), meaning that here *medhā* consists merely of knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman.
Or rather, [it means] "or even."
[Vol. 2, Page 506] Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, First Chapter.

He states the reason: "Because it is a means" (*sādhanatvāt*). The meaning is that since mere knowledge (*jñānamātra*) is the cause for the production of the seven types of food, established intelligence (*medhā*) is not applicable as such. || 17 ||
For the sake of establishing the apprehension of no distinction between scriptural and worldly knowledge.
The apprehension of general knowledge is what is intended to be expressed by the term "medhā. (18)

In that case, one might ask: "Should it not be said that he produced the world through knowledge (*jñāna*), rather than through intelligence (*medhā*)? To this, he says: "By means of scriptural [knowledge].

If it were stated that he produced it "by means of knowledge," there would arise a misconception consistent with the context—that it was produced by meditation (*dhyāna*) alone; therefore, the mention of "intelligence" (*medhā*) is for the purpose of dispelling that [misconception]. It is not [the case that intelligence is redundant].
The meaning is that the very meditation on the seven creations of food is the cause, because it is the cause even for one whose intellect is otherwise prohibited. || 18 ||
If, indeed, by the word "austerity" (tapaḥ) practices such as the Kṛcchra penance are meant;
Nevertheless, the mention of "karma" is for the purpose of explaining the sevenfold division. || 19 ||

He states the meaning of the word *tapas* (austerity) with the words "by the word *tapas*. Because ritual action (*karman*) is the cause for the birth of the world consisting of the seven types of food, it is that [action] alone which is meant here by *tapas*, not the *kṛcchra* penance and so forth; for the mere [performance of such penances] is not the cause of that [world-creation]. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
From the indicative mark "by means of wisdom, by means of wisdom," knowledge and action are both understood.
Wisdom, austerity, and passion are the [qualities] to be grasped, and not others, because the other [qualities] are fruitless regarding what is to be grasped. || 20 ||
By means of the words "medhā" (intelligence) and "tapas" (austerity), he shows that the inclusion of knowledge and action is supported by the remainder of the passage. Regarding the word "dhiyā":

since the remainder of the passage—"by intelligence, by intelligence one generates [the self] through actions"—states that it is the knowledge and action existing at that time which act as the generators, it follows that these two alone are to be understood here, and not the well-known intelligence and austerity. He recalls the previously stated reason for not taking the well-known intelligence and austerity.
"Because that [result] would be fruitless. (20)
For drinking is indeed the primary action, as is the experience of knowledge.
Therefore, having abandoned the irrelevant, it is not proper to include what is not relevant to the subject at hand. || 21 ||

He states that it is not only the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that serves as the means of proof here, but also the context (*prakaraṇa*), saying: "For [the word] *pārka*. Thus, the meaning is that in this case there would be both the abandonment of what is under discussion (*prakṛta-hāni*) and the introduction of what is not under discussion (*aprakṛta-prakriyā*). || 21 ||
Since there can be no other means than intelligence and the removal of heat (affliction).
Therefore, because it is well-known, the Śruti explains [it] directly with the words "for indeed" (ato hi). 22.
Having explained the mantra beginning with "The seven kinds of food," he explains the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "By intelligence" (medhayā hi). Regarding "By intelligence":

since there is no cause for creation other than knowledge and action, and because it is well-known that this [intelligence] alone is the cause therein, the Śruti text beginning with "by intelligence" directly declares, by means of the word "hi" (for/indeed), that the father's status as creator is due to that very [intelligence]. || 22 ||
He fashioned that which is common to this entire assembly of enjoyers.
Having created this single-mindedness, if the Father bestows it here; || 23 ||
This very Brāhmaṇa passage—"this indeed is his"—provides the explanation for the mantra-word beginning with "ekamasya" (one of him). Regarding the word "asya" (of this):
[it refers to] that which is the means (*sādhana*) for you.

Regarding the inquiry— what was that single food which the Creator fashioned after creating the seven foods as common to all living beings?— it is said:
He said: "And that. || 23 ||
That which is constantly eaten by living beings day after day is husk.
Therefore, this is appropriate as it is common to all beings, because they all abide within it.

Anticipating the objection that there might be some other food that is common to all, he clarifies this by saying "yadidam" (that which is this). He states the reason why it is precisely this food—which is eaten daily and regularly by living beings out of thirst—that is common to all, by saying "sarva... (all...). 24.
He who meditates upon this food as having an uncommon form—
Sūtra 206:
"The afflicted person here does not turn away from evil.
(25) He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who [knows this]" (sa ya etat...). For one who makes common food exclusive, there is no [consequence] such as evil and so forth.
"Vṛtti" means subsistence. "Iha" refers to the application of food. "Jñānadaurbalya" means being afflicted by illness. || 25 ||
And here, by the word "upāsana," the scripture intends "tātparya" (the primary purport).
Likewise, in the mantra "mogham annam," there is a censure of the habit [of eating].

"What is that worship? To this he says: "And worship... The word "food" (*anna*) has the sense of the locative case; the intended meaning is the state of being fixed upon that [food] by making it one's own exclusive possession. He provides a mantra as authority for the matter stated by the Brāhmaṇa: "In vain... "In vain" means food...

"The one lacking wisdom finds [only] death; I tell you the truth. This means that if one weak in knowledge obtains food that is unfit for the gods and others—food that is "not for us" (*amotra*) and thus fruitless—that constitutes his death. Since making common food exclusive is contemptible, the meaning is that one should not make it exclusive. If the making of common food exclusive were merely accidental, then [the expiation would be] *prāyaścitta*.
Considering the lightness of the white [stone], it is a term denoting habitual practice. || 26 ||
For that food which is prepared is indeed called the Vaiśvadeva.
For this is not sufficient for the complete cessation of all evils. || 27 ||
Having stated his own position regarding the mantra and Brāhmaṇa beginning with "One of these," [the author] states the position of Bhartṛprapañca: "For it is the Vaiśvadeva.
The meaning is that the food known as *vaiśvadeva*, which is prepared by the householder according to the Smṛti for the sake of the gods and others—that alone is what is common here.

In this context, the word "for" (*hi*) is intended to establish its status as well-known through the Smṛti and the conduct of the learned. How can there be a statement regarding the removal of evil for one who meditates upon that? For indeed—

Anticipating the objection that one who performs the scriptural *vaiśvadeva* rite might still be subject to fault, he says: "Not sufficient" (*nālam*). The meaning is that the rite called *vaiśvadeva* merely removes some small portion of sin and not all of it; therefore, the statement is intended to destroy only a minor amount of evil. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to indicate that [the rite] lacks the capacity to dispel a much greater quantity of sin. || 27 ||
Thus some maintain this view, but it is not tenable according to reason.
Since the established fact "that this is so" is restated by way of anuvāda (corroboration), [it is not a mere repetition]. || 28 ||

He concludes the opponent’s view with the words "Thus [it is said]. He refutes that with the word "That. He clarifies why it is indeed untenable with the phrase "Because it is not stated. Therefore, since the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is something not previously established (*apūrva*), it cannot be the object of a restatement (*anuvāda*); yet here such a restatement exists. Thus, the opponent’s position is not tenable—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Furthermore, it possesses no perceptibility, since it is established solely by means of the scripture (*śāstra*).
Just as [the object] situated within the mouths of all speakers is directly perceived, so too [is it here]. || 29 ||
“Having prepared the Vaiśvadeva offering,
a Brāhmaṇa should daily perform the oblation (homa) in the domestic fire for these deities according to the prescribed rule.”
In the evening, one should diligently offer a bali-oblation of cooked food;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.

Anticipating the objection that, according to the aforementioned Smṛti, because [the Vaiśvadeva] lacks novelty (*apūrvatva*), its status as a restatement (*anuvāda*) is established, he says: "It is perceptible" (*prātyakṣyam*). He states the imperceptibility of the Vaiśvadeva by means of a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): "Just as... Because of the reference to the perceptible food with the word "this" (*idam*), [it refers to] the Vaiśvadeva.

The point is that even if it were seen in scripture, since it is not perceptible, that [scriptural vision] would be impossible; thus, according to the opponent's view, the Brāhmaṇa passage is difficult to reconcile. || 29 ||
And in every living being, the desire "may this be mine" is observed.
Therefore, it is concluded that this [body] is mixed with portions of all living beings. || 30 ||
He states that [the view] is tenable within his own school: "perception" (*pratīti*). After the word *syāt*, the word *iti* should be understood.

He states that the fruit is the attainment of the desired object: "all" (*sarva*). The meaning is that when food is grasped by the general term "of all living beings," it is suitable to be referred to as "this" (*idam*) through perception and so forth; thus, the restatement (*anuvāda*) is easily accomplished. || 30 ||
And there is also the statement of the Smṛti: "One should not cook food for one's own sake."
He who enjoys what has been given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief.
"By eating the food of one who has killed a learned Brāhmaṇa (bhrūṇahā), one becomes [guilty] here"—so says the Smṛti.

Furthermore, if the word "common" (sādhāraṇa) were taken to include the food of all living beings, such as dogs and so forth, then the statement regarding the cessation of sin for one who makes common what was not common, as well as the Smṛti texts, would be consistent. Therefore, considering that our own interpretation alone is logical, [the author] states "common" (sādhāraṇam).
He cites traditional texts (*smṛti*) to demonstrate the faultiness of one who makes [offerings] common property: "Not for oneself," etc. One should not kill an animal in vain;

nor should one eat alone by oneself; and one should not offer [the sacrifice] except according to the prescribed rule—these three quarters of the verse are to be understood. He refers back to the gods mentioned in the statement, "For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, bestow upon you desired enjoyments" (*iṣṭān bhogān hi vo devā dāsyante yajñabhāvitāḥ*). By the word "by them" (*taiḥ*), he means "the enjoyments granted by them."

The meaning is "for these gods. Regarding the first quarter-verse of the *Smṛti* which states: "The killer of an embryo wipes his sin upon the eater of food; the one who falsely accuses a blameless man, or the thief before the king, as long as there is no mixing of falsehood," this is its meaning: a "killer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahā*) is a slayer of an eminent Brahmin. For he will say later: "And here, the slayer of an excellent Brahmin is designated as a 'killer of an embryo'. He wipes his own sin upon the consumer of his food.
Because it is stated that the giver of food purifies and casts off [his] evil, the word "sinful" (*pāṣita*) refers to the other who eats without having made [the food] common [to all].
"But he who, though wise, eats before giving to these— while eating, he does not realize his own devouring by dogs and vultures."
Having worshipped the gods, the sages, humans, the ancestors, and the domestic deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.

[vol2, page 509]
He who cooks for his own sake alone eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from the sacrifice.
"But those wicked ones who cook for their own sake eat this [sin]," and so forth—
this is the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). Here, the phrase "in this world" (*iha*) refers to the fact that making common food one's own exclusive possession is fraught with fault.
Thus it was said. || 31 ||
And because it is included within that [category], it is logical that it belongs to the very pinnacle of all.
Although its two parts were grasped by the planets, it was not cast into their midst in that manner. || 32 ||

For this reason as well, he states that by the word "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), the food of all living beings is to be understood, saying: "Of that too. Since the food of the Viśvedevas is included within all food, and because it is possible to grasp that [specific category], the meaning is that only the pervading [food] is to be grasped. If it is argued that even when the Viśvedevas' portion is grasped, other portions would also be grasped, he says "no," stating: "Of that. The meaning of the particle *tu* (but) is that there is no grasping of the food of dogs and so forth. The reason for this is stated: "There..."

Regarding the phrase "of this [person]": therein, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is "in that manner. The meaning is that just as the food of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is included within the food of the Sarvādya sacrifice, there is no other food within that [latter] in such a manner. || 32 ||
Since non-creation and non-application have been established, when there is the grasping of that [object], [the following occurs].
And that would result in something undesirable for all living beings. || 33 ||

He states another defect in the opposing position: "asṛṣṭa" (uncreated), etc. The word "tat" refers to the Vaiśvadeva [offering]. He refutes the acceptability of this consequence: "tacceti" (and that). The meaning is that both the creation of everything and its application are intended to be expressed. || 33 ||
And there is no turning back from evils when the Vaiśvadeva offerings are not collected.
His statement is not reasonable, because it relies solely upon the authority of the scriptures.

In that very context, he states another defect: "And there is no exclusion" (*avyāvṛttiśca*). The construction is as follows: if the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is taken to mean the *vaiśvadeva* [offering], then the statement that "one who is intent on that is not excluded from sins" is not logical. [For] the destruction of sin results from the performance of scripturally enjoined rites.
He states the reason, saying "of that," because it alone is logical. || 34 ||
Nor is it understood from the word itself that there is even a slight diminution of sin.
Because of the statement "he is not [touched] by evil," it is neither heard nor grasped.

Regarding the claim that this [passage] has as its purpose the destruction of only a small amount of evil, he says: "Even a very small [evil]. The meaning is that it is not logical to abandon what is explicitly stated in scripture and to adopt a procedure not mentioned therein. || 35 ||
However, when both are apprehended, the reason is accepted as being probative.

the ellipsis is to be supplied as "in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. This means, in effect, "those two [offerings] which are the food of the gods. An option between two equal [alternatives] is well-known elsewhere as well.

The word *hi* (for) has the sense of *tu* (but). For this very reason, it is said "equally" (*tulyavat*). Equivalence is the cause for an option (*vikalpa*). However, there is no equivalence between what is based on direct revelation (*śrauta*) and what is based on tradition (*smārta*), because the former is stronger; furthermore, since that [equivalence] would also exist in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [which are both śrauta], an option is impossible. After the explanation of the two mantras beginning with "one," why is the seventh food, the food of animals, explained while skipping the three [foods] beginning with "three" which follow in the sequence?

Regarding this transgression of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), he states the intention of the *Śruti*: "Because they are relevant... Even though the three foods would have been reached at this point by virtue of the order of recitation following the explanation of the food common to all and the two foods of the gods, [they are not explained here].

He states the reason why [these] have been explained with the words "of these" (*teṣām*). Since the three kinds of food are to be accomplished as the fruit in the form of the *sūtra*-self, they are entirely distinct from the aforementioned foods—such as the food of cattle—which serve as means; therefore, [the text speaks of] the fourfold food that constitutes the means.
The meaning is that by explaining [the three foods] immediately after the preceding explanation, there is a transgression of the order of the text. || 46 ||
And because it is easy to understand, and likewise because its scope is more extensive.

The meaning is that by stating "the explanation of the three foods" (*annatrayavyākhyā*) after [the mention of] "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*), comprehension is achieved with ease; therefore, there is no regard for the order of the text.

Furthermore, because the three foods have an extensive scope—pertaining to the internal self (*adhyātma*), the elemental world (*adhibhūta*), and the divine realm (*adhidaiva*)—it is appropriate that they follow immediately after the four foods, which have an extremely limited scope; for this reason as well, he says "moreover" (*bhūyaḥ*) to justify the transgression of the textual sequence. Moreover, [he shows that] the food of animals is distinct from the previously mentioned foods...

One might raise the objection: "In this context, the conquest of death is understood to result merely from performing the Agnihotra oblation with milk for a period measured by a year; it does not refer to another philosophical system (darśana). He states the number of units of time—the days and nights that are parts of the year—by saying "three hundred and sixty. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the year. "There are hundreds of them. Thus, even the days and nights of the year, when divided in two ways, amount to seven hundred and twenty.

The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is as follows: the Śruti states, "Seven hundred and twenty are the days and nights of the year. Regarding the bricks known as *yājuṣmatī*, which constitute the limbs of Prajāpati in the form of the *cityāgni* (the piled fire-altar) that is the year itself, there are three hundred and sixty according to the non-distinction of their application; however, by distinguishing their specific applications, there are seven hundred and twenty. This is the number residing in the bricks. (65)

Relying on the Śruti passage, "So many are the Yājuṣmatī bricks of Agni," he says: "The Yājuṣmatīs also... Then, by means of the commonality of number residing in the channels (*nāḍī*) of the person, those channels—

The meaning is that, having transformed those very days and nights into the form of bricks and thereby connecting the channels (nāḍīs), one who offers the Agnihotra with milk for a year— by means of that very ritual correspondence (saṃpat) consisting of the oblation combined with knowledge— attains Prajāpati, whose nature is the year, and thus conquers death. || 67 ||

The meaning is that since these [offerings] satisfy the householder and are the causes for his victory over death, there is no need to depend on a variety of ritual applications (prayoga-bheda) for that victory, as it follows from a single application alone. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that by the power of knowledge (vidyā-sāmarthya), the wise person possesses the capacity to offer everything to the gods with a single oblation (āhuti). || 73 ||
Thus the entire world has been offered as an oblation; nothing else remains beyond this.
Therefore, from the realization as it has been described, death arises through the attainment of all.
He summarizes the meaning of the cause: "It is offered" (*hutam*). Therefore, other than this world which has been offered, there is nothing further to be offered—that is the sense.

As for the aforementioned vision—the meditation that the entire world is established in milk—having withdrawn the entire world into oneself and attained it as one's own self, and having experienced oneness with all the gods by becoming oneself the form of the food of all the gods, one does not again partake of birth; such is the meaning. || 74 ||
Having reflected in her heart upon what has been said and also upon what is yet to be said, the Śruti [proceeds].
He says "Why food? with the intention of posing a question. (75)
Now, an objection is raised: "Four kinds of food have been explained, while three remain to be explained; since those have not yet been explained, why [is there no question]?

Anticipating this doubt with the word "why," the author says: "as has been stated. Although three foods are yet to be described, nevertheless, intending to show that they are indeed taught in the same manner as the four previously mentioned foods, the Śruti uses the expression "why" with the intention of posing a question.
Thus is the connection [of the verse]. || 75 ||
In this manner, the aforementioned foods are always being consumed by the eaters.
Why do they not reach exhaustion, like grain in a full granary? || 76 ||

He explains the interrogative statement with the words, "being eaten. The meaning of the word *atha* (then) is: after having created the sevenfold food and having distributed it to the eaters. The phrase "as described" refers to the mention of its sevenfold nature. "Always" means every day, as it is being eaten.
This is the connection. He provides an illustration regarding the non-depletion of food while it is being consumed: "As [in the case of] barley," etc. A *kusūla* is a granary for grain. || 76 ||
Why are they called "those" (tāni)? [The answer is] given by the Śruti itself acting as the teacher.
Or rather, by the word "puruṣa," the supreme cause for the imperishable is stated.
He provides the answer to the question: "Why are they [not exhausted]?

The construction is as follows: by the very scriptural statement—"Puruṣa indeed is the imperishable," etc.—which stands like a teacher providing the answer to the question "Why are they?", the uncontradicted cause for the non-exhaustion of the aforementioned foods has been stated. || 77 ||
If food is always being eaten, it is not produced from that [eating].

"The aforementioned defect would apply [only if it were so], but it is not produced here. (78) He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of that [verse] by way of its contrapositive (*vyatireka*): "If it were eaten... and so forth. "From that" means from the eater. "In this world" refers to the time of enjoyment. The remainder of the sense is: "Therefore, there is no fear of the depletion of food. (78)
Because he is the cause of the inexhaustibility of food, the Puruṣa is called Akṣiti.
For he always produces food through a continuous stream of cognition; therefore [it is so]. || 79 ||
1 kha. ...from what has been declared, [one attains] vision; 2 kha. ...from everything, death; 3 kha. ...of whom indeed.
[vol2, page 518] 812 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]

In that context, he states the meaning of the word *akṣiti* (imperishable): "By food," etc. Anticipating the question, "How is that enjoyer the cause of the non-destruction of food? he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "For he [is this]," etc.: "For he," etc. The meaning is that the ignorant person, through the aggregate of scriptural and non-scriptural knowledge and action, becomes the creator of food during the state of enjoyment. Therefore, because he is the cause of its non-destruction, the person is the *akṣiti*; this is the implied conclusion. || 79 ||
For by means of the continuous flow of activity and cognition, the enjoyer [of experience] exists day and night.
That indeed produces food; therefore, food is never exhausted.
Having restated what was previously said, he declares that the fruit of the food is inexhaustible: "The ritual act," etc. (verse 80).
Because it is being created by the very enjoyment of the one who bestows enjoyment.
In this way, there shall indeed be no exhaustion of food, because of the non-distinction between those two.

For the enjoyer, while consuming food, exhausts it; how then can there be the production of that [food] through the continuity of actions and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that which bestows enjoyment. Since both knowledge and action bestow enjoyment, by means of that enjoyment itself, future causes such as attachment are produced; thus, because of the mutual connection between enjoyment and creation, there is no exhaustion of food through enjoyment. This being the case, the enjoyer does not exhaust the food.
Such is the meaning. || 81 ||
The experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is the fruit of prior karma.
In that case, there would be the activity of passion and aversion for the sake of accomplishing another result.

[Verse 82] Regarding the question, "How can enjoyment be the cause of passion and so forth, since it rather causes desire to dissolve? some respond with the word "sukha" (pleasure). The word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to its internal subdivisions. The result of the accumulated knowledge and karma is what is called the direct perception of pleasure and the like; and that—

Furthermore, that [karma] which produces passion and so forth toward objects of a similar class causes one to perform actions that are either auspicious or inauspicious; and since those [actions] bear fruit for the agent, there is no destruction of the food [of karma] by way of a continuous flow—this is the meaning. || 82 ||
For action preceded by passion and so forth arises as something possessing fruit.
But that which is devoid of passion and the like is fruitless, like the speech of one who is asleep. || 83 ||

He states, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that passion and the like are the cause of fruitful action. [The verse begins with] "Passion and the like" (*rāgādi*). Therefore, the remainder of the sense is: "Thus, passion and the like possess the quality of being the cause of fruitful action. || 83 ||
Now, it is asked: what is the cause for its inexhaustibility?
This further question is posed by those who know that for the sake of accomplishing the fruit.
Now, this is being explained: how is it that the person (puruṣa) possesses imperishability? || 84 ||

He restates the preceding [text] regarding the latter [portion] to avoid redundancy: "What is the reason? The meaning is that when the question was asked regarding the cause for the seven types of food—which are constantly being eaten by their eaters—not undergoing depletion, the answer was given in the passage beginning with "Or rather, the person is the imperishable" (*puruṣo vā akṣitiḥ*). He then states that the sentence beginning with "He who knows this" (*yo vaitām*) is intended to declare the fruit for one who meditates upon Prajāpati as the person consisting of the sevenfold food, characterized by the quality of being the cause of non-depletion.

Regarding the word *atha*: he states the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) in order to introduce the passage beginning with *sa hi*. Regarding the word *bhūyaḥ*: since it was previously stated—and is now being restated in the present context—that the person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the imperishable (*akṣiti*), i.e., the cause of imperishability, if one asks again how he is the cause of the imperishability of food, [the answer follows].
(Note: The text fragment ends with *vittipha*.)

The meaning is as follows. To this, he says that the previously stated answer beginning with "For he" (*sa hi*) and so forth is now being elaborated upon by the passage beginning with "For he" (*sa hi*). This—[the text continues].
And so it is said. || 84 ||
For he prepares this food at each respective time by means of that which has been produced [by her].
For by each act of his intellect and by his deeds, a person fashions his own self.

He explains that [with the words] "For he" (sa hi). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of actions produced at their respective times. The meaning of the word "for" (hi) is that knowledge and action possess the capacity to produce that [result] through a succession of prescribed and prohibited [factors], as established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). || 85 ||
Even while being enjoyed from that source, they do not diminish because of their continuous flow. || 86 ||
Just as a person is an absolute consumer of foods, so too is he.
The agent, too, would be absolutely non-existent, because of their mutual non-distinction.

He states the result regarding its production of food through both prescribed and non-prescribed knowledge and action: "Being enjoyed... This means that because enjoyment and creation exist as a continuous stream (*prabandha*) in the form of a flow. Alternatively, he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "Or rather this... by way of its grammatical connection (*anvaya*). He says: "Just as... In that regard, he states the reason: "Mutually..."—because agency and enjoyership are bound to one another.
This is the meaning. || 86 || 87 ||
Thus, in the form of a continuous sequence, there is the definition of the probandum and the probans.
It appears as if stationary to those whose minds are enveloped by the veil of ignorance. || 88 ||

The phrase "by means of thought after thought" (*dhiyā dhiyā*) and so forth refers to the scripture which elaborates upon the solution stated in the passage "for he [is] this" (*sa hīdam*). Since the sevenfold food is an effect, it perishes moment by moment; nevertheless, because it is produced again and again, it is "immovable" (*acalam*) in its nature as a continuous flow (*pravāha*). The intent is that the ignorant perceive it as such. Thus, he clarifies what was stated in the commentary beginning with "prajñā" (wisdom). "In this way" (*evam*). || 88 ||
And this is stated by the Śruti for the sake of achieving dispassion in the person.
For one who is not dispassionate toward saṃsāra, no one here has a desire for liberation. 89.

To the question of why the world is said by the Śruti to perish at every moment, he says: "And this... He also states that [this leads to] detachment: "From the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)... For it is observed that those possessed of attachment to the world have no desire for liberation. || 89 ||
Because the fruit and the cause are always and absolutely non-different from one another.
For what purpose [is it said] that when right knowledge is obscured, there is no cause for the cessation of its causes? (90)

He states the reason why one who is not dispassionate lacks the desire for liberation: "Phala... (The fruit...). Because worldly existence and passion and so forth are always pervasive, the meaning is that for one possessed by passion, there can be no desire for liberation. Anticipating the objection that even for one who is dispassionate, there may be no desire for liberation because liberation is achievable through ritual action (*karman*), and ritual action is dependent upon passion, he says: "Samyak... (Perfectly...). It is knowledge alone that destroys bondage along with its cause, not ritual action, because the latter is not antagonistic [to bondage].
The meaning. || 90 ||
Therefore, having abandoned everything else, one should strive for the attainment of perfect knowledge.
One should exert great effort through the activities of mind, speech, and body. || 91 ||
1. Ma. The station of the mobile beings. 2. Sva. Ga. will be examined.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:

Since knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), having renounced, should be intent upon the repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth for the sake of that knowledge; this is the established conclusion, which he states with the word "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*). The fact that such intentness toward the aforementioned repetition must never be relinquished until the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is of great importance.
...that very [nature]. || 91 ||
For the person who knows the imperishability of the Self, this fruit is declared.
He who eats by means of the secondary function (vṛtti) through the metaphorical indication (pratīka) of "eating bliss," he truly eats [the Self]. || 92 ||

Having explained the passage beginning with "yā dhiyā," he explains the passage beginning with "yo vaitām. Regarding the word "puṃsaḥ" (of the person), he states the meaning of the mantra-verse beginning with "so 'nnam" through the term "vṛttyā" (by means of function). || 92 ||
For food never becomes defective in this manner when offered to him.
Being the primary one, he always eats food according to his desire. || 93 ||

He states the aforementioned point by way of contrast: "Not one such as this. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that while it is appropriate for the ignorant person to be subordinate (*guṇatva*) with respect to food due to the absence of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), for the knower, however, because of the power of knowledge, there is indeed primacy (*pradhānatva*) with respect to food. The phrase "at any time" means before enjoyment, after enjoyment, and at the very moment [of eating]. If the knower lacks subordination with respect to food, how can he be its enjoyer?
To this, he replies: "The primary," etc. (93).
He even goes to the gods and likewise subsists upon their vital energy.
This is the certainty that this praise is for the aforementioned knowledge. || 94 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa vai devān... as "api devān" (even the gods). Since the state of being a god and so forth is already established by the very statement "he eats food," there is no acquisition of any new meaning here; therefore, the point is that this is merely a praise of knowledge (vidyā-stuti). || 94 ||
Now follows this definitive exposition concerning the three types of food that are most excellent.
The nature of the inner self (adhyātma) is described for one who is established in the performance of bodily duties. || 95 ||

The fourfold food consisting of the means of attainment has been declared, as well as the cause for the non-exhaustion of that food through the addition of the quality of being the "abode" (*akṣiti*).

Now, until the end of this Brāhmaṇa, he states the purport of the subsequent section: "Food... etc. That which is "superior" (*utkṛṣṭa*) means that which is distinguished from the fourfold means of attainment. It refers to the three types of food existing in the form of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-kārya*) and the gross body (*sthūla*).

The meaning is that the subsequent text is for the purpose of providing an explanation. He states the specific connection of the portion preceding "the three worlds" with the words "it is described"; the ellipsis to be supplied is "the three kinds of food at the beginning. (99)
The state of being inherent in the preparatory application has been described in the preceding chapters.
And those who are the enjoyers of these [offerings] have also been described by the Śruti. || 96 ||

In order to clarify the very relationship already mentioned, he recalls what was stated previously with the words "In practice," etc. This means: in the aforementioned foods—namely, common food, the food of the gods, and the food of animals—the consumers are, respectively, dogs, cāṇḍālas, and others; the gods, Indra and others; and the animals. || 96 ||
1. Kha: This is its fruit. 2. Ka. Kha: Together with Deṃ.
