Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 815.
Because the previous karmas that exist are inherent in the preparatory application (prayoga).
The subsequent scriptural passage [establishes] that the triad beginning with the mind is an effect, for the sake of that [Brahman]. || 97 ||

Having stated that the fourfold food is the means (*sādhana*) and the threefold food is the goal (*sādhya*), he restates the intermediate division by saying, "because of being inherent in the performance" (*prayogasamavāyitvāt*). He then introduces the commencement of the subsequent section for the purpose of explaining the threefold food which constitutes the result, saying, "for the sake of that" (*tādarthyena*). || 97 ||
Then the father, through his wisdom and austerity, produced three kinds of food.
He likewise employed the mind, speech, and breath for the sake of the Self. || 98 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "three" as follows: "Having produced," meaning having created the seven kinds of food through knowledge and action, [he created] four.

The meaning is that [the Creator], having divided [the food] among the enjoyers, set aside three parts for his own sake. The word "atha" (then) signifies the immediate sequence of the creation of food and the subsequent distribution of the fourfold food. The particle "ca" (and) is used to provide an illustration by comparing it to the distribution of the other fourfold [elements]. || 98 ||
In order to establish the existence of the mind, inference is presented by means of scripture.
And he will also describe its forms as desire and so forth, even though it is existent. || 99 ||

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "elsewhere" (anyatra) as follows: "of the mind" (manasaḥ). That [point] will become manifest later. Having raised the objection—"If the existence of the mind is established through inference, then for what purpose is the scriptural statement regarding desire and so forth?"—he states its purport from a preliminary standpoint:

"and of that which exists" (sataśca). The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is "and of that which is measured" (mitasya ca). The word "also" (api ca) is used to indicate the conjunction of the attribute with the substratum (dharmin). || 99 ||
In this state governed by ignorance, there is the association of attributes, their substrata, and so forth.
It is situated solely within the effects of ignorance, but it does not belong to the inner self (pratyagātman). || 100 ||
He states the intended purport: "Ignorance" (avidyā). || 100 ||
In order to establish this point, the subsequent section of the text is introduced.
An effort is made [to prove this] so that the self may not possess the nature of desire and the like. || 101 ||

"How is this matter established by mere assertion? To this he says: "It is thus. Anticipating the objection that it is incorrect to say there is no relationship between the self (ātman) and its attributes (dharma), since desire and so forth are well-known to be its attributes, he says: "Let it not be. This means: lest the status of being the substratum of desire and so forth be suspected for the self, the Śruti intends to establish that desire and so forth are attributes of the mind (manas).
The meaning is that what is established [by such means] is a delusion contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 101 ||
Question 28: When asked, "Did you see the old ox going along?", the other replied: [he did].
My mind was elsewhere; therefore, I did not perceive what you have said.

Having analyzed the subsequent section and stated its purport, he explains the passage beginning with "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) and so forth. The word "questioned" (*pṛṣṭa*) implies that "the other person speaks. He describes the manner of that person's speech with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). This means "with regard to the 'old ox' (*jaradgava*) and so forth. Even when the cause—the object and so on—is present, the cognition of the old ox arises only occasionally; this necessitates another cause, otherwise [there would be] a contradiction regarding the object and so forth.
The meaning is that the presumption (arthāpatti)—that the arising of knowledge would otherwise be impossible at any time during deep meditation—establishes the existence of the mind. || 102 ||
816 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 522]
The mind is observed to be connected with other objects, just like a jar or similar things.
And that [knowledge] has the self alone as its witness, by virtue of relying on a logical presumption (arthāpatti). || 103 ||

In that very context, he states the direct perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*). [He says] "in another object" (*viṣayāntara*), etc. Having raised the objection—"Even if another cause is established by relying on the aforementioned *arthāpatti* (presumption), how is the mind (*manas*) established?"—he replies with "by the method of elimination" (*pāriśeṣyāt*). [He says] "that," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) [indicates] the direct perception of the witness.

The word "and" (samuccaya) has the sense of conjunction. The meaning of the particle "hi" is that it is well known that a means of cognition (*māna*) is the establisher of its object (*meyasādhakatva*). Nor is it logical to claim that the auditory organ and so forth alone constitute that [means], because even when those organs are unimpaired, the cognition of an object sometimes fails to arise, and because memory is observed even in the absence of those organs, as in the case of the deaf and so on; such is the intended meaning. || 103 ||
The self exists here, having consciousness as its intrinsic nature, and likewise the eye is unimpaired.
And the conscious being does not perceive the cow and horse even when they are right before his eyes. || 104 ||

In order to establish the existence of the mind (*manas*), he states the reason to clarify the inference mentioned here: "It exists" (*asti*). This means that when the object of inquiry, such as a cow, is present; he says "consciousness" (*cit*) to show that the defect residing in the agent is not the cause for the absence of knowledge.

He says "and the eye" (*cakṣuśca*) to show that a defect in the instrument is also not the cause. He further says [the following] to show that even the non-existence of auxiliary factors is not the cause thereof.
Regarding the phrase "along with its illumination": having raised the objection that the effect might also exist when the causal complex is present, he says: "And not... (104).
Therefore, it is inferred that there exists something else, in the absence of which one does not see.
In which all that is aggregated, beginning with the letter *d*, is seen when it exists.

He states [the argument]: "The object of doubt (vimata) depends on something other than the self and so forth, because even when those [self, etc. are present, it occurs only occasionally, like a jar. He says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). He states the result of the inference: "It is established that there exists another cause for the cognition of cows and so forth, distinct from the self and other [factors] commonly accepted. In that very context, he states the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "In which... The term "all" refers to the seer and so forth; "assembled" (*saṃhatam*) means joined together; this is the designation of the agent.
The connection is that "there exists something other than that. || 105 ||
That which exists as the mind must exist through established proof; and that mind does indeed exist.
"Because my mind was elsewhere, I did not see him; it is for this reason [that I am at fault]. (106)

Anticipating the objection that it might be something other than the mind (*manas*), he says "that which... The construction is as follows: since it is another cause, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be the [subtle] body (*puryaṣṭaka*) rather than the mind. Nor is it reasonable to say that it is simply the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), because that [unseen force] conforms to what is perceived (*dṛṣṭānusāritva*). Therefore...

The sense is that [the cause] would otherwise be fruitless, that the non-arising of the effect would be illogical, and that otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). He states that worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is also an authority in this matter with the word "by consensus" (*prasiddhyā*). He states that even the consensus of the arrow-maker is an authority there with the word "it happened" (*abhūt*): "Since my mind was elsewhere, directed toward the arrow and so forth, I did not perceive the king even as he was approaching nearby."
The meaning is that its establishment [is achieved] even through a specific form of conventional renown (prasiddhi). || 106 ||
Even though it exists, the self and all other such things are not causes for seeing and so forth.
For it is by the mind alone that the seer perceives cows and other objects here in this world.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "manasā hi" (for by the mind): "Even though it exists," and so forth. Here, the term "iha" (here) refers to the state of proximity between the self, the sense organs, and their objects.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth) in "darśanādau" (in seeing, etc.), touching and other such activities are included. "Paśyati" (sees) is an elliptical expression for "hears" and the rest. Therefore, the ellipsis to be supplied is "therefore, that [mind] exists. || 107 ||

Having established the existence of the substratum (dharmin) which is the locus of all cognitions without exception, [the author proceeds]. [Vol. 2, Page 523] 5 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri. 817.
For the sake of accomplishing the dharmas such as desire and so forth, "desire" and the rest are thus explained. || 108 ||

Having restated what has been established, he introduces another statement with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The word "hi" (for) is used to indicate the maxim that "the investigation of attributes [is possible] only when the substratum exists. He suggests the operation of scripture as a corroborative factor for the inference: "The mind possesses specific qualities because it is corporeal, like a jar. Then [he says] "atha" (now). || 108 ||
The instruments of the mind, as well as the organs of intellect and action, are indeed means of accomplishment.
Therefore, the mind possesses preeminence over all its respective bases.

One might suspect that desire and the like are not properties of the mind (*manas*), because they are properties of the body and so forth due to water [and other elements] in them; anticipating this, he says: "The means" (*sādhanāni*).

The meaning is that since the body and so forth are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the mind in the production of desire and the like, the mind alone, as the primary factor (*pradhāna*), possesses the status of the substratum (*dharmitva*).
The word "also" (*api*) signifies the stated pervasion (*vyāpti*). || 109 ||
Desire for sense objects is what constitutes desire; there is no reason for it to apply to anything specific.
For one who has perceived an object through the senses, there arises conceptualization and ascertainment. (110)

Having explained the meaning of the word *kāma*, [the author] states that the specific mention in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) as "desire for sexual union with women" is inappropriate; he says: "viṣaya... He explains *saṃkalpa* (volition): "indriya... The meaning is that volition, which is rooted in desire, is the specific determination of what has been perceived in a general way. || 110 ||
A mental state characterized by a lack of certainty is declared to be doubt.
Faith is the conviction that things exist; lack of faith is its opposite.
He explains doubt and the others [with the words] "aniścaya" (lack of certainty) and so forth. || 111 ||
Without fortitude and faith, desire and the other [afflictions] would not exist, for they cannot arise without a cause.
For even desirelessness and the rest are indeed considered to be stated here by implication. || 112 ||

"Why is desirelessness (*akāma*) and so forth not mentioned there, just as lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) and so forth are? To this, he says: 'Firmness' (*dhṛti*). Since an effect cannot be established by itself without a cause, and since desire and so forth are the causes of firmness and so forth—as established through positive and negative concomitance—and since desire and so forth are impossible without them, the absence of desire and so forth is already implied by the statement regarding the absence of firmness and so forth. For indeed, the functions of desire and so forth, which consist of the stiffening of the body and so on, do not exist without faith in sense objects."

The meaning is that they are accomplished. The word "here" (*atra*) refers to the sentence under discussion. The particle *hi* is used for the purpose of stating a well-known fact: namely, that an effect is not accomplished without a cause. || 112 ||
And retention (dhāraṇā) is to be understood as steadfastness (dhṛti), which is the holding fast of an object apprehended by the intellect.
The opposite of that is lack of fortitude; it is designated as *hrī*, or modesty. || 113 ||
Consciousness is determined to be the intellect (dhī), and fear is said to be dread (bhī).
"All this is to be known by the mind"—this is what is meant by identity (tādātmya). || 114 ||

He states the meaning of "fortitude" (*dhṛti*) and so forth: "and sustaining" (*dhāraṇam*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the propping up of the body and other such things is also included. [Note: *na* appears to be a scribal error for *naca* or similar. 103 1 ga. is not mentioned.
818 Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika) [First Chapter] [Vol. 2, Page 524]

Furthermore, there is no tautology with respect to consciousness through the term *saṃkalpa*, because there is a distinction between the general and the particular. Nor can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on the relationship of cause and effect, as this is not observed in cases such as the potter and the jar; it is with this in mind that the term "identity" (*tādātmya*) is employed. || 113 ||
The conclusion is made by intending the identity of the intellect and the mind.
All the sense organs as well are indeed merely the functions of the internal mind.
For the indication of its own function occurs within one's own mind through the tactile sense organ.
Therefore, it should be understood that the mind alone is the aggregate of the body and the senses. || 116 ||

Having abandoned the notion [that desire and so forth belong] to the intellect (*buddhi*), why is it said that they possess identity with the mind (*manas*) through desire and the like? To this he replies: "Of the intellect alone" (*buddher eva*).

The meaning intended by the concluding phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is that, by the force of the aforementioned proofs, the mind—whose form consists of desire and so forth—is established as non-different from the intellect.
He states the meaning of the word "also" (*api*): "the senses" (*indriyāṇi*). He explains the passage beginning with "behind" (*pṛṣṭhataḥ*) as providing the reason for that.

Regarding the word "yataḥ" (since): Alternatively, taking the identity of the two [the mind and the intellect], he says that the concluding statement "all this is the mind" includes the intellect as well—this is expressed by the words "and of the intellect. He prepares the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to explain the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore). Regarding the words "indriyāṇi" (the senses), he explains the passage beginning with "tasmāt" as the reason for that. Regarding the word "yataḥ": whatever is one's own effect produced by means of the sense-organ of touch...

Since it is observed that one perceives what is touched from behind through the mind because of its connection with the mind—therefore, the meaning is that the skin is merely the mind. Having raised the objection that even if the skin is the mind according to the stated reasoning, the other sense organs must still be distinct just like the body, he says: "The mind. The word "therefore" (tataḥ) signifies the equality of the underlying principle. || 115 || 116 ||
For the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of the person, the intellect undergoes manifold diversity.
But the intellect, being intent upon the states of the body, senses, and so forth, [perceives] everything indeed as such. 117.
If everything were merely mind (*manomātra*), then there would be no diversity of bodies, sense organs, or the resulting inequality of experiences; anticipating this objection, he says:

"Of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), all the instruments of experience are included. Since there is no contradiction in the aggregate being of the nature of mind, he concludes with: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 117 ||
When smelling, it becomes the sense of smell; when seeing, it is called the eye.
"By hearing, it becomes the sense of hearing," so too Vyāsa has declared.
He states the proof for the mind abiding in the form of the eyes and so forth: "They smell," etc. (118).
The cognition that "it is white," "it is black," or "it is large" arises through the power of karma.
"Indeed, through the mere authority of duality, the manifold nature of the universe comes into being.
(119) Fearing that one might suspect a difference between the mind and the body etc., as if they were distinct from their objects, he says "the white," and so forth.
The meaning is that the mind, when oriented toward the activity of duality, evolves (*vivartate*) into the form of various objects under the influence of the karma of the enjoyer. (119)
For there is no difference in the whiteness and other qualities of an object due to a difference in location.
Existence is conceived elsewhere than in the innermost reality, which is like the Self. || 120 ||
1. sa. ‘tam ityā’ | 2. ka.
‘laka’ | [vol2, page 525] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled Śāstraprakāśikā composed by Ānandagiri; 819.

If it is argued that consciousness alone undergoes transformation in its entirety, then that very consciousness would be non-dual, which would result in the destruction of the doctrine of the non-duality of the Self; anticipating this objection, he says: "The inner" (*pratyak*).

The meaning is that consciousness itself, having become the inner self, is the substratum of all conceptual constructions; therefore, the existence of duality—consisting of name, form, and action—as distinct from that [consciousness] is impossible. In this regard, he provides an illustrative example based on dissimilarity: "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*). That is, elsewhere than the object to be grasped (*grāhya*).

Just as existence is conceived for the inward-facing [consciousness], that same existence cannot possibly belong to the non-self (anātman) through its distinction from it; therefore, since the mind along with its effects is pure consciousness (cinmātra), it is non-dual—this is the meaning. || 120 ||
Therefore, no entity such as "white" exists; it is only cognition that appears so due to the force of its own activity.
It assumes the form of white and other colors for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human beings.
Having refuted the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), he concludes what was stated starting with "pure" (*śukla*) and so forth: "Not from this," [verse 121].
This cognition is of the nature of an error, since it possesses the form of white and so forth.
Therefore, the wise declare that everything has the nature of the mind alone.

By stating that "the intellect (dhī) assumes various forms for the sake of the person's experience," it is asserted that everything possessing form is nothing but the intellect alone; therein, he establishes this as a matter of common consensus among the learned. [He says: "The intellect. For since this very intellect, having become manifold and possessed of form, is determined to be of the nature of error (viparyaya), the technical designation of the learned—that "everything is form, and that is the intellect alone"—is logical. This is the meaning. || 122 ||
The reality of the entire category of "mine" exists solely for the sake of the self.
I have previously stated that this is because of the true nature of those subtle elements.

One might then object that since the mind (*manas*) also has everything as its self, it must be ultimately real like the Self (*ātman*), which would strike at the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) because two things that have everything as their self cannot coexist; or else, one might suspect that the mind itself is what possesses the nature of everything. Anticipating this, the author recalls what was stated in the passage beginning with "by the distinction of the locus of consciousness" (*pratyak-cid-deśa-bhedena*). He says: "By the purpose of the Self" (*ātmarthena*). Since the superimposed (*āropya*) possesses form only by virtue of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and lacks any form apart from it, the existence of the non-Self, such as the mind and so forth, is through the Self alone.
The meaning is that since this has been demonstrated many times, there is no room for the aforementioned objection. || 123 ||
Moreover, all the sense organs are indeed the mind itself; for that reason, [it is the mind].
Even when touched from behind, a person perceives it through the mind alone.
Having stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "Therefore also" (*tasmād api*), he restates the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) [with the word] "also" (*api*). || 124 ||
Having been touched while facing away, such is this touch of the hand.
"Thus, one attains a particular kind of touch by means of the mind alone.

[Objection: One might suspect that even when touched from behind, one would perceive the touch solely through the power of the external sense organ, without the mind; therefore, he says: "parāṅ" (turned away). [Verse 129]
By the mere touch of the skin, one attains the sensation of touch alone.
But one attains the specific qualities of touch and so forth by means of the mind alone. || 126 ||

One might raise the objection that, because the eye and other senses are not in contact [with the object], even if a specific tactile sensation is not perceived by them, there could still be a perception of the touch of the hand and so forth by the skin (tvak) when it is in contact, even without the mind. Anticipating this, he says: "By the skin. Although the skin, like the eye, is a grasper of substances—[as indicated by the reading *rūpaṃ* in manuscript *ga*]—nevertheless, [the perception occurs] through the skin alone. [The variant *tahāniḥ sa* in manuscript *kha* refers to the loss of that [perception].]
820 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 526]

The meaning is this: although that specific quality of touch can be known by her [the yoginī], nevertheless, for one who is not in a state of meditative concentration (asamāhita), having first perceived the mere touch when touched by the hand or other limbs, and then having reflected upon its specific qualities, the comprehension of it occurs through the mind alone. || 126 ||
For it is by the mind alone that the arising of cognitions regarding the objects of all the sense organs occurs.
"Indeed, everything is mind alone"—thus the Śruti declares.

Therefore, [the author] concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "from that also" by saying "by the mind. Since the arising of cognition regarding the objects of all the instruments—the vital breath, the skin, and so forth—such as the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower or the touch of the hand, occurs only through the mind, therefore all the instruments and so on are the mind.
The meaning is that the Śruti states the passage beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, having established [the mind] as being merely instrumental (*mātram*).

Nor is it correct to argue that the mind is only a common instrument (*sādhāraṇakaraṇa*) for the cognitions produced by their respective specific instruments, and not their specific instrument itself; for if that were the case, the qualification "by the mind" (*manasā*) in instances such as seeing and touching would be redundant, since its status as a common instrument is possible even in the absence of those [specific instruments]. This is the meaning of the word *hi*.

Alternatively, since all instruments are in essence the mind (*manas*), and because there is no difference between that [mind] and the intellect (*buddhi*), the Śruti concludes by stating "all this is indeed the mind," intending to express their identity; thus it says: "by the mind" (verse 127).
The mind has indeed been thoroughly determined, as have the body and the sense organs.
Immediately following that, the explanation of speech is now introduced. (128)

With the words beginning with "anyatra" and ending with "mana eva," he restates what has been said. With "manastāvat," he introduces the subject. With the words beginning with "tasmāt," he recites what was stated. And with "śarīram ca," he means that immediately after the determination of the mind, the aggregate of the body and the senses has been determined as being nothing but the mind. He states the purport of the passage beginning with "yaḥ kaścit" as follows: "of speech. || 128 ||
That which is an unspecified statement such as "it is said" by means of sounds, phonemes, and words.
It has the sense of conjunction, the sense of disjunction, and it is also of the nature of a suffix. || 129 ||
It should be known that he is indeed speech itself; why? Because this [speech] is always [present].
In the case of a common vehicle, speech is the means for the awakening to form. (130)
Having stated the intended meaning—that the subsequent statement is for the purpose of determining the internal [nature]—he restates "whoever" and explains its meaning with the word "yaḥ" (who).
Stating what is established by the mention of "mere sound" (*dhvanimātra*) without distinction, he explains the meaning of "speech alone" (*vāgeva*) with the word "nāda" (resonance).

Sound, which arises from the conjunction of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) with the throat and other [articulatory organs], and which takes the form of resonance (*nāda*) and so forth, as well as the cognition (*pratyaya*)...

The meaning is that everything produced from itself and by means of the other sense organs is indeed speech (*vāk*). Even though sound (*śabda*) is speech, he raises an objection as to how this applies to the cognition (*pratyaya*): "From what? He provides the answer by taking up the word "that" (*sā*): "Because... Since both the object to be manifested and the manifesting agent are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), [speech] makes known the connection between the object to be manifested—which shares the same material cause as the manifesting agent—and the instrument (the sense organ).

Since speech is desired here, and because everything that illuminates mere manifestation is of the nature of the word "speech," all valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of verbal concepts is to be considered as speech itself at all times; this is the meaning. || 129 || 130 ||
How is it understood that speech alone should exist at the beginning of cognition and so forth?
For this [work] extends from its own subject matter until its completion. || 131 ||
1. *Prakriyā* | [Vol. 2, p.
527] | 1. *Brāhmaṇa* | Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 821.
Yet, speech proceeds excessively [toward the jar], like a lamp toward the cognition of the jar.
The purpose of speech is the communication of meaning; there is nothing else besides this. (132)

He raises the objection that there is no evidence for the claim that speech exists solely as the nature of sound and cognition, by stating "speech alone. In this context, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "it exists as its own essential form. He explains the subsequent passage beginning with "For this... as follows: "with respect to its own denotatum," meaning [the relationship] of the signifier to the signified.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to demonstrate that activity culminating in the comprehension of the object is well-known in verbal discourse. To the question, "What is the proof here that speech is the illuminator of the object? he says: "artheti" (the object...). Since speech proceeds until the ascertainment of the object, therefore the knowledge of the object is its effect, and it is not logical for it to have any other effect; this is the meaning. Consequently, both the word and the cognition are the illuminators of the object.

The meaning is that those two do not differ in reality from speech because they are illuminators, just like it; thus, it is logical for anything that is merely an illuminator to be called "speech. || 131 || 132 ||
For indeed, the organ of speech is considered to be that which possesses the capacity for the utterance of sound.
How is it that the word, which has that [speech] as its object, is designated here as "vāc" (speech)? || 133 ||

He raises an objection: "In this context, it is merely the illuminator, not the word 'speech' (vāk), because that would contradict the conventional usage of the elders. [The author] says "for" (*hi*) in order to state that it is capable of producing a cognition; one should understand that this refers to both "the word" (*śabda*) and "the cognition" (*pratyaya*). || 133 ||
Truth is to be understood elsewhere, for its fitness lies precisely there.
But here, it is precisely the state of being the self of all that is intended for the one who is beyond the three [states]. || 131 ||
He accepts the common usage regarding the objects of the senses. [The opponent says: "True. [The author replies: "In that case, the sense organ must be understood here by the word 'speech' (vāk).
To this he says: "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*). This means: having set aside the present context. The reason for this is stated: "Of that" (*tasya*). The meaning is:
because it is appropriate to grasp the organ of speech by the word "speech" in another context, it is grasped as such only there. Of one...
Since it is impossible for a single word to have multiple meanings, he anticipates the objection that the word "speech" (*vāk*) here might refer to the sense organ and says: "But here...

The meaning is that within this context concerning the three foods, the word "speech" does not denote the sense organ alone. He states the reason why the word "speech" here refers to anything that illuminates: "Because of food... (134).
Just as every form that falls within the mind is intended to be expressed, so too [is the case here].
In the same way, every word is intended to be the illuminator of that [meaning]. (135)

Although it is intended here that the three foods constitute the self of all, one might ask: "How is it that the word 'speech' (vāk) is merely an illuminator? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The mind" (manaḥ). The meaning is that just as everything that is illuminated is included within the mind, so too is everything that illuminates established as being included within speech; by the word "sound" (śabda), speech is meant. || 135 ||
For the purpose of establishing that everything which is manifest is indeed of the nature of sound.
For she says "no" to this in order to withdraw the organ of speech. (136)
He states the meaning of "for this is not so" with the words "of illumination. The intended sense is that the word *vāk* (speech) applies to every single illuminator.
The cessation of the organ of speech is intended; for that purpose, this Śruti passage "not this" declares the absence of the status of an organ in speech.
Therefore, the meaning is that "speech" is merely a manifestor. || 136 ||
Just as the eye, being material in nature, is the illuminator of form alone.
Likewise, let speech, which consists of sound, be the illuminator of that very sound.
In order to state Bhartṛprapañca’s commentary on the phrase "for this [is] not," he first states the doubt to be set aside: "consisting of form.
As they have said: "Just as form manifests itself by means of itself, so too should sound manifest itself alone, and not another. (137)
Having anticipated this objection, they set forth the following resolution.
For some indeed say, "This is not [the case]," yet this is not considered to be like a lamp and so forth. (138)
He introduces the rebuttal to that [objection] with the words, "And this [is as follows]. He clarifies the rebuttal itself with the words, "This [light] is not...

The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to the light of the sun and so forth. Just as a lamp illuminates forms of its own kind, this [light] is not like that; rather, it is the illuminator of everything. As they have said: "For this [light] has as its object that which is absolutely luminous, and not..."
The meaning is that sometimes it is perceived without being manifested; therefore, the word "mantra" refers merely to that which manifests speech. || 138 ||
Everything that is perceivable by the collection of instruments such as the ear is called "form" (rūpa).
This [scripture] is merely its illuminator, not its object of illumination, like a lamp. || 139 ||

Regarding the statement "that which consists of form" (*rūpātmaka*) and so forth: that "form" is either well-known [as a specific object] or merely that which is being manifested. Thinking that the first alternative is untenable because the eye is not established as having that nature, he addresses the second alternative with the words "the ear and so forth. When form is intended as merely that which is being manifested, then this speech is its manifestor alone and is never itself the manifested, just as a lamp is a manifestor [and not something to be manifested].
And the meaning is that speech is not like this. || 139 ||
And the mind, in whatever way it may be, is by its very nature entirely luminous.
And it is certain that the Vāgrapa is exceedingly luminous. || 140 ||
Anticipating the objection that, like a lamp, speech too might possess both the quality of being illuminated and the quality of illuminating, he says: "It is only that which is to be illuminated.

The meaning is that, just as it is a fixed rule that the mind—which consists of form—is only that which is illuminated, so too it is proper to restrict speech—which consists of sound—to the status of being only an illuminator. || 140 ||
The form would be only that which is manifested, or else the manifestation itself would be speech.
One should know this, in brief, to be the characteristic of form and conjunction. (141)

He distinguishes [the two] by their definitions for the sake of avoiding confusion between name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). He says "that which is to be illuminated" (*prakāśya*) to show that there is ease of comprehension regarding the definitions as they have been stated; thus he says "in brief" (*samāsena*). || 141 ||
Even a name, when being grasped, possesses the nature of existence, just like whiteness.
And likewise, while manifesting form, it abides on the side of name. || 142 ||
[Vol.
2, Page 529] 5 Brāhmaṇam], accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 823.
Having raised the objection that the definition of "form" (*rūpa*) overextends to "name" (*nāman*), he says: "Name. [He then states that] the definition of "name" overextends to "form"—

He refutes over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "and form" (*rūpaṃ ca*): he states that it is like the inclusion of form within the name of that which makes known. Regarding the phrase "in the same way" (*tadvat*):

the point is that if either form or name is the object to be known (*bodhya*), then it is simply form; and if either name or form is the means of making known (*bodhaka*), then it is simply name. Thus, there is no over-extension. || 142 ||
Having thus correctly explained speech and mind individually, [I shall now explain] the twenty-two [faculties].
The vital breath (prāṇa) that sustains those two is then called the "undefined" (anirukta).

Having restated what has been said, he introduces the passage concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth with the word "Thus" (*evam*). Anticipating the objection—"How can the vital breath, which is of the nature of the offspring such as speech and the rest, be their sustainer?"—and wishing to state the reason, he says: "Unspecified" (*anirukta*).
The word "then" (*atha*) is intended to indicate the sequence: since that which is to be sustained has been mentioned, there is an expectation for the sustainer. || 143 ||
The word "ana" is intended to denote air in its undifferentiated state.
That very prefix *asu-* would acquire a specific meaning through its connection with a preverb (*pra* and so forth). 144.
He provides an introductory context for explaining the meaning of the terms *prāṇa* and so forth. Regarding the word "ana": this will become clear later on.
He states that the terms *prāṇa* and others apply to that very wind denoted by the word *ana*: "That itself... (144).
The emission [of breath] through both the mouth and the nose, as well as the offering of the morsel (piṇḍa) with prostration.
That which is called prāṇa is the movement of Marut; now apāna is being described.
Downward movement of the vital air, downward exhalation, and likewise downward motion of the body [are the results].
This has been described as apāna; now vyāna is being discussed.
It pervades the state of being the cause of energetic action and abides within the body.
This is declared to be the function of vyāna; it is also celebrated by the name uddhāna.
It is the cause of activities such as exertion and likewise performs actions that lead to worldly prosperity.
But the function in the body known as udāna is the cause of upward movement. || 148 ||
He who withdraws the vital functions and remains fixed in the region of the heart like a stake.
He should be known as the "Equal One" (Samāna), who withdraws all effects. || 149 ||

Anticipating the question of how the prefix *pra-* and other prepositions (*upasarga*) impart specific meanings to the word "wind" (*vāyu*), he explains the terms *prāṇa* and the rest in sequence, beginning with the words "emission" (*utsarga*).

[He explains: "The bending of the body" (*piṇḍasya praṇatiḥ*) refers to the bending of the physical frame; "upward movement" (*unnatiḥ*) refers to both [bending and upward movement]; and from these two, [arises] exhalation (*ucchvāsa*), and from that [exhalation], [inhalation].

The meaning is that *prāṇa* is the cause. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves to include the locations of the navel, the breasts, and the big toes. For it has been said: "Prāṇa functions at the tip of the nose, the breasts, the navel, and the big toes. Regarding "of the downward-moving air" (*avāgvāyoḥ*), this means downward motion; the point is that *apāna* is the cause of that exhalation. The word "likewise" includes its location in the back and other such places. As it has been said: "Apāna..."

"The functions [of vyāna] are at the nape of the neck, the back, the anus, and the heels. The word "ca" (and) in the phrase "in the body" (dehe ca) is intended to indicate that its function also extends to the skin, as it has been stated:
"vyāna has the skin as its function. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used to state that all these functions are well-known in the Yoga Śāstra.
1. radhaḥ śvā | 2. ka. ga. dehaṃ |
824 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 530]

The phrase "the cause of activities such as exertion" means that it is the cause for ascending and so forth—meaning it performs actions preceded by enthusiasm (*utsāha*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to its location in the heart and other sites. And it has been said: "Udāna functions in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the head.

He clarifies its status as the cause of excellence (*utkarṣa*) with the words "for prosperity" (*abhyudaya*). Here, "prosperity" (*abhyudaya*) refers to the upward departure (*utkramaṇa*) for that purpose; "excellence" (*utkarṣa*) refers to the nourishment of the body.

The withdrawal of all functions (*sarvakāryopasaṃhṛti*) means the gathering together and conducting back into the body of everything that has been eaten and drunk; that is to say, it is the cause of that [withdrawal]. The mention of the heart is an illustration for the navel and other locations. As they have said: "The *samāna* wind operates in the heart, the navel, and all the joints. (145)
He for whom these modes of conduct have been declared is called one who possesses the proper conduct.
He remained pervading the body, established in the answer to Śākalya’s question.
Having explained the meaning of the word *ana*, he states its location with the words "of which" (*yasya*). He then states what its essential nature is with the words "Śākalya.
The meaning is that when the question "In what is the udāna established? is asked, it is resolved by the answer "in the samāna. || 110 ||
The word "prāṇa" was previously stated to denote merely the function.
"Previously, the meaning would have been that which possesses functions (vṛttimat), because of the statement 'all are breath' (prāṇa).

Having raised the objection that, since the word *prāṇa* in the passage "all this is indeed breath" refers back to the specific functions under discussion, its identity with "all" is untenable, [the author] says "the word *prāṇa*" by resorting to the fact that it does not refer to those immediately mentioned [functions]. Therein, the reason is as follows:

"Everything"—for mere functional activity alone does not constitute "everything. Therefore, the meaning is that the word *sarva* (all) enjoins the state of being everything by referring back, via the word *prāṇa*, to that which is common [to all] and denoted by the word *ana*. || 151 ||
Name-and-form, as well as karma, are conjoined like a triple staff.
Abiding in a state where [the self and the body] are mutually confused, it is said that "the body is the self. || 152 ||

Regarding the statement "this self consists of these," he explains the meaning of the word "self" (ātman) with the words "name" (nāma). Just as three staffs joined together serve as the cause for supporting a wall or the like, so too the triad of name and the rest, combined into a single mass, constitutes the body; and that [body] is what is meant here by "self. He explains the mutual combination of name and the rest with the words "intermingled" (saṃkīrṇa). It exists in a state of being a solid mass through their mutually intermingled functions.
This means "as much as. || 152 ||
The aggregate consisting of the body, the vital breaths, and so forth, is of this extent alone.
Then likewise the one consisting of speech, the one consisting of vital breath, and the one consisting of mind. || 153 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "consisting of this" with the words "this much. Explaining the meaning of "consisting of speech" and so forth, he elucidates its extent with the words "consisting of speech. The word *atha* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). || 153 ||
Here, everything consisting of speech is name, and everything consisting of mind is form.
In the same way, action consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) is the sustenance of this body. || 154 ||

How can a single body possess multiple transformations such as various vocal organs and so forth? Furthermore, since that [body] is accomplished by a single [cause], why postulate many causes? This is the objection regarding the self (*ātman*).

Anticipating the objection that [the distinction] arises from yoga, he demonstrates the division among bodily names and so forth with the words "The name," etc. The word "of this" (asya) is a direct reference to the present subject.
This analysis of the refuge-less has been described with respect to the internal;
now, its analysis regarding the objective sphere of external elements is proclaimed. (155)

Having restated the preceding verse, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "the three worlds" and so forth: "annatraya" (the three foods). He shows the occasion for the subsequent statement regarding the division into the objective (*ādhibhautika*) immediately after the statement regarding the division into the subjective (*ādhyātmika*): "atha" (now). || 155 ||
The Bhūrloka is the Ṛgveda, and this goddess Vāk is the mother.
That which is known here is declared to be the *adhibhūta*, and that is speech (*vāk*). 156.

He summarizes the meaning of the fivefold set of sentences beginning with "Speech indeed is this": "Bhūḥ. The construction is as follows: know that speech which is declared here in relation to the physical world (adhibhūta) to be the Bhūr-loka and the Ṛg-veda; and that which are the gods, that which is the mother, and that which is the known—all that is speech alone. The meaning is that one should perform [the meditation] by means of the word itself upon speech, which is the intellect (dhī) in relation to the physical world, the Ṛg-veda, the gods, the mother, and the known. || 156 ||
The intermediate space is the Yajurveda, and likewise the ancestors are the father.
"Here, that which is to be investigated is the mind; therein, [the mind] is the physical (ādhibhautika).
This summarizes the meaning of the five sentences beginning with "The mind. "Antarikṣam" (the intermediate space). "Iha" refers to the sphere of worldly activity.

"Atra" refers to the inclusion of the worlds under discussion, or the locative case may be used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), as in "among speech, mind, and breath. As before, [the reference to] the intermediate space—
The meaning is that [the syllable] should be meditated upon in the mind, which consists of the Yajurveda, the ancestors, the knower of the fathers, the intellect, and the objective world. || 117 ||
The world of heaven, the Sāmaveda, and human beings together with their offspring.
And whatever is unknown, that is this vital breath (prāṇa) pertaining to the physical realm (ādhibhautika). || 158 ||

He summarizes the meaning of the five statements beginning with "That is prāṇa": "The heavenly world," etc. The meaning is that the functions [of the fires] proceed as before within the prāṇa—the presiding deity (adhibhūta) who is known by the wise—which consists of the heavenly world, the Sāman, and human progeny. || 118 ||
Whatever is known here, that they declare to be the foremost of speech.
The form of the mind is to be investigated, yet that of the vital breath remains indeed unknown.

He explains the passage beginning with "Whatever is known" (*yatkiṃca vijñātam*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Whatever," he supports the consensus among the learned that everything clearly known within the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-bhūmi*) is the form of speech (*vāco rūpam*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Whatever is to be desired to be known" (*yatkiṃca vijijñāsyam*) and so forth as being the form of the mind (*mano-rūpam*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Whatever is unknown" (*yatkiṃcāvijñātam*) and so forth as belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇasya*).
By the word "tu" (but), it is indicated that in both cases, as before, the consensus of the learned is favorable. || 119 ||
In all the worlds, beginning with Bhūrloka, that which is characterized by mind, speech, and breath—
In each case, one should apply three [elements] at a time, as far as possible.

Anticipating the objection—"Since the triad beginning with the 'knower' (vijñātṛ) is seen in each one of the worlds beginning with *bhūḥ*, and since speech (*vāk*) and the other organs are restricted [to specific functions], how can the knower and the rest have speech and the rest as their self?"—the text says: "Bhūḥ. This means that, as far as possible, one should not overstep the triad beginning with the knower. First—104.
826 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter] [vol2, page 532]

The two occurrences of the locative case are for the purpose of specification; the application is that in each one of those [elements], according to what is possible, the support characterized by speech and so forth should be joined as a support. || 160 ||
Because the expansion of speech and the other [organs] with respect to their objective domains is impossible to describe in detail.
Then he made the summary "whatever it may be" by means of stating its defining characteristic. || 161 ||

If speech and the other [organs] were everywhere of the nature of the "known" (vijñāta) and so forth, then the general statement "whatever [it may be]" would be purposeless; for it is appropriate to teach their specific forms individually. Anticipating this objection, he says: "With respect to the elemental" (*adhibhūte*). The phrase "of the expansion of speech and the rest" is to be supplied as the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). The "statement of definition" (*lakṣaṇokti*) refers to the general description. || 169 ||
He is fully perfected by his very characteristics in the collection of material elements.

The certainty is that the statement beginning with "three" (traya) is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha). Having raised the objection that—since the inclusion of the manifestations of speech and so forth belonging to the elemental realm (ādhibhautika) is already accomplished by the general statement "whatever [it may be]," and since earth and the other elements are also included within the categories of the knower and so forth, the statement "this is indeed speech" and so on would be redundant—the author says: "By means of a definition" (lakṣaṇena). By the general statement...

The meaning is that even though the inclusion of the elemental (bhautika) elements has been established, [the text] says "the three worlds" and so forth in order to restrict that speech and the other [senses] are to be meditated upon as having the nature of the earth and the other elements. || 162 ||
But now that this exposition has been introduced, [we shall treat] ignorance from every side.
This is its summary by way of the nature of cause and effect. || 163 ||

Regarding the phrase "whatever" (*yatkiṃca*) as a conclusion, it was previously stated that this is for the purpose of concluding the manifestation of the material elements, such as speech and so forth, which were described by the words "whatever is known" (*yatkiṃca vijñātam*). Now, he states another possible interpretation of that same phrase: that it is for the purpose of concluding the entire world along with its cause. He says: "In the exposition," meaning when the detailed expansion of the ignorance (*avidyā*) briefly mentioned in the aphorism is being set forth for complete and clear elucidation. A few...

The meaning is that, although she has been explained as possessing manifold manifestations (*vibhūti*), there is a summary in the middle with the words "whatever it may be" (*yatkiṃcit*) and so forth, because of the intention to describe her effects according to two groups. || 163 ||
That Brahman, when unknown as the self of vital breath (prāṇa), is called the cause.
But that measure is measured by the self through name, and it is also measured as having the form of the mind. || 164 ||

In this regard, having raised the doubt that even when the effects such as speech are perceived, there is no cognition of the cause, he says: "prāṇa... [etc.]. Having accepted the statement that sound and its cognition, which are illuminators, are included within the denotable object, he says: "nāmni... [etc.]. The word "tat" refers to Brahman in its unmanifest state.
Having accepted the statement that everything which is illuminated is included within the mind, he says: "and in the form of the mind. (164)
For all this, characterized by mind, speech, and breath, is nothing but ignorance.
Therefore, by thoroughly awakening to that reality and having consumed it, one partakes of the nectar of immortality.

He states the intended result of concluding that the world, together with its cause, is essentially the internal ignorance (*avidyā*) accompanied by its appearance (*sābhāsa*). "From which" (*yataḥ*):

by this, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indicated. The meaning is: from the knowledge of Brahman as the reality (*tattva*) of that world—which consists of ignorance accompanied by appearance—as being one's own inner self (*pratyaktvena*). "That" refers to ignorance along with its effects. "The immortal" (*amṛta*) is the supreme Brahman, the imperishable (*akṣara*). (165)
This is indeed other than the known, and likewise distinct from the unknown.
Having consumed both these, Brahman alone remains as the fullness.

One might object that it is untenable to claim liberation arises from the knowledge of Brahman as the Self—which is neither cause nor effect—because such a Brahman lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says "vijñātāt" (from the known) and so forth, stating that this is not so because of scriptural texts such as "That is indeed other than the known. Therefore, he says "etad" (this), meaning that liberation is logical when preceded by the knowledge of reality; the meaning is that both the known and the unknown are encompassed by this. || 166 ||
The deities of speech and the other [senses] satisfy a person who knows the Knower and so forth with their respective enjoyments.
They protect him individually, each according to its own specific nature, such as that of the knower and so forth.

Having explained the passage beginning with "Whatever [is spoken]," he states the meaning of the three sentences concerning the fruits, beginning with "Speech protects him. Regarding the phrase "vijñātādi":

the construction is that the respective deities, assuming their various forms, protect the person who knows the glory of speech, mind, and breath—whether in their known, to-be-known, or unknown states—with their respective distinct enjoyments. || 167 ||
Thus, speech and the other [organs] have been briefly described as pertaining to the physical realm (ādhibhautika).
Now, the explanation of their presiding deities (adhidaiva) is being set forth.

Having restated what has already occurred in the passage beginning with "of that speech," he introduces the next section with the words "Speech and the others. The word "atha" (now) is for the purpose of indicating the sequence. || 168 ||
Its form, consisting of the internal and the elemental, has been described previously.
When there is the intention to speak of the divine aspect, this is the body of that Speech.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Of that speech" (tasyai vācaḥ) and ending with "Agni" (agniḥ), saying: "With reference to the self" (adhyātmam). This means that because of the relationship between the support and the supported, there is a twofold division;
the meaning is that for the divine speech, the earth is the support and Agni is the supported. || 169 ||
The speech that was previously explained here with respect to the internal and the elemental, [is now to be considered].
That [power] is pervaded by speech, which is the presiding deity of all, through its state of non-differentiation.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadyāvatī" (so far as it extends) by saying "adhyātmam" (with reference to the internal self). The meaning is that whatever speech has been mentioned regarding the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth, all of that is pervaded by identity with the two-fold speech—namely, the causal speech belonging to the divine realm (*ādhidaivikī*). Here, "in the middle" refers to the letters beginning with *ga*. The word should be divided as "avibhāgataḥ" (by way of non-distinction). || 170 ||
The earth is said to be the body of speech, harsh and made of copper.
She exists as the foundational support for Agni, whose nature is light. || 171 ||

He recites the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca in order to acknowledge it, [beginning with] "consisting of darkness" (tāmasam). For it has been stated that the earth is the body of speech because of its hardness and density, and thus it consists of darkness. He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "having the form of light" (jyotīrūpam) as follows:
"[of fire]" (agner). || 171 ||
Fire, however, is the sattvic form, which exists in the earth as that which is to be supported.
It exists in a tamasic form; thus, divine speech is indeed of two kinds.

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]: He states the purport of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*)—that "this very [fire] exists in two forms, as earthly and as fiery"—with the words "But fire... The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used because the distinction between the locus and the thing located is well known. || 172 ||
The internal, the elemental, and the divine are all but one speech.
For it is said to be both one and many, according to the distinction between the universal and the individual.
Thus some maintain this view, while others accept a different one as well.
In that case, since it is so, the two forms consisting of speech are of the nature thus explained.

He states the meaning of the commentary [on the point] that "Agni alone is the deity" with respect to both the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the external elements (*adhibhūta*). Regarding the phrase "with respect to the internal self," he states the meaning of the commentary that by taking up Agni as the single deity even with respect to the celestial realm (*adhidaiva*), each individual person takes up the entire deity in its entirety.

He uses the word "hi" (for/indeed) to state that unity and multiplicity are well-known in the world through the distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). She... [the sentence continues].

The deity of speech (vāg-devatā) has been described. He summarizes the opposing view with the word "evam" (thus). He states that the deity of speech is desired by them [the opponents] as existing within the internal (adhyātma), elemental (adhibhūta), and celestial (adhidaiva) realms through the relationship of general and particular, through the state of being a sustainer, and through the relationship of part and whole. He says "tathā" (so it is). Regarding the phrase "tadyāvatī," he explains the meaning of the word "tat" (that) mentioned therein. Taking the word "tatra" from the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca, [he explains] "tasyaivaṃ sati" (this being so for him)...
Having stated the meaning, he clarifies that very point with the words "Speech," etc.; the sense is: "in this way, by means of the nature of the universal and so forth. || 173 || 174 ||
And as for this speech that has been spoken, [it is explained] by the words "of that" and so forth.
Speech that is delimited by the internal self and so forth is considered to be only that much.
He states the meaning of the commentary on the phrase "as much as" (*yāvatī*) with the words "as much as" (*yāvatī*).

By the passage beginning with "of that very speech" (*tasyaiva vācaḥ*), the meaning is that the speech pertaining to the divine (*ādhidaivikī*) which has been explained, and that which is delimited by the internal (*adhyātmika*) and the elemental (*ādhibhautika*), is of the same extent as that speech which is non-different from the divine speech. || 175 ||
Speech, with respect to the internal self and with respect to the objective world, is of such a nature; it is likewise with respect to the divine.
For by each such qualification, it becomes the deity itself. || 176 ||

He states the meaning of the question "What is the reason? with the words "Speech," etc. The sense is: what is the reason for the claim that speech, which exists in the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth, is as extensive as that which exists in the divine realm (ādhidaivika), and that it is non-different from it? He provides the answer through the commentary: "For that very deity of the earth establishes itself in various places in various forms. Therefore, speech—which is limited by the internal self and so forth—is [identical to] the divine.
The word "kavāgabhinna" (broken by a stone) is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. || 176 ||
In each individual section, that very same fire remains fixed.
In some cases, she may exist in the form of earth and fire, or as the essence of speech. || 177 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "this is that very fire" as follows: "In each one. The word *adhikāra* refers to a location. He demonstrates this fixed arrangement with the words "the earth," etc. The expression "where indeed? is a statement regarding the divisions such as the divine (*adhidaiva*) and so forth. For it has been said:
"This very same fire is to be seen in its entirety in each individual place of authority (*adhikāra-sthala*), whether in the form of the earth or in the form of speech."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 177 ||
1 ka. ga. pīryate | [vol2, page 535] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri; 829.
This which has been stated should be applied to the mind, the vital breath, and the self as well.
Because it was taught in the divine speech for the purpose of providing an identical explanation. || 178 ||

In accordance with the two commentaries (*bhāṣya*), having explained the passage beginning with "of that speech" (*tasyai vācaḥ*), he now extends the aforementioned principle to the passage beginning with "of this mind, heaven" (*etasya manasaḥ dyauḥ*) by means of the word "just as" (*yathā*). He analyzes the phrase "as has been stated" (*yathoditam*) with the words "in the divine" (*daivyām*).

He states the reason for extending what was said regarding speech to breath and the others with the word "equal" (*tulya*); the phrase "of the preceding and following sentences" (*pūrvottaravākyānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 178 ||
The internal and the elemental [aspects] are like the offspring of speech and mind.
The meaning is that this same [explanation] should also be stated regarding the deities; such is the supreme scripture. 179.

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "those two are a pair" as follows: "With respect to the self (*adhyātma*)," etc. In relation to the self, the mind is its soul (*ātman*), speech is the wife, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the offspring; and in relation to the individual self (*pratyadhyātma*), the mind is the father, speech is the mother, and the vital breath is the offspring.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that among the elements (*adhidaiva*), the vital breath is the offspring of speech and mind, the same must be asserted for it in relation to the divine realm (*adhidaiva*) as well; it is for this purpose that the scripture begins with the words "those two," and so forth.
Such is the meaning. || 179 ||
For the transformation of the mind into the moon is clearly heard of everywhere.
Why is its connection with the sun explained here? || 180 ||

Having stated the identity of the sun and the mind in the passage "This is the sun," the author raises an objection: the statement that these two form a couple (*mithuna*)—referring to fire and the sun as the forms of speech and mind—is contradicted by other scriptural passages. This is expressed in the words "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*). The meaning is that in various other contexts, such as "the moon was born from the mind" and "therein the moon is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*)," the moon is everywhere associated with the mind. As it has been said: "For everywhere the moon is the mind."

It was stated "for" (hi) with the intention of explaining this very commentary. The qualification "clearly" (sphuṭaḥ) is used to state that the status of the mind as the moon is based on direct scriptural statement (vācanikatva). He states the resulting conclusion: that a statement contradicted by another Vedic text is inappropriate here. [This refers to the phrase] "of that" (tasya). || 180 ||
Therefore, because the identity of the mind and the intellect is intended to be expressed, there is a scriptural statement [to that effect].
The mind is indeed conjoined with the sun, but not with the moon.

He offers a rebuttal by means of the commentary of Bhartṛprapañca: "Because of the non-difference between the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), they constitute the self. Regarding the phrase "because it is intended": in this context, the identity of the mind and the intellect is intended; and since the intellect is the primary of the two because its nature is that of determination (*niścaya*), the Śruti connects the mind with the Sun alone—the deity of the intellect—and does not declare its identity with the Moon. Thus, the Sun is the intellect...
For the meaning is that "he speaks" (vateti) refers to the limit of those who know the Gāyatrī. || 189 ||
And here, because he is authorized to give the impulse, the impulse belongs to Savitṛ.
Therefore, the connection of the mind with Savitṛ alone is praised. || 182 ||

Regarding this connection between the mind and the Sun, he states another reason: "prasava" (procreation). From the statement, "From that, Prāṇa was born," the birth of Prāṇa from the mind is declared. And all of that is caused by Savitṛ, because the word "Savitṛ" is applied to the cause of the procreation of all living beings;
therefore, the meaning is that the mind's union occurs through identity with Him alone. || 182 ||

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter]:
"If there were an expectation of grace, the mind would become the moon."
Likewise, with respect to the divine, the Sun is considered the deity of the eye.

Then, anticipating the question as to what the status of those scriptural statements is which speak of a connection between the mind and the moon, and between the eye and the sun, he says: "By way of favor" (*anugraha*). As they have said: "For where the mind and the intellect are intended to be spoken of as distinct, there the moon is the presiding deity (*devatā*) of the mind whose objects are desire, volition, and so forth; but when [the mind] is engaged in the production of actions and the like..."
At that time, the mind, while engaged in the act of procreation, has Savitṛ as its presiding deity. || 983 ||
For fire alone is held to be the universal illuminator of the world.
And the differentiation of forms is based upon the heating by Tvaṣṭṛ. || 184 ||

By stating the relationship between Āditya and Manas, the passage beginning with "those two" has been explained. Now, in order to explain another interpretation, he states the cause for the production of Prāṇa from Agni and Āditya, who are joined together as the forms of the divine Speech and Mind:
"Agni... [He says: "Nothing whatsoever is born apart from light and pervasion, because birth is the manifestation of a thing, and that light..."

That is indeed fire, and for those things being born, a specific manifestation cannot be established without cooking (*pāka*); and since cooking is produced by that which has the nature of time (*kāla*), the meaning is that all origination is caused by fire and the sun. || 184 ||
Thus, for those two, speech and mind, whose natures are illumination and procreation respectively.
Prior to the union of the two selves as previously described, the vital breath (prāṇa) came into being, moving through the intermediate space.

Then he states the meaning of the verse "From that, Prāṇa was born": "Of those two," etc. This means: such being the case, where the birth of everything proceeds from Agni and Āditya; that is to say, from those two selves in the form of Agni and Āditya as previously described. || 185 ||
Just as the vital breath (prāṇa) exists within the self, so do progeny exist within speech and the mind.
Even in the context of the divine realm, this very procreation of the vital breath (prāṇa) is what is being described here.
He concludes what was introduced in the passage beginning with "the progeny of speech and mind" regarding the internal (adhyātma) and the elemental (adhibhūta): "Prāṇa.
The mention of the internal is intended to indicate the elemental as well. || 986 ||
In this context, the birth of the vital breath (prāṇa) is described with reference to its three names.
However, the birth of the vital breath is designated in relation to the process of digestion. || 187 ||

Having raised the objection that since the *prāṇa* mentioned in the passage "mind is the vessel, *prāṇa* [is the food]" is the cause of speech and the other organs, it cannot be their effect, he says, "No," and so forth. Then, regarding the statement "the *prāṇa* was born," he asks whose *prāṇa* that word refers to, and answers with "But rather... He intends to state that even the result is fivefold (*pāṅkta*) in relation to the fivefold action which serves as its means; therefore, apart from the causal *prāṇa* included within the three groups, what else could there be?
He states that the birth of the wind, designated here as *citprāṇa*, is spoken of in this context as being born from the fivefold [elements], etc.: "pāṅka... (verse 187).
Just as the vital breath is in one's own internal body, so it is in Prajāpati.
The vital breath situated in the intermediate space is this very Supreme Lord. || 188 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since there is no prāṇa (vital breath) capable of being included within the fruit apart from the prāṇa that has become food, how can its production occur—he says:

831. "As it is" (*sa yathā*). Just as within the self (*adhyātma*) and within the elements (*adhibhūta*), the wind arises as the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) of Prajāpati, so too this wind, which is the individual self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belonging to the elemental sphere, exists within space (*ākāśa*) through speech and mind, which belong to the divine sphere (*ādhidaivika*). It is introduced [as follows]:...

The meaning is: "on account of the authority of your word. He explains the purpose of the passage beginning with "He is Indra," which is for the sake of meditating upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which has become the subjects—as possessing the qualities of being Indra and being without rivals, by stating "That is this one" (*sa eṣa*). || 188 ||
Because he is without rivals, he is therefore called Indra.
But surely speech and mind exist for him; how then can he be without a rival? (189)

He establishes that Indrahood consists in being without a rival (*asapatna*). As for the words "since": for a second [being] is indeed a rival; therefore, by the absence of such a one, he is "without a rival" (*asapatna*), and thus he is Indra—this is the meaning. He raises an objection against the claim of being without a rival based on the absence of a second: "But surely... (verse 189).
Speech and mind are not like that, because one continues to live by the very function of the vital breath alone.
Because of the statement, "Since he eats food by means of this," they are therefore called *it* (the breaths). || 190 ||

He offers a rebuttal, stating "It is not so," because those two [speech and mind] are dependent on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and thus lack an opponent; therefore, for that [breath], there is no rival. The sense is that since the vital breath, which has become the offspring, is partial toward them, speech and mind—which are favorable to it—are likewise favorable to it. Regarding their dependence on the vital breath, there is the scriptural passage: "Whatever food one eats by this [breath], by that these [other organs] are satisfied," and "Therefore they are called 'the breaths' (*prāṇāḥ*) by this name."
He validates the statement with the words: "That which by this... (190).
Since speech and mind are also said to be merely modifications of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore, the Prāṇa is without a second, and for that very reason, it is indeed Indra. || 191 ||

Having established that speech and the other [senses] have their cause in the vital breath (prāṇa) because, in reality, there is no difference between the cosmic vital breath and the vital breath residing in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and having thus proven that those two are dependent upon the vital breath, he concludes the result with the words: "Of the vital breath... (199).
He who has truly known the "without-rival" becomes one who has no rival.
How could one who sits near [this] without a rival ever have a rival? || 192 ||

He explains the statement regarding the fruit, beginning with "Not his," and so forth, by means of the words "Not... and so on. The meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) is that the fruit corresponds to the specific quality meditated upon, as established by such scriptural passages as "In whatever way [he meditates]... (*taṃ yathā yathā*). He provides the reasoning for the fact that the fruit for one who meditates on the Prāṇa characterized by the quality of being "without rivals" is the state of being "without rivals": namely, that the fruit follows the nature of the meditation, otherwise there would be a contradiction.
The state of being. || 192 ||
Thus has been described, in accordance with the Pañcāgni-vidyā, that which rests upon speech, mind, and breath.
Now, the process [of creation] is being described according to the division of the non-refuges (anatraya). [Objection:

Since speech and mind are subordinate to the vital breath (prāṇa) due to their quality of being attributes, and since the vital breath is primary, how can it be said that "all these are equal," and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, the author introduces the following by restating what has been said: "It has been said... [and] in accordance with the fivefold action (pāṅkakarma), its fruit—

Having stated the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) located in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) through the passage beginning with "those two are a couple" in order to explain its fivefold nature, the meditation upon it as possessing the quality of being without rivals was taught. Now, the meditation concerning speech and the other [senses] as they exist through the division of the three kinds of food is being described;
therefore, the meaning is that the statement declaring their equality for the sake of that [meditation] is not contradictory. || 193 ||
