The internal self (*adhyātma*), the objective world (*adhibhūta*), and likewise the divine realm (*adhidaivata*).
Let it be understood that all [the senses], beginning with speech, have been described as being equal. || 194 ||
He explains "ta ete" and so forth with the words "adhyātmam. || 194 ||
"In what manner is there equality?"—to this question, he said, "Because they are infinite. (195)
Surely, those [elements] previously mentioned were defined with respect to the internal (adhyātma) and the external world (adhibhūta).
But how can it be asserted here that the sense organs and so forth are infinite? (196)

The statement "all are infinite" is supplied by way of the requirement [of syntactic expectancy]. Regarding the word "equality," he raises an objection concerning the contradiction between what precedes and what follows with the words "But surely... (nanu). || 195 || 196 ||
1.1 This is not so, because all things, as they have been described, are infinite.
By means of speech, which is the presiding deity of all, there is even infinity for the worlds and so forth. || 197 ||

He says that this infinity is unimpeded by way of the *adhidaiva* (cosmic) self: "Not this," etc. "Beings" refers to speech and the other organs. He states the argument *a fortiori*: "Speech," etc.; it should be understood as "by mind and by breath. When there is such infinity of the worlds beginning with *bhūḥ* and of the deities residing within them by way of the cosmic selves of speech and so forth, then [how much more so] for speech and the others when they are limited by the *adhyātma* (corporeal) and other dimensions?
The meaning is: what more need be said about its infinity? || 197 ||
Because everything is concluded within this section on the qualification.
The deity, being uncomposite, possesses no agency either inherently or through others. (198)

He states another reason for the infinity of everything, beginning with speech, in the verse starting with "adhikāra" (authority). "Adhikāra" means authority, which is to say activity; its "pariccheda" is its completion or fulfillment. In that fulfillment of its own activity, everything else is brought together, because a deity that is not conjoined lacks agency. Therefore, since it is conjoined with everything in the production of its own effect, its infinity is logical—this is the meaning. || 198 ||
Upon the complete fulfillment of their own respective offices, the deities [worship] the host of deities.
For indeed, having made everything his own, he performs each respective task.

Anticipating the objection that there is no infinity [of deities] because they are limited even when combined with other deities for the production of their own effects, he says: "By their own office," and so forth. As they have said: "That which is the infinity of the earth belongs to each individual deity."
The internal [treatment] is completed within the section on the external; thus, it is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed) in this very commentary. || 199 ||
In this context, "infinity" is understood as that state which persists until the dissolution of all beings.
For that which exists as the effect of karma, primary infinity is not logical.
He states another meaning for the word *ananta* (infinite): "As long as the world exists" (*ābhūta*). The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the present sentence.
To the objection—"Why should that [immortality] not be absolute eternity?"—he replies with "Karma," etc. By this, the contradiction with scripture (*śruti*) in that case is indicated. || 200 ||
Sthā [vol2, page 539] 5 Brāhmaṇa], together with the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 833.
This being so, he who here constantly worships the infinite with perpetual diligence—
That person attains the infinite worlds of speech and the rest. || 201 ||

Now, one applies the passage beginning with "He who [meditates] on these" and so forth. "In this way" means that since the infinity of speech and the other [senses] has been established, one should understand that the statement regarding meditation along with its fruit is made by breaking the order of the text in favor of the order of meaning. Here, the locative case is used for the purpose of specifying the subject under discussion.
By the term "constantly exerted," the excellence of the threefold qualification of the meditation is intended to be expressed. || 201 ||
But he who worships that which is finite attains what is finite.
Because he contemplates the infinite Self, he reaches the infinite world from every direction.

The passage beginning with "He who [meditates on] these" explains [the preceding]. Regarding the word "worships" (*upāste*): having stated the defects and virtues for one who meditates upon the three foods as being limited or unlimited, he concludes the scriptural meaning with the words "from which. This means that it is because of the meditation on the identity of the Self with the Sūtra-self within the unlimited threefold food. || 202 ||
Here, the qualification for two [persons] regarding the fivefold rite is the subject under discussion.
Likewise, the division of the threefold sequence of processes is also the subject under discussion.

Having raised the objection—“Since the meditation on the three kinds of food has already been explained along with its fruit, and there is nothing further to be said, what is the purpose of the subsequent text?”—the author states the subject matter (*vṛtta*) in the words “The topic” (*adhikāra*). Having stated that in this section the topic under discussion consists of the division of the results of two things—namely, fivefold action and the three kinds of food—he explains that very topic in the words “Fivefold,” etc. This is the method of exposition (*prakriyā*).
The fruit is what was under discussion; "division" means analysis or explanation. The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction. || 203 ||
Therein, the three kinds of food pertaining to the divine have been described in their respective divisions.
The ritual applications (upāsana) of the fivefold [hymn] remain to be stated. || 204 ||

He restates what was mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence for the purpose of specifying the subject matter of the passage beginning with "sa eṣa" and so forth. Regarding the word "tatra": the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The meaning is "according to the division of the fruits of meditation. Alternatively, the meaning is "according to the division of the locus and the located. It should also be understood that [the meditations] are together with their meditative practices (*upāsanā*) and their fruits. He states the subject matter of the subsequent sentence: "of the cooking," etc. (204).
With respect to the divine, however, a triad has been described, characterized by mind, speech, and breath.
The effect of the ripening of karma has not been stated, nor have wealth and karma themselves.

The remaining fruit of the fivefold action (*pāṅkakarmaphala*) must be stated; he shows this by first restating what has already been said: "With regard to the divine" (*adhidaiva*). That which is the fruit of the fivefold action in the domain of the divine must also be described as fivefold. In that context, mind, speech, and breath constitute the mother and the father.
The meaning is that while this triad characterized as "progeny" has been mentioned, "wealth" and "action" have not been mentioned; therefore, they must be stated. || 209 ||
The effect of the act performed for another is not yet understood.
Until wealth and action are mentioned for the sake of establishing the state of being fivefold. || 206 ||

Even though this [world] consists of fivefold effects (*pāṅkakāryatva*), it does not possess the nature of being fivefold (*pāṅkatva*) because a systematic distinction (*vyavasthā*) is possible; therefore, neither wealth nor ritual action (*vittakarmaṇī*) need be mentioned there.
105 1 ga. *bhuyāt*. lo. 2 ka. *asti svavya*.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the fivefold" (*pāṅkasya*). Since the cause conforms to its effect, if the fivefold nature (*pāṅkatva*) is absent in the effect, it cannot be established in the cause either;

thus, the status of the fruit of action as being fivefold is not established. Furthermore, this distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*naimittika*) does not apply here, nor is action itself fivefold.

Since it has been stated that the world is the unprecedented transformation (*apūrva-pariṇāma*) caused by the threefold nature of the self, the subsequent section of the text is intended to explain wealth and other factors for the sake of establishing the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) of the fruit. This is the meaning. || 206 ||
The god named Varāda is the Prajāpati who brings about the dissolution of the world.
The Self pertaining to the worlds (adhiloka) is said to be this very one, whose nature consists of the three kinds of food.

Having restated the intended meaning expressed by the mention of Prajāpati through the term "year" (*saṃvatsara*), he explains another connection for the passage beginning with "He is this" (*sa eṣa*) by means of the preceding commentary, starting with the words "The world" (*loka*). For, by defining the nature of Prajāpati—who is twofold—as consisting of the three foods, his nature as the world (*lokātmatva*) has been defined; thus he says, "Of him" (*tasya*). || 207 ||
But that which is its higher self is called the Moon.
He is the constant agent of the fortnights, months, seasons, colors, and so forth, as well as of all actions.

He says that the subsequent statement, "The remainder, the nature of time (kālātmakatva), must be explained," refers to the phrase "exceeding time" (*adhikālam*). Prajāpati, called Virāj, has been understood as consisting of the worlds, time, and the deities; having first explained his self (*ātman*) as consisting of the three kinds of food with reference to the worlds, it must now be explained that his very self, with reference to time, exists in the form of the moon. Thus, [the text speaks] of Prajāpati in his aspect as the moon.

The meaning is that [the moon] is designated by the term "year. To explain the mention of wealth and action, the passage beginning with "He, this one" was stated. Anticipating the objection—how can there be an understanding of wealth and action in Prajāpati, who is the moon consisting of time?—he first states the perception of action: "In the fortnights," etc. For he is the agent of the continuous performance of actions such as the production of the fortnights; therefore, the action known as its creation appears in the moon.
This is the meaning. || 208 ||
Furthermore, wealth is observed here by way of its nature of decrease and increase.

Time, whose nature consists of moments, divisions of time, and measures such as the lava, transforms the universe; existing as the essence of both the vital breath and the physical body, it persists until the great dissolution.

In that context, he shows the notion of wealth (*vitta*). [The word] "loss" (*hāni*) refers here to the statement regarding the moon. The intention is that because they consist of increase and decrease, Prajāpati is spoken of as being of the nature of the moon, precisely for the purpose of establishing that the digits (*kalā*)—which consist of the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*)—are of the nature of wealth and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the Bhāṣya that these digits, which are divisions of time, have "action" (*karman*) as their cause for the transformation of the world; how then is that action—?

Anticipating the objection that this is merely a statement of what has already been said, he says "kalā" while following the Bhāṣya: "Time, consisting of the Sūtra and the Virāj, having assumed its respective specific forms and bringing about the transformation of the world, remains until the great dissolution; thus, its agency consists in being the transformer of the world. (209)
Just as at the end of a fortnight, a sixteenth part of the moon remains.
Having entered [the womb], every living being is born again from the side. || 210 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "so 'māvāsyām" (that [occurs] on the new moon) as follows: "yaikā" (which is one). At the waning of the fortnight (*pakṣakṣaye*), that is, at the dissolution of the fifteen digits (*kalā*) on the day of the new moon (*amāvāsyāyām*).
1. Of those; 2. *ga* reads *pakṣatī*.

The meaning is "on the lunar day" (tithau). The meaning is "from the beginning of the bright fortnight," that is, from the first day (pratipad). However, if the reading is *pakṣatau*, then that same first day is called *pakṣati*;
the meaning is "in that [day]". For they recite: "A woman's *pakṣati* is the root of her wing. It is born.
That is to say, he becomes endowed with a second digit. || 210 ||
For during this night, Prajāpati enters and dwells within it.
Therefore, one should abandon all violence toward that which possesses vital breath.

Therefore, he explains the passage beginning with "tasmādetām" (therefore, this...). Regarding the word "rātrau" (at night): the word *rātri* refers to a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*). For it has been said:
"The nights themselves are the days-and-nights. || 211 ||
Because it was struck down by its severed digits (kalās), it is known as "kṛkalāsa" (the lizard).
One should not commit violence; moreover, one should not even initiate the act of harming.
He states the meaning of the phrase "even of a chameleon" as follows: "by means of its parts. || 212 ||
One should also avoid [sexual intercourse] at night, even if it has been authorized by one's preceptor.
One should avoid, with great effort, the harming of living beings as well as the infliction of pain on those who have not yet begun their work.
He explains that very point: "Sāmī" [means] "prāṇabhṛt," which is a designation of the agent; it refers to the effort to desist from violence even when a cause for violence exists. || 213 ||
For the violence toward living beings that is naturally well-known to occur among chameleons;
One should not even do that here; what need is there to mention anything else?

[214] He explains the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya regarding the word "even" (api) and so forth. "Krukalāsa" refers to a lizard. "Here" (atra) means on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). "From elsewhere" (anyataḥ) means from another [day]. [214]
The ritual dismissal of this very deity is for the sake of her worship.
For there is no other purpose for the destruction of living beings here in this world than this. (215)

Since a specific prohibition implies the permission of the remainder, one might suspect a contradiction with such injunctions as "one should not harm any living beings"; therefore, the author explains this by saying "of this very [day]," and so forth. The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the lunar day previously mentioned. Although violence is prohibited in general everywhere, its specific prohibition on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is understood to be for the purpose of worshiping the deity Soma; hence [the restriction].
The meaning is that, because there is no permission for the remainder, there is no contradiction with the general prohibition. || 215 ||
For even in the Smṛti, this injury is forbidden for ritual performers on sacred festival days (parvan).
Through association with a distinguished fruit, a statement here may become as if it were true. || 216 ||

It has been stated that the injury of living beings is prohibited everywhere in general, and specifically on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*); now, the author supports the injunction that one must not commit injury on that occasion by citing a *smṛti*: "In the *smṛti* [it is said]:
'He who, when the Soma has entered the trees, should injure those trees...'"
"He is undoubtedly joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo."
“He who causes plants to be destroyed when the moon is situated among the *vīrudha* constellations,” [Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika by Sureśvarācārya, First Chapter, Section 836].
Or if he causes even a single leaf to fall, he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Such is the Smṛti passage. "Of those engaged in ritual acts" means, in other words, of those who are subject to injunctions and prohibitions. Having stated that there is a prohibition against violence on the new moon day for the sake of worshiping the deity Soma, [the author] states another result: "viśiṣṭa... (distinct). Its meaning is as follows: just as in the context of the Darśa and other sacrifices, regarding the rule "one should not speak untruth," there is either a restatement of a prohibition already established as pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*), or [it establishes] something previously unknown as pertaining to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

In the doubt as to whether this is an injunction (*vidhi*) or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a prohibition already established for the sake of human ends by Smṛti texts such as "One should speak the truth" and "One should speak what is pleasant. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is established in the section on the definition of the *śeṣa* (auxiliary) under the sūtra "Or it is an injunction, because of a different connection": since the prohibition studied within the context of the Darśa and other sacrifices, upon examination of its own sentence, is seen to have a purpose related to the immediate sacrifice, and since a restatement is impossible regarding something not already established, it is therefore an injunction.

Therefore, although truthful speech is enjoined without distinction as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it is enjoined specifically [in this context]; likewise, although injury (*hiṃsā*) is prohibited without distinction, it is specifically prohibited on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) for the purpose of accomplishing specific fruits such as the destruction of sin. || 216 ||
Let there not be a fruit consisting of the three types of food by means of mere absolute knowledge alone.
Therefore, because he possesses knowledge of the supreme self, his worship is prescribed. || 217 ||

Having raised the objection—“Since the fivefold nature (*pāṅktva*) has already been stated for the purpose of establishing that the fruit, which consists of the three foods, is the result of the fivefold action (*pāṅka-karma*), there is nothing further to be said; so what is the use of the subsequent text?”—the author states its intended meaning: “Kevalam,” etc. “Kevalam” means knowledge alone, uncombined with action—that is to say, knowledge that has arisen once and does not depend on repeated practice.
For it is not the case that the state of being those [foods] results from the mere knowledge of the three foods without meditation upon them, as there is no evidence for such a thing. Therefore—
The meaning is that the subsequent statement is intended to explain that meditation (*dhyāna*). In this regard, he provides an example by way of contrast: "the Supreme Self" (*parātman*).

For that [meditation] is held to be fruitful merely through the attainment of its own nature (*svarūpa*) via the cessation of ignorance; it is not so with this system of philosophy—this is the meaning. || 297 ||
"Let my digits be equal to the wealth itself; having fixed the constant (dhruvā) myself."
He who worships in this manner then attains the Self consisting of parts (Kalātman). || 218 ||

Since it has already been stated in this context that "all these are indeed equal," one might wonder: why grind what is already ground? Anticipating this objection, and considering that there is a specific distinction—that very meditation must be performed through the identification with the "I"—he states the purport of the passage beginning with "his wealth indeed... as follows: "Wealth. [The meaning is: those fifteen digits of Prajāpati, which are the moon, are my own wealth—consisting of cattle and so forth—precisely because they possess the nature of waxing and waning. Thus, [he identifies them] with his own wealth.

The meaning is that, having fixed one's gaze upon the fifteenth digit (*kalā*) and having conceived one's own body as the sixteenth digit, one who meditates, "I am Prajāpati, possessed of sixteen digits," attains that very state. || 298 ||
The wise one should worship Prajāpati, who possesses the qualities as described.
Having continuously superimposed [the qualities of the Self] upon this body of one's own through that similarity of nature. || 219 ||

With the intention that one cannot meditate on [the Self] thinking "I am Prajāpati" because that Self is not a different entity from oneself—and thus the superimposition of "I" would be improper—he says: "As has been stated. || 219 ||
Wealth alone is its essence; its increase and decrease constitute its activity.
This very body of his is constant; while living, it consists of sixteen parts.
[Vol.
2, Page 543] 1 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri: 837.

A wise person, having superposed upon his own body—on account of its similarity—the *sūtra* (the subtle body) which possesses qualities such as consisting of sixteen parts and being infinite, for a long period of time...

It has been stated that one should worship through both continuity and proximity. He now states the reason for attributing the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) between that [Prājāpati] and the worshipper of the Sūtra:

"Wealth," etc. Those fifteen digits (*kalā*) which belong to that Prājāpati are indeed my wealth; that activity of his, consisting in the power to transform the universe, is my wealth’s very loss and increase; and that which is his constant sixteenth digit—
That body of mine is indeed superior even to my vital breaths; thus, due to this similarity, the superimposition of Prajāpati upon me is appropriate.

Even though the Self is distinct from the thread, its nature [is attained] through meditation on it as the Self, according to such scriptural texts as "In whatever way... and so forth, and because a result is observed through the cognition of the Lord in an image and the like—this is the intended meaning. || 220 ||
"He desired, 'May I be born'; thus the Śruti [declares] to us that these are indeed the means.
"But that [which was said] is not to be accomplished; therefore, the subsequent Śruti speaks for the purpose of explaining that.

(221) Having raised the objection that the subsequent portion of the text is redundant—since it has already been stated that the meditation on Prajāpati as the Self through the "I-grasp" (*ahaṃgraha*) upon the threefold food is fruitful, and thus there would be nothing further to be said—the author states its subject matter: "He desired... (so'kāmayata). (221)
If that which is to be proven is indeed understood by the mere statement of the proof, [then what need is there for further elaboration?]
Nevertheless, a connection with a distinguished fruit is not perceived in that way. || 222 ||

Anticipating the objection that the result has already been stated by the very mention of the means (*sādhana*), since the two are mutually connected, [the author] replies: "By the mention of the means... (verse 222). Even though that [result] is understood in a general sense, it is not stated as "this belongs to this," because it is not understood in its specific form without a specific statement; therefore, he says that the subsequent scripture is for the purpose of stating that.
For means such as sons and so forth would possess [the properties of] arising and so on.
Therefore, the three worlds are the goal to be accomplished; thus says the Śruti: "Or indeed, there are three. || 223 ||

One might raise the objection: "Since sons and the like are causes for liberation, they do not have a connection with the three worlds alone; therefore, how can the subsequent scriptural passage speak of their connection with the three worlds according to a specific arrangement? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Sons and the like. He states the reason why the three worlds are the goal to be accomplished by them: "Because of birth and so forth. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that because liberation is opposed to birth and the rest, it cannot be accomplished by those means.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "of the three worlds alone," by way of being accomplished through sons and so forth. || 223 ||
For only these three worlds are to be accomplished by means of sons and other such instruments.
Therefore, a mendicant who desires liberation must renounce all longings for the sake of freedom.

He states the meaning established by the force of the present scriptural passage itself: "The three. Because they are the causes of only those three, one who desires liberation from *saṃsāra*—which consists of those causes and their effects—should abandon the pursuit [of worldly objects] for the sake of the knowledge that is the cause of liberation, and become intent upon hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; this is the meaning.
The term "ascetic" (*yati*) is used by adopting a prospective designation. || 224 ||
Verse 16: Some explain the connection here in a different manner altogether.
Since the goals of human existence are attained through knowledge alone, ritual actions and their fruits are useless.
He introduces the connection between the passage beginning with "trayo vāva" as stated by Bhartṛprapañca, [saying] "otherwise," and so forth, in order to explain that very point.
1. Thus it is said. 2. Kha. Śeṣaṇo.
[Vol. 2, page 544]
838 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, First Chapter:

He states his opponent’s position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "from knowledge" (*jñānāt*). Knowledge here refers to the meditation on the threefold nature of food (*tryannātma-upāsana*). The goal for the person (*pumartha*) is the state of being that threefold nature of food.
For it has been said: "This person who knows thus—he is indeed Prajāpati. || 225 ||
Because the attainment of the fruit in its entirety occurs through insight alone.
The goal would not be achieved through the hearing [of the scriptures] and so forth, nor would it be achieved through the performance of the five-limbed ritual.

He establishes the futility of sons and so forth with the verse beginning "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). The word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to wife and wealth. Thus, the meaning is: "then," that is, at the time when one has attained the desired goal through the meditation on the Self consisting of the three foods. || 226 ||
To establish the meaningfulness of these two, it is said: "There are indeed three."
Having examined this, it should be accepted by the wise, but not that which is devoid of reasoning. || 227 ||

He adopts that very position: "Of those two," etc. The subsequent passage is intended to establish the purposefulness (*arthavattva*) of the fruit for both son and ritual action when combined with knowledge (*vidyā*). The meaning is that it has been stated that the perceptions of son, wealth, and [the world] are combined for the sake of the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*).

He begins to refute the opponent’s intention through the voice of the proponent [the *pūrvavādin*], starting with the words "having examined" (*parīkṣya*). The meaning is as follows: after deliberating whether a conjunction (*samuccaya*) or a non-conjunction is logically tenable, that which is determined by reason must be accepted; for without deliberation, logical correctness cannot be ascertained. Furthermore, the wise should not accept what is devoid of reason without having first deliberated, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 227 ||
The combination of means that are independent of anything else for their own respective results.
It is not logical [for one to be both], because of independence, like the acts of going and seeing. || 228 ||

Then, raising the doubt as to which [of the two] possesses logical consistency in this examination—whether it is the combination of independent [factors] or that of dependent ones—the author states the fault [in the former case] by saying "svaphale" (in its own fruit). He provides an illustration for that with "gamaneti" (by walking, etc.). Since movement is possible for the blind man and the perception of form and so forth is established for the lame man, there can be no combination of those two independent [factors] in a single instance; likewise, in the case of independent [factors], there is no combination.
The meaning is that it does not go anywhere. || 228 ||
If they were to say that the unity of the action depends on other factors, then there would be a combination;
yet even by Rudra, the combination of a single [action] is not admitted.

It refutes another alternative with the words "anyeti" (if it were otherwise). The meaning is that if the means, such as sons and so forth, were causes of the fruit while being mutually dependent, then because there would be a single means, there could be no combination (samuccaya). || 229 ||
Due to the distinctness of the means—thread, vīraṇa grass, clay, and wood.
In the production of an effect such as a cloth, there would be no conjunction of those [causes].

He clarifies the example stated—that for those things which are independent, there is no conjunction, just as in the case of going and seeing—with the words "tantu" (thread), etc. "Distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*) means mutual independence with respect to a single fruit. || 230 ||
Just as the shuttle, the loom, and the peg are mutually combined for their own respective functions.
This collection is untenable even then, because of the cause of oneness.
He provides an illustration for the case where things that are mutually dependent and combined do not achieve unity: "The pot," etc. [The meaning of this is: it is the combination itself...
[ga. tasyārtho] [Vol.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a combination [of means], he says that even when combined, there is no combination of means, because that which is combined is the reality itself, and that reality is one.
"Even then," [it says]. || 239 ||
If it is held that the attainment of the three worlds occurs through knowledge alone;
Because it is the cause for the attainment of everything, this is not so by way of separate entities. (232)

In the context of the impossibility of a cumulative [combination], the proponent concludes that the ritual action of the son would be futile, stating "of the three worlds. Having raised the objection as to how knowledge—which is the cause for the world of the gods—could be the cause for the three [worlds], he replies, "of that," because meditation on the Self consisting of the three foods is the cause for becoming Prajāpati, the Self of all worlds. In this regard, he states the refutation offered by Bhartṛprapañca: "This is not so," for it has been stated—that through knowledge alone, all...
The attainment of the three worlds occurs through the [respective] transgressions; it is not due to separate causes. || 232 ||
For each means of accomplishment, such as the rite for obtaining a son and so forth, has indeed a distinct objective to be achieved.
It is certain that this cannot be accomplished by a woman alone, but only through knowledge. || 233 ||
He explains how there is distinctness: "individually. He states the result when each [member] of the group, such as a son and so forth, is connected to the fruit separately:
"by herself alone" (ekākinyā). || 233 ||
Therefore, he states the exclusion of other means by saying "by the son alone."
Having raised an objection regarding the word "jyotiṣā," they set forth the following resolution.

He states that the restrictive particle (*eva*) is the means of knowledge for the connection of each [of these] with its respective fruit, using the words "by means of a son" (*putreṇa*). This means, therefore, that because each one—son and so forth—is connected respectively with the world of men and the others. He shows the objection and resolution regarding the restriction of other means, such as ritual action (*karman*), which are distinct from the son, by citing the phrase "by means of light" (*jyotiṣā*) and so on, specifically in the context of the passage "by means of a son alone" (*putreṇaiva*).

The meaning is that they raise an objection—that it is not logical to maintain the restriction "one conquers this world by means of the light" because another cause for the conquest of the world of men is heard [in scripture]—and then they provide a rebuttal. || 234 ||
Because of the occurrence of attainment and transcendence, and because of the differentiation of objects. || 235 ||
This is not so, because here [the result] does not arise apart from the birth of a son.
This world is conquerable by other means; therefore, what has been stated is not true.

He clarifies the rebuttal with the words "attainment" (*prāpti*). The meaning is that through the *Jyotiṣṭoma* there is the attainment of this world, and for one who has attained it, there is the transcendence [of death] by means of a son;

therefore, because the objects [of the two injunctions] are distinct, the restriction is established. He explains the Bhāṣya—which establishes the restriction by stating that there is no conquest of the world of men other than through the procreation of a son—with the words "not this" (*na etat*). The locative case is used in the sense of determining the specific means (*sādhana-nirdhāraṇārthā*).

[The state of being] a son, action, lack of supreme knowledge, the human world, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods.
The mutual restriction [of the means and the ends] has been explained through their connection as cause and effect. || 275 ||

In order to establish that very relationship, he follows up with what has already been stated: "The son," etc. The construction is as follows: it has been explained that there is a fixed rule of mutual correspondence, whereby the triad beginning with the son is the means for attaining the fruit of the three worlds respectively. || 279 ||
Since it consists merely of the act of placing the son [into the fire], there is no other separate means of accomplishment.
A wife and human wealth [are acquired] because they share a single purpose with one's actions. || 276 ||

Since wife and wealth are also mentioned in the context just like sons and so forth, one might object that their application toward a specific result should have been stated even though it was not; fearing that their connection to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) would otherwise be untenable, he says: "Sons... etc. The connection is as follows: "another means" refers to an independent means, and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that [wife and wealth] are not separate from ritual action (*karman*). Since wife and wealth are included within the categories of sons and ritual action respectively, [they do not require a separate statement].
[Vol.
2, Page 553] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri;

The meaning is that even when the connection with the fruit is established, since the connection with that [fruit] is also established for those two which are included therein, there is no need to mention their connection with the fruit independently. || 276 ||
They attain the status of being means of accomplishment merely by the acquisition of their own nature.
How can his son become the means for both ritual action and knowledge? || 277 ||

Now, one might object: "Even though there is thus a restriction to three means of attainment, why is the son described separately, setting aside knowledge and ritual action? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Svarūpa... (The remainder is: "...the means for the two worlds. This means: because they consist of action (*kriyārūpatvāt*). However, the son is not such a cause for the conquest of the world of men (*manuṣyaloka*), because he is a substance (*dravyatvāt*); for a substance not permeated by action is never seen to be a means of attainment. Therefore, regarding his conquest of that world...
He asks, "In what way is it a means? [The answer is] "As a son," meaning: as a son in that world of men. || 277 ||
Thus, this connection of the author of the Bhāṣya, the speaker, is clear.
Since it does not contradict what we have stated, it is not excessively scrutinized here. || 278 ||

To the objection raised in this way, he states the response regarding the inheritance (*saṃpratti*) in order to make known that the son is the cause for the world [of the father]. He says "in this manner" (*ityevam*). The qualification "clearly" (*sphuṭa*) is used to indicate that this connection was not merely hinted at, but was shown directly. He says "our" (*asmad*) to show that this connection is not to be rejected, because it does not contradict the connection stated by us. The statement regarding the inheritance is an auxiliary part of the renunciation of the stages (*kramasaṃnyāsa*).

Therefore, this relationship stated in the Bhāṣya is not contradictory to the relationship we have described; for at the time of renunciation, the conquest of this world is accomplished by means of a son during one’s current practice. Thus, no effort is made to refute the relationship stated in the Bhāṣya—this is the meaning. The word "iti" (thus) is used to indicate that there is no fault here from a superficial perspective. || 278 ||
If a son were properly instructed, the world would be won by him alone.
There is no purpose served here by any other action for the sake of achieving victory in the world of men. (279)
The particle "eva" (only) must be applied for the sake of restriction to the son alone.
The attainment of the worlds of the ancestors and gods occurs through the hearing [of the scriptures] and other means. || 280 ||
If the connection stated in the Bhāṣya is not to be refuted, then one must also accept the explanation given there for the passage beginning with "by action, the world of the ancestors.

Consequently, one might object that the claim that "the attainment of the world of the gods is through knowledge because it is so heard in scripture" and so forth is incorrect. Anticipating this, [the author] establishes that this [connection] applies only where the particle *eva* (only) is heard in the text, by stating: "If the son... Here, the word *atra* (here) is used to specify the human world among the various worlds.

For the conquest of the world of men is twofold: here, the performance of the remaining duties such as study and so forth on behalf of the father, and the enjoyment [of worldly pleasures]. In this regard, if the son is instructed by his fathers with the thought of conquering that world, by that alone is the first [type of] conquest achieved; for neither ritual action nor knowledge has any utility toward the conquest of the world as previously described. Therefore, since the son alone is the means for that purpose, the word "eva" (only) is used for the sake of emphasizing him.

The second [type of] victory, however, may occur even by means of another cause, such as the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa*), according to scriptural texts such as "by the stars... It is with this very distinction in mind that we have stated the restrictive particle *eva* (only) as excluding other means of yoga; this is the intended meaning. He states that the application of the restrictive particle *eva* to the two subsequent sentences is not logical: "the world of the ancestors," etc. For the victory over the world of the ancestors is not restricted solely to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and the like; rather, it occurs through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Nor can it be that the conquest of the world of the gods occurs through knowledge alone, because that would contradict the maxim "due to the hearing of that" (tacchruteḥ), and because of such scriptural statements as "from renunciation comes the station of Brahman."
848. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* [First Chapter]:
Therefore, because it is possible for the conquest of both worlds to depend upon other causes, the interpretation of the two sentences is not achieved by inserting the particle *eva*.
The meaning is "it is logical. || 279 || 280 ||
This very explanation here is faultless, whereas all others are full of defects.
Therefore, only this should be accepted, and not that which is considered to be faulty.
The particle *eva* (only/alone) signifies that [the term] applies to that where it is heard and not elsewhere; this alone is faultless because it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti.

However, the application of the particle *eva* to both sentences is faulty because it contradicts them. Therefore, he states the conclusion: "Our own interpretation alone should be accepted by the learned, and not that of the author of the Bhāṣya. Thus, it is said that the sentence beginning with "by action" (*karmaṇā*) refers to this very point.
Having established that one [view] is free from fault while the other is faulty, he states the resulting conclusion: "This," etc. (289).
Then, immediately after that, from the performance of ritual action and meditative worship as previously described, [the result arises].
Therefore, for the sake of the accomplishment of that fruit, its transfer is ordained. || 282 ||

At this point, having concluded the incidental discussion regarding the statement on the connection between the Samhitā and the Vākya, he explains the passage beginning with "samāpya" and so forth. The word "atha" (now) signifies that immediately after the previously mentioned meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore)— namely, from the performance of ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*)— and upon the completion of those two commenced undertakings, [the following is begun] for the sake of their fruit, as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to them.
The construction is as follows: [this is] the rule for the transfer of property (saṃpratti) useful for the gradual renunciation (kramasaṃnyāsa). || 282 ||
For this world of men is one where the accomplishment of distinguished sons is possible.
Therefore, the ritual for the attainment of prosperity should be explained here to one who desires its fruit.

Therefore, he states another meaning of the word "from" (*yataḥ*). "In this world" (*iha*) refers to the mention of a specific son. "The state of desiring to obtain this world, which is to be accomplished by him" means the seeker's desire for its fruit; the phrase "for the sake of the attainment of that fruit" refers to that seeker. || 283 ||
The accomplishment must be performed by one who is wise, and not by one who lacks discernment.
Therefore, this has not been formulated by the authors of the aphorisms as being impermanent.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say that the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is a transfer [of duties] by means of the service (upāsana) of a lay follower (upāsaka)—because such renunciation could exist independently or as an auxiliary part (aṅga) of the Agnihotra—he says: "By the knower" (viduṣā). Whether it were independent or an auxiliary part of the ritual, this [renunciation] would have had to be formulated as a separate rite by the authors of the Kalpasūtras; yet it was not so formulated. Therefore, this [transfer] occurs by way of knowledge (vidyā).

The meaning is that it is indeed a subsidiary part [of the meditation]. Nor is its status as a subsidiary part even fixed, because it is impossible for one who has no son to perform that meditation; thus he says: "Because it is non-eternal.
"Saṃpratti" is the name for this rite of self-purification.
Or there might be the activity of practicing [a remedy] upon seeing another patient who has recovered. || 285 ||

He states the meaning of the word *saṃpratti*: "It is called *saṃpratti*. The meaning is that, like bathing and other such acts, it is the designation for a rite of self-purification performed by the practitioner.

He states another meaning for it: "It is called *pratipatti*. For a householder who is seized by a severe illness and is about to die, the abandonment of ritual actions follows as a matter of course; thus, just as in the rule "one throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit," if the ritual actions [are to be abandoned]...
1.1 kha.
‘The desire to obtain.
When they are abandoned, then by way of entrusting them to one's son, one should relinquish them; this act of relinquishment is called *saṃpratti*.
Furthermore, renunciation is observed for one who is in a state of adversity; therefore, the meaning is that it is an act of performance, specifically the formal transfer of one's duties. || 289 ||
And by the word "maipyat" (when about to go), the time for this ritual action is prescribed here.
Through a thorough understanding of the Jātaka tales and other such works, it is also possible to know the [proper] time. || 286 ||

Anticipating the doubt as to at what time that action [should be performed], he states the purport of the passage beginning with "yadā" (when), namely: "maipyanniti ca. Here, the word "saptamyā" (by the locative case) refers back to the sentence. It is an injunction of awareness (*bodhana*), but not an injunction of time like that of a sacrifice; for an action is not enjoined with respect to a specific time.
The phrase "time" (kāla) should be understood as referring to "stability" (sthiti). Since the time of death is difficult to know, he asks how its effects can be determined therein, and thus says:

"Jātaka," etc. By the word "etc. (ādi), dreams and other signs indicating death are included. The word "also" (api) is used to provide the knowledge of prosperity and so forth as an illustrative example. || 286 ||
And when the father is about to die, he should call his son and address him with these words.
Being thus enlightened by those words beginning with "Thou art Brahman," he also replied.

Now, demonstrating that very manner [of practice], he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then" (*atha*) and so forth, starting with the words "And one who is about to die" (*mumūrṣuśca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and by being thus, it excludes any other activity for him. The meaning of the word "then" (*atha*) is immediate succession to the state of being about to die (*mumūrṣānantarya*). || 287 ||
One who is about to go forth from worldly activities or who desires liberation is called a *mumukṣu*.
Likewise, the primary meaning of both the root and the prefix may also be resorted to. || 288 ||

In the view that the *saṃpratti* (transmission of one's duties) is an auxiliary part of the gradual renunciation (*kramasaṃnyāsa*), he states the meaning of the word "departing" (*preyan*) as follows: "from works. He points out a distinction here with respect to the position stated in the Commentary: "of the verbal root," etc. When the meaning of "departing" (*preyan*) is taken in the sense of renunciation (*pārivrajya*), the primary meaning of the verbal root *i*, which signifies "going," and of the prefix *pra* would be accepted; namely, "I am going forth from works with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*)."
For in that case, such would be the meaning; thus, this very interpretation is the correct one—this is the sense. || 288 ||
"I am Brahman"—thus had my father previously instructed me.
He would not be able to give a reply unless he had been previously trained by me. || 289 ||
In order to clarify what was briefly stated there—that even he [the son] replied with the intent of the responses beginning with "I am Brahman"—he says: "I... and so forth.

The meaning is that the son, having been addressed by his father with the words "You are Brahman, you are the sacrifice, you are the world," replies to his father with "I am," etc., because he had already been instructed previously that the remainder of his duties, such as study and the like, were to be performed by him. Thus he was previously instructed...
He states its true nature by way of its distinction [from others] with the words: "to answer. || 289 ||
He himself explains to us the meaning of the consecration of the son.
Because the meaning of the mantras is hidden from the Śruti, he said this. || 290 ||
He introduces the passage beginning with "Whatever indeed" (yadvai kiṃca) with the word "putra. Since this very meaning is also intended by the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt), he says:
"Therefore," thinking that the venerable author of the Commentary had this meaning hidden from him, the Śruti proceeds to provide an explanation; thus he said, "from this [it follows]. || 290 ||
Urged by Ka.
and Ga. [vol2, page 556]
850. Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]:
Whatever has been studied and recited, and whatever is intended to be studied—
And regarding that which has not been studied, when it is spoken of as "Brahman," there would be identity [of meaning]. || 291 ||

He connects the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "That which... [with the following]. "Anūktam" means that which has not been studied; that is to say, it is distinct from both [the studied and the unstudied].

The address "tvam" (you) implies its distinction from what ought to be studied because it is not necessarily so; however, this address is intended for the successful study of that [text] according to one's own will. || 299 ||
For it is this meaning of the sentence, "Thou art Brahman," that is intended to be expressed here.
I have fulfilled my duty by bringing to completion the meaning of that which was to be studied. || 292 ||

He states the combined meaning of the sentence "Thou art Brahman" and its corresponding Brāhmaṇa passage with the words beginning "Thou. Here, the word *iha* (here) is coreferential with the mantra; the word *atra* (there) refers to the Brāhmaṇa. The particle *hi* (for/indeed) is used to indicate the consensus among those who know both the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa regarding the meaning of the statement thus explained. || 292 ||
Whatever is established by means of valid cognition as being produced by me, [is so].
"Let that [act] here be performed by you; such was the father's intention. (293)

He states the meaning of the two Brāhmaṇa passages beginning with "ye vai ke na" [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.2.1] with the words "yāvat" and so forth. The meaning is: "Whatever ritual acts such as sacrifices, prescribed by the scriptures, were to be accomplished by me prior to this, let that be accomplished by you. The word "atra" refers to the subsequent time. || 293 ||
For indeed, by common worldly saying alone, when the carrying away of the fruits of sacrifices occurs, [it is understood].
And the mention of "sacrifices" is for the purpose of including the obligatory sacrifices (nitya-yajña). || 294 ||

He raises the objection of tautology with the words "by worldly usage. This means that because [the Vedic rites] have that [worldly fruit] as their result, they possess that [worldly nature], and thus they are pervaded by it.

The ellipsis is: "If [Vedic] grasping exists, what [additional] sacrifices are there?"—thus there is tautology. [This is so] because of the mutual pervasion between the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana).

The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves the purpose of providing an explanation. Since the mention of "worlds" (*loka*) implies the inclusion of the sacrifices that are their cause, one might ask why there is a separate mention of "sacrifices" (*yajña*) for the sake of dedicating them to the son—given that it is only the obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifices that are to be dedicated to the son, otherwise there would be the contingency of dedicating only the optional (*kāmya*) ones, as it is those alone that are recognized as causes of worlds—and furthermore, there can be no dedication of optional sacrifices to a son because they cannot be considered mandatory. To this, he provides the answer: "Nitya... (obligatory).

Furthermore, it should be understood that it is not correct to claim that the mention of "sacrifices" (*yajña*) is redundant for the purpose of including the "worlds" (*loka*), as in the phrase "whatever worlds there may be. This is because, on the view that obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are fruitless, such [worldly fruits] would be absent; and even on the alternative view, since the worlds are intended merely as subordinate elements, their separate mention alongside sacrifices and so forth—without being intended as the primary focus—is accepted as not being redundant. Thus it should be seen. || 294 ||
Thus, the meaning of the words beginning with "Brahman" has been stated in brief.
But now, the meaning of the statement "Thou art Brahman" is being clarified by means of scripture. || 295 ||

He restates the meaning for the three Brahmins with the words "brahma" and so forth. He introduces the passage beginning with "etāvat" with the word "tvam. By the particle "tu," the remaining two sentences are included. || 299 ||
Only this much is to be performed here by the householder who holds the authority.
The Vedas, the sacrifices, and the worlds—no other purpose remains beyond these. || 296 ||
1 kha. 'ttirani' | 2 ga. stvaniṣpa' | 3 kha. retadviva | [vol2, page 557] 851
He states the meaning of the portion beginning with "All this is only so much" (*etāvadvā idaṃ sarvam*). [The word] "only so much" (*etāvat*) refers to the path of ritual action (*karmamārga*).
He demonstrates the extent of what is to be performed [in that path] with the words "the Vedas," etc. The Vedas are to be studied, sacrifices are to be performed, and [worlds] are to be conquered.
"The worlds" is the division. || 296 ||
Desiring to perform the task as described, he becomes absorbed in that very thing through his own will and intent.
"May he not suffer from this binding of authority; may he protect [it]. || 297 ||
Keeping this meaning of the sentence in mind, the father spoke to his son.
No meaning other than this is intended by such statements as "Thou art Brahman. (298)

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "All this is Myself" (*etanmā sarvam*) with the words "As has been stated. The meaning is: desiring to perform the sacrifices and other rites offered by Me as duties to be performed, the son—having that as his primary aim and possessing that resolve—will protect Me from this bond of office which is the cause of the human body.
He states what is indicated by the word "iti": "In his mind... and so forth. He precludes the intention of any other meaning with the words "You are Brahman," etc.
"Of sentences," [so it is said]. || 297 || 298 ||
For it has been said: "One who desires to act and is likewise instructed in such a manner..."
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, the wise call him "putra. || 299 ||

Therefore, regarding the phrase "as a son" (*putram*), he states what is required by the word "that" (*tat*): "because" (*yataḥ*). The meaning is: because, having been instructed and desiring to perform the study and other duties taught [to him], he is absorbed in that and possesses the resolve for that. He connects the passage beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) as follows: "hence" (*ataḥ*). || 299 ||
For when a son is instructed by his father himself, he attains capability.
Therefore, the wise say that a son who has been duly instructed is truly "of the world" (lokya). || 300 ||

Anticipating the objection that "since there is a specific scriptural statement that 'the world belongs to one who has a son, not to one who is sonless,' what is the purpose of instructing him [in the Veda]? he says: "He is instructed. The remainder [of the sentence] is: "with regard to the capacity for the subsidiary acts such as study and so forth. Those who understand the purpose of having a son are the performers of ritual action (karmiṇaḥ) intended here, namely those called *vipaścitaḥ*. (300)
And for this very reason, the ancestors instruct him when he has attained the state of being a true son.
"By means of a son who has been properly instructed, may I become one who has fulfilled his worldly duty"—with this thought, he should exert effort. || 301 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore, him... with the words "And the ancestors... This means that it is precisely because a son who has been instructed is fit for the world (*lokyatva*).

The "existence" of the son refers to his fitness for instruction. He states the intention of the ancestors, who are the instructors, with the words "By one who has been instructed..."; this refers to the effort or intent (*tātparya*) regarding the instruction. || 309 ||
Even one who has transferred the burden of his own person should not abandon the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Thus, this which has been stated by Karmarāga is without authority and is not accepted.

Having explained the injunction for the transfer [of the fires] and its corresponding explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), [the author] restates what was said by Bhartṛprapañca: "Having performed this transfer, as long as one lives, one should not abandon the *agnihotra*. He refutes this with the words "it has been transferred," responding that there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*māna*). Thus ends [this point]. || 302 ||
1 kha. Regarding agency (kartṛtva) | 2 ka. kha. ...ti | or (vā) | 3 kha. ...tyavaśe | [vol2, page 558] 852
In Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, [in the first chapter]:
"On account of the indicative mark of the transmission of the self (*saṃpratti*), the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is intended here."
It is maintained that knowledge is the single means of valid cognition for all the Upaniṣads without exception. || 303 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only the ritual act (*kratu*) has been transferred to the son, while this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) do not permit the renunciation of the *agnihotra* and other rites? Therefore, there is no authority for one who has performed the transfer (*saṃpratti*) to abandon the *agnihotra*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The transfer" (*saṃpratti*). Because the transfer, enjoined as an auxiliary to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) in the *Kāṭhaka* Śruti, is observed here [in this context] for this very reason.

The meaning is that the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is intended here as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the principal act (*aṅgin*), on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). One might object: "Even though renunciation is a subsidiary to the act of entrusting (*samprattiḥ*) in another Vedic text, it is not a subsidiary here; for indeed, all the Upaniṣads do not constitute a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says "niḥśeṣa... (in its entirety), according to the principle of "cognizance through all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya-nyāya*). || 303 ||
Because the attainment of the state of having the three foods as one's own body has already been accomplished while still living.
Since all means of accomplishment culminate in their fruit, why is renunciation being obstructed? || 304 ||

Regarding the statement that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is intended for one who meditates on the self consisting of the three foods (*tryannātman*) within the *Saṃpratti* discourse, he states another indicative mark (*liṅga*).
He provides the reason why the state of being the *sūtra* (the thread) is accomplished by the living person himself: "Of the means" (*sādhanānām*).

This means that because meditations (*upāstayaḥ*) culminate in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of becoming the deity to be meditated upon, there is no further fruit to be gained from their performance. || 204 ||
If its abandonment is not desired until one has attained the scriptural injunction for lifelong [celibacy], then...
Thus, there is no qualification for the aged by means of that which has been completed through application. || 305 ||

He raises an objection that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) cannot be established because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "Performing actions here indeed... and so forth. [The word] "yāvat" [is used];

the word "of actions" (karmaṇām) is to be supplied as the remainder. The pronoun "tat" (in the verse) also refers to that same subject. He states that the aforementioned scripture is not literal: "naiva—" [not at all].

[The opponent] says: "Because the Agnihotra and other rites have fixed times, we observe their interruption at other times. He states the reason: "Regarding the performance... [The author] replies: "No; because for one who is aged," etc. Since even a living person who is incapable has no entitlement [to perform them], this rule does not apply; therefore, the scriptural text refers to householders who are not dispassionate, and not to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
The meaning is "contradictory. || 305 ||
Because rites such as the Agnihotra are concluded in the morning.
But even for obligatory duties, renunciation may indeed take place at that very time.

The author states the reasoning for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) from the perspective of one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*). Regarding the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*): it is stated as an illustration of a fixed time.

Since rites such as the *agnihotra* are completed at their prescribed times, the abandonment of obligatory (*nitya*) and other such rites at times other than those enjoined is established even during the state of non-discernment; however, since this [abandonment] is possible at the time of the formal transfer of duties (*saṃpratti*) during the state of discernment, what more need be said?
This is the meaning. || 306 ||
For one who has transferred the burden of the self, the word "Brahman" becomes meaningful.
Then all actions would cease if one were to remain having renounced them. || 307 ||
He states that even such statements as "Thou art Brahman" serve to establish renunciation for one who has performed the *saṃpratti* (the formal transfer of assets). He says: "Having transferred...
[ka. 'daṅgisaṃ'; kha. 'ntasaṃpra'] [Vol. 2, p. 559].
1 [Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

If the father, having performed the *saṃpratti* rite, remains alive for as long as he lives, and during that time renounces all ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) and stays [in that state], then [regarding] the son...
Even for a father who has surrendered the entire range of his duties to his son, such statements as "Thou art Brahman" become meaningful with respect to the son;
therefore, the meaning is that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is established in the present context even from the aforementioned statement. || 307 ||
Because the entire collection of effects consisting of all things has been transferred to the son.
If it were not intended to be abandoned, there would be a statement regarding its general reinstatement.

How is it that the meaningfulness of the statement exists only when there is renunciation (saṃnyāsa)? To this he says: "The Self of all. Fearing the objection that even upon the abandonment of certain rites, the abandonment of the Agnihotra and other such duties might not be intended here, he says: "If not," [and] "the handing over" (saṃpratti).

If it were not intended in the statement that all actions are to be renounced, there would have been a statement specifying by whom this much work was to be performed after the transfer of duties; since such a statement does not exist, the meaning is that the renunciation of all actions is intended here. || 308 ||
In the Kauṣītaki Śruti, it is stated that this applies only to a householder who is still living.
Renunciation is clearly enjoined; one should dwell happily under the sovereignty of one's sons. (309)

In the case of gradual renunciation (*krama-saṃnyāsa*), as in the case of the sentence regarding the acquisition [of knowledge], and as in the statement beginning with "one who [proceeds] in due order" found in the *Kāṭhaka-śruti*, it is said: "A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), having studied the Veda, or having practiced celibacy after studying the Vedas or the Vedāṅgas, having taken a wife, having procreated sons, having established the sacred fires, having performed sacrifices according to his capacity, and having shared those [possessions] with suitable means of livelihood— then, for him who has been authorized by his teachers, renunciation [is prescribed]," and so on.

He says that even for this reason there is no denial of that [renunciation], because in the Kauṣītaki Śruti, the renunciation of a living householder is heard of without doubt: "One may practice fasting, enter the waters, undertake the Great Journey (mahāprasthāna), go to the hermitage of the aged, or live under the sovereignty of one's sons.
Thus he says, "Kauṣītaki," summarizing the Kauṣītaki Śruti itself with the words, "Under the sons... (verse 309).
Having renounced all actions and having dispelled all defects.
Such things have been stated by Manu as well, yet something contradictory to that is being asserted. (310)
He states that even Smṛti is an authority regarding the renunciation under discussion, saying: "Having renounced... (saṃnyasya).
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of Dharma,
and having studied them, follow them accordingly, go to the supreme goal.
For a twice-born man who practices the Dharma characterized by the ten marks and has heard the Vedāntas according to the injunctions, may renounce his worldly life, being free from debt.
Having renounced all ritual actions and having cast off all defects,
one should dwell happily in the sovereignty of one's sons, remaining self-restrained and practicing the Veda.
Having thus renounced actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
1 kha, regarding renunciation (saṃnyāsa). 2 ka. 'digdhaṃ śrū. 3 ka. nudet. iṃ.

By stating this, Manu also accepted gradual renunciation (*krama-saṃnyāsa*). If even for one who has performed the *saṃpratti* (the rite of transferring one's duties and property to one’s son), there is still work regarding the sacred fires—

He states that if there were an acceptance [of the offering] from the *hotṛ* priest and others at that time, there would be a contradiction with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*: "And that would be contrary to that" (310).
The fruit of his worship is indeed declared here to be like that of a father.
Why is it that the Agnihotra and other such rites are not likewise restored? || 311 ||

Although the abandonment of the *agnihotra* and other rites is intended in both Śruti and Smṛti, yet there is no reason here for such an intention; having raised this doubt, the author elaborates on the statement "if it is not intended to be abandoned" (*na cet tityakṣitam*). He says: "He meditates" (*upāsti*). Just as for one who has performed the *saṃpratti*, only the fruit of meditation is stated in passages such as "And from the earth [the teacher] leads him," and no other duty, so too is the renunciation of all works [the result of] the *saṃpratti*.

If [renunciation] were not intended to be expressed, then even the Agnihotra and other rites would have been restated in the immediately following passage; since that is not the case here, the meaning is that renunciation is indeed intended to be expressed. || 311 ||
Because of the restrictive emphasis on "only one," the father's vow regarding the vital breath is justified.
Because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*), that alone [is intended] and nothing else is desired [therein].

Since the fruit of meditation (*upāsti*) is not mentioned later for one who has performed the *sampratti* (the ritual transfer), and since the vow of the vital breath (*prāṇavrata*) is also observed, one might suspect that this too is a ritual action (*karman*) and thus there is no injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) here; anticipating this doubt, he says: "One. For the vow of the vital breath is indeed either the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇopāsti*) or...

Or [it may be argued that] mere activities such as breathing and so forth do not oppose renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in either case; for since the meditation upon that [breath] is mental, it serves as a cause for the refinement of the person consisting in the cessation of all activities by means of the restraint of the mind, and thus it is conducive to renunciation. Furthermore, because those activities are the cause of the person's maintenance—as they serve as the cause for sustaining life—they are favorable to it through those respective channels. Therefore, the father’s renunciation is indeed consistent with the restriction "only one" [of the two].

Even for one who protects his life, nothing other than that [which is compatible with knowledge] is accepted here by the wise as being contrary to renunciation; therefore, the meaning is that the rule for that [protection of life] is appropriate here. || 312 ||
When one who knows this thus dies, having transferred his sacrificial rites to his son, [he does not perish].
Then, abandoned by his vital functions, he enters his son along with his life-breaths.

Having refuted the view that one who has performed the *saṃpratti* (the rite of transferring one's duties) may still abandon his actions, and having established the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of those actions, he explains the passage beginning with "When he...
by saying "he dies. The meaning is: one who meditates thus, "I am Prajāpati, the self consisting of food," and has thereby directly realized that state.
By the word "kṛta" (performed), it is meant "purified by the impressions of his volitions (*saṃkalpa*)," since all his volition has been entrusted to his son.

The meaning is that because only the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I am Prajāpati" remains, the father, entering together with the refined speech and other faculties that enter everywhere, is designated as "entering into the son. || 313 ||
Prior to the transition of one's own season, the father was the one who grasped the earth.
That very image of his father was reflected in him, his own son.

What is this "entry"? For there is no entry, as in the case of a snake or similar creature entering a hole, for one who is either qualified or solitary. To this he says: "Previously" (prāk). The meaning is that the manner of the father’s volition (*saṃkalpa*)—which he possessed prior to entrusting his own duties to his son—is metaphorically designated as the "entry" of this wise man into his own son. || 314 ||

Just as the reflection of the sun in water occurs due to the delusion of its own appearance.
The [notion of agency] of the inner self arises solely from the cause of external adjuncts, because of its immutability.

[Objection: "But surely, why is a figurative transfer (*aupacārikī saṃkrānti*) postulated there, instead of accepting a primary transfer (*mukhyā saṃkrānti*), as in the case of a reflection in a moving tree? To this, he says: "In water," etc. [The primary transfer] does not belong to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor to the conditioned self (*upahita*), nor to the inner witness (*pratīc*); it is not the first [option], because it contradicts direct perception (*adhyakṣa-virodhāt*), for a body and so forth belonging to a father is not perceived as having been transferred to his son; nor is it the second, because [the transfer] of the sun in water— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, but the translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.*

The meaning is as follows: even for a father who has performed meritorious deeds, because his own resolve for his work appears to be transferred to his son—due to which there arises the delusion that he himself has entered therein—the statement regarding "transference" (*saṃkrānti*) refers to a different kind of transference, as it is contradicted by direct perception. He refutes the third [view] with the words "parā" (the other), etc.;
the meaning is that the transference of the inner self (*pratīc*) is merely conditional (*aupādhikī*), not real, because of its immutability (*kauṭasthya*). || 395 ||
Just as those whose intellects are purified by ritual action possess the state of being witnesses with respect to their own bodies.
In the same way, due to delusion, there arises the misconception of a manifold self within the bodies of one's sons and others. || 316 ||

If immutability were established, one would have to say that transmigration is merely adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); yet that is not the case, because [the self] is subject to modification through its state of being divided.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the seasons" (*ṛtu*). The meaning is that since the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*), characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*) which is permeated by the volition for action, is one as the witness of all bodies, the notion of difference is an error. || 316 ||
Because the father himself enters [the son] through the entry of his own office (adhikāra) into the son.
But he himself, being devoid of authority, remains subservient to destiny.

He summarizes the established point regarding the impossibility of primary entry with the words "svādhikāra" (his own office). The meaning is that because he has entrusted his own purposeful intention to his son, the father is said to have "entered" there only figuratively. He states the result of the father's entry as being merely conditional (*aupādhika*) with the words "ityataḥ" (therefore).
That is to say, being "niradhikāraḥ"—meaning devoid of his own purposeful intention—he remains as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of the fruit.
The meaning is that it "remains. || 317 ||
By means of his internal body, for the sake of completing his remaining tasks.
A father, while performing [rites] through his son, himself becomes the enjoyer of that fruit. || 318 ||
Anticipating the doubt that his departure from the world of men there might be absolute, he says: "By means of the internal [self].

Even though the father is dead, he continues to exist here through the self of the instructed son, performing his remaining duties to the best of his ability for the sake of their accomplishment; thus, he is not absolutely departed from this world, nor has he departed from the other world in the form of its fruit. || 398 ||
One who is endowed with the means provided by destiny remains truly a son.
But the father is indeed the very essence of that fruit, and not merely one who exists in the form of the means.

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a dual nature for one and the same entity?", he says: "Divine," etc. Even a father who possesses knowledge and action, though included within the category of causal factors (*kāraka*), remains in relation to his son; yet he cannot remain there while still maintaining the form of a means (*sādhana*), but rather exists as the fruit itself (*phalātman*).

The meaning is that [the son] is unable to be established as having no nature of its own; therefore, due to the distinction between cause and effect, he is of two forms. Alternatively, here the son is one who possesses knowledge and so forth.

The father exists merely as the essence of the aforementioned results in the next world, and not as the essence of the means; therefore, the meaning is that he moves through both worlds by means of the son’s self—which consists of both the means and the results—and by his own self. || 319 ||
Whatever duty was not performed by the father through negligence—such as the study of one's own Veda—it is called "putra" because he fulfills that [duty] and thereby protects his father. 320.

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "If he... and ending with "is called a son" by means of the words beginning with "No...": the meaning is that because the father protects (*trāṇa*) [the child] by fulfilling through instruction whatever [studies and so forth] he himself failed to perform due to negligence, the child is a "son" (*putra*). || 320 ||
This father, having fully accomplished his own purpose, abides as the divine self.
The son proceeds by fulfilling the work half-completed by his father. || 321 ||

Fearing that, if there were a remainder of duties to be performed, the father—who is himself the fruit—would not be complete, he says: "Complete. The reason for this is stated as "of the father. || 322 ||
Upon death, the world is cut off because of the cause that is the cessation of its means of existence.
Nor should any doubt be entertained regarding the father, for he himself [is that very one].
With his very own body, he remains performing ever-new [deeds]. || 322 ||

He states the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "sa putreṇa" (he [is freed] by means of a son) as follows: "mṛter" (from death). "Loka" refers to the world specifically characterized as the human realm. "Sādhana" refers to the body and so forth. He provides the reason for this with the words "yasmāt" (because). The meaning is that there remains ever-new [duty], such as Vedic study and the like, which must be performed. || 322 ||
Therefore, he says "by the son alone" in order to establish a perpetual entitlement.
The father conquers this world by means of such a son.

He brings forward a scriptural statement to support the stated point: "By means of a son. Since the scripture declares that a father [is saved] by a son alone for the sake of accomplishing the perpetual performance [of rites], the meaning is that because of the performance of those causes, there is no severance from this world even for a deceased father. By means of a son, this world—
He concludes the work with the word "jayati" (he triumphs). The meaning is: by one who is thus constituted, that is, by one possessing the aforementioned instruction. || 323 ||
But victory does not come merely by attaining one's own self, as is the case with knowledge and action.
The word "atha" (now/then) is employed for the purpose of setting aside the authority of the son. || 324 ||

He states the distinction of the son from other means [of attaining the worlds] with the words "But not... (na tu). Just as knowledge and action are causes for attaining both worlds merely by their own acquisition, so it is not the case that the son is a cause for conquering the world of men merely by his own acquisition of form; this is because [the son], being unchanging, does not itself undergo modification.

Regarding the father who has conquered this world through a son who has been duly instructed, he explains the meaning of the word "then" (atha) in the passage beginning with "Then him... (athainam...).

Regarding the word "putra": since the son is the subject under discussion, there might be a doubt that the pronoun "enam" (him) refers to him; therefore, the word "atha" (now/then) is used to preclude that [doubt]. This is the meaning. || 324 ||
The deities—the vital breaths such as speech and the rest—having performed the transfer together, [depart].
Thus instructed, they always enter their father, being permeated by that very state of being.
