The word "atha" (now) has been explained as being for the purpose of marking a break in the section (*prakaraṇa*). Now, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "imam" (this), starting with the words "kṛta" (done).
In response to the inquiry—among those [five fires], which one is entered first, or which one is last—he says: "samam" (equally). Thus they have been described.

This is a statement of the truth. Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for one thing to possess the nature of another, he says: "Always" (sadā). The meaning is: cultivated as the state of the Self within the divine vital breaths (prāṇas) described in the Sūtras. || 325 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "And for the earth him" in the same manner as before.
Alternatively, this word "atha" has the sense of a reason, because [he] has transferred his sacrificial rites. || 326 ||

It was stated that "they enter into this"; wishing to know the manner of that [entry], he says: "And into the earth," etc. By the word "that" (tad), the nature of the entry is referred to. Having explained that the word "then" (atha) in the passage beginning with "then him" (athainaṃ) marks a transition in the context, he states another meaning: "Because," etc. He clarifies the meaning in the form of a reason: "Since," etc. || 326 ||
Therefore, upon separation from that, the gods enter [the body] as previously described. || 327 ||
For that speech which resides in the Śruti, this fifth [vowel] is its supreme form.
Then, for that [consciousness] which has attained its own existence, the first [moment] arises from the cause of birth. || 328 ||

He concludes the meaning of the passage beginning with "having referred to this as having a cause" (*hetumanūdya*) with the words "due to separation from that" (*tadviyogāt*). The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is the resolve regarding what is to be done (*kartavyatā-saṃkalpa*).

The phrase "as described" (*yathoditāḥ*) is a reference to the immortal vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). It has been stated that the divine vital breaths enter the practitioner who remains after abandoning his current gross body; now, the manner of that process is explained through the passage beginning with "to the earth" (*pṛthivyai ca*).

Anticipating the objection that since both earth and fire are divine speech (*daivavāk*), how can there be both the ablative and the nominative case endings in one and the same place, he says: "The scripture says...

That which is seen in the scripture, the subject under discussion, or the accepted speech—which is the previously established thread (*sūtra*) to be meditated upon—is followed by the ablative case endings "from earth" and "from fire. These are ablative endings used in the sense of a source (*apādāna*) relative to the speech-form of the thread to be meditated upon, which functions as the substratum and the contained; they refer to the speech that constitutes the fruit attained by the meditator under discussion.

"Beyond that is the divine speech"—this means "the first. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used to state that the thread-like speech (*sūtrībhūtā vāk*), like the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is an object well-known to practitioners (*upāsaka*). To explain how the attainment of the thread-like speech results in the success of the speech of the practitioner who has reached the fruit [of realization], he says: "Birth... (verses 327–328).
Having heard the speech, he piles up that which resides in the words, consisting of creative contemplation.
Therefore, the speech of one whose self is characterized by creative contemplation (bhāvanā) would be based on direct audition (śrautī). || 329 ||

Fearing that the birth [of the meditator] might not be established through the words of the disciple or the words of the Sūtra, he says: "The word. Having understood the word of the Sūtra—which consists of sentences—from the sentence itself, the meditator (upāsaka), identifying himself as the Self consisting of the three foods, gathers the word as the fruit of meditation.

Therefore, the word of the Sūtra, which is to be meditated upon and is accessible through scripture, becomes the word of the meditator; thus, the meditator who has achieved the state of being the Self consisting of the three foods through meditation becomes the cause of the effect.
The meaning is that speech enters you because it is logical for the effect to enter its cause. || 329 ||
For no entity whatsoever can be established by itself as something other than the Supreme Self.
If that were the case, the treatise beginning with "together with the gods" (sadeva) and so forth would be contradicted.

858 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Adhyāya]:

Having raised the objection that, like the light of a lamp illuminating a jar set apart from it, speech is merely a manifestation [of Brahman] through the destruction of the internal limiting adjuncts (*adhyātmopādhi*), [the author refutes this by showing that] the Sūtra and so forth exist by their own nature—
It vitiates the proof. [The author says] "Not so," etc. The meaning is that the thread and so forth are not established by themselves because they are non-self (anātman), like a jar.

He states the defect in the opposing view (*vipakṣa*), saying "existent," etc.: if the thread and so forth existed as the Self, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1). || 330 ||
"By means of intellect, by means of intellect"—thus [the scripture] itself declares the state of being an effect for the entire universe.
This has been clearly stated by the Śruti itself; therefore, manifestation is not accepted [as the cause]. || 331 ||

He states another reason for its not being established by itself: "By the intellect" (*dhiyā*). According to the Śruti, "It produces the entire world, consisting of the seven types of food, through each act of cognition by means of ritual actions," the fact that the world is an effect is explicitly shown by [the text] itself. Furthermore, since the world is of the nature of a thread (*sūtra*), it is not established by itself; the meaning is that, because it is an effect, it is like a jar. If the thread and so forth lack inherent existence, then the speech of the meditator (*dhyātṛ*) also...

Because of the absence of that [inherence], it is not merely a manifestation for her; rather, the result is stated as being "birth" due to its dependence on the words of the Sūtra. Thus he says: "No. || 331 ||
And because of the scriptural statement regarding those in distress, and because of the teaching that breath and so forth are a mere modification of speech.
The Self is not established by itself like other things, for scripture likewise speaks of its arising and so forth.

He states another reason for the fact that speech and so forth are not established by themselves: "Ārtā" etc. The connection is as follows: speech and so forth would not be established by themselves. (332)
Therefore, it is performed by agents through the acts of bringing-into-being (bhāvanā), cognition, and action.
This entire universe consists of the three foods; therefore, manifestation is not admitted [as a separate process]. || 333 ||

Since [the self] is not established by itself, he states the established meaning: "by the agents. He concludes that there is no admission of individual manifestations from the words of the Sūtra and the words of the meditator: "not therefore" (nātaḥ). || 333 ||
"Indeed, this is Brahman alone; likewise, it is the Self and the Puruṣa"—such is the sacred tradition (Āgama).
This being so, our [scripture] would possess meaning; otherwise, it would be meaningless. || 334 ||
He demonstrates the support of numerous scriptures for the very point that the Self alone is self-established, and not the thread and so forth, by saying "Brahman alone," etc.

In the passage "The Person alone is all this," the first *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction with the two preceding [statements]. The second, however, is for the purpose of conjoining another reason.
"No" means "for us. Otherwise, if even some non-self were self-established—
This is the meaning. || 334 ||
Others have proclaimed the means for accomplishing the knowledge of the supreme son.
They serve for the sake of cessation from the worlds of humans, fathers, and gods. || 335 ||

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "And for the earth," he sets forth the view that is to be refuted, starting with the word "Sons. The meaning is that the Mīmāṃsakas have declared that sons and so forth—which were previously mentioned as the means for attaining the three worlds—are themselves the means for liberation, based on the scriptural and traditional texts concerning the discharge of debts (*ṛṇāpākaraṇa*). Having stated the position of the Mīmāṃsakas, he states the position of Bhartṛprapañca, beginning with the word "Human."
The word "sons and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 335 ||

Regarding what is established by their purpose of turning away from the worlds, he says: "In this way. The meaning is that they declare these [worlds] to have liberation as their fruit through this sequence: by means of the cessation of the three worlds caused by sons and so forth, the two bodies are destroyed, and thereby bondage is destroyed.
He states that both views are contrary to such scriptural texts as "And to the earth," etc., saying: "Scripture. || 336 ||
Having thus introduced the subject that all ritual action is indeed for the sake of desire, [the text continues].
Because sons and others withdraw their application toward the objects to be accomplished for themselves. || 337 ||

He explains how the first position is refuted by scripture: "The optional," etc. The meaning is that since every fivefold ritual action is indeed optional (*kāmya*), and having introduced the subject with the words "This much indeed is desire," the text concludes with the passage beginning "Now, there are three," which assigns sons and the rest individually to specific worlds; therefore, these cannot be sought as causes for liberation. || 337 ||
Therefore, it is understood from the Śruti that sons and the like result only in the fruits of saṃsāra.
Therefore, even the scriptural injunction regarding debts is held to apply only to the domain of the ignorant.

By examining the beginning, middle, and end of the scripture (*śruti*), one understands that sons and the like result in *saṃsāra* as their fruit, and not liberation; thus he states the conclusion with the words "saṃsāra... [etc.]. Regarding the claim that sons and the like result in liberation as their fruit based on the *śruti* and *smṛti* concerning the discharge of debts (*ṛṇāpākaraṇa*), he says "avidvat... [etc.]. The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is used to refer back to the fact that the scriptural statement regarding sons and the like has *saṃsāra* as its fruit. The particle "api" (also) serves to include the *smṛti*.
This is the meaning. || 338 ||
And he will speak thus: "What shall we do with offspring?"
Therefore, for one who has known what is to be known, there can never be any scriptural injunction regarding debt.

He states another reason for the fact that the Śruti and Smṛti concern those who are not dispassionate and are ignorant: "By progeny," etc. The meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ) is that the wise man has no dependence regarding such objects as sons and the like. || 339 ||
Just as these [terms] such as "son" and so forth do not have the purpose of exclusion, so it is with these.
The Śruti itself explains this to us in the passage beginning with "pṛthivyai cainam. (340)
Having refuted the Mīmāṃsaka view by means of its contradiction with the Śruti, he now refutes another view by that same [Śruti]: "They are for the sake of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttyarthāni*).

For one who meditates on the Self consisting of the three foods, the attainment of those [foods] is stated in the passage beginning with "And from the earth," and likewise for one who has performed the *saṃpratti* (transmission of the self) and possesses a son.
The meaning is that the doctrine of Bhartṛprapañca is contrary to the scriptural teaching of that state [of Brahman], as expressed in the word *pāstyā*. || 340 ||
Moreover, it is not logical that liberation consists in the attainment of the nature of the threefold food.
Because it is born of intelligence and austerity, one should hear it again and again. || 341 ||

Anticipating the objection that since liberation (*mukti*) consists precisely in the attainment of the *sūtra*, it follows that karma and other factors which cause that [attainment] are the causes of liberation—and thus how could there be any contradiction with the Śruti?—he says, "And not... He states the reason why the threefold self cannot be produced by knowledge and action: "By repetition... This means: because of the repeated hearing of that [scripture], namely, the scriptural statement that it is produced by action. The underlying sense is: for that which is created cannot be liberation, as that would entail its being non-eternal (*anityatva*). ||241||
1. ga. 'dhyārthe viṃ | [vol2, page 566] 860

Likewise, from the scriptural teaching of its destruction in the passage beginning with "Now, as for this... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7), Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter]—
From the statement "The earth is the body," Prajāpati's state of being embodied is established. || 342 ||

He states another reason for why attaining the *sūtra* is not liberation. "In that way," he says; or rather, because of the scriptural statement, "If one were not to do this, it would perish," and because of the scriptural teaching on the destruction even of the world-form consisting of the three foods, attaining that is not liberation—this is the meaning. Furthermore, because scripture teaches that [the *sūtra*] possesses both cause and effect, the state of being the *sūtra* is not liberation; thus he says, "The earth... (349).
Because the effects of delusion are subsumed within the activity of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). || 343 ||
It may suffice for the liberation of some, while for others it serves only to produce hunger and thirst.
A statement heard but once is unable to establish two things simultaneously and directly.

He states another argument: since ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects—the duality consisting of the triad beginning with name—are subsumed under the three [categories], the state of being the thread (*sūtra*) is included within bondage and is not liberation. He says "name" (*nāma*). Because the attainment of the thread is not liberation, it was stated that ritual action (*karman*) and so forth are for the sake of that [thread] and not for the sake of liberation. Thus, there is a distinction: for the ignorant person who lacks dispassion, even the fruit of attaining the thread results from ritual action and so forth; however, for the wise person who possesses dispassion, it results in the fruit of liberation.
He speaks to dispel this doubt with the words "of someone. This means for the sake of obtaining the state of that which consists of the three foods.
The meaning is that a single sentence heard only once cannot have multiple meanings, according to the maxim: "For in that case, the sentence would be split. || 343 ||
The abundance of meaning in [words such as] "prakāśa" and so forth arises from the very cause that is perception and the like.
But in matters that are accessible solely through scripture, suchness is not determined [by inference]. || 345 ||

[Objection: But surely, according to the maxim cited—"We behold the rising sun by means of the eyes of thieves, yogis, and those who look in all directions"—since light has multiple purposes, that [multiplicity] is observed even in water. For it has been said: "Canals are constructed for the sake of rice, and from them water is both drunk and used for ritual ablution. Likewise, why should a single sentence not have multiple meanings? To this, he says: "bhūri" (abundant). Thus—

This means "you" [the opponent] imply multiplicity; for according to the maxim that "if these were to be enjoined, the sentence would be split," it is not logical for a single sentence to convey multiple meanings. || 345 ||
Because [the sentence] "That white one runs" and so forth possesses multiple modes of expression.
There might be a determination of multiple meanings, but that is not appropriate here.

[Objection: But surely even a single sentence such as "The white one runs" is seen to have multiple meanings—conveying the act of running by both a horse and a dog through the symmetry of its compound and non-compound forms; would it not be the same here? To this, he says: "The white one," etc. Here, in cases such as "And for the earth," etc.—
Such is the meaning. || 346 ||
He alone remains as the single Self of all beings without exception, abiding through the Self of the presiding deities.
Unmixed with actual sins, he attains divine happiness.
Having refuted other views by means of the current discourse, he introduces the passage beginning with "he who is thus" (*sa evaṃvid*) with the words "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*).
By virtue of his meditative realization (*bhāvanā*), abiding in the self of Prajāpati, he becomes the independent life-breath (*prāṇa*), the self of all beings without exception.
[Notes: 1. ka. ga. read *ṃstasyā yauṃ*; 2. ka. kha. read *sūtrasyāmuṃ*; 3. kha. reads *ṃsūtrātmabhāṃ*.]

2, Page 567] 1 Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

The interpretation: Fearing that if [the self] were of the nature of the elements (bhūta), it would be subject to their defects and thus the state of Prajāpati would be unacceptable, he says: "The elements... He will clarify its non-mixture with those [elements] later on. || 347 ||
He has become the self of all beings, seeing the non-difference from all.
He exerts himself as if playing with the creation and destruction of the world. || 348 ||

He explains the statement that has been introduced with the word "sarva" (all). The meaning is as follows: having the vision of non-difference—that "I am He"—regarding Prajāpati, who is the self of the entire world, this wise man exists as the self of all beings, having become their very life-breath; he remains rejoicing, performing various activities such as the creation of the world as if in play. || 348 ||
Speech is the ear of all beings, as are the skin, the tongue, and the mind.
The nose, feet, and all the others [arise] from the cause of the appropriation of all [elements]. || 349 ||
He states that it is not only the wise one who is the *prāṇa* of all beings, but also the self consisting of speech and the rest.
He provides the reason for the wise one, whose nature is the *sūtra*, being the causal self of all: "Because of all... (verse 349).
Just as knowledge is perceived among us as having resistance, or as an effect, so too [is it here].
It is not so for the Lord everywhere, for the very reason previously stated.

Having stated that [the Self] is the self of all because it is the material cause of all, he declares its result—omniscience and so forth—by means of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). He says, "Knowledge... [referring to the knowledge of ordinary beings]. That [knowledge] is "with resistance" (*sapratigha*), meaning it is obstructed. However, he states that the knowledge or the activity of the Lord (*īśvara*) is unobstructed everywhere. He says, "Not so... [referring to the Lord's knowledge]. This refers back to the previously mentioned reason, namely, being the self of all (*sarvātmatva*); therefore, [it is not like the knowledge of ordinary beings].
Furthermore, all beings protect him according to their strength.
Scripture expresses this matter with effort by means of an illustration. || 351 ||

He states another result of the meditation under discussion with the words "Furthermore" (kiñca). The word "him" (tam) is an address by the meditator. Regarding that, he cites the passage beginning with "As he [is]" (sa yathā) as the authority. By the very fact that it is stated while taking hold of this illustration (dṛṣṭānta), the intention of the Śruti—expressed by the word "effort" (prayatna)—is understood in this sense. || 39 ||
Just as they serve a deity manifested from a previous birth.
In the very same way, all beings are always sustained by enjoyments through this Veda.

He explains that [verse] as follows: "The previous," etc. The construction is: just as toward a previously established deity, so too toward a person who possesses the direct realization of that state, all beings protect him with all enjoyments in all conditions. || 352 ||
If it is maintained that one who knows thus attains the state of being the self of all beings;
How could suffering and other such states not belong to him through his association with those who suffer? (353)

He states the doubt to be dispelled by the passage beginning with "whatever" (yad kiṃcit) in the words "all," etc. Thus, the remainder [of the sense] is: "One who knows in this way would lead to misfortune. || 353 ||
1 kha. *sanprājā* | 2 ka. *'kara'* | [vol2, page 568] 862 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter—]
Because his cognition is not limited, there is no experience of suffering and the like for him.
We have not the slightest connection with the sufferings of worms dwelling within the womb. || 354 ||

Clarifying what was stated in the passage beginning with "by real sins" (*bhūtapāpaiḥ*), he provides the answer that there is no connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in individual elements for the Knower who is of the nature of all things. He begins with "no" (*na*) and so on. One might raise the objection: even if the Knower possesses an undivided intellect (*aparicchinnadhī*), since the Knower—being of the nature of the *sūtra* (the thread)—is contained within all beings, there would necessarily be a connection with their suffering and so forth. Anticipating this, he says: "In the belly" (*kukṣau*). Even though [beings] are cast into the belly...

Just as there are worms [in the body], yet even because of the unbearable sufferings residing within them, not even the slightest connection with us is desired; so too, although all beings are included within the wise one whose nature is that of Prajāpati, the meaning is that the wise one has no connection with the sufferings residing in those beings. || 354 ||
If he were to possess the same sense of self-identification as we do, he would be subject to our suffering.
Because he possesses the conceit of totality, he does not have the conceit of being merely ourselves.

An objection is raised regarding the disparity [between the two cases]: that while Maitra—who possesses the conceit of ownership over his own hands and so forth—is joined with their suffering and other states, the same cannot be said for the wise one who is the *sūtrātman* (the cosmic thread-self) and who possesses the conceit of being the self of all beings, his own parts; thus, the wise one should not be joined with their suffering. Anticipating this, he says: "As in the case of ourselves and others. Anticipating the further objection that by the example of Maitra, the wise one who has become the *sūtra* is said to possess that conceit [of ownership], he says: "Of him" (*tasya*). || 315 ||
And because of his lordship, there can be no association with our sufferings.
But our attainment of suffering is indeed caused by a lack of sovereignty.

Anticipating the objection that if [the Lord] possessed the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being the whole, He would remain subject to all suffering and so forth, he says: "Because of His being the Lord" (*īśvaratvāt*).

Even so, one might suspect that because He possesses the conceit of being like us and others, He would be subject to suffering and so forth just as we are; therefore, he states that "non-lordship" (*anīśvaratva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), saying: "Of us" (*asmākam*). By the word "but" (*tu*), the contradiction with such scriptural passages as "The gods do not [die]" (*na ha vai devān*) is implied. || 316 ||
Having taken such reasoning to heart, the Śruti declares: "And so forth."
The phrase "whatever it may be" (yad u kiṃ ca) serves to negate the suffering of the learned (vipra). || 357 ||

Regarding the point already stated, he cites the passage beginning with "whatever" (*yad u kiṃca*) and so forth. The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) refers, by means of the word "iti," to the previously mentioned reasoning, namely that [the Lord] is independent; and by the word "ādi," there is the inclusion of such attributes as being the creator of all and the self of all. He states the purport of that [passage]:
"Clearly," etc. This sentence establishes the non-existence of the suffering of living beings within the Knower who is of the nature of Prajāpati.
This is the meaning. || 357 ||
That all living beings grieve because of internal and other such sufferings.
That suffering is experienced by these very [beings] together with their own selves. || 358 ||

He explains the syllables of that [verse], beginning with "yat" (that which). The meaning is: since all creatures are afflicted by the three kinds of suffering, that [suffering] is conjoined with the very selves of those creatures; therefore, it is to be experienced by them alone. || 358 ||
According to the reasoning already stated, suffering does not coexist with the divine self.
Furthermore, there would be the destruction of what has been done, as well as the acquisition of what has not been done. || 359 ||

Anticipating the question, "How is there such a restriction?", he says: "Just as... The meaning is "of independence and so forth. The word "conjoined" (*saṃyuktam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
He states the obstacle regarding the union with the deity's suffering: "Having done," etc. (399).
Since only merit has been performed, therefore only merit follows him.
By simply not committing evil, one never incurs sin.

Clarifying the sublation [of the opposite view] regarding the counter-position (*vipakṣa*), he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "merit" (*puṇya*). He explains the passage beginning with "Indeed, [the gods] do not [eat]" (*na ha vai devān*) by means of the words "of sin" (*pāpasya*). || 360 ||
Coldness does not approach fire, due to the inherent nature of the substance of fire.
In that same way, through the essential nature of the deity's self, [the practitioner] [destroys] the evil ones and the deities. || 361 ||
He clarifies that very point by means of an illustration: "Fire," etc. For coldness does not touch fire because its inherent nature is heat;
likewise, evils do not touch the deity because her nature is the fruit of meritorious action. This is the meaning. || 361 ||
When it is stated that "all vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed equal," the certainty of their equality [is established].
Since attendance [upon the teacher] is established as an option, the vow is now subjected to deliberation. || 362 ||
Fearing that the sentence beginning with "Then" (*atha*) might be purposeless because there is nothing further to be stated, he states its intended meaning: "All indeed... (*sarva eva*).

Since the sentence beginning with "These very ones" (*ta ete*) establishes the equality of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), a doubt arises as to whether one should meditate on speech, mind, or breath as alternatives.
To state that all three are to be meditated upon, yet not as equals, but rather that the breath alone is to be meditated upon primarily, [the author says]: "All indeed... (*sarva eva*).

The meaning is that, having deliberated on whose action should be maintained as a vow (*vrata*), the subsequent passage is intended to determine that it belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone as an auxiliary to meditation (*dhyāna*). || 362 ||
The attainment of divine speech and other such perfections belongs to one who has died while perceiving the three foods.
Now it is being deliberated: what vow should be maintained by one who lives?

To clarify that very point, he recounts the narrative with the words "By fate," etc. The word "was said" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having deliberated upon which among speech and the other organs the living meditator should maintain as his vow, he states the reply—"of the vital breath alone"—in order to declare it as an ancillary to meditation (*upāsti*).

Once the state characterized by non-action (naiṣkarmya) has been attained through constant application and renunciation, the subsequent section is introduced for the purpose of destroying Māra. || 364 ||

Having stated the purport according to the Bhāṣya, he states another purport with the words "sarva" and so on. The meaning is that since at the time of *saṃpratti* (the handing over of one's duties) all action along with its effects has been relinquished, and liberation (*nirvāṇa*) has been attained, the subsequent sentence is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for that vow which is an auxiliary to the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 364 ||
However, by the very fact of its being mentioned extensively, the prior worship of all [the deities] is established.
"Since it is said 'immediately after these,' therefore this does not depend on what precedes. (365)

If it is argued that this [injunction] prescribes that very [observance] as independent, and not as a subordinate part of the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) because there is no means of establishing it [as such], [the author] says "no," adding the word "tu" (but) after the expression "bahūktyā" (by the statement of many).
The word "tu" is intended to dispel the suspicion that the observance of the vital breath (*prāṇavrata*) is independent. [This is supported by the text: "He who [knows] these as infinite...
[Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.4].

Since the meditation on the triad beginning with speech is established by the plural number, and since the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is thereby established as well, the passage concerning the observance for the practitioner of *prāṇa*—namely the preceding text beginning with "He who [knows] these"—depends upon that; therefore, this [passage] does not independently enjoin a vow.
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of the injunction regarding the dharma of meditating on the vital breath as it has been introduced. || 365 ||
The nature of speech and mind has already been stated previously.
If their worship were not intended [to be primary], it would be like that of the vital breath (prāṇa).

Anticipating the objection that this [passage] is not merely an exposition of the vows (*vrata-vibhāṣaka*), because its purpose is the cessation of the worshipfulness of speech and mind as they have been described, he says:
"Speech... The meaning is that meditation on those two must be undertaken as subordinate to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); otherwise, their mention would be purposeless. || 366 ||
Since speech and the other senses have been seized by Death in the form of exhaustion.
Furthermore, they set and grow weary; for that reason, they are known as the Bhānavas. || 367 ||

Having stated the purport of the passage beginning with "atha" (now), he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) as follows: "By death. The sense is that the organs such as speech, etc., within the body (*adhyātma*), and the deities such as fire, etc., in the divine realm (*adhidaiva*), being active, become exhausted and set; because they are seized by death known as exhaustion, both of these are understood by the wise to have their vows broken. || 367 ||
The middle [level of] austerity is like the wind, free from fatigue and exhaustion.
Therefore, one whose vows are unbroken should take refuge in that very vow alone. || 368 ||

Now, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "athemameva" (then this very one). "Tadrūpaḥ" (of that form) means, in other words, "of the form of death. The two terms "madhyama" (the middle) and "vāyuḥ" (the wind) refer to the wind distinguished as *adhyātma* (internal) and *adhidaiva* (divine). The absence of fatigue and setting for both of these is the fruit dependent upon that very absence.
Having set aside [the objection], he states the established conclusion: "Since... (368).
For speech and the others, as well as fire and the others, set in their courses within the vital breath and the wind.
Therefore, the vow of the vital breath alone is to be maintained, and not that of anything else whatsoever.

Anticipating the question of how there is such an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) as "of that very one," he says: "Prāṇa. Since within the body (*adhyātma*), speech and the other [senses] set into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and externally, fire and the others set into the wind (*vāyu*), but for the vital breath—which is itself the wind—there is no setting; therefore, its action alone is to be maintained as a vow (*vrata*), and not that of speech and the others, or of fire and the others. This is the meaning. || 369 ||
Just as the vital breaths, through their embrace with the one Prāṇa, come to possess its name and form.
"Even one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) would likewise [attain this] through the meditation on the vital breath as the Self.

Therefore, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "Therefore, these... with the words "The vital breath," etc. Since speech and the other [senses] possess the name and form of the vital breath by virtue of being supported solely by the vital breath, its vow alone must be maintained, not those of the others; thus, one who has maintained the vow is a meditator on the vital breath, and being of that nature, possesses the name and form of the vital breath.
The meaning is "it might be so. || 370 ||
Whatever movement there may be in all the sense-faculties, which consist of action;
That [state] is to be known as belonging to the vital breath alone; however, among those [other faculties], it is the manifestation of their respective objects.
Anticipating the objection—"Let it be so for one who worships the vital breath (prāṇa), but how can speech and the other organs possess its name and form?"—the text says: "All," etc.
[The word *mācaret* is in manuscript *ga*; *kali* is in manuscript *kha*.]
[Vol.
2, Page 571] 1 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by Ānandagiri’s commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā*. 865.
The term "foot" (*pada*) is also an indicative mark for light; the word "illumination" (*prakāśana*) also includes speech and so forth. [It refers to] the eleven organs together with the mind.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: whatever degree of vibration exists in those [organs] possessing the powers of action and illumination, all that is to be understood as belonging solely to *prāṇa*, which has the nature of movement;

thus, the activity of speech and the other [organs] toward their respective objects, and the illumination by the eye and the others toward their objects, are to be known [as such]. Since the common movement within the eleven organs has *prāṇa* as its essence, the meaning is that they possess the name and form of *prāṇa*. (371)
Just as [the organs] such as speech [are applied], so too should one apply them with respect to the divine realm.
It is certain that in fire and other such elements, motion belongs to air alone.

It shows the correspondence with respect to the divine (*adhidaiva*) as it was explained with respect to the internal (*adhyātma*). Regarding the word "just as" (*yathā*): just as speech and the other organs are, within the internal self, designated by the name "breath" (*prāṇa*) and possess its nature, so too one should apply the name and form of "air" (*vāyu*) to fire and the other deities in the divine sphere; such is the construction of the sentence. The particle *api* indicates that there is no difference between the two cases. To the question, "How do fire and the others possess that name and form?", he replies: "In fire and the others... [and so on]. Of that...
The meaning is: "because of the inherent nature of motion. || 372 ||
The favoring of speech and so forth is accomplished; however, for fire and the like, it is merely an action.
The Self alone is the vital breath of all the senses, as well as their creation and dissolution.

What, then, is their specific (asādhāraṇa) function? To this he says: "Speech, etc. By the word "only" (kevala), their specific nature is expressed. The phrase "established in the Śrutis" is the ellipsis. The construction is as follows: that very assistance (anugraha) provided by Agni and others toward speech and the rest, which is understood from such Śruti passages as "Agni, having become speech... and so forth, is their specific function. Thus, both with respect to the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata), he has stated the nature of Prāṇa.

He concludes with the word "all. The meaning is that, through their respective roles as the internal (adhyātma) and the celestial (adhidaiva), Prāṇa and Vāyu are the self and the cause of speech and the others, as well as of fire and the others. || 373 ||
Just as speech and the other [senses] are known by means of their designations as "vital breath" (prāṇa) and their respective names.
In the same way, a family of learned men attains renown through the designation of being "knowers of the vital breath. || 374 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tena" as follows: "prāṇa... (374).
And whoever competes with one who knows the vital breath, he follows after death due to that rivalry.
Having reached emaciation, he goes to death; therefore, one should not hate an ignorant person.

1.1 He explains the passage beginning with "ya u ha" (And he who...). As for the phrase "yaśca" (And he who): death, which consists of attachment and evil like [ordinary] death, having reached the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*),...
The meaning is: "it perishes just as [that]. He states the intended meaning of the statement of the proponent of sin (pratyavāyavādin) who competes with the worshipper: "One should not hate... (375).
A verse is cited here to confirm the meaning stated by the Brahmin.
From where this sun rises and where it goes to its setting; || 376 ||
This sentence is in the form of a question, since an answer is being stated.
Having determined that the rising and setting of the sun, as described by the verse beginning with "prāṇāditya," occur through the vital breath (prāṇa) alone—

both from the perspective of the inner self (adhyātma) and the divine realm (adhidaiva)— he then explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha" [verse 377.2], stating that the vow (vrata) of the vital air itself must be maintained. Brāhma-...

Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*, Chapter One, Verse 866:

"...by means of the word 'anu' (after). Because this mantra occurs immediately after the Brāhmaṇa section, the term 'anu' is employed. Regarding the first half of the mantra, [it refers to] the rising of the sun..."
He shows that this is a question concerning the cause of setting. He says "yataḥ" (from which), anticipating the objection that there is no word such as "kim" (what) here to indicate a question;
thus he says "yataḥ. He asks what the grounds are for the rising and setting of the sun from the vital breath (prāṇa). [The answer begins with] "bhānoḥ" (of the sun). || 376 ||
When a person indeed sleeps, speech then enters into the vital breath (prāṇa).
In the same way, the eye, the ear, and the mind are born from that very source.

In order to state the proof for the origin of the sun from the vital breath (prāṇa) and its dissolution therein, [the author] first states the proof for the origin of speech and the other senses from it and their dissolution therein, beginning with the words "When... The word "vai" is used because the state of sleep, denoted by the term "lying down," is well-known to every individual self. || 378 ||
Likewise, with respect to the deities, fire and the other elements originate from Vāyu.
And just as, internally, the vital breath (prāṇa) is superior to everything else, so too is dissolution [superior]. // 379 //

Regarding the origination of fire, the sun, and so forth from the vital breath (prāṇa), as well as their dissolution therein, he cites as authority such scriptural passages as, "When fire departs, it passes into the wind. He states that this applies to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*). Having established that the vital breath is the cause of the origination and dissolution of speech and the rest, as well as of fire and the rest, he declares the resulting conclusion: "He is superior" (verse 379).
The word "prāṇa" must refer to the Self alone, on account of the statement regarding the bondage of prāṇa.
From the statement "this was indeed non-existent," the manifestation of the Self as the sun occurs.
An objection is raised: "How can the well-known vital breath (*prāṇa*) be accepted as the cause of the origin and dissolution of the sun and other elements, given that its power is formless?

To this, he replies: "The Self alone. He states the governing reason for using the word "breath" here for the unknown Self: "Because [it is] the breath... In that context, by the word "mind" (*manas*), the individual soul (*jīva*)—which has that [mind] as its limiting adjunct—is understood; however, it is not the sustainer of the vital breaths in its primary sense.

The meaning is that, just as the Supreme Brahman is designated by the word "prāṇa" because it abides in the vital breath (prāṇa) and is thus the abode of the individual soul (jīva), so it is here as well. To provide further scriptural authority for accepting the unknown Self as the referent of the word "prāṇa," he cites the passage beginning with "asadeva": "In the beginning this was non-existent; it became existent; it developed; it turned into an egg; it burst open," and so forth. Having introduced the Supreme Cause—the source of all things whose name and form were yet unmanifest—by means of the word "non-existent" (asat).

Therefore, after teaching the origin of earth and the other elements from that [Brahman], it is stated that the sun originates from that very same source: "And that which was born—He is that sun. Furthermore, in the *Agnirahasya*, it is said: "When the sun sets, he enters the wind; the moon enters the wind; the quarters are established in the wind; and from the wind alone they are born again. Thus, the origin of the sun from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is declared.

In the present context as well, it is stated that "he indeed rises from breath," thus declaring its birth from breath. Since there can be no alternative regarding that [cause] because it is a real entity, the meaning is this:

according to the Śāṇḍilyavidyā of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the cause of the Sun's origin—which is heard mentioned elsewhere—is none other than the Unmanifest Self (Ajñāta-ātman); therefore, when that [Self] is being refuted, it is referred to by the word "breath" (prāṇa). || 380 ||
And wherever there is origination, therein also is dissolution.
A jar produced from clay does not dissolve into vīraṇa grass or similar materials.
Having explained [the terms] "prāṇa," "āditya," and so forth, he explains [the phrase] "it sets in prāṇa" with the words beginning with "yataḥ. [It means: produced from the potter...
[Vol.
2, page 573] 1. Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri.

Anticipating the objection that—just as a jar dissolves into clay—the sun, though produced from the Supreme, may likewise dissolve elsewhere than that, and thus the restrictive rule [of dissolution into its own source] is not established, [the author], considering that the rule refers specifically to the material cause (*upādāna*), provides an example: "Of clay," etc. (Verse 389).
Because it sustains the group beginning with speech, the wise know Dharma to be the vow of Vāyu.
They performed and maintained the dharma, because it is the fundamental nature of things.

Having explained the first half of the mantra along with its Brāhmaṇa commentary, he now explains the portion beginning with "tam" (him). Regarding the phrase "vāgādi" (speech, etc.): the construction is that those who know the scriptures understand the *vrata*—the duty—of Prāṇa and Vāyu to be such that, just as Prāṇa internally supports the class of speech and the other organs, so too Vāyu externally supports the group of fire and the other elements. The context is the restrictive factor for interpreting the root *kṛ*, which usually means "to do," in the sense of "to support."
He said: "Retention. || 382 ||
Even today that [rite] is performed by them, and its performers are likewise their gods.
At that time, having been defeated, they studied the Yama [Veda].
Today, Agni and the other gods likewise uphold that very same auspicious vow of dharma.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa eva" (that very one) as follows: "Even now," etc. The construction is as follows: by means of those [deities] such as Speech and the rest, that protection of the vital breath (*prāṇavrata*) is performed in the present time; and in the future as well, those deities—Agni and the others who are the performers of that [protection]—will perform this "Vow of the Waters" (*vāsu-vrata*) at other times just as they do now. Alternatively, he explains the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "eta" (these) as follows: "They maintained," etc., [and] regarding the word "amuhī."
Regarding the phrase "the exposition therein" and so forth: that time is indicated as something remote because it is delimited by the Mīmāṃsā;
the word "auspicious" (śubham) expresses its being uninterrupted. || 383 ||
Because the vow of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is unbroken by death, for that reason [it is so].
One should always observe this single vow regarding the vital breath until death.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore" (tasmāt) as follows: "unbroken" (abhagnam). This means the vital breath (prāṇa) and that which is connected to it. He shows the limit for the performance of the vow (vrata) with the words "until death" (ā maraṇāt). Even there, the word "always" (sadā) is used to signify continuity. || 384 ||
The self of the vital breaths (prāṇātman) should inhale and exhale even during activities such as yoga.
Because these [actions] are included within the functions of the sense organs, such as the ear and so forth. || 385 ||

The passage beginning with “He should breathe” (*prāṇyāt*) is introduced to demonstrate the nature of the vow (*vrata*). Regarding the phrase “He should breathe,” it states that the reason for the knower’s engagement in such activity is his identity with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Anticipating the objection—“Since the activities of breathing and so forth are natural to all living beings and cannot be performed at will, how can there be an injunction regarding them?”—the text [proceeds] with the statement concerning eating while facing the east (*prāṅmukha-bhukti-vākya*).

He says "not so" because the sentence is intended to signify the cessation of other activities. Regarding the phrase "in speech and so forth," he explains how, having abandoned the activity of speech and the rest, the activity of the vital breath alone is to be performed: "because it is included within them. (381)
Therefore, in the act of pride, one should observe this very same vow alone. || 386 ||
For this vow consists of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and its sole performer is the vital breath itself.
Therefore, one should always draw [the breath] out from the *māṇya* and the *apānya* until death. || 387 ||

page 574] 868 Sureśvarācārya’s *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* [First Chapter— ]

He states another reason why the one who worships *prāṇa* must perform that very vow (*vrata*), namely that the worshipper is identical with the *prāṇa* being worshipped. [The verse begins with] "prāṇa...

The word "constantly" (*nityam*) expresses continuity, while "until death" (*ā maraṇāt*) indicates the limit. A wise person (*budhaḥ*) is one whose view regarding all activities of speech and so forth is the activity of *prāṇa*; that is to say, he is its worshipper. (386–387)
One should always carry out even the functions of speech and the other organs by means of the vital breath itself, just as those organs do.
Just as there is attachment to speech and the other [senses], may that evil, the demon, not overcome me.
Having this intention, the wise man should practice the vow of the vital breaths (prāṇavrata).
If one has begun the vow of breath-control (prāṇavrata) and desires to perform it, one should bring it to completion.

Fearing that the statement [of the breath] might be purposeless because the vow of speech and the other senses has been abandoned by the restriction "only one," he recalls what was stated in the section on "inclusion" (antarbhāva): "by means of the self of the vital breath" (prāṇātmanā). The meaning is that the restriction is due to the subordinate nature of speech and the others, and the primary nature of the vital breath. He states the meaning of "not me" (mā) and so forth: "speech and the others. This is an example by way of contrast (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). The meaning is: "Do not deceive me, the speaker."

Having raised the doubt as to why one should observe the vow of protecting the vital breath (*prāṇavrata*) for as long as life lasts, he explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "yadi" (if) as follows: "prāṇa... (verse 388).
For by practicing [the recitation] of the *amṛta*, one attains union (*sāyujya*) and other [liberations].
Therefore, this is prescribed for the deity whose self consists of the three foods. || 390 ||
Thus ends the fifth section, the Saptānnabrāhmaṇa, of the first chapter in the *Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika*.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tena*) as follows: "By means of what has been practiced" (*abhyastena*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sāyujya etc. is intended to include *sālokya* and the other forms of liberation. Furthermore, the fruit varies according to the degree of practice. He concludes that because it possesses a fruit, there is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) for one who meditates upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), just as there is for [the meditation on] the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Thus: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 390 ||
Thus ends the fifth section, the Saptānnabrāhmaṇa, of the first chapter in the commentary on the Śāstraprakāśikā, which is a sub-commentary on the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārttika. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth Brāhmaṇa.
Thus has the entire effect of ignorance been described as "this world" (tad-vedam).
Now, the threefold summary of that which was just explained is stated as follows: || 1 ||

One might object: "Since ignorance (avidyā) along with its effects has already been explained as it was briefly indicated (sūtrita) in the section on ignorance, there is nothing further to be said; therefore, it is proper to conclude the chapter.
Anticipating this doubt, the author restates what has already occurred and introduces the next Brāhmaṇa with the words "tad dha" (Now, that...).

In the passage concerning the unmanifest (avyākṛta), ignorance residing in the inner self (pratyagavidyā) together with its appearance and its effects was briefly indicated; and of that [ignorance], which was drawn forth in the passage "atha yo 'nyām," the course [of its development] has now been described.

The meaning is that the subsequent Brāhmaṇa is intended as a conclusion for that subject matter, including its reasons, which has been elaborated upon in the preceding composition. The word "atha" (now) is used to show that there is occasion for a summary after the detailed exposition. Furthermore, both summary and detail are desired for the sake of easy comprehension. || 1 ||
1. ka. kha. 'te | annāṃ | 2. ka. 'nādide | 3. ga. 'vatopāstestasmā | [vol2, page 575] 6.
Brāhmaṇa] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri. 869.
That which has been thus described is the effect of the unknown identity of the Self.
But it does not consist in merely understanding the true nature of the object of cognition once delusion has been destroyed.

But for what purpose is this conclusion stated? Anticipating the objection that it is redundant because [the result] has already been mentioned, the author prepares the ground to state its fruit now at the occasion of the conclusion, since the conclusion of the section on "the Knower" (*vijñātṛ*) and so forth was previously extracted and stated separately. He says: "The unknown," etc.
That which is the unknown identity (*aikātmya*), its effect is the world described below; because it is the effect of a reality untouched by the knowledge of truth, in order to point that out—
The meaning is that it is not possible for that immutable [self] to be its own cause, because its status as such a cause is unestablished. || 2 ||
When this was said, he became dispassionate toward us, desiring liberation and endowed with faith.
It is now stated: "How indeed might one become qualified for the knowledge of Brahman? (3)

This [verse] clarifies the fruit of the conclusion. Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*): when it is established that the world is of a threefold nature and is rooted in ignorance (*āvidya*), a seeker of liberation who is detached from it and who, with faith, investigates its cause—how could he not be qualified for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which are preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and are the means to the knowledge of Brahman?
Since the Śruti contemplates this, the conclusion is made by means of that [word]. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
One whose mind has turned away from the objects of human pursuit arising from ignorance.
A person desiring to know the true nature of the Self should turn away from that [worldly existence]. || 4 ||
Fearing that even one who is not dispassionate might be qualified for this [inquiry] out of mere curiosity—rendering dispassion unnecessary—the author says "avidyā" (ignorance).

The meaning is: one whose intellect has turned away from attainable ends such as heaven produced by ignorance, and whose mind has desisted from the means thereto, becomes a seeker of the Self; how then can one who lacks dispassion have the qualification for knowledge? || 4 ||
One whose intellect is bound to external objects [strives] for the sake of knowing the true nature of the inner self.

"A person is not capable [of knowing the Self] due to contradiction," according to the statement of the Āgama. He states the reason for that person's incapacity regarding knowledge [of the Self] with the word "external" (*bāhya*). The meaning of "due to contradiction" is that there is a mutual opposition between attachment to the non-Self (*anātma-saṅga*) and the realization of the Self (*ātmavedana*). Even a means of valid cognition regarding the non-Self would cause one to cognize the Self as its own substratum.

Anticipating the objection that there is therefore no contradiction between those two cognitions, he says: "parāñci" (turned outward). For the cognition of objects is not capable of making the self known as its own substrate, because it terminates solely in the object; thus, there is a contradiction between those two cognitions—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Ignorance alone is the cause, and not conformity with the nature of the one Self.
It is explained why [the result arises] from the entity as it has been described. || 6 ||

One might object: "If the entire world consists merely of the triad whose nature is ignorance (*avidyā*), then the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth would not be possible; yet even today that has not been established. To this he replies with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*). The genitive case [in *avidyāyāḥ*] refers to the world consisting of the seven kinds of food. He introduces the passage beginning with "the triad" as the answer to that objection, using the word "this" (*etad*). || 6 ||
The direct manifestation of the Self from the unknown has been previously described.
Of that which is devoid of the nature of cause and effect, [the perception occurs] through the forms of name, form, activity, and self. || 7 ||

To explain that, he recalls the subsequent [verse]: "From the unknown," etc. The very nature of the inner self (pratyagātman), which is devoid of the relationship between cause and effect, is [the reality]. [Ka. Ga. reads 'vṛttau bha'.
Whether it be that world, which is devoid of the nature of that [Self], or the Self itself, its clear manifestation as name and so forth belongs to the Self.
The meaning is that it is stated by a knower in such cases as "that is its cause," and so forth. || 7 ||
The nature of this entire world, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects, consists precisely of name and so forth.
But it would not be a separate entity, as it is described here. (8)

He summarizes the purport of the passage beginning with "The triad" [in the words] "Name, etc. Anticipating the objection—how can the aforementioned reality be established by a mere proposition?—he says, "Just as... Here, the word "here" refers to the present Brāhmaṇa. || 8 ||
By virtue of being the cause, being identical [in nature], and being the attainment of its own self.
The fact that this entire phenomenal world consists of name and so forth is now established. || 9 ||
For what reason is it said that the world has name and so forth as its nature? To this, he says: "Because of being the cause," etc. (9).
This world, which has been described as divided into many different categories, is thus differentiated.
Let all this reality of the activity of name-and-form be understood. || 10 ||
Having stated the purport, he explains the syllables beginning with "trayam" (the triad) as follows: "aneka... (10).
This statement, "Indeed, this is threefold," is intended to establish the thesis.
"The subsequent text beginning with 'the statement of reasons' (hetuktiḥ) is for their sake," and so forth, is stated.
Fearing that this would be a tautology—since this very same point will be stated later in the passage beginning with "of those names" (*nāmnām*) and so forth—he says:

"The triad. The construction is as follows: the entire subsequent text, beginning with "this triad of words" (*idaṃ vacastrayam*) and ending with "all the world consists of name and so forth," serves as the statement of the reason (*hetūkti*) for the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) established by the preceding section beginning with "of those" (*teṣām*). Alternatively, [it may be understood] by means of the passage beginning with "of those" (*teṣām*).
The construction is as follows: that which is the subsequent statement [following] the form [of the thesis] is the "statement of the reason" (hetūkti) regarding the matter proposed. || 11 ||
By the word "speech" (vāk), it is intended that mere sound (nāda) is meant.
But because it is not abandoned due to the transformation arising from the sound (nāda), [it remains]. || 12 ||

In the passage beginning with "of those names" (*teṣāṃ nāmnām*), he states the meaning of the word *vāk* (speech). By the phrase "by this [word] 'vāk'," he provides the reason for not perceiving specific sounds: "because it is not occupied" (*apajuṣitatvāt*). || 12 ||
Among these modifications of name, the *uktha* is sound (*nāda*), because it arises from that.
From that [state] called "all names," the sound is designated as the Uktha. || 13 ||

He states the meaning of the phrase "this is their *uktha*" with the word "of these. [The argument is: all specific names do not differ from that [single reality] in terms of their essential being (*sattva*), because they are its effects; and whatever is an effect does not differ from its cause in terms of its essential being, just as a pot does not differ from clay. He concludes this inference with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 13 ||
Likewise, speech in general is the very self of its specific instances.
For no particularity whatsoever is perceived as being extracted from the universal. || 14 ||

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "This is their *sāman*" by saying "In that way. Because speech is the cause, there is an identity (*tādātmya*) between it and its specific effects.
[Vol. 2, page 577]

The meaning is that it is like [the self] being identical with its own nature. Having raised the objection— “Even though speech is a generality, how can the particulars have that as their essence?”— he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

"Not indeed," [it is said]. The meaning is that all specific names are imagined upon their corresponding universal (sāmānya), because each is permeated by that [universal], just as a snake and so forth are permeated by the "this" aspect of a rope. || 14 ||
And because speech is likewise of the nature of the Self, nothing else remains that could belong to it as its own.
Because it is connected here with its own object in its entirety. (15)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "This is their Brahman" as follows: "And because they are its own. The word "likewise" (tathā) means that, due to being the cause and due to being the universal, speech and its particulars possess identity with it. He establishes this very point—that there is no particular of speech other than that—by stating "in its entirety," because speech is the cause for the particulars obtaining their own nature from it. Here, the word "here" (iha) refers to clay and so forth, which constitute the essence of jars and other objects.

Everything that is called "name" does not exist as a separate entity from its universal (sāmānya) in reality; therefore, because it possesses the nature of that [universal], whatever possesses the nature of something is not other than that in reality—just as a pot, which has clay as its nature, is not in reality other than that. This is the intended meaning. || 15 ||
The distinction between cause and effect that is observed in the world is thus established.
This [notion], which is established without critical investigation, is refuted by the Śruti.

Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned inferences contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "The effect," and so forth. It should be understood that this refers to the universal and the particular, as well as the self and what belongs to the self. He states the reason for the negation of difference based on such scriptural passages as "This is their *uktha*": "unexamined," and so forth.
Because of defects such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), the imagined difference is fit for the scriptural negation and is the object of perception; therefore, it is not real.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural authority] in the inferences which negate its difference. || 16 ||
This being so, its status as a valid means of knowledge arises from its cognition of an object not previously known.
Otherwise, it would be a mere restatement, because the act of hearing only conveys an already known object. || 17 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "This scripture teaches non-difference; it does not negate difference. Since it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) if it were intended to convey both meanings, it must therefore be intent upon both difference and non-difference. Anticipating this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is that if the scripture were intent upon negation, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established because it makes known the absence of difference where difference was previously unknown. He states the fault in [the view that] it teaches both difference and non-difference: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). Since difference is already established by common worldly consensus, non-difference— ...[is taught] in order to negate that [previously established] difference. Thus, there is no split in the sentence. Therefore, the scripture is intent solely upon non-difference. This is the sense. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"There is no diversity here at all" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*)—negates difference. And the following scriptural passage—"He who sees any diversity here goes from death to death" (*mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati*)—negates difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"For where there is duality, as it were, there one smells another" (*dvitīyād vai bhayaṃ bhavati*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"From death to death he goes who perceives therein any plurality" (*mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati*)—negates difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"The knower of Brahman attains the highest" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"Brahman is one, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"Being, truly, this was in the beginning, one only, without a second" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam*)—negates difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"How could it see itself, O fair youth? How could it know itself, thinking 'I am it'? (*kathaṃ nu tadvijānīyāt yenedaṃ sarvaṃ vijānāti taṃ kena vijānīyād vijñātāram are kena vijānīyāt*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite" (*yatra nānyatpaśyati nānyacchṛṇoti nānyadvijānāti sa bhūmā*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"Where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else—that is the finite" (*yatrānyatpaśyaty anyacchṛṇoty anyadvijānāti tad alpam*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"The Infinite is immortal; the finite is mortal" (*yo vai bhūmā tadamṛtam atha yadalpaṃ tanmartyam*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"The Infinite alone is below, the Infinite is above, the Infinite is across, the Infinite is the inner self" (*bhūmā hyevādhastād bhūmā upariṣṭād bhūmā paścād bhūmā purastād bhūmā dakṣiṇato bhūmā uttarato bhūmā evedaṃ sarvam*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"But when for him the Self becomes all, then what should he see and through what? (*yatra tv asya sarvam ātmaivābhūt tat kena kaṃ paśyet*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"There is no difference whatsoever here" (*na tu taddvitīyam asti tato 'nyad vibhaktaṃ yatpaśyet*)—negates difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"He who sees even the slightest bit of difference here goes from death to death" (*mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyuṃ gacchati ya iha nāneva paśyati*)—negates difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"One should meditate upon the Self alone as 'I am Brahman'" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi ātmano vā are darśanena śravaṇena matyā vijñānenedaṃ sarvaṃ viditam*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"By knowing Him, one knows all" (*tamevaikaṃ jānatha ātmānam anyā vāco vimuñcatha amṛtasyaiṣa setuḥ*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" (*brahmaiva san brahmāpyeti*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"When there is duality, as it were, then one smells another" (*yadā hy evaiṣa etasminnudaramantaraṃ kurute atha tasya bhayaṃ bhavati*)—negates difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"But when for him the Self has become the whole, then what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (*yatra hi dvaitam iva bhavati tad itara itaraṃ paśyati... yatra tvasya sarvam ātmaivābhūt tat kena kaṃ paśyet*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"O Gārgī, the knower of Brahman reaches the highest" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"The knower of the Self transcends grief" (*tarati śokam ātmavit*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows the bliss of Brahman is never afraid" (*yo vai bhūmā tatsukham atha yadalpaṃ tanmartyam*)—teaches non-difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman" (*sa yo ha vai tatparamaṃ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman which is without sound, without touch, without form, without decay" (*aśabdam asparśam arūpam avyayam*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman which is beyond darkness" (*yasmin dyauḥ pṛthivī cāntarikṣam otam*)—teaches non-difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman which is hidden in the cave of the heart" (*yo veda nihitaṃ guhāyām parame vyoman*)—teaches non-difference. Moreover, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman which is the light within the heart" (*hṛdā manīṣā manasābhiklṛpto ya etadvidur amṛtās te bhavanti*)—teaches non-difference. Furthermore, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman which is the bridge over the waters" (*eṣa setur vidhṛtiḥ eṣāṃ lokānām asaṃbhedāya*)—teaches non-difference. Also, the following scriptural passage—"He who knows that Brahman

The meaning is that because [scriptural statements] such as "the ear-ring is gold" are observed to involve a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the Śrutis asserting both difference and non-difference are merely reiterative (*anuvāda*) since their objects are already known; therefore, they lack authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*). || 17 ||
Here, by the word "eye," the object of the eye is intended.
Because of the connection with "of forms" (rūpāṇām), and because it has the nature of form (rūpātmatva), it is likewise [the same]. || 18 ||

Now, regarding the phrase "of forms" (*rūpāṇām*), he states that the word refers to the eye (*cakṣus*). He says "of the eye. The reason for this is "of forms. In the statement "the eye is the hymn of forms," the relationship is observed such that specific forms are the effects and the eye is the cause. Thus, it is logical that the eye is the universal form (*rūpasāmānya*), because specific forms are not produced from a well-known [particular] eye, whereas those specific forms are produced from the universal form. This is accepted.
This is the meaning: "you" (tvāditi). In that very context, he states another reason: "rūpa" (form), etc. Since the eye is a modification of light and consists solely of form, it is essentially form;
therefore, by the word "eye," the universal property of form (rūpasāmānya) is grasped—this is the meaning. || 18 ||

For whatever is manifested by the intellect, such as sound, touch, and so forth—whatever it may be—[is form].
It should be understood that each takes on such a form because there is no distinction in their fiery nature.

He establishes that its nature is form (*rūpa*) with the words "yadyaddhi" (whatever...). The particle *hi* is used to indicate the appropriateness of applying the term "form" to an object being conceptualized by the intellect. He states the reason why every effect that is being conceptualized possesses the nature of form: "taijasatva" (being composed of light). The meaning is that since all effects are without distinction in their luminous nature (*taijasatva*), and that luminous nature is accepted as having the nature of form. || 19 ||
For indeed, in every instance, the splendor characterized by form and so forth belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ alone.
Therefore, the commonality of the object is expressed by the word "eye. || 20 ||

How is it that the subtle element (tanmātra) alone possesses the nature of fire? To this he says: "The offspring of Tvaṣṭṛ. For every effect, being cooked by the solar light, attains its own self; thus, the meaning is that the effect is indeed identical to that [cause]. Having stated that the eye has the nature of form because of its fiery nature, [he proceeds...]
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. || 20 ||
Through the distinction between the cause and that which arises from it, [the analysis proceeds] by way of the causal relationship between effect and cause.
And from the scriptural teaching that it is a mere matter of verbal designation, the unreality of modifications is stated. || 21 ||

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the scripture which teaches the causal relationship between specific forms (*rūpa-viśeṣa*) and their commonality (*sāmānya*). [The verse begins with] "Because of the cause...

Since the non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) of cause and effect is observed in cases such as clay and a jar, and since in the present case there is the observation of identity (*tādātmya*) due to the reason for that state, and because of the statement that modifications are merely verbal (*vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāraḥ*) which declares the unreality of the effect, specific forms do not exist in reality apart from their commonality.
This is the meaning. || 21 ||
And now it is stated that particulars are included within the universal.
This is common to all particularities, for it is indeed equal to them.

Having thus explained the statement regarding the *uktha*, he states the meaning of the phrase "this is their *sāman*": "And because of inclusion. The word "atha" (now/then) signifies another reason. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "For this... as "the commonality. He establishes that the mere form possesses the quality of being common to its specific instances. This is shown by the words "For it is equal... (22).
For us, there is neither particularity nor generality, neither through difference nor through non-difference.
Likewise, because specific forms consist of nothing but form itself.
For it indeed bears all forms, such as garlands, calves, serpents, and so forth.

Fearing that one who asserts the inclusion of particularities within the generality of form must thereby accept the reality of the relationship between generality and particularity— since otherwise such a relationship would be impossible, which would result in contradicting one’s own tenets— the author says, "No," and so forth. For us, who maintain that a thing is devoid of both generality and particularity, there is no particularity distinct from the generality by way of either difference or non-difference, nor is there any generality [apart from it].

The meaning is that because difference and relation are difficult to explain [independently], and because if there were no difference, one or the other would remain as the sole reality, the status of being a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is imagined; yet this imagined status serves as a basis for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), just like the unimagined. He states the meaning of the phrase "Brahman is their [nature]" with the word "tathā" (so).

Just as the nature of snakes and so forth is nothing but the rope, so too, because specific forms have as their essential nature only the form-in-general (*rūpa-mātra*), they do not exist as distinct from it.
