The meaning is that they exist. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "For this" (*etaddhi*) as follows: "Serpents and so forth.

Just as a garland, as its substrate, supports serpents and the like, so too does the generic form (*rūpasāmānya*) sustain its own particulars as its very self; therefore, those particulars are not merely that [generic form].
The meaning is that it does not exist separately. || 23 ||
In fact,
the identity of name and form has thus been stated in brief.
Now, in the same manner, the unity of action is also established. || 24 ||

Now, having restated what has been previously discussed in the verse beginning with "atha karmaṇām" and so forth, he introduces [the next section] with the words "uktam" (it has been said). The meaning is as follows: the identity of specific names with name-in-general and the identity of specific forms with form-in-general were stated in brief; likewise, the identity of specific actions with action-in-general is now stated in the following [verse]. || 24 ||
The object that is grasped by speech and sight through sound is the domain of those two.
In the same way, the object of the self is grasped by the word "self. || 25 ||

How is it that the Self is specifically designated as the "Uktha" of actions? Anticipating the objection that this is because the Self is the material cause of everything, he states the meaning of the word "Self": "Speech," etc. (25).
The vibration of all our sense-faculties is manifested within our little body.
Therefore, that which has the body as its object is here designated as the "self" (ātman). || 26 ||

Anticipating the objection that "Self" here might refer merely to the action performed by the body—which is designated as the "Self"—he says: "All the senses," etc. This means the body as the object and the movement produced by it. By the locative case, the previously mentioned *uktha* passage is referred to. || 26 ||
"Action is indeed his very self"—thus it was stated previously.
Therefore, in this context, it is the commonality of action residing in the body that is understood. || 27 ||

With the word "ātman," he states another reason: "The self alone. In the preceding Brāhmaṇa, it was stated that for the ignorant person—who is incapable of producing external wives and so forth—the body itself is the action (*karman*). Anticipating the objection, "How does this much suffice to show that the word *ātman* here includes all actions in general? he says: "Therefore, here. The meaning of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the body possesses the designation "self" (*ātman*). Here, the word "ātman"—
He states the reason found in the Bhāṣya—"because of being situated therein" (tātsthyāt) and so forth—for the apprehension of the generality of action by means of truth: "deha... (verse 27).
Name-and-form, as well as karma—these three have been thus described.
This triad becomes one alone, being merely the existent body.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "these three" (tad etat trayam) as follows: "Name," etc. (nāma iti). || 28 ||
In this context,
action exists here as the transformer of the two, namely name and form.
Name and form are established as the instruments for the accomplishment of karma.
Anticipating the question—“If that [Self] is merely the body, in what form do name and the rest abide within the body?”—the author says: “By way of being the agent of transformation.
Here, the word “here” (atra) refers to the body. The meaning is that name and the rest abide here by being mutually cause and effect. || 29 ||
Form alone would always be the basis for both name and karma.
For name and action do not exist without depending upon form. || 30 ||

By stating that the purpose of the qualification is to show mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he introduces the fact that form (*rūpa*) depends upon name and action (*nāmakarma*). He says, "Form.

The phrase "at all times" refers to the period delimited by the existence of both [name and action] within the body. He provides the reasoning for this: "For not... The meaning is that these two lack independence (*asvātantrya*). || 30 ||
The meaning is that the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is thus always the foundation for name and form.
For the acquisition of their own nature always proceeds from their resting upon the identity of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 31 ||

He states that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the substratum of name and form: "The vital breath... and so on. Just as [it was said] that form has name and action as its substrata, the word *sat* (Being) is used here as before. He provides the reason for its mutual dependence upon one another through the nature of general activity: "The vital breath... and so on. The statement that the vital breath is the substratum of those two means that the existence of name and form, which reside in the body, is always dependent upon the vital breath.
This is the meaning. || 31 ||
In the same way, those two—form and action—would have speech as their substratum.
Since those two are always employed when speech is being manifested. || 32 ||

He states that name (*nāman*) is the substratum for form (*rūpa*), action (*karman*), and so forth, with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*). The meaning is: just as form and action are each mutually dependent upon one another. He states the reason why speech (*vāk*), which is merely name, is the substratum for form and the rest, with the words "by speech" (*vācā*). For indeed, form and action have no application whatsoever when they are unmanifested; therefore, it is logical that those two, being manifested, must depend upon their manifester.
This is the meaning. || 32 ||
By way of the relationship between substratum and that which is supported, [there is the manifestation] of those whose nature consists of name-and-form and activity.
Of those [elements] which exist for a single purpose, there would be a combination within the body. (33)

Having explained the existence of name and the other [factors] in the body through their mutual dependence, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "saṃhatam" (composite). He says: "āśraya... (as a support).
The meaning is that those things which serve a single purpose—namely, by bestowing pleasure and pain upon a single experiencer and by initiating a single body—are so situated.
Everywhere, the suffix *ka* used here denotes a sense of contempt regarding that which is generally designated as a "body. || 33 ||
This single, unified self also attains this threefold state.
Since this body is perceived as distinct from the activities of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). || 34 ||

Raising the objection as to how there can be an absence of confusion in worldly transactions if the triad beginning with "name" were merely the body, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Being one... (ātmaikaḥ san).
He says: "Being one... As to why that single body has three forms, he says: "Name... (nāma...). 134.
"This self consists of this," as was previously explained in detail.
All this that is aggregated by these three is designated as "the unmanifest" (avyākṛta). || 35 ||
He states that the threefold nature of the body is not only perceptible but is also established by scriptural statement: "consisting of this" (*etanmaya*).

The word "thus" (*tathā*) means in accordance with the body's being permeated by the aforementioned names, forms, and actions. Anticipating the objection that—since there are many effects and causes—the mere mention of the triad would fail to include all of them, and thus the summary would not be comprehensive, he says:
"Thus much," [it is said]. || 35 ||

This indeed is the Vairāja, consisting of name, form, and action.
But that immortal life-force is concealed by the truth of the nature of name-and-form.

Explaining "that this," he states that it is a composite form well-known from the Śruti and Smṛti. He says "that" (tad). He explains the meaning of "immortal" (amṛta) and so forth by saying "name" (nāma). The meaning is that the subtle body (sautra śarīra), denoted by the word "truth" (satya), is enveloped by the Vairāja body, which is the immortal one. || 36 ||
By the word "prāṇa," the subtle body (liṅgātman), consisting of the instruments of perception, is denoted.
Since this does not perish even upon the death of the body, it is therefore considered immortal.

He states the meaning of the passage "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed immortality" with the words "The vital breath," etc. He explains how it possesses immortality with the words "Of the body," etc. || 37 ||
One should perceive the elements of earth, water, and fire as being designated here by the term "existent" (sat).
But those two, wind and space, should be understood as being designated by that [name] by the great-souled ones. || 38 ||

Regarding the statement "name-and-form is reality" (*nāmarūpe satyam*), he explains the etymological meaning of the word *satya* [in verse 38]: "The earth," etc. This refers, in effect, to the five gross elements. The phrase "by the great-souled ones" (*mahātmabhiḥ*) means by those who desire to fix their minds upon the Great Self (*mahati ātmani*), which is undivided; the word "as a means" (*upāyatvena*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 38 ||
They know that truth, consisting of the five elements, to be both "sat" and "tyam."
The gross sense-base which they call Vairāja; || 39 ||

He states its collective meaning: "And *sat*. Everything consisting of the five elements that have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*), as well as their effects, is called *satya* based on the etymology of "that which is *sat* (existent) and *tyat* (extended). This is the Vairāja body, the effect. It is known by the knowers of Brahman to be the abode (*āyatana*) of the subtle body (*liṅga*) called the Sūtra, which consists of the seventeen instruments formed from the five elements in their non-quintuplicated state and their effects. The meaning is that this is the domain of expertise for those alone who possess knowledge of the scriptures. || 39 ||
Contained within this also is the vital breath (prāṇa), which they know as the conscious self (vijñānātman).
From the beginning of saṃsāra, he has remained constant, stable, and eternally subject to transformation.

With the commentary beginning "But *prāṇa* consists of action," he explains the true nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "of this too": if it were the case that *prāṇa* is simply the Supreme Self in the form of knowledge, he says "no," adding "as long as transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts. By apprehending the identity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that which possesses the adjunct (*upādhimat*), it was called the "self of consciousness" (*vijñānātman*). If so, how can that self, whose nature is action, possess immortality by virtue of persisting as long as bondage endures?

Regarding this, he says: "It is stable" (sthāsnur). The meaning is that for that [Self], whose primary attribute is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), immortality is relative. He excludes its absolute [immortality] by saying: "through transformation" (pariṇāma) || 40 ||
According to one's karma and according to one's knowledge, one takes up a body.
Therefore, this [Self] is described even in the Śruti as being equal to Luṣa and others. || 41 ||

If it does not depart even when the gross body departs, how then does it again take up a gross body? To this he says: "Just as... He cites the scriptural authority beginning with "equal to a mosquito" (*samaḥ pluṣiṇā*) in that regard. By means of mosquitoes and so forth... like the gross body.

The meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is the non-destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The particle *api* (also) signifies that the immortality of the vital breath is not stated only here, but also previously. || 41 ||
This [practitioner] has taken possession of all the elements, possessing the deities of the limbs as previously described.
And the conceit arising from all ignorance is due to the cause of the non-knowledge of the inner self. || 42 ||
He reveals here as well the intention of the Śruti, which withdraws the entire world into the nature of its own two bodies, by means of the words "upātta" (appropriated) and so forth.
He states the reason for possessing the two types of conceit pertaining to the two bodies with the word "kṛtsna" (entire). || 42 ||
One who knows the reality within the body of Hiraṇyagarbha and within the Vairāja body.
This Gārgya, possessed of ignorance, has bound himself with the conceit of selfhood.
Regarding the entire cycle of existence as his own, he remains established in the thought, "I am all this."
The insentient [self], which is the object of the instruction regarding Brahman, is awakened by the Veda itself. (44)

He clarifies that very point with the words, "Hiraṇyagarbha. The intention is that the concluding scriptural passage (*upasaṃhāra-śruti*) is intended to state that one who, through ignorance, identifies with the two bodies, becomes detached from them by perceiving their defects, and thus becomes qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding this, he cites the *Ajātaśatru-brāhmaṇa* as the supporting evidence, beginning with the words "Gārgya," etc. [The opponent asks: "How can Bālāki, who possesses discernment (*viveka*)—which is the cause of detachment—be ignorant?"
She said: "It is inert. The meaning is that it is so because of the absence of direct perception (*aparokṣa*) therein. || 43 || 44 ||
Though himself immortal, he is [conceived] through name and form, which are mortal.
The vital breath, along with the aggregate of the senses, is always concealed and enveloped. || 45 ||
Having concluded the purport of the concluding scriptural passage (*upasaṃhāra-śruti*), he explains the verse beginning with "by those two" (*tābhyām*) and so forth. Regarding the word "name":

the subtle body, though not the Self, is difficult to discern because it is veiled by the gross body; the innermost reality (*pratyag-vastu*) is even more so, as it is veiled by that [subtle body] as well. Thus, the sense is that one must remain vigilant in the knowledge of that [reality]. || 45 ||
However, those who know the tradition maintain here various theories regarding plurality and unity.
They declare that Brahman consists of both difference and non-difference, like the world of names, forms, and so forth. (46)
Having stated his own explanation regarding the passage beginning with "these three," he introduces the interpretation of Bhartṛprapañca with the words "by means of identification" (*saṃpadā*).

The qualifying particle "but" (*tu*) is intended for the purpose of derision; however, it also serves to distinguish this from the previously mentioned explanation. It was stated that "the triad beginning with Name is here";
let them say that the triad of Name and so forth is both different and non-different [from Brahman], but what happens to Brahman itself at that point? To this he replies: "different... (*bhinna...*).

The distinction and non-distinction of name, form, and action are stated as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) for establishing the distinction and non-distinction of Brahman; thus, the meaning is: "How then can there be the monolithic unity (ekarasya) of Brahman? || 46 ||
The triad would be one alone, and that one existence would be just like the triad.
By this very inference, one should know that Brahman is also of such a nature.
Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the words "the triad. He clarifies the application to the subject at hand with the words "by this. In the illustration:
1. always.

"Not so," up to this point [is the objection]. He states: "The object under dispute is both different and non-different, because it is a real entity, like names and so forth"; thus he says, "by means of inference.
And it has been stated by him that, through this observation of unity and plurality, supreme unity and plurality are to be inferred. || 47 ||
Even though there is a multiplicity of powers such as vision and the rest, they know that which is supreme to be truly one.
Because of the identity of power and the possessor of power, it is called non-duality (advaita). || 48 ||
Anticipating the objection that the inference of Brahman’s being both different and non-different contradicts the scriptural teaching of its oneness, he says: "The power of sight, etc. (*dṛg-ādi*).

The meaning is that although there is a distinction among its powers, they are nonetheless one; therefore, the scriptural statement regarding the oneness of Brahman—which is both different and non-different—is not contradictory. Nevertheless, anticipating the objection that this inference contradicts the scriptural denial of duality, he says: "The powers, etc. (*śakti*). That [scripture] is intended for the purpose of negating absolute duality.
The state of being. || 48 ||
Just as "cowness" is established without distinction in the dewlap and other [characteristic] features;
Although the dewlaps and other features are distinct from one another, they are nonetheless non-different from "cowness. (49)

Nevertheless, fearing that the inference [of yours] is contradicted by the reasoning known as "mutual contradiction" (mithovighāta)—insofar as it asserts that something is both different and non-different—he says:

"In the dewlap, etc. Just as the universal "cowness" (gotva) persists through individuals such as the spotted cow (khaṇḍa) while those individuals are mutually distinct, yet they are not excluded from cowness simply because of that mutual distinction—since there is the cognition of non-difference, such as "the spotted one is a cow"—for all entities indeed have a fixed status of both unity and plurality.
The meaning is that this is because of the statement, "those which are situated are apprehended. || 49 ||
Just as the nature of being both different and non-different is observed in gross objects.
In the same way, a wise person should understand even subtle matters by the power of inference. || 50 ||

Having restated the illustration, he states the application to the subject at hand with the words "bhinnaiḥ" (by distinct...). This refers to gross objects such as cows and the like; the meaning is "in subtle objects such as the eyes and so forth.
The term "wise person" (budhaḥ) is intended to mean one who is skilled in the methodology of inference. || 10 ||
Not even a single example can be found in the opposing position.
Therefore, it is certain that every entity consists of both distinct and non-distinct natures. || 51 ||

The argument that "the subject under dispute (the particular) is both different and non-different [from the universal] because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a cow and so forth," is incorrect. Anticipating the objection that this is refuted by the inference: "The subject under dispute is neither different nor non-different [from the universal] because it lacks a commonality (*niḥsāmānyatvāt*), like ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣavat*"), he says: "parā" and so forth. If "being other than the universal" is the reason (*hetu*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a broken pot and the like; if "not possessing a commonality" is the reason, there is a deviation in the case of "cowness" and the like. Furthermore, there is no corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here, as ultimate particularities—[which would be required].

The intended meaning is "because it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*). He concludes with the result of that inference being free from defects: "bhinnaiḥ," etc. The meaning is that every object consists of both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). || 51 ||
Because the entity whose nature is both different and non-different is established solely through inference.
What need is there for scripture here, which merely restates what is already established by logical marks?

Having raised the alternative—whether [the knowledge of Brahman] arises from inference or from the scriptural tradition (āgama) concerning the hero-like Brahman as previously described—he refutes the first position by stating that the authority of the Veda regarding Brahman would not be established: "From inference... (Verse 52).

Nor does the purport of scripture lie in such a thing as that.
It is not gross; it is "not this, not this"; likewise, it is both known and unknown.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "And not... The meaning is that the purport of the Veda does not lie in a Brahman of manifold flavors (nānārasa), because none of the indicators—such as the marks of the six means of proof—are perceived therein. He states that not only does the scripture have no purport toward a manifold-flavored object, but rather its purport lies in an object of single flavor: "Not coarse... Thus, there is no purport of the scripture toward a manifold-flavored reality.
The word "his" (asya) is supplied from the previous context. || 53 ||
Likewise, for the sake of negating a specific self, [there is the negation] of that which has the nature of a universal.
The razor and the earth are established as examples by means of scripture. || 54 ||

He states that Brahman is of a single essence (ekarasa) even by virtue of the introductory statement, beginning with the words "viśeṣa" (particularity). The word "tathā" (so too) serves to carry over the negation. Two examples were stated to describe the entry of Brahman into the body through both the general and the particular; however, Brahman does not possess a dual nature in this way, because such mutual contradiction would result in the absence of any essential nature beyond those two, leading to a lack of finality. Therefore, it is devoid of generality and particularity and is of a single essence.
The meaning is "Brahman. || 54 ||
Ultimate particulars exist as examples even in the opponent's position.
It is now explained how there is no supporting example even within your own position. || 55 ||

Regarding the objection that there is no example for the opponent's position, he says: "The last ones. Since they are established as authoritative by the proponents [of the view], their status as examples is proven; it is not a failure of definition due to the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*). This is because the meaning of being a universal is "not being the locus of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that possesses a universal," while [the final categories] themselves possess such a universal. Having thus stated the example for his own position—that Brahman is devoid of distinctions—...
He states the logical consequence that, because that [reason] is absent in the opponent's position, his own arrow strikes only himself, saying: "In your position...
(verse 55).
98.1650. The particulars (viśeṣas) would be without generality (niḥsāmānya), if "cowness" (gotā) were not distinct from them.
If, on the other hand, "cowness" were to be excluded from them, it would become like a fragment (khaṇḍa). || 56 ||

Anticipating the objection that "just as 'cowness' exists in the dewlap and so forth," an example has been shown in my own position, [the author] raises the following alternatives—whether cowness is non-different from the particulars, different, or both different and non-different—and states the fault in the first case: "They would be devoid of universals" (*niḥsāmānyā*).

If cowness were merely the particulars themselves, they would be devoid of universals; and in that case, they would not even be particulars, because the subsequent triad [of categories] is devoid of universals.

The meaning is that [the universal] would not be established because it is not desired to be non-existent. Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "atha" (now/if). The meaning is that if there were a difference between that [universal] and those [particulars], then because it would fall into the category of a particular, the universal would not be established as distinct from the particulars. || 16 ||
If you state that what is excluded from different things is non-different [from them], then...
"It is excluded, yet it is not a distinct entity—oh, how wondrous is the operation of knowledge! (57)

Regarding the third [alternative], one might wonder whether by the word "undifferentiated" (*abhinna*) it is meant that [the universal] is excluded from those [particulars] or not excluded; having thus raised this dilemma, he restates the first [position]: [In the case of] "cowness" (*gotva*), etc. [it would be excluded].

"Excluded" (vyāvṛttam): since at that time even the universal (sāmānya) becomes a particular (viśeṣa), there is a loss of its status as such; thus he says "contradicted" (vyāhatam) with a touch of irony. "The activity of knowledge" means, in other words, scholarship (pāṇḍitya). || 97 ||
Furthermore, that which is not excluded from particulars is called a universal.
Since the universal is itself a particular, there are only particulars. (58)
He states another alternative: "non-exclusive" (*avyāvṛtta*). He says that even then, the relationship between universal and particular remains unestablished: "of the universal," etc. (18).
For "cowness" is not perceived in its particulars by means of a conceptual construction (*abhidhīyā*).
Since it resides solely in the particularity itself, how can it be called both different and non-different? (59)

Fearing the objection that "the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of particulars [is not established] because the cognition of inclusion (*anugatabuddhi*) perceives even 'cowness' (*gotva*) in them," he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). To the further objection that "in that case, the inclusive cognition would be without an object," he replies: "Of the particulars" (*viśeṣa*). Just as there is an inclusive cognition regarding ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*), so too in the case of [individual cows] such as Khaṇḍā, that cognition has only those [particulars] as its object; therefore, how could it be without a basis? This is the result of refuting the relationship between the universal and the particular.
He said: "It is broken. || 19 ||
Is non-difference their conjunction, or is it identity, that is, being undivided?
There is no non-distinction in the conjunction of two rams; even when joined, they remain as distinct as before.

Having refuted the state of being both different and non-different by means of the refutation of [the categories of] generality and particularity, [the author] now offers a dilemma regarding the meaning of the word "non-different" in the claim that "even in the absence of that [inherence], those two are different and non-different," for the purpose of showing that its referent is difficult to ascertain. He states: "Non-difference. This refers, that is to say, to the relation between those two, namely the generality and the particular. He first refutes [the position] with: "No," [arguing] that the relation is not the object of the conventional usage of "non-difference," because it is a relation, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
He refutes the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). || 60 ||
Whether mixed or pure, the nature of "cowness" (gotva) is apprehended within its various particulars.
There is no non-difference in either case, because of the established nature of its being unique (asādhāraṇya). || 61 ||

To refute the second [position], he analyzes the cognition of those [particulars] regarding it: "mixed. Whether there is a cognition of the universal *gotva* as mixed with the particulars or as isolated, their identity is not established, because both possess distinct natures—one characterized by persistence (*anuvṛtta*) and the other by exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*).
He says: "No, because of the contradiction with that stability. (61)
And that "cowness" (gotva) is either employed within the individuals or exists separately from them.
Whether it be the universal or the particular—what of these two could be designated? || 62 ||

He offers an alternative analysis in order to state another fault regarding the identity (*tādātmya*) of the universal and the particular. He says, "In the particulars. The meaning is that [the universal] is either absorbed within them alone, having been utilized, or it does not exist separately from them. He refutes the identity by stating, "Or the universal," because in both of these two alternatives—whether the cowness (*gotva*) is utilized or not utilized in the particulars—the relationship of universal and particular is not established. || 62 ||
Because it is specific, it is applicable [to that alone], since there is no connection with anything else.
It does not possess the nature of being both different and non-different, because the coexistence of those two forms is impossible.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [in the first chapter], he states the following regarding how the existence of that [universal] is not established in the accepted position: "It is employed" (*upayuktam*). The meaning is this: it is the particular (*viśeṣa*) that is employed, not the universal (*sāmānya*), because the universal is included within the particulars; nor is it the particular, since a particular depends upon the universal and would cease to exist in its absence. Anupa-...

In the case of the [opponent's] position, he establishes the non-existence of those two with the words "of the other as well. The meaning is that because there is no connection with particulars even for that which is not applicable, it does not arise from the universal and so forth. Since the status of being a universal or a particular is impossible for both the applicable and the inapplicable, and since identity is impossible, the result is stated: nothing whatsoever attains the state of being both different and non-different. || 63 ||
In the actual nature of things, there is neither generality nor particularity.
Since [the distinction] is established merely through mutual dependence, like the relationship between cause and effect and so forth. || 64 ||
Furthermore, the inference—"Moreover, those two are not in reality both different and non-different because they are conceptualized, like the blue color of the sky"—establishes the reason.

Regarding the word "vastu" (entity): for the universal and the particular cannot be established without mutual dependence; thus, because they lack inherent existence, their status as conceptualized is proven, just like a snake [imagined] in a rope. He indicates this inference with the words "vyomni" (in the sky). || 64 ||
The non-difference between the "cowness" residing in a hornless cow and that in a horned one is established through recognition.
The distinctness [of the pot] from those [parts] such as the shards arises from the knowledge that they share a single substratum. (65)

The proponent of both difference and non-difference (bhedābhedavādin) says: "On account of recognition" (*pratyabhijñānataḥ*). Because there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) such as "this is that very same [cow]" regarding the cowness (*gotva*) residing in the spotted and the hornless [cows], non-difference is understood. Furthermore, from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the spotted cow" and "the hornless cow," there arises the cognition of non-difference with respect to the individuals.
Therefore, because it is not different from them, it is not different from them either; thus, the meaning is that the two are both different and non-different. || 65 ||
Even so, there is no identity between those two, because their cognitions have different substrata.
Because there is a cognition of non-difference regarding the universal, whereas there is indeed a cognition of difference regarding the particulars. (66)

He refutes [the opponent’s position] by stating that even if there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between those two, there is no identity or non-difference, because the cognitions of the recurring and the excluded are established as having the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) respectively as their objects. He explains this with the word "distinct" (*bhinna*). He elaborates on the phrase "from a cognition whose locus is distinct" with the words "the universal," etc. The sense is that coreferentiality is like [the relation between] the sky and its blueness. || 66 ||
Because it is not apprehended by direct perception, that [recollection] is not an act of seeing.
For indeed, no object whatsoever that has not been apprehended through direct perception is remembered. (67)

As for the claim that there is non-difference [of the universal] on account of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), he replies: "By perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). The apprehension of "cowness" (*gotva*) does not occur through a prior experience whose object was a specific individual such as Khaṇḍa; for since cowness resides in multiple individuals, at the time of perceiving one individual, other individuals are not perceived, and thus it is not established that [the universal] exists in many. Therefore—

The meaning is as follows: there can be no recollection of "cowness" (gotva) regarding that which was not previously experienced, because recollection is impossible for what has not been experienced; and if there is no such recollection, then the perception characterized by recognition—known as the subsequent synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of what was previously experienced—is not established. Therefore, how could there be a cognition of difference or non-difference? || 67 ||
Because grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) depends upon distinct referents.
How can there be a cognition of non-difference between the qualifier and the qualified in that case? (68)

As for the claim that the cognition of non-difference between the universal and its particulars arises from grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he replies: "Of grammatical coreferentiality... Alternatively, even if the oneness of "cowness" is established through the aforementioned recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth, its subsistence [in individuals] remains unproven.

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with specific attributes, there is non-difference; for unlike the case of "blue is yellow," the expression "blue is blue" is not observed, since that [latter] has a different meaning.

Since that [non-difference] is not established by any means of valid cognition, there is no cognition of non-difference between these two; therefore, non-difference is not established on its basis. Thus, how can there be both difference and non-difference?
This is the meaning. || 68 ||
By means of a novel statement, a negation that was previously established is here declared.
Consequently, it follows that there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of that which has been attained and is of a distinct nature.

Anticipating the objection that—whether [the entity] is distinct or non-distinct—it must necessarily be both distinct and non-distinct by force of its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—I consider the point:
does the word "not" negate distinction or not? Having stated the first alternative, he refutes it with the word "non-distinct" (*abhina*). [The opponent] asserts...

Therefore, the meaning of the word "not" (na) is a negation regarding the substrate; thus, the implication is that it is not possible for a single entity to be both different and non-different. ||69||
If it does not negate the distinction between words, it would be like a sentence that expresses distinction.
In this way, the position that [the self] possesses both a distinct and non-distinct nature would necessarily be abandoned. || 70 ||

Having restated an alternative position, he refutes it with the words "the statement" (*vaca*). The sense is that even if both [entities] were mentioned here, since neither difference nor its absence is stated in one place, the well-established meaning of non-difference would be abandoned. || 70 ||
Nor is it determined here that [the Buddha] was Takra-Kauṇḍinya-Vaiyāghrapadya.
Because there would be no opportunity for its abandonment, emptiness alone would consequently follow. || 71 ||

One might raise the objection: "Even if the word 'non-different' (abhinna) serves to negate difference, it does not follow that difference is void everywhere; for when something is prohibited in its cause after having been generally applicable—as in the case where curd is to be given to the Āryas, but the prohibition 'curd is for Kauṇḍinya' applies to Kauṇḍinya specifically—the result is not a total voidness. Anticipating this, the author says: "In that case," meaning that the principle of general rule and exception (utsargāpavāda) relating to that [case] does not apply here.

Stating the reason for the phrase "possessing valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇavat*), he states the conclusion: "In the case of the general rule and the exception" (*utsarga...*). The meaning is that since there would be no scope for both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) in the claim that "everything is both different and non-different," the very negation of difference residing in each respective object by means of the term "non-different" would result in its being nothing but emptiness; thus, the state of being both different and non-different is not established. || 71 ||
Genus and quality are distinct from substance, according to the evidence of one's own experience.
How can non-difference from that [object] be cognized through a means of valid cognition, given its contradiction with it? || 72 ||

Anticipating the objection that because difference and non-difference are admitted only in certain cases such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, and not everywhere, the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavāda*) is established, [the author], while accepting the difference between the universal and so forth and their substratum (*dharmin*), states the non-difference [of the two] by saying: "The two are distinct" (verse 72).
The state of being both identical and distinct is not established in any way whatsoever.
Since it is non-different from its own substratum, how could it have another as its substratum? || 73 ||
Having now accepted non-difference, he rejects difference. He states: "It is non-different. He establishes this by saying: "Because it resides in itself.

The meaning is that since non-difference, being the very nature [of the thing], is internal and therefore more powerful, difference—which is dependent and opposed to it—cannot exist in reality. || 73 ||
Whatever occurs independently of anything else is ultimately real.
Since their distinctness depends upon something else, they are like the blackness of those two [substances]. (74)

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, [First Chapter]: Having stated that there is no room for difference within what is non-different, according to the maxim that "between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger," he speaks of the imagined— [Vol.

2, p. 588] 882. [First Chapter] — Having stated that there is no room for difference within what is non-different, according to the maxim that "between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger," he speaks of the imagined—

To state that between two imagined things, the non-imagined is stronger, he declares the non-imagined nature of non-difference with the words "anyā" (other). He states the weakness of difference due to its being imagined with the words "anyāpekṣam" (dependent on another). Therefore, the sense is that difference is sublated by non-difference. || 74 ||
Cowness, existence, knowability, substantiality, and so forth, appear as if they were distinct entities.
In this context, universals such as "fragment" and so forth are mutually contradictory. (75)

Furthermore, are the universals such as "cowness" (gotva) mutually distinct, non-distinct, or both distinct and non-distinct? Since it is impossible for that which is non-distinct from cowness—such as a broken-horned cow (khaṇḍa)—to possess [properties like] existence (sattva) and so forth, it would follow that they lack existence, are not objects of knowledge, and so on; otherwise, their mutual distinction would be untenable. With this in mind, he states the fault in the second alternative: "Cowness," etc. These [universals], residing in things such as the broken-horned cow, are likewise [mutually] distinct.
They are seen as indeed distinct; thus, they are not non-distinct, because that would contradict experience—this is the meaning. He refutes the third [position] with the words "by that" (*tena*).

If those [particulars] were both distinct and non-distinct from one another, then the genus and so forth would likewise be both distinct and non-distinct from the substratum; thus, your desired conclusion would fail, and there would be a mutual contradiction between your two statements—this is the meaning. || 75 ||
That which is one is not manifold, and that which is manifold is not one; such is the valid cognition.
How can an object that contradicts direct experience be established by force? (76)

In the third [verse], he states another fault: "That which... and so on. There is no valid cognition (*pramā*) that "whatever is one is not manifold," nor is there a valid cognition that "whatever is manifold is one," because it is impossible for a means of knowledge (*māna*), which requires consistency, to have contradictory objects. Therefore, the meaning is that unity and difference cannot coexist in a single locus. In that very context, he points out the contradiction with one’s own experience: "He who has experienced... and so on. A means of knowledge cannot establish an object that contradicts one’s own experience.
The sense is that, without accepting [this], there would be an over-extension (atiprasakti). || 76 ||
If particulars were to become the universal, and the universal were to become the particular, then there would be no distinction between them.
There would be a contradiction with what is well-known in the world, and that [contradiction] too would be purposeless. || 77 ||

Having set aside the mutual difference between the universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, he states that [the opponent's view] contradicts worldly consensus regarding the mutual non-difference of those individuals. He says: "The differences... Anticipating the objection that even this [non-difference] would be sublated—just like the worldly consensus regarding the difference between moons—he replies, "And that," stating that it is not so because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasakti). || 77 ||
If both the universal and the particular are considered to reside in substance;
And those two [existence and non-existence] possess a substance that consists of both the uncommon and the particular. (78)

Furthermore, having raised the alternatives—whether those two [particularity and inherence] are non-different from the substance, different, or both different and non-different—the author refutes the first by restating it:

"And if they are the universal," and so forth. This means that they are dependent on the substance and non-different from the substance; for those two [would then be] mere substance, devoid of its own specific state.

Because of that [dependence], the universal and the particular would be identical; consequently, due to the absence of their own intrinsic nature (svarūpa), they would be non-different from the substance—this is the meaning. || 78 ||
When a substance is dependent upon its qualities, then it is sublated by common usage.
It would follow that even a single substance would incur the state of being manifold. (79)

Furthermore, if there were no difference between the universal (sāmānya), the particular (viśeṣa), and the substance (dravya), one must consider whether the substance is included within those two or vice versa; having raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the words beginning "guṇa. Because they are dependent, the word "guṇa" refers to the universal and the particular; that which is dependent upon them is the [substance]. [Page 589] [The substance would be subordinate to the universal and the particular.]
6 Brāhmaṇam] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Śāstraprakāśikā* composed by Ānandagiri:

"Included" means [subsumed]. He states another defect—just as there is a contradiction with common consensus regarding the inclusion of that which is independent within that which is dependent—in the words "of one."
The meaning is that if the substance were non-different from those two, it would follow that it possesses their multiplicity; yet that is not tenable due to contradiction. || 79 ||
Because qualities are connected only with substances, there is no mutual connection between them.
Because they are not mutually connected, there is no distinction, nor is it otherwise. (80)

He refutes the inclusion of those two within substance by means of the phrase "by substance. Since the two are non-different from that very substance and consist of nothing but it, there can be no mutual difference or non-difference between them; if that were the case, they would lack a connection with each other through that state, resulting in a deviation from their true nature—this is the meaning. || 80 ||
If it is your view that substance is distinct from both the universal and its opposite;
Since that [other] is established by the negation of those [elements], how could there be non-difference from them? (81)

He restates another alternative: "If [it is argued that] the universal," and so on. The construction is as follows: "If it is your view that substance (dravya) belongs to the universal and so forth, and that this [substance] is distinct from the universal. Then, since the universal and so forth are established precisely by the exclusion of that [substance], and substance is established precisely by the exclusion of the universal and so forth, it follows that the one is not non-different from the other, and it is impossible for those two to be non-different from it. Thus, he says: "Therefore, that would be devoid of both universals and particulars. He states: "The negation of that..."
Now, if it is held that the substance is non-different from those two, then its destruction follows from that [destruction].
Neither particularity nor generality can exist without being mutually interwoven.

In the third [case] as well, he refutes [the position] by restating the aspect of non-difference, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The meaning of the restatement is: "If it is thought that substance is non-different from the universal and the particular, and the universal and the particular are non-different from the substance. This is not so; for difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing due to contradiction. Furthermore, if the substance were non-different from them, then because the two depend upon it, they would cease to exist in its absence. Moreover, there would be no relation between them by way of the status of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).

And since those two [existence and non-existence] are not different from the substance, and because there is no existence or non-existence apart from it, the substance would have to be accepted as being devoid of both universals and particulars; such is the meaning. || 82 ||
If there were non-difference from that which is different, then the non-different would certainly become differentiated, just like a physical lump.
Likewise, it follows that the individual entity (piṇḍa) would be omnipresent, because there is no difference from the universal "cowness" (gotva). || 83 ||

Having refuted the distinction between those two and substance, he states the previously mentioned fault regarding the nature of a particular when it is non-different from the universal: "If [the particular] were different... He states the fault regarding the particular being non-different from the universal: "If the individual... (83)
Because they are not mutually distinct, those two would attain identity.
Consequently, there would be a contradiction with direct perception, for that difference is based upon it.
He states the fault in their mutual non-difference: "anyonya... (mutually...). If it is argued that their identity is intended, he says in response:
"tataḥ" (from that). He states the reason for this: "tadbhedo hi" (for the difference between them...). The substratum is the object. || 84 ||
Because it is non-different from its parts when analyzed, the whole object is not even slightly like the individual parts.
One should understand that knowledge possessing all forms is [not possible], because it is contradicted by direct perception. || 85 ||

He states another defect in the case where the universal is non-different from the particulars, beginning with the word "vyasta" (distinct). The meaning is: the object under dispute is not the cause of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttadhī*), because it is non-different from that which is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*), just like those [particulars]; thus, there would be a contradiction with the experience that the universal is the cause of a recurring cognition. || 85 ||
If, even when there is no difference between the individual parts, one were to forcibly produce the cognition of the whole;
Even if not complete when taken part by part, a mountain might still produce the notion of satisfaction.

He states the fault in the opposing view: "Even if there is no distinction when separated" (*vyastābhede’pi*). This means: even if one does not follow the actual mode of being of the object by force. The meaning is that if that which is separate were the cause of the cognition of the whole, it would also have to be the cause of the cognition of the separate [parts], because there is no difference [in their status]. The word *asamastaḥ* (separate) is to be construed with *api*. || 86 ||
Difference in the world is determined by way of its unique form.

Furthermore, the universal (sāmānya) is that which pervades all [particulars], whereas the particular (vyakti) is not so; because their essential natures are distinct, their identity is not supported by valid cognition.
Thus he says: "Asādhāraṇa... (Verse 87).
And because everything is non-different [from Brahman], the cognitions of a snake and so forth occur with respect to a rope.
Just as there would be the cognition of a rope, so too would there be the cognition of that [snake], like the cognition of a snake. // 88 //

Furthermore, [the opponent might argue that] there is either difference-and-non-difference everywhere, or only in the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth. It is not the first case, because the distinction between error and non-error would be established; thus he says: "All... etc. In the doctrine of universal confusion (*sarvasaṃkaravāda*), since everything is non-different from everything else, even the cognition of a snake would be non-erroneous like the cognition of a rope, and the cognition of a rope would be erroneous like the cognition of a snake. Thus, there would be a reversal of error and non-error due to the non-difference between the rope and the snake—this is the meaning. ||88||

"Of the qualifications" (adhikārāṇām) means "of the qualified persons" (adhikāriṇām), who possess the causes for activity and so forth. It should be understood as "non-engagement" and "non-cessation. This has been stated.

"Indeed, this would result in the non-engagement and non-desistance of the entire world; for all [classes], such as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others who are entitled, there would be no distinction in their engagement across all rites—such as the Bṛhaspatisava and Rājasūya—due to the total confusion of the specific notions of entitlement (adhikāra) denoted by terms like 'injunction' (vidhi), which are the causes of engagement and so forth. This is the meaning. || 89 ||
And whatever great effort has been made for the purpose of conceptualizing non-existence as an object of cognition;
That [distinction] has turned out to be fruitless in the case of the established positions of difference and non-difference. (90)

Furthermore, he states that for one who asserts an unrestrained identity-in-difference (*bhedābheda*), there would be a contradiction with their own established tenet (*siddhānta*). He says: "In the absence...

If everything that is both different and non-different were established through perception and other means of knowledge, then since the absence of difference—the referent of the term "non-different"—would be established by another means of knowledge even without the non-perception of the fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*), the presentation of the non-perception of the fit as a means of knowledge for establishing absence would be useless; moreover, it would result in the non-existence of the object of cognition (*meyābhāva*).

For that whose non-existence is not observed, there exists a distinction [from existence] due to the difference in its properties; since there is thus a distinction even from existence, non-apprehension of the fit (yogyānupalabdhi) is ineffective regarding the position of non-existence.

He concludes the refutation of the positions regarding difference and non-difference with the words beginning "No" (*na*). He recalls what was stated in the passage beginning "Because it is established solely by inference" (*anumānaika-siddhatvāt*) with the words "as previously described" (*yathokta*). The meaning is that the claim that the entire world and Brahman are both different and non-different—that they are to be known as such—is neither authoritative nor logical, according to the reasoning already set forth. Thus, since the interpretation offered by others for the passage beginning "Therefore, these three" (*tadevaṃ tadetat-trayam*) is untenable...

Since the world, which consists of the two bodies, is withdrawn into its own nature, it is established that the seeker of liberation—who has become detached from that world through the power of discrimination regarding the one who identifies with it—is qualified for the means of knowledge that cause that [liberation], namely hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). || 93 ||
Those who desire to taste the entire nectar of the Vārttika should resort to the Sarasvatī born from Ānandagiri.
